l2|17.c: Imposter syndrome and fast growth are two sides of one coin, so meet it with curiosity.
l2|17.e: She believes you only feel unqualified when facing unfamiliar problems, and that's exactly when you grow fastest. So rather than trying to get rid of the feeling, seek out fast-growing companies that keep pushing new tasks onto you. Her coping tools: remember almost everyone feels this way, ask for help sooner, and be open about what's hard so others can share the load. Even at senior levels, she says, you keep running into problems you've never seen before.
ex: For her first seven or eight years at Facebook she felt like a fraud almost weekly
Facebook had about 8 million users when she joined as an intern

items.d: A growing company keeps handing you new tasks

items.t: Ask for help and be open
items.d: Everyone feels it; speak up early

l2|17.c: Writing is first a tool for clearing your own thinking, not for building an audience.
l2|17.e: She started writing after a performance review said she had ideas but stayed quiet in big meetings. The root cause was fear of looking stupid in public. So she set a rule: publish one piece a week for a year, with no audience goals at all. Writing worked like letters to herself that sorted out her ideas, and by year's end she was noticeably more willing to speak up in meetings. Her advice: pick a skill, commit to an action like a word count or a time block, try it for 30 days or a few months, then review. Writing to go viral, she says, just comes across as insincere.
ex: Her New Year's resolution: one post a week for a year
Borrowed from NaNoWriMo: hit the word count first, edit later
Later she spent a year writing a weekly Twitter thread to practice being concise

items.d: Has ideas but silent in big meetings
Commit to the action, not an audience
A year later, more vocal in meetings

l2|17.c: Product sense is built through observation and curiosity, then calibrated with qualitative and quantitative data.
l2|17.e: She doesn't see product sense as a gift; it comes from sustained observation. Start by being a user yourself: notice where you get confused, at what step you give up, and what pulls you in. Then take products apart and critique them with other people. Read a lot of deep product analysis along the way. Once intuition forms, test it with user research and A/B tests. A/B tests tell you what causes what, and those lessons feed back and correct your intuition.
ex: She recommends long-form product essays by Eugene Wei and Kevin Kwok
A/B tests teach you cause and effect

items.d: Where you're confused, quit, or hooked
Critique and dissect products with others
Learn how others break products down

l2|17.c: Intuition works when the builders are the target users; the more diverse the users, the more you need experiments.
l2|17.e: She rejects the idea that data and design are at odds: data is how you test design hypotheses. Intuition is reliable only when the people building the product are also its users. Early Facebook was built by college students for college students, so going on gut feel worked. As users spread to other countries and demographics, the team's intuition started to fail. The bigger the user base, the less any single story counts and the more experiments are worth. Founders selling to businesses should interview lots of customers, since one person's experience rarely represents many companies.
ex: Several failed Facebook launches in 2008–2009 exposed the limits of intuition
B2B founders should interview customers widely

marks.d: College students building for college students

l2|17.c: Design reviews aren't about consensus: judge value first, then ease of use, then delight.
l2|17.e: She favors gathering lots of feedback, in layers: fellow designers, the product team, outsiders with fewer biases, and target users reached through research. But every opinion being valid doesn't mean decisions should be made by consensus. What matters is the order of questions. First define the target user and the job they're trying to get done. Then ask in sequence: does this solve the problem, can people get the value easily, and does it exceed expectations? Every review should open by stating what stage the work is at and what kind of input is needed; otherwise people nitpick the visual details of a prototype far too early.
ex: Four feedback sources: fellow designers, product team, outsiders, target users
Open each review by stating the stage and the feedback you need

items.d: Does it exceed what users expect?
Can people get the value easily?
Does it solve the core job?

l2|17.c: When giving designers feedback, explain the problem first instead of handing them a solution.
l2|17.e: Opening with "change this to look like that," she points out, takes away the designer's room to solve the problem themselves. A better approach is to describe where you got stuck and why, agree on what the problem actually is, and only then offer suggestions. She notices product managers make this mistake often, even though they hate it when others do the same to them.
ex: Bad example: demanding "make the logo purple"

items: Designer loses room to solve it
No agreement on the problem itself
Say where you're stuck and why
Agree on the problem, then suggest
Let the designer find the best answer

d.verdict: Suggestions only help once you agree on the problem

l2|17.c: If you want to manage, say so, and practice the skills before you have the title.
l2|17.e: Her advice: tell your manager clearly that you want to lead a team, then work out together what skills you're missing and make a plan. Many management skills can be practiced without the title: mentor an intern, be a new hire's onboarding buddy, or lead the improvement of a process or a meeting. Some obstacles are structural, though. If the company isn't growing and no roles are opening up, you may have to move to another company.
ex: Ways to practice: mentor an intern, be an onboarding buddy, lead a process improvement

items.d: Tell your manager you want to lead
Ask what's missing; make a plan
No open roles? Consider switching companies

l3|18.c: Start a big project by assuming it has already failed and working backward, and you avoid the painful post-mortem.
l3|18.e: Post-mortems are useful, he says, but you should not have to wait for a disaster to learn. The heart of a pre-mortem is the opening prompt: imagine it is six months from now and the project has failed badly, so why? That prompt gives people permission and psychological safety to voice bad news. The format: everyone silently writes down risks, then shares in turn, then votes for the scariest threat someone else raised. The owner ranks them, turns them into an action plan, and is accountable for following through. For a big launch, run separate sessions for engineering and go-to-market.
ex: Tiger: a threat that could really kill the project
Paper tiger: something others fear but you don't
Elephant: the big issue nobody in the room wants to name

items.d: The owner opens with the prompt
Each person lists three kinds of risk
Pick the scariest tiger someone else raised
The owner ranks and follows through

l3|18.c: Sort tasks into leverage, neutral and overhead, and save perfectionism for the few leverage tasks.
l3|18.e: His first three years at Google were brutally stressful, and the root cause was treating every item on his to-do list with the same effort. L tasks return ten or a hundred times what you put in. N tasks roughly break even. O tasks return far less than they cost. The extra time for L tasks cannot come from working longer; it has to come out of N and O work. The same kind of activity can land in different buckets depending on context, so the skill is recognizing the bucket and adjusting effort to match.
ex: An expense report is classic overhead; it does not need to be pretty
Write a thorough report for a severe bug; file a minor one with a screenshot
Decision notes from a contentious CEO review deserve an hour or two of polish

marks.d: Returns far less than it costs
Put in 1, get 10 to 100 times back

l3|18.c: The task you keep putting off is usually the leverage task, and the delay comes from fear of doing it badly.
l3|18.e: PMs usually know which tasks are the L tasks, he says, because not doing them, or doing them poorly, keeps nagging at you: setting strategy, writing the PRD that will not come together, getting two teams aligned. "No time" is often a respectable excuse; the deeper reason is fear of not producing something good, or of a hard conversation. He offers two tricks. For a day or two beforehand, deliberately do only N and O tasks, what he calls placebo productivity, to build momentum. Then, on the appointed day, work somewhere else and let the change of setting force focus.
ex: Placebo productivity: clear small tasks first to build momentum
Move to a cafe or coworking space to attack the leverage task

items.d: The one that makes you most uneasy
A day or two of N and O tasks first

l3|18.c: Product work happens at three levels, impact, execution and optics, and many fights come from mismatched levels.
l3|18.e: A PM explains in a review why customer support will not be ready at launch. The reasons are sound, yet the CEO is unconvinced, because the PM is talking execution while the CEO is thinking about the impact on customers and the brand. They argue details without noticing the mismatch. With this vocabulary, a team can decide which level matters most in its situation: an early-stage team with a solid hypothesis should focus on execution. Optics is not bad in itself, but if an organization keeps rewarding status updates and other optics work, optics becomes the goal.
ex: Early-stage team: impact is invisible for now, so focus on execution
A platform team after an outage: communicate more with dependent teams

items.d: Outcomes for customers, brand and business
How it gets done, hitting milestones

l3|18.c: In high-performing organizations, most execution problems are really strategy, culture or people problems.
l3|18.e: When two teams fall out of sync and slow things down, leaders typically add meetings, review processes and regular check-ins. But misalignment usually has a deeper cause: there is no clear strategy, so each team writes its own OKRs; or the culture rewards only hitting your own OKRs, so helping another team costs you; or the two managers simply do not get along. Fix the symptom and the problem returns a month later in a new form. The tell is that the band-aid keeps falling off, with the same kind of issue recurring. Some execution problems are real, such as aging infrastructure that cannot handle the load.
ex: A real execution problem: aging infrastructure that can't handle the usage
A real execution problem: a zero-to-one PM running a mature business, a skills gap

items.d: No clear strategy; OKRs set in isolation
Only your own OKRs get rewarded
Two managers who don't get along

l3|18.c: High-leverage roles should minimize opportunity cost, not do everything with a positive ROI.
l3|18.e: A high-leverage role has hundreds of positive-return things it could do. ROI puts time in the denominator, so to make the ratio look good people naturally pick short, quick wins and pack the plan with them. Opportunity cost asks a different question: what is the gap in value between the best option and the one you chose? Not "is this worth doing" but "is this the most worthwhile thing to do." He picked this up watching Patrick Collison at Stripe. You do not have to quantify it; what matters is that leaders give teams permission to go after the big opportunities.
ex: Taking over Stripe Connect, he pushed for more flexible platform payments
Quarterly planning: five certain small things versus two fuzzy big ones

items: Dares to try fuzzy big things
Asks: is it the most worthwhile

d.verdict: High-leverage roles should minimize opportunity cost

l3|18.c: Before planning starts, leaders should set rough time allocations that reserve room for big projects.
l3|18.e: Besides explaining the strategy, he says, a leader should give the team a rough split of time before planning begins. He borrows this from Google's 70-20-10 rule during its high-growth years. His usual split is 60 percent on incremental features that improve the everyday experience, 30 percent on one or two big new projects, and 10 percent on stability and infrastructure. The numbers vary by situation, but with the frame in place a team will not fill the big-project share with quick wins too.
ex: Google's 70-20-10: search ads, apps, and other big bets

l3|18.c: Whether a PM outperforms their resume comes down to high agency.
l3|18.e: High agency means not waiting for perfect conditions or blaming circumstances, but finding a way to get the outcome you want. PMs face thin resources, legacy systems, staffing gaps and customer problems every day, so the trait matters even more for them. He has compared PMs with modest resumes and huge impact against PMs with glittering resumes who fall well short of their potential, and the difference is usually this. He breaks it into three parts: a strong sense of ownership, creative execution when stuck, and resilience.
ex: He borrowed the term "high agency" from Eric Weinstein

terms.d: Work around resource and system limits

result.d: Reach the goal without perfect conditions

l4|19.c: There's no single metric for weak positioning; the symptoms are scattered across the whole funnel.
l4|19.e: Weak positioning, she says, drags on several things at once: marketing campaigns get a flat response, leads move slowly through the middle, sales struggle to close, and customers who do buy discover it's not what they expected and churn. That's why no single number pinpoints the problem. The most direct diagnosis is to listen to sales calls. Prospects asking you to explain again, assuming you're just like a well-known competitor, or understanding you but not seeing why they'd pay are all red flags. A new marketing leader should do this on day one.
ex: A prospect asks, "So it's like Salesforce?"
A prospect says, "I could do this in a spreadsheet"

items.d: Prospects are confused or compare you to rivals
Buyers find it's not what they expected and leave

l4|19.c: Most positioning problems aren't wrong positioning; they're a team telling slightly different stories.
l4|19.e: In the companies she works with, the founder, marketing, sales, and product usually each tell a slightly different version. Two patterns are common. Either the founder tells it well but newly hired executives can't, or the founder's view of the market comes from doing the early selling personally, and both the market and the company have since changed, so that view is stale. Positioning therefore can't be a deliverable marketing throws over the wall. The CEO and every function need to hammer it out together until everyone agrees. And because markets shift, positioning needs a regular review.
ex: Postman's current one-line positioning isn't how it originally described itself

items.d: The story lives only in the founder's head
Market and company have both changed
Thrown over the wall; nobody buys in

l4|19.c: Start positioning from competitive alternatives, then work forward to best customers and market category.
l4|19.e: Starting from "why do people love us" just gives you opinions, she says, and starting from the market category gives you nothing to judge by. So the starting point has to be what customers would use if you didn't exist, including doing nothing and sticking with the status quo. Next, list the capabilities only you have, translate each into value customers care about (usually two or three themes), identify the traits of customers who care most about that value, and finally pick a market category that makes the value obvious. B2B buyers have to justify the choice to their boss; if you can't give them a reason, the deal quietly dies.
ex: She estimates about 40% of B2B deals are lost to no decision
Alternatives include spreadsheets, pen and paper, and doing nothing

items.d: Accounts that care most about that value
The context that makes the value obvious

l4|19.c: Positioning has to become a sales narrative, tested on how qualified prospects react.
l4|19.e: She sees many teams that "understand" their positioning but can't tell it, so salespeople improvise. After the positioning document, build a sales storyboard, then turn it into real demos and a pitch so sales, marketing, and product all tell the same story. The test isn't whether an outsider can understand your homepage. It's whether a qualified prospect gets excited and wants to buy after hearing it. Running it past your grandmother, she says, proves nothing.
ex: Help Scout: rivals treat support as a cost; it argues support drives growth
Help Scout fits DTC and e-commerce brands that use support as a growth engine

items.d: See whether they want to buy
Roll out to the team once proven

l4|19.c: Positioning is the foundation under copy and brand; brilliant technology can't rescue vague positioning.
l4|19.e: If you don't know who the product is for, what it's compared against, and what value it delivers, she says, you can't write a homepage. Brand has to sit on top of positioning too, which is why she dislikes the muddled phrase "brand positioning." The cautionary tales are products with dazzling technology and no clear value: users either can't think of a reason to buy or invent wild expectations of their own. Those products only found clarity later, when they narrowed to focused business uses.
ex: Segway promised to revolutionize transport; users didn't even know where to ride it
Magic Leap and Google Glass later pivoted to focused enterprise uses

l4|19.c: Early-stage companies need only a loose positioning thesis; tighten it once customer patterns emerge.
l4|19.e: An early-stage company, she argues, has only a positioning thesis, and part of it is probably wrong. Narrowing too soon can leave you crashing in the wrong market. Better to stay loose and let the market tell you where the product truly fits. Tighten when the customers who pay and succeed start to share obvious traits, like using the same tools or having similar team sizes, and when you can predict which pitch will win a deal. She usually works with companies past roughly $5 to $10 million in revenue; earlier ones often aren't ready.
ex: You wove a net for tuna and may discover it's better at catching grouper

marks.d: Let the market show you the fit

l4|19.c: In B2B, don't build a persona for every decision-maker; win over the champion and arm them.
l4|19.e: She separates two concepts people often blur. Segmentation slices the market by actionable traits like company size, tech stack, or team size, and produces a target account list for sales and marketing. A persona describes one person's goals, worries, and motivations. A B2B deal usually involves five to seven decision-makers, so building a persona for each is wasted effort. The person who matters most is the champion pushing the deal inside the company. If your positioning doesn't land with them, the deal dies early. After that, you arm the champion to convince IT, procurement, the end users, and whoever holds the budget.
ex: A B2B deal typically has 5 to 7 decision-makers

items: Profile all five to seven roles
Misses the person driving the deal
Get the champion to buy the positioning
Then arm them to convince others
Cover IT, procurement, and the budget holder

d.verdict: If positioning misses the champion, the deal dies early

l5|20.c: Great careers aren't a straight climb; do your job well, stay curious, and grab the lucky breaks.
l5|20.e: You have to do your day job well, he says, but the next opportunity usually comes from who you know inside the company and what you know about their work. While working on affiliate ads at Google, he wandered the office one evening and found a group of engineers building a project that matched ads to page content. He offered to be their PM in his spare time; three months later it had grown into what became AdSense. He also gave free advice to colleagues who left to start companies, and one of them recommended him to Jack Dorsey, which led to Square's offer. Help people and build goodwill, and it comes back in unexpected ways.
ex: The side project he PMed grew into Google AdSense
A founder he had helped for free recommended him to Jack Dorsey

l5|20.c: Better to be a regular contributor at the category leader than an executive at a second-tier company.
l5|20.e: He starts with two questions: does the problem and the customer give you energy, and is the founder genuinely committed to the mission rather than just the money. Then he asks whether the company can become number one in its category. A leader's talent density, brand and network all flow back to you, and the outside world grants you a winner's halo. So he would rather be an ordinary PM at Google than head of product at Yahoo. For people early in their careers, the sweet spot is a mid-stage company of 300 to 500 people that has found product-channel fit and is heading toward becoming a platform.
ex: He once advised someone to skip a second-tier exec job and step down a level at Coinbase
Mid-stage: roughly 300 to 500 people, with product-channel fit

items.d: Talent, brand and network flow back to you

l5|20.c: Keep early process minimal; the big trap is founders dictating features and turning the team into a feature factory.
l5|20.e: Early on, plan week by week with a simple spreadsheet; product strategy is just company strategy. After a Series A, add quarterly goals, and only at larger scale do you need annual planning and a separate product strategy document. What never changes is a core squad of six or seven people with a daily stand-up. The most common mistake he sees is a founder who believes they understand customers and tells engineers to build a specific feature. The team then ships one thing after another without knowing whether any of it changed user behavior. Instead, hand the team the problem and let them find the solution.
ex: Instead of "build an iOS app," say "move weekly usage from two times to five"
A feature that ships but changes no behavior is a tree falling in an empty forest

items: Handed a problem, not an answer

d.verdict: Give teams problems, not answers, from day one

l5|20.c: Hire a first PM at eight to ten engineers, when the founder can't keep up, and promote from inside.
l5|20.e: Engineers are a company's most expensive resource, he argues. If the founder is busy elsewhere and nobody is defining problems and setting priorities for them, that resource is wasted. The first PM is really a bridge between the founder and the engineering team, so both sides must trust them. Every first PM he has seen succeed came from inside, converted from engineering, design or analytics; an outsider risks being rejected. If the team can already take a problem, compare options and run experiments, there is no rush, and developer-facing infrastructure products need fewer PMs anyway. Once there are three or four PMs, they should report to a dedicated head of product.
ex: Stripe is known for having few PMs, because its users are developers
To judge a new PM, ask the engineers directly

d.xLabel: Can the team solve problems itself
d.yLabel: Does the founder have time to PM

cells.d: Still needs a partner as the team grows

l5|20.c: Don't just raid competitors; find the companies best at that function and recruit the deputy's deputy.
l5|20.e: To hire a head of some function, first identify three or four companies that serve similar customers and are best in class at that function, not necessarily competitors. Then map their org charts using LinkedIn and friends. The target is not the person at the top but a rising deputy, or even the deputy's deputy. After Square went public, its compliance and risk teams were poached in exactly this way by other fintechs. He also thinks founders should spend about two hours a day recruiting, one on outreach and one meeting two candidates, after designing the process first.
ex: One portfolio company hired executives three times this way
Two hours a day: one of outreach plus two half-hour conversations

items.t: Best three or four at the function
items.d: Say, the best at consumer marketing
Not the person at the top

l5|20.c: Hand out titles as late as possible, and avoid hierarchical ones like Director and VP.
l5|20.e: A young company has a chance to build a culture that cares about scope and impact rather than titles, he says. Hierarchical titles cause the most arguments and resentment, and people even stay just to keep one. And once given, a title cannot be taken back: the VP of Engineering or General Counsel at 25 people is often not up to the job at 250, and then has to be demoted or let go. He prefers labels like Lead or Head of that simply describe the responsibility. At Square, his team never once raised the subject of titles with him.
ex: His title at DoorDash was simply Caviar Lead
Square's approach came from Jack Dorsey seeing titles abused at Twitter

l5|20.c: Angel investing is a bet on people, and missing a great founder costs more than backing a bad one.
l5|20.e: His approach is founder-first: he believes a great founder will create a market or pivot into one. Early on he turned down friends because he was picky about the market, and most of those turned out to be errors of omission. The math is simple: a bad investment loses at most your money, while a miss loses the relationship and the option to back that person's next company. He looks for motivation rooted in a problem the founder has lived, and likes complementary pairs where one builds and one sells. To get into good deals you need to stand out, for instance by writing and sharing non-obvious insights to build a personal brand.
ex: If the first search result for your name is LinkedIn, your brand isn't built yet
More and more founders succeed in the same space after a first failure

result.d: Keeps the option on their next company

l6|21.c: A PM is not a gatekeeper. Most suggestions point at a real problem, so don't rush to say no.
l6|21.e: In her first six months at Asana, she thought a PM's job was to shield the team from every request. She shot down even her boss's design ideas, until he told her to stop blocking him. Her coach gave her an experiment: say yes to everything for two weeks. Yes meant agreeing the problem was real and agreeing to put the idea in front of users. She found the defensive stance was unnecessary and actually got in the way of real collaboration. Even when someone's solution isn't the best one, it can be a clue to the problem and a starting point for brainstorming together.
ex: Her coach's challenge: say yes to everything for two weeks
She only sees a coach when she has a specific problem to work on

items: Treat the idea as a clue

d.verdict: You can say yes and still be a good PM

l6|21.c: Managing people isn't the only way to grow, and senior PMs already earn very well.
l6|21.e: She finds management lonelier. You keep other people's secrets and often get pulled between the company's interests and your reports' needs, which is part of why she burned out after eight years of it. Her advice: if you want to try management, treat it as a two-way door you can walk back through. Many people assume a promotion is the only way to earn more, but senior PMs at big companies already make about what doctors and lawyers make. At smaller companies, switching jobs usually pays better than an internal promotion. Senior individual roles like principal PM are rare and mostly show up on platform teams and large cross-company projects.
ex: Use levels.fyi to see real pay at each level
Senior IC roles cluster on platform teams and big partnerships

root.d: Not only by becoming a manager

items.d: Treat it as a two-way door
Usually pays more than a promotion
More users or bigger social impact

l6|21.c: A complete strategy has three parts: a vision, a strategic framework, and a roadmap.
l6|21.e: She was passed over for promotion at Google for not being strategic enough, and a new product leader at Asana told her the platform strategy she wrote wasn't a strategy. Those knocks led her to three ingredients. The vision is a picture of the future that makes people want to join. The strategic framework says which market you're going after, what success looks like, and the few big bets that will win it. The roadmap works backward from the vision to what gets built over the next few years. A roadmap is not a commitment, she says, but a feasibility check. Most teams lay it out and realize it would take thirty years at the current pace, so they have to place bigger bets and cut optional work.
ex: Asana's vision: be the team's brain, so groups work together like two hands
A roadmap also forces marketing support, fundraising, and hiring plans

terms.d: An exciting picture of the future
Target market, success criteria, big bets
Feasibility check working back from the vision

result.d: Anyone would recognize it as strategy

l6|21.c: A good strategy connects every dot between the top business goal and the specific features.
l6|21.e: Two people recently complained to her that the strategy their CEO handed down was just "grow revenue 50%." In her view, a number by itself isn't a complete strategy. The PM's job is to take the candidate projects collected from customer research, line them up against the top-level goal, and fill in the reasoning in between. Why is this the most profitable move? Is the new-customer market saturated, so the focus should be existing users? What other options are there, and how should effort be split? The only way to find a missing dot is to explain the strategy over and over and watch for the confusion people hide.
ex: "Grow revenue 50%" is a goal, not a strategy

items.d: The number handed down from the top
Because the new-user market is saturated
And be able to say why

l6|21.c: New PMs should leave the strategy alone for six months, then draft one and refine it with teammates.
l6|21.e: Your manager usually hired you to execute an existing strategy. Declaring it all wrong on day one makes people wonder why you joined. So for the first six months, she says, talk to customers, look at the data, ship things, and notice the trends that surface. Then block out half a day with no meetings, start a draft with whichever of the three parts excites you most, and bring it to your engineering and design leads. If the same feature argument keeps coming back and feels like a clash of values, the real disagreement is at the strategy level, and writing down strategic principles will settle it. Staying on one team long enough to see results, and borrowing trade-off frameworks from other products, also sharpen the skill.
ex: Shishir brought the shopping team's consistency-versus-comprehensiveness trade-off to YouTube

items.d: Learn the current strategy and ship
Start with one of the three parts
Discuss with engineering and design leads

l6|21.c: To get promoted, tell your manager the level you want someday and ask what to work on now.
l6|21.e: PMs get endless feedback, and all of it is true, like saying "um" too much in meetings. But most of it isn't what's actually blocking a promotion. Her advice is to state the goal in the future tense: "someday I'd like to reach this level." That keeps the manager from getting defensive and rushing to prove you're not ready yet. Instead they join your side and help you prepare, and the feedback narrows to the gaps that really matter. If your manager decides promotions, follow their guidance. If a committee decides and your manager is new, find a peer of theirs who has been around longer and has helped people get promoted, and ask them the same question.
ex: It works for any goal: senior PM, manager, director

items.d: All true, but not equally important
The few things actually blocking you

l6|21.c: Early on, don't try to dazzle. Nail a narrow scope, and get your level of involvement right.
l6|21.e: She thinks a medium or large company is the better first stop: you learn best practices, build a network, and earn well. The exception is when you're sure you've picked a small company that will take off. New PMs usually get a narrow assignment, and reaching for a grand idea there is a mistake. Doing it well earns trust, and solid work is all it takes to get promoted out of Google's APM program. Common mistakes: looking down on everyday PM work while itching to manage people, turning into a note-taker next to a strong designer, or the opposite, grabbing the lead on everything and crowding teammates out. Peer feedback carries a lot of weight in reviews.
ex: If you're assigned the print dialog, don't reinvent it

l7|22.c: Product strategy means delighting customers in hard-to-copy ways that also improve margins.
l7|22.e: From Reed Hastings he learned that the goal isn't to satisfy customers but to delight them, something close to ten times better. Delight that's easy to copy doesn't last, though, so you also need advantages others can't replicate, and in the end it has to make money. That's DHM: Delight, Hard to copy, Margin. He sees strategy as a set of high-level hypotheses about those three things. Roughly six out of ten fail, and the three or four that work build the value. Netflix's social recommendations failed, while personalization hit all three, to the point that content spending could be sized by predicted viewers.
ex: A family on a couch on the signup page: Blockbuster could copy that in weeks
Netflix bet $500 million on Stranger Things because it predicted 100 million viewers
In B2B, the hard-to-copy advantage is often switching costs

terms.d: Surprise customers, don't just satisfy them
It has to improve profits eventually

result.d: A set of hypotheses waiting to be tested

l7|22.c: When customers all ask for something, test how much that delight is worth, then compare it to the cost.
l7|22.e: In the DVD era, members constantly asked for new releases to arrive faster. Netflix ran a "perfect new release" A/B test: 10,000 members got the disc the day after release. Monthly churn fell only from about 4.5% to 4.45%. Scaled to a million members, that's roughly 5,000 extra people retained. At $100 lifetime value each, times a word-of-mouth multiplier of 2, the gain was about $1 million. The extra inventory would have cost $5 million. The whole answer hinged on the word-of-mouth assumption, and the CFO flatly refused to raise it, because a bigger multiplier meant a bigger spend.
ex: With Amazon's 10x word-of-mouth multiplier, the answer would flip

items.d: To meet day-one demand for new releases

l7|22.c: Cut any feature only about 2% of users touch. Its complexity outweighs its value.
l7|22.e: A feature can only improve retention if enough members actually use it. A feature that serves 2% of users adds one more option for everyone and leaves behind complexity the team will later forget to maintain. So he scrapes these off like barnacles on a ship's hull. Netflix Party, watching together with friends, sounds delightful and even has network effects. But an earlier Netflix feature like it, built with Xbox, barely reached 5% usage and was killed. In his experience a feature needs 10 to 15% usage before it's worth serious consideration.
ex: When streaming launched, they forgot to carry over multi-user profiles from DVD
Social features for friends recommending movies failed the same way

marks.d: Only here can it move retention

l7|22.c: PMs treat every decision as high stakes. First ask how big it is and whether it's reversible.
l7|22.e: Early in the pandemic, Netflix was growing faster than expected. A product manager noticed that about 0.5% of members hadn't watched anything in a year but were still paying, and decided to cancel them automatically. That made customers feel well treated and built up the brand, at a cost of roughly $100 million in revenue. Against $30 billion in revenue, though, that isn't huge, and the policy could be switched off at any time. It's what Amazon calls a two-way door. Once you see the size of a decision and whether you can undo it, he says, many decisions can be made quickly.
ex: Auto-cancelling about 0.5% of inactive members cost around $100 million

cells.d: Big and hard to undo, so be careful
Try it, roll back if it fails

l7|22.c: Whether to add an ad tier depends on whether simplicity or customer choice matters more right now.
l7|22.e: From 2005 to 2008, Netflix ran big banner ads on its site. Tests showed they didn't hurt retention, and they helped the company turn its first profit. But in 2008 Reed Hastings had him cut both ads and the used-DVD business. Google was going to be the best at advertising, while the thing Netflix had to be best at was personalization, and staying simple kept the focus there. In 2022, after losing subscribers, Reed said customer choice now mattered more. Ads can also be handed to many outside partners today without breaking focus, so Biddle expects Netflix to launch an ad tier.
ex: Reed asked just two questions before having him kill the ad business
Password sharing: test in small countries, see how many will pay to go legit

items: Outside partners can run the ads

d.verdict: Same model, different context, different answer

l7|22.c: Getting executives to rank growth, engagement, and monetization is the first job of alignment.
l7|22.e: When he joined Chegg, the CEO was shouting for more growth while the CFO wanted to slow down and prove the business model first. He put the two in a room and made them force-rank growth, engagement, and monetization and agree on the order. They landed on growth, then engagement, then monetization. A few months later the disagreement resurfaced, and the CFO left the company. He sees this as the most common source of misalignment in startups. The hardest part is the engagement metric, meaning how you measure product quality. His approach: start with a rough guess, refine it one-on-one with long-tenured employees, and publish it after about six weeks.
ex: Netflix measured engagement as monthly retention
SWAG: a scientific wild-ass guess, so you have a view before asking for feedback

items.d: A proxy for product quality, like retention
Turning users and product into a business

l7|22.c: You own your career. Treat it like a product: form a hypothesis, run experiments, adjust on the results.
l7|22.e: Your career is your responsibility, not your employer's. He runs his like a product. He once hypothesized that he'd love teaching, and after teaching at Stanford found he liked it but didn't love it, because it tied him to campus every fall. So he shifted to talks and workshops outside the classroom. He urges people to be bold, since you learn most outside your comfort zone, and the easiest way is to start right now. He also relies on a personal board of directors, peers and mentors who help him compare notes and pick companies. To find a mentor, don't lead with an ask. Find a way to help them first.
ex: His first talk was a terrible one at a friend's company
He asked a CFO friend to assess whether joining Chegg was worth it

items.d: Move to talks outside the classroom

l8|23.c: B2B buying power is shifting to end users, and product-led sales will replace top-down selling.
l8|23.e: B2B software used to be built for corporate buyers who never used it themselves, which produced cold products assembled from feature checklists. Now individual users pick the tools first and the organization pays once it sees usage, so the product needs a consumer-grade experience. She predicts that within about a decade, product-led sales will replace top-down selling: acquiring a user is cheaper than acquiring a buyer, usage itself is the sales lead, and expansion opportunities keep surfacing on their own. Buyers still hold the budget, but the influence is moving to users.
ex: Slack and Miro spread bottom-up through their users
She mentions Atlassian closing $200,000-level deals on self-serve
She paid about $24,000 a year for Drift on a credit card without talking to sales

terms.d: Volume, growth, feature breadth, spread within the org
Users ask to buy on their own
The product is the sales tool

result.d: Replaces top-down selling

l8|23.c: Growth has three levers—acquisition, retention, monetization—and product-led growth must nail retention first.
l8|23.e: She breaks a growth model into three questions: how you acquire users, how you retain them, and how you make money. Each can be driven by product, marketing, or sales. Product-led acquisition only works once users have formed a habit. Without activation and a habit loop, there's nothing to build on, so never start with product-led acquisition. Acquisition also requires a product that's naturally collaborative. A single-player product struggles to grow through users bringing in other users.
ex: Collaborative products like Slack, Miro, and Amplitude suit product-led acquisition
A single-player product like Snowflake finds product-led acquisition hard

items.d: Needs collaboration; one user brings many
Activation plus habit loop; the foundation

l8|23.c: When product-led companies move upmarket, the most common mistake is cutting product-led investment.
l8|23.e: The typical path she describes: users love the product and spread the word, self-serve payment works, lots of users inside one organization lead to the first big deal, and management rushes to hire enterprise salespeople. Those headcount slots compete with product managers, and product-led investment gets squeezed out. But only a minority of enterprise buyers are already in your user base, so the pipeline slows down fast. Her advice is to layer the two models rather than swap one for the other. Don't compare the smaller first deal from product-led growth with top-down deal sizes, and keep investing in user growth.
ex: She estimates about 80% of companies drop product-led efforts during the transition
Roughly 30% or fewer enterprise buyers are already product users
SurveyMonkey, Netlify, and Amplitude all went through this

items.d: Most buyers aren't in the user base

l8|23.c: Time-limited trials shut out large enterprises; use a free tier capped by usage instead.
l8|23.e: Freemium and trials are both free usage, she says. The only difference is that a trial adds a time limit, and time is a terrible proxy for value. A seven-day trial works for a small team, but a large enterprise with many dependencies and integrations to configure needs far longer, so the trial effectively excludes them. Capping by usage makes more sense. Trials are better suited to proofs of concept and lowering the activation barrier, while a free tier can play a much bigger strategic role.
ex: MongoDB's shared clusters are free forever; you pay when you go to production
High-setup products like Okta and Snowflake have moved toward offering trials

cells.d: Try as needed; pay at the cap
Too many dependencies to activate in time

l8|23.c: The biggest misuse of a free tier is treating it only as a funnel into paid.
l8|23.e: A free tier, she argues, is first a strategic tool. It can make money indirectly, as free users bring in new users when they share. It can claim a segment you can't monetize yet and expand later. When a feature becomes a commodity that everyone offers, free lets you hold your ground. And it reveals adjacent use cases and user types that feed the roadmap. If you only watch the free-to-paid conversion rate, you throw all of that value away.
ex: Miro's free tier gives three editable boards and spreads through sharing
Most of SurveyMonkey's acquisition comes from free users
LinkedIn's free base supports its paid recruiting and sales products

items.d: Claim segments you can't charge yet
Hold ground on features everyone has
Surface new use cases and users

l8|23.c: Features that drive virality, habits, and aha moments go free; features that add friction go paid.
l8|23.e: She offers a few rules of thumb for deciding whether a feature is free. Anything that drives virality or network effects is usually free. Anything everyone needs and that's close to a commodity is usually free. Features behind the aha moment should at least have a free version that proves the value. Features that form the habit loop, like notifications, are usually free. Features that would create friction in the growth model go behind the paywall. The specific answer depends heavily on the company's monetization strategy.
ex: Habit-loop features like notifications are usually free

marks.d: A free version that proves the value

l8|23.c: Don't hire a growth leader before product-market fit; founders must build the first growth model themselves.
l8|23.e: Growth should start from inside the company, she says: promote from finance, product management, data analysis, or engineering, because they get results fastest. An outside executive needs at least three to six months to understand the product, and copying the playbook from their last company usually fails. In her fourth month at Amplitude she caught herself replicating old experience and stopped. Hire only once you have product-market fit, which shows up clearly in retention after 6 to 12 months. Before that, the growth model, like the first product, can only be built by the founders.
ex: Qualtrics and SurveyMonkey's growth models couldn't be copied from one to the other

items.d: The first growth model can't be outsourced
Retention is visible after 6 to 12 months
Allow a 3 to 6 month learning period

l9|24.c: Hard PM skills just get you in the door. Going furthest takes founder skills.
l9|24.e: Organization, analysis, communication, and some technical ability are the basics that make you a PM, he says. Domain expertise, like being a top payments PM, takes you a step further. But what he's seen decide who reaches the senior ranks is the founder's toolkit: telling a story, firing up a team, making high-conviction calls on problems with no clean answer and leading people through the uncertainty, and leading by example while owning the consequences. His advice is to take on a serious side project, so you personally live through selling, support, and a botched launch, and lose your fear of the technology.
ex: Thirty to forty percent of Shopify's PMs are former founders
Someone who doesn't know HTML can build a Twitter clone from a tutorial in a weekend

l9|24.c: Product thinking belongs to the whole company. The PM's job is to help the team build the right thing.
l9|24.e: Shopify is intensely technical. In the early days even marketers had to commit code to publish a blog post, so every function stays close to the product and the product team isn't put on a pedestal. New PMs get a one-line job description: help the team ship the right thing, the right way, at the right time. The emphasis is on servant leadership, not being the CEO of the product. It does change with level, though. A junior PM balances decisions with design and engineering. At director and above, the PM's only job is to call the direction and own the outcome.
ex: Canada has never produced a truly global tech company, so Shopify deliberately stresses ambition

marks.d: Decides together with design and engineering
Sets direction and owns the results

l9|24.c: Set direction yearly, let teams decide how, and dare to tear up the plan when the world changes.
l9|24.e: Each year Shopify makes an investment plan in big blocks, each about a fifth of the company, and aligns on vision and headcount with the CEO, executives, and even the board. After that, product directors place their own bets, commit by quarter, and win support by persuading peers and bosses. Because things change so fast, the company refuses to be trapped by sunk costs. Something three to six months in the making can still be dropped. When Covid hit, offline merchants' revenue went to zero overnight. The team cut roughly 40 planned items for the quarter down to 3, focusing on lifelines like gift cards and buy online, pick up in store.
ex: About 500 people were moved to ship gift cards within two weeks
Early in the pandemic they permanently closed offices and went digital-first

l9|24.c: The fix for remote work isn't going back to the office. It's making meetups extremely easy.
l9|24.e: After going fully remote, they found face time still mattered, so they created "bursts": each team gathers about once a quarter for a few days of intense creative work and socializing. The company built its own app that books flights, hotels, and meals in one click, with no expense reports. The old offices were turned into community spaces for teams to use. The idea is to flip remote work's weaknesses and keep only the best parts of being in person. The system can also spot teams that haven't met in a long time and nudge their leads to get together.
ex: Employees can work from any country for 90 days a year
He once worked remotely from the Caribbean for five weeks

terms.d: Work together from anywhere, any time
Team gatherings booked in one click
Spot teams that haven't met in a while

result.d: Keep only the best of in-person

l9|24.c: Writing is first a way to think clearly. Publishing it also amplifies your influence inside the company.
l9|24.e: The frameworks in his essays weren't worked out in advance. They took shape while he wrote. Writing things down also clears his head so he can keep thinking on top of them. An essay typically takes him about 40 hours: two for the first draft, the rest for revising, drawing diagrams, and getting feedback, and he's willing to show people rough drafts. Even if a piece never spreads, that payoff alone is worth it. When it does land outside, new colleagues arrive already knowing how he thinks, it's easier to influence a noisy big company from the outside in, and it helped him earn the CEO's trust.
ex: After David Marcus shared one essay, Shopify's chief product officer took him more seriously
He stopped writing as an executive with kids, afraid lower quality would let readers down

items.d: You only figure it out while writing
New teammates already know your ideas
New PMs reach out every week

l9|24.c: First judge how much a decision matters. Dig deep on the few that do; go with your gut on the rest.
l9|24.e: This is the core of his most widely read essay. A PM faces hundreds of decisions at once and only has the energy for a few, so step one is to assess importance: can it be reversed, and does it materially affect a lot of users? The one or two that matter most outweigh everything else combined, and that's where the time should go. For the rest, follow your intuition or delegate. Intuition is right more often than you'd think, and the main thing is not to become the team's bottleneck. After a few "sky is falling" moments where nothing happened, his bar for "important" keeps rising.
ex: The test: is it reversible, and does it materially affect many users?

l9|24.c: Platform PMs must set principles and stakeholder priorities first, and live with much longer feedback loops.
l9|24.e: Platform work takes five to ten times longer to validate than a normal product. You change the underlying systems, open an API, run an alpha and a beta, and end users might not touch it for two years, because you're designing a canvas for developers to create on. So you learn to celebrate milestones along the way. More important is settling your principles up front and ranking developers, merchants, and consumers, or conflicts over data policy and who gets paid will blow up the day before launch. He doesn't think platform and consumer product work is a one-way door. Switching back and forth is where he's learned the most.
ex: The long-press shortcut menu on iOS icons is platform extension design
The CEO once stopped one of his launches the day before

items: Data must flow back to merchants

d.verdict: No right answer, just rank the stakeholders in advance

l10|25.c: Teams moving from shipping features to chasing outcomes need scaffolding like the opportunity solution tree.
l10|25.e: Many teams learned product by being told to build a list of features, which is well-structured work. Being handed a business outcome and asked to figure out what to build is an open, messy problem. The opportunity solution tree works like a decision tree. The root is the outcome you're driving. Below it sits the opportunity space, the unmet needs, pain points, and desires. Below each opportunity come solutions, and below those, assumption tests. It looks simple but is hard to use well. The difficulty is separating the problem space from the solution space and resisting the urge to jump straight to solutions.
ex: She estimates 98% of the "opportunities" people write down are actually solutions

items.d: The business or product metric to move
Several ways to address one opportunity
Check the assumptions behind a solution

l10|25.c: Structure opportunities along the customer's journey. The further down you break them, the more solvable they get.
l10|25.e: Take streaming. First map the whole experience of entertaining yourself with a streaming service, then hang the needs and pain points under each moment, with no solutions anywhere on the map. Keep the top level to three to seven opportunities so it fits in your head. An evergreen problem like "I don't know what to watch" can be broken down layer by layer, say to "I can't tell if this show is good," then to "I want to see the cast first." At that level it's something you can actually act on, and it still contributes to the big problem above it. Opportunities must be specific. "Make it easier to use" gives you nothing to work with.
ex: A specific opportunity: typing a password letter by letter with an Apple TV remote is painful
Netflix and Hulu face a similar opportunity space but make different trade-offs and solutions

items.d: Pick a service, find a title
Read the summary, check the cast

l10|25.c: Interviews should collect stories about specific experiences, not direct questions asked out of context.
l10|25.e: Ask "what do you like to watch" and the brain produces a quick answer that may not match actual behavior. You've collected one fact. Ask instead "tell me about the last time you watched something," then keep probing with "where were you" and "what happened next," and you rebuild the context and hear needs the user never noticed themselves. The most common mistake, she says, is being busy thinking of your next question instead of listening, so you miss a point of friction and rush to the next story. Focus on what people actually did, not what they would do or what they think.
ex: A good interview feels like chatting with a friend over a beer
Done well, customers ask when they can talk to you again

items: What do you like to watch?
Tell me about the last time

d.verdict: Ask about real behavior, not hypotheticals or opinions

l10|25.c: Discovery and delivery aren't two phases. They run at the same time, steadily improving the quality of your bets.
l10|25.e: Digital products are never finished, so decisions never stop, and customer input has to keep flowing in too. When leaders say there's no time for discovery, they mean no time for project-style research, and she agrees with that. Every item on the backlog is a bet, whether you did discovery or not. If a team has never done discovery, don't propose stopping everything to wait for research. That's the fastest way to kill interest in it. Keep placing bets as usual, and add a little interviewing and testing every week. The bets get better over time.
ex: The minimum: one customer interview a week
Only the core experience and differentiating features need heavy discovery

items.d: Track the impact of each release

l10|25.c: Automate interview recruiting so an interview is already on the calendar every Monday morning.
l10|25.e: The idea comes from the book Nudge: make the behavior you want easier than not doing it. Like an in-product NPS survey, ask users inside the product whether they'd spend 20 minutes talking to you. Anyone who says yes lands in a scheduling tool and picks a time. That works for consumers and for end users of B2B products. To reach buyers and decision makers, have the salespeople, account managers, and support staff who talk to them every day extend the invitation, using criteria the team sets each week. The goal is that the product team does nothing except show up.
ex: Tools: Calendly, Qualaroo, Ethnio, Intercom, and others

items.d: Or sales and support extend it

l10|25.c: The PM is not the CEO of the product. A healthy product trio decides together.
l10|25.e: The idea of the PM as final decision maker comes from turf-guarding office politics in business culture, and the result is that nobody really collaborates. She points to the marshmallow challenge: build a tower from spaghetti, tape, and string with a marshmallow on top. Kindergartners often beat MBAs, because kids just start building and learning, while adults argue over who's in charge and make plans. When the PM, designer, and engineer work from shared understanding, disagreements are rare. When one does come up, it means the best solution hasn't been found yet, so keep looking. She guesses only a small fraction of the industry has ever experienced a team like this.
ex: The marshmallow challenge: spaghetti, tape, string, and one marshmallow

l10|25.c: Break ideas into assumptions and run small tests. Small samples are enough to support product decisions.
l10|25.e: When people question deciding on a handful of interviews, she asks how much customer data last week's decisions were based on. Product teams are trying to change behavior, not generate new knowledge, and they have a continuous feedback loop. So you can decide on a small experiment first and get larger-scale data as you ship. Don't test the whole idea up front. That's too slow and too expensive. Instead, break the idea into the underlying assumptions it depends on, rank them, and test only the critical ones. Compare three solutions at once so you don't commit too early to a single answer.
ex: Good teams run six to a dozen assumption tests a week across three solutions

items.d: Compare rather than bet on one

l11|26.c: Skip the five-year plan: make small bets, recover fast, and go where you learn quickest.
l11|26.e: He wanted to be an astronaut and didn't make it, tried a startup that failed, and worked on Hotmail without success, pivoting each time. He later found the method in the book Little Bets: try small things, and when they fail, recover quickly and change direction. Over-analysis makes you miss opportunities; when something gives you energy, go all in. Pick the faster boat, because you won't reach shore before the boat does. Also be clear about what you want to learn, starting from zero or scaling, since big companies and startups each teach different things. His three years at Airbnb, he says, were worth thirty.
ex: Amazon keeps a million employees innovating; a startup can't teach that kind of scale

items.d: Go all in when it energizes you
Carry the lessons into the next round

l11|26.c: In a crisis, shorten planning cycles, dissolve sub-teams, and let the founder carry everyone's belief in the future.
l11|26.e: In January 2020 Airbnb was preparing an April IPO. Six weeks later countries locked down one after another and revenue forecasts fell to single-digit percentages of the prior year. The company laid off about 1,900 people, borrowed $2 billion in debt, and saw its valuation halved. Operationally it switched to planning every two weeks, scrapped sub-teams and moved people wherever they were needed. Leaders told employees honestly that they did not know, and shifted everyone's focus from features and revenue to a belief that travel would come back. What saved the company, he thinks, was the founders staying on the front line throughout.
ex: He laid off 190 people on his own team personally, over Zoom
Airbnb pitched the safety of a whole home for just you and your family against hotels
He compares Brian Chesky to Rocky, Silicon Valley's version of the fighter who won't stay down

items.d: No more quarterly or annual plans
Sub-teams dissolved, people moved as needed

l11|26.c: Decide where the product is going first, then use A/B tests to find the fastest route, not the destination.
l11|26.e: You tell the GPS where to go; you don't ask it where you should go. A/B testing picks the route, not the destination. When Instagram built Stories, Kevin Systrom did not first try to quantify whether the feed would decline. He decided to go all in and iterate from a new baseline. Facebook, by contrast, modeled the impact on existing business first, and its version of Stories never took off. Gut and intuition are data too, he says, just not statistically significant yet, so don't dismiss them. Pair that with being impatient to start and patient to persist, and teach the team to recover fast from failure.
ex: Data showed most posted photos were old, yet Systrom insisted Stories be live-only

d.verdict: Intent first; tests only find the fastest route

l11|26.c: Design an "11 out of 10" experience with no constraints, perfect it in one place, then scale.
l11|26.e: Most teams, he observes, start by squeezing the goal down to a seven based on time, people and budget. Brian Chesky instead asks for a 15 on a ten-point scale first. Take the Airbnb lounge: guests can't check in until 3 p.m., but their flight lands at 6 a.m. The usual approach is to ship an MVP, then add Wi-Fi, then coffee, measuring each step. Chesky's approach was to pick a single location, hire a barista, get the seating and air conditioning right, and build the most lovable version first. Then see what actually works and scale only that.
ex: At Airbnb, running a pile of A/B tests and reporting back would get shot down by Chesky

l11|26.c: Every decision gets one owner who collects written input, decides, and expects everyone to commit.
l11|26.e: At many companies, he says, cross-functional decisions go through endless alignment, and what ships is the option nobody hates most; speed depends on relationships. Coinbase assigns a directly responsible individual, or DRI, to every project, who may come from operations, engineering, legal or product. Each function writes its input into a RAPID document, and the DRI makes the final call based on what is best for customers and the business. Those who disagree can write down why, but once decided, they must push the decision as if it were their own. The system works from the executive team down to the smallest group.
ex: Coinbase's NFT marketplace started with just five people
Coinbase's COO has published a public blog post on this method

terms.d: Each function writes it in the RAPID
Based on customers and the business

result.d: No committee-grade compromises

l11|26.c: Early-stage companies should hire people who know the substance and teach them process, not the reverse.
l11|26.e: What decides a startup's fate, he argues, is not whether it runs Scrum but whether someone knows what to do and when. He calls that content; process is merely how. As companies grow they add process to avoid mistakes, until process becomes the product and executives spend 80 percent of their time managing it. If you attract only process people, the founder ends up carrying all the content alone and the company cannot scale. When Airbnb interviewed executives, it posed a real, hard problem, watched how the candidate would actually solve it, and pressed on what they personally did rather than their team.
ex: Sample interview question: how would you scale Airbnb Plus to millions of listings
He points to the Netflix culture deck's discussion of this

marks.d: Can say what to do and when

l11|26.c: The right people for Web3 can see its potential without being put off by today's imperfections.
l11|26.e: Plenty of famous people call Web3 terrible, and their real complaint is that it is still centralized today. He thinks the path from Web2 to Web3 runs through a 2.5 stage, and most products now sit somewhere between 2.5 and 2.7, but the decentralized ideal is real. It is like the late 1980s, when getting online meant typing an IP address and paying a lot; the people who could imagine video podcasts back then became the builders. He predicts every company will become a Web3 company this decade, and all of them will have to learn to form conviction in a noisy environment with no data.
ex: He sees Ethereum and Bitcoin as the closest to true decentralization

l12|27.c: A good pitch opens like an action movie, at the climax, leading with the insight only you have.
l12|27.e: As a VC she noticed that companies with similar fundamentals felt completely different depending on how well the founder told the story and commanded the room. Deals were often won or lost on relationships rather than rational analysis. Pitches, talks and writing are all stages where you control the narrative, so outline first and work out the story arc. A mediocre pitch starts with market size, but this talk is about you: open with your unique insight to grab attention and get people to put their phones down, then fill in the background later.
ex: Mission: Impossible films always open mid-mission, on the hero's previous job

items: Cuts to the climax like a thriller

d.verdict: Grab attention first; everything else follows

l12|27.c: The clear statement "Slack is a tool for work" made thousands of small decisions obvious.
l12|27.e: Around 2015, plenty of people inside Slack still thought social use cases mattered, and outsiders kept comparing it to Discord. The greatest gift from the early founding team, she says, was the clarity that this was a tool for work. When some users demanded a block feature, she pushed back: workplace harassment belongs with HR rather than being hidden, and blocking could be abused to shut someone out of key discussions and damage their performance. With the positioning clear, arguments like that had a basis for resolution.
ex: Open-source projects and Burning Man groups used Slack, but those were never the core use

items.d: Slack is a tool for work
Should we build a block feature
Work has HR; blocking can be abused
Thousands of small calls resolve themselves

l12|27.c: Collaboration products activate when people arrive together, so invite prompts should appear early and often.
l12|27.e: Slack's growth work started from curiosity: nobody had built Slack before, so they refused to copy other companies' metrics. Some onboarding patterns borrowed from elsewhere simply did not work inside Slack. Regression analysis and follow-up experiments showed the activation threshold was three real humans and 50 real messages; a three-person conversation is exactly where email starts to break down. Having someone there to greet a newcomer mattered a lot. Every user base has natural organizers, and it is easier to get a sharer to send several invites than to coax an introvert into sending one. She draws the line at any dark patterns.
ex: Mobile push notifications pulling new members into the team worked so well they remain today
Longer trials convert better, because buying depends on the customer's timing

result.d: From regression, confirmed by experiments

l12|27.c: Design onboarding alongside the product from day one, and let the product itself teach people.
l12|27.e: When she designed games, she started the whole game from the tutorial, because how something is presented shapes how people understand it. Many teams leave onboarding for last or bolt on a plug-and-play tool, some of which even claim to replicate Slack's onboarding, but what worked for someone else may not fit you. A launch carousel introducing seven features is destined to be skipped, because nobody cares about your product the way you do. Her rule: simplify until it feels a little dumb. If your boss won't buy it, build a few prototypes and compare, and watch real people go through signup every month.
ex: A to-do app's first task reads "check here to complete a task"
Carousels only suit products like Tinder that are already built on swiping

marks.d: Point to a clear next step
Like the to-do app's first task

l12|27.c: Product-led growth works only if an individual can start alone and gets value on day one.
l12|27.e: Whether a product suits product-led growth is mostly decided before any code is written, she says. If the head of HR has to approve it and it plugs into systems full of personal data, it will be sales-led. Something anyone at any level can pick up and try, like a developer tool, can grow product-led. The other condition is value on day zero: a product that takes months to pay off may get people in the door but will not keep them. Hire your first salesperson when the founder is giving everything and still cannot keep up, or when larger customers show up who want to talk to sales first.
ex: You should be able to try it without "borrowing dad's Porsche keys"
Bottom-up: anyone in a 500-person company can just start using it

l12|27.c: Hire PMs on a real work sample; nothing shows thinking quality and storytelling better.
l12|27.e: She treats hiring as a two-way match whose goal is finding people who will thrive at this company, not proctoring an exam from on high. For regular PM roles she insists on a take-home: three real problems, pick one, and the choice itself is revealing. Someone unwilling to spend three hours probably is not a fit for a startup anyway. She looks at whether the proposal is technically feasible, whether it tells a persuasive story, why they made the trade-offs they did, and how they would measure it. At Slack, the people who did outstanding work samples mostly grew into team leads.
ex: Red flag: imagining Slackbot as magic that holds natural conversations
At Slack, the story usually won the argument, not the numbers

root.d: Pick one of three real problems

items.d: Why this option and not another
Knows how to test and build it

l12|27.c: Don't blame the talent pool; recruit for diversity early and it becomes a self-reinforcing flywheel.
l12|27.e: Hiring women alone is not enough, she says; some people actually enjoy being the only woman in the room. In her observation women are, on average, less risk-tolerant, so relying on inbound applications and referrals yields few women, and the earlier and riskier the company, the lower the conversion. The answer is to go out and interview a lot of people. Once more women and people of color are hired early, newcomers are no longer the only one, and they refer their friends. Going from one woman to two on a team, she found, visibly changes the atmosphere and raises mutual respect.
ex: Early Slack was one of the most diverse teams she has ever seen

items.d: Interview widely; don't blame the pool

l13|29.c: Only two things in a career are repeatable: surround yourself with A+ people, and be a technology optimist.
l13|29.e: Looking back on success, he says, people overrate hard work and underrate luck and risk. Only two patterns truly repeat. First, get yourself among A+ talent as early as you can and stay with them for the long run. The same people keep working together across careers, and the trust they build compounds. Second, believe technology is a force for good. That belief pushes you toward projects that solve real needs with technology and can reach enormous numbers of users. The two reinforce each other, because optimists tend to find one another.
ex: After a title, coach Steve Kerr said the secret was "hang around superstars"
He went to Singapore on a scholarship at 16 and started a company with classmates right after graduating
He cites the chapter on luck and risk in The Psychology of Money

terms.d: Find them, then stay close for years
Pick problems that reach huge audiences

result.d: Plus luck and a willingness to risk

l13|29.c: Consumer products are far harder and slower than people expect, so get small wins fast and iterate.
l13|29.e: Because everyone is a consumer, teams assume they can build for themselves and their friends. But you serve a huge, varied population, you can't force anyone to use the product, and you have to earn genuine love and word of mouth. Finding product-market fit takes lots of trial and error and far longer than in enterprise software. His answer is to get a win first: in a low period, shrink the feature and ship it to a handful of customers in a month rather than waiting six, so the team gets its confidence back.
ex: After the dot-com crash his company pivoted repeatedly and his co-founder left
A scaled-down launch in one month, with about ten customers, had the team high-fiving

items: Wait for the full feature set

d.verdict: Wins are energy; get it in front of users, then iterate

l13|29.c: Build one product for the whole world from day one, and localize only at the edges.
l13|29.e: He has watched many companies burn time arguing that users in some market are different and need a dedicated product. In his view, the interfaces and core behaviors of consumer products are now highly universal. Users differ, but the way they use products does not. Language, pricing and legal compliance must be localized, or you have no right to exist in that market at all. Beyond that, don't over-invest in market-specific solutions; build one global product and keep innovating and adapting around the edges.
ex: Facebook, Google Search, Maps and TikTok all ship one global product
India was once called unmappable; it became Google Maps' second-largest country

l13|29.c: At a big company, answer "company-product fit" before you go looking for product-market fit.
l13|29.e: A company, he says, is really a portfolio of products, each with strengths and weaknesses. Before starting a project, assume it succeeds and ask: does it occupy the right place in the portfolio, does it draw on what the company is uniquely good at, and can it be better than everyone else's? "Competitors are doing it" is not a reason. Answer that confidently and the project gets support at the right level; everyone understands it is a strategic bet, people step in to help when it stumbles, and the search for product-market fit faces less interference. The usual failure is linear extension, assuming two more features will carry you to an adjacent customer base.
ex: Anti-pattern: adding two features to an SMB product and expecting to win enterprises
A company's culture closely matches the kind of product it is good at

items.d: Takes the right place in it

l13|29.c: There's no formula for consumer success, but five capabilities can each be graded and built up.
l13|29.e: At Microsoft he is pushing a "consumer capability stack": design-led product, focus and prioritization, metrics and instrumentation, fast shipping and experimentation, and the talent that underpins all of it. His reasoning: too many things must go right in consumer products for anyone to hand you a recipe, but having these capabilities raises your odds. A leader can grade a team from A to D on each one, accept that nobody is all A's on day one, and watch real results arrive as the gaps close.
ex: Solving a problem takes one or two great features, not twenty
Define "active" in DAU once, instrument it, and lock it in to stop the recurring debate

l13|29.c: The CPO is becoming a GM with single-threaded ownership, and purely functional C-level titles will fade.
l13|29.e: Org design swings between functional and divisional structures, he says, and he sees more product leaders running product, engineering, design and data together, so one person is accountable and trade-offs get made fast. The cost is that this person must be strong enough in every function, or the others feel like second-class citizens. The heart of the CPO job is aligning the product vision with the company vision, owning execution personally, and coordinating across functions. Before hiring a CPO, a CEO should decide where they want to spend their own time.
ex: If the CEO still wants to own the roadmap and execution, don't hire a CPO
A similar shift is happening between CTOs and VPs of Engineering

items.d: Runs only product, reports to the CEO
Product, engineering, design and data under one owner

l13|29.c: A PM is ready for more when they show end-to-end impact, bring clarity and energy, and attract followers.
l13|29.e: He looks at both what was achieved and how. The what is verifiable impact across a full product cycle: believe a hypothesis, lead the team through it, and learn even if it fails. The how is creating clarity and energy for the team. The third test is followership: do smart people actively want to work with you? Career inflections usually come at two moments: when you genuinely change a product's trajectory, or when you make the jump from managing individuals to managing managers. Early-career traps include valuing process over progress, self-centeredness and refusing to admit mistakes.
ex: "The PM is the CEO of the product" is a myth; the PM is an enabler
At Google, the PM-to-engineer ratio was about 1 to 8 or 1 to 10

root.d: Judge the what and the how

items.d: Led a team to test a hypothesis and deliver
The team knows what to do
People want to work with you
Change a product's path, or manage managers well

l14|30.c: Early products need one quality metric as a north star to balance the growth metrics.
l14|30.e: At Airbnb she learned that pushing growth without caring about the end experience hurts you over time. Early Airbnb Experiences made review rate its top goal, backed by coaching for hosts and the team personally trying lots of experiences. At Etsy, her seller onboarding flow chased the number of new shops, which dragged down the downstream metric of a seller's first sale. The longer that first sale took, the more likely new sellers were to lose heart. The team actually added friction to the flow so sellers listed items more carefully, and first sales came faster.
ex: Airbnb Experiences used review rate as its top-level goal
Etsy measured seller quality with something like "first sale within 7 days," as she recalls

items.d: Make signup as smooth as possible
Growth and quality back in balance

l14|30.sc: Is this job right for me
l14|30.c: To judge whether a role fits, color-code every meeting red, yellow or green by how it makes you feel.
l14|30.e: Soon after taking a platform role at Shopify she sensed something was off. So after each meeting she recolored it on her calendar: green if it energized her, yellow if it was neutral, red if it was boring or stressful. A few weeks later the calendar was almost all red and yellow, and she decided to leave. Her advice: first figure out which part of PM work you love most, then learn what PMs at the target company actually do day to day, and only go if the two match. For her, the fit is zero-to-one work, finding product-market fit.
ex: Shopify suits PMs who want to learn systems thinking and build platforms
She sees herself as strongest in the zero-to-one stage

l14|30.c: Whether to organize by function or by GM depends on what you're building and the company's stage.
l14|30.e: In a functional structure, product, design and engineering each report to their own functional leaders. It suits organizations where teams face similar problems and need to develop lots of junior people, and it makes cross-functional work easier. In a GM structure, one business leader runs operations, marketing and product together, which suits a new business with unusual needs inside a large company. She believes Airbnb Experiences would probably not have survived in an Etsy-style structure; it succeeded because it had its own space and resources.
