A startup should decide what it is building and what process and people it needs before choosing a structure.
ex: Etsy used functional reporting lines
Airbnb Experiences ran under a GM structure

items: Report to product, design, engineering leads
One business leader owns all functions
Sets its own resources and process
Suits new businesses in big companies

d.verdict: No single right answer; choose by product and stage

l14|30.c: Vision cascades down a pyramid, and OKRs at the bottom pull strategy into the next three months.
l14|30.e: She rejects the director writing strategy alone behind closed doors and then announcing it; the team never buys in. But it cannot be a vote either, and one person has to own the result. She also goes upward to the business lead or even the CEO for organizational context and support. The tool is a vision-mission-strategy-goals pyramid: write the ten-year vision first, make each layer more concrete, and at the bottom use OKRs to spell out the next quarter. The framework does not have to be OKRs, but there must be one goal system shared across functions.
ex: She pre-fills prompts in Miro or FigJam and runs ten-year vision brainstorms with cross-functional teams
Duolingo kicks off next quarter's OKRs in the third month of each quarter

items.d: Where we want to be in ten years
How we make the vision real
What we do in the next three months

l14|30.c: Use second-order thinking to spot one-way doors: debate those carefully, and let two-way doors go fast.
l14|30.e: Today's decisions shape which decisions are available tomorrow. In marketplaces and user-generated-content products, one change ripples out to every user and is hard to undo. So irreversible decisions that constrain the future deserve real discussion and executive buy-in, while reversible small ones should go to the team to move quickly, which gives autonomy and speed at once. Telling the two apart is a skill you build: read about systems thinking, write first principles into your PRDs, and hold explicit discussions of knock-on effects. Early founders often skip this and have to rebuild when they scale.
ex: Airbnb Experiences' quality standard took months to finalize; it was a one-way door
Etsy's definition of "handmade" affected every listing
Even shortening listing titles upset hosts and triggered design changes

d.right: One-way door: touches the whole system

marks.d: Product, policy and training all rest on it

l14|30.c: Run product reviews cross-functionally with three checkpoints, and the first one matters most.
l14|30.e: Most review failures she has seen come from each function reviewing separately: the design lead's feedback and the issues found in technical review never reach the whole team. The better approach merges the gates into one meeting everyone attends, with a pre-read, to judge whether the work meets its goals and quality bar. Ideally there are three: first align on the problem and first principles, then review the solution and technical architecture, and finally confirm it is ready to ship. Small two-way-door changes should skip the gates so the team is never blocked from shipping.
ex: Shopify has a well-developed system of review meetings
A small team without product-market fit can skip formal checkpoints

items.d: What we're solving; the gate that matters most
Does it meet the quality bar

l14|30.c: A strategy the team genuinely owns is the best defense against shiny new ideas.
l14|30.e: She brings the team into quarterly planning. As soon as leadership approves, she records a Loom video covering what was presented, the feedback received and the changes made, and posts it to Slack rather than waiting for the next meeting. Weekly meetings keep checking progress against strategy and goals. Most distraction, she finds, comes from offhand suggestions by executives who are not close to the work, and the reply is that it doesn't serve the long-term plan. To persuade, she borrows a negotiator's empathy: mirror what people say, make them feel heard, and accept you might be wrong. Remote teams need more async updates and fewer video calls filling the day.
ex: Empathic listening from Chris Voss's Never Split the Difference
Slack huddles for 30-second voice check-ins

items.d: If it doesn't serve the plan, skip it

l15|32.c: Most people under-communicate with their bosses, and briefings should start from the last thing the listener already knows.
l15|32.e: During the pandemic he saw many managers struggle with hard problems in silence instead of flagging them. Afterward, executives could neither help nor fairly judge the results. Reporting up, he argues, gives your boss a chance to change the situation, or at least to know what trade-offs you made. He treats a briefing like telling a story. Many people open at chapter six, never explaining which strategy the work serves, which metric it should move, or what assumptions sit underneath. Others spend twenty minutes re-explaining background everyone knows. The right move is to find the last point your audience clearly already knows and start from there.
ex: Like the coded talk aimed at Matt Damon in Ocean's Eleven, teams often can't parse executives' questions

items.d: Tells them how to judge you
Why you're doing it this way

l15|32.c: De-risk important meetings in advance: rehearse what each executive will ask, then talk to them one-on-one first.
l15|32.e: Product managers and designers love a big reveal in the meeting. He argues for the opposite: make the meeting stop being a make-or-break moment. He role-plays the CFO, the CEO and the other attendees in a rehearsal with his team, and weaves the questions they will surely ask into the presentation itself. Then he sets up one-on-one conversations before the meeting so the main concerns surface early. How long this takes varies by person, but the point is to think through every direction the meeting could go and have data ready for each question. Otherwise the odds of a bad outcome go way up.
ex: Pinterest's product head opened with data questions; stumble, and you were doubted all meeting
He writes extensively to master the material, then speaks off the cuff

items.d: Each has a different style and concerns
Answer the inevitable questions in advance
The meeting becomes a confirmation, not a gamble

l15|32.c: As features pile up, aim for perceived simplicity: advanced tools are easy to find but never in the way.
l15|32.e: He borrows Scott Belsky's product life cycle: users flock to a simple product, the product adds features for power users and gets complicated, and users move on to the next simple product. The usual remedies are splitting into several apps, revealing features gradually, actively training users, or segmenting by user type. But Eventbrite's organizers range from first-timers to people running hundreds of events a year, and the same person shifts between types, so none of those fit well. Instead they aim for advanced features that appear the moment you look for them and vanish when you don't, so most people never feel the complexity.
ex: WhatsApp is chat at its core; voice notes and video calls show up when you need them
Eventbrite's automated Facebook ads are fully managed by default, with an advanced path on the side

d.center: Perceived simplicity can break the cycle

items.t: Users move to a new product

l15|32.c: Hard-to-measure work like performance stays underfunded; recruit allies first, then prove its value with data.
l15|32.e: Once a company is at scale, the highest-impact work, such as experience, performance and engineering productivity, is often the hardest to measure, so it chronically loses out on resources. His approach is to first get the engineering manager and design lead on board, so two or three people push together. Then build your own metrics that show the value, prove it with small experiments, and write it into the team's principles. Executives also need a mindset shift: early on everything is about growth, but at scale you can lose what you already have. User expectations and competitors improve every day, and without ongoing investment the product slowly drifts out of product-market fit.
ex: Pinterest stalled after a Facebook change, then got hit hard by a search algorithm update

items.d: Get engineering and design leads to agree
At scale, protect what you have

l15|32.c: Operations roles are patches over inefficiency; the ideal goal is to make the role unnecessary.
l15|32.e: He has nothing against operations people, and Eventbrite has a product operations team. What he opposes is treating operations as a permanent function where people run manual processes forever. Hiring more people the moment a scaling problem appears only amplifies the inefficiency, and it easily turns into empire-building. A good operations role hunts for inefficiencies, removes them with process or software, then moves on to create value elsewhere. People who do this well get fought over by every team, so they need not fear working themselves out of a job.
ex: He ran tens of millions in marketing spend at GrubHub with no marketing ops role
Intercom says the goal of business operations is to not exist

items: Adds people for every scaling problem
Removes them with process or software

d.verdict: Fewer people, work done more effectively

l15|32.c: An execution-focused product manager can't rise past director without learning to write strategy independently.
l15|32.e: He places product managers on a spectrum. At one end are innovators who overflow with ideas but struggle to ship. At the other are executors who deliver a good strategy well but can't come up with new directions. When hiring, he leans toward executors, because there are always too many good ideas. Venture capitalists lean the other way, toward wild innovators. But to manage a group of PMs or own a business area, you have to write the strategy document without him. That is the great filter on the way up. His own path: go wherever the leverage is, refuse to specialize too early, and learn to put the company ahead of your own team.
ex: Early on, what matters most is proving you can ship things users love
Treat executives' questions as them learning, not as a test of you

marks.d: One hit in ten is enough
Knows the field, has ideas, ships

l15|32.c: Unscalable "kindling" tactics exist for one reason: to unlock a growth loop that does scale.
l15|32.e: He splits growth into two stages. Kindling is the hands-on work founders do themselves to get the first users. Fire is the loop, whether content, sales, virality or paid acquisition, that can carry you to millions of users. Only after finding the fire strategy do you hire a full-time owner to scale it tenfold. He also sees founders designing growth loops into the product before product-market fit, because good retention with no way to find new users doesn't count as fit. He thinks data network effects, where more usage yields more data and a better product, are underrated, especially after Apple and Facebook changed their platforms.
ex: Eventbrite merged its self-serve and sales-lead flows, moving toward product-led sales
Pinterest's personalized recommendations and Eventbrite's ad targeting are data network effects

items.d: Founders do things that don't scale
Content, sales, viral or paid loops
Sales lead, growth PM or paid specialist
Push the loop to its limit

l16|33.c: Advice is like a marshmallow, sweet but empty. Senior leaders need a coach, not more advice.
l16|33.e: While advising founders at GV, he noticed something odd: giving advice felt great for both sides, yet weeks later nothing had changed. Advice usually misses the real problem, and what worked elsewhere may not fit you. Coaching is different. The client defines success, the coach has no agenda, and the work is listening, asking and challenging until the client sees their own blind spots and untangles their thinking. New hires need hands-on guidance, he says, but a senior person who already knows every framework can only break through from the inside. A good manager says out loud when they are switching into coach mode.
ex: Try a free first session with a coach; if it doesn't fit, move on
You can find coaches through the International Coaching Federation or BetterUp

marks.d: Needs someone to explain the rules
Breakthroughs can only come from within

l16|33.c: Once you become a leader, you need to rewire how you think, not learn another framework.
l16|33.e: He compares it to learning to drive. As a kid you think the car drives itself, later driving looks easy, and then you sit in the driver's seat and get flooded with complexity while people shout tips at you. The world didn't change; your position did. Psychologists call the capacity to absorb that shift "self-complexity." A career works like a video game, he says: you learn the rules, rack up points and level up, but at the leadership level feedback slows down, the rules blur, and people treat you as the game's designer. Skills still matter, but the shift at this stage is mostly inner growth.
ex: He is currently teaching his 16-year-old son to drive
Frameworks like "hands at 10 and 2" don't help much here

items.d: Someone guides you; failure is cheap
Score points, level up, teach others
Feedback slows; old tricks stop working
Time to rewire how you think

l16|33.c: Leaders driven by curiosity score better on every measure, yet most still operate from fear.
l16|33.e: Different schools use different words, but the idea is the same. Do you see the world through fear, noticing only problems and threats, wanting to be liked and to be right? Or through openness, curiosity and a sense of purpose? He cites research by Anderson and Adams: "creative" leadership correlates positively with every success measure, from performance to brand to profit, while "reactive" leadership correlates negatively. Yet about 75% of leaders run mostly in reactive mode, because changing means rewriting deep beliefs. Reactive mode usually shows up in three ways: pleasing others, insisting you are right, or controlling people.
ex: Other names for the same idea: online vs. offline, brave vs. armored, playing to win vs. not to lose
The Leadership Circle calls them creative and reactive

d.verdict: Works better, but requires rewriting deep beliefs

l16|33.c: What holds you back is often having only one picture of what a leader looks like.
l16|33.e: Early in his career he was a people-pleasing product manager: with no formal power, he kept everyone happy. It worked for a while, but as he rose he gave away too much authority and his decisiveness suffered. People told him to be tougher, yet the only "tough" model in his head was a dictator, so he resisted. The breakthrough was keeping his value of caring about people while changing the goal from "be liked now" to "still have people who want to work with me in ten years." Coaching also showed him he loves helping people grow, which explained why managing 5 people was joyful and 35 was painful.
ex: His performance reviews kept saying "push back more"
A 360 review shows which situations push you into reactive mode

items.d: People still want to work with you in ten years

l16|33.c: A PM leads without authority from day one, so "soft skills" deserve hard practice.
l16|33.e: He noticed that the hard problems executives bring him are almost all about people: persuading, getting teams to work together, dealing with difficult colleagues, explaining a vision. Product managers have no formal authority, which means they practice the hardest part of leadership from day one. The most common blind spot is reaching a role that demands influence and realizing you never trained for it. He argues the "art" of communication and collaboration matters as much as the "science" of managing requirements, and more so as you get senior. You would take a data analysis course, so take one on hard conversations and storytelling too.
ex: PM interviews feel like exam prep, yet nobody checks whether the candidate can rally engineers
Candidates can ask a company, "How do you define the product team?"

result.d: Art counts for more as you get senior

l16|33.c: Impostor feelings are common among PMs, but leaders can't blame individuals for problems in the environment.
l16|33.e: A PM's job spans many functions with fuzzy edges, so there is always some area where a nearby engineer or designer knows more. Almost everyone doubts themselves, and simply knowing that others do too brings relief. But he warns that women and people of color often face real bias and real doubt from others. Telling them "that's just impostor syndrome" dumps a systemic problem back on the individual, and leaders have a duty to fix the environment. On a personal level, treat your inner critic as the loudest member of a board, put your real self back in the chair, and then ask whether the belief behind the criticism holds up.
ex: The HBR article "Stop Telling Women They Have Imposter Syndrome"
Internal Family Systems therapy suggests giving your inner critic a name

root.d: Work on yourself and the environment

items.d: Knowing others feel it brings relief
Leaders must dismantle bias and microaggressions
Treat the critic as one board member
Is "too nice to lead" actually true?

l16|33.c: To get 10x breakthroughs instead of 10% gains, leaders must make failure safe.
l16|33.e: He thinks people usually aim too low. Breakthrough innovation requires daring to try and daring to fail. Failure is often the more likely outcome, but the payoff from success is worth it. This is partly mindset and mostly culture: if employees assume the CEO will kill any big idea, they lower their ambitions on their own. He sees the investment mix as fractal. At the company level you can split bets into core, adjacent and moonshots; at the team level you can still carve out room, say one engineer per sprint doing experiments.
ex: Kodak invented the digital camera but never let it grow
The COVID vaccines were a big bet with no guarantee
Google once split its investment 70-20-10

l17|34.c: Most organizational problems come from unclear goals and strategy, not undertrained employees.
l17|34.e: She has watched software companies move from product-market fit into scale, often going from one product to many. That is the first time a company needs a complete, prioritized strategy, and it has to reach hundreds or thousands of people. Many companies assume the problem is that staff aren't trained well enough. In her experience it is almost always that goals and strategy were never set or communicated, so even well-trained people don't know where to push. A turnaround has to be driven as a whole, with someone at the helm willing to make hard calls.
ex: She estimates she has worked with four or five thousand PMs
Working with Insight Partners, she never spent more than three months inside a company

items.d: First need for a full strategy
Push priorities to thousands of people

l17|34.c: When executives and the board can't tell what product is doing, it's time for a CPO.
l17|34.e: Her warning signs: the board can't say whether tech and product are hitting goals; teams can't explain how their work connects to company strategy; strong PMs are frustrated by lack of direction; the company can't hire PMs; junior PMs have no path to grow. Certain events also trigger the need, such as running multiple products, entering new regions, a major pivot or an acquisition. A VP of product is good at scaling one or two products and building process. A chief product officer must trace the roadmap to revenue, forecast confidently to the board, and run several functions at once.
ex: She usually starts thinking about a CPO at seven or eight PMs
When engineering leadership was weak, she has put engineering under the CPO

items: Good at scaling one or two products
Runs design, product ops and more

d.verdict: Multiple products or a complex platform need a CPO

l17|34.c: Teams working flat out while metrics stay flat means the "missing middle" of strategy is absent.
l17|34.e: The classic symptom: teams work 80-hour weeks and ship constantly, yet business metrics don't budge, and executives see product and engineering as a black box. Teams know which feature they are building, executives know the outcome they want, but nothing connects the two. In her experience the strategy usually exists, it just lives in a few people's heads and was never written down, so everyone gives a different answer. Without priorities, teams get spread across too many things, and no single team has enough force to move a key metric.
ex: A healthcare executive said the vision was "the backbone of healthcare," but nobody could explain it

items.d: No single team can move a metric
Executives see product as a black box

l17|34.c: Write a two-pager at every level and link them into a tree, so every team tells the same story.
l17|34.e: She has the CEO write two pages first: where the company came from, the outside threats and competition, what it will and won't do, and a ranked list of "strategic intents" for the next two or three years, such as moving upmarket, downmarket or into new markets. Directors and VPs then write product initiatives framed around customer problems, and teams write specific solutions. Everything links together so you can read from the bottom to the top. The test: ask any team and they can connect their work to a business metric. Done well, she says, executive infighting drops and trade-off discussions get calmer.
ex: Strategic intents might be: go upmarket, go downmarket, expand geographically, enter a new opportunity
Not a 20-page requirements doc, just what you're doing and why

items.d: What you become in five to ten years
Ranked business directions set by executives
Big customer problems, written by directors and VPs
Specific approaches chosen by teams and engineers

l17|34.c: A good vision is concrete enough to picture, far enough to require exploring, and clear about what's different.
l17|34.e: A tagline is not a vision, she says. A vision should be concrete enough that everyone can picture it, yet ambitious enough that you don't know how to get there today and have to find the way by experimenting. If it describes what you already are, you are just optimizing what you have. Many visions say "be the best" without explaining what makes you different, why you are better or where you will win. Her favorite visions state what the company will not do, which stops teams from copying competitors. The best format is writing paired with a designer's illustrative prototype.
ex: A UX lead and a VP of product once aligned fast by presenting the vision as an untested prototype

terms.d: You have to experiment to get there
How you win, what you won't do

result.d: Writing plus a visual prototype

l17|34.c: Strategy is gathering information, making your best call, then revisiting it and changing course when needed.
l17|34.e: PMs without strategic responsibility can still practice: imagine what you would do as CPO, ask the CPO how they think, ask sales why deals are won and lost, and seek out market and financial information. First-time strategy leaders often don't know where to start, so she suggests hiring a data analyst to pull together internal data, customer research and company goals. Strategy is never certain, she stresses. The hard part is daring to choose, then testing the choice against new information and pivoting when it's wrong. Personal learning works the same way: start from practice, fill gaps, and drop processes that don't fit.
ex: One student kept asking "what would I do?" long before she became CPO
She recommends hiring an ex-McKinsey consultant as a data analyst
If textbook Scrum doesn't fit, replace it

items.d: Test the direction against new information
Admit a mistake and change course

l17|34.c: Scaling product teams need product ops, but it should only standardize the interfaces between teams.
l17|34.e: In scaling companies she sees roadmaps in different formats that can't be rolled up, no career ladder, too many meetings with the wrong people, and the same customers pestered by several teams. She splits product operations into three parts. First, internal data and insights to track strategy and OKRs. Second, customer and market research, aimed at helping more PMs do research efficiently rather than centralizing it. Third, cadences and processes such as strategy reviews and roadmap syncs. How a team runs its standup is its own business, but roadmap formats and how product works with sales and marketing should be consistent.
ex: Athena Health had 350 PMs, and one hospital was asked the same question ten times
She is co-writing a book called Product Operations with a former colleague

root.d: Make insights and cadences reusable at scale

l18|35.c: Simulate the experience by hand before writing code. Real user behavior is the best data.
l18|35.e: She thinks an idea you can't test is mostly useless. People aren't always rational, so the only thing that counts is letting users actually experience something and watching how they react. Gojek's approach was to ask what experience they wanted to create, then stage it the fastest way possible, Wizard of Oz style, with humans behind the curtain. Only after value and conversion were proven did engineering get involved. Even 30 users are enough to run an experiment early on, she says. The trend usually holds; more data just makes it more precise, and 30 beats zero.
ex: Gojek rented a stadium and recruited about 60,000 drivers in a few weeks
Put 100 drivers in a WhatsApp group to sell subscription packs during rides
Overlaid a new onboarding design on screenshots and sent it as an in-app message

root.d: Stage the experience the fastest way possible

items.d: Vouchers and balances handled manually in the back office
Test new onboarding via in-app messages
A personality quiz with no app release

l18|35.c: Don't chase "retention" as a goal. Fix the step right before the user decides.
l18|35.e: Everyone wants to lift retention directly, but "retention" is too vague to act on. It's like asking someone to list every orange thing; narrow it to a construction site and suddenly they can. Her method: every user decision rests on what happened just before, so ask what is missing one step before the conversion. Gojek's food business, GoFood, found users were afraid to try new restaurants, and the root cause was a lack of trust. They used Facebook friend connections to show "your friend ordered here," trial rates doubled, and order volume rose with them.
ex: Showing friends' purchases roughly doubled the chance of trying a new restaurant
She borrows Darius Contractor's model of user psychology to reduce friction

items.d: Get users to try new merchants
The blocker is lack of trust

l18|35.c: A free product should hold weekly retention above 60%, and closer to 80% when only friends use it.
l18|35.e: Her rules of thumb: look at cohorts on the product's natural usage cycle. A free product should keep at least 60% of users after the first week, then flatten out within two or three cycles. Paid products should see 20% to 30%. When only friends and family are using it, retention should be near 80%; if you can't keep the people who care about you, you won't solve a stranger's problem. She also warns about pulling demand forward: a dazzling first week in a new market may just mean you grabbed every likely payer at once, and it only gets harder from there.
ex: Gojek's early retention ran between 60% and 70%
Netflix and Spotify misread first-week numbers in markets where credit cards were rare

marks.d: At least 60% in week one, then flat

l18|35.c: Learn the "physics" of your growth, then find an unused lever and change one thing at a time.
l18|35.e: Her approach has two steps. First, define the constraints: what is your market, your product, your business model and your channels? Second, check whether the inputs to your growth loops and funnels fit those rules. Teams aren't wizards who can change the universe, she says, so start with what already works, find the biggest constraint or an idle lever, and change only one variable at a time. Gojek realized uniformed drivers on the street were themselves a channel. When a driver picked up a passenger who had never used the GoPay wallet, the app prompted and rewarded the driver for helping them top up.
ex: After launch, drivers promoting GoPay drove about 60% of new sign-ups
Kumu uses deliberate friction, like a questionnaire, to spot users who truly want to join a community

items.d: A mobile app connecting both sides
Push, ads, drivers on the street

l18|35.c: If a landing page gets no action, fix the copy. If conversion is slow, shorten the most painful path.
l18|35.e: When users leave before trying the product, the product isn't the problem; the copy failed to hit their pain point. A new, unfamiliar thing has to be tied to a familiar concept. If people convert but use the product rarely, look at those who did complete the key action, find the longest and most painful stretch of their journey, and shorten it. She likes pairing these "sure wins" with bold new features that have no data behind them. Churn needs the right remedy too: if users cancel because they can't use it all right now, add a pause option instead of letting them leave for good.
ex: Printing the virtual account number on a credit-card-style image increased GoPay top-ups
A direct-to-consumer brand eased churn by adding a "pause subscription" option

items.d: Finding friends on Kumu: slow search
Faster search plus more content, within weeks

l18|35.c: Analytics fail when you only track KPIs. Measurement isn't insight; record the context too.
l18|35.e: Many teams treat data like the news, which is really just entertainment: interesting to read, but nothing changes afterward. "Power users order four times more" is an observation. An insight answers why and changes what you do. The key is how you instrument events. A bad spec has lots of events with almost no attributes. A good spec records how many drivers the user saw, which city, whether surge pricing was on, whether a coupon applied. Only then can you segment by situation, form a hypothesis and test cause and effect.
ex: Users who saw only two drivers converted far less than those who saw five
Power users were more sensitive to free delivery on big orders, which shaped marketing

items: You can segment and ask why

d.verdict: Information is what changes your actions

l18|35.c: An early growth team fills gaps the core team can't reach, and statistical intuition is the top hiring skill.
l18|35.e: Gojek grew so fast that the core team was consumed by basic features, so the growth team filled the gaps: choosing which SMS vendor sent verification codes, telling drivers a passenger was new, and so on. Only later were growth PMs embedded in each product team. So your first growth hire doesn't need to build a model from scratch; they should solve known gaps. In hiring she looks first for statistical intuition, meaning they understand sampling and selection bias, tested with a take-home experiment design. She also wants people who favor fast, scrappy fixes over spending six months integrating new tools.
ex: A Python script sending texts through Twilio raised driver acceptance rates by 2%
The take-home experiment design gets five days and should take about four hours

items.d: Problems the core team can't get to
Become owners of part of the product

l19|36.c: Many problems blamed on individuals are really process and incentive problems; fund integration fully or skip it.
l19|36.e: After eBay bought PayPal, she lived through a clash of two cultures: one heavy on process, the other scrappy and flexible. Her conclusion was that neither side lacked effort; they lacked information and support. Forcing teams to compete while demanding they collaborate doesn't work, and scarce resources breed hostility. People simply adapt to the system they're in. So an acquisition has to be treated as integrating people and cultures, not just buying assets. Either resource the integration well and move fast, or don't do it at all.
ex: eBay scheduled work in Tracker, where one "seat on the train" was about 15 engineering days
The same work took about 2 to 5 days at PayPal
Next-gen checkout took about two years; unified checkout was estimated at another two

items.d: People adapt to the system they're in

l19|36.c: The mark of a strong PM is a growth mindset; hire for potential, not credentials.
l19|36.e: Early PayPal hired people with strong product instincts and didn't require product experience. She too values instinct, a learning mindset, and passion over years in the job. Strong PMs seek out feedback and shore up weaknesses rather than only amplifying strengths. Fast-growing companies hand people responsibility beyond their experience, which speeds up growth. She acknowledges that effort rises and falls with life stages, but the most successful people sprint hard when the timing is right.
ex: An analyst with no design background read three books to prepare, then led a design-driven product
Early PayPal PMs joke they couldn't get hired onto their own teams today

terms.d: Goes all in at the right stage

result.d: Beats years of experience

l19|36.c: A PM's output is communication, so introverts must treat speaking up as a skill to practice.
l19|36.e: PMs don't write code, design, or run the research themselves, she points out. Their only output is influence, so "I'm an introvert" can't be an excuse to avoid speaking up or convening people. Expression is a learnable skill: in business school she logged and graded every classroom comment she made, practicing it like a language. She'd rather you swing often and miss sometimes than wait for one perfect remark. Leaders remember the overall impression a team makes, not one awkward sentence.
ex: She told a silent leader: if you don't speak, your whole team stays quiet
Before a meeting, decide what outcome you want and what you'll contribute

items: Stay silent for fear of error

d.verdict: Teams that swing more often win more

l19|36.c: Manage your career like a product: write the vision and a pre-mortem, then work backward.
l19|36.e: Each year she sets outcome-based goals with metrics, grades herself at year's end, and shares the results. For the longer term, she suggests writing a two-year plan, a five-year plan, and a pre-mortem that imagines why you might fail. Then work backward from the goal to the experiences you'll need. With a personal vision in place, every opportunity can be judged by one question: does it bring me closer? She used the same approach at Ancestry, writing a ten-year pre-mortem and two- and five-year product visions.
ex: A mentee aiming to be CEO by 35 worked back to needing a board seat and a big GM role
She shared a ten-year pre-mortem at an Ancestry all-hands

items.d: Write down where you want to be
Judge every opportunity against the vision

l19|36.c: Peer circles reveal blind spots your manager can't see, and they should be standard in the industry.
l19|36.e: A circle has to be made of people at the same level, she says, so they dare to ask each other pointed questions: did you actually ask for the promotion? What are you going to request in your relocation package? Peer feedback exposes blind spots a manager may never notice. She has taken part in several kinds of circles and encourages people to start their own, locally or in their communities, much like a writers' critique group, until it becomes the industry norm.
ex: Lean In circles and executive circles
Facebook's group of women VPs, the "leading ladies"

l19|36.c: Technical requirements and "futurist" interviews kept large numbers of women out of product management.
l19|36.e: Around 2004, she says, the industry made a computer science degree the entry ticket for PM roles, at a time when women earned only about a fifth of those degrees. That cost a generation of women PMs. Facebook's "futurist" interview, which asked candidates to imagine the future, didn't correlate with PM success, yet it favored big-picture dreamers and penalized practical, concrete candidates. Her fixes: drop the degree and technical interview requirements, set up rotation or associate PM programs, and track where candidates drop out at each stage, the same way you'd analyze a product funnel.
ex: Women earn about 20% of computer science degrees
For years she personally interviewed every woman PM candidate who reached the first round
In 2016, about 4,000 people applied for 300 seats at the Women in Product conference

items.d: Women are only about a fifth

l19|36.c: Incubate new businesses small; Marketplace's edge is the trust that comes from social connections.
l19|36.e: She argues for small bets during incubation so a new idea isn't crushed by pressure too early. At the start, the lead still looked after other products. The team noticed that private moms' groups were already buying and selling used goods: supply existed but demand was scattered, so the job was to create liquidity at a larger scale and to tackle fraud and misinformation first. Real identities, mutual friends, and visible profiles made trust the differentiator, which is why Marketplace shouldn't be a standalone app. Success was measured by value to people, not just gross merchandise volume.
ex: Her husband sold a minivan within 24 hours for more than CarMax offered
She says Marketplace now operates in more than 100 countries

items.d: Don't pressure a new bet too early

l20|37.c: Treat it as an experiment first. Raise money only when you can picture ten years and explain the need.
l20|37.e: He often tells founders eager to raise money to slow down. Product Hunt began as an email newsletter and a website experiment, and ran for four or five months before he incorporated. Calling it an experiment means the goal is learning, not success: do users actually want this? Before raising, he tests whether he cares enough by asking if he can imagine doing it for ten years, and he wants a clear answer for what the money is for. Fundraising is like stepping onto a treadmill, he says. Employees can step off early; founders rarely can. So pick investors whose goals match yours.
ex: He raised money to hire people, since he had no capital of his own
Doing it again, he might fund the first year himself
Weekend Fund is named after a side project done on nights and weekends

items.d: The goal is learning, not success
A test of whether you care enough
If you can't say, don't raise yet
Pick investors who share your goals

l20|37.c: Ask why you're launching. Getting customers is often not the only goal, or even the main one.
l20|37.e: Most people assume a launch is for acquiring customers, but launches don't necessarily bring any. He lists other goals: spreading the word, helping with hiring, building buzz for fundraising, collecting feedback, and stumbling into partnerships. One that gets overlooked is team morale: celebrating together and sending the press coverage to your family matters. Positive coverage and a launch page also help your search rankings. Figure out what the company needs most right now, then decide how to launch and how much effort to put in.
ex: He estimates he has seen tens of thousands of product launches

items.d: Positive coverage and a launch page

l20|37.c: Write launch copy the way you'd describe it to a friend, not like a press release.
l20|37.e: School writing classes teach people to use big words and fill the page, he says, so founders end up writing PR-speak that readers tuned out long ago. For a tagline, borrow how users describe you to others, or how you explain it to a friend over drinks; that language is more honest. Keep the maker's intro short, because browsers won't read a long post. The image gallery is the first thing visitors see, so use it like a slide deck to tell a story, such as a before-and-after or how the product evolved. B2B products regularly top Product Hunt too.
ex: There may be more B2B companies than consumer ones on Product Hunt

result.d: More honest, more persuasive

l20|37.c: Looking back at Product Hunt, he'd make money sooner, stay focused on one community, and delegate more.
l20|37.e: One of his biggest regrets is that after raising a seed and Series A, he focused entirely on growth and only started making money after AngelList acquired the company. Once they did start charging, they reached cash-flow break-even in about a year. Had he put even 10% of the effort into revenue earlier, he might have controlled his own destiny years sooner. His second regret was trying to expand sideways into podcast, game and book discovery, underestimating how different those experiences are and how hard it is to move a community. His third was not delegating enough: until shortly before he left, he still edited the newsletter himself every morning.
ex: Reddit is one of the few platforms that successfully expanded into long-tail communities

items.d: About 10% of effort on revenue would do

l20|37.c: Momentum in early companies feeds on itself, so don't write a company off too soon.
l20|37.e: He increasingly sees momentum as one of the most important things in an early startup, and it is self-reinforcing. When a team keeps shipping and things are going well, others feel that energy and want to keep up. When someone slows the pace, the people around them stop caring too. As an investor he has repeatedly watched companies he had mentally given up on come back to life through a pivot, a sudden big partnership or an acquisition. So he bets on resilient founders who can create momentum from nothing, and he doesn't call the game until it's over.
ex: Weekend Fund has invested in more than 110 companies
Returns follow a power law: one company can outweigh all the rest

l20|37.c: Consumer startups are far harder than B2B, and without a unique insight they almost never work.
l20|37.e: Social and gaming are the hardest. Ad revenue requires enormous scale first. You compete for attention with Netflix and everything else. Users have deep habits, and you have to move from external triggers like notifications to an internal trigger where they open the app on their own. User needs are also fuzzy, often boiling down to human desires like wanting connection. B2B is a clear problem that customers will pay for on day one. So consumer products need a unique insight, which you can find by keeping a problem diary, hanging out in niche communities, watching behavior and technology shift, and answering "why now."
ex: DocuSign is an example of B2B with an obvious need
After remote work took off, Airbnb redesigned its homepage around browsing for inspiration

items: Needs huge scale before it pays
Fuzzy needs rooted in human nature
Easier to navigate the idea maze

d.verdict: Consumer products need a unique insight first

l20|37.c: Starting with a narrow audience makes a better product, and chances to expand show up later.
l20|37.e: The narrower the audience, the more precisely you can aim the product experience and messaging at one group's specific problem. Marketing and go-to-market get simpler too, because you don't need a value proposition for everyone. Founders worry the market is too small to support a big company. He leans toward not worrying much, because once you fully serve one group, you usually spot a path to a neighboring community or problem. Airbnb started with couches and spare rooms, something most people would never use, and today, in his view, it's playing in the entire housing market.
ex: Airbnb started with couches and spare rooms
It depends on the situation, of course; this doesn't apply everywhere

items.d: Like Airbnb into all of housing

l21|38.c: Products spread through loops, not funnels; map your loop and clear the friction out of it.
l21|38.e: He believes almost every product has some loop, though some are obvious and some have to be invented. Coda's "black loop" is make a doc, share it, and the recipient makes their own; every document product has it. Its "blue loop" is publishing a doc openly, like a YouTube video, so people with the same interest discover Coda along the way. About a third of users arrive that way. To avoid adding friction to sharing, Coda charges only the people who create docs, not every editor like similar products do. To find your own loop, think back to how you last described the company to a job candidate.
ex: Users describe Coda's gallery as somewhere between Medium and an app store
One of the most popular docs is an Orangetheory workout tracker

items.d: Drawn by the idea, not the tool

l21|38.c: Platform companies can't control the conversation with users; they can only help publishers and sharers tell it well.
l21|38.e: New users reach Coda three ways. A doc shared by a colleague activates best, because it is immediately useful. A publicly published doc comes next. Starting from a blank doc is hardest, with only about one in five reaching the activation point. Yet only that last path has the company telling its own story. On the other two, the sharer or publisher holds the microphone, and they don't care about teaching people Coda. Platform builders have to accept that their connection to users runs through someone else. Like YouTube or Airbnb, the job is helping people in the ecosystem make great content, not controlling everything yourself.
ex: Steve Jobs is the counterexample: the first iPhone had no App Store
Airbnb once photographed listings itself, but ultimately had to rely on hosts

marks.d: Publisher tells the story; middling activation

l21|38.c: Great companies have a few "golden rituals," and rituals are a mirror of culture.
l21|38.e: He borrows investor Bing Gordon's definition: a golden ritual has a name, every employee knows it before their first Friday, and it has a template. Interviewing over a thousand people for his book, he found people love sharing their rituals, and the details make or break them. Asked about company culture, almost everyone answered with a ritual. Coda's golden ritual is Dory/Pulse: in meetings everyone writes their view first and can only read others' after writing, and questions get voted on before discussion. New employees say it makes them feel their voice is taken seriously.
ex: Amazon's six-page memos, Google's OKRs, Salesforce's V2MOM
At Gusto, every interviewer joins the call when an offer is made
Arianna Huffington's team plays a random one-minute "reset" video before meetings

terms.d: Easy to identify with and spread

result.d: Reflects the team's culture

l21|38.c: Rituals must change with company size and wartime versus peacetime; use rider, elephant and path to land them.
l21|38.e: Some rituals work beautifully at a hundred people and fall apart at a thousand. Peacetime and wartime also call for different ones, and many companies have war-room style rituals. Some rituals grow on their own: Dory/Pulse began when a product manager got fed up with round-robin speaking in remote meetings. To introduce one deliberately, he recommends the framework from the book Switch, which maps neatly onto the three criteria: teach it during onboarding (direct the rider), give it a catchy name (motivate the elephant), and build a template that makes it the easiest thing to do (shape the path). When borrowing a ritual, mind the details, such as adding a role column to a feedback form to prevent groupthink.
ex: Coinbase's RAPID decision meetings spell out in advance what each approver must answer
At Facebook, saying "lockdown" is instantly understood by everyone

root.d: Three moves from the book Switch

items.d: Give it a name people identify with
Build a template; lower the bar

l21|38.c: Don't rank questions by importance; first answer the "eigenquestion" that settles the most other questions at once.
l21|38.e: In 2008 YouTube was deadlocked: when someone searched for Modern Family, should it link out to ABC's site? One side wanted to serve users; the other feared good content would never come to YouTube again. He reframed it: ten years out, would online video reward consistency or comprehensiveness? The team bet on consistency, and the link-out question answered itself. The same answer also led them to stop embedding other players and to take the iPhone YouTube app back from Apple. The name borrows from eigenvectors in linear algebra, the directions that matter most.
ex: Google Shopping found users chose Amazon because they valued consistency
About six months after reclaiming the iPhone app, YouTube held roughly 80% share
Coda's eigenquestion: is it more like a document or more like an app?

items.d: Good for users vs. good for business
Still looks right ten years on

items.t: A chain of decisions gets easy
items.d: No link-outs, no embeds, reclaim iPhone app

l21|38.c: Finding eigenquestions is a learnable skill, but you have to practice in low-stakes settings.
l21|38.e: He compares it to learning an instrument or a sport: if you only practice at the recital or the real game, you never get good. Eigenquestions at work are all high-stakes, so he practices with hypotheticals and uses them in interviews. One: you're handed a teleportation device to bring to market, and the scientists will answer only two questions. What do you ask? One product manager asked whether it could safely carry people and whether the cost was in buying it or running it, then sketched four go-to-market strategies from the answers. He finds children often grab the key issue fast, while adults ask things like "how big is it" that change no decision.
ex: He and his daughter debated why one intersection has three gas stations

x: Expensive to buy, cheap to run
Cheap to buy, expensive to run

cells.d: A few units in strategic locations
Put them everywhere; charge per trip
Like transporting a heart for transplant

l21|38.c: Judge people not by scope but by whether they define problems, invent solutions, organize the work, or execute.
l21|38.e: After Google reorganized into business units, he led the effort to unify PM evaluation. He found that level descriptions could only be ordered by scope, but scope is handed down by managers, varies across teams, and pushes people to avoid risky projects. So he switched to PSHE. Juniors receive the problem, solution and approach and simply execute (E). The next level designs how to run the work (H). Above that, people invent the solution (S). At the top, they identify which problem to solve at all (P). Early and late careers are mostly about growing scope; the murky middle is where PSHE applies. It works for engineering, design and even sales.
ex: Cut level descriptions into strips without titles and nobody can tell which level is which
A great salesperson doesn't just hit quota; they find the right problem in any territory

items.d: Deliver the given script with quality
Organize the work and its pace

l21|38.c: In hiring, reference checks are most reliable, real work samples come next, and interviews rank last.
l21|38.e: A reference has worked with the candidate for years, which beats a thirty-minute artificial scenario. Many "H-type" product managers run great meetings and are well liked, but ask who picked the problem or came up with the solution and the answer is often the designer or the CEO. That is hard to detect in an interview and obvious in a reference call. The trick is to give the reference an easy way to be honest: ask without naming names who on the team is best at picking problems, or offer four profiles and let them choose, without revealing your preference. Also ask whether they would hire the person again. In interviews, lean on neutral scenarios, then let candidates present on their home turf.
ex: Do reference checks early so candidates aren't rejected at the final step
Beware home-turf questions: you may just be testing whether they agree with you

items.d: Years of shared work; most trustworthy
Candidates show their ceiling on home turf

l22|39.c: A good name is a bonus, but a bad name won't kill a good company.
l22|39.e: She believes a name's meaning gets poured in slowly by company strategy and years of marketing. Disney was just the founder's surname and now stands for magic; Volvo stands for safety. Names sit on a spectrum: descriptive, suggestive, evocative, and finally "empty vessel" names that say nothing at all. The further right you go, the more marketing spend and time it takes to give the name meaning. She personally prefers suggestive and evocative names. After hearing the company pitch, people think "oh, that makes sense," so the name does part of the marketing for you.
ex: Seesaw: back and forth, fitting an education app connecting teachers, students and parents
Maven is Yiddish for someone who knows through experience
Eero, named after designer Eero Saarinen, is nearly an empty vessel

marks.d: Need heavy marketing to gain meaning

l22|39.c: Position first, then write a brief, brainstorm in bulk, and filter down to three to five finalists.
l22|39.e: Positioning decides what the name needs to convey, so it always comes first. The brief spells out what you are naming, what to convey, what to avoid, and what competitors are called. Then a one-hour brainstorm: start with synonyms, antonyms, foreign words and associations for the words in your positioning statement, then branch out across seven to ten related themes. The goal is a few hundred bad ideas and a few promising ones. Next, grade candidates red, yellow or green on trademark, domain, distinctiveness, timelessness, pronunciation, look and length, and keep three to five. Trademarks can fall through, so never bet on just one.
ex: She nearly used Lattice but dropped it because it sounds like lettuce on the phone
Avoid dated tricks like -ly endings or dropped vowels
The naming firm A Hundred Monkeys quoted about $47,000

items.d: Trademark, domain, sound, look and more
Then run trademark and domain checks

l22|39.c: A brand isn't a logo and a color palette; it's what other people think you are.
l22|39.e: Visuals are just how a brand expresses itself. Brand strategy answers what you want people to think of you and how you will shape that perception. Her stripped-down framework for early companies has three parts: purpose, positioning and personality. Visual identity and tone of voice then follow from those. Most companies' style guides specify the logo, fonts and colors but never say who we are or why we exist. An early-stage company can finish this in a few weeks, and it saves time afterward on everything from the website to day-to-day decisions.
ex: Nothing in Volvo's logo or colors says "safety"
Volvo gave the three-point seatbelt patent away to the whole industry
About three weeks from scratch; naming often takes a month

terms.d: Why you exist; stable for a decade
The place you hold in users' minds
How you show up in the world

result.d: Then derive visuals and tone of voice

l22|39.c: Skip mission and vision statements; all you need is one line that lasts a decade: "We exist to..."
l22|39.e: People remember only one thing, she argues, so she asks only for a purpose: the change you want to make in the world, unrelated to making money. It is far more stable than positioning. It unites employees, helps the company make decisions, gives the public a reason to root for you, and can serve as the headline of your About page. To write it, list the cultural tensions relevant to your business, then list what the brand looks like at its best, and pick one of each. Warm up with "the world would be better if..." and then fill in "we exist to..."
ex: Google: organize the world's information and make it universally accessible and useful
Stripe: increase the GDP of the internet
LogicLoop: make operations data work harder than operations people

items.d: Mood of the times; audience anxieties

items.t: The world would be better if…

l22|39.c: Positioning starts by focusing on one target audience, then the statement has to pass the "bar test."
l22|39.e: Positioning is the place you occupy in your target user's mind. If ten employees or customers give ten different descriptions, or nobody can explain it in one sentence, the positioning is broken. Early companies have limited runway, and the worst mistake is trying to please everyone. Narrow from the total market to the audience you will actively pursue over the next eighteen months, then down to one specific model user. Map that person's problem and their current workaround, and compress it into the classic positioning template. Finally, pretend you are the target user recommending the product to a peer in a bar. If the benefit and the difference come out naturally, it works, and that benefit line is often your homepage headline.
ex: Eero's target audience was the tech-savvy dad
Square Stand: turn your iPad into a point of sale
Don't write words like leverage or empower that nobody says out loud

items.d: People you'll actively pursue in 18 months
One real person with a name, address and hobbies
Say it out loud to a fellow user

l22|39.c: A brand should stand out on two personality dimensions, then add tension with "we are X but not Y."
l22|39.e: A brand is like a person. On TikTok or Instagram, where real people hang out, a brand with no personality looks as awkward as ADP. She borrows Stanford professor Jennifer Aaker's research: strong brands usually stand out on two of five dimensions. But most tech companies land on sincerity plus competence, and stopping there makes everyone look the same. So she adds five lines of "we are X but not Y," where Y is X pushed too far, with tension between the lines. These guide copywriting, illustration and photography style.
ex: Mountain Dew is excitement plus ruggedness; Rolex is sophistication plus competence
Google: playful but not childish

root.d: Strong brands stand out on two

l22|39.c: Seed-stage coverage comes from exclusives and a bigger story, not from a funding announcement alone.
l22|39.e: Get your story straight first: if you can't explain the company in a sentence, a reporter certainly can't. Founders used to pick a launch date and send embargoed drafts to three to five outlets at once. Now fewer reporters and outlets cover seed-stage companies, and a funding round is no longer news by itself, so you usually get one exclusive. Use the round as a hook and lead with a product launch, a marquee customer or a partnership, and place the company inside a larger social trend. Pay attention to local media too; they are hungrier for these stories.
ex: Vitable Health rode the Great Resignation trend into the Philadelphia Inquirer
Square once made its merchants the heroes of local news stories

items: Embargoed drafts to 3–5 outlets at once
Tie to trends and local media

d.verdict: Fix positioning and story first; keep expectations realistic

l23|40.c: Feature teams and empowered product teams are so different they shouldn't even share the PM title.
l23|40.e: A feature team gets a list of features that stakeholders have prioritized for the quarter, then does a little design, writes a lot of code, tests, and ships. Its PM is really a project manager herding cats. An empowered product team gets a customer or business problem to solve, is judged on outcomes rather than output, and treats engineers and designers as equal partners in finding the solution. The gap persists mainly because most people have never worked at a good company and can't picture what good looks like. To start changing, ask your manager to let one team try it for a quarter or two.
ex: From experience he estimates only about 10–15% of commercial software companies are good product companies
Reframe a "build buy-now-pay-later" request as raising conversion or order size

items: Engineers and designers find the solution together

d.verdict: Celebrate solving the problem, not the launch

l23|40.c: A PM owns the two hardest risks: whether it's valuable and whether it's viable for the business.
l23|40.e: He sorts product risk into four kinds: will users want it, can they figure out how to use it, can engineering build it, and does it work for the business. Engineers own feasibility, designers own usability, and the PM owns value and business viability, the two hardest. Viability means the PM also has to understand monetization, privacy, security, and go-to-market. That's why he considers "PMs own the why, not the how" an outsider's view. Decisions should sit with the people closest to the knowledge, a principle he borrows from Netflix.
ex: The four risks: value, usability, feasibility, and business viability

items.d: PM owns it: will users buy in?
PM owns it: monetization, compliance, go-to-market

l23|40.c: As companies grow, sales and finance people get promoted, product people leave, and product DNA drains away.
l23|40.e: He thinks Steve Jobs explained it more sharply in 1995 than he can: once a company has enough market share, people from sales, marketing, and finance get rewarded and promoted, while product people stop being valued and leave for companies that value them. Management grows complacent, adopts a "don't break anything" attitude, and stops taking risks on new products. It's worst after the founder leaves, because successors lack moral authority and don't know what truly matters.
ex: The SVPG article "Devolving from Good to Bad" describes the same pattern

items.d: Growth comes from sales and operations
No risks; just don't break anything

l23|40.c: Discovery creates value and optimization only harvests it; when only optimization is left, the end has begun.
l23|40.e: He notices that companies that have lost their founder tend to fear risk, and the only experiments left are low-risk A/B tests on flows and retention. You need both discovery and optimization, but optimization alone means you've stopped creating new value. A second disease is executives who assume they know best and push feature lists down the organization. Jobs called it the stakeholder disease: believing the idea is 90% of the work, when the idea is only the start and the real work is in iterating again and again.
ex: He says only about 20% of features end up delivering a positive return

l23|40.c: User research should hunt for why people won't use the product, with the PM and designer present.
l23|40.e: He objects to researchers testing a prototype until users finally say they like it. Research should be evaluative, deliberately looking for the reasons a product would be rejected. It also doesn't tell you directly what to build; it keeps refining the team's mental model of the user, and that model guides decisions. Don't spend weeks re-validating a problem the founder already understands either. Customers buy the solution, so most of the time belongs in solution discovery. A report written by a lone researcher usually gets shelved. If the PM and designer won't attend, he'd rather cancel the session.
ex: Quoting Patrick Collison: research exists to refine your mental model of the user
Airbnb ran a host focus group in Paris with engineers and designers in the room

terms.d: Find why users won't use it
Spend less time re-proving the problem

result.t: A sharper model of the user
result.d: Which then guides what to build

l23|40.c: A PM's direct lines to customers, engineers, and stakeholders are sacred and can't be delegated.
l23|40.e: Project management, QA, product marketing, and production operations can all be handed off, he says, but three things a PM must do personally: reach customers and users without anyone filtering the conversation, work with engineers every day, and deal with stakeholders face to face. Anyone standing in between, however well-meaning, hurts the product. So product ops is bad when it handles the data for the PM or only reports what the PM wants to hear, and fine when it handles production issues or builds tools that save time. A PM also has to bring deep knowledge in five areas: users, data, the business, the industry, and strategy.
ex: His coach made him visit 30 customers, 15 in the US and 15 in Europe, before deciding anything
Learning discovery techniques takes about two to three months

l23|40.c: You can only scale through leaders; scaling by process always goes wrong, and SAFe is waterfall in disguise.
l23|40.e: Companies scale either by process or by leaders, he says, and only the second ends well. SAFe flies the agile flag but is really repackaged waterfall, exactly the "beware the process people" disease Jobs warned about. Outside top-tier companies, product management is a mess: many product owners are trained by agile coaches who have never built a product, the blind leading the blind. The better path is turning leaders into coaches. The recent emphasis on coaching at big companies owes a lot to Bill Campbell's influence.
ex: He thinks the mess is worse in Europe than in the US
Google, Microsoft, and Apple all list coaching among a leader's responsibilities

marks.d: People who never built products teaching product

l24|41.c: Readers already agree on the what and the why; what's scarce is the super specific how.
l24|41.e: Writers and teachers, she argues, spend far too long proving that something matters, when most readers already accept the premise. What they want is how to actually do it, with the nuances and examples. For product managers, for instance, don't explain why communication matters; explain how to win support when you have no authority, or how to bring order when several groups are in chaos. By the same logic, cut the preamble. Start the story at the most tense moment, not at the outdoor store where you bought the gear.
ex: Opening rule: start right before you get eaten by the bear
PM topics: winning support without authority, floating a hypothesis to move the team

items: Long argument for why it matters
Readers already agree with the premise

d.verdict: Spend the words on how

l24|41.c: The more interactive a format and the more you face live questions, the less room for fluff.
l24|41.e: She ranks content formats by how much fluff they can hide. One-way formats let an author toss out an opinion and walk away without defending it. In a cohort-based course with live sessions and asynchronous discussion, students push back in real time and weak reasoning shows immediately. It's only a rough guide, she says; quality varies within each format, and some books are padded blog posts while others are rigorous. She also admits she's biased because she builds courses. Viral Twitter threads, in her view, often sound wise but lack depth.
ex: Most to least fluff: tweets, podcasts and articles, talks, books, video courses, cohort courses

l24|41.c: Talks and meetings need a state change every few minutes to pull attention back.
l24|41.e: Sitting on camera through a long monologue is draining. Listeners have to hold their posture and an attentive face, and their minds wander. Her fix is to change the mode of participation every few minutes: ask a question in the chat, switch from gallery view to screen share and back, have people guess before revealing the answer, run breakout rooms, go around the room, or ask someone to unmute. She wants this to be a fixed habit rather than something you do by feel, and it applies just as well to everyday meetings.
ex: She cites research that attention lasts only about 2 to 4 minutes
Nathan Barry changes state every 3 to 5 slides or 3 to 5 minutes

l24|41.c: Politeness masks true reactions; the moment someone's eyes light up is the reliable data.
l24|41.e: People rarely say they're bored, she notes, but leaning forward, a change of expression, energy in the voice, and engaged eye contact all give away real interest. Treat those signals as data and write them down: keep and amplify the lines that excite people, and cut the ones that make their eyes glaze over. The method works for sharpening content topics, sales pitches, and the way you explain a concept. It also works in internal meetings and conversations with your boss, and patterns emerge once you've collected enough.
ex: Signals to watch: leaning in, facial changes, vocal energy, eye contact

l24|41.c: Manage up at every level, and calibrate how much you share by how reversible the decision is.
l24|41.e: Many people think the boss should manage them, so they resist managing up. She argues that doing it proactively earns appreciation, trust, and opportunities. The most senior people are usually the best at it, because it's why they got promoted: they anticipate what the boss will worry about. The practice is to keep your manager informed of your decisions and progress, with enough context to object or approve, without drowning them. Share less on small, reversible decisions and more on irreversible or costly ones. When in doubt, over-communicate, especially when working remotely.
ex: People who think they over-communicate usually land just right for the receiver

marks.d: Full context; let the boss decide

l24|41.c: Lead with the conclusion in writing, and separate what needs a decision from background information.
l24|41.e: Put the conclusion or recommendation first and the background below, she says: people who agree can stop after the opening, and people with questions can read on. That matches the pyramid principle. Listing pros and cons implies you're neutral, and if you actually have a preference, readers lose trust. Better to state your recommendation and then be candid about its downsides. Don't scatter action items through the background; label them separately from what's just for information. If you have no position, ask neutrally rather than with leading questions. She also recommends studying writing craft to avoid mistakes like misplaced modifiers that make reading harder.
ex: The military-style bottom line up front is too blunt for customers and needs softening
She recommends the HBR Guide to Better Business Writing

items.d: Those who agree can stop here

l24|41.c: Instead of saying no outright, spell out what saying yes would cost and share your priorities.
l24|41.e: A flat no is hard for many people. The method she learned replaces refusal with a trade-off: I can do this, but it means that other piece of work slips; is that okay? The conversation shifts from whether you're a team player to how we should prioritize, which protects your energy without the word "no." A former boss gave her a second framework: prioritize, and tell people how you've prioritized. Prioritizing without telling anyone reads as silence; explaining without prioritizing reads as defensive; doing neither is the worst of all.
ex: She learned the method from Alex Peck, her design partner at altMBA
The second framework came from a former boss

l25|42.c: The product picks the engine: high lifetime value means paid, network effects mean viral, long-tail demand means SEO.
l25|42.e: He starts by asking which archetype a subscription company fits. If the unit economics work, lifetime value per user is high (often prosumers who use the product for work), and more than 5% of free users convert to paid, the company can run a paid acquisition loop. If the product has natural network effects, referral and viral loops can be layered on top. If there is long-tail search demand that can be served with programmatically generated pages, SEO can become a durable advantage. Not every product can take every path, and he thinks founders should figure out which one fits early.
ex: Consumer subscriptions at $5–7 a month usually top out at $50–60 in lifetime value
Grammarly and Canva earn hundreds of dollars per user over their lifetime
Early Canva grew on long-tail searches for "make a..." and "...template"

root.d: Set by the product and its economics

items.d: Huge search demand served by generated pages

l25|42.c: Network effects are either built in or very hard to fake; without them, don't count on viral growth.
l25|42.e: He defines a network effect as each user getting more value as more people join; in collaboration tools, that means the product gets better as more of the team uses it. Marketplaces and collaboration tools have this naturally. A solo writing product like Grammarly does not, and trying to manufacture it is an uphill fight. The exception is a premium product with a brand people love. Even without network effects, a give-one-get-one incentivized referral program can deliver meaningful results there.
ex: Dropbox file sharing is the classic referral loop
Laika, an Australian fresh dog food subscription, grew on give-one-get-one referrals

l25|42.c: SEO is worth doing only if two of three conditions hold, and you should timebox the test to three months.
l25|42.e: SEO pays back slowly, six months at the earliest, and historically companies could only afford it around Series B. His rough checklist has three items: do you have a unique editorial angle on what already ranks, is there a way to generate pages programmatically at scale, and do you have proprietary data that can become a search experience. Invest only if two of the three hold, and keep the cost of testing low. The details change fast, so paying an outside firm $5,000 to $10,000 for an audit is good value. With capital scarce, buying growth is no longer viable, and long-term plays like this are moving down to Series A companies.
ex: Programmatic examples: Canva's template pages and real estate sites
Proprietary data example: the personal finance app Monarch Money

items.d: Unique angle, programmatic pages, proprietary data

l25|42.c: Paid acquisition is shrinking short term, but for companies with solid unit economics it's a window to expand.
l25|42.e: After capital cooled, the payback requirement for consumer subscriptions dropped from about 12 months to under 6. Budgets without clear attribution got cut outright, and ad revenue at Meta and Snap contracted. But when competitors pull back, auction prices and CPMs fall, so companies with cash, fast payback and good measurement win. He expects a wave of investment in attribution: media mix modeling for companies spending over $100,000 a month across many channels, and ongoing incrementality tests as the only way to prove cause and effect. As online attribution gets worse, offline channels like out-of-home, podcasts and direct mail become competitive again.
ex: Media mix modeling is back; Recast is a leading example
Incrementality testing tools include Measured and Incrmntal
TikTok also reaches people over 40 with household incomes of $200,000

items.d: Payback requirement drops from 12 to 6 months
Media mix models plus incrementality tests

l25|42.c: Paid ads are either for profitable acquisition or for fast learning, and you must know which one you're doing.
l25|42.e: There are two legitimate reasons to spend on ads: healthy unit economics that return the money, or using ads as the fastest scalable feedback loop to test copy, positioning and features. The common failure is claiming both while spending $100,000 a month that neither pays back nor produces clean experiments. He can tell whether paid can be the main engine from conversion, retention, lifetime value and churn. If conversion is weak and retention poor, keep only a small budget for positioning tests. Open the taps only when the funnel is healthy, the channel isn't saturated, and the runway is long enough.
ex: Prosumer SaaS converts 20–35% of visitors to sign-ups, and 40–50% early on
Free-to-paid under 5% is unsustainable; above 7% is ideal

l25|42.c: Early on, master one channel before diversifying; later, over-reliance on a single channel becomes the risk.
l25|42.e: Early companies have limited resources and a ticking clock. Betting on one thing and being wrong wastes precious time, but trying five things at once means none gets a real test. Worse than a channel failing is declaring it dead without giving it a fair shot. So focus, but set guardrails: a minimum number of impressions, two or three creative directions, and a click-through range. Hit them and continue; miss them and pause. Successful companies often get 80% of growth from one engine. Diversifying while acquisition volume is still small is premature. But a company past $50 million in annual revenue that still gets 90% from one channel must carve out resources to explore new ones.
ex: Grammarly was once over-reliant on performance marketing
Canva depends on long-tail SEO and must guard against Google algorithm changes

items: Don't put diversification in OKRs too soon
Diversification is a blind spot; fund it

d.verdict: Timing depends on scale; earlier isn't better

l25|42.c: Onboarding and user research are almost always high-return investments.
l25|42.e: Most of the companies he works with are prosumer tools that put work once done by engineers, designers or video editors into ordinary hands. They have to be both simple and powerful, and users dropped straight into an editor get lost easily. Capture intent first, tailor the landing experience to it, and don't expose every feature at once. For early companies this can double to quadruple activation, and post-Series B it still adds 20–30%. Research that helps you understand customers always pays off too, giving small teams sharp focus. Attribution spending should match the stage: too little breeds inertia, and chasing perfection isn't worth it.
ex: The editors in Airtable, Canva, Whimsical and InVideo are all complex

items.d: What they came to do, and who they are
Don't show all the complexity at once

l26|44.c: Programming languages are languages too, with tighter rules, which makes them a natural fit for large language models.
l26|44.e: Microsoft and OpenAI had already been working together on large models. The realization came that Python and JavaScript are languages just like English and Japanese, only with a far smaller vocabulary and grammar, which makes them easier for a model. The trigger was GitHub's infrastructure team noticing a huge volume of clone requests and assuming an attack, until they traced it to OpenAI scraping public code. GitHub then handed over a snapshot of public code it had already prepared for the Arctic Code Vault. Researchers quickly found the model could translate English into code and predict what code came next.
ex: Copilot runs on Codex, a code model derived from GPT-3
The public code snapshot was originally made for the Arctic Code Vault archive

items.d: Reuse the Arctic Code Vault archive
English and code translate both ways
From translation to prediction and completion

l26|44.c: An AI coding assistant's core value is keeping developers in flow, and every interaction choice serves that.
l26|44.e: Remembering argument order, looking up syntax and inventing test data are labor, not creation. Copilot's job is to bring that information straight into the editor, so you never switch away to documentation or Stack Overflow. The team tried a right-click side panel offering whole functions, but it still pulled your eyes away. They settled on inline, multi-line completions in gray italics, signaling the suggestion is temporary. Latency is a flow problem too, and their experiments found about 200 milliseconds was the sweet spot that didn't break a train of thought. What context to feed the model mattered just as much, and that is where prompt design grew from.
ex: Suggestion latency of about 200 milliseconds was the sweet spot
Gray italic text signals a temporary suggestion you can ignore

items: Still shifts your eyes and panels

d.verdict: Chose inline multi-line completion with latency near 200 ms

l26|44.c: Isolate moonshot projects to incubate, then move them to product teams in stages once real customer signals appear.
