l26|44.e: GitHub Next works only on horizon-two and horizon-three projects, separate from engineering, product and design (EPD), and carries no profitability, security or availability targets, so smart people can experiment freely. He defines horizons by ambiguity and confidence rather than the calendar, roughly one, three and five years out. When an idea maps to a group of customers with a real problem, and the team has moderate confidence it can solve it in a novel way, they start pushing the prototype to more users. Copilot's technical preview invited tens of thousands and then hundreds of thousands of people, and the amazement on social media and Hacker News convinced them to scale.
ex: About a year and a half from settling the interaction to general availability
The technical preview gradually invited tens to hundreds of thousands of developers

items.d: Moderate confidence in solving a real problem
Scale after hundreds of thousands try it
Only after replacements are in place

l26|44.c: Hand research over when someone can truly take it, not on a date, and product owns the roadmap.
l26|44.e: When a researcher returns to the R&D group should depend on whether a replacement has genuinely ramped up and absorbed the domain knowledge, not on a deadline. The product team taking over sits closest to customer feedback and has to feel in control of its own future; it cannot outsource the roadmap, or innovation itself, to the research group. Engineering fundamentals act as the contract between a research project and an operating product. Researchers find that unnatural, so it takes cultural change management, plus mixing engineers who are good at running services with researchers who carry the vision.
ex: Only after about a year and a half did researchers start returning to Next

root.d: Graduating from experiment to operating product

l26|44.c: Picture the AI as a pair programmer sitting next to you, and the limits on what it should say become clear.
l26|44.e: Who is responsible when an AI produces offensive content is an ethical and legal problem beyond engineering. They framed Copilot as an AI pair programmer. If your partner whispered politics or profanity in your ear, you couldn't focus on code, and that human framing helped the team set rules of behavior. At first there was no filtering at all. Then they added a simple blocklist, which turned the team into language censors and wrongly blocked legitimate contexts like medicine. They later switched to models from Microsoft's Azure responsible AI team that detect offensive content based on context.
ex: Of all his products, this one involved the most time with legal
Microsoft had already seen a chatbot go off the rails and get pulled

marks.d: Risk of the experience going off the rails

l26|44.c: Copilot augments developers rather than replacing them; human decisions and existing quality gates all stay.
l26|44.e: The community raised many questions about training on public code and whether suggestions are safe. He considers that skepticism healthy, since AI can help or harm. The team's stance is that there must always be a person behind the keyboard making decisions, and no safeguard like unit tests or static analysis gets removed. He expects AI to spread across the whole development stack, such as automatically summarizing pull request changes, freeing developers from memorizing syntax and arguments to focus on design and outcomes. The constant need to talk with the community meant the product team grew more than engineering. The other bottleneck is the scarce supply of GPUs.
ex: Copilot writes about 40% of Python code, and 20-something to 40% across languages
More and more varied training data means better suggestions

items.d: Design, outcomes and the final call
Existing quality gates stay in place

l26|44.c: A large team should put roughly 10% into bold experiments, 30% into operations and 60% into incremental improvement.
l26|44.e: As a portfolio manager over several product lines, he says there is no fixed answer for splitting time and resources; it depends on the moment and the state of the organization. But some capacity must always go to bold, experimental research. The rest goes to keeping shipped products up to customer expectations and to steady iteration that turns bets placed one to four years ago into returns. These ratios apply only to large teams. A startup is itself one big lottery ticket, so its split looks completely different.

l27|45.c: Forget marketing's many sub-functions and first ask whether growth is stuck on fuel or on engine.
l27|45.e: She boils marketing down to two halves. Fuel is the valuable stuff you create: positioning, website copy, content, templates, calculators. Engine is what gets it in front of the right people: channels and distribution rules, plus marketing operations and tracking. An engine with no fuel means outbound emails that go nowhere no matter how many you send. Fuel with no engine means content nobody reads. Most projects have both; an email's copy is fuel, while segmentation and trigger rules are engine. Before hiring, ask: if you can't name your best-performing content or positioning, it's a fuel problem. If good content isn't being seen, it's an engine problem.
ex: A community both produces content (fuel) and distributes it (engine)
Top-down sales companies usually have a crude engine in SDRs and lack fuel

d.verdict: Find which side is the bottleneck; logically fuel usually comes first

l27|45.c: Your first marketer should be pi-shaped: expert in one area, strong in a second, strategic across all.
l27|45.e: Early on, hire generalists rather than specialists; specialists can be covered by agencies and contractors. Going a step beyond the usual T-shaped marketer, she wants a pi shape: deep in one of product marketing, content marketing or growth marketing, solid in a second, and able to set strategy for all three and hire the right outside help. Common workable pairs are product marketing plus growth, or product marketing plus content. People strong in both content and growth are rare, since one runs on storytelling and the other on data. Her most frequent recommendation is a product marketer who understands growth channels and can write both long and short copy.
ex: Asana's COO liked to ask candidates, "What is product marketing?"
Product marketing spans both fuel and engine, so it's often the first pick

result.d: The ideal profile for a first hire

l27|45.c: Pick a first marketer for business-model and early-stage experience, not a big name who only knows public companies.
l27|45.e: The business model dictates what marketing does, so matching experience with the model (enterprise sales versus product-led) matters more than industry experience; good marketers learn an audience quickly. Look for someone who worked on a small enough team to see all of marketing, wasn't siloed, and has seen what great looks like. People who only ran launches at big companies have never done positioning or built channels, and aren't used to doing the work themselves. Timing is usually around Series A, with early product-market fit. Product-led companies don't hire sales, so marketing has to arrive earlier. Her test: if the marketer floored the gas, could the product and team handle it?
ex: A common failure: an investor recommends someone who has only worked at Salesforce
No rush while you're still doing discovery customer by customer and changing the product

items.d: Saw all of marketing; never siloed
Sets strategy and does the work

l27|45.c: "Product-led growth" is a misnomer: it really means fewer salespeople and a bigger marketing team.
l27|45.e: What PLG actually means is growth without sales holding customers' hands, so product plus marketing. With no sales team talking to customers, the early marketing team has to be larger, not smaller. Marketing is good at one-to-many communication and should own traffic and website conversion, with the site on a tool like Webflow that marketing can change anytime. Product is good at working with engineering on in-product experiments. Sign-up, onboarding and first use are a gray zone, and the key is the marketing-to-product handoff, just as sales-led companies obsess over marketing-to-sales. Users shouldn't feel two teams talking past each other, like getting a product notification and a marketing email at once.
ex: Whether the form lives on the website or in the product decides who owns it
A website gets changed thousands of times; it can't be buried in the codebase

items.d: Depends if it's on the site or in product
Gray zone; name a clear owner

l27|45.c: Product and marketing collaborate well through clear ownership lists, shared planning and briefs written up front.
l27|45.e: At Asana, everyone keeps an "areas of responsibility" list, separate from their job title, that names what they are directly responsible for. A product manager running a launch can look up exactly who to involve. Before each quarter, a roadmap week opens cross-functional planning meetings to everyone, so marketing leads can sit in on product planning. Before any big project, marketing writes a GACCS brief and shares it with product to align early on audience and channels, rather than discovering the direction was wrong after the work is done. Without a good planning process, she argues, there is no good cross-functional work, and each side has to respect the other's expertise.
ex: Asana's roadmap week and areas-of-responsibility lists
GACCS stands for goals, audience, creative, channels, stakeholders

l27|45.c: Good marketing teams set impact goals rather than activity goals, and watch conversion across the whole funnel.
l27|45.e: A lot of marketing is splatter, not strategy: busy, but blind to impact. A good team can explain three things: the core work that sustains linear growth and how it's measured, the big bets that could produce a step change, and the infrastructure that isn't built yet and is slowing everything down. "Write ten blog posts this month" is a tactic; the goal should be traffic and the sign-ups it drives. Absolute numbers at one stage aren't enough either. As sign-ups grow, activation at the next stage should hold or improve, or you may just be pouring in low-quality users. Marketers also need to report internally at the right level of detail, with less jargon.
ex: Asana's former head of content jokingly called it "content splatergy"

items.d: Aim for a step change in sign-ups or leads
Gaps like lead scoring or a site migration

l27|45.c: Experts who angel invest should pitch their own value as clearly as they would a product.
l27|45.e: Most traditional VCs come from founder, sales or product backgrounds, so investors and advisors who understand marketing are scarce, and founders increasingly fill the gap with angels. She tells founders exactly what she offers: help building the marketing function, writing job descriptions, referring candidates and coaching the hire once they start. With a clear value proposition, people pull her into the right deals, and she says she gets into almost everything she wants. Helping takes less time than you'd think, since she has given the same advice countless times. And refer someone who gets hired, and the founder remembers you for a long time.
ex: Her fund pools more than 50 marketers
She builds a candidate pool through her newsletter, meeting one or two marketers a week

l28|46.c: Improv's "yes, and" habit and its love of specifics work well for cross-team collaboration.
l28|46.e: The worst thing you can do in improv is deny what your partner just set up; the scene dies on the spot. The right move is to accept the premise and build on it. At Uber he often saw headquarters and city teams define the same problem in ways that looked contradictory. Once you accept that both can be true at once, you build a relationship and usually find a better answer than either side had. His other improv rule is "specificity is a gift": the more concrete you are, the easier it is for the other person to respond, and the same goes for positioning. He thinks everyone should take one intro improv class, and he publicly asked his team to catch him saying "no."
ex: MasterClass positioning: satisfy deep curiosity about a person, the way a biography does
How Uber's headquarters teams worked with its city teams

items.d: Give them something to build on
Each side adds to the other

l28|46.c: To judge a new channel, check three things: a three-way overlap, the channel's DNA, and your company's DNA.
l28|46.e: First, look for overlap between what customers need, what the company wants, and what the channel is actually good at. People most often skip the last part and only ask whether the channel is hot. Many B2B companies simply shouldn't chase consumer channels. Second, study the channel's DNA. The earlier it is, the more likely it's a one-time opportunity and the faster its product changes. Also learn how it makes money; if you can help it hit its revenue goals, you can win partnerships and custom resources. Third, look at your own DNA: can you stomach the pain of being an early mover, do you have the people, and have basics like Google and Facebook already hit scale?
ex: Spotify on Clubhouse was a green light, both audio; a photo app would be yellow
Zynga and other games grew on Facebook notifications, then the platform shut them off
Hotel Tonight got into Facebook's mobile ad beta as the non-game example

items.d: Customer needs, company goals, channel strengths
How early, how volatile, how it makes money
Risk appetite, headcount, core channels at scale

l28|46.c: Test a new channel with half a person, fish for a month, and give it a quarter at most.
l28|46.e: How much you invest depends on those three factors. Average fit, a very early channel and a small team means half a person. Only when fit is excellent and you have a twenty-person team is it worth sending three people to try to lead the channel. There's no playbook for a new channel, but within a month you usually get a directional signal; give it longer if content is expensive to produce. Decide up front which momentum metric you'll watch, and if nothing improves after a quarter, put it on ice. These experiments belong on the roadmap and in the backlog, so you can weigh them against other opportunities.
ex: On Clubhouse: can attendance per room grow by about 10% each time?
A video that took three weeks and $20,000 to make deserves more time

items.d: About half a person, not the whole team
Look for a directional signal within a month
If it bites, add a sprint or two
No improvement, put it on ice

l28|46.c: Only about 5% of brand-new channels work; new forms of old channels are a better bet.
l28|46.e: The "emerging channels" that actually worked for him come in two kinds. One is a channel that has existed for ages and can finally be done at scale, like podcasts. The other is a new product from an old platform, like Facebook's mobile app install ads, where the rules changed weekly for the first 18 months or so. Channel by channel: OTT streaming ads are more trackable than traditional TV. Influencer marketing is so precise it reminds him of early Facebook targeting, but it's still very manual. TikTok has crossed the chasm, so any company it suits should be on it. Podcast ads work like radio: pick the right shows and repeat, best for high-ticket B2B. VR is where mobile was before the iPhone 3.
ex: MasterClass used Grin to find and manage influencers
Podcasts struggle to reach the scale of Google or Facebook

marks.d: Only worth it if you have a VR product
Mature ad platform, works at scale

l28|46.c: When the economy shifts, assume you've lost product-market fit before you go hunting for new channels.
l28|46.e: Early adopters are often nothing like the mainstream. Many companies claim product-market fit, but the market they size and the market they validated against are two different groups of people. That's the biggest red flag he sees as an investor. The 2022 shift means the entire customer base changed, not just the next 10% of new customers. So he suggests assuming your fit held only in the old market and validating it again. If you're lucky, a few tweaks will do. But if you treat the problem as "we need a new channel," you're pointed the wrong way from the start.
ex: Clubhouse may have expanded to the mainstream too fast, without proving the demand would last

items: Growth slows, find a new channel
Treat it as an acquisition problem

d.verdict: Fit holds for a specific market; when the market changes, start over

l28|46.c: Product-led companies need a "growth CMO" who ties marketing tightly to product.
l28|46.e: He has watched several excellent traditional CMOs struggle after joining product-led companies. They tend to treat brand as a one-off campaign rather than an investment you keep iterating on. The classic 4Ps of marketing come from an era when products took years to build and marketing handled packaging, shelf space and pricing. Today the product is the company, and marketing has to be woven into every part of it. A growth CMO measures everything with data, brand included, iterates fast in an agile way, and runs experiments across the whole funnel. When hiring, look for someone who can handle chaos and is willing to get hands-on again. He believes most marketers can make the shift once they learn agile product development.
ex: Books like Hacking Marketing cover agile marketing
Coca-Cola's earliest coupons were really a two-sided marketplace tactic

terms.d: Treat every asset the agile way

result.d: Joined at the hip with the product lead

l28|46.c: Burnout shows up as a sudden drop in resilience; losing interest in things you love may be depression.
l28|46.e: At Uber he managed a 150-person team and dealt with hundreds of city managers. He thought he was just tired and went to therapy, where he learned he was overworking because he craved recognition. So he moved toward work that was more impactful and more respected. His test for exhaustion versus depression is to look outside work: when tired, he still enjoyed improv class; when depressed, he cancelled it. If a manager sees a report go from "worth a shot" to "why bother," that's usually burnout. Therapy, meditation and opening up to friends all help. And check whether your company benefits include mental health resources.
ex: He found his therapist through a service Uber offered
The meditation app Waking Up taught him what meditation is about

items.d: Resilience drops, or you cancel hobbies
Therapy revealed a craving for recognition
Do work that is impactful and respected

l29|47.c: In a downturn only visible progress keeps morale up, and as Web3 products mature PMs matter again.
l29|47.e: He believes speeches and perks can't hold a team together in a slump. The only thing that works is shipping constantly, so people can see "this is real." Airbnb went through the same thing when revenue collapsed during the pandemic. He's still optimistic about Web3: the word has only been in mainstream vocabulary for about a year, and new technology never moves in a straight line. Early Web3 teams could grow with a few engineers, a community manager and a rising token. As products get more complex and competitors multiply, product management becomes a competitive advantage again, and more projects are now hiring PMs from big tech companies.
ex: Uniswap has about 100 people and some days out-trades Coinbase, which has thousands
Alchemy hit a record number of developers and added Solana support

l29|47.c: Amazon's press-release documents force clear thinking: replace adjectives with numbers and cut until every word counts.
l29|47.e: His year at Amazon shaped him most, because there the product and the business are inseparable. "Working backwards" means writing a PRFAQ first: the press release you'd publish on launch day, plus a set of questions and answers. The external FAQ answers customer questions; the internal FAQ exists to name the elephant in the room. The writing rules ban empty words like "great," demand you say exactly how much time a customer saves, and require cutting again and again. With fewer words, each one carries more weight and the trade-offs get more deliberate. The customer quote has to come from the real target user's shoes, not from what you wish they'd say.
ex: Every new hire takes a business writing class and keeps a tips card on the desk
When teams switch from slides to docs, they often just write longer fluff

items.d: One paragraph, straight to the pain
What a real user would say
When and where to get it

l29|47.c: The best leaders share three traits: nothing is beneath them, they go deep on details, and they adapt.
l29|47.e: He has watched David Sacks, Jeff Bezos, Brian Chesky and Alchemy's founders up close. First is humility: reading a spec or running a SQL query is never beneath them. Second is craft: you can only make good decisions when you're deep in the details, like running product reviews yourself or placing a test order yourself. Third, they don't cling to a playbook built over twenty years; in a crisis they can shift gears. Humility plus craft is powerful on its own, and adaptability makes it more so. As a company scales, instead of forcing "accountability" down from the top through performance reviews, he'd rather build a culture where everyone feels "this is my product."
ex: Bezos forwarded customer emails with just a question mark, expecting an answer within 24 hours
As Yammer's CEO, Sacks ran product reviews himself
Chesky cares about details like the homepage hero image

result.d: Leaves a mark on the team

l29|47.c: Don't treat disagreement as "pushing back"; find what the other person really wants and reframe your plan.
l29|47.e: The phrase "push back" itself puts you in a combative, say-no mindset. What works better is figuring out what the other person actually cares about, then aligning your proposal to that goal. When Airbnb integrated Luxury Retreats, the team was worn down by a chat feature that kept getting more complicated. A senior colleague realized the goal was a magical experience, not more features, and reframed the concierge as a "trip designer." The experience got more elegant and the scope got smaller. Renaming alone isn't enough, though; you need a bigger idea behind it and a good way to tell it.
ex: Airbnb turned its concierge service into a "trip designer"
At Alchemy he won over the founders with "this is how we hire if we want to win"

items: Fight over features, people and time
Cutting scope looks like giving in

d.verdict: Work backwards from the goal the other person cares about

l29|47.c: Treat your career as a map, not a ladder: be intentional about the big picture and accept discomfort.
l29|47.e: A ladder is about levels, power and titles; a map is about interesting experiences. He treats his career like travel and would rather it be interesting than comfortable, because that's where growth and good stories come from. Many people obsess over the title and pay of their next job but are casual about the direction of their life. Ask what you'll care about on your deathbed, he says, and it gets clear. People also have false certainty about how any one job move will turn out, and ladders can fall over too. But a map doesn't mean job-hopping; people who stay somewhere for years hold institutional knowledge nobody can replace. For newcomers he leans toward a middle path.
ex: After selling his first company he built five or six products alone at his kitchen table
At do.com, an acquisition offer fell through the day before his wedding

marks.d: For a gold star on the resume
Good mentors and lots to do
Hard to build a track record or network

l29|47.c: Run hiring like a business, with marketing, sales and product all in play.
l29|47.e: Rename "hiring" to "choosing the people you work with every day and who define what the company is," and it naturally becomes the most important thing. On the marketing side, had the candidate heard of you before the interview, met your employees, seen what you've shared? That takes genuine word of mouth. On the sales side, understand the one or two things the person cares about most; he admits he failed at outbound sales because he didn't listen to needs. On the product side, a job description is a spec, yet people write it once and never revise it. When a great person doesn't quite fit the role, reshape the role the way you'd iterate on a product.
ex: Alchemy's founders still meet every candidate
Airbnb Plus was iterated by remodeling real homes; roles deserve the same

items.d: Reputation and awareness, company and personal
Hear what the person cares about most
Reshape the role to fit the person and the business

l29|47.c: The most important PM skill is defining clearly which problem actually matters.
l29|47.e: How you define the problem shapes everything: what you build, how you make money, and whether the team is motivated. At Alchemy, you can't compare an SDK against an NFT API in the abstract. You first have to ask whether the problem is developer experience or an NFT market that needs more support. His first company defined the problem as low-income students lacking college-prep resources, so it stayed free for years and earned money from university sponsors. Had it defined the problem as a lack of good courses, it would have focused on teaching methods instead. Like most life advice, everyone understands this; the hard part is applying it to a specific case.
ex: The test-prep company he founded at 15 was free for students and funded by university sponsors

root.d: Define it before choosing a solution

items.d: Free plus sponsors, or sell courses

l30|48.c: Follower quality beats quantity: attract people who come for your ideas, not your curation.
l30|48.e: He splits followers into two kinds. "Idea followers" come for your original insights. "Labor followers" come for the memes you repost and the inspirational threads you crank out. The first group feels closer to you and is more loyal; they show up when you host an event, sell something or push a cause. The second group sees you as interchangeable with any other curation account. He found that cheap threads attracted the wrong people and drove away those who wanted a real exchange, so he nearly stopped posting and now shares only original ideas distilled from his blog. For beginners, though, threads are still the main way to grow, because showing a lot of thinking at once convinces readers you can keep delivering.
ex: Paul Graham built his following on original ideas, not growth posts
He was one of the first to write threads at scale, then chose to stop

d.verdict: Better a few idea followers than many labor followers

l30|48.c: The best growth comes from products that pull in new users just by being used normally.
l30|48.e: He thinks "product-led growth" usually just means self-serve sales. What growth people should really care about is growth that comes from usage itself. Each new user costs nothing extra, it scales, it can form a network, and it isn't at the mercy of a Google algorithm change or swings in ad prices. It's fully in your control. It's also different from referral bonuses, which are an added lure that often attracts people who only want the reward and churn quickly. Mostly this is a question of what you choose to build: if you have several startup ideas, pick the one that has this mechanism built in.
ex: To get paid, the recipient has to sign up for PayPal or Venmo
"Sent from my iPhone" and Calendly links are free billboards
User discussions on Quora and Reddit get indexed by Google and bring search traffic

root.d: Using the product recruits new users

items.d: They must sign up to get paid or receive goods
Content gets shared or indexed by search

l30|48.c: Retention comes from letting users build up "state" in your product, so the more they invest the harder it is to leave.
l30|48.e: He borrows the idea from games: the longer you play, the more gear and skins you collect, the less you want to leave, and the more your stash earns you. In software, state includes reputation you can't take with you (seller ratings), an audience you can't take with you (subscribers), a social graph built over years, and infrastructure wired deep into your code. That's why eBay and Craigslist, with mediocre experiences, have gone unchallenged for decades. He thinks "moat" is overused. The only true moats are government barriers or patent-protected scientific breakthroughs; what most companies call a moat is just a better-than-average retention mechanism.
ex: An eBay seller with tens of thousands of reviews can't easily move elsewhere
YouTube won't give creators subscriber emails; Substack lets you export them
Twilio, Stripe and AWS sit deep in the code, so switching is costly

l30|48.c: Good writing packs in novelty; cut the dead space between one "wow" and the next.
l30|48.e: His definition of novelty has three parts: you haven't heard it before, it matters, and you couldn't have come up with it yourself. Only when all three hold does a reader feel a jolt. Novelty comes in a few types: counterintuitive (so that's how the world works), counter-narrative (what I was told was wrong), shocking, and elegant articulation that compresses a complex idea into one line. He asks about twenty friends to mark the sentences that made them go "wow," then compresses the flat stretches in between so more people finish the piece. When you meet something novel, score its novelty on the spot, because after you've seen it a few times you go numb.
ex: Counter-narrative: reading a lot is the most respectable vanity metric for adults
Counterintuitive: the world isn't run by exceptional people
Naval is great at compressing complex ideas into one line

l30|48.c: Writing quality equals novelty times resonance: build the novel skeleton first, then add stories and analogies.
l30|48.e: Even the most novel idea is just dry trivia if it isn't packaged in a form that sticks in the reader's mind. Resonance comes from examples, analogies, metaphors and stories. So his first draft hunts only for novelty, and the second draft layers in the stories and analogies. He admits his writing is often called too dry, but that's deliberate: too much resonance bloats a piece, and he personally prefers things as lean as a reference manual. The golden rule is to write what you'd want to read. He also keeps updating his handbooks so they stay evergreen.
ex: On Writing Well taught him to cut two-thirds of what he writes

result.d: Draft one for novelty, draft two for resonance

l30|48.c: Pick topics where you have both a clear writing goal and a strong enough motivation.
l30|48.e: Whether you finish a piece depends on whether the goal is clear and the motivation strong. Goals include proving a mainstream view wrong, saying what everyone thinks but nobody says, contributing an original insight from your own research or experiments, or telling a moving story with a lesson. With a goal, one read-through tells you whether you're done, so you don't trail off at the end. Motivations include having something you can't keep to yourself, using the writing to solve a problem that's bugging you, or being obsessed with a topic and wanting company. Pair one goal with one motivation and you'll see it through.

items.d: Such as overturning a mainstream view
Such as an itch to speak or a problem to solve
Stop when the goal is met

l30|48.c: Creativity is a faucet clogged with dirty water: drain the bad ideas first and the good ones follow.
l30|48.e: He noticed that Neil Gaiman, Ed Sheeran and John Mayer describe almost the same creative process. Think of creativity as a pipe: the first stretch is all wastewater, and you have to let it run before clean water comes out. So at the start of every session, write down every bad idea that surfaces and don't judge yourself. Writing bad ideas is itself progress: your brain gradually learns what makes them bad and gets better at spotting fresh combinations. Many people sit down, write a few lines, feel uninspired and leave; they simply didn't finish the process. In practice, start with a crude imitation, find its weaknesses, and iterate until it becomes original.
ex: He spotted the shared method in their MasterClass courses, documentaries and videos

items.d: Your brain learns to avoid the duds

l31|49.c: Funnel thinking is company-centric and stops at acquisition; subscription businesses need the customer's point of view.
l31|49.e: Funnels, pirate metrics, MQLs and SQLs dump every customer into the same bucket and assume all customers and products are alike. They measure value to the company, not value to the customer, and "pushing people down the funnel" is an off-putting idea in itself. For a recurring-revenue business, marketing and growth can't end at acquisition. Yet most of these models ignore retention and expansion, and they skip the "problem stage" customers were in before they ever found you, which is some of the most useful context marketing can have.
ex: She once cheered Dave McClure's pirate metrics, then saw their limits

items: Centered on value to the company
Centered on value to the customer

d.verdict: Design growth around how customers get value

l31|49.c: The fastest win is rewriting positioning and messaging for your best customers; attract the right people and conversion follows.
l31|49.e: Every company she has worked with learned something new from the research, and the most common low-hanging fruit is website messaging that isn't doing its job. One social media tool did only light research, found two customer jobs, focused on one, rewrote its site, and cut the trial from 30 days to 7. They didn't touch anything after signup, yet trial-to-paid conversion rose too, because better-fit customers were coming in. Carrying the same messaging into onboarding and email can lift activation dramatically as well.
ex: The social media tool: website conversion up 89%, trial-to-paid up 40%
Autobooks roughly tripled core usage after adding onboarding emails
SparkToro doubled trial-to-paid conversion

l31|49.c: Survey your best customers who joined in the last three to six months and get the most out of the product.
l31|49.e: Best customers get a lot of value from the product, pay for it, are happy and don't need much hand-holding. They also need to have joined recently enough to remember life before you; long-time customers tend to make up answers from memory. She designs questions using jobs-to-be-done theory: what was going on in your life, what triggered you to look for a solution, what else did you consider, what were your must-haves and worries, and what can you do now that you couldn't before. Interviews are ideal, but a survey is often clear enough. You can have actionable conclusions in two or three weeks, so don't get stuck in analysis paralysis.
ex: SparkToro reached clear conclusions from a survey alone
Founders think they know their customers best, but nobody has finished this research without learning something

items.d: Both get value and pay for it

l31|49.c: Focus on one customer job at a time, favoring the one with high willingness to pay and urgent pain.
l31|49.e: Research usually surfaces several distinct jobs. Try to serve all of them at once and your messaging stops resonating with anyone. The criteria mirror those for best customers: high willingness to pay; an urgent problem, so you're selling a painkiller rather than a vitamin; strong retention and expansion potential; a level of hand-holding that matches your sales model; a group that's easy to reach; or an unfair advantage you hold in that market. Jobs you don't focus on now aren't abandoned, you can add them later. She finds demographic personas unhelpful here. Jobs pull marketing, product and customer success into the same view.
ex: SparkToro chose marketing service providers over analysts chasing data purity
Ozzy Osbourne and King Charles share demographics but have very different motivations

root.d: Pick one of your best customers' jobs

items.d: Needed long term, and the need grows
A gathered audience or an unfair edge

l31|49.c: Map the journey by the milestones where customers get value, and give each milestone a KPI.
l31|49.e: The approach comes from storyboards she saw at Airbnb's office in 2013: told entirely from the customer's point of view, including emotions and life outside the product, and instantly understandable to anyone. Back at Unbounce she shut herself in a room for two days with a co-founder and the head of support to draw their own version, which gave the whole company a shared language. She splits the journey into struggle, evaluation and growth. Keep milestones few, about six, like a documentary of "how I met and fell in love with your product." The struggle stage is measured by visitors and website conversion; in evaluation, the KPI should be tied to usage of the features customers value most.
ex: Storyboards of the guest and host journeys hung on the walls of Airbnb's product area
Unbounce drew its own journey map the same way

l31|49.c: Measurable milestones let you push users forward and pull them back when they fall off.
l31|49.e: If a user hasn't yet reached the feature they personally value most, sending them anything else is pointless; help them reach that value moment first. Because every milestone has a metric, the team can nudge people forward with in-app guides and email, and can also trigger an email or a one-to-one reach-out when someone misses the mark. At SparkToro, the best customers cared most about lists and exports. Those features weren't hidden, but they weren't prominent either, so the team bundled them with core search as the activation criteria. She says that in many products about 70% of users log in once and never return, yet very few companies try to win them back.
ex: First value was defined as five or more searches plus at least one list
After launching an onboarding checklist and emails, trial-to-paid doubled within two months

l31|49.c: Write the messaging guide in your best customers' own words, ordered by what they care about most.
l31|49.e: Internal knowledge is valuable, but it should never come before listening to your best customers. You can't read the label from inside the bottle, so reflect customers' own words back at them to prove you understand their problem. With a hundred or so survey responses you can tally what they care about most and second most, instead of guessing from the features the team finds coolest. The messaging guide she delivers runs five to seven pages: value proposition, competitive advantages, and value themes with their emotional and functional benefits. It connects up to the customer job and down to the marketing and onboarding projects at each milestone, and it's easy to hand to a copywriter.
ex: SparkToro's customer job: uncover opportunities I couldn't see, and look like an expert to the people who matter

items.d: When..., help me..., so I can...
Fix the biggest gap: emails, checklists

l32|50.c: The feature users ask for loudest may not change their behavior, so run a behavioral diagnosis first.
l32|50.e: In one fintech app, budgeting was the most requested feature. The team agreed only to test it first: ten thousand people in three groups, two budgeting designs against a control that simply showed spending. Average spending and its variance didn't move at all. She wasn't surprised. Break "spend less" into its steps and you see it demands repeated effort from the user over a long time. What people say they will do and what they actually do are different things, and any design that pushes work onto the user deserves suspicion. In personal finance, better answers are defaults or a simple rule of thumb.
ex: Budgeting test: 10,000 people, 3 groups, zero change in average or variance of spending
Automatic 401(k) enrollment is the main reason Americans have retirement savings
Rule-of-thumb example: no ride-hailing on weekdays, only weekends

items.d: How much is spent this month

l32|50.c: To change behavior, use the three Bs: pick a specific behavior, remove barriers, and add immediate benefits.
l32|50.e: Companies are good at setting outcome metrics but rarely spell out the exact action they want users to take. The behavior should be so specific that the team argues about it, and "log in" is never the answer. Step two is lowering barriers: operational ones like filling in forms or typing a card number, and psychological ones like aversion to uncertainty or sticking with the status quo. Step three is amplifying benefits. People are present-biased, so the product has to give a reason to act today, such as the satisfaction of checking something off or being seen by colleagues.
ex: Peloton example: take a 10-minute class with each of two instructors within 7 days of joining
One Medical recommended a doctor and a next-day video slot; bookings rose 20%
Asana: the urge to complete tasks and social visibility provide immediate benefits

items.d: An action specific enough to argue over
Give a reason to act today

l32|50.c: Adding an easy question to a sign-up flow can actually raise conversion.
l32|50.e: Less friction usually means more conversion, but questions are the exception. A question plants an idea in the user's head and gets them imagining what the product will do for them, which gives them the motivation to push through the later steps. The condition is that the question must be easy to answer, with a dropdown or multiple choice. Open text boxes are almost always hard to answer and should be removed. Rather than passively showing benefits in a carousel, let users see the benefit as part of setup, for example by asking how quickly they want their bills paid.
ex: Trunk Club said asking questions at sign-up lifted conversion 133%
Removing one open text box raised that page's conversion 40%

l32|50.c: To get people to do less of something, add friction: TikTok cut misinformation by slowing down sharing.
l32|50.e: To get more of a behavior, make it easier; to get less, put obstacles in the way. TikTok moves fast and users are in a "hot state." The team first narrowed the target behavior to sharing, then added an "unverified" label to videos and a pop-up asking "are you sure?" when someone tapped share. That created both operational and psychological friction, and shares of misleading videos fell 24%. The design came from the research literature: reminding people to care about accuracy works only at the moment of sharing, not before and not after.
ex: Elevator study: delaying the doors 16 seconds pushed more people to the stairs
From about 30 designs, 5 pop-ups were tested on over a thousand people on Prolific
In the product, only 2 test groups plus a control were run

items.d: Accuracy prompts; hot and cold states
Different ways to test one hypothesis

l32|50.c: You can drive the right behavior with the "wrong" reason, because people need motivation right now.
l32|50.e: People know they should do many things but lack the push to do them now, so you can offer an immediate reason unrelated to the real purpose. Vaccines protect other people, yet donuts and lottery tickets move people more. Pizza at polling places raises turnout. Deadlines are a gift of the same kind, helping people prioritize, and adding them at several companies raised completion rates. But use restraint: forcing people through steps with error messages, for instance, breeds resentment if overused.
ex: Ohio used a lottery to encourage Covid vaccination
Kiva added a deadline to its borrower sign-up flow and conversion rose
Peloton: people take classes for an instructor shout-out or to keep a streak

d.verdict: Long-term benefits rarely drive action now; add an immediate reason

l32|50.c: Whether these tactics help or harm depends on incentives: tie KPIs to user behavior and lengthen the review cycle.
l32|50.e: Whether behavioral design turns into manipulation comes down to how the team is measured. She once took a pay-for-performance project with LendingClub: she would be paid only if borrower conversion rose five percentage points. She found herself behaving more and more like a predatory lender, legal kept rejecting her proposals, and she reached only 4.5 points. Her two recommendations: tie evaluation to specific behaviors that are good for users, not just activity and retention, and stretch the review period from a quarter to a year or more, so nobody sacrifices users for a short-term spike.
ex: LendingClub bet: target of +5 points, actual +4.5
At the same time she ran a lab at Duke focused on low- and middle-income families

cells.d: Long-term view, but metric misses users

l32|50.c: Teams can do this themselves: run a workshop to fix the behavior, then diagnose it screen by screen.
l32|50.e: Without outside consultants, the most important step is getting the team together to agree on an extremely specific target behavior. Only then can you discuss the psychology that drives it. Step two is a behavioral diagnosis, a souped-up journey map: screenshot every step on the way to that behavior, often two or three hundred pages, and annotate the psychological factors at work on each. Then design interventions for the sticking points, and always compare several options side by side rather than showing users one design and asking whether they like it.
ex: Facing a new problem, spend a day on Google Scholar looking for meta-analyses
Wealthfront: returning users resume where they left off instead of starting over
A common health-app sticking point: people avoid looking at their test results

items.d: Agree on a very specific target behavior
Screenshot each step; note the psychology
Compare options; don't ask about preference

l33|52.c: A growth model is a tool for understanding a business, not predicting it, and half its value is in building it yourself.
l33|52.e: A growth model is a spreadsheet framework describing how a business grows, and because every part has to connect, it's hard to fool yourself. SaaS needs just acquisition, retention and monetization. Transactional businesses add frequency, order value and unit economics. Marketplaces also model the supply side and how supply and demand interact. The most interesting parts are the nonlinear ones, like virality and reinvesting profit into acquisition, which also show that payback period matters more than LTV/CAC for growth speed. Too many market assumptions means garbage in, garbage out, so he favors one high-level conceptual model plus smaller models owned by each team.
ex: He built twenty or thirty growth models while running Basis One
In annual planning, the model turns each team's commitments into a common currency
Thumbtack's model showed repeat rate was key, shifting resources from acquisition to cross-selling

items.d: Add frequency, order value, unit economics
Add supply acquisition, retention and interaction

l33|52.c: Retention is the biggest lever, but you move it through the core product and the early experience.
l33|52.e: Once you build the model, growth turns out to be far more sensitive to retention than intuition suggests, because retention also drives referrals, content and profit. But retention is the result of the whole experience. More emails and push notifications rarely work, and marketplaces usually have to pull core product levers like supply depth. The biggest gains often come from the early experience: find users who had a bad first week or month when they shouldn't have, and bring the below-average experiences up to average. He discounts correlational analyses like "good users all did X," and thinks winning back churned users is far less valuable than serving new ones well.
ex: Uber and Lyft competed to guarantee new drivers' first-week or first-month earnings
An unlucky new driver earning $3 an hour may never come back

items.d: Cancellations; low earnings in sparse areas
Assumes the platform is always like this

l33|52.c: Judge a marketplace's health on four things: GMV, unit economics, liquidity and share of wallet.
l33|52.e: GMV, the total value transacted, combines both sides and is the north star. Unit economics must be broken down clearly, because early marketplaces often lose money on every order. Liquidity matters most: when a buyer or seller wants to transact, can they? Define it in terms of the experience users care about and find the tipping point. Until you reach it nothing else matters, which is why you narrow by geography or category first. Share of wallet measures depth of relationship; the higher it is, the less users multi-home across platforms. For the same 10% growth, he would rather it came from existing customers spending more than from new ones.
ex: Uber's experience changed in kind once wait times fell to about 4–5 minutes
Faire tracks how much of a retailer's shelf came from Faire
Instacart and Uber both lost money per order early on

items.d: North star linking supply and demand
Often negative early; break it down
Can transactions happen? The first metric

l33|52.c: Demand is the hard currency; add supply only until it stops improving the demand-side experience.
l33|52.e: Early on, supply matters more, because supply is the product and suppliers use the platform more deeply. But that tempts people to treat supply itself as the thing to optimize. He believes whoever aggregates an industry's demand wins: merchants and drivers almost never turn down paying customers. So add supply only when it improves the demand experience; once wait times stop falling, you don't need more drivers. Rather than watching a supply-demand ratio, write an ROI formula that captures the two-sided relationship, push acquisition on both sides to an acceptable payback period, and guard only against extreme imbalance.
ex: Uber example: 1 driver per 10 riders, so rider CAC plus 10% of driver CAC
When Amazon adds pet-category supply, it must ask how much is truly incremental

result.d: Compare with LTV to get payback

l33|52.c: Run a marketplace like a gardener, not a builder, and be especially gentle when touching core mechanics.
l33|52.e: In a marketplace almost every decision has second- and even third-order consequences. Take pricing: a SaaS company can plot price against conversion and find the optimum. A marketplace usually takes a commission from the supply side. A higher take rate funds a better demand-side experience but may drive suppliers away, and that relationship doesn't fit on a simple curve. A change you make in one place may show its long-term effect only two months later, when the cause is hard to trace. So in a marketplace that already works, adjust incentives and core mechanics with great care.
ex: The higher Amazon's commission, the more it can subsidize returns and faster delivery

items: Build features and sell them, step by step
Intervening in an ecosystem you can't fully see
Effects may appear two months later
Take rate pulls on both sides at once

d.verdict: Touch core incentives gently, especially when things work

l33|52.c: Expand first into adjacent areas that strengthen your network effects; unbundling big platforms is usually overrated.
l33|52.e: Large marketplaces sit in huge industries, with ten opportunities one step away. Past a certain size the market's size stops mattering; what counts is whether you can win it (is the model similar?) and whether you can reuse the same supply or demand. Conversely, the "unbundle the big platform" thesis rarely comes true. Vertical players offer a more tailored experience but can't beat the big platform's higher customer lifetime value and network effects, unless the niche is itself high-frequency or high-ticket. When expanding, keep the product up to speed and don't let marketing outrun it.
ex: Instacart went into convenience stores before traditional retail; Uber launched Uber Eats
Thumbtack tracked hundreds of vertical competitors and few broke out
Successful unbundling: StockX solved sneaker authenticity; Airbnb came out of Craigslist

cells.d: Shared users, but a very different model
Like Uber Eats: same drivers and users
Amounts to starting a new network

l33|52.c: Newer marketplaces take on more of the work and charge higher fees, and the endpoint may not be a marketplace at all.
l33|52.e: He plotted marketplaces' take rates against their founding years and found newer ones charge more, and do more to earn it: from merely aggregating demand, to building trust, to running logistics and absorbing bad debt. Taken to the limit, the take rate approaches 100% and it stops being a marketplace; Opendoor, which buys homes before selling them, is essentially e-commerce. Which ones go that far depends on whether users want standardization or supplier creativity. Ride-hailing will fully consolidate once cars drive themselves, while Etsy, Faire and Steam will stay marketplaces for a long time.
ex: Pure lead-gen marketplaces like Zillow take about 5–10%
Faire absorbs the risk of retailers defaulting, so it can charge a higher take rate
Few B2B marketplaces: concentrated industries and big orders make it easy to bypass the platform

d.right: Owns supply; no longer a marketplace

marks.d: Builds trust between the two sides
Holds the supply itself; essentially e-commerce

l34|54.c: Don't hire a growth leader by looking for "you, ten years younger"; fill the team's gaps across four skill areas.
l34|54.e: Founders often ask him how to find a younger version of himself. He sees that as pattern matching with no first-principles thinking. His growth skills model has four blocks: growth execution, customer understanding, growth strategy, and communication and influence, each with three specific skills. The goal isn't a unicorn who scores perfectly on everything, but a team with no blank spots overall. The last two blocks are advanced, and junior people needn't master them all. The model also works for interviewing a company in reverse, and it turns vague feedback like "be more strategic" into something concrete.
ex: Wyzant's founder wanted a silver bullet and ended up closing the San Francisco office and laying people off
A key customer-understanding skill: users arrive with emotions, so address those before logic

items.d: Strategic comms, leading teams, managing stakeholders

l34|54.c: For junior growth roles, screen for execution and customer understanding, prefer internal transfers, and hire specialists later.
l34|54.e: Execution is close to a basic executive function and is hard to teach in adulthood, and customer understanding takes years to build, so junior growth hires must already have both. He prefers internal transfers: they ramp faster, you know them, and it gives employees a new opportunity. But if the founder doesn't understand growth, give the new person an advisor, a course or a coach, or an eager hire will keep hitting walls without seeing the door right beside them. "Surgeon" specialists in fields like SEO and paid acquisition, which take years to master, should be hired from outside once the foundation is in place.
ex: Ben Lauzier borrowed an old laptop between interviews to handle work for his current employer
Sean, a Patreon marketer, moved internally into a growth PM role and excelled

items: SEO, paid acquisition and the like
Not the right first growth hire

d.verdict: Build the base with internal transfers, then hire specialists

l34|54.c: Onboarding is the only part of the product that 100% of users go through, so it deserves the most investment.
l34|54.e: Few features ever reach 100% usage, but everyone goes through onboarding. Your brand is the promise you make in the market, the product experience is how you keep it, and onboarding is the first time you keep it. A mismatch leaves users disappointed. At this moment users are most motivated and willing to push through obstacles to use the product, so you can add a bit of friction to learn more about them. Its core job is connecting users to value and forming a habit, and he has seen companies shift their retention curve outward by 10 to 20 percentage points this way.
ex: He ran an onboarding project at every company, including Lyft and Patreon

items.d: They want your product most when they arrive
Add a little friction to gather information

l34|54.c: Serve high-potential users with humans first, then turn what works into opinionated defaults in the product.
l34|54.e: Tens of thousands of creators went through Patreon's onboarding every week. The team had creators connect YouTube, Instagram and other accounts, then used a data science model to flag high-potential ones by audience size and engagement and route them to a human. That human touch raised creators' first- or second-month earnings by 25%, and second-month earnings are a key input to lifetime value. They then productized what the humans had learned: recommended pricing tiers and page copy became defaults. Users could still change them, but straying from the default took a bit more effort.
ex: Three pricing tiers by default; 3–5 is ideal, not one and not 40
An entry tier of $3 or $5 rather than $1
Human outreach lifted creators' early earnings by 25%

items.d: Link social accounts; check audience and engagement
A real person reaches out with advice
Find the setups that work best
Easy to get right, hard to get wrong, still a choice

l34|54.c: Good onboarding may lower conversion slightly while raising retention, so use proxy metrics to balance the two.
l34|54.e: Good onboarding screens out people who were never a fit and would have churned anyway, so a small drop in conversion isn't necessarily bad: those who stay are higher quality. But there is a balance point. If conversion falls too far and retention doesn't make up for it, you got it wrong, so watch both of these opposing metrics in every experiment. Nobody can wait 90 days to see retention, so find early proxy metrics and do qualitative spot checks on whether new users are the right people. And only redo onboarding when you have a new insight; redesigns for their own sake rarely help.
ex: Patreon's proxies: how fast a creator gets their first patron and their first $100
A scaled company should have a team spend a quarter or two each year revisiting onboarding

items.d: Includes people who aren't a fit

l34|54.c: Pick a company with his PMF framework: people, mission and financials, and don't compromise on any of them.
l34|54.e: Job seekers should hold a strict set of criteria too, and his are people, mission and financials. People means colleagues who can argue honestly and resolve disagreements well. Mission means that if the company gets big, many people's lives improve. Financials means spending discipline, not budgets built on pandemic-peak assumptions. Looking back, he evaluated all three properly at Lyft and Patreon and both went well. At Wyzant and Imperfect Foods he settled for two out of three, or misjudged one, and neither ended well.
ex: Imperfect Foods: strong mission and financials, but constant infighting among executives
Wyzant: the founder's expectations and what he could deliver were completely misaligned

terms.d: At scale, many lives get better

result.d: Discount any one and trouble follows

l34|54.c: A job is an investment of your time, so do due diligence on future colleagues the way an investor would.
l34|54.e: You can earn money back, but time invested is gone, so job-search diligence should be more rigorous than investment diligence, and people are the hardest part to assess. First, ask to sit in on an executive meeting, a product review or a team meeting, and watch who talks and whether feedback is constructive or hostile. Second, ask the CEO to describe a disagreement at the most recent strategy meeting and how it was resolved. Third, run back-channel references: talk to current or former employees who aren't part of the interview process, since they have nothing to sell and speak more candidly. If someone refuses to share a list of former reports, that tells you something by itself.
ex: Tal Raviv asked for a list of people he had managed and called each one

marks.d: Not part of the interview loop
Best source on the real experience

l35|56.c: A product community grows by learning together and showing up; a conference is the least forgiving business.
l35|56.e: Mind the Product didn't set out to build a community. It began as people figuring out product management together, and it stayed grassroots while running meetups every month and a conference every year. The founders only knew so many people, so they asked members to find speakers, write articles, and bring in more of the right people. A conference, by contrast, can't be iterated. If something goes wrong you wait a year, one mistake costs thousands of pounds, and weak ticket sales can sink the whole thing. Her trick for selling tickets: run monthly community events for years beforehand, because those events are the marketing.
ex: ProductTank meetups spread to nearly 300 cities
The first conference's party venue went bust three weeks before opening
When food ran short, volunteers bought out nearby sandwich shops

items.d: Get together to work out what no one knows
Keep the same feel as it scales
Ask members to find speakers and writers

l35|56.c: Work out the story before the slides, and remember the audience wants you to do well.
l35|56.e: She used to write talks straight into PowerPoint and ended up led around by her slides. Now she settles the story beats first, then fits the content into slides. Before the conference stage, a speaking coach rewrote her jokes, straightened out her story, adjusted her posture and wording, and made her listen to her own recordings until she could run through the talk while out walking. On the day, she suggests a power pose, walking the empty stage beforehand, and locking onto the people who nod and smile. If you freeze, breathe and start again. The audience wants you to succeed, and a small slip just makes you more human.
ex: Early on she forgot her lines at a 200-person ProductCamp, apologized, and restarted
Mind the Product gives its conference speakers a professional speaking coach

items.d: Settle the beats before making slides
Power pose, walk the stage, find friendly faces

l35|56.c: Timeline roadmaps force a date onto everything; Now/Next/Later matches how work actually happens.
l35|56.e: She used to draw timeline roadmaps too, never shipped everything on them, and assumed the problem was her. The first version of ProdPad was a digital Gantt chart, a plan laid out as bars along a calendar. About a month in, many users asked to shift a whole block of items back a month. When she dug in, nobody had delivered anything on the dates shown. Once there is a timeline, every item gets an implied deadline, and the further out you plan, the more made-up the dates are. So she switched to three columns: Now, Next, and Later. Detail fades as you move right, and individual items can still carry a date when one is needed.
ex: About 70% of ProdPad customers want this roadmap style (with some selection bias)
The tool asks what problem each idea solves and what came of it

marks.d: Work in the next few weeks, dates allowed

l35|56.c: Plan real deadlines separately, then use soft and hard launches to uncouple engineering from marketing.
l35|56.e: This isn't about living in fantasy land. Regulatory deadlines, the Christmas rush, or back-to-school season genuinely need dates. For those, plan early, leave buffer, and soft-launch before the deadline so problems get fixed in time. Everything else doesn't need a date. Engineering soft-launches when convenient, meaning the feature quietly goes live for users. Two weeks late means nothing to marketing, who are still busy promoting last month's feature. Once marketing has a real, working product, they record videos, gather testimonials from early users, and stage a big hard launch when it makes sense. By then engineering has moved on to the next thing.
ex: When GDPR took effect, everyone's roadmap had a hard deadline on it
Fixing dates on everything means sacrificing quality or drowning in over-planning

items: Built on a product already live
Make a big splash when it helps

d.verdict: Keep them separate so engineering and marketing each set their own pace

l35|56.c: A roadmap isn't a plan. It's a prototype of your strategy, and the value is in making it.
l35|56.e: In lean product work, a prototype exists to test assumptions: you show someone a sketch, hear their reaction, change it, or throw it away and start over. She sees a roadmap doing the same job at the strategy level. You lay out the problems you think should be solved, in order, and ask your team, your customers, and anyone who will listen whether that's right. When someone suggests a different order or a problem you missed, you've learned something and the roadmap gets stronger. That's why sticky notes on a wall are enough to run Now/Next/Later.
ex: A product vision can follow the elevator-pitch template from the book Crossing the Chasm

items.d: Lay out the problems to solve, in order
The prototype gets stronger each time

l35|56.c: Product teams should answer for investment and experiments, like sales does, not for predicting delivery dates.
l35|56.e: Only product teams, it seems, are asked for precise delivery dates. A head of sales doesn't promise the board that a particular customer will sign by month end. They ask for a budget to hire people and make lots of calls. Each call is an experiment, nobody knows in advance which one will land, but experience says deals close by quarter end. Product works the same way: spend the investment on experiments with the interface, pricing, and positioning, and enough of them will move the metrics. Hold the team accountable for how many experiments ran and which numbers improved, not for fortune-telling dates.
ex: The sales analogy: ask for $250,000 and bring in about a million in sales by quarter end

terms.d: Some win, some fail, unknown in advance

result.d: Judge by experiments run and results

l35|56.c: Changing a big company's product culture is like chipping away limescale, and it starts with one small team.
l35|56.e: She compares culture to limescale: it builds up in layers, you can't remove it all at once, and you have to chip at it. Find a leader who understands the new approach and a small pocket of a team. Treat it like a startup lab inside the company, produce a working example, then spread it outward. Once a few such groups band together, go talk to senior leadership. The hard part is motivation. Big companies prefer steady quarterly growth and hate dipping before climbing. But in banking, health tech, and similar industries, startups are eating the most profitable business, and companies that don't change lose the ability to innovate.
ex: HSBC's savings and mortgage business is being picked off by startups like Starling
Good teams share traits: user research, psychological safety, regular retrospectives

items.d: A person or department that gets the new approach
A startup lab inside the company
Bring in a VP of strategy or technology

l36|58.c: A team incubating new business must be seen as core, or the organization will reject it like a foreign body.
l36|58.e: He spent years on growth and marketplace teams and has watched new-business teams get rejected wholesale because they looked too different from the rest of the company. He offers three ways to avoid that. First, make sure the whole company sees the work as directly tied to the core mission, not a group playing in a corner, or every fight over resources breeds resentment. Second, when it succeeds, count it as everyone's success. Third, never let people think innovation only happens on this team. Other teams innovate too; the incubation team just picks up what others don't have the bandwidth for.
ex: Reddit's avatar marketplace: creators sell digital avatars, with NFTs proving ownership

items.d: Not a side project in a corner
Everyone benefits, not just the team

l36|58.c: A team that looks like the world builds products the whole world can use, faster.
l36|58.e: He was Facebook's first Black PM and grew up in Trinidad, where ethnicity, religion, and income are all thoroughly mixed. He knew from childhood that "one phone number equals one device equals one person" isn't true, and that insight went into signup design and helped growth for years. On a team with people from many countries, he says a 15-minute argument can settle what would otherwise take two weeks of user interviews. Diversity lasts only when the company genuinely sees its business value. That keeps people around, and hiring gets easier as a result.
ex: Prepaid numbers change often, dual-SIM phones are common, and one phone is often shared
His team included an Israeli engineering manager and a Brazilian tech lead, among others

items.d: Not just bowing to public pressure
Build it into how the company runs
Outsiders see it's not a slogan

l36|58.c: In a controversy, a PM is the team's shock absorber, sorting real problems from the noise of shifting power.
l36|58.e: Changing how people behave always upsets whoever benefited from the old way, and conflict is what the press loves most, so controversy is unavoidable. The PM's job is to absorb shocks: when things go well, remind the team how far there is to go, and when it's getting hammered, remind them it's not that bad. The harder part is telling real criticism from noise. He had little sympathy for New York taxi medallion owners, but drivers going unpaid for the drive to a pickup and the empty trip back was a genuine problem. His approach was to drive for Lyft himself, get close to users, then focus on designs that balanced driver earnings with rider prices.
ex: A 15-minute drive to pick up Rick for a 2-minute ride that mattered a lot to the elderly man
Whether or not California's Prop 22 passed, have a plan that works for drivers and riders

items: No pay for the drive to pickup
No pay for the empty return trip

d.verdict: Get close to users and find the real problem behind the criticism

l36|58.c: Algorithms are good at optimizing toward a goal; people must set the constraints and make the strategic trade-offs.
l36|58.e: At Lyft he led a pricing algorithm that rolled out to about a hundred cities before he realized a single price change took months of wrangling. He had to admit the mistake and rebuild from scratch. The lesson: operator control is a first-order requirement. An algorithm can't see the season, gas prices, a new tax, or a competitor's move, and it doesn't understand long-term effects or product intent. Tell it to grab market share and it will push prices to the floor. Add a profit constraint and the competitor does the same, so a human still has to decide where to win. Software should amplify human intent, not become a black box.
ex: How to price during a Chicago blizzard, and how much to pay drivers, needs human judgment
The mix of ads and friends' posts in Facebook's feed is also a human strategic call

items.d: Hand it all to the algorithm
The game stalls at the constraint

l36|58.c: Growth hacks are a stopgap; big wins come from grinding on a few core actions for years.
l36|58.e: Finding a small change with a big payoff has its place, but stitching tricks together underestimates users, and a product without real value eventually gets found out. What actually worked at Facebook was polishing a few simple things over and over: make the product easy to find, easy to get into, extremely easy to find your friends in, then build a habit of coming back. Some of those were "cannonballs" that needed heavy investment. About 60% of experiments succeeded, but small experiments carry hidden costs. He favors more cannonballs and fewer small tweaks, and the earlier the product, the more you should just go do the big thing.
ex: Cannonball examples: phone-number signup, SMS delivery worldwide, friend suggestions
"10 friends in 14 days" worked because it was memorable and rallied the company, not because the numbers were magic

marks.d: You know the big things, so just do them

l36|58.c: To improve conversion, focus on the marginal user and watch them use the product. Don't trust funnel data alone.
l36|58.e: The marginal user is the person who almost completes the key action but doesn't, such as users in a country with heavy traffic and terrible conversion. He starts with the most extreme case: someone on a feature phone, on a slow EDGE connection, far from any data center, and lists every flaw in the experience. Then he assumes a good device and network and asks which problems remain and can be fixed, and prioritizes those. Data only hints at where the problem is. The answers come from watching and interviewing people, because some problems have nothing to do with the funnel and never show up on a chart.
ex: Indian users signed up with legal full names nobody called them, so friend requests went unaccepted
Common issues: wrong language, misparsed phone-number formats, high latency

items.d: Feature phone, EDGE, far from servers
Assume a good device and network

l36|58.c: The higher you go, the more it's about organizational design and empathy, not personal brilliance.
l36|58.e: He used to assume the smartest, most technical individual contributor got promoted. Then he realized that to have more impact you can't do everything yourself, and anything meaningful takes many people. So he thought back to what he needed when he was most effective and gave his team the same: clear goals, the safety of knowing someone has your back, and smooth processes and collaboration. Empathy applies to colleagues as much as to users. The hard part, he says, isn't putting on someone else's shoes but taking off your own first, understanding their motives and worries, and then finding a shared goal.
ex: His favorite interview question: teach me something you think I don't know

terms.d: Take off your own shoes first

result.d: Find the goal you share

l37|59.c: Pixar taught him that what matters is what the audience sees; the technology is just a means.
l37|59.e: He spent almost seven years at Pixar building effects and tools. At first he insisted on simulating bubbles and sand with real physics. He was quickly corrected: what matters is the image on screen and the emotion and story it carries. The math behind it is only a tool, and you can tweak the numbers so it looks right. He carried that into product work. A beautifully written strategy doc doesn't matter in itself; it is just one input to the final experience. The same goes for courses: a tidy framework matters less than whether it actually helps someone solve a problem.
ex: He worked on Finding Nemo, Cars, WALL-E, and Up

items.d: What the image has to serve
If it looks right, it is right
Backstage tools; bend them for the effect

l37|59.c: There is no shortcut for PMs; you grow through a loop of doing, distilling, communicating, and taking on bigger problems.
l37|59.e: He thinks product management lacks the kind of transferable training engineering has. Much of the skill is specific knowledge you only get by doing the work; courses and reading are a layer on top of practice. He describes growth as a loop. Execute on real projects. Distill what happened into lessons that transfer. Tell people what you did and what you learned. That earns you harder problems, moving from known problems with known solutions toward unknown problems with unknown solutions, and then you execute again. The more senior you get, the more the distilling and communicating steps matter.
ex: Instacart tested very short and very long onboarding; for hard-to-activate products, some friction helps

items.d: Turn experience into lessons that transfer
Let others know what you learned
Move from known problems to unknown ones

l37|59.c: Career jumps come from sponsors, not mentors, and the key is making your impact visible.
l37|59.e: Each of his big career jumps came from someone trusting him with a bigger problem. That is sponsorship, which is different from the day-to-day advice a mentor gives. His formula: impact equals what you actually get done, multiplied by how well you show and explain it. And impact isn't only on users; it includes the organization, like teaching the company how its growth model works. He suggests working on the four or five most important things at the company, because that is where the CEO and head of product are looking. Then stay curious, so you become the person people come to when they have questions.
ex: Nabeel Hyatt, CEO of Conduit Labs, moved him from engineering into product
At Slack, sponsors like Merci Grace kept handing him a bigger scope
Curiosity in practice: two levels up for priorities, two down for tech, sideways to neighbors

terms.d: Real impact on users and the company
Making the work seen and understood

result.d: Earns sponsors and bigger opportunities

l37|59.c: Going from individual contributor to manager means shifting from doer to editor, or you fall into a death spiral.
l37|59.e: Individual contributors get promoted by going deep into the details and doing things themselves. Once they lead a team, the instinct is to keep the most important, most interesting projects and hand the dull ones to reports. The result: you burn out, every decision bottlenecks on you, and the team never gets to grow. He calls this the manager's death spiral. The way out is to start trusting people. Decide for each person, based on their experience, whether to delegate, coach, or direct. And be strategically lazy: ask what the least amount of involvement is that still gets the best outcome.
ex: He calls this gap the product leader chasm

d.verdict: Once you lead a team, your job is making other people's work better

l37|59.c: A product leader has to balance four kinds of product work, not just the kind they are good at.
l37|59.e: He and Casey Winters split product work into four types. Feature work solves more problems for existing users. Growth work connects more users to the value that already exists. Product-market fit expansion takes the same product to new audiences, or sells new products to the same audience. Scaling work covers technical capacity plus issues like trust and safety that only appear once you have lots of users. Individual contributors usually master one type. As a leader you have to allocate resources across all four, rather than treating everything as an experiment the way some growth-trained leaders do.
ex: Scaling example: the new problems Airbnb hit going from 10 hosts to 10,000
PMF expansion examples: going international, new verticals, product bundling

items.d: Solve more problems for existing users
Connect more people to existing value

l37|59.c: Leaders must own the outcome and ask for the resources it takes, rather than accept what they have.
l37|59.e: When you run a small team, the job is to deliver the most value with the people you have. As a leader, the job flips: first define the outcome, then say how many people you need, which departments have to help, and what the trade-offs are. For a senior individual contributor that is a bonus; for a leader it is the baseline. He admits he got this wrong many times. He was busy building roadmaps for the existing team and keeping everyone busy, and forgot to ask whether this was the right team for the problem. He ended up saying "we only have four engineers."
ex: At Instacart his team was tiny, but he never pushed to grow it faster
At Slack, working earlier with marketing, sales, data, and finance would have meant more growth

items.d: What you can deliver with less

l37|59.c: Senior operators can work across several companies, but only with a narrow, world-class specialty.
