l37|59.e: More senior operators are becoming fractional leaders, long-term advisors, writers, or workshop teachers. It is flexible, the upside can be large, and demand is strong; most of Reforge's executives in residence do this. The prerequisite is a niche where you are among the best in the world, distilled well enough that you can help someone in a very short time. To prepare, combine depth with breadth, for example by working the same problem across industries. Then join well-known, rising companies, where results are easier to get and easier to sell. The risks: you lose value the longer you are away from the front line, and you have to keep selling yourself.
ex: His specialty is activation for bottom-up SaaS; he can help in an hour
He dislikes selling and prefers one main job as an anchor

marks.d: Still one day a week doing the work

l38|60.c: Decide on a new category by budget, customer language, and competition, not by wanting to avoid rivals.
l38|60.e: A category is how review sites and directories group products by function, and it usually maps to a set of pain points customers have budget for. Miro wanted a new category because "online whiteboard" was too small and too rarely searched to support a company everyone would use. She looks at three signals: whether customers already have budget for this, how they describe the pain, and whether competitors exist. Many founders want a new category to escape competition. She disagrees: without competitors you don't have a category yet. When others follow and claim the same label, that is the validation.
ex: New categories often follow a technology shift: Deel and Oyster after the pandemic
Earlier examples: marketing automation, and Gainsight's customer success platform

items.d: Do customers already have money for this?

l38|60.c: What customers call you and which budget pays decides it; if you can't rename the category, raise its value.
l38|60.e: Back then, applicant tracking systems (ATS, the software recruiters use) had a bad reputation as transactional tools with no strategic value. Greenhouse tried to position itself as a "recruiting optimization platform," with content and press to match. It didn't matter. Customers still budgeted for and talked about an ATS, even when they agreed the product was different. So the team dropped the new category and spent its resources raising the value of the whole ATS category instead. Together with CultureAmp, that helped push companies toward more professional recruiting and employee experience practices.
ex: A mature company with no clear difference from its peers will usually fail at creating a category

items.d: ATS seen as a transactional tool
Spend on making ATS more valuable

l38|60.c: You can grow a new category bottom-up: sell inside the old one while telling a new story.
l38|60.e: She says you don't have to choose between the old category and a new one. Miro kept optimizing for existing labels like whiteboard, while gathering the many names users used (whiteboard, mind map, diagramming) under one term: visual collaboration. It then packaged use cases for HR, marketing, design, and other teams, and used content marketing until other companies adopted the label too. Her new company Pando is doing the same: on directories it sits under performance management, where the budget is, while it slowly educates the market on a new idea, employee growth.
ex: Marketing automation was built top-down by educating the market, the opposite of Miro's path
CultureAmp's category gradually shifted from people analytics to employee experience

marks.d: Back to ATS, raise its value
Sell as performance management, seed a new idea
Start as whiteboard, grow into visual collaboration

l38|60.c: Building a category means listening to customers, testing with press, winning over analysts, and publishing constantly.
l38|60.e: The best positioning comes from many customer conversations: who they are, how they describe the product, which differences they care about. Then use PR to put the category and positioning out loudly and see whether it resonates. In B2B, analysts like Gartner and Forrester and directories like G2 effectively decide which categories customers see, so you have to go and explain your functional differences to them directly. Finally, a steady stream of content and thought leadership explains why the category exists and teaches buyers to set aside budget for it.
ex: G2 had no visual collaboration category at first; Miro had to explain the difference in person
Try early, and if it doesn't land, drop it quickly

items.d: Learn how they describe the pain
Get G2 and Gartner to recognize it
Teach buyers to budget for it

l38|60.c: Rename early once you have product-market fit, and run the rename like a product project.
l38|60.e: RealtimeBoard was too literal a name for the product's potential; she even made the ability to rename a condition of joining. The right time is after product-market fit but before heavy brand investment. The company had about 100 people and about a million users then. To keep existing users comfortable, the new logo kept the yellow of a sticky note, and early users were asked for feedback on the design. A rename touches legal, contracts, the website, the product, and the domain. She ran it like product development: a sprint team, clear owners, and full transparency across the company, rather than marketing finishing it behind closed doors and then announcing.
ex: The first proposal was a pink M; the final yellow nods to sticky notes
Materials already carried the new URL; miro.com was secured about 48 hours before launch

items.d: miro.com arrives at the last minute
Public debut with a full 3D booth

l38|60.c: A lasting brand is built on company values and a system, not on training each touchpoint separately.
l38|60.e: She says product and brand both matter: a great brand can't save a bad product, and a good product with a thoughtful brand is what keeps people. The more the brand is one with the company and its people, the more authentic it feels, the way Google brings Googlers to mind. Once values are built into the brand, employees act consistently at every touchpoint without being trained one by one. A brand that scales is a system: logo, colors, type, illustration, and voice that combine and extend. The values themselves should be simple and memorable; Miro's original list was too long.
ex: Each letter in Miro has a shape tied to a value, like a wave for flexibility
Setting values: brainstorm, group, vote, then one person writes the draft

l38|60.c: Opinionated software bakes best practices into rules, and fits when a practice is emerging or badly needs fixing.
l38|60.e: Opinionated software builds best practices, even hard rules, into the product so users can't work around them, the opposite of a fully customizable system. There are two ways to do it. Find a practice that is taking off but lacks tooling, as Atlassian did with agile development. Or tell customers there is a better way and help them do it, as Greenhouse did with structured hiring. Pando is the second kind. She argues today's performance reviews are full of bias, and companies patch the gaps with yearly pay adjustments instead of fixing the cause. So the system requires public levels and skill expectations, making both employees and managers accountable.
ex: Greenhouse's structured hiring: a fixed process and interview kits to reduce bias
Pando aims to replace performance reviews with an employee growth platform

items: Point out flaws in today's approach
Lock the new process into software

d.verdict: Both paths need clear principles and values as an anchor

l39|61.c: Ad-funded products must chase time and attention; direct subscriptions make a better experience possible.
l39|61.e: He and co-founder Alex Cornell spent years at Facebook building products that help people share with friends and family. They had a better experience in mind but kept hitting the same wall: an ad model needs huge amounts of time and attention that can be sold as eyeballs. So they started Cocoon to try a paid model for photo sharing among close friends. Substack, they realized, was the same principle working at scale: rebuilding the internet around direct subscriptions between readers and writers. The whole team joined Substack.
ex: Cocoon was a photo-sharing app for a small circle of family and friends
He joined Facebook in 2011 and worked on growth, platform, ads, and sharing
He recommends The Timeless Way of Building: when builders don't live in the house, it gets worse

l39|61.c: Organize teams around customers, not product surfaces, and the structure stays stable for years.
l39|61.e: When he joined, Substack had no product managers, just a few designers and about 15 engineers. A year later it had four PMs and three full-stack product teams. The teams are split by customer: a writers team, a readers team, and a growth team, plus a systems team without a PM that keeps everything scaling. At Facebook he was reorganized roughly every three to six months. Serving writers, serving readers, and growing are problems that never finish, which makes them a more durable way to divide work than surfaces like the app, the dashboard, or podcasts.
ex: Each team has a PM, an engineering manager, data or design support, and engineers

root.d: Split by customer and long-term mission

l39|61.c: Next to a product-minded founder, a PM's first job is bridging the gap between the CEO and the teams.
l39|61.e: When he arrived, the company had just outgrown the phase where one weekly meeting with CEO Chris could set two weeks of work, and it was hiring fast. The CEO no longer knew what each team was doing, and the teams didn't understand his vision. For his first few months he did one thing: get both sides to understand each other and help the teams learn how the founder thinks. Now the two of them spend an hour at the start and end of every week syncing. In a period of fast change, any process goes stale as soon as it is settled, so he just aims to be better each week. That means being comfortable with often not knowing what you're doing.
ex: At an all-hands they rewatched the 2017 YC pitch: podcasts and network effects imagined then are landing now

terms.d: Knows what each team is doing

result.d: One hour at each end of the week

l39|61.c: At a big company, doing A can kill B; at a startup, the trade-offs are mostly time and sequence.
l39|61.e: Facebook had to solve countless problems for countless people on one small screen. The PM's core job was managing trade-offs: shipping A might mean B never ships, or that another metric drops. Put a video tab in the bottom bar and the marketplace tab might lose its spot. At Substack the main variable is time: do this now and that waits. Sequence matters a lot too. Substack is moving from a tool for individual writers to a network, so what you build first can unlock what comes next.
ex: Less of his Facebook experience transferred directly than he expected
General frameworks still hold, like doing high-impact, low-cost work first

items: Doing A may rule out B forever

d.verdict: The frameworks carry over, but the daily job is completely different

l39|61.c: Recommendations kept writers in control instead of using an algorithm, and that created a viral loop built on goodwill.
l39|61.e: The team noticed readers often discovered new publications through a writer's lens, such as guest posts or a commenter's profile. The easy answer was something like Facebook's "people you may know," recommending based on reading habits. But stuffing unrelated content onto a writer's page broke the principle that writers and readers stay in control. So they chose the harder path: ask writers to recommend publications themselves, and show those in the subscribe flow. The CEO worried there were too many steps for it to work. Instead, recommended writers got an email saying who had sent them readers, and they recommended others in turn. Growth far exceeded expectations.
ex: Recommendations have driven millions of new subscriptions for tens of thousands of writers
Over a third of new subscriptions and about a tenth of paid ones come from the Substack network
Next: treat recommendations as a social graph, not just a step in the subscribe flow

items.d: An email says who sent the readers

l39|61.c: Changes that touch the core of the product are built with writers: pilot small first, then roll out.
l39|61.e: This extends the principle of keeping writers in control. Any fundamental change is built alongside writers by default, rather than shipped and announced with a pop-up in the dashboard. For Recommendations, the team first found about ten writers likely to care, built a prototype, listened, and ran a small pilot, instead of going to everyone as soon as the feedback was positive. They now run an invite-only Product Lab, where about a hundred early-adopter writers try features first. What finally ships is often very different from the original idea.
ex: Recommendations was driven by PM Dayne Rathbone

items.d: About 100 writers try it before rollout

l39|61.c: A subscription is a costly signal, so creators should bring their most valuable audience home.
l39|61.e: He thinks the golden age for writers is just beginning. You don't need a million viewers or to play the attention game. If a small number of people value your work enough to pay, you can make a living, even a very good one. An audience locked inside someone else's platform is hard to reach or monetize reliably. Substack may not be where your audience is biggest, but it should be home to your most valuable readers: you get their email addresses and can export them any time. His advice is to just start. And don't worry too much about posting too often, turning on paid, or taking a break; readers are more forgiving than you think.
ex: Early examples: underrated established writers like Matt Taibbi and Bill Bishop
He recommends Kevin Kelly's essay You Are Not Late

items.d: Large, but locked in by the platform
You own the address and can export it
A few true fans can be a living

l40|62.c: For a first product leader, don't chase big-company stars; hire someone still close to the work.
l40|62.e: She says founders are easily drawn to big names. But top product executives at large companies are often far from the actual work. For years their job has been team building, performance management, and operations, with a bench of people executing for them. An early-stage company has limited resources and would have to build that bench all over again. A better fit is someone who can do the job of a senior PM themselves while building the team, ideally with something to prove. The question is who is right for this role right now, not who is the strongest person on the market.
ex: Early in her career she chased "big whale" executives to prove herself
A famous big-company CPO may be wrong for a Series A or B startup

items: Needs a team hired under them
Can build the team over time

d.verdict: Hire for this stage, not the strongest name on the market

l40|62.c: If you can't say what problem this hire solves, the search is doomed from day one.
l40|62.e: Many companies start searching only because the board said it was time for a head of product, without knowing what they need. She sees roughly three kinds of product leader: platform or infrastructure types, core or consumer product types (often owning design and UX too), and specialists in areas like growth or monetization. Asking one person to cover all of it means hunting a unicorn. Her advice is to work backwards: what is this person's mandate, what does great look like, and what should they be doing at 90 days, one year, and two years? Hire for the most urgent piece first; the overall leader can come later.
ex: Building an ad walled garden, doing product marketing, and fixing core UX are three different jobs
The 90-day plan is just the tip of the iceberg

l40|62.c: Early on, "head of product" is enough; save C-level titles for when the company is more mature.
l40|62.e: She sees startups getting more careful with C-level and VP titles. Up to around Series C, "head of" usually marks the most senior person in a function, and VP, director, and CPO titles mostly appear after Series D or E. The reason for restraint: the person you need today may not be the one who takes the company public in two and a half years, and the worst outcome is having to demote someone later. So a candidate who will only accept a CPO title may miss good opportunities. At the early stage, these titles mean roughly the same thing anyway.
ex: Her firm often advises early-stage companies not to hire C-level executives yet

items.d: Mostly "head of"; top person in the function

l40|62.c: Whether or not you're hiring, keep meeting top people so the relationship exists before you need it.
l40|62.e: She thinks both hiring managers and candidates should always know what great looks like. Founders can reach out with no agenda beyond meeting excellent people, and most are happy to share. Then invite them to advise or join product discussions. When you really need to hire, the relationship and trust already exist, so it doesn't feel transactional. Hours spent aren't the point; what matters is whether your approach is different. Cold outreach on LinkedIn is inefficient, and many of the best people aren't there at all. Better to ask people you trust for the best person they have ever worked with.
ex: She once spent seven months slowly convincing a VP of engineering to join
She starts a search by asking about five product leaders she trusts most for introductions

l40|62.c: A famous employer doesn't make someone great; dig one level deeper to find the real top 1%.
l40|62.e: Mapping talent at companies known for a particular strength is a good start. But every company has passengers who were simply in the right place at the right time. In reference checks, clear negatives surface quickly. The hard cases are lukewarm middle candidates, where you need people who worked closely with them. References a candidate supplies are almost always positive, so informal backchannel checks get closer to the truth. Ask why you shouldn't hire this person, whether the reference would report to them, and whether they would put their name behind them. Any hesitation is worth noting.
ex: Only twice has a candidate-supplied reference given her negative feedback
Chosen references are a curated feed; backchannels are the photos other people tag you in

items.d: Probe weaknesses; would they work together again?

l40|62.c: Product people should build breadth, and leave each job with results others can name.
l40|62.e: To become a product leader, get exposure to different kinds of products: platform, user-facing, internal tools, and ideally both startups and mature companies. Avoid logo collecting; leaving every time it gets hard is easy to spot. But don't be loyal to a fault either, staying while the company is clearly in decline. The minimum bar is a result you can point to, one that cross-functional colleagues can describe too, because the industry is small and backchannels are everywhere. Be honest on your resume; hiding a short stint is a bigger red flag than the stint itself. In interviews, don't blame failures on engineering, and rehearse telling your story.
ex: Writing two failed companies up as "two years of advising" hurts more than it helps
"You want to be a CPO? CPO of what kind of company?"

marks.d: Be a little selfish about your career

l40|62.c: A recruiter's biggest mistake is being transactional; build the relationship and trust before pitching a role.
l40|62.e: She says recruiters have a bad reputation for a reason: they forget the person across the table has a family and ambitions. Really listen, and remember what people tell you. If someone says they won't join a crypto company, or has equity vesting in a certain month, don't push a job before then. Keep notes, and reach out at the right moment for coffee or to discuss a talk they gave. Once trust is lost, it rarely comes back. When founders choose a recruiter, describe the role and ask them to repeat it back to test their listening, then ask for a few candidate names on the spot to see how they think. Series A to B is a good time to bring in an outside firm.
ex: She puts candidates' vesting dates on her calendar and reaches out after them
Earlier-stage companies can lean on their investors' talent teams first

items.t: Reach out at the right time

items.d: Lost trust is hard to win back
They listen when you bring an opportunity

l41|63.c: Security can work bottom-up: making developers responsible for it is the only sustainable path.
l41|63.e: Traditional application security is run by a central security team and leans toward audit and control. Tools run late in development, feedback takes forever, and problems get thrown over the wall to developers, so adoption and retention are poor. Snyk's founders bet that security only sticks when developers treat it as part of their job, like performance and quality, and that only happens if the tool creates very little friction. So the product began as a command-line tool that runs locally or inside CI/CD, the automated build pipeline, and something was free from day one. The idea was to bring security into the developer's workflow instead of pulling them out of it.
ex: Founded in 2015, valued at $8.6 billion after its Series F
Over 2,000 paying customers and about 1,300 employees

items: Slow feedback that drags on developers
Early feedback locally or in CI

d.verdict: Developers owning security is what lasts

l41|63.c: Start with one audience and one use case, go deep, and expand only after product-market fit.
l41|63.e: Snyk began by serving a single group: developers building apps on open-source Node.js components who wanted to know whether those dependencies were safe. Open-source code makes up most of a modern app and had become an entry point for attackers. The Node community was growing, yet small enough for a startup to influence. The founders kept dropping one hook at conferences, meetups, and online: "Do you have known vulnerabilities in your app?" He stresses depth first. JavaScript developers don't care whether you support other languages, but they care a lot whether key features for their ecosystem are missing. Resist the urge to expand.
ex: At least 75% of a typical app is open-source components
NPM, the JavaScript package registry, had about 200,000 packages and 2.5 billion monthly downloads
About 5,000 free users before the first attempt at monetization

items.d: A growing community a startup could reach

l41|63.c: Founders should design acquisition loops into the product early on.
l41|63.e: Once you have product-market fit, the question is where new users come from. Without a clear hypothesis you're betting on "build it and they will come." Snyk's core loop: a user connects their GitHub repository, Snyk scans it and automatically opens a fix pull request carrying Snyk's branding and an explanation of the vulnerability. Other developers on that repo see it, click through, sign up, and connect their own repos. It's both an acquisition loop and a retention loop, and it was later extended to Bitbucket and GitLab. On top of that came programmatic SEO pages on open-source package health, free public security courses, and invite and referral loops.
ex: Snyk Advisor auto-generates hundreds of thousands of package pages
Security courses are fully public with no paywall

l41|63.c: Developers loving you doesn't mean companies will pay; after self-serve stalled, Snyk added governance and sales.
l41|63.e: The product was valuable and developer growth and retention were strong, but the first round of self-serve monetization only sold monthly plans to individual developers. Big companies didn't follow, and several investors backed away. The team realized that the people responsible for the whole application estate are security teams, and they need standard governance features like reporting and user management, plus coverage of more languages and tech stacks. Depth-first had hit its limit. Once those gaps were filled and the first salespeople and sales engineers were hired, growth truly took off. He adds that today Snyk has plenty of very large customers who bought entirely self-serve.
ex: Early paying users were mostly individual developers at about $100 a month
Ed Sim of boldstart was one of the earliest committed backers

l41|63.c: Growth teams must be truly cross-functional, with growth marketing embedded in every squad.
l41|63.e: When he joined, engineering and growth marketing had mismatched incentives, so good ideas piled up without getting executed. The new developer growth group was split by outcome into acquisition, activation, and monetization teams, plus a team owning data and the experimentation platform. Each team had engineering, product, design, growth marketing, and decision science support, with shared goals and KPIs. Having growth marketers inside the team brought more ideas and more ways to act on them. One SEO page that needed no engineering performed well, so the team built a tool to scan code without signing up. Signup rate dipped slightly, but total new users and activation both rose.
ex: They started with acquisition and activation only, deliberately delaying self-serve monetization
The group's mission: connect developers to the platform's value through frictionless self-serve adoption

root.d: Split by outcome, not by feature

l41|63.c: Growth strategy uses a loop model to find the biggest constraint, which requires early, trustworthy data.
l41|63.e: High-performing growth teams never lack ideas, he says. Strategy decides where to put the effort. First, build a qualitative model of the big and small growth loops and how they connect, so everyone shares a language. Then use quantitative data to find the current biggest constraint, set priorities for a quarter or two, and keep revising as learning, product, and market shift. Invest in data early. Snyk once collected everything yet lacked trustworthy behavioral data, so it built a tracking plan and validated events against a schema in CI. People matter too: growth suits those who enjoy rapid trial and error and aren't attached to their old code.
ex: Start with simple experiment methods; don't begin with multivariate testing
A loop extension example: copying the GitHub fix loop to Bitbucket

items.d: How big and small loops connect

l41|63.c: Experiments directly produce learning, so fixed rituals should capture it and spread it.
l41|63.e: Teams are ultimately accountable for impact, he admits, but impact is paved by step-by-step learning, and staring only at results makes you lose your way. Each growth team writes its findings from data exploration, experiments, and user research into a weekly "impact and learnings" document. The PM-led weekly meeting spends most of its time on what those learnings mean and where they can be reused, a little on metrics, and none on reporting what was done. A monthly group meeting shares across teams and is recorded for the whole company, so sales and others can use it. A healthy sign: everyone proposes data-based hypotheses and anyone can run an experiment end to end.
ex: Borrowed from the HubSpot meeting rituals Brian Balfour has written about
Before experimenting on a surface another team owns, hold an experiment plan review

terms.d: Share across teams and record it

result.d: Reused across the organization

l41|63.c: Put growth-driving features in the free tier, and define activation as a team forming a fixing habit.
l41|63.e: He agrees the free tier should hold features that power the growth model, while weighing the cost to serve. Each plan should state who it's for and why they'd upgrade. For Snyk that means protecting business-critical code and meeting compliance and governance needs. Trial models deserve regular challenge, since companies of different sizes and regulatory burdens evaluate on different timelines. Activation isn't logging in or finding a vulnerability. It's a team fixing a vulnerability within 30 days of being created, because that strongly predicts still fixing at three months. Security is a team sport, so it's defined per team, not per person. They also track product-led revenue, whose customers contribute more to net retention.
ex: Heroku dropped its free tier because of cost
Activation = a team fixes a vulnerability within 30 days of creation

l42|64.c: Fear gives bad advice. Test it with a low-stakes bet, then do the opposite.
l42|64.e: Most founders, he finds, are run by fear. A frightened brain makes exaggerated predictions that block the hard but necessary actions. His method is to pick something low-risk, have the person predict the outcome, predict the opposite himself, and bet on it. He says he has made that bet hundreds of times and never lost. After that, all it takes is a reminder: "I sense you're in fear." This is fear for the ego, not physical danger, and it helps to check with someone who isn't afraid right now. Anger, meanwhile, is a cover for pain and tends to hurt the people closest to you. A non-judgmental "I sense you're angry" is what snaps people out of it.
ex: A CEO was afraid to tell the board about a problem; coming clean earned their trust instead
His wife tried three phrasings, and "I sense you're angry" worked best

l42|64.c: The smaller the team the better; every added person multiplies coordination cost and morale problems.
l42|64.e: Once a company finds product-market fit and raises money, he says, it hires nonstop. But every new person needs to be kept informed, given context, and listened to, or they feel ignored and morale drops. The friction grows geometrically with headcount. His management system, he admits, only keeps a company from falling apart; the ideal is still a tiny team. He ran his own experiment: he let go of a strong performer whose work a deputy could absorb, and two or three months later things ran better. His test: if you've never regretted firing someone, you don't yet know where the line is.
ex: WhatsApp, Instagram, Linear, and Notion are all known for small teams
In March 2020 a hospitality company laid off 40% of its staff

items.d: The fix looks like more hiring

l42|64.c: Separate the decision from the execution, and actively act as the fired person's agent.
l42|64.e: Managers are bad at firing because they feel they're hurting someone. He borrows a framework from Clipboard Health CEO Wei Deng: when deciding, think only about the key stakeholder, usually the customer. When executing, look one by one at who gets hurt and what they actually want. The person being let go wants a job where they're genuinely needed, so spend an hour or two actively connecting them to opportunities instead of saying "call me if you need a reference." If you dread the conversation, doing it once cures that. If the team grieves, let them express it. Open with "this is going to be a hard conversation" so the shock doesn't trigger an emotional spiral.
ex: Be like CAA agent Michael Ovitz and actively find your client a job
His test: he's still friends with everyone he has ever fired

root.d: Decide for the customer, then care for the affected

items.d: Customers only want the best people
Actively find them a role that needs them
Do it once and the fear is gone

l42|64.c: A layoff succeeds or fails on whether managers tell people one-on-one, and whether you cut once.
l42|64.e: He has been through about 40 layoffs alongside CEOs. The biggest dividing line is whether each employee hears it from their direct manager, one-on-one. Email or group announcements make people feel dehumanized. Give managers a dollar amount to save, not a headcount, or they'll cut the cheapest, often hardest-working junior staff first. Let frontline managers choose their own lists. Hold every conversation that morning, then an all-hands that afternoon for those who remain to answer "am I next?" Cut deep enough to cut once; repeated rounds traumatize the organization. Finally, give each remaining person an hour one-on-one just to listen. Recovery shrinks from about 60 days to two weeks.
ex: Roughly 80% of a tech company's costs are people
One company cut 50% at once and came out stronger

items.d: Warn, announce, listen, be their agent
Address fear; say it's one cut

l42|64.c: There are three levels of making people feel heard; the deepest is saying what they left unsaid.
l42|64.e: The shallowest level: have everyone spend five minutes writing their proposals into a shared document at the same time, then read each one and thank people by name. The second level: after someone speaks, repeat it back in your own words until they say "yes, that's exactly it." The deepest level: behind someone's polite phrasing, guess at their real, stronger view and say it out loud. People often reply, "It's not that bad, but you're on the right track." Being heard also needs a response: if you accept the point, say what you'll do; if not, explain your side. He says all of this has public step-by-step scripts, and doing it once is enough to feel the payoff.
ex: One CEO read his book, implemented all of it, and then declined his coaching

l42|64.c: Big companies should innovate through tiny independent teams that bypass product and engineering and report to the CEO.
l42|64.e: A product at scale has millions of users and must stay stable and secure, so every code change gets strict review. A prototype-stage feature can't move inside that system. His answer is to copy a YC startup: put someone with a founder's mindset in charge, and a YC founder whose company failed is a good fit. Keep the team tiny, have it report directly to the CEO rather than to the heads of engineering, product, or design, and give it its own brand or even a separate legal entity. The key motivator isn't equity, he argues, but control over decisions and creation. Fear can drive people too, but it corrodes them. Only love of the work lasts.
ex: Wei Deng set up five separate companies for new products in two months
She ran an engineering-led team and a customer-relationship team in parallel on the same product

d.verdict: Uncouple new products from the core process

l42|64.c: Do an energy audit: cut what drains you, and you'll drift toward your zone of genius.
l42|64.e: He borrows Diana Chapman's four zones: incompetence, competence, excellence, and genius. The dangerous one is excellence: it pays well and others want you doing it, but it drains you. Look back over two weeks of your calendar and mark each hour as energy up or energy down. For each draining item, ask in order: can it be cancelled, can someone else do it, and if only you can do it, how can it be redesigned to the extreme? For instance, have executives write their updates before the meeting, and a three-hour meeting shrinks to 45 minutes. Repeat until 80% of your calendar is green. He also suggests blocking daily time for your top goal, with an accountability partner if needed.
ex: Brex's two founders used this to split internal and external meetings between them

items.d: Others do it better; hand it off
Anyone can do it; hand it off
Good at it but drained; the danger zone
Love it, unique to you, time flies

l43|66.c: Chaos and crisis are where PMs shine: sort out the facts, tear up the roadmap, reassign work around the mission.
l43|66.e: She believes PMs add the most when they turn a flood of messy input into structure: what's true, where we're confident, what the most important question is, and then get the team pointed at one goal. When she took over news products at Facebook in 2017, the platform only split content into friends-and-family versus public. Her team first had to carve out trustworthy factual information and downrank questionable content. When COVID hit in 2020, she had the team throw out the roadmap, pulled engineers to build a public case database and zip-code lookups for infections and vaccines, and made the critical pandemic coverage free.
ex: At the March 2020 peak, she says about half of America came to the Times
After months of pressure, focusing on a few priorities and less switching helped prevent burnout

items.d: Share the new context with everyone

l43|66.c: Subscriptions need a new bundle: journalism is the sun, and its satellite products together become essential.
l43|66.e: A printed newspaper was a bounded bundle. Once news moved to the web and phones, stories got unbundled and scattered across platforms. Shifting to subscriptions meant building a direct relationship with readers, so the Times put its own destinations first and tried to recreate the breadth of the Sunday paper at digital scale. She uses a solar-system metaphor: journalism is the reason to exist, the source of trust, and the biggest front door, and it spawns satellite products that share its expertise and trustworthiness. The next step is linking them into one family, so anyone entering through one product discovers the rest.
ex: They estimate about 135 million people worldwide would pay for products like these
The goal is 15 million subscriptions by 2027, up from just over 9 million then
In 2011 a consultant predicted subscriptions would top out at about one million

root.d: Source of trust and the biggest front door

l43|66.c: Teams are organized by function times mission, and consumer teams have editors embedded directly.
l43|66.e: She runs two functions, product and design. The functional line owns craft standards, career growth, and promotions, but the real work happens in cross-functional mission teams. There are three kinds. Consumer missions build news, cooking, games, and similar products, with product-minded editors embedded. Monetization missions build subscription accounts that work across the whole bundle, plus advertising based on the Times's own privacy-safe first-party data. Platform missions provide the commerce engine, machine learning and experimentation platforms, and infrastructure. The business side and the newsroom have separate leadership. Product helps stories reach the biggest audience but has no say in what gets covered.
ex: The newsroom has over 2,000 people, and editors decide coverage independently

items.d: News, cooking, games, with editors embedded

l43|66.c: New story formats start as one-off newsroom experiments, and the product team turns the ones that work into platforms.
l43|66.e: The most creative story formats usually begin as one-off experiments by the graphics, visual, and interactive teams inside the newsroom. A reporter brings an idea, and engineers, designers, and data people push that single story as far as it can go. News moves too fast for a roadmap. A separate storytelling product team watches for the formats that work and tests with editors whether they can scale across many stories. That team has to switch between two modes: making quick calls with editors in the moment, and building end-to-end systems that serve both the people producing content and the readers experiencing it.
ex: One story showed readers their own "productivity score" in real time as they read
Live, short updates broke what she calls the tyranny of the article

items.d: Reporter, visuals, engineering on one story
Check with editors whether it scales
Most premium stories built on the platform

l43|66.c: After an acquisition, protect the product's core magic first and only add the plumbing users actually care about.
l43|66.e: The case for buying Wordle: games are a break from the news, Wordle shares DNA with the Times's own word puzzles like Spelling Bee, and it gives people one more daily reason to connect with the Times. The deal closed in a few weeks. The original had no back end; stats and streaks lived in the local browser and vanished when you changed phones. The team kept the board and core gameplay untouched, rebuilt it on the Times's own stack, added free accounts to save stats, and put it in the news and games apps. Midway through the migration, one day's answer happened to collide with a news event and couldn't be changed uniformly, so the team chose to explain publicly what had happened.
ex: The daily answers had been preset by the original creator months earlier
She stresses the Times did not deliberately make Wordle harder

items.d: Shares DNA with the Times's puzzles
Accounts for stats, more entry points

l43|66.c: A news organization's algorithm should learn from journalists' editorial judgment, not just engagement.
l43|66.e: At Facebook, she notes, she controlled only the software and distribution, not content quality, so news ranking could only be trained on engagement. The Times owns content, distribution, and product all at once. Editors curate the home page first, then the algorithm is trained on an "editorial importance" score that journalists assign, and only on top of that does it optimize for reach, engagement, and conversion. That extends editorial judgment to a huge audience. So PMs here need to be more editorially minded, and editors more product minded. She also believes trust in institutions is falling while trust in individual experts is rising, so the Times helps journalists build their own newsletters and podcasts.
ex: She doesn't see the Times as anti-algorithm; the algorithm should reflect editorial judgment

result.d: Recommendations weigh quality and results

l43|66.c: In a news organization, business goals serve the mission, not the other way around.
l43|66.e: She compares her two experiences. At Facebook, impact mostly meant scale, engagement, and revenue. At the Times, subscription growth is just as hard a target, but the business exists to support an informed democracy at a time when people struggle to agree on basic facts. So impact includes the subscriber count, and it also includes a deep investigation that changes policy or leads to a new law. PMs have to move specific metrics and also help stories reach the people who truly need to see them. That gives them a wider view of how business goals relate to the mission.
ex: The mission: seek the truth and help people understand the world

d.verdict: Business growth is a means to the mission

l44|67.c: He left big tech to keep a promise to himself, and layoffs showed him he was just a number.
l44|67.e: In 2016 Uber offered him nearly double his pay, mostly in stock. He promised himself that if the company went public in four years and he had savings, he'd take a risk. When COVID layoffs hit in 2020, excellent people on his team were cut simply for being in the wrong group. As a middle manager he didn't even have budget to adjust his reports' pay. His trust that the company would take care of him collapsed, and he wanted a position where he called the shots. The original plan was to raise money for a platform-engineering startup, but he asked himself what he'd do after getting rich. The answer was write books and share knowledge, so he decided to do that now.
ex: Uber laid off about 20% of its engineers at the time
He used the parable of the fisherman to ask where a startup would actually end

items.d: Pay doubles; a four-year promise to himself
Wants a role where he calls the shots
Tests with books first, then writing

l44|67.c: A paid newsletter can out-earn a big tech salary, and every good article is a raise.
l44|67.e: His best year at Uber paid about $320,000 to $330,000 in total, already very high for Europe. He expected a big pay cut when he left, but the newsletter earns more, and as subscriptions grow there's no theoretical ceiling. In the first year he kept a spreadsheet of how much annualized revenue rose one week after each article. Writing something that resonated was literally a raise. He relies on subscriptions, not ads or sponsorships. The free-to-paid conversion rate is in the single digits but healthy. Growth sped up noticeably once Substack launched its recommendations feature. He also stresses that he's a rare exception.
ex: About 80,000 new subscribers in the last 90 days, close to a thousand a day
Two early ebooks earned about $100,000 in their first year

l44|67.c: A one-person writing business brings freedom and control, but also loneliness, guilt, and no easy exit.
l44|67.e: What he likes most is a calendar with almost no meetings, long blocks of focus time, and full freedom to choose what to write and try new formats. The costs are just as real. He lost the team and office chatter, so he works from a coworking space. Compared with eight meetings a day at Uber, he often feels like he's slacking and feels guilty. Peers are competitors, so sharing isn't as open as inside a tech company. Subscriber counts create external anxiety. The business is tied to him personally, so it's hard to sell like a company. Vacations are hard too; he barely stopped in the first year.
ex: At Uber he took four months of paid leave when his child was born
He estimates a business like this would sell for 4 to 5 times annual revenue

items: Tied to him, hard to exit
Hard to truly take time off

l44|67.c: Self-discipline fails when you work alone, so create pressure with public commitments and external deadlines.
l44|67.e: He considers himself a diligent employee of 15 years, yet working for himself he often wasted whole days. His fix was to promise readers a fixed weekly schedule, then add a Thursday news commentary for even more pressure, so every day except Wednesday now has a deadline. He advises would-be authors to sign with a publisher just to have someone chasing the manuscript. He serializes his own books inside the newsletter, inspired by The Three Musketeers being written as a magazine serial. Other tactics include a 20-minute timer, a script that blocks social sites, and the Centered app. Each trick works for a few months before he needs a new one.
ex: A deep-dive article often takes days to two weeks of research, then feedback and editing
He estimates he wrote the equivalent of four or five books last year

root.d: A substitute for a company's calendar

items.d: Use the newsletter to push big projects
Survive five minutes and you're in flow
Edit the hosts file to kill social sites

l44|67.c: The newsletter's overnight success rested on six years of steady writing.
l44|67.e: A hundred people subscribed the day he announced the paid newsletter, and he had 1,000 paying subscribers within six weeks. But he says anyone copying the move probably won't get the same result. Behind it was The Pragmatic Engineer blog, started in 2015. Inspired by Jeff Atwood's advice to blog three times a week for two years, he wrote six posts and quit. Months later an old post blew up on Hacker News, and only then did he know anyone cared. He kept writing on and off, and posts on performance reviews and the three tiers of engineer pay built a big readership. His lesson: when you feel clear demand, like 20 DMs within an hour of sharing a draft, double down immediately.
ex: The viral old post argued that a code comment is an invitation to refactor
Readers suggested turning his long piece on building mobile apps at scale into an ebook

items.d: A hundred subscribers on day one

l44|67.c: First build real depth in one field, then set goals you control, keep a cadence, and dare to experiment.
l44|67.e: Starting a newsletter without real industry experience makes credibility hard, he argues. So first become an expert in a field, join challenging teams, and collect stories worth telling. A well-known employer on your resume also makes people more willing to listen. Set goals on things you control, like one article a month, not outcomes like subscriber counts. Then keep a steady cadence, and like Steve Yegge, give each new experiment a six-month deadline before changing course. He also notes that fewer people write deep long-form pieces now because everyone has moved to video, which is an opening for writers.
ex: Kent Beck keeps working hands-on while writing, and he sees him as a role model
Steve Yegge tried podcasting for six months, then went back to industry

terms.d: One article a month, kept up
Set a deadline; pivot if it fails

result.d: Though luck still plays a big part

l44|67.c: Run the writing as a one-person business, and deliberately leave empty time for the next spark.
l44|67.e: He no longer makes long-term plans, because three years ago a newsletter was nowhere in his thinking. He treats it as a sustainable one-person business rather than part of the creator economy, and that mindset lets him switch off on weekends. He isn't attached to the newsletter format and will keep leaning on what he likes: talking to people, writing, and software engineering. His takeaway is that this career came out of six months of not job-hunting after he quit. So next he wants to cut his weekly hours from about 50 to 20 and leave room for the next spark.
ex: The newsletter idea, he says, came out of that six-month gap

marks.d: About 20 hours a week, regular breaks

l45|68.c: A new PM doesn't need to master everything. Start with communication, prioritization, and execution.
l45|68.e: He once wrote a long list of what top PMs do: think big, simplify, forecast and measure, understand technical trade-offs, design, and copy. Later he added earning trust, digging into data yourself, saying no well, and adapting to change. But he says he has never met anyone strong at all of them. In the first year, focus on three. Communication is a lifelong practice; when asked "when does it ship," give the date first, then explain. Prioritization decides what you work on. Execution means shaping a proposal into a tight package and taking some responsibility for the team's morale and pace.
ex: He compiled his manager's communication lessons into a "Book of Kim"
Communication tip: answer first, explain second, and sometimes stop after the answer

root.d: The other skills can come later

items.d: Answer first, then explain; grade yourself after
Decide what to do and what not to
Deliver what you promised; carry the team

l45|68.c: Prioritization is a PM's most powerful tool, worth several times the impact all else being equal.
l45|68.e: Prioritization is far more than picking the next project, he argues. It runs through many layers: which themes lead the roadmap, which projects within a theme, in what order, how big each one should be, and where your own time goes, including what you deliberately leave alone. He credits his early success at Amazon to this rather than to being smarter, working longer, or knowing more technology. He badly wanted the business metrics to climb fast, so he led the team to find the highest-leverage projects and concentrate resources there. That made up for weaker memory and a lighter technical background.
ex: He estimates a PM who prioritizes well has about 5 times the impact of one who doesn't

items.d: What gets full effort, what gets dropped

l45|68.c: Senior PMs should first ask "could this be bigger?" and own everything that affects success.
l45|68.e: He quotes Warren Buffett: at our size, we have to hunt bigger elephants. When a PM brings an idea, he first pushes it as big as it could go, then decides whether to start small, while keeping the bigger vision in mind. Thinking big also applies to the edges of the job. Most people stay inside the box of "what a PM does." He prefers to act like a product-leaning general manager, treating marketing, operations, and anything else that affects the product and its customers as his business. If nobody owns something, own it yourself and clear obstacles one at a time. Within reason, though, and without overreaching too fast.
ex: Most of his roles have really been product-leaning general manager jobs

l45|68.c: Trust builds by repeatedly setting and meeting expectations, and it decides how many resources you get.
l45|68.e: This one he added to the list later. Doing bigger things takes more resources, and leaders won't hand them over unless they trust you to use them well. You build trust by stating a goal in advance and hitting it, shipping when you said you would, and owning up to mistakes. Lying, vagueness, and repeating mistakes all drain it. The deeper level is working back from your partners' goals and putting in the effort to align. He reflects on building a customer-support technology platform at Airbnb: convinced the direction was right, he pushed ahead without building enough of an alliance with support leadership, and execution suffered for it.
ex: His wife is a PM at AWS, and he has watched trust work as her superpower

items.d: Forecast a goal and say it out loud
Ship what you said, on time
Be seen as a good steward of resources

l45|68.c: Be driven by impact rather than promotion, and promotions follow as a byproduct.
l45|68.e: Forget politics, promotions, and team size, he advises, and spend each day asking how to have the biggest impact. That changes how you order your roadmap and your day. In his first ten years at Amazon he never discussed promotion with a manager; he just wanted to grow the business he owned, and he was promoted repeatedly anyway. For new PMs impact is a bonus; the more senior you get, the more it becomes the standard you're judged by. Given the choice, work on "offense" projects that directly drive revenue and users rather than just making a cost center more efficient. And pick managers who prioritize well and like to teach.
ex: Executives pay more attention to projects that bring in revenue and customers

items.d: The organization hands you hard problems

l45|68.c: A product leader doesn't just build new things; they run the existing products well.
l45|68.e: From Jeff Wilke he learned the operator's mindset. In the weekly business review, an hour covered the metrics of every North American retail line, and any owner could be grilled about a blip, so everyone had to know their business cold. He brought the same mechanism back to his own teams, and it cascaded down. If you look hard at the product you run, you naturally see where to double down and what to guard against. Wilke also practiced tough love, and he'd spend a few seconds in meetings explaining the mental model behind a decision, so people could apply it elsewhere and find it easier to disagree and commit.
ex: Bezos: when you don't yet know the direction, the process doesn't need to be efficient

items.d: Executives grill key metrics for an hour
Can always explain a blip and the response

l45|68.c: Working backwards means starting from the customer's problem; the PR/FAQ is just a forcing function.
l45|68.e: Amazon's working-backwards method means writing a mock press release and FAQ before building anything. The most common misuse, he says, is starting with a solution and bolting a problem onto it afterward: "these two technologies are similar, what could we combine them into?" It's cooking from whatever is in the pantry, and it's especially common at big companies. An early project of his that linked products by catalog ID went that way and was shut down. Done right, the press release opens with the problem paragraph, then the solution and customer quotes, and the FAQ tests whether there's a credible plan. Tiny features can skip the full process. Elsewhere, adapt to the existing culture; the method usually sways your team more than your bosses.
ex: Bezos's three questions for a new bet: Is it big enough? Should we do it? Is there a credible plan?
When Bezos saw he'd skipped the problem paragraph: no problem paragraph, maybe no problem

items: Start with a technology or solution
Start with the customer and pain point

d.verdict: The template is a tool; the spirit is starting from the problem

l46|71.c: Coaching a PM takes five steps: set the bar, place them, align, plan, and follow up.
l46|71.e: She breaks coaching down into five steps. First, work out what a good product manager looks like in your company. Second, place each report on that map: where they are now, how far they could go, and what "next bigger challenge" would teach them something new. She suggests spending an hour each quarter writing that list, so when an opportunity comes up you can hand it to them. Third, check that the direction you see matches theirs. Fourth, a development plan, owned mostly by the PM, with you helping break it into small steps. Fifth, follow up, like reminding a friend to go to the gym, at whatever pace they want.
ex: She has coached about 130 people one-on-one and about 150 in groups
Lenny's approach: pick a theme after performance reviews, then check in monthly

l46|71.c: Don't wait for a perfect competency framework. Start with development plans and keep it small.
l46|71.e: Many managers get stuck on step one. They want to agree on standards with their peers first, or wait for HR to publish a company-wide version, and that can take forever. Her advice: do it for your own team, because your reports have only one manager, you. The fastest way in is to skip straight to development plans. PMs usually know what they want to get better at, such as storytelling or prioritization. Pick one theme per quarter or every four months, add short check-ins, and it takes very little time. She also suggests keeping a list of coaching questions handy, like a list of emotion words, or "You rate yourself a 6. How do I get you to a 7?"
ex: Investor and CEO coach Matt Mochary's rating question focuses on small improvements

items: Plan for your own team first

d.verdict: Consistency beats intensity

l46|71.c: PMs need far more than T-shaped skills. Managers need a clear map, and hiring must screen for traits.
l46|71.e: Many product leaders she coaches came from marketing, business, data or engineering and never worked as PMs themselves. They don't know the methods the industry already has, and they underestimate how broad the role is. She describes a PM as an "eight-legged creature" that touches everything. So their reports are left to figure it out alone. Her advice is to pick an existing framework that comes close, such as the PM Daisy, Marty Cagan's assessment or her own PMwheel, then customize it deeply, and combine self-assessment with reviews from the manager and peers. Traits like curiosity and empathy are hard to build inside a company, so screen for them when hiring.
ex: The PMwheel has 8 dimensions with at least 15 questions each
Her catchphrase: being in product is not a role, it's a career

items.d: See the problem, find a solution

l46|71.c: Good stories take real time to craft. Drop the jargon and speak to both heart and head.
l46|71.e: What newcomers underestimate most, she says, is how much time good storytellers put in. To explain to the whole company what your team will do over the next three or four months, she estimates two weeks at one or two hours a day, polishing versions for different audiences. Then there's language. Business terms and acronyms make people tune out. Even "product discovery" can wear thin, so say "we need to figure something out" instead. What actually moves people is concrete language: smells, feelings, how life gets better. She believes a PM who can't tell a story or rally a team will hit a ceiling on promotions.
ex: She thinks US schools value public speaking more, and Europeans are generally weaker at it
Her role models: former boss Jason Goldberg and data presenter Hans Rosling

items.d: About two weeks, an hour or two daily

l46|71.c: A story is a design tool: tell it early, watch reactions, then prepare versions of different lengths.
l46|71.e: Don't stare at a blank page too long, she says. Draft something, because changing a story is even easier than changing a prototype. Tell it to people, watch how they react, then adjust. You can borrow proven structures like the hero's journey. To motivate the team, make them the hero, with a monster to defeat and a bright destination. To explain product value, make the user the hero. A story needs three forms: spoken, written and visual. It also needs three lengths: an elevator version, a short one before planning meetings, and a full one for the all-hands. This effort fits quarterly vision and strategy, not every sprint.
ex: The elevator version runs about 75 seconds, the short one about 6 minutes
The full version is about as long as a TED talk

items.d: All-hands, with visuals and a written doc

l46|71.c: To get over stage fright, start with small friendly audiences and work your way up.
l46|71.e: She admits she used to be terrified of speaking in public. Her first time was a five-minute update at an all-hands of about 90 people, and she was a wreck. Her path was to speak to her own team first, then at the company all-hands, then at local product meetups, which are smaller and better for practice in summer. Collect feedback every time. Peers are harsher critics, while strangers are more polite but spot gaps in your logic that you missed. Before going on stage, strike a "superhero pose" backstage or tap your chest to lift your energy, and seat a few friendly faces in the front row.
ex: Local ProductTank meetups sometimes draw only about 30 people

l46|71.c: An internal product community is the cheapest way to grow people, but it can't rest on one or two shoulders.
l46|71.e: Her research this year found that many companies have never considered an internal community of practice, and plenty of people don't even know external product communities exist. A community helps people learn and get better at the craft, so they are more likely to stay, and it takes some of the development load off managers. It is far cheaper than training, conference tickets or outside coaches. Signs of a good one: people build connections, learn something new now and then, share freely and trust each other, and stay friendly and active. To run one, revisit its purpose, values and definition of success regularly, design rituals and incentives, and spread responsibility across several interest groups.
ex: She doesn't think engagement volume is a good metric; signal-to-noise matters more

l47|72.c: Technical audits are SEO's biggest myth; real growth comes from generated pages and human-written content.
l47|72.e: He thinks the most common misunderstanding in SEO is that running a crawler and fixing its list of errors will make traffic grow. Site structure, tags, redirects and page speed are the foundation you must get right, but the foundation itself does not bring visitors. Two things actually move traffic. One is pages generated in bulk from a database, where each extra page costs almost no writing. The other is articles, guides and lists written by people, which almost any company with a real market can do, and which now often outgrow generated pages. Teams, he says, overrate the technical work and underrate the writing.
ex: Generated pages at scale: eBay and Zillow listing and category pages
Editorial content can start at 10 to 25 pieces a month, then scale past 100

items.d: Human-written articles and guides; best route for most
Pages generated from a database at no writing cost
Necessary foundation, not a growth lever

l47|72.c: Invest in SEO only if enough people search for what you do and your site has enough authority.
l47|72.e: He sizes the opportunity by looking at competitors. That means not just companies selling similar products, but content sites fighting for the same readers. Check their search traffic in a tool like Similarweb, multiply by the conversion rate you expect, and compare that with your other channels. On authority, he offers a rough bar: meaningful traffic that does not come from search, plus plenty of other sites linking to you, which shows you are a real brand rather than an SEO farm. Companies with lots of user posts or products compete more easily, but others can start with editorial content. If paid or brand channels already work well, SEO may not be the priority yet.
ex: Rough bar: over 1,000 non-search visits a day and over 1,000 referring domains
A fintech company can treat Investopedia as an audience competitor

cells.d: You can rank, but the traffic ceiling is low
Big opportunity and the strength to compete

l47|72.c: Work from the market down to page types and product requirements, instead of copying competitors.
l47|72.e: His process runs in order. First define who could find you through search. Then pick the topics and keywords to cover. Next, look at which kind of page ranks at the top for those searches and decide what kind of page to build. Then write requirements for it the way you would for any product feature: which components it needs and which subtopics the content should cover. Finally, use internal links so Google can find the pages. Competitors are only inspiration. The real question is what genuinely helps the user, because behavior signals like click-through rate, bouncing back to results, and time on page also affect rankings.
ex: "How to poach an egg" ranks articles, so MasterClass course transcripts could not rank
A store page needs components like a map and a phone number

items.d: Size the opportunity from competitor traffic
Rank by volume, authority, and conversion
See what already ranks in results
Help Google find and recrawl pages

l47|72.c: Build pages around whole topics, covering the full intent, or they will not rank.
l47|72.e: He points out that one page usually ranks for hundreds to thousands of related search terms, so a topic's total search volume can be ten times that of any single keyword. Prioritizing by individual keyword badly undercounts the opportunity. The old habit of one page per keyword variant no longer works and just produces piles of thin articles. To decide what belongs on one page, compare the search results: if two terms return the same results, they go on one page; if not, split them. The page should also cover the subtopics people want and fill in whatever competitors left out.
ex: MasterClass's butter lettuce page added health benefits and beat Food Network
His early shopping site, built on keyword variants, had over 10 million pages

items.d: One page usually covers 200 to 2,000 terms

l47|72.c: SEO is slow and uncertain, so it gets cut from roadmaps, and most "failures" are false negatives.
l47|72.e: He says the typical cycle is about three months to build and launch, then another three to six months before growth shows up. Very high-authority sites may react within days or weeks. Early on, watch leading indicators: new pages first break into the top 20, then climb. Because SEO is slow and uncertain, and because the SEO team often sits outside the product org while every change is a product change, most recommendations never ship. Many "SEO didn't work" verdicts are really poor execution or too little authority. His fix: put SEO inside the product team, get executive backing, and fund it at the scale of advertising. And do not test too early; wait until about month six after launch.
ex: Ranking signal to watch: top 20, then 15, then 8, then 5
Zillow and eBay spend tens of millions on ads; SEO deserves the same scale

l47|72.c: Authority is topic by topic, and standing in one topic spills over into closely related ones.
l47|72.e: He believes Google's authority signals moved well beyond PageRank long ago. They include referring domains and the anchor text they use, traffic that does not come from search, shares and social buzz, and people searching your brand by name. Authority is also not just one site-wide score. A small site that is recognized in a narrow field can beat a big site there. Google's sense of which topics are related is generated by algorithms from signals like co-occurrence and query rewrites, not a fixed taxonomy. So the authority from one breakout article spreads to neighboring topics, and the strategy is to expand outward from a core topic.
ex: One viral Jell-O shot article got a recipe site ranking for vodka and whiskey recipes
MasterClass built authority on Gordon Ramsay dishes first, then expanded

items.d: People looking for you by name

l47|72.c: Most sites pile internal links onto a few pages; flattening them is an early quick win.
l47|72.e: He estimates that more than nine in ten sites have orphan pages, meaning pages that almost no internal link points to. Standard modules like faceted navigation, related items, and popular or newest lists concentrate links on a small set of pages. Google enters a site through the homepage and the popular pages with many external links, so every page should be only a few hops from those entry points. Keep the link graph flat, with at least five and ideally ten internal links pointing to each page. Links in the body text carry more weight than footer or navigation links, so important links belong in the body or at least above the footer.
ex: He estimates about 5% of pages get about 95% of internal links
Redistributing links typically lifts traffic 25% or more, sometimes nearly doubling it
Early data: adding links to under-linked product pages raised traffic about 300%

items: Links pile onto a few pages
Every page a few hops from entry

d.verdict: Redistributing internal links is a quick win; do it early

l47|72.c: Letting AI write pages outright is risky; it only works when grounded in structured facts.
l47|72.e: He generally advises against generating SEO pages in bulk with AI. Models like GPT-3 produce fluent sentences that resemble text already on the web, not verified facts. The result reads smoothly but can be wrong, and on high-stakes topics like retirement planning or cancer treatment, wrong answers hurt people. The exception is content built on structured data or expert knowledge, such as game recaps generated from play-by-play stats. He sees AI as more useful around the writing: clustering thousands of keywords, finding subtopics, drafting outlines, and assessing topical authority and content performance. The actual text should still come from subject-matter experts.
ex: GPT-3 described a soap as "oxide-free," which it was not
Generating text from structured clinical trial data is a sound use

marks.d: Fluent but may make things up

l48|73.c: When visibility is low, plan the year on a conservative baseline and set checkpoints to scale up or down.
l48|73.e: Bravado's quota-tracking data shows the share of salespeople and companies missing quota climbing every quarter, and the market swinging back and forth: a late-summer rebound, then a sharp drop in October. He thinks this downturn is the tech industry's own problem, unlike the pandemic that hit every sector, so it may last longer. Boards generally advise caution, but too much caution leaves a company lurching between "we're doomed" and "we're fine." His approach: plan for revenue to fall, then set quarterly checkpoints. Hit the number and you raise targets and unlock budget; miss it and you cut. Agree on these rules with the board and sales team in advance, to guard against founder optimism.
ex: 76% of companies missed their Q3 targets; he expects over 80% in Q4
Example: $10M this year, plan for $9M next year, with a Q1 checkpoint at $2.5M

l48|73.c: Paying commission only on new deals is outdated. Renewals and customer quality belong in the plan.
l48|73.e: A typical SaaS seller's target pay is half base salary, half commission, with a quota about five times that target and accelerators for beating it. His example: rep A closes $1.5M, earns about $400K and gets celebrated company-wide. Rep B closes $1.2M and earns about $250K. But if most of A's customers churn next year while all of B's renew, expand and agree to be references, neither paycheck changes. That made sense when everyone only cared about new recurring revenue. Now that capital is expensive and retention and efficiency are the focus, he argues for renewal bonuses, comparing each rep's customer retention, and even rethinking the 50/50 pay split for sales executives.
ex: He thinks comp plans often get tangled by ad hoc incentives
Other executives' fixed-to-variable pay is usually about nine to one

d.verdict: Pay should serve customers, company and reps alike

l48|73.c: When new customers are hard to win, move your best sellers to customer success and plug the leaky bucket.
l48|73.e: He sees cold call and cold email response rates at all-time lows, enterprise sales cycles stretching out, lots of deals ending in "no decision," and the ones that close being small, like three-month pilots. In hard times people trust what they already know. So over the next six to nine months, he argues, how much new business you sign matters less. What you absolutely cannot do is lose existing customers, because they are nearly impossible to replace. He knows moving top sellers into post-sale roles sounds backwards, but Bravado is doing exactly that, and he tells his portfolio companies to do the same.
ex: An investor told him average enterprise sales cycles went from about 62 days to about 115

root.d: Plugging leaks beats pouring in more water

items.d: Existing customers more likely to stay

l48|73.c: Turn the data you see across customers into insights for them, and you go from tool to advisor.
l48|73.e: Every vendor can see what similar customers are doing right now, and he thinks that is the most underrated asset a company has. Instead of writing white papers to attract new leads, turn product marketing into a research team, add data analysts, and publish industry insights only existing customers can see. Bravado tells customers whether similar companies are hiring or freezing, and how quotas and pay are shifting. An applicant tracking vendor could share how job cuts and salaries are changing by company stage. He also suggests keeping budget for customer-only events, like taking still-active customers to Napa next February. That measurably reduces churn.
ex: Imagine Greenhouse publishing a report: open roles at companies your stage have halved

l48|73.c: New deals come from warm intros by existing customers, and the intro should be a text, not an email.
l48|73.e: He insists a company either grows or dies. Just trying to survive the winter drains a team's energy, so you still have to find new business. Customer-only events are the perfect moment: between dinner and drinks, ask a customer to recommend one or two peers in a similar situation. Getting a name isn't enough. Ask them to start a three-way text thread right there, because email intros tend to die quietly. Keep the referrer in the thread for the first ten or twenty messages and the prospect feels awkward ghosting you. He once followed up in such a thread every week or two, and after nine weeks signed the sales leader as a customer.
ex: When Webflow's sales leader offered a referral, his only reply was: text thread, please
He is against mixing customers and prospects at the same event

items.d: One or two people in similar situations
Pushes the first meeting to happen

l48|73.c: Top sellers close by teaching the customer something new, staying pessimistic inside and optimistic outside.
l48|73.e: At Glassdoor, Facebook had turned down every pitch for years with the same line. He had data scientists analyze all of Facebook's employee reviews, salaries and CEO approval rating against other big tech companies, packaged it into a nine-page report, guessed every email format, and cold-emailed Sheryl Sandberg with a subject line about Zuckerberg's Glassdoor approval rating. She replied that night. The next day he met the executive team and Zuckerberg, and eventually closed a large deal. Good sellers, he says, don't just listen to the nice things; they actively hunt for signs the buyer won't buy. A CEO is really a full-time seller too, convincing themselves, cofounders, investors and customers.
ex: That approval rating was later added to Facebook's weekly executive briefing
He says he personally signed about 60 Fortune 500 customers at Glassdoor

items.d: Subject line hits the decision maker's concern
Met the leadership team next day

l48|73.c: In hard times, don't survive by tweaking. Stand in the customer's shoes and rewrite the rules.
l48|73.e: Bravado's recruiting business dropped off as the market froze. Instead of accepting it, they looked at it from the customer's side: companies wanted new customers but were afraid to hire full-time sellers, while lots of salespeople couldn't find full-time jobs. So they launched Bravado Flex, which supports commission-only, part-time and contract arrangements. Last month was the best in company history. They also found many sellers actually prefer working for several companies at once. A year ago, with supply and demand reversed, the product would not have worked. He also suggests rethinking pricing, such as turning an annual fee into monthly or even daily billing, rather than just shaving the price.
ex: Pricing example: a $12,000 annual fee becomes $1,000 a month or $20 a day

cells.d: War for talent; no room for Flex

l49|74.c: Don't slap a price on a finished product; test willingness to pay early and let it shape the roadmap.
l49|74.e: He says most companies build the product first, then scramble for a pricing plan, and he sees that as the common root of most commercial failures. Price is a measure of value. Asking "do you like it?" without talking money gives misleading answers. So beyond product-market fit, you need to confirm that people will actually pay, as early as possible and repeatedly. The roadmap should also be ordered by willingness to pay. If you don't know which features are worth money, you over-invest in the wrong ones. That is why he now argues pricing belongs with the product team, not finance.
ex: He says 72% of innovations fail commercially
About 20% of features drive about 80% of willingness to pay
Porsche tested every Cayenne option with prototypes; it now drives over half of profits

terms.d: Which features they will pay for, and how much

result.d: Then order the roadmap by it

l49|74.c: Never ask customers what to charge; use anchors, price thresholds, and purchase likelihood instead.
l49|74.e: Asking "what should we charge?" is useless. His approach: first walk through the sales pitch so the customer understands the value. Then ask them to score your product against a product they already know. Next, ask for three price points, acceptable, expensive, and too expensive to buy, and find the cliff where interest drops. Ask how likely they are to buy on a 1-to-5 scale. Have them pick the most and least important features from several sets, and run trade-off scenarios. About half your follow-ups should be "why?", because the answers tell you what to build and how to pitch it. Repeat at least every six months.
ex: He says about 30-50% of people who answer 5 actually buy; about 10-20% of 4s
For B2B, interview the 20-30 customers who drive 80-90% of revenue
Superhuman used the threshold method to land on its $30 price

items.d: Set it up with the sales story
Score against a familiar product set to 100
About half of questions probe reasons

l49|74.c: Segment by needs and willingness to pay and build for each segment; one size fits none.
l49|74.e: He estimates about 60% of companies claim to have a segmentation strategy, but only about 10% have one that matters. Most segment by demographics or personas, yet a wealthy 70-year-old living in a castle could be the Queen or a rock star, with completely different needs. Useful segmentation divides people by needs, value, and willingness to pay. The test is whether you can treat each segment differently in product, sales, and marketing. The same person also switches segments depending on the situation. Early-stage companies don't need to serve every segment at once; pick one to start.
ex: Uber's X, Black, Pool, and Comfort serve different needs
Apple's iPhone tiers each map to a segment
