A ticketing company split one product into starter, pro, and enterprise tiers

l49|74.c: "Go cheap to grow" is a fallacy; don't use penetration pricing unless your cost structure supports it.
l49|74.e: He sorts pricing strategy into three types. Skimming means entering high and lowering prices over time, with the price itself signaling quality. Penetration means pricing low to win volume, which only works if your cost structure can live on thin margins. Maximization means balancing how much value you capture in the short term. Many startups default to low prices to grab share without a business model that can sustain it. Different businesses inside one company can run different strategies, and execution matters more than which label you choose.
ex: Skimming: Apple. Penetration: Amazon. Maximization: he cites Microsoft
AWS and Amazon retail can run different strategies

l49|74.c: Sort features into leaders, fillers, and killers; stuffing a killer into a bundle lowers everyone's willingness to pay.
l49|74.e: Pick the segment first, then build each bundle around what that segment cares about. He gives features three roles. Leaders are features more than half of customers want; they carry the whole bundle. Fillers are cheap to provide and can be added to the package for a small premium. Killers are features only a minority wants intensely. Put a killer in the bundle and everyone else feels they are paying for something they don't need, which drags down willingness to pay for the whole package. Sell killers separately as add-ons.
ex: Fillers work like a McDonald's Happy Meal bundle
A killer is forcing coffee into a burger combo; better sold on its own

items.d: Over 50% want them; they carry the bundle
Cheap; bundle for a small premium
Only 10-20% want them; sell as add-ons

l49|74.c: How you charge matters more than how much; pick subscription or usage based on the business, not fashion.
l49|74.e: He argues that with the right pricing unit, customers will even accept a premium. Subscriptions fit when usage is steady month to month, when the value is ongoing but use is occasional, or when customers simply want simplicity. Usage-based pricing fits when customers want low commitment, care about fairness and transparency, or get value only in bursts, but it needs a trackable metric the customer accepts. The two can be mixed. B2B companies can also price on two dimensions, seats and departments, so the per-user price improves as usage spreads, which reinforces product-led expansion.
ex: Michelin charges truckers per mile instead of raising tire prices about 20%
Segment switched from charging per API call to per monthly tracked user
HubSpot combines a fixed monthly fee with usage tiers

d.verdict: Choose by the business; mix when needed

l49|74.c: Buyers aren't fully rational, so how you present prices must appeal to both sides of them.
l49|74.e: He notes that in a break-even test where options are mathematically identical, "indifferent" almost never wins; people still lean one way. One SaaS company gave away too much in its entry tier, so most people chose it. After testing showed $99 was the real demand threshold, the company raised its mid and top tiers and added a decoy tier almost nobody buys, and customers clustered in the middle. Other tactics include the compromise effect, restating a monthly fee as a few dollars a day, the razor-and-blades model, a puzzle effect that plays on the urge to complete a set, and selling outcomes rather than feature lists.
ex: With no product changes, MRR and ARPU rose more than 30%
A puzzle-style presentation lifted a financial client's attach rate 40-50%
SmugMug rewrote its pricing page around benefits and grew revenue by double digits

l49|74.c: In a downturn, don't just discount; defend your price with a stripped-down version and non-price levers.
l49|74.e: He believes a discount, once given, becomes the new price. So any price cut has to buy something back, such as removing features, to protect the integrity of the original price. Better still, prepare a stripped-down, cheaper version in advance and keep it in your pocket for customers at risk of leaving; that beats watching them go. Beyond that, use levers other than price: give more value at the same price, trade concessions for a longer contract, or adjust payment terms.
ex: Payment terms can be loosened from 15 days to 30

items.d: For customers at risk of churning
More value, longer terms, payment terms

l50|75.c: Community-led growth ends in being everywhere, which makes enterprise buyers comfortable and lets you move upmarket.
l50|75.e: Her definition of community-led growth is specific: the community pushes awareness so high that big companies feel there is no risk in choosing the product, so teams keep buying more seats. When people hear about Notion again and again on social media, on podcasts and from friends, it goes beyond simply knowing the name. They want to go find out more. She calls that "discovery." To measure it, the metric she cares about most is the number of new visitors coming to the website for the first time each month.
ex: Core metric: net new website visitors each month
Influencer partnerships can be tracked directly, so attribution is cleanest there
Figma's community path is a useful comparison

items.d: Everyone uses it, so it can't be wrong
From one person to the whole company

l50|75.c: If users make something with your product that's worth showing off, community is almost mandatory.
l50|75.e: Her test: if what users create with your product shows off their skill and taste, they naturally want to share it, and a community grows on its own. That's especially true for freemium and product-led growth products, where the product itself brings in users. On the other hand, sales-led companies with high prices, long sales cycles and many touchpoints before a deal closes shouldn't make community their first priority. She also points out that a community doesn't have to be about the product itself. It can gather people around the knowledge your target users need most.
ex: Notion templates and workspaces, Figma and Canva are all shareable outputs
Stripe Atlas gathers founders around startup knowledge
One creator made $35,000 in four months selling a single template

items: Users' work can be shown off

d.verdict: First ask whether you have output worth sharing

l50|75.c: The shape of your community depends on whether you have product-market fit and whether you lean enterprise or consumer.
l50|75.e: She uses a two-by-two matrix to pick a community format instead of defaulting to a big forum. An enterprise product still searching for product-market fit suits a customer advisory board: connect a handful of ideal customers and encourage feedback, and they often become your first evangelists. An enterprise product that already has fit should focus on champions inside customer companies and outside implementation consultants. A consumer-leaning product with fit relies on ambassadors and influencers to spread word of mouth like wildfire.
ex: Salesforce's ecosystem of outside implementation consultants
Notion's Champions community on Slack
The fourth quadrant wasn't covered in the episode

cells.d: A small circle of ideal customers
Listeners can check the original chart

l50|75.c: Don't judge community by ROI early on. Delay monetization rather than kill organic enthusiasm.
l50|75.e: Notion didn't measure its community systematically until quite late, because geographic expansion and user surveys already showed it was working. When you see organic enthusiasm, she says, the worst thing you can do is cut it because you can't calculate the return. Founders need to decide whether the long game needs reach or near-term revenue more. Many successful companies delayed charging for every piece, and once the wave of word of mouth built up, they had more options, not fewer.
ex: Notion founder Ivan Zhao believed in community from the start
Community helped Notion get into networks like Station F in Paris

marks.d: Word of mouth and reach first

l50|75.c: Start an ambassador program with your most active real users, and add only a small batch at a time.
l50|75.e: Just as positioning starts with your real best customers, Notion in 2019 invited only about 20 users who were already sharing on Twitter on their own. The incentive wasn't money but feeling special: early access to new features with the product team genuinely listening, direct Q&A with the founding team, funding for in-person events, and their work featured on official channels. She deliberately kept growth slow, adding one batch a month. When membership jumps to thousands overnight, people feel like they're talking to an auditorium and the conversation goes quiet.
ex: About 20 people at first, then roughly 20 more each month
In-person events are back to about 30 a month
The community lives on Slack, inside users' daily routine

items.d: People already sharing on their own
Early access, being heard, founder AMAs

l50|75.c: Treat content like a product: find content-market fit first.
l50|75.e: Content may be a side product, but she says it still has to answer who the audience is and what worries them most, like how to get promoted or how to avoid failing. Content that works as a painkiller beats content that's a vitamin. Emotional value counts too, like making someone feel they're not alone in their struggle. High quality also means lots of time: connecting scattered bits from interviews into bigger themes. Early on, a few big names help build the audience's confidence.
ex: First Round Review encouraged operators to share their failures
A single piece took about 8 hours of prep and 8 hours of writing
Subscribers skewed toward Google, Apple and other big-company email domains

items.d: Who you really want to reach
Solve a problem or ease loneliness

l50|75.c: Anyone can publish now, but press coverage is still a rare, credible megaphone.
l50|75.e: She still values PR. Very few channels reach a large audience with credible endorsement attached, so an honest, accessible relationship with journalists pays off. Notion's big turning point was an authoritative tech column calling it the only productivity tool you need. Launching on Product Hunt also produced breakthroughs several times. As for whether founders should tweet constantly, she thinks it depends on personality and authenticity. Setting yourself a posting quota is a big mistake. Post when you actually have something to say and it lands better.
ex: Wall Street Journal reporter David Pierce's piece was the turning point
Launches like Notion 2.0 all went on Product Hunt

result.d: Draws users, candidates and investors

l51|77.c: Sales isn't a gift for talking. It's a learnable skill: helping customers see their own pain like a consultant.
l51|77.e: He rejects the old "sell ice to Eskimos" image. Sales, to him, is bringing supply to demand: acting like a consultant who happens to prefer their own solution, asking discovery questions until the buyer sees how serious the problem is, then offering a fix. If a customer isn't a fit, don't sell to them. The hard part is the mindset shift: lots of strangers every day, a fragmented calendar, and living inside a CRM. All of it can be practiced deliberately, from building trust fast to asking awkward questions to shutting up after you quote a price.
ex: Atrium only serves sales teams of roughly 10 to 300 people
An ideal customer profile has two layers: the company and the roles involved in the decision
Practice "speed to trust" on bartenders and baristas

d.verdict: Sales is becoming measurable, like product analytics

l51|77.c: The founder has to sell the first few dozen customers personally. You can't outsource it.
l51|77.e: He sees this as the next step after The Lean Startup. A minimum viable product is usually rough, and it takes many customer conversations to iterate it into something genuinely valuable. Hand that feedback loop to a third party and it becomes a game of telephone. Founders understand the problem far better than anyone else, and learning "good enough" sales is much easier than turning a salesperson into a domain expert. Selling yourself has two other payoffs: you learn what pitch actually lands, and you can package it into a process others can run. B2B companies scale precisely by adding salespeople.
ex: Steve Blank: many companies have to replace their first VP of sales
Think about handing off after roughly 10 to 30 customers

root.d: The first few dozen real customers

items.d: From rough MVP to real value

l51|77.c: Get it working on the founder first, hire two to copy it, then double one level at a time.
l51|77.e: He uses an engineering analogy: the sales process has to run reliably on the founder's "local machine" before you deploy it. The bar is a statistically meaningful win rate with strangers, say 15% to 25% across fifty to a hundred opportunities. Then write down what's in your head and hire two salespeople to see whether they can reproduce it, not ten at once. Ramping ten new hires at the same time means you can't even ramp two properly. Only when those two succeed have you earned the right to go to 4, 8, then 16. Skip a level and something breaks.
ex: Win rate benchmark: 15% to 25%
Closing 1 in 30 opportunities is too low, unless deals are huge
Favor deals from friends or fellow accelerator founders don't count

items.d: Steady win rate, dozens of customers
Only after the previous level works

l51|77.c: Iterate the sales process like software, and use the "second date" rate as your leading indicator.
l51|77.e: He suggests working in small batches: about ten first meetings per cohort, watching where the questions, slides or demo fail to land. Every objection you handle badly earns a new slide, like a commit to the source code. Final win rate is too slow a signal. The simplest early indicator is how many first meetings turn into second and third meetings. If you can't even get a second date, check your message or your target audience. And deals you lose this round can still be won in the next one.
ex: Expect 10 first meetings to yield about 7 seconds, about 4.5 thirds, and 2 to 3 deals
Atrium's stages: discovery, data connection, preview, commercials
Big customer GRIN took three or four cycles to close

l51|77.c: Every B2B company eventually builds a sales team. Product-led growth is lead generation, not the whole business.
l51|77.e: Self-serve products are great at landing and spreading inside an organization. But the people using them usually don't control big budgets. Contracts of $50,000 or $100,000 and up mean talking to whoever holds the budget, and enterprises want someone to walk them through the process. He thinks many product-led companies stalled precisely because they waited too long to add sales. Dropbox is the classic case of product investment outrunning enterprise sales. Even a developer tool that starts on credit cards hits a ceiling eventually. The question is when, not whether.
ex: Atlassian got very far on extremely low pricing
Slack brought in Salesforce-trained sales talent in time
He says Snowflake has about 500 salespeople

items.d: Individuals try it on a credit card

l51|77.c: Hire early-stage "pioneer" salespeople first, not an accomplished VP of sales.
l51|77.e: A VP of sales from a big company has usually managed managers for years, hasn't sold personally in a long time, and is often financially set, so they may not want to grind from zero again. Early on, with no finished scripts or materials, you need people who will roll up their sleeves. Look for early sales hires, not recent ones, at companies that sell to the same buyers at a similar price point. Once two reps are working, hire a sales leader who is still close to the front line, and use data to prove product-market fit to them.
ex: For a recruiting tool, poach early sales hires from Lever or Greenhouse
About 57% of applicants never finish the written screening questions
Jason Lemkin's quip: why would they do it all over again?

d.left: Managers long off the front line

marks.d: First choice: same buyers, similar deal size

l51|77.c: Judge new reps on leading indicators, and sit together early so mistakes get fixed fast.
l51|77.e: The worst outcome is discovering after nine months that a rep isn't working out, when leading indicators would have told you in two. His cadence: month one is training, role-play and shadowing. Month two, count first meetings and the share that turn into second meetings. Month three, see whether deals reach a proposal. Only after that do you look at closed deals. This assumes the founder has supplied the deck, the question list and the demo script. For junior reps, remote work makes the feedback loop too slow. Sitting next to them and debriefing right after a call speeds up learning enormously.
ex: In month two, expect 10 to 20 first meetings with about half becoming second meetings
A rep who can't book a first meeting in a month is almost certainly not going to work

items.d: About half reach a second meeting
Proposals without closes are a warning

l52|79.c: Saying you want something isn't using it: autopilot money management improved retention but never drove acquisition.
l52|79.e: At Wealthfront he ran many interviews with a clickable prototype, sometimes pretending the product was already live. Only when someone wanted to go get their spouse to see it did he believe the demand was real. But asking people to hand all their money movement to software was a high-risk bet: everyone says yes in an interview, then hesitates once it's in their hands. In the end, Autopilot clearly raised savings and deposits and tied cash, investing, and retirement accounts into one system, but it didn't produce explosive organic growth. By Andy Rachleff's definition, that still isn't product-market fit.
ex: Autopilot kept enough for bills, then routed the rest to an emergency fund, an IRA, and so on
Like Tesla's Autopilot: hardly anyone buys the car just for that feature

items: Some fetch family to see it
Made the product set more complete

d.verdict: Good glue for the system, but not a growth engine

l52|79.c: To push a big bet internally, repeat the vision and the user's feelings, and state your motives up front.
l52|79.e: User insight and test data aren't enough on their own. Other teams have to build and promote the product, so you have to act like a founder: repeat the mission at every all-hands and describe how users will feel, not just which features they get. Before pushing a radical idea, say plainly that you only care about the company succeeding and that you don't need to be the one who owns it. That defuses suspicion that you're angling for yourself. He has noticed that the best people care only about impact, not about pleasing their bosses to get promoted.
ex: Andy Rachleff values slugging percentage over batting average: rare big wins beat frequent small ones
He wanted projects big enough to shrink the existing business to a tenth of the whole
Reforge's vision, strategy, roadmap framework is a useful reference

terms.d: Repeat the vision, state your motives

result.d: Teams want to build and promote it together

l52|79.c: Just keep publishing and you beat most podcasts, but only pick a topic you'd do for free.
l52|79.e: There are millions of podcasts, but only a small fraction are still publishing and have more than ten episodes. Put out one episode a week for ten weeks and you're ahead of most of them. Still, statistically, someone without an existing audience probably won't make it work. The first six to nine months bring almost no income, and the workload is far more than "an hour of talking a week." He suggests committing to one eight-episode season as a test, choosing the topic that makes people lean in at a dinner table, and using an outside deadline to force decisions.
ex: He originally planned a dad-parenting podcast, but his interests shifted after his child was born
Kevin Rose pressed him for a show name on air, and he settled it within days
You can start with a private RSS feed and send it to friends

l52|79.c: Be a few people's favorite show rather than everyone's "it's fine" show.
l52|79.e: He treats content quality as a podcast's product-market fit: no amount of launch tactics can rescue mediocre episodes. Podcasting is an intimate medium. People listen while walking, and a regular release becomes a ritual in their lives. Die-hard fans write reviews, share episodes, suggest topics, and even apply for jobs. Following your own excitement when choosing topics often beats chasing big-name guests who "pull numbers." His episodes with obscure guests, he found, drew the most thank-you emails.
ex: A survey around episode 50 showed every episode but one was someone's favorite
Tim Ferriss's episode on violin making split his audience
Keep a fixed release schedule and listeners will nag you for the next one

items.t: Content with a point of view

items.d: An intimate medium with a listening ritual
They suggest topics; you keep refining

l52|79.c: Concentrate your push at launch to hit the charts, then watch the download trend, not the raw number.
l52|79.e: Apple's charts mostly reward the speed of new subscriptions, not total downloads. So prepare two or three episodes, call in every favor at once, and you can briefly spike up the chart. A screenshot of a top-ten ranking can be used forever to invite dream guests. Put your best episode first. Afterward, ignore the first three episodes, which friends propped up, and watch whether episodes four through six are rising or falling, along with completion rate. For a typical show, fewer than half of listeners make it to the end.
ex: He estimates about 3,000 downloads per episode already puts you in the top 1%
At 10,000 to 20,000 downloads per episode, podcast networks start calling
His best episode has a completion rate of about 65% to 70%

l52|79.c: Podcasts have no recommendation algorithm, so bootstrap through channels that do and that already have audiences.
l52|79.e: TikTok and YouTube automatically push good content to more people; a podcast can only grow slowly. His practical moves: build an email list of friends and acquaintances long before launch; find questions about your topic on Twitter and Reddit and answer them properly; cut each episode into short clips for platforms with recommendation engines; guest on other podcasts with content their listeners genuinely need; and put the show in your email signature. Whether clips actually drive downloads is hard to measure, but they build the brand and give you leverage when inviting guests.
ex: His friends-and-family email list, built over many years, had about 1,100 people
Early on, Gary Vaynerchuk answered wine questions online one by one
Danny Miranda got millions of views by posting large volumes of clips

root.d: Make up for the missing algorithm

items.d: Reply to questions about your topic
Tailor your pitch to their listeners

l52|79.c: A few hundred dollars of ads in the Overcast podcast app diagnoses both your packaging and your content.
l52|79.e: Paying to acquire a podcast listener costs roughly $3 to $10, which doesn't pay off early on. But ads in the Overcast app are cheap, priced by demand, and report impressions, clicks, and subscriptions along with industry benchmarks. A click rate below the benchmark means your topic, description, or cover art isn't appealing. Clicks that don't turn into subscriptions mean people heard the trailer or an episode and decided it wasn't for them. You can even test your positioning with only a trailer before recording a single real episode.
ex: The same ad slot cost $200 one week and $700 another
He spent about $1,000 in total for a few hundred subscribers
The benchmark is about 50 subscriptions; once he got only 7

l54|83.c: Early on, PMs get ahead on hard skills. Once the job expands, people skills become the bottleneck.
l54|83.e: He splits skills into two groups. "IQ" skills are execution, product sense, and strategy. "EQ" skills are communication, leadership, and management. As an individual contributor just joining a company, the first group produces results fastest. Once you're promoted to manage people and drive company-level goals across teams, ambiguity and pressure spike, and the second group sets your ceiling. EQ skills are harder to learn and differ for each person, so you need self-awareness first and then steady practice. Many people get stuck at a level because colleagues only mention their lack of EQ in calibration meetings and never say it to their face.
ex: Communication moves from "clear and concise" to storytelling tailored to the audience
A CEO and a CFO care about different parts of the same update

l54|83.c: Interviewing is badly underrated: a great company changes your trajectory, and dozens of mock interviews get you in.
l54|83.e: Working at a great company puts you next to strong people and real examples of good work, and apart from connections, the way in is the interview. Yet most people only read up and rehearse in their heads, never doing a single real mock interview. He recommends dozens, ideally as deliberate practice with people who interview well. Interviews never give you feedback, and the pressure is even higher for candidates from underrepresented groups. So he has his mentees form groups of three to five and practice together, aiming to be good enough to pass even on their worst day.
ex: Over the years he interviewed at Google and Meta several times without success
When he got the Slack offer, he says he "barely" made it

items.d: Practice with people who interview well

l54|83.c: To learn a new skill, set a provable result first, then work backward to the questions and the people.
l54|83.e: When he joined Slack he knew nothing about growth, so he set himself a goal: lift new-user activation by several percentage points through experiments within six months. Then he listed the questions he'd need to answer to get there, skimmed the literature to check he was asking the right ones, and went to the best people in the field for advice. Once he had a framework, he worked with a user researcher and a data analyst to test it. With results in hand, he went back to his mentor, reported, and asked the next question. This forces you to learn, and it's far faster than reading around a topic.
ex: He sought advice from Bangaly Kaba, who came from Facebook's growth team
The framework was understand, identify, execute, with most time spent on understanding
Within six months, changes to the new-user experience lifted activation by double digits

items.d: Like lifting activation in six months
Skim the material to calibrate them

l54|83.c: Reverse-engineer great examples, watch the drafts behind them, and work on one skill at a time.
l54|83.e: He collects the best strategy docs, executive weekly updates, and emails inside the company and reverse-engineers which questions they answer. He also sits in on other PMs' meetings and presentations, and even asks to watch their next strategy doc go from outline to final draft, because the real learning is in the iterations. Practice is one skill at a time: give yourself three to six months, take apart one example a week, then spend a few hours polishing your own version. Reading an article and slipping back into old habits teaches you nothing. Skills are like muscles, and they shrink when you stop training.
ex: Five or six good examples reveal about 80% of the pattern
Read The Pyramid Principle, and keep a folder of excellent emails

items: Try to fix many things at once
Take apart one example a week
One skill for three to six months

d.verdict: IQ skills improve in months; EQ skills take years

l54|83.c: To get honest feedback, ask specific questions and respond to criticism with genuine enthusiasm.
l54|83.e: People only give critical feedback when they feel safe, and employees from underrepresented groups often find that trust harder to earn naturally. His approach: ask about a specific goal, such as "did I come across with executive presence in that update?" Criticize yourself first, then invite their view. However much it stings, thank them warmly and sincerely, and show vulnerability by telling them they don't need to soften it. The most valuable feedback is about subjective impressions, like "when you're concentrating you look angry." Almost nobody says that to your face.
ex: His mentor Lawrence Ripsher pointed out that he goes quiet when nervous
Someone told him that asking questions without context made him seem junior

items.d: Lower the bar for them to speak

l54|83.c: What others keep praising and you take for granted is your strength, and its flip side is your weakness.
l54|83.e: A mentor gave him one question for finding strengths: what do people keep saying you're good at that you think is no big deal? A fish doesn't think swimming is special. Once you find it, ask why you're good at it; in his case the root was curiosity. The bigger insight is that strengths and weaknesses aren't opposites but the same dial, read as a plus or a minus depending on the situation. Once you see that, you only need to turn it up or down for the occasion instead of rejecting part of yourself.
ex: He asks good questions, but without context it can look like he doesn't know
He's good at simplifying, but he goes quiet until the model is worked out

marks.d: Get to the heart of the problem

l54|83.c: Start a mentor relationship with the smallest possible ask, then report back on how the advice was used.
l54|83.e: He picks mentors on two criteria: they're good at exactly the thing he wants to improve, and they can explain it clearly. Such people are everywhere; the hard part is the opening. More than nine in ten people ask for a call right away. He sends one specific question that takes two minutes to answer. After getting the advice, he writes back later to say how he used it and what happened, a step almost nobody takes. Only then does he ask for fifteen minutes on a new problem. Each time he brings a concrete situation, takes notes, refers to the last conversation, and asks what he can do to help in return.
ex: He met Bangaly at a recruiting event and Lawrence at a dinner
He used a CEO's framework to rewrite a nonprofit's mission, then wrote back to thank him

items.d: One question answerable in two minutes
Explain how the advice was used
Fifteen minutes on a new problem
Bring context, take notes, help back

l55|84.c: A great product manager is first a great storyteller who turns messy opinions into one memorable line.
l55|84.e: He breaks storytelling into two parts. The first is synthesis: in a review, everyone has a different opinion, and whoever can pull those into a clear conclusion or a useful way of framing the problem moves things forward. It's a bit like literary criticism, building an argument out of scattered observations. The second is memorability. People give you only a few dozen seconds of attention, so an insight has to be boiled down until an executive can repeat it in a meeting. Only then has the knowledge really landed and started driving action. His practice: clear your own context and retell the story as someone with zero background would hear it.
ex: At Uber, good research insights got casually quoted by CEOs Travis and Dara
As a teaching assistant explaining pointers, he learned to borrow real-world analogies

items.d: Everyone in the review says something different
Offer a framework or a way to see it

l55|84.c: Ideas and solutions can come from anyone, but the product manager alone must own the "why."
l55|84.e: At Microsoft working on Hotmail, he wrote every detail into the spec, down to tables of error handling. When he took over the whole YouTube iOS app, that became impossible. Designers and engineers made small decisions all day without him in the room. The only approach that scales is making sure everyone understands why the work matters and what problem it solves. He also borrows the "five whys" from engineering postmortems: when users ask for a feature, ask what problem sits behind it, then why that problem exists. That often uncovers a much bigger opportunity.
ex: Figma's engineering team runs "five whys" in incident postmortems

items: Falls apart as the team grows
Keeps working as the team grows

d.verdict: Anyone can own what and how; the PM owns why

l55|84.c: Closeness to users is in Figma's DNA, but Twitter is only a canary; balance it with other feedback.
l55|84.e: When Figma started, nobody believed a design tool could run in a browser. Founder Dylan Field kept showing it to designers, fixing what they complained about, and bringing it back, which turned those designers into evangelists. Dylan still reads more user feedback than anyone and often drops a tweet with zero likes into Slack, so the team created a small channel just to catch them. But he warns that a loud minority is not the whole picture. Support tickets skew negative, sales conversations reflect outside perception, and most users aren't on Twitter at all. Research and data fill in the rest.
ex: A private channel called "Concerning Tweets"
Visiting his home, Dylan asked his partner directly what frustrated her about the product

d.right: What users as a whole experience

l55|84.c: Quality comes from the team using its own product heavily and the personal ownership that creates.
l55|84.e: He believes the more time a company spends inside its own product, the better the product gets, because people naturally want to fix the tools they use all day. So he moved the PM team from writing memos to building presentations in Figma, and even runs performance calibration in FigJam. When an engineer personally hits a bug, it feels embarrassing and they fix it. Fixes engineers propose themselves also get estimated at about half the time of ones a PM assigns, so he tries not to block bottom-up work. The cautionary tale is branching and merging: built for large organizations unlike Figma, rarely used internally, and adoption after launch fell short.
ex: Uber employees took Ubers to work, so driver-side problems were visible
Branching and merging saw weak early adoption

items.d: Decks and calibration live in the product
Hurts more than reading a ticket
Fix it yourself, with shorter estimates

l55|84.c: Call them OKRs or not; good goals are readable, make you want to act, and reflect real work.
l55|84.e: Working on core product experience, he kept facing a dilemma: pick a secondary metric you can move but can't prove matters, or pick an important business metric several steps removed, where you can't show you moved it. Figma's OKRs once degraded into a task list, so he switched to a one-line "what we want to be true" plus a self-assigned grade. When a data leader joined, OKRs came back, but they felt like after-the-fact packaging of projects already decided, and engineers couldn't say what the team's goal was. They then tried calling them "commitments." He admits he still hasn't found the answer, only three criteria.
ex: On Uber's rider app he was once asked to own "incremental trips"
A self-graded "report card" that explains how the score was reached

terms.d: Clear at a glance, not an obscure metric
Makes you want to change what you do

result.d: Whether called an OKR or a commitment

l55|84.c: He hires PMs for three things: explaining a conflict, zooming between levels, and predicting experiment results.
l55|84.e: His favorite question is "tell me about a controversial product decision you were part of." Someone who presents both sides fairly and explains why the disagreement existed can hold different perspectives at once. A second test: after hearing them describe the problem, do you want to go work on it? That reveals storytelling ability. Next he looks for whether a candidate can move quickly up and down the tree of possible solutions, handling the big picture and the details. The third comes from former Uber product head Jeff Holden's "fast-forward to the future": imagine the experiment's result first, and if no outcome would change the decision, skip the experiment.
ex: Interview question: describe a controversial product decision you took part in
Jeff Holden: assume the experiment has already run; what did it show?

root.d: What he probes for in interviews

items.d: Present both sides of a dispute fairly
Make a dull problem feel urgent
Move quickly across levels of detail
Predict the result, skip wasted work

l55|84.c: Figma's product-led growth is really community-led: users rallying behind a new way of working.
l55|84.e: What actually spreads Figma inside a company isn't sales; it's the designers there who love it. Sales exists to arm those champions with data and stories and connect them to the rest of the company and its leadership. Early on, Figma deliberately built community: users could share design files publicly, so outsiders could see how other companies worked. Later came Friends of Figma groups around the world. Deeper down, the product has to inspire almost irrational love and carry a contested new idea, like multiplayer editing and a fully transparent process. Then users aren't defending a tool; they're defending a way of working.
ex: An early designer said, "If this is the future of design, I'm changing careers"
Friends of Figma groups meet regularly on Discord around the world

items.d: Designers who love the new way of working

l56|86.c: You can't retrofit collaboration; crossing from single-player to multiplayer lifts acquisition, retention and revenue together.
l56|86.e: She thinks Evernote's design philosophy was almost anti-social: it positioned itself as a personal second brain, and that capped its growth. Everyone at a company might use it, yet it never turned into a large enterprise contract. Once a product carries a shared workflow, referrals and collaboration bring in new users on their own. Colleagues agree that "this is where the work happens," so stickiness jumps. Revenue grows with the number of people using it and how deeply. Many bottom-up SaaS products get stuck at exactly this gap, from individual to team to enterprise.
ex: Figma for design and Jira or Linear for planning became default team platforms

l56|86.c: The three most common monetization mistakes: charging too late, pricing too low, and never revisiting it.
l56|86.e: A free trial early on can be treated as part of R&D cost, but many companies wait far too long to shift from building a product to building a business. Willingness to pay is the real signal of product-market fit. Not charging makes a product look cheap, forfeits feedback on what people will pay, and invites backlash when you finally do charge. Pricing too low isn't just a low base price; it includes having a single paid tier with no plans designed for different customer groups. Pricing should be treated like a roadmap and revisited every six to twelve months, around major releases.
ex: Evernote took years before it fully overhauled pricing

root.d: What she sees most often in startups

items.d: Missing feedback on willingness to pay
One tier, money left on the table

l56|86.c: Features that get users to the aha moment and build habit must be free; day-100 features can be paid.
l56|86.e: Free exists to shorten time to value, build habits, and create advocates. Free users also bring organic growth, which lowers the cost of acquiring customers. Paid features need sorting. "Day-one features," whose value is obvious on first use, can sit in an entry-level paid tier. Advanced features that depend on accumulated data shouldn't compete for a new user's attention; put them in higher tiers and monetize through upgrades. If there's a clear bridge to the enterprise market, it's worth giving up revenue at the individual level, which is exactly what Figma did.
ex: After Invoice2go repackaged tiers, upgrades doubled and the Pro price rose about 30%
Once Figma moved into enterprise, more than half its users weren't designers

items: Value is clear on first use
Put in free or entry tier

d.verdict: Map pricing and packaging to the user journey; keep it simple

l56|86.c: Price should track value: pick the right value metric, then tier prices by how much value people perceive.
l56|86.e: A value metric is the unit in which users receive value, such as API calls, storage, or messages sent. The more they use, the more they pay, a natural escalator. Evernote's research found that many people paid mainly because they used it so much they felt guilty not paying, a sign the free version was too generous. New users treated it like the notes app that came with their phone, while power users found $45 a year absurdly cheap. So the team redesigned plans around what each group perceived as value. Pure usage-based pricing has a catch, though: finance teams want predictable budgets.
ex: Evernote originally had one tier: $45 a year
She says only about 5% of companies are purely usage-based; most use a hybrid

marks.d: Treat it like a built-in notes app
Many devices, work and life depend on it

l56|86.c: Pricing should be led by a cross-functional group that ranks what customers need, then tests willingness to pay.
l56|86.e: Pricing shouldn't belong to a single department. In a product-led company, a growth PM and a data scientist can lead it; in enterprise software, bring in sales, finance and revenue operations. Step one is talking to customers: have them sort features into must-have, nice-to-have and don't-need, or give them 100 points to spread across features, because conversion usually hinges on one or two of them. Step two is taking the must-have bundle and running the Van Westendorp method, asking four price questions and plotting the curves to land on a price.
ex: Four questions: suspiciously cheap, a bargain, expensive but worth it, too expensive
The 100-point allocation measures each feature's relative value

l56|86.c: Pricing is an underrated growth lever: dare to raise prices and keep experimenting.
l56|86.e: She cites industry research: about half of companies that changed prices grew annual recurring revenue by at least 25%, and a 1% improvement in monetization affects profit roughly four times as much as a 1% improvement in acquisition. The biggest gains come from reworking pricing and packaging as a whole, not tweaking one price. In enterprise sales, keep probing the ceiling; losing 20% to 30% of deals on price is acceptable. For self-serve pricing pages, build the ability to run experiments, roll out region by region, and watch long-term effects such as churn the following year.
ex: Envoy's founder quoted 10x the price on the spot and the buyer didn't flinch
Invoice2go tested in Canada and Australia first
Judge a first-year discount by second-year retention

l56|86.c: The "modern growth stack" spares teams from building growth infrastructure and frees people for the core product.
l56|86.e: She sees the modern growth stack as the layer on top of the modern data stack: once data is in the warehouse, these are the workflow tools that use it to drive growth and revenue. Her own teams used to spend huge amounts of engineering time building experimentation, billing, metering and personalization systems in-house. Now there are dedicated products to buy. She looks for three things: breaking down data silos, letting business users self-serve, and proving hard returns in cost savings and new revenue, which matters even more when budgets tighten. Generative AI for marketing and sales copy also looks likely to deliver attributable returns.
ex: Product-led sales: Endgame, Pocus
Experimentation: Eppo, Amplitude; billing: Metronome, Orb
Reverse ETL: Hightouch, Census

items.d: Spot expansion-ready customers from usage data
Tied directly to revenue and core metrics
Reverse ETL breaks down data silos

l57|87.c: Low-performing teams fail in the same ways; high-performing teams succeed in very different ways.
l57|87.e: He borrows his friend Josh Arnold's "anti-Anna Karenina principle," a reversal of Tolstoy's famous line. Bad teams share the same anti-patterns and are easy to spot, while good teams reach the same principle by very different routes. Take "make better decisions faster." Some companies rely on strict process and red teams that challenge every plan. Others count on diverse perspectives colliding at the right moment. Still others let the CEO decide and attract people who buy the vision. Good product leaders vary too, from humble listeners to forceful debaters. So understanding the principle matters more than copying the practice.
ex: Josh Arnold's "anti-Anna Karenina principle"

items.d: Red teams challenge, layers of review
Diverse views collide at the right time
Attracts people who share the vision

l57|87.c: Top teams share a few traits: structure fits strategy, strong opinions loosely held, and faith in product compounding.
l57|87.e: He sees several common threads. Org structure, incentives, budgeting and even technical architecture line up with the current strategy; when they don't, hiring smart people and talking about empowerment won't help. These teams are almost stubborn about a few core beliefs and open about everything else. They believe today's results come from decisions layered up years ago, a devotion to craft that no data or ROI calculation can justify. Their leaders' words match their actions. And their skills fit the specific business context. It sounds like common sense; the hard part is actually doing it.
ex: Bezos: today's success was planted three years ago
AppFolio's founders refused to sacrifice quality and stayed close to customers

items.d: Nearly stubborn about a few beliefs
Aim for nine out of ten, not seven

l57|87.c: Whether people or systems decide success is unsettled; leaders should know their beliefs, then stretch a little.
l57|87.e: A room full of geniuses still fails under incoherent leadership and structure, while plenty of first-time founders succeed. High-performing companies either screen everyone ruthlessly or are very good at keeping people for years and growing the ones with potential. He admits he used to blame the environment for everything, and he urges people who insist on "only A-plus talent" to reflect too. Crediting success to a heroic leader is equally simplistic. A founder torn between investing in process or talent should first work out what they truly believe, be a coherent leader, and then shift slightly toward the other view.
ex: He thinks Satya Nadella's turnaround also relied on Microsoft's existing talent and structure
High performance is a moving continuum, not a state you reach and keep

marks.d: Shift a little away from your comfort zone

l57|87.c: Silicon Valley advice needs context: big companies should let small teams run full loops first; frameworks only help.
l57|87.e: Most product advice online comes from purely digital Silicon Valley companies whose main challenge has been scaling. Many executives at large enterprises have never shipped a product, and they carry annual budgets and sprawling IT systems. He suggests carving out small teams and letting them run several complete ship-and-learn cycles. Frameworks are learning tools that keep a team pointed in the right direction, not the goal. He also notes an attribution bias: successful people underrate luck and momentum, while people inside big companies overrate the system's resistance and underrate what's possible.
ex: Anheuser-Busch's B2B ordering app BEES
Angela, a product leader at LEGO, doing great work through a hard transformation

items: Practice the loop in small teams

d.verdict: Learn how Figma does it, then adapt to your context

l57|87.c: Skill is knowledge times practice, so run more full product loops instead of hoarding advice.
l57|87.e: He thinks ability equals knowledge times practice, moderated by environment, habits and motivation. Yet people mostly accumulate knowledge, and many managers feel perpetually inadequate under the weight of the advice industry. The data-informed product loop he taught at Amplitude goes: have a strategy; build a qualitative model and add measurement; decide where to focus; design bets; measure impact; and feed what you learn back into the strategy and model. Missing any step jams the loop. What matters is how many full laps you complete. Listening to podcasts is valuable mainly because you learn that a given topic is a real discipline.
ex: The North Star framework is one example of a qualitative model
He did roughly 800 one-on-ones in four years at Amplitude

items.d: For example the North Star framework

l57|87.c: Even a waterfall company has learning loops; don't wait until you quit to say "it was a mess."
l57|87.e: Even when a boss simply orders "build X," you can write a one-pager that argues for X as one of five options. Ask executives what they expect to observe if it works. List the assumptions and risks. These small moves build a portfolio while you work; otherwise, two or three years later you'll be in an interview shrugging that the company was terrible. He also distinguishes chronic from acute problems. Facing the same pandemic, companies that actively designed a response were visibly healthier than those that waited for normal to return and postponed organizational decisions.
ex: He watched 15 to 20 companies handle the pandemic differently

items.d: Argue X as one of five options
What would you see if it works?
Build a portfolio as you go

l57|87.c: Stop judging who has "product sense"; break it into specific skills that can be taught and practiced.
l57|87.e: He used to say "product sense" and "product thinking" too, but now deliberately breaks them apart: modeling a problem, systems thinking, deciding under uncertainty, facilitating discussion, reading the competitive landscape, and so on. Some people only ask "can we build this?" while others ask "should we?" Rather than sorting people into two camps, figure out which skills the second group is using, such as separating current tactics from optimal ones. He also wants more non-celebrity leaders to be visible, so people who don't buy the strong-individualist style have role models too.
ex: "Can we build it" versus "should we build it"
You can ask ChatGPT to read one situation through five different worldviews

result.d: Teachable and practicable

l57|87.c: Measurement exists to reduce uncertainty around key decisions; start small with analytics tools.
l57|87.e: He endorses Douglas Hubbard's view: measurement isn't copying the metrics competitors track, it's reducing uncertainty enough to make the next decision. Product is more like a game with permanently incomplete information than an exact science. So he keeps trying to persuade customers not to spend months cataloging every question and metric and turning instrumentation into a giant project. Hook up twenty or so events on the free plan and start using it, even if you throw it all out later. Much of the time you only discover what you don't know once you're using the tool.
ex: He recommends Hubbard's book How to Measure Anything
The book Accelerate modeled team performance with large-scale surveys

items.d: Even if you redo it later

l59|89.c: A startup's speed is low latency, not high output, so decide on informed conviction instead of waiting for experiments.
l59|89.e: After leaving Tinder to start a company, he at first felt slower: fewer engineers, no existing users to study. Then he realized big companies can always do more things at once, while a startup's edge is the very short wait between having an idea and testing it. His analogy: a fast car has a wide turning radius. A small company also lacks the traffic to run statistically significant experiments, so leaning on them too early just slows you down. Better to move once you have enough information to form a view, then see if you were right. He also found his big-company network favored deep specialists, so founders should join early-stage communities soon.
ex: Measure latency: how long until you learn the result of changing a button's text
Communities to join: Indie Hackers, Everything Marketplaces

items: Short wait from idea to test

d.verdict: Break big plans into small pieces so you get data daily or every two weeks

l59|89.c: Separate mission, strategy, roadmap and goals into five layers: build top-down, debug bottom-up.
l59|89.e: When a product manager can't choose between two features, the root cause is usually a strategy they haven't absorbed, or one that was never defined. He splits commonly confused terms into five layers. At the top is the company mission, an aspirational vision. Below it is company strategy, the rigorous logic for achieving that mission. Then product strategy, which connects company goals to day-to-day work. Then the roadmap, and only then the goals. You build the stack top-down. When a goal is missed, you work bottom-up to find which layer broke. Comparing Tinder and Hinge shows when to look like a competitor and when to differ.
ex: Vision can fold into the mission; one clear sentence is enough
Tinder deliberately skipped filters for height and income

items.d: Tinder: make single life fun / Hinge: designed to be deleted
Similar monetization; growth via influencers vs TV ads
Light swiping vs rich profiles and prompts
Some overlap, like both adding video chat

l59|89.c: A strategy document needs wireframes; with words alone, everyone imagines a different product.
l59|89.e: When he led trip-planning strategy at Tripadvisor, he set a rule: a strategy document without wireframes (rough sketches of the screens) wasn't finished. His analogy: nobody hires an architect who won't produce a blueprint. Describe a strategy only in words and everyone pictures a different product. One test is to ask what belongs in the four or five slots of a mobile app's bottom navigation bar. Different answers mean different ideas about where the value is. Not having a designer is no excuse. A product manager can sketch by hand or use a tool like Balsamiq and have concept wireframes in an afternoon.
ex: Trip planning is a problem many startups have failed to crack
The litmus test: which four or five tabs go in the navigation bar

terms.d: Like a blueprint; low fidelity is fine

result.d: Shared view of limited screen space

l59|89.c: Data only spots anomalies; interviews explain them. Tinder's biggest spenders weren't rich.
l59|89.e: Tinder noticed a small group of users driving a large share of one-off purchase revenue, spending hundreds of dollars a month on Super Likes and Boosts. The team assumed they were wealthy people showing off. One-on-one interviews showed their incomes weren't higher. Their need was just more urgent: military members, salespeople who travel constantly, people who had just moved to a new city. They didn't compare the price to other subscription apps. They compared it to the cost of dating itself. That insight led to a higher-tier subscription and Super Likes with an attached message, priced far above what the team had expected.
ex: New product: Tinder Platinum
Super Like with a message lets you write someone before matching

items.d: A few users spend hundreds a month
Urgent need; compared to dating costs
Premium tier, Super Like with message

l59|89.c: Set goals after the roadmap, and pick the type of goal based on what the team understands.
l59|89.e: Setting goals first is like planning a road trip by saying "drive 250 miles" without picking a destination. At Tripadvisor, teams chased immediate bookings and undermined the strategy of getting users to return directly and plan trips on the site. He also argues goals should match the team's risk. If you don't yet know what drives retention, set a goal to understand it. If you understand it but lack tools, resolve the dependency. Once resources are in place, measure execution. Only then test whether the strategic hypothesis holds. And when you miss a goal, you should know why.
ex: He prefers NCTs (narratives, commitments, tasks) over OKRs
A 2x2: did you hit the goal, and do you know why

items.d: Don't yet know where the levers are
Know the levers but lack tools or resources
Test whether the hypothesis is right

l59|89.c: Product management breaks into four areas and twelve skills, the same from APM to CPO at different depths.
l59|89.e: The framework came out of Tripadvisor's product rotation program. Hiring a senior product manager in Boston took three to six months, so they hired new graduates and trained them, which forced the team to define what a PM must actually be able to do. The four areas are product execution, customer insight, product strategy, and influencing people, with three skills each. An associate PM focuses on personal execution; a CPO builds the system that lets whole teams execute well. He suggests you and your manager each score every skill. Wherever you disagree is the place to dig in. That turns surface-level feedback into root-cause feedback that compounds.
ex: The rotation: four six-month stints over two years
Three ratings: needs focus, on track, exceeds expectations

root.d: Same structure from APM to CPO

items.d: Data fluency, voice of customer, UX design
Business outcomes, vision and roadmap, strategic impact

l59|89.c: Micromanaging isn't a sin: dive in briefly when direction is off, teach the framework, then step back.
l59|89.e: New managers fail in two common ways. Some treat reports as extensions of themselves and get involved in everything, which damages trust and caps how many people they can lead. Others let go entirely without giving context or guardrails. He argues that becoming senior doesn't mean getting more abstract; it means widening your "dynamic range." Steve Jobs, Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg all go deep into details. The ideal is that you trust the direction and the team runs itself. When you don't, step in briefly and specifically, and explain the framework behind your decision. The goal is a team that eventually judges better than you do.
ex: Your relationship with your own boss also rests on alignment and confidence in you

items.d: Low confidence in the team's direction
Help the team see why this choice

l61|92.c: Engineers moving into product must unlearn the reflex to say no and first try to make ideas work.
l61|92.e: Engineers spend years paying for half-baked ideas, maintaining the code and taking the on-call pages, so they develop an immune response that rejects new ideas on sight. In product, though, ideas come from everywhere in the company. New ideas are fragile, and a hard "that's impossible" can kill a direction with huge reach and impact. His practice is to first spend real time imagining how the idea could work, and to write those attempts down. If it genuinely doesn't hold up, then say no. A no that comes after honest effort carries far more weight.
ex: He suggests engineers spend 10 minutes imagining how an idea could work
Saying no is often good instinct; the key is trying first

items.d: Map a real path, not a token effort
So the judgment has a paper trail

l61|92.c: Fund new products with profits, not people pulled from the core, or competitors will overtake the core.
l61|92.e: Mixpanel used its existing SDKs and event collection to expand into messaging and data infrastructure. But the people came from the core analytics product, and its features fell behind competitors. His lesson: a leader should keep outspending everyone on the core, then use the profits from it to fund new lines. Adjacent categories each have strong incumbents, so you end up sixth or eighth, and together they add little revenue. And shutting down a business that has had some success is far more painful for the organization than anyone expects, so think hard before starting one.
ex: Adjacent categories: CDPs, messaging, feature flags
He estimates such add-on products bring in only 5 to 10 percent of revenue

items.d: Rivals invest more in the core
Killing a modest success is very painful

l61|92.c: In a crisis, rank the roadmap by churn reasons and ARR for speed; once stable, switch to design-led work.
l61|92.e: In 2018 the core product was losing about 40 percent of its revenue. Customers still needed analytics; they were leaving for competitors with more features. The company cut the other two lines, grouped the churn reasons that sales and customer success had logged for years, sorted them by ARR (annual contract value), and made the top ten the roadmap, with engineers talking directly to customers. That works when competition is fierce and what's missing is table-stakes features. But it stopped working fast: shipping without overall design meant every feature had low usage. So they opened a second, design-led track to rethink the product's core building blocks.
ex: About 100 features shipped in the first year
Retention rose from about 60 to 90 percent; NPS went from 16 to 50
His line: don't mow the lawn while the house is on fire

items.d: Top ten churn reasons become the roadmap

l61|92.c: Product success often comes down to architecture, so give designers protected time away from firefighting.
l61|92.e: In high-speed shipping mode, design got called in at the end of each project to polish, and often slipped in a simplified version too, so scope kept growing. As engineering manager, he made a deal with the head of design: for the next three months, projects wouldn't depend on design. A group of designers instead worked out the product's core building blocks: how many there should be, how users discover them, how they relate, and the fewer the better. Once charts and interactions were unified, any improvement applied everywhere automatically. Usage multiplied, and things like dark mode became possible.
ex: Notion's page-plus-blocks architecture can carry a huge number of features
With unified chart interactions, new visualizations inherit every improvement

result.d: Also easier to use and discover

l61|92.c: Don't let confidence and effort scores kill big ideas too early, and replace estimates with a time appetite.
l61|92.e: RICE scoring is simple and robust, but innovative ideas with big reach and impact naturally have low confidence and unclear effort, so they sink to the bottom. He has the team look only at reach and impact first, then spend about a week attacking the idea across functions. That often turns up a safer, cheaper approach. Then they add confidence and effort back in and score, balancing innovation, incremental improvements and tech debt. Estimation works the same way. Instead of quoting a timeline before the problem is understood, set an appetite, then compare what you'd do with four weeks versus eight. That forces the team to tackle the core of the problem first and review honestly when time is up.
ex: RICE: reach, impact, confidence, effort
Basecamp's Shape Up: appetite instead of estimates

items: Fuzzy confidence and effort sink ideas

right.t: Set aside C and E first
items: Filter only by reach and impact
About a week of cross-functional work
Then add C and E back and score

d.verdict: Give big ideas a fair shot, then mix innovation, increments and debt

l61|92.c: Raw customer feedback should flow unfiltered to everyone, so engineers can follow up with customers directly.
l61|92.e: In 2018 a sales engineer set up an automatic Slack feed of the feature gaps that sales and customer success were logging. It was raw and unfiltered by product managers, and took about 20 minutes a day to read. Engineers would flag an item, email the customer directly to ask more, and then improve the product themselves. That took the gatekeeping burden off PMs. Later the sources grew to include Twitter, NPS surveys and win-loss notes, all flowing into BigQuery, enriched with the account's ARR and its customer success manager, then pushed to Slack and Notion. The cost is learning not to react to every single piece of feedback.
ex: An email emoji marks "I'll go ask this customer"
BigQuery plus Census pushes the data back into everyday tools

items.d: Which brings a new round of feedback

l61|92.c: Track events on the server by default, not through client SDKs, so the data is reliable and maintainable.
l61|92.e: Many people equate product analytics with installing an SDK in the website and app. He calls that the biggest mistake. On the web, ad blockers and the like drop 20 to 30 percent of events. On mobile you write tracking twice, once per platform, which creates duplicate events with slightly different meanings, and new tracking only reaches users who upgrade, so old broken events linger for years. Server-side tracking works across platforms and can be updated everywhere at once. An event is just a log line with a user ID, something engineers already know how to write. He also believes the data warehouse is becoming the company's center of gravity for data, with events as the universal model for analytics.
ex: Web tracking loses 20 to 30 percent of events
Snowflake, BigQuery and Redshift are becoming the data center of gravity

items.d: Structured events with a user ID
One source of truth for the company

l62|93.c: A temporary organization works through a one-sentence mission, relentless repetition, and a laughably small MVP.
l62|93.e: Early in the pandemic, vaccine eligibility was chaos. VaccinateCA had volunteers call pharmacies and put the answers on a map. The data ended up more complete than the federal government's and most states', and fed Google Maps. She draws three lessons. First, the ideas that pull people in are simple ones everyone grasps instantly and knows how to help with. Second, repeat the same few points over and over, or people fill in the blanks themselves. Third, phones and a spreadsheet were enough to start, and doing it revealed that most of her assumptions about tools and regulation were wrong. Once the goal was met, they deliberately shut the organization down.
ex: Messaging as simple as "pick up the phone, help save lives"
She estimates she repeated the same three points about 5,000 times

items.d: Everyone gets it and knows how to help
Otherwise people fill in the gaps
Phones plus a spreadsheet; learn as you go

l62|93.c: A small company wins trust beyond its size by making every touchpoint look more considered than it needs to.
l62|93.e: Airtable handles critical workflows and sensitive data, and customers only hand that to companies they trust. Every touchpoint, from word of mouth and ads to landing pages and support, adds or subtracts trust. So beyond shipping fast, someone should proofread the emails, the images should look right, and sample data should use industry in-jokes rather than a list of Jane Does, so users feel the product was built for them. In public, talk about the larger trend you belong to. Her method: appoint one person as the "quality avatar," give them a simple checklist, and spend about 15 extra minutes each time.
ex: At 15 people, they took visiting customers out to eat so the office size wouldn't show
They bought leftover billboard inventory in New York for as little as a few thousand dollars each

terms.d: Proofread emails, decent images, industry-specific examples
Talk about the trend, not just the product
Like a billboard near a customer's office

result.d: Customers hand you a six-figure budget

l62|93.c: A do-anything product spreads through internal champions grown at scale, and the champion rarely holds the budget.
l62|93.e: Airtable can be used for anything, but "build your own software" sells nothing in the abstract. The magic is in specific use cases. Early on, they piped new sign-ups into Slack, emailed them with one click to set up a call, and helped them build their first base. Whoever succeeded went on to help colleagues with other problems, became a hero inside the company, and effectively sold Airtable for free. The champion is the person building tables on a Friday night, not the budget holder. Six months later, with hundreds of people already using it, you go to IT and ask them to pay. Spreading within a company is the real superpower.
ex: A "tinkerer" psychographic, targeted on Facebook by interest group
Champions got branded swag at the AirPods level
Inside one company, usage went from 10 to 1,000 people in a year

items.d: Over-invest to make one person succeed
Hundreds of people already using it

l62|93.c: Customer success and marketing are fundamentally the same job, so B2B companies should invest in it early.
l62|93.e: Both identify needs, get customers to see the product as the solution, remove friction in getting value, encourage sharing, and turn one person's insight into a resource anyone can use. The only difference is one works at scale and the other one-on-one. Airtable built customer success before it had a sales team. The key is a conveyor belt: the systems customer success builds for big accounts get distilled into templates and blog posts that the next small company can pick up directly. Her informal metric is how many people got promoted because they used the product well.
ex: Informal metric: how many people got promoted thanks to Airtable
If you won't listen to customer success, don't hire them
The founder sent 3 outreach emails a week for 10-minute calls

items.d: Help a customer build their system
Blog posts and templates for small customers
Bring back new needs and insights

l62|93.c: For a horizontal product, templates narrow the "what is this for" gap; don't expect them to drive acquisition.
l62|93.e: If a product that does everything doesn't instantly show someone how it solves their problem, they say "cool, I'll come back later" and never do. A few well-matched templates connect the user's problem to the product, and they also help it spread inside a company. But many people wrongly assume templates were Airtable's traffic source. They never did SEO on them, and the templates were hard to even find in search. If you want templates to acquire users, treat it as a major programmatic SEO investment the way Zapier did, and decide your goal and how you'll measure it first.
ex: Airtable had only about 50 people from 2015 to 2018, so it had to choose
Zapier gets huge traffic from programmatic SEO

marks.d: Narrow the gap, help internal spread

l62|93.c: Creating a new category is usually a waste; elevating a profession is far more powerful.
l62|93.e: Two claims she is willing to stand behind. First, unless your industry runs on trade shows, flashy event sponsorships are almost always a waste. Send people, but don't pay to hang your logo. Second, treating category creation as the pinnacle of product marketing is often not worth it. In B2B software it's an enormous undertaking, and buyers don't buy just because you have "no competitors." What works better is elevating a profession. A job is an identity and people will fight for it, while a category is just a line in a budget. Build community around the profession, promote yourself less, and you become part of that identity.
ex: Gainsight made "customer success" a recognized profession
DevOps was reshaped into a job people aspire to
Datadog and Notion have done community well

d.verdict: Make the customer the hero of the story, not your company

l62|93.c: PR doesn't bring users, only credibility, and launches should be a series rather than a single event.
l62|93.e: A big press feature often buries its one link in the twelfth paragraph. Few people click, and few search for you afterward, so as an acquisition channel it barely works. PR's real value is credibility, best used where you send it yourself and can measure the result: recruiting emails and cold outreach. Coverage for its own sake mostly boosts internal morale. Launches don't need to be tied to PR either. Rather than betting on one big launch, ship something new every month or two, ride people's response to novelty, and keep showing up in the right communities.
ex: Two sound uses of PR: recruiting and lifting cold-outreach reply rates
The link in a TechCrunch story is often buried in paragraph twelve

items.d: Almost none, so use PR for credibility

l63|94.c: Stripe's success came from consistently getting many decisions right, not from one or two big calls.
l63|94.e: She has traced back Stripe's turning points and concluded that even with different choices, the company would likely have ended up in the same place. The real difference was a culture that kept producing good decisions. First, deep respect for thinking: everyone asks why, and nobody gets away with "industry best practice." She still writes memos imagining how co-founder Patrick Collison would push back. Second, a writing culture: if you can't write it clearly, you haven't thought it through. Third, not overthinking: rigorously identify which decisions are truly irreversible "trapdoors," and decide everything else fast.
ex: Pricing is often treated as one-way, but you can grandfather existing users
Titles are one-way doors: hard to take back once given
One operating principle: micro-pessimist, macro-optimist

terms.d: Slow down only for trapdoor decisions

result.d: Rather than nailing one or two turning points

l63|94.c: Teams don't think big because they fear failure, drown in firefighting, and never get permission to think.
l63|94.e: Nobody wakes up wanting to ship a mediocre incremental improvement. The problem is that organizations put up barriers without meaning to. Leaders want the upside of innovation but won't accept the cost of failure, so talk about failure openly and lower the stakes with small teams and early customer feedback. If a team is buried in tech debt, product debt and outages, help them dig out first. And thinking big is genuinely hard, so build explicit permission to think into the process.
ex: Rename postmortems to retrospectives
Send failures to the all-company "shipped" mailing list too
In planning, ask what you'd do with 20 percent more time or double the team

root.d: Barriers the organization sets by accident

items.d: Share failures openly, lower the stakes
Diagnose, then clear debt and outages

l63|94.c: Incubate new products with one or two people, run them like company-funded startups, and keep them apart from the core.
l63|94.e: Retool launched three new products in one year, Workflows, Mobile and Database, and at least one came from a "crazy ideas" document collected from the whole company at the start of the year. The approach: each direction starts with one or two people who spend about six months immersed in customers and prototypes, and only gets more people once there's signal. Retool acts like a VC, providing resources and existing customers, and the team has to show a return in engagement or even revenue. Early on, they deliberately operate apart from the core team. The cost is integration work later. She also reflects that having all three mature at once drained the organization, and staggering them would have been better.
ex: About 3 to 8 items from the crazy-ideas doc ship each year
Only after running separately did Mobile find its customers differed from the core product's
Retool had about 300 people at the time

items.d: About six months of prototypes with customers
The company invests like a VC

l63|94.c: Process reduces variance by definition, so keep it minimal and leave an escape hatch for your best people.
l63|94.e: Companies add process because they worry about too much variance and want everyone at the same standard. But while process raises the floor, it also pulls the most creative people, who never needed it, back toward average. Using AI as a lens, she notes we keep asking humans to be more machine-like and formulaic, and the price is losing the real peaks. So write at the top of every template that it's only a floor and can be skipped when it doesn't fit. Managers should spot the people who don't need process, give them cover, and decide whether they're willing to "break the org" for that person.
ex: Former Stripe COO Claire Hughes Johnson's question: would you break the org for this person?
The five-paragraph essay taught in school is a formulaic example

d.verdict: Before adding process, make sure you can afford its cost

l63|94.c: Every level, company, function and team, needs a charter, goals and a roadmap, written top-down.
l63|94.e: At Stripe they asked companies like Amazon and Atlassian about their planning processes, only to find big-company methods don't transplant to a small one. Her view is that at any stage, every level needs three documents. The charter covers mission, vision and strategy. The goals say what to achieve and how to measure it. The roadmap says what to ship. Many teams work backward from the roadmap; she argues for writing the charter first. The charter's time horizon stretches with maturity: before product-market fit, look three months out; a well-running company can look ten years ahead.
ex: Before product-market fit, a charter looks about three months out
A mature company's charter can look about ten years out

items.d: What to achieve and how to measure it

l63|94.c: Build for your best users, ship a skateboard before an axle, and split R&D seventy-twenty-ten.
l63|94.e: Early on, don't distort the product for a few abusers or ill-fitting users. Onboarding, for example, should serve the people who get it right away. An MVP has to deliver complete value end to end. Her analogy: when building a car, make a skateboard first, not just an axle. Retool Mobile targeted only companies whose frontline staff manage inventory. On resources, seventy percent goes to the core product that already has product-market fit, including maintenance and tech debt; twenty percent to non-core projects that are strategically necessary; ten percent to bets.
ex: Founder David Hsu's line, via Anthony: if abuse becomes a problem, that's a good problem
"Build the skateboard, not the axle" comes from design lead Ryan

items.d: Includes maintenance, bugs and tech debt

l63|94.c: Managers shouldn't hire in their own image; build a PM team whose strengths complement each other.
l63|94.e: Managers tend to hire people like themselves, because those are the skills they recognize and value. But the best product teams are complementary. She balances home-grown PMs, who know the product and carry the culture but lack outside experience, with PMs from other companies, who bring more disciplined product methods. She also balances executors with visionaries. Every six months she lists the team's strengths and gaps, hires specifically for the gaps, and asks each product area lead to hire people unlike themselves.
ex: Retool has three product areas, each with its own lead
Many Retool PMs previously held customer-facing roles

items.d: The team beats the sum of individuals

l64|97.sc: Every PM is an AI PM
l64|97.c: Every product manager will soon be an AI product manager and must learn to partner with research scientists.
l64|97.e: She believes almost every product needs personalization, good recommendations and automation. Finish a show, and the product should suggest similar ones. AI becomes the default. So PM teams will include research scientists who build models, and PMs have to get used to the uncertainty of research. Unlike ordinary work, where you build and ship, a research effort can run for a year, fail, and start over. In her view, a good AI product sits where three circles overlap: users want it, the business can sustain it, and the technology and research can actually deliver it.
ex: Netflix-style recommendations are table stakes for every product
She suggests spending an hour a week shadowing research scientists

terms.d: A real need and pain point
Can become a business and make money

result.d: Only worth building where all three overlap

l64|97.c: Avoid the shiny-object trap: find a problem that deserves a smart solution before you talk about AI.
