l64|97.e: Doing AI for its own sake often means six months of work before discovering the payoff is tiny. Her framing: a generalist PM helps the team build the right product, while an AI PM helps the team solve the right problem, sometimes owning a problem rather than a product. So first confirm there are users, a pain point, and that the pain point genuinely needs an intelligent solution. Sketch a high-level approach, then talk to data scientists about how to build it. Idle data you already have is the starting point. A team without even a dashboard should start collecting data; that's step one toward AI.
ex: Intelligence you can add: safety, personalization, fraud detection, recommendations
You could start by hiring a data science intern

items.d: Real users with a real problem
Does it require a smart solution?
Decide what you're trying to build

l64|97.c: Don't train a model for your MVP; fake the AI with a prototype to validate demand.
l64|97.e: Training a model ties up data scientists and expensive compute for weeks, which is a poor way to prove a market exists. Many early founders ask her whether to train a model first to demonstrate demand. Her answer: build a Figma prototype and fake what the AI would do, then show it to users. Once you have data of your own, or can borrow it from an adjacent product, build the real thing, like recommendations or automation. After that, the PM personally has to decide how accurate the model must be before launch, a new question nobody has answered before.
ex: The PM sets the launch bar: 70% or 80% accuracy

items.d: Your own or an adjacent product's
PM decides how accurate is enough

l64|97.c: How much data you need depends on the task; public datasets only get you the same quality as everyone else.
l64|97.e: She compares a model to a child's brain: show it enough examples and it learns to recognize new ones, reporting how confident it is. Simple image classification might need only fifteen or twenty labeled pictures. Speech recognition or complex natural-language tasks need thousands upon thousands of examples, and some teams even synthesize fake data to train and test. Ready-made datasets are available for purchase, but since everyone buys the same ones, everyone ends up with the same quality. That's why big companies building services like voice recognition must collect more, and more varied, data of their own.
ex: Is there a dog in this picture? About 15 to 20 labeled images
Models output confidence, such as "70% sure it's a rhino"

marks.d: Anyone can buy; same quality for all
Thousands; needs your own varied data

l64|97.c: ChatGPT augments product managers rather than replacing them, clearing repetitive work so they can focus on strategy.
l64|97.e: She doesn't think GPT will put PMs out of work. It frees up time for more strategic thinking and may even open new kinds of work. She regularly asks ChatGPT to rewrite mission statements, because a mission has to be understood by executives, new hires, other departments and even competitors, and it writes more plainly and more inspiringly. She also asks it to list user segments with their motivations and pain points, and it often surfaces groups she hadn't considered. The rule is to start with your own thinking and let it polish and expand, not do the job for you.
ex: For a screenless wristband, it listed time-starved young professionals and other segments
Content shared across several project docs can be handed to it

root.d: Start with your idea, then augment

items.d: Clear and inspiring to every reader

l64|97.c: PMs don't need to train models themselves, but should learn some coding to understand how their tools are made.
l64|97.e: Non-technical people shouldn't be intimidated. PMs rarely need to write code to train a model, and no-code training tools exist. Still, she encourages learning a bit of programming and training a small model yourself, the way her childhood piano teacher insisted on classical fundamentals before free creation. That's how you understand where the tools you rely on every day come from, instead of trusting them blindly. Depending on how you learn best, pick a self-paced course or a coding bootcamp with a cohort.
ex: AutoML: upload labeled images and it trains a model
One student built a small X-ray reading model in three weeks
Drone photos plus AutoML cut inspections from weeks to hours

l64|97.c: AI PMs must withstand uncertainty and agree upfront that progress won't be measured by launches.
l64|97.e: She flags four difficulties. Training results can overturn your assumptions, so the PM has to be the captain who keeps the team motivated. Direction changes often, and managing a pivot upward with leadership is hard. Good data is hard to get; you may literally have to ask people on the street to contribute it. And ordinary PMs get promoted on launches, while research-heavy work ships rarely, so define what counts as progress with your hiring manager from day one. When asking for a big investment, she draws analogies to adjacent products in the company that seemed crazy but worked, and lays out a rollback plan and the worst-case impact.
ex: To win support: cite a successful precedent plus a rollback plan
The PM bridges research and product by finding a way to monetize

items: Build and ship on a set rhythm
Has to find ways to gather data

d.verdict: A great chance to build zero-to-one skills

l65|98.c: Customer obsession has to become policy: every employee delivers orders, which also filters out poor fits.
l65|98.e: Founder-led companies take on the founder's personality, and CEO Tony Xu is humble, competitive and obsessed with customers. So DoorDash requires every employee to personally deliver food at least four times a year, or do customer support if delivering isn't practical. He does it about once a month and almost always finds a problem, which goes straight into a dedicated Slack channel. It doubles as a culture filter. Not every engineer wants to drive McDonald's orders around, so interviewers say so upfront, and that attracts humble, customer-obsessed people.
ex: His daughter complained to Tony about an 18.5-mile sandwich delivery; a fix was underway by the time he got home
Telling a candidate "you came across as a jerk" to see how they take feedback

items.d: Deliver food at least four times a year
Like routes measured as the crow flies
A dedicated Slack channel, or the CEO

l65|98.c: For 10x results, put a generalist over an unfamiliar function, hire the best experts, then step aside.
l65|98.e: The first time he was asked to run a function he didn't know, he felt like an impostor and wanted to decline. Tony had him read the book Range and explained: hire a domain expert and you mostly get the usual playbook and incremental gains, while an outsider is more likely to redesign the whole system. His approach was to trust that he could add value, then tell candidates honestly, "I don't know this field as well as you; here's how I'll help, and then I'll get out of the way." That attracted top experts. Everyone says to hire people better than yourself, but few talk about what comes next: gradually stepping back.
ex: He went from managing about 1,500 people to leading 12
The brand leader he hired became CMO; the legal leader became general counsel

items: Hires the best experts to help

d.verdict: Generalist sets the stage, experts perform; better odds of 10x

l65|98.c: Write down how to work with you, and promise to help your reports find their next job.
l65|98.e: When headcount doubles or triples every year, culture is hard to replicate, but written things scale. His document covers three things: the traits he sees in successful people, the flaws he's working on (as a former lawyer, arguing for the sake of arguing), and his commitments to the team. One commitment is helping you find your next job, even outside DoorDash. Reports then tell him earlier when they're thinking of leaving, so he can line up a successor. Reference checks hear "he puts you first." And plenty of people come back. He even forwarded recruiter pitches to his own head of legal.
ex: The last 10 minutes of every one-on-one are reserved for career development
Kofi, a well-known marketer, joined after reading the document

items.d: My expectations and what success looks like here
Feedback received, like arguing for sport
Including helping you find your next job

l65|98.c: Have each side argue the other's case, then name the decider and a deadline, and hard decisions move.
l65|98.e: Disagreements among executives usually come from different metrics they own and different experiences. So step one is understanding motivations and making everyone feel heard. He often asks the person pushing for profit to give three reasons growth should come first. That instantly creates empathy, and sometimes people talk themselves into the other side. If there's still no consensus, be clear about who decides, whether the CEO, a business lead or a product lead, and set a date for the decision. Once it's made, everyone executes. His reputation for not building an empire and just wanting to win gives him standing to call this out.
ex: One business line pushing profit versus a new business pushing growth

items.d: Give the other side's three best reasons
Who decides if there's no consensus

l65|98.c: Managers should ask for critical feedback and publicly report what they changed because of it.
l65|98.e: Many new managers avoid giving critical feedback because they want to be liked. In one-on-ones he first asks reports to critique him, pressing if they hold back, and only then gives his feedback. Once he opens the door, two-way conversation gets easier. He learned this from Uber's T3B3: every review had to list three strengths and three things to improve. When you receive feedback, say thanks, but more importantly act on it. Treat it like customer feedback: report the three things you did and track progress. Nothing deflates people more than a survey that ends in a slide deck and no follow-up.
ex: Uber's T3B3: three strengths plus three areas to improve
For the lowest-scoring survey item, report back three concrete actions

items.d: Here's what I changed; is it better?

l65|98.c: Hard times make companies: they filter out opportunists, force cost discipline, and make hiring easier.
l65|98.e: His board once told him that hard times build companies. When Uber entered food delivery and DoorDash fell to fourth place, the opportunists left and the people who stayed believed in the mission. Having less money than rivals forced them to watch unit economics from the start. Talent is also more available in a downturn. Internal surveys showed employees actually liked crises, because there was one goal and resources were concentrated. In fundraising they only promised numbers they were confident of hitting, accepting a slightly lower valuation to earn investors' trust. Nearly out of cash before the Series D, everyone said no, but they only needed one yes.
ex: After the Series D, almost every round's lead investor had previously turned them down
Early in the pandemic, Tony waived about $100 million in restaurant commissions

root.d: The board: hard times build companies

items.d: Those who stay believe in the mission
Unit economics from the early days
Good people are looking for their next stop

l65|98.c: BD shouldn't customize the product for every deal; validate with manual workarounds first, then build a platform.
l65|98.e: Product and engineering capacity is DoorDash's most precious resource. Bring product in too early and they burn cycles on deals that never close; too late and you may have already conceded terms you shouldn't have. So he keeps the deal pipeline visible to them at all times. Product leader Rajat taught him that instead of building custom features for every DashPass partnership, it's better to build a scalable platform first, which also clarifies what you can promise in negotiations. The other rule is "dream big, start small": test with scrappy tactics like handing out promo codes, then ask for product resources.
ex: A hotel-chain deal to replace room service failed because franchisees wouldn't cooperate
DashPass partnerships with Chase and others moved from custom builds to a platform

items.d: Kept transparent to the product team
Single-store pilots, promo codes at the door

l66|100.c: Growth teams don't need to A/B test everything; experiments are mainly for de-risking big changes.
l66|100.e: Experiments serve two purposes: measuring impact precisely, or controlling risk when you make a big change. Knowing whether activation rose 6% or 7% rarely helps the business beyond a performance review, yet it eats engineering, analytics and product time. She argues for experimenting only when necessary and putting the effort into product development itself: talk to customers, define the problem rigorously, and test prototypes until you're confident you could ship to everyone tomorrow. This only works if the organization rewards real customer impact rather than just the numbers.
ex: Airtable shipped a feature letting form submitters keep a copy without an A/B test
After launch, attribution analysis was used to assess the impact

items.d: Precision often isn't worth the cost
Truly needed only for big changes
Customer interviews, prototypes, rigorous problem definition

l66|100.c: Redesign onboarding with one wizard that serves 90% of users, then personalize by how people learn and build.
l66|100.e: Airtable's problem was that building even a basic skeleton took too much effort. The team built an immersive wizard: pick your project type and what you want to track on the left, and a workflow takes shape on the right in real time. That was the single most effective change. They added personalization by use case and a "Mole" that pops up from the bottom of the screen for ongoing education, while removing a batch of tooltips. For segmentation, grouping people by learning style and how they build worked better than by function like marketing or product. Advanced features such as automations don't need to be taught on day one.
ex: Six to eight months of combined changes lifted activation by about 20%
Next she wants to distinguish builders from people invited in to collaborate

terms.d: Watch the workflow form as you click
Grouped by learning and building style
The Mole takes users from basic to advanced

result.d: Six to eight months of combined investment

l66|100.c: Set a high bar for activation; an activation rate of 5% to 15% is actually better.
l66|100.e: Airtable's team activation metric is "week-four multiplayer active": in week four, more than one person on a team is active in a workflow and contributing content. The analytics team showed it correlates strongly with long-term retention. The high bar means users have really built something, keep collaborating, and come back weekly. If 40% of users hit your metric, only a fraction of them will stick around long term. Better to pick one that only 5% reach but nearly all of whom stay, because moving it from 5% to 6% or 7% is a big deal. In practice, break the metric into its component steps to find leverage, and pair it with individual retention and build complexity.
ex: Supporting metrics: individual week-2 and week-4 retention, a build complexity score
Collaborative, per-seat products suit a team-level metric

items.d: Join as a team or an individual
Two or more people really contributing

l66|100.c: Change your north star as opportunities shift: find the biggest opportunity first, then make the metric reflect it.
l66|100.e: Growth teams need to stay nimble, and watching the same metric for too long often means you're not chasing the biggest opportunity. She thinks a north star should hold for at least six months to build momentum and expertise, but once it feels stale, change it. The method: draw the funnel on a whiteboard, combine it with analytics, find where the team's resources can move the needle most, then define a metric that reflects the output of that work, rather than letting a metric drive every decision from the start. Airtable's growth organization once switched its north star from revenue to user growth, because focusing on revenue led to short-sighted decisions.
ex: In product-led sales, it's better to defer revenue and let sales convert the account

items.d: Map how the business works on a whiteboard
Where can the team move the needle?
Reflects the output of that work
At least six months; swap when stale

l66|100.c: Use a reverse trial: new users get every premium feature first, then drop to a free plan when it ends.
l66|100.e: A free trial is time-limited and ends in a paywall; freemium offers a permanently free tier. She recommends combining them: give new users a full premium trial up front, use onboarding to show everything the product can do, and when it expires, drop them to the free plan so they keep using it. Before deciding, don't rush to competitors' pricing pages. First get clear on your company's monetization philosophy: if you care about millions of people using the product and building the brand, a free tier is worth it. You only get a few chances to ask for a credit card or a sales call, and using them too early burns trust.
ex: Trials can run 7, 14 or 30 days
Products that can't be self-serve can offer a sandbox or interactive demo first

items.d: Land directly in the premium plan
Self-serve payment or talk to sales

l66|100.c: Onboarding should serve what users need, not what the company wants to push: don't name features or sell by pricing tier.
l66|100.e: The common trap is employees designing onboarding around their own assumptions. One version is naming features, like a pop-up saying "this is Automations," which means nothing to a new user who hasn't found their footing. Better to explain what it does for me, and ideally turn it on with one click and carry the user through to completion. Another version is designing around pricing and packaging: people who use premium features pay more often, so onboarding pushes them hard, which isn't what a new user needs. Stay focused with the north star, and add guardrail metrics, for example investigating if an onboarding change cuts revenue by 10%.
ex: Guardrail metric: if an onboarding redesign drops revenue 10%, trace the cause

d.left: What the company wants to push

marks.t: Explain what it does for me

marks.d: Take users straight to the value

l66|100.c: A product-led business can be understood as join, evaluate, upgrade, expand, and teams can be organized around those steps.
l66|100.e: The framework describes a user's whole life in a product-led product. They join through Twitter or a colleague's invite. They evaluate whether the product deserves to become a habit, a step she deliberately doesn't call "activation." Once they see premium value, they upgrade through self-serve or sales. Then they expand across the organization, driving net revenue retention, renewals and new referrals, which loops back to join. It shouldn't be mapped mechanically onto four KPIs, but it lets everyone say which step an investment targets. Airtable started with acquisition, activation and monetization teams; expansion emerged as an opportunity only once large-company users grew.
ex: B2B growth has fewer, weightier customers, so it leans more on interviews and betas

l67|103.c: Product ops is both a system that keeps a product team running well and a partner role to PMs.
l67|103.e: She gives product ops two meanings. First, it's a thing: the system a product leader or PM builds so the team runs well, and no dedicated person is required. Second, it's a role, more common in recent years, meaning a person or team that works closely with PMs. As it matures, that role becomes a strategic advisor to the chief product officer, using qualitative and quantitative data to help product leaders make better-grounded decisions. The distinction matters because when problems appear, the first instinct should be "we need to build a system," not "we need to hire someone."
ex: After Pendo's bad launch, her first thought was to build a system, not create a job

items.d: A strong PM can build it alone
A dedicated person owns the ops work
Informs the CPO's decisions with data

l67|103.c: Product ops emerged naturally as the product function matured, just as sales and marketing grew ops roles.
l67|103.e: The problems were always there; people who had been PMs just felt them most. At Pendo, demand clearly exploded in the summer of 2019. Customer feedback needed consolidating, and internal alignment and transparency toward revenue teams were poor almost everywhere. During the pandemic many industries grew fast while shifting toward product-led growth. At the same time, the CPO's job changed from "ship, ship, ship" to owning business outcomes. Having PMs moonlight as the liaison to every ops team came at the cost of their own product goals, so someone was needed to build the structure.
ex: A colleague called summer 2019 "the summer product ops was born"
She cites Marty Cagan on moving from feature teams to outcome-driven teams

items.d: Many industries expanded during the pandemic

l67|103.c: Product ops does four main things: voice of the customer, the tool stack, content and education, and process.
l67|103.e: Mature teams value voice of the customer most: pulling qualitative and quantitative signals from sales, customer success, NPS and feedback tools together for PMs, then handing them to research to confirm or refute. It also tells revenue teams that not every problem needs a product change. Second is managing the PM tool stack, so data from systems like Salesforce flows into product analytics. Third is making content and in-app education part of the definition of done. Last is planning process, often the entry point for teams with no process at all, and the part most easily mistaken for project management.
ex: Getting sales and customer success in one room to reconcile their asks
New product teams need little process and fast feedback; one person can cover two or three

items.d: Connect the data systems PMs need
Part of done; supports product-led growth
Unified planning; often mistaken for project management

l67|103.c: To win PMs over, ask whether they'd rather spend time fielding internal questions or with customers.
l67|103.e: PMs often worry about another stakeholder who has to be in every meeting, or about losing the interesting work. Her approach goes back to basics: what do you hold PMs accountable for, and how do you measure them? Their most valuable time belongs with engineers and customers, so everything else has to give way. The most persuasive point is that PMs stop constantly firefighting for revenue teams. Companies that made it work had support from the CEO or CPO level. The one thing PMs should never give up is time with customers, seeing their pain firsthand. If you don't want that, don't work in product.
ex: Small change, big impact: bring engineers into customer meetings
She fell in love with product watching users struggle with a keyboard and mouse

items: Time with customers, seeing their pain

d.verdict: Give PMs' time back to customers and engineers

l67|103.c: Ops roles aren't a sign of inefficiency, but once systems are built they should be automated or handed off.
l67|103.e: Growth expert Casey Winters once argued that ops roles are often a band-aid over inefficiency. She disagrees with the premise: ops roles grow as functions and organizations mature, which signals growth and opportunity. But she accepts the other half. Product ops should build the processes and systems that are needed, hand them to other teams or automate them, and then get out of the way to do more strategic work, such as improving retention, the in-app experience, and voice-of-the-customer programs. That's exactly how she moved into the role, so she tells candidates upfront they must be willing to drop what they're doing at any time.
ex: After building the systems at Pendo, she moved on to more strategic work

items.d: To other people or to tools

l67|103.c: The signal you need product ops is missing transparency and readiness: knowing a launch is coming isn't knowing what to do.
l67|103.e: In her fifth week at Pendo, the company shipped the biggest launch in its history. It had been about eight months in development and went badly. Everyone inside knew it was coming, but nobody knew how big the impact was or how to get customers ready, and there was no testing or feedback loop. Afterward they surveyed how much time PMs spent firefighting for revenue teams and how often those teams came with questions, and introduced product briefings focused on how to prepare. The split with product marketing: marketing owns positioning and helping sales sell; product ops makes sure internal teams understand the new value and how to use it.
ex: One measure: the quality of questions revenue teams ask product
Product marketing teaches people to sell it; product ops teaches them to understand it

terms.d: Value, usage, how to tell customers

result.d: Both the company and customers are prepared

l67|103.c: People who love healthy teams and solving problems suit product ops; its leaders should have been PMs.
l67|103.e: If you enjoy creating a healthy cross-functional environment, or as a PM you kept feeling there had to be a better way, the role fits. Day-to-day practitioners often come from management consulting, customer success and technical support, and more PMs are switching over now. She strongly believes whoever founds a product ops team should have hands-on product experience, so they know where to put the effort. When job hunting, first decide whether you lean toward data and consulting or technical analysis, then read the job description closely. If it doesn't say how success is measured, that's a red flag.
ex: One of her former PM reports moved into ops and came to love studying the business

items.d: Mostly former product leaders or directors
Growing in number; no longer seen as a threat
From consulting, customer success, tech support

l68|106.c: Everyone says team matters most, then accommodates everyone; values have to involve real trade-offs.
l68|106.e: He found that the average tech manager lasts about 15.7 months in a role, and employees spend under 11 months with the same manager, which suggests nobody truly prioritizes the team. Much of HR also grew out of defensive self-protection. The team should serve the mission, not keep everyone happy. Values need explicit trade-offs that say who they're for and who they're not: "optimize for the long term" means giving up some short-term revenue. ProfitWell practiced "most generous interpretation": in a conflict, assume good intent or talk it out directly. People who couldn't do that were helped to find another job, and interviews made this clear upfront.
ex: Final-round scenario: someone says something offensive in Slack; what do you do?
About one in ten candidates argued for zero tolerance, opening a conversation about culture fit

items: Afraid to state trade-offs in interviews
Conflict handed to HR and policy
Values say who they're for and not for
Assume good intent, talk it out

d.verdict: The team serves the mission; help poor fits find another job

l68|106.c: Bootstrapping suits cash-flow businesses; if you want a billion in annual revenue, raise money.
l68|106.e: He admits this take annoys everyone, but goals, business model and funding have to match. ProfitWell wanted to be a big company yet became obsessed with efficiency and kept putting off fundraising. In hindsight that was a mistake; they could have moved faster and grown larger. The reverse is also true: many ideas should never take venture money. Founders who sell a company for $400 or $500 million may end up with less than the owner of a business they control that throws off $50 million a year. His test is whether there's a clear path to a billion dollars in annual revenue, even if it takes twenty years.
ex: His next company will bootstrap for 18 to 24 months, ideally raising only after product-market fit
Building a software company with $10 million in annual revenue is a remarkable achievement today

marks.d: Freedom, and it can grow over time
Sold for $200M+; should have raised earlier
Get on the treadmill only with a clear path

l68|106.c: Pricing doesn't need a big overhaul; do one thing each quarter to push revenue per customer up.
l68|106.e: Growth has three levers: acquisition, monetization and retention. Companies pour effort into acquisition and retention while monetization goes almost unmanaged. He suggests making it concrete with one metric, average revenue per user, and doing one small thing per quarter to raise it: price, packaging, add-ons, discounting, localization or the free tier. Set up a pricing committee and a calendar reminder that repeats every three months. The most important piece is the value metric, meaning what you charge for. If internal politics are messy, start with a price increase to open the door.
ex: With the right value metric, churn runs about 20–25% lower and expansion revenue roughly doubles
If your NPS is above 20, raise prices once a year

items.d: It should climb steadily every quarter
In a two-person company, the two founders
The number rises as you go

l68|106.c: Product teams focus on strategic retention and ignore tactical retention, which drives 25–40% of churn.
l68|106.e: Strategic retention is what product people are good at: ideal customer profile, time to value, roadmap, polishing the experience. Tactical retention is failed payments, contract-term optimization, the cancellation flow and offboarding. After product-market fit it usually accounts for 25% to 40% of churn problems and can be fixed in two months, yet it's always neglected. He suggests handing it to the finance team. His company analyzed about two million cancellation flows: once someone clicks cancel you have 18 to 30 seconds. Ask two questions, then use their profile and usage data to offer a save discount or a pause.
ex: Daily-use workflow products and products that deliver value without logging in retain best
Only about 1 in 100 free-text answers is useful, so use multiple choice

l68|106.c: Your tempo framework matters more than your org chart; first agree on what good looks like.
l68|106.e: Real professionals ship continuously, whether in marketing, product or operations. When a team seems smart but is always planning, or leadership gets it while the rest drift, the cause is usually no shared standard for tempo. ProfitWell set the mission, a mission metric and guiding principles at the top, and each function's leader defined a good cadence from there: so many content pieces a month, a medium release every month, a major release every quarter. Management then becomes discussing why gaps exist and fixing them one by one, often just two teams not talking. Otherwise, nine months later you suddenly decide someone isn't good enough, when the real problem is organizational.
ex: Mission metric: the total revenue running through ProfitWell
Product gives marketing something launchable every month

items.d: Most helpful brand; do it for you
What to deliver monthly and quarterly

l68|106.c: Markets are getting crowded, so neither customer research nor competitive intelligence is optional anymore.
l68|106.e: He cites data showing only one company in five has an ideal customer profile or buyer personas, and one in ten does quarterly customer research. Those that do have better NPS, willingness to pay and LTV-to-CAC ratios, and grow about 15% to 20% faster. When capital was plentiful, brute force could work; not anymore. Research doesn't mean doing what customers say, but understanding them and combining that with judgment. "Ignore the competition" is good advice for a product team but outdated for a company: there are about 16 times as many competitors as a decade ago and acquisition costs have soared, so at minimum know who they are and set a strategy.
ex: The minimum: 10 non-sales customer conversations a month
Survey competitors' customers' NPS under a third-party name

l68|106.c: The middle of the funnel is the new growth opportunity: grow the prospect pool with freemium, content and meetups.
l68|106.e: Eighty percent of sales and marketing budgets go to the top and bottom of the funnel, but both have become far less efficient over the past decade. Deals now hinge on timing: the customer knows you but isn't ready yet. So keep prospects engaged in the middle for the long haul, and when the time comes they walk themselves to the bottom. One tool is freemium, since the product is the best content. Another is media like podcasts and video; ProfitWell had eight niche shows when it was acquired. The third is in person: breakfasts, lunches and meetups are cheap, and prospects you've met are clearly worth more.
ex: Customers who convert from free retain about 10–20% better and have roughly double the NPS
Prospects met in person show 10–30% higher willingness to pay and about 20% less churn
Top-priority leads get one-on-one coffee; lower tiers get invited to meetups

result.d: Walk to a deal when the time is right

l69|108.c: A product manager in a newsroom has to thrive in chaos, and that starts with pausing before reacting.
l69|108.e: People say product managers must handle ambiguity, but in a news organization you face outright chaos. She believes much of the conflict and frustration at work comes from knee-jerk reactions. If you can stay calm through the highs and lows and pause before responding, you see the situation as it really is and decide quickly. That calm helps with managing stakeholders, keeping team morale up, and reading user feedback. Power comes from managing your own emotions, not from trying to control other people. There is no substitute for meditation, and the benefits compound if you keep at it.
ex: A starter practice: when brushing your teeth, do only that, with all your senses
Her recommended tool: the free version of Insight Timer

items.d: The situation as it really is
Point the team through the chaos

l69|108.c: Your internal users have day jobs, so build buffers into every plan and be ready to change course.
l69|108.e: Journalists and editors are her customers, but they do not exist to serve the product team. Getting editors from around the world together for a user test takes real effort, and the moment news breaks, the meeting gets cancelled. That is normal. So every phase has a backup plan and a buffer. The buffer might be a day or two, or anywhere from a week to a month. If a phase finishes early, the team moves straight on. This is why migrating off the old platform looks slow on paper: training, testing, round after round of conversation and feedback, and only then the actual move.
ex: The team's goal: rebuild the content management system and move every editor onto it
Goals run two to three years out, then break into quarters, months, weeks, and daily sprints

items.d: Run real workflows on the new platform

l69|108.c: Four standing touchpoints capture editors' requests, and people who were involved accept "no" more easily.
l69|108.e: After watching for a while, she set up four kinds of touchpoints. A weekly demo day explains existing features, previews new ones, and doubles as marketing to the whole company. Workshops let each editorial group rebuild its own workflow on the new platform. Breaking-news rehearsals stress-test the system. Office hours help anyone who is stuck. Incoming requests fall into three buckets: improve an existing feature, build something new, or explain that it cannot be done. Because editors took part in discovery all along, trust is already there, so they usually understand when the answer is no.
ex: Each group gets three to six workshops, two hours each
She calls them "workshops" rather than "user testing" because it feels like collaboration
Politics, entertainment, and health teams have wildly different workflows

items.d: Each group rebuilds its real workflow
Simulated events to stress the platform
Troubleshooting once or twice a week

l69|108.c: A platform that can't survive breaking news is useless, so rehearse it from a script and push it hard.
l69|108.e: Rehearsals follow a script that spells out the event and which teams take part. It starts with an email from the newsgathering desk, then video, article, and photo editors all work at once until someone hits publish. The whole thing takes a few minutes. Engineers and the editorial support team watch, noting what breaks and how far each feature can be pushed. No two breaking stories are alike, so this yields a lot of feedback in a short time. Planning for the worst pays off: during the 2020 election, the unfinished new platform served as a backup layer and actually caught a failure.
ex: A rehearsal runs about three minutes, but the preparation is substantial
Election season is like the Super Bowl times a hundred

items.d: Set the event and the teams
Engineering and support log the problems

l69|108.c: Treat engineers as partners, not resources, and bring the tech lead into discovery from day one.
l69|108.e: She has the tech lead sit in on user testing, design discussions, and planning meetings with editors. When engineers understand what journalists need as well as product does, they define the "how" more clearly and accurately, and their calls on technical feasibility rest on firmer ground. The tech lead then passes that understanding to the rest of the engineering team, so a journalist's pain point becomes shared knowledge across the whole team. Pulling engineering in early makes the whole process more efficient, not slower.

d.verdict: The earlier engineering joins discovery, the smoother it goes

l69|108.c: For a product manager, communication starts with listening and then speaking the other person's language.
l69|108.e: When she moved into product, her boss said what stood out was that engineers would listen to her and she listened to them. People assume good communication means being articulate or writing well, but none of that works without listening. Mindful communication means being fully present in the conversation in front of you. When a journalist complains that a feature isn't working as expected, she stays quiet, hears them out, and then distills the root cause. She avoids technical terms and uses the nicknames and shorthand journalists have for the system. And she warns against thinking you are the user: she has freelanced for CNN, but she is still only a proxy. Talk to users as often, as consistently, and as early as you can.
ex: A product manager doesn't need every answer, just to know where to find it
Product and editorial went from working in silos to one unified partnership

result.d: Earns trust and respect

l69|108.c: Product management in journalism is still young, and small newsrooms need ready-made product practices most.
l69|108.e: CNN, The New York Times, and The Washington Post have mature product teams, but most newsrooms around the world are stretched thin. They cannot afford product or technical hires, so journalists end up doing product, engineering, and sometimes even writing code themselves. During the pandemic, a group of media executives founded the News Product Alliance to spread product thinking, bring more diverse people into the field, and offer resources that fit a newsroom. Something as simple as a basic product requirements template can get an editor's project on track. In last year's mentorship program, many mentees were creating a product manager role for themselves from scratch or building a product practice where none existed.
ex: The Slack community has a few thousand members, plus a job board
Her favorite interview question: what exists only because you pushed for it?

items.d: About 400 applied to the mentorship program

l70|110.c: There are four ways into product management; the most common is moving internally after raising your hand.
l70|110.e: The formal routes are applying to an associate product manager (APM) program or applying for a junior PM opening inside your own company. The informal routes are working closely with a PM and becoming the go-to expert on one area of the product, or joining an early-stage startup where everyone wears many hats. Of the people she has brought into product, most came from adjacent roles like support, implementation, or sales engineering. They said openly that they wanted the job, took on extra work, and showed what they could do before they had the title. Those who make it tend to be curious, love products, and sometimes have side projects.
ex: Big-company APM programs are very competitive, so look at earlier-stage companies like Box
APM programs are rare because interviewing, training, and placement all take real investment
Search Glassdoor for "associate product manager"

cells.d: Become the expert, do the work first

l70|110.c: Narrowing your market and target user is the hardest and most effective move, and it requires saying no.
l70|110.e: When she joined, Calendly served freelancers, salespeople, recruiters, customer success teams, educators, and many more, so PMs struggled to choose between feature A and feature B. She started by spelling out the market, the segment, and the persona, and settled on externally facing teams as the core customer. Most companies think they already know this, but it gets fuzzy at the level of an individual PM because saying no is scary. Yet only by saying no can you build something excellent for the people who matter most, instead of something that feels fine to everyone. It worked partly because "focus wisely" was already a company value, baked into the templates people use.
ex: Small businesses wanted a Venmo integration; it was deprioritized because they weren't the target persona
The product review template keeps asking who the target customer and user are

items.d: Freelancers, educators, teams of every kind

l70|110.c: Strategy is an integrated set of choices, and resources should shift across three horizons year by year.
l70|110.e: She borrows from the book Playing to Win: a good product strategy answers what winning looks like, where to play, and how to win. Its real value is forcing you to say where you will play and where you won't. Calendly's aspiration is to be the best place to schedule, prepare for, and follow up on external meetings, and the team mapped out three horizons: today's business, the next one, and the longer-term bet. In year one, horizon three got no investment, just a known direction. Each year after that, resources moved from horizon one toward two and three. The horizontal product had been the wedge for viral growth, so shifting to horizon two meant making real trade-offs.
ex: Horizon two: go deep on teams, departments, and specific industries

l70|110.c: Commit only to dates you control: promise one phase at a time, not a delivery six months out.
l70|110.e: Promising a ship date for a project six months away, before discovery and design are done, is guaranteed to be wrong. She splits product work into four phases: discovery, solution, build, and launch-measure-iterate. In each phase the team commits only to what that phase can deliver. During discovery you can commit to when the research will finish, but not to building anything. Only once a solution is chosen do engineers estimate and give a delivery date. So a roadmap can say "finish discovery on problem X" this quarter, and if things go well, move to the next phase the quarter after.
ex: There is a PM-only forum for debating whether to pursue an opportunity; she deliberately stays out
The company sets about three annual objectives with quarterly milestones

items.d: Only now estimate and set a date

l70|110.c: Layering sales onto product-led growth changes your people, processes, product, and culture.
l70|110.e: A purely self-serve, product-led business runs on a well-tuned product, and departments can operate fairly independently. Once you add direct sales, teams have to work in tight coordination, and the kinds of people you hire, the processes, and the product itself all change. Early on, sales mostly handles inbound inquiries and product-qualified leads (users whose activity signals they are ready to buy), so you want nurturing sellers rather than heavy outbound hunters. The buyer is a head of sales or recruiting, not the CIO, so don't start by hiring big-company reps who sell to CIOs. The buyer will move from team lead to IT to CIO over time, but that takes years.
ex: Two years ago, product-led growth was 99% of annual recurring revenue
Sales-driven revenue is now about 20% of ARR and the fastest-growing part
The company grew from roughly 150 people to 600

d.verdict: The sales team must match both how customers arrive and who buys

l70|110.c: Calendly grew through a viral loop, and the team business was pulled out of how customers used it.
l70|110.e: Founder Tope had spent years in sales and knew the pain of scheduling meetings, so he used his own savings to hire an outsourced team in Ukraine to build it. The first ten users were support staff at another of that agency's clients, a school. They used Calendly to book parents, parents used it for parent-teacher conferences, and it spread through the whole school. The product was completely free at first, partly because they couldn't build a billing system. Today about 70% of signups come from the viral loop of shared links. Individuals then invite teammates, and team leads either ask about pricing or show up as product-qualified leads, which is where sales steps in to expand the account.
ex: The teams business is growing faster than the individual business
Once revenue is in the hundreds of millions, the law of large numbers slows growth

items.d: Sales approaches the team lead to expand

l70|110.c: Sales is a PM's best source of customer insight, but dig into the problem behind each request first.
l70|110.e: Some product teams see sales as a distraction. She sees it the opposite way: salespeople talk to ten times as many customers a week as a PM does, so they can be the voice of the customer. Building enterprise products at Box, she spent a lot of time on customer sites, and the biggest lesson was learning to ask the right questions to understand why a customer wants something. If you build exactly what customers A, B, and C each ask for, you do the work three times and hurt the end-user experience. Instead, find one scalable solution that serves a broad set of customers. Product, design, and research report to the same leader so they can look at the end-to-end experience.
ex: Glassdoor had about 60 million monthly unique visitors; she learned consumer growth and A/B testing there
Competitor war games: small groups each track one competitor for a quarter

terms.d: Ten times a PM's customer contact

result.d: Serves many customers without hurting the experience

l71|111.c: Startups fail because founders don't talk to users; they avoid it out of fear, yet only one in ten will care.
l71|111.e: If you don't talk to customers, you don't know what matters, so you never find product-market fit, and nothing else counts. Many founders treat getting into YC or raising money as validation, so on day one of the batch they are told that most of them do not have product-market fit yet. Technical founders tend to reach for software to solve everything and dread rejection. But in any customer group, roughly nine in ten are not early adopters; their job incentive is to avoid risk. You have to reach ten people to find one who will take a call. Those conversations usually turn into the first customers, so the selling has already happened.
ex: Talk to 25 to 50 people, not the five founders imagine
Paul Graham asked the Airbnb founders why they were here when their customers were in New York

items.d: About nine in ten are not early adopters

l71|111.c: Judge how painful a problem is by watching how people work, not by asking if it's hard.
l71|111.e: Ask someone whether a process works for them and they will usually say it's fine, because they have no idea it could be better. A more reliable approach is to have users share their screen and walk you through their daily workflow, so you can see them repeat the same manual steps over and over. Better still, go use the existing solution yourself. He also points out that the most common reaction from users is not hatred but indifference: everyone is busy, and they sign up and forget. Being ignored is not fatal, and you can go back to them once the product improves.
ex: People who can't script click through Excel a million times by hand
A team building EV charging should rent an electric car and try a non-Tesla charger

marks.d: Feel how bad it really is

l71|111.c: A technical co-founder can't be replaced, because products come from endless iteration, not a spec.
l71|111.e: Non-technical founders often treat engineering like "I have an idea for a song, I just need a musician," underestimating the hardest part. Giving yourself 90% of the equity and an engineer 10% on the application is a sign you don't value engineering. A product is not a service you spec out and receive; most of the decisions are technical, and iteration depends on engineers. That is why he can't recall a company that succeeded with an outsourced team. The fix is to learn to respect engineering first, then approach the strongest engineers you know; many of them are hoping someone will show up to handle the business side. You can also teach yourself to code well enough to build a prototype.
ex: YC runs a co-founder matching service
Successful non-technical teams give core engineers equity so they feel like founders

d.verdict: YC rarely admits teams that can't build their own prototype

l71|111.c: Successful founders share determination, technical skill, customer closeness, and clear communication, but outliers defy prediction.
l71|111.e: The successful founders he has seen are determined to win and don't back down when things get hard. That inner drive is contagious, which is how they build good teams. The more technical the team, the better its odds. They don't wait for investors or YC to approve anything; they make progress every week and work for customers, not investors. They are also good at explaining complex ideas and turning them into a story, which is tied to enjoying fundraising. But these are table stakes. The truly huge companies need something harder to name: outlier ideas tend to look unreasonable, which is why so many investors turned Airbnb down.
ex: Founders' motivations vary widely, and any of them can work
Don't treat starting a company as a career step on your resume
Many of Airbnb's early PMs were former founders

l71|111.c: Small companies have no strategy, just one top priority and execution; growth thinking comes after the product works.
l71|111.e: Strategy is a word from business schools and big companies. It assumes you can do several things at once, while a small team can only do one. Wanting a strategy meeting usually means the priorities aren't clear. Before product-market fit, making people genuinely want your product is the entire strategy. Speed and quality aren't opposites either: talking to customers quickly is how you learn what quality means to them. Coming from a growth team to YC, he had to reset his thinking. Early on, founders should do things that don't scale. Only once thousands of people sign up every day do scalable distribution and growth tactics come into play.
ex: Confidence and humility aren't opposites either: project confidence, treat people humbly
Founding teams should agree on how decisions get made so they aren't relitigated

items.d: One priority; do things that don't scale

l71|111.c: YC can't predict who becomes a giant, but the strongest signal is new progress every two weeks.
l71|111.e: In one-on-one office hours he asks a single question: what is slowing you down? No status updates, no strategy talk. That question forces out the real priority. In group office hours, six or seven companies sit together and each reports whether it hit the goals it set two weeks earlier and what got in the way. Founders are competitive and hate showing up empty-handed, which creates accountability and eases the loneliness of building a company. YC is good at spotting failure patterns it has seen hundreds of times, but it cannot pick winners. If every meeting brings something new, like the customer from last time has paid and more are in talks, that is the best indicator there is.
ex: An interview question: what have you built since you submitted the application?
Hot sectors and press coverage have almost nothing to do with success

l71|111.c: Climate tech is no longer charity; it is a trillion-dollar economic transition.
l71|111.e: Governments have already decided to remake the energy system, and the only question left is how. He believes that means trillions of dollars will move from things that emit carbon to things that don't, a shift bigger than the software industry. Two things changed in the past two years: the United States passed the Inflation Reduction Act, and large companies became real paying customers. They have promised shareholders and governments they will cut emissions, and they are afraid of becoming the Toyota that refused to go electric. So you don't need to convince everyone, just enough companies to change their habits, which is why founders should focus on business customers. General engineering and product skills are just as scarce here, and deep domain expertise isn't required.
ex: YC has backed more than 130 climate companies
Enode: the Plaid of EV charging and home energy, connecting devices and services
Heart Aerospace: battery-electric passenger planes

items.d: Meeting emissions pledges, fearing being left behind

l72|114.c: Product-market fit means you have a product, not a company; build the company like a house, foundation first.
l72|114.e: Many companies fail not because of the product but because the company wasn't built well. Headcount grows badly, cultural bonds weaken, and that damages the product and the mission. She pictures company structure as a house: the foundation is a set of founding documents, the beams are supporting structures like goals, business reviews and planning, and the plumbing is the operating cadence. These should nest like Russian dolls, the way OKRs cascade from the company down to each person, and there should be few of them. Build them late and every team invents its own; after a dozen additions in two years you have to tear the house down.
ex: Stripe had about 160 people when she joined; now it has more than 7,000
Build a leveling system early; one company waited until about 800 people and it hurt
The Collison brothers often asked: who have you talked to? What have you read?

items.d: A work rhythm driven by calendar or events

l72|114.c: You need only three founding documents: a mission, long-term goals and operating principles, to guide everyone's choices.
l72|114.e: How a person spends each day should be guided by what the company is trying to achieve. If employees don't know that, they can't choose well. The mission is one sentence. Long-term goals add detail about why the company exists. Operating principles describe how work gets done, and can be shared with candidates so both sides can screen each other. Long-term goals are directions, not numbers, but when writing quarterly or annual goals you can derive three to five standing categories from them. The signal that it's time to write them down is new hires repeatedly asking what matters and why things are done this way. The story you tell investors should also be told to your own people.
ex: Stripe's mission: increase the GDP of the internet
One long-term goal: advance the frontier of developer tools
Another long-term goal: accelerate globalization

terms.d: One sentence on what you're building
Concrete directions for why you exist

result.d: Employees make the right calls themselves

l72|114.c: An operating cadence is itself a stabilizer: a few consistent rituals beat constantly new processes.
l72|114.e: A fast-growing company is full of chaos, and handing out work ad hoc only adds to it. Shared rituals such as quarterly goals, business reviews and launch processes give people something to hold onto when customers churn or a launch is tomorrow. She has run very different teams, including product, industrial design, operations and business development, on the same underlying operating system. The cadence needn't be quarterly: if nothing has changed between two reviews, they're too frequent; if the content is already stale, too sparse. Young teams keep trying new tools and abandoning them halfway. Better to do a few things well and revise them once a year.
ex: Quarterly reviews for a new product line were switched to every six weeks
Metrics reviews share a live dashboard instead of a prepared deck
An internal event about six months before the customer conference forces progress

l72|114.c: Management starts with you: know your own values and working style before you can build mutual understanding.
l72|114.e: People assume management starts with the team, and founders assume it starts with the product. She says it starts with yourself. Her first principle is building self-awareness to achieve mutual awareness: ask for feedback, learn your motivations, strengths, blind spots and tendencies, and let others know them too. One exercise is narrowing a long list of values down to three, ideally with someone pressing you on why; you'll find a story behind every one. Then take the various assessments to see whether you lean introverted or extroverted, task-focused or people-focused, and assemble all of it into a guide to how you operate.
ex: One manager held transparency as a core value because nobody told him when his mother was dying
Take them all: MBTI, DISC, Enneagram

l72|114.c: Say what you think you can't say, but as questions and your own observations, not judgments.
l72|114.e: In every meeting, each person has a column of harsh commentary running in their head. You can't say it as is, but you shouldn't filter all of it out either; detoxify it and say it. Two techniques help. Start with a question, such as "is there anything we haven't discussed?" Then frame it as your own observation rather than a judgment about the person. This is also the heart of management: a manager isn't a lecturer but an explorer, forming a hypothesis from partial data and testing it with the other person, like holding up a mirror, and stepping back if they disagree. Speaking up often opens the door for others who were holding back.
ex: The "left-hand column" idea from Fred Kofman's book Conscious Business
A report told Reid Hoffman "I wouldn't let you run a McDonald's"; he took it as honest feedback

items.d: Sharp, but can't be said outright
Treat it as a hypothesis to test

l72|114.c: A COO isn't a cure-all; a good COO and CEO need just the right amount of tension.
l72|114.e: Most companies have no COO; she estimates fewer than 20% to 30% do. The role is more common in hypergrowth or in operations- and manufacturing-heavy businesses. When a founder is finding product-market fit, building the company and hiring a layer of leaders all at once, a COO adds leverage. But don't mythologize it. Start by hiring a head of business operations, give them a few functions, and see whether they grow with the company. If a founder just wants to dump everything they dislike on you, they may be avoiding changes they should make themselves. The sign it's working isn't harmony but trust and forward motion, along with the willingness to say no and give each other feedback.
ex: Apple-style coordination of hardware, software and manufacturing needs a strong operating role
She and Patrick were described as having "just the right tension"

items: Takes over what the founder dislikes
Shares the load with the founder

d.verdict: Greater than the sum of its parts, through friction plus forward motion

l72|114.c: Make the implicit explicit in decisions and meetings; if you're unsure who decides, it's probably you.
l72|114.e: The bar for calling a meeting is far too low. The real work is explaining why it's happening, whether it's for a decision or an update, who needs to be there, and even asking who can skip it. Decisions work the same way: pick a model such as SPADE, spell out what's being decided, who decides, by what criteria and who gets told, then follow the process, noting if needed how it could be revisited. Use Bezos's type-one and type-two framing to judge how big and how reversible a decision is. Many teams stall because people aren't sure they're the decision-maker, and that slows the whole company. If in doubt, ask; don't stop.
ex: Product managers: enormous responsibility, little authority, one of tech's hardest jobs
Staying aligned works like marketing: repeat the message across many channels

items.d: Confirm there is actually a decision
Pick a model and follow it
Type one or type two decision

l73|115.c: Don't wait for your manager or a job ladder; bring customer insight to executives and open your own doors.
l73|115.e: The usual path is to work hard in your current role and wait for a review. She finds that too passive: it depends on whether your manager fights for you and whether a slot exists, and a new manager resets everything. Her approach starts from a fact about executives: they are smart, but far from customers, and the bigger the company the less they hear from the front line. People close to customers can fill that gap. Keep sharing customer findings tied to the company's north-star metric and you become "the person who knows the customer best," so new opportunities come to you. It also gives your manager more to say in promotion discussions.
ex: At Bandwidth she pitched self-serve purchasing from a sales role and was made e-commerce manager
Andre, Twilio's seventh employee, became her key ally

items.d: Noticed that Twilio was hard to get started with
Her briefing gained more and more subscribers
Executives and even the CEO attended

l73|115.c: Not all friction is bad: the right kind calms new users down and raises conversion.
l73|115.e: Twilio's sign-up used to ask only for a username, email and password. Everyone inside believed developers hated any obstacle, and as a result the company knew nothing about who signed up. One Friday night she quietly shipped four dropdown questions: which language you write, which product you want, what you are building, and whether you are a developer. The team expected conversion to drop. Instead sign-ups rose about 5%. The reason is psychology: someone trying a new product expects it to be hard, and these questions reassure them that "it supports my language" and "I'm in the right place." User mindset matters as much as product and market.
ex: The "non-developer" group later led to low-code quick deploys worth tens of millions in pipeline
Language data also helped the docs team see trends early

items: They confirm "I'm in the right place"

d.verdict: Bad friction is bad; good friction is good

l73|115.c: Wrap the step that scares users inside something familiar, like hiding a pill in a hot dog.
l73|115.e: They built a step-by-step onboarding flow and it did only okay. Interviews revealed why: developers are comfortable with APIs, code samples and docs, but phone numbers and telecom configuration were the scary "monster," and step one was "go buy a number." In a live class nobody minds because someone is there to help; alone at home, people bail. So they tried a minimal version that looked absurd: send users out of the console to a docs page that shows code first, with number setup tucked inside. Conversion improved. Only after it proved out did they build it properly into onboarding.
ex: When a logical flow converts poorly, it is often fighting user psychology

result.d: Users dare to keep going

l73|115.c: Over 80% of ideas fail, so iterate in small steps and kill bad ideas cheaply first.
l73|115.e: Data from Microsoft, Netflix and others shows eight or nine out of ten hypotheses are wrong. The reason is simple: you have to get the problem, the audience, the timing, the solution and the wording all right, and one miss means no effect, however smart the team is. A six-month redesign behind closed doors ships most of those mistakes at once. Iterating turns each failure into a compass. A/B tests are the most expensive check, needing design, engineering and waiting time, so start with fake-door tests and prototypes shown to users, and only send filtered ideas into an A/B test.
ex: Her team's motto: the first version should be embarrassing
Visual tools like Builder let non-engineers change pages themselves

items.d: Eight or nine in ten will fail
Test interest before building the feature
Only for ideas that passed the filter

l73|115.c: Growth experiments needn't demand 95% confidence; running more tests nets more, if rules are set up front.
l73|115.e: She once did research in an academic lab, where a wrong call distorts findings on education and bias, so 95% confidence is mandatory, and the same goes for drug trials. But a wrong call on a conversion or upsell test costs little. If relaxing the threshold lets you run twice as many experiments in a year, the year's total result is better. Run only ten tests a year and, given failure rates, maybe two will work. Two conditions: decide the success criteria before the test starts, and back a relaxed threshold with qualitative feedback, never bending data to fit the hypothesis afterwards. She also thinks growth teams should commit to yearly results across high, medium and low-risk bets rather than weekly numbers.
ex: Tools like Hotjar collect qualitative feedback to complement the numbers

marks.d: A wrong call is very costly
Relax the bar, add qualitative evidence

l73|115.c: Going product-led isn't slicing up the enterprise plan; start from the self-serve user's problems.
l73|115.e: She sees growth and sales as two sides of one coin: growth sells with the product, sales sells with people, and a company needs both to convert customers. Many sales-led companies that move to product-led growth just strip features from the enterprise product, argue about pricing and put it online. She thinks you should do what a good salesperson does: first understand the particular problems and mindset of the people entering the self-serve flow. At Amplitude, for example, startups almost never have analysts, so CEOs and product managers build reports themselves. What they want most is confidence that they are setting up the right metrics and dashboards.
ex: Existing knowledge can be reused: the best way to build reports, industry benchmarks

root.d: Let the product do the selling

items.d: It's more than trimming and repricing
Their problems differ from big customers'
No analysts, afraid of wrong reports

l73|115.c: Developers own the tools they pick, so they must test them themselves; self-serve is your sales team.
l73|115.e: Developers often skip the website and go straight to sign-up, like someone who opens the IKEA box and only reads the manual when stuck. They also avoid salespeople hard. She traces it to accountability: if the service goes down, the integration breaks or they get paged at 3 a.m., it's on them, and they can lose the team's trust or even their job. So they can't take a sales pitch or marketing copy on faith; they have to build a proof of concept themselves. That means they are deep into the self-serve flow before they'll commit, and a company must invest in that experience the way it would build a sales team.
ex: A team at a big tech company ran in production for months without contacting sales
An engineer at a large retailer signed up with a personal email to dodge sales

items.d: Outages and broken integrations land on them
Go deep into the self-serve flow
Treat it as the sales team

l75|117.c: A new social network needs high-status people the old platforms neglect, then homegrown stars.
l75|117.e: He borrows from Eugene Wei's essay "Status as a Service": a new network is like a new country, and it has to attract interesting, high-status people others want to be near. But people already well served by an older platform won't move, so you go after the ones being neglected. He notes that every big platform has its own breakout personalities, usually rising on a new skill; short-video apps made stars of people who could dance or be funny. Imported celebrities aren't enough. What matters more are creators native to the platform. Their own show grew out of Clubhouse.
ex: Kylie Jenner on early Snapchat
The Rock and Cristiano Ronaldo on Instagram
Charli D'Amelio on TikTok

items.d: A new network is like a new country
Only they have a reason to move
Rise on a new skill on the new platform

l75|117.c: Networking is genuine relationships with no agenda, plus constantly putting yourself out there online.
l75|117.e: He used to think doing great work was enough, then noticed opportunities kept flowing to people better at building relationships. His method is simple: have coffee with every peer you don't work with directly, and with your manager's peers, with no agenda, asking about their story, how you can help, and who else you should meet. Twice a week, and after a few years you know hundreds of people; follow up regularly. The other half is putting yourself out there, whether tweets, videos or GitHub, a beacon to the world. Ignore "am I qualified" or "is this cringe." Post daily like going to the gym, tell your real story, and write about niche topics you've truly gone deep on.
ex: When he joined Facebook he cold-emailed every executive for coffee
His most popular thread was about how to write a cold email
Feedback like "you're over-branded" should simply be ignored

items.d: No agenda, just learn about them
One person leads to the next
Check in every six to twelve months
Draws in people you'd never expect

l75|117.c: Run a community like a party: set the tone, pick the guests, mind the quiet ones, keep rituals.
l75|117.e: He dislikes the abstract word "community" and prefers to think of a dinner party. First the host says whether this is a bar crawl or a formal dinner; otherwise everyone makes up their own rules, which he thinks early Twitter never settled. Second, mix the guests: famous but busy executives, young people who know everyone, quiet thinkers. Third, keep reading the room and hand newcomers a topic they can jump into. Finally, hold it together with rituals, like the Tuesday Zoom gatherings during the pandemic. He runs over a hundred small online groups, and the smaller they are, the closer they feel.
ex: His advice: start by pulling a few people you like into a WhatsApp or Slack group

root.d: That is the heart of community

items.d: Tell people what kind of party it is

l75|117.c: In an executive review, first say how much you care, why, and what kind of meeting this is.
l75|117.e: Going from doing the work to being reported to is a shock: a stray comment can make someone feel dismissed, and you hesitate to say no for fear of hurting people. At Facebook he learned a habit from Mark Zuckerberg: open each meeting by saying where you sit on the spectrum of caring about this decision, and why. Then the team knows the decision can change if they can break your chain of reasoning. Be clear whether it's an update or a decision meeting, and watch for teams pushing a hard call onto you. Send pre-reads, invite the right people, make sure everyone speaks, and replace high-pressure "hero meetings" with a regular cadence.
ex: Audience Network, which he pitched to Zuckerberg, became a large mobile ad network
The term "hero meeting" is borrowed from Gokul Rajaram

marks.t: I'd like you to do this
marks.d: Convince me and I'll reverse it

l75|117.c: Jobs-to-be-Done is a terrible framework; real products are full of trade-offs that need systems thinking and intuition.
l75|117.e: The famous milkshake example looks at one user and one job. But he says real products involve many parties affecting each other: competitors, supply chains, different user groups. Facebook's "People You May Know" sacrificed your experience to help new users reach enough friends. Twitter's algorithmic timeline was hated by power users yet saved the company, because it served ordinary new users. Jobs-to-be-Done can't answer trade-offs like these. He prefers systems thinking: list every participant and their incentives, then have a rational debate about what's worth it. Big breakthroughs, he thinks, usually come from one person's intuition about user psychology combined with systems thinking.
ex: Facebook's goal: get a new user to 10 friends in 14 days
Amazon stopped listing package contents in emails so Gmail couldn't harvest the data
Duolingo's streaks could never come out of Jobs-to-be-Done

d.verdict: Product breakthroughs come from intuition plus systems thinking

l75|118.c: Technology gave them everything they have, so she struggles to see why anyone wouldn't be optimistic about it.
l75|118.e: Both grew up in middle-class families in an ordinary Indian city, where parents saved for a long time to buy them a first computer. They learned to code online, met on Yahoo Messenger, and both started their careers at Microsoft building developer tools, then moved through Seattle, the Bay Area and startups. She has watched technology lift the careers and lives of people around her, and she is living proof herself. Sriram adds that technology is imperfect and its benefits uneven, but most of the good things of the past century or two are tied to it, and the richest person and an ordinary person carry the same phone.
ex: Sriram's father held the same job from age 25 until retirement
Google Search and ChatGPT don't care how much money you have

l75|118.c: Personal brand isn't a dirty word: speak up, but admit some content is bad and keep improving.
l75|118.e: In big companies people are told to keep their heads down, build good products, let the work speak and skip the personal brand. She now thinks that's wrong: what you stand for, your values and where you go next are things only you can decide. A personal brand isn't bragging. It means highlighting what you're genuinely good at, then choosing writing, video or tweets to tell it. But she disagrees with Sriram that there is no such thing as cringe content. Bad content exists, so stay self-aware, change course when nothing lands, and keep grinding every day like Rocky.
ex: Both she and Sriram have been told they care too much about personal brand

items.d: Writing, video or tweets, your choice

l75|118.c: Start a community with a small niche, and figure out how it makes money early.
l75|118.e: She often sees founders set out to build "the world's largest community of X" and start with the scaled-up version, which sets them up to fail. Better to do things that don't scale, find a small group unusually passionate about something, and grow from there. Her second point may be controversial: if the community is a business, think about monetization early. Many communities wait until they're big to start charging, then lose a huge share of members and discover that their supposed stickiness couldn't survive a price tag. Design it early and monetization becomes a weapon rather than a crutch.
ex: She led the creation of Facebook Stars, the platform's creator tipping feature

terms.d: Don't wait until you're big to charge

result.d: Monetization as weapon, not crutch

l75|118.c: You beat impostor syndrome not with reassurance but by finding what you're genuinely great at.
l75|118.e: From school through Microsoft she worried she'd be found out one day. At her first startup people said good founders are great fundraisers, yet she struggled; the seed round dragged on for about eight months and she nearly quit. Then she discovered she was unusually good at acquiring customers cheaply. She wrote the approach up as a playbook, and investors passed it to other portfolio companies. That's where her confidence came from. Sriram did something similar: at Microsoft he retreated to the topics he knew best, open source and developer communities, and expanded from there. Amplify your strengths instead of patching weaknesses.
ex: She was told her accent was too thick and nobody would fund her

l75|118.c: Don't chase whatever investors are hyping, especially when your product is working; the market wins in the end.
l75|118.e: At her startup she saw "sharing economy" become the hot phrase and had her tiny team spin up a side project letting users rent out their own belongings. But that required entirely different skills and fulfillment, and it took months to shut down when it should have ended sooner. She sees the same problem in companies slapping an AI label on themselves today. A four-person team doing consumer and B2B at once has to face the trade-off. At Netflix she also ran a 3D streaming experiment and killed it because the experience was poor. In hindsight, when something feels clearly better, trust that instinct over senior people's judgment.
ex: Netflix's 3D experiment covered only about seven films
Her company then sold consumer electronics online and partnered with Best Buy

items.d: The topic investors are buzzing about
A small group starts a side line

l76|120.c: OKRs are a vitamin, not a medicine: they strengthen a healthy company and expose problems in a sick one.
l76|120.e: She has noticed that companies that succeed with OKRs already have a clear strategy, empowered teams, and psychological safety. OKRs are just a layer on top that makes those stronger. Given that base, they deliver four things: they turn strategy into concrete numbers to move this quarter; they create a rhythm of progress; they make the whole company clear on the one thing that matters most; and the end-of-quarter grading creates a learning loop. Focus on retention for a quarter or two, then move to acquisition, and what you learn accumulates. OKRs are like "eat less, move more": simple to state, hard to stick with.
ex: A healthcare client focused with OKRs and brought in robots to lift heavy loads for staff
She has run her own life on OKRs for years and finds health slips whenever she gets busy

items.d: They decide how to do it
A strong hypothesis about how to win

l76|120.c: The smallest unit of OKRs is a question: what can I do this week to get closer to what I want?
l76|120.e: A mission needn't be eternal, she says; think of it as what you hope happens within five years. Strategy is a strong hypothesis about how to win, answering questions like physical or digital product, subscription or one-time sale. From there you work down to this year, this quarter and this week. She argues for a "half-formed" strategy: too much ties your hands, too little lets events push you around. So write detailed key results for the first quarter, only objectives for the later ones, and decide once you see results. Time landmarks like Mondays and the start of a quarter are moments to stop and look up, which fights "I'll do it tomorrow."
ex: In her peer group, the one person who asked about direction weekly went from PM to well-paid life coach
A quarter is long enough to get things done and short enough to remember what you did

items.d: What you want to see in about five years
A strong hypothesis about how to win
A year of exploring or polishing
The level with the most impact
One step closer to the goal

l76|120.c: Objectives should inspire; key results answer "how do we know we succeeded," not list tasks.
