l76|120.e: Objectives tend to fail in two ways: so vague they mean nothing, or so dull they read like "ship feature X." A good objective makes you want to get out of bed when the alarm rings, without being absurd. The most common mistake with key results is writing them as tasks. She likes three key results that check each other: a hard metric, a softer quality metric, and one tied to money. Spend ten minutes brainstorming every possible way to measure; odd ideas often lead to good ones. Set the target so people feel slightly uneasy but not hopeless, and hitting about 70% counts as success.
ex: Home magazine example: build an interest profile for users this quarter
Key results: about 30% of readers become members; each likes 3 products a week
A user panel every two weeks to measure how much people love it

root.d: The vision to run toward this quarter

items.d: Such as active users or reach

l76|120.c: The cadence is the most valuable part of OKRs: commit on Monday, celebrate Friday, learn over grading.
l76|120.e: Every Monday, answer what you'll do this week to move the objective; every Friday, celebrate the best things that happened. Many CEOs feel the mood shift just from starting Friday celebrations. The weekly status covers only three things: confidence in each key result, what you did last week, and what you'll do next, with at most three top priorities. Record why things didn't get done and you learn far more, ideally visible to the whole company. At quarter's end, don't agonize over precise grades; focus on why you fell short. Keep planning short, and replace approvals with asking three related teams for feedback within 24 hours.
ex: At MySpace, the consolidated weekly report went unread
Zynga's short, subscribable status reports told her who to go talk to

items.d: How to move the objective this week
Share the best things of the week

l76|120.c: Failing OKRs are a diagnostic signal; the usual cause is rolling out too fast, so pilot with your best team.
l76|120.e: If OKR reviews are boring, she says, leaders are stuck in the details. Look only at each team's few most important initiatives and leave the rest to them. Then keep asking why: why don't you trust your people? Is hiring the problem? When teams bring you small decisions, it's often not timidity but that you are scary. If the whole company is confused, the problem may be you. The failure she sees most is speed: someone reads half the book, hands it to HR for a company-wide rollout, and later declares OKRs don't work. Instead, let your best cross-functional team try it for a quarter, learn what doesn't fit your culture, then spread it gradually.
ex: Don't use OKRs to fix a bad team; people will just come to hate OKRs
She recommends the book "The Five Dysfunctions of a Team"

items.d: Unclear strategy, or people fear you

l76|120.c: Stories and sketches reach the oldest part of the brain, the fastest route to shared understanding.
l76|120.e: For most of human history knowledge passed by word of mouth, so stories deliver attention, understanding and memory at once. A bare list of facts is soon forgotten, especially facts that clash with what the listener already believes, but facts wrapped in a story stick. The structure can be simple: open with a hook such as a mystery, a secret or a surprise; put the information you need to convey in the middle; close with success and celebration. Afterwards ask someone you trust how it could be told better. Sketching works the same way. Words are abstract, and an ugly whiteboard drawing is better, because others grab the marker to fix it and soon everyone sees the same picture.
ex: Most TED talks are stories with facts tucked inside
She'd rather designers sketch with engineers than spend hours on wireframes

items.d: A mystery, a secret or a surprise
The information you need to convey
How could it be told better?

l76|120.c: PMs serve the business first; young people lack product sense and should build business knowledge and experience.
l76|120.e: She teaches a PM course at Stanford, and many students finish it realizing they'd rather do interaction design. PM education today borrows heavily from UX, and being human-centered is fine, but in the product triangle the PM represents the business: understanding the business model, the target market and industry trends, and knowing why you'd choose subscriptions or in-app purchases. Product sense is intuition, and intuition is compressed experience; young people don't have enough yet, so they should study which patterns work and why. She suggests starting as an engineer or designer and asking around at small companies. PMs have no authority, only influence, so if you don't like people, don't do it.
ex: Teresa Torres's product triangle: business, experience, technology
The best product cultures are often at 250-person companies in niche markets

items: Thinks the PM is in charge
Know the business model and market

d.verdict: PMs are responsible for the company's survival and health

l77|123.c: Build for how users feel, not for graphs; use metrics only to check you're being honest with yourself.
l77|123.e: At Facebook he saw Silicon Valley's obsession with graphs and metrics. It works, but it misses a lot. The people who created Nike, Disney and Apple thought about people, not curves. So for every feature they first ask: should the user feel delighted, fast, organized or focused? Pick the right feeling and it usually moves the metrics you care about anyway: a feature that surprises people gets screenshotted and shared, which is why the company has no growth team. He admits that feelings alone have blind spots too. You need both; it's just that the Valley has drifted too far one way.
ex: Facing Snapchat, Facebook watched share counts when it should have asked if people felt closer
Their one metric: people using Arc at least 5 days a week, growing over 10% weekly
The Peek feature was designed to feel light and effortless

items: Ask: did the line go up?
Decide the emotion you want first
The right feeling moves the metrics

d.verdict: You need both, but create with the person behind the screen in mind

l77|123.c: Values shouldn't be slogans; write down traits the team already has and the team will ship them.
l77|123.e: He used to dislike corporate values, which felt like fortune-cookie lines. About two years in, he kept hearing the same traits in anniversary conversations with employees. So he interviewed everyone on the team, and almost every word came from them; he then wrote it up as an essay about road trips, which took about three months. He thinks the team ships fast precisely because it lives these values: come with a chip on your shoulder, assume you don't know so you start moving, first ask what else this could be, and make people feel something.
ex: The values essay is called "Notes on Road Trips"
A co-creator of the first version of Chrome has the strongest beginner's mind on the team

items.t: Ask what else it could be

l77|123.c: Treat the team itself as a product and celebrate each member publicly, and top people snowball in.
l77|123.e: He admits he never cared about browsers. Looking back over ten years with his co-founder Hursh, their best memories came from time spent with a group of people. So they decided to pick a problem that would attract the strongest people in the industry and work in a way they believed in. In interviews he often talks people out of joining. From the very first hire, they announced each new teammate publicly like a product launch, and when they ship a feature they name the people who built it instead of crediting the CEO. Senior people join as individual engineers or designers, he thinks, because they want to make career-defining work.
ex: A co-creator of Chrome 1.0 and someone who ran Chrome for 16 years joined as individual contributors
Tumblr's first designer and Slack's former SVP of design also joined as individual contributors

items.d: One the best people want to work on
Trust them to do it their way
Credit goes to whoever did the work

l77|123.c: Building in public isn't about transparency; it's about rebuilding trust when tech has lost it.
l77|123.e: They film internal meetings, even board meetings, and post them. A browser holds a person's most sensitive personal and work data, and public trust in tech companies has been damaged again and again, so even the best privacy policy isn't enough. Their bet is that once you know the imperfect, ordinary people behind the screen, you'll believe them when they ask for a permission that it's for your benefit. He calls this radical trust-building rather than radical transparency. He also worries the experiment has gone too far and put him, the CEO, too much at the center of the story.
ex: A video responding to MKBHD's review became their most-watched YouTube video
When someone on Twitter assumed the worst about them, he found he understood why

items.d: Believe it's for the user's good

l77|123.c: Redefine and rename a team from first principles and you shed the industry's assumptions about the role.
l77|123.e: At Facebook he most admired the user research team, yet felt research was treated as a service department. So they merged support, customer success and user research into a "membership team" that owns a person's whole journey from first contact to long-term use. A "storytelling team" faces people who don't use Arc yet: investors, press and the public. There is no PM department either; PM is a role assigned per project, so an infrastructure engineer runs the performance project. A new name makes people ask what the job really is. He admits this has started to break down in places.
ex: The three-person storytelling team includes a former Verge reporter and an independent filmmaker
They like "hybrid" hires, such as a head of data who also acts as PM

l77|123.c: Not every product deserves obsessive polish; they chose browsers because experience decides the winner there.
l77|123.e: As an investor at Thrive Capital he learned that each idea has one attribute that decides success or failure. Browsers have three traits: they are among the most universal consumer software, used by parents and kids alike; they are nearly interchangeable, since most run the same Chromium code; and they are extremely profitable. That means the only way to win is an emotional connection that makes people irrationally prefer you, so caring about delight and animation is a pragmatic, even capitalist choice. By contrast, nobody cares about rounded corners in cybersecurity software sold to governments, and a beautiful remote-collaboration tool still loses if its latency is worse than Zoom's.
ex: Tuple has a simple design and better audio quality than Zoom
The browser market is mostly held by Google, Apple and Microsoft

terms.d: Each extra user costs almost nothing

result.d: Experience and brand are growth and revenue

l77|123.c: Computing is moving to the cloud, and Arc wants to be the internet computer, as the iPhone was to phones.
l77|123.e: His and Hursh's first company underestimated the mobile wave. What's underestimated now, he thinks, is computing moving wholesale to the cloud: most apps are web apps, your files and photos are really URLs, nothing is lost if you smash the device, and hardware is becoming an empty shell. So they're building not just a replacement browser but a new interface to cloud computing. Long term, the developer platform matters more than built-in features. The web is free, works across devices and takes no cut, yet loses on experience. Apple wants you in the App Store and Google wants content it can index, so neither has an incentive to make the web feel like native apps.
ex: A Figma blog post invited users to "see you in the browser"
Google treats the Chrome extension platform as a loss leader

items.d: Arc: a stronger interface than a browser
Apps, files and photos are all URLs
Just a shell to look through

l78|125.c: Ideas spread because people want to repeat them, not because they're doing a company a favor.
l78|125.e: People repeat things to entertain others, to seem interesting, or to express who they are. Nobody wants to run errands for a company. So package the message as a joke, an analogy, a short phrase you say over and over, a vivid image or a small story, and go easy on subjective adjectives. The test is whether a second-grader gets it instantly. Compress the mission into one sentence, strip out the clichés, add a metaphor or an image, and you're most of the way there. The worst mistake is throwing an inside joke that only you understand at the public.
ex: "Move fast and break things": ordinary words in an unusual combination
"Hide the pill in the cheese": you see it the moment you hear it
In her thread, the tweet quoting a book review's "ocean" metaphor saw likes plunge

root.d: Zero mental effort for the listener

items.d: Something you can see in your head

l78|125.c: Don't try to change what your audience cares about; graft your message onto passions they already have.
l78|125.e: Changing someone's worldview or passions is extremely heavy lifting, and she has almost never seen anyone pull it off. Reshaping your own topic to fit a frame they already care about is far lighter. Your audience cares about X and you offer Y, so the communicator's job is to build a bridge from X to Y. She also says to accept that some people simply aren't your audience, and not to waste effort on them.
ex: Kamala Harris tied K-12 education to defense: enlisting requires a tenth-grade reading level
Rebutting a false story, Substack argued free speech rather than the company's grievance

items.d: How X relates to your Y
If you care about X, you should care about Y

l78|125.c: A startup's enemy is the status quo, so make errors of commission rather than errors of omission.
l78|125.e: Comms people often manage risk by doing nothing, she says, but that hands victory to the status quo, your biggest opponent, without a fight. An error of commission is visible immediately, so you can review it and improve fast. An error of omission can't be seen or learned from; the opportunity just quietly slips away. She compares it to investing: holding cash looks safe but inflation makes you poorer, while investing is volatile yet far better over time.
ex: While on maternity leave she tweeted a thread on Substack's free-speech stance that got over 30,000 likes

items: Can't be observed or learned from
Visible at once, fast to fix

d.verdict: Act, and turn mistakes into learning

l78|125.c: A message starts with you and moves outward in concentric circles, and you can't skip a ring.
l78|125.e: First she boils the thousand facts in her head down to one to three clear messages. Then she wins over co-founders, executives, employees, investors and power users in that order, and only then the outside world. Outer rings assume inner rings know more: if employees aren't excited, why would anyone else be? And if insiders feel they were sold a bait-and-switch, the backlash is worst from them. In practice, list five or six audience groups on one page, rank them by influence and credibility, and write down what each cares about and where it gets information.
ex: Substack gave power writers like Lenny early access to Recommendations, and they promoted it themselves
Outer rings include reporters who cover media, writer-influencers and investors

items.d: Boil it down to one to three messages
Get the innermost ring aligned first
They follow the inner rings' attitude

l78|125.c: Work backwards from the business goal: who must act, what they must believe, and where they listen.
l78|125.e: Comms results are often judged by feel, so she pushes for as much discipline as possible. Start from a business goal such as revenue or market penetration, not impressions or a viral hit. Then decide which people, how many, taking what action. Next, what do they need to believe first? Then figure out whom they listen to and which accounts and podcasts they follow. You end up with a full equation: deliver this message through these channels to these people to drive this action, instead of shouting into the void.
ex: Selling a new running shoe: people must first believe their feet hurt now and the new tech is real

items.d: Whom they listen to, what they watch

l78|125.c: Pressure equals force over area: a small company should narrow its audience and win ten superfans first.
l78|125.e: Her metaphor is the physics formula. Force is the money, time and even credibility you put in, and it's limited; the smaller the area, the more pressure the same force creates. At one end of the spectrum you move a single person; at the other is "world peace is good," which everyone agrees with and nobody feels. Startups should sit near the narrow end, build a "mini-monopoly" in some corner of the internet, and let superfans carry it outward. Don't worry the market is too small; in the digital age the denominator is huge. Try to please everyone and you get averaged into mediocrity.
ex: Spending $100 to reach the 100 people who matter beats spending a million to reach a million
Balaji's new book hit number one on Amazon through his own channels and superfans
Her closing advice: give the product free to people who will obsess over it and have influence

l78|125.c: Founders should speak directly in a human voice, and early on go deep on the one channel they're good at.
l78|125.e: People don't trust or love companies; they trust and like people, so a faceless corporate voice gets ignored. A direct channel has to be tied to an executive speaking in the first person with a real voice, allowed to make mistakes and show vulnerability. On defense: anyone going against the grain will be attacked and has no institution to back them, so build the audience and the posting rhythm in calm times so it doesn't look odd in a crisis. On offense: someone doing something genuinely new tells the story better than any reporter. Start with the one format the speaker is best at, whether long posts, video or short posts, prepare a week or two of content to launch, then value consistency over chasing hits.
ex: Flexport's Ryan Petersen became the human face of his company
She estimates about 95% of LinkedIn is congratulations, so good content is scarce
The beauty brand NYX spends almost nothing on marketing and relies on influencers

terms.d: First person, authentic, allowed to err
Build it early on one channel

result.d: Offense: tell the story; defense: defend yourself

l79|130.c: Super apps are overrated: if users can't see how the services connect, cross-selling fails.
l79|130.e: A "super app" (dozens of services inside one app) looks great on investor and consultant slides: cheaper customer acquisition, easy cross-selling, better retention. But Gojek's user research found those benefits often didn't show up. Users understood Gojek as "the guys on motorbikes," so moving from rides to package delivery, food and groceries felt natural. Once the company launched services that had nothing to do with drivers, users were confused. Gojek had to spend on ads to educate them again, acquisition costs went back up, and the home screen turned into a giant grid of icons.
ex: Over 95% of users needed phone top-ups, yet only 30-40% knew Gojek offered them
After launching home massages, users asked whether the driver would do the massage
At its peak the app held nearly 30 services

items: Users didn't know the service existed
Had to re-educate users; costs rose again
Home screen became a giant grid

d.verdict: Services must share one idea users already understand

l79|130.c: In consumer businesses, product and brand matter most; brand kept Gojek alive with 100x less money.
l79|130.e: He thinks treating brand as a soft, afterthought item is one of the biggest mistakes consumer tech companies make. A good brand makes users associate you with more than a transaction. It becomes part of who they are, and that loyalty isn't easily bought away by a rival's discounts. The way to build it is consistency at every touchpoint: ads, in-app copy, even the design of the interface. Gojek was first to run self-deprecating ads that poked fun at local culture, and it built local customs directly into product features.
ex: Rivals had far more money for user discounts and driver subsidies
GoFood let you send food far away, handy for sending a meal to a crush
Apple fans and Nike sneakerheads show how a brand becomes identity

items.d: Raised in the first six months after launching the app
Already raised in the same period

l79|130.c: The best brand exposure shows the service happening, not just a name to remember.
l79|130.e: Giving drivers branded jackets and helmets is, in his view, one of the most important decisions the company ever made. It wasn't only that the brand became visible all over the city. People saw the service in action: someone stuck in traffic watched a passenger on a Gojek bike weave past, or saw a driver delivering food and packages, and instantly connected the brand with what it could do for them. Opportunities like that are rare, which is why lazy billboards and pay-per-click ads are so common. Rivals who entered motorbikes from a car mindset didn't brand their drivers at all at first.
ex: If an airline dressed pedestrians in its logo, people would only remember the name
Lenny compares it to Lyft's early pink mustaches on cars

items.d: I could get around like that

l79|130.c: Every advantage gets copied eventually; doing hard, valuable things is what rivals struggle to match.
l79|130.e: He dislikes the word "moat" (an advantage others can't copy), because skills, features and channel partners all erode with time. But hard things stay hard, and as long as they create value for users, rivals can't easily steal those users. Early on, motorbike taxi gangs attacked Gojek drivers with bricks and machetes. Instead of hiding behind "drivers are contractors," the company ran its own security for years: a hotline, patrols in hot spots, a response within 5 to 10 minutes. Drivers came to believe the company truly cared, and later rivals couldn't poach them even with more money.
ex: Partnered with a private security firm to patrol hot spots in Jakarta
Before digital payments existed, built cash counters where drivers collected pay with their ID
Only later connected to banks and ATM networks

l79|130.c: A founder should do every job once to learn what great looks like and whom to hire.
l79|130.e: In a market short on experienced talent, you can't just hire "the person who did X at company Y" and trust they'll be good. So he did the jobs himself, running ad campaigns and writing push notifications, saw how bad he was, and learned what good actually looked like. Then he hired people several orders of magnitude better. Driving a motorbike taxi was different: that was about empathy. He was the platform's first driver, once took a passenger on a detour to a laundromat for very little money, and later pushed hard for waiting fees and multi-stop trips.
ex: Ran amateur performance marketing, buying ads on Facebook and Google
After the laundry detour, backed waiting fees and multi-stop rides

result.d: Then hire people far better

l79|130.c: Outside Silicon Valley, solve problems with people first, go remote early, and don't copy America.
l79|130.e: Southeast Asia draws global giants into the fight, yet local talent and capital are thin. His lessons: first, solve problems with operations and manual work, because waiting for a technical fix takes too long. When security engineers were scarce, Gojek simply built the most popular features of knock-off driver apps into its official one. Second, get good at remote work early and build teams where talent is deep. Third, don't copy. Gojek isn't an Uber clone; it grew around a uniquely Indonesian thing, the motorbike taxi driver. The population is young and the pain points obvious, so a product that fits grows astonishingly fast.
ex: Opened an engineering center in Bangalore in 2015
Grew over 100% month over month for 16 to 18 months after launch
eFishery built a full fish-farming system, with about $250 million in revenue and profits

items.d: Build teams where talent is deep

l79|130.c: Whoever owns the outcome makes the call; that beats "good ideas can come from anyone."
l79|130.e: A lot of product writing describes teams as places where "good ideas can come from anyone." He thinks the intent is right and everyone should contribute ideas. But when it's unclear who owns a decision and who makes it, execution slows down a lot. Gojek made the decision-maker explicit for every item in its product process, and made that person the one accountable for the result. Execution improved noticeably.

l80|32.c: Cheap money made startups run like Google, producing PMs who follow process and never take risks.
l80|32.e: When money was easy, every company staffed PMs as if it had Google's margins: engineers, designers, researchers and analysts on every team. PMs got used to demanding full data and user interviews before proposing anything, and nobody took risks. But he thinks the fastest way to learn is usually to ship, and for simple problems you can just look at what the leading companies do. In interviews he skips the resume and gives a real scenario, to see whether a candidate can come up with a few ideas without research and design a quick test. Only PMs who just apply frameworks and wait for promotion will be replaced by AI.
ex: A candidate said they couldn't propose anything without seeing data and interviewing customers
Interview red flags: plans that take months to show a signal, no guardrail metrics
Notion AI invented a stint at Google for his bio

items.d: Everyone spends like a public company
Research, analytics, design on every team
A whole quarter with no launches

l80|32.c: User research is scarce: consumer apps run experiments, enterprise talks to customers, the middle must choose carefully.
l80|32.e: For large consumer products, users aren't experts and experiments and data are cheap, so research steps in only when results are hard to interpret. Large enterprise customers are sophisticated and rational and pay six figures or more, so talking directly to them and to the sales team is research in itself. The hard case is the middle: many customers who are also fairly expert, such as small businesses. There, research goes only to two high-value kinds of questions: a problem that's big but poorly defined, or a problem that's clear but where you're unsure the solution will land.
ex: Eventbrite focused its research on the business event organizers
Redesigning a login page needs no research; copy what top companies do

marks.d: Research only when results confuse you

l80|32.c: Founders should direct new leaders closely until those leaders prove they know better.
l80|32.e: A founder who has found product-market fit has built up a lot of intuition that's hard to put into words. A new executive, however experienced, doesn't understand the business as well, so "handing it to the experts" too early is a mistake. Once the company scales, the founder can only go broad, not deep. Employees start to know specific areas better than the founder, and that's when to delegate. Scaling also means stop iterating on new products and focus on growth. Employees should signal clearly too. If overruled, find the kind of evidence the CEO accepts: an experiment, customers, an outside adviser. If that fails, disagree and commit, or leave.
ex: A rival Grubhub acquired ran everything through its founder and scaled more slowly
Grubhub's founder insisted on building a driver app, which proved far-sighted
Eventbrite had "drivers" and Whatnot has DRIs: once decided, it gets done

items.d: Team surpasses the founder in their areas

l80|32.c: Network effects come in three kinds: direct, cross-side and data. Social networks end up needing the last two.
l80|32.e: A network effect means a product gets better as more people use it. Direct: every new user benefits everyone. Cross-side: more people on one side makes the other side more valuable, and vice versa. Data: more data means better quality or lower cost. Social networks are usually seen as direct, but only pure messaging tools stay that way. Once you sell ads and separate creators from consumers, you've become cross-side. Once you personalize recommendations, you depend on data. Network effects are the best defense a company has, but they don't make it immune to disruption.
ex: WhatsApp: direct
Grubhub's restaurants and diners: cross-side
Pinterest's signals from users saving pins to boards: data

root.d: Better as more people use it

items.d: Two groups make each other more valuable

l80|32.c: Against an existential threat, the only rational response is to overreact and assume the disruptor is right.
l80|32.e: A cross-side marketplace usually gets disrupted when a rival massively expands the choice on the supply side. Grubhub was an asset-light, high-margin matchmaker. DoorDash and others built their own delivery fleets, lost money on every order for years, started with suburban restaurants that never delivered, and even delivered without restaurants' consent. By the time they entered cities, their selection far exceeded Grubhub's. Grubhub assumed the model was structurally unprofitable and the VCs would eventually stop funding it. Instead, the rivals kept raising money, signed national chains, and the pandemic made them profitable. He thinks the only way out was to buy DoorDash early.
ex: Grubhub raised $80 million before going public and $100 million at IPO
Rivals raised roughly $100 million every six months
Rover quickly copied Wag's high-frequency dog-walking use case and did it better

items.d: Leads New York on corporate lunch budgets
DoorDash starts in suburbs, expands choice
Rivals turn profitable; office orders vanish

l80|32.c: A marketplace can easily add SaaS tools, but a SaaS company rarely grows a marketplace.
l80|32.e: For SaaS to become a marketplace, two things must already be true: your service touches both your customer and your customer's customers, and those end customers recognize your brand; and buyers have a reason to deal with multiple sellers, so they need to discover new ones. On top of that, you must build new capabilities for a completely different audience. The reverse is much easier: a marketplace adds SaaS as a tool to acquire customers, run workflows or stop people from going around the platform. To tell whether something is a real marketplace, ask whether suppliers join mainly because it brings them extra business.
ex: Eventbrite drives 25% of ticket sales; he thinks it needs nearly 50% to work
Faire built the wholesale marketplace first, then used free SaaS to pull in retailers
OpenTable sold for about $2.6 billion and was later written down below $1 billion

items: Must build tools for a new audience
SaaS as a customer acquisition tool

d.verdict: Crack the hard marketplace first, then expand nearby

l80|32.c: Consumer subscriptions have no net revenue retention, so paid acquisition plus freemium can't last.
l80|32.e: The appeal of B2B SaaS isn't just predictable revenue. Businesses are rational and can be screened, and the ones that stay spend more every year. Consumers are unpredictable, churn more, and won't pay more in year two. So annual retention has to be 60-70% or higher, and only a handful manage it: Netflix, Prime, Spotify, Duolingo. Paid acquisition gets worse with scale, because you always capture the best users first. The way out is to add social features, bring in a supply side, build network effects or organic growth loops, and push acquisition costs toward zero.
ex: Calm stayed around 10 people and barely lost money while Headspace grew to hundreds
Duolingo relies on a data network effect
Apple's ATT privacy rules hit paid acquisition hard

items.d: Blue Apron when it went public
Blue Apron at recording, by his account

l81|132.c: Product-led growth and sales aren't either-or; most B2B companies end up with both.
l81|132.e: She has never agreed that PLG is the only future and sales will disappear. PLG lowers the barrier to trying a product and widens reach; it's a volume game. Sales locks in large customers and big contracts; it's the solid base of revenue. If you only have sales, a rival that adds PLG can get into your accounts through individual end users. If you only have PLG, someone else may win the big accounts first. Adding sales on top of PLG is easier than the reverse. PLG took off because the people using B2B software are ordinary consumers who are used to trying before buying.
ex: Defense software has only a few target customers worldwide, so PLG doesn't fit
Sales-led pioneers like Salesforce are adding self-serve paths too
Zoom: meeting attendees use it first, then sign up and pay themselves

marks.d: Only a handful of target customers
Customer value can't support a sales team

l81|132.c: PLG is really data-led growth; without a data foundation you're just giving the product away.
l81|132.e: Giving the product away for free should buy you two things: wider reach, and behavioral data from free users, meaning which features correlate with higher conversion and retention. Companies that sell through sales often lack fine-grained usage data, and they still need to connect it with marketing campaigns and the CRM into a full picture of each customer. She advises not rushing to pick tools. First audit your event tracking and build a data dictionary so every event has one agreed definition; otherwise it's garbage in, garbage out. The basic stack: a data pipeline, product analytics, experimentation, and lifecycle marketing tools.
ex: Segment as the data pipeline; Amplitude or PostHog for product analytics
Optimizely or Eppo for experiments
Clearbit or ZoomInfo to fill in which company a user works for

terms.d: Free lowers the barrier to entry
Which features drive conversion and retention

result.d: Without data, it's a giveaway

l81|132.c: Adding PLG requires a free entry point, fast time to value, self-serve checkout, data and simple pricing.
l81|132.e: On many B2B websites the most prominent button is "book a demo," which cuts off the self-serve path entirely. Step one is a low-barrier entry point: a free tier, a trial, open source, or at least a realistic interactive demo. Next, shorten time to value by giving users a warm start and a small delight. Then self-serve checkout. Then use data to understand the gap between activation and paying. Pricing also needs to be simple. Red flags: treating PLG as just launching a free trial, assigning one person part-time, or doing it because it's fashionable. She suggests committing for at least one to two years.
ex: Amplitude once used an interactive demo to move toward PLG
Give trial users a sample video or sample workflow to create a small aha

items.d: Free tier, trial, open source or demo
Warm start and a small aha
Buy the moment you want to
See the gap from activation to paying
No need to ask sales for a quote

l81|132.c: A PLG funnel treats product usage as the leading indicator, not scores for marketing engagement.
l81|132.e: In a traditional sales funnel, marketing scores leads on actions like opening emails or reading white papers. Once a lead scores high enough it becomes an MQL and goes to sales, because nobody can use the product before signing. A PLG funnel looks more like B2C: after sign-up, what matters is whether people use the product, and marketing emails are only support. From usage there are two paths to revenue. If the price fits the budget, users buy with a credit card. If usage is high and the account fits the ideal customer profile, it becomes a product-qualified lead (PQL) that sales nurtures toward a bigger contract.
ex: GitLab: developers use the free tier on personal projects, then push their company to trial it
Teams run a 30-day trial as proof of concept; small teams self-serve a few seats

items: Self-serve, or PQL handed to sales

d.verdict: Map both funnels first and find the missing pieces

l81|132.c: Walk the whole funnel as a user to find leverage; activation and checkout are usually the best starting points.
l81|132.e: Growth work is about finding leverage: small effort, big result, and momentum for later experiments. The first thing she does for a client is go through the whole journey as a prospective buyer. Is the landing page compelling? Is sign-up smooth? Do you reach the aha moment quickly? Can you actually buy when you want to? Then she reads the first few emails and checks the data at each step. Most B2B software was never designed for quick onboarding, so activation is usually the best place to start. Checkout can borrow from e-commerce. The PQL path is more complex and better left for later. Collaboration products can prioritize product-led acquisition.
ex: A checkout form asked everyone a question only UK customers needed to answer
One company added a payment option and success rates in India jumped
Miro takes about five minutes from sign-up to finishing a task with a template

l81|132.c: To define the aha moment, find behaviors that correlate with conversion and retention, then test for causation.
l81|132.e: The aha moment is when a user first experiences the product's value. GitLab started by listing about ten high-value actions that might represent value, such as merging a first pull request or running a first pipeline. Then it compared users who did each action on 90-day conversion and 30-day retention, looking at both together. Because the platform has many features and teams arrive with different goals, it ended up with a composite metric. Data only shows correlation, so the next step is experiments that push more users to complete those actions and checking whether the metrics actually rise. For complex products, users don't have to get there on day one.
ex: GitLab: 2 users using 2 features within 14 days
Facebook: 10 friends in 7 days

items.d: Such as merging a first PR
Can be a combination of actions

l81|132.c: Retention is the messy middle, and it can often be reframed as adoption of a high-frequency use case.
l81|132.e: Retention plays out over long cycles, users can leave at any time, and it's hard to test quickly, so it's usually not the first place to start. Fundamentally the product needs to be frequent enough, collaborative, or embedded in a workflow; email reminders only help at the margins. At Acorns, the passive investing philosophy meant users had no reason to come back. So she first identified the feature most correlated with retention, recurring investments, and pushed it hard, then added high-frequency use cases like retirement accounts and a debit card. Expansion is part of retention too: upgrading tiers, adding seats, adding usage, all triggered by data at the right moment.
ex: Acorns: recurring investing correlated strongly with retention; the better-known round-ups didn't
GitLab expansion: upgrade tiers, add seats, buy more CI/CD minutes

items.d: Embedded in workflow; the base of retention

l81|132.c: Start PLG with a growth PM and an analyst; formalize a cross-functional PLG org after early wins.
l81|132.e: The usual starting point is hiring a head of growth or a senior growth PM, backed by dedicated engineers, data and design as a core squad. If the first priority is something like PQLs, which touches data and sales, a temporary tiger team can go first. She would even hire the analyst first, because experiments without insight have no direction. Prefer internal people who are interested; when hiring externally, match experience to your starting point. After early wins, formalize it: three leaders from different departments jointly own the same funnel.
ex: One client moved its former head of investor relations into the head of growth role
Every ticket states the success metric and the growth lever it targets
Interview question: which experiment surprised you, and what did you do next?

l82|133.c: Trello won through progressive disclosure: start with a simple problem and grow as users' needs get complex.
l82|133.e: Trello started out simple in design, easy to pick up, with no configuration needed, usable alone or with others. That drew small businesses, families and people planning weddings. As users' problems got more complex, the product grew with them. Many competitors did the opposite: complex from day one, so making them simple meant stripping things out yourself. She believes productivity software can never satisfy the different definitions of efficiency held by product, design, engineering and data at once. You get 80% of the core right first, then pick the 20% your core users care about.
ex: She joined Trello to build the enterprise business, scaling from three to five collaborators to twenty
Small teams still brainstorming and prioritizing suit Trello; once decided, break tasks down in Jira
Power-Ups integrations are often underrated

items: Add features as users need them

d.verdict: Let the product grow up with its users

l82|133.c: Have product, design, engineering and data each write down what they expect of each other, as a contract.
l82|133.e: When building a strong team, she starts by making roles and responsibilities clear. Each function's lead writes down their own responsibilities and what they expect from the other three, then everyone reviews and argues until they agree, and the contract rolls out level by level across the organization. It takes time and sparks debate, but it stops everything from piling onto a vaguely defined PM and shows which responsibilities are shared. Ideally you revisit it every three to six months; in practice it gets reopened when conflict or a gap appears, and the most common sticking point is execution speed.
ex: Project management shifted gradually from Scrum Masters to engineering managers
Embedding data scientists in teams saved PMs from begging for resources
In Shanghai, PMs were expected to have every answer; she shared that load with the team

l82|133.c: Overemphasizing outcomes neglects output; shipping speed is itself a leading indicator of outcomes.
l82|133.e: For years everyone has chanted "outcomes, outcomes, outcomes." The direction is right, she says, but many teams, hers included, went too far and forgot that output is an indicator of outcomes. You can nail the ideation, the decisions and every brief, but if not enough reaches the market fast enough, it means little. More attempts mean a higher chance of getting it right. Break the speed problem apart: PMs often get stuck on decision speed, engineering on not slicing tickets small enough. She sees driving urgency as product's job.
ex: She asks only: what shipped this sprint, and how long is the cycle?
A warning sign: something doable in a week or two still being discussed two quarters later
Many founders claim "no competitors," and years later rivals are all shipping good products

result.d: You need both

l82|133.c: PMs are getting more technical, designers more business-minded, engineers more user-focused, so collaboration deepens.
l82|133.e: Product management has gone mainstream, with degrees, courses and a whole industry around it. That has benefits, but may also sand off some quirkiness and creativity. In terms of roles, PMs have swung from "everyone is a generalist" back to being expected to know more about technology, though she doesn't think they must write code. The best designers are shrewd businesspeople. Engineers care more and more about the product and its users. When each function keeps its expertise but cares about the others' domains, good ideas can come from anywhere.
ex: "Product manager" now shows up in elementary school career-matching exercises
Her interview question: artist, scientist or general manager, which are you most?
Advice for newcomers: join a small company and touch every function

items.d: Taking coding and data analysis courses
Design as a means to an end

l82|133.c: She doesn't chase work-life balance; she asks what she is optimizing for right now.
l82|133.e: PMs are expected to be good at everything, have answers at all times and stay calm. She tells her team again and again "I know this is hard," and focuses on one thing at a time. As a mother she has dropped the word "balance" for "optimize": what am I optimizing for today, this quarter, this year? And she accepts that not everything can be good at once. Early in her career she would sprint for weeks before a big release, then recover with things like morning runs. Life stage shapes choices too; right now she wouldn't join a very early startup that demands long hours in person.
ex: One week she owns the school run; the next she goes all in on work
In quarterly planning she also asks: given what Q1 taught us, what are we optimizing for?

items.d: Start at ten after a long run

l82|133.c: Remote teams run on documents and async work, and gather in person for two days when a hard problem hits.
l82|133.e: She has spent her whole career on distributed teams. The foundation is strong documentation and the ability to work asynchronously, plus a fixed window of overlapping hours; new hires onboard in person for about a week. She has found it far harder to solve tough problems remotely with people you've never met, argued with or shared a meal with. So when a thorny issue comes up, she brings everyone together in person for 48 hours: agree the agenda in advance, meet during the day, eat dinner together at night to build trust, then go back to remote.
ex: One strategy shift went back and forth in documents across time zones for days without resolution
The breakthrough at that offsite came when the data colleague explained the data to everyone
An earlier company gathered the whole team globally two or three times a year for a week or two

l83|135.c: A self-driving car must drive like a human yet more safely, and rider trust comes from many small designed details.
l83|135.e: Waymo trains deep models on human driving data but removes the bad driving examples, so the car feels natural rather than robotic while being safer than a person. The model has to read where pedestrians are looking and which way they're facing, understand signs and hand gestures, and learn the social norms that differ by city and intersection. Riders are usually amazed for the first five minutes and then find it unremarkable, and that naturalness is deliberately designed. The in-car screen shows what the car sees, and a support agent calls if a seatbelt is unbuckled; each detail builds trust.
ex: When merging, the car nudges in slowly, like using body language to ask for room
Going down steep San Francisco hills it drops below the speed limit, which matches rider expectations

l83|135.c: In self-driving, the MVP idea still applies, but the safety bar is raised extremely high.
l83|135.e: Compared with typical software, PMs here must go deep into technical detail, tolerate far more uncertainty and ambiguity, and have the stamina for a long game, improving continuously until the vision is real. The team self-selects too: people are driven by the mission of making roads safer. The idea of shipping a minimum viable product and iterating through real deployment still holds, but you can't cut corners on safety, so the bar for an MVP is simply much higher. Waymo went for fully driverless from the start rather than driver assistance that relies on a human ready to take over.
ex: About 1.35 million people die in road crashes each year, mostly from driver error and distraction
Her teams span in-car software, simulation and validation, and ride-hailing commercialization

d.verdict: Same philosophy, completely different bar

l83|135.c: Progress in self-driving is measured by both business operations and driving performance, with safety and efficiency in tension.
l83|135.e: Waymo already charges for rides in Phoenix and is open to the public in San Francisco, so it's no longer a pilot. That means tracking weekly trips, active users, funnel conversion at each step, and operating cost. On driving performance, the core goal is to be safer than humans, measured against benchmarks like human collisions per 100,000 miles. But "never moving" isn't the goal: they also watch whether the car slows unnecessarily, how often it needs rescue, and whether it holds up other traffic. Earning long-term investment, she says, depends on real progress in both technology and commercial deployment.
ex: She thinks L4 at scale can deliver the vision without waiting for L5
Driving in snow is still a capability to be solved

l83|135.c: Work backwards from customer problems, decide what not to build, and as a big company disrupt yourself first.
l83|135.e: At big companies and startups alike, she says, the core is working backwards from the user's problem: who it's for and what it solves, because technology for its own sake doesn't go far. Amazon makes PMs write the press release for launch day before work starts, which forces you to think through the value proposition. Just as important is being explicit about what you won't do; a product that tries to satisfy every request from every customer usually goes nowhere. Big companies are often the share leaders, so strategy tends to turn incremental, and they must disrupt themselves before a challenger does.
ex: Amazon's PR/FAQ: write the press release first
She was the first PM on Honeycode, Amazon's no-code development platform

terms.d: Write the launch press release first
Refuse to be everything to everyone

result.d: Avoid the innovator's dilemma

l83|135.c: Listening and empathy are underrated PM skills; to get promoted, stop wanting it and focus on business impact.
l83|135.e: People usually name influence, prioritization and writing as core PM skills, but she finds listening and empathy harder: absorb and understand first with a beginner's mind, hold back your own ideas, and actively challenge your assumptions. If there's no disagreement at all, you've probably missed the signal. On promotion, too much calculation shows and splits your attention. Focus on what genuinely matters to the business and go all in, while letting your manager know you want more challenging projects.
ex: Interviewing executives, she asks: when did you fail, and what did you learn?
The seven-email rule: if it's still unresolved after seven emails, call or meet in person

items.d: Do what's right for the company
Full commitment is visible on its own
Let your manager know you want a stretch

l84|137.c: In a marketplace, the supply side is the real product; serve them first and growth follows.
l84|137.e: Airbnb once thought its product was the technology, she says, then realized it was nothing without hosts. So it created a Hospitality team to support, recognize and hold hosts to standards. The key was getting the internal culture to believe this first; otherwise you build tools for their own sake and stare at booking numbers. Once the company built tools genuinely for hosts, users brought more users. She took two more lessons with her: energy is a company's currency, and a strong story can make even the smallest feature feel meaningful.
ex: At Airbnb she ran customer support, the Dublin office integration and global host operations
Fully remote Bobbie keeps both personal and work check-ins

items.d: Not just to sell more bookings

l84|137.c: In a crisis, slowing growth to keep existing customers' trust matters more than grabbing new ones.
l84|137.e: In 2022 a dominant formula maker issued a recall and the US ran short of formula; Bobbie's customer count doubled in the first week. Her head of growth saw inventory draining far faster than it could be replenished, with existing subscribers' babies running out in about six days. She decided to shut the website, take no new customers for six months, rename the growth team the "slowth team," and even email some subscribers suggesting they cancel. Bobbie became the only formula company that never let existing customers run dry, which earned deep loyalty. Earlier, when the FDA halted their pilot and products were pulled for relabeling for nearly a year, that was another patient pause.
ex: About 70,000 subscribers never missed a shipment
At Davos a customer told her in tears, "You saved me"

items.d: Pulled and relabeled for nearly a year

l84|137.c: A brand should answer what keeps customers up at night, without converting skeptics or putting others down.
l84|137.e: Someone once told her: think of the three things your customer worries about most when she wakes up tomorrow, and if your brand doesn't solve one of them, it's just noise. Bobbie's positioning and creative all center on parents' feeding struggles in the first year, with the goal of taking the guilt out of formula. "If you're explaining, you're losing," so she doesn't try to persuade people convinced that breast is best. Instead she amplifies the 83% of parents who use formula. The brand only talks about why it exists, never attacks competitors or other feeding choices, and leans on credible third parties when needed.
ex: She couldn't breastfeed, read the ingredient label on a can, and decided to start the company
Economist Emily Oster uses data to debunk breastfeeding myths

items: Put down competitors or other methods
Explaining puts you on the back foot
Talk only about why you exist

d.verdict: Spend your energy on the people who truly need you

l84|137.c: Give a dull internal process a brand name and people anticipate it, remember it and care about it.
l84|137.e: She calls "branding the mundane" her secret to getting things done, a trick learned at Airbnb, where analysis of support tickets was packaged as Air Dives and everyone looked forward to the new edition each Friday. At Bobbie, legal has to regularly check that marketing claims are compliant, so she turned it into a "secret shopper program": the regulatory team sweeps through like mystery shoppers once a month and reports back. That's far more appealing than a meeting called "legal reviews claim errors." Projects and Slack channels get code names too.
ex: Air Dives: Airbnb's deep dives into customer support pain points
Project code names like Shamrock and Lumberjack

result.d: The team is more motivated

l84|137.c: A dash of naivety is the secret to innovation; hire "optimistic doers" who act and don't fence themselves in.
l84|137.e: When she entered this heavily regulated, stigmatized industry she knew almost nothing about how hard it would be. Precisely because she didn't fully understand the status quo, she could see it differently. The same goes for hiring: generalists make the world go round, and slightly naive, seemingly unlikely people often have the biggest impact. She looks for curiosity, fast decisions and no fear of outcomes, because the secret of a startup is keeping momentum, and chasing perfection means missing the moment. A candidate who keeps saying "that's not my job" is a big red flag.
ex: Her head of marketing was an Emmy-winning news anchor who asked what CAC meant on day one
Her interview question: teach me something, to see if they can explain it clearly

items.d: See the status quo with fresh eyes
Unafraid of outcomes, not seeking perfection

l84|137.c: D2C isn't dead; paying for every customer is. Put content and community ahead of commerce.
l84|137.e: "D2C is dead" is too simple, she says. What's outdated is paying for every customer and being hooked on performance ads, a drug that only gets more expensive. Bobbie flipped the usual order of commerce, then content, then community: five years ago it launched a separate blog, Milk Drunk, answering questions like how to mix formula and how long it keeps, and today it ranks on the first page of search results alongside the CDC. She estimates 60% of growth comes from the product and brand themselves and 40% from how you spread the word. The mom-to-mom flywheel has to rest on that 60%.
ex: She resisted calls to add another $100,000 or $300,000 a month in ad spend
Her fear: getting distracted by the 40% while the 60% stays mediocre, like fast fashion

l84|137.c: Leaders shouldn't just maintain momentum but create it, and an artificial deadline is fine.
l84|137.e: Momentum is everything, she says, and a leader's job is to create it deliberately, even putting pressure on yourself early on. People often ask why something must launch on a given day, and her answer is "because we said so." Without a date, it might never happen. Artificial milestones are fuel that keeps the team moving. Lately she also speeds things up with asynchronous work: twenty people pile into Slack for a focused hour, make the call and move on, rather than relying on meetings or stacking up process tools.
ex: A one-hour Slack sprint where twenty people settled a decision on the spot
Home runs on systems too: she and her husband plan the schedule every Sunday

l85|139.c: Before a big decision, run a "curiosity loop": ask several people in a structured way so advice fits your situation.
l85|139.e: Most bad advice isn't malicious, she says; it just doesn't fit your situation, like whether to quit and chase a dream or build experience first. She borrows from customer advisory boards in marketing. First, ask a good question: specific, asking for reasoning, and without revealing your own leaning. Second, pick two kinds of people: experts in the domain and people who really know you. Third, keep the ask light so busy people can answer in minutes. Finally, digest what you heard, then circle back to thank them and share the outcome. The goal isn't to obey the advice but to find surprises and strong objections you had missed.
ex: For this episode she sent about 10 friends 9 topics, asking each to pick two with reasons
Debating when kids should inherit money, she asked around and nobody picked 18
A bad question: "What should my next career move be?"

items.d: Domain experts plus people who know you
Look for surprises, don't just obey

l85|139.c: Use your ranked personal values as an inner scorecard to resist outer scorecards like titles and fame.
l85|139.e: She gives every coaching client a 10-to-15-minute values exercise: tick the words on a list that resonate, group them, rank them, and write three to five sentences. That becomes an inner scorecard, measuring how you spend your day, whether you were kind, whether you took risks, rather than status, wealth and what others think. When an opportunity looks like an obvious yes, test it against the scorecard. She once turned down a glamorous role because constant travel and very long hours would have wiped out all three of her top values.
ex: Warren Buffett's inner scorecard versus outer scorecard
One of Lenny's values is "choose adventure," but a long book project may no longer count as adventure
The worst ending: trapped by your lifestyle late in your career, unhappy when you look in the mirror

items: Were you kind, did you take risks

d.verdict: Choose by your own ranked values

l85|139.c: Early in a career, explore with a hypothesis each time; once you strike a rich vein, switch to exploiting it.
l85|139.e: She borrows "explore and exploit" from growth work: when much is unknown, try things, but with a hypothesis behind each move. In seven years she went from entry-level sales at Microsoft to SVP of marketing at SurveyMonkey. At Microsoft she found big companies too slow. She tried marketing at a startup and discovered she loved marketing and small teams. At 23 she felt she could afford to lose, so she became a founder. After LinkedIn acquired the company she switched to exploit mode, telling her manager "I'm here to learn to be a better founder," and deliberately filled her gaps in growth and subscription pricing instead of chasing titles.
ex: While working with LinkedIn's growth team, membership grew from 100 million to 200 million
The mix of startup, big-company, growth and subscription experience made SurveyMonkey come to her

items.d: Fell for marketing and small teams
Head of marketing in her late twenties

l85|139.c: Don't be the frog in warming water: use learning and growth as your yardstick and watch the temperature trend.
l85|139.e: Inertia traps people easily, she says. Small discomforts pile up while you tell yourself a new manager or one more promotion will fix it. Her test for staying or going is whether you're still learning and growing. If you're challenged every day and the work matters, twenty years at one company is fine. If you disagree with the company's direction, your role is boxed in, or you've stopped learning, it's time to change something. That needn't mean quitting: first tell your manager what you want to learn and ask for the right projects. If that hits a wall, treat the time freed up by mastery as a gift and use it to build relationships or learn new skills.
ex: At LinkedIn she asked for and got experience running growth and the subscription business

marks.d: Talk first, then consider a change

l85|139.c: Most people don't need a coach; fast-growing founders and sensitive problems are where one pays off most.
l85|139.e: She starts by "un-selling": picture the ideal outcome six months from now, then ask whether another route gets you there better. If you want a mentor, a coach is one opinion, and a curiosity loop gives you several. If you want to learn a subject systematically, a course is more complete. If you want emotional support, a community you can lean on long term is better. Founders, though, live in chaos with no structure, where impostor feelings are justified and learning must be very fast, and a coach is a shortcut. Sensitive topics like interpersonal conflict suit coaching too. Talk to at least two or three coaches; fit matters more than credentials.
ex: Of 80-plus people she interviewed, about half simply hired the first coach they spoke to
You can hire a short-term specialist, like a pitch coach before fundraising

items.d: Run a curiosity loop, hear several views
Where a coach is most valuable

l85|139.c: Nobody states the rules of success, so dare to give hard feedback and practice weak spots like eating vegetables.
l85|139.e: Becoming an executive or a funded founder is like competing at the Olympic level with nobody telling you the rules, she says. Sensitive feedback about appearance or impressions is the worst gap, since managers usually stay silent because speaking up only carries downside. She once worked up the courage to tell a brilliant female founder that her casual dress was making people underestimate her. The founder was grateful, adjusted, and the reactions around her clearly improved. People aren't powerless: you can study the rules and point them out to each other. Her other trick is "eating your vegetables": separate disliking something because you're bad at it from truly disliking it, and repeat it ten or so times before judging.
ex: New to Silicon Valley, one event a week: no leaving before 10 cards handed out and the back wall reached
"LinkedIn 30": posting every day for 30 days
She estimates 70 to 80 percent of podcasts never get past episode one

items.d: Such as one event a week

l85|139.c: Co-founding with a partner goes very well or very badly; the keys are complementary roles and arguing about ideas, not people.
l85|139.e: Startups are already intense, volatile and unstructured, and adding a romantic relationship makes an unstable mix; among her friends the results have been mixed. She and her husband Sachin have now built two companies together and were product-and-marketing partners at LinkedIn too. At the start they set 30, 60 and 90-day checkpoints to ask specifically whether this was hurting their relationship. The ingredients for success, she thinks, apply to any co-founders: complementary skills, clear decision rights, and the ability to have constructive conflict, hearing "this plan isn't good" as a comment on the plan, not on you.
ex: Sachin runs product, design and engineering; she runs marketing, operations and finance

result.d: Applies to any co-founders

l86|141.c: How fast a company grows depends a lot on how much room competitors leave you.
l86|141.e: After twenty-plus years in collaboration software, he has noticed that almost every growth spurt or slowdown traces back to competition. The classic pattern: a category leader is growing nicely, then a giant with distribution and pricing power walks in and the curve changes. How hard it hits depends on three things: whether the rival's product is good enough, how many users it can reach, and how aggressive its pricing and bundling are. The answer is not to ignore rivals but to make sure customers know what makes you different and how you fit alongside other tools. That is why Miro put product marketing inside the product org.
ex: He saw giants enter the market at both Adobe Document Cloud and Box
When FigJam launched, many people wrote Miro off

terms.d: Is the rival's offering usable enough?
Channels and how many users they touch

result.d: Decides how much growth is left for you

l86|141.c: A product never stands still: every release gains or loses points against rivals in customers' minds.
l86|141.e: His starting point is simple: as long as direct or indirect competitors exist, customers compare you to them, whether they mean to or not. Every feature you ship makes the product better or worse, and rivals are shipping at the same time. So every move is like a point scored or lost in a long game. Looking at the roadmap this way makes it clear to the team where to invest and why. Eventually the market consolidates and a company standardizes on one tool, and those points decide which one.
ex: Only brand-new markets with no rivals are the exception; most products have competitors

l86|141.c: In a crowded, innovative market, be the first to hit the brick wall; speed decides who wins.
l86|141.e: His reasoning: when you are building an experience that exists nowhere else, nobody knows whether users will accept it. The most valuable thing is learning before everyone else that a particular path is a dead end. Hit the wall first and you can turn 10 or 30 degrees before anyone else does. Stay one or two insights ahead of rivals and you keep the lead. He respects the saying "slow is fast," but thinks it only applies in certain mature areas. When exploring new experiences, an organization should deliberately speed up.
ex: The idea was inspired by Frank Slootman's book Amp It Up

items: Try new experiences early, fail early

d.verdict: When exploring new experiences, speed decides who wins

l86|141.c: Teams aren't slow because they don't want to be fast; leaders' job is to clear the blockers.
l86|141.e: His observation: people who choose to be product managers naturally want challenges and want to move fast. What slows them down are technical, organizational, and prioritization blockers. So leads should be able to raise a hand at any time and say they are stuck, and leadership should fix it quickly. Each fix starts a virtuous cycle: the team sees results, gains courage, learns to recognize the pattern, and handles it alone next time, escalating only the harder problems. People who seem ten times more productive, he says, simply know better where to start, whom to ask, and how to scope the work.
ex: Miro Connect is a live demo session every other week
An engineer passing by built a feature in 3 hours that was planned for 3 months

items.d: Say what is blocking you, any time

l86|141.c: One line, "deliver high-quality customer value faster," drives everything from reviews to metrics.
l86|141.e: He breaks the motto into three parts, each with its own measurement. Customer value only counts when customers actually use the feature, so after launch the team checks how much the original target metric moved. "Faster" is measured by cycle time at each stage: projects are bucketed as small, medium, or large, and the mean, median, and variance are published so teams can benchmark themselves. He compares speed to golf, where you only compete against yourself. "High quality" means measuring up to the best apps in each category. Performance reviews and rewards are built around the same sentence.
ex: The process runs product strategy, then P0 problem, P1 solution, P2 validation metrics
A "small" project is one that can ship within a month

items.d: After launch, did the metric move?
Measure cycle time per stage, publish it

l86|141.c: "High quality" is hard to define in writing; sorting real examples into good and bad works better.
l86|141.e: A year earlier, everyone at Miro kept saying they wanted high quality. Leaders wrote long documents defining the attributes, which turned out heavy and hard to act on. So they switched: each month the design leadership team sorts what shipped into two buckets, high quality or not, writes down why, and shares it with designers. His analogy: someone who has never seen color cannot tell pink from red by description, but a few examples make it obvious. It works like training a classifier. First calibrate the leaders, then gradually open it up to the whole organization.
ex: One design leader is responsible for running this regularly

l86|141.c: A rolling six-month roadmap: firm near term, flexible far term, serving customers without losing agility.
l86|141.e: Large enterprise customers always want to see a roadmap, but committing too firmly kills agility. Miro's answer is a roadmap refreshed every three months. The first three months are meant to be delivered at 80 percent, the next three at only 50 percent. That lets teams adjust to customer needs, competitor moves, or technology shifts like large language models without being penalized. Above the roadmap sits an annual strategy paper that explains the company's key bets and why. OKRs moved from quarterly to every six months, tracked monthly, to cut the overhead of constant re-planning.
ex: Resources split roughly 70/20/10 across three time horizons
20 to 40 percent of capacity goes to architecture and maintenance

l87|23.c: Product-led sales is a bridge from individual self-serve use to company-wide value that sales must explain.
l87|23.e: Her starting point: self-serve payment has a ceiling. Credit cards get blocked at around ten thousand dollars, and individuals won't front that much money for their employer. Users arrive to solve a personal task. Enterprise-level value, like building a data-driven culture or company-wide collaboration, is hard for the product to explain on its own. Sales has to tell that story and raise the perceived value to land contracts worth tens of thousands to over a hundred thousand dollars. She hopes products will eventually walk users up this escalator themselves rather than relying entirely on sales.
ex: At Amplitude, individuals want data insights; the company wants a data-driven culture
Going from individual usage to an enterprise contract usually takes 12 months or more

items.d: Solve one task on your own

l87|23.c: Don't hire sales until users ask to buy, but that demand peaks fast; 90% means finding buyers outside.
l87|23.e: In product-led companies, she notes, sales usually begins when a user contacts support and says they want to buy for the whole company. That is the moment to hire salespeople to handle the demand. The catch is that end users are not the people who sign company checks. Relying on internal champions to close deals caps your growth quickly. She estimates 90 percent of product-led sales is reading usage signals to spot a meaningful sales conversation, then finding the decision-maker outside the account and connecting them to the usage already happening inside their company.
ex: Miro hired its first salesperson at roughly $5-7 million in annual revenue; before that, support closed deals

items.d: They ask to buy for the whole company
Serve the demand that comes in
Use usage signals to reach decision-makers

l87|23.c: Adding product-led sales means moving upmarket for PLG companies and downmarket for sales-led ones.
l87|23.e: Her reasoning: the smallest contract a sales team will traditionally touch is about $15,000. That means you also need deals worth $100,000 to $200,000, which come from mid-size companies of 200-plus people and enterprises with thousands. If your product serves freelancers or tiny startups, who are price-sensitive and prefer self-serve, don't rush to add sales. Sales-led companies go the other way: they add product-led sales because customers want to see value before signing, or because moving downmarket makes fixed sales costs unaffordable and the product must automate the human steps.
ex: The floor for a sales team is roughly a $15,000 contract

items: Start from a personal use case

d.verdict: Both roads lead to product-led sales, from opposite directions

l87|23.c: Leads come in three kinds; treating a brand-new signup like an MQL and calling them is the classic mistake.
l87|23.e: She separates three kinds of leads. A product-qualified account (PQA) is a company whose usage has crossed a threshold. A product-qualified lead (PQL) is a PQA where someone with buying power is already using the product. A marketing-qualified lead (MQL) is a buyer that marketing has found. The further upmarket you go, the further users sit from buyers, so you often see great account usage with no buyer in sight. Sending sales after ordinary users just annoys them; marketing has to find the buyer and connect them to the usage. Then there are pure top-down leads with no usage at all. Each kind has different conversion rates, playbooks, and even sales teams. A new signup is solving a personal task; asking about budget ten minutes after signup is badly timed.
ex: Her meme from The Shining: five minutes into the product, sales breaks down the door with an axe

cells.d: No usage context, sell the whole package
A decision-maker is among the users
Marketing finds an MQL, connects usage

l87|23.c: A PQA shows in user count, usage thresholds, and growth rate; run it by hand before automating.
l87|23.e: The strongest signal, she says, is how many people at one company are using the product, and seven is often the dividing line. So make sure new signups from the same company join the existing account instead of creating their own. Next come usage thresholds, then sudden changes in growth rate, which are hardest to measure but best for timing. Behavioral signals also work, like an admin change or someone reading the terms of service page. Start modeling from sales intuition, then compare hand-raisers with people who look like them and run a simple regression. Understand the data manually first and keep a tight feedback loop with sales. Don't dump every user on sales, and don't buy a platform on day one.
ex: Amplitude watches event counts; Miro watches the number of boards
MongoDB has confirmed the same behavioral signals

root.d: The moment sales should step in

items.d: About 7 people is a common threshold
Event counts, boards, and so on
Admin change, reading the terms page

l87|23.c: In product-led sales, product must own the pipeline; putting it under marketing fails within six months.
l87|23.e: She contrasts two models. In the traditional one, marketing builds pipeline, sales sells, and product only cares about retention after payment, throwing features over the wall. In product-led sales, product acquires users, activates them, and creates the pipeline, so the tightest partnership becomes product and sales. She argues product leadership should carry revenue targets while individual PMs own input metrics: free-to-paid conversion, packaging, and the PQA rate, meaning the share of active ideal-customer teams that reach PQA. Marketing is still essential: it finds buyers, runs account-based marketing, and shares the pipeline target with product.
ex: Miro's head of growth product carries a self-serve revenue target
She thinks B2B product teams have gotten too comfortable about revenue

terms.d: Activate accounts, push them to PQA
Keep mining signals that predict deals

result.d: Predictable and sustainable

l87|23.c: To lift free-to-paid conversion, first make users aware of what you sell; change pricing last.
l87|23.e: She claims about three quarters of users in a freemium product have no idea what the paid version offers. So most of the work is awareness: feature gates, usage limits, trials, and consistent, visible upgrade prompts that each user sees at least three times. Second comes conversion optimization, such as the pricing page, checkout, currencies, and payment methods. Only last should you touch the monetization model itself, because changing plans, prices, and upgrade paths affects the most things. One simple habit: in design reviews, look at every new paid feature from the free, low-tier, and target-tier user's point of view.
ex: SurveyMonkey made all upgrade prompts gold and made sure users saw them three times
Track awareness as the share of activated accounts that have viewed the pricing page

items.d: Show users the paid value; the biggest lever

l88|145.c: Hypergrowth takes three things: a product people love, word of mouth, and leaders who keep pace.
l88|145.e: She has watched many companies grow at extreme speed and sees three things in common. First, the product has to be something people genuinely love, with ChatGPT as the extreme case. Second, growth has to spread on its own: one person starts using it and pulls in colleagues, which beats any sales pitch. You can't buy that kind of growth with ads and stay healthy. Third, what she calls "riding the lightning": these companies cross in one or two years what takes others five to ten, so they must keep bringing in leaders who have already seen the next stage, or lean on advisors and mentors.
ex: Whiteboard photos were once the most-uploaded attachment in Jira, and Miro built on that need
1Password's chief product officer brought Productboard in and the whole company adopted it

terms.d: Hire leaders who have seen the next stage

result.d: Paid ads can't replace this

l88|145.c: How fast you rise depends largely on the company's momentum, so pick one using hard numbers.
l88|145.e: She believes reaching the executive level takes more effort than the people around you: grab the work nobody owns, tie your job to revenue, learn to talk finance the way the CEO and board do, and rotate through departments to understand the whole system. But the company's momentum matters just as much. A fast-growing company hands you bigger responsibility sooner, and the colleagues you meet there bring you opportunities later. Her advice: early in your career, join a well-known, high-momentum company; later, pick later-stage companies, because momentum is easier to verify there.
ex: Her sticky-note checklist: Rule of 40, investor quality, NPS, and net revenue retention
She also checks growth rate, burn rate, whether it leads its market, and Glassdoor reviews

items.d: Led the team for five years
Led the team for four years

l88|145.c: In a downturn, don't settle for a bad company; follow the industry wave and speed up.
l88|145.e: When you're out of work, there are more candidates than jobs, so it comes down to endurance, and nearly every great executive has been through a low point. But don't take a job at a bad company just to land somewhere, because every job and every brand on your resume sets up the next one. The industry you choose sets your ceiling: the best antique shop earns a margin of one or two percent, the worst oil and gas company earns over thirty, and software earns more. If you're still employed, this is the moment to take on projects nobody owns while others pull back, worry less about title and pay for now, and cash in when things recover.
ex: The 2000 and 2008 downturns were when she grew fastest
