The Millionaire Next Door compares profit margins across industries

l88|145.c: Brand ads only amplify; they can't fix a weak product, and they work best small and steady.
l88|145.e: She ran global brand campaigns worth hundreds of millions of dollars at Oracle and spent millions more at Atlassian. Her conclusion: ads only pay off after years of repeated exposure, and what really decides the outcome is the product experience. Oracle's ads were everywhere, and plenty of people still disliked the company. So keep your advertising consistent over the long run, even if it's only in a few places. Good ads tend to be a bit funny, a bit surprising, and honest about the product, or they put the customer in the starring role.
ex: HipChat's parody ads mocking Slack couldn't fix its own reliability problems
Snowflake kept a single billboard on Highway 101 for years
Oracle's fixed layout made its ads recognizable without a logo, several times over

d.verdict: The product is the base; ads only amplify it

l88|145.c: Word of mouth speeds up with three things: visible experts, useful content, and your own community.
l88|145.e: She points to early Atlassian: the founders spent their time in developer forums, and the CEO was still answering posts when the company had one or two hundred million dollars in revenue. Dedicated evangelists came later. Employees with real expertise kept publishing blog posts and new ideas, so users got knowledge along with the product. The best salespeople are happy existing customers. Letting customers talk to each other while prospects listen in works far better than a pure sales event. Atlassian just paid for beer and pizza, and user groups in different cities organized themselves.
ex: Weights & Biases has its technical experts blog and run the community
HubSpot's content and its certifications for marketers

items.d: Founders and experts as thought leaders

l88|145.c: Don't hire sales too early; Atlassian put that money into R&D and let the product sell itself.
l88|145.e: Atlassian's founders took almost no outside funding, so nobody could push them to build a conventional sales team. They put the money into R&D instead, spending two to three times what comparable companies did. Sales mainly handled renewals for existing customers, and only later moved into large accounts and cross-selling. It almost never did cold outreach, the most expensive way to win customers. Her warning: sales looks like predictable revenue, but when the product doesn't resonate, a sales team is a huge drain, sometimes just an expensive service department hiding product problems.
ex: Miro and Airtable wait until 20 to 40 paying users in an account before sales steps in
Atlassian tried bundled deals, which slowed product-led growth, then went back to single products

items: Two to three times the R&D spend

l88|145.c: Moving upmarket and other big growth levers are company strategy, not one department's job.
l88|145.e: She says the growth levers look similar everywhere: add products, enter new segments or industries, expand abroad, open new channels. But they only work once they become a company-wide strategic goal. To go after enterprise customers, marketing has to bring the right leads, product has to prioritize enterprise features, and support and sales need new people and new approaches. Many companies blame marketing or sales for a lack of leads when the real problem is that the company never chose a direction. CMOs often get fired because they weren't tied to revenue and couldn't explain the growth levers. Win the CEO's trust with metrics, strategy, and market judgment.
ex: She often runs company offsites to set shared OKRs for moving upmarket

items.d: The company never set a direction
Product, support and sales change together

l89|147.c: Top talent comes from a clear mission, patience, and hands-on managers, not a hiring pipeline.
l89|147.e: Stripe's mission is to build infrastructure for the internet economy and quietly help users succeed. He thinks that attracts self-starters who like digging into unglamorous hard problems and think long term, so Stripe says so openly when recruiting. For key roles they will meet dozens or even hundreds of people, and when someone is right but the timing isn't, they keep the relationship going. Managers get to know candidates deeply themselves. Interviews are structured, have no trick questions, and mirror real work. He puts special weight on reference checks: interviews total about eight hours, while former colleagues have thousands of hours of observation.
ex: Engineering interviews feel like pair programming, and you can Google freely
Product managers do a timed written exercise

root.d: Hiring is not an assembly line

items.d: Wait for the right person and moment
Thousands of hours from former colleagues

l89|147.c: Build products with the right early users and only scale once they are delighted.
l89|147.e: Early Stripe was almost all engineers, but everyone stayed close to users the way a product manager would. When building Billing, the team noticed existing customers like Figma and Slack were already running subscriptions and pushing the limits of the product. So they set up a shared Slack channel with them, demoed often, gathered feedback, and only rolled out more widely once those alpha users were very happy. He thinks a fast feedback loop with users makes it hard to build the wrong thing, and many teams simply lack one. Product managers synthesize user insight, pull in partners like legal and risk, and hold the long-term strategy.
ex: Stripe Connect grew out of work with Lyft and Shopify
The Atlas team got the IRS to issue EINs instantly at registration

items.d: Pushing limits and fitting the strategy
Scale only once they are happy

l89|147.c: Attention to detail has to be selective: friction logs show you where polish matters most.
l89|147.e: Chasing perfection everywhere stalls progress. So he starts by stepping into the shoes of one specific user, say an engineer at a large SaaS company integrating Billing, and walks the whole path from dashboard to docs to writing code, jotting down every snag as it comes. That is a friction log. Then the team concentrates on fixing those snags, and calls out what works well too. Before he joined, Stripe's error messages linking straight to the relevant docs impressed him; the code handling those edge cases outweighs the main path. In payments, improvements are often measured in basis points, but small checkout gains add up.
ex: Merchants who switched to Stripe Checkout and related tools saw revenue rise 10.5% on average
For years he has walked the new-user signup flow monthly and written a friction log

items.d: Decide exactly whose shoes you're in
Note the experience as it happens

l89|147.c: Values alone aren't enough; they need fixed practices and rhythms to become real.
l89|147.e: Stripe's operating principles were distilled from how its most effective early people behaved, but each one comes with a concrete practice. In group UX reviews, the team, along with support staff and executives, walks through a flow as a user, and anyone can add to the issue list. The company-wide Friday Fireside sometimes does a "walk the store" session to examine a key flow together. After an incident, remediation items take priority over the rest of the roadmap. Like a chef tasting the soup or a film studio watching dailies, regularly looking at the product together builds shared standards and a shared language.
ex: No fixed ratio; each team decides how much time to reserve for polish and operations

d.verdict: Values need predictable, fixed routines behind them

l89|147.c: Managers should edit the team's plan, and even the CTO should regularly ship code.
l89|147.e: Stripe's problems depend heavily on domain knowledge, so managers must know what the front line is really like. But doing individual contributor work every day costs you the big picture. His approach is to clear his calendar for three or four days at a time, decline every meeting as if on vacation, join a team, and with a buddy's help take a small feature from start to production. He gets to feel the tools, the build, code review, and documentation firsthand, then writes and shares a friction log. He recommends new engineering managers do this within their first three to six months.
ex: He had never written Ruby when he joined and learned it from his buddy
The experience showed that working across time zones needs more docs and more automation

items.d: Three or four days, like a vacation

l89|147.c: Reliability comes from automated tests, gradual rollouts, and systematic reviews, not fewer changes.
l89|147.e: Stripe handles money that is the lifeblood of its customers, at a scale now equal to all of e-commerce when Stripe was founded. But user needs change too fast to stay safe by freezing changes. So they rely entirely on automated testing, not manual QA. Each change moves through increasingly realistic environments, and a release goes to a small slice of traffic first before ramping up. A commit reaches production automatically in about 45 minutes, so feedback received in the morning can be fixed the same day. After an incident, they ask how to rule out that whole class of problem, and fixes get scheduled first. In recent years they added chaos testing.
ex: An auto-merge checkbox, and a "crying octopus" feedback button in the dev tools
The host cites 16.4 deploys a day on the core API on average

l89|147.c: Large models let Stripe serve AI companies while upgrading its own products and internal work.
l89|147.e: Stripe has long used machine learning in Radar, its fraud product, and brought in Transformers over a year ago. AI companies face high compute costs and need revenue from day one, and many run on Stripe. Outward-facing, Stripe uses GPT-4 to read all of its documentation and answer developer questions, and lets Sigma turn plain-language questions into SQL. Internally it built a governed GPT-4 interface where prompt presets can be shared company-wide, so people in marketing, support and other non-engineering roles can use it too. After a strict trial, Copilot was opened to everyone, and it saves the most effort on writing test cases.
ex: OpenAI uses Stripe for ChatGPT Plus subscriptions
He uses a shared preset to write blog posts in the right tone

l89|147.c: The bigger the organization, the fewer decisions you touch, so hire well, trust by default, delegate.
l89|147.e: Thousands of decisions happen every day and he is present for almost none of them; meddling would grind everything to a halt. So the key is hiring people who can operate with real autonomy, extending generous trust from the start, and then letting accountability prove them right. He often delegates a bit more than feels comfortable. He also manages his time deliberately so the inbox and calendar don't run his day. He tries to show up in a consistent state every day, because a leader's behavior is the culture. And he manages his energy by keeping some work that recharges him.
ex: For ten years, every Sunday night he writes what a successful week would look like
Planning runs in an inverted W: teams propose, leaders synthesize, then it goes back down

terms.d: Trusted to run on their own

result.d: Not dependent on the leader's calls

l90|149.c: Paid ads are like stocks: they only become a drug if you bet everything on one channel or loophole.
l90|149.e: He treats the marketing budget as capital that has to earn a return, with himself as the fund manager. A fund manager wouldn't put a client's savings into one stock, and a company shouldn't put its whole budget into one ad channel and ride out wild swings in click prices and market conditions. The real blow-ups he has seen usually came from scaling fast on some quirk in a platform; when the loophole closed, the business collapsed. His "first rule of performance marketing" is not to forget offline and traditional channels: email, direct mail and SEO all work, and paid search and SEO are not an either-or.
ex: Early on he ran ads on Uber's brand keyword for referral bonuses, and later won Uber as a client
Thrive manages about $500 million in ad spend a year

d.verdict: Manage marketing like an investment portfolio

l90|149.c: How far paid growth scales depends on product-market fit plus creative, people, and technical resources.
l90|149.e: Early on, check for product-market fit: if other channels work, paid will most likely work too. Later the question shifts from "does it work" to "how big can it get," which depends on creative resources and a feedback loop, marketers who know the channels, and engineers who can fix tracking and attribution. He warns against survivorship bias: every unicorn of the 2010s did performance marketing, but not every company doing performance marketing succeeded. For a first paid-growth hire he values a technical or quantitative background, hands-on channel experience, and staying calm under pressure more than years of experience.
ex: Grammarly and Athletic Greens have scaled almost entirely on paid in recent years
His interview question: how many windows are in New York? It tests reasoning and composure

items.d: A testing loop with the ad buying
Someone in-house who knows the channels
Tracking and attribution that actually work

l90|149.c: In B2B, don't chase the cheapest lead; score leads by eventual revenue and bid accordingly.
l90|149.e: The common mistake is assuming more and cheaper leads mean more MQLs, SQLs and closed deals, so teams keep pushing cost per lead down. But customers vary enormously in value: leads for high-value customers cost more and pay back far more. B2B sales cycles run anywhere from two to twelve months. The fix is to pipe revenue data from the CRM into a database, join it with channel data, and see which audiences actually bring in enough revenue. Then build a lead-scoring model and bid up in real time on audiences more likely to become high-value customers.
ex: Thrive built its own data pipeline tool, Thrive Stack
Off-the-shelf alternatives include data connectors like Supermetrics

items.d: Judge by revenue, not lead count

l90|149.c: With bidding and targeting automated, ad creative is now the biggest lever in paid growth.
l90|149.e: Over the past seven to ten years, Google and Meta automated most of the levers that once took a "rocket scientist" to operate. The one thing still driven by people is creative. The usual problem is a brand team handing over a pile of polished assets that follow brand guidelines but ignore how ads actually work. The right approach is to design for the funnel: spark interest at the top, move the conversation forward in the middle based on what the audience does, and prompt action at the bottom. Blasting the same message at everyone just causes banner blindness and wasted spend.
ex: User-generated content shot on a phone often beats polished brand video

items.d: Top: open a conversation with new audiences
Change the message based on site behavior

l90|149.c: Test one variable at a time with comparable metrics, make the winner the new baseline, repeat.
l90|149.e: On Meta, he puts one audience in an ad set with two nearly identical ads that differ in a single variable, such as the copy or the image. The algorithm often gives the two ads different amounts of exposure, so you compare them on normalized metrics like click-through rate or impression-to-conversion rate. The results go back to the creative team, the winner becomes the new control, and a new challenger goes up against it, round after round. What matters is a repeatable testing process, not one genius's lucky idea. Most of this can be done inside the platforms with no special tools.
ex: A furniture brand put a dog on the sofa and its social ROAS doubled or tripled

l90|149.c: Everyone buys Google; TikTok is cheap but burns through creative, best for direct-to-consumer brands.
l90|149.e: By Google he means YouTube too, and Meta includes Instagram. Those two are the most mature, and not one advertiser he has worked with over the past decade skipped Google. TikTok's ad system feels like Facebook six or seven years ago: attribution is still weak, but fewer advertisers means cheaper clicks. Direct-to-consumer brands have to study it; nobody has cracked it for B2B SaaS. The biggest barrier is how fast creative wears out. You need several new assets a week, and spending a million dollars a month requires a content machine. Amazon suits D2C, and Snap is losing users.
ex: What works on TikTok: founder-shot handheld video and creator partnerships
In one quarter, Google made about $70 billion in revenue and Meta about $32 billion

l90|149.c: There is no single truth in attribution; you triangulate, keep investigating, and sometimes disprove yourself.
l90|149.e: Attribution means working out the link between what you did and what happened afterward. He sees it as part art, part science, with judgment calls built in, and the first step is deciding whether the company wants profit or growth. Last click, first touch, and weighted multi-touch are all human choices. In 2021 Apple let users refuse to share the IDFA, Meta's data shrank sharply, and audiences, testing and revenue readings all suffered. Today you combine cookie-based attribution, media mix modeling (MMM) and customer and audience surveys. His team once used MMM to prove that a carefully built campaign had no real effect.
ex: Wanamaker's line: half my advertising is wasted, I just don't know which half
For MMM tooling, there's Recast

items.d: Users can refuse to share the IDFA

l90|149.c: AI hasn't shrunk agency headcount, but the work shifted from execution to modeling, validation and creative.
l90|149.e: The ad-buying business was already reshaped by Google's and Meta's automation more than a decade ago, and the result was shifted jobs, not lost ones. Thrive has more people than ever, but they spend less time tweaking keyword bids and doing manual analysis, and more time building models, validating results and asking the right questions. Today they use ChatGPT to generate copy variants and draft RFP responses, and Dall-E and Midjourney to mock up proposals; a week's work now takes an afternoon. He compares it to the printing press, which replaced scribes without reducing the number of writers.
ex: Fed 100 old RFPs, the AI produces drafts that are about 80% usable
Mock-ups take roughly 1% of the time they used to

result.d: No AI layoffs so far

l91|152.c: Cash App won by doing ten things at a world-class level at once, not through one secret.
l91|152.e: When he joined, Cash App had under 50,000 monthly active users; today it has more than 50 million. People want a single reason, but he thinks many things were done best in the industry at the same time: a small, very senior team, extreme focus, strong fraud prevention, and separation from the rest of Square with support from the top. Every trade-off put the consumer first, even when it upset the merchant business. Design got deep investment. Doing any one of these well might have kept it alive, but the lead it has today came from stacking them. He admits it's hard to know which lessons transfer.
ex: For three or four years, Cash App was the fastest, cheapest way to send money between people in the US

root.d: Many things done best at once

items.d: Walled off from the main business

l91|152.c: Real differentiation is different and better, better where users care, and in a domain that matters.
l91|152.e: Being merely different is easy: look at what exists and do something else. Being merely better is easy too: improve a little and charge more. The real bar is being better on a dimension the user or buyer actually cares about. Even then, the product may be a beautiful "art piece" that can't scale, so the domain itself has to matter, the economics have to work, and delivery and distribution have to function. Cash App's breakthrough was instant money: cash out, get a card, sell stock or bitcoin, and the money is usable right away.
ex: Asked why not Venmo, he'd say: send me a dollar right now and see

items.d: On what users truly care about

l91|152.c: Inside a big company, a small, senior team that trusts each other beats piling on headcount.
l91|152.e: People say intrapreneurship isn't real because there's no fear of missing payroll, so teams get used to asking for resources. If the leader is good at winning headcount, the team grows faster than the project's actual results and potential justify, and becomes a long-term burden. Cash App's early team was about eleven or twelve people and stayed that size for roughly a year. They were experienced and trusted each other, so little was lost in communication. The leader knew the organization, knew whom to pull in, and won the team room to experiment. Every seat had to be earned: build a business of real scale first, then staff to match.
ex: Square's CFO at the time was strict about approving new headcount

items.d: Good at winning headcount, so it grows
Out of step with the potential

l91|152.c: Deliberately hiring former founders raises output a lot, at the cost of blunt criticism and short tenures.
l91|152.e: He has seen many highly capable founders fail to last at big companies, and hiring funnels screen out anyone who doesn't fit the elite-school, big-tech template before a manager ever sees the resume. So at Carbon Health he wrote "former founders welcome, even if you failed" straight into job descriptions, and about 15% of hires are ex-founders. The bet has paid off, but the costs are real: any waste or nonsense in the organization gets called out on the spot. They are ambitious and usually leave after two to two and a half years. Overall it means higher output and higher turnover, and it raises the level of the whole team.

d.verdict: He's sure it's worth it, costs and all

l91|152.c: In hiring you pick the people but they pick the timing, so create value for them first.
l91|152.e: Many people on his team joined months after they first met, one of them a year and a half later. So when he meets someone he'd like to work with, he says openly that he hopes to work together someday, then asks what they need right now and helps with introductions to opportunities or people, so he's more than "someone I met on a Zoom once." His creed: everyone wants something, and if you happen to have it and it costs you almost nothing to give, not giving it is indefensible. Over a long enough time, that goodwill comes back.
ex: He made about 600 introductions last year
Someone once passed on investing in him but introduced a string of investors, which helped enormously

items.d: Find people you'd like to work with
Say you hope to work together

l91|152.c: In complex, regulated fields, keep asking until you hit bottom; whoever executes must become a real expert.
l91|152.e: Building the first Cash Card, the vendor samples fell far short of the design, so he visited card factories around the country and studied thousands of settings on laser engraving machines. The so-called expert is often just the most senior person, and their answer can be wrong without being malicious, so don't stop at the first answer. This isn't about doing everything yourself; the person responsible for execution has to master every detail. When someone says "the rules don't allow it," ask what the contract or regulation actually says and what happens if you break it. Don't let old habits become an excuse for a worse user experience.
ex: Cash App would put regulations on the screen and discuss them line by line
He insisted on replacing ambiguous null values in the database with explicit labels

items.d: Often most senior, not most knowledgeable

l91|152.c: Healthcare startups run on relationships, but a very specific use case gets you to the real decision-maker.
l91|152.e: In healthcare, whether something moves forward often depends on relationships rather than the merits of the proposal. Some companies got data or partnerships nobody else could simply because the founder knew the CEOs of the big insurers. So first figure out whether yours is that kind of business. Carbon Health sells directly to consumers, not to insurers or employers, and its founders had succeeded in direct-to-consumer before, so the fit is strong. For teams strong on technology but weak on connections, he advises defining the use case very precisely, because that's how you find the person in the organization who actually holds the button.
ex: Carbon runs the full stack: its own clinics, physicians and software, about 130 clinics

terms.d: Say exactly what problem you solve

result.d: Less waiting on promised introductions

l92|154.sc: Product sense and the first mile
l92|154.c: Product sense comes from empathy for users, and the first-mile experience is the most underrated battleground.
l92|154.e: He sees teams fall in love with their own solution instead of feeling what it is like to be stuck with the problem. The solution may be 30 degrees off, and empathy is what reveals the fix, so sit next to users and watch them work in real situations. Product experience, he argues, is psychology. In the first 30 seconds, users are lazy, vain, and selfish: they want a quick win, want to look competent in front of others, and won't read a tutorial. Yet most teams think about the first mile only at the very end of development. And every new cohort is different. Later, more pragmatic users are pickier, so onboarding has to be rebuilt again and again.
ex: When Photoshop dropped to about $10 a month, a flood of unskilled new users arrived
Every screen should answer: how did I get here, what am I doing, where do I go next

root.d: The first 30 seconds decide who stays

items.d: Get people to a quick win fast
Know where you are and how to go back
Choose boldly for users; ask less

l92|154.c: Nobody talks about a product working as expected; people only talk about what surprised them.
l92|154.e: Product leaders often hope users will spread the word because the product is "good," but nobody tells friends that a product did exactly what it was supposed to do. People share the unexpected: easter eggs, hidden features, a little holiday touch. So whether you build for consumers or businesses, he thinks it is worth deliberately designing for moments users don't see coming. Borrow from Hollywood: a bit of mystery, suspense, and delight builds an emotional bond with the product, and that bond is what drives word of mouth.
ex: Tesla owners talk about easter eggs they found in the dashboard, not how smooth today's drive was

l92|154.c: Consumer products last only with a real underlying edge; a clever interface alone gets copied by big platforms.
l92|154.e: He points to two durable examples. Uber activated idle capacity that had always existed and built network effects, since more riders meant more drivers. Pinterest caught a new insight, that people want to express themselves through interests rather than selfies, and sent traffic back to every source website, so sites added the Pin button themselves. By contrast, many recently hot apps are just clever interfaces for a moment. They are spending venture money doing R&D for platforms that already have distribution and network effects. Users today also tolerate more complexity and don't mind features buried in menus, which makes it even easier for platforms to absorb new ideas.
ex: BeReal-style features showed up on TikTok quickly
He was Pinterest's first seed angel investor and product advisor

items.d: Fun, but easy for platforms to copy
Like a driver network or sending traffic out

l92|154.c: Build only half the features you planned, and optimize for the problems you want to have.
l92|154.e: His thinking: when you build a minimum viable product, requests like "support this platform" or "let me share this" from users who are already hooked are exactly the problems you want. You don't need to solve them yet. Just remove the walls people crash into, such as signup, login, and connecting accounts. When Behance launched in 2008, it was stuffed with features to hedge against uncertainty. Then they cut the tips section and project postings went up. They cut groups and postings went up again, so they kept cutting. When a product revolves around one thing, the core action runs several times faster. Whenever you add something, ask what you can replace or remove.
ex: Removing custom portfolio colors drew complaints for only 24 hours
Good product leaders are naturally minimalists

items.d: Like the tips section and groups
Users all do the same thing
Before adding, ask what to remove

l92|154.c: AI turns workflow into flow, and amplified human creativity means companies need more people, not fewer.
l92|154.e: He is an optimist. What holds people back, he says, is repetitive work and friction, and AI removes exactly that. Some companies have announced thousands fewer hires because of AI, but the history of engineering productivity shows companies simply expect more from people and build more products. AI is good at restating the center of what already exists; finding the edges that will become the center still takes humans. AI also flattens the organizational stack: nobody needs to route every question through a data analyst, so everyone can chase answers themselves. That is why small teams beat big companies. He expects promotions to reward creativity rather than headcount.
ex: He discussed IBM's claim that it would hire 8,000 fewer people with Howie from Airtable

result.d: Companies can build more products

l92|154.c: AI's biggest value is letting designers and product people explore far more possibilities in less time.
l92|154.e: The best designers and product people he has worked with all set aside time to diverge into many possibilities, narrow them to a few, gather feedback, refine, and finally bring the team two or three recommendations. Every step is limited by time. Generative AI widens the exploration enormously. Even when you don't use its output, it helps you rule out directions you don't want. His own career "secret" is bringing design into the process earlier, into user research and value-proposition discussions, to build the golden gut for trade-offs. His advice to PMs is one word: play. Try the tools with your own hands.
ex: A Hollywood director asks ChatGPT for five plot options and gains something even if none is used
Photoshop uses generative AI to extend an image beyond its edges

l92|154.c: Survive the messy middle by manufacturing progress; if your conviction is weaker than at the start, let go.
l92|154.e: The middle years of a startup, or a new venture inside a big company, are full of lows, obscurity, and anxiety, he says, while human instinct craves immediate reward. You have to short-circuit that reward system with mission, team, and small milestones. Leaders also need to narrate progress, like a driver calling out where the car is to passengers in the back with blacked-out windows. On whether to quit, he asks one question: knowing everything you know now, is your conviction in the problem and solution stronger or weaker than when you started? Stronger, keep going. Weaker, pivot. And never make a big decision on a bad day.
ex: Scarcity forces resourcefulness, and that stays with you like a muscle
He prefers founders who are optimistic about the future and pragmatic about the present

items: Just haven't found the solution yet
Keep going; this is the messy middle
Knowing this, you wouldn't have started

d.verdict: Let today's conviction decide whether to stay

l93|157.c: The internet moved from curation to recommendation to generation, and each leap forces a product rethink.
l93|157.e: He divides the internet into three eras. First, people, books, and music were digitized and users curated them on their own. Then algorithms took over recommendation, forcing Spotify and others to rebuild the user experience and even the business model. Now comes the generative era, and he tells his teams not to treat it as "more machine learning" but as something entirely new. Large models can improve recommendations and classify podcasts nobody has heard for safety. But the one feature that could not exist without generative AI is the AI DJ. It serves users who have no intent at all, like turning a radio dial. Its principle: talk as little as possible and get people to the music.
ex: The AI DJ uses a digitized real human voice to personalize transitions for hundreds of millions of users
The AI DJ was proposed bottom-up by the personalization team

items.d: The content itself comes from a model

l93|157.c: Design the interface around the model's real hit rate, and always give users an easy way out.
l93|157.e: In the recommendation era he saw countless mockups with one big play button, but that assumes perfect prediction, which never happens. His approach starts by measuring how accurate the model really is. If it is right one time in five, the screen should show at least five options so the right one is probably in view. And when the prediction is wrong, users need one tap back to their own library. He borrowed this fault-tolerant interface principle from investor Chris Dixon and thinks it applies just as well to generative AI.
ex: Midjourney quickly returns four low-resolution images, hinting that about one in four is a hit

items.d: Learn how the model really performs
Low hit rate means more options
One tap back when it's wrong

l93|157.c: Generative AI will be a more powerful instrument, but music needs a new business model, as after piracy.
l93|157.e: He points to Avicii, who made music only with software on a computer. The record industry said it wasn't real music; today everyone recognizes his talent. Generative models are likely another, more powerful instrument that lets people who play nothing make something new, maybe even a new genre like EDM. He expects the line between AI music and human music to disappear, leaving only the question of what share is AI. Since models are good at imitating existing work, mediocre music gets easier and truly original music gets harder. On copyright, he sees a precedent: piracy was a technological shock, then new business models made the industry bigger than ever. That could happen again.
ex: At the time, an AI song imitating Drake and The Weeknd had sparked debate

terms.d: Let creators share in the revenue

result.d: Music grew past its old peak after piracy

l93|157.c: Autonomy works best at the VP level, not in frontline squads and not in a single leader.
l93|157.e: Early Spotify squads had about seven people, were full-stack and highly autonomous, which helped recruiting. At scale the overhead got too high; teams are now two or three times bigger with fewer roles. His logic: hiring smart people means renting expensive brainpower, so they deserve room. But push autonomy all the way to the edge in a young organization and a hundred squads produce a hundred strategies, which only generates heat. Concentrate all power at the top and you get a bottleneck. Their compromise is the VP layer: dozens to a hundred senior people with the authority to set strategy and place bets.
ex: The VP of podcasts defines the podcast strategy
Swedish decision-making is like a circle with no center

l93|157.c: Whether to centralize depends on strategy; Spotify chose more centralization to keep the experience simple.
l93|157.e: He describes two extremes. One is Amazon: two-pizza teams with as few dependencies as possible, even competing internally. Ideas reach users fastest, but you "ship your org chart," with several search boxes on one page. To stop teams hiding code from each other, Bezos forced hard APIs between systems, which happened to create AWS. The other is Apple: functional organization, everything decided at the center, an experience that feels made by one person for one person, at the cost of speed. Both became trillion-dollar companies; the good spots are usually at the extremes. Spotify blends music, podcasts, and audiobooks in one app, so recommendations and interface are centralized.
ex: Double-clicking the iPhone power button opens Apple Pay; someone has to make that call for everyone

items: Hard APIs grew into a platform
Easy to expose the org chart to users
Feels made by one person for one

d.verdict: One app with many content types, so Spotify leans centralized

l93|157.c: A redesign is forced on everyone, so separate broken habits from decisions that were actually wrong.
l93|157.e: Users often complain about being stuck in a taste bubble, but recommending a brand-new genre naturally has a low hit rate. Background listening needs about 90 percent hits; exploration only needs one in ten, which calls for a feed you can swipe through quickly. That part worked as expected. The mistake was putting it on the home screen. The old home was 90 percent about finding what you were already listening to; the test nearly flipped that, people couldn't find their playlists, and traffic flooded into search and the library. A new feature is opt-in, but a redesign is forced on everyone. Compare new users with existing users to tell the two kinds of feedback apart, and commit fully to a hypothesis until the data says no.
ex: He has done three major redesigns: one failed, two succeeded
It is like rearranging a desk someone has used for 12 years

l93|157.c: Product judgment must be explainable; a gut feeling you can't explain usually means unfinished thinking.
l93|157.e: He deliberately says product is 0 percent art and 100 percent science to force people to articulate their thinking. Historically, "art" and "magic" were labels for things we couldn't yet explain, and genetics, quantum physics, and even creativity have all turned into science. Explaining something to others is the best test of whether you understand it, and once explained, the knowledge can be shared across the organization. His promise to employees: you don't have to agree, but you have the right to know why a decision was made, and nobody gets to pull rank. He favors Socratic debate so the best idea wins rather than the most senior one.
ex: He walks and talks with remote colleagues wearing AirPods
Planning takes under 10 percent of time: about two weeks per six-month cycle

items.d: If you can't explain it, you haven't thought it through
Disagree, but still know the reason

l94|161.c: Don't pitch "you have a pain, I have the cure, mine is better"; start with a shift in the world.
l94|161.e: The pitch structure taught in business school, he says, sounds like an arrogant doctor: you're sick, I have the cure, and my cure beats the others. It slides naturally into bragging. Movies work differently. They always open with a change in the hero's world. Applied to business, that means declaring that an old game is over and a new one has begun, and inviting the listener to join a movement rather than just having a problem solved. Competitors you get compared with are then placed on the side of the old game.
ex: Salesforce: software is dead, the cloud is the new game, and if you want the old game, buy Siebel
A VC scored his 1998 pitch deck 1 out of 10; a movie-style rewrite got a term sheet

items: Rivals belong to the old game

d.verdict: Defining a movement beats solving a problem

l94|161.c: A strategic narrative has five parts: the shift, the stakes, the new game's goal, the obstacles, and the magic gift.
l94|161.e: He breaks the story into five moves. First, name the old game and the new game in the simplest possible words; slight exaggeration beats a long comparison table. Second, lay out the stakes, ideally by pointing to winners already playing the new game. Third, boil the new game's goal down to a few words, often framed as a question like "how might we..." so listeners become fellow explorers. Fourth, describe the obstacles on the way to that goal; this is where "the problem we solve" gets repackaged. Only at the end do you explain how the product helps people get past those obstacles.
ex: Zuora: from transactions to subscriptions, with the goal of turning customers into subscribers
Gong: stop selling on opinions and embrace reality
Airbnb: Belong anywhere, and later, Live there

items.d: Old game to new game, as simple as possible
Winners already play the new game
A few-word rallying cry, maybe a question
Frame the problem as a monster in the way

l94|161.c: "Engaging emotion" means showing customers a future that splits into a very good and a very bad path.
l94|161.e: He compares a hesitant buyer to Luke at the start of Star Wars, who says he has to go home and work. The buyer talks about innovating but says there's no budget this quarter. Luke changes his mind only when his aunt and uncle are killed and staying put becomes a dead end. A pitch has to create the same realization: the future won't just be "fine." Miss the shift and things get bad; catch it and things could be great. Present the obstacles after this life-or-death framing, and a plain "problem" suddenly carries emotional weight.
ex: Zuora used data on the shrinking lifespan of Fortune 500 companies to build a sense of crisis
A buyer saying "no budget this quarter" is the hero refusing the call

items.d: Like the companies that died out; a bad ending
Like the winners already ahead; a bright future

l94|161.c: Once the narrative is set, it becomes the north star for filtering feature requests and content.
l94|161.e: Sales and customer success keep bringing back feature requests, he notes, and product teams lack a rule for choosing among them. The narrative draws that line: whatever advances the new game's goal comes first, and whatever doesn't gets pushed back or dropped. Salespeople stop listing features out of context, because the product becomes a prop that makes the story come true. Marketing gets an endless supply of material, with most content about how the industry is moving to the new game rather than about the company itself.
ex: Gong turned down feature requests for recording reps' personal opinions
About 80 percent of Zuora's early website was trend pieces on industries adopting subscriptions
360Learning prioritizes by whether something helps companies upskill from within

items.t: Does it advance the new goal?
items.d: Check against the new game in the story
Requests that belong to the old game

l94|161.c: A category name is just shorthand; what makes a company different is the movement story behind it.
l94|161.e: He is not against category design, and the book Play Bigger itself admits a category is really a story about moving from an old world to a new one. The problem is that people fixate on those two or three words and assume a name alone makes them stand out, then end up holding a category name with no story to tell. Movement and category are nearly independent: the category changes as the business expands, while the movement stays the constant thread. If others start using your movement as the category name, that's a bonus.
ex: Gong's CEO joked the category could be called "strawberry intelligence" for all he cared
HubSpot's inbound movement spans two categories, marketing automation and CRM

items.d: Like outbound to inbound; stays constant
Like marketing automation to CRM; changes
Props that make the story come true

l94|161.c: Strategic narrative fits enterprise B2B sales best; for consumer products bought on specs, it matters less.
l94|161.e: His reasoning: enterprise purchases are made by a group of people, who need one shared story. The products are complex and change so fast that feature-by-feature comparison means little anyway. The arrogant-doctor pitch comes from the era of shelf goods; canned soup or cars barely change, so comparing specs makes sense there. He turns away most consumer companies that approach him. Three signals say it's time to work on the narrative: the founder can no longer brute-force every meeting (often around Series B), the old story no longer fits after an expansion or acquisition, or the business is pivoting.
ex: After OneTrust expanded beyond data privacy, it needed a bigger story
When he bought a Fitbit, he still compared specs line by line

l94|161.c: The CEO must personally lead the narrative, and expect the first draft at workshop two to look bad.
l94|161.e: Looking back at past projects, he found the narrative only became a true north star when the CEO personally wrote it. So he now insists the CEO lead, and product leaders need that air cover from the top. The process starts with a kickoff that collects lots of ideas, followed by customer interviews and a one-on-one drafting session with the CEO. At the second workshop, the draft has cut most of the ideas and is inevitably wrong, and the team is disappointed. But a bad first draft is far more useful than a pile of good ideas. Then it gets tested on a handful of sales calls to see whether customers pick up the thread themselves.
ex: The narrative team is at most four people, usually heads of marketing, sales, and similar
A salesperson can simply ask: am I crazy, or are you seeing this shift too?

items.d: Small group breaks down the five elements
Talk to customers, draft with the CEO
Draft gets criticized; the necessary low point
Do customers agree the shift is real?

l95|162.c: The audience is the hero of the story; the presenter should be the mentor handing them tools.
l95|162.e: She used to think the person on stage under the lights was the hero. Then she realized the power to accept or reject an idea sits with the audience. The presenter is more like the mentor in a myth, walking beside the hero and helping them out of trouble with both an outer tool and inner resolve. What you ask an audience to do is usually hard, and unless you first understand their situation, they won't act for you. Before her own annual vision talk at her company, she does listening interviews and a gap analysis, then rehearses a rough draft with her next layer of managers.
ex: In Star Wars, Obi-Wan gives Luke a lightsaber (outer tool) and the Force (inner strength)
Her annual kickoff: listening tour, rough-draft rehearsal, feedback, then the real talk

items: Say only what you want to say
Give outer tools and inner resolve

d.verdict: Put the audience in the lead role and they will act

l95|162.c: A great talk keeps moving between "what is" and "what could be," then lands on a "new bliss."
l95|162.e: She once analyzed classic speeches by hand on graph paper, including Steve Jobs's iPhone launch and Martin Luther King Jr., and found they all rise and fall between the present and an ideal. Lay out what is, paint what could be, go back and forth a few times to build tension and desire, and end with a picture of the world once the idea is adopted. That is the three-act shape of beginning, messy middle, and end, and human brains are wired to follow it. The framework works far beyond big stages: meetings, phone calls, even getting her husband to do chores. The key is adjusting how long you dwell on "what is" for each audience.
ex: Jobs went back and forth comparing the iPhone with the BlackBerry
The Gettysburg Address was a few hundred words; the photographer hadn't set up yet
Her husband is detail-oriented, so she spends longer on "what is" with him

items.d: The world once the idea is adopted

l95|162.c: Help the audience see what you mean; sometimes the best visual is no slides at all.
l95|162.e: Leaders usually carry a complete picture in their heads while the team sees only a few pieces of the mosaic, so you have to draw the idea out so everyone sees the same thing. Options include a memorable "STAR moment," like a shocking statistic, a moving story, or one great image; a diagram of how the parts of a technical architecture connect; or a sketch on a napkin or whiteboard when there are no slides. But in a high-stakes, face-to-face ask, a screen separates you from the other person. Better to close the laptop and draw on paper as you talk, so they can see your eyes and your passion.
ex: One CEO turned a process into a single picture and rolled it out to about 100,000 retail employees
A country head for India ditched slides, drew by hand, and won a $100 million budget
Dr. King's "I Have a Dream" needed no slides

items.d: A number, a story, or an image
Show the parts and how they connect
Draw together on a napkin or whiteboard
Let them see only you and your words

l95|162.c: The whole deck serves one big idea, each slide makes one point, and density depends on the audience.
l95|162.e: Start with the audience journey and the big idea: what is your point of view, and what is at stake if they adopt it or don't. That is the organizing spine of the whole deck. Each slide supports one point under the big idea; anything that doesn't support it stays out, and you shouldn't cobble slides together from old decks. Before opening the software, storyboard the narrative with boxes on paper. There is no universal rule on density: dense tables are fine for an internal team used to them, while a "slide doc" passed around by email should use full sentences and a long appendix. Leading with the conclusion suits executives and fundraising, though she prefers opening with the new bliss.
ex: A slide doc: five pages of core content plus an appendix of a hundred pages
The Minto Pyramid Principle, conclusion first, fits executives and fundraising

items.d: Point of view and stakes; rules everything
Together they support the big idea
Stage, meeting, or document all differ

l95|162.c: Nervous speakers often have deeper content; the key is a personal ritual that resets your body.
l95|162.e: Stage fright, she explains, is the fight-or-flight instinct: your body treats the stage like a wild animal. People who get nervous are usually more thoughtful and have something worth hearing. She suggests sitting in the audience first and looking at the stage, then imagining yourself as the friendly, smiling face out there, replacing the picture of everyone judging you. Pre-talk rituals vary by person. Since her own energy already runs high, she hides in a dark spot backstage and breathes deeply, or watches saved funny videos to shift her body chemistry from tense to laughing. Others pump themselves up with heavy metal.
ex: She once jumped around to psych herself up, then couldn't catch her breath on stage and worried the client
Breathe all the way in, sip a little more air, then let it out slowly

marks.d: For people who need a lift

l95|162.c: Leading change is a five-act movement, and every act needs talks and rituals to refuel people's emotions.
l95|162.e: A single talk, she says, is usually just one part of a larger movement. She and her co-author studied major movements in history and found five acts: dream, leap, fight, climb, arrive. The leader is like someone carrying a torch into a cave, seeing only a few steps ahead, but that light is enough to drive away followers' fear. Once people commit, they enter the long fight and climb, where it starts to feel harder than expected. That is when speeches, stories, rituals, and symbols have to keep supplying emotional fuel.
ex: The framework is in her book Illuminate, co-written with Patty Sanchez
She checked it with Marshall Ganz, who studies social movements at Harvard

items.d: Paint the future you're heading to
A long grind that needs fuel

l95|162.c: Product teams need someone who can tell the "why" at every stage, from exploration to launch.
l95|162.e: Every step of the product process, from early idea exploration to mass-market launch, can be pushed forward with a story, she argues. Walking frame by frame through a day in the user's life exposes strategic blind spots. At handoff, if you can't explain the reasoning and passion behind a product, years of work can get rejected. Apple's big launch events are themselves a story about the moment of unveiling. She has also noticed that casual, information-rich videos get more attention than polished productions. People want the content, not the production value.
ex: Airbnb hired a Pixar artist to draw the user journey and realized it had to go mobile first
A designer at a sportswear brand spent a year or two on a shoe and could only say "it's red"

terms.d: Why it was built this way
A day in the user's life, the unveiling

result.d: Makes the roadmap and wins the market

l96|165.c: To stay fast as you grow, use small teams, strong platforms, hands-on leaders, and the right people.
l96|165.e: His observation: when hundreds of people work on one thing, communication overhead crushes speed. So break big problems into pieces and let small teams attack them with a clear mission and little cross-team coordination. Put shared capabilities into a platform with clean interfaces so product teams face fewer decisions, but keep refining the platform. Leaders shouldn't direct from above; they should pick the hardest piece and work on it alongside the team. He also recommends regularly checking team composition: people who excel at zero-to-one may not enjoy, or be good at, scaling a few years later.
ex: Dunbar's number: past a certain headcount, communication breaks down
The thicker the platform, the more engineers can do with fewer people, so speed goes up

items.d: Clean interfaces, fewer decisions to make
Tackle the hardest part with the team
Zero-to-one and scaling need different people

l96|165.c: Hand a new product line to one founder-type engineer plus a designer, and ship in six to nine months.
l96|165.e: A new business line at Rippling usually starts with a one-page idea. Then they find an engineer who understands systems, thinks like a product person, and can decide quickly with incomplete information, whether from inside the company or outside. That engineer spends a few months on other teams learning the platform and picking the brains of people who have launched products before. Meanwhile they hire two or three more engineers with the same zero-to-one mindset and add a designer who knows the component library. The CEO or Jeremy himself reviews designs every week or two. Before launch, they decide whether to keep the team small or grow it to a dozen or more.
ex: The time-and-attendance product: about four people, roughly nine months
This playbook has been repeated more than a dozen times

items.d: Usually a category that already exists
Learn the platform and from past launches
Owner reviews designs every week or two
Stay small or grow to a dozen

l96|165.c: For a company with a platform, an MVP bakes in bad architecture; design for the hardest case first.
l96|165.e: He doesn't deny that a minimum viable product helps a startup that hasn't validated its market yet. But an MVP is optimized for speed. Engineers consider only the simple cases and make architectural assumptions to match, and then hundreds of decisions over the following months pile on top of those assumptions, which become nearly impossible to unwind. Better to think through both extremes at once: a two-person company and a global firm with tens of thousands of employees. The first version doesn't have to support the latter, but the architecture must not block it. A little more time upfront saves far more later.
ex: Global payroll launched with six very different countries from the start
About 80 percent of the capability lives in the global payroll platform, 20 percent is per country
Country differences can be configured by compliance and legal staff without code changes

items: Copy the US version, tweak it for the UK
V1 may not support it, but doesn't block it

d.verdict: A little more time now, much faster later

l96|165.c: A compound startup's hard-to-copy edge is that every product shares one employee record.
l96|165.e: Payroll, benefits, IT, and time tracking could each support a multibillion-dollar standalone company, he notes. But when you buy them separately, the same employee data gets copied everywhere and never stays in sync. Rippling put that data into a single system of record from day one, then built shared capabilities like workflows, reporting, and permissions on top, which every product line uses. The upfront cost was enormous; the founding team built first versions of nearly everything at once. But once it's done, you can do things other companies simply cannot.
ex: Ask "who is this person's manager" and the system always has the right answer
Others export a spreadsheet and upload it, and it's stale the moment the org changes

items.d: Payroll, benefits, IT, time tracking, and more
One database holds all employee data

l96|165.c: Fast decisions depend on every PM going deep enough to be the top expert on their own product.
l96|165.e: At Rippling, meetings decide what they can on the spot. If they can't, the key people get pulled into Slack, and once a quarterly planning deadline passes, nobody waits. This works because PMs own an entire product line and are expected to know it better than anyone, so they can answer questions in the room. One leadership principle, "go and see," means tracing issues all the way to the engineer writing the code and the actual regulatory detail. He estimates that kind of digging should take half a PM's time; otherwise the documents they write are meaningless. Process frameworks should be just enough, never a substitute for deep product thinking.
ex: The payroll lead personally studied tax rules in the UK and in places like Ohio
Product people dig in first; tax experts are hired afterward
The company-wide "must do" list has only about ten items

items.d: Read the code, read the regulations

l96|165.c: Start international expansion earlier than you think, and treat every country as its own market.
l96|165.e: He believes HR software that isn't global won't exist in ten years, and the pandemic sped this up by turning even small companies into multi-country teams. To pick countries, Rippling first looked at where its existing US customers already had employees and ranked by demand, then weighed build difficulty, strategic value, and risks like approval timelines. The resulting initial list only needed small tweaks later. The most underestimated part is localization: other countries resent having the US approach copied onto them, and a small slip costs credibility instantly.
ex: British users notice whether "colour" has a u in it
A US Social Security number field showing up in a demo to a foreign customer lost points on the spot

items.d: Where existing customers already employ people
Fine-tune the order as you go

l96|165.c: When interviewing PMs, watch how they react to a changed assumption and the questions they ask; juniors need humility.
l96|165.e: Rippling's case questions are deliberately too complex to prepare for. Midway through, the interviewer changes an assumption. Some candidates immediately reason through a chain of consequences; others freeze. Another signal is the questions candidates ask. Good questions show how invested they are and can make the interviewer stop and think. For early-career PMs, he values humility most: building product means nobody knows the right answer yet, so you have to stay curious and admit mistakes. If you'll work with a strong-willed founder, confirm they accept being challenged, then adapt to them.
ex: Kyle Boston proposed building several platform pillars in his interview and now runs platform products
His favorite interview question: what would you like to ask me?

items.d: Gauge interest and depth of thinking
Grounded in the company's real business
Can they trace the ripple effects?

l97|168.c: Plan your career like a product: work backward from the job after next and pick a specialty early.
l97|168.e: People often leave because they dislike their boss or the company never ships. He thinks those frustrations usually follow you to the next company, and a lateral move is not progress. A better approach is to treat your career like a product: decide what kind of builder you want to become, then work backward to what the job after next requires. Your current role and promotions should serve that. Early on, pick one kind of product ambiguity and get world-class at it, such as polishing experiences, opening new markets, coordinating complex organizations, mastering a domain, or leading teams. Also prepare the story you will tell later: what you solved and what you learned, said as "I," not "we."
ex: His community The Skip tells people to study their boss's boss's job
It's like Amazon writing the press release before building the product

items.d: What kind of builder you want to be
The experience and skills it needs

l97|168.c: If a company is valued at hundreds of millions but still searching for product-market fit, leave soon.
l97|168.e: Cheap money produced a flood of unicorns. Now that the music has stopped, he says, many of those companies still have plenty of cash, so they neither lay people off nor raise money, yet they are quietly searching for a core product again. Comparable companies that went public in the same period are often worth about a tenth of what they were, so the stock options at these private companies will likely shrink too. He offers two questions: are we scaling a product customers are pulling out of our hands, or still looking for that pull? And is the valuation in the tens of millions or in the hundreds of millions? Still searching at a valuation in the hundreds of millions means the opportunity cost of staying is too high.
ex: Product-market fit shows up as pull: users arrive with almost no marketing spend
Good reasons to stay: a rare chance to learn as an executive, or loyalty to the team
Bad reason to stay: fear of not finding another job

cells.d: Customers want it, valuation still low

l97|168.c: A stalled promotion usually comes down to one of four causes; get honest feedback to find out which.
l97|168.e: First, nobody sees your value and fights for you. Then change projects, managers, or even companies. Second, the next-level role simply doesn't exist, which is common now that growth has slowed. Third, high performers used to a promotion every year get impatient, but leadership impact shows up late and is harder to measure. Fourth, in about half of cases, there is a real gap: the manager missed it, the promotion committee caught it, and the person doesn't want to hear it or fix it. Telling these apart requires informal, candid feedback, cross-checked with peers, managers, and reports.
ex: Formal reviews and candid private conversations send very different signals
Jules Walter can repeat criticism back more precisely than it was said

items.d: About half of cases; person won't change

l97|168.c: A new manager should ride sidecar, sharing the handlebars, and wait to be invited in.
l97|168.e: Tech assumes that if you can code or build products, you can manage people, so it barely trains managers. He calls this an epidemic. New managers often picture management as divide and conquer, or as teaching someone to ride a bike: hold on, then let go. He prefers the motorcycle sidecar: you ride alongside, offer advice, and share the steering. Formal authority is not the same as the report's acceptance. Like a vampire, a manager has to be invited in. If you're turned away, wait patiently; once invited, pick one or two areas to work on deeply. He thinks structured training is weak everywhere, so a safe, candid community is how new managers really learn.
ex: He treats his team meeting like a product, shipping a new version every 90 days; now on version 7
His community of chief product officers grew from 6 members to 28

marks.d: You go there, I go here

l97|168.c: The senior individual-contributor path is good for the industry; builder experience beats early management.
l97|168.e: Over the past decade, companies grew by adding managers, so many promising individual contributors (ICs) were promoted too early, received no training, and became mediocre managers with unimpressive building stories. When he hires, he wants people who stayed ICs and went from learning to mastery in one kind of ambiguity, because his hard problems are cracking complex markets or aligning teams with conflicting goals, not managing people. Engineering and design have long had expert tracks, while in product everyone became a manager. He believes this mistake is being corrected for good, though the career ladders still need time to mature.
ex: Engineers can become CTOs or senior engineers; designers can manage or keep crafting

d.verdict: Builder and IC should mean the same thing

l97|168.c: An executive's biggest weakness often hides behind their superpower, because that strength is their identity.
l97|168.e: He quotes the line: what got you here won't get you there. Someone rises on one strength, and at a higher level the same tool stops working, but they never think to change, because that strength is who they believe they are. For example, a person once rated the best collaborator may have simply gotten along when everyone agreed with them. Once they become a leader who must take positions, they start clashing with other functions. The fix is to dig out the feedback you dismissed as a fluke and take seriously the opinions that contradict your strength. He changed only after a trusted peer told him the truth directly.
ex: People great at growth struggle to innovate; great storytellers struggle to get into details
As a founder he decided fast on little information; as an executive he had to give everyone context

l97|168.c: A career can last 60 years, so find a new north star for the third act before you hit your goals.
l97|168.e: Desk workers can keep working into their seventies or eighties, so after twenty or thirty years you may be only halfway. He sees three acts: in the first you learn to build, and in the second you build the factory that builds the cars, meaning teams and organizations. Many people reach their goals and then feel lost, like a racing greyhound that finally catches the fake rabbit and never runs again. Without a new goal, people keep working but grow unhappier, start fights in peacetime, or pick up bad habits. The third act has two broad directions: chase greater wealth, or give back. He finds the second more fulfilling and plans to spend his own third act coaching and giving back at scale.
ex: At the dog track, a greyhound that catches the fake rabbit never races again
Lenny went from engineer, founder, and PM to content creator

items.d: Learn to build the car yourself
Build the factory that builds cars
New north star: wealth or giving back

l98|170.c: Organizations should reward impact only, not effort or how busy people look.
l98|170.e: Three months into Facebook, he sat in a half-year review and Mark Zuckerberg's first question was when results would show up. He thinks Facebook became an execution machine because performance reviews, strategy, and reviews all centered on impact. The word is broad enough to cover any work that advances the mission, yet specific enough that you can keep asking what was actually produced. Effort correlates with impact, but many companies habitually celebrate activity and long hours. Growth work is highly measurable, so it deserves constant checks on whether the strategy is moving the north-star result.
ex: His personal goal: impact so large the next board deck needs a slide to explain it

d.verdict: Only companies truly focused on impact break through

l98|170.c: Once you lead, hiring is a skill to master; look for repeated signals of excellence.
l98|170.e: You no longer do the work yourself, so your team's success depends mostly on who you hire. He splits hiring into three chapters: finding, assessing, and closing. Past performance predicts the future best. Stars usually have done remarkable things several times, inside and outside work, so he looks for about three signals of excellence while watching for red flags. One strong signal: a former boss left and later came back to recruit the person. For closing, he learned three things from Zuckerberg: mobilize the whole executive team, include the spouse and family, and never let the momentum drop.
ex: Facebook spent seven months convincing him to move from Canada to Palo Alto
Shopify's Tobi talked with him on and off for over ten years before they worked together

items.d: All execs in, include family, persist

l98|170.c: The right growth advisor can change a company's path in one sentence, once you have product-market fit.
l98|170.e: Doing growth before product-market fit means pushing an unfinished product onto lots of users who try it once and never return. If you truly need real-user signal, test small in a remote English-speaking market first. A good advisor's value is judgment built over years of experiments at high-traffic companies, and passing it on takes seconds. To vet one, ask why they think a tactic works, and see whether they recite playbooks or understand the principles. If you don't know growth, ask a trusted expert to help interview. Don't be swayed by online fame; look at their track record and the context they achieved it in.
ex: A now-public company changed its landing page on his one suggestion and saw big results in three weeks
Done right, growth can deliver gains of hundreds or even thousands of percent

terms.d: Years of experiments at companies like Pinterest

result.d: Can multiply growth several times over

l98|170.c: Pay advisors in equity with front-loaded vesting and a three-month cliff, aiming to make the team independent.
l98|170.e: He prefers pure equity so the advisor and founder want the same thing. Vesting should be front-loaded, since the advisor's value is concentrated early. He always sets a three-month cliff: if it's not working, both sides tear up the agreement, which lowers the risk for everyone. Ideally the advisor teaches everything quickly and trains the team, so within about a year the company no longer needs them. He recommends one strong internal owner for the channel, a few advisors around them, and agencies last. For advisors, pick companies the way an investor would, judging the odds of an exit, and negotiate a ten-year window to exercise options.
ex: Where to find advisors: investor networks, other founders, and the companies best at that channel
His first advisory role paid nothing; he traded it for Bay Area connections

items.d: Tear it up if it isn't working

l98|170.c: Products that generate pages automatically suit SEO best, and one keyword can carry a whole business.
l98|170.e: Existing demand on Google is enormous, so almost every company has an SEO opportunity. A site with few pages should optimize the pages it has, then use content to answer its audience's questions. User-generated content sites and marketplaces with thousands of pages have far more room, and ideally pages are created automatically as users grow. Ranking first drives far more traffic than people expect. Entire companies in his industry were bought and sold for a single keyword ranking, so having the whole team chase one keyword isn't crazy. Pages already ranking well can improve quickly; new content usually takes three to twelve months, and no progress after a year means something is wrong.
ex: His startup TravelPod had the better product but lost to a rival ten times its size
They held the number two spot for the term "travel blog" for years

d.center: Viral loop feeds the SEO loop

l98|170.c: AI search is the biggest shift since Google began, and informational keywords will take the first hit.
l98|170.e: When he saw Google put an AI answer box at the top of results, he immediately recalled Google building its own flight and hotel search and what that did to travel sites: good for users and the platform, bad for content providers. Keywords come in three kinds: transactional, navigational, and informational. Informational queries, where the question gets answered directly, are the most exposed. Sites may have to pay for that traffic or get almost no clicks at all. The new optimization goal is making the AI understand what you do and why you're best. He defines growth as doing whatever moves the metric, not any one channel. Most companies scale on one main channel, so you must shift to new platforms in time.
ex: Half of his everyday searches already go through ChatGPT
Scaling on one channel: Priceline on search ads, Tripadvisor on SEO

marks.d: Question answered right on the results page

l98|170.c: An hour of structured self-reflection every day is the most valuable habit of his career.
l98|170.e: He gets up at five, exercises, stretches, meditates, takes a cold plunge, and then spends a fixed hour reflecting: what went well, what he messed up, why, and what he plans to do about it. The "why" is usually the most important part. He keeps a red-yellow-green dashboard tracking the experiments he's running as a friend, husband, father, and leader. For example, he had never asked his kids how he was doing. When he did, his son said he wanted more time together, so they now have a one-on-one date every two weeks. He also hosts themed dinners for five to eight people at home to meet talent, which doubles as a hiring and reference-checking tool.
ex: Books he recommends: Spark on exercise and the brain, Smart Brevity on concise writing
Growth teams also just ship a few sure-thing changes instead of testing everything

root.d: Red, yellow, green for each role

items.d: Themed dinners to meet interesting people

l99|173.c: Dropbox's lessons: hire well, execute carefully, stay focused, and make the whole company care about growth early.
l99|173.e: She was at Dropbox from about 200 people to 1,500. Hiring went right: they valued first-principles thinking and humble collaboration, and everyone was trained to interview and sell the job. On execution, the first growth experiments in 2013 went nowhere because the team copied best practices that didn't fit, instead of starting from users and hypotheses. Focus fell short: consumer and business lines ran in parallel without an early plan for how they connected, so enterprise sales started late and competitors caught up. Growth and revenue were seen as slightly unseemly, and growth ended up as a layer bolted on top of the product.
ex: She joined at a roughly $1 billion valuation; the IPO was around $10 billion
Hiring smart people with no sales background to sell led to creative go-to-market ideas

items.d: Don't let growth be a bolt-on layer

l99|173.c: Easy, viral products should start product-led, then add enterprise sales as big customers demand it.
l99|173.e: Early companies usually have to lean one way. If a product is intuitive, has a low learning curve, needs no human onboarding, and spreads virally, it suits a product-led start, using scale to gather user signal. Large companies will appear among self-serve users and keep asking for single sign-on, security, and other enterprise features. That list becomes the case for building enterprise sales. Other products are naturally sales-led, because they need customization or enter through legal or finance, and many of those are now simplifying onboarding to become more product-led. The key is to pick a starting point and map the full journey from consumer to enterprise early.
ex: Dropbox, Miro, and Figma all have product-led DNA
Big customers kept knocking, asking for SSO

items: Collect enterprise needs from self-serve users

d.verdict: Pick one starting point; map the whole journey early

l99|173.c: Caring deeply and demanding results aren't in conflict; direct feedback is how you show you care.
l99|173.e: Some of her former reports have worked with her at three companies. She credits genuinely caring about people and investing in their careers. At the same time, team goals are clear and broken down to each person's levers, so everyone knows how success is measured. When a new hire was moving too slowly two or three weeks in, she said so directly and laid out a path, starting with "I believe you can do this and I'm here to help," then sticking to observed behavior and its impact rather than blame. The person was grateful afterward. Development runs end to end: hire for a growth mindset, set 90-day goals, help land early wins, give steady feedback and visibility, and stay in touch after they leave.
ex: Kim Scott test-ran her Radical Candor material at Dropbox
She has reports record 5-to-10-minute Loom videos for executives to gain visibility

terms.d: Everyone knows how success is measured
State intent first, then the behavior

result.d: Former reports join you at new companies

l99|173.c: High-performing teams combine clear goals and mission with results focus, team-first spirit, ownership, and fun.
l99|173.e: Across Dropbox, Canva, Grammarly, Miro, and Webflow, she saw the same pattern. First, clear goals: annual recurring revenue (ARR) as the north star, broken into leading indicators like activation rate. Then a mission that explains the why. Culturally, teams should be results-oriented but team-first, so members don't compete with each other or optimize only their own corner. They need ownership: when blocked by another team, ask what you can still do yourself. And they need fun. Ownership only works when each person has an area big enough to own independently.
ex: Each Dropbox growth PM generated over $1 million in ARR per year
Finance wanted to double the team on that math; she objected because there weren't enough big problems to divide up
At Webflow she took on pricing and packaging when nobody owned it

items.d: ARR north star broken into levers
Don't take it too seriously under pressure

l99|173.c: When interviewing PMs, coach candidates on their presentation first and watch how they absorb feedback.
l99|173.e: Communication and cross-functional work are table stakes; she cares more about first-principles thinking and a growth mindset. The hiring manager's first screen is live problem-solving, such as opening the company's pricing page and asking what the candidate would change, with repeated whys. This round eliminates the most people. The final round is a presentation prepared over a week on a real problem they would tackle in the job, not a past project. Before it, she calls the candidate, shares data, and gives notes on the draft. That helps them succeed and previews what working together feels like. If none of the feedback shows up, they're probably not a fit.
ex: Presentations run 30 slides at most: 30 minutes plus 15 minutes of Q&A
A candidate who has barely used Webflow's product is a red flag

items.d: Share data, give notes on the draft

l99|173.c: Common growth mistakes: copying best practices, mis-sized experiments, and growth and product working in silos.
l99|173.e: Many companies never plan their go-to-market model and pricing early, then face painful migrations of existing users when they change prices at scale. Many teams take a course and copy another company's playbook instead of forming hypotheses from their own data and user interviews. Experiments are often the wrong size: an early company testing tweaks worth 0.5% is pointless, while rebuilding a page from scratch without a hypothesis means you can't explain the failure. Growth teams sit closest to users, so their insights should feed the product roadmap. Use DACI, a framework for who drives and decides, plus a steady meeting rhythm to spell out how teams fly in formation.
ex: Early at Dropbox she rebuilt the checkout page in one go, and couldn't explain why it failed
At Webflow, growth marketing owns signups and product growth owns everything after signup

marks.d: Too many variables; failure can't be explained

l99|173.c: After product-market fit, the first growth hire is usually an acquisition lead who tests channels like a portfolio manager.
