l99|173.e: Before product-market fit, everyone does growth, focused on nailing the ideal customer and the buying decision-maker. After that, you need to acquire the first thousand customers at scale, so the first dedicated hire usually owns acquisition. They test channels like a portfolio manager, find the one or two that drive 80% of signups, and make sure those users monetize. She values analytical skill, user understanding, and creativity over deep channel experience, because too much experience can bring false precision. Activation and pricing don't need dedicated people early; for activation, think-aloud tests with five target users are enough.
ex: Options: a junior person with acquisition experience, a smart Reforge grad, or add an advisor
Try an advisor for one quarter and part ways if it isn't working

items.d: Everyone does growth; nail the ICP
User testing is enough; no dedicated hire
Add paid-media experts and growth PMs

l100|175.c: Ramp's channel mix isn't unusual; the difference is an early shareholder network and engineering behind every channel.
l100|175.e: The co-founders had a successful exit before, and this time they brought many founders and influential operators onto the cap table. Those people's companies became the first customers, which Sri calls using the cap table as a growth strategy. Investor introductions mattered less than recommendations from peers who had actually used the product. Today most of Ramp's growth still comes from new customers, mostly mid-sized and large companies. The channel mix looks like any company at this stage. The real advantage is a dedicated growth engineering team that uses third-party data and automation to make every channel more efficient.
ex: Sales-support engineers share pipeline and payback targets with the sales team
Each funding announcement is treated as a market moment and brings in substantial leads

terms.d: Outbound, paid ads, field events, SEO, and more

result.d: Far higher output per person than peers

l100|175.c: A speed culture means making decisions in smaller units of time: days, not quarters.
l100|175.e: The CEO shows the number of days since Ramp was founded at every board meeting and all-hands, a reminder to work in days rather than years, quarters, or weeks. If something can be done today, don't leave it for tomorrow. Day to day, people respond very fast on Slack, and even when they can't finish right away they name an owner and a deadline. The growth team runs two-week sprints like a product team and prioritizes across groups together. To limit interruptions, the company offers a calendar-audit template to check whether your time matches your priorities. He thinks hours aren't the issue; autonomy, flexibility, belief in the mission, and celebrating wins decide whether people burn out.
ex: days.ramp.com shows the live day count; about day 1,529 at recording
Participation in the Zoom chat during all-hands is close to 100%

items.d: Name the owner and the deadline
Drawn in and kept by this pace

l100|175.c: The growth engine runs on culture and rhythm, with every team's metric converted into one north star.
l100|175.e: He sees debates about team structure as a distraction. What matters is a simple north star, data-driven hypotheses, and a fast test-and-learn rhythm. Keep at most two north-star metrics, one for scale and one for efficiency. They should tie directly to value while letting frontline teams see how their work moves them. Teams track local metrics they can directly influence day to day. At planning time, finance and data teams apply conversion factors to translate those into the north star, giving a common currency for allocating headcount and budget across teams. The conversions only need to be 70 to 80 percent right, factors are refreshed every six months, judgment still rules at the margin, and a long-term holdout group checks the cumulative effect.
ex: Instacart's north star: monthly active ordering users
Ramp's growth team north star: sales-qualified pipeline value

items.d: Scale plus efficiency, at most two
Finance and data set the factors
Load time, search count, and so on

l100|175.c: Judge customer acquisition by contribution-margin payback period, not by CAC.
l100|175.e: Customer acquisition cost (CAC) alone looks at spending, not value, and driving CAC down often means attracting less valuable customers. Lifetime value over CAC is better, but for a young company lifetime value depends on as many assumptions as a discounted cash flow. Overestimate retention and you spend freely, only to discover a year or two later that churn was higher than you thought. Payback period has assumptions too, but they rest on recent data and can be checked faster. Calculate it on contribution margin, after all variable costs. Executives and the board set an acceptable ceiling, and then everyone works to shorten the blended payback period.
ex: Spend $5,000 to acquire a customer who contributes $500 a month, and payback is 10 months

d.verdict: Get everyone shortening blended payback

l100|175.c: B2B channels should start with founder-led sales; each later stage is pricier, more effective, and more scalable.
l100|175.e: He thinks most B2B companies should follow a similar path. The early team learns to sell first, then hires the first few salespeople. Next comes cheap, targeted marketing such as content, communities, and small events, then PR, and only at the end paid ads and brand. The order works because later channels cost more, but as you understand your customers better they also become more effective and easier to scale. SEO is cheap, yet he suggests starting it alongside paid ads, because without domain authority, backlinks, and media coverage, content can go nowhere for a long time.
ex: Newsletters and podcasts help with hiring and reaching tech founders; traditional PR reaches broader customers

l100|175.c: With small B2B samples, push the treatment to the maximum so that even failures are conclusive.
l100|175.e: About 30 percent of the growth experiments he's seen succeed, so risk-taking should be encouraged, and the real failure is not learning anything. Half-hearted experiments can't give answers, and the same idea gets retried by every new executive. For a result to be significant, you need either a large sample or a strong treatment effect. B2B rarely has the former; what Facebook can learn in two hours might take B2B two years. So throw every tactic you can think of at a hypothesis. If the best possible version still doesn't work, drop it for good. If it works, strip tactics away one by one to cut cost. This applies to big, slow, expensive experiments; small things like web copy can be tested quickly.
ex: For account-based marketing, Ramp maximized both the number of target accounts and the ways of reaching them

cells.d: All tactics in; even failure is conclusive
Unexplained failure, retried again and again
High traffic makes small changes testable

l100|175.c: Talent density comes from targeting the right companies, paying top performers tenfold, and quickly letting misfits go.
l100|175.e: There are two ways to find people. Work your network until you've identified the twenty or thirty best people in a field. Or use public data to find companies truly good at a channel, limited to those one or two stages ahead of you, and recruit from there. He opposes compressing pay bands, arguing a small team of top performers beats a large group of average ones, so a tenfold contributor should earn tenfold. Interviews misjudge people often, so talent density also depends on retention, performance management, and letting the wrong people go promptly. He also hires for slope rather than starting point, and only when the team is genuinely overloaded.
ex: Hiring a CRM marketing lead? Check SimilarWeb for companies with a high share of email-driven traffic
His favorite question: what are you bad at but still doing anyway?

items.t: Companies a stage or two ahead
items.d: They've lived the stage you're entering
Such as a high share of email traffic

l101|178.c: The most common mistake is falling in love with a solution first; that is what sank Airbnb Plus.
l101|178.e: The first thing she corrects in her class is students wanting to build a specific product before understanding a real user's problem. She also reminds them that a PM is not the CEO and has no formal power; the job is more like editing among possibilities. Airbnb Plus set out to solve guests not knowing the quality of a listing. But the team, spooked by competitors who managed properties themselves, went straight to in-person inspections and managing inventory. That was not an operational strength of a platform, and the unit economics rested on the fantasy that scale would fix them. Better to return to the real problem and solve each listing type's specific pain cheaply.
ex: Mailing hosts a lockbox is cheaper than sending an inspector
Partner with local cleaners and fold the cost into the nightly rate

items: Build operations you're not good at
Use the free review system you already have
Ask more detail at listing upload

d.verdict: Nail the real problem, then pick the solution that fits a platform

l101|178.c: The vision can be huge, but cut it into short phases, each with learning goals and a go/no-go point.
l101|178.e: Without a big vision it is hard to innovate, she says, but the vision needs careful execution alongside it. Her approach is to tell the team exactly which phase they are in: for example, three months devoted to learning a few specific things, when doing things that don't scale is fine. Set milestones and go/no-go decisions every quarter, so you never spend two years before being forced to cut, and you avoid the sunk-cost trap. If you are convinced an idea is wrong, you have a responsibility to say no. To persuade a deeply invested founder, first agree with what they are trying to achieve, then come back with data and a better plan.
ex: She herself left the Plus team to go improve the review system

Get fast signal in the prototype stage
Write down what success looks like

l101|178.c: In an age of endless choice, build a minimum lovable product; the bar depends on users' alternatives.
l101|178.e: Her reasoning: a product that barely clears the bar won't win over users who have many options, so figure out what experience your target users would actually love. The bar varies. If you are replacing a manual spreadsheet, a product missing 15 features may already be good, even lovable, and should ship fast. Users like designers demand far more from their workflow. She would rather polish 5 things to a high shine than do 15 things clumsily. Resources are limited, so sprinkle the extra "pixie dust" in only a few places.
ex: Webflow's keyboard shortcuts for power users
During an Airbnb redesign, templates were prefilled with content hosts already had
Webflow shipped memberships first and let ecosystem partners add the lovable parts

marks.d: Depends on how many alternatives they have

l101|178.c: A roadmap should tell a story through themes, and OKRs should first describe in words what great looks like.
l101|178.e: A common trap, she finds, is treating a RICE spreadsheet full of impact, cost, and effort scores as the roadmap. What people really need is to understand why these things are being built. She asks teams to write a document: what the goals are, which few themes get investment, the big projects under each theme, and links to the Jira boards the team actually uses, so nothing goes stale. When new insight arrives, the story and the themes are what change. OKRs often turn conservative because people fear hurting their promotion, so every metric is green while users feel nothing. She would rather see all red and yellow, as long as there is an ambitious north star and a quarter-by-quarter milestone path.
ex: If every OKR is green, the goals weren't ambitious enough

items.d: What to achieve for users and the business

l101|178.c: Early in your career, become known for one thing; responsibility and opportunity follow that reputation.
l101|178.e: You can be known for orchestrating the most complex cross-functional launches, she says, or for cracking the hardest technical or regulatory problems. The specialty lets you deliver projects exceptionally well, a reputation builds, and people naturally hand more responsibility to someone known to be great at something. Moving from consulting to a gaming company, she established herself through analytics, then discovered she was strong at execution, and at Dropbox earned more responsibility by shipping an urgent cross-platform launch with a small team. Once she started managing people, being the best executor was no longer enough; the core strength had to stretch into new forms.
ex: In interviews she looks for candidates who can build structure and a path out of ambiguity
The best advice she ever got: leaders also have to ask for help

l101|178.c: As a new leader, bank trust before pushing change, and gate hiring behind milestones so you don't overhire.
l101|178.e: At WeWork she hired aggressively for six months, then spent the next six deciding who stayed. The lessons were empathy and not overhiring: hit milestones and show results first, then unlock the next round of hiring. When she joined Webflow, she had only 90 days before maternity leave, so she ran intensive interviews across functions and levels, wrote a plan that said what would continue and what needed study, and told the board plainly that engineering was understaffed. In hindsight she pushed change too fast: trust is like a piggy bank, and you save before you spend. She also traded deep product learning for understanding how the team worked together.
ex: About 40 to 50 one-on-one interviews in the first 90 days
During WeWork's layoffs she gave up her own role to protect reports on work visas

items.d: Build context across functions and levels
Make sure execs and the board know
Then spend it to drive change

l101|178.c: The lesson from all four companies: know exactly why users love you, then double down on it.
l101|178.e: Every company she has worked at, she believes, got pulled off course at some point by market hype or competitors, spreading investment beyond the core with disappointing results. The right question is why users choose you and what your unique strength is, then keep investing so that strength stays real. Companies will of course build multiple products, but each new one should ask how to draw on the core strength rather than starting from scratch.
ex: Dropbox tried to build Slack-style chat but underinvested in sync performance
Airbnb branched into experiences and transportation without perfecting listing descriptions

items.d: Simple, fast syncing of your files
The space itself, not fancy keycards

l102|180.c: Nest planning into pillars, areas, and teams, and re-plan the next 12 months every six months.
l102|180.e: As the organization grew, Asana added an "area" layer between pillars and teams. Each area targets specific customers and problems and has its own metrics, so the roadmap is organized around problems rather than features. Planning moved from once a year to every six months, each time covering a rolling 12 months: high confidence for the first half, lower for the second. That makes it easier to align with sales and marketing and to double down quickly when technology shifts. Roadmap projects can be cut or pivoted, and dates aren't locked to quarters, which avoids hacking scope just to hit a date.
ex: The Coordinate area tracks weekly active users in paying organizations and healthy project usage
At most three reviewers, and only one of them can block
When a meeting passes 10 people, the extras are asked to leave and the decision is written up instead

items.d: Aimed at specific customers and problems

l102|180.c: The double diamond forces you out of opinion: pick the customer, then the problem, then the solution.
l102|180.e: Every step diverges and then converges: which customers exist, pick one group; which problems they have, pick one; which solutions are possible, pick a starting point. She says this breaks decision-by-opinion and ties success criteria to customer outcomes rather than teaching-to-the-test metrics like "the feature got used." Asana maps its various reviews onto the turning points of the diamonds. The exception is large language models: a dedicated team builds prototypes directly, quickly sees which ones far exceed expectations, and hands those prototypes to the team that knows the problem best.
ex: Review checkpoints in order: kickoff, direction, design concept, spec, experience review
The LLM prototype team skips the double diamond and hands results to teams like status reporting

items.d: List customer groups, then choose a target
List pain points, then focus on one
Choose a starting point among concepts

l102|180.c: A young PM earns senior colleagues' trust by bringing insight, not by pretending to have seniority.
l102|180.e: She was often the youngest person in the room. Her approach was not to act experienced but to know the customer, market, competitors, numbers, and product cold, and walk in with observations nobody else had, which sparks curiosity and then trust. She borrows Anne Raimondi's trust equation: credibility plus reliability plus authenticity, divided by how much self-interest the other person perceives. The fastest route for a new PM is to befriend user researchers and watch users firsthand. Companies that heavily use their own product should be especially careful not to mistake themselves for the user.
ex: Trust = (credibility + reliability + authenticity) / perceived self-interest
Reliability is your say-do ratio: how often you do what you said

result.d: Then divide by perceived self-interest

l102|180.c: The most common new-PM trap is rushing to look all-knowing and sliding from inquiry into advocacy.
l102|180.e: PMs eager to seem professional, she notes, do discovery and specs behind closed doors, then announce "this is the right answer." Others either challenge it on the spot or, worse, keep their doubts to themselves. Holding a review while not wanting feedback is performative collaboration. Real confidence comes from openness: be fully present in the meeting, watch everyone's face, and end by asking what was missed. When feedback comes, sort it into must, should, or could. You don't need to ask for a promotion either; results speak for you.
ex: Three tiers of feedback: must do, should do, could consider
End meetings with: is there anything we should have covered but didn't?

items: Finish behind closed doors, then announce
Ask the question behind the question

d.verdict: Openness signals more confidence than constant forcefulness

l102|180.c: You grow through experience, exposure, and education, and exposure is the most underrated of the three.
l102|180.e: Early-career people, she finds, tend to think first about education, then about hands-on experience, which is too linear. Exposure is like sitting in the car without holding the wheel: if you stay present and keep analyzing, you learn far beyond what your role requires. That is why she prefers to lead by example. People internalize through repetition, so she runs meetings the way she would want to attend them. Education comes from mentors, like a business unit head at Intuit who told her to answer the question the other person should have asked and look at the whole picture one level up.
ex: Intuit's manager training taught the situation-behavior-impact feedback method
She urges early-career people not to screen themselves out; apply boldly

items.d: Do it with your own hands
Sit in the car and watch others drive

l102|180.c: As a manager, teach reusable patterns, and say the bad news out loud instead of only the good.
l102|180.e: After moving from individual contributor to manager, she realized a precise instruction works only once; you should teach a way of thinking that repeats, or it becomes micromanagement. Reports know you're the boss and won't interrupt you, so the discipline has to be yours. She brings a stack of sticky notes to meetings, writes down what she wants to say, waits for others to say it first, and only adds what is still worth saying before the meeting ends. Another lesson: her natural optimism made the team think she didn't see the problems and wasn't being real. Now she says plainly, "this plan is 70 percent done, and here are the three missing pieces."
ex: The sticky-note method: write it down, let others say it first
She told an area lead frankly that a strategy brief was only 70 percent done

items.d: The boss speaking shuts down discussion
Only what's still worth saying at the end

l102|180.c: Judge a job by its learning curve, environment, and problem; passion is built, not found.
l102|180.e: She plans her career around the skills and experiences she wants, not titles or company names, and is just as deliberate about staying as about leaving. Three checks. First, is the learning curve still steep? Even if you love the company, watch for the moment you stop growing. Second, does the environment set you up to succeed: enough people and tools, someone who advocates for you, and no toxic manager? Third, does the problem itself make you curious? It doesn't have to be glamorous. When torn, she asks herself how the opposite might be true, a way to escape a scarcity mindset.
ex: Her question to herself: how might the opposite be true?
From Conscious Leadership: above the line you seek learning, below it you seek to win

items.d: Judge by skills and experience, not title
People, tools, advocates, no toxic boss

l103|184.c: Joining an early startup is like investing: judge the people, market, product and distribution.
l103|184.e: She says she evaluates a startup to join the same way an investor evaluates a deal. People: can you trust the founder to steer the ship? Market: is it growing, and is there room for a newcomer? Product: do users love it so much they can't stop recommending it to coworkers and other companies? Distribution, meaning how the product reaches customers, may matter even more than the product itself. A company should be great either at bottom-up adoption or at genuinely complex enterprise sales. No company scores perfectly on all four, so you should also ask which gap you can fill.
ex: dbt founder Tristan can paint the industry vision and still dig into daily analytics engineering details
In 2019, Snowflake's valuation jumped from $4 billion to $12 billion
dbt users treat it as part of their identity, not just a tool

l103|184.c: Selling a company means building plan Bs early: press where buyers hurt, stay friendly, and be honest when money runs low.
l103|184.e: She says the best negotiating position is being able to survive on your own, because then you can always choose not to sell. Most companies can't, so they should prepare fallback options early. Usually only two or three buyers truly see you as a strategic asset. Hurt them where you are strong, enough that they can't ignore you, but act like a partner and don't close doors too soon. While you still have runway, never mention a sale, only partnership. Once cash is running out, say openly that you are looking for a home and widen the list of buyers. Investors already expect some companies won't return their money.
ex: Transform pressured dbt on the semantic layer while acting as a partner, and dbt eventually acquired it
List about a dozen possible buyers and ask their corporate development teams for intros to product or business leaders
She guesses the M&A market, which peaked in November 2021, is close to recovering

l103|184.c: Stick to your vision, grow the whole market, and refuse to give ground only on core standards.
l103|184.e: dbt Labs wrote its view of competition down as three principles. First, stay true to your own vision; competitors' jabs are mostly noise. Second, work with partners in the ecosystem to grow the opportunity instead of slicing the existing pie thinner. Data, for example, is moving beyond reports into day-to-day operations and training machine learning models, so the market itself is expanding. Third, play to your strengths while leaving room for others. They take a long view of competition and insist on owning only two things: the standard for transforming data and the semantic standard, because the two work best together for users.
ex: Transform founder Nick Handel led the effort to write down these three principles
The two things dbt insists on owning: the transformation standard and the semantic standard

l103|184.c: dbt won by being simple yet powerful, with open source creating a loop where more users make it more valuable.
l103|184.e: Early on, many people dismissed dbt as a tool for templating SQL, but she argues simplicity is its strength. An analyst who only knows SQL can now push clean data into production with guardrails, work that used to belong only to data engineers. Open source makes trying it nearly effortless, and users spread the word inside and outside their companies. The variety of uses let dbt grow into a horizontal platform, and the huge user base attracts partners who build around it. Timing mattered too. And the founding team spent almost two years as a consulting firm, fixing these exact problems for clients by hand.

l103|184.c: Price by first understanding the value you create, then charge only a small slice of it.
l103|184.e: She says that in the zero-interest-rate years, many companies chased GitHub stars and usage and never thought about making money. But the pricing conversation has to happen eventually, and sooner is better, ideally before you build the product. dbt's principle is to create value before capturing it. Customers estimate that dbt is worth roughly 20 to 35 percent of what they spend on their cloud data warehouse, and dbt deliberately charges only a fraction of that. For its first price change, the team measured price sensitivity by talking with dozens of customers about relative value, asking what price would feel cheap, fair or too expensive.
ex: Quoting pricing expert Madhavan: you can't avoid the pricing conversation, only choose when to have it

l103|184.c: Shipping something slightly worse is better: launch, learn from users, and treat technical debt as a good sign.
l103|184.e: She fights perfectionism with two mantras: perfect doesn't exist, and you only truly learn how people use a product once it ships, no matter how much you plan. The first version of the dbt Cloud scheduler was embarrassingly basic: it looped over a table of jobs and ran each one when its time came. The team felt sheepish about it, but it worked. Only after real scale arrived did they rewrite it, several times. Technical debt means people are actually using the product. On launch day, nobody needed a distributed scheduling system.
ex: The scheduler now serves about 8,000 companies

l103|184.c: Product managers should borrow investor habits: build a network, be a T-shaped generalist, and bet big on power laws.
l103|184.e: Venture investors see many companies a day, switch contexts constantly, and lean on their networks to learn from smarter people. She says these habits work just as well in a product job. She keeps meeting operators at companies slightly ahead of dbt, asks them about open source, pricing and acquisitions, and brings back what applies. Her broad background in finance and business also makes her more persuasive when pushing things through inside the company. Investing follows a power law, where a few big winners produce most of the returns, so she keeps placing bets on directions that could change the company's trajectory.
ex: Her favorite interview question: how did you last teach yourself something new?

l104|185.c: A clear north star makes decisions simple, even in an ecosystem of many interlocking marketplaces.
l104|185.e: LinkedIn runs a content feed, hiring, marketing and subscriptions at once, so decisions across businesses could be messy. But everyone knows the test: does this help connect people to economic opportunity? He joined through an acquisition, and his first product review was torn apart. When he redid it by reasoning backward from that north star, it sailed through. Leaders repeated the goal for years until it became an immune system in the culture. It also shows up in each marketplace's output metrics and in the "members first" value.
ex: His metrics: hires made, and people who learned a skill, measured by learning hours

l104|185.c: Hiring for skills instead of job titles is changing how talent moves, and it outlasted the downturn.
l104|185.e: When the pandemic hit in March 2020, hotels laid off huge numbers of workers while customer service jobs went unfilled. The market should have balanced itself but didn't, because employers searched only by fixed job titles. So LinkedIn pushed hard to translate experience into skills, letting employers search for people who can negotiate or calm an upset customer. That made workers from other industries visible. He believes this shift won't reverse when the market swings back. Another lasting change is people choosing jobs by values and interests. The product's job, he says, is to amplify signals users already send, not force them.
ex: Hospitality workers already have about 70 percent of the skills a service job needs; the rest can be trained
About 47 percent of recruiters explicitly use skills when searching for candidates

l104|185.c: Show both proof of your skills and clear intent for the role; industry experience sets you apart.
l104|185.e: Recruiters look at just two things, he says: your skills and abilities, and your intent and interest in the role. For intent, turn on Open to Work and spell out the kinds of roles you want, or express interest on a company's page so they see your signal when a job opens. For skills, attach evidence such as work samples and recommendations under each skill a job requires, so a recruiter sees at a glance why to pick you. Product manager roles are crowded, so knowing the industry, like having worked in autos before building car software, helps you stand out.

l104|185.c: Sort products by complexity; in a highly connected system you must think through second- and third-order effects.
l104|185.e: He classifies products by complexity rather than hardware versus software or consumer versus enterprise. A children's picture book is finished when it's written. On LinkedIn, any change touches people on the other side: if you publicly say you're Open to Work, how do others see you, does engagement change, and how will business customers use that data? Each layer has to be thought through and measured over time. Few people can manage systems like this, so when hiring and promoting he looks for people who see the whole picture and work across teams, not just those who grew their own corner.
ex: Open to Work went from a private signal to a public post to a photo frame

l104|185.c: A complex organization needs circuit breakers: one named decider per decision, plus time limits for escalating.
l104|185.e: With several marketplaces and business models intertwined, many people have a stake in each decision, so there must be a way to break ties. LinkedIn uses RAPID, a chart that spells out who recommends, who must agree, who gives input and who decides. The key, he says, is that the decide column holds exactly one name. His personal rule: after three rounds of email, pick up the phone; after 20 minutes on the phone, go straight to the decider and aim to settle it within an hour. A five-day rule requires managers to escalate anything they can't resolve within five days.

l104|185.c: The feed, jobs, connections and courses feed each other, so LinkedIn has to be built as one whole.
l104|185.e: Outsiders see LinkedIn as a pile of separate products, but inside it's run as several marketplaces within one ecosystem: hiring connects job seekers and employers, learning connects learners and instructors. Showing interest in the feed can trigger a job recommendation; when you apply, your connections help you get in the door; and when you want to go deeper on a topic, a course picks up from there. LinkedIn Learning exists for the same north-star reason: job seekers often lack a required skill, so help them get it. He sees quiet systems like skills and values as serious social infrastructure.

l104|185.c: Great product managers live at a corner of the skills triangle; don't sand yourself down to fix weaknesses.
l104|185.e: He draws PM skills as a triangle: the creator, like Spielberg; the data scientist who sees patterns and the future in numbers; and the general manager, which matters more the more senior you get. He has never met a great PM sitting in the middle, so he advises figuring out which corner you're in and picking roles to match. Newcomers should try to work once on a product users truly love, to know what the bar looks like. Working PMs should dare to claim a product and shape it with their own hands, and keep side projects going to stay in building shape.
ex: He was on the Ford team that built the Escape Hybrid, America's first hybrid SUV

l105|187.c: With a strong product founder, turn their taste into written principles, then involve them in a U-shaped curve.
l105|187.e: If the CEO is an expert at your own job, he says, you'll learn the most and feel the most frustrated. His approach is to distill the founder's instincts into product principles the whole company shares; otherwise every review feels like guessing hot or cold. The founder's involvement should follow a U shape: deep at the start, to agree on strategy, goals and anti-goals; hands-off in the middle, so the team can explore; and deep again at the end, when the founder tastes the soup, ideally in working code, hunting for problems and polishing details together with the whole team.
ex: Slack principles include "be a great host" and "don't make me think"
Sometimes more clicks are better, because they give users confidence; don't just cut steps

l105|187.c: An AI product's interface should promise only what its data can deliver, and usage should feed back into accuracy.
l105|187.e: About 15 years ago at Google he worked on what became the Knowledge Graph, which gives direct answers in search. What's new with large language models, he says, is that machines can now talk back in natural language. The principle he set then still holds: the more confident the interface looks, the more reliable the underlying quality must be. Today's models sound sure of themselves even when they hallucinate, which erodes trust, so products should admit uncertainty and show their sources. The second principle: make training data a byproduct of normal use, so the product gets more accurate the more people use it.
ex: Netflix's early ratings system was exactly this kind of feedback loop
Step four of Slack's 2014 vision was to build AI magic on top
His vision: Slack as a personal chief of staff that summarizes updates by importance

l105|187.c: Make bigger bets: spin up separate teams to incubate new areas and judge them by learning speed, not KPIs.
l105|187.e: Feature teams, he says, easily slip into nudging a metric up 1 percent a quarter, like being stuck in a valley where you only see the next small hill, not the mountain range behind it. So before a new area matures, Slack builds a team from scratch to incubate it. These teams skip the usual quarterly planning and reviews and are judged only on prototypes and how fast they learn from users, then they pilot and ship. For AI right now, central machine learning and search teams provide the foundation while several small squads prototype in parallel. He expects AI, like mobile before it, to eventually land on every team's roadmap.
ex: During the pandemic, customer demand led Slack to incubate huddles and clips
Argue less over static mockups; prototype in real software as soon as possible

l105|187.c: Look at your product through the eyes of someone who doesn't care about it, to build for the next wave of users.
l105|187.e: Slack employees are the heaviest Slack users in the world, so it's hard for them to feel what a newcomer feels. In a complaint storm, the whole team shares a screen, walks through a complete journey and writes down every point of confusion or friction, practicing first on a neighboring company's product and then on their own. Usability tests moved online: the whole team reacts in real time in a single Slack thread, which becomes the first draft of the research report. The most frequent complaints heard by customer support are piped to product teams, and two-week customer love sprints fix the small, delightful things.
ex: Customer-facing teams run a customer love sprint about once a quarter
Pilot programs include thousands of customers, chosen for variety and tolerance for rough edges

l105|187.c: Be customer obsessed and competitor aware, and build something users will pull their coworkers into.
l105|187.e: Slack never set out to kill HipChat, he says. It was ten times better on a few specific axes: a mobile experience that synced seamlessly across devices, search that actually worked, and consumer-grade touches like emoji reactions brought into the workplace. Behavior shifted on its own. Discord serves communities, a different audience from teams that work together. Microsoft Teams began as a defensive move to protect Office and later became more of a video meeting tool; many customers use both. The root of Slack's growth is users willing to spend social capital pulling a team of 5 to 50 people onto it.

l105|187.c: When growth stalls, throw out the roadmap, trade short-term impact for learning, and pick a new north star.
l105|187.e: In 2019, Slack's self-serve cohorts started looking worse. Most tech-forward companies were already customers, and the users arriving next had different needs and less maturity. The team threw out its roadmap, proposed a fresh set of hypotheses, and accepted six months of almost no impact in exchange for learning. What worked: helping new users understand and want Slack faster, letting free users try the paid version for the first time, and changing the north star to "successful teams," a signal that shows up before payment but isn't at the very top of the funnel. He sees product-market fit as S-curves stacked on top of each other.
ex: Users who hit the successful-team bar were 400 percent more likely to upgrade within six months
Growth in new paying customers doubled over the following years

l105|187.c: Great PMs are amplifiers, not mini CEOs: nail execution first, and lean on writing as you get senior.
l105|187.e: He calls "the PM is a mini CEO" the most dangerous advice in the field, because it breeds dictators. A PM should amplify the team and raise the speed and quality of decisions, not act as the referee every time. Newcomers should focus on what they control: flawless execution, impact even if it's local, and fluency with data and research. Senior PMs must drive high-quality decisions, live in the future and work strategy backward from it, and write well, because writing is the only way to influence an organization at scale. Data fluency plus product taste, he says, is a powerful combination.
ex: Ben Horowitz's line: do what you say, and explain why when you can't
He recommends Stephen King's "On Writing"
Larry and Sergey at Google kept asking: how would this work at 100 times the scale?

items.d: Work strategy backward; a senior focus
Amplify the team instead of refereeing

l106|188.c: Most product ideas fail, and teams are far worse at predicting experiment results than they think.
l106|188.e: The numbers he has seen firsthand are brutal. At Microsoft overall, about two thirds of ideas failed to move the target metric. At Bing, a search engine already tuned for years, about 85% failed. At Airbnb search, the failure rate was 92%. Booking.com and Google Ads have published figures in the 80-90% range too. Every team that starts experimenting believes it will be the exception, and every team gets humbled. Occasionally a small change nobody believed in produces a huge win, but most gains come inch by inch. So he recommends turning surprising results into institutional memory, reviewing them regularly, and recording the unexpected losers as well as the winners.
ex: Moving Bing ads' second line into the title raised revenue about 12%, after sitting in the backlog for months
About 250 Airbnb search experiments added up to roughly 6% more revenue
Bing's search relevance team aimed for about 2% improvement per year

items.d: The highest failure rate he has seen

l106|188.c: Every change should go through an experiment; break big redesigns into small steps and don't ship flat results.
l106|188.e: His reasoning: even a small bug fix can have surprising side effects, so every code change should be tested against a control. In his view you cannot run too many experiments. Treat resources like an investment portfolio: most goes to steady incremental improvements, with a slice reserved for high-risk, high-reward bets, accepting that about 80% of those will fail. Wholesale redesigns usually fail. It is better to break them apart and test one factor at a time. A change that shows no effect should not ship either, because it only adds code to maintain. For changes required by legal, try several versions and pick the least harmful.
ex: Bing spent about 100 person-years integrating Twitter and Facebook content, then abandoned it
Moving the Windows indexer offline made it more accurate, but testing showed it drained batteries

items: Six months before you learn anything
Sunk cost pushes you to ship
Keep only the changes that help

d.verdict: Big bets are fine, but expect 80% to fail

l106|188.c: Optimize a single metric that causally predicts customer lifetime value, not short-term revenue.
l106|188.e: He argues that chasing revenue alone invites bad behavior. Cramming more ads onto a search page always makes more money this quarter, but it hurts the experience and drives users away. So the overall evaluation criterion (OEC) needs counterweights, such as how quickly users find a satisfying result or the share of successful sessions. Another option is to turn it into a constrained problem: give ads a fixed pixel budget, and only count it as a win if revenue rises within the same space. Airbnb could fold in post-stay ratings and use a model to predict them early. His test for a bad OEC: if people cannot even agree which direction the metric should move, throw it out.
ex: Amazon's recommendation emails were judged only on revenue, so teams blasted out email
Once unsubscribe losses were counted, over half of email campaigns were net negative
Microsoft.com once chose time on site, but nobody could agree whether longer was better or worse

terms.d: Retention, time to result, cost of unsubscribes

result.d: Causally predicts customer lifetime value

l106|188.c: Start building an experimentation culture at tens of thousands of users; it really works at about 200,000.
l106|188.e: His logic is simple: with too few users, the statistics cannot detect a difference. His rule of thumb: for a typical e-commerce conversion rate, detecting at least a 5% improvement takes roughly 200,000 users. Startups should be aiming for 5-10% improvements anyway, not 1% tweaks. With tens of thousands of users, you can build the platform and the culture and test only large effects. The platform's goal is to push the marginal cost of one more experiment to nearly zero. Third-party tools are good enough now, so most companies mix buying and building. When rolling it out, start with teams that ship often and have clear goals.
ex: By 2019 Microsoft ran about 20,000 to 25,000 experiments a year
To speed up: cap extreme values, and use CUPED to borrow pre-experiment data to reduce noise
Bing was the beachhead; people moving to Office carried the practice with them

items.d: Build platform and culture; test big effects only

l106|188.c: An experimentation platform lives or dies on trust, and results that look too good are usually wrong.
l106|188.e: He sees the platform in two roles: a safety net that quickly stops bad launches, and an oracle that tells you the truth. Trust is hard to build and easy to destroy. Early on, Optimizely let users watch p-values in real time and stop as soon as a result looked significant. That pushed the real false-positive rate far above the nominal 5%, and many users stopped believing it. The most common warning sign is sample ratio mismatch: you designed a 50/50 split but the numbers are off, usually because of bots or a broken data pipeline. Then there is Twyman's law: if a metric that normally moves under 1% suddenly jumps 10%, don't celebrate. Odds are you will find a bug.
ex: He estimates that peeking at p-values and stopping early pushes false positives to about 30%
About 8% of Microsoft's experiments had a sample ratio mismatch
When a mismatch is found, every number on the scorecard is struck through in red so nobody screenshots it

items.d: Stop at first significance; false positives soar

l106|188.c: A p-value is not the probability you won; in low-success teams, significant results are often false positives.
l106|188.e: He points out a common misunderstanding: a p-value of 0.02 does not mean a 98% chance the treatment is better. A p-value is the probability of seeing data like this if there were actually no difference. To get the number people really want, you need Bayes' rule, plugging in your team's historical success rate as the prior to compute the false positive risk. With Airbnb search's roughly 8% success rate, about 26% of results with p below 0.05 are false positives. That is why he requires any result with a p-value between 0.01 and 0.05 to be replicated, and then combines the p-values from both runs.
ex: Combine p-values with Fisher's method or Stouffer's method
Track your own team's historical success rate to use as the prior

l106|188.c: Evidence comes in levels, with controlled experiments at the top, and a crisis is no reason to stop testing.
l106|188.e: He often walks friends and family through the hierarchy of evidence. Anecdotes deserve no trust. Observational studies, which look at patterns without a control group, deserve a little. Natural experiments, controlled experiments and replicated controlled experiments are each more reliable than the last. Plenty of observational findings were later reversed by controlled experiments. During the pandemic, some argued there was no time for experiments and decisions had to be made fast. He pushed back: if intuition is wrong two thirds to 80% of the time normally, it does not suddenly get accurate in a crisis, and you still need to check whether changes hold up once things return to normal. He believes Airbnb would have done better by experimenting more, while admitting that is an unprovable counterfactual.
ex: He believes the online experiences pushed hard during the pandemic had weak early numbers
Amazon replaced slide decks with structured narrative documents for decision reviews

l107|191.c: Speed and stability improve together; shipping small changes often is actually safer.
l107|191.e: Many leaders assume that staying stable means slowing down, say by putting every change through a two-week approval process. She calls that an old belief with no evidence behind it. DORA's data shows the two are strongly correlated. When you ship small changes frequently, each one has a small blast radius, problems are easy to pin down, and recovery is fast. Batch up a big release instead and debugging gets hard and merge conflicts get painful. Waiting longer does not make the code any better.
ex: She calls "two-week change approval for stability" an old wives' tale
Big-batch releases bring painful merge conflicts

l107|191.c: Track two speed and two stability metrics; benchmarks are for navigation, not shaming.
l107|191.e: DORA measures speed with lead time for changes and deployment frequency, and stability with time to restore service and change failure rate. The benchmark numbers don't need to be precise. What matters is knowing where you stand and whether you are improving, and separating slowness that is a business choice from slowness caused by technical limits. The research found no significant difference between large and small companies. The only significant finding was that retail does better, and she suspects an industry shakeout left only the capable survivors.
ex: Elite teams deploy on demand, with lead time under a day
Elite teams restore in under an hour, with a 0-15% change failure rate
Try the free Quick Check at dora.dev

cells.d: Share of releases that cause failures

l107|191.c: DevOps is a set of capabilities, not a toolchain you buy; work backward from outcomes to capabilities.
l107|191.e: Vendors package DevOps as a product, but she describes it as a combination of capabilities across technology, architecture, culture, and lean management. To get faster and more stable, first decide which business outcome you want: more revenue, faster feature launches, or better reliability. Then work backward to the capability that is holding you back. It might be continuous integration and delivery, trunk-based development, automated testing, a loosely coupled architecture, or using the cloud well. DORA sits on top of a whole research program; the four metrics are only the surface.
ex: Key capabilities: CI/CD, trunk-based development, automated testing
Loosely coupled architecture and a healthy organizational culture
See her book Accelerate for the details

l107|191.c: Measure creative work on at least three dimensions so the metrics keep each other honest.
l107|191.e: SPACE is not a fixed list of metrics. It is a framework that helps teams pick a balanced set for complex, creative work. The most dangerous mistake is measuring activity alone; lines of code, for example, is a metric she never uses. Chasing a single efficiency number can also backfire. Frequent alerts interrupt focus, so alert frequency should be paired with focus time to offset it. Satisfaction often drops before the other dimensions do, making it an early warning signal. DORA is essentially SPACE applied to the outer loop of delivery.
ex: She never uses lines of code
Measure alert frequency and focus time as a pair
DORA is an instance of SPACE on the outer loop

root.d: Pick at least three dimensions that balance

items.d: Often the first signal to drop
Outcomes of the process, like reliability
PRs, commits: easy to collect, easy to misread
Time and handoffs through the system

l107|191.c: Triangulate surveys with system data, and when they conflict, the surveys are almost always right.
l107|191.e: Engineers have no incentive to lie on a survey. If a system is broken, they want it fixed, so self-reported data is trustworthy. Surveys also reveal what systems can't see, such as a deployment that only works because one person heroically handles it by hand. System data has blind spots; at some companies, large amounts of critical code are not even in version control. Early on, start with surveys and interviews, which are fast and cheap. As you mature, add system data that scales, but still run a survey at least once a year.
ex: Google uses surveys and telemetry together; in conflicts the surveys are nearly always right
One company's critical code sat outside version control, invisible to telemetry

d.verdict: People first, then systems; triangulate over time

l107|191.c: The biggest metrics trap is a vaguely defined problem; write it in words before finding data.
l107|191.e: She estimates that for about 80% of the teams she works with, the hardest part is defining the problem. A directive like "improve developer experience" can mean culture to one team, inner-loop friction to another, and tooling to a third, so they spend months talking past each other. Her four-box method puts words in the top row: define the concept and the outcome you want to move, and confirm it with stakeholders. The bottom row then picks a data proxy for each concept. When results disappoint, you can tell whether the data was bad, the proxy was wrong, or the hypothesis itself was wrong, and you avoid fishing for correlations.
ex: Example: customer satisfaction as the concept, repeat customers as the outcome
About 80% of her partners get stuck on defining the problem
Rollout needs executive support and engineer buy-in at the same time

items.d: Make sure it is clearly recorded
A measurable metric for each concept
Bad data, wrong proxy, or wrong hypothesis

l107|191.c: AI coding tools free up mental capacity; they should not be used as a reason for layoffs.
l107|191.e: Tools like Copilot are shifting developers' work from writing code to reviewing it. A Microsoft Research paper found about half of developers' time now goes to review. One experiment showed building an HTTP server about 50% faster with AI help. But she argues productivity is not just speeding up individual tasks; the bigger win is freeing up cognitive space to tackle harder problems. She is also studying whether SPACE needs a trust dimension, along with new questions about over-reliance, learning, and how novices differ from experts.
ex: Microsoft Research: about half of developer time shifted to reviewing code
Building an HTTP server was about 50% faster with AI assistance

terms.d: About half the time spent reviewing

result.d: For harder problems, not layoffs

l108|194.c: Speed comes from small single-threaded teams, big goals on tight deadlines, and shielding them from chaos.
l108|194.e: In the early pandemic the market opportunity was huge, and he felt the question was not which path to take but how fast to move. So velocity got written into Ramp's processes, incentives, hiring and promotions. His reasoning: a team that iterates fast will eventually reach impact, speed attracts people who actually want to ship, and moving fast lowers the cost of any single decision. In practice, a small group wakes up every day thinking about one goal, with plenty of resources, an ambitious target and a short timeline. Ramp may not even announce the project company-wide until it has early traction. A product engineering on-call rotation and a product operations team keep bugs and busywork away from them.
ex: About 8 engineers built a corporate card to rival Amex in three months
Three engineers, one designer and one PM built an accounts payable product to rival Bill.com in three months
Benchmarking against public companies and a vision prototype video made big goals credible and exciting

terms.d: Wakes up for one goal only
A public company as the benchmark
On-call and product ops absorb the busywork

result.d: About $100M in annual revenue in roughly two years

l108|194.c: Leaders should align upstream on goals, data and assumptions, and leave solutions to the team closest to the work.
l108|194.e: Looking back, almost every early mistake he made came from dictating a solution before aligning on the goal and the assumptions. Junior leaders love to argue about solutions, he says, but the real debate belongs upstream: is the goal right, how should the data be read, and what are we assuming. His contract with each team is their strategy and roadmap. After that, his job is to keep filling in context the team lacks. The team's job is to surface risks and bring him the one-way-door decisions, the ones that are hard to reverse. The one point where he gets deeply involved is the move from beta to general availability, before sales starts selling.
ex: His direct reports post their weekly goals every Monday and review each other's
One-on-ones cover only what the other person needs from him
CTO Karim stays almost entirely out of specific product decisions

items.d: Debate how to read the evidence
Why this should reach the goal
Left to the team closest to the work

l108|194.c: Velocity has magnitude but no direction, so guard it with customer feedback and operational burden metrics.
l108|194.e: To keep fast shipping from breaking the business, Ramp gives every team the same set of controls. Every piece of negative feedback goes back monthly to the tech lead, PM and designer. Teams report NPS and CSAT. They also track operational burden: the share of support tickets their product generates, normalized by how many people use it. Bugs go straight to the on-call engineer so the pain is felt directly. When these metrics turn red, especially when too many tickets come from confused users, the team pauses new features and fixes the experience first. As long as the metrics hold, teams can work however they like.
ex: There is no bug backlog; bugs get fixed as soon as they are found
When confusion-driven tickets run high, shipping new features is off limits

items.d: Complaints, NPS, tickets reach the team

l108|194.sc: For PMs told to speed up
l108|194.c: If you want speed, give real autonomy, kill status meetings, and force leadership to choose between goals.
l108|194.e: Many PMs are told by their boss to "move fast like Ramp." He starts with an honest caveat: Ramp's speed comes mostly from top engineering and design talent. Engineering has to be a first-class citizen, and the CEO sets the vision but stays out of sequencing. Second, adding status meetings and process only kills morale. He has never run a status meeting; progress is shared asynchronously in the tools. Third, leadership tends to say "we want it all." PMs should lay out the trade-offs as a menu and make them choose, because doing four things is far faster than doing eight. He also believes burnout comes from effort without visible progress, not from speed itself.
ex: A founder dropping a quick "this is amazing" in a project channel is hugely motivating
The CTO spent almost all of his first year hiring the best engineers and designers

items.d: Progress shared asynchronously, in real time

l108|194.c: Planning precision costs time, so buy it only for big cross-functional launches and spend the rest executing.
l108|194.e: He tells every new hire that joining Ramp means signing an implicit contract: speed comes before almost everything, and some chaos is unavoidable. Precision in planning takes time, so it should only be bought for high-value moments, such as a big launch where product, marketing and sales have to move together. Exactly which day a single feature ships does not need to be precise. Ramp used to run quarterly OKRs tied to financial metrics. That ate about a third of everyone's time and became political. Now it is a one-page list of priorities every six months, and the product team's contract is the financial plan and the roadmap. Vision and strategy, by contrast, should stay stable for the long term.
ex: A strategy doc covers goals, assumptions, right to win, metrics, initiatives and risks
Right to win: a bill is just an invoice to a company, so existing payment rails and risk controls apply

marks.d: Roughly every quarter or half year

l108|194.c: Reason from first principles instead of copying past experience, such as treating every support ticket as a product failure.
l108|194.e: Ramp is a credit card company, a payments company and a software company at once, growing through both self-serve and enterprise sales, so there is no playbook to copy. Internally, saying "at my last company we did it this way" is considered an anti-pattern. The processes he brought with him were designed for a B+ engineering team, and with an A+ team he had to throw them out. One example is having customer support report to product. If the product were perfect, nobody would need to contact support, so support's goal is to reduce tickets, not just handle them. When he faces a hard problem, he closes his laptop, writes the question at the top of a page, and thinks it through himself before looking anything up.
ex: More than 400,000 users served by fewer than 30 support agents
He blocks time every Friday to think about the most important question for next week

items.d: Every ticket is a product failure

l108|194.c: Keep PMs few and strong: designers and engineers think like PMs, and PMs own only vision and priorities.
l108|194.e: Ramp has about 13 PMs for more than a hundred engineers. He says the leverage comes from three places. First, designers and engineers also take on spec writing and trade-off decisions. Second, Ramp built a product operations team early to absorb project management, launches, enablement and customer research. Third, low-value work gets cut: PMs never write tickets. A PM's core job is vision, priorities, building the pod's culture and shielding the team from distractions. The signs of a great engineer, in his view: they want to win the market, care about the business, set their own pace and fix problems unprompted. He hires for hunger for impact and depth of thinking, not experience.
ex: To move into PM, first prove yourself in an adjacent role like product ops or solutions engineering
A six-month trial, with the engineers and designers you work with deciding whether you stay
A favorite interview question: what is the hardest thing you have ever done

items: Writes tickets and breaks down tasks
Runs status meetings to track progress
Owns every detail of the spec
Sets vision, priorities and a rough spec

d.verdict: A PM's leverage is making everyone think like a PM

l109|196.c: To get invited to the table, think one or two levels above your team and bring a point of view.
l109|196.e: When he joined HubSpot in 2016, the company had just launched its free CRM but had not figured out how to make money from it. As a growth PM he recognized this as product-led growth before anyone used that name. He was willing to take risks and cared about strategy a level or two above his own team, so he hung around the sales floor and chatted with other departments looking for problems his team could help solve. At a company party in Dublin, he and a designer pitched the COO a brand-new approach to pricing and packaging. He was then invited to present it formally to the executive team.
ex: The proposal was not adopted wholesale, but parts of it later made it into the pricing model
After that, he was regularly pulled into important decisions

items.d: Hang out with sales and other teams
A new take on pricing and packaging
Pitch the COO at a party

l109|196.c: Growth PMs need curiosity and resilience first, and a high experiment win rate means the bets are too small.
l109|196.e: The trait he hires for above all is relentless curiosity: people who are not afraid to admit they don't know something but cannot rest until they figure it out. Second is resilience. Most growth experiments fail, and people without resilience get desperate for a win and start placing only tiny, meaningless bets. Third is coachability, because growth product management is still young and every company does it differently. Fourth is creativity: caring only about outcomes, not how elegant the solution is. People who love building beautiful little widgets are not a fit for growth.
ex: His rule of thumb: roughly 20-30% of growth experiments succeed
Interview question: what would your recent coworkers say about you behind your back
His creed: details matter, and taste means digging deep enough to have a strong opinion

marks.d: Thinking too small, chasing easy wins

l109|196.c: Where you break into product matters, and the real accelerator is a sponsor, not a mentor.
l109|196.e: He got into product by accident: he heard the founder wanted to hire a PM, looked up what the job was, and volunteered. His first few years were spent on B2B2C products, too far from end users, and he shipped a lot of bad product. Only when he joined a running app under Fareed Mosavat, with direct access to users and data at scale, did he understand what a PM should be. His advice for career changers: pick a place with structure and a senior manager above you. Or help existing PMs with their grunt work, watch how they operate, and earn a sponsor who will stake their reputation on you. The key is to drop your ego and welcome the harshest feedback.
ex: He thinks he interviewed poorly with Fareed, who bet on him anyway
He often talks to users who didn't pick the product or churned, and finds their decisions are often emotional

items.d: Take the grunt work, watch how they work
Someone who stakes their reputation on you

l109|196.c: Decisions that hurt customers usually reflect a short horizon; find the customer problem before solving the business one.
l109|196.e: He has watched plenty of heated debates inside HubSpot, and they all come down to what is best for the customer. In his view, a decision that hurts customers but helps the business is usually only looking at the short term. Unless you have a total monopoly, you cannot keep growing while working against your customers, so decisions should be judged by their results two or three years out. In practice, documents cannot just say "problem." They must label it as a business, customer or efficiency problem. For a business problem, you ask why it hasn't fixed itself, what customer problem sits underneath, and you list the assumptions and knock-on effects.
ex: Staying in the mid-market: revenue is spread out, so no single big customer can hold the roadmap hostage
Publishing the culture code and regularly stress-testing whether it still holds

items: Label what kind of problem it is
Ask why, and who it affects
Judge by results in two to three years

d.verdict: Long term, what's right for customers is right for the business

l109|196.c: A growth team should treat every problem as its own and take over high-leverage areas nobody is watching.
l109|196.e: When he joined, the growth team was nominally responsible only for activation of the sales tools. But the team decided not to be boxed in by its charter: if they spotted an opportunity nobody owned, they acted first and asked forgiveness later. At the time self-serve subscription revenue was tiny, and nearly every product lead was handed to sales. They found a neglected purchase page inside the product, which the original team was happy to give up, and rebuilt it completely. The shape of the funnel shifted in a step change. Taking ownership made the company trust them with more, and it matched what buyers wanted: to try and buy on their own.
ex: HubSpot's original product-led DNA came from Brian Balfour
His early metrics: activation rate, and how much demand the team sent to sales

terms.d: How users find the purchase page
Make the value for sale clear

result.d: A step change in the funnel's shape

l109|196.c: Product-led growth is not all self-serve: let the product drive revenue and have humans fill the gaps, not the reverse.
l109|196.e: Many founders confuse product-led growth with pure self-serve, but most successful PLG companies run a hybrid. He suggests deciding module by module along the customer journey: who the customer is, how they usually buy, whether decisions come top-down or bottom-up, how complex billing is, how familiar they are with the category, and whether the product is intuitive enough to need no hand-holding. Something as intuitive as Loom can be fully self-serve. A customer dealing with IT security or data migration will happily try and activate on their own, but wants a person when it is time to buy. Forcing self-serve on them serves the company, not the customer.
ex: Small teams migrating from spreadsheets or sticky notes often never talk to anyone
First ask why you want PLG: top-of-funnel demand, relief for a stretched team, or revenue efficiency

cells.d: IT security, data migration want a person
Step in where the cost model allows
The cost structure has to support it

l109|196.c: Common PLG mistakes: no resources, impatience for payback, messy data, and giving up for lack of data.
l109|196.e: The classic mistake he sees is hiring a head of growth, giving them no engineers, designers, tools or data, and handing them a scary number. The second is treating PLG like another sales headcount and expecting a short-term return. It is really an R&D investment and needs patience. The third is poor data hygiene: incomplete tracking, messy data, and waiting in line for an analyst to pull a number. The fourth is assuming you cannot do PLG without huge volumes of data. In his experience, talking to ten customers often reveals the why better than any quantitative dataset.
ex: The heart of PLG is a product that explains its own value proposition
He discusses these issues regularly with founders backed by OpenView

items.d: Treating R&D like a sales hire

l109|196.c: HubSpot's flywheel gives value before extracting it: free products and word of mouth bring in new customers.
l109|196.e: He thinks true growth loops are hard to build in B2B SaaS. HubSpot relies instead on a big flywheel: attract, engage, delight. The core of inbound marketing is giving value first. Early on, blog posts, white papers and ebooks filled the top of the funnel. Later that shifted to a large amount of genuinely useful free software. Heavy users eventually hit the limits of the free tier, and paying becomes the natural next step. Happy customers then recommend it to peers. He stresses channel diversity: an algorithm change or generative AI could hit SEO hard, so HubSpot keeps testing new channels, such as free tools.
ex: Free tools like Website Grader open a conversation about what to fix next
Cutting prices and friction during the pandemic actually accelerated the free and starter tiers
ChatSpot, built by cofounder Dharmesh, unexpectedly drove meaningful signups

items.d: Peer word of mouth brings new users

l110|197.c: Martech is product management for internal systems, and past 100 people a company needs someone owning the tools.
l110|197.e: He defines marketing technology as a role spanning product, growth, engineering and marketing: half people and process, half first-party and third-party systems. At 30 or 40 people, a growth person can set up tools and everyone maintains them together. At around 100 to 150 people, that village-style co-ownership breaks down. Someone has to know how data flows through each tool, what every field means, and who owns the contracts. A common signal: the engineer who originally wired everything up is overwhelmed, and nobody dares touch the system.
ex: Read contracts for the price at scale: 500 monthly active users is cheap, but what about a million?
The ideal: as the business grows, tool cost per employee actually falls
Two thousand dollars and two days to set up single sign-on can prevent a data leak

items.d: Tipping point: someone must own it

l110|197.c: In consumer companies, centralize martech under growth; in business-to-business companies there's no standard answer.
l110|197.e: In a consumer company, the tools mostly serve the growth team. He recommends one central role under the CMO, sitting beside the head of growth or reporting to them, as long as that person is technical enough to represent growth in conversations with product and engineering. The alternative, operations people scattered across departments, tends to spawn more systems and should be avoided unless the company is huge. B2B is messier, especially B2B2C, where you serve businesses and their users. Ramp has moved the function back and forth between revenue operations and the CMO's organization. The question is who it serves and whether its resources get spread too thin.
ex: At Postmates, martech reported to the growth team
Ramp's revenue operations splits into business technology and marketing technology

cells.d: Next to the head of growth; his top pick

l110|197.c: Once data warehouses got cheap, the stack shifted from a central customer data platform to the warehouse plus reverse ETL.
l110|197.e: The consumer stack settled between 2017 and 2020: a customer data platform (CDP) in the middle, fed by an SDK in the app, sending data out to ad, email and analytics tools. After 2020, data warehouses became much cheaper, so a company could model its data centrally without a big data team. Reverse ETL tools, which push warehouse data back into everyday tools, took off. His advice: if engineering is scarce and you want simplicity, buy a CDP; if you already run Snowflake and dbt with a strong engineering culture, move to reverse ETL. B2B still revolves around Salesforce, and B2B2C, where users must be matched to company records, is the hardest problem today.
ex: With several data pipelines in parallel, decide when data moves and from where
Running HubSpot and Salesforce together makes field mapping the biggest headache
His recommended stack includes Amplitude, Snowflake and Hightouch

items.d: Leads into Salesforce, then outbound tools
Segment in the middle, routing data
Small teams can model data centrally
Data flows from the warehouse to tools

l110|197.c: Collect data for multi-touch attribution from day one, so upgrading your model later doesn't mean waiting for data.
l110|197.e: Most companies start with first-touch or last-touch attribution, crediting one channel per customer. When someone later complains their channel gets no credit and asks for multi-touch, they discover the data was never captured. His advice is to lay the groundwork early. On every visit, record the landing URL, the referring page, each ad platform's click parameters and all UTM tags. Store both first and latest UTMs on the device, updating the latest on each visit. Write them to the user profile and also attach them to every page-view event, so the warehouse can rebuild the full path. Most third-party tools only know users and events, so design around that.
ex: Make a checklist of every ad platform's click ID parameter and capture each one
Snowplow is one of the few CDPs that allow custom schemas

l110|197.c: The golden decade of deterministic attribution is over; marketers must learn to decide on probabilistic data.
l110|197.e: From 2010 to 2020, Apple's IDFA identifier told you exactly who saw an ad and then installed your app. Almost nobody opts in now, so app attribution is mostly aggregate numbers. The web is getting harder too: browsers strip URL parameters, users block cookies, and a lot of paid traffic gets counted as organic. Much of his work now is building models on the roughly 30 percent of people he can still see and extrapolating to everyone. He thinks most companies aren't ready for marketing mix modeling; they need multi-touch attribution plus better probabilistic modeling, and geo-based holdout experiments when it matters.
ex: Platforms grading their own ads is a conflict of interest, which is why AppsFlyer and Branch exist
He is watching the Threads ads API and Reddit's conversion API

d.verdict: Accept uncertainty and let models, not exact matches, guide spending

l110|197.c: Tools only exist to solve problems: start with the problem and the people, and choose buy and build, not buy or build.
l110|197.e: He keeps telling his team that tools are just a means of solving problems; you don't have to buy one, let alone a specific one. When a request comes in, he breaks it down in order: problem, people, system. What is this person actually trying to solve? Whose approval and training does it involve? Only then design the system, rather than handing out admin access. Framing it as build versus buy puts people on opposing sides from the start. Better to buy a third-party tool that covers 90 percent, then spend engineering effort on the differentiating 10 percent on top. Vendors are more willing to work with you that way too.
ex: When a company wanted to build its own A/B testing tool, his financial model showed buying and extending was cheaper
His gray-area thinking: don't reach a conclusion until a decision is actually required

result.d: Faster, cheaper, everyone wins

l110|197.c: Hire martech people for curiosity and scrappy engineering skills, not for which tools they've used.
l110|197.e: There are too many tools for anyone to master them all, so he looks first for curiosity, then for enough engineering to get by: some JavaScript or Python, and the ability to read API docs and make a request. He studied civil engineering and taught himself to code, and figures six months is enough to catch up. The role coordinates up, sideways and down, like a quarterback calling plays across departments. He asks how candidates prepared for the interview to test systems thinking, and assigns a report due Friday on what the company should change, to spot tool bias. Resume gaps and school names, he says, are misleading shortcuts.
ex: When job hunting he asks for the company's financials; a refusal is a red flag
A favorite question: what's the hardest thing you overcame in the past year?

items.d: Too many tools to ever finish learning

l111|201.c: Fans already want to pay, but creators are shy about pricing, so platforms should handle monetization for them.
l111|201.e: Musicians especially, she finds, carry a starving-artist mindset and would rather give everything to fans for free. But making a living from creative work requires an exchange of value. Because the work is tied up with emotion, creators struggle to think like merchants about what the market will bear. That's why a platform stepping into the middle, aggregating fans and taking over pricing, payments and taxes, is close to an ideal marketplace solution. Subscription models like Patreon and Substack also smooth out the highs and lows of creative output and give creators predictable income.
ex: Spotify gives top listeners exclusive merch discounts and early access to buy
Fans treat being a creator's patron as a badge of honor
Patreon and Substack smooth out creators' income

l111|201.c: Creating is a hamster wheel that's hard to get off, so platforms should help creators take breaks.
l111|201.e: Creators start out of love, but once they charge money and fans buy an annual subscription, stopping becomes nearly impossible, because income drops to zero the moment they do. Inside Patreon this was called the content-creation hamster wheel. She sees it as an opportunity for platforms to add value: make the creative process less effortful, offer financing that banks won't extend to creators, or automatically aggregate data and generate summaries, so creators can pause during important moments in their lives.
ex: Financing products designed for creators
Automatic roundups and summaries that cover some of the posting

l111|201.c: Winner-take-all platforms are inevitable, but the number of people making a living from creating will keep growing.

Together they inevitably produce a large population of people who live off content; Twitch and TikTok are the giants that grew out of this wave. Creators can also build lasting intellectual property that spins off comics, film and merchandise, and that space is far from fully explored.

l111|201.c: Creators succeed on three things: consistent output, collaborating with each other, and attaching to the right curators.

Third, in a world with far too much content, people rely on tasteful curators, much as they once relied on record labels or radio stations. Creators should find curators whose sensibility and audience match theirs and tie themselves to them.
