l111|201.c: Run a sale like a fundraising process, and start building relationships with potential buyers from day one.
l111|201.e: Her company Kit wasn't snapped up; it went looking for a buyer. That meant managing it like a fundraise, with several potential acquirers in a funnel at once. Her biggest regret is reaching out too late: the first meeting was already about an acquisition, and the other side knew nothing about her. Had she shared her vision earlier under the banner of partnership, there would have been a relationship by the time it mattered, and the buyer would have had time to think it over. l111|201.c: A marketplace isn't a chicken-and-egg problem: build supply first, or no amount of polish on the demand side matters.
l111|201.e: At ride-hailing company Hailo she ran supply, the driver side, and led the U.S. launch of a private-car service to compete with Uber. Real-time rides showed her firsthand that when there aren't enough drivers, when drivers are unhappy, or when strikes or regulators shut things down, the business suffers immediately. If a rider opens the app and no car comes, it doesn't matter how beautiful the interface is or how well marketing worked. So she believes a marketplace always starts with supply. Later you can decide which side to favor when interests collide, but you can never ignore the supply side's real pain.
ex: Hailo launched a private-car ride service in the United States
The cautionary tale is eBay, which aggregated buyers and then squeezed sellers on terms

l111|201.c: Test the riskiest big bets first, and let leaders own the failures when they don't pan out.
l111|201.e: From Marty Cagan she learned dual-track agile: discovery and delivery run side by side, with fast experiments constantly testing assumptions instead of designing behind closed doors for months and tossing it to engineering. On a two-by-two of risk and reward, she argues for doing discovery first on the top-right big bets, because always picking the safe small improvements means never truly innovating. That isn't comfortable, so leaders have to absorb the consequences when bets fail and give teams permission to try. Once the risk has been worked out, the idea moves into the delivery track.
ex: Marty Cagan's dual-track agile
Twilio's value "draw the owl," meaning figure it out and build it

Fine to do, rarely a breakthrough

l112|205.c: People hire products to make progress, so your real competitors show up on the demand side, not the shelf.
l112|205.e: After nearly thirty years building products, he found that "build it and they will come" doesn't work. Jobs to Be Done starts from a simple premise: in a given situation, a person hires a product to get a particular outcome. By ingredients and calories, Snickers and Milky Way are rivals. But look at the moment of purchase: Snickers is fast fuel when you skipped a meal and still have work to do, while Milky Way is comfort after an emotional moment, eaten alone to decompress. Their real competitors are completely different. Analyze competition only from the supply side and you'll be fighting on the wrong battlefield.
ex: Snickers competes with protein drinks, Red Bull, coffee and sandwiches
Milky Way competes with a glass of wine, a brownie, even a run
On tech company snack shelves, the Snickers always disappear first

items: Eaten alone after an emotional moment

d.verdict: Same shelf, hired for completely different jobs

l112|205.c: Demand comes from moments of struggle, not from products, so roadmaps should list struggles, not features.
l112|205.e: He argues the link between supply and demand is far looser than people assume. Products don't create demand; struggling moments do, and those moments can persist for years with nobody solving them. A struggle isn't just a pain point either. It's a context plus a desired outcome, which together point in a direction of progress. He recommends writing features on a roadmap only for the next 90 to 120 days, and beyond that listing the struggling moments you intend to crack. That way, when something unexpected like ChatGPT arrives, you still have several solutions to choose from.
ex: Southern New Hampshire University started with 50 or 60 "anomalous" students who only took online courses
SNHU later grew to more than 200,000 students
Intercom and Basecamp build roadmaps around struggling moments

items.d: Today I have to do something

l112|205.c: People switch only when push and pull outweigh anxiety and habit, and reducing friction often beats adding features.
l112|205.e: People don't change for no reason, he says. Four forces are at work: F1, the push of the current situation, and F2, the pull of a new outcome; and beneath the surface, F3, anxiety about the new thing, and F4, attachment to old habits. Only when the first two outweigh the last two does anyone act. Most people assume more features mean more pull, but every added feature raises the worry about whether you can actually use it. Building houses taught him that cutting friction often requires no change to the product itself, just making the purchase easier.
ex: Offering packing, moving and two years of storage let him raise prices and still lift sales more than 30 percent
Leaving room in the floor plan for the dining table people couldn't part with lifted sales 22 percent

root.d: F1 plus F2 must beat F3 plus F4

items.d: Worry the new thing won't work

l112|205.c: Design sales around the buyer's stage in the purchase: help people buy instead of selling at them.
l112|205.e: In his book "Demand-Side Sales" he argues you should design the process around how customers want to buy, not how you want to sell. A purchase moves through stages: first thought, passive looking, active looking, deciding, first use and ongoing use, and each stage needs something different. Autobooks used to push every lead into a demo and then press for a close. He had the team first ask which stage the customer was in and split the demo into three versions. The sales cycle nearly halved and conversion rose to about four times what it had been.
ex: Autobooks' three demos: explain the landscape, compare options, or offer a choice
The sales cycle nearly halved and conversion rose about fourfold

items.d: Know the problem, not the solutions
From first use to a new habit

l112|205.c: Interview only people who actually switched, and reconstruct their buying story like a detective.
l112|205.e: What people say they will do in the future can't be trusted, and complaining isn't the same as switching. So he interviews only people who have already tried to change, including users of competing products. There's no fixed script; he uses the four forces as a frame and keeps pulling on the story. Deliberately repeating something back wrong makes people say more as they correct you. Answers start as pleasantries, then become exaggerated dreams or nightmares, and the job is to keep dragging them back to what actually happened. Cause-and-effect patterns start repeating after seven or eight interviews, so 10 to 12 is enough.
ex: Basecamp users demanded Gantt charts but never left over them
One man agonized for 18 months over a $137 coat rack
93 percent said they wanted an energy-efficient house; all chose a finished basement instead

items.d: Old car at 280,000 miles, repair after repair

l112|205.c: One product is often hired for several conflicting jobs; cluster them and choose your trade-offs deliberately.
l112|205.e: After the interviews, he doesn't segment by demographics. He clusters people by their combination of pushes and pulls into a few distinct paths. The same product usually carries three to five jobs at once, and they conflict: some people want speed, others want thoroughness. Intercom discovered customers hired it for four quite different reasons, so it turned off irrelevant features for each path and priced each against that path's own competitors. He stresses choosing on purpose where to be worse, because 90 percent of failed products made trade-offs their customers didn't agree with.
ex: Intercom priced against HubSpot for customer acquisition and against Zendesk for support
Intercom was later valued at more than $2 billion

l112|205.c: Jobs to Be Done is research for forming hypotheses; jobs dreamed up in a conference room are always wrong.
l112|205.e: Mainstream research at big companies starts with a hypothesis and tests it. Jobs to Be Done does the opposite: it begins by admitting you don't know far more than you know. He and Clayton Christensen share the same roots, but Christensen leaned toward theory and mental frameworks while he focuses on tactics. Tony Ulwick's school starts from product functions and involves many steps, which suits process-heavy organizations. He insists only people have jobs; products don't. And where there's no real choice (health insurance from your employer) or habits run very deep (a detergent used for twenty years), the method has nothing to dig up.
ex: Peter Drucker in 1953: what the business thinks it sells is not what the customer buys
He worked with Christensen for 27 years, with a long conversation every quarter

marks.d: Starts from functions, hundreds of steps

l113|208.c: The cheapest way to win customers is to go where people ask questions and answer them well first.
l113|208.e: B2B products usually exist because of a real problem, she says, and buyers don't want a pitch, they want an answer. On her first day she set up keyword alerts on Reddit, and the team, co-founders included, answered questions personally, never with automation. A good answer first explains whether something can be done and what to watch out for, and only at the end mentions that Deel can help. Because the answer stays on a public page, it gets seen again and again. Before investing, estimate the ceiling on a community's size and confirm people are actually asking.
ex: Community answers were about 15 percent of the funnel early on, later under 5 percent
Unpaid channels were 80 to 90 percent early; now about half
Reddit, Quora, Twitter and closed communities like Y Combinator

l113|208.c: Good SEO content ends the search; rank topics by intent with a traffic-light system.
l113|208.e: Stuffing keywords is the most common mistake. What search engines actually care about is whether a reader goes back to Google to keep looking after finishing your article. Her team digs up as many as 700 related keywords, sorts them by search volume, then judges the intent behind each one. Green means someone looking to buy a solution, yellow is fifty-fifty, red is just research. They write green first, then yellow, and rarely get to red. Before writing, they check what Google currently returns for the term, and they use tools to bring the text down to an elementary-school reading level.
ex: Searching EOR returned "enhanced oil recovery," not employer of record
Five new articles and five refreshed old ones every week

l113|208.c: Build the skeleton before the makeup: a fast, findable website comes before any ad spend.
l113|208.e: Early on, she says, go back to fundamentals. Do you have a website? Is it fast? Does the search engine know it exists? Then, can people find it? If not, write content. Only once all that is handled should you consider paying for ads. Your positioning also has to pass a test: if the sentence works just as well on another company's site, it fails. Her first move after joining was migrating the hard-coded website to a platform she could edit herself, so she could quickly A/B test different value propositions.
ex: A site that takes more than four seconds to load can't run paid ads well
"We handle the complicated stuff" could describe 90 percent of B2B companies

l113|208.c: Early B2B companies shouldn't rush into brand ads: capture existing demand first and judge channels by payback.
l113|208.e: A good brand awareness campaign takes a lot of strategy and creative work and may still miss, she says. Early on, before your message is even validated, it's easy to waste a month. B2B has existing demand waiting to be captured, and she estimates it takes at least six to eight months to fully work the bottom of the funnel before speaking to a broader audience. Paid ads need fresh creative every month to fight ad fatigue, and it's worth spreading across many small long-tail platforms. Evaluate channels not by lead count but by the whole chain from lead to closed deal to revenue a year later.

l113|208.c: Pick partners not just for audience overlap, but for whether your users would turn to them for advice.
l113|208.e: Many companies partner with anyone who shares their audience, but she says that's only the starting point. What matters is whether users would actually go to that partner when they face this particular problem. For Deel, venture capital firms are ideal partners: a startup that just raised a round needs to hire, and founders ask their investors what other portfolio companies use. Another tech company might have exactly the same audience, but nobody asks it for advice on hiring and employment, so the partnership delivers far less.

She also asks them to plan for budgets of zero, $10,000 and $100,000. When hiring from big companies, check how large the company was when the person joined, because people who arrived in flush times often won't get their hands dirty. Deel prizes "small hands," meaning anyone at any level will do the most tedious task. To expand, hire one lead to validate the idea, then let them build a team, so you never have to lay people off when a plan doesn't work.

l113|208.c: An intense culture runs on speed, default optimism and caring about customers, and it pays back with freedom.

Employees bring "Deel speed": customer questions answered within 24 hours, and features everyone wants shipped in a tenth of the time competitors take. They default to optimism, asking first why something could work and then dealing with the risks. And they genuinely care about customers, because payroll and contracts affect people's livelihoods. In return, the company gives people the freedom to choose where and when they work. These values were written down only about a year after founding, as a way of naming a culture that already existed.

l114|210.c: A culture shift needs one clear north-star metric and a story leaders repeat over and over.
l114|210.e: When Josh Silverman became CEO in 2017, layoffs came with him. Many employees had tied their identity to Etsy, and the company was moving from a consensus culture built on deep debate to one that prized speed, which felt existential. The most important step, he says, was making GMS, gross merchandise sales, the north star: it came up in every meeting and measured every launch, so arguments about priorities quickly resolved. The second was looking from the outside in, benchmarking against the other places buyers spend money. Leaders also had to keep telling the same story. Say it three times and people understand; three more and they internalize it.
ex: The north-star metric was GMS, gross merchandise sales

l114|210.c: The pandemic made Etsy Black Friday overnight; after catching the traffic, the job was keeping the new buyers.
l114|210.e: In April 2020, when the U.S. recommended wearing masks, Etsy's traffic and sales jumped overnight to Black Friday levels. Sellers who could sew wedding dresses quickly switched to masks. The next challenge was showing the flood of new and returning buyers that Etsy was more than masks. The team shifted to retention and purchase frequency, which forced a group used to A/B tests to learn to measure results over 30 to 90 days.

l114|210.c: With over 100 million unique items, Etsy doesn't lack supply; the hard part is giving buyers confidence to choose.
l114|210.e: In its early years Etsy focused on sellers, visiting their studios and inviting them to hack weeks. Later the focus moved to the buyer experience, because GMS is buyers purchasing from sellers, and the marketplace's core job is to bring qualified buyers. Overall, more than 100 million listings means supply is fine, with gaps only in specific categories. The difficulty is that every item is one of a kind and sellers have no brand recognition, so buyers lack confidence. Reviews with buyer photos and signals like "only one left" both work well, and search ranking nudges sellers to add photos and reply quickly.

l114|210.c: A/B testing is the gold standard for validation, but it shouldn't be the only way.
l114|210.e: Etsy has a deep engineering and experimentation tradition, and the vast majority of changes get A/B tested, because a test comes close to proving that a change caused a metric to move. But he thinks this is exactly where the team needs to grow. Retention has to be read in cohorts over months. SEO can't be tested the same way. And a single step toward a much bigger new direction says little about the whole. Some things must be done out of respect for sellers, such as showing a discount whenever a seller sets one, and those can only be judged with before-and-after analysis.

l114|210.c: Acquisition came from seller word of mouth and long-tail inventory; retention comes from turning favorites into a habit loop.

Referral rewards were free listings; the 20-cent listing fee is tiny, but still a barrier worth removing. On the buyer side, the enormous long tail of inventory powers SEO and Google Shopping, meeting very specific needs, and sellers often become buyers themselves. For retention, Etsy uses a trigger-action-reward habit loop: favoriting an item signals intent, and when the price drops or it's almost sold out, a notification pulls the person back to buy.

l114|210.c: Etsy's brand is its supply, and keeping commerce human is what separates it from Amazon.
l114|210.e: Etsy coexists with eBay and Amazon because the brand stands for unique items in people's minds, backed by policies that protect the marketplace's integrity. Almost all content is created by sellers and buyers, so deciding what can and cannot be sold is itself brand-building, and policy enforcement is never finished. To help sellers who can't keep up with demand, Etsy allows production partners, but the seller must know exactly who is making the item and how. l114|210.c: Product teams should be led five ways, not by a PM acting as mini CEO, but the PM makes the final call.

l115|211.c: Figma's playbook: make individual designers love the product first, then let them spread it inside their companies.

Using it isn't enough; they have to love it, because recommending a tool to coworkers means staking your professional credibility on it. These people become internal champions: they start free, then pay with their own credit cards. Once the product has spread far enough, they come to Figma themselves and ask for help getting through security review and procurement. That makes the sales conversation completely different.

l115|211.c: You can't optimize your way to product-market fit early on; look for strong signals, not small-sample metrics.
l115|211.e: Figma spent three years in stealth, and the team needed a milestone to lift morale, but multiplayer, the core selling point, was still a year away. A visiting Notion team even asked how they could launch without it. She and Dylan went door to door giving demos, and the test was the designer's emotional reaction. When people grabbed the laptop out of Dylan's hands to try it themselves, and a few teams were already using it full time, she decided it was time to launch. l115|211.c: Designers don't want to be marketed to; earn credibility with deep technical content and advocates drawn from users.

So instead of traditional marketing, she had the CTO write technical posts about WebGL and had the design team break down the design decisions behind features like grids and vector networks. Her bar: if she could have written it herself, it wasn't deep enough. Six months after launch, her first hire wasn't a marketer but a designer advocate who loved the product and whose job was to meet users, make content and bring feedback back to product. l115|211.c: Early on, don't wait for users to find you; go where they already gather, and ask for feedback, never sell.
l115|211.e: In the early days nobody knew Figma, so users weren't going to show up in your community. Designers already lived on Twitter, swapping best practices, so the team bet on that one channel. Dylan wrote a scraper that started from a few prominent designers and mapped who followed whom, revealing clusters around icon design, graphic design, product design and so on, plus the influential people in each. The team then messaged them one by one asking for feedback. Founders and engineers answered questions on Twitter themselves, so users could follow along passively before switching and keep getting pulled back to the product.
ex: They never pitched the product; they only ever asked for feedback
The same map came out again later when launching new products

items.d: Starting from a few prominent designers

l115|211.c: Even at scale, keep building with users and stay transparent instead of hiding behind a brand account.
l115|211.e: Early on, everyone answered users in Intercom, and engineers debugged and fixed problems on the spot. As Figma grew, it ran engineering quality weeks to knock out the small annoyances users complained about on Twitter and in forums, bundled them into an annual release called Little Big Updates, and linked each fix to the original post that prompted it. Transparency has to hold too: after a string of outages, Figma published a technical postmortem. The day the acquisition was announced, social media erupted, and the next day the team hosted an open-question Twitter Space to face users directly.
ex: Designers use it eight hours a day, so saving a single click is a big deal
Little Big Updates is one of the most popular releases

items.d: Link each fix to the original post
They see themselves in the product

l115|211.c: The free tier must not choke the growth engine: limit files, not collaborators, and keep viewers free.
l115|211.e: If a product spreads through sharing, you can't put a gate on collaboration. About two years after launching pricing, Figma found that the starter plan, unlimited files but only two or three collaborators, was hurting growth. Switching to three files with unlimited collaborators showed up immediately in the metrics as smoother sharing. Only editors pay; viewers are free, so product managers and others can come in and comment. Going from free to Pro has to be fully self-serve, while Pro to Organization is driven by the needs of scale, so users can step up as their confidence grows.
ex: Pro is bought with a credit card; Organization and Enterprise go through sales
Most sales leads come from free and Pro users

items.d: Through sales; design systems and more

l115|211.c: Turn the biggest obstacle to adoption into the reason to upgrade; that's what happened with design systems.
l115|211.e: Large companies depend on design systems: buttons, fonts and spacing defined once, updated everywhere, and matched to code. Early Figma couldn't share components across files, which became the biggest barrier to getting into big companies. Rather than avoid the topic, the team invited design systems practitioners to informal meetups, learned from them, then built the features and wrote the content. Today design systems are the core reason teams move from Pro to Organization, and the people who run design systems inside companies have become key champions for spreading the product.
ex: Figma runs the website DesignSystems.com
It hosts Schema, a conference devoted to design systems

l115|211.c: This playbook needs technical users, an existing community, and a leader who truly believes in it.
l115|211.e: Reusing the playbook for FigJam and Dev Mode, she identified the preconditions. The audience is technical and cares about its tools. A single person gets a lot of value from the product alone, so there's something to talk about beyond collaboration. The target group already has a community that can serve as a distribution channel. Core users have many touchpoints inside their organizations, making them natural super-spreaders. On the team side, the most important thing is a leader who genuinely believes, because the approach is hard to prove with metrics in the short term, and during scale-up you have to keep newly imported traditional tactics from crowding it out.
ex: Designers and engineers both deeply love their tools
Someone on Designer News once said that if this was the future, they'd change careers

root.d: FigJam and Dev Mode reuse it

items.d: No need to lead with collaboration

l116|213.c: A child who learns that achievement earns love can be hurt by that same habit as an adult.
l116|213.e: When he was 10, his mother, who had bipolar disorder, died. A child can't process that kind of trauma, so he buried it. He noticed that top grades and scoring goals earned him love from family and everyone around him, so he staked his entire self-worth on achievement. That got him out of the dark and powered more than a decade of career success. But a coping mechanism you haven't noticed keeps going too far. Work stress and the old buried pain surfaced together: first panic attacks, then a heart scare, and finally 45 days in a mental health facility.
ex: Frequent panic attacks while at Twitter in 2010
Nearly had a heart attack at 35 and turned down the Wealthfront CEO job
Earned high six to seven figures a year as a venture capital partner

items.d: The better he did, the more love

l116|213.c: Everyday stress is survivable, but broken sleep, strained relationships and failing health mean stop now.
l116|213.e: He compares people to animals: when the basics like eating, moving, playing, socializing and sleeping go off, something is wrong. The same goes for us. If you sleep badly for months, your relationships are always tense and your body keeps getting worse, those signs are easy to see, and you can't claim you didn't know. The body keeps score, and whatever you push down eventually comes out as chronic illness. He estimates that at least half the people who have worked in tech for five to seven years or more carry some kind of mental health struggle, but like a frog in slowly heating water, they haven't noticed.
ex: Ground his teeth so badly he had all his molars redone twice
His cardiologist warned he'd become another CEO felled by a broken heart
He recommends the book The Body Keeps the Score

items.d: Poor sleep for a long time

l116|213.c: Deep change happens in four steps: suffer, find the truth, be kind to yourself, then to others.
l116|213.e: He believes almost every big transformation starts with suffering, and the deeper the pain, the bigger the change, like what people in recovery call hitting rock bottom. Next comes years of digging into why you suffered. Most people find the root cause was never their fault; as children they simply read what happened as "I must be bad." Only once you understand that can you forgive yourself and treat yourself kindly. From there it becomes natural to see that other people were shaped by their pasts too. Identity, he says, is the foundation under everything else: where you live, who you're with, what you do. Rebuild the foundation and everything on top can change.
ex: More than 90% of people only need small shifts, like a new job or a move
A full identity rebuild happens to fewer than 1% of people, he estimates

items.d: Rock bottom gives you courage to change
Dig up the root of the pain
Realize it was never your fault
See they were shaped by their pasts too

l116|213.c: To find your truth, start with a therapist you feel safe with, or keep asking yourself why on paper.
l116|213.e: In the West the usual first step is a therapist. He describes them as routers: they send you on to the right specialist, such as somatic therapy or breathwork. Pick one like speed dating, trusting your gut about who makes you feel safe. A shaking dog at the shelter, he says, is in no state to learn tricks. He also wants the therapist to be genuinely smart. If therapy isn't for you, use pen and paper. List the recent moments when your emotions flared up. Every reflex has a reason behind it, so keep asking why until you either feel deeply uncomfortable or suddenly understand.
ex: The first time someone said "that's a panic attack," he felt relief
Unstructured writing works too, whether one sentence or ten pages

items.d: List recent moments of strong reaction
There's always a deeper reason behind it

l116|213.c: Decades of inner narrative can't be rewritten overnight; you interrupt it in small daily moments.
l116|213.e: Low self-worth, he says, is the deepest groove in the brain, and rewriting it takes time. Once you're aware of it, you can catch the reflex the moment it appears and choose a different response. A former boss once told him to say only "thank you" when praised, and he still does it today. Small actions like that, repeated day after day, add up to a new story about yourself. There are more intense routes too: long silent meditation retreats, psychedelics, extreme physical challenges. The transition in a big change often takes years; Eckhart Tolle spent seven years becoming a spiritual teacher.
ex: He used to run ultramarathons and cried after almost every one
He sits on the board of a nonprofit funding psychedelic therapy for veterans

items.d: See the old core belief clearly
Look them in the eye and say thanks

l116|213.c: We trade our individuality for acceptance, so the biggest barrier to change is fear of losing love.
l116|213.e: He thinks humans are born with two needs. One is to be loved and accepted, which for mammals matters even more than water for survival. The other is that each of us is one of a kind. Society runs on shared beliefs and tells you from childhood who you should be. To avoid being cast out of the tribe, we hand over our individuality in exchange for acceptance. One of the key truths in any transformation, he says, is realizing that who you are is mostly what the world made you. Then you consciously choose your own path and accept the risk of no longer being accepted. That is exactly what makes it so frightening.
ex: He's a San Francisco Giants fan only because he was born into a Giants family
He quotes psychologist Carl Jung: if you don't know who you are, the world will tell you

terms.d: There has never been another you

result.d: The biggest barrier to change

l116|213.c: Life isn't a series of mountains to conquer; it's a river you relax into and float down.
l116|213.e: For the first half of his life he treated life like mountaineering, believing the summit would bring lasting satisfaction. Instead, every peak revealed another one, and he was exhausted. He notes that most people who die on Everest die on the way down. Now he practices the "mummy position" from whitewater rafting: float on your back, arms crossed, feet forward, and don't fight the current. Plan less, stop over-optimizing your life, notice the signals around you and feel where the water wants to take you. As a Thai farmer told him, everyone wants to get to Bangkok; the point is to take your own road there.
ex: After losing his luggage, he spent days in the clothes he was wearing
He followed his gut to Vietnam and is waiting to see where the current goes next

items: Expect the summit to satisfy you
One peak after another, no stopping
The descent is the most dangerous part
Take your own road to Bangkok

d.verdict: Drop the over-planning and let the current carry you where you need to go

l117|214.c: Map a workflow by how many teams use it and how often, and you can predict B2B success.
l117|214.e: The last decade of startup advice focused on validation and rapid experiments, but he believes the problem space itself still predicts success. He uses two dimensions: how many departments a workflow touches, and how often it runs (daily or several times a week counts as high frequency). High-frequency, company-wide workflows make the most money, but Microsoft and Google guard that territory. High-frequency, single-department workflows are the richest ground for B2B software. Landing in a low-frequency box isn't fate either. The strategy is to move up: find the department that treats you as mission-critical and build a high-frequency module for them.
ex: Email and Slack are high-frequency, company-wide; Jira and sales tools are high-frequency, niche
Typeform is trying to move from a low-frequency box into high-frequency niche

cells.d: B2B software's main battleground, like Jira
Most profitable, but giants guard it

l117|214.c: Pick a sharp problem: your product must make a workflow two to three times better before anyone notices.
l117|214.e: A sharp problem is one that genuinely steals customers' time, energy, money or attention. People work to buy back leisure, so a tool that's 20% better goes unnoticed. You have to cut a workflow by two or three times, or double the output in the same time, before people will switch tools and pay for it. The test is simple: draw your target user's workflow today, draw it again with your product, and measure how much shorter it got. A customer asking when they can pay you is another good sign. When you solve a sharp problem, customer enthusiasm covers your mistakes. When you don't, one mistake can be fatal.
ex: Counterexample: the pandemic-era camera app mmhmm was fun but not sharp
The best customers aren't price-sensitive and get it instantly

l117|214.c: Customer input comes in three layers: targeted discovery, weekly routine conversations, and gathering existing signals.
l117|214.e: He separates three activities. Discovery means finding the right people to study when you want to improve a specific workflow. Continuous conversation means customer interviews show up automatically every week on the calendars of PMs, designers, engineering managers and product marketers, because the moment there's friction, nobody keeps it up. The most neglected layer is customer listening. Social media, app store reviews, churn surveys, NPS comments, bug reports, support tickets and won deals in the CRM are generating signals all the time. Processing them efficiently is a major goal of product management.
ex: Calendly built a signal-gathering system out of workflow tools plus Slack
Invite people during activation or conversion and even churned users will talk

items.d: Find the right people for a specific workflow
Interviews land on the calendar every week
Gather reviews, tickets and other existing signals

l117|214.c: Onboarding is the salesperson you can't hire: keep required setup short and measure activation in tiers.
l117|214.e: With thousands of customers, onboarding stands in for sales reps and account managers. At its core it's about understanding the evaluator's psychology: grasp the value, judge whether it's simple enough, try it, decide. The required part should contain only instructions and the few settings needed to succeed, ideally no more than three screens. Everything else becomes optional content people can return to. Click-through tours don't help much; one or two good examples work better. During a trial, users should always know which step they're on. Set several activation milestones and watch the drop-off between each one.
ex: Calendly requires just two things: connect a calendar and set available hours
Twitter measured activation by whether a new user followed someone or got followed

items.d: Third: make sense of the responses

l117|214.c: Virality means customers do your marketing, and it only works on a great product that solves a sharp problem.
l117|214.e: Many people think virality is the little promo line at the bottom of every Hotmail email. But Hotmail was first a revolutionary web-based inbox. If you rely only on engineered "synthetic virality" and users arrive to find a bad product, it's over. Early Slack couldn't even share across teams, yet it spread through lunchtime word of mouth. Scheduling tools existed before Calendly; it won by being simple and respecting the invitee's time. Once that foundation is solid, referral programs, network effects and exceptional support multiply the effect.
ex: Atlassian spends 10 to 20 percentage points less on marketing than peers
Uber was pushed out of Austin for a year, then crushed rivals on return without any campaigns

terms.d: A great product is the foundation
Make people want to recommend you

result.d: Spend the savings on product

l117|214.c: A network effect past critical mass is almost impossible to kill; the real weak spot is revenue.
l117|214.e: A network effect means passive members benefit whenever someone else joins: the more people use Word's format, the more documents you can open. Past critical mass, people come because everyone else is there, and that's the strongest feature a product can have. Threads didn't topple Twitter, and the telegraph had to be deliberately shut down in 2016, more than a century after its invention. But the business can still die. When advertisers leave, users remain, yet there's no money to improve the network, and a downward spiral begins. He thinks Threads will also need a revenue flywheel to win, not just active users.
ex: Threads could win by tapping Meta's more usable ad marketplace
He believes Friendster is still alive somewhere

l117|214.c: Operators should regularly step out of execution for "forest time," recalibrate, then dive back in.
l117|214.e: As a consultant he could see the whole picture, but as an operator the daily grind pulled him in and he could only see the trees. So every month he gives PMs and functional executives one or two days. It isn't a holiday. They work through a worksheet that surveys the whole landscape: what problems exist, what alternative paths they haven't seen. Aiming takes maybe a tenth of product development time, yet it decides where millions of dollars of people's effort go next, so it's well worth it. He also warns that frameworks are mental shortcuts: understand how they were derived and adjust them to your company's stage.
ex: A PM's job swings back and forth between finding problems and directing execution
Bridgewater taught him to read people on three axes: skills, traits and values

items.t: One or two days a month

l118|217.c: In tech, the category leader takes 76% of the value on average, so competing means fighting over 24%.
l118|217.e: He says most people make a decision without noticing it: compete with a better product in a market where demand already exists. Thousands of marketing and strategy books teach how to win that fight. But none of the legends got there that way. He and his co-authors studied every venture-backed US tech company from 2000 to 2015 and found that the leader in each category captured 76% of the category's total market value on average. So the real choice is whether to fight over the remaining 24% or design your own category and take the lion's share.
ex: The research was peer-reviewed and published in Harvard Business Review
Everyone knows Bob Marley; nobody knows the 17th-best reggae artist

items.d: Fought over by all the rest

l118|217.c: Category design isn't shipping first; it's getting the world to accept your definition of the problem.
l118|217.e: People often confuse category creation with being the first product to ship a feature. That's why he prefers the term category design: if you can design a product and a culture, you can design a market. The key is getting a meaningful share of people to agree with how you define the problem, because they'll then accept your solution. The founders of Gojo found the shared bar of soap in factories disgusting, so they changed the question from "how do we wash hands" to "how do we wash hands without bar soap," and invented liquid soap. Later they asked "how do we wash hands without water," which gave us hand sanitizer and Purell.
ex: MySpace and GeoCities shipped first but didn't win their categories
Gojo was founded by a married couple and is still family-run today

l118|217.c: The "better trap" is fatal: a better version of a known solution to a known problem gets no switchers.
l118|217.e: Threads had the strongest distribution in history and a top brand, and for a while grew faster than ChatGPT, yet it emptied out fast. It offered a copied "better Twitter" for a problem everyone already knew and already had solved. In his view, problems make categories. You either solve a new problem or reframe an old one in a radically different way; only then do people open up to a new solution. That's also why he calls product-market fit a dangerous idea: you should design a category for your product instead of squeezing it into an existing market.
ex: Threads hit so-called product-market fit faster than anything in history and still failed
He predicts copycat AI startups will burn enormous amounts of venture money

root.d: Known problem plus a better copy

items.d: Failed despite top distribution and brand
Category makes brand, not the reverse
A copy of the Apple Store

l118|217.c: Win a small slice of a big category first, then expand the vision or get pushed to the margins.
l118|217.e: An emerging mega-category starts out as many small niches, and no single company can serve all of it. A startup claiming to offer the full suite on day one isn't credible, so Gong starting with one slice of the emerging revenue space and nailing it was smart. But a few years into success, a company's biggest growth obstacle becomes its own category. If it doesn't expand the vision and set the agenda for the larger category, someone else will define it, leaving only two options: stay trapped in the niche and slowly shrink, or upgrade late and look like a copycat.
ex: He thinks Clari defined the broader revenue category first, and discloses he works with them
Microsoft proved more than 30 years ago that "best of breed" loses to the suite

cells.d: Set the agenda for the big category
Take one slice and become number one
A startup claiming the whole suite

l118|217.c: Think about your thinking: reject the premises and reason back from a successful future, not forward.
l118|217.e: The first law of category design, he says, is to think about your thinking. Borrowing from Roger Martin, he separates reflection from reflex: most people believe they're thinking when they're only reacting, assuming the future will extend the past. Planning a hike from start to finish makes sense, but doing that with a startup is a disaster because the reference point is still the past. He admires Mike Maples' approach: reject every existing premise, imagine wild success five years out, then stand in that future and look back at what you did to get there. The word "disruption," he adds, also keeps the reference point locked in the past.
ex: Mike Maples says great founders are visitors from the future
A design class assignment: design a bicycle you can't ride

l118|217.c: Whoever creates the category's language wins, and new words must start from what people already know.
l118|217.e: Many founders describe something new in old words, so people can't see the value. But pile on too many new words and nobody understands you. The trick is to start from how people already think about the category and move them forward. Otis first called its product the "safety elevator"; people found it interesting but didn't see why they needed one. Renamed the "vertical railway," it instantly suggested a new kind of building. Starbucks used its own invented cup sizes and drink names to sell ten-cent coffee for three dollars. Draw a line in language, he says, and you draw a line in thinking and in perceived value.
ex: OpenAI made "large language model" the term the whole industry uses
Order a grande latte at an independent cafe and you'll get an eye roll

marks.d: Old words; nobody saw the need
A familiar idea pointing to a new use
Too new for anyone to understand

l118|217.c: Category designers don't compete with rivals; they compete with the status quo and redirect demand.
l118|217.e: Positioning today usually means telling a distinctive story relative to competitors. To him, that's volunteering to fight over the 24% someone else designed, which is why he says positioning is for losers. A category designer's opponent is the status quo. Spinning said: why risk getting hit by a car when you can ride indoors? Peloton then said: why drive to the gym when you can ride at home? Neither attacked a rival; they intercepted demand that was flowing to the old way. The electric guitar didn't kill the acoustic guitar either; it grew the whole market.
ex: Brand is about us; category is about the customer
Nielsen data shows personal growth is the best-selling nonfiction category

items: Move from the old way to the new
Intercept demand headed the old way

d.verdict: The enemy is the status quo, not a brand

l118|217.sc: Lightning strikes and word of mouth
l118|217.c: Instead of spreading budget evenly all year, concentrate it in a few lightning strikes aimed at superconsumers.
l118|217.e: Most marketing spreads budget evenly across quarters like peanut butter, following a century-old "reach and frequency" playbook. With tens of thousands of messages hitting people every day, that approach can't break through. He borrows from Hollywood movie launches: once or twice a year, concentrate everything where your target audience gathers so you become impossible to ignore. Aim at superconsumers, the 8% to 10% of buyers who generate most of the profit and set the trends. Spread your point of view on the problem as an educator, and word of mouth takes care of the rest. He says he has never seen word of mouth as a line item in a marketing plan.
ex: B2B companies should do one or two lightning strikes a year; B2C two or three
Sometimes emailing just 300 people produces a sales breakthrough

terms.d: Concentrated in time, impossible to ignore

result.d: Big growth for little money

l119|219.c: Google+ lost by betting everything on belief; Gmail's tabbed inbox won by validating before investing.
l119|219.e: Google+ was a top-down strategic bet: a division of nearly a thousand people, with Gmail, YouTube and Search all wired in. After years of iteration nobody really needed it, it was shut down, and Google missed mobile social opportunities like WhatsApp and Snapchat. The tabbed inbox started with no believers. The team went back to the user problem and found most people never clean their inbox; they're passive readers. Then they validated step by step: trying it themselves, internal use, external tests, and finally machine-learning classification. He believes great companies use evidence to strengthen human judgment, not replace it.
ex: Google+ peaked at around a thousand people and shut down in 2019
Roughly 85% to 88% of passive users liked the tabbed inbox

items: Validated from self-test to external test

d.verdict: Use evidence to strengthen judgment instead of betting on opinion

l119|219.c: Even a founder's idea deserves the question "where's the evidence," and evidence lets managers push back.
l119|219.e: Founders contribute the most important ideas during a company's early and scaling years, he says, so the goal isn't to suppress them but to examine them critically. In a pure battle of opinions, the most senior person usually wins. Bring hard data to a "continue or pivot" discussion and the quality of the conversation jumps. Show the results of an experiment you ran quietly on your own and most bosses will be persuaded. If instead they just get angry and send you back to work, that person is unreasonable and you should think about leaving. He also points out the iPhone was really a discovery process of many iterations: Steve Jobs initially opposed building a phone and multi-touch, and changed his mind when he saw the evidence.
ex: Jobs was more an architect who integrated others' work than an original inventor

items.d: "I talked to three customers and I get it"

l119|219.c: Vague goals, no user metrics, roadmap obsession and disengaged teams all signal you're not evidence-guided.
l119|219.e: Many teams think they run experiments and look at data, but they don't really. He checks a few signals. Goals are too many, too fuzzy, or just outputs. The only metrics are business ones like revenue, with nothing that measures users. Leaders and PMs spend huge amounts of time polishing a perfect roadmap. Experiments are rare, and even when they happen, nothing is learned. Engineers are judged only on what they ship, so they're disconnected from users and the business and don't much care. All of these symptoms, he says, improve once you bring in an evidence-guided system.

items.d: Too many, too vague, or just outputs
Few experiments, and no learning from them

l119|219.c: A North Star metric should measure value delivered to users, then split with revenue into a metric tree.
l119|219.e: The usual pattern is a revenue target at the top and separate departmental goals below, which pushes people in different directions. He proposes a "value exchange loop" as the shared company goal: create as much value for the market as you can, then capture as much of it back as you can, with each feeding the other. The North Star metric measures value created, not just "the most important number." Top-level KPIs measure value captured. Both break down into a metric tree, and the sub-metrics where the two overlap matter most. Those can be owned by teams long-term, and you may even reorganize teams around them.
ex: WhatsApp long tracked messages sent
Airbnb tracks nights booked
Amplitude tracks weekly learning users

items.d: Measured by the North Star metric
Top KPIs like revenue and profit
Each drives the other toward fast growth

l119|219.c: In ICE scoring, confidence is the most overestimated input; score it by strength of evidence, not gut.
l119|219.e: Ideas come from founders, stakeholders, competitors and everywhere else, and they're usually settled by debate or seniority. He recommends Sean Ellis's ICE framework: Impact, Confidence, Ease. Impact and ease are estimates, but discussing them separately already beats arguing in the abstract. The trouble is people score confidence on gut feeling and inflate it, which breaks the system. His confidence meter sets rules: self-conviction, a polished document and fit with a hot theme add up to at most 0.1 points. Reviews and estimates score a little higher; anecdotes and market data higher still. Only building and testing earns medium-to-high confidence. A competitor doing it does not count as validation.
ex: Self-conviction is worth 0.01 out of 10
"It's an AI project" doesn't prove an idea is good
PMs can use it to say no gently

l119|219.c: Measure time to outcome, not time to ship, and start validating with nearly free methods.
l119|219.e: People assume a choice between shipping fast and learning slowly, but under uncertainty the metric that matters is time to outcome: shipping the right thing. Many organizations believe they must first build an MVP that isn't minimal at all before they can learn. In fact there's a whole ladder of validation: cheap assessment first, then mining existing data, then fake-door style tests, then rough versions, internal use, controlled experiments, and even a staged launch. This quickly kills most ideas and saves investment for the ones with positive evidence. Small, low-risk changes can simply ship.
ex: The early tabbed inbox was an HTML shell with humans sorting mail, zero code
Fish food: try it inside your own team first
All of Microsoft dogfooded an unreleased Outlook

items.d: Fit to goals, ICE, map assumptions
Fake doors, Wizard of Oz, alpha, dogfood
Staged rollout with a holdback group

l119|219.c: Free developers from the agile "cage" with a GIST board and outcome roadmaps that link planning to execution.
l119|219.e: Many organizations split into two worlds: managers make roadmaps while builders push tickets to done, and PMs are squeezed in the middle with no time for research or testing. He suggests every team keep a GIST board: at most four key results, the ideas in play with their ICE scores, and the next validation steps, discussed at least every two weeks. Teams pick ideas themselves based on ICE, and steps are learning milestones rather than engineering milestones. Release roadmaps that promise features by date kill learning, so he recommends outcome roadmaps instead.
ex: Goal example: cut average onboarding time from 5.5 days to under 2
Idea example: an onboarding wizard, prototype-tested for usability, then A/B tested

items.d: The end state and metrics to hit
Concrete work on the board and in Jira

l120|222.c: Raising customer scores beats optimizing conversion: each extra point doubles the number who refer friends.
l120|222.e: His starting point: money is the ultimate commodity, so Wise's low prices mean thin margins and little budget for paid marketing. The only channel that scales and costs almost nothing is word of mouth. Wise asks new users at sign-up how they heard about it, adds tracking data, and finds about 70% come from friends. Lining up invite data against NPS (how likely you'd recommend us, 0 to 10) showed that people scoring 6 or below barely refer anyone, and each point above that doubles referrals. A conversion win pays once; a higher score lifts how much the whole user base brings in new people. Every week the company sends NPS comments to all staff, and users keep asking for the same three things: faster, cheaper, easier.
ex: About 70% of new customers heard about Wise from a friend
NPS comments went to the whole company weekly for three or four years
Three product pillars: price, speed, ease of use

l120|222.c: To earn referrals, build an experience users didn't know was possible, working back from the theoretical limit.
l120|222.e: Most teams stop once the product works, or they polish conversion, and that buys only a little extra growth. For people to tell friends, the experience has to be so good they didn't know it was possible, roughly ten times better. When Wise entered the US, pricing just below rivals would have won users who never talked about it. Being eight to ten times cheaper is what makes people spread the word. Launching a new market on someone else's payment rails is fast, but it never produces hockey-stick growth. The right question, he says, is what the theoretical lowest cost and fastest speed are, and then spending years getting there directly.
ex: Pricing at 5.9% when rivals charge 6%: people use it but don't talk
NPS around 70, above the iPhone; banks sit near -30
Opening accounts directly at central banks like the Bank of England

marks.d: Never seen before; this gets referrals

l120|222.c: Trace every cost to the transaction that caused it, charge heavy users more, and cut prices for everyone else.
l120|222.e: People assume Wise's low prices mean it loses money on each transfer. In fact every transfer is profitable, and the company has been profitable for years. In the pricing project he led, every bill the company receives gets allocated back to the customer or currency route that caused it; add a margin and that is the price. Typically 20% of customers create 80% of the cost, so those customers pay more and everyone else pays less. Meanwhile engineering keeps pushing costs down, which opens up new customer segments. At the transaction level there are only three costs: people, risk and partner fees. He treats people cost as the price of poor quality, to be removed through automation and clearer product design.
ex: Retail rates run about 6–7%; Wise started at 0.5% and now charges about 0.35%
An Australian customer's support call is charged to the AUD/GBP route
The cost of currency risk has halved in recent years

terms.d: Support and operations; the price of poor quality
E.g. rate moves while a rate is locked

result.d: Add a margin and that is the price

l120|222.c: A sincere mission gets customers to help you, feeding a loop of lower costs and more users.
l120|222.e: Beyond rational reasons like price and speed, people refer for emotional reasons, and he prefers to call that mission rather than brand. People trust friends most, so word of mouth gets around trust problems that are otherwise hard to solve. During the first rebrand, Wise emailed customers a plain statement of its mission, with no button and no call to action. That email got forwarded and brought in more new customers than any marketing campaign, because people could tell the founders genuinely wanted to fix overpriced transfers. When Singapore's regulator required in-person identity checks for every customer, users complained to the regulator themselves. A year later Wise received the world's first eKYC license, allowing online identity checks.
ex: The Singapore waiting list reached about 20,000 people
The team stationed staff in Singapore for a year to verify identities in person

items.d: Word of mouth brings new customers

l120|222.c: A/B tests can't show whether users will love you; build conviction first, then make big changes.
l120|222.e: If you break a price cut into small incremental tests, the short-term numbers rarely prove it will earn enough back, so you move very slowly. Wise's core bet is that if it has the lowest cost, highest speed and best quality, the world's transfer volume will come to it. That conviction is what justifies years of investment in price and speed. He doesn't believe in throwing everything at the wall to see what sticks. When a PM wanted to test every element on a page, he asked her to pick one thing within three weeks, form a view through customer interviews, then ship and verify. Data still matters, as a guard against conviction turning into arrogance.
ex: The company keeps one list, ranked by impact on customers
A co-founder rejected the currency converter; the team built it anyway and it drove huge traffic

items: Price tests show little short term
Interview users to form a view
Pick one thing and go big

d.verdict: Build conviction from insight and data, then bet big

l120|222.c: Value users don't notice doesn't count; close the gap between delivering it and making it felt.
l120|222.e: Wise ran its referral program for 12 years and tried nearly every reward. Then a PM talking to users spotted the real issue: the transfer-complete email said how much they had saved, and users believed they saved money but didn't believe the number. He and a designer took sketches to the coffee shop downstairs, showed them to strangers, and iterated until they had a comparison chart that broke out the fees banks hide in the exchange rate. Putting that chart on the success page with a share button tripled the share rate. Instant transfers with an animated notice also lifted referrals. He calls this product marketing inside the product.
ex: The sweet spot for referral rewards is roughly invite three friends, get $100
Wise opened about 70 bank accounts worldwide to keep comparing prices

items.d: Users don't believe the savings number
Show sketches to strangers in a coffee shop
Break out fees banks hide in the rate
On the success page with a share button

l120|222.c: One global codebase plus deep local infrastructure, with local teams changing the global code directly.
l120|222.e: International banks run a separate local system in each country, which gives them deep connections to local payment networks. PayPal runs one global stack but lacks those deep local links. Wise wants both. Take onboarding: regulations differ so much by country that you can't gather all the requirements up front. So the global product team owns overall conversion, regional teams own local conversion and KYC (identity-check) costs, and regional teams commit changes straight into the shared codebase. The system's design emerges from that feedback. Once there were about 30 teams, all-hands planning stopped working, so Wise moved to squads and tribes organized by product.
ex: Opening an account in Japan means photographing an ID's front, back and side
Most fintechs go deep in only one market

items.d: Owns overall conversion and similar KPIs
Own local conversion and KYC costs
Local teams commit to the global codebase
Grouped by product after about 30 teams

l121|223.c: Teams building creator tools must make their own podcasts, or they never feel users' real pain.
l121|223.e: She sees creator tools as close to B2B, because the podcast is the user's livelihood. Priorities ranked from a feature-request list and dashboards come out different from the ones set by people who have lived the problems. She started in customer support and instinctively sides with users. Being a user herself also gives her the confidence to defend space on the roadmap for things that help customers today, not just strategic bets two years out. In practice she publicly celebrates colleagues who have podcasts, builds podcast recording into team offsites, and keeps a short list of tips for first-timers.
ex: She has made 4 podcasts; her Stephen King show peaked at about 5,000 listens per episode
Recording late one night she found a small iOS bug, DMed an engineer, and it was fixed the next day

root.d: Set priorities from pain you've felt yourself

items.d: Celebrate podcasting teammates; help tell their stories
Use the company's own tools at every team event
Record shows yourself; report bugs as you go
Record with a partner, don't read a script, no 30-second tests

l121|223.c: Intuition is a kind of data too, if you explain where it comes from; projects pushed by rank alone fail.
l121|223.e: She worries that product management has become so process-heavy and scientific that teams build for the sake of building and forget how users feel. Data is valuable; the problem is relying on it alone, and different stages call for a different mix of data and intuition. At a big company you have to influence many people who don't report to you. Going on intuition doesn't mean saying "trust me." It means laying out as objectively as you can where the instinct comes from: past experience, your own testing as a user, user stories. She has watched leaders override both the team and the data, and those projects were doomed from day one.
ex: Before the acquisition Anchor had no data scientist; engineers ran the queries

result.d: More evidence, more right, more buy-in

l121|223.c: Keep the mission, change everything else: Anchor twice walked away from products users already loved.
l121|223.e: Anchor 1.0 was a voice-based social app with strong retention and devoted users. But she and CEO Mike decided it was too niche to reach the mission of letting anyone tell their story. On instinct they pivoted to a 2.0 focused on content creation. Existing users were hurt, but the numbers took off after launch. Her rule is to build for the 80%, not the loudest 20%. During 2.0 the team resisted the word "podcast" and sat on the top request, export as a podcast, for about six months. A small test showed hockey-stick growth, so they rebuilt the whole app around RSS, the feed format podcasts run on.
ex: Early features had nautical names, deliberately avoiding the word "podcast"
Any small change could turn out to be a life-or-death moment for the company

items.d: Voice social; good retention, low ceiling
Gut-driven pivot to a creation tool
Rebuilt around RSS and podcast distribution

l121|223.c: Do things that don't scale, package them as one-tap magic, and grab share in a commodity market.
l121|223.e: Back then, submitting a show to Apple Podcasts meant understanding RSS, proving you owned the feed, and having an Apple ID. For anyone non-technical or without an iPhone, that was a high bar. Anchor was small and short on money, so it hired a few college interns. Users tapped one button in the app, and behind the scenes interns created accounts and submitted shows by hand. She stresses the packaging mattered: "someone will contact you in three days" has no magic in it. That let Anchor quickly take share in a hosting market where rivals all looked the same. It stopped only when it became unsustainable.
ex: People assumed a secret deal with Apple; really interns submitted hundreds of thousands of shows
One of those interns was hired full time and is now a PM on her team

items.d: Asks to distribute the show everywhere
Create Apple accounts, submit one by one
Feels automatic and magical to users

l121|223.c: After an acquisition, keep proving your value to the parent and balance independence against integration.
l121|223.e: Anchor had the creators and Spotify had the listeners, and both were stuck inside the limits of RSS, so the visions lined up. She has seen many acquisitions fail because the original vision no longer fit the new strategy. Anchor's approach was heavy internal evangelism, building relationships, volunteering to help other teams, and keeping up through dozens of strategy shifts. Daniel Ek told them not to slow down, to speed Spotify up instead, and suggested declining meetings for the first year. The result was a team that felt it didn't belong. Afterwards they dropped the Anchor name and collaborated deeply. Slower, she says, but worth it.
ex: At acquisition Anchor had about 20 people and about 40% of new podcasts
Today Spotify hosts over 75% of new shows
A "small" Spotify project takes about a quarter; Anchor used to ship a feature every two weeks

marks.d: Skipped meetings, moved fast, felt isolated
Dropped the Anchor name; more collaboration, slower

l121|223.c: Acquired founders often fall into depression and an identity crisis, and almost nobody helps them through it.
l121|223.e: From the outside an acquisition looks like a pure happy ending, and she didn't expect the low that followed. After talking with many other founders Spotify had acquired, she found it was common. Running a startup means fighting for survival every day, and that fight is itself the meaning. Once things are stable you no longer know what your job is, and you fear becoming a cog in the machine. Eventually everyone has to choose: stay and adapt, or leave and start again. She stayed and found her footing by holding onto her core values, but she wishes someone had talked with her about it at the time.
ex: Nearly five years into Spotify, she has come to like big companies

items.d: The daily struggle is gone; who am I?
Stay with your values, or leave and start again

l121|223.c: Feedback works when you genuinely care and challenge directly; poor performance is usually a role mismatch.
l121|223.e: Radical Candor is the book she recommends most and requires every manager on her team to read. Its point: caring without challenging, or challenging without caring, makes feedback useless. She treats feedback as a gift, and specific feedback delivered with care is almost always accepted. With someone underperforming, she doesn't assume they are lazy or bad. She assumes the role is a poor fit. Opening that way makes people more willing to listen and helps them find a next step. For herself, everything goes into a to-do list, and every night she clears her head by sorting items into do, defer, delegate or delete.
ex: Her standard interview question: what would your podcast be about? No answer is a red flag
She logs everything people ask of her in Todoist

cells.d: They never learn what to fix
Care and say it straight; feedback is a gift
They get defensive; feels like an attack

l122|228.c: A PM's core job is turning ambiguity into clarity, and default-on systems do that better than goals.
l122|228.e: Product work is ambiguous everywhere: the role, the problem, the target user, the prototype are all uncertain. He uses a Jerry Seinfeld story to make the point. After Seinfeld threw out his old material, what worked wasn't the goal of building up an hour of new jokes. It was the system: write every morning for an hour, perform every night. Teams are the same. Put "interview 10 customers this quarter" into your OKRs and it may vanish next quarter. Teams that meet customers every week by default develop noticeably better customer instincts.
ex: Early Coda had customers visit every Friday, which forced the team to always have something to show

items.d: Meet customers at the same time every week
Always bring a prototype or design
Doesn't rise and fall with a quarter's OKRs

l122|228.c: Teams should feel they're building a cathedral, not laying bricks, and each person needs a different view of it.
l122|228.e: At YouTube he once complained that his team wasn't living up to its potential. Shishir, his manager then and later Coda's founder, asked whether the team knew what cathedral it was building. PMs easily fall into handing out task after task and forget to widen the team's view. Surprisingly, one vision document is rarely enough; different people need to see different sides. So when planning, lay out the written strategy, the metrics, directional design mocks, even a future billboard or homepage. He also separates strategy discussions from setting OKRs, and caps planning at about 10% of the execution period.
ex: The parable of three bricklayers: only the third says he is building a cathedral
The "10% planning rule": about three days of planning for a month of work

root.d: Take the mystery out of the direction

items.d: Spell out the vision and strategy
Say where you're going in numbers
Roughly what the product will look like
How you'll tell the world later

l122|228.c: Tag each piece of feedback with how much you mean it, so teams don't treat a hundred comments as mandatory.
l122|228.e: Feedback gets over-read or ignored, especially when a leader tosses off a remark and the team rushes to act on it. He likes the four-level scheme from HubSpot co-founder Dharmesh Shah, which frames weight as whether this is a hill you'd die on. Coda added a dropdown to its feedback form, with the definitions right beside it, forcing people to decide how much they actually care. In meetings people ask outright, "is that a suggestion or a plea?" That lets you spot the one plea among a hundred comments and move ahead confidently on the rest.
ex: The four levels: FYI, Suggestion, Recommendation, Plea

marks.d: No hill here; just so you know
A view, not a stand; for your consideration
Thought hard about it; don't ignore
Rarely used; please trust me on this

l122|228.c: Reviews suffer from fixed attendees and one topic at a time; hold open slots and run topics in parallel.
l122|228.e: Review meetings have two problems that are easy to miss. First, the attendee list is fixed, so either too many people show up or the person who knows most is absent. Second, they handle one topic at a time, so they either drag on for three sleepy hours or take two weeks to schedule, slowing the whole company. Coda's answer is Catalyst: three one-hour slots each week that the entire company keeps open by default. Each topic lists four roles, calendars get swapped the day before, and non-conflicting topics run at the same time. Likewise, project discussions should move from one-on-ones to small tag-ups with core partners, so nothing gets lost in relay.
ex: The four roles: Driver, Maker, Braintrust, Interested
The Braintrust idea is borrowed from Pixar

items: Either too long or hard to schedule
Three open hours a week for everyone

d.verdict: More throughput, and the right people are always there

l122|228.c: Instead of debating a decision for months, test both extremes and learn by building, not talking.
l122|228.e: As a brand-new PM he inherited the project nobody wanted: skippable ads. Advertisers and sales were against it, the idea was unproven, and that kind of thing can be argued over for years. His manager Phil Farhi told him to start an experiment the next day and test the extremes to see the ceiling and the floor. One group got a tiny skip button, another got a huge one covering the whole player. Within weeks, directional data gave the team confidence. He thinks this applies at every level from new hire to CEO: prototypes, docs and mocks beat going round in circles, and the outcome is almost never as bad as you feared.
ex: YouTube was then facing a billion-dollar lawsuit from Viacom, and advertisers were staying away

items.d: A tiny skip button and a giant one
See the ceiling and the floor

l122|228.c: Work discussions are moving from one-way docs to two-way docs, where feedback becomes part of the content.
l122|228.e: He sees three eras of discussing work: the PowerPoint era, the one-way doc era brought by Google Docs and Amazon's six-page memo, and the two-way doc era arriving now. One-way docs have problems. You don't know who has read it, so you watch for the executive's avatar. Important debates get squeezed into a comment column a hundred pixels wide, and the title alone can draw dozens of comments. Two-way docs add a "read it" button, a question table people can vote to rank, and a sentiment table everyone fills in, so the people who stay quiet in meetings get a voice too.
ex: A proposal he thought was a sure thing got a frowning face from a quiet head of design

items.d: Discuss by presenting; often long and dull
Read buttons, question voting, sentiment tables

l122|228.c: Measure growth by how often you've recently felt out of your depth, and start your career facing customers.
l122|228.e: "Are you growing?" is too vague, he says. Borrowing from Seth Godin, he asks instead: in the last six months to two years, how many times did you feel you didn't belong or weren't qualified? If you haven't been stretched like that in a long while, it's worth a rethink. To learn a new skill, find the best person in that area and break down what they do, then jump into the deep end. He began reviewing AdWords ads and answering support calls, and a mentor told him his whole career would be about serving customers. Knowing customers is the strongest asset for moving into product from another role, and it taught him users don't care about the product itself, so communicate more sparingly.
ex: Three or four years as a product specialist, sitting in with seven or eight core product teams
Four or five years from joining Google to becoming a PM

items.d: Learned preparation, checklists, staying calm in a crisis
Faced every kind of customer daily
Watched many teams; a PM masterclass
Google, YouTube, then CPO of Coda

l123|229.c: Judge people by the work they have produced, not by the impression they make in conversation.
l123|229.e: He thinks conversations are full of bias and a poor way to gauge real ability. At Reforge, 80 to 90 percent of hiring decisions rest on portfolio reviews or simulated tasks, and every time he made an exception he regretted it. The same goes for promotions. Rather than relying on a manager's retelling of someone's self-promotion, keep a simple running log of what the person shipped, with a few screenshots. What counts is work that actually reached end users. A beautifully polished internal document that never launched does not.
ex: He credits the framework to Frank Slootman
80-90% of Reforge hires rely on work reviews or simulations
Reforge Artifacts is a platform for sharing and reusing real work

items: A log of what was shipped
Only output that reached users counts

d.verdict: Hire and promote on the work itself

l123|229.c: Ask what it takes to win before discussing cost, and align on a picture of the end state.
l123|229.e: Ideas get filtered and watered down as they travel up an organization, so he wants to hear the undiluted version first: what would it actually take to win? Only then does he discuss cost and trade-offs. Teams should sketch the ideal end state and iterate toward it, revising it regularly. The picture is for aligning direction, not a precise spec. Early on, when things change fast, drawing the target experience works better than writing OKR documents. Plans will change anyway, so settle the big pieces and move.
ex: Reforge lost a year to a planning process that failed
80-90% of today's planning output is visual mockups of the target experience
Used for six months at about 75 people; he is unsure whether it scales

l123|229.c: Strong players shouldn't be pushed into management; senior ICs should stay on the field as captains.
l123|229.e: He objects to what he calls the manager death loop: people take on managing for the title, pay, or promotion path when they neither want it nor are good at it, and the best players get pulled off the field. He splits roles three ways: players who do the work, coaches (managers) who guide from the sidelines, and captains who play while owning the hardest strategic problems. Reforge flattened its org and turned many managers into captain-level individual contributors, with the same titles and no pay penalty. He expects AI to amplify individual leverage, making teams smaller with less coordination, and captains may one day earn more than managers.
ex: A Reforge value: small teams doing bigger things
Much of leadership is firefighting; the problems never stop

root.d: Don't force good players off the field

items.d: Does the actual work on the field
The manager, guiding from the sidelines
Senior IC who plays and owns strategic problems

l123|229.c: Growth is a system where acquisition, retention and monetization interact, so the cause often sits elsewhere.
l123|229.e: Change one part of the growth system and the others move with it. When a metric breaks, the root cause is often in a different stage. That is why he argues for good friction: deliberately adding steps that improve downstream results, even if short-term conversion dips. Teams tend to resist this. Reforge, for example, turns away applicants who are unlikely to have a good experience, to protect its reputation. In two-sided marketplaces, these system effects get amplified.
ex: Airbnb found repeat bookings depend on trip quality and disbanded its standalone retention team
Early HubSpot had poor renewals, so off-target deals stopped earning commission
Reforge's application asks whether you want networking or content

items.d: Which kind of users you bring in
Experience quality decides who comes back

l123|229.c: Map what everyone else is doing, then deliberately do the opposite to find open space.
l123|229.e: Reforge's early courses ran against the MOOC trend: small cohorts, in person, expensive, live, and not self-serve. They sold well. His method is to study the mainstream approach and ask what its opposite would be. The goal is to find white space, not a guarantee that the opposite will work. He is skeptical of the idea that great companies always create new categories, and thinks category creation is rarely the right answer. HubSpot co-founder Dharmesh Shah sees it the same way.
ex: HubSpot peers published about 10 posts a day; he wrote infrequent long-form pieces
For ads, study competitors' creative, then design the reverse
His Unsolicited Feedback podcast skips interviews and reviews products instead

l123|229.c: Build around a use case rather than a persona, and write down who you are not serving.
l123|229.e: Most products serve several personas. But serving several use cases at once, he argues, does far more damage than focusing on one use case shared by multiple personas. A use case map should spell out the problem, who has it, the alternatives, why they would pick you, how often the problem naturally occurs (which drives retention and activation), and how often people adopt (which drives acquisition). It should also state whose problem you are not solving. Otherwise adjacent use cases keep getting rationalized in.
ex: Harvard case: early HubSpot had four use cases and bet only on mid-market marketing VPs
SaaS buyers enter the market once every few years, so content builds the relationship early
