Reforge workshops often produce about 8 use cases, which he thinks is too many

items.d: Mid-market marketing VP, compliance, small business owner, technical marketer
Write down who you don't serve

l123|229.c: Find sparring partners for your career, not just mentors or coaches who give generic advice.
l123|229.e: Mentors and coaches often give generic advice, charge by the hour, and do not share your goals. Sparring partners share your goals, operate at a similar level with complementary strengths, play in the same arena, and push back hard. Candor is rare because people want to please each other, so the opening tone matters: when a few senior members share heavy personal things honestly first, the others follow. As members' paths diverge, regroup periodically.
ex: He has run a five-day founders' trip to Mexico every December for about seven years
Former co-founders Aaron White and Ariel Diaz are his sparring partners

terms.d: Goes straight at the core issue

result.d: More useful than mentors and coaches

l123|229.c: Change takes effect far more slowly than you expect, so give new bets more than double the sustained investment.
l123|229.e: People overestimate how quickly change kicks in. SaaS buying cycles run from months to a year, so moves made in the second half rarely affect that year's numbers; the year is decided in the first half. Existing businesses have momentum, so a new bet has to grow far faster than the baseline to matter. The common mistakes are dabbling or adding resources a little at a time. But throwing too much money at it all at once brings too many voices. You can't skip steps on new things: start with a small team, then keep adding.
ex: If an old channel grows 50% a year, a new one must grow several times faster to show
Airbnb's homepage once showed Trips side by side with listings
HubSpot made small bets on many products; only CRM and sales tools survived

marks.d: No skipped steps; enough activation energy
Too much money, too many voices

l124|230.c: Craft isn't perfectionism: ship early to yourselves and a few customers, then polish before the real launch.
l124|230.e: If craft means chasing perfection from day one, he says, you usually end up shipping nothing. Linear's approach is to put an early design into production within the first week, visible only to the company. Then customers who opt in get to try it, and rough edges are fine at that stage. Serious polishing happens only right before the full release. He personally clicks through every state, and if he finds problems the launch slips a few days. It rarely means starting over.
ex: Linear improved its roadmap feature together with Vercel
A comment-threads demo looked fine, but he found broken animation and scrolling, so the launch slipped

items.d: In production about a week after the first design
Try every state yourself; catch the flaws

l124|230.c: Craft comes from people: founders must agree on what quality means, then leave the details to the builders.
l124|230.e: If a company doesn't value quality, nobody bothers with the details. Co-founders from different companies can carry very different quality cultures, so they have to align first and then pass it on to every new hire. Linear has a single PM, head of product Nan Yu, who sets direction rather than joining every decision. Each project is staffed by engineers and designers, and the project lead can come from either side. The people staring at a feature all day are best placed to see how it could be better, as long as they have ownership and room to act.
ex: Engineer Andreas built a dynamic safe zone for right-click submenus so the mouse can move diagonally
The company has about 50 people and one PM

root.d: Starts with people who care about it

items.d: One company can't hold several quality cultures
Pass the quality bar to every new hire
Engineering plus design; lead regardless of title
The one PM stays out of most decisions

l124|230.c: The more crowded the market, the more design matters, but design is an amplifier, not a company.
l124|230.e: When something genuinely new appears, the first products don't need great design. Once there are hundreds or thousands of similar products, design becomes the bar for being considered at all. Users facing many options, unsure which features they need, tend to pick the one that looks the highest quality. The product still has to be better or different, though. Like good technology, design only amplifies, and it has the most effect early, the way packaging and a website set expectations before anyone uses the product. Brand goes further: it has to be real, built up through everyday words and actions, not a new logo and color scheme.
ex: Nobody today would use the web pages Google and YouTube launched with
Airbnb and Nike: brands that stop people considering alternatives

items.d: The first products survive with rough design
Design becomes the price of being considered
Attract users, keep them, be remembered

l124|230.c: Productivity software should be opinionated and set a default workflow, not be endlessly flexible.
l124|230.e: The point of productivity software, he says, is to get people doing work that actually matters to the company. Overly flexible tools make every team spend hours figuring out ten ways to use the same feature. His design principle is to design for one person; designing for everyone yields a generic compromise. Linear ships the defaults its team believes are best, so users spend less thought on the tool. Cycles work the same way: they run automatically on a fixed rhythm, help a team pick what matters out of an endless backlog, and leave a record when something jumps the queue.
ex: They're called cycles, not sprints: "we're not sprinting anywhere"

marks.d: Every team works out its own usage

l124|230.c: No A/B tests, no per-feature metrics: get everyone to understand customers deeply, then decide on instinct.
l124|230.e: Linear sets company-level goals like weekly active users but no metrics for individual features. Customers differ in size and culture and use things differently, so success means the customer feels the problem is solved. He calls the approach science plus magic. The science: user research on every project, the whole team in shared Slack channels answering customer questions, and looking at data with a specific question in mind. The magic: once people understand deeply enough, they decide by intuition. Many teams over-rely on data out of fear of choosing wrong. He would rather be wrong occasionally and fix it.
ex: Linear sees itself as a retention-and-trust business, not a one-off transaction
Contrast with Ramp's speed and metrics: Amazon and Apple both won in different ways

terms.d: User research, customer Slack, data with a question

result.d: Be wrong and fix it, rather than let data choose

l124|230.c: Focus means constantly asking whether something matters now, pushing the main quest and skipping side quests.
l124|230.e: He follows the YC advice that founders should only talk to customers, build product and exercise, and anything else is probably a mistake. Lots of things sound good, so he asks whether they matter now or later. Security certification, for example, will be needed eventually, but early on they simply told customers who asked that they didn't have it yet, and most accepted that. The team borrows role-playing game language to judge ideas: does this advance the main quest or a side quest? If it helps neither customers nor the product, it waits. He allocates his personal time by the same test.
ex: Asked about SOC 2 early on, they just said it would come later
He even put off podcast appearances until the company was the right size

items: Don't move product or customers forward

d.verdict: Ask first: does this matter now, or can it wait?

l124|230.c: Small, strong teams do better work; hire people who exceed their title, and finish with a paid work trial.
l124|230.e: The founders had seen the chaos that comes when fast-growing companies pile on headcount. They believe a few excellent people beat a crowd of average ones, so they barely hired in year one and have never more than doubled in a year since. They want people who are a bit more than their title: engineers with product judgment, marketers who can tell a story. Product sense is tested by probing the reasons behind decisions in past projects. The final step is a paid work trial: an open-ended problem that the candidate scopes, builds in the real codebase and presents. Both sides see each other clearly.
ex: Trial candidates get Slack, Notion and meeting access, and very few decline
Trials can run on weekends or holidays to limit disruption for the candidate

l124|230.c: Win product-market fit one customer segment at a time, starting by becoming the default tool for startups.
l124|230.e: He treats product-market fit as a spectrum measured segment by segment. Linear's announcement was written in the founders' own voice, explaining why they were building it. The waitlist came with a survey, so they could pick people by current tools, company size and level of interest, and invite a batch each week. They fixed what one batch reported before inviting the next, so everyone didn't hit the same bug. The first two years went to early-stage startups, the next two to filling in what larger companies need. Borrowing from Zoom, whenever a segment works, they double down on it.
ex: About a month after the announcement, the waitlist reached roughly 4,000 people
During the private beta a pay-what-you-want slider let some people pay $1 per seat
Profitable for two years running, with more cash than the company has ever raised

items.d: One or two hundred users, about 10 companies
Fit for companies of hundreds to a thousand

l125|231.c: Press is a supplement to growth, not a strategy; like fundraising, know what you'll use it for.
l125|231.e: He has heard founders say one article outsold a whole month of paid ads, and others say coverage did nothing at all. Press is too unpredictable to be your main growth strategy. It's worth chasing only when you can name a specific use: launching a product, entering a market, repositioning the brand, building a founder's authority, supporting a fundraise, or attracting partners. "I work hard and deserve coverage" isn't a business reason. And picking the wrong outlet wastes the effort entirely.
ex: A Washington hot-dog truck wanted Entrepreneur coverage, but 99.5% of readers can't buy its hot dogs
Big companies pitch the magazine to look like they care about small business owners

items.d: The food section of a local publication
Don't chase a national business magazine

l125|231.c: Editors don't care about you, only about their readers; understand the publication's mission before pitching.
l125|231.e: Many people treat media as a service that provides coverage, asking how to get in the magazine the way they'd order a burger. He says editors serve readers, and you get picked up only if you can give their audience something useful. Every publication has a different mission. At Fast Company he looked for stories that showed where business was heading. Entrepreneur is a magazine about thinking, so it wants stories of counterintuitive decisions and hard problems solved while running a business. You can break your story into pieces and pitch each piece to the outlet it fits.
ex: A butter-dish founder couldn't afford $10,000 of research, so she interviewed people at airport gates
The same product: Cosmo might cover the product, Entrepreneur the founder's decisions

items: I'm a founder, so I belong in the magazine
Push the story I want to tell
Pitch even a new company president
Pick the slice useful to its readers

d.verdict: You get coverage when you help editors serve their readers

l125|231.c: Don't email the editor in chief; find who actually covers your area, and freelancers are often hungrier.
l125|231.e: People go straight to the top editor because that name is easiest to find. But the editor in chief mostly vets ideas that editors bring in and isn't out looking for stories. Instead, search the publication's site for your category or your competitors, look at what form those articles take and who wrote them, and judge whether you can realistically land a feature or a seasonal gift list. Freelancers make a living selling story ideas and get far fewer pitches than staff editors, so the odds they read your email are close to 100%. A bio that says "contributor," or a quick Google of their portfolio, tells you who they are.
ex: A peanut-butter brand targeting millennial moms searched Cosmo for "snacks" and found only holiday lists
He gets thirty to fifty pitches every time he records a podcast episode

items.d: Who will buy what you sell

l125|231.c: Most PR people aren't good; good ones have real media relationships and say no. Run from anyone guaranteeing coverage.
l125|231.e: A PR firm saves you a lot of research and pitching, but it's expensive, and he says much of the industry is lazy, running on mass emails and outdated ideas. A classic trap: they charge you to write a press release, push it out over a paid wire service, then hand you a report saying you "appeared on Yahoo Finance" when almost nobody saw it. Coverage is entirely an editor's subjective call, so guaranteed placement is empty talk. Good PR people contact editors only when they truly have a fitting story, know your industry, and will tell you straight when your story doesn't suit a publication.
ex: He told a PR industry conference most PR people are bad at the job, and the room nodded
PR firms tend to specialize by sector: health, hospitality, consumer goods, tech

items.d: Says when a publication won't fit
And no selling of wire releases

l125|231.c: Coverage is often worth less for its readers than as an endorsement you reuse in your own channels.
l125|231.e: A big publication's site may get millions of visitors a month, but that doesn't mean your article gets read. Most likely five to ten thousand people see it. That isn't necessarily a problem. Many people turn the article into a paid social post aimed precisely at the people they want to influence, or add an "as seen in" section to their website. When the podcast company he's part of was covered in Variety, nothing came of it directly. But every email to advertisers and partners since has included the link, and people clearly take them more seriously. A funding story in TechCrunch works the same way.
ex: Money News Network got a Variety story and now puts it in every business email

terms.d: Maybe only a few thousand actual readers

result.d: Often worth more than the article itself

l125|231.c: Keep the pitch short and obviously written for that person, and in interviews be honest about struggles, not wins.
l125|231.e: An editor decides whether to delete based on a glance at the subject line and preview, so the opening has to show the email was written specifically for them. Mention something they've written, but don't pretend to be a fan. Keep it under three paragraphs and get straight to the story their audience cares about. Interacting naturally on social media beforehand, so they recognize your name, also helps. Then be candid in the phone interview. He hates success stories and loves problem-solving stories. The more you try to control the narrative and sound like you're reading talking points, the more the journalist resists, and the harder the piece may land.
ex: Canadian painter Meg O'Hara pitched him using the problem-and-solution structure of his own podcast
When the pandemic closed ski resorts, she started painting skiers' favorite mountains for them

items.d: Why this publication and this section
The part their readers care about
Problem and solution, not a success story

l125|231.c: You can get press without being the subject: be the expert, publish data, or become part of a bigger story.
l125|231.e: An obscure B2B company rarely gets a story of its own, so rather than forcing it, change the angle. When news breaks, offer a reporter expert perspective in exchange for a quote, or submit a bylined article. Smarter still, create or point to a bigger context. You may not be interesting on your own, but the trend you're part of or the data you hold might be, and when that gets covered you naturally take a prominent place in it. This route also lets you put "as seen in" on your website.
ex: A cat-toy seller exposed Amazon-to-eBay arbitrage, which led to a 4,000-word article
Barbara Corcoran built a Manhattan housing report from her own firm's sales data
Zapier publishes an annual list of the fastest-growing business apps

d.right: You are part of the backdrop

l125|231.c: Things nobody asks you to do but you could (opportunity set B) grow you more than your actual job.
l125|231.e: He splits the opportunities in front of you into two sets. A is what others expect of you, and doing it well is the basic measure of success. B is what nobody asks for but you could do anyway: take on a new responsibility, develop a hobby, start a podcast. Doing only A makes you better at what you already do. Growth happens in B. People skip B because the payoff is unclear and time is short, but he finds these things always turn into opportunities or lay groundwork for later. Once he became editor in chief, nobody asked him to speak, podcast or write books. He did all three, and redefined himself as an entrepreneur who helps entrepreneurs.
ex: The idea is a chapter in his book Build for Tomorrow

items.d: Nobody asked, but it's within reach
No longer just a magazine editor
Direct income or groundwork for later

l126|233.c: A new leader should listen and earn trust first, then change things together with the team.
l126|233.e: When she took over a design team of about ten at Airbnb, she had heard in interviews about poor collaboration and low morale, so she started making big changes right away. About a month in, half the team booked a meeting with her and HR and took turns reading out their complaints. She resisted the urge to defend herself and heard the common thread: she hadn't earned their trust yet. They didn't know she cared about them or shared their goals. From then on she learned what motivated each person before pushing changes. A few months later, the team's engagement score was the highest in the company.
ex: She calls it the biggest lesson of her career as a leader

items.d: Five designers plus HR, face to face
Make changes together with the team
Highest in the company months later

l126|233.c: Quality is growth: getting the details right lifts conversion and revenue directly, no trade-off needed.
l126|233.e: She describes quality in levels: first it works, then it is bug-free and complete, and at the top it exceeds what users expected. Users always ask for new features, and measurable projects are tempting. But companies that treat quality as a baseline don't play that numbers game. It's like exercise: one session shows nothing, but the long run decides your health. The fiercer the competition, the more details matter. Cars today compete on stitching and the sound of a closing door. Stripe's growth team is almost obsessive about experience, and improving the onboarding flow directly raised activation.
ex: A study found errors in the checkout flows of 99% of top online stores
The new checkout brought merchants 10.5% more revenue than the old one
A clearer invoice button meant fewer people contacting support

items.d: Does the basic job, offers real value
Does what users didn't know to ask for

l126|233.c: Beauty and function aren't rivals: beauty makes products easier to use and earns trust in details users can't see.
l126|233.e: She cites the book "Beauty": over two hundred years, the word has appeared far less often in books, reflecting a function-first mindset that treats beauty and usefulness as opposites. In fact, beauty makes things easier to use and more approachable, and people broadly agree on what is beautiful. Stripe sells financial infrastructure to businesses, yet still puts beauty first. When users see care in the visible details, they trust you with the invisible ones. Beautiful interfaces and invoices get better results. Beauty also rubs off on users, and it draws in people who care about craft.
ex: Tweets sent from New York's Penn Station are more negative than those from Grand Central
The TV show "The Bear" has a scene about peeling mushrooms

items.d: Visible care hints at invisible care
People who care about craft want in

l126|233.c: Quality decays over time, so assign owners to each key user journey and walk and score it regularly.
l126|233.e: She believes organizations naturally drift toward mediocrity, so quality has to be a group effort, not the job of one genius or a QA team. A product meets the bar at launch, then every team ships its own things and the whole gets worse. It's like renovating one room and making the others look shabby. Stripe picked its 15 most important user journeys and gave each an engineering, product, and design owner. Every quarter they walk the journey as a user would, from a Google search to the website, docs, and dashboard. They log every point of friction, file bugs, score with colors, and then calibrate standards across teams in a product quality review.
ex: Scores cover usability, usefulness, attractiveness, and delight
She often walks random flows with David Singleton, Stripe's CTO, who codes

items.d: From search to docs to dashboard
Teams agree on one quality bar
For example, search ranking and wording

l126|233.c: Performance equals potential minus interference, so a manager must raise potential and keep clearing interference.
l126|233.e: She learned this formula at Airbnb. You raise potential by hiring good people and developing them. But even great people, weighed down by process and organizational problems, wither like a muscle in a cast and end up burned out and underperforming. When a team grows, old processes stop working. She will even let a team run "hot" on purpose to see how people really work before changing anything. For more than ten years she has had designers regularly drop screenshots or prototypes into a shared slide deck sent to product and engineering leads, so everyone spots duplicated or conflicting work early.
ex: The shared deck moved from every two weeks to monthly so it wouldn't become a burden
Her motto: a prototype is worth a thousand meetings

result.d: Performance = potential − interference

l126|233.c: Designers should sit with product and engineering, while keeping a design community and creative space.
l126|233.e: When she joined Lyft, the design team sat in a beautiful but locked studio of its own. The creative energy was great, but product and engineering were outside setting direction in hallway conversations. Designers would finish work, bring it out, and find it didn't match the goal, which meant lots of waste and rework. She listened first, got everyone on board, then took down that wall. Designers now sit with their engineering and product partners by area, such as driver, rider, and safety, while keeping space for critiques and workshops. Her image: everyone wears two T-shirts, one for design and one for their cross-functional team.
ex: She admits Apple and others keep design separate, but that needs many other supporting decisions

items: Cut off from product and engineering

d.verdict: Two T-shirts: design community and cross-functional team

l126|233.c: Dare to have a bold vision: picture the ideal whole, work backward, and ship it in steps, not just increments.
l126|233.e: At companies of any size, people fear big ideas. Big changes are hard to measure, while incremental improvements are controllable, fit in a quarter, and look better in performance reviews. But users judge quality by their whole experience across products and over time, and polishing your own corner rarely improves the whole. She argues for visions that actually ship: draw the ideal version of the full journey, like Chesky's "11-star experience," then work backward to a two-year path, release it in pieces, and adjust as you learn. That takes an "editor" who sees the whole, and the courage to say "not good enough yet."
ex: Building a house starts with blueprints, an architect, and a general contractor
At Airbnb, founder Brian Chesky plays that editor-in-chief role

marks.d: Measurable, but the whole rarely improves
Draw the ideal, work backward, ship in pieces
Aim for day one, easy to give up

l126|233.c: Hire designers for taste and character first, then humility and courage; tools are the easiest to teach.
l126|233.e: She thinks tools and process are easy to teach, while taste and character are not. So she looks at how often a candidate's judgment is right and how their taste was formed. Next comes humility, which is what makes someone respect teammates and genuinely care about user feedback. Then courage: proposing a better idea on a blank page, or saying "this isn't good enough, let's redo it," takes nerve. Early-stage companies often agonize over hiring a doer versus a senior leader. Her advice: hire a full-time doer and add a senior design advisor, so user-centered habits are there from day one.
ex: Her interview question: what work are you most proud of?
She sees design as intent, and anyone in any role can decide with intent

items.d: Proposes new ideas, dares to start over
Easiest to learn on the job

l127|235.sc: The A side and B side
l127|235.c: People only show the A side of their careers; the B side's setbacks are just moments you get through.
l127|235.e: She says the working world rewards telling only the highlights, so what you hear on podcasts and stages is an edited life, and anyone in a slump can conclude they're finished. Her own resume looks shiny, but behind it is a string of setbacks. What she learned: doing meaningful work isn't enough. You also need to understand what others value and know how to tell your own story. Most of all, you need resilience, the habit of getting back up. Latin America is similar: people see the danger and chaos and miss the enormous opportunity in tech.
ex: At 26 she thought her career was over
As a new head of growth, she learned the job from investor Andrew Chen's blog

items: Dropped out of college while depressed
Lost her visa twice, was laid off and fired
Went six months unpaid at Tumblr

d.verdict: Lows are just moments; resilience carries you to the next A side

l127|235.c: When everyone is chasing ads, the landing page is the neglected lever, and its gains compound.
l127|235.e: The Bloomberg campaign was spending about a million dollars a day on ads, and talented people were everywhere, so ad creative was crowded. She moved to the next step that nobody owned: the landing page people saw after clicking. Doubling landing page performance doubles the return on every ad dollar spent before it. The huge traffic meant she could reach statistical significance several times in a single day. Her rules: design for mobile first, with the key copy and button above the fold. People skim, so keep copy minimal and make the headline and button understandable on their own. Match the ad. Mind the emotion, and use images only as background.
ex: In a campaign, dark, slightly threatening imagery drove more action than funny imagery
Her warning: too much money makes teams careless about efficiency

items.d: Conversion rate of one landing page

l127|235.c: Duolingo made consumer subscription work through mission obsession, frugality, a focus on retention, and data rigor.
l127|235.e: Back then almost nobody believed language learning or education could make money. She lists reasons that are hard to copy. First, obsession with the mission: learning English in a developing country can double or triple your income, which made users and talent want to follow. Second, long-term frugality; she had no budget at all when she joined. Third, treating retention as the test of whether the product delivers real value. Fourth, obsession with product and data. Many people copied Duolingo's interface without a team that watches the numbers and forms hypotheses every day. It's like copying the answers without knowing how to solve the problem.
ex: Based in Pittsburgh and unable to match Google salaries, it still hired top talent
Adding "your payment helps others learn for free" to the paywall raised conversion

items.d: Years of no paid ads, organic growth
Retention is proof of real value
Own hypotheses and experiments, not copied answers

l127|235.c: Relying on paid acquisition early is like an addiction: costs rise, you can't stop, and retention problems get hidden.
l127|235.e: Duolingo didn't start charging subscriptions or showing ads until about year three. With no lifetime value per user, calculating acquisition cost was meaningless. Even if buying users is cheap at first, the cost climbs once the most receptive audience is used up. And the growth that ads bring has to be shown to investors and fed into experiments, so it becomes hard to stop. The sneakier problem is that measuring retention on bought users hides who is truly benefiting from the product. Paid ads are good for testing copy, images, and value propositions. Once you find your ideal users, figure out how to attract them organically.
ex: A founder bragged of 10-cent acquisition costs; she warned that number rises with scale

l127|235.c: When an experiment fails, try it yourself first: a sloppy badge test was misjudged and real badges came a year late.
l127|235.e: After studying popular games, the team wanted badges, but whenever they ranked ideas by expected return, badges looked too expensive, so she held them back for six months. To keep it lean, they finally ran a minimal test: one badge for signing up. Nobody is proud of signing up, and there was nothing to collect or show off, so it did nothing, and the team shelved the idea for about eight more months. Only later did they realize the growth team never tried its own experiments. The real badge system lifted almost every metric in the company. Her other lesson: trust your own confusion as a user, because many others probably share it.
ex: More than half of A/B tests fail
In China, about a million downloads on day one, then the app was blocked and buried in one-star reviews
Indian users with phones set to English were mistaken for English speakers learning other languages

items.d: Ranked by return, shelved six months
One badge just for signing up
Realized the test itself was bad

l127|235.c: A lovable brand rests on mission and a distinctive voice, and when it goes viral, lean into it.
l127|235.e: She thinks most startups underrate brand and PR. A brand has to stand for something: Duolingo's social media calendar had one post a week on learning results and one on the mission. The voice has to be distinctive. For every line of copy, ask "could any other company have written this?" and aim for a smile or a double take. When the passive-aggressive reminders after missed lessons and the crying owl Duo became memes, some people inside worried about the image, but the team chose to run with it. Duolingo's TikTok success today grows out of that brand DNA and a culture willing to take risks.
ex: The push after five missed days: "These reminders don't seem to be working. We'll stop for now."
They once A/B tested the size of Duo's tears and the puddle beneath him

items.d: When a meme lands, run with it

l127|235.c: When going international, treat the world as one market, because people are far more alike than different.
l127|235.e: Every time she entered a new country, she heard "it's different here": green is unlucky, owls are bad omens, people here don't trust free. She agrees cultural differences are real, but mostly they are the last 5% of understanding people. If a startup builds a version per country, the cost in code, process, people, and time multiplies, and every experiment has to run on several versions. Duolingo's default was to roll out what worked in one place everywhere, capturing the big 80% first, with exceptions only in a few cases like China and India. Regulated B2B industries are a different story.
ex: For a startup, she says, time matters almost more than money

marks.d: What works in one place ships everywhere
Censorship and language settings need special handling

l127|235.c: Tech is a far smaller share of Latin America's economy than in big countries, so the low-hanging fruit is plentiful right now.
l127|235.e: Latin America has about 660 million people and a 6 trillion dollar economy, but tech's share of GDP is roughly a third of India's, a tenth of China's, and a thirtieth of America's. Much of what is already digital in developed markets hasn't been built there. Latin American founders are naturally scrappy and resilient. But founders are lonely, information and capital are hard to reach, and cross-border incorporation and currency exchange are a hassle. That is what Latitud set out to fix. Venture money keeps flowing in, and veterans of local unicorns are returning to start companies. There is room in fintech, services for small businesses, and her favorites, healthcare and education. Emerging markets may also leapfrog old stages.
ex: Only about 3% of Brazilians speak English, so going straight to Silicon Valley rarely gets taken seriously
Latitud's community has about 1,500 founders and has backed about 100 companies

terms.d: Much is still done on paper
Unicorn and big-tech veterans start companies

result.d: High risk, but bigger rewards for success

l128|19.c: Most software pitches are just feature tours that never answer "why pick us over the others?"
l128|19.e: When she does positioning work with clients, she finds their sales pitches look almost identical: click through every drop-down menu, feature after feature. The customer walks away thinking "it's sort of like a shared inbox, sort of like a ticketing tool" and can't tell the difference. A better approach starts with where you sit in the market and what you believe about it, then presents features inside a frame of differentiated value, so every part of the demo answers why they should choose you.
ex: Help Scout's view: for digital businesses, support is a growth engine, not a cost center
One alternative, shared inboxes, is easy but companies outgrow it
Ticketing systems do everything but turn customers into numbers pushed to cheap channels

items: Open with a market point of view
Weigh the alternatives' pros and cons
Organize the demo around differentiated value

d.verdict: A pitch must answer "why us"

l128|19.c: A good pitch has a setup and a follow-through; the setup is short but decides whether the customer buys your worldview.
l128|19.e: The setup isn't about you, it's about the market. Give an insight, lay out the pros and cons of each type of alternative, then propose the few things a perfect solution would need and ask whether the customer agrees. If they nod, the second half only has to prove you deliver. The follow-through starts with your category, then walks through each value point and how you deliver it, which takes more than half the call. Then come proof, answers to the objections nobody voiced, and a clear ask for the next step. The setup is also where discovery happens, so it should be a conversation, not a monologue.
ex: Proof usually means customer stories or third-party data
Silent objections: too expensive, IT won't approve, too hard to roll out

items.d: Agree on the criteria with the customer
Each value point, with a demo
Stories, defuse worries, clear next step

l128|19.c: The biggest rival in B2B sales isn't the status quo but the buyer's fear of choosing wrong and deciding nothing.
l128|19.e: She cites data showing that 40% to 60% of B2B purchases end in no decision. Most of the time it's not because the old way seemed better, but because the buyer couldn't choose with confidence. The person assigned to evaluate options is often buying this kind of software for the first time, drowning in information, and worried that a bad pick will make the boss think less of them, annoy colleagues, or even cost them their job. So "let's revisit next year" becomes the safest exit. And sellers make the overload worse by piling on more features.
ex: 40% to 60% of B2B purchases end in no decision
The market leader wins by default: nobody gets blamed for picking it

items.d: Never bought this kind of software
Dozens of options on review sites
Worried about blame from boss and peers

l128|19.c: Piling fear of missing out onto a hesitant buyer backfires; instead, teach them how to buy and remove the risk.
l128|19.e: The usual move is to scare the customer: "your competitors are already using this." She points to Matt Dixon's research: when a customer is already hesitant, adding fear of missing out lowers close rates, because now both acting and not acting feel dangerous and the person freezes. Two things work. First, give them tools to decide: map the whole market and tell them a company like theirs only needs to care about three or four things. Second, lower the risk: break a big deal into smaller pieces, offer money-back guarantees, and promise service support if something goes wrong.
ex: Dixon's "The JOLT Effect" analyzed about 2.5 million sales calls recorded in Gong
In Bob Moesta's terms, the champion has another job to be done: don't get fired

terms.d: Market map plus the key criteria

result.d: Instead of pressure from FOMO

l128|19.c: Win over the internal champion first, then arm them to handle vetoes from every other department.
l128|19.e: A typical B2B purchase involves five to seven people, but only one, the champion assigned to evaluate options, actually cares about the value. The others can't push the deal forward, yet they have countless ways to kill it. So positioning and the pitch should be designed for the champion first. Once the deal is in motion, prepare the champion's answers for IT, procurement, the boss, and end users. Sellers have been through many deals and know what each group will ask, so they should flag it in the first meeting and hand over the ammunition.
ex: For IT: SOC 2 compliance and integration plans
For the boss: a ready-made ROI calculator
For end users: training and onboarding plans

root.d: The only one who truly cares about value

l128|19.c: Differentiated value starts with "what would customers do without us," then keeps asking "so what?" of each unique capability.
l128|19.e: First, name the real competitive alternatives, which often include the status quo, like Excel or an intern doing it by hand. Then list the capabilities nobody else has, whether features, pricing models, or service. For each one, keep asking "so what?" The answer is the value, and because the underlying capability is unique, competitors can't easily copy it. If you have active, happy customers, differentiated value exists; it just needs digging out. The market insight that opens the pitch can also be worked backward from that value.
ex: LevelJump: the only sales enablement tool built on Salesforce
So what? Enablement data joins sales data, so new-rep ramp time can be measured
The ultimate value was faster revenue, and Salesforce later acquired the company

items.d: Dig out the outcome customers care about

l128|19.c: Let your best salesperson test and tune the new pitch first, then have them win over the rest of the team.
l128|19.e: Even salespeople who dislike the old pitch have it memorized, and anything marketing tosses over the wall will be rejected on some excuse. Her approach: involve sales leadership in building it, have the best rep rehearse it repeatedly, then test it on qualified new prospects rather than existing customers, with a debrief after every call to change wording and reorder. When that rep says they'll never go back to the old pitch, record a demo and let them teach the others, backed by their own pipeline results. The whole process takes two weeks at the fastest, usually about a month.
ex: She finishes a positioning workshop within a week
One client doubled the number of first calls that turned into opportunities
When she was in-house, revenue once doubled within two quarters

items.d: Learn it cold, pitch the sales leader first
Once convinced, roll out to the team

l128|19.c: Creating a category isn't the only road to a great company; most winners first carve out a niche in an existing one.
l128|19.e: Google didn't invent search and Facebook didn't invent social networks. Many category pioneers were overtaken by well-funded fast followers. The more common path is Geoffrey Moore's bowling pin strategy: win a niche the giants ignore, expand into adjacent niches, and only after you dominate, widen the category's boundaries. Many so-called category creation stories are really companies that reached hundreds of millions in revenue and then renamed themselves to expand.
ex: Qualtrics was survey software until about 300 million dollars in revenue
Snowflake started as a cloud data warehouse, then expanded into the "data cloud"
Her early company began as CRM for investment banks and was later bought by Siebel

items.d: Investment-bank CRM: a niche the giants ignored
Retail banking, then all of banking

l129|237.c: Products built out of fear of a competitor rarely work; good products start from real user pain.
l129|237.e: At Google he worked on social products like Buzz and Google+. The motivation was fear that Facebook posed an existential threat, not a desire to build something good for people. He had actually done about 18 months of formative research and kept seeing that people wanted better ways to talk with small circles of family and friends. In hindsight that was the need WhatsApp met, but the project started from the wrong place. Google+ was sealed off in its own building with separate badge access, and the internal rivalry was intense. Fear-driven projects, he believes, warp every decision.
ex: Google Buzz was a privacy disaster
His research method: mapping dozens of people's social networks and communication channels
Google Maps and Android from the same era were excellent products

items: Solve problems people feel strongly about

d.verdict: Projects born from fear don't end well

l129|237.c: To judge AI's impact, return to what your product is fundamentally for, then ask if AI can replace or enhance it.
l129|237.e: He compares AI to an incoming meteor and thinks its impact may exceed mobile and even the internet, so anyone not exploring it seriously will be left behind. Don't get distracted by flashy demos. Start by answering why the product exists and what problem it solves. Then check that against what AI can do today: write, summarize, answer questions, see images and hear audio, and soon take actions. The answer will be fully, partly or not yet, which maps to replacement or enhancement. Almost every B2B SaaS product with a workflow is in the path.
ex: A reporting tool's future may be nothing but a question box
Project-management tools could be upended by a new approach just the same

items.d: Why it exists; what problem it solves
Decide how deep the strategy change goes

l129|237.c: The day ChatGPT shipped, Intercom tore up its old strategy and bet on AI customer service.
l129|237.e: On the day ChatGPT launched, Intercom's head of machine learning concluded everything had changed. The company rewrote its strategy almost from scratch, starting from why customer service exists, and built Fin, an AI-first support bot, with a bet-the-company mindset. Older bots needed support managers to hand-script conversation flows; large language models can read and reason on their own. The technology now runs ahead, and the hardest problem is helping support teams through the organizational change, which has created new roles like conversation designer. He admits the financials haven't shifted dramatically yet, but the evidence convinces him the direction is right.
ex: For some customers, Fin resolves 50–70% of incoming questions
Fin also sits in the inbox suggesting replies to human agents
About 900 people, yet hunting for an exponential curve like a startup

items.d: Fin as the first line of response
Fin assists agents in the inbox

l129|237.c: Don't bolt AI onto one specialist team; every product team has to learn to use it.
l129|237.e: Great AI products start with strong machine-learning engineers. Model providers supply only the foundation, and you have to adapt it deeply to your own use case, so Intercom's ML team is bigger than ever. But most of the work is front-end and interaction design: when should the AI assistant jump in, how does it coexist with human agents? Those are hard design problems, solved by ordinary product teams with help from the ML team. He draws the lesson from the mobile wave, when a small mobile team in London was ignored by headquarters. So he opposes a standalone AI group and prefers generalists who can learn new things.
ex: Product teams run about 1 PM to 5 engineers
At Google, the mobile team was about 20 people against about 200 at headquarters

items.d: Every team understands AI; no bolt-on
PM, design and 3–5 engineers build the experience
Adapts the foundation model to the domain

l129|237.c: Two forces drive switching: differentiation attracts buyers, and table-stakes features decide whether they can buy.
l129|237.e: This is his simplified version of the Kano model for classifying features. Differentiation has to be different and better in a way users care about; Google Wave was innovative, but nobody cared. Table stakes are dull basics like reporting and permissions, easy to neglect, but without them customers can't buy even when they want to. A startup entering a mature category can only win on strong differentiation, getting customers to buy it alongside the incumbent. Only years later, after filling in table stakes, can it replace the incumbent outright. Intercom now splits effort roughly half and half, though it has swung to 70/30 in both directions.
ex: Early customers bought Intercom on top of incumbents like Zendesk
It lost deals for lacking basic reporting and permissions

l129|237.c: Organizations overcorrect when they fix a problem; you only find the boundary by crossing it.
l129|237.e: When you step back, notice something is off and fix it, the pendulum tends to swing to the other extreme. Too much differentiation leads to a frantic push on table stakes, and then the product loses its appeal. Hiring works the same way. Intercom once felt nobody in-house had done these things before, so it hired lots of experienced people and specialists. They brought their old companies' cultures with them, and specialists struggled in a highly ambiguous environment. Today it prefers people who have done a bit and have some depth. Swings can't be avoided, he says; the key is limiting their size: cross the line, feel the pain, and correct with humility.
ex: At Google he spent a year stuck in privacy debates and shipped nothing
Facebook's view: you only find the boundary by crossing it

items.d: Step back and see something is off

l129|237.c: A good product in the right market can still fail; what's missing is usually a clear story.
l129|237.e: Product people think too little about the market side, he says. A market is a group of people, their problem, and how much they care about it. You need many people with the same problem and real energy to solve it. But he has seen good products in good markets fail anyway, because the explanation was too complicated to hold anyone's attention. So designers, PMs, researchers and data people should all learn to explain the product the way product marketers do; it matters as much as learning to build it. Jobs to be Done should stay simple too: focus on what the user is trying to get done, and skip the arguments between schools of thought.
ex: Rdio had a beloved product but lost to Spotify, which told a better story
The four forces model: Intercom's founder used it to talk him into leaving Facebook

terms.d: How many people care, and how much
Whether you can explain why it's better

result.d: Missing any one can sink it

l130|241.c: Lean Startup is mostly descriptive, not prescriptive: name what's already happening, then derive the practices.
l130|241.e: Early on, VCs asked him to teach the "magic" that made engineering teams so productive. He was just describing what actually happened at his company IMVU, and was often told it was impossible. Startups are experiments by nature, and strategy changes every day; naming these things is what lets people discuss and reason about them. The prescriptive practices are deduced from assumptions and then tested by experiment. So he treats Lean Startup as a scientific theory: any new practice shown to work should be absorbed, rather than its proponents being treated as heretics.
ex: IMVU deployed about 50 times a day when monthly releases counted as advanced
He first blogged anonymously after being warned it would end his career
His favorite interview question: name a best practice, then say when it doesn't apply

items.d: Work out what to do from the assumptions
Practices that work join the theory

l130|241.c: An MVP isn't a shoddy product; it's the least effort needed to test your key assumption.
l130|241.e: An MVP has nothing to do with quality level, he says. The only question is how to test the assumption fastest. If users have a high bar, build just one key feature and build it to that bar. Quality is defined by customers, and if you don't know who they are, you can't talk about quality. Shipping a product isn't the same as launching it to the market: get 10 customers to try it and tell you what's wrong, which costs very little. MVP is a U-shaped curve, and roughly near the optimum is good enough. Most teams do one to two orders of magnitude more work than validation requires.
ex: IMVU avatars couldn't walk, only crudely teleport, and users praised it as cutting edge
A data-center team met customers with a brochure first, saving 3 years and $18 million in R&D
LTSE's MVP took 10 years to build

items.d: Small enough to make you uncomfortable
Let them tell you what's terrible

l130|241.c: Caring about craft is fine, but craft must not become an excuse to avoid user feedback.
l130|241.e: He breaks "craft" into three meanings. Engineering craft, meaning clean code and the right abstractions and tools, preserves your options and makes you faster, and you should never trade it away for speed. Then there are core values: if a design philosophy is something the company would rather die than give up, don't pretend to test it, and precisely because so much is invested there, everything else needs experiments even more. The real problem is the third meaning: people with neither taste nor a design philosophy who use craft as a reason to keep not shipping. Building the wrong value proposition to a high standard is nothing to be proud of.
ex: A beautiful product converted at zero due to a sign-up button bug, yet the team blamed the value proposition
The dozens of buttons nobody presses on a cheap microwave also took plenty of craft

items.d: Don't test these; experiment everywhere else
Hiding from feedback in the name of polish

l130|241.c: A pivot changes strategy, not vision, but the vision itself gets discovered along the way.
l130|241.e: He uses the basketball pivot foot as the image: one foot stays planted on what you've learned while the other changes direction. Starting over with no continuity isn't a pivot. From outside, pivots often look strange, but inside there's a coherent thread, such as tool B, built to make product A possible, turning out to be more valuable than A. A founder's vision also evolves while building, and a startup is largely a process of self-discovery. Memory quietly rewrites the past too, so write your hypotheses down the way a scientist would.
ex: On an old whiteboard he found a bad idea in his own handwriting, one he remembered opposing
As he heard it, Zuckerberg and friends were still working on other projects when Facebook took off
He can tell the same stretch of IMVU history as all wrong or all right

marks.d: One foot planted on what you've learned

l130|241.c: If you're asking whether to pivot, you probably know; go all in for a fixed period, then end it gracefully.
l130|241.e: Companies with product-market fit are too busy to ask the question. He suggests giving the current direction a fixed deadline, ideally six weeks, even just a weekend, with everyone working on the single most important thing. If that still fails, have each person say what they would build if starting over, then pick a direction everyone can rally behind or try them one per month. Failing, in his view, is far from the worst outcome. Worse is being trapped in a zombie company you hate but can't leave. Separate your ego from the company; if needed, shut down and return the money, or bring in a new CEO.
ex: A metric creeping from 10% to 10.65%: growing, but nowhere near enough
In a big company, assign at least one full-time person, not a part-time committee
Like Kuhn's paradigm shifts: experiment where results are still coming

items.d: Growing isn't the same as enough
Six weeks or a weekend, one thing only
Each person's answer to starting over
Shut down, return money or change CEO

l130|241.c: AI is fundamentally a management technology: it amplifies an organization's values and reshapes its hierarchy.
l130|241.e: What people really fear, he argues, is corporations wielding AI. Software mirrors the structure of the organization that builds it, and training an AI passes on that organization's values, while tech companies have a huge governance debt. AI agents often behave like middle managers, subcontracting work down the chain until they fall into infinite recursion. Because AI is good at summarizing, structures built on large middle layers that roll information upward will be rewritten. Facing an unpredictable future, he favors actions that hold up across many scenarios, such as more transparency and stronger state capacity.
ex: Asked for a 30-day course, an AI wrote two days and spawned sub-agents to "fill in the rest like this"
Someone used GPT-4 to write personalized sales emails to 10,000 Shopify stores
He imagines AI screening supplier emails fairly according to purchasing preferences

items.d: One prompt summarizes the whole company
Used to take many people reporting upward
AI passes the buck too and needs managing

l130|241.c: No individual can make promises for an organization; a credible mission must be written into governance.
l130|241.e: He sees an organization as a living superorganism in which the founder can be replaced at any time. A commitment is kept in the founder's absence only if it is built into the structure. Companies are good at what they structurally care about: filing quarterly reports on time is near certain, while "don't be evil" is something nobody can guarantee. Shareholder primacy, he argues, is wrong even on pure returns. Lawyers always say to do this governance work later, but by the time of an IPO it's too late, so bring them concrete scenarios early.
ex: Self-test: a tobacco company offers $1 more per share to buy you; are you obliged to accept?
He cites Danish research finding foundation-owned companies perform better financially
Tools: public benefit corporations, board mission commitments, mission-aligned SPVs

items: Easy to sacrifice the long term

d.verdict: Centering human flourishing is both right and more profitable

l130|241.c: Growth isn't only viral loops; why users come back can be modeled just as precisely.
l130|241.e: His law of sustainable growth says new customers are a natural by-product of what existing customers do, and he distinguishes three growth engines: viral, paid and sticky. He once expected the engagement loop to become better known than Lean Startup itself, but it never caught on. People return to a product for only a few reasons: a reminder the product sends, a notification triggered by someone else's action, or the product's place in their mind that makes them think of it on their own. With so few sources, return visits can be measured and studied the way viral loops are.
ex: PayPal's "you've received money" email had an extremely high click rate
Facebook's "someone tagged you in a photo"
People play World of Warcraft with no reminder at all; that's positioning

items.d: The user is busy with something else
A product reminder, someone's notification, or memory
Use it and leave a trace of activity
That activity sets off new notifications

l131|242.c: Amazon treats process innovation as seriously as product innovation, and its mechanisms came from experiments.
l131|242.e: Between 2003 and 2007, he notes, Amazon launched most of its famous products, and all but one of its key processes were born in the same four years. The company was turning from a fast-growing bookstore into a complex organization with many categories, many countries and a third-party marketplace. The CEO couldn't attend every meeting or interview every candidate, so there had to be mechanisms. Bezos worked like a scientist: form a hypothesis, try it, keep what works. Many practices were borrowed from elsewhere, and processes were how the leadership principles got put into practice.
ex: Kindle, AWS and Prime all emerged in the same period
A new process needs CEO backing and months of persistence before it pays off
His life motto: slow is smooth, smooth is fast

items.d: Can't attend every meeting or interview
Iterate on process like a scientist

l131|242.c: Give a team full ownership of one small business rather than half ownership of a long list of projects.
l131|242.e: As the company grew, departments fought over centralized resources like engineering. Coordinating through endless meetings was slow and produced piles of documents built on wrong assumptions. Amazon switched to long-lived teams that own an area: one leader with dedicated cross-functional people, who sets their own controllable metrics and roadmap, so executives only have to make resource decisions a few times a year. The precondition was breaking the monolithic codebase into services and APIs. The cost was functional expertise, so central technical leaders still set the standards for code review, hiring and promotion.
ex: The search team watched click-through on the top three results and page-load milliseconds
Prime Video split teams by TV, game console and phone, down to a team just for Xbox
As a business generalist, he couldn't review an engineer's code

items.d: Decide team resources a few times a year
Fully owns one line and its metrics
Engineering, design and product in one group
Uniform code review, hiring and promotion

l131|242.c: If you have new information you must speak up; once you're understood, commit for real.
l131|242.e: He calls this the hardest of the original ten leadership principles to use well. Dissent is valuable because it brings information the decision maker hasn't considered, and on important issues you're obliged to escalate it all the way up. Once the leader can restate your reasoning and explain why other factors outweigh it, it's time to stop arguing. Real commitment isn't agreeing out loud while disagreeing inside; it's understanding the reasons well enough to explain them to your own team. If you still disagree, find the core of the other person's idea and work to make it something that can succeed.
ex: Advice from his boss Steve Kessel: find the kernel of Bezos's idea and build on it
Being "right a lot" comes from experience; the same data can be read to support any conclusion

items.d: Bring information the decision maker lacks
The leader restates it and explains the trade-off
Your input is now part of the decision
Able to explain the reasons to your team

l131|242.c: Start from the customer's need and work back: a PR/FAQ spells out the customer, the problem and the solution.
l131|242.e: Most companies work forward from resource constraints or revenue targets, and that leads them astray. Amazon's creed is that if you serve customers well, the financials follow: first figure out the best solution for the customer, then work backward to the engineering and cost problems you'll have to crack. The PR/FAQ, a mock press release plus FAQ, isn't a real press release. Its core is three sections: overview, problem, solution. The hardest parts are defining a specific customer and quantifying the problem. The writing must avoid hype and carry data, and the imagined launch date itself signals how complex the project is.
ex: "Every restaurant is my customer" is a failed customer definition
Cutting costs doesn't help customers unless it becomes lower prices
Separate "deciding what to build" from "delivering it efficiently" as two processes

root.d: An internal decision document, not a real press release

items.d: Specific down to the segment and the city
Quantified, and worth paying to solve
Hints at how hard it is

l131|242.c: Build a product funnel, not a tunnel; failed products are mostly a solution looking for a problem.
l131|242.e: A PR/FAQ is reviewed in concentric circles, from the author to the manager to wider groups and finally the CEO, and many get thrown out along the way. A tunnel process outputs whatever goes in. A funnel compares and filters, backing only the best few like a venture investor, so the scarcest engineering resources go where they matter most. He sees the Fire Phone as a case of having a technology, the 3D display, and then hunting for a problem. When a product fails and the execution was fine, nine times out of ten it didn't solve a meaningful problem.
ex: Imagine 100 PR/FAQs a year, with about 20 reaching the CEO
Slots, an early search-ad idea, failed for lack of scale but would work today
Bezos wrote up a voice-controlled "puck" in 2004; the Echo came a decade later

items.d: Writing it down exposes weak ideas
Good ideas may yield to better ones

l131|242.c: Watch input metrics, not revenue: improve what drives the customer experience and the outputs follow.
l131|242.e: Around 2000, whenever Amazon was about to miss a quarterly target it ran last-minute promotions and price cuts. They barely helped, mostly pulling next quarter's revenue forward and scattering attention. Inspired by Good to Great, the team drew its growth flywheel and listed selection, low prices, delivery speed and ease of finding and buying as inputs, each one measured. Good input metrics are things the team controls that touch the customer experience; you instrument the whole customer journey and keep refining how you measure. He opposes weighting several metrics into one composite, because that hides cause and effect.
ex: The key metric for selection was measured wrongly for several years
The method borrows DMAIC from Six Sigma
An early weighted "fitness function" was eventually abandoned

items.d: The rest were mostly input metrics

l131|242.c: Encouraging risk takes pay, performance reviews and the CEO's personal cover, not slogans.
l131|242.e: Many companies say they tolerate failure, but anyone on a failed project loses their bonus and damages their career. Amazon has no performance bonuses; pay is tied mainly to the stock price. When he moved from the biggest business, books, to digital media with zero revenue, his pay was unaffected. Reviews also focus on what you built and which inputs you improved. Beyond that, a big company's approval structure naturally crushes small innovation teams, so you put your strongest people in charge and the CEO gets deeply involved to clear obstacles for them.
ex: Steve Kessel led digital media and Andy Jassy led AWS
Citing Loonshots: innovation teams need a different approval structure
Kindle was heavily doubted inside the company at the time

result.d: How AWS and digital media got started

l131|242.c: An outside Bar Raiser guards the hiring bar and offsets the hiring manager's urge to fill the seat.
l131|242.e: During the 1999 hiring boom, new hires were hiring new hires, and a manager one week into the job could only apply their previous company's standards. So Amazon added a Bar Raiser to every interview loop: someone outside the hiring chain who runs the debrief and makes sure candidates are judged against the leadership principles using behavioral interviews, not gut feel. The Bar Raiser nominally holds a veto, but good ones never use it; they guide with questions, and the hiring manager still makes the call. To introduce it, pilot in one department and pick people who care about hiring, interview well and hold a high bar.
ex: In years as a Bar Raiser and 15 at Amazon, he never saw the veto used
Being a Bar Raiser could take 10 hours a week
The idea was borrowed from Microsoft's "As Appropriate" interviewer

items: Leadership principles as the shared standard

d.verdict: A bad hire costs far more than extra interview time

l132|246.c: The best product managers simplify, follow up on results, and do the unglamorous work.
l132|246.e: She has worked on consumer and business products, at big companies and startups, and says the standout product managers share three traits. They can pick the one thing that matters out of a pile of priorities and see it through. They come back after launch and report how it actually went, which executives almost never see. And they will happily do support, sales, copywriting or project management when it is needed. Communication and analysis are table stakes, and real strategy work is maybe 5% of the job. The people who ship more and practice more win. When in doubt, assume the task is yours.
ex: A big company has hundreds of OKRs and endless projects; you must pick one
She prefers "bets" to "ownership" because ownership hides the risk
PMs are often the team's emotional center and have to keep morale up

terms.d: Find the one thing and finish it
Support, sales, QA, whatever it takes

result.d: Ship more, practice more

l132|246.c: Simplifying is a skill: write what you would say, lead with the conclusion, cut the opening.
l132|246.e: Writing is most of what a product manager produces, and the usual problem is documents that wander. People can explain something in one sentence out loud but cannot get it on the page, and her answer is always "then just write that sentence." Her tools are simple. Read the draft aloud to hear where it drags. Put the conclusion first, then the reasons. Almost every document can lose its first two paragraphs. Keep conclusions and next steps to three at most. And get reviews from many people, including your boss and the founders, who started the company because they understood this market and probably know more than you.
ex: Her father edited her essays by removing page one: "start here"
She and two other product leaders run a three-person Slack group to edit each other
In interviews she checks whether a candidate is a simplifier or a complicator

root.d: Documents are a PM's main output

items.d: Hear where it wanders or breaks
Lead with the answer, no warm-up
The first two paragraphs rarely help
For conclusions and next steps alike

l132|246.c: Strategy means laying out the reasoning from mission to priorities so disagreements get specific.
l132|246.e: She kept hearing women in product described as "not strategic enough" and decided to pin down what strategy actually is. The trigger was an engineer who kept asking why they were building something. So she wrote a document that works its way down: the company and team mission and goals, a picture of the market and competitors, an honest look at the current product and technology, the biggest opportunity, the assumptions that have to hold, and finally the plan, with a short summary at the top. It can run 20 pages and is mostly homework for herself. Once it is public, pushback changes from "I disagree with you" to "I disagree with this point."
ex: She first asks her engineering partner to tear the document apart
Comparing it to the roadmap often shows most effort going to work unrelated to the strategy
A single feature needs no strategy; the higher the level, the more it does

items.d: Why the company and team exist
Market, rivals, customer voice, tech debt
Where your unique strengths let you win
Three items at most, in order

l132|246.c: The key part of a spec is why this problem matters and why it must be solved now.
l132|246.e: Designers deliver designs and engineers deliver code; the one-page spec is what a product manager delivers. She thinks the opening matters most: the background, the problem, why it matters, and why now. Get that right and the rest follows, and the document becomes the place where the team records its decisions. Her worst project was the one where she skipped this step. The team arrogantly decided to rewrite a core legacy product without enough discovery or technical research, and could never catch up with what the old product already did. Her advice is blunt: do not run a parallel rewrite.
ex: She always asks interviewees about the worst product they ever built
Laughing about a failure shows humility and enough reps
Keep a decision log: on this date we chose to solve only this part

items.d: Rewrite of a core legacy product
Still unfinished after two and a half years

l132|246.c: A team that keeps saying "data-driven" often does not understand its users.
l132|246.e: In her view, when an executive says "we make every decision from the dashboard," it usually means the team trusts numbers over observation, rarely does its own user research, and does not know the people using the product. You should instrument everything and measure results at scale. But data only tells you what happened, not why, and without the why you cannot figure out the next move. Unless you run a high-traffic business where experiments are cheap, talking to 10 users teaches you more than any dashboard. And if something is obviously better, just build it.
ex: Adam Medros at TripAdvisor stopped a review meeting: if it is obviously better, ship it

d.verdict: Data is essential but cannot replace understanding people

l132|246.c: There is no shortcut: ship a lot, watch what your decisions cause, and show your results.
l132|246.e: After two years rotating through TripAdvisor she thought she had it figured out, then became the only product manager at a startup and realized she had no idea. So she went to Drift to learn from a strong product team, and it took about five years in total before she felt confident. Almost four years at Drift let her watch two or three full cycles of the same product, which taught her more than job-hopping would have. After a launch she sets calendar reminders at two weeks, one month and six months to check the metrics and share them, because your boss will not notice on their own. To break in, join a startup or move internally, and take any role with the PM title.
ex: Her first hiring question is whether you have been a PM; the second is what you shipped
An MBA graduate kept contacting her and eventually got hired at the startup
They sat side by side at a WeWork for four months to get him up to speed

items.d: Two years; thought she had it
Saw two or three product cycles

l132|246.c: Product frameworks get misused, but publishing your own thinking is the best career investment.
l132|246.e: To turn real product work into readable content, she says, you have to sanitize it and squeeze it into a framework. Readers then treat applying the framework as the goal and forget that the point is impact. The best people make the call from instinct and data precisely when no framework fits. Yet she hosts a podcast and writes, and calls it the best decision of her career. It built a network, brought opportunities, kept her employable, and made candidates come to her when hiring. Most of all it forces her to reflect. The start is always awkward; the key is to be genuine. What feels obvious to you may be exactly what someone else needs.
ex: Someone once challenged her with her own podcast line about not believing in roadmaps
Her hand-drawn slide-outline method saved a colleague 75% of their time
She graduated in 2008 and has wanted to stay employable ever since

items.d: Think it through, make it interesting
Go back and do the job better

l133|247.c: Marketplaces do not sell rooms or rides; they sell removing the friction of finding each other.
l133|247.e: He explains it with the economist's idea of transaction costs. Someone who wants a ride or a place to stay has no idea who is willing or available. That friction can be bad enough that no deal happens at all. The fee a marketplace charges is the price of removing it, which is why hosts and drivers are customers just as much as guests and riders. Trajan's Market in ancient Rome was built in stone; today's markets can be redesigned with data at any time. Every marketplace, he says, has to do three things: help people find candidates, help them make a match, and learn from how matches turn out, feeding that back into the first two steps.
ex: Active data is a five-star rating; passive data is checking out early
At oDesk, employers had to screen large numbers of remote applicants

items.d: Help both sides filter and rank
Better search and matching next round

l133|247.c: Without scale on both sides you are not a marketplace yet, so solve one side first.
l133|247.e: The biggest failure mode, he thinks, is thinking like a marketplace before you are one; he is suspicious of the phrase "marketplace founder" itself. The test is whether both buyers and sellers have scale. If neither does, focus on growing one side, exactly like any other startup. Once you have one side, use it to attract the other. Your early value proposition should target a specific pain that exists when there is no liquidity yet. He also warns against locking in the future too early: a flat take rate on every transaction can feel unfair once a relationship matures, pushing both sides to go around the platform.
ex: UrbanSitter started by simply letting parents pay babysitters by card
Early oDesk used work-hour verification tools to solve remote trust
Stitch Fix's in-house stylists show controlled labor can beat an open market

cells.d: Or just keep growing the buyer side
Now talk about search and matching
Run it like a normal startup
Uber subsidized drivers and gave free rides

l133|247.c: Predicting what will happen is not deciding; data science should ask what an action adds.
l133|247.e: His first task at oDesk was predicting which applicant would get hired. He later realized that ranking by that prediction just reproduces past patterns. Prediction looks for correlation; decisions depend on cause and effect. Nobody gets fired for sending the biggest coupon to the customers with the highest lifetime value, but the real question is who spent more because they got the coupon. Evaluating search ranking works the same way: do not ask which algorithm best recreates historical bookings, ask which one produces more bookings and better matches once it is live.
ex: In an executive class, a CMO also instinctively chose to send coupons to top-LTV customers
Judge a hiring match by the rating afterward and whether they hire again

items: Measure the lift a coupon creates

d.verdict: A data scientist's job is to help the business decide

l133|247.c: Marketplaces are whac-a-mole: every big change moves attention around and creates winners and losers.
l133|247.e: Attention and inventory in a marketplace are limited, so many changes simply move them from one group to another. One company he worked with wanted new supply to have a better experience, so it steered newcomers toward experienced users on the other side. The veterans' experience got worse, and adjusting again just pushed the problem somewhere else. Badges often work the same way, pulling attention away from everyone without one, so it is no surprise that short-term Superhost experiments at Airbnb came out flat. The real question is whether the winners you create matter more than the losers, combined with leadership's beliefs about long-term value.
ex: Upwork's former CFO: every important change has winners and losers
He prefers "quantitative" to "data-driven": combine beliefs with data
Superhost's long-term retention value is hard to detect in a short experiment

items.d: New supply does not stick around

l133|247.c: Run experiments to learn, not to count wins, and the samples spent on learning are not waste.
l133|247.e: Companies that claim to test everything often grade data scientists on how many wins they get, so people test only incremental tweaks and let experiments run too long. Microsoft's research on fat-tailed returns suggests the opposite: try bolder ideas and move faster. A failed experiment that tested a clear hypothesis is just as valuable. He favors a Bayesian approach, where past experiments become your prior and a failed test that moves the prior deserves credit. Learning has a cost, and complaining afterward that the control group was wasteful is like complaining you ordered too much food once you are full.
ex: A manager at a real-estate platform secretly kept a holdout group costing about $2 million a year
That money told the company for the first time what its marketing team was worth
His PhD students in data science often get stuck on peripheral business problems

result.d: Decide whether to keep betting

l133|247.c: Nobody has solved ratings yet: scores inflate over time, and simple averages punish newcomers.
l133|247.e: He thinks no one has really gotten rating systems right. Ratings inflate: after meeting someone face to face, people feel bad leaving a low score, standards drift, and eventually four stars feels like an attack. One fix is to ask whether the experience exceeded expectations, or to compare it with the person's past experiences. The other problem is simple averaging. It barely affects an established seller, but for a newcomer the first bad review can be devastating to income. Blending a newcomer's score with a prior gives them a fair chance. Reviews that never get written carry information too.
ex: eBay research: a first review that is negative cuts expected short-term revenue by about 8%
Tadelis counts missing reviews in an "effective positive rate" that predicts sellers better
John Horton's paper documents median ratings rising steadily

items.d: A newcomer's first bad review can be fatal
A missing review is information too

l133|247.c: AI multiplies the hypotheses and options on the table, so human judgment matters more, not less.
l133|247.e: He rejects the idea that AI will automate data science away. Writing code and making charts is certainly faster, but AI vastly expands what you can propose and test: 10 explanations for a pattern become 100, 10 ad creatives become 1,000. Deciding which deserve attention and what counts as good enough now falls entirely on people. The flood of AI-generated text can also mislead people doing analysis, which makes data literacy more important. He also urges people to slow down and build a mental model of how the business works first.
ex: He requires students to use generative AI on every weekly assignment
Since November 2022 he no longer gives coding questions in interviews

items.d: A person stays in the loop

l134|251.c: Airbnb didn't cut product managers; it merged them with product marketing, because telling the story is part of building.
l134|251.e: Reports said Airbnb got rid of product managers. He says nobody was fired; the job changed. Product managers used to drive development internally while product marketers explained the product to the outside world. Now one person does both.
