The coordination and scheduling work moved to actual program managers, and program management became a high-status role. The new product team is smaller and more senior, doesn't manage design or engineering, and works through influence. His reasoning: if you don't understand the market, you can't build a good product. Many products that "were tried and didn't work" simply never reached users or were never explained well.
ex: 5,000 designers cheered the change, a sign design is often treated as a service team
He says many famous design leaders are really "design administrators" running process
UX writing and marketing writing were merged into one writing team

root.d: Fewer people, more senior, works through influence

items.d: Knows how to build and how to tell

l134|251.c: Splitting a company into self-contained divisions slows it down; Airbnb used the pandemic to go back to a startup structure.
l134|251.e: He describes how big companies decay. Teams depend on each other and wait in line, so each builds its own resources and becomes a division. Divisions compete for resources through relationships, which breeds politics. Further subdivision brings bureaucracy, no clear owners, and complacency. In 2019 Airbnb had about ten divisions and the app had barely changed in years. When the pandemic cut business by 80% in eight weeks, he reorganized the company by function (design, engineering, marketing), killed most projects, removed layers, and made only domain experts managers. The whole company now works from one rolling two-year roadmap with two big releases a year.
ex: Airbnb has under 7,000 employees; he estimates Uber has about 30,000
He had everyone list their projects in a spreadsheet and kept only about 20%
Someone described working 80 hours a week with only 20 of them productive

d.verdict: Make a thousand people build like ten

l134|251.c: Leaders must be in the details. That isn't micromanaging, and delegating too much actually slows teams down.
l134|251.e: He noticed a strange loop. The less he was involved, the vaguer the goals got, the fewer resources projects had, and the slower they moved. Yet people assumed the problem was that he was too involved, so he stepped back further and things got worse. He separates micromanaging from being in the details. Micromanaging is making decisions for people. Being in the details is knowing what's going on, the way a board understands what a CEO does without doing the CEO's job. Without the details, you can't judge whether work is good. Now he reviews every project on its own cadence and sees exactly where it's stuck. The first year or two meant far more work. After that, everyone rowed the same way and he had more free time.
ex: He thinks the CEO of a product company should be its chief product officer
He quotes investor Ben Horowitz: don't let founders delegate what they're best at
Today nine out of ten surprises at Airbnb are good news

items.d: Assume the leader is too involved

l134|251.c: Marketing is really about teaching people what you built; performance ads are precise but build no lasting advantage.
l134|251.e: He borrows a metaphor from co-founder Joe Gebbia. Performance marketing is a laser: good for lighting up one corner, such as balancing supply and demand in a city. But it isn't an investment, unless you run it as a high-return arbitrage business the way Booking does. To light the whole room you need the chandelier, which is brand. He thinks most companies never tell users what's new, so new features go unnoticed and teams drift toward ever smaller tweaks. Airbnb now works out the story first, and the story often shapes the product. Growth optimization still matters, but about 80% of the effort should go to big, long-pass moves.
ex: In 2019 Airbnb spent about $1 billion on Google search ads
A/B tests need a hypothesis; don't test the sofa and ignore the whole living room
He quotes designer Charles Eames: understanding cannot be delegated

marks.d: A laser: precisely balances supply and demand
Explains why a new feature matters
A chandelier: builds up over time

l134|251.c: "Add a zero" forces new thinking; leaders should set the pace and see potential their people can't see yet.
l134|251.e: A common phrase inside Airbnb is "add a zero." It isn't a hard demand for 10x goals. It asks people to imagine the thing ten times bigger or ten times better, and to notice that today's process would break. Then the only option is to take the problem apart into its basic pieces and rebuild it, which is first-principles thinking. He believes a company's speed depends more on how fast decisions get made than on hours worked. If something can be decided in the meeting, don't push it to next week. He quotes legendary basketball coach John Wooden: leaders should see potential in people that they don't see in themselves. Saying "this isn't good enough yet" means you believe they can do better.
ex: He cites former Intel CEO Andy Grove: performance depends on ability and motivation
In a growth-minded organization, being pushed means being trusted

terms.d: Settle it in the meeting; set the pace
Believe the team can do better

result.d: Instead of a slow bureaucracy

l134|251.c: Reliability has been Airbnb's weak spot; he wants review data to make listings both unique and dependable.
l134|251.e: Every Airbnb listing is different, but guests only learn whether it matches the photos when they open the door. That's exactly where hotels win: predictable, even if bland. The Guest Favorites feature launched this winter combines reviews, customer-service tickets, and host cancellation data to pick out the best-loved listings. He argues that a good guest experience starts with good tools for hosts, so the listing management page was rebuilt too. Changes that span guests, hosts, and marketing like this only happen in a company that works as one unit. He also predicts flat design is on its way out, and interfaces will return to color, texture, and depth.
ex: Listings are selected using about 370 million reviews and other signals
An AI photo tour, trained on 100 million photos, sorts pictures by room automatically
No more separate guest and host teams; designers and engineers move between projects

l134|251.c: Don't let your inbox run your calendar. Plan your time on purpose and protect your health and relationships.
l134|251.e: He used to spend all day reacting to emails and meeting requests, so passively that he drifted away from old friends. Now he reminds himself that life is finite and decides deliberately whom to see and what to do. He says no to "fake work," the kind that looks like work but moves nothing forward. He treats health, work, and relationships as three pillars: he exercises, takes every other week off, and travels regularly with friends from high school and college. He also keeps a beginner's mind, researching where the divisional structure originally came from and asking for help from people even just a year or two ahead of him.
ex: A roughly 85-year Harvard happiness study found healthy relationships matter most
Helping OpenAI's Sam Altman is his way of passing on Michael Seibel's earlier kindness
He hopes to still believe about 70% of what he says today a few years from now

items.d: There's less time than you think
Don't let email set the agenda

l135|34.c: Product ops doesn't take decisions away from product managers; it clears the busywork so they can focus on strategy.
l135|34.e: She stresses that product ops only informs decisions; it never takes decision-making away from product managers. Writing SQL or spending dozens of hours scheduling interviews is operational work that doesn't itself help you decide what to build. What PMs keep: deciding what to build and getting the team to ship it, doing user research themselves, handling hard tradeoff conversations, and owning the outcome. Product ops isn't program management either; it won't track your sprint progress. Companies face a choice: hire lots of PMs who spend only 30% of their time on strategy, or build an ops team that provides shared systems.
ex: Early on at OpenSky she learned MongoDB just to pull data, then never used it again
After simulating the PM job, many of her Harvard MBA students gave up on the career
Many CPOs are busy picking roadmap templates instead of doing strategy

items: Make product decisions and drive delivery

d.verdict: Product ops is the PM for the PMs

l135|34.c: Which pillar comes first depends on stage: fast-growing companies fix data first, big enterprises start with governance.
l135|34.e: She has noticed that fast-growing companies usually start with business and data insights, so they can monitor progress and feed strategy. Large companies in the middle of a transformation often have no product operating model at all, so they need process and governance more. For example, roadmaps from every team need to roll up into one view so the CPO can see what everyone is doing and whether the money is well spent. Jira can't do that. Data insights matter most for executives: breaking ARR (annual recurring revenue) down by customer segment, product line, and feature adoption is the only way to test whether a strategy like "move upmarket to enterprise" is actually working.
ex: ARR broken down by segment and product line is more useful than total ARR
Forsta's CPO: board materials must be reproducible, or they're stale as soon as you use them

marks.d: Roll up roadmaps, build the operating model

l135|34.c: Product ops should be a lean shared service: start with one person, and a 1:1 ratio with PMs is wrong.
l135|34.e: She suggests finding the most painful pillar and putting one person on it. That alone usually frees up a lot of PM time. Add people only when you hit a new bottleneck the first person can't solve. If product instrumentation is poor, you can temporarily assign a data analyst to each product director. Once instrumentation is solid and PMs can pull their own data, the team can shrink again. In her view, product ops should fill gaps with software, tools, and process, then make those systems run on their own. So the role won't disappear, but headcount should stay small. One ops person per PM is definitely wrong.
ex: Denise adds that a 1:100 ratio is just as wrong
Replying to investor Casey Winters: automated systems still need someone to maintain them

items.d: A few people maintain self-running systems

l135|34.c: Hire for the expertise each pillar needs, plus an instinct to turn repetitive work into systems.
l135|34.e: People doing business and data insights don't need a product background. They need to interpret data and tell a story with it. Former consultants or analysts who know BI tools are ideal, not database engineers. People running process and governance must have been product managers; an agile coach who never did the job tends to slide back into optimizing Scrum. People doing customer insights ideally come from research operations. Her favorite interview question: tell me about a task you hated and how you automated or systematized it. Product ops should report to the CPO. If the leader has no time to coach, hire experienced people.
ex: Fidelity's Jen Cardello built a participant pool and tiered certifications for researchers
A growth-stage CPO's very first hire can be product ops

terms.d: Data analysis, product management, or user research

result.d: Reports to the CPO

l135|34.c: Training product managers can't fix system-wide problems; Athenahealth filled the gap with product ops.
l135|34.e: At Athenahealth she trained every product manager. Even after their skills improved, some problems training couldn't fix remained, like the CEO digging through hundreds of thousands of Jira tickets to see what teams were working on. So they taught people to write meaningful epics, chose software to roll everything up into a portfolio roadmap, and built OKR dashboards. The company created a VP of product operations and, while instrumentation was still weak, paired each director with a data analyst. Several people moved into data or research roles after the training. The company has reorganized many times since and kept product ops every time.
ex: A product director typically oversaw 5 to 8 Scrum teams
The company was rolling out Amplitude across the organization at the time
The current CPO says she'll never join a company without product ops again

l135|252.c: Product ops has three pillars, and all of them exist to make product decisions faster and better.
l135|252.e: She points out that many product managers spend 20 to 30% of their time gathering and cleaning data. Product ops exists to send them back to the strategy work they were hired for. The framework has three parts. Business and data insights supply quantitative inputs like engagement and revenue. Customer and market insights handle qualitative input and make sure PMs hear from more than one or two customers. Process and practices establish consistent ways of working. Which pillar comes first depends on the company's biggest opportunity and pain point. Customer insights is the pillar most often neglected and the one with the most room to grow.
ex: No need for a separate BI team; add a product lens to the data you already have
Program managers run long-term programs; project managers run projects with deadlines

l135|252.c: Process owners need high emotional intelligence: suggest methods rather than mandate them, and keep checking they still work.
l135|252.e: She believes the person running process and practices has to read the unspoken tension in teams, judge how much method to introduce, and roll it out as a suggestion rather than a mandate. PMs usually welcome it, since they no longer have to worry about roadmap templates and cadences. Process isn't set once and forgotten; it needs constant checking to see whether it still works. In their research, interviewees kept naming go-to-market as a major pain point. Product ops can be the bridge between sales and product, breaking down silos with simple templates and training, and help the CPO build a consistent narrative for the board and quarterly reviews.
ex: At a large enterprise she's working with now, silos are the biggest problem
Check whether each team's quarterly review tells the same strategic story

items.d: Are the tools and process still useful?

l135|252.c: Product ops usually grows organically: listen first, grab quick wins, then make the case for more people.
l135|252.e: She rarely sees a company build a full team from day one. More often a product manager feels the pain, carves out some time to build support systems for colleagues, finds they enjoy it, and moves into the role. She cites Shintaro Matsui at Amplitude: start with a listening tour and a research sprint, find the fastest wins within one person's reach, celebrate the small ones, and be clear about what one person can do versus what needs a bigger team. When hiring, don't judge by title alone; many people have done this work under a PM title.
ex: In 2020 about 60% of her students were just curious; now about 60% have the role in place
Blake Samic built product ops at Uber, then Stripe, then OpenAI

items.d: What one person can do vs. a bigger team

l136|255.c: There's nothing wrong with the default path; the problem is never noticing you're following a script.
l136|255.e: The "default path" is the script in your head about how life should go: good school, good job, house and family, then uninterrupted work through adulthood. He isn't against it. He wants people to see its costs and its unspoken contracts, like still feeling you must sit at a desk eight hours a day after you've quit. He also argues that everyone is already on a pathless path: companies reinvent themselves every two years and solid middle-class jobs are shrinking. Planning your life around a smooth promotion curve actually narrows your options.
ex: A friend listed four priorities using the book's method and found his current job met three
He cites MIT economist David Autor's research on the shrinking of middle-class jobs

items: Rearrange how work fits your life
Trust that things will work out

d.verdict: It's not about switching paths, but choosing awake

l136|255.c: Work doesn't have to be something you endure; you can design your life around work you genuinely love.
l136|255.e: For his first thirty-odd years he assumed work was a grind you simply tolerate. After quitting, he planned to escape work altogether and moved to Asia, cutting his living costs to about $1,000 a month. Instead he unexpectedly fell in love with writing and creating in public, and realized he could build his life around work he loved. He thinks it's hard to find meaning inside a "job-shaped container"; it usually runs out after seven to ten years. Now he makes decisions by the rule "aliveness over achievement," which is why he turned down a second-book deal from Penguin.
ex: In Asia he cut his monthly spending to about $1,000
He turned down Penguin so he could write his second book his own way

items.d: Endure it and find small pleasures
Public writing brings energy and connection
Protect the work you truly want to do

l136|255.c: A three-month break is easier than you think; at minimum, steal three hours on a weekday for yourself.
l136|255.e: Adult working life runs about 500 months. Taking three of them to get to know yourself isn't extravagant; people save for far harder things, like a house. In his experience it takes six to eight weeks just to shake off work mode. He has talked with more than 500 people about work, and almost all of them found a break worth it. If you can't manage that yet, block three hours on a weekday to wander aimlessly or pick up a childhood hobby. Then notice where the guilt of sneaking away comes from, and ask yourself why you work at all. A step further: find someone a bit ahead of you on a similar path and have a "path expert" conversation.
ex: Intel gives employees six weeks off after seven years
Before the pandemic he opened his calendar every Wednesday and talked with 500+ people

items.d: It has to be a weekday
Do something you loved as a kid, aimlessly
Where does the guilt come from?

l136|255.c: Doing what you love pays better in the long run, but expect your income to drop for the first few years.
l136|255.e: For three years after quitting he deliberately optimized for exploration rather than income, living on freelance work and low expenses. Only in year five did he get close to his old salary. Then the year he published his book, his income hit a new high, with the book alone bringing in close to $200,000. He suggests naming the cost of your exploration, say a "life MBA": business school also means two years without pay and well over $100,000 in fees, yet people praise you for it. Another reframe: treat savings from your old job as a gift from your past self. You can also make room by living abroad or turning your current job into a three-day-a-week contract.
ex: Business school costs about $150,000 to $200,000 over two years with no salary
Employers are more willing than you'd expect to convert a full-time role to contract work

items.d: Near old salary only in year 5

l136|255.c: Fear never goes away. Count the cost of inaction, and learn to talk with the fears that stay.
l136|255.e: He borrows Tim Ferriss's fear-setting exercise: write down what you're afraid of and how you'd cope, and, most importantly, estimate the cost of not acting. That pushed him to hire a community manager quickly, because not hiring would have drained his creative energy. But for existential fears about health or money, he no longer expects to get rid of them. When one surfaces, he acknowledges it and reassures himself: I've lasted six and a half years, so I can probably last a lot longer. He also notes that people mostly regret what they didn't do. Mistakes can be fixed; things never tried can't be.
ex: Inspired by Lenny hiring a community manager, he hired one too
Most people get creative fast once the income stops

root.d: Without going back to a job to kill it

items.d: Count the cost of inaction, then act fast
Acknowledge them and live alongside them
People regret what they didn't do

l136|255.c: Run low-risk experiments before quitting, follow what gives you energy, and don't build yourself a job you hate.
l136|255.e: Years before quitting, he was already testing side projects: editing resumes, career coaching, writing on Quora and Medium. He couldn't explain why they mattered, but each one gave him energy, and that made him brave enough to leave. His rule is "ship, quit, learn": build the smallest version you can walk away from, like committing to only five podcast episodes and continuing if it feels good. A few early consulting gigs taught him to set guardrails so he wouldn't recreate a job he disliked. Today 95% of his days have no meetings, he works with contractors asynchronously, and his consulting-skills training is a self-paced course that funds his exploration.
ex: He committed to just five podcast episodes and kept going only because it felt right
His StrategyU self-paced course was his main income for two to five years

items.d: Build the smallest version you can quit
Did it charge you or drain you?
Don't build yourself a bad job

l136|255.c: Don't worry about everyone quitting: most people would hate this life, and work itself is becoming gig-like anyway.
l136|255.e: Some people object that if everyone took the pathless path, nobody would be left to work at companies. He doesn't buy it: most people's first reaction to his lifestyle is "absolutely not." Meanwhile work itself is becoming gig-like. He cites economist David Deming's research showing that labor-market growth from 2005 to 2015 came from nontraditional work arrangements, and companies increasingly move people around by project internally. He thinks businesses still underestimate freelancing and the creator economy. In the future people may move more easily between modes of work. Many who try it and return to a job are happier, because they've learned where their limits are.
ex: David Deming: labor growth from 2005 to 2015 came from nontraditional work arrangements
People who try it and go back to a job are often more content

marks.d: Three days a week, more autonomy

l137|257.c: Career satisfaction comes from products you love and people you admire, not from being a founder.
l137|257.e: Looking back, his satisfaction had almost nothing to do with external measures like user numbers or financial returns. It tracked two things: whether he loved what he was building and whether he liked the people. When judging a team, trust your gut. Every time he joined a company and found a values mismatch, he had sensed it beforehand and talked himself out of it. His contrarian view is that the industry has too many founders. Plenty of smart people take a $2 million seed round into a company that was never going to work. Joining a team that needs your skills and whose equation adds up can bring the same recognition, reward and impact.
ex: He has never been a founder, yet did his best work at several young companies
The founders of Pandora and Zero called him founder-like; he politely declined the label

terms.d: Build something you truly care about
Market and business model add up

result.d: No seed round required

l137|257.c: Raising too much money is itself a burden; it drags competitors into an arms race nobody wins.
l137|257.e: Three online pet retailers each raised more than $50 million and all treated the market as zero-sum. When one bought national TV ads, the others followed, and in the end nobody won. He thinks the critique that selling dog food online could never work is wrong; Chewy later proved it works fine. The problem was timing: about 80% of American internet users were still on dial-up. The company went from founding to IPO to shutdown in roughly 19 months. Management chose to wind down deliberately and return the remaining cash to investors rather than burn the last dollar.
ex: Chewy was bought by PetSmart for about $3 billion and is now worth around $9 billion
The failure became his way into Pandora

l137|257.c: Quibi's business equation never added up, so no amount of execution or iteration could save it.
l137|257.e: Quibi bet about $2 billion on building a library of mobile-only shows big enough to make people subscribe and stay. The team made 70 shows in 18 months, with daily content eating about a third of the budget, then launched two weeks into COVID and had to shoot in hosts' garages. The model also required hitting the top ten of the app store at launch and staying there. Hollywood marketers thought that was easy; Silicon Valley people knew it was brutally hard. He had assumed they could spend a year or two tuning the funnel like a normal startup, but a billion dollars a year in content meant it had to be a hit immediately. In hindsight he should have pushed harder on the risk in the distribution assumption.
ex: He estimates it really needed $6 billion to $10 billion
Even Uber, spending heavily on acquisition, could not stay in the download top ten

items: A year or two to tune the funnel
Mediocre retention can be fixed over time

d.verdict: A broken equation; execution and iteration cannot fix it

l137|257.c: A company is an equation that turns investment into returns; model the whole thing, then find the biggest levers.
l137|257.e: Early on he saw software as art: find people with insight into human nature, build something stunning, then optimize with numbers. Only in his fifties, as CEO of Zero and also running financial planning, did he truly see the company as an equation. His instinct was to stare at the bottom of the funnel, install to signup, signup to trial. Then he built a model that pulled all the data together and could play out future scenarios, and only then could he see which variables had the most leverage. It also solved a long-standing puzzle: boards rarely ask about features because investors are looking at the equation.
ex: Zero chose to grow by raising lifetime value per user rather than paying to fill the top of the funnel
Zero has over a million monthly actives and 100,000-plus subscribers with zero paid acquisition

items.d: Move variables but not the equation

l137|257.c: You only get forced to master one thing in a culture with clear lanes that judges your own output.
l137|257.e: He spent four years at Apple while Jobs was gone. The culture rewarded weighing in across functions, so he became the guy with an opinion on everything, six miles wide and an inch deep, and the features he wrote took four years to ship. He then moved to Berkeley Systems, maker of You Don't Know Jack, where his only job was shipping quality software on time. His clever opinions on gameplay and packaging counted for nothing in his review. That constraint made him write a lot of code, learn to manage, and become a real engineer.
ex: A folder-blink effect he hacked together at 2am is still in macOS 30 years later
You Don't Know Jack is still getting sequels nearly 30 years on

l137|257.c: Pandora won by treating users like people, and lost by betting on radio instead of streaming.
l137|257.e: In its first year Pandora had no support team. The support inbox went to the whole company, whoever saw an email first answered it, there were no templates, and staff were free to criticize the company's own product decisions. At the height of the iPod era, being a real human rather than a polished brand became the word-of-mouth engine, and during his tenure they never paid for a single user while growing to 80 million. But they treated the much larger ad-supported radio market as the main prize and relied on a government statutory license. They missed that all music would eventually stream from the cloud on the labels' terms. After the IPO the company lacked the capital to take risks, and Spotify took the lead.
ex: The support@ address was literally the all@ address
The biggest digital music exit at the time was only about $400 million (Musicmatch)

l137|257.c: Capital and standing let founders make bold bets, but in small teams a CEO should use a light touch.
l137|257.e: At Snap he mostly executed Evan Spiegel's vision, and the biggest lesson was risk-taking. With deep capital and solid investor relationships, Evan could buy game-changing technology and ship speculative features that would have been cut anywhere else. When enough land, nobody remembers the misses. He also understands why a product-minded CEO at a big company makes the calls himself: Apple without Jobs had too many smart people and "a thousand to one was a tie," until Jobs came back and stopped holding votes. But small teams should be steered lightly. The CEO should know the details deeply without dictating outcomes, because a casual question from the boss usually turns into an assignment.
ex: After one morning of interviews, Snap offered him the VP role on the spot
Labeling the strength of opinions, Coda-style, still only helps so much

l137|257.c: Lasting decades without burning out comes from loving the work, not performing long hours.
l137|257.e: He measures work with the Japanese idea of ikigai: the overlap of what you love, what you are good at, what the world needs and what pays. Choices that cover only three of the four tend to feel slightly off. Software is both his job and his hobby, which is why he has sustained it for decades. As a young engineer he got praised for all-nighters, but a teammate who arrived at 8:30 and left on time contributed more, so at Pandora he made a point of not rewarding performative effort. After leaving Pandora he traveled the world and realized he cared most about relationships, and on Monday morning everyone he cared about was at work.
ex: He once planned to live three months each in London and Mexico City
His interview question: what does a really great day look like for you

root.d: The overlap of four things lasts longest

l139|259.c: AI replacing developers is overrated; AI writing your tests is badly underrated.
l139|259.e: She thinks the idea that generative AI will replace people and solve everything is overrated. Innovation and creative thinking still belong to humans, and AI itself depends on the data people generate by using tools, so a human has to stay in the loop. What is underrated is AI-driven testing. As AI multiplies the amount of code and the number of applications, and every company becomes a software company, verification matters more. Expecting people to write complete unit, functional, load, security and penetration tests by hand is not enough; AI should generate fuller test suites.
ex: She cites data that about 92% of developers already use AI tools

d.verdict: Copilot is a copilot, not a pilot

l139|259.c: Once AI handles simple code, developers should think in systems and architecture from day one.
l139|259.e: She expects that within three to five years the developer's focus will move from writing code to the bigger picture: systems, architecture, how experiences connect, and how to use AI tools well. Today that mindset mostly belongs to senior engineers, because newcomers first spend years learning to write simple code. With an AI assistant doing that part, a new developer can start understanding the system, the runtime environment and the product on day one. She also thinks AI's hunger for compute will make hardware and code optimization mainstream, and integrating with AI will become a basic skill for every developer.
ex: Compute demand will push CPU, GPU and code optimization into the spotlight

items.d: New hires understand systems on day one
Architecture and AI integration as basics

l139|259.c: Start from the problem you need to solve, not from asking what you could do with AI.
l139|259.e: She sees two common mistakes. One is assuming that handing out a tool makes it work, ignoring change management. The other is getting swept up in the hype and constantly asking what to do with AI. GitHub started from a problem: developers were buried in chores and spent too little time coding. Only then did it decide to plug in OpenAI's models to automate part of the coding. Copilot's design followed from that. Developers are already overloaded, so any tool that requires extra invoking, waiting or learning will not get used; it has to blend into the workflow. GitHub also insists on using its own products, polishing features internally for months before release.
ex: GitHub's finance, legal and HR teams also collaborate through pull requests and Discussions
In 2020 internal engineers and designers built Copilot together with OpenAI

root.d: Not AI for its own sake

items.d: Tools do not work by themselves

l139|259.c: Do not judge an AI coding tool only by time saved; the real goal is developer happiness.
l139|259.e: No single metric tells the whole story, she says. Developers often spend less than 20% of their time writing code; the rest goes to meetings, waiting for builds and reading old code. Giving them back half an hour a day means more coding, room to breathe, and space for collaboration and innovation, which is why it should not be an excuse for layoffs. But time alone is not success, since you can write bad code quickly. Each area needs its own measure, such as how many leaked secrets a security feature catches. She likes time-to-value as the link to business goals, and rolls everything up into developer happiness.
ex: Surveys show coding about 55% faster with Copilot, and 88% of users feel less frustrated
More than 37,000 organizations and 1.5 million developers already use it

result.d: The thing to optimize for

l139|259.c: General-purpose models will not do everything; the future mixes specialized models with several large ones.
l139|259.e: Her early career was in specialized AI that took years to tune, and she never expected generative AI to put AI in the hands of people who know nothing about it. But she thinks the industry is betting too heavily on general-purpose models. They are limited by their training data, give statistical recommendations, and try to be everything to everyone. In fields like aviation and automotive, with strict safety regulation and fine-grained tuning, she does not see autonomous driving models being built on ChatGPT. She predicts a return to a hybrid world: several large models combined for their strengths, alongside custom models built for specific scenarios.
ex: She used to tune sensor filtering in the aerospace and automotive industries

marks.d: Several LLMs, each for its strength

l139|259.c: A research team needs freedom to look far ahead, but must be tied to product from day one.
l139|259.e: Copilot came out of GitHub Next, an applied research team that looks three to five years out, writes papers and runs experiments. She thinks similar teams elsewhere usually fail in one of two ways: they become a "university" that produces papers but nothing that ships, or they get treated as a tactical team told to build something in six months. GitHub's balance is to pick the right people and mindset, give them real freedom, and keep a two-way conversation with product and engineering. Ideas also come from customers, the open-source community and frontline teams, and employees can pitch research proposals to get resources for a proof of concept. But she is against structuring innovation.
ex: Counterexample: mandating 15 minutes a day for innovation
The Copilot Workspace vision was announced six months to a year early

items.d: Proof of concept, virtual team, or Next
Plan for shipping from day one

l139|259.c: A CPO must understand the business, think in systems, and explain why before driving change.
l139|259.e: A chief product officer, she argues, is far more than head of product. You need to understand the business, the market and sales, apply the systems thinking she learned from her first boss in aviation, and use influence to get engineering and revenue teams moving toward one vision. Her biggest lesson came at TomTom. As the new leader she immediately saw a long list of problems and charged in to fix them all, without first building agreement on why change was needed. The team told her she was moving too fast and had to explain her reasons. Newcomers spot the flaws veterans have stopped noticing, but they have to build the communication bridge first.
ex: In her first multinational job she found her personal style did not fit every culture
Her favorite interview question: what is the most innovative thing you have done

items.d: See each part inside the whole
Get others acting on the vision

l140|260.c: A good vision is big yet reachable, free of today's constraints, and rooted in a real user problem.
l140|260.e: Every product manager needs a vision regardless of level, she argues, just as passengers need to know where the plane is going. A vision is the picture of the destination you paint after traveling to the future; the mission is why you set out and what principles guide the trip. A good vision has four ingredients. It is big enough to be both scary and exciting. It is realistic enough to be within reach. It is not bound by today's technology or conditions, so you can look back from the future and see what is missing now. And it rests on a clear, strongly felt user problem.
ex: Uber's vision: a city that no longer needs parking, which takes up about 25% of a city
The mountain analogy: the view from the summit is the vision, why you climb is the mission

root.d: A picture of the future destination

items.d: A clear, strongly felt user pain

l140|260.c: Sell a vision with stories, not numbers: a story template, then a future headline, then a drawing.
l140|260.e: Storytelling is a product manager's most powerful skill, she says; humans pass down stories, not statistics. The simplest tool is a template: "Once upon a time... until one day... because of that... until finally..." The next step is traveling to the future and writing the headline and subhead a publication would run once you succeed, which forces you to name the pain you solved. The step after that is drawing it. Not having a designer is no excuse: sketch on sticky notes, or draw the four hero screenshots in blank App Store frames. People usually end up drawing the same two or three key ideas.
ex: Her design partner sketched cash top-ups for Uber at corner stores; it shipped four years later
She once wrote the imaginary headline "Uber will replace your Clipper card"

items.d: Once upon a time... until finally
Design mocks or even a concept video

l140|260.c: Keep a list of "ten things you should know" so the whole team agrees on the top problem.
l140|260.e: The first step in building a vision is empathy. She asks product managers to use their own product (eat the dog food) and competitors' products (eat the cat food), opening several accounts to walk through the new-user experience. Research should supply the foundational questions a few cycles ahead rather than make the judgment for you. Each PM keeps a quarterly-updated list of questions, qualitative or quantitative, including technical debt, because infrastructure is a product too. Before a strategy session she has marketing, support, data and others submit ten questions each in the same template, then refines them into one final list.
ex: At Uber she called the list "Mo' Money, Mo' Problems"
One insight on it: the average American reads at about an 11-year-old's level

items.d: The team agrees on the answers

l140|260.c: Clarity comes from writing: two pages covering insights, strategy and three to five big rocks.
l140|260.e: She separates vision from narrative. The vision paints the world once the problem is solved; the narrative is like a startup explaining to investors why it exists, how it will work and what it will deliver. She often runs a three-day strategy session, focusing in turn on insights, strategy and big rocks, and requires the result as a two-page document. There can be only three to five big rocks. Like putting ice in a cocktail glass first, the roadmap cannot be a long list; the small things are sand that fills the gaps. The narrative comes before the roadmap and lives as an evergreen document. When someone asks her for a briefing, she sends them to read it first.
ex: Planning rule: any problem needing fewer than three engineers gets merged
The evergreen document has a short link everyone remembers

terms.d: What: three to five big things

result.d: The roadmap follows from it

l140|260.c: Spread a vision from the inside out: your team first, then stakeholders, then as high up as possible.
l140|260.e: She pictures evangelism as three concentric circles. The core is the whole team, not just the PM: tell the story several times, leave time for it to sink in, and open the document to comments so friction polishes the idea. The second ring is stakeholders and neighboring teams, who will push back from the angle of support volume or immediate needs. The outer ring is leadership: go as high as you can and aim big, letting your managers pull you back. A vision should last at least three years, so you do not rewrite it every year, you just keep raising the fidelity. Her Vision 2026 at YouTube only entered the planning cycle a year and a half later.
ex: As an L5/L6 at Uber she presented "one wallet for every service" at an all-hands
Ask everyone for their ten things early, and they feel heard when you evangelize

items.d: PM, engineering and design all on board
Neighboring teams bring challenges and views
Go as high as you can, think big

l140|260.c: The PM craft is clarity plus conviction, and a conviction you cannot state clearly is not one.
l140|260.e: She reduces product management to two things. Clarity means filtering out the noise so people understand the problem and what you want; even an email should say whether it is an FYI or a request for help. Conviction is a feeling about how the world should be, not certainty. If someone says all five things should be done, they do not have conviction yet. She asks, "if you had almost no resources, which one would you do?" to force the trade-off, then spends research where conviction is weakest instead of spreading resources evenly. She also refuses to let a team hand the pros and cons of options A and B to leadership to decide.
ex: If dumping the research into AI would produce the PRD, the PM has not done their job
Career-switch advice: list the top ten problems with apps you use to build product sense

items: A little of all five things
Hand the A/B choice to your boss
Pick one path even with few resources
The team makes the trade-off itself

d.verdict: Conviction without clarity is not conviction

l140|260.c: A culture that is not deliberately evolved drifts on its own, and culture decides how a product can change.
l140|260.e: She saw three cultures at three companies. Early Uber was a strong monoculture: hire the right people, give them autonomy, and encourage anyone at any level to argue their case. Her team used data and tests to overturn Travis Kalanick's objection to cash payments. But the culture was never revisited and updated, and it eventually led to the #DeleteUber crisis. Netflix deliberately keeps evolving its culture, using written debate and a single informed decision-maker, which is how a product devoted to pure subscription finally accepted ads. Google is like a city: a loose overall culture with micro-cultures in each business, which lets it run Cloud and YouTube at the same time.
ex: About 400,000 people deleted the app during #DeleteUber
She was Uber employee number 1024 and started as a city general manager

marks.d: Autonomy and debate, but never evolved
A city where each district has its own culture

l140|260.c: Aim to be loved, not liked: care about people and hard feedback lands.
l140|260.e: She and her engineering and design partners spell out the team culture: freedom with responsibility, act like an owner not a renter, and one informed decision-maker per decision rather than consensus. She believes vulnerability is a strength. She defines love as giving of yourself for someone else's growth, which is not the same as being easygoing and includes hard conversations. As long as people are sure you care about the person behind the role, direct feedback reads as kindness. Know your engineering manager's birthday and why they do the job, she suggests, and help each other polish PRDs.
ex: She and her EM at the time, Gergely Orosz, went from disliking each other to close friends
On her Uber team she borrowed the values from the Netflix culture memo

d.center: Care about the person behind the role

l141|261.c: India has huge numbers, many languages and low spending power, so picking paying users is the core skill.
l141|261.e: India only started building products for its own consumers around 2010, he says; before that, engineers mostly wrote back-end code for Western clients. Early e-commerce executives came from consumer goods and manufacturing and assumed resources in meant predictable output, and it took a few cycles to learn that software is not a machine. Jio drove data prices close to zero and brought a wave of new internet users, while UPI and other digital infrastructure made small payments routine. But India is extremely diverse in language and culture, and income per person is only a little over $2,000. Traffic is easy; paying customers are hard. Finding users who will pay a delivery fee or buy pricier goods takes much more work.
ex: The saying goes that language and culture change every 15 miles
He estimates US income per person is about 30 times India's

items.d: Cheap data brings new users online

l141|261.c: New users are lazy, vain and selfish, so onboarding decides more than core features do.
l141|261.e: He borrows Scott Belsky's framing: today's internet users are lazy, so they leave unless something dazzles them; vain, so they will not change their habits for you; and selfish, so they only care what is in it for them. Product managers stare at their product all day and assume users care just as much. That is why copy, onboarding and the first welcome often move the needle more than core features built for loyal users. At Swiggy they reconstructed the moment a user hears about the app and downloads it, carried the marketing promise seamlessly into the onboarding screens, pitched a single value proposition, and only later steered people toward other services.
ex: PMs are in the business of influence, inside and out, so think like a marketer about prospects
Jupiter users often use one service; cross-selling has to follow the value they already found

items: Users think about the product all day
Build good features and they will come
Selfish: what is in it for me

d.verdict: Design onboarding for lazy, vain, selfish users

l141|261.c: The point of a press release is to get dates, goals and every team agreed on one page.
l141|261.e: Amazon's press release method, in his view, works backwards from more than user value: it works backwards from how the whole machine runs on launch day. With one page and a date, you can ask the engineering lead whether they can deliver on time, use the customer quote to pin down marketing and pricing, and use the business owner's quote to lock in the three-month target. If someone says it cannot be done, you adjust the date or the goal together. The FAQ bakes process in, such as always asking whether compliance has signed off on a financial product. He has teams write three very different press releases and recommend one, so every view is visible and leaders get a real choice.
ex: Swiggy's FAQ always asks about the impact on restaurants and delivery partners
Think harder first: most experiments should stay thought experiments

items.d: Work back to what must be ready
What customers and business owners say
If not, change the date or goal

l141|261.c: Put a specific person's whole journey, in a real situation, up on the wall instead of describing it.
l141|261.e: This extends working backwards. He skips abstract personas and picks a specific person: how old, what income, what happened with this category in the last three days. Then he asks what triggers them to open the app at 11am, and from there every pixel and every line of copy has to serve why they came; half of his product reviews are spent here. In a real-time marketplace you also play out the 30 minutes after the order: the food is late, the rider gets a flat tire, what is the customer thinking? The leadership version draws the company's whole growth loop on one page, again in three versions to compare. The biggest payoff is that everyone ends up aligned.
ex: The rule: a specific person, not a persona
The wall became a shared place for deep discussions with every function

items.d: Why they open the app at 11am
Each pixel and line of copy
Emotions in the 30 minutes after ordering

l141|261.c: How to split resources across types of work is strategy, decided by the product head and CEO together.
l141|261.e: He sorts product work into four buckets. Brilliant Basics is technical debt and core platform, and a good name keeps it from being dismissed. Bread and Butter is the iteration, bug fixes and experiments a PM prioritizes on their own. Big Bets need sign-off from several teams and a written PR FAQ. Breaking Bad means redefining the company, like a food delivery business moving into groceries. He insists this is not a tactical PM ranking. You take 100 points of attention to leadership and negotiate the split, spelling out what each mix costs, for example that underinvesting in basics means accepting more outages.
ex: Swiggy expanded from food delivery to groceries, then to convenience services
Every PM assigned to a Big Bet helps write the PR FAQ

l141|261.c: In a three-sided marketplace the sides trade off against each other, so OKRs and A/B tests break down.
l141|261.e: A three-sided marketplace is not one plus one, he says; it goes from flat to three-dimensional. Charging users more for delivery, taking more commission from restaurants and paying riders less are three levers tied to each other. Split them into OKRs for different teams and the goals clash forever; a Big Bet that explains the whole picture sets direction better. Network effects also make it hard to isolate an A/B test on the rider side. His rule is to first keep every side stable so nobody leaves, then let the company vision decide whom to serve first. Swiggy changed "customer first" to "consumer first": riders, restaurants and the platform together serve the person ordering.
ex: Amazon leans toward consumers; Taobao's mission is serving millions of sellers
A PM building rider tools still has to speak for the consumer side

l141|261.c: Things fail for only three reasons, and 70 to 80 percent of the time the leader set people up wrong.
l141|261.e: He diagnoses with a three-way split. "Can't do" is a capability problem: coach the person or move them to a better fit. "Won't do" is motivation or alignment: find out whether they disagree with the vision or simply have no time. "Not set up to succeed" is the leader's own fault. He finds 70 to 80 percent of cases fall in the last bucket, such as OKRs whose organizational impact nobody thought through, or a poorly designed org. As Conway's law says, you can guess the org chart by looking at the product. He also says bluntly that most PMs should not be PMs: intelligence can mostly be learned, grit is hardest to build, and influence is non-negotiable.
ex: He recommends Team Topologies, which builds org design on Conway's law
His creed: do not externalize problems; you are the source of your own pain

l142|264.c: Radical candor means caring personally and challenging directly at the same time; drop either and it fails.
l142|264.e: She explains it with a two-by-two. The vertical axis is how much you care personally, the horizontal axis is how directly you challenge, and only both together is radical candor. Challenging without caring is obnoxious aggression: it hurts and it does not work, because the other person goes into fight or flight and stops listening. When people realize they went too far they often retreat into fake agreement, which lands in the worst quadrant, manipulative insincerity. Caring without challenging is ruinous empathy, where she estimates 90% of people make 90% of their mistakes. The framework should work like a compass to guide a specific conversation, not as a way to label yourself or others.
ex: The common misuse: being a jerk in the name of candor, which is just obnoxious aggression

cells.d: Most common: staying silent to spare feelings

l142|264.c: Staying quiet to spare feelings hurts more in the end: ruinous empathy is the most common and most damaging mistake.
l142|264.e: She once hired Bob, who was funny and likable but did sloppy work. She was afraid of hurting him, and afraid he would cry and make her look mean, so for ten months she only said "maybe make it a little better." The team ended up redoing his work, deadlines slipped, her best people were ready to leave, and she had to fire him. He asked why nobody had told him. Her takeaway: the job is not to be liked, it is to care, and in the long run silence is the unkind choice. Now she first asks the person to diagnose the problem themselves, then names the issues one by one, and keeps going if they brush her off.
ex: Caring in practice: three 45-minute career conversations about past, dreams and action plan
People overestimate how upset others will be, a kind of negativity bias

items.d: Could not bring herself to be harsh

l142|264.c: Give feedback humbly, helpfully, immediately and in person, using context, observation, result, next step.
l142|264.e: She refuses to give scripts, because copying one will not sound like you, but she offers principles. Be humble: your candor is your view, not the truth. State that you intend to help. Say it immediately, because waiting for a better moment usually means never. Say it synchronously, where a phone call can beat video, and feedback over Slack is guaranteed to go wrong. Praise in public, criticize in private. Talk about behavior, not personality. For the wording she uses CORE: context, observation, result, next step, which works for praise too. Praise matters more than criticism, and these two-minute impromptu moments should not wait for a one-on-one.
ex: The mnemonic HHIIPPP: humble, helpful, immediate, in person, public praise, private criticism, not personal
Her boss's "you say 'um' so much it makes you sound stupid" was a complete CORE

items.d: It made you sound less smart

l142|264.c: Ask for criticism before you give it, and when you get it, reward the candor.
l142|264.e: Radical candor has an order of operations, she says, and step one is asking others to criticize you. It improves the relationship more than anything and makes your own feedback easier to give later. "Any feedback for me?" only gets "everything's fine," so prepare a specific question in your own words, such as what you could do or stop doing to make working together easier. Then shut up and count to six. Listen to understand rather than to rebut, and ask clarifying questions. Most important, reward the candor: if you agree, fix it and say so publicly, then ask whether you overcorrected; if you disagree, first acknowledge the ten percent you can agree with, then come back with a reasoned explanation.
ex: One manager saves the last five minutes of every one-on-one for this question
Never accept "nothing"; ask them to bring one item next time

items.d: Your own words, not a script
Clarify, do not rush to argue
Fix it publicly, or explain the disagreement

l142|264.c: Candor is measured at the listener's ear, so watch the reaction and adjust as you go.
l142|264.e: Communication happens on an emotional and a rational level at once, she says, so give feedback where you can see how it lands. Start in the middle rather than with your harshest wording. If the person brushes you off, move further toward challenging directly, the way her old boss had to say it three times before she took it seriously. If they get upset, move toward caring personally and ask how you could have said it better, but do not take the point back, or they end up both sad and confused. If they get angry, stay curious instead of angry, acknowledge that your delivery may have been off, and keep the problem on the table.
ex: Her boss first asked "did you notice?", then suggested a coach, and only then said the harsh line

items.d: Add care, but keep the point
Stay curious; the problem still stands

l142|264.c: You do not have to choose between jerk and pushover; you can be successful and kind.
l142|264.e: She criticizes Bridgewater for criticizing employees publicly and personally in meetings and circulating the recordings, calling it the darkest form of obnoxious aggression; Ray Dalio's hundreds of pages of Principles devote only a few to caring about people. She does not put Steve Jobs in the same category. He could be brutal, but he had deep relationships with his direct reports, and what looked like cruelty to outsiders read as caring between them. Having to choose between a competent jerk and a kind incompetent is a false dilemma. With leaders who do not know how to care, she first tells the story of her own jerk phase, then explains in terms of enlightened self-interest how the behavior holds them back.
ex: When Jobs had cancer, Tim Cook offered part of his liver
Jokingly calling an old colleague a "dumbass" scared bystanders out of making mistakes

d.verdict: You can be both successful and kind

l142|264.c: Candor does not cost everyone the same, and without respect there is no caring or challenging.
l142|264.e: A Black woman CEO told her that even her gentlest criticism got her labeled an angry Black woman, so practicing candor was far harder for her. That made Scott realize she had not been a good upstander as a colleague, and that she had been denying the bias and bullying she had experienced and even inflicted. Becoming a leader makes it easier to bully people without noticing. As a woman raised in the American South, she had herself been mislabeled as aggressive because of the bias that women cannot be both likable and competent. So she wrote Radical Respect, arguing that everyone plays different roles at different moments.
ex: Radical Candor has sold over a million copies and been translated into 23 languages

items.d: Create a respectful environment for the team
What to do when facing bias or bullying

l144|267.c: Every good story is built around a five-second moment of change; everything else is setup.
l144|267.e: He believes almost every story worth hearing is about one moment: a person changes, or their mind changes. Change feels slow, but it builds up and then flips in an instant. The story's job is to let the listener live that instant with the teller, and about 98% of the story is just setting it up. So start from the ending: find the moment first, then make the beginning its opposite. Most people simply report their lives in order, which is hard to connect with. Focus on the change and the story becomes interesting even when the subject has nothing to do with the audience.
ex: A student named Eileen teased him, which told him she finally had enough confidence
In Star Wars, Luke switches off his targeting computer and trusts the Force instead

items.d: A new self or a new understanding

l144|267.c: A good story has change, passes the dinner test, and is your own story.
l144|267.e: He uses three tests. First, something has to change. Second, the dinner test: what you say on stage should be only a slightly polished version of how you'd tell it at the dinner table. Don't open with a floating quote or a sound effect; that's performing. Third, tell your own story. Someone else's experience plays like fiction and can't show your vulnerability. When he teaches descendants of Holocaust survivors, he has them center the story on how their elders' experience changed them. Vacation stories usually bore people unless they contain a change, and then you tell only that moment. As Vonnegut said, start as close to the end as possible.
ex: His most common note: the story started in the wrong place

items.d: Most are just a log of events
A moment of transformation or realization

l144|267.c: Assume nobody wants to listen, then layer in stakes so people need to hear the next line.
l144|267.e: He starts from the assumption that nobody ever wants to hear him talk. Business people often mistake a seated audience for a listening one. Stakes are whatever makes listeners worry, hope, or wonder. His tools: open with an "elephant" that makes people curious right away. Use a "backpack" to lay out your plan, so listeners feel it when the plan goes wrong. Drop "breadcrumbs" as hints. Use a "crystal ball" to predict a bad possible future. At the key moment, flip the "hourglass" and pile on detail to slow time down. Don't dump all the stakes up front; keep adding them through the first half.
ex: Every story opens with a place and an action, which signals "the movie has started"
His demo story "Charity Thief" uses almost every one of these tools

items.d: Make people curious from the start
Slow time down at the key moment

l144|267.c: If you don't tell stories at work you'll be forgotten; standing out is how you're remembered.
l144|267.e: He says most business communication is deliberately smoothed into something round, white, and flavorless, because people fear that leaving the herd gets them eaten. The price is being forgotten. Brains don't hold on to pie charts, data, or slogans; they remember things attached to an image. He and his wife once watched an education conference where one speaker pulled out her childhood lunchbox to talk about her parents' sacrifices, and it stuck. Another executive spoke fluently and confidently, and fifteen minutes later nobody could recall a word. Only four things keep people listening: stakes, surprise, suspense, and humor. Use none of them and the audience is already gone.
ex: The best surprises are unexpected yet feel inevitable
Steve Jobs' product launches are a model of carefully engineered surprise

items.d: The surest way to stand out

l144|267.c: Everyone wants to seem funny but few risk a joke, yet humor follows learnable formulas.
l144|267.e: He thinks almost everyone at work wants to be funny, but what they really want is to have already been funny. Trying a joke is a risk, and a joke that dies hurts. One executive cut every joke from his talk because the two speakers before him weren't funny. Dicks saw that as exactly the moment to stand out. He has catalogued 26 humor strategies, and two work best in business. One is nostalgia, like recalling how in 1983 you found a job through the classified ads on the back of the newspaper. The other is "which one doesn't belong": give two expected items, then a surprising third. If the joke doesn't land, the story simply carries on.
ex: A CEO rejected a nostalgic opener saying "nobody cares about the 80s"; he calls that a mistake
The rival hardware store also sells shovels and nails, but only has self-checkout machines

terms.d: They have all kinds of nails too
But there isn't a single person inside

result.d: The third item breaks the pattern

l144|267.c: Don't scramble for a story when trouble hits; collect your own stories and match them by theme.
l144|267.e: He splits workplace storytelling into two kinds. Asking someone to invent a story when a problem comes up is a Band-Aid; next time you'll need help again. Building up your own stories over time and then deploying them in the business, as factory owner Boris does, is laying bricks. Boris told his sales team about his son striking out in a championship game and heading off for ice cream with friends minutes later, to show them how to bounce back from a lost deal. The trick to finding stories is adjacent matching: don't match content to content, match the theme, meaning, or message, then click it back onto the product. When Slack's head of communications added a personal story about a lonely night, the audience's response changed completely.
ex: List your interests: "married" reaches many people; "ran a marathon" reaches few but bonds strongly

items: Talk about test tubes as test tubes
Forgotten as soon as it ends
Tell a story about buying apples for family
Click it back to custom test tubes

d.verdict: The apple-story scientist got more leads than the other four combined

l144|267.c: Write down one story-worthy moment each day and you'll never run out of stories.
l144|267.e: He worried that storytelling would use up his material, so he gave himself "Homework for Life": every night, in a spreadsheet, he writes a sentence or two about the day's most story-worthy moment. He asks himself: if I had to tell a story about today to get my family back, what would it be? He hoped to find one a month. Instead he found more stories than he could ever tell, his eye got sharper, and old memories came back. About one in ten entries becomes a story. The rest still matter: days stop disappearing, and patterns show up, like realizing he picks "secret fights" with his wife through housework.
ex: A dull note about a neighborhood barbecue later became the opening of a story about two divorces

items.d: Moments recorded per day, on average
A sharper eye, not a more exciting life

l144|267.c: Most nerves hit before you start talking, and the doors that scare you deserve a look.
l144|267.e: He says about 98% of nervousness happens before you open your mouth, and most of it fades once you start. Just knowing that helps, and almost everyone gets nervous. To prepare, record your talk and play it back while grocery shopping or folding laundry. People rarely forget content; they forget transitions, so memorize how you move between scenes and never memorize word for word. On opportunities, say yes first. Saying no assumes you already know what's behind the door, and a yes can always turn into a no. He agreed to try stand-up comedy because it scared him. Now he performs often, while the friend who invited him never went on stage once.
ex: His belief: the things that scare you most are often the best for you

items.d: Especially to things that scare you
A yes can always become a no

l145|268.c: Most software companies don't need venture capital, and taking it leaves only one path: get huge.
l145|268.e: He thinks businesses that must buy equipment and pay rent up front, like carmakers, factories, and restaurants, genuinely need capital. Software needs a few computers and a few people, and should run at 80 to 90 percent gross margins. Yet Silicon Valley has turned the most profitable kind of business into the least profitable, spending everything on headcount and customer acquisition. The bigger problem is that venture capital accepts only one ending: become enormous or wither. Between a small business and a unicorn there are plenty of places to land, and a self-funded company gets to choose. He isn't telling everyone to copy him; he just notes that almost nobody makes the venture path work.
ex: Physical businesses that must blanket many cities fast, like Airbnb and Uber, do need capital

marks.d: Can stop anywhere along the way
About 75 people, tens of millions in profit

l145|268.c: Chase efficiency instead of growth: one product, one price, and 75 people can serve 100,000 customers.
l145|268.e: Competitors employ thousands. 37signals has about 75 people, a similar number of customers, and a profit every year. The difference is that they optimize for efficiency, not growth. No sales team, no enterprise deals, no custom work for a client paying $300,000 a year. Basecamp costs at most $299 with unlimited users, and one codebase serves everyone. Each feature is built by one programmer and one designer in at most six weeks, so there are no fifteen-person meetings and no slow decisions. He admits that handing him a thousand people, or even five hundred, would sink the company.
ex: "Hire more because you can afford to" is a Silicon Valley habit he deliberately avoids
His target customers are the "Fortune 5,000,000": ordinary small businesses

l145|268.c: Success means wanting to do it again, and the hard part of a business is staying in it.
l145|268.e: His definition of success is simple: after doing something, ask whether it was enjoyable, whether it was worth it, and whether you'd do it again. In business he only checks that overall the company earns more than it spends. No profit and loss by product, no OKRs or KPIs, no revenue or growth targets. Saying thank you doesn't need an A/B test. He sees the business as a job he wants to keep doing forever. Reselling electronics at 15 and selling software today are the same thing, so he won't take money that assumes a sale in five years. Starting is easy; surviving plateaus and competition is hard. Independence means they never need anyone's approval.
ex: The company's first principle is independence; everything else grows out of it
He rejects war language like "conquer the market" and "crush the competition"

items.d: The way you like doing it
Earn more than you spend overall

l145|268.c: Set an appetite instead of an estimate: two people, six weeks max, and usually drop what isn't done.
l145|268.e: Their Shape Up method never asks how long something will take, because people are bad at estimating and work expands to fill the time available. Instead they decide how much they're willing to spend: at most six weeks and two people. A lead shapes the work first, then the team breaks it down itself and makes its own trade-offs when surprises come up. If the deadline arrives and the team is still "uphill" figuring things out, they usually drop the project rather than let it drag on, since endless projects kill morale most. Each cycle is followed by a two-week cooldown. He dislikes the word "sprint," and he thinks committed dates, especially "by end of year," are the root of much that goes wrong.
ex: The hill chart: uphill is figuring it out, downhill is just execution
Try a new method on a non-critical project first; don't flip everything overnight

items.d: Two people, six weeks at most
Describe direction, not a task list
Fix bugs, shape the next round

l145|268.c: Every decision is really a judgment call, so admit it and trust your gut.
l145|268.e: He says he only knows how to decide by gut, and believes everyone does. Unless a machine makes the call, a human decision draws on thousands of experiences nobody can fully articulate, and data is just one input. Companies hire executives for judgment and experience, not spreadsheet skills. So at 37signals they ask "what do you think, how does it feel" and rarely demand "prove it." When hiring designers, he gives finalists a paid one-week project, then asks what they'd do with two more days, to see whether their instincts extend on the spot. He also thinks post-mortems on failures are often self-deception, because nobody truly knows what went wrong.
ex: Investor Charlie Munger told him: when doing something unfamiliar, trust your gut
He likes asking candidates whose work they admire, and why

terms.d: Your gut takes in far more than you can say

result.d: Every human decision is one

l145|268.c: Bootstrapping forces you to practice making money from day one; too much cash just breeds sloppiness.
l145|268.e: He says having money doesn't make efficiency impossible, but it breeds sloppiness. When you don't have to earn or be efficient, you hire more and buy more ads, because investors gave you money to spend. The most basic business skill is making money, and like guitar, the longer you practice, the better you get. Companies fattened on funding never practice it, so when capital tightens and they try to turn on the profit tap, often nothing comes out, and layoffs and confusion follow. Constraints are what make you resourceful. He cites the advice RXBAR's founder got from his father: go sell a thousand bars first, then we'll talk.
ex: His father's advice: nobody ever went broke making a profit
Give him $10 million and a thousand people, he says, and he'd just waste them

d.verdict: Knowing how to earn beats knowing how to spend

l145|268.c: Bootstrap by staying as small as possible, doing it yourself, and picturing the worst case first.
l145|268.e: He admits bootstrapping is hard. His advice is to stay as small as you can for as long as you can, because cost is the only thing you control. The market, competitors, the economy, and ad prices are all out of your hands. Before hiring a second person, do as much as possible yourself. Each hire is another mouth and another personality, and if it's a bad hire you cover the gap anyway. Don't spend on branding or an office; build your site with off-the-shelf tools. Things are simple until people complicate them. Finally, borrow the Stoic practice of negative visualization: picture the worst outcome, make peace with it, and then you can move freely.
ex: Worst case for ONCE: six months of exploring, and having fun doing it
His strategy: make good things, control costs, price fairly, share what you learn

items.d: For as long as you can

l145|268.c: Much software is now a commodity sold at luxury prices, so pay-once software will swing back.
l145|268.e: He and his partner David think the pendulum will swing back. For a decade, business software has been rent-only, yet most of what you pay for each month existed years ago. Many categories offer dozens of near-identical options at luxury prices. ONCE aims to be the high-quality generic version in these categories: nail the core 80 percent, with two people building each product in about three months. Customers pay once, install it on their own servers, and get the source code to modify. 37signals carries no hosting costs. The first product revives Campfire, their 2006 group chat tool, priced under $1,000, useful as a Slack backup or inside an isolated network.
ex: He once thought Basecamp alone was enough, then admitted he's a maker and started building again

items.d: Pay once, run it on your own server

l146|269.c: People dislike product managers mostly because they've never worked with a truly competent one.
l146|269.e: He believes a PM's authority comes from competence: knowing the customer, the data, the industry, the business, and the product better than anyone else in the room. Many PMs never reach that level, so colleagues who feel they know more simply make the decisions instead, and the company ends up sales-driven or executive-driven. He doesn't blame culture or leadership. The profession has to raise its own standard and earn the right to decide. He often asks CEOs to imagine every team having a version of the long-tenured employee they trust most.
ex: The CEO's most trusted veteran, "Bob," is what a competent PM looks like
Good PMs come from only two places: a painful failure, or a great boss

l146|269.c: Of the four product risks, value risk matters most, gets skipped most, and decides whether to build.
l146|269.e: Product teams face four risks at once: value, usability, technical feasibility, and business viability. The PM mainly owns value and viability. Value is the hardest and the one most often skipped. Teams get handed a feature roadmap, and whatever the boss asks for is assumed valuable. In that setup you don't really need a PM at all. Being able to use something is not the same as buying it, choosing it, or actually using it, and what people say rarely matches what they do. The PM is like a quarterback, not because they're special, but because they have to answer whether the thing is worth doing.
ex: A test with 300 users scoring 84 to 90 percent still doesn't mean anyone will buy
Customers pay you back in four ways: revenue, engagement, loyalty, or referrals

cells.d: Will they buy, choose, and use it?
Does it work for the company?
Can we build it in time?

l146|269.c: You've reached product-market fit when enough reference customers will publicly vouch for you.
l146|269.e: A reference customer is someone who has used your product and loves it enough to stake their reputation on recommending it. Most people won't go first; they follow once someone like them approves. The method: find early adopters who truly have the pain, iterate with them until they'll write a review or record a testimonial. Asking for the endorsement forces their real objections out. Build only what all of them want; if one doesn't want a feature, leave it out. His bar is 6 to 8 companies for B2B and 15 to 25 people for B2C, which may mean working with 30 to 50. If you can't recruit them, the problem isn't worth solving.
ex: He says he's worked on about 205 products this way and it has never failed
Every app launched with 25 five-star reviews already on day one
Marketing copy lifted straight from customers, like "super fast but hard to read"

items.d: 6 to 8 for B2B, 15 to 25 for B2C

l146|269.c: The best way to learn to solve a problem is to solve it by hand first, before it scales.
l146|269.e: At an hourly-hiring company, Starbucks' head of HR asked for help: after acquiring a bakery chain, nearly 800 employees might walk. He got in a car with a designer and an engineer. They first checked whether a new McDonald's site and Macy's had the same pain, then recruited for McDonald's by hand with flyers, newspapers, Craigslist, and phone calls. Once they learned that about half of applicants never show up for interviews, they scaled up. The designer and engineer were there from the moment the problem was defined. He never wrote a requirements document, and the product shipped in about nine months.
ex: They hired 784 people for Starbucks in one week
An airport project dragged on nearly three months before they ruled airports out
The product signed about $32 million in its first 90 days

items.d: Recruit by hand, learn show-up rates

l146|269.c: The fastest way to earn trust: ask the most influential person to teach you, or offer to help them.
l146|269.e: Trust inside a company rests mostly on competence, but people only learn you're competent by testing you, often publicly in meetings. His "teach me or let me help you" trick: take a new hire to the loudest, most influential person in the company and ask them to let the newcomer shadow them for a week. The newcomer borrows that person's trust and network. The influential person now has a stake in the newcomer's growth and won't casually say they're no good. The newcomer also sees the real business skill behind the influence. After that, keep doing discovery so everyone sees you learning every day.
ex: Fill a new hire's calendar with a week of quietly sitting in on a senior leader's meetings
If they're too busy, offer to be their "intern"

items.d: Shadow for a week or intern
Your failure means they taught badly
Let people see you learn daily

l146|269.c: Building the product is the PM's job; making the PM better is the manager's daily coaching job.
l146|269.e: Vision, strategy, and hiring are one-off acts. Coaching is the manager's everyday work, like a coach on the sideline watching a player on the field. Most people can't coach because they were never coached well themselves, so they copy whatever they saw. Companies also rarely give people room to practice; they just expect you to show up ready. If you have no good coach, find a "pickup game" such as a nonprofit or community project to practice solving problems with others. And if you send staff to a communication course, the manager should take it and practice alongside them.
ex: One CEO screamed at people in public only because his old boss did it to him
