He has coached his son's soccer team for eight years and won many championships

items.d: They assume this is how it's done
And pass the bad habits on

l146|269.c: Don't promote people into jobs they can't do; let them do the job first, then give the title.
l146|269.e: A common story: a great engineer gets promoted to manager because there's no other path up, having never interviewed, fired, or led anyone. When a hard problem appears, they jump back in and do it themselves, which is the most common source of micromanagement. New managers are afraid to say "I don't know," so they search for a framework online and follow it, and their reports copy the bad habits. His approach: have people do the next level's work before they have the title. Mistakes are cheap then, and someone has their back. Give them one report to prove it, then four.
ex: Want to be a director? "Go do director work; you don't need the title"
The group PM role is supposed to be exactly this test of whether someone can lead people

items: Copy a framework from the internet
Already doing the job when promoted

d.verdict: A promotion is to do the job, not to learn it

l146|269.c: Africa has the talent; what it lacks is enabling technology and the product mindset to face problems head-on.
l146|269.e: He noticed that problems North America solved long ago are still unsolved in Africa; some people still find jobs through newspapers. Locally you often have to solve a chain of prerequisites, like electricity, devices, and software, before you can even reach the real problem. That's why he sees government as the biggest public-private product platform. Hard conditions teach many people to work around problems or profit from them, like buying a generator when there's no power. But Africa's population is young and growing fast, and he notes it has produced seven unicorns with under 30 percent of people online. So he started a foundation and a conference to train product talent.
ex: A Tesla towing a portable generator behind it
The Inspire Africa conference drew about a thousand people from 31 countries
He plans to launch an angel fund for early-stage founders

items.d: What you actually set out to solve
People who solve problems with technology
Under 30 percent of people are online

l147|273.c: A consumer product must first pick its one core action; MAU and downloads are vanity metrics.
l147|273.e: She sees founders point to rising signups, downloads and monthly active users, numbers that say nothing about whether the product will last. The real foundation is the core action: once a user completes it, they understand what the product is for and are likely to come back. Pick it by asking whether enough users can do it and where optimizing the roadmap around it will take the product. Onboarding succeeds when a new user starts doing that action. Pinterest settled on its core action by running two kinds of analysis at once.
ex: Adding a friend on Facebook, pinning on Pinterest, taking a note in Evernote
Users who pinned in a given week came back the next week over 90% of the time
YouTube later found its core action was subscribing, not watching

terms.d: Rank actions by completion and next-week return
Ask what the product really exists for

result.d: Pinterest's weekly active pinners

l147|273.c: Engagement builds in layers: a core action first, then a product that improves with use, then self-perpetuation.
l147|273.e: The test for the second layer is that the product gets better the more you use it and leaving gets more costly. Pinterest personalizes your home feed from what you pin, so more pins mean better recommendations, and the recipes and book lists you have saved make you reluctant to leave. She has thousands of documents in Evernote and is stuck there for the same reason. The third layer turns the energy users put in back into the experience: network effects are the strongest, followed by growth loops and re-engagement loops. Checking each layer after launch helps founders focus on the lever that actually matters.
ex: Pinterest's recommended home feed may have been the first algorithmic feed in a social product
A "someone pinned your pin" notification can bring dormant users back

items.d: Network effects, growth and re-engagement loops
Better with use, costlier to leave
Users truly get it and return

l147|273.c: Without self-perpetuation you can only buy growth, and a badly designed loop can unwind itself.
l147|273.e: Getting a consumer product to hundreds of millions of users through marketing takes enormous capital. Apart from TikTok, almost every social product grew organically through loops, and even TikTok only spent heavily once the first two layers held and it already had millions of users. Evernote had no loop where users brought in or benefited each other, so it had to pay for acquisition and eventually ran out of steam. Houseparty and Clubhouse looked like flywheels that spin faster with more people, but live products depend on push notifications. Follow more people and the notifications flood in, users start ignoring them, and the flywheel stalls.
ex: TikTok spent over $1 billion on acquisition after proving the first two layers
Evernote's attempt at collaborative notes never worked either

items.d: A bigger network should be more valuable
Live products rely on pings to tell you when to join

l147|273.c: Purely anonymous products have no accumulated value and no cost to leaving, so they rarely clear retention.
l147|273.e: She distinguishes pseudonymous from purely anonymous. A pseudonymous account on Twitter or Reddit has a persistent identity, can build followers, and costs something to abandon. Pure anonymity has neither. It also invites bad behavior that drags a community down, so the network effect works against you. A user who deletes the app and comes back three months later finds exactly the same experience. Early growth in anonymous products is often a lot of fun, but many talented founders have hit the same wall, because without a lasting identity there is nothing to keep people.
ex: Purely anonymous apps like Secret have struggled to last

l147|273.c: Build a marketplace backwards from dominance; step one is reaching "happy GMV" in a small market.
l147|273.e: A marketplace is like running two companies at once, one for supply and one for demand. The pain is worth it because a dominant marketplace is hugely profitable, while a marginal number one has to fight for every point of share. The only scalable path to dominance is tipping a market, and tipping requires first saturating a constrained one. Capital and founder attention are scarce, so focus like a laser, not the sun. GMV is not a measure of health. What matters is how happy users are after a transaction and whether they come back, which she calls happy GMV.
ex: DoorDash went after suburbs nobody served; Postmates spread across cities and categories at once
$1 million split over 10 cities loses to a rival that bets it all on one
Test product-market fit with the Sean Ellis question: over 40% would be very disappointed

items.d: Reach minimum viable happiness in a small market
After saturation, supply and demand lean toward you
Repeat the playbook, one market at a time

l147|273.c: Tipping a market takes two kinds of loops: growth loops pull people in, happiness loops reward good supply and shed bad.
l147|273.e: Tipping usually shows up first at a micro level: individual suppliers or buyers start leaning toward you, cohorts improve, and organic growth appears. REKKI began by sending people out to persuade London chefs to order through it; later, suppliers tired of listening to voicemails sent over their customer lists and asked to be connected. Good founders stay close to both sides, notice the lean, and double down. Alongside growth loops you need a happiness loop that filters like a kidney: healthy churn on the supply side, with search ranking and reputation rewarding good suppliers and weeding out bad ones.
ex: REKKI suppliers sent CSVs of their customers and asked to be onboarded
Uber's driver referral bonuses were rich enough that bloggers made money recruiting
Early Uber Eats ranked restaurants by how fast they prepared food

root.d: Two kinds of loops working together

items.d: Hipcamp bookings let you invite companions
Reward sellers who deliver good experiences
Let poorly rated supply fall away

l147|273.c: Not every market can tip: concentrated supply or interchangeable supply keeps the flywheel from turning.
l147|273.e: She lists six conditions that make a market easier to tip. If supply is already highly concentrated, the incumbents are comfortable and will not lean toward a new platform, so there is no hungry new supply to drive the flywheel. B2B marketplaces have a bigger problem: supply is interchangeable, so one more unit of supply does not improve the buyer's experience, and the model is easy to copy. The competitive landscape matters too. Facing Grubhub plus Seamless in New York, where restaurants already delivered, was far harder than the suburbs. And after tipping you cannot relax, because a stagnant experience gets disrupted.
ex: Mechanical Turk feels the same with 100,000 workers or 5 million
Grubhub never changed the atomic unit of supply and got disrupted
Airbnb listings are all different, so more supply means more value

l147|273.c: The best markets look small from the outside but have a current pushing them forward.
l147|273.e: Most people picture a market as still water and compare surface area. She cares more about the force of change: in a river, even a plank gets carried forward. An underestimated market has no competition early on and is easier to tip, but it cannot be a dead end; there must be a bigger adjacent market to expand into. Hipcamp started by serving hardcore campers. Once landowners made money, they added bathrooms, treehouses and yurts, and the market grew to include glampers who never wanted a tent. The counterexample is Etsy before its IPO, which chased GMV by letting in mass-produced goods and damaged trust on both sides.
ex: She is bullish on dollar stablecoins, where she sees a strong current
She suspects LLMs can automate onboarding long-tail supply and change the atomic unit

l148|275.c: The opposite of distraction is not focus but traction, and the only difference is intent.
l148|275.e: He calls any action that moves you toward your plans, values and the person you want to be "traction," and any action that pulls you off plan "distraction." The only test is intent. Browsing Reddit or watching YouTube is not a waste if you planned to do it, and there is no reason to look down on it morally. The sneakiest distractions are the work-related ones: answering email first, checking Slack, reading industry news. They make you feel productive while urgent, easy tasks crowd out the important, hard ones.
ex: He quotes Dorothy Parker: time you plan to waste is not wasted time
Checking work email is more deceptive than playing Candy Crush

items: Planned in advance, done with intent
Moves you toward values and goals
Urgent and easy crowds out important and hard

d.verdict: One word separates them: intent

l148|275.c: Ninety percent of distraction comes from discomfort inside; procrastination is an emotion-regulation problem, not a character flaw.
l148|275.e: Research suggests only about 10% of distractions come from external alerts, he says; the rest come from internal feelings like boredom, loneliness, fatigue and anxiety. He switched to a flip phone with no apps and bought a used word processor, and still found himself tidying his desk and taking out the trash, which shows the problem is not the technology. At the level of the brain, everything we do is an attempt to escape discomfort, and even the desire for pleasure is a kind of discomfort. High performers feel all of this too; they just use the discomfort as fuel, while distractible people click away the moment they feel it.
ex: Plato was discussing "knowing what to do and not doing it" 2,500 years ago
"The carrot is the stick": chasing pleasure is also escaping discomfort

items.d: Boredom, loneliness, anxiety and the like

l148|275.c: When you want to give in, don't say no; say "in ten minutes" and let the urge pass like a wave.
l148|275.e: After more than a decade of writing he still finds every word hard, so he does not believe in building a writing habit. Whenever he wants to look something up or check the news, he sets a ten-minute timer. He can either return to the task or "surf the urge": acknowledge the discomfort, tell himself "this is what getting stronger feels like," and wait for the feeling to crest and fade. Hard bans tend to backfire; "not yet" is more sustainable. Most of the time the urge is forgotten within ten minutes, and over time he can stretch it to twenty. More importantly, it proves that attention is not stolen from you; you hand it over.
ex: Carol Dweck's research: willpower only runs out for people who believe it does
It adds one step to the Pomodoro technique: dealing with the emotion

items.d: Notice the discomfort, let it pass

l148|275.c: Replace the to-do list with a timeboxed calendar, and measure whether you did what you planned for as long as you planned.
l148|275.e: You cannot call something a distraction unless you know what it distracted you from, so turn your values into time on a calendar. Every Sunday evening he spends about ten minutes laying out the coming week across three domains, you, relationships and work, including time with his daughter, social media and sleep. Within work, block time for reflective work that needs deep thought. A to-do list has no constraints and only tracks output, so you never finish and you pick the easy items. The better measure is whether you did what you said for as long as you said without distraction. That teaches you how long things really take, and you get more done.
ex: Research finds tasks take about three times as long as people estimate
Bring the calendar to your boss to sync and ask for help prioritizing

items.d: Partner, kids, friends, not just leftover time
Sleep, exercise, reading and other self-care

l148|275.c: Becoming indistractable takes four steps in order, and pacts are only the last line of defense.
l148|275.e: Step one, master the internal triggers. Step two, make time for traction. Step three, hack back the external triggers. Step four, prevent distraction with pacts. The order matters: skip the first three and pacts will not work. Hacking back external triggers means more than turning off notifications; it includes unnecessary meetings and email, and interruptions from family. Pacts come in three kinds. A price pact attaches a financial penalty. An identity pact makes being indistractable part of who you are. An effort pact adds friction to the distraction.
ex: His wife wears a "concentration crown"; his daughter waits 30 minutes unless there is blood
A timer cuts off the home router at 10pm every night
Growing trees in Forest, or working alongside a stranger on Focusmate

items.d: Deal with the discomfort you want to escape

l148|275.c: Distraction at work is a symptom of a dysfunctional culture, and the fix is culture, not banning tools.
l148|275.e: His research found email is the biggest workplace distraction, followed by group chat tools. So he visited Slack headquarters expecting the most distracted company on earth, and found the opposite. Indistractable companies share three traits. Employees feel psychologically safe enough to say "being expected to reply instantly keeps me from doing good work." There is a forum for discussing these problems. And leaders model the behavior themselves, because culture flows downhill like water. Of the three, leadership modeling matters most.
ex: Slack has a #beef-tweets channel where emoji reactions mark complaints as fixed or seen
A sign in Slack's cafeteria reads "Work hard and go home"
BCG introduced "predictable time off"

terms.d: Safe to raise distraction problems openly
A dedicated channel or regular meeting

result.d: Treat distraction like any other business problem

l148|275.c: For most people phone use is distraction, not addiction; the answer is personal responsibility plus new social norms.
l148|275.e: He thinks the methods in Hooked work, but they are not magic and certainly not mind control. Addiction means a compulsive dependency that harms you, and he estimates it affects 3% to 5% of the population; those people and children deserve special protection. Everyone else who calls their problem an addiction is shifting responsibility onto tech companies. Society dealt with smoking through new norms: his mother removed the ashtray from the living room and started calling herself a nonsmoker. He expects similar social antibodies to form around phones, along with new tools built to fix the problems of the last generation of technology.
ex: Paulo Coelho: a mistake repeated more than once is a decision
He wants companies to adopt use-and-abuse policies for pathologically addicted users

items.d: No phones in meetings or at dinner

l149|277.c: Researchers got laid off in droves because the field did too much interesting but unusable middle-range work.
l149|277.e: He splits user research into three layers. Macro research looks at markets, competitors and where the company is headed long term. Micro research tests whether a screen is usable or explains why an A/B test came out the way it did. The middle layer asks how a certain kind of user thinks and behaves. That middle layer is fascinating, he says, but it rarely lines up with the funnel, the strategy or the quarter's goals, so nothing happens with it, and it gets waved off with "we already knew that." In the zero-interest-rate years companies hired lots of researchers without knowing how to use them. That model is over. Research itself isn't dead, but it has to evolve.
ex: A middle-layer question: how Airbnb hosts feel about payout methods
A macro example: Airbnb's yearly "concept car" built from pooled insights about five years out

items.d: Interesting but hard to act on; overdone
Usability tests, explaining experiments; fast payoff

l149|277.c: Treating research as a service desk creates a vicious cycle; the fix is embedding researchers from start to finish.
l149|277.e: Many companies hire researchers and then hand them requests only at the end of a project. Researchers who aren't in the room can't help shape the right questions. So research ends up reactive and on topics that don't matter much, and its impact is small. Executives conclude research is useless, push it to the margins or cut it, and that makes it even harder to embed, round and round. His fix is to tie researchers to product, design and engineering for the long haul, sharing the same success metrics instead of separate research OKRs. His test of a good researcher: the team can't hold a decision meeting without you.
ex: A researcher at full load handles about three things: two big, one small
Grow the team by having partner teams fight for researchers, not by arguing research matters

items.d: Called in only at the end

l149|277.c: Much "user-centered" work is theater; research should try to prove itself wrong, not right.
l149|277.e: He calls research done to look user-focused, with no intention of changing a decision, "user-centered performance," and he thinks it's everywhere. Asking a researcher to "quickly validate our assumptions" right before launch is just checking a box. Executives sitting in on focus groups mean well, but it's mostly a show. Underneath is confirmation bias (hearing only what supports you) and ego. Intuition matters, he says, but biases and blind spots hide inside it. So slow down, bring together people with different sources of information to test each other, and let researchers do what they're good at: running that conversation.
ex: He estimates about 97% of executive listening sessions are performance
PMs can walk through the product and list issues, but shouldn't prioritize by gut

marks.d: Actively hunting for where you're wrong

l149|277.c: Researchers must learn business language and find questions where user needs and profit overlap.
l149|277.e: The UX field has long stressed empathy, and he agrees with that. But there is an overlap between what users need and what the business needs, and researchers have to go looking for it. Concretely: read the quarterly earnings, listen to shareholder calls, study the internal half-year strategy and OKRs, and really understand the metrics and the conversion funnel. Then you can say in a meeting "the problem is at this step of the funnel" or "a competitor is taking these users." He adds this isn't only on researchers. Plenty of PMs perform user-centeredness too, and fixing the system takes change from everyone.
ex: The most surprising pushback on his essay came from people who think research shouldn't discuss profit

result.d: Ask questions where the two overlap

l149|277.c: The best researchers are generalists with at least five methods in their toolkit.
l149|277.e: Early user research was mostly qualitative, and he thinks that model has to evolve. The ideal researcher is a Swiss Army knife. If all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail. In interviews he poses an open research question and watches whether the candidate can offer several approaches, and how they'd tackle it with a day, a week or a month. Individuals can go deeper on one or two tools, and the team as a whole covers the gaps.
ex: He built his teams at both Meta and Airbnb around these five tools

root.d: A Swiss Army knife, not a hammer

items.d: Field work aimed at new opportunities
SQL, and today maybe prompt writing

l149|277.c: Research isn't slow; a few dozen hours of micro research can return real money.
l149|277.e: He lists the lines researchers hate most. "Research is too slow" doesn't hold: research can take a day, a week or a month, and shipping the wrong thing and redoing it is slower. "I can do research myself" ignores that one user can be very unusual, and garbage in means garbage out. "Just A/B test everything" tells you what happened but rarely why, so data science and research should work together. And "users would just ask for a faster horse" misreads research: good researchers never ask users what they want directly.
ex: Facebook's "super hiders" hid every post they'd read, chasing an empty feed
"We already knew that" is hindsight bias; he recommends Duncan Watts's book

items.d: Users feared the button would charge them instantly

l149|277.c: Stop using NPS; a simple satisfaction question gives cleaner data that tracks the business better.
l149|277.e: He calls NPS (the "how likely are you to recommend us" score) the marketing industry's best piece of marketing for itself. By survey-science standards it gets almost everything wrong: 11 options from 0 to 10, usually with only the ends labeled, when precision drops past five to seven options, and on a phone some options fall off the screen. Questions like "would you recommend this operating system to a friend" make little sense anyway. Companies ask it differently, swings are hard to explain, and even industry benchmarks don't really work. He and Airbnb's head of survey science checked their own data: satisfaction measures were more precise and more tied to business outcomes.
ex: His recommended question: overall, how satisfied were you with this experience?

items: Hard to explain swings or benchmark
Simple question, can be made specific

d.verdict: Skip NPS, ask about satisfaction

l150|281.c: Systems thinking is a great learning tool, but when the model and reality disagree, the model is wrong.
l150|281.e: Systems thinking means modeling a problem as stocks and flows, like fish in a lake and the people fishing it. Applied to hiring, you map how candidates convert from sourcing to screening to offer, then compare that against the real history in your recruiting system. That shows where things actually get stuck instead of changing the process on a hunch. But he has watched many smart people decide that reality must be wrong. He did it himself at Stripe, running incident analysis and getting so absorbed in measuring that he forgot to improve anything. Once the model is good enough, stop and go do the work.
ex: Hiring can stall because managers won't extend offers, offers get declined, or there are too few candidates
He recommends Donella Meadows's Thinking in Systems

items.d: Lay out the stocks and flows

l150|281.c: Every company has an engineering strategy, usually unwritten, and good ones are often boring.
l150|281.e: Strategy always exists, he says; it's just often unwritten, and sometimes bad. Writing it down lets you tell whether people misunderstood it or the strategy itself doesn't fit. He uses Richard Rumelt's definition: a diagnosis, guiding policies and actions. The value of an engineering strategy is that it constrains future decisions. Good ones are often boring, like "only use the tools we already have." Some engineers will grumble, but it focuses limited energy on the problems the company actually cares about. Bad strategy usually comes from refusing to accept an honest diagnosis, such as believing every project can happen at once.
ex: Uber stuck with its own data centers instead of the cloud, and launched in China in about three months
Stripe stayed with a single large Ruby application for years
Carta's strategy is a "standard toolkit" written down by its engineers

terms.d: An honest view of the situation and constraints
Trade-off rules built on the diagnosis

result.d: Decides where limited energy goes

l150|281.c: Writing for the long haul means only writing what energizes you; the biggest risk is quitting.
l150|281.e: He has written for 16 years, around a thousand pieces. The secret is to write only about what genuinely energizes him right now, not for money or deadlines, and to drop a book that stops working. When writing lines up with the day job, it becomes a way to think through hard problems at work rather than a burden. Different goals call for different methods. Everyone feels they're too late, but if you keep producing good work, an audience builds slowly and moves with you across platforms. He doesn't see other writers as competition.
ex: Before writing, decide whether the piece can be published; if not, skip it
Don't try to "debug" a stranger's harsh review

items: Polish two or three pieces carefully
No need for a weekly blog
Publish almost as soon as it's done
Ten years beats one big burst

d.verdict: Know why you write before deciding how

l150|281.c: EM-PM fights mostly come from not understanding each other; sharing a performance rating puts them on the same side.
l150|281.e: His rule is that there are no villains at work, only people with complicated incentives. Engineering and product managers sometimes do have misaligned incentives, but more often they start arguing before understanding what the other side really cares about. Dig deeper and you can usually find a plan everyone likes. At Carta, the EM and PM on a team get the same performance rating by default, calibrated together with the product leader. He also thinks the zero-interest-rate years coddled engineers in ways that hurt them. Now they can be held accountable like adults and trusted with more senior roles.
ex: Carta's CEO has business, product and engineering leads share one rating as a "triad"
A growth team wants 50 experiments while engineers want to build a brand-new system

items.d: First learn what the other side needs
EMs must find the team interesting work

l150|281.c: Don't wait for perfect metrics; report imperfect numbers and use the questions to teach.
l150|281.e: When a board asks about efficiency, comparing R&D spend against companies at the same funding stage gives a defensible answer, but it doesn't help you run the team. To really know whether a team is effective, keep talking to the engineers. Externally, tie engineering's evaluation to product goals and show the substantial things shipped in the last six months. DORA metrics (a standard set measuring software delivery speed and stability) are better for diagnosis than for proving the company is doing well. Experts often measure nothing because every metric is flawed. He'd rather report imperfect numbers and, when challenged, explain the messy reality behind them.
ex: Reporting sprint points to a board is, in his words, completely fake
The DORA metrics from the book Accelerate are a reasonable starting point

l150|281.c: Good values are honest, applicable and reversible; otherwise they're just identity statements.
l150|281.e: Copying values doesn't work. He has seen executives tour Facebook and paste its values onto their own walls. Good values pass three tests. They are honest: the company really acts this way. They are applicable: they guide specific trade-offs. And they are reversible: the opposite would also be a reasonable way to run a business. Nobody argues against "we build good software" or "we care about customers," so those are identity statements. Executives enjoy discussing them, but they're useless. If a value wouldn't exclude anyone, there's no point writing it down.
ex: Stripe's "global optimization" versus Uber's implicit "take care of your own team first"
Netflix's "we're a team, not a family" is partly reversible

items.d: The company really acts this way
The opposite is also a sane choice

l150|281.c: Full rewrites almost never work, but a struggling company teaches you the most.
l150|281.e: Digg feared being overtaken by social networks, so it rewrote the whole site as V4 with social features built in. On launch day the team waited around sushi and champagne for the site to come back. Instead, most features stayed broken for a month, and in the end only about five people were still fixing things. The company eventually went to zero. But as people left, he ended up running the entire engineering team after just two and a half years there. He calls that experience the starting point of his whole career.
ex: Changes to Google search hurt traffic and ad revenue, which forced the rewrite
He thinks the social news product Digg wanted to build is still missing today

l151|282.c: The more disruptive an idea, the dumber it looks at first; love-it-or-hate-it reactions signal impact.
l151|282.e: Everything around us was disruptive when it first appeared, he says. New things threaten people's view of the world, so people invent reasons why they can't work. That's why the most disruptive ideas look like bad ideas at first. When someone says "it's just a toy," it often means the thing is a real threat. To judge impact, look for polarized reactions: some people love it passionately, others want it gone. Mild reactions usually mean an incremental product. It isn't a vote. As long as somebody loves it, the number of detractors doesn't matter.
ex: With millions of Writely users, a Google executive still wanted it shut down
In his first week at Google an executive refused him servers; his contract saved him

marks.d: The whole world loves or hates it

l151|282.c: Optimism is a deliberate choice: first ask "what if this works," then break down the obstacles.
l151|282.e: He describes himself as a natural pessimist who chooses optimism on purpose. Looking back, he missed far more by being pessimistic than he lost by being optimistic. With a new technology, first ask what the world looks like if it works, push the curve out as far as you can, and figure out what it would mean. Only then go back and work through the specific reasons it might fail. Optimism still needs grounding: you must be able to point to real value for users. He thought hard about crypto and couldn't see user benefit even in the best case, so pessimism there seems fair to him.
ex: SpaceX: what happens to the world if launch costs fall dramatically?
Generative AI is expensive and hallucinates, but that doesn't stop the what-if question

items.d: Work out what the best case means
No value even then? Drop it
Then tackle each "why not" in turn

l151|282.c: Sharpen your tools so experiments are cheap, then aim the tinkering with a concrete goal.
l151|282.e: Writely's two co-founders were industry veterans who initially decided a browser couldn't support a word processor. But a prototype took only days, so they tried anyway, and were surprised by how cool simultaneous editing felt. That made them willing to tackle the very hard problem of merging everyone's changes. If they had seen the difficulty before the value, he says, they probably would have quit. An optimistic mindset helps you notice results that fail in interesting ways. Aimless play produces little, though, so he gives teams a concrete north-star goal.
ex: Giving multiple AI agents a shared "whiteboard" memory made them noticeably smarter
Example goal: have a coding agent finish an intern's entire summer project on its own

items.d: A prototype in a few days

l151|282.c: Users are lazy, so a product's benefit must far outweigh everything it costs them to adopt it.
l151|282.e: Users only care whether their lives get easier, not about your mission or your logo. He thinks of adoption like thermodynamics: add a little value and it spreads slowly; add a lot and it explodes. Teams fixate on the new feature itself and forget that users first have to hear about it, remember it when they need it, learn it, and build a habit, and every step costs effort. Only when the payoff far exceeds that effort, ideally tenfold, do people adopt. Writely fought a full-featured Office with zero installation and collaboration, trading features for convenience.
ex: Early Writely didn't even ask for an email until about two minutes of typing
He says a consumer product has 15 to 30 seconds to prove its value
They cut too far once: students' first complaint was no word count

items.d: People have to know it exists
Recall it at the right moment

l151|282.c: Do the thing you feel guilty getting paid for, and do it with everything you have.
l151|282.e: People undervalue what they're good at. They assume work should hurt and that anything easy and fun can't be worth much. His advice: find the thing you enjoy that people will pay for, then do it at maximum intensity. Carefully managing risk only earns linear returns; extraordinary returns need bigger bets. He sees younger people as more afraid of failure. The internet presents one-in-a-million success as normal, childhoods are heavily scheduled, and there's less unsupervised play. But if you're afraid of looking silly, you can't dance.
ex: He often sends Satya Nadella odd ideas, then admits a week later he was wrong
When he moved into management his boss said: wherever you go, things get better
His motto: get virtue from your mistakes

d.xLabel: Good at it and enjoy it?

cells.d: Good at it, not all in

l151|282.c: AI will make pixels free, and future software will be built around expressing intent.
l151|282.e: He calls himself a builder of apps and tools: he uses models rather than training them. To him GPT-4 is essentially a random pure function, text in and text out. Turning it into a program needs state, control flow and orchestration, which is why his team built projects like Semantic Kernel. The internet made distributing information free; AI will make generating interfaces free. Add planning, multiple modalities and personal memory, and people will use software mostly by saying what they want, like directing a team of capable assistants. Adding AI to a product only adds value at the margin. The big value comes from apps that can't exist without it.
ex: His line: AI isn't a feature of your product; your product is a feature of AI
"Bot as document": let an AI interview you for an hour, then write the document
He admits a quarter or more of these predictions may be wrong

items.d: Generative AI builds interfaces on demand
Software that adapts, knows you, converses

l151|282.c: AI is in its one-to-N phase; to learn it, set yourself a concrete goal.
l151|282.e: "Go play with it" isn't enough. The best way to learn a new technology is to pick a specific goal and pursue it stubbornly, such as building a custom GPT that does part of your job. The exhausting feeling of not keeping up is itself a sign that something big is happening, much like the early internet. Zero to one is the hardest part; it takes luck, talent and grinding in the right place. Once something is proven possible, the one-to-N optimization gets pushed forward by huge numbers of people in parallel, incredibly fast. So pick your battles, read and think a lot, and accept running out of breath.
ex: Someone joked that AI found more use cases in a week than crypto did in ten years

d.verdict: Generative AI is now in the one-to-N fill-in phase

l152|283.c: Grow your career by helping your manager succeed, then tying their needs to your goals.
l152|283.e: The loop is for people who don't know how to move up, or whose manager is too busy or not very good. First, make sure your manager thinks you're doing your current job well. Then ask what you can do to help, and do it even if it's tedious. After a few rounds, share your own goal and ask whether there's work that helps them and moves you toward it. Then repeat. It works because almost nobody offers to help their manager, and people naturally help those who helped them. Managers also often assume you want to stay put or follow their path. What a manager "should" do doesn't matter; this loop is in your hands.
ex: A laid-off worker in the UK used it to land an offer with a $30,000 raise
A mid-level engineer grew into an executive running 800 people in 8 years
The more senior you are, shift from asking how to help to doing it and reporting back

items.d: Even if it isn't work you enjoy
Find work that helps both of you

l152|283.c: Promotion takes two things: you can do the job, and the organization actually needs the role.
l152|283.e: Getting stuck at senior manager is common. A director may have six to eight senior managers, and there are only so many seats above them. Fast-growing companies used to carry people up like an elevator; that elevator has slowed. The deeper reason is that the requirements change. You reach senior manager on expertise and execution. Director and above depend more on influence, coordinating across teams, and letting go of details. Whether a role exists is often out of your control, but you can practice next-level skills early, such as volunteering for strategic projects, so you're the one of eight who gets picked.
ex: He went from managing 6 people to 800 in nine years, which he calls riding the elevator
One client's two peers were laid off and both teams were folded under her
Book recommendation: What Got You Here Won't Get You There

terms.d: Show next-level skills ahead of time
The organization really needs the layer

result.d: Be the one of eight who gets chosen

l152|283.c: Invention can be a system: two focused hours a month, combining two things that already exist.
l152|283.e: When he joined Amazon he didn't think of himself as an inventor. Seeing principles like "invent and simplify" pushed him to work out a method, and over 15 years he earned more than 70 patents. First, you need to know the field well. Second, step away from every device and set aside time that forces you to think. The most direct route isn't creating from nothing but combining two existing things. A good idea often takes years to build and refine, so two hours a month is enough. You don't need many ideas to look extremely creative.
ex: From aircraft carriers: trucks as mobile airports launching delivery drones
Prime is still evolving after twenty-plus years; he says it now bundles about 25 benefits

items.d: Two hours a month, no devices
Take one good idea all the way

l152|283.c: Show enthusiasm in interviews, and explain the impact you made rather than how much you did.
l152|283.e: He has interviewed more than 2,500 people and believes appearance and enthusiasm are the two biggest factors. Even if you haven't decided whether you want the job, go in aiming to get the offer. Remote interviews need the same commitment: don't take them from your car, don't turn off the camera, and eye contact and gestures still count. The more senior the candidate, the more they tend to describe what they did and how hard it was instead of why it mattered. Leaders hire to solve problems. Showing how you changed the business is what makes you look like a leader.
ex: The best preparation might be a good night's sleep and a pot of coffee

items: Show the change for company and customers

l152|283.c: You can recover from a disaster: own it, report hourly, and repair the relationship in person.
l152|283.e: He ran the Amazon Appstore launch. Jeff Bezos had written the launch letter himself and was pushing the "test drive" feature, which let people try apps without downloading them. At 6 a.m. it still didn't work, Bezos grew angrier with each email, and layers of executives got copied in. He immediately admitted the failure and took responsibility, then sent hourly updates on progress and next steps, buying trust one hour at a time and keeping micromanagement at bay. He accepted help from AWS while the team worked in shifts. A week later he deliberately sat next to Bezos in a meeting; Bezos greeted him first, and the relationship was repaired.
ex: Jeff Wilke told him: if you didn't know you were gambling, we're discussing whether you stay
He regrets not consoling the new graduate who wrote that code and later left

items.d: Anger spreads up the cc chain
Earning trust one hour at a time
500 extra machines to hold the line

l152|283.c: Owners never say "not my job"; lean toward action, but watch out for the headlines.
l152|283.e: When Amazon merged several lists of values, "ownership" got dropped. He and a few directors objected and were told to draft it themselves. His line, "owners never say that's not my job," stayed in the leadership principles, and he calls it the most influential sentence he has written. He also champions bias for action: most decisions are reversible, and in competition being right is nice but being fast is required. Speed needs balance, though. After the Appstore incident he gave his team a rule: first ask whether this could end up on the front page of the New York Times.
ex: Afterward they replaced surprise launches with extensive beta testing

items.d: Most decisions reverse; speed is required
Extra care when it could make news
Surprise launches only surprise you with bugs

l152|283.c: Remote work has far more room to improve than offices, so it will win in the long run.
l152|283.e: Many executives at his level push for a return to the office. He bets on remote work because of its room for innovation. The first purpose-built office building went up in London in 1726, so offices have been refined for nearly three hundred years, and big improvements are hard to find; even open-plan layouts remain controversial. Remote work is young and full of unexplored ways to get better. His other contrarian habit is doing business on a handshake: most coaching clients sign no contract or NDA. Occasionally someone lets him down, but guarding against everyone costs more.

items.d: Since London's first office building in 1726
About 20 years since the internet took off

l153|286.c: Team change is unavoidable, so accept that teams evolve and get good at changing them.
l153|286.e: She spent about 20 years at fast-growing software companies and kept reading advice to keep teams stable. But the startups she worked at grew from a dozen people to over a thousand, and the teams never stopped changing. Companies that are growing or shrinking shouldn't fight that natural evolution, she argues. The classic team-development model also misses a stage: stagnation. Stay on one team too long and people get tired; switching teams can feel like a new job. Good teams are worth treasuring, but companies and teams have life cycles, and nothing stays the same forever.
ex: Her image: even a great team is like ice cream melting in your hand
She recommends Adizes's Managing Corporate Lifecycles

items.d: The stage the classic model misses

l153|286.c: Team change falls into five patterns, each with its own practices and pitfalls.
l153|286.e: She avoids the word "reorg" because it carries top-down, take-it-or-leave-it baggage, and one person switching teams to learn something new is team change too. When someone joins, help them feel they belong, and look after existing staff so a suddenly parachuted-in manager doesn't unsettle them. When a team grows, meetings get longer, decisions get harder and the work starts to diverge; that's the signal to split. Splitting creates new dependencies, though, such as a single PM serving two teams. When merging, have both teams map their histories together to build a shared past and a shared vision.
ex: Give a newcomer a pairing partner on day one so they never sit alone
When merging, build a "story of our team" timeline together

root.d: Happen from individual to company level

items.d: Someone joins or leaves the company
A big team divides into two or more
A small separate team builds something new

l153|286.c: You can put a reorg plan out in the open for feedback, but keep the discussion strictly time-boxed.
l153|286.e: She prefers transparent reorgs. At Procore, a platform department of about 80 people needed to go from two big groups to three. Leaders drew the future structure on a whiteboard, wheeled it out, and listed each team's name, mission, open roles and current members, then invited everyone to look and comment. Employees spotted mistakes in the design and saw opportunities they wanted to pursue. Transparency comes in degrees; more open companies have teams pitch themselves and let people choose. Whichever you pick, set a time limit, and err on the short side so people don't lose focus.
ex: The idea came from how Spotify reorganized its infrastructure teams

marks.d: Decide, then announce in one email
Procore: public draft, open to feedback

l153|286.c: What matters most in a change is clarity on who decides; RIDE sorts out everyone's role.
l153|286.e: Not every change can be participatory. When a company is acquired, employees get no say. But a team-level split can absolutely come from the team itself during a retrospective. The key is that everyone knows their role. She recommends the RIDE framework she learned from former colleague Pat Wadors: who recommends, who gives input, who decides, who executes. William Bridges's transitions model helps too: first an ending, then an uneasy neutral zone, and only then a new beginning. Leaders should explain what the new reality means in order to lift morale.
ex: She recommends William Bridges's book Transitions

l153|286.c: Isolating a small team with freedom over its process is a good way to incubate a new product.
l153|286.e: As employee 15 at Expertcity, she watched the company's tech-support marketplace fail to sell, and the CEO told her to stop and "go to the beach." She was then moved into an isolated team that validated the market using The Four Steps to the Epiphany, escaped the slow waterfall process, iterated faster, and built GoToMyPC, which she believes saved the company. For an isolated team to work: give it its own space, have leaders tell everyone else to leave it alone, free it from standard process, and have it report to an executive with real decision power. It can go wrong, too, for instance by leaving others to maintain something they had no say in.
ex: AppFolio's SecureDocs was incubated by an isolated team, then spun out and acquired
McDonald's Chicken McNuggets were also rescued by a small isolated team

items.d: The CEO said it made about $6 last month
Remote PC access that saved the company

l153|286.c: Pairing and rotation spread knowledge, which is both a safety net and a source of fulfillment.
l153|286.e: Switching is tied to learning and fulfillment. Changing teams or systems can make people feel new again and extend how long good employees stay. It is also a safety net: pair people up and rotate partners regularly so several people know every system. Then knowledge doesn't walk out the door when someone leaves, and it's easier to pull people onto important new projects. Expertcity once suffered when the only person who knew a system left. AppFolio handles huge volumes of rent payments and relies on pairing, rotation and test-driven development to keep that safe. Rotation shouldn't be arbitrary, though, like forcing a swap every two weeks.
ex: Menlo Innovations pairs everyone and rotates partners regularly
AppFolio engineers started rotating pairs on their own after a team split

result.d: No more single-person "knowledge towers"

l153|286.c: Splitting people by percentage, moving them without warning, and breaking up great teams are anti-patterns.
l153|286.e: She lists several common anti-patterns. Allocating one person by percentages across several projects looks efficient, but the percentages rarely add up and people can't switch context that often. People appearing or vanishing with no communication is just as damaging. And AppFolio CTO Jon Walker once tried spreading the members of a high-performing team across other teams, hoping to replicate the magic. It didn't replicate, and the original chemistry was destroyed. A great team is like a band; the chemistry doesn't survive being taken apart and transplanted.

items: Breaking up great teams to "seed" others

l154|288.c: Strategy is a design for a high-stakes challenge: diagnosis, guiding policy and coherent action, all three.
l154|288.e: To him, strategy is fundamentally problem solving, not applying analytical tools like the five forces or a 2×2 grid. A complete strategy starts with a diagnosis of the situation and a judgment about what deserves attention. Then comes a guiding policy: what to do and what not to do. Finally it has to land in concrete actions that don't work against each other. Leave out any one of the three and you have something else, but not a strategy.
ex: Microsoft's AI response: bet on a leading model company and plug it into search
Goals like high growth plus high return on equity often contradict each other

terms.d: What the challenge is and why it's hard
What to do, and what not to do

result.d: Missing one, it isn't strategy

l154|288.c: The most common roots of bad strategy are a missing diagnosis and goals dressed up as strategy.
l154|288.e: What companies call strategy is often a string of performance targets or a wish list. "We're not growing fast enough" is a value judgment; it says nothing about what is holding growth back. Without a diagnosis you can't act. Fluffy language and actions that contradict each other are bad strategy too, though less common than the first two. A good diagnosis says "because of this," and when people disagree, it actually commits to one explanation.
ex: The "strategy" of 17 US intelligence agencies was to "collaborate more effectively"
One client listed 17 priorities at the same time
US students lag on PISA tests, yet the prescription was "more college"

root.d: Documents or slogans that look like strategy

items.d: A list of ambitions instead of actions

l154|288.c: Power comes from an asymmetry, and it must be focused on a single target that can actually be moved.
l154|288.e: An evenly matched fight is a coin flip. Strategy exploits some asymmetry: moving first, reputation, relationships, an invention, network effects or scale in data. But that power only works when it's concentrated, like a magnifying glass focusing sunlight, on a target that can genuinely be influenced. Chase too many targets at once and the power dissipates. Yesterday's advantage can also turn into a burden, so keep asking what exactly tilts the odds in your favor.
ex: Burning a thread with a magnifying glass needs the sun, focus and something that can ignite
IBM recovered on big-customer relationships, then those ties held it back in the cloud era
Want to open a restaurant? Without a real edge, buy the S&P 500 instead

items.d: Something you can influence and advance
From a coin flip to a real edge

l154|288.c: Don't call it strategy; call it an action agenda: pick the challenge that's both important and addressable.
l154|288.e: The word "strategy" has been mangled by mission statements, visions and values documents, so he suggests simply writing "what we're going to do about this problem." Acknowledge all your ambitions first, then ask of each: can we make progress on this today, and what makes it hard? The challenge you choose has to be both important (close to your ambitions) and solvable. Then list what you'll do over the next one to three years, not the goals you hope to hit.
ex: His ambition list at 25: become a famous professor, drive a Morgan sports car, climb big mountains
Asking clients "what makes this hard" is when the real answers surface

cells.d: Important, but nothing you can do now
Doable, but far from your ambitions

l154|288.c: Good solutions come from insight gained by immersing yourself in the hardest part, not from picking off a menu.
l154|288.e: "Crux" is borrowed from climbing: the hardest move on the route, and if you can't make it, don't climb. Designers and engineers learn that if you stare at what makes a problem so hard, you often suddenly see a way around it. Insight is frightening because it isn't guaranteed to show up. But it isn't mystical either. It comes from soaking in a problem for a long time, and it may arrive while you're driving or in the shower.
ex: I. M. Pei solved the Louvre's entrance problem with a glass pyramid

l154|288.c: There's no scientific formula for strategy; you build diagnostic skill through historical analogy and rethinking.
l154|288.e: Strategy has no equations the way structural engineering does. It leans heavily on analogy to past human experience, which is why he recommends business history, biographies and military history. Faced with a messy situation, people grab the first explanation like a drowning person grabs a plank. The most important habit of mind is to think again: is there a better explanation? He once read newspaper front pages day by day from 1928 onward to feel how nobody at the time understood the Great Depression.
ex: His guess: the Depression was tied to saturation of durable goods like cars
Business schools prefer teaching theory because it's easier than teaching how to think

l154|288.c: Office politics and fear of acting are strategy's biggest obstacles; someone must finally make the call.
l154|288.e: Executives usually know most of what they need to know. The disagreements are about priorities, and about the fact that any action shifts power inside the company. That's why organizations need hierarchy: someone has to say "this is what we're doing, and here's who owns what." Today's leadership culture makes managers embarrassed to give orders. Donald Rumsfeld: every piece of intelligence comes with someone's private agenda

l154|288.c: A founder's strategy is a bet: believe you'll win, yet stay ready to change course at any time.

l155|289.c: The chasm exists because pragmatists only trust their peers and never treat visionaries as a reference.

Pragmatists are the opposite: they buy only after seeing what companies like theirs have bought. Many startups assume a visionary success story will win over the mainstream, but pragmatists see visionaries as odd and prone to leaving messes behind. So nobody wants to go first, like a middle-school dance where no one steps onto the floor. The sales pitch has to change too, from "we believe what you believe" to "we need what you have."

l155|289.c: Each adoption stage needs its own playbook; reusing the last stage's winning moves will fail.
l155|289.e: In the early market you sell a technology vision, a powerful executive sponsor conjures a budget from nowhere, and you deliver as a project. In the bowling alley you target one customer segment's pain and use a whole-solution approach to move budget away from the old way of doing things. In the tornado the category becomes something everyone needs, budgets already exist, and you grab share with a standard product. On main street the product has become a commodity and innovation shifts to services. The wrong playbook backfires, such as qualifying early-market customers by whether they already have a budget.
ex: Valuation logic: you capture roughly 10% of the "trapped value" you release
Juniper couldn't be the gorilla, so it became the "chimp" of telecom

l155|289.c: A beachhead must be big enough to matter, small enough to lead, and matched to your core strengths.
l155|289.e: A small company only gets partners to rally around it by being the big fish in some pond. So pick a segment where you can take 30% to 50% share within two years. A segment is bounded by the same geography, the same industry and the same profession, plus a use case that forces customers to act faster than usual. You can't attack several segments at once; when you're campaigning in New Hampshire, votes in Vermont don't count. The prerequisite is one flagship customer that makes your name.

l155|289.c: After the beachhead, expand only into adjacent segments, concentrating your fire like lighting a campfire.
l155|289.e: Stuck in the chasm, people get desperate and will sell to anyone. That's like waving a match back and forth under a whole log; it never catches. Hold the match on the kindling until it burns. Then expand only to what's adjacent: a new use case for the same customers, driven by customer referrals, or the same use case in a new industry, driven by partner introductions. This takes a company from tens of millions to hundreds of millions in revenue. Logs in another room are no use.
ex: Documentum's start: a new-drug application could run to 500,000 pages
Each day of delay cost a drug company roughly $1 to $2 million in patent value

l155|289.c: Selling to the mainstream means centering on their compelling reason to buy, not your features.
l155|289.e: A pragmatist's procurement process exists to keep new vendors out. Only when a problem is bad enough that the boss's boss knows about it will the owner push against that inertia. So in the bowling alley the conversation is never about you. Close the laptop, skip the demo, and ask: "Companies in your industry tend to have this problem; do you?" Let them talk and take notes in front of them. What's most valuable at this stage is your understanding of the problem domain. They won't say no; they just keep not saying yes.
ex: Ransomware gave every company an urgent reason to buy security
Qualify leads with a list like "seven symptoms of fatal churn"

items.d: Verify the problem, find the real owner
No discounts; promise to take the problem away

l155|289.c: Crossing the chasm, position as the technology leader for this specific problem; no discounts, no enterprise reps.
l155|289.e: The incumbent vendors understand the business but lack the new technology. Your technology peers may have better tech but don't know this domain. Your position is the one box that has both, and you don't ask the customer to throw out the incumbent. Discounting doesn't lower the buyer's risk; it makes them worry the service will be cut back, and nobody wants discount heart surgery. Enterprise salespeople used to covering accounts horizontally are also the wrong fit for the chasm. You want people who diagnose well, more like sales engineers.
ex: One of his "seven deadly sins": discounting before you've crossed the chasm
Targeting mistake: find the economic buyer, not just the end user

cells.d: Know the business, lack new tech
Strong tech, blind to this problem

l155|289.c: You've crossed the chasm when cash flow turns positive and you no longer need to raise.
l155|289.e: Venture money exists to change a company's value state so the next round is worth two to three times more. Otherwise, however much good work you do, you raise flat or down. Crossing the chasm means going from a cool possibility to a going concern in the accounting sense: loyal customers, a partner ecosystem, and clear customer acquisition cost and lifetime value, perhaps at $10 to $20 million in revenue. Raising after that is about ambition, not about running out of cash. He also thinks most software companies should bootstrap as far as they can first.
ex: You only need VC when the technology is too expensive or the window too short
Each funding round removes a different risk

items.d: Removes the risk you can't build it
Removes the risk the company dies

l156|292.c: To calm down, change your body's state first, not the story in your head.
l156|292.e: There are roughly four times as many nerves running from the body to the brain as the other way. So the body's state largely shapes your thoughts and emotions, and the brain often just invents a reason for a state that's already there. Instead of telling yourself the talk will go fine, change physical signals like your breathing first. Once the state shifts, thoughts and feelings follow. Anxious thoughts and shallow, fast breathing reinforce each other into a downward spiral. Mindfulness meditation can widen the gap between stimulus and response, but adjusting the breath directly works far faster.
ex: About 4 times as many nerves run body-to-brain as brain-to-body
He did 15 minutes of breathwork before his TEDx talk and walked on calm

items.d: Chest breathing, through the mouth, rushed
Triggers the stress response and hormones
The mind explains the body's state

l156|292.c: Breath is the nervous system's lever: longer exhales calm you, stronger inhales wake you up.
l156|292.e: Breathing happens automatically, yet we can also control it deliberately. When the exhale is about twice as long as the inhale, you drift toward calm; when the inhale is stronger or longer, you drift toward alertness. He suggests building a personal "if this, then breathe like that" toolkit for different situations: a quiet 4-4-8 (in for 4, hold 4, out 8) before a meeting, humming after too long at a screen, fast nasal breathing for the afternoon slump. The key is practicing a few minutes each morning for a week or two. Otherwise, when you're actually nervous, you won't remember to use any of it.
ex: 4-4-8 breathing: the ratio matters, so 3-3-6 works too
Humming releases nitric oxide and stimulates the vagus nerve, which helps the body relax
"Espresso breath": about 30 breaths per round, 2 to 3 rounds

marks.d: Relaxes the eyes, stimulates the vagus nerve
Exhale twice as long as the inhale
Fast nasal exhales instead of afternoon coffee

l156|292.c: Interoception is a trainable sixth sense; a quick APE body scan catches problems early.
l156|292.e: Interoception is the ability to sense what's going on inside your body. It can be trained, the way a chef trains their palate. The finer your perception, the earlier you catch the first signals before anxiety escalates. His check-in is APE: is your Awareness narrow or wide, how is your Posture, and what Emotions and sensations are in the body, plus your Breath. Noticing a tight stomach before a meeting isn't noise, it's data. It might be your gut warning you the deal is wrong, or a sign something someone said just triggered you.
ex: Research suggests traders with stronger interoception make better decisions and more money
"Email apnea": unconsciously holding your breath while reading messages
After noticing tightness in his chest, he pushed podcast recording to the summer

items.d: Narrow means tense, wide means relaxed
Posture directly shapes how you feel
Emotions and where you feel them
Ideally through the nose, into the belly, effortless

l156|292.c: Burnout warns you in three stages, feather, brick, then dump truck; adjust at the feather.
l156|292.e: At first the body only taps you lightly, like waking up a bit tired. Ignore that, and a few weeks later come brick-level signals such as picking fights or losing your temper. Keep going and the dump truck arrives: a serious health crisis or even getting fired. Early signs include overreacting to small things, worse sleep, and strain in close relationships and at work. One key marker is needing alcohol or CBD to come down in the evening, which means your load has crossed the threshold you can handle.
ex: The dump truck can be a health crisis like type 2 diabetes
Needing a drink to unwind after work is a red flag

items.d: Health crisis, breakdown or getting fired

l156|292.c: Stress cycles that never finish pile up as emotional debt, and talk therapy alone won't clear it.
l156|292.e: Stress mobilizes the body. If there's no relaxation to close the cycle afterward, the load gets stored, much like technical debt: necessary early on, but if you never pay it down it keeps growing until it pushes you past what you can tolerate and you crash. He's skeptical of talk therapy that stays purely intellectual. The suppressed emotions need to be fully felt, in a setting that feels safe. The path is to build interoception first, then learn self-regulation, then practice letting emotions move through, ideally alongside a body-oriented therapist.
ex: He did about 200 breathwork journeys in Bali
He recommends two body-based therapies: Somatic Experiencing and Hakomi
Neuroscientist Damasio's idea of "somatic markers": the body tags experiences with feeling

items.d: First know what the body is holding
Come down when emotion rises; don't drown
Let every emotion run its full course

l156|292.c: Emotions are key information for decisions; choices made to avoid a feeling come out badly skewed.
l156|292.e: He rejects "just the facts, not the feelings." Neuroscientist Damasio studied a patient named Elliot who lost his emotional capacity after tumor surgery and then couldn't even decide what to have for lunch; his life fell apart. The brain makes predictions from signals the body sends up, and ignoring them throws away information. People who fear conflict or anger unconsciously pick whichever option avoids those feelings. It also helps to know whether you freeze and withdraw or fight back when triggered. Come down and find safety first, then talk and decide.
ex: Elliot went from successful businessman to divorced and bankrupt
He himself leans toward freezing and is practicing expressing anger in a healthy way

items: Choose the option that dodges conflict
Decide while in a reactive state
Discard what the body is signaling
Accept in advance how the decision will feel

d.verdict: Only people who can sit with emotion make unskewed decisions

l156|292.c: Burnout is badly underpriced; hard work has to be matched by an equally serious rest ethic.
l156|292.e: He surveyed leaders who had burned out and asked them to estimate what it cost their companies. The median was about $100,000, from lost talent, missed opportunities and poor decisions made in the run-up to burnout. A CEO's emotional state spreads to the team; the organization's nervous system mirrors the CEO's. He isn't against intense work, but it should be like taking on technical debt deliberately: a few months at high intensity, then a month or two to come down, with recovery practices like NSDR (non-sleep deep rest) along the way.
ex: Leaders he surveyed put the median cost of burnout at about $100,000

Quoting Kevin Kelly: a good work ethic needs a good rest ethic

result.d: The organization steadies as the CEO does

l157|296.c: When a team's ideas turn cautious, the problem is usually fear, so rebuild safety first.
l157|296.e: She noticed her team starting to give feedback anonymously and over-polishing everything before showing it to leaders. Correcting course that late wastes a lot of work, and the ideas kept getting more incremental. Inspired by mindset coach Ben Crowe, she believes the opposite of play isn't work but fear. Only when people feel safe does the mind open up and reach a state of flow. So she and her PMs designed mechanisms: small-group peer reviews of rough drafts, a twice-yearly offsite where executives talk about their failures, and a "split $10" game to check everyone's priorities.
ex: Signs of disconnection appeared when the PM team reached about 15 people
"Fight Club": 30 minutes a week where she and the engineering and design leads argue on purpose

l157|296.c: Remote work needs deliberate gatherings, protected deep-work blocks, and fully asynchronous status updates.
l157|296.e: Atlassian believes you don't need an office to build world-class products, and that flexibility isn't a perk but something that changes lives. Early on, people worried about reaching each other and packed their calendars with meetings, which wrecked productivity. A PM needs three or four uninterrupted hours to get into a creative state. She and her leadership team lined up two long blocks each week, and meetings are reserved for solving problems. Status rolls up asynchronously in Atlas, decisions go into Confluence, and across time zones people communicate with recorded audio and video.

result.d: Meetings only for real problems

l157|296.c: Getting buy-in is a journey, not something one perfect pitch meeting delivers.
l157|296.e: Many people assume a well-written proposal and one meeting will get approval, and that mindset is wrong from the start. Her approach is to find the people who will be affected, positively or negatively, as early as possible, then keep going back to them with designs, data and user-test results, folding their concerns into the plan. Executives get one-on-one conversations before the meeting so they show up as supporters. In the meeting itself, say up front whether you need a decision or feedback, tell one storyline of current state, proposed change and impact, and know your data cold.

Open by saying whether you want a decision or feedback

With designs, data and test results
Clear ask, one storyline, solid data

l157|296.c: To push unglamorous improvements, start small and win people over with data and real user pain.

When platform teams she depended on couldn't fit it into their roadmaps, she asked each to send a "shepherd" to review code and design while her team did the building. Then she showed the pain with videos of customers struggling, started small, and kept shipping to maintain momentum.

It performed well after launch. What she missed was that automation would be useful for every role and every product, and could have been built as a general service. Years later the company had to pay a lot to acquire a company that did advanced automation. l158|297.c: OpenAI builds general-purpose capability, so startups should build for specific industries, not general assistants.

So a startup building a general assistant will eventually compete head-on with OpenAI, unless it can fix ten of ChatGPT's pain points at once. OpenAI will not, however, build something like an AI sales rep. l158|297.c: Prompting is like talking to a person: the model is smart but knows nothing about you, so context decides everything.
l158|297.e: Models are trained to answer whatever they're asked. Ask something vague and you get something vague back, like asking a stranger "how's it going" and hearing "fine." He compares the model to a human-level person with zero background: it doesn't know who you are or what you want, and it is too eager to answer to tell you it needs more. So feed it material. l158|297.c: Priorities start with whether something advances AGI and reliability; revenue is just a means to compute.

l158|297.c: When compute is the constraint, the research team should stay small; another researcher can slow everyone down.
l158|297.e: OpenAI's growth has gone mostly into customer-facing roles and the engineering that keeps ChatGPT running, while the research team is kept deliberately small. Unless that person makes everyone meaningfully more productive, it's a net loss. Product engineering is different: one more engineer writes more code, which is usually a net gain.

Many products just bolt on a simple chat window. The real move is to rebuild the core experience from the ground up, so a user can ask a question and get a summary backed by data. l159|299.c: Pick one highlight for the day, then run the highlight, laser, energize, reflect loop as an experiment.

In the morning, imagine being asked that evening "what was the highlight of your day," pick one thing, write it on a sticky note and block 60 to 90 minutes for it. Then use tactics to block distractions and look after your energy, and check in that night. The rest of the day can be messy; a day with a highlight just feels different. l159|299.c: Big important projects naturally lose to small urgent tasks, so you have to make room on purpose.
l159|299.e: The "A project" you really want to do is big, hard to start, slow to pay off in any dopamine, and nobody is chasing you for it. The small tasks in front of it are the opposite: obvious how to do, instantly satisfying, and seemingly urgent. Email, meetings, short videos, even items on your OKRs can all be that kind of task. So getting more efficient just means doing small things faster. He trusts that people have good instincts about where their time should go, even when the thing isn't on their boss's radar. l159|299.c: Delete the bottomless apps, feel the relief once, and you'll know you can let go.
l159|299.e: In 2012, playing with his kids, he caught himself scrolling without meaning to and deleted every app with an endless feed: email, social, news. Deleting them felt bad; afterward it felt like relief. Keeping them around leaves "attention residue," like carrying the One Ring and constantly wanting to touch it. His analogy: your highlight is a good meal a few steps away, and the apps are candy stuck to your face. Push the candy farther away than the meal and you'll naturally eat the meal. The cost is slower replies and fewer followers, which he thinks is worth it.
ex: The idea of attention residue comes from researcher Sophie Leroy

A timer on the router switches off home wifi on schedule

items.d: A no-wifi office or a router timer

l159|299.c: Reset expectations with a signature and slow your inbox; what really changes is your own guilt.
l159|299.e: Put it in your email signature or auto-reply: "Because I'm focused on an important project, I check email once or twice a day." You can add an emergency contact or not. The word "because" matters, since people are more forgiving of a request that comes with a reason. On the surface this resets other people's expectations, but the bigger effect is renegotiating with yourself. Most of the pressure comes from feeling you're not good enough if you don't reply instantly. The faster you reply, the more mail comes back. Slow down and the whole cycle slows.
ex: The photocopier study: say "because" and people are more likely to let you cut in
Inside Character, most communication moved into Notion documents

l159|299.c: A design sprint builds and tests a prototype in five days, replacing guesswork with real customer reactions.

l161|303.c: Talent density is the foundation of everything else in Netflix's culture, maintained through the keeper test.

l163|310.c: Use your manager more: your job is to get the thing done, not to prove you can do it alone.

l163|310.c: The failures worth regretting are the ones that hurt people; meet disagreement with curiosity, not ego defense.

The long-term vision stays fixed; how to get there is constantly tested

items: Global expansion rooted in the US

d.verdict: Market closeness and a truly global view set TikTok apart

l164|311.c: Algorithms do the heavy lifting, but going global still means sending people in and letting local talent tune the machine.
l164|311.e: He grants that the recommendation algorithm does a huge amount of the distribution work in each market, but technology is ultimately a tool. The real difference is whether you're willing to show up: send teams, hire locals, understand the culture. Culture drives behavior, and if you don't understand the culture you can't read the users. So TikTok adjusts the content supply market by market, and for ad creative it combines machine tagging with human business judgment.
ex: Early research in Thailand: consumers didn't care about print quality from premium ink cartridges
In Japan, food and consumer electronics content beats dancing
A coupon sticker on a product sometimes works better than a price cut

items.d: Send people in to tune the machine
Creative relies on human business judgment

l164|311.c: Give people context instead of control: everyone should treat the whole business as their own problem.
l164|311.e: Boxing people into job descriptions creates artificial walls between departments and slows everything down. TikTok shares the full picture so that everyone thinks like an owner of the business, not a part that keeps the machine running. The companion principle is to think proactively and execute together: if you have an idea about someone else's area, go talk to the owner rather than doing it for them. He admits that early on he drew "can do / can't do" lines for his team, and it only slowed things down.
ex: The Lego analogy: you can't build the whole thing without seeing the full picture
The goal isn't to deliver a go-to-market plan but to land it together with sales

terms.d: Treat the whole problem as yours
Bring the owner in and push forward

result.d: No artificial department walls

l164|311.c: Product, engineering and sales have to sit close together for a big company to keep startup speed.
l164|311.e: He has never seen a company where engineering, product and sales work this closely. If engineers don't know what the market wants and PMs don't hear customer feedback, you can't build the right product or tell a good go-to-market story. Structure makes it real: a quarterly cross-functional meeting of about 180 people, where everyone reads documents and writes comments to sync up. PMs and engineering leads at every level also go out to meet customers and feel the pain points firsthand. Add a "Day One" mindset, and anyone can go straight to a co-founder with a suggestion.
ex: Memos and Day One came from Amazon; OKRs came from Google
Last year he broke up his own team and embedded it directly in sales
The goal: run the second half of the marathon faster than the first

items.d: Sales brings back real pain points

l164|311.c: Hypergrowth is the worst time to lower the hiring bar, because the wrong people only slow the team down.
l164|311.e: When he joined in 2020, the ads go-to-market team had two people and needed to hire about 100 within six months. The pressure cascaded down, and both he and his managers lowered the bar at times. In hindsight, the wrong hires slowed the team down. He hires for curiosity, discipline and the ability to prioritize, because a context-rich culture falls apart without discipline. The other lesson is that managers can't drift away from the front line and only manage people; their judgment gets worse and they lose their edge in the job market.
ex: His last interview question: what are your goals for the next three to five years
Joining a rocket-ship company is a lifestyle, not a nine-to-five

l164|311.c: Advertising is really about discovery; TikTok is digital word of mouth that can carry people all the way to purchase.
l164|311.e: He distinguishes the three platforms as Google's intent graph, Meta's social graph and TikTok's content graph. Because distribution works differently on each, copying the other two's playbooks often fails on TikTok.
