Digital advertising makes people think everything can be measured precisely, but he sees advertising's essence as getting discovered by people who don't know you and creating demand that wasn't there. Word of mouth leads to action, so TikTok isn't stopping at brand awareness; with e-commerce and shopping ads it is moving to the full funnel.
ex: The hashtag "TikTok made me buy it" has billions of views
He downloaded Duolingo after seeing a video and kept a 40-day streak

l164|311.c: New advertisers should build an organic account first, then run broad targeting and test at least 10 creatives a week.
l164|311.e: He suggests spending time as an ordinary user first to absorb the platform's culture, then opening a business account and posting organic content that is authentic rather than polished. Once ads start, run them for at least a month to get through the learning curve, ideally with ten or more different creatives a week. If resources are tight, use CapCut or a certified creative partner. The most common mistake is starting with retargeting or narrow targeting, which boxes you in. Broad targeting usually performs noticeably better early on. Later, use A/B tests or geo splits to measure incremental lift.
ex: Some advertisers have built creative teams dedicated solely to TikTok
He made an anniversary video for his wife with CapCut

items.d: Post from a business account to test
10+ a week for at least a month

l165|40.c: Pandemic over-hiring, expensive money and AI have combined, and the reckoning for product management has begun.
l165|40.e: He sees several forces arriving at once: massive over-hiring with a lowered bar during the pandemic, rising interest rates that made money expensive, uncertainty from generative AI, and remote work dragging on speed and innovation. Big companies outside Silicon Valley have it worst, with agile coaches, product owners, assorted project managers and PM assistants stacked on top of each other, plus heavyweight process frameworks like SAFe, at staggering cost for little result. Good companies do more with far fewer people, which is why these roles are the most exposed in layoffs.
ex: Ten years ago he wrote "Epic Waste" criticizing the proliferation of these roles
Treating product ops as the PM's errand runner is a red flag

items.d: Expensive money plus the AI shock

l165|40.c: Feature teams deliver output and empowered teams own outcomes; the former don't really need a PM.
l165|40.e: A feature team gets a roadmap of features, often from executives or big customers, and its job is to design, build and ship them on time. That's project management, and engineers and designers can do it themselves, which is why so many people conclude PMs add no value. An empowered product team instead gets one or two customer or business problems each quarter, and is measured on whether the problem got solved, not whether something shipped. His line for CEOs and CFOs: what matters is time to money, not time to market. You only truly need a PM when the team is accountable for outcomes.
ex: "We don't want PMs" is the biggest tell that you're looking at a feature team
Ask PMs to define their job and you often hear "coordinating, communicating, herding cats"

d.verdict: Output is easy, outcomes are hard; outcomes are where PMs add value

l165|40.c: A PM is a creator alongside design and engineering, responsible for value and business viability.
l165|40.e: Engineers own whether something can be built. The PM owns value, meaning whether customers want it, and viability, meaning whether the business can sell it, market it, support it, and do so legally and within compliance. He dislikes the line "my job is to explain the why"; the why should come from product strategy. To do the job, a PM has to become the expert on customers and data, understand the constraints from sales, finance, compliance and legal, and know the market deeply. Otherwise the team ends up pulling 20 stakeholders into a room and sliding back into design by committee.
ex: Before he became a PM, he was required to visit 30 customers, 15 in the US and 15 in Europe
Airbnb's hard problem wasn't acquiring users but making San Francisco listings legal
Until a startup has about 20–25 engineers, a founder should be the PM

items.d: Go deep with users and customers yourself
How usage and buying behavior change

l165|40.c: AI will first replace backlog administrators and feature-team PMs, while empowered PMs become more essential.
l165|40.e: He grants that AI is hitting engineering and design sooner, and the timing is hard to call, but the direction is clear. Product owners who only manage a backlog in Jira are the most at risk. Most of a feature-team PM's work is administrative and will be heavily automated too. PMs responsible for value and viability matter more, not less. For instance, once software goes from deterministic to probabilistic, deciding where a "probably right" answer is acceptable involves legal and ethical judgment. He has also changed his advice: work out your own answer first, then use ChatGPT to challenge it, because people trust AI output too readily.
ex: Certification courses teach Jira, which is like learning to use Google Docs
Top product designers and tech leads will also become more important

l165|40.c: Empowerment isn't teams picking their own direction; leaders set strategy and bets, teams find solutions.
l165|40.e: Boz described Meta as fairly top-down, and Cagan thinks that is exactly what a good company looks like, though he wouldn't call it top-down. Pushing a feature roadmap onto teams is the real top-down. Product strategy is the product leaders' job: deciding where to focus and what to bet on. Then they hand problems to serious cross-functional teams and give them room to figure out how to solve them. If every team decided for itself what to work on, 50 teams would do 50 different things. That's anarchy.
ex: He rates Zuckerberg as very strong at product strategy
Much of this confusion comes from misguided agile coaches

items.d: Own the solution to a problem

l165|40.c: About 90% of PM content comes from the feature-team world, so practitioners have to think critically.
l165|40.e: What made him "spicier" was the largest PM certification body publishing a chart of what a PM does that was almost entirely project management. He estimates that about 90% of PM content online comes from feature teams or worse. Even well-meaning people in communities mostly share what they learned at weak companies, so the pattern copies itself. The way out is personal: don't see yourself as a victim of your company, filter what you read critically, research your prospective manager before taking a job, and deliberately raise your skills to the level of a real PM. That often leads to promotion, and sometimes to the company running a pilot.
ex: One of the few good books: Teresa Torres's Continuous Discovery Habits
Most sales-driven B2B products are bad because the CEO isn't a product person

items.d: They think this is what a PM is

l165|40.c: The product operating model is a set of principles, not a process; transformation hinges on strategy, discovery and delivery.
l165|40.e: The new book answers the question readers ask most: our company is so far from this, how do we change? They chose the non-threatening term "product operating model" and avoided "product-led," which sounds like a power grab. The core is 20 principles, such as innovation over predictability, learning over fear of failure, giving teams problems to solve, embracing rapid experimentation, and small, frequent, independent releases. In practice it comes down to three things: how you decide what to build, how you solve problems, and how you build and deliver. It also takes four new competencies: real PMs, product designers, tech leads and product leaders.
ex: Every case study is from outside Silicon Valley, such as the UK's Trainline
Saudi travel agency Almosafer captured more than 80% of its market
Most companies release quarterly, which serves customers poorly and learns too slowly

terms.d: Find solutions that are valuable and viable

result.d: 20 principles plus 4 new competencies

l166|316.c: Speak up for the company as a whole, even if it means cutting your own project or adding a boss above you.
l166|316.e: After YouTube acquired his startup, he told management within about three months that, given the company's overall plan, it made no sense to put 50 engineers on rebuilding his product. Later he ran the creator side and reported directly to CEO Salar Kamangar, but found he couldn't keep up with how Salar thought about problems. So he asked to report to Hunter Walk instead, adding a layer above himself, and grew faster for it. He could do this because he had absorbed the company's strategy and trusted that a healthy team rewards decisions like these. If it doesn't, that is worth finding out early.
ex: When to quit: most projects die because the team runs out of stamina, not money
His first job taught him to recognize a high-caliber team

result.d: Cut your project, change your boss

l166|316.c: When customers and the business conflict, rank them by principles set in advance, not what helps right now.
l166|316.e: Ideally what is good for customers is also good for the business, but not always, so you need guiding principles agreed ahead of time. At Thumbtack, a marketplace for hiring local pros like plumbers and photographers, the order was customers first, pros second, the company last. You might think a marketplace should look after its supply side first. But what pros need most is more good customers, so improving the customer experience ends up helping pros and the company too. Raising prices for revenue in a way that hurts how easily deals get done is the opposite: optimizing one piece at the expense of the whole.
ex: "Thumbtack last" is easy to say and hard to actually do

items.d: The whole wins, not one part

l166|316.c: Growth masks every problem, and a company that depends on one channel will eventually get hurt.
l166|316.e: Thumbtack grew up on Google search traffic. When he joined, growth was in the triple digits. After several Google algorithm changes it fell to double digits, and then the company saw its first year-over-year decline ever. During the fast years, a lot of customer demand went to waste because there weren't enough pros, and the team knew but didn't feel urgency. Only when growth turned negative did the organization really face its problems. He thinks every PM should live through at least one downturn. Now he asks of any product: does it rely on a single channel, and what comes first if growth goes negative? In hard times, everyone on the CEO's team has to engage with product strategy, not watch from the side.
ex: Sequoia's Brian Schreier called it the prettiest smile curve he had ever seen
The CFO and head of HR should leave fingerprints on product strategy too

l166|316.c: Thumbtack turned around by rebuilding its core loop: from a 24-hour wait to instant quotes from pros.
l166|316.e: In the old flow, a customer described the job and was told to expect replies within 24 hours. Thumbtack then sent the request to pros, who had to pay before they could quote and be seen. That worked early on, but the company had outgrown it. Customers were left hanging at the moment they most wanted help, and pros paid without knowing whether the customer was serious, which created a bad cycle. The team rebuilt both the core loop and the way it made money: pros could quote instantly, and the charge moved to a new point in the process. Advertising changed too, from targeting one small local market at a time to casting a wider net and optimizing afterward.
ex: Similar to Airbnb moving from request-to-book to instant booking
A product that spans online and offline is exponentially harder to run

items: Pros pay before they can quote
Ads targeted one local market at a time
Charge at a new point in the process

d.verdict: Swapped the engine mid-flight and turned growth around

l166|316.c: Don't judge a big company's incubation team only by whether it found the next Instagram.
l166|316.e: He helped start Facebook's New Product Experimentation team (NPE) and thinks it is unfair to measure such teams by whether they hit the jackpot. At Facebook's scale, running an experiment with just a hundred users is nearly impossible, and a PM who wants to sit next to users has to go through layers of intermediaries. NPE let the organization practice doing things that don't scale again, exposed obstacles in the main product process, served as a hiring magnet, and produced ideas that later became features in other products. The most important piece is incentives: evaluating a zero-to-one team with the regular twice-a-year performance review kills it before it starts.
ex: Ideas like Threads were floating around inside NPE at the time
Nike's incubation lab uses separate hiring and incentives, then plugs winners into Nike's distribution

root.d: More than finding the next big business

l166|316.c: Grammarly has stayed profitable through a frictionless, install-and-go experience and a bootstrapped focus on revenue.
l166|316.e: Grammarly is 15 years old, has been profitable since day one, and is bigger than people assume. For years it was seen as "a feature inside your word processor," which kept it off the giants' radar. He thinks users love it because you install it and immediately write better, without changing how you work, and it helps you in dozens or hundreds of text boxes every day. He calls it a huge AI achievement disguised as a small UX improvement. The team started in Ukraine and never planned to raise money, so everyone is used to asking how their work turns into revenue. At today's scale, though, it also has to invest ahead in new products, new channels, and a shift toward enterprise customers.
ex: Once large language models arrived, it found itself at the center of the storm

items.d: Work has to turn into revenue

l166|316.c: Pick the painful job that stretches you, but keep one or two strengths to stand on.
l166|316.e: He admits it is hard to predict which job will succeed, but you can tell whether the people around you are excellent, and you can find a place that forces you to do things you've never done. The promised land is usually on the other side of the pain. Still, don't pick a situation where everything is new. If you are managing a big team for the first time, do it in a product area you already know, lean on one or two strengths, and learn the rest. He barely tweets or writes a newsletter; he meets people by working with them. Do real work that gives you energy, and you are more likely to become one of the best at it.
ex: His life motto: we are meant to struggle
In interviews he likes solving a problem together, like how to rebuild email today

marks.d: One or two strengths, rest is new

l167|318.c: For B2B companies, press is mostly third-party validation, not a direct source of signups.
l167|318.e: Lenny had been featured in several big outlets without seeing growth, and she says that is normal. For companies selling to businesses, the value of coverage is that someone else is vouching for you. Buyers of an early-stage product worry you might disappear tomorrow, so a news article attached to a sales email or a recruiting message is far more convincing than self-praise. Reporters like founder stories and company culture, which may not sway customers but can help hiring. Consumer products depend on the case: if the product is dead simple and you get it after one try, organic press alone can drive growth. Categories that live on review rankings rely more on affiliate marketing.
ex: Perplexity spent almost nothing on paid marketing; press drove a surge in signups and paying users
Recruiters have limited space on LinkedIn, and a link to coverage carries weight

items: Attach links in sales and recruiting

d.verdict: First decide which audience the coverage is for

l167|318.c: Funding news can always land if you do it right: keep it simple, offer an exclusive, follow up politely.
l167|318.e: Many founders assume TechCrunch will cover their round automatically. But another PR firm once counted that in one week TechCrunch published only 9 funding stories while roughly 50 rounds were announced. Her approach is to keep the message plain: say clearly whether it is a product launch or a funding round, offer it as an exclusive, state the amount, the space, and the investors, and find the reporter who actually covers that space. If there is no reply, follow up after three or four days with one new piece of information, then move to the next reporter. Three or four well-chosen reporters is usually enough.
ex: The count came from a tweet by another agency, Propeller PR
She says she has never had to abandon a funding announcement because it couldn't be placed

l167|318.c: Match the outlet to the story type, because each publication only takes certain kinds of pieces.
l167|318.e: She warns that media changes fast, so this is a snapshot. TechCrunch suits funding news and a company's first feature, and its conferences and podcasts are other ways in. Axios only cares about deals, so don't pitch product launches there, though its local editions are worth a try. Business Insider takes pitch-deck stories, founder journeys with numbers, and all kinds of lists. VentureBeat focuses on AI, and Fast Company leans toward the future of work and design. To get into The New York Times or The Wall Street Journal you usually have to disclose valuation and revenue; otherwise an early-stage company gets a sentence or two at most.
ex: Forbes lists and its contributor network have a lower bar for early companies
TechCrunch recently stopped accepting outside opinion pieces

root.d: Match it to the story type

l167|318.c: Relationships with reporters matter less than you think; a well-written cold email works just as well.
l167|318.e: Journalists change jobs too often for a contacts-based approach to last. A relationship gets your email opened and maybe answered, but good reporters don't cover you out of friendship. The hard part is writing a thoughtful, short message to the right person: put your intent and the relevant section right in the subject line. Her most successful pitch ever was three sentences. If a reporter asks for sources on Twitter, a dozen words and a link are enough. You can also point out a gap in their coverage or offer a contrarian take. Once you've worked together, then invest in the relationship.
ex: She and Lenny had never met; this appearance came from a cold email
Clockwise's CEO wrote that Shopify cutting meetings treats the symptom, not the cause

items.d: Know their beat and what they haven't covered
Exclusive, contrarian, or a gap filled
New info, or a different channel

l167|318.c: Don't call yourself a category creator; compare yourself to a famous giant so reporters get it instantly.
l167|318.e: Many companies want to position themselves as the creator of a new category. She thinks this almost never works in PR, and it is usually not true anyway. What works better is saying you do what some household-name product does, but better for specific reasons. That hands the reporter a ready-made frame of reference. Even without a big-name rival to borrow, you can find the single most interesting thread, in your customers, your partnerships, or your founder's story, and focus on that instead of cramming in every marketing message.
ex: Ramp positioned its bill-pay feature as a challenger to Bill.com and landed CNBC coverage
Column Tax focused on tax filing for low-income families and got into Fast Company
Entropy told the story of immigrant founders blocked from renting and what it reveals about credit

result.d: Like "coming for Zapier"

l167|318.c: Write in plain language, drop the traditional press release, and make growth numbers specific and believable.
l167|318.e: She estimates that at least half of press releases are full of empty phrases like "AI assistant," "human-in-the-loop collaboration," and "powerful multiplayer experience," simply because that is how marketing people are used to writing. Her fix is to first answer out loud: what does the product do, for whom, who are the customers, why should anyone care, and what is new this time. Then cut the jargon and read it aloud. Paying $300 to $2,000 to blast a release over the wire reaches almost no one; early and mid-stage companies are better off publishing a blog post under the founder's name. For growth, don't say "700% growth since coming out of stealth." Say revenue is in the six figures and growing about 30% a quarter.
ex: Gamma built its funding announcement in its own presentation tool and got TechCrunch coverage
Public-company earnings and similar cases still call for a press release

items.d: What it does, for whom, what's new
Ask what each term really means
Shareable, and you set the style

l167|318.c: Podcasts and newsletters are now standard PR channels, and social works through executives, not brand accounts.
l167|318.e: She pitches podcasts and newsletters alongside traditional press. To find podcasts, search the industries your customers are in, then filter: do they host vendor executives, are they still publishing, how good are they and who has been on before. You can also just ask customers what they listen to. If you sell to CFOs, send your own CFO on the show. Open with a one-line question, "are you open to guest suggestions?", which gets a higher reply rate. On social media, brand accounts struggle to build a following because people follow people. It is only worth investing if an executive is willing to take strong positions. She posts on LinkedIn at least once a month, and every post brings in client inquiries.
ex: A tweet from Box CEO Aaron Levie once directly led to a news story
Morning Brew's workplace column has a submission form; she says about half her pitches get in

l167|318.c: Don't be dazzled by big-name agencies; ask about month one, read recent samples, and start six weeks early.
l167|318.e: Big agencies are used to serving household-name brands, so they tend to be reactive and control-focused, the opposite of the fast experimentation a startup needs. She suggests asking exactly what the agency will do in the first month, requesting recent writing samples, and meeting the team that will actually do the work. Skip the big formal RFP, because good agencies won't do lots of free work. Start a major announcement about six weeks ahead, and let your top-choice reporter's schedule set the date rather than clinging to your own. On budget, boutique firms start around $10,000 a month, hers starts at $15,000, and a Series C company rarely needs to spend more than $30,000.
ex: One company stuck to its launch date, sent the release, and got zero coverage
A one-off project runs about $10,000 to $20,000

l168|320.c: A new product must score at least 4 points more efficient than the old way before users switch for good.
l168|320.e: "Ten times better" can't be measured, so he uses scores instead. Ask people to rate the old way and the new way from 0 to 10; the gap has to be at least 4. A taxi might be a 3 and Uber a 9. Once you hit Delta 4, three things happen: the switch is irreversible, users tolerate occasional failures, and they can't help bragging about it, what he calls a unique brag-worthy proposition, so customer acquisition costs are very low or zero. Below 4, the opposite holds: users switch back, forgive nothing, and tell no one. And moving something online does not automatically make it more efficient.
ex: Buying a suit online: Lenny scored it 5 online versus 7 in a store
He sees large language models as a true Delta 4 product, like magic
The framework grew out of his thinking on entropy and evolutionary biology

items.d: Word of mouth, near-zero acquisition cost

l168|320.c: Indian-born CEOs succeed by preserving the founder's dharma and switching between two roles when needed.
l168|320.e: He first points to the immigrant drive to prove oneself and India's reverence for math. Then he borrows a framework from mythologist Devdutt Pattanaik, a two-by-two of values versus obedience to rules. Krishna has strong values but breaks the rules, like a founder. Rama has strong values and follows the rules, growing an enterprise by its established dharma, its guiding principles. Many incoming CEOs want to rename the company or change the logo to leave their mark, and end up doing damage. Indian-born CEOs tend to stay humble and carry the founder's principles forward, switching into Krishna mode during a crisis and back to Rama afterward.
ex: Satya Nadella played Krishna during the OpenAI leadership crisis
Tim Cook has carried on Steve Jobs's dharma

cells.d: Obeys on the surface, no values

l168|320.c: In India users come easy but revenue per user doesn't, so the Western mass-user playbook fails.
l168|320.e: He argues that revenue per user tracks income per person. India's annual income per capita is about $2,500, so you cannot make $100 a year from each user. Traffic is cheap and smartphones are everywhere, so global giants harvest huge user numbers here to support their valuations while making very little money; India has become a "monthly-active-user farm." The deeper reason is how people think about time. Indians have never been paid by the hour, so they can't say what an hour of their time is worth, and many Indian languages have no word for efficiency. That makes it hard to charge for saving time.
ex: He estimates Meta earns only $3 to $4 per Indian user per year
The mass of paying subscribers Netflix and Spotify expected never showed up
Someone earning $100 an hour will still spend an hour to save $10 on a flight

items.d: No sense of what an hour is worth

l168|320.c: In a low-trust market, focus is a curse, because trust pools in super apps and super brands.
l168|320.e: When each user brings in little money, you have to do several things for them. But the bigger factor is trust. He calls places where institutions offer little protection and consumers are afraid to try new things low-trust markets, and most developing countries are like this. In the US you can sue if you slip in a coffee shop; in India nobody would think of it. When trust is scarce, it concentrates in a few names. So one app does hundreds of things and one brand sells everything from salt to cars, and the fun of trying something new is far weaker.
ex: Tata sells salt, cars, and jewelry, and people buy on the brand name alone
Many old Indian brands carry their founder's name, like Chyavanprash

items.d: New brands struggle to earn trust
One brand does hundreds of things

l168|320.c: Indian society doesn't yet reward risk takers, but first-generation founders are rewriting the rules.
l168|320.e: Societies that think long term are naturally averse to risk. Arranged marriages are still common in India, and a failed founder struggles to find a match. Inside big companies, someone who tries a zero-to-one project and fails gets neither promoted nor poached, while the person minding a legacy brand with built-in tailwinds climbs steadily. Family businesses are mostly buy-low-sell-high trading, so the public keeps asking when CRED will turn a profit and doesn't grasp the internet playbook of building distribution and brand first and monetizing later. Online mockery is common too. He says envy is like Wi-Fi, it only reaches people nearby, and he only takes criticism seriously from people doing better than him.
ex: In Portugal's churches, explorers are buried alongside royalty
He says tech is about 27 to 30% of US stock market value, versus 2 to 3% in India
India now has a national startup day, and the prime minister talks about entrepreneurship publicly

items: Minds a legacy brand with tailwinds
Tries zero to one and fails

d.verdict: A country moves forward when risk takers get the highest status

l168|320.c: Founders absorb uncertainty for everyone, and the bigger the company, the more stability everyone needs from them.
l168|320.e: CRED's core insight was that India's time-valuing, high-purchasing-power population is concentrated in about 25 million households, so it built only for them, rather than feeding investors the "next China" scale story. His previous successful exit is what let him raise a $25 million Series A to bet on that view. As the company grew, he found that being good at zero to one doesn't make a company good at ten to a hundred, so the founder has to evolve. Investors go from seed funds to growth funds to sovereign wealth funds, each demanding more stability, while the company still can't lose its zero-to-one DNA.
ex: Where profits sit reflects a country's values: only two or three retailers rank among India's 1,000 most profitable companies
Mark Zuckerberg has lately played Shiva: tear it down, then come back stronger

items.d: Need a high degree of stability

l168|320.c: Curiosity and second-order thinking are the strongest forms of adaptability, and good questioners will have the edge.
l168|320.e: He thinks curious people don't show off their expertise and get excited by problems they know nothing about. Curiosity requires safety, so even a CEO has to be willing to ask in the group chat what a word means. He once asked GPT why sharks and crocodiles have survived for hundreds of millions of years, and got three answers: they can lower their metabolism, they hunt with a high hit rate, and they adapt to drastic change. Companies are the same. Second-order thinking is the ability to trace chain reactions accurately, like predicting the butterfly effect; the brain resists it, so it has to be trained from childhood. In the AI era, people who ask good questions will have the advantage.
ex: His interview question: if everyone vaccinated against COVID died tonight, what would the world look like in a year?
His "Whyfi school": ask your kids one why question at every meal
He asks executives monthly: what was the hardest problem you solved last month?

terms.d: Burn less energy in a crisis
Chase less, catch what you chase

result.d: Survive like a long-lived species

l169|323.c: Nerves are normal, and relabeling them as excitement actually makes you perform better.
l169|323.e: Researchers broadly agree that being nervous about speaking in public is human nature, and knowing everyone feels it takes some pressure off. Harvard's Alison Wood Brooks found that anxiety and excitement are almost the same physical arousal; the difference is the label. Tell yourself the racing heart means "I'm excited to share my ideas," and you relax while listeners rate you as a better speaker. Pair that with a modest mantra, and rehearse in your mind the whole sequence of walking up, speaking, being well received, and walking off, so the moment itself feels familiar.
ex: His mantra: "I have value to bring"
Research on visualization to reduce speaking fear began at the University of Oregon in the 1980s
A reader he met at an airport said just knowing the book existed was reassuring

items: Racing heart read as a threat
Seen as a chance to share ideas

d.verdict: Same body, different label, different outcome

l169|323.c: Calm your body first and bring your attention back to the present, and the nerves settle on their own.
l169|323.e: He cites research showing that what the body feels shapes what the brain concludes. Breathing is the fastest tool, and the exhale is what matters. His rule is to exhale for twice as long as you inhale, say in for three counts and out for six. Tongue twisters pull you into the present instead of worrying about what comes next, and they warm up your voice. Some research even suggests swearing a little relieves anxiety. Most people are most nervous in the minute before they start and the first minute after, so open with a short video, a question, or a story to take the eyes off yourself for a moment.
ex: People holding a cold drink judge others as colder
A Google executive opened with "let's watch a video" and became the discussion host
Opening with "today I'll answer three questions" lets you ask and answer yourself

terms.d: Breathe out twice as long as in
Get present, warm up your voice
Open with a video, question, or story

result.d: Get through the two hardest minutes

l169|323.c: Dare to be dull: aim for connection rather than perfection, and you'll communicate better.
l169|323.e: The phrase comes from improv, and improv is not really about being funny; it is about staying present and working with others. When we speak off the cuff, we want to give the best answer or the cleverest feedback, constantly judging ourselves against a perfect standard. That is like a computer with too many windows open: less bandwidth is left for the content and the audience. Give yourself permission to just get it done: answer the question, give the feedback, join the small talk. With the self-judgment turned down, you usually end up speaking better.
ex: The brain is like a CPU, and self-judgment eats up processing power

l169|323.c: Spontaneous speaking rests on preparation: organize what you say with ready-made structures, then practice.
l169|323.e: Most of our communication is spontaneous, yet many people assume you are either born a good speaker or not. He insists anyone can improve, and that you should prepare to be spontaneous, the way athletes and jazz musicians train so they can perform in the moment. The brain is bad at lists, forgetting anything past four items, but it is built for stories and logical connections. With a structure in hand, all you have to figure out in the moment is what to put in it, which halves the load. Practice comes down to repetition, reflection, and feedback, for example retelling a podcast episode using a structure right after you listen.
ex: PREP: point, reason, example, point again
A product update: what it is, why it matters, what comes next
He recommends Toastmasters and improv classes for regular practice

items.d: Believe you can improve; prepare to be spontaneous

l169|323.c: In small talk, be interested rather than interesting, and keep how much each person shares roughly equal.
l169|323.e: Small talk has a bad reputation, but many important relationships begin with it. His favorite advice comes from Rachel Greenwald, a scholar and matchmaker: be interested, not interesting. Treat it like hacky sack, passing the ball back, rather than spiking it every time. Self-disclosure should deepen gradually and evenly on both sides; going too deep too soon is awkward, and only asking without ever sharing is awkward too. Lean on supporting responses that ask for more detail about the other person, with a few shifting responses that share something of your own.
ex: Supporting response: "You went to Costa Rica? Did you get to the beach?"
Shifting response: "You went to Costa Rica; I went to Hawaii"

l169|323.c: Feedback is really joint problem-solving, and the four-I structure helps you organize it fast.
l169|323.e: Apart from behavior that has to stop immediately, most feedback is a chance to solve a problem together, so invite the other person to help instead of handing down a verdict. He admires Kim Scott's Radical Candor and adds that structure helps you package the message. For simple cases use what, so what, now what. The fuller version is the four I's: state the information, describe the impact on you, issue an invitation to work on it together, and spell out the implications, good or bad. Tone can vary with the situation; the four steps keep your thinking straight in the moment.
ex: "This is the third time you've been late... what would help you come prepared next time?"
After a meeting: you spoke too fast on the implementation plan and gave too little detail

items.d: Say what the feedback is about
Ask them to work on it with you

l169|323.c: Toasts, Q&A, and apologies each have a ready structure: WHAT, ADD, and AAA.
l169|323.e: For a toast, use WHAT: why we are here, how you are connected, an anecdote everyone can follow, and thanks. Keep it short, let the story carry the emotion, and for big occasions try it on someone first, what he calls minimum viable communication. For answering questions, use ADD: answer directly, give a detailed example, and describe why it matters to the asker. Don't say "great question" every time or keep asking "does that make sense?" For apologies, use AAA: acknowledge what you did rather than saying "sorry you feel that way," appreciate how the other person feels, and make amends with a specific fix.
ex: After giving his father's eulogy, he wrote an article on what he learned
He suggests rewriting a company's FAQ in the ADD structure

root.d: A starting point when put on the spot

l170|326.c: Skip management if you're bad at it and hate it, but break unavoidable skills like speaking into parts and grind.
l170|326.e: He has been CEO twice and concluded he is not good at managing people; years of effort would only get him to barely passing, so his energy is better spent on things he is both good at and enjoys. In the first week of HubSpot he agreed with his co-founder that he would never have direct reports, not even temporarily. The result: he was happier at 7,000 employees than at 70, enjoying the big bets that scale allows without carrying the management load. Public speaking, though, a founder cannot avoid. He believes talent only sets the slope of the learning curve, so he broke speaking into sub-skills, tackled one a year, and measured progress with data.
ex: More than 7,000 employees, and his direct report count has always been zero
He wrote software to count laughs per minute; above 1.2 is elite for a business talk
Put the punchline on the last word of a passage, then stop and let the audience laugh

items: Not good at it, doesn't enjoy it

d.verdict: Fix weaknesses only where unavoidable; bet the rest on strengths

l170|326.c: Founders overrate the downsides of an IPO: public markets give you a real valuation and let everyone share the growth.
l170|326.e: Many founders see an IPO as the start of a nightmare. He admits it brings compliance work, but the benefits are underrated. While private, your valuation depends on how VCs feel about your sector. Public markets are reasonably efficient: the price swings around real value and tracks it over time, so the team can just focus on creating value. The other reason is letting customers, partners, and supporters take part in the growth. Going public also doesn't have to change the culture. HubSpot registered every employee as an insider and kept sharing its financials with the whole company.
ex: Lawyers said companies usually have five or six insiders; they found there is no legal cap
Bezos's first shareholder letter: if you don't share our long-term view, don't buy the stock

items.d: Shared by a few private investors

l170|326.c: Make few contrarian bets, only where you have high conviction and little agreement, and stick with them.
l170|326.e: He thinks "first principles" is overused; most so-called principles are just founding assumptions. You should be contrarian on more than zero dimensions, but not many. HubSpot's core bet was focusing on small and mid-sized businesses. For 18 years people asked when they would move upmarket, and they insisted it was not a stepping stone. The SMB market combines the paying model of enterprise software with the huge customer count of a consumer market. Software has a "reverse gravity" that pulls every competitor toward big customers, so staying put means less competition. Their other contrarian move was building the full suite in year one: customers lack integration skills, so if one product cracks the top three in its category, you have over-invested in it.
ex: No revenue concentration with SMBs, full control of the roadmap, short feedback loops
In year one they built SEO, analytics, blogging, and content management at once
They later dropped the no-titles experiment: titles carry signal to the outside world

cells.d: Most things, done the usual way

l170|326.c: Complexity kills companies slowly but reliably, so simplicity has to be won with rules and constraints.
l170|326.e: He borrows the second law of thermodynamics: left alone, any system gets messier. A young company fights not to die, a middle-aged one fights not to stall, and after that it fights complexity, as layers, headcount, and pricing tiers all swell. HubSpot's slogan is "fight for simplicity," but slogans fade, and structural constraints last longer. In the early years, every feature added meant one removed, and the freemium model forced the product to stay simple. When judging a new product, count not just the cost to build and maintain it, but the extra dimension it adds to every future decision.
ex: After the second product, hiring, marketing, and every report had to be split by product
New hires drew lots for seats, up to several hundred people, which killed office politics
Full transparency comes from simplicity: sharing everything is an easier call than picking what to share

items.d: Things get messier on their own
More reliable than any other cause

l170|326.c: A founder's offhand remarks get amplified, so use graded tags to say how strongly you mean them.
l170|326.e: Leaders have a megaphone problem: a passing comment can send a team off to work on it for months. In emails he adds one of a set of escalating tags to show how much weight an opinion carries. Even the top level is not an order, because HubSpot believes in autonomy and a single directly responsible person for every decision, and he has used the top tag fewer times than he can count on one hand. On decisions, data informs but people decide, so first settle who the decider is. Once decided, the rule is debate, decide, unite, which goes further than Amazon's "disagree and commit" in asking everyone to stand on the same side.
ex: The tags are searchable, so you can look back at how past suggestions turned out
Debate, decide, unite is adapted from Amazon's "disagree and commit"

items.d: #plea: a considered request, still not an order
#recommendation: explain if you don't take it
#suggestion: I'd consider it; no reply needed

l170|326.c: Judge an idea by potential first, then probability, then ask about passion and your unique edge.
l170|326.e: He makes decisions like building a spreadsheet: list the factors that matter, and even without weighting them, just ranking them gets you 80% of the value. Effort should scale with the consequences, which extends the one-way-door, two-way-door idea into a continuous spectrum. For startup or product ideas he scores four P's from 0 to 10. The common mistake is looking at probability first and killing ideas too early, when a 10% shot at a huge outcome can have the higher expected value. Passion doesn't have to exist up front; it can grow once you dig in. Prowess answers the question, why us.
ex: A 50% chance of making $10 million is worth $5 million in expectation
His default to new things is no: saying yes to one means removing another

items.d: Odds of success; don't start here
Do you care enough for years?

l170|326.c: Culture is a product a company builds for its employees, so keep improving it rather than guarding it.
l170|326.e: When he was asked to take on culture, all he wanted was to describe what already existed: if you could write a function predicting whether a new hire would succeed at HubSpot, what would the variables be? That became the Culture Code. He thinks a company builds two products, one for customers and one for its team. If culture is a product, you listen to users and treat problems as bugs. The most common founder mistake is believing the job is to preserve the culture, when what employees need changes with scale. Core values work like federal law, with departments allowed state-level variations. Items you haven't yet achieved can be labeled aspirational; new hires act on them, and they slowly come true.
ex: In the employee NPS survey, the top reason people are happy is their coworkers
Every quarter all anonymous feedback is published and answered at the all-hands
When he first raised the word culture, people recoiled, fearing posters on the wall

items.d: What to fix, what is by design

l170|326.c: AI scales human thinking, so software will shift from step-by-step commands to simply describing what you want.
l170|326.e: He has been in the industry almost 30 years, and the last time he was this excited was the arrival of the internet. The PC scaled computation, the internet scaled distribution, and AI is the first thing to scale cognition. Software claims to be intuitive, but users still have to translate the goal in their head into a sequence of clicks and drags. AI lets you describe the result you want, the way SQL replaced hand-written loops with a single condition. His GrowthBot project six-plus years ago had the same idea but failed because the technology wasn't ready. To keep up with AI, pick a problem you genuinely care about, use AI to solve it, and learn in public.
ex: For example: "give me a report of European customers signed last quarter with over $100K in annual revenue"
GrowthBot wasn't feasible then; ChatSpot is now

items.d: Cognition at scale; describe, don't click

l171|328.c: Design your own career: know what you want, and frame your promotion as solving a problem for the company.
l171|328.e: She boils career acceleration down to knowing what you want, saying it out loud, and making it easy for your boss to give it to you. Don't say "I want direct reports." Explain what the company is missing, what this role would deliver, and why you are the best fit, and time it with the company's promotion cycle. Organizations are fluid and reshape themselves around capable, motivated people. PMs are generalists, so a sideways move followed by a step up works well too. Still, talking about promotion should be a tiny slice of your conversations with your manager; in the end the work has to speak.
ex: When the marketing lead left, she drew an org chart merging product and growth and nominated herself
On joining LaunchDarkly she told the CEO her next job would be CEO
She sold her startup at 34 weeks pregnant by first getting into the room with the acquirer

items.d: Current role and the next one
The work has to speak for itself

l171|328.c: Sustainable performance comes from staying in your zone of genius, not taking on more; promote late rather than early.
l171|328.e: She argues that what makes a career sustainable is not the workload but whether you are working where you are exceptional, hard to replace, and deeply satisfied. If most of your time goes to shoring up weaknesses, that is unfair to both the organization and you. To find your zone, look back over a month or two of your calendar, sort activities by how much you enjoyed them, and focus only on the top tier, finding ways to do more of it. Then ask what you can do that nobody else in the organization can. Managers should be careful too: piling responsibility on high-potential people too early leaves them neither effective nor happy.
ex: Her strength: spanning product, engineering, design, data, and revenue, and switching between strategy and detail
Even with several hats on, she protects builder time to make things herself

items.d: Find ways to spend more time there
Hard to copy, like a differentiated product

l171|328.c: Late-stage companies can move like startups: stop letting the meeting calendar set the pace, and pull every deadline in a notch.
l171|328.e: She says she is brought into late-stage companies not to teach them to act like big companies but to remind them they can still act like startups. Organizational speed tends to decay into calendar speed; "let's decide at the next meeting" is a fake deadline the calendar invented. The better question is how much information the decision actually needs. She asks every leader, before stating a deadline, whether it could be one notch sooner. Once expectations are clearly raised, teams usually rise to them. She also sets herself a personal response-time commitment so she never becomes the bottleneck for decisions and approvals.
ex: Her motto: fast beats right

l171|328.c: A high talent bar rests on measurable level expectations, routine feedback, and acting quickly when someone isn't a fit.
l171|328.e: She splits high standards into a people layer and a product layer, and the people layer starts with writing the standard down. Many senior level descriptions are vague, like "manages multiple departments," so you can't tell whether someone meets them. Write them like OKRs, as measurable expectations. Next, a culture that avoids conflict and feedback lowers talent density. Being clear is the kind thing to do, and you should make it explicit that challenging an idea is not a judgment on someone's ability. Finally, when someone truly isn't a fit, act fast. It makes the team healthier and is better for the person too.
ex: Two product and engineering leaders clashed publicly; she said change or leave, and one became a model manager
She cites Brené Brown: clear is kind

result.d: A healthier, happier team

l171|328.c: The hard part for women leaders isn't impostor syndrome but structural problems, and the fix starts with visibility.
l171|328.e: She stresses that her ability was proven long ago; the issue is not self-doubt but that the numbers in the industry work against women, and that this keeps happening even at the executive level. Her approach is curiosity: separate what is structural, cultural, or external from what she herself brings into the room that doesn't help, then look for levers the way you would in a product. She frames it as economic participation: when women are absent, the industry misses out on innovation and growth. The simplest change is making diverse technical leaders visible, so people's picture of who counts as technical starts to loosen.
ex: She cites Carta: women made up about 13% of founders last year
She coded solo for 12 months and ran engineering teams of hundreds, yet still gets asked if she is technical
A VC once told her not to get pregnant

root.d: Stay curious and break it down

items.d: Who counts as technical in media and kids' books
Things done to me or around me
What I bring in that doesn't help

l171|328.c: A combined product-and-engineering leader can optimize for the whole rather than one function, if they truly know technology and org design.
l171|328.e: She says the CPTO job is not babysitting engineering with generic leadership skills. You own architecture, infrastructure, and engineering efficiency, and in reviews you look at the PRD and GitHub side by side. You also need to be good at org design and operations, because engineering teams are bigger, hire more, and get paged at night. There are two reasons for the role. Product, engineering, and design are one group of builders, and putting them together ends the fight over who comes first. And R&D spending is expensive, so having one person accountable for it gives the CEO a lot of leverage. But there is no perfect structure; if the CEO can handle both, keep them separate.
ex: Her team's principle: there are no lanes, and the lines between roles are dotted
Early startup experience is the shortcut to cross-functional skills

items: Works when the CEO has capacity
Optimizes for the whole and the customer
Must know tech and org design

d.verdict: Design the org around the talent; no structure is perfect

l171|328.c: AI will take over lowercase communication that just relays information, shifting a PM's value to being right, fast, and effective.
l171|328.e: She is pessimistic short term and optimistic long term: PMs won't vanish next year, but the PM-to-engineer ratio and the skills required will change, probably faster than expected. The first thing to go is lowercase communication, the summarizing and relaying of information for coordination. Capital-C Communication, persuading people, being bold, and carrying a group forward, is hard to replace. PMs need to let go of the identity that their value comes from their ideas, and focus on whether they got it right, got it done fast, and made an impact. To keep up, learn to build non-deterministic AI products, the way PMs who bet early on mobile got ahead.
ex: About 60% of ChatPRD use turns ideas into PRDs, and about 30% improves existing documents
She has heard of teams spending a week trying to automate a role before opening a req for it

marks.d: AI is good at this too

l172|329.c: Real product-market fit needs demand, satisfaction, and efficiency together, and efficiency is the one most often ignored.
l172|329.e: He finds most online advice about product-market fit vague, and thinks sales-led B2B is more predictable than consumer. He defines the end goal as extreme PMF: broad demand, a product that meets a critical need, and the ability to deliver it to every customer repeatably and efficiently. Many people look only at the first two, but a boom bought with subsidies doesn't count. One test is the marginal customer: as PMF strengthens, winning and serving the next customer should get easier and easier.
ex: WeWork and Casper had demand and satisfaction but never got efficiency right
Brett Berson's image: a vending machine that pays out $100 for every $1 you put in

result.d: The next customer keeps getting easier

l172|329.c: PMF isn't on or off; it's a four-level ladder, and each level calls for optimizing something different.
l172|329.e: The three ingredients pull against each other: pouring money into marketing lifts demand but hurts efficiency, and over-automating can hurt satisfaction, so you can't chase all three at once. Level 1 is about satisfaction, Level 2 shifts to demand, Level 3 starts on efficiency, and Level 4 needs all three strong while expanding the market through new segments or new products, which is like finding PMF again. Top enterprise software companies usually take four to six years to reach Level 4. Each step up means spinning more plates, and the earlier dimensions can't slip.
ex: ARR: under $500K at Level 1, up to $5M at Level 2, up to $25M at Level 3
Net revenue retention: at least 100% at Level 2, over 110% at Level 3, over 120% at Level 4
Level 4 expansion: Verkada went from cloud cameras to alarms and door access readers

l172|329.c: At Level 1, just make three to five customers extremely happy; inefficiency is fine, but watch for polite customers.
l172|329.e: At this stage the team is under 10 people, and the job is to find a handful of paying customers with an important, urgent problem and deliver on the promise they care about. You can do it entirely by hand; efficiency metrics like burn multiple and gross margin don't apply yet. Most customers come through warm introductions and conversion is hard, which is normal. But if you're stuck for six to twelve months and see certain yellow flags, you picked the wrong problem. He recommends what Persona's founder did: take early customers aside and ask them to drop the politeness and say whether the product is truly essential.
ex: Vanta had no product at first; the founder filled out SOC 2 forms by hand and won big deals
About 20 warm intros per customer, so three to five customers means at least 50 conversations

items.d: Customers shrug if the product vanished
Bought but rarely used; churn is coming

l172|329.c: When stuck, adjust the four P's: persona, problem, promise, and product, and pivot completely if you have to.
l172|329.e: The four P's have to line up: the product delivers a promise that solves a specific problem for a specific kind of person. When stuck, you can change a few of them or all of them. He prefers selling before building: confirm with customers that someone will buy, then write code. So the focus goes on the first three P's, and the product's job is to deliver on them. Think of a market as a group of specific people willing to pay, and get close enough to text them and meet them on weekends. At Level 2, the problem is usually that the pain isn't painful enough or the promise isn't valuable enough, and founders tend to make only small changes.
ex: Lattice kept the head-of-HR persona but pivoted from OKR software to performance management
Plaid kept its bank-connection code but pivoted from a budgeting app to a developer API
Jack Altman: most people pivot 10% when they need to pivot 200%

items.d: How you pitch it; your positioning

l172|329.c: Level 2 is about unlocking demand, and repositioning within an existing category is usually easier than creating one.
l172|329.e: Willpower can get you to five or ten customers, but to pass 25 the product has to do much of the pulling, and a scalable acquisition channel has to appear, such as cold outbound, content, or community events. He thinks creating a new category is very hard. If you bring something new to an existing category, buyers are already looking and already have budget. Signs of being stuck include churn above 20%, deals lost late in the process, and customers with no urgency. "No budget" or "let's talk next year" is a no. A slow sales cycle combined with a low price is the death quadrant.
ex: Ironclad only started closing deals after renaming itself from "AI legal assistant" to CLM
Looker spent 20 to 40 hours of pre-sales modeling per customer and closed about 75%

cells.d: Slow and cheap; the math doesn't work
Six-figure deals can take 3 to 6 months
Fast close and a big deal

l172|329.c: Most companies get stuck in the first two levels, and the choosing at Level 1 deserves the most time.
l172|329.e: By their count, most seed-stage companies stall at Level 1 or 2; about 30% reach Level 3, and only there does a company have a real shot at becoming great. He quotes a partner: founders spend 99% of their time doing and 1% choosing the market, problem, and customer, yet that choice sets the ceiling for the next decade. So it's worth spending 12 to 18 months at Level 1 getting the four P's right. On the flip side, if you've been at it four or five years and still feel no pull from the market, a miracle turnaround is the exception. Returning money to investors or finding a soft landing is nothing to be ashamed of.
ex: Ideal pace: 12 to 18 months at Level 1, a year at Level 2, one to two at Level 3
Going from 5 to 25 customers within a year is almost always a sign of strong PMF

l172|329.c: Run customer interviews around money: validate extreme value first, then ability to pay, then willingness to pay.
l172|329.e: Customers are polite and bad at predicting whether they'll buy, so casual conversations give weak signals and make it easy to hear only what you want. Step one: ask about their goals and struggles, then present your promise and watch for a "wow" or for action, like booking a follow-up or asking for materials. Step two: confirm ability to pay. Are they already looking for a solution or did they try building one and fail? Where would budget come from? How does procurement sign off? Step three: ask about three prices, reasonable, expensive, and prohibitively expensive. The people who actually pay usually land at "expensive." You've done enough interviews when you can predict 70 to 80% of the next person's answers.
ex: The three-price question comes from Madhavan Ramanujam of Simon-Kucher
The best customers know they have the problem and have tried and failed to build a fix

items.d: Who approves, what triggers a bake-off

l173|331.c: Make everything public by default except customer data and security flaws; the upside dwarfs the occasional slip.
l173|331.e: GitLab records a huge number of meetings, and some stream live to a public YouTube channel. The handbook, direction pages, and most issues are visible to anyone. He sees many benefits: people focus on outcomes, nobody worries about missing information, anyone can catch up asynchronously, alignment improves, there are fewer late surprises, and you never have to remember who heard what. Community members and customers who watch the meetings also file issues, give feedback, and even contribute code. The cost of occasionally publishing something by mistake, he thinks, is small next to all that.
ex: The public issue tracker holds about 72,000 open issues
At a previous employer, public feature requests sharpened the roadmap and lifted retention and expansion
Start by recording one team meeting, then add weekly or async updates

root.d: Recorded meetings, handbook, issues, direction pages

items.d: Catch up anytime; no need to ask who heard
Community and customers file issues, write code

l173|331.c: The handbook is editable by anyone, like source code; management guides rather than directs.
l173|331.e: GitLab's handbook is public down to its source, and anyone can open a merge request to change it. New product managers often spend their first weeks fixing errors in it. Big changes do get approval: adding a product category needs his sign-off, and structural changes also need the CTO and others. Each team writes a smaller handbook that references the main one. Their efficiency principle pushes responsibility to the lowest possible level: he sets the three-year and seven-year strategy, teams decide how to get there, and anything good enough ships first and improves later.
ex: One company forked the UX section of GitLab's handbook outright
A release ships every third Thursday; about 149 releases in roughly 12 years

items.d: The CPO sets the 3- and 7-year direction
Single source of truth; vote and comment

l173|331.c: Assuming good intent plus "short toes" keeps candid feedback about the work, not the person.
l173|331.e: Kindness here means assuming the other person means well and that everyone is there to help each other. Negative feedback goes one-on-one in private, while public channels are for thanks. Short toes means you are hard to step on: feedback is about the work, not about you, and he treats criticism of his own videos as a chance to improve. Transparency, he says, has to rest on these values, and the two reinforce each other, starting with the CEO. He rejects the combative "move fast and break things" style of culture.
ex: A dedicated thanks channel reinforces recognition
Other values include a results focus and efficiency
Humor can defuse a tense conversation, but you have to read the room

terms.d: Default to helping; criticize in private
Feedback targets the work, not the person

result.d: People dare to speak up and can hear it

l173|331.c: Remote work should be judged on results, not hours, and you should over-communicate at 150%.
l173|331.e: Remote isn't for everyone, but when it fails, the cause is usually a missing face-to-face connection rather than ability. His coach reminded him that a message you think is clear may land at only 60 or 70 percent, so you have to communicate twice as much. The practice is async first: write the requirements down before work starts, ask questions right in the issue or merge request instead of waiting a day or two for standup, and switch to video when text isn't working. Key decisions wait for the directly responsible individual. Meetings are optional, recorded, and documented.
ex: About 1,100 people before the pandemic; now over 2,000 across more than 60 countries
The roughly 140-person product team meets in person in two cities
Almost no internal email; issues are the single source of truth

items.d: Put the ask in writing before work starts
In the issue or MR, not at standup

items.t: Switch to video if text fails
items.d: Avoid a day or two of back-and-forth

l173|331.c: A PM is not an order-taker; success means users adopting the product, not features shipped.
l173|331.e: Product sits at the hub between departments, and if people are a little annoyed with you, that may mean you are doing the job well. You can't take every request at face value; you have to read the use case and pain behind it. Success should be measured not by what launched but by adoption and use-case coverage, such as the share of customers using a given product area, and you should check early whether the goal has already been met. Product work is hard and rarely applauded, but the payoff is big. The core skill is putting the customer first.
ex: Example goal: get 60% of customers using a product area
Interviews use a "bicycle requirements" question, with an engineer role-playing the customer

items: Treats launch as the finish line
Digs out use cases and pain

d.verdict: Measure PMs by whether customers actually use it

l173|331.c: Build a platform wide first, then go deep in core areas, which lifts the adjacent ones.
l173|331.e: Early on, GitLab had to go broad to assemble a complete DevSecOps platform. Last year it shifted to going deep in core areas: source code management, code review, CI/CD, security governance, planning, and AI. He believes depth in the core raises adjacent areas too; once MLOps is deep enough, only a light connection to data tools is needed. New directions still get explored with breadth first. He says HubSpot takes a similar view and deliberately avoids racing into the top three of any single category.
ex: Without the platform, a customer might stitch together about 75 tools
Observability and service management are still being built out

l173|331.c: AI should span the whole software lifecycle, with different models matched to different tasks.
l173|331.e: He estimates writing code is only about a quarter of the software development lifecycle, so AI can't stop at code completion; it also has to serve PMs, testers, operations, and security. The second principle is transparency and privacy: publish which models are used and how they were trained, and never train or fine-tune on customer code. The third is efficiency. Don't force one hot large model into every feature. Inline completion needs to be fast, while generating a block of code can take twenty or thirty seconds. That is why GitLab uses about 16 models.
ex: About 16 models serve different use cases
Google Cloud and Anthropic are its commercial model partners
The 2021 UnReview acquisition brought in-house machine learning capability

items.d: About a quarter of the lifecycle

l174|332.c: The core of startups is not dying, and most companies die because founders quit, not because the money runs out.
l174|332.e: He says nearly every successful company had moments when quitting would have been the rational choice, and survived several near-death experiences through almost irrational persistence before looking like an overnight success. Founders fear running out of cash, but the more common death is that the idea isn't working, the co-founders have a blowup, or they just don't want to do it anymore, while money is still in the bank. As long as you refuse to accept failure, there are usually plenty of moves left. But if you're unhappy, no longer like your team or customers, and are only hanging on to save face, nobody will remember if you shut it down, and the cost to your life is bigger.
ex: Airbnb probably should have shut down three or four times before YC
The two weakest-looking companies in the W17 batch became Brex and Retool

l174|332.c: A good pivot is like going home: closer to what you truly know, built on what the last idea taught you.
l174|332.e: Successful pivots usually move closer to the founders' expertise and reuse what they learned from the previous idea. Many winning ideas were ones the founders could never have thought of at the start; they accidentally became experts along the way. Sometimes founders resist the field they know best and need a push. As for when to pivot, look at how many untried growth ideas the founders have left. If there's still a real one, keep trying. When all that's left is "maybe get an influencer to post about us," it's time.
ex: Brex pivoted from VR headsets to fintech; the founders had worked in finance in Brazil
Retool grew out of an internal dashboard the founder built for a peer-to-peer payments product
Zip's approach: find incumbent software customers hate in a very large market

items.d: Learned analytics on the first idea
Built just to ease trials of the competitor

l174|332.c: Tar pit ideas look unsolved and get warm feedback, but they have trapped countless founders for decades.
l174|332.e: Everyone listens to the same podcasts and reads the same tweets and blogs, so with the same information diet they come up with the same ideas. A tar pit is different from an obviously bad idea: it gets early validation, everyone says they want it, and the argument sounds great, which is exactly why people get sucked in and can't get out. The better approach is to leave the crowded city center and dig into your own unusual experiences and interests. YC's Requests for Startups exist partly to disrupt that shared diet and put rarely-pitched areas in front of founders.
ex: Classic tar pits: apps for coordinating hangouts with friends, and music discovery
His own first company did music discovery too
RFS areas include ERP, open source, space, and glue for enterprise systems

cells.d: Like procurement software or Funko trading
Gets hot fast once it works, like trucking
Everyone loves it; it never works

l174|332.c: Investors mostly say no because they make so few bets, and the earlier the stage, the less market size matters.
l174|332.e: He suggests founders put themselves in investors' shoes: they fund only a few companies a year, so they may like yours and still pass because it isn't the one that makes them say "this is it." The feedback you get is usually just a polite way of not investing, with no hidden truth behind it. How much market size matters depends on stage; the later the round and the higher the valuation, the more it counts. At pre-seed, calculating TAM with precision means little, and many great companies started in tiny markets. He cares more about how you get customers, how you grow, and whether you've built something users want.
ex: When Razorpay started, almost nobody in India used credit cards
Whatnot's early Funko Pop collectibles market was not large

marks.d: Acquisition and growth first, TAM later
Many balk at the leap of faith on TAM

l174|332.c: You can't outsource caring about users: don't hire shiny executives too early, and give customers 20 to 30% of your calendar.
l174|332.e: Investors often push founders to scale the team and hire executives from big companies, and one day the founder wakes up to find everything has drifted. That's a common first-time founder mistake: delegating too soon. He thinks if you genuinely care about customers and the product, your instinct for allocating time will be right, and schmoozing investors is what should get cut. Everyone claims to talk to customers, but many hide behind landing pages and ads because they fear awkwardness. The self-check is whether 20 to 30% of your calendar is customer meetings. And a customer saying "we'll buy" isn't the end; follow through until they're actually live.
ex: The Collison installation: go to the customer's desk and set up Stripe on their computer yourself
Zip's founders booked lots of calls with procurement heads and pre-sold before building

items.d: Make sure at least one person will use it
A sale isn't the finish line

l174|332.c: What founders of big companies share isn't a personality type but a conviction that grows out of the data.
l174|332.e: He has seen successful founders who are introverts and extroverts of every kind, and doesn't think there's a personality template worth copying. What they share is wanting it badly and believing they will succeed, even when the data and the employees say otherwise. That inner gravity pulls the people around them into believing too. But nobody has that conviction before they have an idea or a customer, so feeling unsure doesn't mean you're not cut out for this. Usually it's only after pivoting to an idea you care about and launching that customers and data keep telling you you're right, and the conviction builds.
ex: As he recalls, Stripe's founders only became sure it would work a year or two in

items.d: Customers and problems you care about
Put the product to the test

l174|332.c: Growth hacking and A/B testing at the earliest stage are a waste; study how similar companies went from zero to one.
l174|332.e: Much of the startup advice online is written for Series A and B companies, and seed-stage founders who copy it end up more confused. With no customers yet, studying split tests and reading big-company growth playbooks only pulls you away from the real job: finding your first customer and talking to them. People coming from big tech tend to bring these habits with them. The right move is to find comparable companies and study what they did to win their first thousand users, not what they're doing today.
ex: Whatnot didn't pour money into Instagram ads; it focused on the buyer side first
Facebook won all of Harvard before expanding

d.verdict: Advice has to match the stage; too early, it does harm

l175|334.c: Vision is everything: blend research, design, and engineering into one visual vision so every step counts as progress.
l175|334.e: She sees product development as messy and full of ups and downs, and only a shared vision turns pivots and setbacks into learning rather than blows. A good vision can't be built behind closed doors. User insight, design prototypes, and engineering feasibility have to collide, instead of research, design, and development handing off to each other in a line. Words alone don't persuade, so she structures proposals as rounds of pain point, solution, and evidence, and has the whole team produce one artifact together rather than each preparing their own update. At Figma, the habit is to prototype before a project is even approved: seeing is believing.
ex: FigJam's vision: bring the democratic feel of a brainstorm into every meeting
Figma's internal product reviews, Gantt charts, and bug bashes all happen in FigJam
AI lowers the barrier to design, and Figma wants to be everyone's design co-founder

items.d: User quotes that make people feel it

l175|334.c: Form an opinion fast and put it out there; even a wrong one moves things further than slowly gathering insights from zero.
l175|334.e: She thinks the most important thing a PM creates for a team is momentum, and since most software decisions are reversible two-way doors, you should dare to have a view and let people react to it. Product sense is ultimately intuition, built from endless curiosity about users; after enough conversations you have a library you can draw on anytime. Junior PMs often hold back because they feel they lack the credentials, but people react far more to an idea than to a blank page. Pair high conviction with strong opinions, weakly held: the moment outside signals point the other way, drop your favorite idea.
ex: Figma CPO Yuhki's advice: go into user research with at least an A-minus idea
Meta boils PM skill down to two things: product sense and execution

items.d: Ask how people use the product, even at dinner
Push if right, pivot if wrong
Upgrade to A-plus or drop it

l175|334.c: A PM with strong opinions should label how sure they are, and make sure feedback flows both ways.
l175|334.e: High conviction has side effects. When her design partner first met her, he wondered how one person could have so many opinions. Worse, if people assume the PM is dug in, they stop speaking up. Her fix is to state her confidence level every time, from strongly held to medium to "it's your call." She never sugarcoats, and she tells new teammates up front to push back on her directly. Directness only works when it goes both ways: before giving someone feedback, ask what feedback they have for you, act on it quickly, and they will do the same.
ex: Meta's mantra: feedback is a gift
She and her design partner had an hour-long one-on-one almost every day last year

marks.d: If you feel stronger, you win

l175|334.c: Bottom-up projects have to generate their own hype, and you can only hype what you genuinely believe in.
l175|334.e: Projects that leadership loves get carried by executives. For a bottom-up zero-to-one project, keeping the energy up falls entirely on the person driving it. She sees hype as helping others see what you see, so grab every company-wide stage to demo, even when the product is rough. Exposure that seems premature looks like a distraction but actually brings more signal and gets the whole company excited. External hype has to connect emotionally and fit the product's personality: FigJam is playful, while Figma wins with hard features that fix long-standing designer pain.
ex: With only about 10 people using the new product, she insisted on demoing it in the annual sales kickoff keynote
For FigJam's first birthday, new features were hidden in gift boxes for users to hunt

items: Use Maker Week and sales kickoff
Make people feel it's built for them

d.verdict: Hype only works if you believe it yourself

l175|334.c: The most valuable user conversations ask non-users why they don't use the product, and feed insights into the roadmap systematically.
l175|334.e: She asks people around her how they use Figma at every chance, and makes a point of asking non-users why they don't. Whether a product spreads depends not just on how good it is but on how people perceive it and how it's marketed. When users are hard to reach, early-stage companies have to hunt them down themselves, while in a big company you work closely with sales and sit in on sales calls. She talks regularly with FigJam's sales team: their signals shape her priorities, and her own usage turns into sales material. Feedback she can't act on yet goes into a backlog she reviews weekly.
ex: A former colleague said he only used FigJam occasionally, which led to an onboarding flow for non-designers
She recorded a video of how she used FigJam for a week, and sales sent it to customers
Reacting with an Asana emoji in Slack turns feedback into a backlog task

root.d: Where insights come from and go

items.d: Blind spots in perception and marketing

l175|334.c: PMs can shape culture from the bottom up, and affection for teammates keeps a team together when things get hard.
l175|334.e: She thinks passion for work comes from two things: believing in the vision you're building, and liking the people you build it with. Roadmaps and products change, but human connection makes a team instinctively huddle together in hard times instead of jumping ship. Culture can be set from the top while innovation bubbles up from below; Figma lists play as a core value, which makes room for these rituals. Everything she has started cost almost nothing. What matters is daring to do it, and using it to learn what motivates each person.
ex: Hot seat: two minutes per person for any question, which later spread to the executive team
The Figgies awards trophies came from Amazon and the show took an hour to set up
When a new engineer joins, she asks directly how involved they want to be in product decisions

terms.d: Trust built through culture and rituals

result.d: Huddle together, don't jump ship

l175|334.c: Your scope is the world: if you can't find passion in your project, step outside it, inside the company or out.
l175|334.e: She doesn't treat the project she's assigned as her boundary. First understand the company's vision and its users, see whether there's a direction in there you care deeply about, then decide whether to pursue it inside the company or outside. Building inside gives you the company's distribution and technology platform with less risk; the cost is that every decision needs buy-in, and you assemble teams and pitch to different people.
