She quotes Julie Zhuo: disagreements about strategy come from different assumptions. So whether top-down or bottom-up, align on the assumptions first. The more deeply you believe, the more natural the passion.
ex: In college, campus groups wouldn't fund her, so she built Design Nation from scratch with cold emails

items.d: You can build outside the company too
Is there something you care about?

l175|334.c: Whoever drives a zero-to-one product keeps the flame: find the right idea, win support, then let it spread like wildfire.
l175|334.e: She says a company stays competitive only by keeping a startup mindset, and many of Figma's important features came out of hackathons. The person driving a new idea is like Hestia, the Greek goddess who tends the hearth. The idea comes from constant user conversations and has to line up with the company's big goals. Winning support takes almost delusional optimism and hearing "no" as "not yet"; her pitch failed twice and only stuck the third time, at Maker Week. Finally, let colleagues use the product internally for a long time and help shape it, and they become fellow evangelists.
ex: At Maker Week she changed two lines of code to swap in the new product's icon in the file browser
Both Jambot and the widgets platform started as hackathon projects

items.d: Vision, optimism, demo on big stages
Internal use lets everyone shape it

l176|335.c: How well you handle people decides your career, because business is always done between people.
l176|335.e: The course lives in a business school, not a psychology department, because she believes business is ultimately people dealing with people. She pictures relationships on a spectrum. At one end you have contact without real connection, or a relationship that has broken down. At the other end is an exceptional relationship. Not every relationship needs to get there, but everyone should learn the skills to make a relationship robust. Leaders should ask: why would anyone follow me? Vision, product and money all count. But for lasting influence, you need to become the kind of person others want to be. People let that kind of person influence them.
ex: Exceptional relationships have six parts: knowing each other, disclosure, honesty, handling conflict, helping each other grow
The course is mostly learned by experience in groups of 12 students plus 2 facilitators

marks.d: Only a few relationships go this far

l176|335.c: Relationships deepen through gradual disclosure. Each time, go just 15 percent past your comfort zone.
l176|335.e: Disclosure and vulnerability are reciprocal, she says: if I hold my cards close, you hold yours even closer. You only learn outside your comfort zone, but students fear jumping straight into the danger zone. Hence the 15 percent rule. Say something that makes you slightly uneasy, and see whether the other person responds. If they do, both comfort zones grow, and you can step out another 15 percent. Disclosure is a dial, not a switch, and you adjust it to the person and the setting. And when people lack information about you, they make up a story. Sharing more gives you more say in how others define you.
ex: A class exercise: ten minutes of "help me know you," then debrief, then talk again
Her catchphrase: in the absence of data, people make stuff up

items.d: Saying it would scare you both

l176|335.c: The right kind of vulnerability makes leaders stronger. Anger pushes people away and usually hides fear or hurt.
l176|335.e: A leader who shows no emotion cannot inspire anyone, she believes, and people leave the moment they have another option. But vulnerability has to be appropriate. After several bad quarters, don't say "I don't deserve to be your VP," and don't pretend everything is fine. Admit you don't have the answers yet and that you need the team now more than ever. Feelings give meaning to facts, so she urges people to expand their emotional vocabulary. Anger is treated as the safe emotion at work, but it creates distance. Naming the fear or hurt underneath is what brings people closer.
ex: In 1975 she was told to leave feelings in the parking lot; ten years later a report asked, "You're human?"
A founder skipped the Monday blowup, said he feared only he cared about the delay, and the team fixed it

items: Draws people in, makes them want to help

d.verdict: Anger is usually secondary; find the real feeling underneath

l176|335.c: Beliefs that served you early in life keep running, and you rarely notice when they start costing you.
l176|335.e: Early on, she says, we form beliefs like "if I do this, that will happen." They work at first, then nobody updates them, and the cost goes unnoticed. Three are common. One: disclosing more will get me exploited or make me look weak. Two: giving feedback will damage the relationship, which usually means you've never seen good feedback. Three: a small annoyance isn't worth raising, but if you stay quiet the other person keeps doing it and you just get angrier. She suggests working backward from the outcome to the behavior, to the choice behind it, to the belief. And when you say "it's not worth it," swap "it" for me, you or us, and ask again.
ex: Raise small frictions while they're small: a pinch left alone becomes a crunch
"Leaders must have the answers" is another belief worth testing

items.d: Every action starts with a choice

l176|335.c: When giving feedback, describe the specific behavior and your own feelings. Never guess at their motives.
l176|335.e: Every interaction has three realities, she says: my intent, my behavior, and the effect on you. I know only the first two, you know only the last two, and only the behavior is visible to both. So picture a net between you and stay on your own side of it. "I feel like you don't care" is not a feeling; it's an attribution about their motives, and it triggers defensiveness instantly. Calling someone rude is labeling. The point of feedback is not to fix the other person but to move into a problem-solving conversation. Feedback comes in two kinds, constructive and appreciative. Both are data, and more is better.
ex: After she changed her wording, her husband asked for a buffer when he got home; they settled on 15 minutes
Quick check: if you start with "I feel that you" or "I feel like," you've probably crossed the net

terms.d: When you did this particular thing
What I hope for between us

result.d: Find something that works for both of us

l176|335.c: Ask before you advise. Advice widens the power gap and usually misses what the person actually cares about.
l176|335.e: The root of "inquiry" is to seek, she says, which assumes you don't know what you'll find. Asking questions to confirm what you already think isn't inquiry; you have to suspend judgment first. Yes-or-no questions are limited, and "why" puts people on the defensive, so start with what, when, where or how. Leaders often think they must have the answer, but their real job is to make sure the best answer gets found. Jumping to advice deepens the power gap and breeds dependence. And nine times out of ten, the advice doesn't address what the person really cares about.
ex: Before advising, ask yourself: is this for you, or to make me look smart?
Same with friends: first ask what they've tried and where they're stuck

items.d: You can't be curious with a conclusion in hand
Use what, when, where, how instead

l176|335.c: You can't change your personality, but you can change behavior. When things go wrong, ask what they heard.
l176|335.e: People control their own behavior, she believes, so she won't accept "I can't," only "I won't." Even the best techniques only raise your odds, and you will still mess up sometimes. What matters is knowing how to repair. When someone reacts strangely, ask what they heard. It's often not what you said, and once you know, you can say it again differently. She calls failure another growth opportunity, and her first question is always what you learned. After long COVID forced her to hand off her duties step by step, she saw it confirm her view that a leader should never make the organization depend on them.
ex: She is naturally extroverted, so she learned to talk less and let others speak
Psychologist Carol Dweck's advice: add "yet" after "I can't"
AFOG: another f-ing opportunity for growth

items.d: They react in an unexpected way
Ask: what did you hear me say?

l177|340.c: A functional org without a strong decision-maker stalls, and culture change has to start at the top.
l177|340.e: When he joined, Twitter was organized by function: separate heads of product, revenue, engineering and design. He ran only the consumer product managers, with no engineers or designers of his own. A functional structure, he argues, needs a CEO or GM who is deeply involved and makes calls quickly. Otherwise a group of strong personalities can only move by consensus or get stuck. His first year as head of product felt like walking through mud, with huge energy spent on cross-functional politics and consensus-building. His takeaway: you can't change culture from one corner of the company. Alignment has to come from the top down.
ex: When Parag Agrawal became CEO he switched to a GM model and made him consumer GM
At 19 his company was acquired by Blackboard, where he learned patience inside a big company

items: One person owns product, eng and design

d.verdict: Without one strong, unified leader, change just slows down

l177|340.c: Treat the sacred cows as a roadmap: challenge each untouchable, while keeping the growth from polishing the core.
l177|340.e: When he arrived, Twitter's product strategy was "polish the core": the ranked timeline, better recommendations, better notifications. It worked and daily active users started growing again. But it also made the organization more risk-averse, while outsiders complained the product hadn't changed in eight years. His approach was to keep polishing the core and pair it with a set of bets that would add new capabilities. The long list of things you "couldn't change" was itself a ready-made roadmap. Challenging them one by one also surfaced the cultural fears behind each one.
ex: When building hidden replies, an engineer warned the PM it would be bad for their career
New instrumentation revealed SMS verification was broken in some countries, blocking many new signups

items.d: Challenge the untouchables one by one

l177|340.c: Buying small teams and letting founders lead the riskiest projects is a shortcut to changing a big company's culture.
l177|340.e: The most effective accelerator he found was small talent acquisitions. Bring in founders who have urgency and ambition but also know how to get things done inside a big organization, and let them lead small teams on the riskiest bets, the ones least like the existing product. Management's job is to carve out protected space so an impatient big company doesn't kill the project. He benefited from exactly this kind of bet: after Periscope was acquired, he eventually ran product. It's expensive, but it fit Twitter at the time. And throwing people into the deep end is how they grow fastest.
ex: Community Notes was led by Keith Coleman, who came in through an acquisition
Creator projects like Super Follows were led by Esther Crawford

root.d: Put them on the riskiest bets

items.d: When to follow rules, when to break them
Keep the big org from smothering it

l177|340.c: Staff a project with people who truly believe in it, not whoever happens to be free.
l177|340.e: In a functional org, different people allocate headcount, so teams often end up on projects they don't believe in. Building something from zero is hard enough; a team that doesn't believe is almost guaranteed to fail. Risky projects especially need people who are both capable and obsessed with finding out whether it solves a real user problem. During a culture change, leaders also have to keep repeating the vision and the reasoning behind each bet, and quickly judge who is on board. Either convince them fast or let them go. He admits Twitter lacked that structure and nerve back then, while Elon went to the opposite extreme.
ex: High performers have limited patience; drag them into internal friction and they go elsewhere

marks.d: Lacked structure and nerve, slow change
Very little tolerance for dissent or low performance

l177|340.c: Any framework taken to the extreme becomes dogma, and metrics can even excuse user-hostile experiences.
l177|340.e: He disagreed with how Twitter rolled out Jobs-to-be-Done. Its real value is forcing you to see things from the user's point of view and consider the real alternatives, which common sense can also do. Letting OKRs alone decide what to build is just as risky. Product decisions ultimately balance what's good for the company against what's good for the user, and sometimes only judgment and taste can make that call. Two signs a framework has gone too far: the team keeps making decisions that are obviously bad on a gut level, and bets the team wants to make get squashed by the incentive system.
ex: The timeline toggle reverted to ranked after about 24 hours, purely because that helped the metrics
The Spaces bar at the top pushed down tweets and ads, hurting DAU and revenue short term
Community Notes ran like a seed investment, not measured by OKRs

cells.d: Like Spaces, hurts DAU short term
Like the toggle that reverts to ranked

l177|340.c: A live-only social product can't last. Synchronous video needs an asynchronous social graph underneath it.
l177|340.e: He sees several layers to Periscope's failure. Explosive growth in one country after another masked a retention problem, the team didn't prioritize it, and some changes made retention worse. More fundamentally: how many times a day can a person go live? A live-only app gives people no way to stay connected when they're not broadcasting. Merging into Twitter could have fixed that, but it took far too long. Meanwhile Facebook focused hard on copying it and paid top broadcasters to switch. Vertical live products like Twitch and Whatnot are a different story and have their own staying power.
ex: Growth exploded first in the US, then France, Turkey and the Middle East
Reportedly Zuckerberg pulled 300 people off their work to build live video

terms.d: Stay connected when nobody is live

result.d: Like live video inside Instagram or TikTok

l177|340.c: Twitter kept spotting consumer trends early, then botched execution by building competing projects internally.
l177|340.e: Twitter correctly called short video, live video, even the opportunity Instagram seized, he says, but fumbled the execution. After acquiring Vine, it built a separate native video team to compete with it. After acquiring Periscope, it had another team build premium live events like NFL games on a different tech stack, and it took ages to re-integrate them. The root cause was the lack of one unified, opinionated leader. Having learned that lesson, the team made Spaces, inspired by Clubhouse, the company's top priority. Borrowing ideas is fine, he says. The key is to borrow with taste and make something your own.
ex: Most Periscope users weren't "teleporting" to see the world; they wanted someone to talk to
Spaces grew out of an internal project called Hydra, from 6 people to the company's top priority

items.d: Built an internal video team to compete with it
Huge waste of time and resources

l177|340.c: The shortcut to better consumer product taste is being a voracious user: try everything, judge slowly.
l177|340.e: To build good products, he thinks the team should be heavy users themselves, starting from their own pain points and building what they want to use. There isn't much science to developing taste. You have to use lots of new products and notice which ones are merely pretty, which are ugly but useful, and which are both, until it becomes muscle memory. He tries things that look dumb too, because some things that seem dumb at first turn out to matter. His first boss, when he was a teenager, told him to sweep the floor if he had nothing to do. It taught him there's always something that moves things forward.
ex: Perplexity is one of the few consumer AI products that actually kept him coming back

items.d: Start from your own pain points

l178|342.c: Learn humility from Kahneman: actively hunt for where you're wrong, and work with your strongest critics.
l178|342.e: Kahneman had enormous influence yet was deeply humble, she says. He always wanted to hear other views and was happy to change his mind. When studies cited in his book failed to replicate, he was the first to admit it, rather than defending them as many academics do. He also pioneered adversarial collaboration: find someone whose conclusion contradicts yours, design a study together that can settle the disagreement, and publish it jointly. That restless curiosity about "where am I wrong?" is, in her view, more worth copying than any of his academic achievements.
ex: He said openly he wished he hadn't written about priming, because it didn't replicate
On income and happiness, he teamed up with Killingsworth, who had found the opposite

items.d: Like: above some income, happiness stops rising
A researcher with the opposite finding
A study that can settle the dispute

l178|342.c: Use mental time travel to escape the heat of the moment, and "nevertheless" to listen without caving.
l178|342.e: Two general tools she distilled from parenting. First, mental time travel. As Kahneman put it, nothing is as important as it seems while you're thinking about it. Ask how you'll see this in a week or in ten years, and the magnifying effect of the moment fades. Second, "nevertheless": let the other person feel fully heard, then stick with the decision anyway. Managers responding to complaints about a decision can use the same move. She also warns against judging by outcomes. A well-behaved kid is mostly temperament, not great parenting.
ex: To her kids: when you're 40, this will be a great story at Thanksgiving dinner
Only after four children did she see how little parents shape a child's personality

terms.d: Repeat back their reasons and acknowledge them
Don't change it because of complaints

result.d: They feel heard and know the decision stands

l178|342.c: Only by writing your intuition down as explicit criteria can you discover when it's wrong.
l178|342.e: She isn't against intuition. It's sometimes right and sometimes wrong; the problem is that unless you write it down, you can't tell which is which. Early in his career, Kahneman took the hiring instinct of "I just know who's right" and broke it into explicit criteria, a scoring sheet and structured interviews. Letting interviewers use their gut after that raised the hit rate noticeably. The hard part is that almost nobody actually does this, which is exactly the edge for those who do. At First Round she found the same thing: partners pounded the table for several factors, and some predicted outcomes while others didn't even work for the partner himself.
ex: She works with only a few clients, spending three to five years deeply with each

l178|342.c: Meetings should only be for discussion. Collect opinions independently before, and decide independently after.
l178|342.e: People habitually use meetings to collect opinions, discuss and decide all at once. The three interfere with each other, and the loudest, most confident person wins. Her alternative is the nominal group technique: before the meeting, everyone independently submits their rankings, estimates and reasons. These get compiled, and the meeting discusses only the disagreements rather than everyone agreeing with each other. The decision goes to a single decision-maker or a private vote. She thinks "alignment" is a terrible word. People never naturally agree, and chasing agreement turns meetings coercive. You speak to convey your reasoning, not to persuade.
ex: The facilitator only repeats back and confirms understanding, never opines, so everyone feels heard
If the senior person says three months first, you'll never hear someone's private four weeks

items: Private vote or one decider afterward

d.verdict: See the full shape of disagreement, not surface agreement

l178|342.c: There's no such thing as a long feedback loop. Track intermediate signals tied to the final outcome.
l178|342.e: Many VCs say an investment takes ten years to play out. Her response: do you just go to sleep for ten years? Along the way there are plenty of necessary-but-not-sufficient signals, such as raising a Series A or B, finding product-market fit, revenue, retention and the talent you attract. If you explicitly predict those signals when you decide, you calibrate your judgment much faster. She thinks the long-loop story is psychologically comforting. Someone who backed a star company early doesn't want to know whether it was skill or luck. People would rather feel good now than find out soon that they were wrong.
ex: Every First Round exit above a billion dollars had raised a Series A
First Round now predicts the probability of a Series A for every deal

l178|342.c: A premortem only really helps when it's tied to kill criteria and pre-committed actions.
l178|342.e: Her research with scholars at Penn found that a premortem on its own usually doesn't change plans or behavior. Its better use is setting kill criteria. Imagine the project has already failed, look back for the signals you should have seen, then commit in advance to an action for each signal. Once a project is underway, people are very slow to quit. Counting on being rational in the moment you see the signal isn't reliable; think of climbers pushing for Everest's summit in a blizzard. Pre-commitment fights that inertia, and gives salespeople cover to drop hopeless deals.
ex: Sales team rule: if they only talk price and refuse a demo, walk away
Can't get to the decision-maker? Offer an executive meeting; if refused, walk away

items.d: Six months on, the deal is dead
What signs were visible back then
See the signal, quit or push

l178|342.c: By the time you start thinking about quitting, you probably should have quit already.
l178|342.e: Starting and stopping are both decisions made under uncertainty, but people want certainty before they walk away, so they often wait until there's no choice, like when the money runs out. Several biases pile on. Sunk costs make you want to protect what you've already put in, even though waste is really about the future. People value things they built themselves more highly. And they fear being seen as a failure. The right question is whether you would start this today. Sticking with something that isn't worth it also has a hidden cost: you can't see the other opportunities.
ex: For every heavy Glitch player, 95 to 99 people played for a few minutes and left
After Stewart Butterfield shut down Glitch, the internal chat tool became Slack

items.d: Won't leave until there's no choice
We overvalue what we built ourselves
Fear of looking like a failure

l179|344.c: Strategy shouldn't wait until after product-market fit. Start thinking about it from day one.
l179|344.e: He used to say find product-market fit first, then worry about strategy. Talking with many founders changed his mind. Early on, the question isn't a full strategic plan. It's whether a candidate business has the underlying traits that tend to produce power, his term for a structure that sustains above-average returns. That only improves your odds; it guarantees nothing. After product-market fit, you use your understanding of where power comes from to establish a competitive position. In the stable phase, you defend it. Great companies often have a second act, and then the whole cycle starts over.
ex: Second acts: AWS at Amazon, Intel's shift to CPUs, Apple's iPhone
In takeoff, product managers should grab the new features and segments a technology wave opens up

items.d: Judge which ideas are likelier to yield power
Repeat it all in a new business

l179|344.c: Power needs both a benefit and a barrier. A moat is only the barrier half.
l179|344.e: He narrows strategy down to the fundamental drivers of a company's value, meaning the present value of its expected cash flows far into the future. That makes strategy a long-horizon idea: Pearl Harbor was a tactical triumph and a strategic disaster. Power, in his sense, is an economic structure that lets a company keep earning high returns despite competitors trying to arbitrage them away. It needs a cost or price advantage, the benefit, and a reason rivals can't take it from you, the barrier. A moat describes only the barrier. A moat around a worthless piece of land is worth nothing.
ex: Content is about half of Netflix's costs, so more subscribers means lower cost per subscriber
In Buffett's castle-and-moat image, the castle is the benefit

l179|344.c: Almost every startup should start with counter-positioning, then pursue scale, switching costs or network economies.
l179|344.e: Power has a time dimension, he says. Brand and process power only become available in the stable phase, and name recognition bought with a Super Bowl ad isn't brand power. Cornered resources, like a patented drug, are a different kind of business. The remaining four come in sequence. Product-market fit is essentially satisfying an existing need in a new way, replacing the old way. At that point the biggest threat is an incumbent capable of copying you. Counter-positioning means your approach would hurt the incumbent's existing business, so they choose not to follow. Only later do the three powers that depend on relative scale come into play.
ex: Amazon versus physical stores and Google versus Yahoo were both substitutions
A cornered resource: the drug company that first made Viagra

items.d: Only available in the stable phase

l179|344.c: Data scale and flywheels are often overrated. What matters is whether the effect is material.
l179|344.e: Judging whether a company has power is hard; his team often spends weeks on a single company. Data does have scale economies, but existing players are usually already so large that the cost curve has flattened and the gaps between them are small. Flywheels are everywhere, but ones that meaningfully change returns are rare. He separates network effects from network economies. Most platforms have some network effect: more users, more useful. It only counts as power when the added value is big enough to support a clear price premium and higher margins over the long run.
ex: His guess: Uber and Lyft have network effects but not network economies
Uber won through modest city-level scale economies plus a war of attrition
Early on, Uber wrongly defined its business as global transportation

d.verdict: Only the latter counts as power

l179|344.c: Operational excellence is a treadmill you must keep running on, but it usually isn't power.
l179|344.e: He agrees with Michael Porter that operational excellence is not strategy. Best practices can be filled in by hiring consultants or by poaching people from competitors who already know them. But during takeoff, when you're fighting for position, operations decide almost everything, and if you stop you get crushed. A process only becomes process power when it's both material and opaque, so rivals can't even figure out how it's done. That is rare.
ex: When Blockbuster moved into DVDs by mail, it nearly copied Netflix's interface outright
Toyota's car-making and TSMC's new fabs may be the exceptions

marks.d: Huge investment, but rivals can copy it

l179|344.c: Generative AI won't create an eighth power. Its biggest impact will be in remaking old businesses.
l179|344.e: He sees the seven powers as an empirically complete list, and AI hasn't changed it so far. But AI does affect which business models work. Billion-dollar model costs are a scale-economy question. Learning across users could create network economies. An AI that knows you could create switching costs. He sorts the beneficiaries of any new technology into three groups: those who make the technology, those born because of it, and those who use it to remake existing businesses. He leans toward the third as where AI's biggest value lies, much as electricity remade the factory floor, which took enormous redesign and investment.
ex: The semiconductor analogy: Intel, then Microsoft, then the car industry
Business process re-engineering in the 1990s
A 50 percent gain in programming productivity would be hugely valuable by itself

items.d: Like cars; the biggest impact, he thinks

l179|344.c: America's debt trajectory means no ammunition left for the next crisis, and startups will suffer too.
l179|344.e: Over the past thirty years there has been a crisis roughly every decade, he notes. In the financial crisis and the pandemic, the government propped up employment with massive deficit spending. But with debt climbing steadily, it may be unable to act next time. When capital markets freeze, starting a company gets very hard. He thinks the problem is hard to solve because it sits between capitalism and democracy. One side sees transfer payments as a fair correction for inequality; the other worries about government's ever-growing share of the economy. The result is neither higher taxes nor lower spending.
ex: Three crises: the dot-com bust, the financial crisis, COVID
He sees entitlement spending as the root cause

items.d: No tax hikes, no spending cuts
No room for another deficit rescue

l180|345.c: New PMs should nail output first, then outcomes, then direction. And never lose the craft on the way up.
l180|345.e: Many people start by obsessing over impact, goals and strategy, but what a new PM can actually deliver first is output: shipping features, running experiments, contributing to a launch plan. Once you know how things get built and how people work together, you can judge which outputs matter and take ownership of outcomes. Direction comes after that. Even at the most senior levels, he says, keep your individual-contributor craft and roll up your sleeves when needed. That is also how you build credibility with the team.
ex: One PM ranked homepage content sources by difficulty, and it went straight into the overall strategy
He once wasn't picked to lead a business he had grown, because the other person's output skills were stronger
Proactively draft the first version of a leader's summit brief or review materials

items.d: Owning the goals of a product area

l180|345.c: "What you bring" is your influence on the impact, and you prove it with high-quality product documents.
l180|345.e: A product line doing well doesn't mean you'll get promoted. You have to show you actually contributed to the result. When he diagnoses a stalled PM, he asks for their recent PRDs, product notes, strategy docs and the problem-prioritization brief they gave design. Usually one of these is missing or sloppy. The four pillars of the job, data, design research, technology and strategy, all show up through these artifacts. At a deeper level, some people bring arguments and pushback, while others channel everyone's concerns into clear strategic choices. The second kind grows faster.
ex: Jira tickets with a title and no description are a common red flag
Sprint planning meetings that go badly are another signal

l180|345.c: Three rules for working with people: raise hard issues, don't self-promote, drive decisions instead of owning them all.
l180|345.e: Going from mid-level to senior, what matters most is communication, collaboration, organization and community. The "mini-CEO" idea has led plenty of PMs to push too hard on stakeholders. His three rules sound simple but are hard to live by daily. The people who push back most effectively, he's noticed, pull a discussion away from emotion and back to logic, so everyone can talk on a more equal footing. He has also revised an early belief: good intentions aren't enough. How you speak and act communicates who you are just as much.
ex: Occasionally a loud "battle cry" style rally is needed, but only in a few situations

items: Raises hard issues, easy to work with
Pushes big issues without taking credit

d.verdict: The three rules apply at every level

l180|345.c: Mid-level and senior PMs stall mostly on mindset: fixating on the uncontrollable, slowing down, and telling themselves the wrong story.
l180|345.e: Junior PMs focus on what they can do. By mid-level and senior, the conversation often turns into "why won't the organization give me a chance," even though most of what shapes a career is within your control. Juniors change dramatically every six months; more senior people start picking their projects and avoiding risk, and once the rate of change drops, growth slows. The sneakiest trap is self-labeling. People who call themselves high-agency excuse recklessness; people who call themselves great collaborators excuse indecision. Find those stories, ask someone you trust to point them out if needed, and fix them.
ex: He changed his own label from "high agency" to "agency with awareness"
Seeing yourself as a learner is an empowering story to tell

root.d: Most common at mid and senior levels

items.d: Blaming the org and other people

l180|345.c: Benchmark against the best in the industry so your self-rating drops. Only then do you see room to grow.
l180|345.e: If you think your data skills are already a four out of five inside your company, compare yourself with the best in the industry and the score drops on its own, which makes the gap visible. For collaboration, compare yourself with people in other functions. When he joined Gojek and saw the data skills of Crystal's team, he realized how far behind he was, and that became motivation. Feedback comes from everywhere, so map it onto specific skill dimensions and pick only the highest-leverage one to work on at a time. Trying to fix too much at once is overwhelming. Obvious weaknesses, though, come first.
ex: Soft skills like communication, collaboration and community take a lifetime of practice
He still thinks time and effort are a precondition for growth, even if that's unfashionable to say

items.d: Top people in the industry or other functions
Work on one skill at a time

l180|345.c: To move into PM, first build the skills your background lacks. Prove two, then go after strategy.
l180|345.e: He breaks PM skills into dimensions like data, design research, technology and strategy, each rated zero to five. Starting out, pick one from data or technology and one from design research. People from a research background should add data or technology; people from data or engineering should add design research, because that's what they've practiced least. Once two are solid, turn to strategy. Senior people switching careers move more slowly, and a good product leader to learn from helps a lot. A slower start often means faster progress later.
ex: A PM from growth led the redesign of the "find a driver" screen
A PM from research first won over the engineers, then turned a contested feature into a full plan

items.d: One from data or tech, one from design research

l180|345.c: When the PM role is fuzzy, use this rule: whatever is blocking the product from moving forward is the PM's job.
l180|345.e: Product management still has no single concrete definition. It differs across companies and even across teams in the same company, and other functions often ask whether something counts as PM work. His answer: if it's holding up the product, it's the PM's job. The PM is the only role that pairs with data, design, technology and strategy at the same time, which gives a whole-picture view nobody else has. Think of yourself as playing a role rather than holding a title. Once you join, the team's overall output should go up.
ex: Like acting or dance, the craft of product management can be learned through method and practice
Product strategy: others decide which mountain to climb; the PM decides how to climb it

items.d: Anything blocking progress is the PM's job

l181|346.sc: Where word of mouth comes from
l181|346.c: To make customers love you fanatically, start with a deep pain point and a culture built around it.
l181|346.e: Most of Nubank's growth comes from referrals, and he thinks the roots lie before product craft. First, it tapped Brazilians' widespread resentment of highly profitable big banks. Second, the company made "customers who love us fanatically" its first value, and that value really shapes daily trade-offs, tilting toward the customer when it's close. Only on top of that comes the craft: discover what users need, innovate on their behalf, observe rather than just ask, then measure honestly whether they truly love it, and iterate again and again.
ex: In 1997 a friend in São Paulo pointed at his own bank and said he hated it
Five values: fanatical customer love, challenge the status quo, diverse teams, smart efficiency, ownership

items.d: Fanatical love is the first value

l181|346.c: Don't scale until product-market fit is proven. A PM's job is often to say no.
l181|346.e: Every post-launch product review at Nubank asks for the Sean Ellis score: what share of users would be "very disappointed" if the product disappeared. After launch they watch NPS and churn to avoid a leaky bucket. Big companies have huge user bases, he says, and funneling traffic can make any new product look good for a year or two. That's just beating a dead cat. Scale a small problem and you get a big mess. When the whole company is itching to scale, the PM, as owner, should deliver the bad news early, because they'll be held accountable in the end anyway.
ex: NPS usually sits in the 70s and 80s, and hit 94 to 95 in Mexico's first years
The design lead's catchphrase: good enough isn't good enough; it has to be great

items: Big traffic dresses up the numbers
Small problem becomes a big mess
Sean Ellis score clears the bar

d.verdict: Get it right small before making it big

l181|346.c: Mine the score for the small group that loves the product most, then move the product toward them.
l181|346.e: The usual Sean Ellis threshold is 40 percent; he raised it to 50 in Brazil because Brazilians are more polite and optimistic. When the payments assistant launched, the overall score was only around 40. Sliced up, though, a small group that had linked four or more bills across at least two payment channels scored 70. The team ran dozens of iterations so users could import bills from multiple channels at once, turning that bullseye group into the mainstream. He also tells PMs not to spend three weeks surveying a thousand people. Call ten users yourself.
ex: Brazil has four bill-payment channels, and a missed payment hits your credit record
The payments assistant went from hundreds of thousands to over ten million monthly users in about 15 months
By the fifth call you can usually predict what the rest will say

l181|346.c: Start user research with a clear hypothesis, act as judge rather than advocate, and observe more than you ask.
l181|346.e: He admits this is the least reliable part of product development. Without a clear hypothesis, research is just an interesting conversation that neither confirms nor refutes anything. With one, you tend to fall in love with it and turn into its defense lawyer. In interviews, hunt for problems instead of pitching solutions. Ask from several angles, even argue the opposite, and let the user convince you. A single concrete user story, he finds, is often closer to the truth than a detailed analysis.
ex: P&G's Swiffer: people were so used to the pain of mopping they couldn't articulate it
Joint accounts are over a century old, yet shared savings goals are harder than shared playlists

root.d: The hardest part to do consistently

items.d: A user story often beats the data
Don't fall for your own hypothesis

l181|346.c: Great execution multiplied by the wrong strategy is zero. Strategy has to be specific and clear.
l181|346.e: He rejects the Silicon Valley dogma that strategy is easy and execution is everything. People see the legendary companies that got both right, not the ones whose great execution was multiplied to zero by a bad strategy. Borrowing from Richard Rumelt, strategy is neither a vision nor a financial target. It's a coherent plan that uses your own strengths to attack the crucial problem. Even if it's not entirely right, clarity lets you notice sooner when you've drifted. Startups should concentrate their bets, not hedge. Getting conservative once you have a cash cow is a slow death.
ex: Instagram's Kevin Systrom: we may not be right, but at least we're clear
The 2014 strategy: a branchless, digital no-fee credit card for young urban professionals

terms.d: Young urban professionals with thin credit files
Hate annual fees, can't get credit
Branchless and cheap, so no-fee cards work

result.d: The fewest moves that are truly necessary

l181|346.c: At the company level you must be fundamentally different and define a new category. Incremental improvement can't break through.
l181|346.e: In the debate over category design, he's on the pro side: Google, Netflix and Airbnb all created new categories. Nubank made two concentrated bets. It built a branchless bank on the back of smartphone adoption, and, unusually, it started with credit, which is far harder and riskier, rather than with accounts. Even when entering an existing market, you should reshape the category. A challenger can't fight on the incumbent's ground. The market keeps getting noisier, and only something fundamentally different gets heard.
ex: Payroll-secured loans for civil servants: Nubank sold direct, cut out middlemen and slashed prices
This runs against Todd Jackson's advice to enter a category where people already spend money

marks.d: Not every feature can be disruptive

l181|346.c: The next stage is a private banker for everyone, built AI-native rather than bolted on.
l181|346.e: Nubank started with a single credit card in Brazil, grew into a full-service bank across three Latin American countries, and is now entering a third phase. He lists several still-unproven hypotheses: a bank should cover every financial stage of life, from spending and saving to investing, borrowing and protection; a global bank can be built on a single codebase; social mechanics around money and "autopilot" automation will matter, with AI accelerating all of it. Everyone, he believes, lives a wildly unoptimized financial life. The goal is to give everyone the private banker that only a wealthy few have had.
ex: He draws on how Fidji Simo moved Facebook ads to mobile-native
Early Google required products to launch in 40 languages

items.d: A single credit card in Brazil
Full bank across Latin America, into Mexico and Colombia
An AI private banker in your pocket

l181|346.c: Tenacity is badly underrated, but while you persist, stay clear-eyed about your odds.
l181|346.e: In 2006 he dropped out of Harvard to join Google and work on an acquired radio advertising business. The hypothesis fell apart fast. Radio ads serve brand goals, not direct response. Inventory was scarce. Sellers were concentrated and held the bargaining power. His team was hit by layoffs and he nearly lost his job. Then Google bought YouTube and DoubleClick, and with the brand advertising knowledge he'd picked up, he took over display ads using real-time bidding. That business grew into Google's second largest.
ex: Coldplay and Jay-Z's remix of Lost: just because I'm losing doesn't mean I'm lost
His life motto is also to be fundamentally different: don't tick boxes to meet others' expectations

items.d: Bring the search-ad auction to radio
Brand ads, scarce inventory, concentrated sellers
A low point after dropping out and moving west

l182|349.c: Not daring to ask for what you want is, at bottom, being dishonest with yourself.
l182|349.e: Everyone thinks they know how to ask, but many people fool themselves about whether they're really pursuing what they want. He frames it as integrity: keep asking and keep listening to the answer, and even when you don't get it, you know you've honored what's inside you. Asking doesn't guarantee the outcome; it spares you the suffering of self-deception. In coaching he watches for signs that someone needs this skill: being stuck for weeks repeating the same approach, frequent conflict with others, and treating everything as life-or-death while just trying to escape the fear.
ex: If you've sat on one sentence for three or four days, you've already lost integrity
As a founder he found it far harder to back down than he had at Adobe

root.d: What he watches for in coaching

items.d: Either bottling up or bossing around
Focused on fear, not the goal
Decided you're right before the meeting

l182|349.c: Asking is a three-step loop you repeat: get clear on what you want, ask deliberately, accept the answer.
l182|349.e: The process itself isn't hard, he says. The hard part is the resistance: fear that not getting it means you've failed, and fear of not knowing how to face yourself after a no. He treats it as an iterative exploration. The world says no most of the time, and every no is data for the next round. He borrows the "parts" idea from Internal Family Systems therapy: don't be ashamed of the scared or complaining part of yourself. Acknowledge and understand it. Only then does the fear soften enough for you to get unstuck.
ex: In IFS language: "part of me thinks this, another part thinks that"
Wanting to make sure nobody gets upset first is itself a form of resistance

l182|349.c: Behind every complaint hides a dream. Work backward from the complaint to what you really want.
l182|349.e: People-pleasers are bad at describing dreams but great at complaining. He lets clients complain freely, then asks what the world looks like once the problem is solved. Then comes the test: is this dream big enough to outweigh the fear behind it? Controllers are the opposite. A goal like "everyone does what I say" collapses as soon as it's spoken, so he keeps asking what that would give them. It usually lands on something emotional, like wanting a team that trusts each other and fights side by side.
ex: The "I'm fine" trap, like the cartoon dog saying "this is fine" in a burning room
"I want to speak up more in meetings" is usually not a complete dream

items.d: The world once the problem is solved
Motivating enough? Can you say it aloud?

l182|349.c: Ask clearly and humbly. Your personal opinion is enough to count as a request.
l182|349.e: People-pleasers hope others will read their minds, and controllers are used to giving orders. Neither works. He suggests stating your position clearly while acknowledging the decision isn't yours, then asking whether they'd be willing to reconsider. PMs lean on data to back themselves up, but the relationship itself is influence, and the intuition of the expert in the room is important information too. When you speak, stick to your own thoughts, feelings and the facts you observed, not stories like "you're a jerk."
ex: It's in the spirit of Nonviolent Communication and the DEAR MAN skill from DBT
One step beyond radical candor: don't just give feedback, name the outcome you want

cells.d: Never says it, hopes you'll guess
Clear position, admits it's not my call
I knew this project would fail
I'm the boss, just do it

l182|349.c: It's not a yes unless it's a hell yes. Take a no at face value, no more and no less.
l182|349.e: Accepting the answer is the hardest part, he thinks. People want a yes so badly that they treat a reluctant "maybe" as agreement, and then the other person never really commits. The right move is to treat any lukewarm answer as a no and ask what it would take to get a wholehearted yes. Don't over-accept, treating one no as never. Don't under-accept either, deciding they just don't get it or must obey. Genuinely respecting a no and letting it have consequences actually gives you more influence. The key is regulating your own emotions.
ex: The CTO said "maybe May 1st," and sure enough it wasn't done by then
Say you'll hand the project to someone else, and people often change their answer
Even kind founders have to be willing to ask for "disagree and commit"

marks.d: One rejection and the dream is dropped
Just this person, this time, this way

l182|349.c: He was fired three times at Slack, each time for not being clear, not asking, or not hearing the no.
l182|349.e: In 2014 he became Slack's first PM, arriving with a former founder's confidence. He never asked what success looked like or what was expected, and was fired after six weeks. He apologized and was reinstated. Then he turned into a people-pleaser, never once saying what he wanted in a year of one-on-ones, and was told the product function would be eliminated and he'd move to user research. This time he wrote a proposal and fought for it, and was back within a week. Finally, he couldn't hear management's repeated no, blamed the CEO instead, and was formally fired after HR stepped in.
ex: Looking back, he says he wasn't a victim and Stewart Butterfield wasn't a villain
A confused first PM can imagine that the founder is living in constant fear
He advises founders to have a "how we'll work together" talk with their first 10 to 20 hires

items.d: No clear goals, fired in six weeks
Never asked for anything in one-on-ones
Wrote a proposal, back within a week

l182|349.c: Fear and discipline only work short term. Sustainable motivation comes from a vision you truly want.
l182|349.e: Many high achievers believe the fear of not being good enough is exactly what makes them excellent, and worry they'd slack off without it. He points out that fear was designed for being chased by a tiger; there's no real danger in an office video call. His contrarian view is that he doesn't believe in discipline. Drill-sergeant pressure, like people-pleasing, is a short-term coping strategy. It gets you to the gym for a week, not a year. People who stick with something for years do it because they genuinely want to.
ex: He refuses to be his clients' drill sergeant
The tennis documentary Break Point: top players have similar skills; the difference is mindset

d.verdict: Try following a vision that genuinely inspires you

l183|351.c: Impact equals environment times skills. Score the six environment factors every year; your manager matters most.
l183|351.e: The framework came out of a stretch at Facebook where he worked harder and harder with nothing to show for it. What you should optimize for is impact, he argues; level and pay are byproducts. Environment has six parts: manager, resources, scope, team, compensation and culture. Each year he scores every one from 0 to 2 and looks honestly at what's holding him back and whether it can change. The manager matters most, because only the manager can move the other variables. On skills, communication comes first, and the rest you build through reading, mentors and watching others.
ex: At Facebook he led 30 engineers on friend recommendations, with too much scope and a revolving door of managers
Have three or four mentors at once, rotating through them on different Fridays each month
He copied his predecessor's post-meeting debrief: call out what each person contributed

terms.d: Manager, resources, scope, team, pay, culture

result.d: Level and pay follow from it

l183|351.c: Understand first, then identify and execute. Slowing down is how you speed up.
l183|351.e: The common anti-pattern is identify, justify, execute: someone has an idea, the team finds data to back it, and after months of work the metrics don't move. Facebook's approach was to understand the problem from first principles first. He writes "understand work" explicitly into the roadmap, assigns it to specific people, and runs it alongside execution. Each cycle uses the results and new insights to plan the next, so win rate and speed compound. The less familiar the team is with a problem, the larger the share of understand work should be.
ex: By the time he left Instagram, roughly 60 to 70 percent of experiments were positive and shippable
At YouTube the split started around 60/40 execution to understanding, later about 80/20
In India many people share the same name, so Westernized profile fields didn't help

items: Idea first, then data to back it
Understand work goes on the roadmap
Runs alongside execution; win rate compounds

d.verdict: Slow down to speed up

l183|351.c: Change needs five ingredients. Whichever one is missing, the team shows a matching symptom.
l183|351.e: Whenever he takes over a team or reshapes a culture, he brings the managing-complex-change framework: vision, skills, incentives, resources and an action plan, all required. He observes the symptoms the team shows, works backward to the missing piece, then looks for the easiest lever inside it. Action plans are the easiest to fix, with things like PRD templates and meeting rituals. Vision and skills are the hardest. His YouTube team lacked a shared understanding of product quality, so he built a deck to give everyone a common language.
ex: The framework diagram comes from an old slide deck from around 2006
He carries a deck of skills and frameworks to get a team on the same page fast

l183|351.c: Managing PMs is coaching. Use Bloom's taxonomy to diagnose which level someone is stuck at.
l183|351.e: He spent six years in education and sees PMs as similar to teachers: the people in front of you owe you nothing, so all you have is communication, a clear vision and influence. He rejects the "PM as CEO" idea and treats product as a team sport that needs good role players. He's proud of his coaching tree, the people he developed who now develop others. He uses Bloom's taxonomy to tell whether a team lacks knowledge, understanding, application or higher-order thinking. Managers should sit at the top of the pyramid, synthesizing and evaluating across multiple teams.
ex: Persuading 24 seven-year-olds was harder than pitching growth strategy to Instagram's founders
Former reports went on to lead growth at Stripe, Instagram Stories and more
A common block: knowing only one way to do something, unaware there are others

l183|351.c: Growth comes from the adjacent user, the next group not yet on board. Use the product as they would.
l183|351.e: During hypergrowth, today's users and the users a few months from now are completely different people. At Instagram he proposed the adjacent user framework: understand who uses the product now and why, but more importantly predict who's next and why it isn't working for them yet. One signal is that retention curves for new signup cohorts get worse even though the product hasn't changed, because new users are less tech-savvy or come from new markets. Use the product the way they do: create a fresh account to see the cold-start experience, and visit them at home. It applies just as well to companies whose growth has slowed.
ex: Instagram grew from about 440 million to 636 million monthly users in 2016
After five Instacart orders, 90 percent are identical, yet reordering took seven or eight taps
A beauty company might simply lack shades for certain skin tones

items.d: Buys for the team every week
At home with children, relies on delivery

l183|351.c: Most growth opportunity is in activation and habit. Acquisition needs several loops that reinforce each other.
l183|351.e: Opportunity, he finds, hides in the stretch from signup to habit, and many teams can't even articulate their own aha moment. If you can't retain people, a bigger top of funnel is just a leaky bucket. For acquisition, build compounding loops that amplify each other. Outsiders assumed Instagram grew on word of mouth alone. In fact the partnerships team taught celebrities to use it, their posts got covered by media that linked back to Instagram, the web version and embedded posts brought in search traffic, and friend invites and paid marketing stacked on top.
ex: When Instagram launched its web version, growth jumped about 10 percent right away
The two founders initially didn't buy the idea of a web version

items.d: Teach celebrities to tell their stories

l183|351.c: A simple insight can drive huge growth, like connecting new users to real friends first.
l183|351.e: Early Instagram treated every follow the same, and recommendations skewed toward celebrities. New users followed a bunch of famous people, then posted for the first time months later and no friend saw it. Stuck in an echo chamber, they left, and the retention curve dipped again seven to nine months in. The team convinced the founders to make the connection pivot: new users get connected to real friends first, with celebrity recommendations saved for people who already have a social graph. Retention doubled over a year and a half, he says. Making it easier to get back into your account is another example.
ex: Being locked out of accounts was costing Instagram roughly 10 to 12 million users a year
A unified login box, SMS confirmation and saved credentials added about 15 to 20 million monthly users a year
They stumbled on how active secondary accounts were, which led to a multi-account team

items.d: New users connect to real friends first

l183|351.c: Do understand work before taking a job too, and listen to both current and former employees.
l183|351.e: He doesn't count his time at Instacart as a success. He arrived with a big product vision, wanting to build systems, processes and a talent pipeline, while the operations-driven company needed a hands-on, tactical leader deep in the details. The two sides gradually deadlocked. The lesson is to do understand work before joining. Current employees give you the best version of the company and former ones the worst, so triangulate for yourself. In his first 90 days in a new role, he sits in on meetings and learns everyone's name and story.
ex: His interview question: rank the five skills this role needs from your strongest to weakest
A line he often quotes: you don't rise to your goals, you fall to the level of your systems

marks.d: Tend to show the company's strengths

l184|352.c: Most lost deals are lost to no decision. Customers fear messing up far more than missing out.
l184|352.e: His team used machine learning on 2.5 million sales calls and found that 40 to 60 percent of qualified opportunities end in no decision, usually after the customer says they want to buy but before they sign. Salespeople are trained to break the status quo bias, so they stress what the customer will miss, create urgency and offer limited-time discounts. Yet doing that made a loss more likely 87 percent of the time. Only 44 percent of no-decision customers actually prefer the status quo; 56 percent want to buy but are afraid to. People fear being blamed for an active decision that goes wrong. That's omission bias.
ex: When a customer hesitates, 75 percent of salespeople respond by piling on FOMO
The research began in March 2020, just as sales meetings all moved online

items: Broken with pain points and costs
Fear of blame outweighs fear of loss
Needs confidence and a safety net

d.verdict: First tell indifference apart from indecision

l184|352.c: Fear of failure has three sources: choosing wrong, new information surfacing later, and promised returns not materializing.
l184|352.e: First, customers worry they've configured the solution wrong: contract length, implementation approach, integrations. Second, they worry new information will surface after signing and make the decision look foolish, so they research endlessly. Third, they worry they won't get the promised return. Their name is on the contract, and they could lose their job over it. He warns big-brand vendors not to assume they're safe. More options, more outside opinions and bigger deal sizes amplify all three fears.
ex: A startup won a seven-figure deal, then lost it two weeks later over a middling Gartner Magic Quadrant position
"Nobody gets fired for buying IBM" is comforting, but it isn't immunity

items.d: Did I pick the right solution and setup?
Will the promised return actually come?

l184|352.c: First judge how indecisive the customer is. Use "ping and echo" to get their fear onto the table.
l184|352.e: JOLT stands for judge the indecision, offer a recommendation, limit the exploration, and take risk off the table. It isn't a linear process, though. The J is like a probe that tells you which of the other three to do next. Indecision, he says, is like carbon monoxide: colorless, odorless and everywhere. Almost every buyer considers themselves decisive, yet the data shows the vast majority are moderately to highly indecisive and embarrassed to admit it. Top performers don't ask directly. They hypothesize the sticking point, say something like "many customers feel overwhelmed by the options at this stage," and listen to the response to confirm or rule it out.
ex: Like a surface ship sending out a sonar ping to detect a submarine
Sample line: are you and your team clear on what should be in the solution?

l184|352.c: Stop asking customers what they want and recommend directly, so they don't carry the decision alone.
l184|352.e: Options cut both ways. Early on, let a thousand flowers bloom. At decision time, prune them, or the customer will fear picking wrong and pick nothing, or sign and then backtrack. Salespeople worry a recommendation seems pushy, but the customer rarely makes this kind of decision while the rep lives in it every day, which makes the rep the better guide. A good waiter recommends the signature dish and offers a lighter alternative. That's the delegation effect: the recommender shares the blame if it goes wrong, so the customer feels safer and decides more readily.
ex: Offer three tiers, recommend the middle one, and expand after year one
Counterexample: a waiter asking "what are you in the mood for tonight?" just hands the problem back

items.d: Trade shows and first demos: show many options
Say clearly which one to pick

l184|352.c: To stop endless research, earn trust by being candid, then show your own expertise.
l184|352.e: Some customers always believe the answer is in the next white paper or reference call. Underneath is the fear of being blindsided later, plus a suspicion that the salesperson won't tell the truth. Top performers expose their weak spots early, admitting a feature gets mixed reviews or a competitor is stronger in a certain scenario, to show they only want to help the customer decide well. Then they demonstrate expertise themselves rather than bringing a carload of experts and playing host. Otherwise the customer sees you as a coordinator, and you lose the standing to guide the choice.
ex: The "clown car" approach: showing up with a solutions engineer, a product manager and an executive sponsor

terms.d: Know it more deeply than the customer

result.d: The customer stops playing expert themselves

l184|352.sc: T: Take risk off the table
l184|352.c: To de-risk the deal, lower expectations first, then give the customer a safety net.
l184|352.e: Average reps love it when a customer gets fired up by a 10x case study. Top performers cool it down: that case had everything go right and plenty of resources. Better to build the business case on the 5x every customer can reach, then try to over-deliver, so the customer isn't embarrassed in front of the CFO later. The safety net can be pulling in implementation and customer success before signing to map out a six-month roadmap, or positioning professional services as insurance. In some industries you can also offer exit clauses or special contract terms.
ex: Hitting 7x should count as a big win, but gets questioned if you promised 10x
His metaphor: be the customer's tandem skydiving instructor

items.d: Build the business case on a safe multiple
Milestones and owners set before signing
Positioned as insurance if things go wrong

l184|352.c: Challenger selling tells customers what should keep them up at night, then leads to what only you can offer.
l184|352.e: Most salespeople dig for what keeps the customer up at night. A Challenger instead points out the risk the customer should be worried about but hasn't noticed, because a rep sees more similar customers in a week than the customer sees in a year. It isn't free consulting, though. The insight has to funnel into value only you can provide. You light a fire, then be the only fire extinguisher dealer in town. The starting point is knowing what only you can do, and under what conditions the customer would pay a premium for it.
ex: The Challenger Sale was based on a study of 6,000 salespeople
Dentsply's cordless handpiece cost about three times more, and leading with the product kept failing
They switched to opening with hygienists' repetitive strain injuries, absences and workers' comp costs

items.d: Hygienists suffer frequent repetitive strain injuries

l185|354.c: Canva stays profitable so it never has to beg for money just to survive.
l185|354.e: In a funding round at a valuation of about $100 million, every other investor had signed and wired money. Two days before signing, the lead investor demanded the valuation be cut in half, saying they could get a better deal. The two co-founders flew to Silicon Valley that night and found a new lead a week before Christmas, on better terms than before. That episode made them decide to stay profitable. Canva has now been profitable for about seven years and raises money only on its own schedule. Board meetings are almost entirely about product.
ex: Board decks have one page of financial curves; the rest is product and roadmap

items.d: Demands half the valuation two days before signing
Overnight flight to Silicon Valley, new lead found
The replacement deal was actually better
Never again beg for money to survive

l185|354.c: Don't copy big companies: PMs connect people and ideas, and ideas must become visible prototypes.
l185|354.e: He thinks the kind of product you make shapes how you think. Spotify works in sound, so its teams push ideas forward through discussion. Canva is about visual communication, so an idea only counts once it is drawn as a prototype or mockup, and people who can't express themselves visually often struggle. He deliberately avoided Google's engineering-centered PM model, and Canva didn't even have a PM title until year six or seven. At Canva a PM's job is to connect the team, the ideas and the data, and keep adjusting as new constraints appear. Executives hired from outside should listen for a few months before changing any process.
ex: Most leaders grew up inside Canva; some outside executives left within months
For the first four or five years, the founders were the only product leads

items: Start from what tech can do
Show the vision as a prototype

l185|354.c: As the company grows, everyone hands off their old work, and everyone gets a coach in their own craft.
l185|354.e: Canva grew from three people to more than four thousand, so every role has to keep leveling up. The first email copywriter can write every email by hand for a year, but with hundreds of millions of users and a hundred languages, they have to hire, build systems, and learn to enjoy leading people. Just telling people to grow doesn't work; you have to give them opportunities and support. Canva has almost no traditional managers. Instead, each person has a coach in the same discipline who helps build skills and judge when to move up a level. Whoever brings a good idea gets to pull a few people together and build it.
ex: Roughly 800 to 1,000 internal coaches, plus about five full-time coaches
Performance is judged by 360-degree peer feedback, now every six months
The idea came from the founders hiring outside coaches early on

root.d: Let go of old work to have bigger impact

items.d: Watches your skills and timing for promotion
Idea owners assemble a team and build it

l185|354.c: The first version needn't be perfect, but it must delight people, or word of mouth never starts.
l185|354.e: When the lean-startup idea was everywhere, investors kept pushing them to launch early. They polished for about a year instead, because the experience is the product, and word of mouth has been Canva's biggest source of growth for years. He has two tests: build something you genuinely love and would use yourself, and make it exciting enough that people want to pay right away and tell their friends. Six months of user testing before launch showed social media managers were the most excited group. It also led them to rebuild onboarding so people wouldn't freeze in front of a blank page.
ex: Onboarding starts with searching "monkey" and making a design in a few steps
Test users said, in effect: I never thought I could be a designer
The first version only made social media images and blog graphics

l185|354.c: Design the whole path from a Google search to the moment of delight, and go international early.
l185|354.e: Early on, search-engine growth (SEO) was just one slide in the fundraising deck, until Andre joined. The team mapped what users were trying to do, say searching for "Halloween poster," and designed the whole path: rank first in search, then the landing page, the template, simple edits, and the download. Search can't save a bad product. As an Australian company with a small home market, Canva started localizing about three years after launch. Users in Brazil ran their businesses from phones, which pushed the team to take the Android experience seriously.
ex: Brazil, India and Indonesia are all top-five markets, growing faster than the US

l185|354.c: The free tier comes from the mission; subscriptions are what made revenue take off.
l185|354.e: Canva's mission is to let everyone in the world design, and many people can't afford design software, so a free version was planned from day one. But the company also had to pay its own way. The first revenue came from selling stock images one at a time: exporting a design that used a paid image cost one dollar, and revenue grew about 30 percent a month for the first two years. About three years in, they launched a subscription, Canva for Work (later renamed Canva Pro), and it soon outsold the single-item purchases. Folding the stock images into the subscription later produced a second jump.
ex: One-dollar images let many people afford stock photos for the first time

items.d: Main revenue for the first two years

l185|354.c: AI can't just be a chat box bolted on; Canva builds, partners, and opens an ecosystem.
l185|354.e: He sees AI as the next key technology after mobile and cloud, but it can't be the whole product. What matters is still what the user is trying to make, with AI helping them design faster and better. The first pillar is training Canva's own models in design and imagery, where its data and understanding give it the biggest edge. The second is handing commodity capabilities, such as large language models, to the best partners. The third is an open app platform so AI developers can reach Canva's roughly 170 million monthly users.
ex: Partners include OpenAI, and RunwayML for video generation

terms.d: Design and imagery, where Canva's data is strongest
Commodity capabilities like large language models

l186|356.c: Fall in love with the problem, not your solution; the problem guides the whole journey.
l186|356.e: He thinks a startup exists to create value, and solving a problem is the most direct way to do that. Loving the problem keeps you from drifting, and it makes a better story: nobody cares about "crowdsourced navigation," but everyone cares about "helping you avoid traffic jams," and they'll want to help you succeed. His method: find a problem that annoys you, then ask who else has it, and leave your comfort zone to talk with strangers. If someone corrects how you describe the problem, it's worth digging into. Without enough passion, you won't survive the hard journey.
ex: If someone says "I know people with that problem," it isn't real enough for them
Auto-rebooking cheaper flights: consumers wouldn't bother, so he sold businesses 10% travel savings
The iPhone is an exception: it didn't start from a clear problem

About 20 conversations is enough to check
If it works, you've created value

l186|356.c: A startup is a long journey of failures, so fail fast and settle for good enough.
l186|356.e: He describes a startup as a roller coaster, with far more ups and downs than an ordinary business. It is also a string of failures, because you are doing something nobody has done before. Two things follow. First, if you are afraid of failing, you have already failed, because you won't try. Second, fail fast, so you have time for many more attempts, like half-court shots: the more you take, the more likely one goes in. Perfect is the enemy of good enough; start with something not good enough and keep iterating. The longest stretch is finding product-market fit, which often takes years.
ex: Ben Horowitz: founders sleep like babies, waking up crying every two hours
Japanese proverb: fall seven times, stand up eight; teach kids to fail

items.d: Widely known only after about six years

l186|356.c: Product-market fit has one measure: retention. If users don't come back, you created no value.
l186|356.e: He says that once a product finds product-market fit, its core stops changing: we use Google and Waze today the same way we did the first time. After succeeding in Israel, Waze went global at the end of 2009, but it was only good enough in a handful of countries, and elsewhere users tried it once and left. The team kept calling drivers who had churned, rebuilt the product on their feedback, and failed again and again. More than a year later it started working, city by city in the US and country by country in Europe. What users valued most turned out to be certainty about arrival time, not saving minutes.
ex: For a frequent-use product, 30% to 50% retention at three months is a good sign
Users usually convert only on their third or fourth use
Japanese house numbers follow construction order, so crowdsourced maps struggle there

items.d: Good enough only in four countries like Czechia
Grew city by city, country by country

l186|356.c: Do one thing per stage: first product-market fit, then growth or revenue depending on usage frequency.
l186|356.e: At the idea stage you can think about everything, but once you start building, there is only one job: find product-market fit. At that point you don't need sales, business development, or even marketing, just a product lead iterating with developers. Growth and the business model come after. A product people use often spreads by word of mouth, so do growth first. A product people use rarely will always have to buy users, so figure out how to make money first. When the stage changes, the whole company has to shift gears or it gets stuck. Focus means deciding what not to do.
ex: Waze planned to sell map and traffic data, then switched to ads
Ask people how they heard of Waze and most say someone told them
Airbnb is used rarely; early on it won word of mouth by being cool

items.d: Solution, vision and business model all at once
Frequent use: grow first; rare use: monetize first
The whole company refocuses each stage

l186|356.c: Put your strongest point first and last, and let the CEO pitch alone with a detailed story.
l186|356.e: Fundraising, he says, is a roller coaster in the dark, and you ride it several times. Investors usually form an impression before you sit down, and early-stage checks almost always come down to liking the CEO and liking the story. So the CEO should go alone. The first slide gets the most time, so it carries your strongest point, and the closing thank-you slide repeats it. A good story works through emotion and detail; investors are users too, so start from the problem. About 30% of customers you pitch will buy, but only about 1% of investors will invest, so get used to a hundred rejections.
ex: Waze raised about $50 million in total, $12 million in the first round
His microwave-doesn't-fit-the-cabinet story had enough detail that investors remembered it
Don't argue after a rejection; treat it like being turned down for a date

items.d: A VC sees one or two hundred startups a year
About 1%; survive a hundred nos first

l186|356.c: Learn to fire before you learn to hire: at day 30, ask if you'd hire this person again.
l186|356.e: He has asked many failed founders what went wrong, and about half blame the wrong team, and almost all of them knew within the first month. The real problem is a CEO who won't make the hard call, so the best people get fed up and leave. His fix: put a reminder in your calendar for a new hire's 30th day and ask, knowing what I know today, would I hire this person? If yes, tell them they're exceeding expectations and give them more equity. If no, fire them right away. If unsure, ask your top performers how much it would hurt if this person left.
ex: Ask references one question: would you hire this person?
Same advice for his kids' jobs: still unhappy after 90 days, quit
An employee who gets zero bonus shouldn't still be at the company

root.d: Knowing what I know today, would I hire them?

items.d: Tell them, and give more equity
Fire now; better for both sides
Ask top performers if losing them would hurt

l186|356.c: Watch users who aren't like you; to win the change-averse majority, always simplify.
l186|356.e: Different people use the same product in completely different ways. Product people are mostly innovators or early adopters, and they can't understand everyone else without watching them. He suggests observing new users, and whenever someone doesn't do what you expected, asking why. Talk to people who dropped off halfway through the funnel, not just the ones who succeeded. The early majority is about a third of the market, and winning them means winning the market. But they fear change and fear looking stupid, so the answer is always to simplify, including deleting features nobody uses.
ex: Wozniak saw him take a selfie with the volume button and said: finally, someone uses it

However good Salesforce is, the early majority asks what's wrong with Excel

About a third; win them, win the market
Adopt only when they have to

l187|360.sc: Rule one: get out of your way
l187|360.c: Thinking power is dirty, or that you don't deserve it, is the first wall blocking your rise.
l187|360.e: Research shows that political skill goes with higher pay, faster promotion, and less stress. Power, he says, is like a knife: a surgeon uses it to cut out cancer, a mugger uses it to rob you, so don't confuse the tool with its use. The less advantaged you are, the more you need it. Common ways people block themselves: feeling like an impostor, apologizing before they speak, and putting being liked first. If you feel you don't belong, that attitude leaks out and others start doubting you too. The job is to get things done, not to be liked.
ex: Gerald Ferris built the political skill inventory; later studies back it up
A top spine surgeon: his patients don't care about his personality
Casino executive Gary Loveman: if you want to be liked, get a dog

items.d: Thinking you were admitted by mistake
Opening with "this may not be useful"
Forgetting you were hired to deliver

l187|360.c: Top jobs are scarce, and nobody promotes someone they've never heard of, so stand out on purpose.
l187|360.e: Organizations are pyramids: the higher you go, the fewer the seats, and decision makers can't pick someone who isn't in their heads. So do things that make people remember you and that also create value for the organization, instead of only doing your job quietly. You need both visibility and substance.
