Visibility alone gets seen through; substance alone goes unnoticed. You can also think of it as amplifying your team's work and sharing what you know at scale, rather than bragging.
ex: Keith Ferrazzi set out to lift Deloitte's brand awareness from 1-2% to 30%
Tristan Walker landed the Starbucks partnership for Foursquare first
Investor Laura Chau made partner in four years through writing, podcasts and a distinctive style

cells.d: No substance and no one knows you
Nobody knows what you can do

l187|360.c: Rules mostly serve those who wrote them; break them to be remembered, and ask for help boldly.
l187|360.e: Unexpected behavior is memorable, he says, and existing rules usually favor the people who made them. Like companies, individuals break through by being different and playing to their strengths. The most over-obeyed rule is "don't ask for help, look self-sufficient." Research finds people overestimate how many others they must ask before someone helps. Being turned down is no worse than not asking, and if you don't ask, you certainly won't get it.
ex: Flynn's paper is titled "If You Need Help, Just Ask"
Investor Jason Calacanis makes many small bets and has no partners
Southwest Airlines skipped the hub-and-spoke routes everyone else used

items: Wait your turn under existing rules
A no is no worse than not asking

d.verdict: If you don't ask, you won't get it

l187|360.c: The first rule of networking is generosity: be a connector and know plenty of weak ties.
l187|360.e: Many people find networking distasteful because they picture it as taking. The real core is: what can I do for you, and whom can I introduce you to? The more people you know, the more connections you can make and the more information you hold, and the broker at the center of a network is the most valuable person in it. Weak ties bring fresh information that close friends can't. For people on your critical path, don't judge whether you like them; just remember you need their cooperation. Once your contempt shows, cooperation is gone.
ex: Omid Kordestani's network made him Google's 11th employee
Sociologist Granovetter found good jobs often come through acquaintances
He connected Esther Wojcicki with Leanne Williams

items.d: The ones most critical to your goal
Host dinners, send articles, make introductions
What can you do, whom can you introduce
Sit at the center of the network

l187|360.c: Looking powerful is a learnable skill: people judge looks first, voice second, words last.
l187|360.e: Evidence suggests people react mostly to appearance and body language, then to voice, and least to the actual content. Speaking without notes, holding eye contact, keeping it short, gesturing, open posture, a loud voice, humor, and even anger all make you look stronger. None of this is about personality; like tennis, it comes from practice and coaching. His class walks students from denial through anger and frustration to acceptance, by pushing them a little outside their comfort zone each time.
ex: Watch BP's Tony Hayward and Goldman's Blankfein on mute and you can guess who keeps his job
Lobbyist Jack Valenti never brought notes to congressional hearings
Marketer Regis McKenna turned a poor public speaker, Steve Jobs, into a master pitchman

l187|360.c: Power feeds on itself: using it to deliver brings more resources, and success makes the past forgotten.
l187|360.e: You are put in a position of power to make things happen, he says. Use resources to get things done, and because people want to stand with winners, you'll get more assignments, more resources, and more followers. The world doesn't rebalance by pulling the successful down; it is self-fulfilling. When others believe you have power, you have more of it. People want to be near money, power and success, and they'll overlook your flaws to get there. He stresses this describes the world as it is, not as it should be.
ex: Senator Lindsey Graham went from attacking Trump to following him, to keep his influence
Martha Stewart went to prison, yet her brand is worth more than ever

items.d: Marshal resources and get things done
People want to be near success

l187|360.c: You can't have both power and autonomy, and he personally chooses control over his own time.
l187|360.e: His late colleague James March taught him this. A top position means an assistant controls your calendar and duty comes first, even when a family member is gravely ill. It also means living under a microscope, losing privacy, and never being sure whether people are close to you for who you are or for your position. Families pay a price too. He held an academic administrative job exactly once and decided never again. His homework for listeners: if any of this feels uncomfortable, get a coach or a personal board of directors rather than toughing it out alone.
ex: A business school dean whose wife was critically ill still had to meet alumni and fundraise
To get Jack Valenti to guest lecture, he had to book through Valenti's assistant
Education official Rudy Crew's daughter described the cost of being a powerful person's family

marks.d: Duties fill your calendar and life
Runs his own calendar, no assistant

l188|361.c: Don't assume what made you successful before will work in a new market; test it first.
l188|361.e: Atlassian grew up on a bottom-up playbook: technical teams adopt a tool first, then it spreads to the rest of the business. So the company bet HipChat would spread the same way. But customers were already saying their engineers used HipChat while business teams preferred Slack, and the team never tested that assumption early. Slack rode the consumerization wave and invested in playful onboarding, emoji and polish, exactly the things the HipChat team dismissed as trivial but that decided what non-technical users chose. His lesson: spell out why you succeeded, then find a way to test whether that carries over.
ex: Atlassian's stock went up after it sold the product to Slack
Before building Jira Product Discovery, a Jira newsletter ad drew over 3,000 waitlist signups in two weeks

items.d: Engineers adopt first, then the whole company
Thought a chat tool would spread the same way
Sold the product to the rival

l188|361.c: Chasing a rival's features means copying what they were thinking a year ago.
l188|361.e: When Slack was on a roll, the team instinctively felt it was always one feature behind, so it followed along and lost its real strength: serving one group of users well. A rival's shipped feature is just the tip of the iceberg, he says. Underneath is research and customer understanding you can't see, and what you're looking at is a decision they made about a year earlier. These days he glances at competitors about once a quarter, only to check for threats. Whenever the team gets rattled by competitor news, they rewatch the last few weeks of user interviews together and get back to their own customers.
ex: When a rival launched AI features, the whole team rewatched three weeks of user interviews
You don't have to be first or shiniest; you have to actually solve the customer's problem

l188|361.c: Don't rewrite and build a shared platform at the same time; win the problem first, then extract the platform.
l188|361.e: To fight Slack, HipChat suddenly got flooded with developers and product managers, the old architecture buckled, and the team decided on a full rewrite, with every component built on a new microservices platform for the whole company to reuse. By the time the rewrite, Stride, shipped, Slack was far ahead and Microsoft Teams had entered by bundling with Office. His rule: if the platform is ready, use it; if not, hack something together, iterate with customers, and move to the platform once the idea is proven. Buying a small company with limited traction, shutting its product and rebuilding on your platform is a different story.
ex: He estimates about 70% of that code still lives in Atlassian's platform today
Confluence's current editor grew out of the HipChat-era work

items: Hundreds of thousands of users with expectations
The acquired product had little traction
Like delaying takeoff to switch planes

d.verdict: With lots of existing customers, never rewrite

l188|361.c: Integrating an acquisition is mostly a people problem; treat it like hiring a team.
l188|361.e: After being acquired, a startup suddenly loses control of its fate. The CEO may become a product lead who gets asked for a three-year plan, and a team that used to be one unit is split by function into product, engineering and design under different managers. Leadership says to keep things as they were, yet each function keeps asking for performance reviews, OKRs and revenue forecasts, which eat the time for building product. So expect a sharp slowdown before any speedup, and design the integration the way you'd design hiring. Next time he'd rather do a small technology acquisition: shut the product down, rebuild it on the platform, and gain a year of time to market.
ex: Statuspage became a big success inside Atlassian, but the integration period was painful
A "frankenstack" of separate technologies stitched together isn't what customers want

root.d: From controlling your fate to being surrounded by process

items.d: Portfolio and platform choices no longer yours
Reporting by function to different leads

l188|361.c: To win internal support, explain why it must happen now, and show steady, visible momentum.
l188|361.e: He once pushed Atlassian to invest more in IT operations, pitching everyone from business leads up to the CEO. Everyone liked it, nobody decided, and after months in limbo he gave up; a year later the company entered that market anyway. Big companies have too many opportunities, so plenty of analyses get shelved. What's missing is an urgent trigger for why now. For Jira Product Discovery, he posted a short weekly update in the internal tool Atlas, demoed new features, cut a few minutes of customer interview clips, and even held finished features back for next week's demo. That created a train that never stopped moving, and nobody wanted to stand in front of it.
ex: Hundreds of colleagues subscribed to his weekly updates
Internal use started after two months; the first lighthouse customer got it in month five

terms.d: Show the opportunity has an expiry date

result.d: Survive the ugly-baby phase

l188|361.c: Keep telling the company the project will probably fail, so scarcity keeps away help that comes with strings.
l188|361.e: A startup's advantage is hunger, while a big company tends to over-invest: other teams volunteer to adapt their services for you, but help always comes with conditions, and that usually means slowing down. His line was that the company's appetite for this was exactly these seven people, and odds were the thing wouldn't exist in six months. That freed the team to build prototypes that didn't scale, broke the design system and ignored the target architecture, just to test with customers. It's also responsible with company money: prove it's worth it before dragging in 50 people. He spent years of accumulated trust on this, breaking rules without breaking trust.
ex: He admits the number was made up: a 70% chance of being gone in six months
No engineering manager, contractors hired in France, sidestepping rules like 15% on reliability work

items.d: Lowers others' urge to get involved
Not dragged by process and planning
Validate the idea with customers first
Platform and headcount only after proof

l188|361.c: Run incubated projects with a shared vocabulary of stages, so everyone knows what to expect when.
l188|361.e: Atlassian realized its innovation had long depended on acquisitions, so the founders launched an internal incubator, Point A, to rebuild that muscle. Projects move through Wonder, Explore, Make and Impact: first prove the problem, the market and why now; then validate a solution with prototypes; then ship in alpha and beta; finally measure business impact. Each gate requires a six-page document reviewed live by the founders and business-line leaders, who can pass it, send it back, kill it, or fold it into another product. Because the whole company speaks this language, nobody rushes to argue about architecture while a project is still in Explore.
ex: Of about 100 proposals, only three products made it through every stage
Whiteboards came out of Point A and were later folded into Confluence
Members are borrowed from other departments and can go back if the project fails

items.d: Prove the problem, the market and why now
Validate the solution with Figma prototypes
Watch the real effect on the business

l188|361.c: Get the product right with 10 lighthouse customers, then scale to 100, then 1,000.
l188|361.e: If a new product is measured on monthly active users, it gets pushed into the open too early, and customers who have a bad first experience are hard to win back; Reforge calls this the safety funnel. So he built a separate experience inside Jira and opened it to only a few customers. First, 10 people prove they represent the target customer. Then 100 cover the range of use cases. Then 1,000 show people can get started on their own. Lighthouse customers also talk directly to the whole team. Once engineers know named customers and their situations, they start proposing what to change themselves, and everyone becomes a product engineer.
ex: Inspired by Noah Weiss's incubate, iterate, integrate approach, like Instagram's Explore tab
Early on he reported to stakeholders with customer video clips rather than metrics

items.d: Prove they represent the target customer
Cover every use case and security need

l189|364.c: Don't pick a job from a spreadsheet; try it on and see if you feel lucky and at home.
l189|364.e: She admits she never had a career plan and once thought that held her back. What has worked all along is following her gut: going where it feels like home and working with people who feel like friends. She still writes out the tradeoffs in a spreadsheet, then tears it up, because those factors don't decide whether she'll do the job well. More useful is imagining she starts tomorrow: what she'd think about on the commute, who she'd eat lunch with, what problem she'd solve. The emotional reaction tells her more. The core is trust. When she believes the people around her will back her and let her take risks, she tries more things.
ex: In 2007 she had a friend walk her through Facebook, then joined as a contractor
She once feared she only worked at Meta; Faire put that worry to rest

items: Project where you'll be in five years
Hunt for the one right answer
Ask whether you trust these people

d.verdict: Do the spreadsheet, then tear it up

l189|364.c: When you disagree, start with "fascinating": value the outcome over being right, and dig for what they know.
l189|364.e: Growing up, being right was part of her identity. At work a former manager pointed out that figuring everything out alone is exhausting and often wrong anyway, because other people hold information she doesn't. So she changed her goal to getting the best outcome and deliberately built a positive loop: get curious, learn something new, reach a better result, and both sides feel better. The instinctive resistance still shows up. The trick is to pause first, let her body calm down, and then treat it as a chance to learn. Everyone in the same meeting walks out with a different version of it, and that alone is worth exploring.
ex: Meta executive Boz says her "fascinating" breaks down the walls between different views
For a few years she had to rotate words, because everyone knew it meant she disagreed

items.d: What do you know that I don't?

l189|364.c: Come to product reviews with a recommendation; the goal is shared principles, not answers to each question.
l189|364.e: She jokes that executives have a small dinosaur brain that holds only three things at once, so they can't dig into every question the way the team can. The team should write everything up, then cut most of it, keeping only the minimum needed to make a clear recommendation, which forces them to take a position. Managers bring pattern matching plus company and industry context; the team brings the recommendation; the two complement each other. If a review just hands every decision up the chain, the organization never gets stronger. Instead, discuss who you're optimizing for, over what time horizon, and how much risk you can take, and leave with principles.
ex: Her line: "My manager owns the context, I own the recommendation"
Keep the room small and cross-functional; record it for anyone who wants to learn the principles

result.d: No need for another review next time

l189|364.c: Unite the team around one metaphor about how the product should feel, and consistent design follows.
l189|364.e: A former boss taught her to ask two questions: how should this product make people feel, and when did you last feel that way? The bigger the team, the more the story matters. Rather than dictating every decision, get everyone to believe the same story, and icons, interactions and tone fall into line on their own. WhatsApp's metaphor was face-to-face conversation, because it had to serve everyone from high-end phone owners to people online for the first time. The typing indicator is like someone drawing a breath to speak; the double check marks lighting up are like seeing a reaction on their face.
ex: Video calls used "sitting around the living room," which led to calls anyone can drop into
The hill-climbing metaphor: leave the small local peak, cross the valley, climb a higher one
She builds mental simulators of mentors: Boz talks principles, Rob Goldman checks dashboards

items.d: How should users feel using the product?
When did you last feel that way?
Design and interactions line up naturally

l189|364.c: Execution beats strategy: a good-enough direction plus great execution lets you iterate the strategy until it's right.
l189|364.e: Strategy is seductive, she says, but customers only care about the product in their hands. A perfect strategy with bad execution never reaches the market, and you learn nothing, because you can't tell what went wrong. A roughly right direction with excellent execution may not win at first, but you know the execution was sound, so you can go back, fix the strategy, ship again, and repeat until you win. She suggests spending about 20% of your time on strategy and the rest shipping, testing and tuning the execution machine, even in senior roles. A strategy is only useful if it actually changes the team's behavior and priorities.
ex: A common Meta saying: execution eats strategy for breakfast
She asks her leadership team: how much revenue will small businesses bring in three years?

cells.d: The strategy never reaches the market
Execution is solid; revise the strategy

l189|364.c: Don't shrink yourself to be liked; keep adding tools so you can fit different people and problems.
l189|364.e: Around the time she became head of ads products at Facebook, she kept hearing that it didn't matter how smart she was if people didn't like her. So she deliberately toned herself down, voiced fewer opinions, and even wore only earth tones for two years. It worked for a while, until her team needed her to make calls and she realized she had to find her opinions again. Women, she says, get more feedback about style than substance, and much of it contradicts itself, so she first decides whether to act on it at all. Today she doesn't give that kind of feedback; she tells people to add tools, more keys to open more doors.
ex: The feedback often contradicted itself: be more decisive, but give fewer orders
She sees "you must find mentors and sponsors" as an extra burden put on women

items.d: Fewer opinions; two years of earth tones
Don't get smaller; add new keys

l189|364.c: Give each team its own input metric, so everyone isn't chasing the same ball.
l189|364.e: If everyone is measured only on revenue or GMV, people pile into the few scenarios that are certain to move the number, tripping over each other like toddlers playing soccer while nobody touches the ball. Better to build a metric tree along the customer journey, with teams owning visits, conversion, reorders or different surfaces, as long as each metric truly connects to the final outcome. Different incentives and disagreements between teams are healthy tension; as long as the end goal is shared, debate it openly and rationally. She adds that there is no optimal org. The more senior you are, the more only unsolvable problems reach you, so you pick the least bad path and explain the principle.
ex: "Toddler soccer": everyone chasing the same ball
In her first year at Faire she wrote the CEO a "radical ideas" doc every quarter

root.d: The outcome the company and customers share

items.d: Each team owns a different scenario

l190|365.c: Screening out obvious jerks early is why YC grew into a community of alumni who help each other.
l190|365.e: YC's other three partners were technical and focused interviews on product and technology. She kept time, walked founders in and out, and watched: did the co-founders interrupt each other, would they really quit their jobs, did they understand their own product? Early batches had only ten or twenty companies that ate dinner together every week. Occasionally she'd say she couldn't face dinner with this person every week, so they passed, and she never regretted it. That set the tone of older batches helping newer ones and making introductions. Today a question posted on Bookface, YC's internal network, always gets answered.
ex: She warned Paul Graham not to invest just because he loved the idea; the founders weren't going to quit
Early interviews lasted 10 minutes, and she mostly said nothing

items.d: Older batches help newer ones and make intros
Thousands of alumni who answer any question

l190|365.c: A founder who gets defensive when questioned is almost always a bad sign.
l190|365.e: Building something new means being challenged constantly, she says, for instance "there's already something like this on the market." The founder's job is to educate the other person, not defend themselves. The first idea is usually wrong, so you have to be open enough to see what users actually want. The best founders love learning from others; when they ask a question, they really listen to the answer, and the conversation feels like a tennis rally. Defensive people usually aren't open, so she watched for it closely in interviews.
ex: PayPal began as money transfers between PalmPilots, then moved to the web version users adopted on their own
Stripe's Collison brothers ask a question and then genuinely listen to your answer

items: Can't see what users really need
Explains what they've already figured out
Willing to adjust to what users need

d.verdict: Defensiveness is almost always a bad sign

l190|365.c: People matter more than ideas: back relentless founders even when the idea looks doubtful.
l190|365.e: In the winter 2009 batch, right after the financial crisis, YC only funded founders who could survive on almost nothing, like cockroaches, or start charging quickly. When Airbnb interviewed, nobody liked the idea of sleeping on strangers' air mattresses, and Paul Graham wanted to talk them into something else. But the team's energy and their story of selling homemade cereal boxes convinced her they'd do whatever it took to make the company work. GOAT's two founders were then building an app for dinners with strangers and had previously run a cream puff shop. She pushed to fund them, and they later pivoted into a sneaker marketplace.
ex: Airbnb's Obama O's and Cap'n McCain's cereal boxes, sealed with a glue gun
She also likes industry insiders fixing their own field's problems, like HR software maker Zenefits

cells.d: Airbnb and GOAT were bets on people
Great people and a great idea
Neither the people nor the idea
Don't fund just because you love the idea

l190|365.c: She values sincerity over charisma: saying "I don't know" is what real confidence looks like.
l190|365.e: She avoids the word charisma, because plenty of charismatic people are full of hot air and just think startups are cool. Charisma helps with sales, hiring and fundraising, but there has to be substance behind it. What she values most is sincerity: genuinely caring about the problem and the users. Sincerity shows up as humility and candor. When stumped, say you don't know, then explain what you've thought about and how you'll find out. That is confidence. YC's three months exist to turn these founders into a company truly worth betting on.
ex: A team of men around 45 building a fashion app for teenage girls was clearly just chasing money

marks.d: No feeling for the field at all
Then explains how they'll find out
Deeply invested in the problem and users

l190|365.c: Founders must burn the boats and go full time, and co-founders should ideally share a history.
l190|365.e: Starting on the side is fine, but sooner or later you have to burn the boats. A founder still drawing a salary and health insurance often won't quit when things get hard, or that co-founder eventually leaves. She spent a huge amount of time at YC mediating co-founder disputes, and many companies died or nearly died because of them. So in interviews she hunted for signs of friction, like contradicting each other on the spot or one person blocking the other from answering. She prefers teams of classmates, former colleagues or siblings, who trust each other, know each other's weaknesses and want the same thing. Dropbox is the exception where near strangers made it work.
ex: The application flags signals like lopsided equity or not quitting, so interviewers can probe
One founder put out an arm to stop his partner: I'll take this question

root.d: Not automatic rejections, but worth probing

items.d: Keeps salary and insurance; bails when it gets hard

l190|365.c: Reading people takes attention and follow-up: watch with a mental checklist, then check your instincts years later.
l190|365.e: She can't say where the skill came from, maybe a childhood habit of puzzling over relationships and motives; Paul Graham used to call her Detective Livingston. Her advice for anyone who wants to practice: you don't need clever questions, just notice small signals. Do they get along? Do they understand the product? Do they get defensive when pressed? Then ask how they met and whether they've worked together. She tracks whether her instincts proved right years later, and so far nobody she firmly rejected has gone on to huge success. But she misjudges too; some founders shine in the interview and then can't carry it off.
ex: On the reading-the-mind-in-the-eyes test she scored 36 out of 36; Paul Graham scored 25
Ten-minute interviews are usually enough; stretching to 20 is just waiting around
She didn't spot that Ilya Lichtenstein would later steal a fortune in bitcoin

items.d: How they met, whether they've worked together
A strong gut feeling, fund or pass
Check right and wrong; recalibrate the radar

l190|365.c: The batch model came from inexperience, and sometimes not knowing better is how you discover something new.
l190|365.e: YC started as pure experiment: could you fund young founders with small checks? None of the four partners had ever angel invested, so they decided to fund a whole group in one summer to learn, planning to switch to ordinary one-off investments afterward. The batch turned out to have its own magic. Founders became friends, had dinner every week with guest speakers, and pitched investors together at the end, so they kept doing it. She misses that pure early period when nobody paid attention and nobody attacked them. Press and investors didn't take YC seriously until Reddit was acquired.
ex: The first batch included Sam Altman, Emmett Shear and the Reddit founders
Her podcasting lesson: the host should talk often, but briefly

items.d: Fund one batch to learn how to invest

l191|314.c: Design is art in service of solving problems, and in the AI era distinctive design is what sets products apart.
l191|314.e: He agrees with the definition of design as art applied to problem solving. Design involves creativity and distinctive expression, but it has to serve what users need. Solve the problem without the art and you're left with something purely utilitarian and soulless. At Config he also admitted that Figma's one-click design generation produces the most conventional answer. As more and more software gets generated by AI, he expects the conversation to shift toward craft, quality and distinctive design, which is where products will differentiate.
ex: By his own account, Make Design only produces the most conventional option

marks.d: The most conventional answer, nothing distinctive

l191|314.c: Intuition is a hypothesis generator: propose, debate, check the data, then settle on a working hypothesis.
l191|314.e: Colleagues say he has a sixth sense for what will work; he breaks that intuition down into a process. He and others keep generating hypotheses, put them on the table to debate, look for data that supports or kills them, and converge on a working hypothesis to move forward with for now. To feed his intuition he absorbs everything he can about Figma, from Twitter to support channels, and keeps asking until he reaches the root problem, because when a user asks for X, what they really want may be Y or Z. He encourages his team to do the same.
ex: He reads what users say about Figma everywhere, from Twitter to support tickets

items.d: Put the hypotheses on the table

l191|314.c: To persuade him, bring concrete artifacts and examples; if it's not fatal, he'll let you try.
l191|314.e: The more concrete the artifact and the more debatable the thing in front of him, the more persuasive it is. He asks for examples and pushes on details to make sure he understands the problem from first principles. When someone can't answer a follow-up, he sends them off to find out before continuing. Some people find that slow, but come back with data and things move. He admits this is a kind of perfectionism, with the condition that it must never stall the organization. For decisions that aren't fatal, he'll say "go ahead" even when he has doubts, attach his feedback, and often the other person turns out to be right.
ex: He still thinks Pages isn't elegantly implemented, but users clearly need it

items.d: A prototype or example to debate
No answer? Go find out first
Test it, carrying his doubts along

l191|314.c: A good PM builds an opinionated framework that carries everyone toward the same destination.
l191|314.e: The lines between product, design and engineering were always blurry, he says: PMs and designers need to understand technology, designers and engineers need to understand the business and users, and engineers and PMs need taste and craft. PMs fail when they treat the job as process and forget the problem they're solving. Good PMs meet users, have a strategy and a point of view, and wrap it all in a framework so everyone knows the destination and the path. Hitting the milestone while everyone is miserable also counts as failure. Right now everyone is doing a bit more of each other's jobs, but he thinks all three roles will remain.
ex: All three should talk to users directly; research can be the fourth leg of the stool

terms.d: Clarity on how to reach the goal

result.d: Everyone knows the destination and the path

l191|314.c: Complexity accumulates: every local decision can be right while the whole thing spirals out of control.
l191|314.e: His co-founder Evan pointed him to the idea of irreducible complexity: one plus one sometimes equals not three but one and a half, and the more you add, the harder it is to stay coherent. Tools are especially prone to this. Making Figma more powerful without making it more complex is extremely hard, and it can turn into a monster if you're not careful. He and his product leads often find a system where every individual decision was right, yet the sum is too complex, and the only fix is to go back and rethink the whole system. Simplicity is everyone's job: keep simple things simple and make complex things possible.
ex: Dev Mode looks simpler than FigJam, but it took at least three times as long to build

items.d: One plus one equals one and a half

l191|314.c: Ship fast to get feedback: pick two of quality, features and deadline, and build a minimally awesome product.
l191|314.e: Figma took three and a half years from first code to launch, and about five years to its first paying customer. He says flatly that was too long, and it would have been faster if he'd learned to hire sooner; a newly hired engineering lead spelled out the gap in his first week and pushed the launch through. Now he believes the earlier you ship, the more you learn, and both FigJam and Figma Slides were built quickly. Evan taught him that a new product gets two of three: quality, features, deadline. Software can keep improving, so sometimes you ship features on time and fix quality later, and sometimes you protect quality and cut features.
ex: Their phrase for it is the "minimally awesome product"

d.verdict: A new product must know which one it gave up

l191|314.c: Find the most central people in a field and ask for feedback; it beats growth tricks.
l191|314.e: When Figma was starting in 2012 and 2013, he borrowed a network visualization technique he'd seen as a LinkedIn intern, scraped Twitter data to find the most central designers in the design community, and then invited the ones he genuinely admired for coffee. Outsiders called it growth hacking, but he says the intent was to learn as a fan, show them the product and hear their feedback, and designers happen to be great at giving feedback. Those people became early users and evangelists. His definition of mentor is broad too: the community, employees, interns, even people he has mentored all teach him.
ex: He tested vector networks on Tim Van Damme's icons; today Van Damme makes icons for Figma's UI3
The first team customer was Shishir's company; when it broke, he turned around to go help

items.d: Find the central nodes in the design world
Study their work, approach as a fan
Show the product, listen to feedback

l192|369.c: Business is never fair; startups win not by being better but by forcing people to choose.
l192|369.e: Incumbents start with the advantage and keep it by default. "Better" is just an extension of the present, and it assumes the future looks like today. Big companies make money by compounding, widening their defenses, and doing the same thing well over and over. A startup has nothing to compound, so it has to change the subject, reject the existing rules, and propose a radically different future. Nobody who has taken a ride-share compares it feature by feature with a taxi; the difference is obvious. When people either love it or shrug, that's a sign it's different enough.
ex: Don't build an apple that's ten times better; build the world's first banana
Nobody compares a Cybertruck with a Ford F-150 line by line

d.verdict: Force a choice, not a comparison

l192|369.c: An inflection is an external turning point, and you should stress-test it with three questions.
l192|369.e: An inflection, in his definition, is an external event that for the first time makes a radical change in how people think, feel and act possible. Smooth improvement curves like Moore's law don't count. Inflections can come from technology, regulation or beliefs; during the pandemic, telemedicine across state lines became legal and people became willing to see a doctor online. He asks three questions: What specifically is new? Whom does it empower, and how? What conditions have to hold for that empowerment to work? Too early and the conditions aren't there; too late and everyone can see it. The window is in between.
ex: The GPS chip in the iPhone 4S let drivers and riders locate each other, which made Lyft possible
The wheel lay flat for pottery for about 500 years before anyone stood it up to build a cart

items.d: Such as a phone with a GPS chip
Anyone with a phone can be precisely located
Users share location, government allows it
Too early it fails; too late it's obvious

l192|369.c: An insight must be non-consensus and right: most people dislike it, a few fall in love instantly.
l192|369.e: The insight comes from the founder: a non-obvious truth about how to use the inflection to change people's behavior. Ideas that are consensus and right earn ordinary returns, because when everyone likes something, it's too similar to what already exists and to what incumbents do. The best ideas repel or bore most people while a small group falls irrationally in love with them. Ordinary companies extrapolate from the present; pattern breakers assume the future must be radically different and reason backward from it. The hard part is that at first you only know you're non-consensus, not whether you're right.
ex: Lyft's insight: with phones that know their location, you can build Airbnb for cars
He once passed on investing in Airbnb at a valuation of about $1.5 million

cells.d: A few people fall in love at first sight
The price of taking the risk

l192|369.c: Secrets are earned: tinker at the frontier and treasure surprises instead of confirming what you believe.
l192|369.e: There is no recipe for breakthroughs, he says; recipes only exist for things already discovered. Vision isn't a better telescope. It comes from diving into some frontier yourself, obsessing over it until you think about it falling asleep and waking up, and noticing what's missing that others can't see. Experiments designed only to confirm an existing idea teach you nothing; treat surprises as gifts. Non-consensus also doesn't mean contrarian, since being contrarian is still a form of conformity. When customers aren't in a hurry, figure out which it is: if the insight is wrong, stop; if the implementation is wrong, change it; or you may have the wrong customer.
ex: Intuit founder Scott Cook always asks: what were the three biggest surprises in this plan?
Chegg tested textbook rental prices with a fake website and found students would pay $75
Okta moved from cloud systems management to identity: right insight, wrong implementation

items.d: Notice what nobody else has seen
Keep the insight, change the implementation

l192|369.c: Good ideas aren't brainstormed: live in the future and notice what's missing there.
l192|369.e: There's no standard best founder, he says. What matters is who understands this particular future best, who is most intrinsically motivated, and who is best connected in its ecosystem. A young Andreessen built the browser with a beginner's mind, while Applied Intuition, selling big contracts to carmakers, needed founders who grew up in Michigan and had worked at car companies and Waymo. He always asks whether the idea comes from the future; if you aren't living there, your opinion about it doesn't count. Three ways in: build what you yourself are missing, serve lighthouse customers who already live in the future, or deliberately leave the present.
ex: Maddie Hall spent a year as Sam Altman's chief of staff, then started a genetically engineered tree company
Justin Kan built the law startup Atrium more for status than passion

terms.d: Surrounded by people living in the future

result.d: Reaches product-market fit faster

l192|369.c: Treat early believers as heroes: use a movement and a story to lead them to a new future.
l192|369.e: Asking people to give up what's familiar is itself a provocation. Early customers, employees and investors follow you not out of pragmatism but because they share your belief. A movement channels a minority's frustration with the majority's rules, gathers fellow believers to migrate to a new future, and turns the incumbent's biggest strength into a weakness. Storytelling can follow the hero's journey: the founder is Obi-Wan, not Luke, and investors, customers and employees each get a version built around their own journey. In a pitch, slide one says what you do in plain words, slide two gives the insight, slide three gives the evidence.
ex: Airbnb never said hotels were bad, just that you could live in Paris like a Parisian
Lyft's pink mustache eased the fear of getting into a stranger's car
A "Frankenpitch" stitched together to answer every objection buries the insight

items.d: Taxis are scarce, dirty and slow
Afraid to get in a stranger's car
Believing the old world can be beaten

l192|369.c: Startups are inherently disagreeable, and good founders accept being disliked for the sake of the mission.
l192|369.e: To break free of conformity you have to be willing to stand out, and to give up your place in the social hierarchy for the mission. He's wary of founders described as coachable. Twitter founder Ev Williams listened carefully to his advice, then did what he himself thought was right, and it worked. That's the right kind of disagreeable: understanding the advice but believing a different truth. Demanding leaders with high standards actually motivate great people. Before success you endure the loneliness of a mocked idea; after success you're accused of cheating or being too aggressive. Startups are messy inside, and movements always are.
ex: "Mike's law": however much you raise, you'll spend it in about 18 months
In Jonathan Livingston Seagull, the gull who wants to fly ever faster is cast out of the flock

marks.d: Understands the advice, trusts a different truth
Doesn't even grasp what's being said

l192|369.c: Big companies need small, hidden bets: a separate team, a maverick leader, and permission to fail.
l192|369.e: Pattern-breaking projects differ from the regular business in how they're led, how they go to market, and how risk works. The usual mistakes are demanding the project become a third of the business within two or three years, or making it so visible that failure ends someone's career. Either way, the parent company's gravity pulls it back to the old path. The successes are almost all independent units led by mavericks: the iPhone, AWS, Lockheed's Skunk Works, the IBM PC. With acquisitions, decide up front whether you're buying something to break your own pattern or to extend the existing business.
ex: Investor Vinod Khosla argues for putting about 10% of profits into bets that may fail but have huge upside
The flip side of the "can't lose" coin says "can't win big"

root.d: Don't manage them like the regular business

items.d: Run apart from the core business
A maverick leader with complete control
Don't expose it to the parent early

l193|370.c: You need both go-go-go urgency and the patience to build things that compound over years.
l193|370.e: By nature he acts immediately: homework always got done the night before, so why not make the deadline tomorrow, and that energy is contagious. But some goals can't be solved in an afternoon; they need layers of infrastructure underneath. For Stripe's first seven or eight years, the number of new countries and payment methods stayed flat no matter how hard the team pushed. So they stepped back and asked what had to be true in ten years, slowed down to build internal platforms, and sent people to live abroad and use those payment methods themselves. Only then did the curve bend upward. Investments you'll never regret, like lower API latency, should keep compounding.
ex: Payment methods went from about 10 to 50 quickly, and now exceed 100
For the 83(b) tax form, an engineer first mailed a blank page to the office, then they built vendors

items: Figure out what ten years out requires
Invest in capabilities you'll never regret

d.verdict: Deliberately pair the two speeds

l193|370.c: Craft is dessert after the meal: first make sure customers truly can't live without you.
l193|370.e: Early in his career he built a SQL analytics tool. Once the service went down for ten or twenty minutes, and the team high-fived for recovering fast. A year later he realized that customers hadn't been furious or banging on the door, which was exactly the sign that there was no product-market fit, and he burned several more years because of it. People get out of bed for their number one problem, not their second. If something shouldn't exist, no amount of craft, beauty or delight will save it. First find the problem people will drop everything to solve; polishing comes after.
ex: Hearing only a few scattered complaints during an outage is a sign you lack product-market fit

items.d: Customers drop everything to fix it

l193|370.c: Don't pitch when you talk to customers: listen in silence, respond fast, and turn critics into friends.
l193|370.e: Opening with an introduction and a product demo means guessing the customer's number one problem for them, and you'll miss the real burning issue. Instead ask what's in their inbox, what annoyed them most last week, and what they'd remove first with a magic wand, then stay quiet. A customer who spends time complaining about your product is giving you a huge gift, so he'll step out of a meeting to reply right away. When something breaks, don't just fix it; turn that person into a referrer. Even serving millions of businesses, you only need to text with five to ten customers at the leading edge.
ex: An Atlas document mistakenly said 25 shares instead of 25%; the person who caught it became a product partner
An impromptu bug hunt brought in 65 videos in three days

items.d: Ask open questions, then stay silent
Fix the problem and make a friend

l193|370.c: Only listen to target customers who pay; saying you'd pay is not the same as paying.
l193|370.e: Product people are easily drawn to praise from friends, but a friend liking you doesn't mean they have a real problem. So he made a rule: feedback from friends counts for zero. He only cares about a specific target customer, like a particular employee who must solve a particular problem by 4pm today. Payment is a forcing function. When you say it costs $10,000 with a full refund if unhappy, that's when people tell you where the real value is. The same goes for a big company promising a large contract: ask them to pay first, refundable any time, and their hesitation is itself the signal.
ex: He asks founders to invoice him one dollar on the spot
Feature lists from big customers often fall apart before the contract is signed

l193|370.c: A good metric measures value from the customer's side; customers would smile at your dashboard.
l193|370.e: A PM's job, he says, is to produce product-market fit, and the evidence is an up-and-to-the-right curve plus customers tweeting praise. Metrics shouldn't be internal views like login counts; they should show whether the customer accomplished what they came to do. Using only a few metrics also forces trade-offs. When he took over Atlas, support tickets were almost all complaints. He figured that people who finished without filing a ticket were the ones who'd recommend it to friends, so he set the share of zero-ticket companies as the core metric. Each ticket category went to an engineer to investigate and solve, with separate metrics for specific tactics, such as how long risk review takes.
ex: Zero-ticket share went from 15% to 85% in about 18 months, and market share traced the same curve
Almost every application now gets a risk decision within an hour

items.d: Founders who incorporated with zero tickets

l193|370.c: If you don't know what to measure, count "bad days" for users, then eliminate them one by one.
l193|370.e: Any event that could ruin a user's day, like a 404, a payout arriving a day late, or a dozen declined charges in a row, gets logged and rolled into a stacked bar chart. Anyone can add a new reason, and the team then picks which ones to eliminate completely. Discovering a new cause of bad days is the most exciting thing that can happen. Metric names should make people feel something, like "zero-ticket companies." Hygiene matters too, down to decimal places and axes, so people want to open the dashboard every day. He only looks at metrics on the shared platform, and how often a team checks its own dashboard predicts how customer-focused it is.
ex: His rule: if it isn't on Go Metrics, the shared platform, he doesn't look at it
A new metric needs a few weeks of skepticism and fixes before people trust it

items.d: What would ruin a user's day?
Pick a cause and root it out

l193|370.c: Products quietly decay, so use an unnatural but fun ritual to recover the customer's point of view.
l193|370.e: A year after launch, a product iterated on by many teams drifts into a maze where the doors don't work, and teams rarely find time to look at it the way a customer does. His Study Group pulls four to eight random colleagues together, invents a company and a goal, picks a CEO, and has them accomplish it using Stripe. Rule one: you don't work at Stripe, and if you use insider knowledge you start over. Rule two: don't fix anything in the room, just practice empathy. Findings feed into the normal bug process. Watching a colleague fail to use your own product hits harder than any customer feedback.
ex: More than 25 sessions this year, with over 250 participants
Best to be the customer yourself; next, sit beside one; next, play one
Craft-related P0 bugs must be acknowledged within 7 days

terms.d: You don't work at Stripe; don't fix anything

result.d: See the real product after entropy sets in

l193|370.c: Start something new in a big company by letting customers ask, making it work once, then showing metrics.
l193|370.e: The most common failure is doing nothing at all. His approach is to make the idea not his own: bring the shared demand of dozens of customers, sketch the unconstrained ideal with a marker, skip the big headcount request, and get one version to work once, because existence is proof. Publish the metrics so people watch progress themselves instead of waiting for long write-ups, and explain why the economics are sustainable. Atlas only takes on work it can automate and hands the rest to vendors. He treats competitors as alternatives his customers could choose, and his candid relationship with AngelList ended with them sending their users to Atlas.
ex: Atlas has about 10 people and incorporates roughly one in six new Delaware companies
It has filed more than 10,000 83(b) forms, all on time
Stripe co-founder John Collison: I need you stuck on problems one and two

items.d: Dozens of customers asking for the same thing
Mail the first sheet of paper

l194|371.sc: What a data team is for
l194|371.c: A data team should help drive the business, answering not just why but what to do next.
l194|371.e: She believes analytics deserves a seat at the table alongside engineering, product, and operations, rather than being a service desk that answers tickets and builds dashboards. The real value of the team is spotting opportunities and having a point of view on what to do about them: now that we know this, what comes next? That seat has to be earned by consistently bringing opportunities the whole company wants to chase. So her analysts share the same goals as their business partners, dig deep into problems, lay out trade-offs, and point to where growth is most efficient.
ex: A ticket-and-dashboard data job is one she says she wouldn't want herself

marks.d: Come to the table with recommendations

l194|371.c: Data people should report centrally but sit in small groups aligned to the business, getting the best of both.
l194|371.e: She is firmly against scattering analysts to report into individual business lines. DoorDash tried it, and it created more problems. Her model keeps the reporting line inside the analytics org but splits the team into pods that mirror product, operations, and marketing. Each pod shares goals with its business partners and works side by side with them every day. That gives business leaders the sense of ownership and control over the roadmap they want. The centralized side brings bigger wins: one hiring bar, the ability to rotate and get promoted across areas, one way of defining metrics, early visibility into shared problems, and a real community of peers for data people.
ex: No need to build six separate churn models in six different teams
The team still calls itself the A-Team today

root.d: One reporting line, embedded day to day

items.d: Rotate across areas, move into management
Peers to review and learn from

l194|371.c: Deliberately protect time for exploration, and make trade-offs visible instead of quietly absorbing every request.
l194|371.e: There are always more requests than hours, she says, and open-ended digging with uncertain payoff is the first thing to get cut. So she protects it with explicit goals and hackathons. In one hackathon, the team found that the referral channel had a weak average return. Instead of cutting the budget, they referred each other and even tried to game the rewards. They discovered the returns were split in two: good customers referring good customers paid off strongly, while people posting referral codes online for freebies dragged the average down. The fix was fraud controls and caps. When ad hoc requests come in, she prefers laying out the trade-off and letting the requester decide over simply saying no.
ex: To collect referral rewards, the team ordered the office a pile of cupcakes
Occasionally knock out a small request to build goodwill

items.d: Look at the distribution, not the average

l194|371.c: Technical skill is just the entry ticket; hire for curiosity, how people take correction, and willingness to decide.
l194|371.e: The technical screen is table stakes, she says. What separates the best candidates is curiosity: after answering the question, they keep pulling on the thread that looks off, without being told to. Her interviews use real cases from DoorDash's history, sometimes with a planted flaw to see whether the candidate notices. Most people make a wrong assumption somewhere. How they absorb new information and change course once it's pointed out is a strong signal. She also pushes: if you had to decide right now, which would you pick? The team happily takes people moving over from operations, engineering, and finance. The more varied the backgrounds, the more people teach each other.
ex: Analytics is a net importer of talent, often from business teams
You want startup hustle and people who have seen scale

items.d: Coding and fundamentals are the bar
Break down a vague problem in a structured way
Do they notice what looks off?
Adjust when corrected, and commit to a call

l194|371.c: Own the outcome completely: don't hide behind your job title, and if a call is needed, make it.
l194|371.e: She has no formal data science background. In DoorDash's early days she taught herself SQL and Python so she could set targets and track how each city was doing, and worked her way up to running analytics. She credits a habit of solving the problem in front of her from first principles, rather than deciding what organization to build first. The spirit comes from founder Tony Xu: in the early days someone took out the trash on Saturday nights, and when the whole site went down, all twenty or so employees answered support calls. She still expects the team to own results. When a change doesn't work, a data scientist will pick up the phone and ask customers why.
ex: Winter 2014, she handed out promo codes at dawn in Boston, with sales colleagues alongside
Everyone delivers or does support at least four times a year, called WeDash

items: User interviews are someone else's job
Wait for engineers to hand over data

d.verdict: The goal is to find out what actually happened

l194|371.c: Pick simple proxy metrics you can move short term, then convert every lever into one common currency.
l194|371.e: Retention is a terrible goal, in her view, because you can barely move it in the short run. Instead, find the inputs that drive it and run experiments to prove that improving those inputs really does improve the long-term result. Data scientists love weighted composite scores, but nobody knows whether a merchant health score of 0.35 is good or bad. Replace it with "did the new merchant get an order within seven days," then track photo coverage and accurate hours separately. Three metrics beat one nobody understands. She also converts every lever, a dollar off, a minute faster delivery, one more restaurant signed, into order value and order volume, so marketing and logistics can compare trade-offs directly.
ex: Everything gets converted to GOV (gross order value) and order volume
Even signing one Thai restaurant in Sacramento can be valued in GOV

items.d: Like retention; hard to move short term
Convert to GOV to compare trade-offs

l194|371.c: Don't just watch averages: set goals for rare, expensive failures, and ask what data you're missing.
l194|371.e: Averages hide the extremes, she warns. A "never delivered" order is very rare and invisible in average delivery time, yet it drives customers away outright, and the company still has to refund, remake the food, and send another driver. The cost far outweighs the frequency. So DoorDash paired its quality analysts with product, engineering, and operations in one team whose goal was to eliminate never-delivered orders, chasing down causes from human error to fraud. Missing data is the other trap. You never see the orders a churned customer would have placed, and a user who fails to log in never enters the denominator. So keep asking: what data are we not seeing?
ex: Never-delivered orders are a tiny share, yet a dedicated team works to eliminate them

cells.d: Like never delivered; set a goal to eliminate

l195|374.c: Good products don't win on their own; timing and marketing decide, so failed ideas deserve another try.
l195|374.e: Once a product succeeds, it looks inevitable in hindsight and marketing's role gets forgotten. But many good things in history were only accepted after years of promotion or a social signal from the right people. Plenty of good products also failed because they arrived too early or told the wrong story. So an idea that failed in the past isn't necessarily a bad one; the timing may simply have been off. He sees Steve Jobs as fundamentally a salesman rather than a technologist.
ex: Meta Portal cost about $120 and worked well, but reviews fixated on privacy
Google Glass launched too early and went to developers first
The smallpox vaccine won trust only after royals had their children inoculated

items.d: Quiet and fast, but seen as cars for women
One campaign ran for about 30 years

l195|374.c: Keep the slightly odd details in a product; distinctiveness is worth more than consistency.
l195|374.e: Small deviations and a little friction grab attention and make things memorable, so he thinks a quirk's value should be counted double. One test is the stand-up comedian test: if a comic could build a joke around it, it is distinctive. He objects to sanding these edges off in the name of consistency. Even too much perfection can backfire; an electric razor that is too quiet makes people doubt it is working at all.
ex: Jaguar's reversed indicator stalk in the 1990s, which Ogilvy fought to keep
Veuve Clicquot's yellow label began as a printing error
MCI's Friends and Family plan got more talk than a plain price cut

items.d: A detail or friction that breaks the norm
Like a small splinter that sticks

l195|374.sc: Just the right amount of odd
l195|374.c: New things should be "most advanced yet acceptable"; the right dose of strangeness gets adopted.
l195|374.e: He cites industrial designer Raymond Loewy's principle: consumers accept evolution more readily than radical reinvention. Too conventional and nobody notices; too alien and nobody understands. The sweet spot is familiar enough to follow and strange enough to feel fresh. The iPhone building on the iPod softened the leap. Scandinavian TV dramas sit in exactly this zone too.
ex: He recalls BBC4 buying The Killing for roughly $20,000 to $30,000
The show later moved to BBC2 and was sold to Netflix
The iPod paved the way for the iPhone

l195|374.c: Humans evolved for uncertainty, so rules of thumb that look irrational are often the rational choice.
l195|374.e: Business and education train people to think in linear, reductionist terms, as if every question has one right answer. But psychology is a complex system: small causes can have big effects, and two opposite ideas can both be right. Economics assumes information is certain, while real decisions are made amid uncertainty and distrust. In that environment, copying your neighbors, sticking to habits, buying electronics a little later, and even being deliberately unpredictable are all efficient survival strategies.
ex: People install heat pumps once a neighbor does; social proof beats the spreadsheet
Hares zigzag at random to escape dogs; submarines run the "Crazy Ivan" maneuver
The French "captain's age" experiment: children force an answer from irrelevant numbers

d.verdict: Understand people through complex systems

l195|374.c: Numerical targets distort behavior; human standards and self-governing small teams work better.
l195|374.e: Measuring staff on things like call length makes them work for the number instead of the customer, and strips away autonomy and the pleasure of the job. He goes as far as comparing quarterly-target capitalism to Soviet-style planning. Work is also where people exercise judgment and morality. The better approach is a clear overall goal, small teams that own their own results, and human yardsticks like "would your mother be proud of you?"
ex: Zappos doesn't measure call length; one customer call ran seven hours
Shopify organizes support into sports-team-style groups of about 10
AO.com: treat the customer the way you would treat your own grandmother

terms.d: About 10 people, accountable to each other
Value judgments instead of speed metrics

result.d: Happier and more engaged

l195|374.c: Fame pays off disproportionately, and a brand compounds like a pension.
l195|374.e: His advice to founders is to be consistent, be distinctive, and be famous. Past a certain point, fame reaches escape velocity: customers come to you and even discover new uses for your product. Hiring gets easier, customers extend trust, and executives return your calls. In B2B, fame also reduces the risk of being blamed. Brand building is slow at first and substantial later, and short-term metrics badly undervalue it. His rough guess is that marketing's true value is about four times what the metrics show.
ex: Pick a famous auditor and nobody blames you when things go wrong
Coca-Cola: customers assume it is available everywhere
He admits "four times" is a very rough estimate

l195|374.c: Marketing and innovation are two sides of one thing; a product must work psychologically, technically and economically at once.
l195|374.e: Companies borrow assembly-line thinking: build the product first and hand it to marketing last. But innovation isn't linear, and the success stories told afterward simply edit out the failures. There are two routes to making things people want: figure out what customers want and deliver it cleverly, or start from what you can make and cleverly make people want it. The most successful companies do both. Features should also be few and clear; one obvious purpose beats a pile of functions.
ex: Sony's Akio Morita refused to add recording to the Walkman
Wrigley went from selling soap, to giving away baking powder, to chewing gum
McDonald's trimmed its menu to speed up service

root.t: A product must work three ways

items.d: People want it and talk about it
It can be built and works well

l196|375.c: Strategy is a set of choices that fit together to get customers to willingly do what you want.
l196|375.e: His starting point: a company can decide to build factories, fund R&D, run ads, and hire, but it cannot control whether customers pay. Strategy is making choices about what you do control in order to induce, not force, customer action. Michael Porter said you must be differentiated or low cost but didn't say how to get there. Between 1987 and 1995 Martin filled that gap with five questions that must be answered together and adjusted against each other. The winning aspiration should be anchored in what customers lack. "That market is big and we want a piece" is a terrible reason, and it's how many foreign companies failed in China.
ex: FigJam: start from core Figma customers finding Figma too narrow
Four Seasons left real estate development and ownership to only manage hotels
App makers complain about Apple's cut, but they chose their spot in the value chain

items.d: Customers, products, channels, value chain stage

l196|375.c: Strategy is hard because choices must fit together and involve sacrifice, and mainstream business-school theory barely helps.
l196|375.e: He breaks the difficulty into three parts. Intellectually, strategy is a set of answers that must reinforce each other, like designing a whole diet rather than ordering lunch. Emotionally, trade-offs mean killing options and owning the decision, which is scary. In training, academics, jealous of Porter, caricatured him as the "positioning school" and promoted the resource-based view instead. But that theory can't tell you which resources to invest in building. In 42 years of consulting he has seen someone use its VRIO analysis exactly once. Consulting firms, he adds, hardly do strategy anymore either.
ex: Even as dean he wasn't allowed to teach a for-credit strategy course
He says Rumelt's talk misdescribed what happened at P&G

root.d: Most people were never trained for it

items.d: Kill options and own the outcome
Schools and consultants don't teach usable strategy

l196|375.c: There are only two ways to win, differentiation or low cost; without either, rivals push you around.
l196|375.e: The test of whether you are really playing to win is what customers do, he says. If a shopper at the shelf could flip a coin between you and a rival, you are not differentiated. If matching a rival's price would lose you money, someone else owns the low-cost position. A company with neither gets squeezed step by step by stronger players and eventually exits. Both routes are legitimate, but low cost almost always requires dominant scale in your arena. Differentiation depends on brand and R&D spending, which also increasingly reward scale, so niche differentiation is getting harder.
ex: Lego: kids think a toy store without Lego isn't a toy store
Vanguard used enormous scale to offer the lowest fees
Southwest entered roughly $1,000 routes at about $200

items: Customers ask for your brand by name
Relies on brand and R&D spending

d.verdict: With neither, rivals push you around until you exit

l196|375.c: Saying "we'll be better" isn't a strategy; you need capabilities rivals can't or won't copy.
l196|375.e: "Sell pet food online and be the best at it" is not a strategy, he says. Anyone who can build a website can do it, and when everyone piled in, they all collapsed. You have to answer the second question: why can't my "better" be copied quickly? Either rivals can't do it, or they won't. The second matters just as much. Walmart had the capability to do e-commerce well but feared hurting its stores, sat on the sidelines for a decade, and handed its scale advantage to Amazon. Legacy carmakers couldn't see how to make money on electric vehicles and gave Tesla a ten-year head start.
ex: Westlaw has summarized case law for a century, now with about 1,500 full-time lawyers
Olay moved into mass retail; Clinique wouldn't follow for fear of upsetting department stores

terms.d: Rivals can't or won't do it

result.d: An edge others can't take away

l196|375.c: The more facets your capabilities and systems have, the more rivals decide life is too short and compete elsewhere.
l196|375.e: He rejects the idea that competitive advantage is fleeting: Tide has been number one for 77 straight years. Advantages are fragile when they rest on one thing. Build the world's biggest polyethylene plant and a rival can build one twice as big next door. Four Seasons, to deliver service that makes up for being away from home, rebuilt hiring, onboarding, and career development, cutting employee turnover from an industry norm of about 80 percent to about 10 percent. A rival would have to start from scratch to copy it, so they choose a different position instead. The best way to compete, he says, is to never be forced to.
ex: Southwest: one aircraft type, point-to-point routes, high pay in exchange for flexibility
Continental Lite and Ted copied half the model and became clumsy imitators

marks.d: Dead once a rival builds a bigger one
Rebuilt everything from hiring to development
Changed fleet, routes, and labor model

l196|375.c: The customer tide always wins, so even incumbents with a threatened cash cow must move with it now.
l196|375.e: When core profits are threatened, companies instinctively hope the new thing fails, like gas-car makers facing EVs or Google facing AI search that gives direct answers. His advice never changes: you might hold it off for a while, but water flows downhill, customers win in the end, and the later you start the harder it gets. P&G's A.G. Lafley kept working with Amazon even when big retailers threatened to pull his products. Vanguard's Jack Bogle disliked ETFs but eventually went all in. Microsoft's PC operating system share held up, but measured by time people spend looking at smart screens, its share has shrunk dramatically.
ex: Vanguard ended up a leading provider of index ETFs
He thinks no Windows update since Windows 95 has excited users

items.d: Microsoft's share, last time he checked
Microsoft's share, last time he checked

l196|375.c: Treat strategy as a problem-solving tool: close the most painful gap first, and get good through practice.
l196|375.e: Your current results, he says, are the natural product of your past choices interacting with the competitive environment. Nothing improves unless the choices change. So don't try to fix everything at once. Pick the most painful gap between what you want and what you're getting, and use the five questions to ask which choices you could change. Close that gap, then move to the next one, and the gaps keep shrinking. He has never met a natural-born strategist. Lafley is called a genius because he started practicing back in the Navy. People who say they'll do operations first and strategy later never amount to much.
ex: The professor who wins the teaching award most often cuts the worst-rated lecture every year

l197|377.c: Every company should run paid ads, at minimum paid search triggered by what users actively look for.
l197|377.e: Free traffic keeps getting harder to earn, he argues. The top of Google's results page is now filled with ads and AI content, and on Meta hardly anyone sees your posts unless you pay to promote them. Paid search only appears when someone types a relevant query, so it captures demand that already exists. Meta, YouTube, and similar channels are interruptive media, slipped in while people are looking at something else, and whether they fit depends on the stage of your business. Even influencer marketing is paid at heart. So the question isn't whether to pay, but which kind to pay for.
ex: The top four Google results are all paid ads
Meta is close to pay-to-be-seen

items: Shows up only when someone searches
Inserted while people browse other things

d.verdict: Paid search should be every company's baseline

l197|377.c: Check where users already come from, then run small "signs of life" tests built on your own customer data.
l197|377.e: Start by opening your analytics and seeing which platform existing users arrive from, he says. That's where paid can turn up the volume on something already working. For a test, upload your customer list and have the platform build a lookalike audience. If budget is tight, target only the closest 1 percent. Once you see a positive signal, build creative, campaigns, and copy tailored to that platform before you scale spend. How long to test is mostly a budget question, and small results can be extrapolated to estimate returns at larger spend. Users have a different mindset on every platform, so a failure is nothing to beat yourself up about. You're either winning or learning.
ex: Hairstory: testimonial creative that worked on Meta flopped on TikTok
Lookalike tiers of 1%, 2-4%, 5-7%, 8%+; the 8%+ tier rarely works

l197|377.c: Start with Google search, then Meta; save expensive LinkedIn for high-value customers.
l197|377.e: His order for beginners: Google search first, then Meta (Facebook and Instagram), then YouTube if you have video, and TikTok if the data shows your users are there. LinkedIn looks about three times more expensive than other channels, but it lets you target by job title, industry, and company, which suits high-value business customers. Even then, test Google and Meta first. Among newer channels, podcasts and connected TV perform well for teams that know how to measure them. As for ads in VR and inside AI products, he'd rather let someone else be the guinea pig.
ex: SoftLayer chasing Coca-Cola: LinkedIn targeting plus a Los Angeles geofence
He's bullish on video if you can keep producing creative

items.d: First choice; users come to you
Depends on having the right creative
About 3x the cost, but precise targeting

l197|377.c: Whether and how to advertise depends on whether demand already exists and whether your product can convert it.
l197|377.e: If you want results fast, start paid now, he says, because SEO takes time. But nobody searches for a brand-new category, so using search ads to build awareness is a mismatch. Use display media instead. If similar products already exist, you can bid on competitors' brand terms and ride their coattails. The flip side: if the product hasn't found product-market fit, or users literally can't pay you, advertising only leaves a bad first impression that's hard to undo. So he advises against spending heavily before product-market fit.
ex: A hotel-room decorating service only took off after switching from search to Google Display Network
IBM in Africa only took US dollars; focusing on South Africa and accepting rand lifted conversions

cells.d: No one searches for a new category
Currency, payment methods, and so on

l197|377.c: Watch only the metrics tied to the campaign's goal, and don't drown in the data platforms hand you.
l197|377.e: Platforms dump reach, frequency, CPM, CPC, and more on you. The hard part is knowing what's signal. Start by asking what the campaign is for: if it's conversion, watch clicks and conversions; if it's awareness, watch reach. He doesn't chase impression share, which he calls vanity marketing. He prefers click share, meaning whether you keep showing up in front of the right people. Google's quality score breakdown points to the holes in the boat: fix whatever is below average first. Pausing one bad ad can lift the whole account. For industry benchmarks, ask your platform rep for an anonymized competitor comparison.
ex: Going from below to above average gained roughly 12% more impressions, as he recalls
PPC Hero's "true competitive metrics" help spot which rivals are real threats

items.d: Brand-term ads in a sample account
Brand-term ads in a sample account
The weak spot to fix first

l197|377.c: Attribution is biased by nature; a channel's real value has to be corrected with incrementality experiments.
l197|377.e: He prefers multi-touch, time-decay attribution. People quickly forget where they first saw you, so the first touch deserves some credit, but it isn't what drove the sale. Yet no attribution model can answer the key question: would this person have bought anyway without the ad? That takes geo experiments or a platform's Conversion Lift test to measure incrementality, from which you derive an incrementality adjustment factor (IAF) per channel. Platforms are happy to help, since visual ads are usually under-credited. But below roughly $50,000 a month in spend there's too little signal to make it worthwhile.
ex: eBay cut nearly all brand-term spend after an experiment around 2012
In a lift test, you win the auction but deliberately show no ad, creating a control group

terms.d: Measured by geo or lift tests

result.d: Allocate budget on this basis

l197|377.c: Creative is badly underrated, and even "perfect" copy should be settled by testing.
l197|377.e: Good creative tells a story and stirs an emotion, he says, whether humor or warmth. People act later only if they remember you, so on YouTube start with emotion. Copy should be a collaboration between the media buyer and the creative team, and no idea should be rejected up front, because the person writing it usually isn't the target customer. Assets need constant refreshing to keep the flywheel turning. He also notes AI has long been at work in smart bidding and recommendations, and its biggest impact next will be on producing content and creative.
ex: ADT: an ad crammed with features lost to "$0 installation, $0 setup"
Dollar Shave Club's video is the classic case of creative winning

items.d: Humor or warmth makes it memorable

l197|377.c: Start with an agency, then build an in-house team as spend reaches a meaningful scale.
l197|377.e: Agencies often run templates and juggle dozens of clients, he observes, so they don't have time to dig into your conversion path and landing pages. It's fine to start with an agency or consultant, but think forward and plan backward: agree up front on the milestone for bringing it in-house. His rule of thumb is to start hiring at about $50,000 a month in spend. The first hire should be good at pulling signal out of data; anyone can be taught the platforms. Then come a brand-minded designer and a dedicated data scientist. Before adding headcount, check a capacity sheet for several quarters of overload, and cut useless meetings first.
ex: An operating cadence sheet: big buckets like keywords, with sub-tasks marked weekly, biweekly, or monthly
In interviews he throws candidates a pile of data; good ones first ask what the campaign goal is

items.d: The founder can't watch the dashboards daily

l198|379.c: Product and ops are twin engines: ops iterates on the ground first, and tech takes over when people can't keep up.
l198|379.e: He compares the two to a twin-engine jet: one engine can keep you flying for a while, but both together are far more efficient. A product manager in San Francisco can't know thousands of cities. Local ops teams move fast, sit close to customers, and bring qualitative insight. That's why Uber created a product operations role that reported into ops but sat with the product team. Early on, ops runs a process by hand. Once scale breaks the manual process, technology takes over, and the people it frees up move on to the next hard problem.
ex: Early surge pricing was set by city GMs by hand: when to turn it on and off, and the cap
He mostly agrees ops is a sign of inefficiency, but notes people shift to new problems

items.d: Thousands a week, documents checked by OCR

l198|379.c: The core product job is finding what truly matters in a flood of signals and betting scarce engineering there.
l198|379.e: Good ideas can come from support, customers, executives, field visits, even a video, he says. A product manager's real job is telling noise from what will actually move customers, and saying no to plenty of good ideas as a result.
