In an ops-heavy company's early days, engineers are scarcer than people, so you have to bet explicitly on the highest-leverage piece, say openly where you won't invest yet, and let small fires burn elsewhere. Every idea should still go into the backlog, so whoever raised it knows they were heard and considered.
ex: Early Uber engineering went almost entirely into dispatch and pricing
uberPOOL first matched commuters by employer, then quickly learned liquidity was everything

items.d: Into the backlog; respect the source

l198|379.c: A product review exists first to make the product better, not to serve as a firing squad.
l198|379.e: Ops-driven companies are used to weekly business reviews, he explains, and rarely look up at longer-term product direction, which makes product reviews especially important. They can double as accountability and information sharing, but the main goal is helping the team think the problem through. The people closest to the problem have the most context. Senior leaders should ask more questions, add background the team lacks, and be clear about which comments are ideas rather than orders. Keep the discussion under ten people, but circulate the document widely. It also makes good onboarding material.
ex: Two sign-up slots a week, so each area gets a turn roughly every quarter
Template: context, problem, proposal, risks and pre-mortem, how success is measured

items: A few hours a week on this
40 to 60 hours a week on it

d.verdict: Breadth plus depth is what makes a review improve the product

l198|379.c: When employees rarely use their own low-frequency product, jobs-to-be-done forces the team onto the customer's side.
l198|379.e: He treats jobs-to-be-done as one tool in the kit, not a universal hammer. Uber employees took rides every day and could build on their own intuition. But Americans sell a home only about every seven years, so most Opendoor employees aren't their own users. They need a framework to understand the customer and the months-long journey around the product, with agents, family, and friends involved. The template is only a starting point. What matters is making it cultural: keep asking whether the "job" you wrote down has the company's own business goals smuggled into it.
ex: "Get an Opendoor offer" isn't the real job; one level deeper, it's price discovery
He finds the Twitter debates about JTBD overly dogmatic

items.d: Get the user to request our offer
Learn what the home is worth and sell it simply, with certainty
A months-long journey, agents, advice from family and friends

l198|379.c: With small samples, don't force A/B tests; build confidence other ways, and ship on judgment when you must.
l198|379.e: A/B testing is still the gold standard, he says, but home transactions are few, and anything deep in the funnel or inside operations is especially hard to test. Start with a power analysis and an honest estimate of how long the test needs. An important experiment with no substitute can be worth running for six months. The real danger is pretending you'll have an answer in a month. You can also interview more customers and use difference-in-differences, sister-city comparisons, geographic splits, a lower confidence threshold, or long-term holdout groups. When none of that works, ship on intuition, but pair it with a feedback loop that can tell you whether you were right.
ex: Drop confidence from 95% to 80% and accept being wrong one extra time in ten
The feedback loop can be support ticket volume or feature adoption

items.d: What effect you can detect, and how long it takes
Key experiments can run six months
With a feedback loop to check yourself

l198|379.c: Pay attention to competitors without being driven by them; the real rival is the traditional way of selling a home.
l198|379.e: When Zillow entered the same business, the pressure was intense, he admits. But the vast majority of people still sell the old way, and housing is the largest asset class in America. Focusing on the customers you already serve well brings steadiness, and the same was true of Uber versus Lyft. He won't pass judgment on Zillow, saying only that the business demands pricing, product, operations, risk management, and capital markets all working at once, and Opendoor was vertically integrated from day one. Today Zillow's traffic and Opendoor's transaction service complement each other, and the two now partner.
ex: Early in Covid, Opendoor paused buying homes for months and returned with a fully online process

terms.d: Online flow plus in-person home visits

result.d: Miss one piece and you can't deliver

l198|379.c: Passing stress down to the team only makes everyone tense; calm is built through repeated experience and reflection.
l198|379.e: Early Uber felt like firefighting every day, he recalls. When a leader's emotions spill over, everyone tightens up, and the results don't get any better. Reminding himself that things are never as good or as bad as they seem keeps his head clear. That composure can't be rushed. You have to face the high-pressure moments rather than avoid them, then reflect afterward on which tools actually helped, so next time you can say, "I've been through this." When you haven't lived it yourself, founder biographies and other people's stories fill in some of the gap.
ex: The night before uberPOOL launched in Chengdu, matching crashed and wasn't fixed until about 5:30 a.m.

l199|381.c: The voice in your head that keeps criticizing you is always wrong; don't suppress it, respond differently each day.
l199|381.e: That voice nagging "you should exercise more" is never accurate, he says, even when there's a grain of truth in it. No boss who yelled at you every few minutes would make you more productive. It's more like a five-year-old having a tantrum, or the parent who once scolded you. Most people try to make it shut up, which doesn't work. The better move is to treat it as an experiment and respond a different way each day: soothe it, sing to it, or simply refuse to believe it. An experiment can't fail, which sidesteps the brain's "mess up once and give up" wiring.
ex: His favorite response: I see you're scared, don't worry, I'm right here with you

items: Tell it to shut up, try to control it
Give up at the first failure
The more you resist, the more it digs in

d.verdict: Once you truly understand it, the critic fades on its own

l199|381.c: Decisions happen in the emotional brain; the more emotions you can tolerate, the more options you can see.
l199|381.e: He cites the book Descartes' Error: people with damage to the brain's emotional centers keep their IQ but agonize for half an hour over what to have for lunch. In his view, we make decisions to feel successful and avoid feeling like failures. Logic only helps us predict how we'll feel. There's no such thing as a purely logical decision. When you can't bear a certain emotion, you automatically rule out a whole set of options. Fear of being disliked keeps you from telling the truth. Avoiding conflict keeps you from building an A-team, because anything alive needs tension.
ex: Another tool: life principles, at most five, each tried for five days, like "embrace intensity"
Feeling overwhelmed usually isn't too much to do; it's an emotion you haven't felt

root.d: Determine which solutions you can see

items.d: So you can speak truth and set boundaries
So you can build an A-team
So you can set high expectations

l199|381.c: Emotions are like water in a pipe; the goal is to let them flow freely, not to manage them.
l199|381.e: When an emotion gets kinked, he says, it comes out distorted. The same anger can become yelling, passive aggression, or guilt-tripping. Unkinked, it looks like Gandhi or Martin Luther King: a clear boundary held with love. Losing control is itself a sign you're still resisting. Non-judgmental awareness is a good step but not enough. You have to welcome the emotion the way you'd welcome a child home, and let the body move and make sound, the way mammals shake off fear. He says he can tell what someone is holding in from the lines between their brows and their raised shoulders.
ex: "Emotional inquiry": explore a feeling with the curiosity of a kid picking up a toad
Sitting still without expressing it works too, but it can take decades

marks.d: A good step, but not enough
A clear boundary held with love

l199|381.c: Whatever emotion you try hardest to avoid, you end up inviting into your life in the same way.
l199|381.e: An executive who fears losing control avoids conflict, he explains. Decisions get delayed, tension never releases, the whole organization tightens up, and he feels even more out of control. You can trace any problem backward this way: in an argument you don't want to feel shame, so you defend yourself, the defense sparks a fight, and the fight brings more shame. The way out is letting yourself feel the emotion. The state you respond from matters more than what you say. Many "problems" also rest on unexamined assumptions, and it's often shame that locks a bad habit in place.
ex: A friend called him an asshole; he owned it, and within weeks he'd softened a lot
Executives afraid of the CEO: there's always one person who speaks up and doesn't get yelled at

items.d: Blamed for not taking out the trash

l199|381.c: Enjoyment is an efficiency tool: enjoy the moment 10 percent more and both output and quality rise.
l199|381.e: A Ferrari is fast, not efficient, he says. Real efficiency is finishing a task with more energy and wanting to do it again. So keep asking, "How could I enjoy this moment 10 percent more?" People usually take a deep breath, relax, and listen better. The order matters: first learn to enjoy what's in front of you, and then you naturally gravitate toward what you love. He knows billionaires who spent fortunes arranging their lives and still didn't enjoy them. By the same logic, "should" produces shame and stagnation, while "want" drives growth. An oak tree never needs to be perfect at any particular moment.
ex: He estimates only about 10 to 15 percent of people actually follow through on their "shoulds"
He keeps stressing: don't copy advice, test it as an experiment

items.d: How to enjoy this moment 10% more
No need to wait for enjoyment

l199|381.c: Meetings and decisions are a company's atomic structure; make every meeting five-star and problems surface on their own.
l199|381.e: A company is really just a set of relationships and ideas among people, he says, so when he enters one he interviews a few people and sits in on a meeting or two. The goal is for everyone to leave every meeting feeling great. Wherever that isn't happening, the problem is hiding, and the same goes for frustrating steps in decision-making. Executives usually take about two months to get every meeting to five stars, and the number of meetings often halves along the way. He also recommends short pulse surveys to track each team's culture as a leading indicator of performance.
ex: A content creator fixed a terrible weekly YouTube meeting and the numbers soon took off
Some meetings open with: what are you afraid to say?

l199|381.c: Trade seven minutes of gratitude with someone daily, especially about what you feel you lack, and life shifts fast.
l199|381.e: This isn't making a list, he says. You first genuinely feel grateful, then let that feeling do the talking, going back and forth with a partner or family member for at least seven minutes. After a few weeks, aim it at whatever you feel short of, whether time, love, or money. Early on he meditated seven or eight hours a day and still worried about money constantly. Then he and his wife began expressing gratitude daily for what they already had. He went from someone who lacks to someone who has. Even a streetlight reminded him that twenty companies made money from it.
ex: Credit card debt paid off in about 3 months; around $60,000 saved six months later

items.t: Credit card debt at the start

l200|383.c: The brain is like a university, and most people lean too hard on the "history department" of old answers.
l200|383.e: The brain is built to save energy, he says, and retrieving a known answer is the cheapest option, so people send every question to the history department. If you deliberately route a question to the science department that runs open experiments, the art department that imagines freely, or the humanities department with its empathy, you get a very different answer, especially in product work. He thinks about the brain in layers: at the bottom, three systems for safety, reward, and meaning; above that, how focused you are; above that, capability, meaning how much real-world context, reasoning, and imagination you bring. Each layer is a lever you can pull.
ex: He cites National Geographic: the brain is more complex than any known structure in the universe
Imagination exists to generate alternatives and rehearse their consequences

items.d: What a person or team produces
From open and loose to deep and narrow

l200|383.c: The safety and reward systems narrow your thinking; only the meaning system engages the whole brain.
l200|383.e: One unsettling remark in a meeting, he says, switches the other person's goal from contributing to restoring their sense of safety. The reward system is transactional. "That's not my job" is the reward system talking. The meaning system sounds fuzzy, but its conditions are concrete: understanding the impact of your work and caring about the people affected, even for something as small as an email. So when you answer "why are we doing this," consequences and rewards work less well than naming who is counting on us. Demanding accountability actually triggers the safety system, and you get a movie-set house with nothing behind the facade.
ex: In his view, demanding accountability is often the surest way not to get it

items.d: Something bad happens if not; self-protection
Something good if you do; transactional
Someone is counting on us; whole brain engaged

l200|383.c: Vision debates blow up because people's "unimaginable" thresholds differ, so first know your own personality.
l200|383.e: The brain sorts ideas into buckets, he says: already believed, believable, imaginable, and unimaginable. Where the lines fall depends on experience and personality. Many vision discussions trip someone's unimaginable response right away, and that's a personal issue, not a flaw in the idea. In the Big Five personality model, people low in openness have abstract creative thinking wired to pain circuits. Highly conscientious people also see blue-sky talk as a waste of time. The best approach is to admit your weak spot, ask others to translate the vision into concrete terms, substitute trust for agreement, and find colleagues who cover your gaps.
ex: Canva replaced managers with coaches, which most leaders find hard to believe
Asking the ROI of good docs: Stripe's payoff comes through retention and referrals

l200|383.c: Warm a meeting up first by aligning on purpose and principles, then decide; skip or reverse that and you get squabbles.
l200|383.e: A meeting has two parts, warm-up and decision, he says, but many jump straight to deciding, assuming everyone shares the same information and goals, which is almost never true. The warm-up can go in the invite and take three minutes to read: is this about generating options, creative problem-solving, or efficiency? Which principles apply? Are we protecting or slaughtering the sacred cows? Mismatched principles are the deadliest problem. One person optimizing for speed and another for accuracy will fight, so debate principles before tactics. His students often save half a day to a full day each week after changing how they run meetings.
ex: "I totally disagree" fires the amygdala; "how do those two connect?" fires the prefrontal cortex
Common anti-pattern: converge at the start, then circle back to purpose late in the meeting

items.d: Rather than converging at the start

l200|383.c: To influence someone, pick your role and your speed first; the faster the approach, the more it depends on trust.
l200|383.e: It's like picking a character in a video game, he says: the devil's advocate, the person who tests ideas with a sledgehammer, or the voice of the user. Choose the one that fits your personality and get the group's permission up front. Then there are three speeds. Slow means watching someone head for the wall and letting failure teach them. Medium borrows from the book The Challenger Sale: hand them a new piece of knowledge and let them live with it for a few days before talking again. Fast means creating cognitive dissonance on the spot by asking "why do you believe that," reaching the belief behind the behavior. Fast only works with enough trust and a culture that allows candor.
ex: The Abilene paradox: nobody wants to go camping, but everyone assumes the others do
Admitting "I'm not good at this" often finds you a partner within 30 seconds

items.d: Offer new knowledge; let them sit with it
Probe the underlying belief on the spot

l200|383.c: Relationships rest on capability, trust, and the experience of being around you, and experience weighs the most.
l200|383.e: Capability determines how useful you are to others, he says. Trust is really a judgment about personal risk, from trusting you to grab a bag of chips, to trusting you'll do it as well as I would, to Spielberg handing the score to John Williams and walking away. But once you've hurt someone, even strong capability gets quarantined: information and authority route around you. The surprising factor is experience, meaning whether being around you is pleasant. A bad experience keeps capable, trustworthy people out of the room. So the first question to ask is: am I a bad experience?
ex: He admits he's too blunt, so his feedback often takes six months to land instead of six minutes
Poor relationships slow replies; across a company that becomes operational inefficiency

terms.d: How useful you are to others
Do people want to be around you?

result.d: Sets how much influence you can have

l200|383.c: Don't build culture on performative mission, vision, and values; derive it from who is glad you exist.
l200|383.e: He quotes Dan Pink: the gap between what science knows and what business does is organizational dysfunction. Mission, vision, and values are like an airline that mostly fails to reach its destination, because they depend on an inspiring performance. A more reliable approach is deductive. First answer who is glad you exist and why, then derive the value you deliver, the definition of done, and the quality bar, and replace a bias for action with a bias for impact. He prefers the word "role" to "mission" because it carries responsibility and makes people picture the specific humans affected.
ex: Warby Parker: no more choosing between ugly-and-cheap and good-looking-and-expensive
An AI document client: about 95% of documents converted to structured data automatically

items: Derive value and definition of done

d.verdict: Build culture by logic, not by inspiration

l200|383.c: Most teams are stuck in busy beta mode and should spend about a quarter of their time in open or deep thinking.
l200|383.e: The waking brain has roughly three modes, he says. Alpha is open and idle, like hearing the small sounds of the house late at night, which is why ideas arrive in the shower. Beta is production mode: answering email, running meetings. Gamma is intense deep work, tearing down and rebuilding a framework. Most teams cycle only between safety-plus-beta and reward-plus-beta, and a beta brain can't produce the other two kinds of ideas. His rule of thumb is about 25 percent of the year in alpha and gamma. Schedule a quarterly deep-thinking offsite, and park the scattered interruptions until then.
ex: "We can't debate this forever" is a line that drags people back into beta
Conscientiousness favors beta, openness favors gamma; he calls it the conscientiousness crisis

cells.d: Worries and sparks that come in the shower
Where vision and new products come from
Knowing who is waiting on the result

l201|388.c: A PM's job is converting a team's potential into customer value, so start in engineering, design, or sales first.
l201|388.e: He borrows potential and kinetic energy from physics. A team of engineers and designers is full of potential energy, and the practice of product management converts it into real value with as little loss as possible. Early on, the people best placed to do that are the builders themselves, plus sales and support. So he tells people not to go straight into product management. First do the jobs whose responsibilities you'll later take over. Good salespeople are the best at listening and translating customer problems. Not every team needs a PM. Companies building for themselves can skip the role, but someone still has to do the work.
ex: Stripe, Twilio, and Figma are classic cases of building for yourself
Moving into PM isn't settling; it's doubling down where you might be world-class

terms.d: The energy of engineers, designers, and others

result.d: What actually reaches users

l201|388.c: Writing is clarity at scale, and a PM must write in the user's voice in a way that moves people.
l201|388.e: A PM has to create clarity both inside and outside the company, he says, and the outside half is often neglected. His bar: if you can't sell or support your own product, he doesn't believe you can build it well. Learning to write is like Anthony Bourdain's advice on learning to cook. You have to eat a lot, and tolerate the occasional bad meal. Read writing that moves people to act, not other people's product requirement docs. Build taste first, then write, then refine by comparing against others. Internal memos also need rhythm, alternating long and short sentences, so readers don't drift.
ex: He recommends Paul Graham's essays and long-form pieces by writers on Twitter
Silent doc-reading meetings: comment and reply on the spot; slower feels faster

items.d: Writing that moves people to act

l201|388.c: A PM must both draw clear boundaries around the problem and own every detail of what finally ships.
l201|388.e: The PM's job, he says, is to draw the edges of the problem space: who you serve, what job they need done, which platforms you cover, and how you trade things off in principle. The clearer the constraints, the more freely engineers and designers can work inside them. The best decision is one you never have to make. But a PM can't hover at the strategy level. The three roles are meant to overlap, and the PM should obsess over whether value actually reached the customer. He'd rather hire one more designer than one more PM.
ex: Square's restaurant POS: a week tuning milliseconds on a menu-group animation, launch pushed three times
A five-course restaurant versus a taco truck leads to completely different solutions

items.d: The box is too big to start
Fine dining or a taco truck
What to do, on which devices

l201|388.c: Product sense is making good calls with too little data, and you build it by practicing with a decision log.
l201|388.e: Like a pianist practicing scales no matter how senior, he says, a PM needs as many decision reps as possible: make a call, write down the reasoning, then see the result. Your own job offers only so many decisions, so make calls about other teams and other companies, write them down, and set a reminder to check months later. Start light: ten minutes every Sunday placing one bet on the news or Hacker News, then build up until it's a habit. It's a supplement, though, not a substitute for building products yourself.
ex: He predicted Shopify's Shop app would move into the purchase flow, and it did
One big text file as a daily log, with decisions tagged #decision

items.d: And set a reminder to revisit

l201|388.c: Send an "unsell" letter with every offer, laying out the truths most likely to cause regret.
l201|388.e: During Square's rapid hiring, several people said six months in that the job was nothing like they'd expected. They left, underperformed, or transferred and left a hole. So throughout the interview process he quietly collects the concerns candidates don't say out loud. At the offer stage he sends an email of no more than eight points that tells the honest truth about the place. Anyone who reads it and is just as excited is an A-plus hire. For items that give someone pause, he's happy to get on a late-night call and talk it through.
ex: A Series A company might spell out: online at 10 p.m., occasional weekend meetings
Good companies revisit interview scores at 6, 12, and 18 months after someone joins

items: Discover the mismatch six months in
Tell the truth before the offer
Lost about 30% of candidates at first

d.verdict: Better to part at the offer stage than six months later

l201|388.c: A PM must touch raw user signal directly, and the work of booking interviews can be automated.
l201|388.e: Research reports, sales anecdotes, and market studies are all bent glass, he says, processed by someone else. A PM needs the raw material. If a company forbids PMs from contacting customers, that's a structural problem to fix first. Lack of time is no excuse. In B2B you can use userinterviews.com to get a steady supply of participants matching your profile, and you should treat the sales team as a research team. "I already understand my users well enough" is a seductive lie, because users' lives keep changing.
ex: Reading a research report about chefs is nothing like standing next to one
The system came from Beth Hills, a PM he hired at Mutiny

items.d: A sales call mentions the topic
With customer name and the quote
Interview lands on the calendar automatically

l201|388.c: A layoff or rough patch doesn't mean you're bad; separate "company doesn't need it," "wrong fit," and "not good enough."
l201|388.e: He was laid off from his first real PM job in a series of rolling cuts, with his wife nine months pregnant, and decided it proved he wasn't a PM. What got him out was separating the causes. Maybe the company doesn't need that skill right now, which means they hired ahead of their needs. Maybe how you work clashes with how the company runs, and you'd thrive somewhere else. Only what's left over calls for improvement or a change of career. He got his confidence back at Square, building a product that had restaurant owners texting him to say thanks.
ex: He wrote his favorite essay, Finding Swagger, about this period
Performance conversations should be framed the same way, not as "you're bad"

items.d: They hired ahead of need; not on you
You might shine at another company
Only this calls for improvement or change

l202|36.c: Whoever keeps learning eventually passes today's experts; the trick is alternating between learning and having impact.
l202|36.e: School has a perfect score, she says, but work doesn't. Someone will always present better, strategize better, or execute better than you, so keep learning from the best, ask for feedback, and get a little better every day. She admits she wasn't fully qualified for any job when she started it. She'd play student until she mastered it, then move somewhere new and be the beginner again. In the role you know best you have the most impact but stop learning. While learning, impact is hard to come by. So climb by alternating between the two. When she started she didn't even know what a PM was. What carried her was love of the problem and curiosity.
ex: Picked product on a whim at a 2002 job fair; admitted day one she didn't know what a PM did
Job-search advice: fall in love with the problem, not the product

items.d: Start again with what you know

l202|36.c: The most successful people aren't the ones with smooth paths; they turn stumbling blocks into stepping stones.
l202|36.e: Among the people she has managed, those who went furthest weren't promoted every cycle. They were the ones who took harsh feedback or shipped a failed product and bounced back, like trees that grow sturdy by weathering cold winds. She herself was passed over twice for a Facebook role she wanted, and Zuckerberg told her flatly she would never get it there. She chose to shape the job she had into the one she wanted. Perfectionism, in her view, is not trusting yourself to recover, and feedback usually comes from someone trying to connect with you. A coach or a peer support group helps you digest it.
ex: Her creed: life is 10% what happens to you and 90% how you respond
For years feedback said she was too transactional and not warm enough; she slowly changed

items.d: Like missing out on the role you wanted
What is the person really saying?

l202|36.c: Building zero-to-one inside a big company means staying out of the spotlight, allowing time to iterate, and accepting half will fail.
l202|36.e: A new business inside a big company gets few resources but too much attention, she says, with weekly questions about progress and strategy. It's being loved to death. She'd rather be low-profile, under-resourced, and free to fail, because new things are built through repeated iteration, and the hardest stretch is the long slow climb, which is exactly when a company tends to kill it. She tells new PMs that working on the core product is just as respectable. Pick a new venture and a year later you may have nothing but lessons; a 50 percent success rate is good. Build fundamentals early, then, when ready, take two or three years for a big bet.
ex: The first mobile app install ad took five or six versions and became a billion-dollar business in about 18 months
When the venture was nearly cut, she also took back the old payments team and carried both

items: A year later, maybe only lessons
Career stories come from big bets

d.verdict: Build fundamentals first, then pick a two-to-three-year big bet

l202|36.c: Run your career like a product: write a career spec and measure every opportunity against it.
l202|36.e: Many of the best PMs are the worst at managing their own careers, she observes. Their products have plans, timelines, and metrics, while their careers just drift. Looking back, her own path from PayPal to eBay to Facebook was almost entirely accidental. It worked out, but that's survivorship bias. Opportunities arrive one at a time with deadlines to respond. Only once you know what success looks like in five years can you judge whether each one moves you closer or further away, then work backward to the first step the way you'd break down a feature. She also believes the most important career decision is who you marry, because an unbalanced home swallows a career.
ex: A founder who wanted a Fortune 100 board seat: a ten-year plan, broken down from step one

items.d: Where you need to be along the way
Does each opportunity bring you closer or not?

l202|36.c: Workplaces favor people who speak up, so introverts must learn to sell the light, and organizations should make room for the quiet.
l202|36.e: A brilliant PM on her team struggled to speak up in groups, and every promotion calibration someone asked, "What did she actually do?" Her framing: you build the light bulb, but you sell the light. A great product nobody talks about might as well not exist. Speaking up is a learnable skill. You don't have to like it, but you have to do it. Reframe self-promotion as making sure your manager knows what the team accomplished and winning resources for the team, and the mental block shrinks. Leaders should also install bias interrupters, like having everyone score and comment in a doc first, or going around the room so each person weighs in.
ex: Her boss Bos had her write one post a month: if you keep repeating something, write it down
She formed a writing accountability group with Ami Vora and others

terms.d: Explain the value to the team and users

result.d: Resources, promotions, and support

l202|36.c: Growth is won inch by inch through many small experiments, not by hunting for one silver bullet.
l202|36.e: Improve a key step by 1 percent every week and it compounds into multiples, she says. Single-digit gains are often the ones that matter most. On growth teams in payments, ads, and Marketplace she kept a list of a hundred-plus hypotheses and picked the top ten each cycle. Rather than perfecting a battle plan, ship more experiments. Plenty of failures are fine, because you get more wins overall and learn what doesn't work. Growth is an optimization layer on top of a core product that already works, getting users to value faster. It isn't the core itself.
ex: Facebook added a "create ad" link next to ads, and it became a major growth source
Ancestry's core is search and hints; growth gets people to them faster

items.d: Her example of a carefully planned team

l202|36.c: In the first 90 days of a new role, diagnose before prescribing: listen and learn, then align, then execute.
l202|36.e: She hadn't changed jobs in 11 years, so before joining Ancestry she turned every onboarding guide she could find into a template, and blogged her reflections as she went. The first 30 days are a listening tour. After talking with more than 60 people she wrote a state-of-the-business summary so everyone knew they'd been heard. Next comes aligning on which problems to solve, and only then execution. When meeting a new team she asks, "What's one thing I can do for you this week?" to build reciprocity. If your boss is pushing for results, publish the plan and negotiate about 20 percent of your time for listening.
ex: Someone listed five wishes at their first meeting; she finished all five the next year and wrote back

items.d: Align on the problems to solve

l203|390.c: Build social apps for teenagers, because adults almost never invite friends or try new apps anymore.
l203|390.e: He has built 15 apps for every age group and found that users over 22 rarely get the flywheel spinning. Teenagers' habits are still forming, they love bringing friends in, and they see each other every day, which is essential for a social product. He observed that from age 13 to 18, invites per user drop about 20 percent with each year of age. One study found the number of people you text peaks around 21 and falls sharply after graduation and marriage. If users don't invite others, you're left buying ads, which a seed-stage company can barely afford, let alone build network density with.
ex: His first product, Politify, showed voters how policies would affect them personally; about 4 million users

marks.d: Invites drop about 20% per year of age

l203|390.c: Look for latent demand: people already getting some value in an awkward, roundabout way.
l203|390.e: A high school user told him kids were playing a "TBH" game on Snapchat, using emojis to compliment each other. At the same time, the number one app in the US was Sarahah, an anonymous messaging app entirely in Arabic. To him, that's the strongest possible signal that people badly want something. The motive he distilled: people want to hear nice things about themselves. But anonymous messages invite bullying, so he only let users answer pre-written positive polls. Message volume exploded. One school sent 450,000 messages in the first week, about 60 per user on day one, when a typical messaging app sees three or four.
ex: People download apps to make or save money, find a partner, or escape reality, in his view
tbh sold to Facebook for over $30 million nine weeks after launch

items.d: A Snapchat game; an Arabic app at number one
People want to hear nice things about themselves
About 60 messages per user on day one

l203|390.c: Since hits are unpredictable, a repeatable testing process cuts risk more than any single idea.
l203|390.e: Success in consumer products is highly random, he says, so focus on getting more at-bats. Their first mobile app took a year to build; the last one took two weeks. Tests must strip out confounding variables. They concentrate ads on a target school, use a dedicated Instagram account to follow students whose bios name the school, and get the first 100 people to join at the same time. Then they ask whether people find it valuable once everyone has ten friends. He stresses this is a testing tactic, not a growth tactic. The app also had 24-hour live support, which doubled as the best user research.
ex: He found users typically need to see a marketing message about three times before downloading
tbh launched at a Georgia school with the earliest start date in the country

items.d: From a year down to two weeks
Scale if it works, else move on

l203|390.c: At each stage, perfect only the one link you're testing and let everything else be rough.
l203|390.e: By the time he built Gas, regulations had changed. Servers could no longer send texts on users' behalf, the old growth system broke, and it took about nine launches to get it working again. His method is to ask layer by layer: if this link holds, what must be true of the next one? Perfect the polling experience first, then tackle spread within a school, spread between schools, and payment. That prevents scope creep and makes every test yield a signal. The more things that must be true, the riskier the plan, so he tries to keep it to about four. Even the name affects invite rates.
ex: Called Crush with a pink icon, boys wouldn't invite; renamed Gas with a black flame icon, invites rose
Gas reached about 10 million downloads and roughly $11 million in revenue

items.d: Jump from one school to the next
Pay to see who voted for you

l203|390.c: Most big-company PMs are really team secretaries, while consumer products live and die in the pixels.
l203|390.e: After tbh was acquired he spent four years as a PM at Facebook. The functional org kept PMs separate from design and data, so the job was mostly writing docs and shepherding approvals through departments. He considers himself a designer at heart, and his skills atrophied. Zero-to-one is hard inside a big company too. You can't openly admit a motive like "build a flirting app for teenagers," ideas without market evidence rarely get funded, so teams end up copying what's on the charts, and responding to a new threat takes 12 to 24 months. Anyone building a new app should personally design the hierarchy, the pixels, and the flows.
ex: Facebook sent about 80 people to acquire tbh; on his side it was just him
He credits Snapchat and Apple's novel products to being designer-led

items: Only follows products with existing evidence
Wins or loses in the pixels

d.verdict: For new consumer products, the owner has to get down to the pixel level

l203|390.c: Whether a social product lasts is nearly random, but making a product grow and go viral can be a science.
l203|390.e: Basic utilities like messaging and broadcasting are locked up by the giants' network effects, he says, and building an experience an order of magnitude better is extremely hard. A social product that retains for years is a once-a-decade black swan. On the other hand, with enough craft you can make an app grow and spread virally with real confidence. Product-market fit is also nearly binary: when it works, you see metrics you've never heard of, like hourly active users. He'd rather have a small team ship something and watch it sweep the country than spend ten years managing a large organization.
ex: Some founders, after IPO and many rounds of dilution, net about what he made from a 90-day app
He advises about 35 companies now, and roughly half have been big successes

l203|390.c: Growth tactics must be above board, or the internet fights back as if it were alive.
l203|390.e: He borrows the Gaia hypothesis, which treats Earth as a self-regulating organism: growth tricks that harm users eventually get punished by the internet itself. So he never quietly abused contact lists or sent invites on users' behalf, and tbh never auto-texted anyone when they were voted for. Gas also deliberately surfaced people who hadn't been voted for in a while, so everyone received compliments, and nearly every day a user said it had talked them out of self-harm. When a rumor spread that the app was used for human trafficking, they booked reporters, got principals and police to retract, and made explainer videos. The principle: make the rumor travel slower than the app.
ex: Nearly every viral app he's seen faced a similar rumor, and some companies shut down over it

items.t: Deletion rate at the rumor's peak
items.d: Briefly enough to kill the app
Reporters, schools, and explainer videos together

l203|390.c: Compress the aha moment into seconds, and make marketing and in-product growth tell one story.
l203|390.e: People now give you about three seconds, he says. Show no value and they're gone. A social app has to let a new user see that their friends are there the same night. That takes creative use of what the phone's operating system allows. Asking users to swap usernames to add friends is unrealistic; one-tap contact sync is what works. He also sees marketing and product growth as one thing: the ad creative, the community you join inside the app, and the invite copy should all point at the same group of people. With iOS 18 letting users pick which contacts to share one by one, he expects contact sync to lose much of its power, making the giants even harder to dislodge.
ex: Dupe: prepend dupe.com to a product URL to find cheaper lookalikes; millions in annual revenue within 60 days
Contact permission rates across apps used to average about 65%

terms.d: Like adding dupe.com before a URL
Sync contacts instead of typing usernames

result.d: See the value within three seconds

l204|394.c: Spend your time only on the company's top priority; if your work isn't part of it, consider changing roles.
l204|394.e: Every day he asks: what matters most to the company over the next few months, and how can I actually move it? That means setting aside time to understand what drives the business and which user behaviors you can influence. Every project gets a rough estimate of its potential impact, along with a written list of what you would have to believe for it to succeed. As companies grow, people start fixating on what other teams should do for them. He argues for focusing only on what you control, and for saying no early.
ex: Instant Book, around 2014, came from breaking down one core problem
Saying no costs goodwill briefly, but earns respect once the reasoning holds up

items.d: Most of it just scatters your attention
What matters most in the coming months
Estimate the impact, then go all in

l204|394.c: Ask questions before arguing a position, and once you've done the homework, dare to challenge senior people.
l204|394.e: Don't walk into a discussion leading with your position. Ask questions first, listen, and then see whether you still disagree. If you have done the homework and still disagree, don't censor yourself, even when the other person is senior. The worst case is limited, and putting the information on the table helps the group decide better. He admits he has been wrong in some of these arguments, and learned from it.
ex: He opposed putting every kind of supply, like hotels, on the platform, fearing it would hurt long-term differentiation
At an all-hands he defended the shift from request-to-book to Instant Book, answering objections one by one

d.verdict: Inquire first; with the homework done, challenge upward

l204|394.c: Don't hire well-rounded generalists; find people with sharp strengths and combine different spikes into a team.
l204|394.e: He doesn't look for people who are decent at everything. He looks for people who are exceptional at one critical skill, then assembles complementary spikes into one team. As an investor, his first question for founders is the same: what is your spike, and does it match the problem you are solving? In hiring, commitment to the mission matters more than domain experience. Skills can be taught, but only the mission carries people through hard stretches like a strategy shift or the pandemic.
ex: Example spikes: marketplace mechanics, sales packaging, process coordination, product design
A warning sign: executives who do lots of outside investing, speaking, and advising
He favors people who enjoy hard problems and don't need outside validation

result.d: Stronger than a group of generalists

l204|394.c: Trying to do everything means you don't know what matters; deliberately let some fires burn.
l204|394.e: Every Monday his leadership team agrees on one to three priorities for the week, and on which things are allowed to go wrong. When a team asks for more resources, the first question is what they can deprioritize. But three kinds of fire can never be left alone. Critical timelines: slip one once and everyone assumes deadlines are negotiable. Strategic disagreements: they spread and drain the team's sense of meaning. Senior hiring: let it drag and the whole team slows down.
ex: Each Monday: set 1-3 priorities and name what can be left to burn

root.d: Everything else can be left on purpose

l204|394.c: Too much calm is dangerous; manufactured chaos and extreme goals can force breakthroughs.
l204|394.e: Even when the numbers looked great, Brian Chesky felt things were too quiet, so he asked for a host onboarding project planned over several weeks to be designed within 24 hours. An artificial deadline forces a team to rely on intuition and creativity and drop its dependence on the organization. It doesn't always work, but it often produces breakthroughs, and it became his favorite team experience. The value of a huge goal is in working backward from it: probe the extreme and ask what the world would need to look like. In interviews he says up front that hours are long, direction changes often, and projects get killed.
ex: Host onboarding went from a multi-week plan to a 24-hour sprint
Chesky gets misread as autocratic; he actually asks a lot and changes his mind

items.d: Weeks of work squeezed into 24 hours

l204|394.c: In hypergrowth you have to reinvent yourself every few months, and reorgs rarely fix the real problem.
l204|394.e: His role changed every three to six months: from individual contributor, to leading 20 people, to leading hundreds. The skills and processes that worked at one stage often failed at the next. Most early employees can't keep up with that kind of growth. Every org structure has trade-offs, and reorganizing rarely cures the root cause; the energy belongs in people, process, and culture. When he was promoted quickly he under-communicated, so he later started writing regular updates and over-explaining context. Making the "why" clear lets others make better decisions on their own.
ex: Data from an Index Ventures book: at 1,000 people, only two or three of the first 10 employees usually remain
He is an introvert; communication was a learned skill
Chesky modeled it by openly seeking help from experts

items.d: The old approach starts to fail
Lead through writing and explaining why

l204|394.c: Don't copy other companies' operating models or values; choose your own and apply them everywhere.
l204|394.e: Every company runs differently, he says. What's worth copying is not a particular method but the act of choosing one clearly and explaining it, because people arriving from other companies bring conflicting expectations. Leaders should go deep into details where they have unique insight and hand the rest to people they trust. Values should describe what the company actually is, not an aspiration; Airbnb cut values it wasn't living up to and built the rest into hiring, performance reviews, and promotions. He also backs Airbnb's choice to slow down on purpose, raising the quality bar before speeding up again.
ex: Dedicated core-values interviewers in the hiring process
New hires walk through a "human tunnel" of cheering colleagues on day one

items.d: Choose it, explain it, don't copy
Drop the ones you don't live up to

l204|394.c: Tying your whole identity to work leads to burnout; doing a bit less makes you more effective.
l204|394.e: Around 2018, as Airbnb grew at full speed, he was overworked and unhappy, and worried he wouldn't make it through the year. The root causes were perfectionism and an identity he couldn't separate from his job. He lost friends, hobbies, and time with family. After changing course, he worked fewer hours, reconnected with friends, spent more time with his wife and parents, and picked up gaming again. He ended up happier, more focused, and more productive per hour. He also reminds people that success depends heavily on luck, so don't be too hard on yourself.
ex: He wrote worries on paper and threw them in a "trash can," with a rule against fishing them out
A sticky note with the Serenity Prayer reminded him what he could and couldn't control

l205|396.c: Ask users how disappointed they'd be without your product; when 40% say "very," it's time to push growth.
l205|396.e: He thinks retention curves are the most accurate test of product-market fit, but they take months to read. Asking "how disappointed would you be if you could no longer use this product?" gives a signal on day one, with no data infrastructure. The 40% bar came from sharing the survey with a batch of YC startups and noticing a pattern. It isn't precise. Its real value is getting the team to agree on when to step on the gas. Who you ask matters: randomly sample people who have used the product at least twice and were active in the last week or two, and collect at least 30 responses. It doesn't work for one-time purchases.
ex: The question came from Xobni: executives rarely admit to being "satisfied," so ask it backwards
Nubank uses a 50% bar, and even tests individual features this way
In a pessimistic market like Hungary, he suspects 30% might be enough

items.t: Active in the last week or two

l205|396.c: When the score is low, don't rebuild the product; reposition around your must-have users and fix onboarding.
l205|396.e: At Lookout, his first survey found only 7% would be very disappointed. Digging in, nearly all of those people cared about one thing: antivirus. So the team repositioned the product as mobile antivirus, which filtered out people who were never going to care. Then they made the first step after signup "set up antivirus" with a message that you are now protected. That set the right expectations and shortened time to value. He says to ignore the "somewhat disappointed" crowd. Chasing them makes a product fine for everyone and great for no one. Superhuman's later refinement only targets fence-sitters who value the same core benefit.
ex: Lookout hit 40% in two weeks and 60% within six months, then became a unicorn
As a marketer, he found reordering onboarding easier to push through than cutting features

l205|396.c: Ask users the main benefit they get and why it matters; that's the raw material for growth.
l205|396.e: Passing 40% only tells you that you haven't built something nobody cares about. It doesn't tell you how to grow. So he first asks an open question: what is the main benefit you get from the product? Then he turns the answers into a four-option multiple choice for a fresh set of users and asks why that benefit matters, which reveals the situation users are in. Next he asks what they would use instead. People who are only somewhat disappointed usually have a generic use with ready substitutes. A must-have is both valuable and unique. Between small and passionate versus big and lukewarm, he picks small and passionate, because an innovator's biggest enemy is irrelevance.
ex: Xobni users kept writing "drowning in email," which became the hook for acquisition copy
Grouped by use case: one group was 60% very disappointed, another 35% but far larger

items.d: Let users describe what they get
Ask a fresh set of users

l205|396.c: After product-market fit, fix activation first, then engagement, referral and revenue, and only then push acquisition.
l205|396.e: New users are curious but skeptical, and they are most likely to leave before they experience the core value. If all you keep is an email address, you'll have to acquire them again later. Acquisition is also brutally competitive. Without efficient conversion, retention and monetization, you won't find a channel that scales profitably. At LogMeIn he found that 95% of signups had never started a single remote-control session. The CEO froze the entire product roadmap so product, engineering, design and marketing could all work on getting signups to actually use the product. That said, before joining a company he still lines up two or three plausible acquisition ideas.
ex: Within three months, usage among signups rose from 5% to 50%
Monthly spend on the same channels grew from $10,000 to $1 million, paying back in three months
After that, about 80% of new users came from word of mouth

items.d: Shorten the time to core value
Follow the product's natural usage rhythm
Existing users bring in new ones

l205|396.c: To improve activation, find out exactly why people drop off, then raise desire and remove friction.
l205|396.e: He likes to quote GM engineer Charles Kettering: a problem well stated is half solved. At LogMeIn, users from one cheap channel were dropping off at the download step at a 90% rate, and a dozen A/B tests didn't help. Then the team, posing as customer support, asked people who hadn't downloaded. The answer: free seemed too good to be true. So they placed a paid trial next to the free version, and suddenly free looked credible. For defining the activation point, he suggests starting with a qualitative judgment about when users really experience the product, then checking that it correlates with long-term retention. It should come early and be something the team can act on.
ex: Download rate rose 300%, and the channel started working
An investor asked when he last spoke to a customer; he's combined interviews and data ever since
Counterexample: defining activation as "100 uses" gives the team nothing to act on

terms.d: Keep reminding users of the benefit ahead
Fix the step with the biggest drop-off first

result.d: Built from many small wins

l205|396.c: Pick channels that fit your product, and remember referral rewards only amplify word of mouth that already exists.
l205|396.e: People tend to copy whatever worked at their last company, but every product opens different channels. LogMeIn's competitor educated the market with radio and TV ads, and LogMeIn used its free version to catch that demand in search results. At Dropbox, nobody was searching for cloud storage yet, so growth had to come from users bringing in users. Dropbox already had strong word of mouth before its referral program; the two-sided reward just sped it up. Freemium works the same way: the free version has to be good enough that people talk about it, and the paid version clearly better. Many companies cripple the free tier out of fear nobody will pay.
ex: Bounce: search harvested existing demand, street signs created new demand
80% of LogMeIn's new users came from word of mouth; he didn't dare add rewards and risk breaking it
Ask users how they found you and how they usually look for products like yours

items: Show up at the right moment

d.verdict: Find the channel your product uniquely opens; don't copy last time's playbook

l205|396.c: A north-star metric should count units of value delivered to customers, not revenue.
l205|396.e: He starts from the must-have value identified in the survey and gives the team a time-boxed discussion. With the right inputs and a checklist, 30 minutes is usually enough. A good metric is not a ratio, can keep rising for years, and grows alongside revenue without being revenue. It should have a time window, otherwise a cumulative number always looks good. What you measure is what you manage. When Facebook switched its goal from monthly to daily active users, teams started asking how to bring people back every day, and the product became extremely addictive.
ex: Amazon tracks monthly purchases: a TV and a toothbrush count the same
Uber tracks weekly rides; he suggested Eventbrite track weekly tickets sold

items.d: The result of doing things right, not a daily guide
A unit of value with a time window
The core benefit from the survey

l205|396.c: Growth is now hard because it's cross-functional, and AI's unbiased advice can cool turf battles.
l205|396.e: Early on, being data-driven and running tests on acquisition was enough to win. Now every marketer tests, and competing requires efficiency across conversion, retention and monetization. That takes marketing, product, sales and support working together, which is hard to bolt on late. He invented ICE scoring (impact, confidence, ease) to gather experiment ideas from across the company and make trade-offs clear. RICE added reach, which he thinks impact already covers. He expects AI to estimate the odds an experiment works, point out weak spots without ego, and ease the analysis bottleneck that comes with running lots of experiments.
ex: He has ChatGPT draft a first pass at "how would Sean Ellis answer this?"
Growth hacking originally meant examining how everything the company does affects growth

items.d: Collect experiment ideas from every team
AI can ease the analysis bottleneck

l206|398.c: A team can be wrong but never unclear: it only has a chance if everyone pushes in one direction.
l206|398.e: He learned this from a founder whose company was failing: once a direction is set, if everyone still hedges, you are relying on luck. In thinking, define the problem down to a specific audience and specific details, and build plans on principles with teeth, meaning you say what you are willing to sacrifice. In meetings, figure out whether people disagree or simply misunderstand. Clear up misunderstandings; don't waste time on disagreements. In execution, the stated top priority has to show up in how people are staffed, or the decision never really happened. Clear goals are also what make it possible to look back and learn.
ex: Leaders call something the top priority while every engineer is on a migration
Americans often say "I don't quite follow" as a polite way of disagreeing

root.d: Obsess over clarity, not being right

items.d: Define problems in detail; principles state trade-offs
Priorities show up in staffing and top talent

l206|398.c: Set goals by working back from the product's potential, not forward from today's numbers.
l206|398.e: He pictures a goal as a mountain. You need a clear view of the summit and a clear base camp; the middle can stay fuzzy and get worked out along the way. When he took on the feed, the data at the time made "millions of daily viewers" look absurd. Instead he worked back from how many professionals worldwide would want to share and discuss content. He admits he is an optimist by nature: conviction leads, then evidence tests the conviction. As he sees it, LinkedIn is an economic-opportunity platform built on a social graph, and a billion members is still small.
ex: Former CEO Jeff Weiner's "vision to values": how is the world different if you succeed?
About seven people get hired through LinkedIn every minute

items: Ask what it could ultimately become

d.verdict: Stay grounded in reality without being tied to it

l206|398.c: Turning a product from negative to positive is hard because of internal inertia; prove it first with a small slice.
l206|398.e: LinkedIn's feed started as updates about who changed jobs and who connected with whom, and it naturally slid into self-promotion. He volunteered to take it on and redefined it as a place for exchanging professional knowledge, not a springboard for driving traffic to other products or selling things. But experimenting on everyone at once alarmed the teams that depended on feed traffic, and he spent his days handling escalations. So he carved out two million members and built the new experience just for them, free from site-wide metrics. Months later their behavior had clearly changed, proving the pie could grow, and the change rolled out to everyone.
ex: He also ran a negative test showing a purely promotional feed makes engagement decay
Success was measured by deeper downstream engagement, not session counts

items.d: From traffic springboard to knowledge exchange

l206|398.c: AI is the ultimate matchmaker: getting content to the right people matters more than chasing traffic.
l206|398.e: In a marketplace, satisfying the other side's need is the magic. At the time, LinkedIn's AI teams ran independently with different goals, so he pulled them into one group serving the product's goals. LinkedIn doesn't compete with Meta on scale. It tries to get your content in front of the right people, even at the cost of some unhealthy engagement. After the algorithm's objective shifted from clicks to downstream conversations, the team still had to work hard to clean out the spam that showed up. When creators get seen by the right people, they gain reputation and business, so they share more.
ex: A post complaining about the "Olympics of business" got reshared by an NBC executive
A professor who posted daily earned roughly half her salary in speaking fees

l206|398.c: AI-first is a mindset: product leaders must personally understand the algorithm's objective, features and data.
l206|398.e: He compares it to whitewater rafting. The paddlers on the sides add speed, but the two oars held by the person at the back set the direction. Those oars are AI, and the product leader should be holding them. In practice, it's often someone else. Many PMs treat AI as a black box and hand it to engineers. He expects PMs to write the algorithm's objective function on a whiteboard, explain which features it learns from, and know how much is invested in data collection and fine-tuning. They should even pay attention to infrastructure, which can be a bigger lever than adding another button.
ex: In 2020 he created an AI academy required for all PMs, like mobile-first in 2014
The chef analogy: in the AI era you supply ingredients and guidelines, not every detail

items.d: Math you can write on a whiteboard
Which signals the algorithm learns from
Can be a strategy of its own

l206|398.c: When generative AI arrived, he dropped the roadmap, returned to goals, explored widely, then narrowed to a few big bets.
l206|398.e: In fall 2022 he gathered his leaders and asked them to set aside their roadmaps. Start from the problems you want to solve and ask how the new technology lets you solve them better, rather than taking a cool technology and hunting for a use. Then he let teams run, even tolerating overlapping projects, because there was no playbook yet and things like prompt engineering had to be learned by doing. A few weeks later, leadership narrowed top-down to four or five of the biggest bets and concentrated resources. With compute and cost constrained, only those projects got reviewed each week.
ex: Some of their prompt-engineering lessons were ahead of the market and shared with OpenAI and Microsoft
A job-search coach feature: private, personalized, so job seekers feel less alone

items.d: Return to the goals you're solving for
Focus on about five big bets

l206|398.c: Choose work by conviction and impact: take the core grind over the glamorous side project.
l206|398.e: Early on he picked paths by society's standards: the hardest, the hottest. After moving to the US for graduate school, he started asking what he cared about and where his conviction could leave a mark. So he started a company while carrying student debt on a student visa. Later he never sent LinkedIn a resume. He told the head of product exactly how mobile should be done and was hired to run it. Product people are lucky, he says: you're judged only by the products you shipped and their impact, like musicians by their albums. Between interesting but peripheral and boring but core, he picks core without hesitation.
ex: No resume: he pitched the head of product directly on a mobile plan
His interviews ask only what you did, what you learned, and what happened

l207|399.c: Don't search alone: anxious job seekers who form a small group and ask for help turn anxiety into momentum.
l207|399.e: Every public-company CEO and CPO he has worked with was anxious while job hunting, and searching alone amplifies that feeling. His answer is a council of six to eight job seekers. They start with a candid "meeting zero" to build trust, then work through a shared method together. Fear turns into hope, accountability and confidence. The thing to manage in a job search, he says, is not your resume but your emotional balance sheet. He sees the councils as a grassroots safety net for the side effects of creative destruction, and he runs them completely free.
ex: More than 2,000 councils formed, with roughly 20,000 volunteer hours
Council members find jobs in about three months, versus three to six nationally
Inspired by a teachers' support group his mother started in 1960 that ran for 50 years

l207|399.c: First figure out your fit with today's market; being leveled down is the market, not a verdict on you.
l207|399.e: A job search is a market with supply and demand. With tech layoffs piling up, a director who could land a VP role two years ago might now only qualify for senior manager. That is the market, not a judgment of you, and many people feel relieved when they hear it. After a layoff, don't rush to apply everywhere. Write a two-page document on what you want and don't want, and share it with your council. Then go on a listening tour: ask former colleagues about your strengths and fit, ask your wider network what they would do in your shoes, and ask recruiters what you are suited for. People you have sincerely consulted start caring about your success and become lookouts for opportunities.
ex: The "Mnookin two-pager" is named after former Intuit executive Allison Mnookin
Take recruiter calls even while employed, to build relationships early

items.d: What you want and don't want
Your council reviews the final version
Tell your network, post on LinkedIn

l207|399.c: You need a spear, not a net: one sentence with three or four specific attributes.
l207|399.e: People instinctively write a broad positioning, the way product builders want to serve everyone. But product-market fit teaches you to focus. He suggests picking three or four attributes from company stage, industry, level and function, and culture, and writing them as one sentence. People can extrapolate outward from a narrow pitch, but they can't narrow down from "any product role," and a vague ask simply isn't remembered. As the market shifts, the positioning should shift too.
ex: A designer targeted only companies with no design team or one that needed rebuilding
A chief data officer searched alone for a year, then got three offers three weeks after positioning
A Nike product VP resisted until a VC told her she had to get specific

l207|399.c: Take a step down to get near the technology frontier; staying far from it looks fine now but traps you later.
l207|399.e: Under creative destruction, new roles and opportunities cluster near the technology frontier, and the further you are from it, the worse your long-term prospects. An EVP running streaming at a traditional media company learned that top streaming firms would only take him as an individual contributor. He accepted, and his career turned. Another person insisted on a COO title, interviewed at 50 companies over a year and a half, and the 50th hired him shortly before going bankrupt over fraud. The better path was to return to VP of product and rise from inside.
ex: There are more jobs at startups than at the big companies doing layoffs
Early in his career at Moody's he built websites on the side to move toward the frontier

marks.d: A step down, but on the frontier

l207|399.c: During interviews, privately draft a job mission with OKRs and walk the hiring manager through it.
l207|399.e: Most job descriptions are badly written, and companies often don't know what they want. Draft your own job mission with OKRs that spells out which outcomes you would own. It helps you ask sharp questions. After a round or two, ask the hiring manager to review the draft with you in person or by phone, not by email. This demonstrates, rather than claims, that you are proactive, accountable and able to get things done. It often decides who gets gold versus silver, and it catches the mismatch where you are hired for job A and end up doing job B. He estimates half his readers skip this step.
ex: An Amazon executive who has hired over 2,000 people said he'd hire on the spot
For senior roles, ask whether the company has had executive hires fail, and why

items.d: Learn what the job really is
Refine the draft with the hiring manager
Tie resource asks to agreed OKRs

l207|399.c: Before talking salary, negotiate the resources you need to succeed, then calmly ask whether they can do X.
l207|399.e: Once you have an offer, first work out with the hiring manager what it takes to hit the OKRs you agreed on: a budget for technical debt, training money, or headcount. Junior people can ask for a mentor, training and conference trips. Companies usually appreciate this, and if they resent it, that is a warning sign. Then talk money. No hardball needed; just ask whether a specific number works. He says long-run data shows that asking usually gets you more, even if the room is smaller right now. Always do it in person or by phone, never email.
ex: Historically, asking gets you more about 87% of the time
Jason Fried of 37signals responded by adopting fixed salary bands

items: Cleared the tech debt in six months
Promoted to GM, later considered for CEO

d.verdict: Not being set up to succeed costs far more than an awkward ask

l207|399.c: Emotions are part of your decision system; manage them with deliberate practices instead of being dragged along.
l207|399.e: Anxiety erodes confidence, which directly hurts interview performance and costs you offers you should have won. He has people draw a "gratitude house" listing everyone who has helped them, then imagine bringing those people into the interview room. Give your inner critic a name so you can catch its lies. Debrief with someone right after interviews and negotiations, because people misjudge their own performance. And be the "I" in the village: drive the process yourself and send your network a progress update every month.
ex: A group searching for over a year had stopped networking and quit their councils, going passive
He named his own inner critic after a childhood nickname

root.d: The thing to manage in a job search

items.d: Bring your helpers into the room
Stay invested in your network and proactive

l207|399.c: Asking for help is confidence, not weakness: do your homework, state the request plainly, and people gladly give.
l207|399.e: He was drinking at 12 with a broken home, and he got out by asking teachers and friends for help. He draws four counterintuitive rules: asking for help takes confidence and builds it; done well, it gives the other person the feeling of being respected; it makes you more independent; and it raises your reputation rather than hurting it. The conditions are that you do your homework, ask for perspective rather than having someone do the work, and say plainly, "I have a request." In a new job, pair with a peer in the same role for first-90-days coaching. To get promoted, ask people one level up.
ex: After losing $300 million, Intuit's Brad Smith realized he hadn't asked for help
Bradley Horowitz openly asked Sundar Pichai for advice after joining Google
Marissa Mayer brought new products to a council for feedback first

items.d: Credit promotions to asking for help
Avoid asking for fear of looking weak

l208|401.c: What engineers hate most in PMs: taking credit, dismissing details, playing messenger, and hoarding the ideas.
l208|401.e: PMs are usually the public face of the work, so it's easy to soak up the credit. Instead, put engineers on stage to present their own contributions. Engineering success lives in the details. You don't have to understand all of them, but acting as if they don't matter shows a lack of empathy. Constantly relaying questions between stakeholders and engineers wastes time and garbles the message; when it happens a lot, let the two sides talk directly. The sneakiest habit is hoarding all the ideas: engineers shut out of the creative work redirect their creativity into technology choices and start over-engineering.
ex: Good PMs welcome engineers' ideas and help them see why the PM job matters
She thinks GraphQL is often used to dodge collaboration between frontend and backend

items.d: Let engineers present their own work
"Why does something so small take so long?"
If frequent, connect the two sides directly

l208|401.c: Rewriting from scratch rarely works; most of the time, evolve clearly bounded modules in stages.
l208|401.e: Engineers often decide the only escape from a hard-to-maintain legacy system is to start over, and they badly underestimate migration time, especially when there are outside users and integrations. During the rewrite, the old system still needs maintenance, and product teams won't accept a year or two without new features. Old systems are full of undocumented business rules and data formats, and reproducing them is far harder than it looks. She suggests first asking: if we leave this alone for a long time, does the business suffer? If it truly needs to evolve, pick a part with clean interfaces, like a recommendation system, and upgrade it step by step.
ex: PHP and simple SQL are fine for a one-person project, maybe not for a hundred engineers
Frameworks born inside big companies often waste time outside their original context

items: Old and new systems run in parallel for ages
First ask whether leaving it hurts the business
Keep shipping features while you evolve

d.verdict: Rewrites are sometimes necessary, but as a cure-all they almost never work

l208|401.c: Move into management once your technical skills are in your bones, which takes roughly ten years.
l208|401.e: Like a fluent second language or an instrument you played for years, deep skills come back quickly even after you get rusty. Solid coding experience keeps your technical confidence and your empathy for engineers after you switch to management. Her own count was undergrad plus grad school plus four or five years of full-time coding, roughly ten years. Being pushed into managing straight out of school because you communicate well is often a shortcut trap, especially for women and minorities whose technical skills get underestimated. Once managing, stay sharp by asking good questions and keeping close to hands-on engineers, not by dictating which library to use.
ex: She keeps listening to frontline discussions through chat groups, meetings and former colleagues
If you still enjoy writing code, don't rush into managing

items.d: About ten years of school plus work
Come back fast even when rusty
The first year or two will feel anxious
Ask good questions, listen to the front line

l208|401.c: Management is a service job, so don't burn your time on one-on-ones that don't scale.
l208|401.e: The biggest surprise for new managers is that their time is no longer their own, and they can't just give orders. In tech companies, command-style management provokes pushback; managing is more like guiding, encouraging and setting guardrails. One-on-ones with your direct reports and your own boss are sacred. But meeting individually with peers, product and design partners, and every stakeholder grows linearly with the number of relationships. And in a one-on-one, an unhappy person can't see that others are satisfied, and when you relay that, it sounds defensive. Before booking, ask whether there is really something to discuss. People who are good at building rapport through small talk should hold even fewer.
ex: She ran internal platforms for years, where stakeholders are especially numerous
She says she's bad at aimless coffee chats and earns respect through the work itself

items.d: Only when there's a reason, not by default
Use group settings and open information

l208|401.c: Overworking is a way to avoid deciding what matters most; fewer, focused hours get more done.
l208|401.e: Everyone knows it's best to do only the most important things. The hard part is judging what's important, and long hours let people dodge that question. She suggests setting boundaries on purpose, like logging off at six or stopping at four on Fridays, then reviewing what got done, auditing your task list regularly and cutting what doesn't matter. Delegate more, too. Teaching someone takes longer at first, but if you never hand things off, the team never learns and you drown. Early in her coding career, intense focus and a refusal to work late are exactly what built her skills.
ex: Always testing your limits brings back the nightmare of the forgotten homework assignment
She gets into focus with lyric-free music and a steady caffeine routine

items.d: See where the time actually went
Invest in teaching, then free yourself

l208|401.c: A platform is a product, so a platform team needs software engineers and product managers.
l208|401.e: A team made up only of ops and SREs can maintain cloud resources and write scripts, but it can't assemble a coherent platform. A platform should be judged like a product, by impact and outcomes: does it shorten engineering cycles, remove obstacles to launching and scaling products, and deliver real cost savings, rather than chasing whatever is trendy online. She gave every platform team a product manager, because someone running a big team and writing code can't sustain product work on the side. A platform team usually makes sense once you pass about 50 engineers and start seeing duplicated work or scaling bottlenecks.
ex: Platforms include CI/CD, cloud resources, storage, web and mobile frameworks, and billing
Platform teams can run with a lower PM-to-engineer ratio

result.d: Makes the whole company's engineering faster

l208|401.c: Platform work means embracing migrations and stakeholder management, and good solutions often start in business teams.
l208|401.e: Platform projects run longer and get more complex than agile product iterations, and migrations are everywhere; even a cloud vendor's version upgrade forces application teams to change code. So you have to care about smoothing the impact on your customers and the company. The hardest and least rewarding part is stakeholder management, since someone is always questioning whether the platform is worth the money. Good platform solutions often emerge inside an application team; the platform team's job is to spot them, take them over, stabilize them and spread them. That suits people who like one-to-many more than zero-to-one. If a business team meets a platform team with no PM, it can quietly do the product management for it.
ex: Facing a difficult platform team, build a relationship with the group inside it that works well
Platform engineers should spend half their effort on operational quality

items.d: Builds a fix for its own problem

l209|403.c: AI answers will swallow top-of-funnel searches, pushing SEO's value to the middle, where intent lives.
l209|403.e: It used to be that whoever wrote the longest "best beach vacations" article and piled up enough backlinks won the first click. Now AI gathers unstructured content into a direct answer and then suggests what to search next. He expected a catastrophe, but it hasn't shown up yet, partly because Google only recently extended AI Overviews to logged-out users and algorithm updates mask the effect.
