The hardest hit are sites that sell ads against generic information, like health explainers. E-commerce sites that sit at the buying stage are affected much less.
ex: "Top podcast tools" gets an AI answer; "Riverside pricing" still depends on SEO
Review-list sites like G2 and Capterra will be heavily disrupted

items.d: "What podcast tools exist?" AI answers it
Narrowing to a few choices, SEO's main ground
Searching a specific product's price and specs

l209|403.c: SEO is a product problem, not a marketing task; PMs should build it from the user's search journey.
l209|403.e: The usual pattern is to finish the product and hand it to marketing to "do SEO," which produces content that doesn't match what users actually search for. His approach has three steps. First, become the user and understand why they would search at all. Second, decide what asset to build for them. Third, build it like a product, with design, engineering, user research and a PM. If you can't say what the user would search for, don't do SEO. And when the product itself is weak, no number of blog posts will save it.
ex: Zapier built pages at scale for combinations like "connect Gmail to Salesforce"
Tinder framed itself as solving loneliness and built "online dating in [city]" pages
Some SurveyMonkey employees worked there for years without ever sending a survey

items.d: What page to build for these users
Design, engineering, research and PM together

l209|403.sc: Should you do SEO at all?
l209|403.c: Many companies, especially B2B SaaS, shouldn't do SEO: there's no search journey, so spend elsewhere.
l209|403.e: SEO isn't free. A decent agency costs at least around $10,000 a month, plus a CMS, engineering, design and content. Many SaaS products either solve a problem users don't yet know exists, which is really a brand problem, or require integrations, approvals and committee decisions to buy, so nobody orders straight from a search result. Treat it like any product opportunity: tally the full cost, then compare whether the same money pays back faster in brand, influencers or paid ads.
ex: Mixpanel's content ranked well but didn't convert
A gardening SaaS spending $15,000 a month on SEO would do better with a trade-show booth
He thinks even a restaurant may not need a website

cells.d: First make people aware the problem exists
Put the money in other channels

l209|403.c: Measure SEO by business conversions, not rankings or traffic, and set product-style milestones.
l209|403.e: Paid media never reports just rankings or clicks, and SEO should be held to the same standard: media companies track page views, SaaS tracks qualified leads, e-commerce tracks sales. Traffic that doesn't convert is worthless, and the idea that more traffic makes Google value you more is a myth. He has told clients to delete whole sections of non-converting content. Time to results depends on what you're doing: a big brand sees results at launch, a small company may wait months or years. So set milestones for ideation, requirements doc, development, launch and indexing. If one is missed, the problem is execution.
ex: Quora opened up its answers and added an HTML category sitemap; traffic quadrupled within months
An HR marketplace found most of its SEO traffic landing on the side that doesn't pay

items: Page views only for media sites

d.verdict: SEO must tie to a conversion metric the business actually cares about

l209|403.c: Programmatic SEO only works when you have both scale and real search demand.
l209|403.e: Programmatic SEO assembles many pages from multiple data sources; editorial content is written one piece at a time. TripAdvisor combines hotel data, city data and user reviews into a page for every hotel. Zillow merges government, transaction and school-district data to estimate every home's value. Writing those by hand would be unaffordable. But generating a page for every zip code, or every "software × city" combination, is scale with no one searching. Copying another site's template doesn't work either. Each page has to lead people toward the product you actually monetize.
ex: Canva's templates lead to paid upgrades; templates that don't monetize are just free content
SurveyMonkey has about a hundred popular templates, not a long tail of tens of thousands

terms.d: Enough to assemble a huge set of pages

result.d: And it must lead to a product that makes money

l209|403.c: AI-written content isn't the problem; usefulness is the test, and both backlinks and AI Overviews depend on brand.
l209|403.e: AI is just a tool. A filler article you used to buy for $50 on a freelance site is still worthless when AI generates it for free. But using AI for useful content, like e-commerce product descriptions or summaries of earnings reports and sports results, is fine, and Google's own documentation says it judges usefulness. Being named in an AI Overview is a brand outcome; appearing only as a link means your content got taken. Cheap purchased backlinks don't help rankings either. The real "backlink" is being mentioned because your product is good.
ex: CNET faced a backlash after admitting it used AI to write articles
His personal site outranks Amazon for searches of his book's title
His LinkedIn poll: about half of respondents click links inside AI Overviews

marks.d: Not fancy, but useful and time-saving
Serve searches for the product name

l209|403.c: Defaults and habit make Google hard to dislodge; SEO won't die, but informational publishers will suffer most.
l209|403.e: He read all 286 or so pages of the Google antitrust ruling. Neeva had a better experience but failed without default distribution. Apple said it wouldn't switch to Bing at any price. When Mozilla switched to another engine, users switched back to Google. So he doesn't think an LLM startup can unseat Google on quality alone, and he sees AI Overviews as mostly a show for Wall Street. People still want to choose their own answers, and the total volume of transactional needs won't shrink because search changes. The real losers are publishers who repackage public information and monetize it with ads.
ex: The ruling says 63% of Gen Z search on TikTok, yet they still book hotels and flights on Google
His survey 12 years ago put DuckDuckGo at about 1%; the ruling puts it near 2%

l209|403.c: Forecast SEO top-down from the market; keyword tools can be off by a factor of ten.
l209|403.e: The common bottom-up forecast pulls search volume from a keyword tool, estimates ranking, click-through and conversion rates, and scales it up. The result is usually too small for anyone to invest in, and the starting number itself may be wrong. Every tool is guessing with its own algorithm, and he has seen them overshoot or undershoot by ten times. When sizing a new country at Faire, he went top-down instead: start with population, filter down to the target demographic and the share who buy online, then multiply by penetration, purchase frequency and order value. Each assumption can be corrected later.
ex: For the term "WordPress," no tool's volume matched the company's actual analytics
A board member cited third-party data to say traffic lagged, when internal data showed it had quadrupled

items.d: A forecast you can correct over time

l210|405.c: Pick a job by whether you can't wait to start work, not by level or headcount.
l210|405.e: He never had a deliberate career plan; he only asked whether a job made him eager to get going in the morning. Watching managers' days, he saw a life he didn't want, and many colleagues he respected moved into management only to ask to come back to IC roles. Product work itself, he argues, satisfies three intrinsic motivators: a high degree of autonomy, a craft that keeps changing and transfers across industries, and the meaning of seeing something get built well with your own eyes. It still stings when peers get promoted, but he wouldn't trade places.
ex: His father, a research professor, never chased administrative titles
He credits the idea of a transferable craft to Marty Cagan

terms.d: A craft that stays fresh and transfers

result.t: A job you want to start
result.d: A better test than the title

l210|405.c: Senior ICs should be priced on their own value, and companies need an IC ladder parallel to management.
l210|405.e: Engineering long ago accepted that a senior IC can earn more without managing anyone, and product should too. After the "great flattening," founders want experienced people who do the work themselves, and a senior PM's scope and impact can be large. When a recruiter says pay will rise once he moves into management, he says plainly that he isn't planning to, and the number should reflect what he is worth as an IC now. Companies, for their part, should publish IC levels and the criteria for each. Product is usually the last function to add that ladder.
ex: He notes Amazon has a Distinguished PM level
In Meta's layoffs, IC-style PMs were more likely to be kept

items.d: Only a few companies have this level
Published criteria and a promotion path

l210|405.c: With AI, documentation work that once took a director and a team can be done by one IC.
l210|405.e: After his team switched to strict Scrum, it needed lots of user stories in Jira written in Given/When/Then format. He gives ChatGPT the template and the context, then uses Whisper to dictate a walkthrough like the one he'd give at a project kickoff, and gets detailed stories that need only light edits. Deciding how to split a big change into sensible stories still takes human judgment, and the team lead does that part. The upstream work, usability research, design, and vision, doesn't use AI either.
ex: Whisper is OpenAI's free, open-source speech-to-text tool
Pasting raw meeting transcripts works less well; he is still iterating

l210|405.c: Keep deep work strictly separate from back-and-forth, because most messages don't need to go out right away.
l210|405.e: He splits the day into deep work and ping-pong-style real-time communication, and for about eight years he hasn't opened Slack before noon. Messages he thinks of in the morning get written out in full and parked in his to-do list, then sent after noon. Most, it turns out, never needed to go early. For true emergencies, close colleagues can call, which happens about twice a year. He also keeps a product scrapbook: tickets, support escalations, screenshots, and other evidence filed by theme. When an opportunity comes up he has real backing, and the people involved feel heard.
ex: Genuinely urgent calls come about twice a year
A large Notion database holds every opportunity and its evidence

items.d: Kept up for about eight years
Send after noon; most aren't needed

l210|405.c: Product is a team, not a role; the PM should be valuable but not something everyone depends on.
l210|405.e: He rejects the hub-and-spoke model where the PM controls every flow of information. Look for the places where you have become the bottleneck: information relayed through you, decisions waiting on you, DMs that could have been public, and working meetings with just you and one other person. He answers DMs with "great question, post it in the channel," so discussions become public, searchable, and snowball. When teammates do PM-like things, cheer them on. When someone asks a question, pull up the data or create the ticket together on the spot. Over time, people start doing it themselves.
ex: At a previous company, customer success moved questions to a shared channel and began answering each other
That team culture resists sales and support going straight to engineers with requests

items.d: No longer relayed through the PM

l210|405.c: Most tech companies win on about two departments, so figure out whether product is one of them.
l210|405.e: A product team that is ten times better doesn't necessarily produce a company that is ten times better; a ten-times-better marketing or sales team might. To find out, ask about the growth model and its levers, look at what customers are really paying for beyond the product itself, and watch which team is actually pushing growth. Being in a department that drives growth brings more status, stronger colleagues, and faster promotions. If product is a supporting function, then a PM who mostly builds things for other teams is doing legitimate work, not failing.
ex: Pairings he cites: design plus support, brand trust plus payments, and so on
His Olympics analogy: product may just be a supporting muscle group

items.d: What are customers really paying for?
Sets your status and growth rate

l210|405.c: Decisions need book smarts and street smarts; how customers feel matters as much as the logic.
l210|405.e: Data, frameworks, and logic are book smarts. Street smarts means giving equal weight to how customers will perceive a change and react to it emotionally. One pricing change he worked on was modeled correctly, but customers saw only the immediate downside while the upside came later, so it triggered an online backlash and was rolled back. To build this sense, spend time in community forums and support tickets. Before a sensitive launch, he has the team stay off social media for two weeks while reading every ticket and mention; complaints that persist after two weeks are the real problems.
ex: A premium feature shown to lower-tier users but locked behind a paywall was reworked into a gentler, staged rollout
A redesign that cut clicks made the value hard to show in sales demos, spotted in Gong call recordings

d.verdict: Weigh both equally to avoid post-launch backlash

l210|405.c: Don't skimp on research and testing; the safer a high-stakes change looks, the more it needs validation.
l210|405.e: His growth team once failed 12 A/B tests in a row because it copied playbooks from Groupon, Amazon, and Booking while its own users had completely different motivations. Qualitative research up front would have saved months. A referral program that interviewed only active users and skipped the people who hadn't adopted it was rushed out and failed too. He also skipped testing on a change that seemed perfectly logical, and payments went down for a week. One more lesson: when you keep disagreeing with your boss, learn to disagree and commit.
ex: 12 consecutive A/B tests, all failures
Skipping an A/B test broke payments for about a week
He says he nearly got fired three times

marks.d: Skipped the test; down for a week
Start from first principles and test

l211|407.c: Skip the five-year plan: do your current job well, read people, and follow the best people.
l211|407.e: To get promoted, first do your current job exceptionally well. The bar isn't finishing tasks; it's moving the business and building things people actually use. Moving into leadership also means reading what motivates people. Her father, a psychiatrist, would quiz her on the drive home: why did that person say that? When choosing a job, go where the best people are. They shape what you learn more than the field does. You can predict who is excellent and what you'll learn. Financial returns are the hardest thing to predict, so changing jobs for money is a big gamble.
ex: Before starting her first management job, she argued the team shouldn't exist
Advice for leaders: pick a job where the people you hire will build careers on it

marks.d: Once you see it, follow them
Skills survive even if the company fails

l211|407.c: A company doesn't have to run well to win; what matters is product-market fit, distribution and enough cash.
l211|407.e: She has seen companies with constant executive turnover, endless reorgs and unhappy employees grow at astonishing rates, and well-run companies with great CEOs stall. In hypergrowth, infrastructure and communication break, and half the staff may have joined within six months. But once you have product-market fit, failing to scale fast means growth stops. So separate what truly matters: a product people crave, distribution and a sales team that can sell it, and enough money in the bank. No product-market fit is a death sentence. Only at five or ten thousand people do you need professional managers running a tight ship. Chaos from constantly changing strategy, though, is never acceptable.
ex: Many of Slack's "most important" features went unused after launch
MySpace declined because the product got slow

result.d: Internal chaos isn't the deciding factor

l211|407.c: Top leaders taught her two things: consistent principles make big organizations work, and prototypes reveal the real experience.
l211|407.e: At Amazon, Bezos waited for every executive to speak before he did, applied the same principles every time, and always centered the customer. After a few meetings, everyone knew what he would ask, and the large organization ran better for it. When she complained that a competitor had ten times the people, he said that was her advantage, and that products should be built on a seven-year view. At Slack, Butterfield drew a four-box master plan in 2014 that didn't change for years. He insisted you can't feel the real experience from a design mock; you have to prototype. That requires engineering foundations and a mindset that allows throwing code away.
ex: Slack's plan: build a product people love, a network, a platform, and AI magic
Butterfield had the team try hiding everything in the interface behind one button
Benioff polishes the Dreamforce keynote the way you'd polish a product

root.d: Her lessons from Amazon and Slack

items.d: The whole organization knows what to do
Fewer people can be an advantage
You only know the experience by building it

l211|407.c: A product leader's most important move is picking the right engineering partner, with clear roles and one voice.
l211|407.e: A great idea you can't build is just talk, so she meets and approves her engineering partner before taking a job. The two of you need to spell out who owns what, so teams can't play mom against dad. If something is in your partner's domain, send people to them. Disagree face to face, never by complaining to your reports afterward. At Slack she did every review together with the CTO. When OKR reviews had eaten more than 300 hours, they switched: teams submitted a document plus a short time-limited video, the two of them watched together, then followed up in the team's channel.
ex: Mondays covered only red projects; green ones got no discussion
The review process itself was iterated every quarter, like a product

items.d: A document plus a short timed video
Book meetings only for key projects

l211|407.c: Don't let a vocal minority of existing users hold you hostage; design for tomorrow's users, but explain honestly.
l211|407.e: Whenever you retire a feature or change the interface, a small group of heavy users gets very upset, and PMs can get trapped by those voices. But unless you are Google-sized, tomorrow's users vastly outnumber today's. If a change makes things simpler for new users, make it. What matters is how: give people transition time and choices, explain the real reason sincerely rather than in marketing speak, and don't dismiss early users. People react very differently when they feel heard.
ex: Google's communications chief Rachel Whetstone personally called an unhappy engineer
Slack gradually replaced its original calls with Huddles

items: Heavy users of an old feature

d.verdict: Change for the many, but be honest, give time, and listen

l211|407.c: People underestimate how much AI changes work: execution-only PMs will be replaced, and those who use it well will pull far ahead.
l211|407.e: She has a master's degree in AI and still assumed the shift was far off, until she saw GPT-3. It won't happen overnight, but people who figure out how to use it first will move much faster. Within five to ten years she expects the lines between PM, design and engineering to blur. Execution chores like updating Jira and maintaining release calendars will be automated, and PM jobs built on those will disappear, while strategic and creative PMs stay in demand. She doesn't think fewer people will be needed; they'll just get more done. Trying it once, declaring it useless and going back to old habits is the dangerous move.
ex: One PM fed an entire Discord channel into Gemini to analyze feature requests
Glean automatically summarizes customer requests from Gong sales calls
She writes prompts that pull together tickets and discussions to judge whether a feature will ship on time

items.d: Like adopting mobile apps back then

l211|407.c: LLM products need guidance and guardrails, and they should get better as the models improve.
l211|407.e: A chat box leaves people unsure what to ask. Glean often gets questions it couldn't possibly answer, like "what should I prioritize next week?" Search took years to teach users through autocomplete and query suggestions, and AI products need the same built-in prompts and guardrails. Enterprise CIOs play with ChatGPT on weekends but expect deterministic results from software at work, so users need educating. Models improve so fast that work done purely to patch a model's weaknesses eventually becomes obsolete, so it can't be your differentiation. Real differentiation gains value as the models get stronger.
ex: Glean started with BERT and vector retrieval for enterprise search, adding chat later
She has heard ChatGPT's retention isn't high

items.d: Show users what they can ask

l212|408.c: Before product-market fit, skip marketplace theory: go deep on the hardest side and bootstrap the other.
l212|408.e: Many founders dive into supply-demand ratios and economics papers before they have product-market fit. He says forget all that at first and focus on the core value exchange. Find the side your team knows it needs but doesn't know how to acquire, which is supply eight or nine times out of ten, and build a reliable way to grow it. Let the other side ride on existing channels for now, almost in single-player mode. Other common ways to grow supply include retaining it with value-added services or converting demand-side users into suppliers.
ex: Thumbtack and Airbnb both used Craigslist early on to get the other side
OpenTable kept restaurants with its reservation-management software
Turning riders into drivers didn't work well at Lyft, but it did at Uber

items.d: Supply, eight or nine times out of ten
Is there enough supply in each market?

l212|408.c: Liquidity is how marketplaces win, so find a leading "marketplace health" metric that predicts it.
l212|408.e: Liquidity is the ability to match buyers and sellers efficiently, usually measured as the share of high-intent demand that ends in a transaction. It's also the ultimate engagement loop. But conversion gets knocked around by outside factors like weather and competition. A more actionable approach is a leading indicator that plateaus and correlates strongly with conversion and retention. At Lyft that was pickup time: once the nearest driver could arrive within two minutes, conversion basically maxed out. Also watch for accidentally fragmenting supply. Too many hard filters for users makes wait times balloon.
ex: Sidecar let riders filter by things like car age, which wrecked pickup times
Only 5% of DJs had a fog machine, so Thumbtack turned that checkbox into a ranking boost

items.d: A good experience brings repeat visits

l212|408.c: A marketplace has two product-market fits to measure; fragmentation, uniform demand and hard matching make it worth building.
l212|408.e: Product-market fit and marketplace dynamics are independent, he argues. You can measure fit the traditional way, like asking how disappointed users would be without the product, but you have to do it separately for supply and demand. A common pattern is happy demand and unhappy supply because the take rate is too high. Three signals say a marketplace makes sense: both sides are a long tail with no few giants in control; demand is fairly uniform and supply can be standardized to some degree; and the two sides find it hard to find and vet each other. Service marketplaces are especially hard because supply is fuzzy and changeable.
ex: A Thumbtack electrician takes only certain jobs, only when free that day, and might cancel

terms.d: Long tail on both sides, no giants
Hard to find and vet each other

result.d: Aggregation adds real value

l212|408.c: Marketplaces mostly fail for three reasons: density never arrives, one side gets ignored, or quality has no standard.
l212|408.e: Building enough density takes time and money, and without a diagnostic framework you run out of both. He felt that pressure at Lyft to reach critical mass first. Many large marketplaces run as one-sided businesses for years, watching only the demand funnel. Marketplace feedback lags, so by the time network effects decay and sellers leave, the product needs a major overhaul. Quality doesn't have to be the best, but a marketplace is by definition a filter, so set standards deliberately. Otherwise you keep lowering the bar to add supply until the whole platform looks sketchy.
ex: Toptal claims to accept about 3% of applicants, and reportedly the real number is lower

items.d: Money and time run out before critical mass
Sellers are users too; feedback lags
The bar keeps dropping to add supply

l212|408.c: Rather than controlling supply, set guardrails and empower them, and intervene heavily only where gaps remain.
l212|408.e: Marketplace operators tend to sit in an ivory tower thinking "if only everyone did X," but people don't always respond logically. When Thumbtack switched from selling leads to selling booked appointments, the math said pros would earn about 20% more, yet they hated it, because they enjoyed the thrill of winning the job. In the US, too much control can also get your supply classified as employees. His approach: set quality standards, a rating system and coaching tools first, then bring heavy interventions to the specific gaps.
ex: Lyft's car-rental partnership with GM became the fourth-largest rental fleet in the US in about 18 months
He says about half of US job seekers and benefit recipients don't have a car

items.d: See where it still falls short
Like renting cars to people who lack one

l212|408.c: Outgunned, Lyft had its best drivers onboard new ones; community leverage beat building its own teams.
l212|408.e: Around 2014 and 2015, Uber was roughly 30 times Lyft's size, so every Lyft employee had to be ten times more efficient to survive. Uber opened offices in each city for centralized vehicle inspections and training. Lyft instead paid top drivers $35 a session to inspect the car, check documents and take the new driver on a ride. A veteran driver's experience and phone number were more persuasive than company copy. Expanding to a new city only required a small team to vet ten or twenty mentors. Becoming a mentor felt like a promotion, which also improved retention of the best drivers.
ex: Later, drivers could claim leads to win back people who dropped out, earning $20 per activation
He thinks Lyft's narrow focus on rides and its bet on carpooling lost to a diversified Uber in the pandemic

items.d: About 30x in revenue, staff and liquidity
Matched coverage with a tenth to a twentieth of the resources

l212|408.c: France's job market moves slowly, and its product teams lack the American sense of ownership and accountability.
l212|408.e: In the US, talent moves fast. A PM gets a piece of the business and real autonomy on day one, and gets replaced if it doesn't work. In France, changing jobs is hard and firing is expensive, so companies prefer "prove yourself first, then get authority." PMs have little autonomy, founders struggle to let go, and many companies simply outsource to product studios. Business-school culture puts business above technology, and stock options are often seen as worthless. He suggests educating people about equity, being clear about the company's trajectory, and building teams that truly own a slice of the business rather than just shipping features.
ex: French executives' options are often under 10% of total pay; in the US, often over half
The French government plans to invest about $2.5 billion in domestic AI by 2030

items: Own a piece of the business on day one
Options often over half of executive pay
PMs have little autonomy, get micromanaged

d.verdict: Build ownership through equity education and end-to-end accountable teams

l213|409.c: LLMs are magical duct tape, overturning the old assumption that software is expensive to write and cheap to run.
l213|409.e: The industry is taking mature playbooks from the end of the last technology era and forcing them onto a new technology. LLMs make it much cheaper to write software that is good enough, but running it carries real marginal cost, and ad-supported consumer products can't cover inference bills. An LLM is like a soft computer: it doesn't follow instructions exactly, but it roughly does what you want. A product that is great 90% of the time and occasionally punches the user in the face doesn't work. So don't treat it as an oracle; design on the assumption that it won't be fully accurate.
ex: It's like the room tilting five degrees: everything looks the same, but gravity points differently
A prototype that took three months now takes almost no time, so it's no longer a differentiator
He wants to use LLMs to break the lock-in of app silos and aggregator platforms

items: Expensive to write, cheap to run
Good-enough software is cheap to write
Real cost every time it runs

d.verdict: Use it as duct tape, not an oracle, and rethink what you can build

l213|409.c: Early AI rewards curiosity, play and taste, and taste means differing from the model's average output.
l213|409.e: This is the community-garden phase of the technology, not industrial farming, so play with the weird things that could only exist because LLMs do. The cost of producing information has collapsed, and most output is mediocre. What stands out is taste: how different your expression is from what the model would say to the same prompt, while still resonating with people. AI makes individuals more capable, but mostly in the long tail where organizations can't see it. People don't necessarily want to tell their boss they are twice as fast, so it looks like nobody is using it.
ex: He talks to Claude about 20 times a day and calls it an e-bike for the mind
WebSim: type in a URL and the model improvises the entire website

terms.d: Different from the model's average output

result.d: Standing out in a flood of content

l213|409.c: Kayfabe, where everyone knows it's fake but acts as if it's real, piles up until the organization becomes a zombie.
l213|409.e: Kayfabe comes from professional wrestling. A little optimism lubricates an organization, but reporting a yellow light as green because you're confident you can fix it is a reasonable little lie that compounds at every level. By the top, the picture can be off by orders of magnitude. Anyone who tries to press the truth button gets talked out of it or pushed out, and the path of least resistance is to sincerely believe. So everyone privately knows it won't work while the organization marches on. The root cause is that you can't make your boss look stupid. The fix is letting disconfirming evidence arrive in small, non-fatal doses.
ex: The more powerful someone is, the more they're surrounded by confirming evidence manufactured for them
He insists this isn't cynicism; you have to see the system clearly to move it

items.d: A fixable yellow gets reported as green
Leaders are off by orders of magnitude
Everyone privately knows it won't work

l213|409.c: Work like a gardener, not a builder: plant cheap seeds with compounding potential, then water whatever grows.
l213|409.e: A builder controls everything according to plan, so the value produced can never exceed the effort put in. A gardener looks for things that can grow on their own and only guides and waters them. Done right it looks like luck, but it's really farming miracles. It applies to anything with network effects or a compounding loop: spend three hours on a small open-source tool, and if nobody uses it, no harm done; if someone does, invest a little more. At Google he had his team spend 70% of its effort on work everyone agreed was valuable, so nobody asked what the team was for, and the other 30% planting seeds.
ex: Let a junior PM chase the idea they're obsessed with; even if it fails, they grow
After making director he stopped chasing promotions, and his impact grew about tenfold

l213|409.c: Organizations are more like slime mold: coordination cost grows with the square of headcount, so drive the vehicle you have.
l213|409.e: Even when everyone is capable, collaborative and hardworking, finding a project that busy people can all commit to carries a coordination cost that grows with the square of the number of people involved. A small company is a sports car the founder can swerve at will. Once it has grown into a semi truck, swerving like a sports car hurts people inside and out. One option is to turn less often, invest more in project management and leave buffers. Another is to break into a fleet of autonomous sports cars, at the cost of outsiders noticing the teams don't talk. Tech companies that prize employee autonomy are more like slime mold, and it's better to embrace that than fight it.
ex: A semi truck doesn't have to drive slowly; it has to turn more deliberately
Perplexity's co-founder said they organize their team the slime-mold way

d.right: A fleet of autonomous sports cars

marks.d: Many different approaches, but robust overall

l213|409.c: Start a voluntary "nerd club" so insights emerge bottom-up from low-stakes discussion.
l213|409.e: At Google he faced a dozen teams working at cross purposes with strategies that canceled each other out. Instead of expensive, performative pairwise executive reviews, he built a secret, voluntary discussion group. The rules: only "yes, and"; if you disagree, offer another angle with "I wonder whether..." Each week, bring in one to three newcomers from different backgrounds. Start with a few people who already love to talk, meet in person so there is energy in the room, and send notes afterward to create fear of missing out. The facilitator also has to prune, like a gardener.
ex: A community where nobody posts is dead; one where one person posts just hasn't noticed yet
The test of a good metaphor: people from very different backgrounds all go "aha"

items.d: A few people who already love to talk
One to three newcomers a week
Send notes, create fear of missing out

l213|409.c: The adjacent possible is small but freely chosen; paired with a distant north star, it traces a long arc.
l213|409.e: The adjacent possible is the set of actions within reach that are almost certain to succeed. It's far smaller than the tech world assumes, but every step rearranges the world. A chain of safe small steps can reach outcomes that looked impossible, while avoiding the risk of big leaps. Pure incrementalism gets dragged into a random walk by whatever local need is steepest; pure long-range thinking builds castles in the air. So set a three-to-five-year, low-resolution north star that people find both believable and exciting, pick the step that points most toward it each time, and don't chase false precision.
ex: Arguing whether it's 93 or 95 in five years is pointless; compounding outcomes are either 0 or 1,000
He quotes Tim Urban: happiness equals reality minus expectations

items.d: Three to five years, believable and exciting
Pick the step that points most toward it
Within reach, almost certain to work

l214|412.c: Emotions are signal, not noise: let them pass through first, then read what they're pointing at.
l214|412.e: He agrees with an early coach of his: what you resist persists. A stressful thought triggers fear, fear brings more thoughts, and the two feed each other in a loop. Suppressing it only locks it in; letting it come and go loosens it. Going a step further, he thinks every emotion is useful. Fear says pay attention to a risk, sadness means it's time to let go, anger means something is off, and joy deserves a pause to celebrate. So he objects to leaving emotions at the door. When OKRs are behind and someone admits they're scared, the whole mood of the meeting changes.
ex: He used "don't think of a pink elephant" to show his daughter that suppressing thoughts doesn't work
At Waymo, worry about safety margins was a fear worth listening to

items.d: Something no longer serves the mission
Something new wants to be born

l214|412.c: Once he stopped seeking approval and focused on the product, he got noticed and promoted faster.
l214|412.e: Early at Uber he was fixated on polished demos and being the most right person in the room, and he stayed stuck at senior PM for years. Only after he let go of how he came across and what others thought, and focused on the product itself, did promotions start. He compares chasing approval, control and security to a hungry ghost that can never be filled. Perception isn't irrelevant: executives allocate resources largely on it, and the more senior you are, the more it counts. But it's the finger pointing at the moon. The real result is the product.
ex: Uber Pool: the carpooling product he built the first version of and helped name
He cites the Buddhist line: don't mistake the finger pointing at the moon for the moon

items: Fear the boss thinks I'm not good enough
Aim to build a great product

d.verdict: Let go of ego and the work improves and gets noticed

l214|412.c: Good vision comes from a field you love and years of depth, then reasoning from first principles to ten years out.
l214|412.e: Step one is finding a mission you genuinely love; passion is the fuel for breaking through to a good strategy. Step two is going deep for a long time. He spent ten years in mobility, and six months isn't enough. Then ask from first principles why the status quo is so inefficient. Close your eyes and picture a city five to ten years from now, and derive the trends that are certain regardless of who wins. Self-driving will arrive and keep getting cheaper, but streets full of single-rider robotaxis will induce more demand and worsen congestion, so pooling still matters. This kind of thinking needs long blocks of time away from back-to-back meetings.
ex: Ask why we move one person three miles in a 4,000-pound car
Induced demand: when texts went from 50 cents to free, usage exploded
He incubates alone on runs and hikes, then spends a full day at a whiteboard with eight people

items.d: Ask why the status quo is inefficient

l214|412.c: Balance vision and execution by stage, and if forced to choose, lean toward action.
l214|412.e: Both extremes go wrong. Around 2017, Uber tried to unify driver pricing, incentives and surge into one elegant system. The whiteboard diagram was beautiful, but engineers felt it was boiling the ocean and had no idea where to start. DoorDash, by contrast, sometimes went "ready, fire, aim," bursting through a wall without knowing whether it was the right wall. His approach: when a turn is needed, ease off and think strategy; once the strategy is set, execute at full speed. If he had to pick one side, he'd rather hit the wall, because action at least produces feedback.
ex: Uber's early "future pricing" project got stuck in theory
DoorDash jokes internally about ready, fire, aim

marks.d: Perfect on the whiteboard, hard to ship
Adjust by stage, lean toward action

l214|412.c: Uber is built around the rider and DoorDash around the merchant, and it's hard to be both.
l214|412.e: A company's origin sets its center of gravity. Uber began with getting a ride whenever you want one, so everything revolves around the rider. For a time it treated drivers as interchangeable commodities and later had to reinvest in the driver side. Adding restaurants to Uber Eats was about giving users choice. DoorDash founder Tony Xu grew up in the kitchen of his parents' restaurant, and the mission is helping small merchants succeed. Delivery was just the first form, and broad selection is a byproduct of thriving merchants. Both are good strategies, he says, but trying to do both well means losing focus.
ex: Analogy: Uber is to Amazon as DoorDash is to Shopify

l214|412.c: Building a self-driving car that works is only step one; running a fleet at scale is a different craft.
l214|412.e: Waymo has largely solved driving itself in San Francisco, but building cars on a test track and operating thousands of them are different problems: cleaning, charging, maintenance, vehicle financing, plus the app, customer acquisition, matching and pricing. The core company focuses on perception and planning, so the commercialization team feels like outsiders, and hiring and culture are hard. Uber built the big iceberg below the waterline, which is why it now positions itself as an aggregator. Self-driving companies must weigh owning the network and capturing all the value against using Uber to raise vehicle utilization faster. Most are currently betting on both.
ex: Waymo runs its own Waymo One service while also plugging into Uber in Phoenix
Waymo engineers once couldn't understand why Uber needed thousands of engineers

items.d: Safe, reachable pickup and drop-off points

l214|412.c: Make your life's objective function explicit, and check today's choices against your future self and your mortality.
l214|412.e: He builds matching and pricing algorithms, so he thinks in objective functions, and he noticed most people inherit their life's objective function from parents, church or community without ever examining it. Clayton Christensen observed that many highly successful executives end up with broken families because every Sunday night they chose polishing Monday's presentation over time with their kids, and a string of short-term optimal choices added up to long-term failure. His method is to look back from his five-years-older self and, like the Stoics, remember that life is finite. He also urges stepping out of victimhood and taking responsibility for how you see the world.
ex: Recommended reading: How Will You Measure Your Life
Viktor Frankl felt compassion for his guards even in a concentration camp

terms.d: Write down your values and principles
What still matters in five years
A reminder that time is limited

result.d: Time with his daughter beats one more slide edit

l215|414.c: A hit product can start as a side experiment and grow with a tiny team.
l215|414.e: NotebookLM began as a Google Labs experiment called "Talk to Small Corpus": using a large language model to chat with a single document. At first it was just her and one engineer who did most of the technical work, later joined by the writer Steven Johnson. When it first appeared publicly as Project Tailwind, the team was three engineers plus her as product manager and a designer. For the past year there were roughly seven or eight engineers, and only recently did they hire more to cover the roadmap.
ex: She previously led AI Test Kitchen, one of Google's first public AI launches
She sees the writer Steven Johnson as her de facto product partner

items.d: Three engineers plus PM and designer

l215|414.c: Labs moves fast because leadership sets clear goals, teams are tiny, and normal approvals are skipped.
l215|414.e: Google Labs is about three years old, and its job is to build AI products and grow them into businesses. There is very little process. She admits it may be too little: PMs, engineers and designers write the doc together in one meeting, and engineers start building while the meeting is still going. She thinks this works only because leadership set clear expectations, the team is small, it is allowed to skip the usual approvals, and it can try unconventional tools. She does not think the approach would transfer easily to all of Google.
ex: Labs was founded by VP Josh Woodward
She previously worked on payments and ads, and at startups

terms.d: Write the doc together, build during the meeting

result.d: The cost: maybe too little process

l215|414.c: Build AI products by asking what the model can do, guessing a form, shipping, and iterating until it feels right.
l215|414.e: Audio Overviews was not something users asked for. The team was exploring a new Gemini model and an audio model from another Labs team, and kept asking what these models could actually do. They found that feeding in a single link or a résumé produced a surprisingly good audio show. Her advice: form a hypothesis about the product's shape based on the technology, ship it to learn, then keep iterating until users feel the form is right.
ex: Audio Overviews was previewed at Google I/O in May 2024
She listened over and over; her husband could not tell it was AI

items.d: New Gemini plus an audio model
Until the form feels right to users

l215|414.c: Hearing information changes how people relate to it, so fun is a real product goal.
l215|414.e: She believes presenting information as audio changes how people engage with it and how they feel about the tool. So she deliberately treats delight as a goal, not a side effect. Early users were mostly educators and students, but working professionals now make up a large share. Daily, weekly and monthly retention have all risen noticeably, though she did not share the numbers.
ex: Someone turned their mother's autobiography into an Audio Overview and study guide
A community favorite: a PDF containing only the word "chicken" still produced a show

root.d: Turns sources into a two-host conversation

items.d: Turn course material into an audio guide
A pep talk from performance notes or a résumé
Understand dense papers and keep up

l215|414.c: The real difference is the content studio layer; the long-term goal is any input to any output.
l215|414.e: Audio Overviews runs on Gemini 1.5 Pro with a powerful audio model layered on top. But she thinks the real edge is the "content studio": the layer that shapes sources into a specific format. The current "Deep Dive" conversation is just the first format. People pick their medium by situation, listening on a walk and reading at work. So the long-term vision is an AI editor where any input can become a blog post, a tutorial, a chatbot or anything else, and can be reshaped from one format to another.
ex: One engineer led the work of polishing the laughs, interruptions and tone
Next for monetization: enterprise features like SSO and SOC 2 compliance

items.d: Gemini 1.5 Pro plus an audio model

l215|414.c: The controls users ask for can't just be sliders; the product's magic has to survive.
l215|414.e: Users want to adjust things: go deeper, be more upbeat, be less serious. But when she saw mockups that simply added sliders, they felt completely unmagical. So she would rather wait and find an interaction that gives control and still delights. Mobile is the other big gap. She wants to explore audio you can interrupt at any moment, more like a conversation, and the team is testing what an interruption should feel like.
ex: Near-term focus stays on educators, students and knowledge workers

d.verdict: Better to go slower and keep the magic

l215|414.c: Building in public on Discord and staying close to users beats guessing from inside the company.
l215|414.e: The team iterates in public on Discord and X and puts user feedback at the center. She had worried nobody would join their server. She also recommends spending long stretches with users, like sitting with students while they do homework. The weekend a clip of the AI hosts "realizing they were AI" went viral, she read all of Reddit and Twitter and concluded users had planted instructions in their sources to test the limits, not that the model was self-aware. So she kept the feature up. If it were truly unsafe she would pull it, and the red team would add test cases.
ex: The Discord server has about 60,000 members
One company found staff using it on personal Gmail and asked for an official rollout

l216|416.c: Humans are built to speak; learning to present means fixing bad habits, not starting from zero.
l216|416.e: He thinks the biggest misconception about speaking is how much it can change your life. It works like fitness: you train one thing and the whole person benefits. Once your speaking improves, you feel different at work, with friends, among strangers, even with family. Humans are born speakers; babies need no lessons. But small setbacks while growing up put bugs in the software, people start avoiding it, and the software stops getting updates. So the job is not to learn from scratch but to debug and upgrade what is already there.
ex: Like fitness: you train muscles, but energy and confidence improve too

items.d: Work, friends and family all feel different
The speaking ability evolution gave us

l216|416.c: If speaking isn't fun, your method is wrong. Fix the root cause, not the filler words.
l216|416.e: People talk easily with family and old friends, then switch into a stiff "presentation voice" in business settings and try to control every word in advance. He says that fights the nature of speaking, which is a subconscious skill. So he uses enjoyment as a barometer: discomfort usually means overthinking. His best talks happened when he wasn't thinking about speaking at all, only about what he wanted to get across. So don't count your filler words. Fillers and rushing come from being afraid to slow down and pause under pressure. A flat voice comes from not trusting that you can let go without losing control.
ex: His prompt to students: forget about us, just think out loud

items: Build the safety to let go
Get into flow and stay there

d.verdict: Fix the cause and fillers and rushing disappear on their own

l216|416.c: Three small changes work right away: look up when thinking, land your endings, and never leak your doubt.
l216|416.e: First, looking down while you think reads as unsure and invites interruption; looking up reads as thoughtful and confident. Second, near the end of a talk people snap out of flow, doubt creeps in, and the voice trails off or adds "I hope that made sense." Audiences remember endings most, so plan the landing and stick it, using an opener like "to sum up" to force your brain to wrap up. Third, the audience can't see your nerves. Apologizing or laughing nervously is like a pilot announcing a flashing red light: it creates doubt. Keep it in, and you get treated like a confident speaker, which makes you one.
ex: He keeps a "think up" sticky note on his computer
Brain scans of freestyle rappers: they drop out of flow as the end approaches

l216|416.c: You can't learn speaking without speaking. Short rounds with instant feedback are what actually works.
l216|416.e: Nobody learns to cook by reading recipes, yet people treat speaking as something you pick up from articles and short videos. Even when people do practice, they usually pick one of two weak options: giving lots of talks, which is too unfocused, or memorizing a polished script, which is like knowing one dance routine. Ultraspeaking's games are short rounds with instant feedback and another go, and they are fun, because fun is what keeps you practicing. He compares them to a flight simulator that creates turbulence on purpose to expose weak spots. Easy rounds teach little; the rounds that feel hard are the ones that count.
ex: He gave over 100 talks in 7 months and reviewed every recording
When a test audience checked phones, he rewrote the whole talk in five days and won the semifinal

l216|416.c: Set your energy first; the emotion follows, and the words fill themselves in.
l216|416.e: In the Conductor game you keep talking while shifting your energy to match numbers from 1 to 10 on screen, with a surprise "breathe" page that forces a pause. From it he draws a sequence: energy drives emotion, and emotion brings out content. To be more convincing, first get into a state of conviction and the stories and examples show up on their own. Different energy levels even surface different ideas and memories. The game is also a mirror: some people are good at turning it up, others at turning it down. Daring to slow down means daring to take up everyone's time and attention.
ex: No app needed: have a friend call out random numbers while you talk
Lenny calls himself an introvert, yet high energy came more naturally

items.d: Stories and examples appear on their own

l216|416.c: Most people should speak with more conviction. Fearing you'll become a bullshitter is proof you won't.
l216|416.e: What people with presence share, he says, is that you can feel they believe what they are saying. He estimates only about one in ten people at work need to tone it down. Most never really stand behind their views, so the ideas of louder, more convinced people win. Many feel an immune reaction the moment they try, afraid of becoming slick talkers. But that worry proves you are highly sensitive to bullshit, and that sensitivity will keep policing you. The goal is to speak as well as the bullshitters while actually having the goods.
ex: The conviction-prompt game: start with "I truly believe" or "what surprises me is" and let your brain finish

l216|416.c: Prepare a talk by speaking, not writing: squeeze it down to 30 seconds, then expand it back.
l216|416.e: The usual approach is to write a dozen pages, turn them into a script and memorize it. But what you memorize is written language, like a poem learned as a child: miss one line and everything stalls. The accordion method prepares out loud instead. Give the talk in 3 minutes on a timer, then 2, then 1, then 30 seconds, staying in character and landing the ending each time. By the end only the essence is left. Then expand back up to 3 minutes, deliberately adding content. It is like emptying a living room, keeping only your favorite sofa and lamp, then furnishing it with care. The talk ends up internalized, and you can give it at any length.
ex: One client said going back to 3 minutes felt like having a football field in his head
Works for a whole talk or one section, and takes about 15 minutes

items.d: Stay in character, land the ending

l216|416.c: Audiences usually remember one thing. Start by deciding what that should be, not what you want to say.
l216|416.e: Think back to your last all-hands or talk: most people remember one thing at most. So start by writing the "arrow," the single sentence you would be happy for the audience to leave with. Having it is like carrying a compass. But you can't throw the arrow by hand; you need the "bow" to give it force, meaning the anecdotes, data or stories that support it. Bow and arrow sharpen each other during accordion practice. The same test works for every slide: if a slide can't be summed up in one point, either cut it or split it.
ex: Before going on stage he writes just four lines: one core sentence and three bookmarks

terms.d: The core idea in one sentence
Stories, data and anecdotes that give it force

result.d: The audience leaves with that one thing

l217|419.c: Even in a terrible situation, find the fun. An abundance mindset matters more than any technique.
l217|419.e: She once had to replace her entire team of direct reports in a short time and was scared at first. Advice to "find the fun at work" shifted her perspective and got her through. In practice that means asking what she can learn, opening meetings with a little humor, and passing that mindset on to the team. She believes mindset depends on energy, so she schedules by energy rather than by time. With difficult people, she swaps irritation for curiosity and gratitude: first figure out what they really care about, then connect what she needs to what motivates them.
ex: Her energy bottoms out at 5 to 6 pm, so no hard meetings or strategy docs then
She journaled daily from 13 to 23 and still writes to unpack negative emotions

terms.d: Ask what you can learn, add humor

result.d: You see more possibilities

l217|419.c: With a hands-on founder, a product leader should use the founder as leverage and still go deep on details.
l217|419.e: Good founder mode, in her view, means knowing the business deeply and knowing when to use founder authority to adjust course or change it completely. As CPO she treats the CEO as an ally for pushing key initiatives. When the founder wants a specific idea built, she first finds out the goal behind it. If the approach is wrong she offers alternatives, and she decides in advance which hills are worth dying on. She goes deep herself too: she gathers lots of information but mostly holds back, stepping in only where the risk is fatal or the opportunity is biggest. She has the team present strategy first, then asks questions and floats hypotheses, so it never becomes a one-person show.
ex: A hypothesis she might float: "The security leaders on our customer advisory board say this. What do you think?"

root.d: Knows the business, uses authority well

items.t: Treat the CEO as an ally
items.d: Use founder power to drive change
Offer alternatives if the approach is wrong
Team presents, then she floats hypotheses

l217|419.c: Being strategic means two things: a simple, compelling why, and pushing for hard, big changes.
l217|419.e: She was told she "wasn't strategic enough" both in performance reviews and when interviewing for CPO roles. After studying what people meant, she boiled it down to two parts. First, being able to give a simple, convincing reason for where the company and product should go. Second, being willing to be a change agent who pushes for things that are hard to execute but best in the long run. You need both. A beautiful rationale attached to small ideas isn't strategy, and pushing big ideas without a clear why isn't either.
ex: Rubrik is in fast-moving cybersecurity, and she is working on a three-year plan

l217|419.c: Summarizing well in meetings gets seen as strategic; push the idea one step further and big ideas appear.
l217|419.e: Big ideas rarely come out of thin air. Her daily tool is the summary: in meetings she pulls the different voices together as "here is the customer problem, here is how we'd solve it, here is why we'd win, so here is what we do," then ends with "does everyone agree?" That breaks circular debates and makes people feel heard. Even without adding anything new, a good summary gets read as strategy. After the meeting she tries to improve the idea by one notch, thinking outside-in from the customer problem and how the product gets sold, ignoring technical difficulty at first. That is where big ideas show up.
ex: When she can't get a word in, she writes the summary on a whiteboard or in Zoom chat
Her team uses Dovetail to summarize and search user research calls

items.d: End with a question to confirm
Refine the idea after the meeting
Start from customer problems and go-to-market

l217|419.c: What matters is deciding, not deciding right: commit at 70 percent and correct as you learn.
l217|419.e: It is easy to fall into analysis paralysis, always wanting one more data point. But product leaders always decide with incomplete information. Only after you commit do you leave the thought experiment behind and get high-quality new information. If 70 percent is right, the other 20 or 30 can be iterated, and even throwing away 20 percent of the work beats not deciding. To make teams comfortable taking risks, spell out the assumptions behind each decision, check them afterward, and reward what was learned rather than the outcome. She also recommends being the company "historian" who understands past decisions and the scar tissue they left.
ex: They shipped a high-value feature without charging, and had to figure out packaging later
Before building for a new user segment, work out who will sell it and how

items.d: What you know and don't know

l217|419.c: Take hard feedback by letting emotions pass, then returning curious. Give it by showing you care, then being direct.
l217|419.e: When she receives tough feedback she lets herself feel bad but doesn't push back on the spot. Hours or days later she comes back with curiosity, asks where it came from, and if needed consults a colleague who knows the situation better. All feedback reflects a real perception, but not all of it needs acting on; the filter is what the company needs most right now. When giving feedback, you can't control the other person's reaction, only yourself. Say plainly that you care about them and want them to succeed, then be direct, with no hedging or passive aggression. Ask about their career goals first, frame the issue as how others perceive them, and work out next steps together.
ex: Someone aiming to be a CPO gets different feedback from someone who wants to stay a top individual contributor

items: Act on what the company needs
Frame it as how you're perceived

l217|419.c: The best way into PM is an internal move. New PMs need to learn to resolve ambiguity, not tools.
l217|419.e: Switching company and role at the same time is hard. Inside your own company you already have credibility, so do your current job well, then raise your hand for product-related projects and get to know the product leaders. Support people know customer pain points, salespeople know what sells and how to handle objections, engineers know the implementation details, and all of that is valuable. Most of her Stanford students got in from product-adjacent roles or from "PM plus everything else" jobs at small startups. Students often want to learn tools like Figma, but the real skill is taking an ambiguous situation and steadily creating more and more clarity.
ex: She moved from engineer to product herself when LiveRamp had 20 people

items.d: Take product projects, meet product leaders
No need to relearn the business or tech

l218|420.c: Early companies shouldn't spend big on brand. Use a good-enough logo, then refine once the business works.
l218|420.e: She is a contrarian in branding circles, where people often say brand is everything and worth heavy investment from day one. But working in Bay Area tech, she has seen too many companies pivot because of competitors or technology shifts, so betting early on a full brand vision can be money wasted. A logo can't carry company culture anyway; product and team do that. Early on, an internal team making something good enough for a pitch deck is fine. Once the company has traction, she comes in to keep the original character while fixing practical problems like scaling and avatars, so the brand grows up.
ex: Signs it's time: a major redesign, printing merch, or hosting a conference
A logo set in a free, popular font is easy for copycats to clone

items.d: Good enough for the pitch deck
No big bets on brand yet
Keep the character, fix practical issues

l218|420.c: How much brand matters depends on the company: for some it is everything, for others it should disappear.
l218|420.e: Some companies don't do anything new; their value is repackaging something to make it approachable, like an author who turns medical papers into a popular book. For them brand is everything. But most products should let brand step back and let the product be the star. Sometimes the greatest delight is that nothing gets in the way. Founders with limited resources certainly shouldn't spend half their budget on brand exploration. Her pricing also differs from brand agencies: she separates the copyright buyout from the creative process, so exploration is cheap and flexible and the buyout fee applies only to the final chosen design.
ex: She thinks brand suits an on-demand expert model, possibly paid in advisor equity

items.d: Her example of an early company

l218|420.c: Start a logo redesign by setting goals and scope, then narrow further and finer with each round.
l218|420.e: Some clients just want to fix things they notice that users never will. Others want to reach a new audience without alienating existing users. Once the scope is set, everything else follows. Exploration starts with overall feel, then narrows round by round to stroke weight, letter height and fine details. She hands over files early so clients can try them in real contexts, and she lets them mix pieces of different options. If a client wants to see a purple version, she makes it, because some people need to take the detour to confirm the first direction was right. Readability is a common goal: a new brand has to be read correctly at a glance.
ex: Jeni's Ice Cream's old logo had a J and apostrophe that read as a rude word
Lenny's logo had to stay clear at podcast-thumbnail size

l218|420.c: Non-designers sense type better than they think. Look at lots of fonts and keep asking why.
l218|420.e: People absorb patterns all the time. It is like noticing something moldy on your plate: your body knows before your brain does. So a non-designer can feel that a logo is off without being able to say why. To train the eye, browse a font library, write down the first feeling each typeface gives you, then group fonts that feel similar and look for what they share. Then break your intuition down the way you would break down a song, asking what it reminds you of. This also reveals industry stereotypes: once an industry claims a style, using it means picking a side.
ex: Rounding Helvetica slightly makes it look printed on paper, softer and more vintage
A wedding-invitation script doesn't fit an edgy food-packaging brand
Fintech loves green, so a brand that wants to stand out uses teal

items.d: MyFonts or the fonts on your computer
What does it remind me of
Follow or avoid the industry look

l218|420.c: Good fonts break rules to look right: mathematically perfect letters look imperfect.
l218|420.e: When people with engineering backgrounds learn type design, everything snaps to a grid, and she can spot it instantly. Professional fonts do follow rules, but they break them constantly to counter optical illusions. Where two strokes meet, the join looks dark, so it gets thinned. Geometric sans-serif fonts look perfectly regular but are adjusted everywhere. Her rule: first make it perfect, then deliberately make it imperfect, and only then does it read as perfect. Blow up a lowercase letter to fill a page in Figma, draw a few lines to compare thicknesses, and you will see these tweaks.
ex: The shoulder of a lowercase n or r is often narrower at the top to shed weight
The bowl of a two-story a cuts into the stem to offset extra weight

d.verdict: Make it perfect, then make it look perfect

l218|420.c: A good brand system looks drawn by one hand and is simple enough to need no thick brand book.
l218|420.e: Many clients' brands are like a soup where the ingredients never came together, and her job is to cook it into one dish. Illustration and type should share the same line quality, and colors should stay consistent, because when you squint at a brand, color is what you recognize first. Assets should work like a wardrobe where pieces mix and match, with usable elements for headlines and subheads. Her top goal is a logo so easy to use that normal people get it right, with the assets themselves showing how to use them. If it takes a 500-page brand book to keep things in line, the brand is too complicated.
ex: Lenny's new logo drops the microphone and keeps the campfire and marshmallow
The typeface is Degular, designed by James Edmondson

terms.d: Illustration and type share a line quality

result.d: No thick manual, hard to get wrong

l218|420.c: Variety prevents burnout, and decisively accepting near-perfect beats chasing perfection.
l218|420.e: Early on she had a day job and freelanced at night. The two were so different that it felt like two eight-hour shifts rather than one sixteen-hour one. Now, when her energy fades, she switches to another project, using fresh work instead of rest. The more uniform the work, the faster burnout comes. Her other strength is decisiveness: every problem has ten good answers, so she sorts them into a few categories and picks one that is good enough, without looking at every gray sofa. That last 0.2 percent can eat a lifetime, so she settles for nearly perfect. She also won't hand slow work like adjusting curves to AI; that is her relaxation time.
ex: She asked Claude to list 50 emotions to pick a theme for a new children's book
She opened a physical shop in Oakland so people can touch her work

l219|422.c: Spot real product-market fit, keep knocking, and do the job before you have the title.
l219|422.e: Her Stanford thesis was about why Facebook would win: classmates were obsessed and schools were lining up to get access, which meant the product already fit the market. With no technical background, she simply went to the office and asked for a job, five to ten times. She lost out on a job as Sean Parker's assistant, then got a marketing role and turned down an offer from LinkedIn to take it. She wanted to be a PM, so every evening she went up to the second floor where engineering and product sat and took on work. After months of doing it unofficially she applied, and when she moved downstairs the whole floor gave her a standing ovation.
ex: Sheryl Sandberg's line: when you get a seat on a rocket ship, don't ask which seat

l219|422.c: A leadership team needs more disagreeable givers so a successful CEO still hears the truth.
l219|422.e: She thinks the gap between public perception and the real Zuckerberg is bigger than for anyone else, though it is closing because he learns faster than anyone she knows. In one year he got his Mandarin to about an eighth-grade level, and he also became a good public speaker. His inner circle, the small group, is picked by the most important projects rather than reporting lines, and most members have been there for years and work for the mission rather than promotions. Borrowing Adam Grant's two-by-two, the most dangerous people are agreeable takers and the most valuable are disagreeable givers. The latter push back and argue, which keeps the CEO's feedback loop accurate.
ex: One open-ended strategy meeting and one structured operating meeting every week
Zuck is a learn-it-all, not a know-it-all

cells.d: For the company and easy to work with
Hard to work with and selfish
Pushes back for the company's sake

l219|422.c: Growth accounting showed churn and resurrection dwarf new signups, so retention is where growth is won.
l219|422.e: The early growth team focused on acquiring new users. But once they computed daily net growth as new users minus churned users plus resurrected ones, they saw that churn and resurrection were far bigger lines than new signups. The focus shifted to engagement and retention. They looked for the variable most correlated with retention, found it was adding friends, and set an activation target: 7 friends in 10 days. Whether it was 7 in 10 or 10 in 14 didn't matter much; the value was everyone optimizing toward one clear goal. That goal also produced the new-user onboarding flow for uploading a profile photo and finding friends.
ex: Churned meant no login for 30 days; coming back after that counted as resurrected
After open registration even her father was confused, which showed onboarding was needed

result.d: Churn and resurrection are the big numbers

l219|422.c: The growth team's secret was using data and product to solve problems that used to belong to business teams.
l219|422.e: At the time people assumed new users came from marketing and PR. The growth team believed the product itself was the biggest growth lever, so product and engineering should optimize signup, invites and onboarding. In January 2009 the team paused everything on the roadmap except instrumentation and added tracking to every step of signup and onboarding. First understand what is happening, then identify drop-offs and opportunities, then execute by building product. The same method was later applied elsewhere. Instead of a traditional foundation, social good became a fundraising product. Instead of hiring translators, the user community translated the site directly on the page.
ex: The fundraising product has raised billions of dollars for charities
Community translation got Facebook into more than 100 languages

items.d: Worked for social good and translation

l219|422.c: Growth is mostly removing barriers, but product-market fit deserves far more credit than the growth team.
l219|422.e: She admits the growth team's contribution may be overrated. Facebook had enormous demand, and the team mostly worked at the margins. The recurring theme was removing barriers. At the macro level: from college students only, to high schoolers, work networks and any email address, then to feature phones and Internet.org for people without connectivity. She insisted on not building a separate site for high schoolers, because there is only one social graph. At the micro level it was friction in the flow. For example, 20 percent of users got stuck at email confirmation, so clicking any notification email was made to count as confirming.
ex: They nearly built a separate "Facebook High" for high school students
About 20 percent of signups got stuck at email confirmation

items: Identity: college only to any email

d.verdict: With strong demand, growth means clearing barriers

l219|422.c: A PM is the orchestra conductor, and the first job is extreme clarity: everyone shares the same facts.
l219|422.e: A team has sections like engineering, design, data, legal, policy and communications. The PM makes sure each plays its part correctly and in the same rhythm, without being the star. She finds that many conflicts are really misunderstandings, so she pushes for extreme clarity: people can disagree, but they must share the same understanding of the facts, the options and the trade-offs. Her method is to make everything canonical. Every project has one canonical doc that lays out the workstreams, a single owner for each, the collaboration process, one set of meetings and chat groups, and a glossary. In meetings she projects the doc, edits decisions live, and numbers every list.
ex: People confuse alignment with accuracy: you can all be aligned and all be wrong
Decision meetings get three options plus a recommendation, in a red-yellow-green table instead of pros and cons
Agenda and pre-read 24 hours before, notes 24 hours after

root.d: The one source of truth for a project

items.d: Break the work into clear pieces
One person per piece, all the way down
One set of meetings and chats
Write down what each term means

l219|422.c: Taking on a complex project, build a kindergarten-to-PhD pyramid and start from the basic building blocks.
l219|422.e: She often joins a project at kindergarten level while everyone else is operating at PhD level. So she identifies the most basic building blocks first, then adds complexity back layer by layer, filling in the curriculum at each level. This is not oversimplifying, she says, and the process usually exposes what most needs attention. She has also found that about 80 percent of problems are people or process problems, not strategy. So aim for flawless execution first. If execution is poor and you fail, you can't tell whether the strategy or the execution was wrong. If the strategy is wrong but execution is perfect, at least you learn something.
ex: Teen accounts: users under 16 need a parent's approval to change default settings
She argues Apple and Google should provide age to apps at the operating system level

l219|422.c: A PM can't outsource judgment to process. You have to form your own point of view and state it clearly.
l219|422.e: She leans toward consensus, drives things through people and process, and prefers to be the quiet conductor backstage lifting up the team's first violin. The growth feedback she received was to know when to step forward and lead from the front. She agrees that the PM is closest to what the founder wants, so after hearing everyone out, the PM has to synthesize a judgment unique to that role and express it clearly. To make room for that, she asked her assistant to change the goal of her calendar from efficiency to thinking time: two or three hours of unbroken time each day, plus one or two trusted people to think out loud with.
ex: She often works through ideas with her chief of staff and her head of data
A lesson from surfing: when you're scared, that's when you stand up and face the wave

marks.d: Have a view and say it clearly

l220|18.c: Past a certain level, busyness comes from the scope of the job, and no productivity trick can fix it.
l220|18.e: In roughly 20 years in product, he spent 16 or 17 of them in a constant state of stress, always leaving work feeling something was unfinished. The pressure even turned into physical pain. He tried every technique: to-do lists, his own LNO framework for sorting tasks by how much they matter, working off the calendar. But as you get promoted, the scope grows until no amount of prioritizing is enough. He thinks you have to face that immovable force and ask where the busyness really comes from, instead of hunting for the next productivity hack.
ex: He hurt his back playing tennis and was down for three days; later he realized it was stress

l220|18.c: With a real product strategy everyone has agreed on, annual planning shrinks from four to six weeks to three days.
l220|18.e: Annual planning often eats four to six weeks of filling templates, holding meetings and untangling dependencies. Then a few customer escalations arrive in January and the plan changes. By late February nobody remembers the original, and someone quotes the line that plans are useless but planning is essential. When he ran Stripe Connect, he built a real product strategy at the start of the year and got everyone aligned on it first. Planning then took three days, and he simply skipped templates that added nothing. With a strategy in place, prioritization and escalations have a basis, and nobody argues about eight engineers versus nine, which is false precision anyway.
ex: Stripe Connect, a large Stripe business where he set the product strategy

result.d: Peers took four to six weeks

l220|18.c: Most decisions that look like two-way doors are one-way doors for a product leader.
l220|18.e: Teams often say "it's a two-way door, let's just decide" and start building without working out why users would want it, how it differs from alternatives, or how it reaches users. Sometimes the choice comes down to which engineer is free. In reality the feature ships after six or seven weeks and few people use it. At the quarterly business review, the PM points to praise from a couple of users, sales says it still misses the basic bar customers need, and someone commits more investment on the spot. A feature that should never have been built keeps absorbing work, and the debt piles up. That is where the busyness comes from. His advice: pause for two minutes, two days or two weeks before deciding.
ex: Two-way doors are only truly two-way at Bezos's level
Thinking is cheap, so think more, not less

items.d: Ships and almost nobody uses it

l220|18.c: Taste is recognizing what's good before the results are in, including which ideas you choose to believe.
l220|18.e: When people talk about taste they usually mean pixels and user experience. He cares more about taste in ideas: what you choose to believe shapes how you manage, lead and decide. During his Google years he believed strategy was for MBAs and his job was execution, and he used that line to brush off a colleague who tried to warn him. Around 2014, six months or so into Twitter, he finally saw that a company with a great product, network effects, brand and talent was underperforming because it lacked a real product strategy.
