Stripe confirmed it. Calling Jensen Huang a genius today takes no taste, he says; seeing it in 2010 did.
ex: Game recognizes game, but you have to recognize it before the game starts
Trashing everything once you're senior takes no taste either

items.d: Saw the real problem was product strategy
Early products need clear strategy even more
Examine what you choose to believe

l220|18.c: To really think from first principles, separate an idea from its packaging and who endorsed it.
l220|18.e: He found he was as easily swayed by form as anyone. "Reversible and irreversible decisions" never caught on, but "one-way and two-way doors" did, and the only differences are a memorable metaphor and Bezos's authority. "Fail fast" would be less appealing as "fail quickly" simply because it loses the alliteration. Complex charts and math nobody understands also command respect, and some executives use that deliberately. Stripping away social proof and authority and judging the idea on its own is what critical thinking actually means. That shift was an important part of his growth.
ex: Fail fast and fast follow spread because they alliterate

root.d: Rather than by the idea itself

l220|18.c: Work frustrates you when you spend too long outside your natural level. Plan your career around your superpowers.
l220|18.e: He loved being a product leader yet felt frustrated every day, and the role was unusually lonely. He analyzes work in three levels: impact, execution and optics, meaning how you and your team are perceived. Everyone has a preferred level, and his is impact. The higher you go, the more time goes to optics. He could do it, but willpower is finite, and working against your nature for long leads to frustration. So when his team at Stripe grew to about 50 people, he decided that was enough and went back to earlier-stage products, rather than planning his career around social expectations and LinkedIn comparisons.
ex: Once a team hits 50 or 100 people, optics work almost inevitably grows

d.verdict: Your best work comes from being true to yourself

l220|18.c: Paraphrasing and eye contact aren't listening. Real listening separates world-class leaders from everyone else.
l220|18.e: He finds this the hardest of the four questions. He used to think he was a good listener: he paraphrased, kept eye contact, and said "here is what I'm hearing." Later he realized there is a completely different level of listening, and only people who reach it have a shot at becoming world-class leaders. With almost no time left on stage he didn't elaborate, and instead pointed people to what Rick Rubin and Peter Drucker have written about listening.
ex: Recommended reading: Rick Rubin and Peter Drucker on listening

marks.d: He once thought that was enough
Know the other level of listening

l223|427.c: Getting a product to people matters as much as building it; the key is turning attention into paying demand.
l223|427.e: Many product managers obsess over the next feature and ignore how the product reaches the market. He says the real question is whether you have an unfair advantage: can you grab attention and turn it into profitable demand? AI keeps making products cheaper to build. A prototype can be thrown together with a large language model and Figma. That leaves distribution as the scarcest, riskiest step, so effort should go into docs, adoption, and the parts that are hard to change later.
ex: Blockbuster had streaming before Netflix but never saw the logistics angle

items: Building is cheap, reach is scarce

d.verdict: PMs should treat distribution as part of the product

l223|427.c: Subversion isn't doing evil; it's using a system in ways its designers never intended.
l223|427.e: Starting a company already means rejecting the status quo, so incumbents often call founders "evil." The book's title came from a conversation with Lenny at Year One Labs. Lenny's Q&A product had no questions, and Croll suggested seeding questions himself to show people how it worked. Be just evil enough to push through the change that needs to happen. He sees the ability to subvert as three parts, and says being disagreeable is a skill you can practice.
ex: Netflix treated the US Postal Service as a high-bandwidth, high-latency network
Stanford's $5 challenge: the winners sold their three-minute presentation slot

terms.d: Know the rules you live inside
Find a new move within the system

result.d: It can be learned

l223|427.c: Find your own "zero-day" marketing exploit; once everyone copies it, it's just normal marketing.
l223|427.e: He dislikes the term "growth hacking" because those tricks have nothing to do with the product and anyone can copy them. A zero-day exploit, borrowed from security, is a move nobody has used before and that belongs only to you. Once it is widely used it becomes ordinary marketing, and once it is banned or stops working you drop it. Many clever tricks are only a temporary turbo boost. Lasting growth eventually comes from changing the value chain or the business model.
ex: Coinbase's Super Bowl ad: 60 seconds of QR code, about 20 million visits, servers crashed
IKEA's flat-pack boxes handed assembly over to the customer

items.d: Lasting only if the value chain changes

l223|427.c: Product-market fit is overrated; you also need product, medium and market to fit together.
l223|427.e: The same product can succeed on one platform and flop on another, and the reason is usually the medium: the platform itself and its norms. His scouting canvas has three columns, product, medium and market, and three rows, the objective, collective and subjective views. You fill in the current state cell by cell, then look for a subversive opening in each cell. When generating ideas, think like a supervillain for a while: ignore the guardrails, embrace the absurd, and only afterwards prune with rules to keep the best.
ex: Supporting methods: TRIZ, construal level theory, pre-mortems, counterfactuals
He used the framework to find go-to-market strategies for four startups

items.d: Features and the message they send

l223|427.c: Subversive plays fall into 11 categories, from turning a flaw into a feature to redrawing the scorecard.
l223|427.e: The eleven are: turn a flaw into a feature, change the buyer, borrow a channel, bait and switch, combine, arbitrage, aggregate, reframe, exploit the rules, appropriate a system, and shift the window of what people accept. He thinks reframing means drawing the whole coordinate system, while positioning as April Dunford describes it is a single point on that system. Better to have customers choose you than to have them pick you out of a lineup of competitors.
ex: Salesforce turned fewer features and browser access into a selling point against big vendors
Magic Eraser was aircraft insulation; bridge-inspection drones ended up sold to insurers
Tom's of Maine led with natural ingredients, sidestepping the Colgate-Crest scorecard

items.d: Sell to whoever values it more

l223|427.c: Rules and defaults are levers; rewriting or exploiting them can change behavior dramatically.
l223|427.e: Much of human behavior is set by institutional defaults, so a subversive founder can start with the rules: either push to rewrite them or use the gaps inside them. His classic example is organ donation. With the same kind of population, opt-in and opt-out defaults produce wildly different results. Community activists have also used legal loopholes to turn curbside parking spots into tiny parks. The condition is that you never break the law itself or the intent behind it.
ex: Germany requires opting in; about 12% are donors
Austria defaults to donating; about 99.6% are donors

l223|427.c: "Just evil enough" has hard limits: no lying, no dark patterns, no picking on the weak.
l223|427.e: The goal is to change the world without hurting anyone. His list of no-gos: don't assume consent, don't act without permission, don't lie, don't use dark patterns (interfaces designed to trick users), don't break the law or its intent, don't damage reputations, and don't bully the vulnerable. Afterlife, which scraped obituaries, got sued, and GetSatisfaction's model was close to extortion. Both were too evil. Chrysler built the PT Cruiser partly to lower its truck fleet's fuel-economy average. Legal, but he thinks it crossed the line.
ex: He agrees with Rory Sutherland: do the rational things first, then leave time for irrational ideas

items.d: No lies, dark patterns or bullying

l224|428.c: Progress in AI products is hard to predict, so plans have to leave room for uncertainty.
l224|428.e: Both CPOs had recently stepped into new roles, and they talked about the surprises of enterprise AI adoption and timelines that keep getting disrupted. Models improve so fast that product intuition built up in the past can lead long-range plans astray. So development cycles should be designed around uncertainty, with course corrections along the way, rather than locking in a plan and executing it.
ex: Chapter: surprises and shifting timelines in enterprise AI
Chapter: product intuition when models advance this fast

items.d: Last version's judgment goes stale quickly

l224|428.c: Model outputs vary, so judging progress depends on evals that keep evolving.
l224|428.e: An AI system can give different answers to the same input, so the traditional approach of writing acceptance criteria once and freezing them falls short. They treat evals, the test sets that check how well a model performs, as the core tool for measuring AI progress and shaping a good product, and the evals themselves have to evolve along with the product and the model. Feedback from real users is a key source for filling the gaps the evals miss.
ex: Chapter: why good evals matter
Chapter: how evals are evolving and the PM's role

items.d: Define what a good result is

l224|428.c: AI product managers need to write evals themselves and prototype directly with models.
l224|428.e: As evals evolve, the PM's role in them grows heavier. The conversation named two must-have skills for future AI PMs. One is writing evals by hand, which turns product intent into testable standards. The other is prototyping directly with models, which lets a PM quickly learn what a model can and cannot do, and then make product calls based on that.
ex: Chapter: essential skills for future AI product managers

result.d: Makes product calls amid uncertainty

l224|428.c: For enterprises to use AI well, end users have to be taught and organizational change has to be managed.
l224|428.e: A capable model does not mean a company can actually put it to use. The conversation spent time on how to teach end users to work with AI products, and on change management inside the organization. Both companies' internal use cases were used to illustrate what AI can do today and which capabilities are coming next.
ex: Chapter: educating end users and managing enterprise change
Chapter: internal use cases and future capabilities

items.d: The model can already do the task
Teach end users how to use it

l224|428.c: AI will become proactive and asynchronous, and a model's personality and relationship with users will matter more.
l224|428.e: In the closing outlook, the two discussed how interaction with AI is changing. AI will increasingly take the initiative and complete tasks asynchronously in the background, rather than only answering on the spot when asked. As people interact with models more continuously, the model's personality and the relationship it forms with the user will become an important part of the product experience.
ex: Chapter: the future of proactive and asynchronous interaction

d.verdict: Interaction is shifting from Q&A to proactive, asynchronous work

l225|429.c: Shopify doesn't fight churn. It lowers the barrier so as many people as possible try starting a business.
l225|429.e: Shopify's mission is more entrepreneurship on the internet, and most businesses eventually fail. It charges a subscription, but most revenue comes from payments tied to merchant sales, so it grows along with its successful merchants. The strategy is therefore to make opening a store as easy as possible and get more people in the door. Many fail the first time, but a few who grow into big brands make the whole cohort a success, the way angel investing relies on a handful of winners. The measure is a cohort's total GMV, the money merchants sell, over several years, not whether any single merchant stays.
ex: Shopify is about 10 percent of US e-commerce, with roughly $235 billion in GMV in 2023
Brands that grew up on Shopify include Allbirds and FIGS

items.d: Get as many stores started as possible
A few winners decide a cohort's success

l225|429.c: Many short-term experiment wins add nothing a year later, so you need long-term holdout groups.
l225|429.e: He estimates 30 to 40 percent of experiments that lift short-term metrics show no incremental GMV a year later. Usually they just pull forward something that would have happened anyway, or bring in low-value users. Some flip negative, and occasionally one reveals a group of high-value merchants the short-term metric missed. So every quarter Shopify keeps a 5 percent holdout on all changes. Experiments that only affect new merchants run 50/50, get called after about three weeks, and the winner ships to everyone, but the original groups keep being tracked and the system automatically sends updated results at 3, 6, 9 and 12 months.
ex: Without long-term tracking, still ship short-term winners, just don't overstate the impact
He has seen neutral turn positive, never negative turn positive

l225|429.c: Give teams absolute-number goals, not conversion rates, or they'll quietly tighten the step before theirs.
l225|429.e: The growth organization has about 600 people, and once teams are split by funnel stage, each one tends to treat its own conversion rate as the north star. But the easiest way to raise a conversion rate is to make the previous step harder. Make signup harder and the people who get through are more motivated, so activation goes up on its own. So he has every team look at the absolute number of people who complete their part of the journey. Teams then discover the best move is usually to let more people in. Conversion, retention and lifetime value drop, but acquisition cost drops more, which means more money can be spent to bring in more people.
ex: The overall goal is a cohort's total value over three or four years, within a payback requirement

items: Count people who finish your stage

d.verdict: Ratios are a tempting trap; totals are the goal

l225|429.c: Short-term metrics and long-term GMV often diverge, so a neutral experiment can ship if intuition says it helps merchants.
l225|429.e: Failed-payment reminders were a classic growth win with a clear short-term lift, yet 6 to 12 months later there was no extra GMV. People who let a payment fail were never that committed, and updating the card didn't make them stick around. The reverse also happens. Pre-filling the store editor with images, text and product sections didn't improve paid conversion, but six months later it clearly increased the number of merchants making sales, because a better store that sells early keeps people going. So they ship neutral experiments when intuition says they help merchants. Reducing financial friction also often keeps good merchants who would otherwise have quit.
ex: Financial friction includes trial length, incentives and pricing
Collecting more information at signup to personalize onboarding

cells.d: Far more merchants selling after six months
Up short term and long term
Short-term lift, nothing after a year

l225|429.c: The core product runs on taste and a hundred-year vision with no KPIs, which only works with strong gatekeepers.
l225|429.e: Shopify deliberately has different groups think on different time horizons. Core product builds the foundations of commerce a hundred years out, merchant services build medium-term tools like payments and shipping, and growth owns the end-to-end merchant journey. The core team has no KPIs or OKRs and judges its work by conviction and taste, which lets it take bigger risks, at the cost of sometimes subjective debates. Founder Tobi Lutke believes how you build something technically shapes strategy more than what you build. Abrams's conclusion: either hold teams accountable with metrics or have a very strong founder define taste. Having neither, with teams building whatever they like, is the worst state.
ex: Every launch needs an explicit okay from the group lead
Every six weeks all R&D leads review projects one by one with Tobi
Most of today's big brands will be gone in a hundred years, so bet on new entrepreneurs

root.d: Decides whether teams build the right things

items.d: A few people like Tobi and Glen set the bar
Everyone builds at random, the worst state

l225|429.c: Once self-serve and sales merge, attribution has to be rebuilt, and only incrementality tests show cause and effect.
l225|429.e: Once Shopify's product could serve large companies, it added a sales team. At first self-serve and sales were two separate funnels that never referred to each other. Then merchants were allowed to move freely between them, which broke many metrics and role definitions. For example, someone arrives from an ad, signs up self-serve, then gets handed to sales. That value no longer flows back to the ad, because the two sides use different lifetime value models, so spending gets cut on ads that deserved more. He thinks multi-touch attribution only shows who was involved, while incrementality tests show cause. Get each channel to the incrementality level, then adjust bids and budgets.
ex: Incrementality test: hold back Meta ads from some people and compare results
Large customers are few, so working with sales relies more on qualitative insight

l225|429.c: A high list price with a deep discount signals value and satisfies the feeling that buying is progress.
l225|429.e: When he joined Udemy around 2012, nobody knew what an online course was worth. Listing courses at about $100 evoked college classes and suggested quality. Frequent discounts to about $10 made buying as easy as picking up a book, and limited-time offers added urgency. He thinks education purchases are strongly aspirational. For many people the job to be done isn't just finishing the course but feeling that they are improving, and the act of buying satisfies that on its own. So people come back and buy again, and retention is strong.
ex: The usual deal was 90 percent off, and clearance sales went as deep as 99 percent

result.d: Emotional payoff drives repeat purchases

l226|34.c: The product owner role came from Scrum, not product management, and was meant to help developers prioritize.
l226|34.e: The Agile Manifesto was written in 2001 by a group of software developers, with no product managers involved. The Scrum Guide introduced the product owner, responsible for maximizing the value of the work and defining and ordering the backlog. The first version mentioned in passing that in commercial development the product owner might be the product manager, but the 2013 version most companies used for their transformations dropped that line and never said where the backlog comes from. When big companies transformed, business people, business analysts and project managers were renamed product owners overnight and sent to a two-day class on splitting backlogs and running standups, with nothing on experiments, market research or data.
ex: She first encountered Scrum in 2011 at the startup OpenSky
Other agile methods like Kanban and XP have no product owner at all

items.d: Written by developers, no product managers
Said the PO might be the product manager
Dropped that line; became the transformation blueprint

l226|34.c: Scrum is fine used loosely; followed by the book it breeds endless meetings. Small teams don't need it.
l226|34.e: At OpenSky she never used Scrum dogmatically. Two-week sprints felt too long, so they released weekly. Everyone talked all day, so they skipped standups. The real value of Scrum, she says, is forcing a team to talk about the work and break it down. If you already do that, you don't need the framework. Follow it by the book and meetings crowd out the actual work. That is when to go back to Scrum's own "inspect and adapt" and cut whatever isn't serving the team. Big companies turned to Scrum because they didn't come from software and needed discipline at scale, but it is only one piece of delivery, not a plan for transforming everything.
ex: Some SaaS companies prescribe no methodology and focus on quarterly themes and roadmap breakdowns

marks.d: Too many meetings to get work done

l226|34.c: She doesn't recommend SAFe: it turns product owners into order-takers and replaces product management with process.
l226|34.e: SAFe has the best marketing of any framework and hands executives a big plug-and-play map. But it splits the job in two: product managers do discovery while product owners sit with the development team writing user stories to keep the backlog full. She met a bank product owner who spent nearly all her time writing stories for a login API that already worked. Teams commit at quarterly big-room planning without having done discovery, sprints run back to back, nobody has time to see customers, and developers learn to wait for instructions. Everyone she knows who succeeded with SAFe eventually dismantled it and turned it into something else.
ex: A Dutch water company stuck in SAFe process couldn't collect payments and went bankrupt
Developers with nothing to do should pay down tech debt rather than wait for the PO

items.d: Tells the PO what to build

l226|34.c: Digital transformation needs a product operating model, not just a development operating model.
l226|34.e: Agile methods only cover how software gets built, not go-to-market or product management. When she works with a company she looks at a wider set of questions. Is there a good product strategy? Is the organization built around products, with qualified product managers at every level? Is there product operations infrastructure so teams can get data and reach customers? Do culture and incentives reward output or value? Can a product owner rise all the way to running a product line? Process itself is not the enemy; a company with four thousand teams needs roadmap tools to see the whole picture. Transformation has to be set from the C-suite, because middle-management roles are hit hardest.
ex: Capital One added product management on top of its agile transformation and turned around its credit card business

items.d: Does it connect to company goals
POs can rise to run a product line

l226|34.c: Transformation means training existing staff and seeding experienced people so everyone sees what good looks like.
l226|34.e: Many leaders who buy SAFe have never run a large technology organization and use it as a crutch. She argues for both: invest in developing your own people and bring in people who have done it at every level. Outside courses don't work if people come back with nobody to learn from. At Athenahealth she took 365 people with all kinds of titles, trained them all as product managers and had them practice. Many realized the job meant constantly influencing others and chose to move into operations, data or user research, and nobody was laid off. Then she assessed who was doing well and which teams lacked veterans, hired senior individual contributors or directors to fill gaps, and within a year or two the place looked very different.
ex: Shruti Patel brought what she learned at Shopify to US Bank
Melissa Douros led the transformation at Discover

items.d: See what the work really is
Visible within a year or two

l226|34.c: Product owners should push for strategic work and write resumes about value, not agile process.
l226|34.e: She recommends companies standardize titles to associate PM, PM and senior PM instead of running product owners alongside product managers. As a product owner, ask leadership about your career path, push to join product managers on user research, and ask of every feature what should happen after launch and how it will be measured. She saw one product owner get promoted for saying out loud that the team was building the wrong thing. On your resume, don't list ordering backlogs and writing user stories; describe the problem you solved, who you worked with and the results. A CSPO certificate from a two-day course won't help much with tech companies. Getting onto a strong team, inside or outside your company, is the better route.
ex: CSPO certification costs about $2,500 per person for a two-day course
She saw one company with 47 different titles for product managers

items: Who you worked with and how

d.verdict: Hiring managers look for the value you created

l226|34.c: Software strategy belongs on the C-suite agenda, and big non-tech companies need a chief product officer too.
l226|34.e: Banks, insurers and pharma companies often say "we're not Google." Their approach will differ, but they can still learn the principles of companies that have built software at scale for a long time and adapt them. Today software and digital strategy are deeply woven into company strategy, so pushing it down as IT work means missing out on innovation. Someone at the C-suite table needs to ask how software can make the company ten times stronger and pull ahead of competitors. Big companies have lots of money and little urgency, so they move slowly, and small high-growth startups are disrupting them because of it. She also warns to stay skeptical of people who make money selling certifications and consulting.
ex: She often follows McKinsey into companies to clean up after agile transformations

items.d: A CPO asks how software makes the company 10x stronger

l229|432.c: AI PMs come in three types: platform, model-as-product, and AI-powered. Most PMs will soon be one of them.
l229|432.e: The core job hasn't changed: represent the customer's problem and coordinate design, engineering and sales to deliver impact. What differs is the relationship to the model. Some PMs build tools for AI engineers. Some build products where the model is the core. Most build features on top of existing models and use AI to do their own work better. He expects AI to become a standard component of software, like a database, so nearly every PM will end up with an AI side sooner or later.
ex: Arize moved from monitoring traditional machine learning to tooling for large language models
ChatGPT and NotebookLM are model-as-product examples

root.d: Still about representing the customer's problem

items.d: Builds on existing models, works faster

l229|432.c: Becoming an AI PM is easier than it used to be; the best calling card is working prototypes.
l229|432.e: He studied mechanical engineering and never took a computer science or machine learning class; he taught himself. Building AI products used to require deep ML knowledge, but today you can assemble an app with tools in an hour. His path: learn the fundamentals, follow your curiosity into specific tools, and always keep one customer problem in view. There is no PM degree, so hiring comes down to three questions: can you do the job, do you love it, and are you easy to work with? A portfolio answers the first two before the interview.
ex: He built a subscription landing page on his phone with Replit in five minutes
Karpathy's intro videos on LLMs, which NotebookLM can condense
Cursor and V0 for prototypes, Midjourney for visual storytelling

items.d: How LLMs and machine learning work
Such as a real-time voice API
Fall in love with the problem, not the tech

l229|432.c: AI makes building easy, so a PM's value shifts to deciding what to build and explaining it clearly.
l229|432.e: AI tools are very good at building what you describe, so the bottleneck moves to finding the real problem and stating the requirements clearly. Executives tend to reuse playbooks that worked before, and an AI PM's job is to steer the company toward the uses that actually pay off. Prototypes also amplify a PM's influence. Bringing something clickable to design, engineering and leadership is far more effective than a document. Design, engineering and product are converging into one.
ex: Figma's Mahika Kapoor combines design, engineering and product skills

items.d: Pick the problem, state the need
Steer the company to use AI well

l229|432.c: Top AI PMs don't jump on the chatbot bandwagon; they ask what interface the problem needs.
l229|432.e: In 2023 many companies built internal chatbots on their knowledge bases, and he doubts many people actually used them. A good PM asks whether the solution fits the business need. An AI interface doesn't have to be a chat box; it might quietly speed up a manual process in the background. The same goes for agents: decide whether to build the agent layer yourself or leave it to the foundation model companies and focus on making AI so seamless in the product that it doesn't feel like AI. Many ideas are solutions without a clearly stated problem.
ex: Arize automated its internal data analysis; a small chatbot was only for learning the technology

items: Make AI not feel like AI

d.verdict: Fitting the interface to the problem is where PMs innovate

l229|432.c: Good AI products lower the bar to creating, but leave knobs so users still feel in control.
l229|432.e: He recommends studying products that already succeeded. When cake mix removed almost every step, sales fell; they recovered once customers had to add their own egg. People value what they helped make, which is the IKEA effect. So AI products shouldn't cut the user out entirely. Alongside the automation, keep some knobs and levers people can adjust.
ex: Betty Crocker put the egg back into its cake mix
Waymo riders can still adjust the air conditioning and music
Blue Apron sells the feeling of cooking, not just a meal

terms.d: AI does most of the work

result.d: The IKEA effect: ownership through participation

l229|432.c: PMs must deliver customer value while protecting time for experiments, and can count experiments as a metric.
l229|432.e: The business won't reward exploration on its own, so PMs have to actively protect time for prototypes, hackathons and teardowns of great products. AI features often lack a clear business metric, so start by measuring how many AI experiments the team has run. Hackathons get everyone hands-on and quickly expose which ideas look simple but don't work. Failure is part of iterating, the way a chef in training inevitably cooks some bad dishes.
ex: Arize's on-call Slack bot failed because it lacked context
Weekly live teardowns of products like NotebookLM

items.d: Feed it into the next round

l229|432.c: When the path is unclear, IC PMs should wander and get hands-on instead of waiting for the next model.
l229|432.e: Many companies wait for the next model release before acting; he thinks PMs should explore proactively to find direction. When his team hesitated over betting on LLMs, he personally sent LinkedIn outreach to people with AI in their titles. He learned the sales pitch, understood customers, and showed the team he would get into the details. He also used long-context models to analyze Gong call transcripts in bulk and pull out common pain points. Bringing positive energy into meetings reduces friction, and keeping it fun makes everyone iterate faster.
ex: Be a player-coach, like LeBron James
CPO Aparna: zero-to-one work always feels murky until you find the direction

marks.d: Let the market set your direction
Talk directly to customers and sales

l230|438.c: "That's interesting" means nothing. Asking about price, requesting a trial and introducing colleagues is real pull.
l230|438.e: People naturally prefer to hear yes, and a prospect facing a room of smart founders has no incentive to say "I don't get it." The real signal, she says, is the customer pushing for the next step: asking how pricing works, how soon a proof of value can start, and who on their team you should meet. In B2B the product also has to get through the teams that deploy and test it, and without "we need this now" energy it won't. Putting a little friction in the customer's way actually tests their commitment, and when the product is still rough you shouldn't push hard anyway.
ex: A Fortune 10 company wanted a proof of value and returned a long technical questionnaire the next day
Before the pivot, customers mostly said "keep us posted"

marks.d: Drives it forward, fills in questionnaires

l230|438.c: Saying "I don't get it" can save a company: the first PM couldn't explain the original idea, which forced the pivot.
l230|438.e: The company started just as pandemic lockdowns began. Executives were all at home, so the team could book 10 to 15 customer meetings a day. As the first product manager she sat in for two weeks and still couldn't say what exactly the company would build. She assumed she was the only one confused, then worked up the courage to ask. That exposed the real problem: the story was far too broad. A five-hour discussion followed, the team moved back to cloud security, which it knew best, and customer reactions changed immediately. It depended on a flat culture where saying "I don't understand" is fine at any level.
ex: The company was first registered as Beyond Networks and focused on network security
The founders had previously built Adallom and sold it to Microsoft

items.d: Executives were home during the pandemic

l230|438.c: If the core team hasn't made something work once, hiring an outsider to fix it is wishful thinking.
l230|438.e: Once Wiz found its direction, growth came so fast that the founders and she were closing contracts themselves before there was a sales team. That taught them how a real sales conversation works. Her observation: thinking "if the message isn't clear, hire product marketing; if deals won't close, hire sales" never worked at Wiz. If the core team, with the most context and the most motivation, can't make something work end to end, an outsider will find it even harder. Selling first also gave the first salesperson confidence that it could be done.
ex: The founding team sold to roughly a few million dollars in ARR before hiring sales

d.verdict: Core team makes it work end to end, then hands it off

l230|438.c: A company's heat moves from product to engineering to sales to marketing, and good people should follow it.
l230|438.e: At first the heat is in product, where everyone waits to learn what to build. Then it moves to engineering, which has to build the thing people want. After the first customers sign, it moves to sales. Once there is product-market fit and sales can sell, it moves to marketing, because the field starts asking for more leads. At two and a half years old, Wiz was winning almost every proof of value, yet customers kept saying "if we'd known about you, we wouldn't have signed with the competitor." Awareness had become the bottleneck, so the CEO asked her to take over marketing. However complex a B2B product, she says, buyers are people and brand still works.
ex: She never compares specs when buying an iPhone; she just knows to buy it
The CEO asked her to run marketing in a freezing server room

items.d: People want it, build it fast
Nobody's heard of us, need more leads

l230|438.c: Features can't be taken back, but marketing experiments cost almost nothing, so be bold and make noise.
l230|438.e: Product requires restraint. A new feature eats the most precious resource, engineering time, and in B2B once a customer uses it you can never remove it. Marketing is the opposite: if nobody likes a video, swap it the next day, with no maintenance cost or technical debt. She took over just before the RSA conference. She turned the booth into a Wizard of Oz theme with actors, and swapped the red-and-black scare tactics typical of security brands for pink, bright blue, optimism and "magic." Same spot, same budget, five times as many visitors as the year before.
ex: RSA is considered the Super Bowl of the security industry
They change the booth theme every year, and few other security companies have followed

l230|438.c: Product people underestimate how much a message distorts outside the company. External messaging must be black and white, no jargon.
l230|438.e: Inside product, when someone asks "can we do this," you can be vague and move on. But every layer the message travels, from product marketing to sales to the buyer, amplifies the vagueness until it is lost in translation. Teams live in a company bubble of acronyms and internal names; customers don't. She requires all copy to assume the reader knows nothing about Wiz. She also pushes back on changing a headline or color scheme because the team is tired of it, since customers have only just started to remember it.
ex: Internally they say CNAPP; buyers google "cloud security solution"
No phrases like "the Wiz graph database" that only insiders understand

items.d: In the bubble, vagueness slides by
Needs clear lines they can repeat
Don't know acronyms, search plain words

l230|438.c: Don't wait to cure impostor syndrome. Accept it, expect to fail, and try anyway.
l230|438.e: She admits she expected to fail at almost every job she took, and doesn't think "just become more confident" is a realistic option. What works better is accepting that everyone feels like an impostor and not letting it drive decisions. If someone rejects you, let them; that is their problem. The mindset comes from her mother, who believed you shouldn't invest in what you are already good at and should push children toward what feels uncomfortable, because friction is good. Letting go of the need to succeed made her more willing to take on new roles.
ex: She took the CMO job with zero marketing experience, binged podcasts over a weekend and called several CMOs
Her mother sent a bookish, introverted kid to swim and make friends

items.d: Admit you feel like an impostor
Push into what you're bad at
The bar is lower next time

l232|220.c: The hard part of software is the editor, runtime and deployment chores. Only an end-to-end platform lets everyone build.
l232|220.e: Most people who fail to learn programming don't get stuck on code. They get stuck on installing an editor, setting up a runtime and package manager, and then figuring out how to deploy and share what they made. Most AI coding tools cover only one slice of that cycle. Cursor, for example, is an editor, and you still need somewhere to run and deploy. Replit chose to cover everything from writing code to deployment and monetization. The cost is being too opinionated to fit into a big company's main development pipeline. He accepts that trade-off in exchange for PMs, designers, operations and legal people being able to build software themselves.
ex: About 34 million users worldwide, with an enterprise plan launched in July
Users include lawyers, sales operations and HR operations staff

items: Cover one slice of the process
Easy for big companies to adopt
You still set up runtime and deployment
From code to deployment and revenue

d.verdict: Give up the enterprise pipeline so everyone can build software

l232|220.c: AI agents need a computer interface designed for them; reusing human interfaces is costly and inefficient.
l232|220.e: At the bottom, Replit has a runtime that can install packages for any language. On top sits an editor built for real-time collaboration, and the agent is implemented as just another user on the platform. Beyond human-computer interaction, he says, a new discipline is emerging: the AI computer interface. Large models are like aliens, and having them operate human interfaces through screenshots is expensive, so it is better to turn feedback from the terminal and editor into text tools the model can use. Above that sits multi-model collaboration. Back in 2022 he predicted products would be made of a "society of models."
ex: Anthropic's Sonnet does most of the coding, with OpenAI models used for review
The embedding model used for search was trained in-house

items.d: Terminal and editor feedback turned into text
The agent is just another user

l232|220.c: When building software gets dramatically cheaper, people build far more of it rather than just saving on engineers.
l232|220.e: Most AI developer-tool startups do the math as "make engineers 20 percent more productive and take a cut." His math is to turn everyone into a developer. When cost falls, total consumption rises, the way cheaper electricity leads to more electricity use. Users say getting started is far easier than hiring someone on a freelance platform, so they build ideas they would never have pursued. One-size-fits-all SaaS often doesn't fit, so small businesses are building their own back-office tools. Inside big companies, PMs build a v1 to test with users, then hand it to engineering to put on the roadmap.
ex: A PM at a public company used Replit to build a v1 for user testing
A marketing lead at SpotHero built an app that monitors competitor prices
A partner engineer at X prototypes APIs quickly for customers

root.d: Lower cost and barrier, ideas get built

items.d: Test with users, then hand to engineering

l232|220.c: Once building is no longer the bottleneck, how fast you can generate ideas becomes the key skill.
l232|220.e: Think of work as a pipeline: ideas, turning ideas into something real, then handing it to others to use and collaborate on. In the past there were plenty of ideas and the middle step, building, was the bottleneck. Now that building is unblocked, people are limited by how fast they can come up with new things, and he finds himself running out of ideas to build. Founders benefit most. Instead of describing an idea to engineers busy with the existing product, they can build a concept prototype of the next product themselves. He suggests deliberately training the idea-generation muscle.
ex: Andrew Wilkinson of Tiny is a heavy user
In the demo the agent finished in minutes; he estimates an engineer would need days

items.d: New bottleneck: train the generation muscle
Old bottleneck, now unblocked by AI

l232|220.c: The return on learning to code doubles every six months, but learn AI-native coding, not the traditional curriculum.
l232|220.e: What people call Amjad's law is his claim that the return on learning a bit of programming roughly doubles every six months, because the same skill drives ever more capable AI. Traditional bootcamps start with tools like Git, handing students tools before they have hit the problems those tools solve. An AI-native approach would skip much of the computer science foundation and teach how an application is structured, how to prompt an AI with what you need, and how to read code and debug. Debugging is especially valuable, since an engineer's value shifts to getting agents unstuck. Nobody has built this kind of school yet, he says, and it would be a big business.
ex: Co-founder Haya, originally a designer, spent her first day of coding class entirely on Git

terms.d: How the basic pieces fit together
Read code, get the agent unstuck

result.d: Return doubles about every six months

l232|220.c: Build for the model that arrives in six months. On that curve, a billion-dollar company with zero employees could appear within years.
l232|220.e: In 2022 they trained their own model for code autocomplete and optimized it hard, then realized the interaction model was wrong. When they switched to agents, the models weren't good enough yet, so he told the team to build for the model six months out, and six months later reasoning caught up. If that pace holds, AI will handle maintenance, debugging and migrations, and the next bottleneck becomes reliable architecture at scale: sharding, queues and the like. He imagines someone running a billion-dollar company with no employees within five years. But he warns that when software gets very cheap, prices come under pressure, so staying ahead still depends on fast iteration and generating new ideas.
ex: Current weak spot: database migrations can produce unrecoverable errors
The Bounties feature lets you hire a human programmer to finish the job

items.d: Can build and deploy an MVP
Sharding and queues, the next bottleneck

l232|220.c: Companies should drop fixed roadmaps, break down design-product-engineering walls, and communicate with working prototypes.
l232|220.e: Design, product and engineering talk through language and Slack, which carry little information, so misunderstandings and handoff gaps pile up. The shared language everyone ends up in is code. Once anyone can build a working prototype, communication gets concrete. At Replit, roles move along a spectrum from designer to engineer: design engineers join design reviews and designers sit in engineering meetings. New AI capabilities can land at any moment, so they keep no firm roadmap. When Anthropic released computer use, they tore up their plans and built on it right away. He admits this fluidity is uncomfortable for many people.
ex: A Figma plugin turns design mockups into working React code
PM Aman moved over from a designer role

l233|440.c: Early on the founder is the product, so founder-led sales is about learning fast, not revenue.
l233|440.e: An early company has no brand, no marketing engine and no customers to point to. What moves the market is the founder's unique insight into a problem. She sees three advantages: only the founder can tell the vision, the market wants to talk to the top of the company, and the founder can catch the early signals in conversations. The day-one vision is almost never the one that ends up with product-market fit. Hand sales to someone else and it becomes a game of telephone, and when things go wrong the salesperson gets blamed instead of the vision. So first sell to learn, earn the right to sell, and only then sell for revenue.
ex: Hand-off point: roughly $500K to $1M in annual revenue, depending on how fast you got there
She prefers not to hire salespeople before Series A

items: Correct the vision against the market
You know who to sell to and what to say
Hand to a sales team to scale

d.verdict: Earn the right to sell before chasing revenue

l233|440.c: A cold email should explain relevance and pose a counterintuitive question, never pitch a solution or claim "better."
l233|440.e: She boils effective outreach down to a few points. Start with why this matters to the person's role, which beats piling on personalized details. Then offer a counterintuitive point that makes them pause. Talk only about the problem and why the current way falls short, and hold back the solution so they want more. Keep it to three or four sentences, no scrolling on a phone. Never say you are "better": it can't be defined, a procurement lead will ask how you measure it and then decide to wait another year. Before sending, have Gmail read the email aloud to hear how it sounds.
ex: She landed JJELLYFISH's first 20 customers through cold email
Her hook: "zero-to-one sales talent doesn't exist"
Cold calls often get a higher response rate than email

terms.d: Three or four sentences, no solution

result.d: Leave them curious for more

l233|440.c: Low reply rates usually mean weak insight or a problem that isn't painful, not poor sales skill.
l233|440.e: She warns against staring at one conversion number in isolation. If your win rate is high, a lower outreach reply rate is fine. A low win rate is when you need more opportunities. Mature outreach gets roughly 5% to 7% replies. When the founder sends it and the problem is real, 8% to 15% is possible. She ran two projects at the same time with identical tactics, and the reply rates were 2% and 12%. The only difference was the founder's insight into the market. People say email and LinkedIn are dead, but when the problem is genuinely felt, people reply and get on the phone.
ex: Those benchmarks assume a win rate of 15% to 30%
Exception: blasting thousands of emails with Clay damaged the domain's reputation

l233|440.c: Before any tooling, hand-pick 30 people and write to them carefully, then learn who to target from the replies.
l233|440.e: Engineer founders love stitching sales tools together and blasting emails, then send thousands a day and wreck their domain. She suggests starting with 30 people you genuinely want to learn from, spending 15 to 20 minutes on each email, and reaching them by email, LinkedIn and phone. The search itself is a signal: if 30 are hard to find, thousands will be harder. Then look at what those people have in common and how many replied, and adjust the message or switch to a different role for another round. Once the parameters are clear, expand in small batches, and only at the end let tools do the enrichment.
ex: Targets like high-net-worth individuals are hard to look up, which drags conversion down

items.d: Whether you can find them is itself a signal
Change the message or the role, try again
Run a campaign on the validated group
Enrich with the parameters you learned

l233|440.c: On a first call, admit you're early, hold the demo, and use a few gates to test whether the pain is real.
l233|440.e: Say you're early and have a lot to learn, and people tell you the truth. Say the product is finished and you get polite nothing. The demo is the only card you fully control, so don't play it on the first call. Let the buyer picture the solution themselves first. Then walk through the gates in order: is the problem growing, are they measuring or managing it, and what have they tried, such as hiring someone or buying a tool. When they start pulling colleagues into the next call, they've shifted into buyer mode. Book the next call before hanging up. "I'll follow up by email" usually means a polite no.
ex: Don't ask "what keeps you up at night"; the answer changes every day
Demo cheap tools quickly; slow down for deals worth hundreds of thousands

items.d: A static small problem never gets priority
If not, move on to the next person
Hired someone, bought a tool, or nothing
They're now pushing it forward as a buyer

l233|440.c: About 40% to 50% of B2B companies must first sell a time-boxed service before they can sell technology.
l233|440.e: When you sell top-down, a buyer with no process or strategy for the problem simply cannot buy technology for it. So sell a consulting-style service first: help them design the process and build the internal case. You prove buying intent, get a logo, earn revenue, and get paid to educate the customer instead of watching someone else win them 18 months later when they're ready. Cut the service into 90-day blocks and reassess at each one. New technology like AI especially needs this step: who is in the loop, how success is measured, and what the risks are.
ex: A traditional-industry customer hadn't changed vendors in five or six years, so it paid for process design first
One team was paid to build the customer's pitch to their own boss

items.d: Design the process, write the scope together
Get the logo, shape their thinking

l233|440.c: Win procurement by doing their work and stating your limits; once inside a big company, returns compound.
l233|440.e: Procurement people are professional buyers, and your deal is a small one on their pile, easy to shelve or redirect to an existing vendor. You need to look different, not just better. Drop the jargon, fill in their forms for them, and say clearly what you do and don't do, or you'll be labeled high risk and handed the harshest contract terms. You can split the deal into a services contract and a technology contract and start with services. Know who signs early and prepare their talking points, and don't expect money before the signature. Get through it and you become the preferred vendor, able to expand into other departments.
ex: A CFO asked "what am I signing?" at signature and cost her an extra month
One enterprise deal started at $60K and reached $280K four months later
The sweet spot for a first annual contract is about $50K to $200K

root.d: A second sale inside the enterprise sale

items.d: "Just better" gets you sent to the existing vendor
Fill in forms, simplify the paperwork
Or you get labeled high risk
Services first to carry the technology deal
Prepare their points, avoid a second queue

l234|443.c: Research should target a comically narrow "bullseye customer," not a broad ideal customer profile.
l234|443.e: The bullseye customer is the small slice of your market most likely to adopt the product first. It is a learning tool, while the ideal customer profile (ICP) is the larger group you will eventually sell to. Founders instinctively resist narrowing. But only when the target is narrow enough does the team know what to build first, how to filter feedback, and whom to understand deeply. He finds typical ICP descriptions still too broad for research and adds specific, measurable attributes.
ex: Amazon started with books; Facebook started with college students
The phrase "comically narrow" comes from investor Andy Johns
Gong's and Linear's early ICPs still needed narrowing, in his view

d.verdict: Lock onto the bullseye for research; expand later

l234|443.c: Five customers, three prototypes and one day of interviews are enough to show a team its direction.
l234|443.e: By the fifth interview you reach saturation: the same reactions start repeating. Packing the interviews into one day makes the patterns stand out. With the whole team watching live, shared empathy and understanding replace a research report. Good times to run a sprint: before a big build, when entering a new market or customer segment, and when growth is flat after launch with feedback that is polite but not enthusiastic. Sprints can be repeated.
ex: He has run more than 300 sprints for GV portfolio companies
One founder ran three rounds, then killed a hardware-plus-software subscription project

result.d: No report needed

l234|443.c: Define the bullseye by working back from your key questions; exclusion criteria and triggers are hardest.
l234|443.e: Start with a roughly 45-minute meeting to list what the team most wants to learn, such as what keeps the customer up at night and what has to be true for the product to succeed. The questions decide whom to recruit: to study onboarding, recruit new users. Teams usually agree on inclusion criteria; exclusion criteria are where an outside push helps most. Trigger events determine whether someone is ready to act right now. You end up with about seven attributes. The first version is a hypothesis, and after the interviews a key distinguishing trait often appears that nobody had noticed.
ex: Specialty pharmacy delivery: cold-chain patients care most about predictable delivery windows
Exclude healthcare workers and people whose spouse manages their prescriptions
A newly hired CSO or a marriage or new baby are classic triggers

items.d: Industry, size, role and so on
Experts, people locked into a competitor
What makes them ready to act now

l234|443.c: Be ruthlessly picky when recruiting; if a group is nearly impossible to find, that's a warning sign.
l234|443.e: He turns every criterion into a specific, measurable screener question and hides the "right" answer so nobody can game it. Platforms like User Interviews bring in hundreds of responses in three or four days, and he picks from them in a spreadsheet. Pay a full standard hourly rate, and pay professionals their own hourly rate. Confirm the NDA and send repeated reminders so people actually show up. If the target group is almost unreachable, either loosen the criteria a little or ask whether you could really sell to these people.
ex: Standard pay is about $125 an hour; lawyers about $400
Oncologists require associations, conferences or snowball referrals

items.d: Compare line by line in a spreadsheet

l234|443.c: Make three very different bare-bones prototypes and test with words, not features.
l234|443.e: Each prototype stands for a different value proposition or feature mix. Most are just a static landing-page image or a PDF, and the key part is one headline that says clearly what problem it solves. Give the three distinct color schemes so observers can follow along, and proofread carefully, because typos undermine credibility. He warns against over-polishing just because AI can produce prototypes quickly. Keeping them simple avoids committing too early to one direction. Letting people compare three options, like shopping for a couch, draws out the best part of each.
ex: Competitors' products are free prototypes
Green, blue and red to tell the three options apart

l234|443.c: Past behavior beats stated intent, and only visible excitement counts as a real demand signal.
l234|443.e: Each hour-long interview has two halves. The first covers the person's past and present experiences, attitudes and specific stories. Only in the second half do the three prototypes come out, and the first half gives context for the reactions. People are bad at predicting their own behavior, so if interest in a prototype contradicts someone's history, he is skeptical. Polite, neutral encouragement really means no. Someone asking whether they can sign up right now is a strong signal. Interviewers should use humble inquiry instead of selling, which founders find hardest.
ex: Edgar Schein's humble inquiry
Open with a big smile and ask where they're calling from

l234|443.c: The whole team watching live, after writing down predictions, drives action better than any report.
l234|443.e: He interviews over Zoom while the team watches backstage, taking turns at handwritten notes. AI note-taking is banned so nobody half-listens. Between sessions everyone fills in a debrief sheet organized by the key questions. Before the sprint each person writes predictions and compares them with the results afterward, to counter hindsight and confirmation bias. At the end everyone silently writes takeaways, then the decision-maker walks the group through the patterns. He warns that domain experts overestimate how much customers know, how much pain they feel and how much they'll pay, and that research usually fails because recruiting wasn't picky enough.
ex: The biggest watch party was about 40 people
Core product team members must attend the whole day

items.d: Compare with predictions, set next steps

l235|444.c: Being a founder is a state; being a CEO is a craft, and "founder mode" excuses not learning it.
l235|444.e: He has asked many investors three questions. What does the ideal founder look like? Courage, resilience, insight. What does a great startup CEO look like? All skills: building product, selling, hiring, fundraising, financial planning. How does a founder learn those on the job? Nobody has an answer. He believes each stage, from launch to growth to scale to exit, demands different abilities, so you have to keep learning the whole way. What makes founders special is that they can dive into any detail and make a difference. The key is knowing when to dive in and when to get back in the cockpit.
ex: Stage one: build something people will buy; stage two: build a company around it
He finds that well-run companies all share the same operating rhythm

terms.d: Courage, instinct, persisting despite the doubters

result.d: Both matter equally; neither is optional

l235|444.c: Most CEO failures come from a few recognizable personality traps, and everyone has a bit of each.
l235|444.e: Companies die for a few reasons: the wrong market, the wrong product, founder infighting (he says more companies die by suicide than murder), and poor execution, which ultimately lands on the CEO. His firm gives the failure types playful names: the Robot who denies emotion, the People Pleaser who wants to be liked and won't decide, the Perfectionist who stalls for fear of mistakes, the Angry One who takes it out on others, the Delegator who hires good people and vanishes, the Micromanager who trusts no one, and the ones who ride the brake or the gas the whole time. Most CEOs mix several. Admitting it is the first step to being coached.
ex: The Perfectionist ships the most beautiful product minutes before going bankrupt
Employees are either adults or children; micromanaging treats adults as children

items.d: Wants passion from staff but cuts off emotion
Seeks consensus, won't decide, hides bad news
Fear of error slows everything; no one takes risks
Either nobody manages, or nobody is trusted
Afraid to spend, or burns it all fast

l235|444.c: The most common failure is "fire, then aim"; the cure is choosing the summit and planning backward from it.
l235|444.e: Cheap capital used to hide bad execution, he says, and now investors want founders to be better operators. At any moment a company is heading toward one of four endings: an exit, the next funding round, profitability, or shutting down, and you must pick one. If it's the next round, write down what has to be true to raise it, turn that into measurable outcomes, then set the actions, cadence, resources and accountability, and check direction with weekly and monthly feedback loops. He also objects to setting a revenue target and back-filling funnel numbers. Instead, project forward from the last few months of real data, then talk about the gap.
ex: "I have to hit $3M or I'm dead" means, he says, that you're already dead
His old boss's line: do what you've always done, get what you've always gotten

items.d: Exit, next round, profit, or shut down
Write it down, in words and numbers
Who does what, how often you review

l235|444.c: The best early exit isn't a formal sale process; it's making someone at the buyer fall for a future fantasy.
l235|444.e: He turned independent banker Ezra Roizen's Magic Box method into a teachable process. A traditional sale means listing buyers, sending letters, waiting for bids and getting ground down on price, all based on past results. Magic Box is built on the future. Big companies want the small company's technology; small companies want the big company's distribution. Someone inside the buyer is already imagining what happens if they own you. Three steps: understand that person's fantasy, help this champion get evidence they can take upstairs, and then invite them to model the future business with you. Once they start responding to your model, you've won.
ex: Instagram sold for about $1 billion with almost no revenue
A construction-tech company with under $2M in revenue was bought by a public company

items.d: Give them evidence that passes committee
Model it together; talk future, not past

l235|444.c: Advance an acquisition by seduction, not pressure, and never negotiate live with corporate development.
l235|444.e: Enterprise sales often closes by manufacturing urgency, but in this kind of courtship, waving other buyers around is usually a negative signal until the very end. A better line: I was planning to raise my next round in Q1 and stay independent, and the valuation then may make this deal no longer make sense. Know the roles on the other side too: the champion fights for you, friendly bystanders only provide intelligence, blockers can veto, and the buyer only looks at numbers. Corporate development teams are skilled negotiators and can give the deal momentum, but move the negotiation to writing, asynchronously.
ex: First contact: founder title plus one line, "got 30 minutes to chat?"
Host an expert forum, invite the target's CEO on stage, and meet as a peer

d.verdict: Make the champion want to say yes; give no reason to say no

l235|444.c: Don't hire from a job description; define success a year out and find someone who has already done it.
l235|444.e: A CEO has three jobs, he says: make sure everyone knows where you're going, pick the right people, and give them the tools to win. Following the book "Who," start by writing down how the business will be different a year after this person joins, then look for people who have already achieved those things. Check whether former bosses keep pulling them into their next job, and use a culture interview to test values. Executives come in three kinds: architects who write the playbook from scratch, optimizers who make it more efficient, and scalers who find leverage for 10x. Same title, very different skills. To hire an architect, find someone who has been one.
ex: Screening question: how many former bosses would call to rave about you?
For junior sales hires, look for any experience selling anything

items.d: Are they your kind of people?
Have they done it, and which kind are they?

l235|444.c: Go-to-market breaks into four parts, and the costliest mistake is selling before defining the ideal customer.
l235|444.e: He breaks the messy move from founder selling to a sales machine into four parts. First, the ideal customer profile: who qualifies, what discovery questions to ask, and what disqualifies someone. Second, positioning: what makes you different from competitors or the status quo, and how the brand expresses it. Third, demand generation: list every channel and run high-impact, low-cost experiments. Fourth, the sales playbook: discovery, objections, demos and closing. First-time founders, he says, are like kids at their first bar, wanting to date anyone who glances at them. Find the customer who loves you most, focus on a small band of fanatics, and leave adjacent markets for later.
ex: Amazon started by selling only books
Use written brainstorming to tone down the founder's megaphone effect

items.d: Who qualifies, what to ask, who to drop
What sets you apart from alternatives

l235|444.c: In life-or-death moments, don't let fear decide; trust the small voice you hear when things go quiet.
l235|444.e: CEOs keep facing existential moments: whether to sell the company, split with a co-founder, or fire a key employee. Fear and the "lizard brain" are terrible decision-makers, he says. The small voice you hear alone, on a walk or during exercise is the real you; the brain is just a pattern-matching tool. He separates this from founder mode: the sudden urge to take over and fire three people is a fear response, while a judgment reached after sitting quietly and backed by data is intuition. Hearing real intuition requires sleep, good food and people who love you.
ex: One founder heard that a partner was wrong early on, yet took a year to split

marks.d: Am I going to be ruined?
Do it myself, fire three people
Backed by data and gut feel

l236|447.c: Quality means meeting the spec; high standards means raising the spec for users, not withholding for perfection.
l236|447.e: He defines good taste as knowing what other people want a little before they do. A weird thing only you like isn't taste. Quality isn't luxury or perfection; once you meet the spec, you're done. If the spec isn't good enough, change the spec. Holding back something that already meets the spec in the name of perfection is really hiding. At Spinnaker, the team's standard was to satisfy the buyer they had described in advance, not to please the boss. If you only work for your boss, he says, don't expect rewards beyond your job description.
ex: Licorice dipped in peanut butter: you're allowed to eat it, but it isn't good taste

items: Won't ship even after meeting spec
Ship when the spec is met
Keep raising the spec for users
Judged by whether the buyer is happy

d.verdict: Improve the spec instead of delaying the launch

l236|447.c: A brand is a promise, not a logo; AI will soon be like electricity, so win by keeping a hard promise.
l236|447.e: Hyatt has a logo, he says; Nike has a brand. We can picture a Nike hotel, but nobody can imagine Hyatt sneakers. Building a brand means standing for something and saying what you won't do. The test is loyalty: would you pay more for it? Airlines keep people with miles, and that's a bribe, not a brand. He expects AI to become infrastructure like electricity, so companies should ask what benefit they give users, then make a difficult, excellent promise and keep delivering on it. Overpromise to consumers and you only get to break it once.
ex: He'd pay more for Claude because it's humble and says clearly when it doesn't know
He finds ChatGPT often overpromises and underdelivers

terms.d: Stand for something, say what you won't do
You only get to break it once

result.d: People will pay more for it

l236|447.c: Choosing your customers, competitors, source of approval and channel is choosing your product and your future.
l236|447.e: Product people often treat these four as givens, which means giving up the most important freedom they have. Choosing the smallest viable audience decides the product's language, price, technical bar, and even who you deal with every day. Choosing a competitor chooses the battlefield; compete with Walmart and don't complain when it cuts prices. Choosing your source of approval means one conversation with your boss agreeing that the 400 target customers are the ones to satisfy, not the boss. Change the channel and everything about the product changes. People avoid these choices, he says, mostly out of fear.
ex: Humane's AI Pin chose customers who expected an Apple-grade finished product
Find 400 tinkerers on Product Hunt and you can improve as you go
A two-person team wanted both Shopify and enterprise channels; he told them to pick one

root.d: Not choosing means giving up control

items.d: The smallest viable audience shapes the product
Decides which battlefield you fight on
Please the boss, or the target customer?

l236|447.c: Good strategy runs on tension, not stress: make a promise that might fail, so people root for you to keep it.
l236|447.e: He separates stress from tension. Stress is two needs pulling against each other, like hating your boss but needing the job, and nobody should seek it. Tension is "this might not work." It's the unfinished melody the listener wants to complete, and he sees it at the heart of every art form and every innovation. When you launch a product and say it can do something, people start imagining how their life would change. Once they fall for that possibility, tension appears: are you telling the truth? The future you paint must rest on empathy. It has to be where they want to go, not where you do.
ex: As a kid, PF Flyers sneakers promised he'd outrun the bullies, and didn't deliver

items.d: Life might change because of it
Is it true? Will it work?

l236|447.c: Only things worth remarking on spread by word of mouth, so decide in advance what you want users to say.
l236|447.e: To judge whether a startup has a chance, he first asks whether users stick around, then whether they tell friends and what they say. "Remarkable" literally means worth making a remark about. It isn't a stunt or a viral video; it's that talking about you makes the user's own life or status better. For a SaaS product, if telling others about you makes the product work better for the user, the marketing problem is mostly solved. Otherwise, don't expect Apple to recommend you. Marissa Mayer insisted Google's homepage have only two buttons, which is itself a promise to take you straight where you're going, and he happily sends lost friends there.
ex: While he was at Yahoo, Yahoo had the chance to buy Google for $10 million
Word beat WordPerfect because coworkers needed the same file format

d.unit: Links and buttons on the homepage

items.d: Lets users browse on their own
Promises to take you straight there

l236|447.c: Strategic thinking means seeing the system; what scares you is often what the system wants you to fear.
l236|447.e: People can't cooperate without systems. Handshakes, zip codes and the metric system are all useful. But once a system forms, it runs to protect itself and invents a culture of "this is how we do things here." So when something scares you, he suggests asking which system would be offended, and whether you should go along with it or have enough leverage to change it. You don't have to be reckless, but you do have to recognize the system. If you can't see it or name it, you just repeat the past.
ex: One company's last four hires had all captained Ivy League tennis teams
Early on, people warned him downloadable software would be pirated; he thought it worth trying

items.d: Born for cooperation, useful at first
This is how we do things here
Can't change what you can't see

l236|447.c: Buzz doesn't sell products; you win customers with things that genuinely change their experience.
l236|447.e: Jaguar didn't rebrand, he says; it changed its logo and threw away a lot of what people already knew about it. A new carmaker spends a fortune earning trust, and Jaguar already owned a much-loved brand. IHOP's fake name change and Oreo's timely tweets got plenty of attention with no evidence they sold more. By contrast, the early Model S's pop-out door handles got strangers talking, and owners could invite them in for the brutal acceleration, which made a story worth telling. The Cybertruck deliberately divided people and wasted the pickup truck, the biggest vehicle category in America.
ex: In Ludicrous mode, the Model S went from 0 to 60 mph in about 2.4 seconds
In some years the Ford F-150 made more profit than Ford as a whole

cells.d: Model S door handles plus the acceleration ride

l239|451.c: A streak threshold should match the product's unit of use: too hard punishes real users, too easy attracts the least engaged.
l239|451.e: Originally the streak required hitting a self-set XP goal. Users who did several lessons in a day still lost their streak because they'd set the goal too high. Switching to "one lesson a day" produced a big jump in daily active users without cheapening the streak, because a lesson is exactly Duolingo's unit of use. They later tried counting a single exercise, and DAU didn't move at all. It only captured the least engaged users, who did one or two exercises and left, so it was turned off quickly. Before designing a streak, he says, decide which habit you're building and how engaged a user you're serving.
ex: More than 9 million users currently have streaks of over a year
XP still powers the weekly leaderboards of 30 users each

marks.d: Matches the unit of use; DAU jumped
A high goal breaks streaks by mistake

l239|451.c: The first seven days decide retention, and letting users choose and commit to a goal beats choosing for them.
l239|451.e: The data shows retention jumps sharply with each day of streak from one to seven. After day seven, loss aversion kicks in and the curve flattens, so the team poured experiments into that window. The streak goal feature started as a single line of copy. They tested different day counts, then added an "I can't do this" opt-out button. Surprisingly, adding the opt-out was itself a big win, because saying yes became a conscious commitment. Later they pre-selected a harder goal on the choice screen to speed things up, and it clearly lost. The act of choosing, he says, is where the commitment comes from.
ex: The copy: people with a 30-day streak are about 7 times more likely to finish the course
Changing the button from "Continue" to "Commit to my goal" was a big win

items.d: A 30-day streak makes finishing more likely
Actively saying yes was itself a win

l239|451.c: Flexibility is the biggest DAU driver, but tighten it as streaks grow, and someone must guard the streak's meaning.
l239|451.e: Going from one streak freeze to two was a big win. It lowered same-day retention, but people who missed a day came back far more often. Three freezes were no better than two, because people gone three days are much harder to bring back. Giving new streaks two freezes up front worked remarkably well, since a short streak that breaks just restarts, and the goal is to get people to day seven. A free "streak repair" beat paying gems to fix it, because users felt they'd earned it. But long-streak users don't need much flexibility. Make it too easy and people stop caring, so someone has to protect the streak's sanctity.
ex: The perfect streak turns gold after a week with no freezes; no reward, yet it works
Changing how freezes are bought sometimes costs a little revenue

cells.d: Teaches skipping; the streak loses value

l239|451.c: Making the streak understandable beats a clever metaphor, but leave room for moments of celebration.
l239|451.e: Many users genuinely don't understand how streaks and freezes work. His first winning experiment after joining was eight words at the bottom of the streak screen explaining the rules, which added tens of thousands of DAU and ranked among the top three retention wins. The flame metaphor got no reaction in user research in India, so the redesign made the ticking number the hero. The more the calendar at the bottom looked like a real calendar, the more users understood it was a daily thing. Clarity doesn't have to kill delight: animation and haptic feedback make people pause on key screens and enjoy the achievement. Complex features wait until a user has made it past day seven.
ex: The copy, roughly: do a lesson every day to extend your streak; miss a day and it resets
Duolingo recently bought a Detroit animation studio just for motion and haptics

items: New users don't get the rules

d.verdict: Form follows function; save celebration for key moments

l239|451.c: Notifications should follow real behavior and what users care about; even a late-night nudge can feel kind.
l239|451.e: Users used to set their own practice reminder time, but life always got in the way. The team found the best predictor of when someone will practice is when they practiced the day before. They tried many elaborate approaches, and "23.5 hours after the last practice" won every time. The other notification is a 10 p.m. streak-saver reminder. It looks annoying, but users care about their streak, and most see it as timely help. Whether a notification is welcome, he says, depends on whether the feature it's tied to feels positive or negative to the user.
ex: At a company party, everyone was rushing to finish their lesson after 11 p.m.

items.d: Real behavior is the best predictor
Last chance; most users see it as kind

l239|451.c: Run many small experiments with a hypothesis, kill neutral results, and reset when you hit a local maximum.
l239|451.e: In four years the streak feature went through more than 600 experiments, roughly one every two days. About half failed, but all taught something. Hypotheses usually come from wins already proven by other teams or by games. The bigger the change, the stronger the hypothesis needs to be, while copy tests are cheap enough to just try. They deliberately avoid a big, complete V1, isolating the core hypothesis first and layering on from there. A new element with a neutral result gets turned off to avoid adding cognitive load. A win that hurts the core experience may not ship either. And once optimized into a local maximum, they rebuild a simpler version that performs just as well.
ex: Showing XP inside lessons won, but was stopped because it distracted from learning
CEO Luis reviews every experiment and often says "if you want to try it, try it"

items.d: About half fail; kill neutral results
Dig deeper when you strike gold

l239|451.c: Organize teams around metrics, not features; a streak can only amplify a product people already want daily.
l239|451.e: Duolingo's north-star growth metric is DAU. Research showed the strongest lever on DAU is whether existing users come back the next day, so the retention team owns that metric. Streaks just happen to move it most, so the team has "soft ownership" of the streak and other teams can change it too.
