A streak, he says, is an engagement hack built on loss aversion, and almost any app with a usage frequency can use one. But if the core experience isn't worth opening daily, building a streak only wastes focus. Board member Bing Gordon reminded them that users care about the streak because Duolingo itself treats it as important everywhere in the UI and messaging.
ex: Peloton uses weekly streaks to fit a few-times-a-week rhythm
His predecessor PM said the streak wasn't even 30% optimized

items.d: What moves the returning rate most
Users already want to come daily

l240|452.c: When you have a choice, take the harder path: even if you fail, you learn and meet smarter people.
l240|452.e: Take the easy path and win, fine. But if you fail, you're left with nothing: no skills built, and few smart people met along the way. Take the hard path and even a failure means you did hard things, worked with strong people and picked up skills you can carry. The condition is choosing the right people, not hardship for its own sake. He also wrote down his own job-choosing framework to resist the pull of titles and pay, and has quit when it was violated. Knowing he's bad at ten-year vision, he pairs with people who have "unreasonable" foresight and pushes things forward 1% a week himself.
ex: Instead of sending 10 resumes a day, build an app on the Shopify API
He minored in electrical engineering in computer science, and in financial engineering during his MBA

cells.d: No learning, no strong people met

l240|452.c: Not caring about looking stupid is a superpower; asking dumb questions and trying dumb things is how you learn fast.
l240|452.e: He regularly asks what others call "the dumbest question," and keeps asking until someone says they've explained it three times already. The point isn't to annoy people but to actually understand. Half the time others had the same question and were afraid to ask. He credits his tolerance for rejection to an early commission-based retail job: get turned down, move to the next customer. Experiments need guardrails, though. Don't take Shopify down to try a new config. His motto is "everything you know is wrong," meaning you should be able to rebuild your understanding from first principles.
ex: He screenshots messages from people calling his question stupid
At home he tries random washing-machine modes; he's ruined clothes and found time-saving settings

items.d: Others often wonder the same thing

l240|452.c: Intensity means doing more per minute, not working longer hours, and pair programming is the most underrated tool.
l240|452.e: An hour is an hour for everyone. Rather than stretching the day to 12 hours, burn more energy in 8. In pair programming two people share one computer, so nobody browses the web, and newcomers often sleep ten-plus hours the first few nights. Less code gets written, but the bottleneck was never typing; it's finding the elegant solution. Pairing also spreads knowledge and leaves fewer single points of failure. Shopify is an exploration-type company, and people pair roughly 4 to 8 hours a week. AI coding assistants now act like a pairing partner too, but he still wants two humans plus an AI.
ex: Like Shaq refusing underhand free throws: it works but looks silly
Top performers produce high-quality work in less time

items.d: Tobi and the CTO set a one-hour timer
You understand it best right after writing

l240|452.c: Frequent check-ins aren't surveillance; they're leaders solving problems with the team to keep up the pace.
l240|452.e: He believes in Parkinson's law: work expands to fill the time given. So every Shopify project posts a weekly update, ideally with a demo you can try. A director and then a VP confirm the direction and the architecture, and every six weeks CEO Tobi reviews all projects. Feedback from a review gets acted on the next day. At Shopify, he says, "micromanagement" isn't an insult; it means a leader with wider context pairing with the team on a problem. Reorgs land within a week or two, with no drawn-out change management. If two or three projects aren't on fire, you aren't taking enough risk.
ex: After one review he asked in a shared channel, and the model vendor raised the output limit within an hour
PMs record "friction log" videos, giving feedback while using the beta

items.d: Text plus a demo you can try
Does it fit the overall architecture?
Walk through every project with Tobi

l240|452.c: Periodically deleting every recurring meeting and moving announcements out of chat cut engineers' meeting time in half.
l240|452.e: Recurring meetings have inertia; once they exist they rarely die. Once a year, on a random day, Shopify deletes every internal recurring meeting with three or more people, except one-on-ones, interviews and external meetings. For the next two weeks nobody may create a new one, which forces everyone to rethink whether a meeting is needed and how often. The other move was taking status updates and broad announcements out of Slack and into a feed-style tool people read when they choose, which cuts interruptions. Those two changes alone sharply reduced meeting hours for frontline engineers and bought them more focus time.
ex: The meeting purge was originally inspired by Dropbox
Announcements moved to Workplace, which was later discontinued; they're still looking for a replacement

d.unit: Meeting hours per week (his rough recollection)

l240|452.c: Instead of building one feature, build a platform where anyone can build it in an hour, and keep deleting code.
l240|452.e: During the crypto boom, merchants wanted a "you need this NFT to enter the store" feature. The team estimated two or three weeks. Tobi instead had them spend two or three months building an open API layer so anyone could build that kind of feature in an hour, because nobody knows what else will grow on top. Every piece of work, he says, should first be classified as an experiment, a feature or infrastructure. When Tobi says something "could be written in a day," he means: what has to be true first for that to be possible? Code is a liability. A lean codebase gets performance, reliability and maintainability for free.
ex: At hack days a team always just deletes code, often over a million lines
He'd rather see Copilot delete a million lines than write a million

items: Anyone can build it in an hour
Unknown use cases can grow too

d.verdict: Fill the tank and everyone drives further

l240|452.c: Interviews barely predict performance, so make hiring look like real work; trials and internships work best.
l240|452.e: At his startup he hired two people at once: a PhD from a top school, and someone he met in a coffee shop who had never worked in software. The PhD left within weeks as a poor fit; the other is still an outstanding Shopify engineer. Like picking a race-car driver by putting them in the car, he prefers work trials: 90 days to see whether it fits, with honest conversation on both sides. In interviews, a "life story" section asks why each choice was made, to test curiosity and breadth. Internships are trials at scale: four months of real output beats eight hours of interviews.
ex: At his previous company, about 20% left within the 90-day trial and under 1% after
Shopify plans about 1,000 interns in 2025, in the office three days a week
He once hired a great waitress who went on to become an HR director

marks.d: Performance often unrelated to the job
Asks why they made each choice

l240|452.c: Hedging is the worst choice; not taking a risk deserves more criticism than taking one and failing.
l240|452.e: In his first week in 2019 he had to pick a technology for rebuilding the point-of-sale system, and he hedged: native Swift on iOS to make sure the product shipped, React Native on Android to learn. A year later the iOS version succeeded. Six months after that the Android version was done, and the team realized React Native was the future, so iOS had to be rewritten. He estimates it wasted about 100 engineers for 18 months. Tobi's response was to have him tell the story to everyone, saying he only punishes people who don't take risks. His lesson: he never does anything halfway, so he should have trusted that a fully committed path wouldn't fail.
ex: Shopify has since become a core contributor to React Native

items.d: Native on iOS, React Native on Android
React Native turned out to be the future

l241|455.c: In a noisy world, try every tactic first, find the one that works, then scale it into a strategy.
l241|455.e: When launching Agentforce, he didn't know which move would matter most, so he tried them all at once: turning the entire Dreamforce conference into an Agentforce event, having celebrity friends shoot ads and posting them on Twitter first to gauge the reaction, making Salesforce's own help center "customer zero," training the sales force, running competitive marketing against Microsoft Copilot, and hiring one to two thousand new account executives. Once you find the move that catches fire, it becomes the strategy. It's the same way a comedian tests jokes in small clubs before recording a big special.
ex: In 2000 he hired actors to protest outside Siebel's conference with "end of software" signs
He also staged a fake news crew, "KNMS," to interview the protesters

items.d: Test on Twitter and similar channels first

l241|455.c: The expert's mind holds only a few possibilities; keep a beginner's mind and treat the old company as a startup.
l241|455.e: He has written code for 45 years, and what he fears most is the expert's mind. Once you start saying "this will definitely work" or "we have to do it this way," you're about to fail. He clears his head with decades of meditation and often visits Ryoan-ji temple in Kyoto. Place matters, he says: find somewhere you can get quiet and receive ideas. He also never looks at the stock price; it only reflects the end of the journey, and the journey is the reward. To him, 25-year-old Salesforce with 75,000 people is still a startup, just getting started in the digital labor business. When a new wave comes, look forward to it instead of complaining.
ex: At 15 he sold a program that taught juggling to a cassette magazine for $75
He sat in a temple with Neil Young, who wrote an entire album in his head

marks.d: Welcomes new waves and new failures

l241|455.c: Agents are a digital workforce that remembers you and acts for you, the layer after automation and data.
l241|455.e: His picture of an agent is the store in "Minority Report" that recognizes a customer and recommends products based on their history. It has memory, knows your preferences and makes suggestions on its own, whether as software on your phone, a home robot or a car that knows you. Healthcare makes it obvious: after a scan, nobody reminded him to drink water to flush the contrast dye, while nurses stay up late handling patient messages. Agents can take over that follow-up and leave the face-to-face empathy to doctors. Salesforce first automated customer touchpoints, then pulled the data together, and is now adding the agent layer. Everyone building agents is a good sign; being alone would mean something's wrong with the market.
ex: Salesforce's help center resolves 83% of inquiries automatically, with human escalations cut in half
He said AI transactions that week were around 2 trillion

l241|455.c: AI and jobs is a tale of two cities: urban white-collar roles get reshuffled, small-town blue-collar work stays untouched for now.
l241|455.e: He says plainly that Salesforce needs to reallocate people: with an automated support layer, it needs fewer support engineers, while it is hiring many account executives to drive growth. He doesn't think jobs will simply be replaced. Many fields, like healthcare, are already short of people, and new jobs are appearing that nobody can fill. He owns a house in a blue-collar town where restaurant, trucking, grocery, construction and landscaping work won't be affected for a long time. In San Francisco, though, the impact is already visible.
ex: At Salesforce today: fewer support roles, more sales roles

items: Hard to replace for a long time

d.verdict: Different places will see very different effects

l241|455.c: A CEO can't just play the clarinet; they must conduct the whole orchestra of product, sales, marketing and every stakeholder.
l241|455.e: He rejects the label of Salesforce as a sales-driven company. This year was supposed to be the year of Data Cloud, but when he saw agent technology arriving faster than expected, he pivoted at once, buying back Airkit, a company once spun out of Salesforce, to speed up development and shipping Agentforce in time for Dreamforce. Founders who focus only on product or only on sales don't get far, he says. You have to look after employees, customers, investors, shareholders and everyone else at the same time. Limiting yourself shortchanges not just you but everyone.
ex: Airkit was spun out by the RelateIQ founders and later bought back
At an all-hands he listed six things to drive Agentforce

terms.d: Get the technology into customers' hands

result.d: The CEO conducts rather than solos

l241|455.c: When stuck, ask the masters: one line from Steve Jobs led to the AppExchange.
l241|455.e: He interned at Apple in college and later became friends with Steve Jobs. When early Salesforce hit a wall, he went to Jobs for help and got three demands: grow ten times in 24 months, sign a big customer like Avon, and build an "application economy." He turned that phrase over and over until he decided it meant an app store, so he bought the appstore.com domain, trademarked the name, and built AppExchange on the Salesforce platform. When the iPhone got its App Store, he gave the domain and trademark to Jobs.
ex: When testing the name, customers said it was an "exchange," not a "store"
Jobs actually disliked that he was building enterprise software

items.d: 10x growth, big customers, an app economy
After Apple launched the App Store

l241|455.c: Success is never a straight line; even a mature company hits moments when it must make a painful turn.
l241|455.e: Business boomed during the pandemic, and Salesforce, like the rest of Silicon Valley, hired too many people. About two years ago, he says, it felt like both pilots had vanished from the cockpit and someone had jumped out with a parachute. The company had to pull off a financial transformation and a product-innovation transformation at the same time, including its first large layoff of 10%. He communicated again and again and still got hammered by the press and on Twitter, which thickened his skin. After 23 years at the helm he never expected a crisis like that. But if you want smooth sailing, he says, don't start a company.
ex: His joke: that was my first pandemic; next time I'll understand economic cycles
Quoting a close friend: there is no linear success

l242|456.c: A PM's value is outside the building: think from the customer's and competitor's view, and systematically hunt for disconfirming evidence.
l242|456.e: Product management is a leverage job, he says: a 10x PM multiplies 10x resources, so returns can differ a hundredfold. Yet after twenty years the craft is still wildly inconsistent. Most PMs get pulled into internal politics, agile process and delivery. Doing those well never earns top marks, because the real job is finding differentiated value nobody else can offer. He asks that every document start from the customer, market and competitive view, backed by anecdotes and data. People who claim to talk to customers often do it sporadically, with no analysis, and never look for proof that they're wrong.
ex: Steve Blank's rule: spend 80% of your attention outside the building
Interviews saturate at 7 to 14 people; 2 is too few, 22 too many

result.d: Leverage jobs have extreme spreads

l242|456.c: When using an LLM for research, ask specifically where things don't match, not for what you hope to see.
l242|456.e: This is the best time ever for PMs to analyze huge amounts of information, he says, as long as the research itself is sound: a sensible sample size and no leading questions. He feeds interview transcripts along with his own strategy into a model and asks it to point out where customers disagree with the strategy, or which competitor their needs sound closest to. Give a model a competitor's public materials and it can often infer their roadmap. At Confluent, an LLM clusters hundreds of inbound requests by meaning to show which needs are heating up and which are cooling off.
ex: Sachin Rekhi's "feedback river": immerse yourself in feedback
Confluent uses LLMs to cluster hundreds or thousands of customer requests

l242|456.c: Ninety percent of an AI product is data management: getting timely, high-quality context in front of the model.
l242|456.e: Models are both brilliant and dumb, he says. They know only what they were trained on and what you hand them right now, and information like customer feedback or competitor moves goes stale fast. The model is largely interchangeable. Prompts deserve ongoing polish but aren't the core. What really decides the experience is the context. Take an HR assistant: it needs employee records, benefits, the laws of each country and company policy, all linked together. Anyone who thinks you just plug in a model and run a pipeline will spend years stuck on getting accurate, timely, well-structured data. That's where 90% of the effort goes.
ex: Imagine the data chain Workday would need for an HR AI assistant
10% inspiration, 90% perspiration

items.d: Worth ongoing work, but not the core
Timely, high quality, structured: 90% of the work

l242|456.c: AI makes cloning SaaS easy, but the lock-in is years of accumulated business rules, so the strong get stronger.
l242|456.e: Calling Jira, Workday and Salesforce "forms on top of a database" isn't wrong. But the lock-in isn't in the fields or the interface. It's in the business rules customers have configured over many years. The longer they use it, the more the software becomes the company's own process, until even the customer can't explain how it works. Even if an agent replaces the interface, it still has to follow those rules. So more look-alike apps only push buyers toward the leader. A new entrant faces harder distribution because of AI-generated junk, and has to be "good enough and different," for example by embedding outcome data into the workflow.
ex: Ashby embeds hiring outcome data into the applicant tracking flow
Even Salesforce can't fully describe its own sales process

marks.d: Years of configuration; agents must obey them

l242|456.c: Data is a compass, not a GPS: when a result defies intuition, suspect the data first and verify it.
l242|456.e: He used to call himself data-driven. Now he thinks treating data as the answer is both wrong and slow; data is better for disproving things. Intuition is itself a lot of accumulated experience. When data and intuition clash badly, Occam's razor says the data is probably broken, and only occasionally is it gold. His check has three steps: look upstream at what happened and whether the sample is normal, look downstream at whether the effect lasts, and look up a level at whether it serves the real goal. A flawed analysis torn apart in public costs more credibility than not presenting it.
ex: One intervention looked amazing but only reached 2% of new users
Week-two retention went up, then everyone churned in week three
He once kept a 10% global holdout group that never joined any experiment

items.d: Is the sample normal and representative?
Does the effect last in later weeks?
Does it serve revenue, price and the real goals?

l242|456.c: B2B companies can't abandon product-led growth: with nobody rewarded for caring about end users, the experience rots.
l242|456.e: In 2012 he built the first B2B growth team at Atlassian. B2B naturally tilts toward the buyer: decision-makers drive purchases and request features, and nothing in the company pulls attention toward the end user's early experience. People do what they're rewarded for. If nobody owns user success, the experience inevitably decays and competitors get an opening. The key is balance: product-led growth feeds leads to sales, and sales routes immature leads back into the self-serve funnel. Companies with both lots of customers and lots of revenue are the hardest to dislodge.
ex: Atlassian reached about 80,000 customers with no sales team by the time he left
Confluent has both self-serve signup and direct sales to large accounts
Growth team stages: prove it works, systematize, scale, embed in the organization

cells.d: PLG and sales feed each other

l242|456.c: Treat your career like a bingo card: deliberately move to adjacent but unfamiliar areas and go deep in several.
l242|456.e: Looking back, every job change filled an empty square: enterprise software, then Atlassian with no sales team, then consumer insurance, then Salesforce's distribution machine. The more patterns you've seen, the faster you recognize a new problem. The condition is some adjacency; don't jump out of a plane before learning to skydive. He dislikes the "T-shaped" idea and thinks the best people are deep in several areas. Decisions need balance too: deciding with too little data is fatal, and waiting too long is equally fatal. He once watched a zombie product drag on for a year and a half before killing it.
ex: A general counsel's one remark pulled a product strategy debate back on track
A green energy product ran for two years and was killed only when a customer wanted to pay
Colin Powell's rule: deciding with under 30% of the information is too early, over 70% too late

l243|457.c: Product teams are small pods organized around user tasks, and each pod decides how to solve them.
l243|457.e: Around 2016, when the company had 50 or 60 people, they didn't organize by function like front end and back end. Instead they tried one pod of a PM, a designer and a few engineers, and once it worked they kept copying it. Pods form around user tasks, such as sales engagement, conversation insights or deal summaries, rather than around a metric first. Once the agenda is set, the pod picks its own approach. Leadership stays informed by talking to customers often, not by approving each item.
ex: Today there are about 25 to 30 pods
Each pod has a PM, a designer, an engineering lead and five to seven engineers

items.d: Such as conversation insights or deal summaries
Define the problem and the experience
Copywriting and data analysis as needed

l243|457.c: Every feature gets 6 to 12 design-partner customers, so customers, not executives, steer the product.
l243|457.e: Partners are mostly existing customers. Gong searches its own library of recorded calls for people who mentioned the need, then a dedicated research coordinator segments them by the PM's profile, sends small email batches and books meetings. A new product is demoed to partners every week or two. Even if a button still throws an error, customers like seeing progress. He believes customers understand their pain best but not necessarily the solution. After seven to nine conversations the requests start repeating, so you want a dozen partners, not one or two.
ex: Eleven of the first twelve partners said they'd pay when charging began
He estimates over 95% of shipped features see significant use
Partners rate the current state from 0 to 10; the goal is to push that score up

items.d: Find customers who raised the need
Show work in progress every week or two
They repeat after about 7 to 9 partners

l243|457.c: Autonomy requires leaders to let go and tolerate mistakes; the payoff is speed, morale and better products.
l243|457.e: He treats autonomy as a personal belief: people produce more when they can work their own way, within boundaries. In practice, teams decide for themselves whether to act on a customer request, and a good-faith misjudgment is never punished. There is a weekly review meeting, but teams have to ask for it. The precondition is that leaders accept more mistakes, and colleagues in sales and finance must trust the model too, since they get less visibility and have to make their own case for an investment.
ex: A family picnic where everyone brought what they wanted turned out richer
AI fine-tuning ideas start in hackathons and get full funding only after validation
He never installs monitoring software on his kids' devices

items: Leaders let go and tolerate errors

d.verdict: Trade some visibility for speed and better products

l243|457.c: Near 50-50 decisions turn out about the same either way, so decide now instead of gathering more data.
l243|457.e: He thinks people naturally overthink. Spending more time doesn't improve the decision, and deciding is tiring, like physical effort. For a true 51-49 choice, picking wrong costs little, so just pick. Obvious choices need even less agonizing. He and the CEO once passed on acquiring a company, and in hindsight it made little difference either way. He does concede that highly regulated or high-risk decisions deserve more care. In an unfamiliar field he learns first, because intuition is only reliable within his own expertise.
ex: Asimov's short story "The Machine That Won the War"
Whether to open an office in China: obviously no

marks.d: Just decide; a miss isn't fatal

l243|457.c: Don't assume LLMs solve everything or hire a data scientist for every project; build measurement first.
l243|457.e: He warns against two extremes: hiring a data scientist for every small project, or assuming a large language model can do everything. Predicting whether a deal will close, for example, needs a dedicated model. Without measurement you can't prove version two beats version one, so Gong has people whose job is defining the evaluation method, and it borrows a chess-style rating system to compare versions. Accuracy changes the shape of the product, so PMs need domain knowledge to judge what's feasible and how to design it.
ex: A mix of in-house models, internal fine-tuning and prompt optimization
Three pods have embedded AI experts for fast iteration
Early on, "AI" had a bad name, so launches deliberately avoided the word

items.d: Large and small models tuned internally
Specialists refine prompts and edge cases

l243|457.c: Learn a new field by asking each person who to talk to next, until you hear nothing new.
l243|457.e: He compares learning to annealing, the slow cooling that lets metal settle. Talk to one person, ask at the end who else you should meet, and keep going. At first almost everything is new. By the fifth person you understand about half. After that, people start repeating what you've heard, which means you've reached the core and can form a view. You test whether you've learned by whether the views converge, not by anyone's title. Later, user research can dig deeper.
ex: He taught himself deep learning this way
It helped him separate account managers, new-business reps and call-center sellers

l243|457.c: Early target customers should be so narrow they know each other; don't scale sales before repeatable product-market fit.
l243|457.e: Gong started by targeting only US, English-speaking sales teams that sold software over WebEx video calls, with deal sizes from $1,000 to $100,000, about 5,000 companies. The circle was small enough that customers talked to each other and word of mouth spread naturally. His previous company, founded around 2000, had technology that was too horizontal, and customers in different industries spoke different languages. With only three customers in three different segments, investors pushed them to hire about 20 salespeople, and most of them failed.
ex: A prospect's rep said he'd only work at companies using Gong; that company then bought
This matches the advice in Crossing the Chasm

items.d: Small enough that customers know each other

l244|460.c: Hard conversations are hard because of the meaning we attach; avoiding them robs the other person of a chance to improve.
l244|460.e: What people fear is rarely the conversation itself, she says, but the meaning they give it: that the other person will be hurt, that it will cause trouble, that they might be wrong. She suggests first asking yourself what exactly you're afraid of, then checking your motive: are you trying to help them get better, or to vent? If it's venting, wait. If you never speak up, the other person never gets to see the problem, change the behavior or repair the relationship. And on the other side of the discomfort there is often something new.
ex: A client worried her report would cry, and the report did cry
The next day the report said thanks: if only someone had told me 15 years ago
Her own low point: crying on the floor for an hour, then getting up to make calls

items.d: What am I actually afraid of?
To help them grow, not to vent
Practice until the words come easily
New possibilities wait past the discomfort

l244|460.c: Base feedback on observable facts and clear expectations, keep the tone ordinary, and end with agreed next steps.
l244|460.e: Her script: open casually, lay out the specific facts you heard from colleagues or observed yourself, connect to the shared goal that "we both know what success looks like here," and ask them to leave with a clear improvement plan. The calmer and more matter-of-fact you are, the less the person thinks "my manager hates me." The more observable the facts, the less it feels like judgment, so it's easier to say and easier to hear. She also advises giving specific praise as carefully as you'd prepare criticism, because that builds the trust that lets bad news land later.
ex: Colleagues said he missed deadlines without warning anyone
For unstructured writing, give 3 or 4 excellent examples to learn from
Writing quality reflects thinking quality

items.d: I want to talk about some collaboration feedback
We both know what success looks like

l244|460.c: Turn down a promotion directly, explain why and offer hope; when emotions flare, pause the conversation yourself.
l244|460.e: First work out why the person thinks they deserve it, such as having done a year in the role or being the only internal candidate. Then, with empathy, state the decision up front, give the reasons, and show you care about their career. People rush to get bad news out and forget that the person across the table needs hope for the future. If they push back with reasons unrelated to the decision, repeat what they said to show you heard it, then explain that the company's stage calls for something different. If they get defensive or tearful, stop: restate your intent, name the shift you're seeing, and ask whether to continue or pick it up another day, rather than letting it become an argument.
ex: Reason for hiring externally: the role needs someone who has done it several times before
Promise that the new boss will help them build the missing skills
You can say: "I feel the temperature between us has changed"

terms.d: Lead with the decision, no circling
What the role needs and what's missing

result.d: They still see you as an ally afterward

l244|460.c: Getting fired should never be a surprise: hold a "pre-firing conversation" first, with a deadline and consequences.
l244|460.e: Managers often think they've been clear, but when asked whether they said it explicitly, they hedge, which means they weren't. Before firing someone, have an unmistakable conversation: these issues have been raised several times, they're still happening, and they must be fixed within 30 days or we part ways. Also say you believe they can change and value their strengths, but these two things are deal-breakers. Most people then get a real chance to improve, and if it comes to firing, it's simple: recap the history, announce the decision, and let HR handle the rest. This is about the culture of the whole company, she says, not just one person.
ex: After six months of feedback, give a 30-day deadline to fix it
Have HR in the room when firing, and consult a lawyer beforehand

items.d: Name the problems and expectations clearly
The firing talk is short and no surprise

l244|460.c: A leader's job isn't to make people happy but to lead the team to win; satisfaction comes from a winning culture.
l244|460.e: Many first-time founders want to be the boss everyone likes, so they won't push people or give negative feedback and hope problems disappear on their own, which eventually sinks the company. Real engagement, she says, comes from a culture of winning: clear structure, everyone knowing the impact of their role, and celebrating once milestones are hit. Founders often try to reinvent management, then end up back at process, hierarchy and goals. Those paths are well worn, so move through that phase quickly. When a project stalls, a leader also has to tell patience from a broken process.
ex: It started with avocado toast afternoons and turned into a clique culture
Visionary founders lack people who build structure and track goals
Founders abolish process and hierarchy, then reinvent them

items: Perks and socials fill the calendar
Writes down how we work and what's expected

d.verdict: People who want to win show up, and the team engages

l244|460.c: End every meeting with three questions: what did we decide, who does what by when, and who else needs to know.
l244|460.e: The most common flaw in meetings is a lack of continuity: next time, everything gets discussed and decided all over again. Ask six people to write down what was decided and you'll often get six different answers, and surfacing that disagreement is valuable in itself. Executive teams also tend to make decisions without telling the people below them. She suggests reserving five to ten minutes at the end as a fixed ritual, owned by whoever loves follow-through. You don't have to be running the meeting to start it, and over time it becomes a team habit.
ex: A six-person meeting often produces six versions of "the decision"
In a large meeting, just ask two or three people to restate the decisions

l244|460.c: Sign a "prenup" before co-founding: talk through values, what success looks like and how you handle conflict.
l244|460.e: She cites Noam Wasserman's research that 65% of startup failures come from conflict within the founding team, yet most people pick a co-founder far less carefully than a spouse. The key questions: what are each person's core values, what does success for the company look like, how does each of you handle conflict (ask the people around you), who decides when you disagree, and what culture do you want. Having talked it through in advance gives you a way to handle disagreements when they come. Colleagues who aren't founders can exchange a "personal user manual" describing how they like to work.
ex: Unanswered weekend messages: one wanted balance, the other wanted excellence
Five or six years in, one founder finally said he didn't want to scale further
A user manual might say: here's how to get a gold star from me

root.d: Get aligned before starting the company

items.d: Narrow 20 down to 3 to 5 and compare
Talk right away, or process first?
Whoever cares more or knows more decides

l245|461.c: Early growth came from engineering word of mouth, not from buying distribution.
l245|461.e: Following the "Guerrilla Marketing" playbook, he asked what Paul Graham did every day, made a demo video and posted it to Hacker News, where it stayed on the front page for two days and got him into Y Combinator. Before launch he made another video packed with internet in-jokes for Digg and Reddit, and the waitlist exploded overnight. Then he applied the same engineering rigor used to make sure wedding photos never get lost to the viral loops: the referral program, shared folders. The model was Facebook's growth approach, borrowed from epidemiology. For the first seven years, users doubled or grew tenfold every year.
ex: The waitlist went from 5,000 to 85,000 overnight
Valuation: about $6 million in 2007, $4 billion in 2011
Printed user counts covered the walls, then the ceiling

items.d: A Hacker News video caught Paul Graham's eye
The live demo failed; the waitlist carried it
The referral program drove viral growth
The giants' rival products had all shipped

l245|461.c: Big-company competition is a python, not a shotgun; at a strategic inflection point, go all in on one direction.
l245|461.e: When iCloud, Google Drive and OneDrive launched, Dropbox's numbers barely moved. The real threat was relentless iteration plus platform bundling, tightening a little at a time. The giants copy your product, bundle it into their platforms, then use free to destroy your economics. Google Photos offered unlimited free storage for life and blew straight through Carousel, Dropbox's photo app. He reread Andy Grove, and like Intel abandoning memory chips, took the view of "what would a consultant tell me to do," killed Carousel and Mailbox, and bet everything on work, since 80% of paying users were already using Dropbox at work.
ex: In 2011 Steve Jobs said by name that Dropbox would look outdated
Netscape wasn't killed by IE 1.0 but by IE 4.0 plus bundling
The lesson of "Playing to Win": don't be second in every market

items.d: They see the demand you've proven
Pre-installed on devices and operating systems
Cut side bets, focus on work

l245|461.c: Most wounds are self-inflicted: a CEO's strengths and weaknesses both get amplified into company culture.
l245|461.e: Bill Campbell told him Netscape wasn't killed by Microsoft; it killed itself. He realized the company had hired lots of smart people who were doing dumb things, and that he had steered the ship onto the rocks. The Enneagram, a personality framework based on motivation, showed him he's a Type 7, the Enthusiast. Every strength comes with a shadow, and left unaddressed, a founder's blind spots become company-wide dysfunction. The fix is either to change yourself or to hire people who don't share those weaknesses, so the company isn't overexposed to the founder's flaws.
ex: The Enneagram is about motivation, which he finds more useful than descriptive tests like MBTI
A coach's 360 review matched each strength to a corresponding development area

items.d: → Avoids conflict, doesn't tell hard truths
→ Chaos; the team doesn't know what to do
Change yourself or hire to compensate

l245|461.c: Challenges are unavoidable but suffering is optional: founders must separate their identity from the company.
l245|461.e: Once a company succeeds, the founder's identity fuses with it, and when the company struggles, the person collapses too. He learned to accept that there's no "up and to the right forever" button. Many heroic founders went through a wilderness period, and that's exactly the forge that shapes them. He was stuck on a treadmill of meetings and email, "too busy firing to aim," with the big questions always at the bottom of the to-do list. He built a support system of meditation, therapy, a coach, mentors and founder friends, and regularly steps away for think weeks. Burnout, he says, is the real killer.
ex: Bill Campbell would take him to dinner, dust him off and send him back onto the field
His 18-year-old self would say: you made it, what are you complaining about?

items.d: Meetings and email fill every hour
Big questions sit at the bottom of the list
You notice the wrong turn years later

l245|461.c: Founder mode is a journey: don't refuse to let go, but don't drift too far from the product either.
l245|461.e: He cites Ben Horowitz's "product CEO paradox": companies die one way when the founder won't let go, and another when the founder gets too far away. He was the second kind. After hiring executives who knew sales and marketing better than he did, it was easy to stop setting direction. He gathered more and more feedback, his own list of things to improve got longer than anyone's, and executives used that to dodge accountability while the roadmap became a negotiated compromise. Once through the learning curve, a founder gains the conviction that comes from firsthand experience, re-engages deeply, and stops apologizing for the company they want.
ex: He hired a Google executive who had run a $10 billion business, then didn't know how to give direction
Steve Jobs and Elon Musk both went through wilderness periods

marks.d: Far from the product, fuzzy direction

l245|461.c: Our tools have gone from amplifiers to suppressors, and attention is now the scarcest resource in knowledge work.
l245|461.e: He realized it wasn't just him; everyone was on the same treadmill. Even SpaceX's head of engineering said they were getting to Mars on a mountain of email and documents. Once work moved onto screens, constant interruptions and busywork made focus nearly impossible, and collaboration tools became empty calories. So Dropbox changed its mission to designing a more enlightened way of working, went 90% remote as a "virtual first" company, and open-sourced its work handbook. On the product side it launched Dash, which connects your SaaS apps for unified search and natural-language questions, and uses Stacks to gather scattered content. At heart it's the same old problem: find, organize, share and protect my stuff.
ex: At home you have one search box; at work you have ten
Imagine Einstein interrupted by Slack and LinkedIn notifications
Dropbox acquired Command E, which built universal search

items.d: Browser tabs and hundreds of SaaS apps

l245|461.c: A second act often stalls because the organization lags: success breeds complacency, and talent gaps slow learning.
l245|461.e: Many SaaS companies face the "second album" problem. Building multiple products in a functional structure loses accountability, so you have to move to business units plus a shared platform. Success also breeds complacency and entitlement: new hires think they hit a home run when they started on third base. He had to deliver the cold truth that the only change customers had seen in three years was a price increase. Once the press turned negative, the talent flywheel ran backward, and the company filled roles by promoting from within and hiring people two levels up, which created a seniority gap. He thinks experienced hands and high-potential newcomers should be roughly half and half for the organization to learn fast enough.
ex: Cash-flow positive in 2016, $1 billion in annualized revenue in 2017, IPO in 2018
He recommends Geoffrey Moore's "Zone to Win"

terms.d: Doing this for the first time
Have done it; not their career's biggest stretch

result.d: Roughly half and half, no seniority gap

l245|461.c: A CEO's personal growth curve has to stay ahead of the company's growth curve.
l245|461.e: Borrowing from StarCraft, he says running a company means playing three levels at once. Micro is the detail of product, engineering and distribution. Macro is the business model, the market and the competition. The meta-game is the constant change in cycles and rules; for example, social media and direct reach now beat traditional media for launching a product. To stay ahead: read a lot of history; befriend founders at your stage and 2, 5 and 20 years ahead of you; work backward from what you'll wish you had learned one, two and five years from now; and run toward discomfort. Smart people especially should beware of explaining away failure; try assuming you're fully responsible.
ex: Netscape's lesson played out at Dropbox in 2014
The article "Teaching Smart People How to Learn"
"15 Principles of Conscious Leadership"

items.d: Cycles and rules shift, like marketing channels
Product design, engineering and distribution detail

l246|463.sc: When to hire the first PM
l246|463.c: Seed-stage founders should be the PM themselves, and hire one only when they become the bottleneck.
l246|463.e: Hiring a PM too early hands over customer conversations, product direction and even the company's personality. Mercury ran well for a long time with no PMs, relying on engineers and designers with product instincts who stayed close to customers, and early Square was similar. The signals to hire: everything waits on a co-founder's decision; partnerships, compliance and risk work in banking leave design and engineering exhausted from pushing projects; or the company is entering a new product area or customer segment. She thinks Mercury made the switch too late.
ex: Mercury had its first formal PM at about 400 people; she thinks it should have been under 100
The company now has about 30 PMs

items.d: Compliance and risk drag on design and engineering
Someone must deeply learn new customers
People doing PM work instead of their own

l246|463.c: PMs are pioneers, settlers or town planners, and you should match the type to the product's stage.
l246|463.e: Pioneers are good at zero to one. Settlers build out fundamentals and run experiments during growth. Town planners optimize mature products, where a small change touches huge numbers of customers. When founders say they don't want PMs, they are usually picturing town planners, while what they lack is a pioneer. Even at Mercury, the mature core banking business needs careful, conservative planner types. To tell which type a candidate is, look at what they have actually done, not just the résumé.
ex: Square Invoices grew from a hack week project, driven by the mobile app and search traffic
Break a vague problem into levers like acquisition and churn reduction, then push each one

l246|463.c: To hire top PMs, define level criteria, verify real work, then pitch to where they are on their career curve.
l246|463.e: Mercury first wrote a leveling ladder that combines values like humility and low ego with PM skills. Interviews then test against it: product sense, obsession with customers and quality, analytical ability and systems thinking. Candidates also give a presentation on a topic of their choice, which reveals detail and passion. To attract people, study candidates the way you study users. Senior people moving along their S-curve want either a more ambiguous problem or a bigger scope. Strong peers and an honest account of the good and the bad matter just as much.
ex: One candidate explained how airplanes are built, right down to the bolts
She plans to add a writing exercise, since writing shows depth of thinking

cells.d: Same kind of problems, larger scale

l246|463.c: Quality and speed aren't a trade-off; the more boring the industry, the more detail builds a lasting edge.
l246|463.e: She rejects the split between data-driven speed and design-driven beauty. In a boring industry like finance, precise, thoughtful details build the trust customers need before handing over their money. A single detail may not move a core metric, but details compound into a competitive advantage and also attract talent. Founders have to set this as culture from the start. She adds that quality is only one way to stand out; price, features and target audience work too.
ex: In Bill Pay, the view zooms to the matching spot on an invoice as you verify each field
Linear, Mercury and the procurement tool Zip win on design
Jira stands out on features

items.d: Each one may not move a metric
Customers trust you with their money
Users love it, great people join
Adds up to a durable edge

l246|463.c: New products need a separate expansion org, or the mature product's roadmap swallows them.
l246|463.e: A seedling product sitting next to a mature business gets pulled into its roadmap, maintenance work and prioritization, and never grows. So Mercury created an expansion organization that she runs: cross-functional pods of engineering, design, product and data, sharing support, risk and operations as common platforms. New teams have no fixed deadline. Every quarter or half year they review against goals and financial projections, can pivot, and keep getting investment as long as the path looks viable. The rhythm is two-week sprints with weekly syncs.
ex: In 2024 Mercury launched personal banking, Bill Pay, invoicing and spend management
Each launch went from concept to release faster than the last
Personal banking had about three times as many engineers as invoicing

d.verdict: A seedling needs its own soil to grow

l246|463.c: Expand into areas right next to the core, give them away for retention first, then charge for complexity.
l246|463.e: She looks at three things: market size, existing demand signals, and whether Mercury has a distribution advantage. Pick areas adjacent to the core rather than scattered features. Invoicing grew out of a "payment request" feature that was gaining traction, so existing users became the first audience and launch costs dropped sharply. Core money movement stays free. New products also start free to build usage and retention, and charging begins when customers need more complex capabilities, usually 6 to 18 months later.
ex: Bill Pay is cross-sold inside the payment flow to customers who need it
Willingness-to-pay research, drawing on Madhavan Ramanujam's pricing ideas

terms.d: Existing users are the first audience

result.d: Free first, charge for complex needs later

l246|463.c: PMs should talk to at least one customer a week, observe neutrally, then confirm with prototypes and data.
l246|463.e: Mercury's baseline is at least one customer conversation per PM per week, and teams in exploration mode do twenty or thirty. Leaders engage customers directly on X, churn reasons stream into Slack in real time, and PMs listen in on sales and support calls. But customers tend to be polite. They praise the product or blame themselves. So look for patterns without preconceptions, then confirm with prototypes, betas and data. Stay anchored to business reality too: customers always want things free, and the company has to survive.
ex: A research team books interviews, and PMs sometimes block out a "research week"
The same bottle of water costs different amounts at a cooler, a hotel and on a plane

items.d: At least one customer a week
Look for what repeats across interviews

l247|464.c: Ask what you would do if you could not fail, and never let "not now" become "never."
l247|464.e: About half the students who come to him ask what to do with their lives. They usually arrive with a pros-and-cons list, their heart set on option B, while talking themselves into option A. His "genie exercise" assumes a genie guarantees that whatever you fully commit to will work out, only slower and harder than you expect. That strips the fear of failure out of the answer. A gentler version is "nine lives": write down nine lives you could start today that all excite you, then pull the one with the most energy into your current life, even as a side project. Nobody admits to giving up a dream. They just say "not now," and the right moment never comes.
ex: A Brazilian student left consulting to start an education nonprofit back home
One student is building a theme park in Texas
Naval's question: what feels like play to you but work to others

items.d: Nine lives you could start today that excite you
The one you would pick if you could not fail
Slower and harder, but you will be glad
Start as a side project; stop waiting

l247|464.c: Most people live on autopilot. Write your limiting beliefs down and fear turns into a to-do list.
l247|464.e: He estimates that 95 to 98 percent of our thoughts come from the subconscious, which has been programmed by media, parents, bosses, and social networks. So a busy day is not necessarily a day you chose. To get off autopilot, first make some space and ask: ten years from now, what do I wish I had already started? Then make your calendar reflect that intention. Limiting beliefs are most dangerous while they stay hidden in your head. Put them on paper and they lose most of their power. "How would I ever raise the money?" stops being a vague dread and becomes a problem you can plan around.
ex: His own day: gym, traffic, meetings, email, none of it chosen on purpose
"How will I support myself?" became "design a fundraising plan"

items.d: Programmed from outside; you don't notice it
It loses most of its power at once
"How to raise money" is just a question

l247|464.c: Everything is hard, so suffer for something you care about. Excitement itself is a superpower.
l247|464.e: Out of school he ran an expected-value calculation and joined a big private equity firm: great resume, steady income. But that was an outside scorecard, and it brought friction, anxiety, and burnout. People can grind through that on willpower for years. When he switched to work that genuinely excited him, he found he would work longer, think about it in the shower and on runs, and others joined because of his enthusiasm. He performed far better than on the "should" path. Both paths involve the same amount of suffering: the travel, the long hours, the missed family time. The only difference is what you are suffering for.
ex: The safe job after graduation also meant travel and long hours
After moving into buying companies, he thought about it in the shower and on runs

items: Pick the safe job by expected value
Willing to stick with it longer

d.verdict: Same suffering, but for something you care about

l247|464.c: Everything you want sits on the other side of "worse first," and it takes far longer than you expect.
l247|464.e: Whether it is getting fit, changing jobs, or ending a bad relationship, the first step is always a step down. If you only want tomorrow to feel better than today, you stay put on a plateau. Instead, ask what your five-years-from-now self wishes you were doing right now. What people who fail usually lack is time. Alpine's first fund lost money, then the financial crisis hit, and five of the first eight investments lost money. He has backed about 600 companies and never seen an overnight success. When should you quit? When you have not seen the vision for a long time and no longer believe in it. Otherwise, find what is working and make it bigger.
ex: The Heath brothers' book Switch: find the bright spots and build on them
Quitting high school wrestling after one loss is the only real failure he counts

l247|464.c: Accountability is the key: hire a coach, fill in a weekly sheet, write daily goals. Three months beats three years.
l247|464.e: If you want to get fit, you hire a trainer. For life goals, the equivalent is an executive coach. He hired his first one in 2009, at the bottom of the financial crisis, for two reasons: to force himself to make time for the big questions about career, relationships, health, and kids, and to have someone hold him to what he said he would do. If you cannot afford a coach, pair up with a like-minded friend. Saying a goal out loud engages more of your brain than thinking it or writing it. In college he wrote "I am the number one rower in the country" every day, followed by three things to do that day. His students now submit a sheet like that twice a week.
ex: One coach required him to fill in yearly goals and weekly progress before every call
On walks with his business school roommate, they discussed his dream out and the roommate's back

items.d: A personal trainer for your life
Goals, last week's work, next week's plan
The substitute when a coach is too expensive
Write the goal and three tasks

l247|464.c: Outside achievements change nothing inside. The real game is internal, and it starts with "I am enough."
l247|464.e: In 2015 the last company in Alpine's second fund was sold, and for the first time he could relax about money. The excitement lasted a few days. Then he noticed nothing inside had changed: the same problems, the same self-doubt, and for the first time, depression. He came to see that "I will be worthy and happy once I achieve X" was just a story he had written for himself. Seeing that was frightening at first, then freeing. His two sons leaving for college also forced him to face impermanence. He turned to meditation and spiritual exploration, and gave himself more permission to spend time on what really matters.
ex: An angel-investor friend felt nothing after several successful exits too
He recommends the book The Untethered Soul

items.d: Elite schools, good jobs, fund returns
See through the story; keep your own scorecard

l247|464.c: Private equity's extra returns come mostly from management: the industry can be merely good, the team must be great.
l247|464.e: After the financial crisis, he and his coach sliced the portfolio every way they could: valuation, growth rate, debt structure, geography, industry. The only thing the three best companies had in common was that they started out terribly, so badly that Alpine had sent in its own people to run them. The conclusion: the management team is what matters. Today Alpine installs the leadership at every company it owns, and runs a program that trains people in their twenties and thirties to become CEOs. You cannot pick the wrong industry, since no team can save a typewriter business, but the industry does not have to be perfect. And in the boardroom, the CEO and the investors are on the same side.
ex: The three best companies had all been bad enough to need a takeover
A program that trains people in their twenties and thirties to be CEOs

terms.d: Not perfect, but not the wrong one
Alpine installs and trains the CEO

result.d: The extra return comes mostly from the team

l249|23.c: A growth team can only amplify product-market fit. Hiring too early or as a rescue both fail.
l249|23.e: Head of growth is one of the most frequently fired roles, because people expect magic. Finding product-market fit and selling the product cannot be outsourced. The founding team should own growth from the first million to ten million in ARR. Some companies wait until one or two hundred million, and the longer you wait, the more the whole company gets used to owning growth. Two things must be true first: product-market fit with good retention, and enough data to analyze and run experiments. Sales-led companies should hire sales first. And if the business is declining, a growth team can add maybe ten-something percent. Core product and marketing have to stop the bleeding first.
ex: Ten customers is not data, it is a spreadsheet
A declining mature company that funds a growth team may get a one-to-one return at best

cells.d: Fix the product and market problems first
Experiments and optimization speed things up

l249|23.c: Redesigns, button colors, social login, a single email, and simplifying for its own sake are not growth tactics.
l249|23.e: She has never seen a website redesign or rebrand improve conversion. The best case is flat. The usual story: a new CMO redoes everything to personal taste, spends over a million dollars on an agency, takes eight to ten months, and performance drops at launch. If there is a real strategic reason, budget for the loss up front and plan three to six months to optimize it back. Testing button colors is an early-2000s move. Social login is a nice experience, but only developer products truly need GitHub login. One email has too low an open rate to move any metric. And "simplify onboarding" is a tactic, not a problem. First say where users actually get stuck.
ex: Average email open rates are about 25 percent; the best reach 40 to 50
The best redesign outcome is neutral, but easier to optimize afterward

root.d: Big investment, almost no incremental growth

items.d: Drops first, then 3 to 6 months to recover
Make it readable, pick one, move on
An experience fix, not incremental users
Needs a series and an overall strategy
A tactic, not the actual problem

l249|23.c: Use competitors for inspiration, but copying them is the fastest way to mediocrity.
l249|23.e: She signs up for products with thousands of email addresses to tear down their flows, and checks web archives to see how competitors evolved. But what you see may be one experiment arm or a personalized version. Their flow was built for their users and their channels, so copying it outright fails more than nine times out of ten. The right approach is to extract the elements many companies share and use them as input to ideation, then still do your own design, research, and experiments, and add your own innovation. Otherwise you will never lead. Industry benchmarks are just as risky, because every company defines visitor, signup, and activation differently.
ex: People begged to copy a Dropbox activation page that was ten years old and performed badly
Her Miro board collects onboarding flows and pricing pages from many companies

items: What you see may not be the real version
Fails about 95 percent of the time
Use them as a starting point

d.verdict: Competitors are input, not the answer

l249|23.c: Your problem is not unique. Find someone who has solved it, hire advisors, and adapt the pattern.
l249|23.e: She is almost certain someone has already faced whatever growth problem you have. Figuring it out from scratch wastes time to market. People love sharing what they know, so ask them on LinkedIn or X. Start from the known pattern to get about 60 percent of the answer, then personalize the rest. When she built a community at Miro, she asked someone who had built Atlassian's, and learned that communities come in three kinds: users, agencies, and partners. That saved more than six months of wandering. She thinks any growth team without advisors is running inefficiently. Before signing an advisor, pay for one workshop first, then reassess every month.
ex: Atlassian's community lead suggested starting with an agency or partner community
Every time she takes an operating role, she hires an advisor for herself

items.d: Drop the ego; don't start from zero
People love talking about their experience
Watch the advisor work before signing

l249|23.c: A growth team's first job is building channels you earn yourself, not renting Google and algorithms.
l249|23.e: SEO, paid search, and social ads all amount to paying to borrow someone else's distribution, and an algorithm can take back what it gave. Earned channels run on virality, word of mouth, and user-generated content, which competitors cannot buy. AI is becoming a new interface layered over content, sending less traffic back to the source, so companies that rely on search will only see acquisition costs rise. Earned channels are not cheap. They take product, engineering, and marketing people. But almost every product can find at least one of collaboration, referral, or user-generated content. Keep doing paid and SEO, but diversify, and never hand your growth to someone else.
ex: More than half of Dropbox's new users came from sharing
Miroverse, Miro's user template library, drives both activation and acquisition
B2B products can design a report meant to be forwarded to your manager

marks.d: The algorithm can pull it anytime
Traffic still belongs to search and AI

l249|23.c: Every growth model decays. Try a new engine every 18 months, because once growth slows it is too late.
l249|23.e: Product-market fit expires, and so do growth models. Optimizing the same spot over and over runs into what Andrew Chen calls the law of shitty clickthroughs. Most growth loops lose their power in five to seven years. Dropbox's sharing loop running for 17 years is the exception. So you keep stacking product-led, marketing-led, and sales-led motions, and every five years a new engine should be carrying a big share of growth. She sets aside 20 to 30 percent of her growth team's time each year to test new loops, with no revenue or acquisition targets early on, or they get killed in the crib. If you wait until growth slows to look for the next engine, you are usually too late.
ex: Miroverse got metrics only after about 18 months
A new loop usually takes six to eighteen months to show revenue

items.d: 20 to 30 percent of team time each year
Carries a big share of acquisition or revenue
Saturates after five to seven years

l249|23.c: If you can't reach sample size in a month, skip the A/B test. Testing everything paralyzes a team.
l249|23.e: Experimentation is the growth team's method, but requiring scientific proof before every launch slows speed and learning, and makes teams afraid to ship anything untested. Data only helps when there is enough of it. If a test needs eight months to conclude, just ship it and compare before and after, checking at 24 hours, 7 days, 28 days, and even a year, and roll back if it fails. Only two cases deserve rigorous testing: major strategic shifts, and high-traffic surfaces where a 0.1 percent difference is worth millions. Statistical significance is a directional signal at best. People should trust their intuition more.
ex: Her rule of thumb: no test if you can't hit sample size within a month
Her motto: progress over perfection

items.d: Default to shipping and comparing before and after
Consider a test only with enough traffic
Reserved for a few key decisions

l249|23.c: Full-time employment is not the only way to monetize your skills. Aim for optionality, not a title.
l249|23.e: Her contrarian view: most people assume full-time employment is the only path, but it ties you to one company that may not fit you. Advising, fractional work, interim executive roles, contracting, courses, and newsletters are all options. She herself is better suited to working across many companies and pattern-matching. Many people aim for VP or CEO, then arrive and discover they do not enjoy managing people. The better question is: if I stay another year, do my options grow or shrink? The prerequisite is building real skills in full-time roles first. That earns you the right to unlock these options, and the door swings both ways.
ex: If you don't like managing people, a management job is a bad job
Humor and memes lower defenses and make complex situations easier to explain

items.d: Have something to show for it
A menu of options; the door swings both ways

l250|468.c: Strategy is not a talent. It sits between vision and roadmap, and it is about focus, what not to do, and why.
l250|468.e: As VP of product at Headspace, the founder told him many people did not understand why they were building what they were building. He realized what was missing was a written strategy. The one he wrote took Headspace from a meditation app to a broader health service. He rejects the idea of a "strategy gene." With a clear definition and a repeatable process, anyone can learn it. Strategy sits between mission and vision on one side and the roadmap on the other. It forces you to put scarce resources where they matter most, like finding an object's natural frequency to create resonance. It names a few pillars, the areas you will not touch, and the reasoning behind both.
ex: Resonance in physics: finding the natural frequency of product and market
Headspace's next-generation product: content library, personalized home, incentives

items.d: Why you exist and what success looks like
Pillars + what not to do + the reasons
What to build in what order, with what resources

l250|468.c: A two-year "small-s strategy" needs 8 to 12 weeks, run in five phases.
l250|468.e: People assume strategy takes two weeks. After all the iteration it ends up taking 8 to 12, which is not much for something that lasts about two years. Preparation takes about four weeks and can run alongside day-to-day work. The strategy sprint makes the hard choices in under a week. The design sprint, led by designers, produces illustrative concepts that make the strategy tangible, not feature mocks. Then the PM alone weaves everything into a three-or-four-page document, with no roadmap in it, since resource allocation belongs to the roadmap phase. Rollout takes two to three weeks and is about landing the strategy, not reopening the debate. Frustration and self-doubt along the way are normal. The person leading it should be a synthesizer with low ego and some playfulness.
ex: Rollout: one-on-ones with two or three gatekeepers, then a review, then roadshows of 8 to 10 people
The appendix holds the full scoring table to answer "why these pillars"

items.d: About 4 weeks to gather every input
Under 1 week to pick the pillars
About 1 week to produce illustrative concepts
1 to 2 weeks; the PM weaves the story
2 to 3 weeks, from gatekeepers to roadshows

l250|468.c: Form a working group for prep, and ask leadership what they want before you start.
l250|468.e: Instead of a PM working alone, he forms a strategy working group with at least engineering, design, and data, with the PM driving. At kickoff everyone gets homework. The data person turns past analyses into a meta-analysis. Design leads a synthesis of user research plus signals from support and social channels. People split up the leadership interviews. Someone does competitive analysis and maps adjacent teams' roadmaps. And everyone observes one real user to build empathy. Leadership interviews are the step most often skipped, yet leaders usually love being asked and often have a pet idea tucked away. Everything rolls up into a single prep reader that stays internal for now.
ex: The fruit analogy: ask whether leadership likes fruit before serving mango
Interview questions: what success feels like, what failure looks like, how it is measured

items.d: Ask about success criteria and pet ideas
Where rivals and sister teams are investing
Build empathy, write down what you learned

l250|468.c: The key day: cluster problems, flip them into opportunities, then score on four criteria to pick three pillars.
l250|468.e: On day one, everyone presents their prep work while the group notes the problems blocking users and growth. Day two matters most. People freely list problems, cluster them into 10 to 15 groups, then rewrite each cluster as an opportunity, so "can't find things" becomes "discovery." The group then scores each opportunity together on four criteria: expected impact, confidence in that impact, whether there is a clear lever, and whether that lever is unique to you. The top three become the strategic pillars; the rest are explicitly out. Arguing over the scores is itself what gets everyone on the same page. On day three, each person writes a news headline from two years out, and these merge into a winning aspiration.
ex: Example opportunities: discovery, relevance, social connection
Meta's privacy team aspiration: drive user trust
Each pillar then breaks into several "how might we" questions

items.d: Rewrite each problem as a positive
Scored on impact, confidence, lever, uniqueness

l250|468.c: Zynga's strength was that the whole company ran on the same pillars and the same list of what not to do.
l250|468.e: As a junior PM at Zynga, he saw every game share three elements. Social viral loops were built into the core gameplay, so you could not progress without active friends. Pay-to-complete pricing meant players paid only for the last 20 to 30 percent of progress, which covered different levels of willingness to pay. And games cross-promoted each other, so the network mattered more than any single title. High-fidelity graphics and complex mechanics were explicitly not priorities, and the data infrastructure and central product team all reinforced the pillars. The model resonated strongly with the Facebook platform, until the shift to mobile broke that resonance. It was so ingrained that he only noticed at Headspace that he had never exercised the strategy muscle himself.
ex: He recalls Zynga as the fastest company to reach a billion dollars in revenue at the time
New genres like match-three and action strategy still followed the three pillars

terms.d: Pay only for the remaining progress

result.d: Until mobile broke it

l250|468.c: A strategy has no value on its own. Execution tests it, and you must honestly double down or pivot.
l250|468.e: At Meta's Reality Labs he ran the same process for two growth teams: the Oculus Quest 2 headset and Portal, the video-calling device. Both aimed to drive hardware sales through software features, and both arrived at nearly identical pillars and similar features, such as referral programs and syncing Facebook memories. About 18 months later the outcomes could not have been more different. The Oculus work succeeded and the team was folded into the VR division. Portal barely moved and the team was redeployed. His takeaway: a strategy is just a few pages of words. Its value comes from the results execution produces, and it takes honesty, humility, and courage to admit what worked and what did not.
ex: The Oculus referral program
Portal showing Facebook memories and Facebook feed ads

items.d: Pick the pillars and the no-gos
Admit honestly what worked and what didn't

l250|468.c: Beyond the problem-solving small-s strategy, you need a big-S strategy that works backward from the future.
l250|468.e: He quotes Elon Musk: life cannot just be about solving problems. Small-s strategy starts from today's problems and is led by PMs. Big-S strategy works backward from the future, looks 5 to 10 years out, can take up to six months, and is led by design and user research. You start by studying cultural, social, competitive, and technology trends, then ask leaders what a user's day looks like in five years and why the world is better. Those answers cluster into three very different futures, which become concept-car style prototypes to test with users. Elements that work feed into the live product. The two tracks run in parallel, like two tributaries flowing into the same roadmap.
ex: Three futures of transportation: fully autonomous, ultra-fast, and virtual travel
VRChat runs small-s and big-S tracks at the same time

items: About two years; 8 to 12 weeks of work
Works backward from an ideal future
5 to 10 years out; up to six months of work

d.verdict: Two parallel tracks feeding one roadmap

l250|468.c: AI can already write a thorough simulated strategy, but the hard choices still need a human, for now.
l250|468.e: He says to use AI for prep research today: mine competitors' changelogs to infer where they are investing, analyze reviews, and build comparison heat maps. Asking a model for a "simulated strategy" works surprisingly well. But its strength is also its weakness: the suggestions are comprehensive, and strategy is about focus. Cutting down to a few areas still takes judgment grounded in your company's context. Medium term he imagines several agents working together, say generative AI designing onboarding variants that feed into a multi-armed bandit experiment that optimizes itself. He believes there is a crossover point ahead where a machine weighing many signals at once will judge better than a person.
ex: Tesla processes six cameras at once; a human can only look left and right in turn
The PM's job shifts to designing product architecture where agents can do their work

items.d: Pick a few pillars using company context
E.g. auto-generate and test onboarding variants

l251|470.c: Speed and quality aren't a trade-off: speed comes from skill, and you need a working version 10 percent in.
l251|470.e: People think you must choose between fast and good because they confuse fast with rushed and sloppy. Top chefs, programmers, and construction workers get faster as they get better, and software quality depends largely on how many iterations you get. At Linear, a feature budgeted for a month must have a version that runs and tests the key assumption by the end of week one, instead of discovering the assumption was wrong at 80 percent done. Nobody expects the first version to be good, and engineers don't get stuck on design details. Then usage expands ring by ring. If nobody uses it, you missed.
ex: The longer the renovation drags on, the bigger your hotel bill
No pixel-perfect design needed, just something usable you can learn from

items.d: Test the assumption 10 percent into the budget
The team runs on Linear every day
Just don't break data or look too rough
Already used by several rings before launch

l251|470.c: Linear flatly refuses middle managers' reporting customizations: they ruin the frontline experience and corrupt the data anyway.
l251|470.e: Enterprise software gets bloated from one kind of request: middle managers wanting extra fields and customizations for their reports, at the cost of worse workflows for the engineers doing the work. Linear doesn't debate these. It says no, and that is its core promise. Engineers are judged on code, not ticket hygiene, so a required dropdown just gets the first option picked at random. Of the ten items on a buyer's checklist, usually only three really matter, and those three should be built natively and done extremely well. A tool really sells a way of working: Linear turns what high-performing teams already agree on into a button other teams can use.
ex: Basic scale features like SAML and SCIM still get built
A buyer's no is often not now; many come back two years later

items.d: More fields to fill, more clicks

l251|470.c: Trace every request to a real person and a real job; you often find a better answer than what was asked.
l251|470.e: When Linear discusses a feature, someone has to name whose workflow it is: a real name, an email, a person you can go ask, not an invented persona. PMs often produce elegant solutions without checking whether reality is equally elegant. After launch, feedback works like annealing, exposing which assumptions didn't match the real world. For big, loudly requested features, they break the request apart to see whether a concentrated use case deserves a deep solution. Many customers asked for custom fields. When asked why, about 40 percent wanted to track requests from a particular big customer, so Linear built a native feature that links customers automatically.
ex: Customer Requests pulls the requester in from support tools and the CRM automatically
Capacity planning sits in the backlog until they know how big a slice to solve

items.d: A generic ask from many customers
What are you actually trying to do
Auto-link the requester; no burden on engineers

l251|470.c: In a crowded category, the opportunities hide in the moments when users feel bad.
l251|470.e: At Everlane, Mode, and Linear he was always in a red ocean, where the opportunities you can reach through goals and jobs-to-be-done had already been picked clean. So on sales calls he keeps asking until he feels as bad as the customer does and reaches the emotional layer: "so I'm not getting promoted." PMs and engineers lean rational and tend to avoid those feelings. Users also have a drudgery blind spot: they are numb to their own daily grind, so an outsider has to spot what hurts every day and every week. Group the bad feelings that share a root cause, and a single solution often appears.
ex: Marketing hated date-only deadlines, so Linear added fuzzy targets like a quarter or a month
Triage: assigning by hand is exhausting, but leaving it alone spirals out of control

items: Already picked clean in a red ocean
Dig until you reach the moment that hurts
See the user's drudgery blind spot
Solve bad feelings with a shared root together

d.verdict: Find why users feel bad

l251|470.c: Push one trait to its extreme and actually build it, and you finally see options beyond the default.
l251|470.e: The biggest risk in a decision is never seeing the right option at all, because of constraints in our heads we don't notice. His approach resembles the "11-star experience": imagine the most absurd version along one trait, ignore cost and feasibility for now, and actually build it fast so you can feel it. For saving drafts, they first built the fastest version: close the window and it's gone, never a popup. It felt too unsafe. Then the safest version: autosave after a single keystroke. That left abandoned drafts everywhere. The final answer sat in between: prompt to save on a new item, autosave inside an existing draft.
