ex: His motto: the right amount is too much minus one
Where the extreme lies depends on the product's promise; "always a car" means surge pricing

marks.d: Prompt on new; autosave inside drafts

l251|470.c: The PM sits at the center of a double triangle, owns the external wording, and treats a few deadlines as P0.
l251|470.e: The usual triangle is PM, engineering, and design. He thinks the other half matters just as much: the PM also connects to sales and marketing, bridging the building side and the selling side. Linear's users are experts and sensitive to wording. The PM knows the customer's language best, so the PM should drive release notes and marketing copy, which sales then validates in the field. Deadlines should be rare, but once set they are P0: nobody gets pulled off, and the PM cuts scope hard so something decision-ready exists on the day. They rarely estimate; the week-one working version does that job. There are only a few dozen moments a year to speak publicly, and a missed one doesn't come back.
ex: The product team has a dedicated product marketer who owns every changelog
The influence most PMs miss is on the sales side

root.d: Bridges the building side and the selling side

items.d: PM drives wording and release notes
Tests whether the pitch works in the field

l251|470.c: When job hunting, find the hiring manager's burning problem and show you are the solution.
l251|470.e: PMs do a bit of everything, so they can't be ranked on one dimension. The hiring manager is really trying to fix a specific headache. So put on your discovery hat in the interview, figure out the job this role is meant to do, and show that you are the answer. That turns the manager's question from "which of these people" into "do I hire the solution to my problem or not." A friend's advice to him was to act as if you already work there: ask about this quarter's OKRs and how you could help hit them, and ask to talk to the relevant engineering managers. It also shows you where you could over-deliver the most.
ex: This is how he got the job at Mode
Everyone claims to have no weaknesses, so you are just one of the crowd

terms.d: Ask about OKRs and real difficulties
Propose ideas as if already hired

result.t: From one of many to the one
result.d: Hire you, or roll the dice

l252|472.c: When a project feels wrong, stop it and restart right away, compressing the change into a short window.
l252|472.e: What employees call the "Tobi tornado" compresses the conflict, candid conversation, and change management into a very short window. A project might be stopped on the spot, with the same people becoming the founding team of the next version, built a different way. His reasoning has three branches. If he is wrong, he has to understand why. If he is right, letting people keep building something doomed to fail is unfair to them. Looking away would be abandoning his responsibility as CEO. A career is only about forty years, so you should spend it on as many things you will be proud of as possible. He holds his views firmly, changes them when persuaded, and tries to free teams from sunk cost.
ex: Keynes: when the facts change, I change my mind
In the debate over merging Shopify into one codebase, "Tobi said so" saved a lot of time

items.d: Must find out why and update my thinking
Letting people continue is unfair to them
Abandons the CEO's job; not acceptable

l252|472.c: Nobody is close to their potential. Hold people to what they could do, not what they do now.
l252|472.e: He believes everyone is far more capable than they think. What limits them is methods they haven't found yet and environments that aim at mediocre targets. He often sees someone's potential more accurately than they do. So he keeps reminding people and holds them accountable to it, saying things like "you knew path A was right and took B because it was easier." It stings, but it is enormously valuable, and he is harder on himself. School teaches fixed content in fixed time and grades by score, which is like overfitting a model. His one criterion for his kids' schools is preserving curiosity. In a career, follow your curiosity and stack a few unique skills until you cannot be ignored.
ex: He went from a snowboard web shop to Shopify by following his curiosity
Goodhart's law and overfitting are the same thing
Hiring JIT-compiler PhDs to speed up Ruby, then giving the work back to the community

items: Name the path you knew was right

d.verdict: People held to their potential surprise even themselves

l252|472.c: No KPIs or OKRs: a metric stops working once it becomes a target, and fun and love are the strongest forces.
l252|472.e: By Goodhart's law, no single metric can capture the tensions inside a complex business, and once it becomes a target people game it. That doesn't mean Shopify ignores data. It has spent heavily so that any newly formed cohort can be sliced to the finest detail, and its release system keeps control groups running for a long time. But data is the cockpit instrument panel; the pilot still makes the decisions. He estimates only about 20 percent of what matters in a product can be measured. Taste, quality, and love cannot. If the metrics are falling but everyone says the product is more fun now, he trusts the metrics will follow. If they don't, adjust.
ex: Pessimism sounds smart; optimism always sounds naive
The suit, the accent, and pointing at pie charts don't equal results

items.d: His estimate of what metric-watchers can reach

l252|472.c: Existing solutions are products of their history. Re-derive the answer from today's building blocks.
l252|472.e: A proposal that says "we looked at how others do it, let's build a better version" makes him wary. Existing products rest on compromises made at the time, and many of those premises no longer hold. To do better you have to do it differently; he treats that almost as an axiom. The right question is: given every building block available today, how would you solve this problem? If the derivation reveals more wisdom in the status quo than expected, fine, but you cannot skip the step. Shopify itself was born this way. Today they are rebuilding search with new models, because the old approach is stuck in a local optimum.
ex: E-commerce software in 2004 existed to port traditional retailers' complex logic online
Enterprise software overfits to procurement checklists: every box ticked, unpleasant to use
Autoregressive models bypassed linguistics' grammar-first approach

items.d: Spot path dependence and stale compromises
How would you solve it from zero today
Keep the status quo if it's smarter

l252|472.c: When a base assumption flips, rerun the whole decision tree. Good decisions alone can still lead to a dead end.
l252|472.e: He compares a product leader to a thermostat, but one that periodically re-derives every base assumption against new information. Office location is a decision tree: same table if possible, then same floor, same city, same time zone. Shopify was already spread across four or five cities, and he sometimes spent a whole day in meetings with nobody physically beside him. That awkward hybrid state was the sum of a series of good decisions. The pandemic flipped the boolean of whether people could leave home, and the company needed to hire everywhere, so they went permanently remote. It is like running a marathon at altitude, harder, but the better trade-off.
ex: Don't move the office online; bring the internet into the company
Wikipedia and World of Warcraft guilds prove fully remote cultures can be good

items.d: One step back as headcount grows
Ottawa's talent pool wasn't big enough
Already spread across four or five cities
The new steady state after the pandemic

l252|472.c: On a hundred-year horizon, play positive-sum games with customers and partners, and value position over tactics.
l252|472.e: Shopify's hundred-year mission is to make entrepreneurship more common, and he has never considered selling. When Shopify and Stripe were both tiny, they agreed to assume both would win and to work together for the long run. That is a repeated prisoner's dilemma, where cooperation beats a one-time betrayal over time. He describes the company as a cockpit full of monetization levers, and his job as adding levers without pulling them, because customers notice value extraction. Business is like chess: there are tactics and there is position. First survive, then focus on position, meaning whether merchants trust and rely on you more. Companies that only play tactics drain their position and decline.
ex: Bankers said he had huge pricing power; he said he would leave if he were the customer
Infinite game: founders design winnable finite games for their teams
Long term, positive-sum games with customers are the ultimate growth hack

cells.d: Borrows from the future; customers notice

l252|472.c: Every time something complex becomes simple, a new wave of businesses appears on the platform.
l252|472.e: Software that makes people feel stupid betrays the purpose of a tool, so he sees good user experience as close to a moral duty. First-time founders are usually short on money, scared, and surrounded by people telling them not to. One day they hit an incomprehensible API or a tax setting, close the browser, and give up. Shopify's data confirms that every reduction in complexity brings a new cohort of businesses onto the platform, which turned his intuition into conviction. The scarcest thing in the world is not IQ or genius but courage. So the job is to lower the courage required to start, and that is worth a lifetime.
ex: Shopify has almost no tax configuration pages; the system just gets it right
Instagram testing Reels with a few hundred people outside your circle lowered the courage bar

terms.d: Taxes, payments, and fraud handled automatically
Make trying safer and more private

result.d: A mission path confirmed by data

l252|472.c: Product quality comes down to how much the team cares, and leaders must keep adding heat to the system.
l252|472.e: Most companies run at room temperature. Only exothermic people, founders and the best leaders, add heat and let a company outperform its peers. Every builder should know where their energy comes from. Michael Jordan ran on confrontation; he runs on dissatisfaction with the status quo, since today is the dystopia of the future. A product's quality ultimately reflects how much the people building it care. A PM's job is to see around the corner for the team and infect it with their own caring. To him, "founder mode" simply means adding heat: a founder as boss can protect the exothermic people who usually get pushed out.
ex: Only build products you care about, or you won't deliver what you want
At hackathons he codes late into the night with engineers, headphones on

marks.d: Business as usual; can't beat peers
The boss protects them; innovation lasts

l253|474.c: Training a model is more craft than science, and conflicting data leaves the model confused.
l253|474.e: She says data quality matters most in training, and debugging a model is a lot like debugging software: you trace which batch of data taught the strange behavior. During Claude 3 training, some data told the model it had no body and could not act in the physical world, while other data taught it to call tools and set alarms. The model could not tell whether it was able to set an alarm, so it often just refused. Training is always a balance between being more helpful and avoiding harm, with the goal of a model that behaves robustly across many different situations.
ex: Claude 3: "you have no body" data clashed with "set an alarm" data
The result was over-refusal, with the model saying it couldn't help

result.d: Unsure of its abilities; over-refuses

l253|474.c: Pretraining data is finite, but post-training can teach endless tasks. The bottleneck is now evals.
l253|474.e: The "data wall" argument is about pretraining, where a model compresses knowledge and learns to model the world by predicting the next word, and there is only one internet. New approaches like o1 shift the weight to post-training, using reinforcement learning to teach tasks such as search, computer use, and writing. Tasks can be expanded without limit, so she does not expect a wall. The real constraint is evaluation: frontier benchmarks saturate quickly, and new hard problems are needed to measure progress. Meanwhile distillation keeps making small models stronger, and the cost of intelligence is falling fast.
ex: GPQA scores are around 60 to 70 percent, close to PhD level
Claude 3 Haiku is smarter than the larger Claude 2

items.d: Compress the internet, model the world
Keep teaching new skills on endless tasks
Benchmarks saturate; new frontier tests needed

l253|474.c: To build an AI feature, break it into core behaviors, then train them fast with synthetic data.
l253|474.e: Canvas was the first OpenAI product where researchers and applied engineers worked together from day one. She broke the feature into a handful of core behaviors, then used o1 to generate the conversations, documents, and user instructions that became training data, instead of collecting human labels. That is cheaper and scalable, and once the core behaviors are learned, the model generalizes. After the beta launch, the team adjusted the synthetic data to match how real users actually used it. That is the path from beta to general availability.
ex: Early on they biased the model toward full rewrites, since rewrite quality was higher
Canvas took about four to five months from zero; Tasks took about two

items.d: Long text and code, yes; Q&A, no

l253|474.c: The product team's new job is prototyping with prompts and defining "correct" with eval sets.
l253|474.e: She has PMs and the emerging "model designer" role fill in a table: current behavior, ideal behavior, and why. Evals come in two kinds. Deterministic ones have a right answer, such as whether Canvas should trigger, or that "7 pm" must mean 7 pm. The other kind has humans compare outputs from different models and count win rates. A good eval set should score lowest on a prompt-only baseline, climb steadily with training, and not damage other capabilities. The prompt itself is also the fastest prototyping tool: try the idea in a prompt first.
ex: She built a 100K-context file upload demo in a local browser with just a prompt
Generating conversation titles in the style of the user's last five chats

items.d: Validate the idea and the interaction first
Tool JSON schema and ideal behavior
Deterministic scoring plus human win rates
Adjust data to the real usage mix

l253|474.c: Models will catch up on coding, while taste, creativity, listening, and management are harder to replace.
l253|474.e: She moved from frontend engineering into research precisely because she saw Claude getting better and better at frontend code. She thinks models will struggle with taste and genuinely creative writing, because there are too few examples of high-taste humans to learn from. Strategy work, like synthesizing data, connecting dots, and producing a plan, is something models are actually good at. The durable advantage is listening to users and iterating fast. Even AI research itself is constrained by research management: deciding where to bet limited compute with the most confidence.

Cursor won by iterating fast and listening to users

l253|474.c: Familiar products plus AI magic are the strongest form, and the next step is async agents earning trust.
l253|474.e: Tasks is nothing new in itself; reminders and notifications are familiar to everyone. Canvas looks like Google Docs. But the model is general enough that adding AI capability to a familiar form becomes powerful, and the product improves on its own as models get stronger. Interaction is moving from synchronous Q&A toward agents that run in the background, but trust has to build slowly, as it does between people. l253|474.c: The two labs are more alike than different: Anthropic polishes, OpenAI is more bottom-up.

Claude is like a nerdy librarian, which came from the team's careful work on its character, ethical behavior, and curated data. When Anthropic was small it felt like a family, with extremely strict prioritization. OpenAI is bigger, more willing to take risks, and gives researchers a lot of freedom, to the point that someone can work full time on teaching the model to write novels. l254|356.c: Only two crises can kill you: running out of cash, and losing product-market fit. The second is worse.
l254|356.e: He defines a crisis as suddenly losing something important you had. A cash crisis is when the cash plan breaks: a big customer leaves, investors vanish, prices swing. Worse is losing product-market fit, when regulation, competition, or a market shift means the product no longer creates value. Everything you thought you knew is void and you go back to square one. Product-market fit has exactly one metric, retention. And it does not help that the whole industry is hit, because you only have your one company.
ex: Order.chat, a food-ordering chatbot, shut down when restaurants closed in the pandemic
Fibo got tax filing under 3 minutes and grew the market 25 percent, then regulators stopped it
Microsoft declared the iPhone would fail and lost mobile operating systems

items.d: Lost customers, investors pull out, price shocks
Losing an A-player hurts but isn't one

l254|356.c: In a cash crisis, ask three questions and decide today. Every day of delay eats your options.
l254|356.e: Ask what is affected, how long the shock will last, and how much runway you have left, then redo the plan. Timing is everything: the later you cut, the less runway you buy, and after a few months there is almost nothing left to cut. In his example, a company with 5 million in annual revenue and 200K monthly net burn loses half its revenue. Cutting half the costs today gives 12 months, waiting three months gives 9, and not cutting gives 6. Even if you decide not to cut and go full speed, tell the team clearly. Everyone knows something happened, and if nobody is holding the wheel, your best people leave first.
ex: WeSki assumed two lost ski seasons, cut the team, and had existing investors reinvest
Example: 5 million in annual revenue, 200K monthly net burn, half the revenue gone

l254|356.c: Cutting costs means cutting people. Layoffs or across-the-board pay cuts depends on team culture.
l254|356.e: In a startup, 70 to 75 percent of the budget is people and the rest is noise. Saving money by canceling office coffee only signals that management is afraid of hard decisions. To cut costs by 30 percent, you can lay off 30 percent of the people or cut everyone's pay by 30 percent. Teams with strong mutual commitment prefer a shared pay cut; more individualistic organizations lean toward layoffs. Management should cut its own pay first, which saves money and shows leadership.
ex: When Waze nearly ran out of money in 2010, only management took a pay cut

items: Usually better than a universal pay cut
Fits teams committed to each other

l254|356.c: In a crisis the team needs transparency most, and extra equity buys loyalty and staying power.
l254|356.e: The team is what carries a company out of a crisis, and what the team values most is transparency. Don't sugarcoat. Say what is really happening, such as "I met dozens of investors and they all said no," and give specific numbers when asked. Key metrics should be public in normal times anyway. When cash is tight, he dilutes all shareholders to grant employees much more equity, and says plainly that if the company makes it everyone wins, and if not everyone loses together. Leadership is not built during the crisis. It comes from everyday transparency, recognition, and putting the team first.
ex: At several companies he diluted shareholders to give employees 5 times their original equity
Asked how many investors he had met, he answered "37"

terms.d: Key metrics and bad news out in the open

result.d: Most stayed even when payroll couldn't be met

l254|356.c: Never giving up is a startup CEO's most important trait, and only two situations justify quitting.
l254|356.e: The first behavior of a successful CEO is never giving up, and the second is making decisions with conviction, because otherwise the team will not follow. He does not say the founder is to blame; he says the founder is responsible. Blaming interest rates or an industry winter does nothing for your success, while taking responsibility means owning your fate. Only two situations call for quitting: the problem you set out to solve has disappeared and the mission no longer holds, or the team is wrong and cannot be changed, for instance when a toxic investor controls the board.
ex: FairFly's CEO: we are like cats, we have nearly died nine times
Pontera is 12 years old, has pivoted twice, and nearly died twice

l254|356.c: After losing product-market fit, ask if you'd start this today, then validate the pivot step by step.
l254|356.e: A pivot admits that your underlying assumptions were all wrong, so you walk the path as if starting for the first time. Validate the problem first, looking for strong emotion like "I hate this." Then check whether your technology, team, or industry knowledge gives you a real advantage. Then ask whether you have the energy to start over. Next, check it with the team, because the new direction often comes from the employees closest to customers. Only then go back to raise money. Passion does not need to come first; once the problem is validated, the passion grows.
ex: Pontera gave its board two options: return the money or try a new direction
Investors didn't want a refund; they invested for a big return

More attractive with assets in hand

l254|356.c: You can't prevent a crisis. The only preparation is more cash in the bank.
l254|356.e: You never know where the next crisis will come from, so you cannot prepare for it specifically. What you can do is analyze fast, act fast, and stay well funded. With too little runway, the CEO does nothing but fundraise instead of creating value. His general advice is about 18 months. Risk-takers can live with 12, and some CEOs prefer two or three years so they have room to pivot or grab a new opportunity. Luck matters too, and he defines luck as opportunity meeting preparation.
ex: When Google launched free navigation in 2010, investors urged Waze to sell
Microsoft and Qualcomm unexpectedly invested, and Waze survived on a different use case

l255|205.c: Nobody switches jobs at random: pushes give you the energy to leave, pulls decide where you go.
l255|205.e: In interviews people often credit a new job to luck, but dig deeper and certain experiences had prepared them to see the opportunity. That is why he says employees hire companies. One frustration is not enough to make someone leave; it usually takes three or four pushes stacking up. But with only pushes and no pulls, people either just complain or jump into an equally bad role. Pulls act like a compass that tells you what progress means to you. Once people stop making progress in their career, they start looking for the next job.
ex: Over 15 years and a thousand-plus interviews, he found 13 pushes and 14 pulls
Of people who said they left for more money, 53 percent didn't get more
If his daughter can name four pushes, she is already job hunting

terms.d: Boredom, feeling overlooked, no path ahead
The progress and outcomes you want

result.d: Without pulls you land in the same hole

l255|205.c: Every job seeker is in one of four "jobs," and each calls for a completely different kind of role.
l255|205.e: All of his interviews fall into four buckets. People who want to "get out" are drained of energy and should take an easy transitional job, a jobcation, with a set end date, to recover. People taking "the next step" need to make sure the step is big enough, and should plan around the job after next. People trying to "regain control" mostly lack time and need more balance. And people who need to "regain alignment" have been pulled into work they are bad at, and should get back to what they do best and what energizes them.
ex: After leaving private equity, he became VP of home sales and ate dinner at home every night for four years
He once shrank a company of nearly 50 people to 5 to get back to building products

root.d: First figure out which one you're in

items.d: Take a jobcation and recover first
Make it big; plan for the job after next
Get your time and balance back

l255|205.c: Dig out what energizes you and what drains you, and treat them as design requirements for your next job.
l255|205.e: Look back, even to high school, and find the meetings and projects you entered with one unit of energy and left with two or three. Then ask what in that situation excited you. Do the same for draining moments and break down their causes. The key is to abstract to the causal level: liking the beach may really mean liking having people around. He treats the job seeker as a product and writes these findings up as a requirements list. Everyone has draining work, but the ratio can be changed.
ex: Your bottom five StrengthsFinder themes reveal your energy drains best
Put process and gamification on the work you hate, not the work you love

The little joy you get in return
At 40 to 50 percent it stops feeling like work

l255|205.c: Pay and title are static features that depreciate. What keeps people is the experience of the work.
l255|205.e: Like products, jobs have features and experiences. A title looks important at first but depreciates: after a while as VP you want to be a C-level, and the title becomes a new push. Money often stands in for something else: wanting respect, paying off debt, feeling behind. He has also noticed that overpaying people makes them conservative, afraid to lose the job and doing only what they are told. His own approach is reasonable pay plus big bonuses, which attracts people who come to learn.
ex: To keep an employee who wanted to become a coach, he added a coaching business

items.d: The moments that charge or drain you

l255|205.c: Prototype your career like a product: go broad, interview people, then accept the trade-offs.
l255|205.e: Most people assume they can only find a similar role in their own industry, but the skills you are good at apply in many places. Start by imagining a wide range of roles, then find people doing them on LinkedIn for informational interviews. Those conversations test your assumptions and give you practice talking about yourself. Then narrow to one direction and write your resume around what you can do rather than where you have been. No job ticks every box, so decide what you are willing to give up, and put a time limit on that choice.
ex: A neuroscientist found that a geographic expedition coordinator is basically a travel agent
Someone gave up a 350K to 400K salary to be chief of staff to a well-known founder at 200K

l255|205.c: Weaknesses often create superpowers. Don't sand down your flaws; find partners who complement you.
l255|205.e: He had several head injuries as a child and read at a third-grade level at 18, so he could only learn by asking questions. Asking questions became his superpower. He sees innovation as a contact sport full of conflict, and being told to improve at "harmony" would only weaken his strength. So build a team with people who love what you hate, instead of hiring people like yourself. Anyone who wants to be a founder needs that same self-knowledge first, to work out what kind of founder they are.
ex: His business partner of 25 years is his complete opposite and his best friend
He tells his own career story using the Pixar story template

items.d: A way of learning forced on him
The core of interviewing and innovation

l255|205.c: Hiring should fit the job to the person, and job descriptions should describe the experience, not list requirements.
l255|205.e: Job descriptions are mostly made up: the manager stuffs in everything they want and everything they don't want to do, so everyone hunts for a unicorn and forces people to fit the job. He argues for the reverse: when you find a great person, reshape the job around them. People who love their work don't leave. A description should explain the context, what progress means in the role, and what you get in return. Requirements like "five years of experience" are lazy and scare off people who are qualified at three. In interviews, you can ask candidates directly about their pushes and pulls.

After his wife hired a resume writer, she got three interviews in a week

l256|489.c: Community Notes has to be the people's voice, not the company's, and fully transparent.
l256|489.e: In the past, misleading posts were judged by fact-checking organizations or an internal trust-and-safety team. He felt neither had the scale, speed or public trust to work. So he set rules that sounded crazy at first. The company has no button to change a note's status; if a bad note appears, the system itself needs redesigning. Anyone with a verified phone number can be randomly admitted as a contributor. Any post can get a note, with no exemptions. The scoring code and data are all public, so anyone can rerun and audit them. Because the team never made exceptions, people across the spectrum came to trust it.
ex: Posts by Elon Musk, government figures and advertisers all get notes
In 2024, about 95,000 notes were viewed roughly 30 billion times
There are about 950,000 contributors

items.d: Company can't change a note's status

l256|489.c: To build something new inside a big company, run the team like a startup; Twitter called this a "Thermal."
l256|489.e: A Thermal was Twitter's internal startup-style setup. The team has one clear owner who reports to an executive who can make decisions. Members work on it full time, so an algorithm idea from the morning can show results by afternoon. There are no OKRs; the team sets its own pace around the next key milestone. Everyone on it asked to join. To start, you only need one person each for frontend, backend, machine learning, design and user research. At X he learned teams can be even smaller than he thought, and people who chose to stay act more like owners.
ex: He still goes straight to Elon Musk when he needs a decision
X's Spaces team scaled up in two or three weeks; old Twitter might have taken a year
The team runs on one long-lived Google Doc, not heavy task-tracking tools

terms.d: Plus an executive who can decide

result.d: A tiny team runs a huge product

l256|489.c: Managing more people doesn't mean more impact; going back to a small team building from zero often does.
l256|489.e: In his first three years at Twitter he helped turn the company profitable, then ran a large PM organization. He put in a lot of effort but didn't see the product changes he wanted. After paternity leave, he asked his boss to let him drop his job and focus on misinformation instead. His own reasoning: staying put would have produced maybe a dozen more pages of OKRs, while Community Notes has become an industry standard. His career has zigzagged this way more than once: build something new on a small team, let it grow, then jump back to a small team.
ex: When he joined in 2016, about a third of Twitter's staff left each year
Blake Scholl left Groupon to build supersonic planes

l256|489.c: Letting data prove the product at every step is why it won people over and survived four CEOs.
l256|489.e: First they showed mockups to people across the political spectrum to confirm they would read notes criticizing their own side. Then they ran crowdsourcing tests to see if ordinary people could write good notes. Then they opened a pilot to 1,000 people to see if gold could be sifted from the mud. Quality came first: better to miss a good note than show a bad one, with speed and scale added later. Every expansion came with data that convinced the team itself. Because the output helped people of every persuasion, each successive leader could get behind it.
ex: Only about 8% (7% to 11%) of proposed notes end up shown
In the first three days of the Israel-Gaza war, about 500 notes went live, half within 5 hours
When Elon Musk saw the prototype in 2020, he replied it was worth a try

l256|489.c: Anonymity actually makes people more willing to cross party lines; real names don't add credibility.
l256|489.e: The team first assumed notes would only be trusted if contributors signed them with real accounts. The pilot showed the opposite. Many people feared harassment for writing notes on hot-button topics, so good notes simply didn't get written. And a public identity made people afraid of looking like traitors to their side; anonymously, they were more willing to rate a note against their own camp as helpful. Other quality mechanisms in the system were enough to keep note quality high without names.
ex: He believes about 80% of society can actually agree on most things

items: Fear of attacks, so people don't write
Don't want to look like a traitor

l256|490.c: A note shows only when people who usually disagree both find it helpful, not by majority vote.
l256|490.e: Showing every note, or picking by majority vote, would both produce biased notes. Instead the algorithm uses matrix factorization, a math technique that finds the underlying viewpoint dimensions in the rating data. A note appears only when a solid share of raters on both sides of that divide call it helpful. That makes notes more neutral and accurate, and naturally hard to game. A separate algorithm checks whether people broadly agree a note is inaccurate. Raters who consistently go against the consensus stop having their ratings count. The thresholds are deliberately conservative, because the team believes the product lives or dies on note quality.
ex: Most ML engineers at the time thought it had to be closed-source and rely on fact-checker labels
The display threshold is 0.4 on an arbitrary scale

items.d: Better to miss than to mislead

l256|490.c: The algorithm was chosen by testing on pilot data; the real problem was polarization, not vote rigging.
l256|490.e: The first version he shipped was a variant of PageRank, Google's early web-ranking method, built to stop groups of accounts from upvoting each other. Its flaw: it amplified the bias of whichever side had more people. Real data from the pilot showed the main problem wasn't manipulation but users split into opposing camps. So the focus shifted to finding agreement that bridges those camps. Once the requirements were clear, he ran an internal Kaggle-style competition and only then brought in more engineers. While the problem was still being figured out, a single ML engineer was actually the right size.
ex: Part of the inspiration was a researcher's list of accounts liked by both parties

items.d: Stops vote rings but amplifies bias
Shows polarization is the core issue
Add people once the need is clear

l256|490.c: Notes don't downrank posts, yet user reactions alone cut the spread of misleading content sharply.
l256|490.e: X's core ranking algorithm doesn't use "has a note" as a signal. But once users see a note, like and repost rates drop noticeably, which is an unusually large effect for an A/B test. Outside researchers also found that seeing a note changes how much people believe the post's central claim. Authors of noted posts are more likely to delete them. He has mixed feelings about that: the best notes end up unseen, and the same claim may keep circulating elsewhere.

l256|490.c: Small teams must regularly delete code, because small incremental wins often become permanent maintenance burdens.
l256|490.e: Whether for promotions or just human nature, engineers like to run a month-long A/B test and bank a small, measurable win. What they rarely notice is that each one adds maintenance cost the team carries forever. When a team is forced to shrink, it has to audit the system and remove whatever costs more to maintain than it delivers. No full rewrite is needed; clearing out the extras and keeping the core works well. After X's big layoffs the whole company did this, and the systems got leaner and needed fewer people.
ex: He recalls Asana meetings spent mostly grooming a backlog of irrelevant tasks

l256|490.c: Open source lets outsiders improve the algorithm, and LLMs can rewrite notes at scale under human review.
l256|490.e: Staying open source has a cost: the system must let anyone download the data and reproduce the results on a single machine, so the architecture differs from a normal online service. The payoff is collaboration with outside researchers. Supernotes is one example: it feeds existing notes to a large language model to generate many variants, then uses a simulated jury, built from each contributor's past ratings, to predict who would find each version helpful and pick the one most likely to pass. The open question is whether human raters will still check sources as carefully once AI is involved.
ex: Reproducing it on one machine takes about 500GB of memory and a day
Ethereum founder Vitalik Buterin once wrote an article verifying the algorithm

l257|492.c: Open source is this generation's most important idea: software runs our lives, so without software freedom we aren't free.
l257|492.e: He grew up in Houston, read Hayek, Adam Smith and the American founders in high school, and discovered open source while building websites for musicians in exchange for music lessons. His view is that software controls more and more of life, and if that software doesn't come with basic freedoms, people aren't truly free. He thinks the founders would be open-source advocates if they were alive today. WordPress uses the GPL license: anyone can use, study, modify and redistribute it for any purpose, but if you share your changes, you must pass those same freedoms along.
ex: WordPress itself began as a fork of an abandoned project called b2
WordPress powers over 40% of websites, about 10 times the runner-up

items.d: More and more decisions are made by software
Shared changes must carry the same freedoms

l257|492.c: Llama isn't open source: past a user threshold you need Meta's permission, so you've lost the freedom to use it freely.
l257|492.e: Meta's Llama can be downloaded and run locally, which he credits. But its license says that above a very high monthly-active-user count, you need Meta's approval. In his view, the moment you might have to ask permission, you're at that company's mercy. The definition of "user" is fuzzy too: WordPress has few registered users but billions of monthly visitors. The Open Source Initiative also says Llama doesn't meet the open-source definition. He suspects Meta insists on the label partly because European regulators treat open-source models more leniently.
ex: He recalls the threshold being around 750 million monthly active users
Meta is also a major contributor, with React and improvements to the PHP engine

marks.d: Code can't be seen or changed
Downloadable, but permission needed at scale

l257|492.sc: Open source in the AI era
l257|492.c: Proprietary software will trend toward worthless; AI should customize a maintained open-source core, not start from scratch.
l257|492.e: Large models learned to code from open-source code, which is also the safest training material. He expects most code in open-source projects to be AI-assisted within five years, and automated scanning to make the huge plugin ecosystem far more secure. Writing code is just the start; maintenance is the real life of software. His ideal: when someone asks a model to build a site, it installs WordPress first and customizes on top. That way the core engine's security audits and updates come along automatically, which beats generating fresh proprietary code every time.
ex: About 25% of Google's code is written with AI assistance
Some 60,000 plugins and themes; the core has had no remote vulnerability in years
He calls himself "the most dissatisfied WordPress user"

items.d: Change looks and features as needed
AI can scan them for security issues
Continuously audited and updated for free

l257|492.c: Don't just build a product, build a movement; you're a real platform when the ecosystem earns more than the core.
l257|492.e: Economics taught him about systems and incentives, and jazz taught him collaboration. Success comes from giving people a belief and a worldview: the "Code is poetry" footer, every release named after a jazz musician, plus meetups, forums and Q&A sessions where people can take part and contribute. A CMS core, he says, is something a few developers could write in weeks, but nobody can replicate 60,000 plugins and themes. That is the advantage no one can copy. Proprietary platforms often pull the rug out when developers get too successful; open source guarantees no one can take it away.
ex: He once said that even if he grew devil horns, WordPress would still belong to everyone

items.d: An advantage no one can copy
More than the core: a true platform

l257|492.c: Open source sometimes has to stand up to bullies, or free riders will destroy the whole ecosystem.
l257|492.e: He accuses WP Engine, a WordPress hosting company, of stopping its contributions to the core after private equity firm Silver Lake took control. He says its use of the trademark led many users to assume it was the official company, and that it turned off revision history, essentially the undo button, to save money. The two sides talked for 18 months; he believes WP Engine was pretending to negotiate while preparing a lawsuit. After he spoke out publicly at WordCamp, WP Engine sued him personally, WordPress.org and Automattic. He stresses this kind of conflict happens once a decade; issues with other hosts get resolved by talking.
ex: Surveys showed 20% to 40% of people thought WP Engine was the official WordPress
He says about 45,000 sites have already left WP Engine

items.d: WP Engine sues and hires PR

l257|492.c: Social algorithms amplify anger, so complex issues need long conversations, not short posts.
l257|492.e: He says about 1% of people used to think he was terrible, and now it's maybe 4% to 5%. But negative sentiment feels seven times stronger than positive. His team ran sentiment analysis and found the share of negative comments varied wildly by platform, suggesting algorithms may favor controversy. A rumor got 700,000 views; the correction got 20,000. So he argues less on Reddit and Twitter and uses long formats like podcasts to explain the details. Support from core contributors keeps him grounded: 98% of core developers have stayed.

Mainstream media coverage was actually more balanced

l257|492.c: Great software isn't designed by committee; have one leader, and let the community's right to fork keep them in check.
l257|492.e: Hundreds of volunteers do the daily work, but someone has to make the final call. Had there been a vote, he says, most people would have rejected the Gutenberg block editor, yet unpopular long-term bets like that carried WordPress through the social, mobile and other technology shifts. He compares himself to a mayor rather than a CEO: the community can leave at any time, or fork the code and go its own way, and that is the check on his power. The trademark is split three ways, between the foundation, himself and Automattic.

l257|492.c: Acquisitions mostly speed up products that already work; a Tumblr-style turnaround won't happen again for years.
l257|492.e: Most acquisitions, he says, take something already good and make it better, or bring a strong team into an existing project, with founders often staying for years. Tumblr was different: the sticker price was tiny, but it came with lawsuits, investigations and a large team burning cash. He led the turnaround himself and eventually replaced most of the staff. Now they're moving half a billion Tumblr sites onto the WordPress backend and testing subscriptions and first-party promotion instead of ads. Whether private equity is good or bad, he says, depends on whether it takes control and what it actually does.
ex: WooCommerce had about 35 to 40 people and now drives most of roughly $500 million in revenue
