l258|301.c: Most people don't care about your grand vision; hide it inside something they already use every day.
l258|301.e: Inspired by early computing pioneers like Douglas Engelbart, he wanted everyone to be able to create their own software. So he first built a friendlier developer tool, and it took about two years to realize most people just want to finish the report in front of them and don't care about making software. The turn came when he hid the vision inside everyday productivity software: notes and docs on the surface, with no-code building blocks underneath. He calls it "broccoli wrapped in candy." He admits the first version was more what he wanted than what people wanted.
ex: He got into a good school after placing second in a Beijing programming contest
People describe Notion as "the Lego of software"

terms.d: Notes and docs everyone uses daily

result.d: The deeper you go, the more it can do

l258|301.c: Don't fear starting over; better abstractions compound and quickly make up for the sunk cost.
l258|301.e: Early on they bet on Google's Web Components, which turned out too new and unstable to tell whether a bug was theirs or the library's. They had to cut the five-person team down to him and Simon and rewrite on more proven technology. He says a reset isn't just a feel-good slogan. People think linearly, but good abstractions compound like math: a tiny core can produce complex behavior, so what you've already invested gets recovered fast. The real danger is letting momentum push you into working on things that don't matter.
ex: After the layoffs they sublet their San Francisco home and office and went to Japan to code
Smalltalk, inspired by Lisp, had a tiny core but enormous influence

items.d: Let go of code already written
A small core yields complex behavior

l258|301.c: Products need a balance between "building to win" and "building for value"; leaning too far either way fails.
l258|301.e: Building to win is like competitive sports: the market is the arena and users and revenue are the scoreboard you optimize. Building for value means bringing your own taste and values into the world. He found the second more lasting, and it carried him through the dark periods. But lean too far toward yourself and you have a research project; lean too far toward commerce and you become a commodity like everyone else. He calls the balancing act craft, like finishing a wooden cabinet, weighing aesthetic direction against technical ability over and over.
ex: Notion's meeting rooms are named after classic tools like the iPhone and a Toshiba rice cooker
The company's philosophy is called "craft and values"

marks.d: True to yourself, useful to others

l258|301.c: Bolting on features that violate your product philosophy, just to compete, gets rejected by users and the team.
l258|301.e: He admits that for over a year Notion shipped things that weren't good enough. Project management is a core use case, and to catch up with competitors they hard-coded concepts like sprints directly into the product instead of designing them as new composable blocks. The result was weaker than rivals, clashed with the rest of Notion, and even the engineers found the code awkward. It took him nine months to a year to see the problem, then they returned to block-based building. His rule: work with the system and it helps you; work against it and it fights you.
ex: He feels Notion only got quality, speed and values back in line in 2024

d.verdict: Build by your values or the organization rejects it

l258|301.c: Replace headcount with systems and tools; small, dense teams move faster and turn a profit.
l258|301.e: He believes the main cost of growth is internal communication, so anything a system or tool can handle shouldn't be solved by adding people. Notion is itself a tool for making tools, and the company runs almost entirely on it. Staying lean brings profitability, and profitability means not raising money every year or two, so the team can focus on the product. They track revenue per employee and talent density, because great people want to work with great people. His metaphor is a small bus: the smaller it is, the better it turns and accelerates, and the leader has to pick who rides.
ex: First salesperson hired after $10 million in revenue; first PM at 50 people
During COVID a single Postgres instance neared its limit, weeks from going down

l258|301.c: A horizontal product must sell enterprises the Lego kit, not loose bricks, and win users through billion-person use cases.
l258|301.e: He doesn't regret building a horizontal product, one that works for every industry, but he wouldn't recommend it. Only hardcore fans care about the bricks; most people want a kit they can assemble out of the box. For enterprises you have to become a solution that shows up on the customer's P&L, and he regrets making that shift too late. Vertical software has natural market boundaries; a horizontal product has no walls, so you have to build your own. Their approach is B2C2B: win people with note-taking, a billion-person use case, and let those individuals bring Notion into their companies.
ex: About half of enterprise customers started as individual users
Notion ranked second for project management in Lenny's survey
After calendar, they're building email, another billion-person use case

l258|301.c: AI naturally favors horizontal tools where information is concentrated, and it can assemble the Lego for users.
l258|301.e: He compares large language models to a new material, like aluminum for aviation. Stage one was embedding writing AI where people already write every day. Then they found AI is good at retrieval and reasoning, and works better the more information sits in one place, so they built Q&A and connectors to outside apps. Stage three excites him most: assembling the blocks was always Notion's weak point, and AI writing code is essentially assembly, so it can generate custom software and agents on top of years of accumulated knowledge-work blocks. He sees SaaS unbundling reaching its end and the market swinging back toward bundles.
ex: He says AI coding improved noticeably starting with Claude 3.5 Sonnet
PCs unbundled software, Microsoft Office bundled it, SaaS unbundled it again

l259|497.c: AI's biggest value isn't faster engineers; it's letting the 99% who can't code build products.
l259|497.e: All his life friends have asked him where to find good engineers. Technical skill has always been the bottleneck between most people's ideas and reality. When ChatGPT arrived, colleagues doubted AI would change programming, so he built the open-source GPT Engineer to prove it. Many companies use AI to make engineers more productive, but he believes the bigger positive impact is serving people who can't code. So he and former colleague Fabian founded Lovable, aiming to build "the last piece of software," the one that builds all the others. He expects a Cambrian explosion of new startups.
ex: GPT Engineer has more than 50,000 stars on GitHub
A designer named Harry shipped apps to clients with it, then started his own company
At peak it created about 15,000 GitHub projects a day and got temporarily banned

items.d: Less than three months after launch
Almost all from word of mouth

l259|497.sc: The law of not getting stuck
l259|497.c: The key for an AI coding tool is never getting stuck; fixing each sticking point makes it reliably better.
l259|497.e: His "scaling law" is simple: the more work you put in, the more reliably the product improves. AI-built apps often start out impressive, then one bug appears and the user never climbs out. The team works hard to find the most common sticking points, such as adding login, persisting data or connecting Stripe payments, then tunes the whole system with measurements and keeps a very fast feedback loop. Knowing how to rescue a stuck AI is a useful skill today, but the boundary where AI gets stuck is receding fast, so that skill will matter less and less.
ex: He says users call Lovable the most reliable tool of its kind
Next step is more agentic: writing tests, running them and fixing bugs on its own

l259|497.c: Foundation models are oil someone else discovered; Lovable's own work is the interface and packaging.
l259|497.e: He doesn't take all the credit: the underlying capability comes from foundation models. What his team obsesses over is how to present it so people get the most out of it. For example, you can click to change text and colors directly, like in Wix, instead of waiting for the AI to rewrite. One click connects the open-source backend Supabase or deploys to Cloudflare. Code syncs to GitHub, so engineers who want to go deeper can edit in Cursor while everyone else stays in Lovable. Growth comes from people loving the product, plus sharing progress openly on social media.
ex: In the demo, the two-word prompt "Airbnb clone" produced a UI in about 30 seconds
The name went from "minimum lovable product" to "absolutely lovable product"

items.d: Engineers can take over in Cursor

l259|497.c: The future bottleneck isn't engineering but taste and user intuition, so everyone on the team must be a generalist.
l259|497.e: As building gets easier, finding real pain points and judging what's good matters more. Engineers won't be replaced, but they should see themselves as translators of human problems into technical solutions and move up a level of abstraction, rather than guarding the frontend. When building a product team, he wants everyone to understand system architecture, design, product taste and talking to users. The best investment anyone can make, he says, is becoming part of the top 1% at using AI tools: spend a full week building one thing end to end with AI.
ex: Dig in with equally obsessed friends and you can reach the top 0.1%
Tell the AI what you expected and where it fell short, not just "this doesn't work"

items.d: Understands what people really care about

l259|497.c: Hire for people who genuinely care, then verify with a one-day to one-week work simulation.
l259|497.e: What matters most is caring, even obsessing, about the product, users and working as a team, rather than coming along as a passenger. They also want generalists who learn fast, plus one standout strength, which for them is usually squeezing the most out of large language models. In interviews they dig into things candidates have obsessed over before, pose an unfamiliar hard problem to watch them think, and almost always run a work simulation of at least a day, often a week. The job ad is modeled on Shackleton's call for Antarctic explorers: long hours and a fast pace, stated up front as a filter.
ex: The team is about 18 people, at least 12 of whom write code
Sweden has plenty of raw talent but lower average ambition, which he wants to raise

l259|497.c: Focus only on today's biggest bottleneck, fix it fast, skip long roadmaps, and let engineers lead.
l259|497.e: His algorithm is simple: find the biggest problem, actually solve it, then pick the next one, without dreaming up long roadmaps. Figuring out the biggest problem isn't easy; it takes talking to users and reading the feedback board. Because the right solution is usually tangled up with technical details, engineers lead decisions and there are no product managers yet. Priorities are set every Monday and results demoed at the end of the week, and the roadmap is only clear about a month out. Most work happens in the office, and lunch together is the most efficient time for ideas to collide.
ex: They once rewrote a service built in a scripting language for performance, pausing new features
One week's theme was just fixing bugs and polishing

l259|497.c: Design the end-to-end experience first, then add AI; retrofitting AI into someone else's product rarely works.
l259|497.e: Early in his career he was the first employee at an AI education company in Stockholm. Its premise was that personalized teaching could lift learning outcomes by two standard deviations, a huge gain. The company built a personalized-learning API, but it required other education products to swap their engines for its AI. Retrofitting cost too much and the results disappointed. His lesson: start from what the user's complete experience should look like, then decide where AI solves a specific problem, instead of carrying a cool technology around looking for somewhere to put it.
ex: They've imagined a "Lenny mode" that asks users whether anyone actually wants what they're building

items: Sell an API for others to retrofit
Costly to retrofit, hard to land

d.verdict: Start from the user's whole picture, then place the AI

l260|445.c: Running the dev environment in the browser, on the user's own computer, is the only way to be fast, stable and cheap.
l260|445.e: Competing products spin up a cloud virtual machine for every user. It takes minutes to boot, often hangs, and sends people to support. Free tiers get abused for crypto mining and attacks, so they keep shrinking. StackBlitz spent years building a WebAssembly operating system that boots inside the browser and uses the user's own CPU and memory. He points out that Figma and Google Docs also compute locally, and that this is the only model that has ever scaled to a billion users: there are fewer than 100 million rentable virtual machines in the world, but billions of devices.
ex: In the demo, a working Spotify clone appeared in about 60 seconds
Deployment also builds in the browser, at almost no cost to the company

d.verdict: Only local computing scales to a billion users

l260|445.c: If you bet on deep technology, keep burn low and take many shots, so you survive until it finds its use.
l260|445.e: He and his co-founder saw a path in early Figma: new browser capabilities plus a homegrown engine built over years. So they bet on an operating system inside the browser. Developers loved the technology but wouldn't pay for the existing uses, and for years there was no business model. They bootstrapped for the first two or three years and spent little even after raising money. When everyone was hiring in 2020 and 2021, they refused to follow, or they would have died. His rule: until you see users fighting to get the product, the default answer to spending is no.
ex: His previous company bootstrapped until it was acquired
At 19 he secretly lived in AOL's offices, spending a dollar a day

items.d: Bets on a full toolchain in the browser

l260|445.c: Code can be checked automatically, so language models will improve faster at coding than in other fields.
l260|445.e: They tried building Bolt about a year earlier, but the apps the models generated often didn't run or looked bad, so they shelved it. Seeing Claude 3.5 Sonnet brought it back. In fields like law, he argues, judgments depend on society and juries, which makes reliable training data hard to create. Code either runs or it doesn't, so you can generate apps at massive scale for reinforcement learning, where the model improves through trial, error and reward. The logic holds up technically, and every major lab is now racing on coding, because rewriting the software world is a trillion-dollar opportunity.
ex: He sees Sonnet as the first model where AI became the main act rather than a sidekick
When ChatGPT first launched, they couldn't find anywhere worth adding AI

l260|445.c: Users will pay more for extra AI compute when the payoff is clear, so flat monthly subscriptions no longer fit.
l260|445.e: Bolt launched with a single $9 tier. Users burned through it in two days and begged to pay more, so within a week the team shipped upgradeable tiers, which competitors later copied widely. Earlier tools like Copilot chased Netflix-style flat pricing, which forced them to minimize inference cost and ruled out agent-like experiences. Now the value of AI output is plainly visible, and people will pay for more of it. The product was rushed out in 90 days with many basics missing, servers were overwhelmed, and he and his chief of staff spent about 90% of their time on support.
ex: They hit $20 million in annual revenue before the product even worked on mobile
At one point Anthropic had no more GPUs to give them

l260|445.c: Few people, each holding the full picture, is the only kind of team that survives explosive growth.
l260|445.e: The core five to seven people have worked together for more than five years, rare in Silicon Valley and the reason they could place long-term bets. They believe in fewer people with more context each: deep mutual trust, everyone able to solve a problem end to end, and engineers who can change the UI while on a call with a user and ship it on the spot. After the explosion, the whole company meets on Zoom for an hour every morning. It looks expensive, but almost nothing gets lost in communication. Product requirement docs stay short and often come with a working Bolt prototype.
ex: The team is about 15 to 20 people, with only three in support
Most employees came from the StackBlitz user community and work remotely, mostly in Europe

result.d: No layers of approval

l260|445.c: Product managers are the best suited to direct AI coding, and software org charts will be rewritten.
l260|445.e: They assumed users would all be developers, but about two-thirds aren't. The non-developers who do best are often strong PMs: they understand how the technology works, scope things well, describe requirements without losing detail, and help debug. Those are exactly the skills needed to direct an AI coding agent. He expects PMs and designers to take over interface work and effectively write the code, while developers review it and tackle the hard problems. His advice is to talk to the AI like writing a Linear ticket: be specific where it matters and give it room everywhere else.
ex: A founder who can't code built a CRM in three weeks for about $300
An agency had quoted $30,000 and six months for the same thing

items.d: Tweaks with AI down to the pixel
Mostly product and design, few engineers

l260|445.c: Prioritization has to balance user feedback with gut bets on things users don't know to ask for.
l260|445.e: He compares a product team to a restaurant chef: you handle customers saying a dish is bad, and you also launch the signature dishes you believe in. Many capabilities never get requested because users don't know they're possible. Native mobile app support was a bet against the feedback, and it became their best-received launch. That judgment, he says, comes from years of getting beaten up by the market. They also launched Bolt Builders, where certified engineers help users by the hour when the AI gets stuck.
ex: With Expo, you scan a QR code to try the native app on your phone
Planned: put bolt.new in front of a Figma link to turn it into an app

marks.d: Like a developer on the team

l261|500.c: Introverts prefer less stimulating environments. That's not shyness, and there are more introverts than people think.
l261|500.e: She offers two self-test questions. After two hours at a party you're enjoying, do you feel energized or start looking for the exit? On a completely free weekend, how many people do you want around, and how close? Many people have conformed to extrovert norms so long that they've forgotten their real preference. Introversion and extroversion form a spectrum, with ambiverts in the middle. Shyness is the fear of social judgment, which is a different thing. She estimates introverts make up a third to a half of the population.
ex: Research she cites shows the most successful salespeople are ambiverts
Psychologists find people generally grow more introverted with age

l261|500.c: You can learn skills like public speaking without becoming someone else; being at ease as yourself is the real power.
l261|500.e: She went from shy to confident on stage by acquiring skills and managing fear, not by turning extroverted. The method is desensitization in tiny doses. In a speaking-anxiety class, her first assignment was just to say her name and sit down. Then she practiced in low-stakes settings like Toastmasters until her brain stopped treating the stage as a threat. Finding role models who are like you matters too. People can tell when you're performing a persona, and being fully at ease makes you more convincing in interviews and on stage.
ex: She modeled herself on Malcolm Gladwell's thoughtful style of speaking
Warren Buffett, shy and introverted, took a Dale Carnegie course at 21
Bill Gates and many Silicon Valley founders are introverts

l261|500.c: Introverts are often underrated at work, so make your contributions visible and state your ambitions plainly.
l261|500.e: Companies lose introverted talent largely because nobody sees what those people contribute. She suggests writing to make your work visible, using small doses of exposure to earn outsized visibility, and building trust through one-on-one relationships, one person at a time. Say your ambitions out loud, or people may read you as unambitious. Introverts often have deep passion and expertise, which earn trust and connections on their own. Networking doesn't have to be broad; one or two real conversations per event are enough.
ex: Write for the company blog; host internal talks
Kathy Fish, former head of R&D at P&G, built trust one conversation at a time
Ask a mentor for 10 minutes to discuss your 1-, 3- and 5-year goals

l261|500.c: Prepare beforehand, speak early, and only say what you truly believe, and a positive cycle follows.
l261|500.e: Introverts aren't great at improvising, so think through your points and questions in advance. Speaking early sets the direction of the discussion, and afterward people naturally look to you, which makes each contribution easier. She used this in law school by jumping in first. People respond to conviction, not volume, so before you speak, check that you actually believe it. Managers can rotate who speaks, discuss agenda items beforehand with reflective colleagues, or have everyone write down ideas before talking.
ex: "Brainwriting": write ideas on sticky notes first, then share them
No-meeting blocks or work-from-home days to protect deep work

items.d: Work out your points and questions
Set the direction of the discussion

l261|500.c: Before saying yes, ask: would I still want this if it were tomorrow? Default to no.
l261|500.e: It's easy to agree to things that are far off, so imagine you'd have to do it tomorrow. Creative people block out requests that interfere with their work. The more invitations success brings, the more they crowd out the work that produced the success. Her default for events, talks and podcasts is no, with exceptions about 5% of the time, and she keeps a template for declining. Another test is physical: if you'd feel relief imagining the event got canceled, you have your answer.
ex: The creators Csikszentmihalyi studied routinely turned down invitations
Naval's reminder that success crowds out the source of success

items.d: Would you still want it tomorrow?
The rest get a polite template

l261|500.c: Confidence comes from mastery, not the other way around, and introverted kids need a longer runway.
l261|500.e: She disagrees with the idea that you need confidence before you can do something well. Get good at something and confidence follows. So help kids find activities they genuinely love. Introverted children need a longer runway, and you can take it in small steps: walk a little closer to the school each day, or dip just a toe in the pool first. Parents can also share their own experiences openly, which takes the shame out of being shy.
ex: Arrive at the party early and settle in before the crowd

items.d: Rather than being required up front

l261|500.c: Pick work that fits your temperament. Long-term dread is an alarm, and goals and paths can be designed separately.
l261|500.e: If you dread going to work most days, the job doesn't fit your temperament. She suggests separating the outcome you want from the path to get there: keep the goal, redesign the path around your personality. She herself hires no full-time employees, prefers loose part-time collaborations, and has a rule of no meetings before 3 p.m. She also objects to treating volume as evidence of a good idea; humble introverts shouldn't underestimate their own intelligence.
ex: A TED speaker who wanted a startup but not a team designed around management
No meetings before 3 p.m., with podcast recordings as the exception

items: Keep the goal, change the path

d.verdict: Don't let the wrong path kill the goal

l262|503.c: No product is truly viral; sustainable growth comes from word of mouth.
l262|503.e: At LinkedIn he asked the head of growth and learned something sobering: no product sustains a viral coefficient above 1, meaning each user brings in more than one new user, and every referral mechanic eventually tops out. What actually drives growth is word of mouth, which can't be measured: users recommending the product on their own. So Superhuman wrote the raw ingredients of growth straight into its company values: create delight, deliver remarkable quality, and build something extraordinary that people can't help talking about.
ex: Facebook's peak viral coefficient was about 0.7, and it lasted only about a year
LinkedIn's address-book import had a lifetime viral coefficient of about 0.4
Referrals give both sides a free month; some people invited hundreds

items.d: About as high as it gets

l262|503.c: The apparent slowdown was half market expansion and half an avoidable management structure.
l262|503.e: He splits R&D into "deepening the solution," which makes existing users happier, and "widening the market," which lets more people use the product. In email, covering every platform and Outlook is painfully slow, and during that stretch users feel updates have dried up. You have to push through, but the payoff is a technical lead that's hard to match and a ticket into the enterprise market. The avoidable slowdown came from the eight direct reports he had by convention: time tracking showed only 6% to 7% of his time went to product, design, engineering and marketing. After hiring a president to run operations, his reports dropped to two and that share rose to 60% to 70%.
ex: His "switch log": every task switch gets a Slack message starting "TS:" to track time
Direct reports went from eight to two
The president acts like a "grown-up co-founder" and strategic partner

items: Main arena when finding product-market fit

d.verdict: Widening feels slow but is worth pushing through

l262|503.c: Position the brand on a single attribute; for Superhuman, that attribute is speed.
l262|503.e: Influenced by the marketing classic "Positioning," he believes every famous brand stands for exactly one thing. In the first year he interviewed hundreds of potential users, and many complained that Gmail and Outlook were slow. He then tested the positioning point by point. Was it unique and unclaimed? Since Chrome, almost no software had led with speed. Did it reinforce the product strategy? The competitors were huge companies with heavy architectures, the ones least able to match on speed. The final test was listening to how users described the product to friends at a party.
ex: Chrome's launch compared page rendering against lightning in slow motion
Users' pitch to friends boils down to one line: it's ridiculously fast

items.d: Hundreds complain email clients are slow
Few apps sold speed after Chrome
Heavy incumbents can't easily speed up
How users pitch it to friends

l262|503.c: Mandatory one-on-one onboarding early on creates superfans, but you have to know when to stop.
l262|503.e: Early on you couldn't use Superhuman without a one-on-one onboarding session, and at the peak about 20 people did nothing else. There were two benefits. First, engagement, retention, product-market fit scores and word of mouth all ran well above industry benchmarks, and early superfans lit the brand on fire. Second, when capital is plentiful, people can stand in for onboarding and activation flows you haven't built, so engineers stay focused on finding product-market fit. The condition is that onboarding itself pays for itself. Once the funnel widens and some people simply don't want to be taught, you need a first-class self-serve experience ready.
ex: About 20 people ran manual onboarding at the peak
He saw competitors spend nearly half their engineering effort on self-serve flows
Email is mission-critical, so you can't ship a half-finished product

root.d: Mandatory early; nearly all self-serve now

items.d: Retention, PMF score, word of mouth above benchmarks
People instead of building activation flows
Funnel widens; some refuse to be taught

l262|503.c: To find product-market fit, deliberately ignore most early users and listen only to the right small group.
l262|503.e: Start by measuring product-market fit with Sean Ellis's question: "How disappointed would you be if you could no longer use this product?" Companies where more than 40% say "very disappointed" tend to grow fastest. To push that number up, don't over-serve people who already love the product, and ignore those who wouldn't be disappointed. Focus on the "somewhat disappointed" users who value the core benefit, such as speed, and politely set aside everyone else's requests. Each planning cycle, spend half the effort doubling down on what users love most and half removing the obstacles holding that group back.
ex: 40% "very disappointed" is the dividing line between fast and slow growth
Changing the survey method invalidates old data, so you have to reset the baseline
They now run the engine separately for sub-products like the sales edition and collaboration

items.d: Like it, but stuck on small issues
People who like it for speed

l262|503.c: Business software should be designed like a game, but points-and-badges gamification doesn't work.
l262|503.e: He used to be a professional game designer. He cites a Stanford experiment: children who expected a reward spent half as much time drawing on their own as children who didn't. External rewards crowd out internal motivation, which is why bolting points, levels and badges onto software fails. Real game design focuses on goals, emotions, toys, controls and flow, the state of total absorption where you lose track of time. Good games are built from good toys: features that invite exploration, are fun even without a goal, and often surprise you.
ex: Stanford study: the no-reward group drew 17% of the time, the reward group 8%
Time autocomplete: type "never" and an email will never remind you again
Five areas: goals, emotions, toys, controls and flow

terms.d: Invites exploration; fun without a goal

result.d: Fun at the toy level and the game level

l262|503.c: Position first, then price: charge where users start to find it expensive, not where it feels like a bargain.
l262|503.e: Superhuman positioned itself as the best email tool for high-performing individuals and teams, backed by before-and-after usage data. He then used the Van Westendorp price sensitivity method, asking about a hundred early users four pricing questions. Most startups price at the "bargain" point to widen the funnel. But a best-in-category position calls for the point where people start to find it expensive yet still buy once they do the math. The median there was $30 a month. Working backward, a billion-dollar valuation needs roughly $100 million in annual revenue, about 300,000 subscribers, which he judged achievable.
ex: Users process email twice as fast, reply one to two days sooner, and save over four hours a week
A top consulting firm measured 3.3 hours saved per partner per week
The method comes from the book "Monetizing Innovation"

l263|504.c: Every engineer ships one marketable feature a week, by cutting scope rather than quality.
l263|504.e: "Marketable" means something a user might download or pay for on its own, not table stakes like feature parity between platforms. When time gets squeezed, people quietly lower quality instead. The right move is to go item by item asking "is it still useful without this?" and keep cutting until one more cut would make it useless. What's left is a week's worth of work. After launch, users complain about whatever is most missing, and you add that next week. Silence is the real warning sign. Directions that prove themselves across many experiments get more investment.
ex: For "add an image," they cut background removal, color tools and cloud picking, keeping only the system photo picker
User complaints go straight into next week's priorities

items.d: Stop when one more cut breaks it
The minimal version goes to users

l263|504.c: A startup's job is to take on technical debt, trading future engineers' time for speed today.
l263|504.e: Big companies either pay their debt immediately or are still paying off debt from their startup days, and startups outrun them precisely by borrowing. His question is: does this problem have to be solved today, or can engineer number 50 or 500 solve it? If the company fails, that engineer will never be hired. But every debt charges interest, eating 1% to 2% of the team's time each day. Once interest piles up to 80% or 90%, all you can do is keep the lights on. So you have to create enough value before the technical-debt runway runs out.
ex: Every Q4 is infrastructure season, when they pay down debt in bulk
One-way-door decisions still get real care; two-way doors can be casual
The team mostly uses Cursor and has tried Devin

items.d: Leave the problem to future engineers
Each debt costs 1% to 2% of time daily
Create value before the runway ends

l263|504.c: Competitors know every feature users ask for; winning takes a secret roadmap of things nobody requested.
l263|504.e: The public roadmap comes from collecting user feedback and prioritizing it. But whatever users ask of you, they ask of every competitor too, so even great execution yields only small wins. The secret roadmap holds ideas nobody has ever requested, ones users may even dismiss on first sight. They come from the team's own understanding of users, problems and technology, and they aim to change behavior so people can't go back. Ideas come from company-wide brainstorms every quarter, get voted on, and the product team assesses feasibility. The biggest wins usually come from here.
ex: Eye Contact, built with Nvidia, redirects a teleprompter gaze to look at the camera
The demo video was translated into many languages and still has millions of views

d.verdict: Breakthrough wins mostly come from the secret roadmap

l263|504.c: Every function should deeply understand the one next to it, and PMs should own the work all the way into marketing.
l263|504.e: Early Snap had no product managers. A dozen or so designers with no direct reports doubled as PMs, which let Evan Spiegel control every user-visible change through them. Still, he thinks Snap succeeded despite not hiring PMs rather than because of it, since things nobody truly owns tend to fall through the cracks. What he values is crossover: designers who think like PMs, engineers who understand product. Captions goes a step further and has PMs understand marketing, because search and feed ads are really the product's front door placed on another platform, and the user journey starts there.
ex: When Snap had five or six thousand employees, design was still only 10 to 12 people
Strong product-market fit hides bad decisions and teaches the wrong lessons

root.d: Innovation often appears where two crafts meet

items.d: Snap: designers reported straight to the CEO
Captions: ad slots are the product's front door

l263|504.c: Big companies can test with prototypes and let them go viral internally; alignment follows on its own.
l263|504.e: Once Snap grew to thousands of engineers, every new product took hundreds of people half a year, so a wrong bet was very expensive, while copycats kept forcing it to innovate. He founded a design engineering group where one person handled everything from design to code. They embedded prototypes directly in Snapchat, tested them with small groups in Australia or a few high schools, got real data, and only then handed validated ideas to a large team to scale. The unexpected bonus: at a company that size, employees behave like a user base. Good prototypes spread internally from engineers all the way up to Evan, and consensus formed by itself.
ex: Only after validation would about 500 engineers spend six months on it
Evan didn't fight copycats; he kept growing the pie

items.d: One person does design and code
Australia, or a few high schools
From engineers up to the CEO
Hand to a large team for six months

l263|504.c: AI video should serve storytelling; in "recording reality" it does nothing but harm.
l263|504.e: He divides video into two kinds. One is documentation: private moments like a get-together, or public ones like news and disaster footage. Faking those with AI only deceives. The other is storytelling: ads, social content, film and TV, even reality shows. Audiences already know it's fiction, so letting more people tell stories is purely good. Captions is deliberately designed to make the first hard and the second easy. He estimates it will take a few more years before AI video is fully indistinguishable from real footage, at which point society may fall back on physical evidence and spoken testimony.
ex: Nobody thinks the Geico gecko is really selling insurance
Captions focuses on "talking videos" with dialogue, not silent B-roll

l263|504.c: AI adoption is far slower than people think, yet AI-generated ad creative already beats footage of real people.
l263|504.e: He believes even astonishing technology spreads slowly. In India, his parents are the only people in their neighborhood using ChatGPT. So winners have to push their product in front of the people who need it. About a year ago, Captions' AI-generated video ads drew comments calling them "too fake." Once the technology crossed the line, the complaints vanished, and generating 30 or 40 variants at once and picking the best now outperforms a single human-shot ad. Localizing with straight AI translation performs close to the original too. He imagines a fully AI-generated social feed appearing within about five years.
ex: Generate 30 to 40 creatives at once and pick the winner
Three steps: find a problem, solve it with technology, find the people who have it

items.d: Comments said AI ads looked "too fake"
Translated versions perform near the original
His dystopian vision of a social network

l264|506.c: Decide how much time you're willing to spend first, then shape a solution that fits inside that limit.
l264|506.e: The usual approach picks a big concept and asks for an estimate, and the work drags on and on. Shape Up flips it: first ask how much time the business is willing to spend on this at most, which he calls the appetite, like setting a budget before house hunting. Then, within that fixed time, adjust the scope and shape a workable solution. Finally hand the complete idea to the team and let them break it into tasks themselves. Six weeks is a ceiling, not a fixed cycle: long enough to build something substantial, short enough to expose most unknowns before starting. Small changes can take two.
ex: DHH could only code 10 hours a week at first, which forced a method that wasted no engineering time
Scrum slices an idea into hundreds of tickets, which he calls "the shredder"

items.d: Max time to spend, up to six weeks
Team sees the whole, splits tasks itself

l264|506.c: If the time box ends unfinished, don't slash scope to ship; send it back to shaping.
l264|506.e: You promised six weeks and the end still isn't in sight. Cutting the parts that make the feature valuable makes everyone feel the work was wasted, hurts morale, and carries a sense of debt into the next cycle. Basecamp's answer is the circuit breaker: cancel it outright and rethink. Few teams can stomach that. The more practical move is to stop pouring effort into something that wasn't thought through, pull it from building mode back into shaping mode, bring in different people or questions to find out exactly what's fuzzy, and then decide whether to start again.
ex: Quoting Bob Moesta: you can't fit ten pounds into a five-pound bag
Giving a team six weeks with no shaping and making them cut scope is, he says, "cruel"

items.d: Basecamp's way; few can take it
Clear up the fuzzy parts first

l264|506.c: Shaping produces a solution explained in ten or fewer moving parts, not a Figma file or a PRD.
l264|506.e: Polished designs often get bounced the moment engineering sees them, because a screen's surface doesn't show how things flow or what mechanism sits behind it. A beautiful renovation rendering is useless until someone checks whether there's wiring in the wall; cost and schedule can change completely. PRDs are full of correct sentences that nobody reads, and reading them still doesn't tell you what to build. Good shaping lets engineering, product and design all say "I know what to do now": breadboards and fat-marker sketches that explain the flow and the parts, with high-fidelity design saved for later.
ex: The calendar example: a two-month dot grid, a scrolling agenda below, and a new-event button
A fat-marker sketch must not turn into a "blurry Figma"

items: No more than ten moving parts

d.verdict: Shaping is done when everyone knows what to build

l264|506.c: Shaping sessions must include a senior engineer who knows where the landmines are buried.
l264|506.e: At Basecamp he combined the technical and user-experience perspectives himself, and the designers all coded, so he never hit the wall between design and engineering. After leaving, he found many teams following the book and still running over, and the root cause was shaping without an engineer in the room. He argues for putting a senior engineer who knows the legacy code, a product person who knows the business context, and a designer together. Like a veteran plumber who insists on opening the wall before quoting, they open the code before committing, expose the time bombs, and turn surprises into trade-off discussions.
ex: A fintech thought it could drop one onboarding step; the code branched three ways by bank
A session runs about three hours, and about three sessions settle a solution

terms.d: Knows what's hard and where the mines are

result.d: Risks exposed before work starts

l264|506.c: How much detail to give the team is a dial, and in practice the most common failure is too little.
l264|506.e: People worry that too much detail reduces engineers to order-takers. But the failure he sees most often is the opposite: not enough detail, with engineers later complaining they were given too little. The right amount depends on who's on the team. Junior members often won't ask when they don't understand, and hide their confusion until it blows up late in the project. More direction helps them succeed and grow, and you loosen the reins over time. Seasoned veterans can get less. If someone feels they should be part of the fundamental decisions, just bring them into the shaping session.
ex: Specifying the database schema for a senior engineer only breeds resentment

cells.d: Like designing their schema for them
Blows up late in the project
Experts fill in the gaps themselves

l264|506.c: At kickoff, the builders split the solution into at most nine pieces, instead of someone else writing tickets.
l264|506.e: In Scrum, the people writing tickets usually aren't the people doing the work, and tickets that look reasonable hide unknowns. A Shape Up kickoff hands the shaped, complete solution to the team, like giving blueprints to a construction crew without teaching them how to swing a hammer. For teams of mixed experience, he suggests drawing a three-by-three grid and having the builders list at most nine major pieces of the implementation: six weeks is about 30 working days, so each piece is roughly four days. This exposes oversized scope on the spot and gives senior people a chance to correct junior thinking.
ex: "Nine" comes from the "seven plus or minus two" limit on what people hold in mind
Beyond ten pieces, it degrades into a ticket list

items.d: Catch oversized scope or flawed thinking

l264|506.c: The best time to introduce shaping is when founders first let go, at 30 to 50 people in product and engineering.
l264|506.e: While the founders do everything themselves, any process works. Problems start when the founding engineer hands off a project for the first time, or the CEO first delegates to a PM. He often gets called in when product and engineering number about 30 to 50: all the hires are made, yet things keep getting slower. The other case is an organization with years of Scrum, a wall between product and engineering, and endless refactoring and paying down technical debt, where leadership needs an honest conversation about how time is spent. He doesn't fear the "feature factory"; shipping steadily is healthy. The more common disease is dragging on with no end in sight.
ex: Pain signals: requirements that keep ballooning, designs bounced back, more problems the further you go
If the method just feels unfamiliar, wait until it hurts more

marks.d: 30 to 50 in product and engineering; ideal
Stuck in refactoring and debt; needs leadership

l264|506.c: In Shape Up, the PM moves upstream to frame the problem instead of chasing projects.
l264|506.e: In many teams, PMs spend their time inside the time box pushing progress and unblocking people, which makes them project managers. Once Shape Up runs smoothly, the PM moves upstream: understanding the business context, going back and forth with the CPO, and finding the slice of the problem most worth a few weeks of work. Further up is demand-side research, where he recommends Bob Moesta's jobs-to-be-done approach to find where users are struggling. Shape Up itself covers the supply side: turning an opportunity into something that can ship in a reasonable time.
ex: For a demand-side primer, he recommends "Demand-Side Sales 101"
For the full picture of jobs-to-be-done, read "Competing Against Luck"

items.d: PM narrows the problem, picks a slice
Team delivers within the time box

l265|41.c: When you don't get the reaction you wanted, first ask what you failed to make clear.
l265|41.e: She often sees people communicate vaguely and then act surprised that others are confused, skeptical, or indifferent. Her advice is to keep the agency on your side. If someone doesn't respond, ask how you could have been clearer, more persuasive, or better at anticipating their questions. Communication is a way to get results, and it is a skill you can practice. Don't save your best effort for meetings with executives; take every colleague seriously so you get enough reps. The measure of progress is simple: how many back-and-forths it takes to get the reaction you want, and whether that number is shrinking.
ex: Can seven rounds of back-and-forth shrink to two or three?
Practice one technique at a time, not thirty at once
Keep a "smart phrasing" file to train yourself to notice what works

d.center: Get the reaction you want, faster

items.d: A note, a doc, or a meeting
Change one technique at a time

l265|41.c: Get people to want it before you explain how to do it; don't assume they already agree.
l265|41.e: A common mistake is to launch into process details before the other person has decided to do the thing at all. When nobody responds, people add even more detail. She separates the two steps: selling is getting someone to want to do it, and execution is telling them how. The order matters. Even when someone agreed long ago, a few sentences on why, why now, and what you need from them are worth it, because their head is full of other things. The reverse also holds: if they are nodding by page four, don't insist on finishing page thirteen.
ex: An ops lead asked executives to fill in weekly reports, opened with the form and deadline, got silence
A better opener: this is a chance to recognize people on your team

items.d: What problem it solves, and why now
Tie it to their own goals

l265|41.c: Concise is not the same as short; rambling usually means you haven't finished thinking.
l265|41.e: Concision is about information density. Three hundred words can be bloated and a thousand can be tight. "Lead with the conclusion" only works if you know what your conclusion is, so the real bottleneck is thinking it through. The most reliable fix is preparation, even one minute before a meeting to ask why you're there and what you want to say. After writing, remind yourself to trim; you can usually cut twenty percent or more. Fragmented bullet points look concise but push the work of interpretation onto the reader. Turning them into full sentences is a good test of whether your idea is actually baked.
ex: A vague message in a 15-person channel has a far bigger blast radius than you think
Bolding 30 percent of your text emphasizes nothing
Use signposts: for example, because, next step, first, second, third

items: Shows the logic in full sentences

d.verdict: Think it through first, then trim

l265|41.c: Say exactly how sure you are, and weigh your proposal against the company's real priorities.
l265|41.e: Overconfident people present assumptions as facts, and teams take them at face value and spend real money. Overly modest people offer a good suggestion and then add "feel free to ignore this," which is just as irresponsible. Her rule is to speak to the evidence: say whether this is an early hunch or backed by data, and lay out your reasoning so others can poke at it. She also warns against becoming a lone martyr. One growth client complained that no one would lend him engineers, then realized the company's priority that year was retention. Put the company first, and scale back your ask when that's what it calls for.
ex: "This will improve X" and "this might improve X" are two different statements
Try opening with: "Based on what I know so far, my gut says..."

marks.d: A good idea goes to waste
View, evidence, and how sure you are
The team takes it at face value

l265|41.c: Before you speak, think of the most obvious objection; when stumped, answer the question behind the question.
l265|41.e: She calls it the MOO, the most obvious objection. Many so-called ambushes in meetings could have been predicted with two minutes of thought, sometimes a few seconds. Once you see the objection, you can build the answer into your message or change how you frame it. Sometimes you discover a real hole in the plan and can fix it first, because communicating and thinking are tangled together. When you're asked for a number you don't have, an experienced person doesn't just say "I'll get back to you." They offer the closest data they do have, then probe what the asker is really worried about. Repeated questions on the same point usually signal a deeper concern.
ex: Write your MOO on a sticky note and keep it in view
Asked last month's mobile share? Try "roughly 60 to 70 percent this quarter, and rising"

items.d: A few seconds on the obvious objection
Fix the hole before you speak
Find out what really worries them

l265|41.c: The more senior you are, the more managing up matters, and the best lever is offering your own view.
l265|41.e: She used to think managing up was for junior employees. Then she found it matters more the higher you go. Assignments get vaguer, often just "move this number," so you have to tell your boss how you plan to do it. Rather than a weekly list of what you did, bring a point of view. Asking "what should I do?" shifts the thinking onto your manager. Saying "here's what I recommend, where are the holes?" gives them a draft to edit. People closest to customers and data should be the ones voicing what they see.
ex: When you share a report, add your own insights and conclusions
Try "I've noticed this keeps happening, and I think it's because..."

result.d: And proof that you're thinking ahead

l265|41.c: Feedback is a strategy, not self-expression; its only goal is to get the other person to change.
l265|41.e: She used to avoid conflict, bottling things up until she couldn't stand it, then booking a one-on-one that turned into venting. The other person either deflated or got defensive. Later she set a single goal: produce a change in behavior. Anything that doesn't serve that goal gets cut. What stays is whatever makes the person want to change and see the benefit for themselves and others, which usually means cutting ninety percent. Vent the emotion somewhere else first, with a partner, a friend, or a therapist. Otherwise one raised eyebrow can set you off.
ex: She calls the framework "strategy, not self-expression"
She cites Einstein: repeating the same thing and expecting a different result

items.d: Clear the emotion before the talk
Drop anything that won't drive change
What makes them want to change

l265|41.c: Run through the CEDAF checklist when you delegate, so you can let go without lowering the bar.
l265|41.e: CEDAF stands for five steps. C is comprehension: does the person have everything they need, including account access and a picture of what done looks like? E is excitement: explain why it matters and tie it to their career goals or the quarter's priorities. D is de-risking: anticipate what is most likely to go wrong and flag it up front. A is alignment: leave room for questions, and you'll often discover you left out something key. F is feedback: shrink the feedback loop as far as possible, checking in after a day rather than a week. She notes that AI tools also pause to confirm in stages, which is the same idea of tightening the loop.
ex: Worried they'll waste time on 100 rows? Have them do 10 first and see how long it takes
When she drafts replies with Claude, stating her intent first works far better

l266|509.c: The foundation under AI products changes every two months, so build for what models can almost do.
l266|509.e: In the past, the technology under a product barely moved; a database might get 5 percent faster in two years. With AI, every couple of months the model can do something it couldn't before. Its inputs and outputs are fuzzy, and whether accuracy is 60, 95, or 99.5 percent leads to completely different products. OpenAI practices what he calls model maximalism: don't spend much effort building scaffolding around today's flaws, because a better model in a few months will wash it away. If a product sits right at the edge of what the model can do, keep going.
ex: The o-series ships a new generation every three or four months, each a leap in ability
He estimates API costs fell about 100x in two years while intelligence went up
The model you use today is the worst model you'll use for the rest of your life

items: Get it right once, it stays right

d.verdict: Design for what's coming, not around today's flaws

l266|509.c: Writing evals is becoming a core skill for product people.
l266|509.e: An eval is like an exam for a model: it measures how good the model is at creative writing, science, coding, and so on. Intelligence is multidimensional. Being great at competitive programming doesn't mean being great at front-end work or migrating COBOL. Most of the world's data and workflows aren't in public training sets, so you teach the model with data from your own setting and measure it with custom evals. For deep research, the team first wrote down hero use cases and ideal answers, turned them into evals, then fine-tuned the model and climbed the score. Only when the numbers kept rising did they know they had a product.
ex: Deep research takes 20 to 30 minutes to do what used to be about a week of work
The models can help write your evals, and they're pretty good at it

items.d: Questions you want asked, ideal answers
Teach it with your own data
Rising numbers mean a real product

l266|509.c: Model labs can't cover every use case; industry data and custom models are startup territory.
l266|509.e: He quotes Twitter co-founder Ev Williams: no matter how big your company is, there are more smart people outside it than inside. OpenAI focuses on making its API great because every industry has countless workflows AI could improve, but the data and domain knowledge sit inside companies and governments. OpenAI doesn't have the people to do it all and doesn't want to. Just as a new hire needs two weeks to learn how a company works, a model needs that setting's own data. His picture of the future: a smart general model, plus specialized ability built by fine-tuning on domain data and measured with custom evals.
ex: About 3 million developers already build on OpenAI's API
OpenAI itself doesn't want to become an enormous company

items.d: Startups build for a specific sector

l266|509.c: In the AI era, plan lightly, let teams decide bottom-up, and keep PMs few but strong.
l266|509.e: He lives by the line "plans are useless, but planning is essential." Every quarter the company pauses to review and untangle dependencies, but nobody expects to ship exactly what the document said three months later. Teams work bottom-up: the people who best understand the model make the calls, and launches don't wait for him or Sam Altman to sign off. Research and product have to be one team, or the company is just another API customer of its own models. There are only about 25 PMs. He'd rather give each one more engineers than drown in docs and micromanagement. He looks for high agency, comfort with ambiguity, and the nerve to make the call when nobody else will.
ex: The model names are a mess, everyone knows it, and it's not the most important thing
The chief people officer vibe-coded an internal tool herself using Windsurf

items.d: See a problem, go fix it
Nobody draws your lane for you
Drives a decision when no one else will

l266|509.sc: Reason about it like a person
l266|509.c: When designing AI experiences, you can often reason about the model the way you'd reason about a person.
l266|509.e: Reasoning models were the first to need time to think before answering. Twenty-some seconds is too long to stare at, but too short to go do something else. The team borrowed from how people behave. Asked a hard question, a person doesn't go silent for twenty seconds, and doesn't narrate every thought either. They say "good question" and share a bit of progress. So the interface ended up showing a one- or two-line summary of the reasoning. By the same logic, having several models answer and one model combine the results looks a lot like a brainstorm. Chat looks primitive, but like talking to a person, it is general enough to hold any level of intelligence.
ex: After DeepSeek showed its full chain of thought, they settled on a short summary instead
Telling the model to act as a world-class marketer also changes how it behaves

marks.d: 400 million users may not want it

l266|509.c: Break problems into pieces and let specialized models cooperate, rather than handing one model the whole thing.
l266|509.e: He is surprised how few companies use fine-tuned models. Inside OpenAI, ten problems often become twenty model calls. Each call uses whatever fits the latency and cost budget: a bigger or smaller model, a dedicated prompt, or a fine-tuned model, and the results are stitched together. Customer support is the example. A model trained on the knowledge base and tone guidelines answers automatically. When unsure, it drafts a reply for a human to review, and the human's edits become new training data. From this he concludes that nearly every product team will soon have a research engineer who knows how to fine-tune.
ex: Over 400 million weekly users, and he estimates a support team of only 30 or 40 people
Putting a few question-and-good-answer pairs in the prompt is poor man's fine-tuning

items.d: Split the big task into specific subtasks
Like the division of labor in a company
Edited answers feed back into training

l266|509.c: AI won't make a great film for you, but it lets creators explore far more options first.
l266|509.e: He says he draws worse than an eight-year-old, yet with image generation he can make things he never could by hand. A well-known director told him that designing a sci-fi transition shot used to cost $100,000 and a month of waiting for two versions, and you picked the less bad one. Now he brainstorms in Sora prompts, gets fifty variations, iterates, and only then hands it to a VFX house for polish, starting from a far better place. Creativity and taste still matter. What AI adds is the ability to explore much more.
ex: When image generation was in internal testing, usage inside the company exploded
If nobody inside your company is obsessively using your social product, question the direction

items.d: The director iterates in prompts himself

l266|509.c: Every child in the world should already have an AI tutor; the models have been good enough for a while.
l266|509.e: He sees personalized tutoring as one of AI's most important uses. Research consistently shows that regular schooling plus one-on-one tutoring speeds up learning by several standard deviations. The models are now good enough, ChatGPT is free, and Android phones are everywhere, yet no product serves the world's 2 billion children. That surprises him. He is optimistic about the technology's long-term effect but admits there will be pain along the way. Society has to take care of everyone who gets hit, and ChatGPT itself is a good retraining tool.
ex: His kids take self-driving cars and talking to AI for granted
He teaches his kids to be curious, independent, confident, and thoughtful

result.d: He's surprised it doesn't exist yet

l267|209.c: AI can expand who can ship a product from tens of millions of developers to 100 million people.
l267|209.e: He has always built developer tools that make hard things easier, but users still had to know how to code. His rough numbers: about 5 million React developers, about 20 million JavaScript developers, and at least 100 million people who want to build products. His reference point is Slack's roughly 100 million monthly users, who spend all day talking about what they want to build. ChatGPT was good at writing Next.js and Tailwind code from day one, because those open-source tools were already in its training data. That's where v0 came from: describe what you want, and it produces a prototype or even a full product you can launch.
ex: More than 1.3 million people have used v0
The community feature drew over 20,000 projects in under a month, all forkable
He calls it social building, a nod to social coding on GitHub

l267|209.c: Jobs that translate designs into code will disappear; understanding how things work and knowing the vocabulary will matter more.
l267|209.e: He used to hire people specifically to translate design mockups into CSS layout code. He sees that as a translation task, and Transformers, the architecture behind today's models, came out of machine translation. With every new model generation he tests it on his own personal website. The previous generation needed about ten prompts to recreate it; the latest needed two, and its accessibility markup was better than his own. Still, knowing how systems work and using precise terms lets you steer the model far better. Memorizing every CSS property is no longer necessary.
ex: A designer said the word "turbulence" and got exactly the animation she wanted
Useful style words: neo-brutalism, minimalist, newspaper, retro

d.verdict: Go broader and shallower, but know how things work

l267|209.c: Kids should learn math, speaking, and showing their work, and low-level infrastructure is still hard-won skill.
l267|209.e: He has five children. He values math because it trains you to understand the logic behind things. He values speaking and vocabulary because prompt enhancement can't replace your own thinking; you need the right words to steer a model toward the references you have in mind. He takes his kids to hackathons to watch people present their work, because as software gets cheaper, having an audience and a personal style matters more. For those who want to go deep into coding, JavaScript is the place to start. Infrastructure like compilers, clouds, and frameworks is something models can call but struggle to rewrite from scratch, so those engineers will stay in demand.
ex: JavaScript is the English of programming languages, reaching billions of devices
Limited by context and compute, an LLM won't write a cloud from scratch

root.d: What he hopes for his five kids

items.d: Build an audience and a style
Hard for models to rebuild from zero

l267|209.c: Once anyone can ship, working prototypes replace documents as the way teams collaborate.
l267|209.e: The deepest change, he thinks, is that conversations with customers and colleagues will center on an interactive artifact instead of departments waiting on each other. Of Vercel's 600 people, about 150 could code; now everyone can build, and some of the best v0 projects come from marketing, sales, and product. PMs use v0 to make a living PRD that demonstrates the error state, the success state, and the slow-loading state, and people respond with "just ship it." A weekly Demo Friday gives everyone permission to step outside their comfort zone.
ex: A designer's v0 demo of infrastructure interactions became one of his most popular posts
He looks forward to not talking about AI separately: AI is just software

items.d: If you can imagine it, you can deliver it

l267|209.c: With v0, ask for a lot, describe only the experience you want, and when stuck, say "try another way."
l267|209.e: He suggests making the boldest request you can and steering with references and inspiration. If you're out of ideas, fork something from the community. Technical people should suspend their skepticism and describe what the user should experience, not how to implement it. Iterate back and forth as you would with an outside agency; many times a single "try a different approach" got him unstuck. Keep an escape hatch, too: the code is always visible and editable. One design engineer got stuck after about 120 iterations, pasted the code into o1, and found the fix.
ex: On a flight, in two hours on a $20 plan, he built a live flight radar
It chose Canvas to render tens of thousands of flights and drew routes along the Earth's curve

items.d: It may know more than you do
Read the code, edit it, ask another AI

l267|209.c: One big advantage of AI products is an extremely tight user feedback loop.
l267|209.e: His number one piece of advice for founders is to put feedback entry points everywhere in the product. Early Vercel copied Stripe and built an embedded feedback box with four emoji faces that posted straight to Slack. AI products get a constant stream of feedback; users will even point out which step of the model's reasoning went wrong. That feedback improves the next version's model, prompts, examples, and retrieval. Products without AI struggle to match that pace of iteration. He is also bullish on expert AI tools for specific professions, because people who know the field vouch for them and keep refining them.
ex: After DeepSeek, showing the reasoning process became a killer feature
Legal teams love GC AI, whose CEO is himself a lawyer
Vercel open-sourced its AI SDK and templates so others can build a v0 for doctors

items.d: Thumbs up or down, flag the wrong step
More people rely on it daily

l267|209.c: Taste is trained: watch real people use products, and be stingy about adding features.
l267|209.e: He doesn't believe taste is innate. Vercel has an internal principle called increasing exposure hours: count how much time you spend watching people use your product or other people's. Everyone overrates their own product, so you have to put it in others' hands and face the real pain points. About a third of his meetings this week were customer meetings, and he often asks customers to demo live. A good product is a thousand details. Adding a feature is like adopting a puppy that grows into a big animal needing daily care, so for every yes you should say nine nos.
ex: Grok's web app: Enter adds a line on mobile, but sends on desktop
Midjourney's mobile website proves the web can be polished to the extreme

terms.d: Break down the small choices in good products

result.d: A skill you can build

l268|513.c: Your first startup idea is probably wrong, and when the premise changes, the whole company must turn at once.
l268|513.e: Founders, he says, must be irrationally optimistic and uncompromisingly realistic. The company started in GPU virtualization and compiler software, betting that model architectures would stay diverse. By mid-2022 it had millions in revenue and positive cash flow. Then generative models took off, architectures converged on the Transformer, and infrastructure stopped being a way to stand out. All eight people pivoted overnight, using their own inference stack to offer free code completion. Later, because VS Code limited what AI features could do, they built their own editor. His lesson is focus: you can't do something you don't believe in and build something big at the same time.
ex: At the pivot they had raised $28 million and managed over 10,000 GPUs
His biggest regret: many decisions should have come a few months earlier

items.d: A VS Code fork built for agents

l268|513.c: The value is in the application layer: same model, new interface, and acceptance rates tripled.
l268|513.e: When everyone runs the same kind of model, infrastructure is hard to differentiate, but developer experience and workflow have almost no ceiling. Inside VS Code, their completions were limited by the extension API; the only way to show an edit was to generate an image next to the cursor. Once they moved into their own editor, Windsurf, the model stayed the same and acceptance rates tripled. They train their own models only where they have a real advantage. High-level planning goes to Sonnet; retrieval and fast edits use in-house models, because they get tens of millions of feedback signals an hour and hold rare data like half-written code.
ex: A 100-million-line codebase is about 1.5 billion tokens, far beyond any context window
They won't train a model for vanity if they can't make it the best

l268|513.c: As AI takes over the how and the doing, the engineer's core job becomes deciding what to build.
l268|513.e: He splits engineering into three layers: what to solve, how to solve it, and actually implementing it. AI will take over most of the implementation. As it understands codebases and company conventions more deeply, it will gradually cover the how as well. Engineers return to what they should have been doing all along: judging which business problems and product capabilities matter most. A computer science degree still has value, because it trains you to solve problems under constraints. The most underrated trait, he thinks, is agency: a PM with an idea can now change the code and open a pull request instead of being boxed in by a job title.
ex: Someone who took an operating systems class understands why an app is slow
The sales and marketing team built its own tools and saved over $500,000 in SaaS spend

items.d: AI takes over as it learns the codebase

l268|513.c: AI writing 90 percent of code isn't 10x productivity, and higher returns on tech mean you should hire more.
l268|513.e: Engineers don't just write code. They review, test, debug, design, and deploy. He borrows Amdahl's law from parallel computing: if writing code is 30 units out of 100, shrinking it to 3 only brings the total down to 73, a gain of about 27 percent. Internally they see roughly 30 to 40 percent. For a company whose upside from technology is high, more output per engineer means a higher return on investing in technology and a bigger cost to not investing. The rational move is to invest more, and in the short term even hire more engineers.
ex: JPMorgan Chase spends about $17 billion a year on software with over 50,000 engineers
He thinks even 200 engineers would be too few for the company long term

items.d: The rest is review, testing, deployment

l268|513.c: Keep the company dehydrated: hire only when a team is about to drown.
l268|513.e: He isn't obsessed with staying small; he wants the smallest team that can meet the ambition. You hire only when a function is clearly overloaded, because extra people invent unimportant work and lobby for it, which creates infighting. Being short-handed forces ruthless prioritization: a team will say it can only do one thing and then pick the most important one. A company doesn't need good grades in every subject, only an A-plus in the one that matters most. A person's value isn't the size of their team; the people to reward are those who pull off the craziest projects with the fewest people. He also tells candidates up front that the job is intense.
ex: Engineering offer rate is about 0.6 percent; the take-home alone filters 10 to 15x
About 160 people: 50-some engineers, 80-some in sales and marketing

Hire one person only when truly swamped

l268|513.c: Technical founders shouldn't shun sales; selling to the Fortune 500 means building enterprise sales early.
l268|513.e: In the GPU business he hired no salespeople, because he himself didn't know how to turn selling into a repeatable process. With Codeium, large companies came knocking. He and his colleagues personally ran dozens of parallel pilots, confirmed there was real demand at scale, and hired a VP of sales by the end of 2023. Enterprises want more than autocomplete: they need security, the ability to understand enormous private codebases, and a fit with their existing tools. l268|513.c: Every 6 to 12 months, make your own current product look outdated.
l268|513.e: From the outside, people see updates every few weeks, but most of the company's bets are on things three to nine months out. Incremental improvement feels safe, like adding a dropdown a user asked for, but that's table stakes, not why you win. They were the first agentic editor, and that lead will lose value fast, so they must keep proving themselves in ways users never asked for. At the same time, you can't ignore users entirely; you have to hold both ideas at once. He also urges people to start using these tools now, because those who can will have a huge advantage over the next year.
ex: He asks that each new bet make the current product shape look dumb

items: Add the button users ask for
Bet three to nine months out

l270|516.c: A competitor's breakthrough is a gift: it proves that what you thought impossible can be done.
l270|516.e: The team executed hard back then, and the weekly updates were always long. One morning they discovered a competitor had shipped 30 new column types at once, while monday had 5, each taking about four months. The hardest part was admitting that after all that work, nobody could name the single most meaningful thing from the past three months. To him that meant a focus problem. Once the competitor proved it was possible, the team lost its excuse. They set a goal of 25 columns in a month, shipped 30 within six weeks, and then repeated the approach for dashboards and automations.
ex: First define what every column shares (export, filter, sort), then build a common foundation
A hackathon: each developer built one column type in a day, shipped two weeks later

l270|516.c: Ambitious goals create real speed, not the fake speed of skipping steps and working longer hours.
l270|516.e: If the goal is just to turn four months into three, people hear "work harder and longer." He separates two kinds of speed. Fake speed means doing the same thing while skipping steps and cutting quality. Real speed means doing only what actually moves the metric, and doing it in a different way. So the goal should be one where, in the first minute, everyone knows they couldn't hit it even by sleeping in the office. That forces a complete change of approach. After a few wins, the team gains confidence and starts applying the same discipline to things nobody has done before.
ex: A team that has lived through an impossible goal starts to believe anything is possible

items: Do only what moves the metric
Goals high enough to force new methods

d.verdict: Speed comes from doing the right thing, not trying harder

l270|516.c: PMs own the impact; shipping the feature does not mean the job is done.
l270|516.e: A good PM, in his view, keeps pushing until the impact is verified. The PM's first job is to get the team aligned on what would make a difference for customers and how they'll know the metric moved, before any talk of solutions. With a real goal, arguments over solutions also shrink, because everything gets tested against reality. Vague phrases like "enhance" or "expand the value" are red flags. Sometimes the biggest impact isn't another feature but making existing value easier to use, such as unblocking the go-to-market process.
ex: Every team has a daily numbers broadcast that gets discussed in Slack

l270|516.c: Radical transparency doesn't hurt morale; it makes everyone a partner who brings their brain.
l270|516.e: Before the IPO, office screens showed paying accounts, churn, and signups in real time, visible even to job candidates. Friends and family warned him that bad news would demoralize the team. He saw it the other way: a leader carrying bad news alone into a cheerful office is the dark side of the moon, and the most draining thing of all. The company wants everyone's brain, not one central brain plus a crowd of hands. Many problems were spotted by employees looking at the numbers. After going public they still share as much as possible, and PMs who see sensitive data are put on pre-scheduled stock trading plans.
ex: Getting started takes an hour: a daily numbers broadcast and a TV in the office
Every new paying account triggers a Simpsons sound effect on the screen

l270|516.c: Not taking a big risk is itself a risk: go multi-product all at once, not with a quiet test.
l270|516.e: Users were building CRMs, dev-tracking systems, and more on top of monday, so the company decided to go from a project management tool to a multi-product platform. The intuitive move is to quietly release one new product and see. Instead they announced five at once, despite internal worries about confusing users, hurting conversion, and how to price and sell. In hindsight, some products took off and others were folded back into the core product, but perception inside and outside the company, and the competitive landscape, changed fast. Had they tested one product and it happened to flop, they might have wrongly concluded that multi-product couldn't work.
