l270|516.c: A crisis that keeps coming back deserves a strategic investment that turns the weakness into an edge.
l270|516.e: Users pushed boards to the limit, from a few columns and hundreds of rows to hundreds of columns and tens of thousands of rows, and performance tickets spiked again and again. The first two times, everyone dropped what they were doing to firefight and barely got things under control. The third time he changed course: he pulled a few of the most talented people off features to rebuild the underlying data infrastructure for 100 times the scale. That seems to contradict a goals-and-data culture, but some decisions are about what kind of company you want to be, and you take the risk on instinct. MondayDB, launched about a year and a half ago, dramatically improved the experience and made monday an enterprise-grade platform.
ex: He considers performance the number one feature that makes people want to use a system

l270|516.c: Set a time trap for yourself; the first version should get feedback that it's not good enough yet.
l270|516.e: He has found that more time rarely produces a better product, just more problems and more confident assumptions. In bottom-up planning, teams compete to spot risks and keep adding scope until the timeline becomes two years. Asking instead "what can we ship before the next earnings call" focuses the conversation on core value immediately. When customers called the alpha of their enterprise project management product "too early," he praised the team, because that directional feedback was priceless. He also warns to read feedback in context: early on they offered no free trial and listened only to paying customers.
ex: If the first version's feedback is "perfect," you built too much and weren't focused

result.d: Know what's missing next

l270|516.c: The superpower that got you here may be exactly what blocks you from the next stage.
l270|516.e: He has always led product and technology, but the role has changed dozens of times, as if he had worked at dozens of companies. When the company was small, knowing every detail was his biggest strength. At scale, the same habit became harmful. After one quarterly business review he thought he had been thorough and clear, but a colleague said the message was lost entirely; people just wanted the three most important things to remember. His advice is to keep reassessing what the role needs now and to dare to drop old superpowers. He admits he often doubts whether he's up to the job, and gets through low points by picturing himself six months ahead and recovering quickly.
ex: Co-CEO Roy admits he might not hire himself to run a 2,500-person public company
He uses running and other non-work activities to get back to center

marks.d: Adjusted to what the role needs

l271|519.c: Programming is heading past code: people express intent in high-level logic close to English, while staying in control.
l271|519.e: He rejects two popular visions. One assumes we'll still be typing text in formal languages like TypeScript and Rust, which underestimates how far the technology will go. The other imagines talking to a chatbot that does everything, but that lacks precision; people can't control software in fine detail that way. His picture is that software logic gets written in a terser representation, something like pseudocode, that a person can point at, edit, and iterate on quickly. The path there runs through today's professional engineers, step by step, with humans staying in the driver's seat. That's also why they built their own editor and control the whole interface.
ex: He argues against the "message the engineering department in Slack" model
Background agents suit tasks like bug fixes that are easy to describe and verify

items.d: Formal languages and text editing; underrates progress
Change an app with a sentence; too imprecise
Editable high-level logic, human in the driver's seat

l271|519.c: Engineers become logic designers: carefulness matters less, taste matters more, and demand only grows.
l271|519.e: Software has two halves, how it looks and how it works. Tools like Figma can describe the look, but logic can only be expressed in code today. Once AI takes over the translation, engineers spend more time defining what to build than how it works underneath. By taste he doesn't just mean visual aesthetics but sound judgment about what should be built. Today's vibe coding hides the details, and once a project grows it becomes impossible to change, so the key is letting people control the details without reading code. He believes demand for software is nowhere near satisfied, so engineers will be needed more, not less.
ex: Building internal tools for biotech companies early on, demand far outstripped capacity
Simple productivity software costs as much to build as a blockbuster movie

items: Translate intent into code by hand

d.verdict: Still needed, and able to do far more

l271|519.c: Don't hide in a niche; a hot field with a high ceiling and unambitious incumbents still leaves room to leap.
l271|519.e: In late 2021, the Copilot beta and the scaling-law papers convinced the team that AI products were now feasible. They mapped out the future of various kinds of knowledge work, then deliberately picked a field they assumed nobody was competing in: mechanical engineering. After about four months they realized they didn't know the industry, lacked 3D data, would have to train their own models, and had no passion for it. Looking back at programming, little had changed and the existing players weren't ambitious enough, so they pivoted to Cursor. They built it by using it heavily every day, hand-wrote an editor from scratch, shipped in about three months, and later rebuilt on VS Code based on user feedback.

Within five weeks the team was using its own editor full time
Built on VS Code the way many browsers are built on Chromium

l271|519.c: Every magic moment in Cursor involves a custom model, built to cover what frontier models can't.
l271|519.e: At first they costed out model training and had no plan to do it. Now model development is central to hiring and product quality. The rule is to pick the right spots and not reinvent the wheel: start from open-source pretrained models and do post-training, sometimes tuning in partnership with closed-model providers. Custom models serve two roles. One is tasks frontier models can't handle for speed and cost reasons, such as autocomplete that predicts your next edit across files. The other wraps around the big model: on the input side a retrieval model finds relevant code in the codebase, and on the output side an apply model turns the big model's rough edit into a complete diff.
ex: Autocomplete must return within 300 milliseconds and re-predict on every keystroke
The retrieval model is like a mini Google built for your codebase

items.d: Finds relevant snippets in the codebase
Sonnet, Gemini, GPT do the high-level thinking
Turns a rough edit into a full diff
More accurate on each task, faster overall

l271|519.c: In a market with a very high ceiling, any barrier can be leapfrogged, so you can only keep building the best product.
l271|519.e: He compares AI coding to search engines in the late 1990s and the early PC market: another hour of a smart person's time or another dollar of R&D still pays off, which creates economies of scale in research, and user feedback data flows back into the product. Such markets are unkind to incumbents. Products are far from commoditized, users can try and switch at any time, and bundling doesn't work. He thinks Copilot fell behind partly for these structural reasons and partly because its original team gradually left and coordination across departments was hard. In the end, one company making a general-purpose tool will become a generation-defining business.
ex: He draws the analogy to the search engine market around 1999
The old IDE market was fragmented, but the new market is far bigger

items.d: There's always something useful left to build
Talent and research both pay off
Users can easily try it and switch

l271|519.c: Break tasks into small pieces, and in a safe setting push hard to find the model's limits.
l271|519.e: The most successful customers today are actually fairly conservative. They lean heavily on next-edit prediction and break the work they hand to AI into small chunks: write a bit of spec, let it write a bit, review a bit. They don't write one enormous instruction and then either accept everything or walk away disappointed. At the same time, he suggests deliberately pushing AI to its limits on side projects, where failure doesn't matter, to learn what it can really do, because many people haven't given it a fair shot. The two mistakes run in opposite directions: junior engineers over-rely on AI to do everything, while senior engineers underrate it and cling to old workflows.
ex: Every new model has its own quirks, so you have to rebuild your intuition
Inside companies, adoption is often driven by senior developer-experience teams

marks.d: Small tasks; test the limits on side projects

l271|519.c: Early hiring was too slow and too narrow; the right people replace a lot of process and keep the team focused.
l271|519.e: What he most wishes he'd known earlier is about hiring. The team was extremely picky, so it hired too slowly at first, and it leaned too hard toward young people from elite schools with shiny resumes, only to find that some late-career people were just as good. Now they pursue top talent over the long haul, sometimes for years, and bring candidates in for two days of real project work. He has found that much of what people try to achieve with organizational tools can be achieved by hiring people who are curious, honest, level-headed, and not chasing outside approval. That also lets the team ignore most of the AI hype and focus on the few changes that really matter.
ex: About 60 people, heavily weighted toward engineering, research, and design
They assumed the two-day work trial wouldn't scale, but still use it

terms.d: Finish a small task end to end
Work, eat, and get to know each other

result.d: Candidates get won over by the team too

l272|343.c: Devin is an asynchronous junior engineer with jagged intelligence, improving half through capability and half through interaction.
l272|343.e: Devin is built as a fully autonomous engineer you can tag in Slack or Linear. It works on its own and opens a pull request on GitHub when done. Over a year it grew from the level of a high school computer science student to an intern to a junior engineer. But its abilities are uneven: it can search and digest huge amounts of code far better than a person, yet some of its decisions are way off. Half the progress comes from model capability, half from learning how people and agents should work together, such as planning interactively and letting you jump in mid-task. He thinks raw intelligence is mostly there; the hard part is teaching the model the messy details of real engineering.
ex: When it launched in early 2024, few people believed agents could work at all
Devin Wiki maps a codebase's architecture automatically and is often used to onboard new hires

items.d: At the first launch in early 2024

l272|343.c: Each engineer runs a team of Devins asynchronously and steps in only where expert judgment is needed.
l272|343.e: Cognition has only about 15 engineers, and most of them run up to five Devins at once. They list the day's tasks, hand each one off, and get involved only to define the problem, make key architecture calls, or do final testing. Sometimes Devin finishes entirely on its own; sometimes a human adds the last 10 to 20 percent. He expects work to get more asynchronous, because reproducing bugs, reading logs, and rerunning checks take real-world time that autocomplete can't shrink. Only an agent-style workflow delivers multiples of improvement. Devin can also split a big task and delegate pieces to other Devins through its API.
ex: Devin merges hundreds of PRs a month into the company's own codebase
About a quarter of PRs come from Devin today, expected to pass half by year end

items.d: Say, five things to get done
Merge if good, else a line or two of feedback

l272|343.c: AI turns engineers from bricklayers into architects, which is not the same as managing a team of Devins.
l272|343.e: The heart of software engineering, he argues, has always been defining the problem and thinking through the solution and architecture, yet that is maybe 10 percent of a typical engineer's time. The rest goes to chasing Kubernetes errors, migrations, upgrades, and bug fixes. Devin is meant to take that part over so people can focus on high-level design while still owning the full spec. He dislikes the manager analogy: management is hard because of the context, responsibility, and emotions you carry, whereas working with Devin is more like handing off tasks through one more layer of abstraction. Further out, a person might just look at the product and say what should change.
ex: He guesses the coding-agent experience has about 20 more generations to go
He compares it to how Python changed the way people described tasks

items.d: The most fun part of engineering

l272|343.sc: Should you still learn to code?
l272|343.c: Yes, still learn to code: software is a textbook Jevons paradox, so there will be more engineers, not fewer.
l272|343.e: Studying computer science is less about syntax than about learning to break problems down logically and understanding abstractions like databases, garbage collection, and network protocols. To someone 50 years ago, Python would have looked like telling a computer what to do in English, yet it produced more programmers, not fewer. The next jump in abstraction will be faster and bigger, but people who can peel back the layers and think precisely about details will still have the edge. Zero-sum thinking says 10x efficiency means 10x fewer engineers. He expects people to build far more than 10x the software, with a flood of personalized products.
ex: For performance work, some people still drop down to assembly
Jevons paradox: when the price falls, total spending goes up

terms.d: The same work, many times faster
Society always finds more software to build

result.d: Output grows faster than efficiency

l272|343.c: Give Devin tasks, not problems: start with work that is well defined and easy to verify.
l272|343.e: Devin does best on jobs with a clear goal and a fast test-and-iterate loop, like small front-end requests, bug fixes, tests, and documentation. It can handle bigger projects, but expect to spend more effort steering. Many new users stare at the blank page and ask it to refactor the whole codebase. The right approach is to treat it like a new junior engineer: set up the repo, linting, and CI so it can check its own work, give it one or two small tasks to learn the environment, then ramp up. Inside companies, a few enthusiastic early adopters usually pave the way, and others join once they see it shipping PR after PR.
ex: Tag a ticket in Linear and Devin first proposes a plan with a confidence level
Claire Vo at LaunchDarkly uses it to scope tasks and pull data

l272|343.c: AI apps don't really have moats; what matters is stickiness, and Devin learns your team and codebase the more you use it.
l272|343.e: From foundation models to the application layer, he sees no hard barrier that keeps competitors out. What does exist is stickiness: once something works for you, do you want to switch? Coding agents naturally compound. An engineer on day one and a five-year veteran who wrote half the codebase are worlds apart, and Devin likewise keeps learning your codebase, stack, and processes. Coding is also a team sport: colleagues add context in Slack, comment on PRs, and have it onboard new hires, so the value grows as more of the team uses it. He isn't trying to lock anyone out.
ex: Usage-based pricing measured in ACUs
New hires can ask Devin the questions they're embarrassed to ask a mentor

Knows the big picture like a veteran

l272|343.c: AI isn't held back by hardware rollout, so it spreads far faster than PCs, the internet, or phones.
l272|343.e: Every major technology revolution of the past 50 years was limited by hardware distribution. Markets grew steadily year by year with the number of people online or owning phones, which is why winners like Apple and Microsoft started early and grew slowly. AI doesn't have to wait for hardware; once it crosses the tipping point it spreads exponentially. He believes AI coding has already crossed that point, and engineers who don't use AI at all are falling behind. Because change is so fast, engineers need to keep up with progress and actively teach the AI what's in their own codebase.
ex: The internet started out connecting just a few universities
Apple and Microsoft were founded at almost the same time, early on

items: Exponential spread past the tipping point

l272|343.c: Startups usually live or die by three to five old truisms; the hard part is doing them far beyond expectations.
l272|343.e: The team is about 27 people, 18 of whom have started companies before. He has found that success rarely comes from a thousand clever tricks, but from pushing a few basics to the extreme: move fast, hire the best people, build what users want, stay close to customers, and look at where things are heading. To recruit an MIT junior, they flew to North Carolina to have dinner with his parents and worked out a plan for him to work full time while finishing his degree. For another candidate they helped write every letter declining other offers. He also cautions: go all in, but don't tie your self-worth to any one outcome.

He says building Cognition felt like compressing eight years into one

l273|523.c: Asking how you've been complicit in what you say you don't want is about reclaiming agency, not blame.
l273|523.e: He deliberately says complicit rather than responsible: you're the one driving the getaway car, not the one holding up the teller. The question isn't an invitation to take ownership of every bad thing in your life. It's about spotting where you've been lying to yourself. If you say you don't want to be so busy but feel anxious the moment your calendar opens up, ask what busyness buys you and whether there's a more conscious way to get the same feeling. Even people with little power can ask: what do I get out of this organization's dysfunction, and why do I keep ending up on teams like this?
ex: His metaphor: you drove the getaway car, you didn't rob the bank
Saying you don't want to be busy, then fidgeting when the calendar isn't full

d.verdict: The question is meant to wake up agency

l273|523.c: Practical skills plus radical self-inquiry plus shared experience equals better leadership and more resilience.
l273|523.e: People usually come to a coach wanting the how-to. He asks about their father instead, and about their relationship to money and self-worth. The third term, shared experience, comes from the CEO bootcamps he ran early on: a circle of people who genuinely care about you, hear you tell the truth, and don't rush to fix you. That's rare, because startup culture runs on fooling others and yourself. The equation really points at resilience. In his thirties he looked successful and was so depressed he considered suicide. What he cares about most is that people don't destroy themselves on the way to becoming good CEOs.
ex: He improvised it on a whiteboard during a talk at Naropa University
A 19-year-old in the audience summed it up: you can succeed without being a jerk

l273|523.c: The questions that make you hold your breath are the gold; dodging childhood baggage always costs you eventually.
l273|523.e: What we learn growing up is how to go around things, not how to see them. We fear that asking the question means leaving a relationship or a job, so we slap on band-aids: the gym, workaholism, substances, even flying to Peru for ayahuasca, which he calls spiritual bypassing. He points to Bruce Springsteen's 25 years of psychoanalysis to make the case that everyone carries unexamined childhood baggage, and leaving it unexamined has a price. That price might be depression, or a founder who quietly believes "I don't deserve success" and wrecks the company with their own hands. You never have to share the answers with anyone. What matters is being honest with yourself.
ex: What am I not saying that needs to be said?
What am I saying that isn't being heard? What am I failing to hear?

items.d: Asking might mean leaving a relationship or job
Childhood patterns keep steering your life
Depression, or wrecking your own company

l273|523.c: Busyness and growth muffle the voice saying "I'm not enough," and clinging to outcomes only deepens the pain.
l273|523.e: He presses Lenny: when things grow you feel great, when they stall you doubt yourself. Busyness is really a way to drown out the inner voice that says you're not worthy. In Buddhism's second noble truth, the things we do to push suffering away end up increasing it. Buying a big house is fine, but if it's meant to prove you're lovable, safe, and belong, you'll live in constant fear of losing it. His advice is to treat your career as an art project, enjoy solving the puzzle for its own sake, and unhook your self-esteem from wins and losses. He has read only two reviews of his own books, because he writes first to answer his own questions.

He often asks himself what kind of ancestor he wants to be
A child's worth shouldn't depend on getting an A on the spelling test

Quiets the voice for a while
Winning or losing decides if I matter

l273|523.c: Even a growth mindset can harden into dogma; stay attached to growing, not to the mindset itself.
l273|523.e: A growth mindset is good in itself. The trouble is that the ego turns it into a new doctrine for judging right and wrong, and at that point it has become a fixed mindset. He quotes Peter Senge: it is almost impossible to challenge the assumptions that made you rich. Founders start with a beginner's mind, but after a taste of success the ego, afraid of failure, decides "this is how it's done," and panics when the world changes. Asked whether letting go of attachment kills ambition, he says using anxiety to keep yourself from slacking is a childhood habit. Self-compassion and enjoying hard work for its own sake are stronger motivators.

He works seven days a week because he loves it

items.d: The ego decides this is the right way
Hard to question what made you successful
Anxiety whenever you leave the old path

l273|523.c: Teams rarely fail for lack of talent or strategy; they fail because members replay their unexamined personal patterns.
l273|523.e: A team is a group, and groups always produce roles like the scapegoat and the truth-teller. When members haven't examined themselves, the group re-enacts each person's family-of-origin patterns. At one software company's leadership meeting he noticed that whenever the conversation got painful, someone cracked a joke and changed the subject. The CEO said on the spot that this was exactly how his family worked. To build a high-functioning team, do your own work, starting with the most powerful person, because more power means a greater moral obligation to self-reflect. One CEO of a 15-person company complained that her staff ran every decision past her; the root cause was that she couldn't stand anyone making a decision she disagreed with.
ex: Jung: until you make the unconscious conscious, it will direct your life
Parker Palmer: if you won't look inward, stay out of work that involves other people

items.d: Looks like a talent, strategy, or execution problem
Scapegoats, jokes to dodge the pain
Family patterns, above all the leader's

l273|523.c: AI may burn away what doesn't matter, so that presence, connection, and ideas count for more.
l273|523.e: He admits AI unsettles him more than the internet wave did, and coaches worry about being replaced by ChatGPT. But he compares AI to a sharp new pair of glasses. He uses ChatGPT as a writing and thinking partner while keeping a human writing partner too. A colleague fed ten years of journals to Claude and asked it to hold those pointed questions up as a mirror, and came out a better coach. His optimistic guess is that presence, connection, and strategic thinking will be elevated, and that AI's best use may be handing you more questions worth asking yourself. He also admits he could be completely wrong.
ex: He has gone from 1200-baud dial-up to a world where the fridge has an IP address
Growth is a practice of continual inquiry, never finished once and for all

items.d: Much of it doesn't really matter

l274|525.c: A hiring signal that scares most people away is what leaves you with independent, curious, fiercely competitive people.
l274|525.e: While everyone else was building social and mobile apps, Palantir talked loudly about defense, intelligence, and protecting the West. That put many people off, which is exactly the point: it drew the ones who wanted the hardest, messiest problems. He thinks a good hiring signal has to repel some people or it isn't filtering anything. The company looked for independent thinkers who would argue back, had wide interests, and badly wanted to win, and founders kept interviewing candidates themselves for years. It also tapped a talent pool nobody valued then: veterans leaving the military, people used to getting hard things done in bad conditions.
ex: The internal slogan was "Save the Shire," borrowed from The Lord of the Rings
Co-founder Stephen Cohen's interviews were often ninety-minute philosophical conversations
Project principles had to be things others would disagree with; "move fast" didn't count

items.d: An odd pitch in the social-app era
Probe how someone thinks, check the fit

l274|525.c: Without titles, nobody can game the ladder, and everyone has to keep earning their place.
l274|525.e: He cites Peter Thiel's argument in Zero to One: once titles exist, they become the thing people fight over, and everyone starts optimizing for whatever metric gets them promoted. A classic case is launching a new product to earn a promotion instead of fixing the old one, which just confuses users. This is Goodhart's law: once a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. In Palantir's early years, everyone except the CEO and a few directors was called a forward deployed engineer. The downside was that competition shifted to winning a senior executive's favor, and your resume made little sense to outsiders. The upside was that responsibility followed performance, and nobody could sit on a title.
ex: Early on, only the CEO and six directors had titles
People leaving and calling themselves SVP on LinkedIn became an internal joke

d.verdict: He favors the no-titles approach

l274|525.c: On-site engineers who iterate four or five times a week were Palantir's forge for PMs and founders.
l274|525.e: Forward deployed engineers spent about four days a week in the client's office or factory. The job wasn't to sell software but to solve problems: meet the key people, earn their trust, and build new software on the spot when needed. Demo by day, rebuild by night, four or five feedback loops a week. Within weeks they'd have something the client would pay serious money for, priced against the value it created. Palantir only promoted PMs from people who had proven themselves in the field, to avoid what they called "Google Docs syndrome," writing requirements documents without ever building anything. And a new PM still had to earn the engineers' trust.
ex: Helped Airbus raise A350 production at least fourfold within a year
He lived in France for about a year and a half for that project
Of the twenty-some people in his starting cohort, at least six went on to found unicorns or near-unicorns

items.d: Walk into the client's building Monday
Write software for the real problem

l274|525.c: Palantir stopped looking like a consultancy only when it turned its engineers' internal tools into products.
l274|525.e: The company has long measured itself by revenue per employee, which it calls product leverage. The logic is simple: if every new client means hiring more people, you're a consultancy. The more general the product, the more clients one person can look after. Early engineers showed up with little more than a laptop and crude data tools, then kept building tools for themselves. Executive Shyam Sankar then ordered every project to get clients using those internal tools by a deadline. It was painful, but it forced product discipline, and Foundry emerged three or four years later. The Airbus work of mapping cryptic data tables onto parts, work orders, and aircraft grew into the core module, Ontology.
ex: Gross margins above 80%, versus roughly 20–30% for consulting firms
Today you can sign up for its AI platform, AIP, with a credit card

items.d: A laptop and crude data tools
Clients use the tools by a deadline

l274|525.c: In big organizations, analysis is the tip of the iceberg; most of the pain is getting and cleaning data.
l274|525.e: Spend a few days inside a large company and you'll see that even calculating quarterly sales means filing an access request and waiting six to eight weeks. Once the data arrives, it still has to be cleaned, joined across tables, and standardized before it's usable. The actual analysis is the last 5–10%. Palantir built a product for every one of those steps, such as a universal connector that reads any data source and tools that let non-technical people join tables. The resistance usually comes from gatekeepers: security teams locking data down with good intentions, and people whose jobs depend on owning it. Its biggest competitor is really clients building their own systems.
ex: SAP table names are cryptic and must first be mapped to concepts humans understand
In the AI era, access to private data puts Palantir in a strong position

l274|525.c: To copy forward deployment, know your deal size, and let engineers build products and learn the client's business.
l274|525.e: Palantir-style on-site work only pays off when each client pays a lot. Companies with smaller deals can have one person cover five clients instead of moving into a factory. The key is that these people must be real engineers who can build a product from scratch, not solutions architects who only deploy what already exists. They also need face time with clients, real friendships, and a deep grasp of how the business works; hospitals, for example, care a lot about turning beds over quickly. He finds founders more often make the opposite mistake: clinging to their original product idea when the client has a more urgent problem. AI coding tools have also made this model far cheaper.
ex: Retool took off only after repositioning as "build internal tools easily"
Hex CEO Barry McCardel argues most companies don't need forward deployed engineers

items.d: Free to build new products from scratch
Small deals: one person, five clients
Hospitals also need to turn beds over

l274|525.c: Place many bets, test them fast, ask for big money early, then tackle the messiest real-world problems.
l274|525.e: He thinks of a startup's odds as two numbers multiplied: how many bets you place, times how likely each one is to work. So place several bets and rotate quickly. When you show something to a customer, ask them to pay a large sum right away; if they won't, move to a different problem instead of dragging it out for three weeks like most teams. Second, build a distinctive culture with real trust. People who have worked at a top company carry an internal yardstick for what good looks like. Third, go after messy real-world fields like healthcare: since ChatGPT, big institutions are more willing to give small companies a chance, and on-site deployment costs five to ten times less.
ex: His interview question: what's the hardest you've ever pushed to get something done?
Architect Christopher Alexander's advice: aim for Chartres Cathedral

terms.d: Test early by asking clients for big money

result.d: More likely to land on a truly big problem

l274|525.c: With controversial work like defense, walking away is rarely right; stay in the room and think hard.
l274|525.e: At Palantir he worked on the US COVID response and cancer research, which he sees as good work that couldn't have happened elsewhere. On the defense controversy, he thinks walking away is rarely the right call. Google pulled out of the Pentagon's AI project, but that stance was further from the average American's view than people assume. Better to stay in the room and make the process more precise and less error-prone than to be absent. That isn't unconditional: if the country turned dark, he'd reconsider. He criticizes tech for long refusing to examine itself politically; engineers optimizing short-video engagement, for instance, rarely thought about the effect on kids.
ex: From 2016 to 2020 there were often protesters outside the office
He believes the real world still needs credible deterrence

marks.d: Make the process precise; keep reflecting
Refuse to think about the impact

l275|527.c: A Revolut product owner is a local CEO, responsible end to end for the product, the business, and customer happiness.
l275|527.e: Revolut calls its PMs product owners, not in the Scrum sense but to stress ownership: this product is yours. Every team has engineering, data, analytics, design, and operations built in, and the product owner is everyone's direct manager and decides what to build. Functional managers decide how to build it and set the quality bar. Product owners write roadmaps that move business metrics and take part in company strategy, but above all they have to execute relentlessly. After a feature ships, they make sure support, sales, and marketing actually use it. Otherwise it's just a useless feature nobody knows about.
ex: Roughly 150 to 170 product owners
About six or seven thousand employees, operating in about 50 countries

terms.d: Decides what; functional managers decide how

result.d: Follows through like a founder

l275|527.c: UX, technical, and data product owners differ by only 10–15%; the rest of the skill set is shared.
l275|527.e: UX product owners handle consumer-facing experiences and lean on taste and industry experience. Technical ones usually come from engineering and dig deepest into details. Data science ones come from data science and stay very hands-on. People move between the three often, because what decides success is the shared foundation. That means problem solving, both step-by-step reasoning and creative answers to non-linear problems. It means customer empathy you can pass on to the team. It means digging to root causes, even reading code alongside engineers. And it means business sense: knowing what will move the metrics. In finance there's one more: making the product satisfy regulators and getting everyone to sign off.
ex: Data science product owners are becoming more important
Specialization accounts for about 5–15%; roughly 85–90% is common ground

root.d: The three roles are mostly alike

items.d: Understand the situation; pass it on
Find root causes; read code if needed
Know what will move the metrics

l275|527.c: Dig all the way into one or two cases first, then step back and turn them into a repeatable process.
l275|527.e: Revolut was opening branches across Europe, in France, Germany, Italy, and more. Each one involved compliance, regulatory reporting, and local payment systems, with sub-projects nested several layers deep. Only a handful of people were available, yet the work had to scale to 50 countries. So they went all the way down on two branches, Ireland and the Netherlands, worked backward to the best approach, then zoomed out and froze it into an algorithm-like process with steps, quality gates, and lead times for hiring. He sees the key skill as switching freely between the details and the helicopter view, while thinking about second-order effects.
ex: Ireland and the Netherlands came first, then the other countries
The process spells out how far ahead to hire whom

items.d: Work through Ireland and the Netherlands
See if the messy details can simplify
Steps and quality gates, many countries

l275|527.c: A new product can drop features, but never quality or experience, or you won't know why it failed.
l275|527.e: When a rough MVP doesn't take off, you can't tell whether the idea was wrong or the product was just bad. Requiring every product to be something people love removes that uncertainty. Revolut's new-project framework lets anyone pitch, as long as they explain the market, the business logic, and why they'd win. The founders take part, so decisions come fast. A small team ships a first version quickly, polishes it with a small group, and only after retention and similar metrics clear the bar does it roll out to fifty million users. His own early movie-ticketing startup spent everything on hardware and expanded before validating anything, and it folded.
ex: Joint accounts passed one million active users after launch
The founders review weekly and have seen every screen that ships

items: Hard to diagnose when it stalls
No compromise on quality or design
Scale once metrics clear the bar

d.verdict: Cut features, never quality

l275|527.c: Match competitors on the basics first, then layer on differences and delight so users truly love the product.
l275|527.e: Take a savings account. At the bottom are the table stakes any bank needs; without them you aren't even considered. Next, the interest rate has to be competitive and the bad experiences have to go: withdraw any time, interest paid daily, no lost interest when you take money out. Then come features that surprise people, like higher rates for saving in multiple currencies. On top is the icing: custom wallpapers, savings goals, rounding up spare change. Products working together is another kind of delight, like spending crypto you received directly on a coffee with your card. He thinks this kind of care is exactly what fintechs most often skip.
ex: Savings in Brazilian reais earn around 12%, versus 2–3% in euros
The points program in Europe gives real rewards on card spending

l275|527.c: Raw intellect and hunger to build beat senior experience; former technical co-founders fit best.
l275|527.e: He has interviewed around four or five hundred product owner candidates, and found that people with glossy resumes ramp up more slowly in the role. They have to adjust to a new culture, sometimes rest on past wins, and their high pay raises expectations. Veterans of big companies often lack the drive to change the status quo, which takes blood, sweat, and tears. The ideal is someone who has founded a company and built a product hands-on with engineers. They take one concrete problem, earn the team's respect, then take the next one, growing step by step. Internal transfers from operations or engineering also tend to do well, since the culture and domain knowledge are already there.
ex: The recruiting team runs in sprints, poaching from companies behind products they love
His advice for fast growth: start a company or join the most entrepreneurial one you can

items.d: Quickly solve a real customer pain

l275|527.c: With a hundred projects running, he goes code-deep on only seven to ten and trusts the rest to run themselves.
l275|527.e: He runs both the product function and the retail business, with close to a hundred projects in flight. Chasing status on each would eat the week in updates. Instead he picks the seven to ten with the biggest customer impact right now and goes deep, down to reading code with the engineers. Counterintuitively, this works. Teams know which areas are under scrutiny and what the company's priorities are, and they know that if they slip, they're next. So they discipline themselves. A team that can explain its decision logic earns trust even when the numbers aren't there yet, and gets to keep doing things its own way.
ex: The credit team is about 300 people and launches loans or cards in a new country every month
He estimates a traditional bank's credit division in one country has two or three thousand people

items.d: Other teams hold the same bar

l276|530.c: Enterprise AI means straddling two cars: the technology moves weekly, but people's work habits change slowly.
l276|530.e: After moving from consumer to enterprise products, she found every use case is really two: the feature has to work well, and it has to be governable. Sharing a document link should be easy, but also secure and auditable. The common mistake is to serve only one side, or to weaken the experience for the sake of control. AI is also the most compressed technology cycle in history, measured in weeks and months, while work habits and organizations change far more slowly. Her answer is not to hold back the early adopters: alongside careful rollouts, a Frontier program gives them experimental features first, making "living a year ahead" an institution.
ex: A deep research agent post-trained specifically for work tasks
An internal "fake company" where employees try frontier features

marks.d: Early adopters get experimental features first
Pharma and law firms need trust and stability

l276|530.c: A good agent has three things: autonomy you can delegate, capacity for complex tasks, and more natural interaction.
l276|530.e: She takes a practical product view of agents. We've moved from the app era to an era where the person sits in the driver's seat with an assistant, and as reasoning improves, you can hand over more. Autonomy is a spectrum, and what matters is how high-level a goal you can delegate. Complexity means going beyond summarizing a document or generating an image to building a prototype or helping you win a meeting. Interaction means more than chat; you can pull the agent into a meeting and talk it through. It should also work asynchronously, getting things done while you're away.
ex: Having a research agent analyze each attendee's views and design a persuasion plan
She describes the help as adding synapses she didn't have

result.d: From saving time to bringing new insight

l276|530.c: NLX is the new UX: conversation has grammar and structure, and it needs deliberate design too.
l276|530.e: Graphical interfaces are inherently unnatural, so they've always been carefully designed, but they're rigid. Natural language interfaces are flexible, yet people often assume the model is the product and chatting is enough. She argues a conversation, like a meeting, has grammar, structure, and invisible interface elements. The prompt itself is today's version of the dropdown menu. An agent should offer a plan you can edit. Showing its reasoning takes judgment: too verbose feels like reading a script, too terse leaves people without confidence. Proactive follow-up suggestions need the right dose too. Over time, she expects all of this to be personalized.
ex: DeepSeek showed its full chain of thought, and people loved it
After generating black-and-white clip art, the product should suggest the next step

d.verdict: Conversational interfaces need real design too

l276|530.c: If you aren't prototyping, you're doing it wrong; with ideas abundant, a PM's value is taste and editing.
l276|530.e: She requires every new project to come with a prototype and a prompt set, which she calls the new PRD: demos before memos. The point isn't to turn everyone into an engineer but to show what's in your head at the highest bandwidth. First demos arrive faster, but full deployment is slower and the bar is higher. With ideas and prototypes flooding in, a few people with taste have to edit, or the product becomes Frankenstein's monster. PMs who only run process get questioned; the right to decide has to be earned. Good ideas from engineers and designers get unlocked too. She's convinced coding isn't dead, just operating at a higher level of abstraction.
ex: She expects "software operators" to outnumber programmers tenfold
She often asks AI to simulate how Satya would react to a proposal

items.d: Replaces the PRD; demos before memos
Pick what's worth building from many prototypes
Takes longer, with a higher bar

l276|530.c: Keep refreshing your outdated sense of what AI can do, and make reaching for AI a reflex.
l276|530.e: She sees "intelligence overhang" everywhere: the capability is there, but people aren't using it. The hard part is updating your priors. A year ago image generators misspelled words and models couldn't reason or analyze data. People tried once, got scarred, and never tried again, not realizing the baby had turned fifteen in a month. She sees this as an arbitrage opportunity for product people: drop the old impressions, keep raising your demands on AI, and you unlock more. She even built a browser extension that asks, every time she opens a new tab, whether AI could do the thing she's about to do.
ex: She built the extension with GitHub Copilot in about 10 minutes
Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke calls this "reflexive AI usage"

items.d: The model really couldn't do it then

l276|530.c: Zero to one means solving first and scaling later: welcome big pivots, and don't impose mature metrics early.
l276|530.e: She tells teams to solve first, then scale, and the two phases need different postures. In solving mode you swing widely. Google Lens started as a plant identifier, and two weeks later the team realized the technology was better at translating foreign text. From outside it looks chaotic, but the team should embrace it, or it will climb a small local hill too early and spend years stuck there. Setting metrics too soon is false precision: with a thousand users, click-through and retention tell you nothing. Nail one or two things completely before claiming you can do everything.
ex: Voice assistants were really good at timers, music, and answering questions
Big companies also get stuck on the wrong hill for years

items.d: Watch qualitative signals, not false precision

l276|530.c: To answer "why now," a new product should hit at least two of three shifts: technology, user behavior, business model.
l276|530.e: From building new categories she has a rule: a good product rides at least two of three inflection points. First is a step change in technology, like deep learning for Google Lens, speech recognition for conversational search, and today large language models and reasoning models. Second is a shift in user behavior: once storage was nearly free and everyone carried a phone, the camera became a keyboard for the real world. Third is a shift in business model, like pay-per-click in search or SaaS subscriptions, and now per-seat, per-usage, and per-outcome pricing in AI. A better interface alone won't make people switch.
ex: Robinhood: the phone became the primary device, plus zero commissions
Google Now was too early: the interface was ahead of the intelligence

root.d: At least two of three shifts

items.d: The camera as a real-world keyboard

l277|532.c: Binance's flat structure and nightly leadership meetings meant no decision stayed stuck for more than a day.
l277|532.e: Within six months of launch, Binance was the largest crypto exchange, peaking at around 2,000 people and a valuation near $400 billion, with teams of fifteen or twenty running businesses that made billions in profit. Founder CZ at one point had 55 direct reports, and most employees were one layer from the CEO. Leadership met late every night, weekends and holidays included. An urgent problem got an owner that same night, who went all in and reported daily, with no resource limits other than time. He thinks the model only works under certain conditions: hypergrowth, very high incentives, and employees who genuinely believe in the mission.
ex: Fifteen financial licenses in fifteen countries within three months
Bonuses ranged from 0 to 500%, so nobody cared about a 10–20% raise
His nightly meeting was at 11 p.m. in Singapore, 1 a.m. for colleagues in Sydney

items.t: Assign an owner on the spot

l277|532.c: Only work on things with a tenfold upside or downside, then swallow your pride and dig into the details.
l277|532.e: There are always more problems than time, so he only picks the ones with a tenfold positive or negative impact. In fintech that's usually growth or compliance. Once picked, he goes all the way down. When crypto moved to strict regulation, signup conversion collapsed. Binance laid out the top 50 countries and top 10 document types in a grid of about 500 cells and worked through them one by one. CZ refused to give up a single user, and the KYC team grew from 20 to 500 people in three months. The founder of White Pages had no fixed desk; he moved it to whichever department had the most leverage, and once spent three months as the SEO product manager.
ex: He'd be asked why the approval rate for Kenyan driver's licenses suddenly dropped
A packed calendar is a disgrace, not a badge; leave room for high-leverage problems

items.d: Always more than there is time
The two usual kinds in fintech
Down to every screen and cell

l277|532.c: Pick a job on three things: how fast you'll learn, whether it uses your strengths, and whether you enjoy it.
l277|532.e: He compares growth to compound interest: at the same rate, compounding daily versus yearly looks very different after two years. A fast-growing company has you shipping and learning every day, whereas the product he built as a Microsoft intern still hadn't launched when he left. Second, play to your strengths rather than grinding on weaknesses, especially early on. For the first 15 years, don't decide based on a 10–20% pay difference; if you end up an executive or founder, 90% of your earnings come in the last five years. If you can, spend your early career where talent is densest, like the US West Coast.
ex: Agoda once paid about $5,000 per PM candidate for a six-hour assessment
Ray Dalio's assessment compares your self-rating with how colleagues rate you

terms.d: The role hinges on what you're good at
The more fun, the more you put in

result.d: Do more, get better, repeat

l277|532.c: Decide early whether you really want to be an executive; founding, deep expertise, or a balanced life are just as valid.
l277|532.e: Many ambitious PMs assume the goal is to climb to CPO without asking whether they'd enjoy the climb. His test isn't how much you're willing to sacrifice. If you can't look at any product without thinking how to improve it, and work energizes rather than drains you, the executive path fits. Once you start agonizing over work-life balance, it probably doesn't. Other good paths: start a company if you're fed up with constraints you can't control, knowing a CEO spends most of their time not doing product; become a deep expert in something like KYC, fraud, or card networks; or find your meaning outside work.
ex: Seventeen of his twenty working years were spent working for founders
He quotes Bezos, who dislikes the phrase "work-life balance"

items.d: KYC, fraud, loyalty, and so on

l277|532.c: Product strategy is overrated; a PM's real strategy is getting from hypothesis to data as fast as possible.
l277|532.e: He thinks product strategy only ever reaches two conclusions: double down, or don't do it, and experiments are the fastest way to tell which. Strategy built from slide decks and Porter's five forces is mostly dressed-up intuition, and the most senior or loudest person usually wins. Google's Jonathan Rosenberg liked to say: bring data, or we do it my way. An experimentation culture gives PMs their own science, so they can answer everyone's ideas with results. Read the data by cohort and use control groups to strip out market swings. Only irreversible or very slow-to-validate decisions, like European pricing or compliance, deserve deep deliberation first.
ex: When Bitcoin crashed, overall conversion fell, but the test group still beat control
Booking grew from about $10 billion to $170 billion in a decade, still selling flights, hotels, and cars

d.verdict: Only irreversible or slow-to-test decisions need heavy strategy

l277|532.c: Fintech PMs must please both users and regulators, and banking naturally hedges against the economic cycle.
l277|532.e: N26 is one of a handful of top companies in Europe, a big fish in a small pond that attracts the best people. As one of the first mobile banks, it faces problems nobody has solved before. Fintech has two customers, users and regulators, and pleasing one often upsets the other; every trade-off is existential, which trains PMs to balance. Banking is also a "100% product" that everyone needs, so the market has no ceiling. When rates are high, people spend less but deposits earn money; when rates are low, spending and borrowing rise. N26 pushed savings to acquire users during high rates and is now leaning into lending as rates fall.
ex: Very few companies truly master experimentation; the skill can carry a whole career
Colleagues who share early success form a dense network

l277|532.c: Avoid big bets that take six months or a year to judge: decisions aren't right or wrong, just fast or slow.
l277|532.e: His biggest career failure was being the first PM on Google Hangouts. Thousands of people worked on it and Larry Page was personally involved, yet it never became a great communications product. In hindsight he blames company DNA in part: some companies struggle to win certain categories, like Microsoft in mobile or Google in social. At Agoda, a hotel payment terminal was delayed six to nine months by licensing and launched right into the pandemic. You can't control the macro, so he prefers small, fast moves that produce early signal. As long as a decision is reversible and won't kill users or the company, being wrong quickly and correcting beats spending months finding the "right" answer.
ex: WebRTC, invented by the Hangouts team, now powers almost all web audio and video calls
The payment terminal started on $50 Android devices bought at a mall

marks.d: Know quickly if you're wrong, then fix it
Could kill users or the company; be careful

l277|532.c: Right now AI is a game changer in three places: coding productivity, customer support automation, and fraud detection.
l277|532.e: He admits he hasn't found an AI tool that makes him a better CPO; making decisions and owning the consequences is still a human job. But at the company level, three areas are transformative. Coding assistants hooked into the codebase noticeably speed up development in large codebases. AI support already handles most basic questions on its own, like why a card was declined or why a replacement hasn't arrived. In fraud, Binance used AI to spot the language patterns scammers use in peer-to-peer trades. He also jokes that some writing tools are "reverse compression": a few sentences get inflated into a long piece, which the reader compresses back down.
ex: N26 uses Writer to generate copy for its multilingual interface
He used Suno to turn a Hindi poem he wrote into a song

l278|534.c: There's no marketing playbook to copy; first figure out where your funnel is actually stuck.
l278|534.e: Founders often ask her what Stripe or OpenAI did, and she resists answering. Copying someone else's output ignores the inputs: the competitive landscape and the climate at the time. ChatGPT had no awareness problem; the issue was people didn't know what to use it for, so marketing became creating "oh, it can do that" moments. When a founder wants to hire a demand-gen lead, she asks about close rates first. If most people who come in the door buy, the product is working and you should invest at the top of the funnel. If prospects keep asking about price and competitors, the bottom is leaking, and you need product marketing for positioning and sales enablement.
ex: When ChatGPT Enterprise opened a contact-sales form, leads jumped 40x overnight
She wrote a lead-scoring script with ChatGPT that ran in production for a long time

items.d: Product works; invest in top of funnel

l278|534.c: Market in four steps: diagnose, analyze competitors, take a different path, and experiment.
l278|534.e: She started as an engineer and brought that mindset to marketing. Unlike Stripe or OpenAI, Retool didn't have customers showing up on their own, so marketing sat directly between the company and revenue. Diagnosis showed that leads from paid social rarely turned into sales opportunities. Competitors mostly did content and events, so Retool went a different way and led with large enterprise customers who paid real money and kept expanding, letting them tell the story. Imitators can't copy that. Then came experiments with webinars and sales dinners, scaling what worked and cutting what didn't, without being held hostage by sunk costs.
ex: Clicks, views, and impressions are mostly vanity metrics; watch signups, leads, and revenue
Retool opened its self-hosted version to self-serve so pilots could build confidence

l278|534.c: Competing on price is a race to the bottom; the heart of marketing is deliberately taking a different path.
l278|534.e: Models keep getting cheaper and more capable, and nearly every company is becoming an AI company, so low prices won't be a lasting advantage. Users don't need yet another tool; they want something that fits their values and goals. Understand what they need, then pair a great product experience with an equally great marketing experience, and that's a one-two punch. When Stripe launched Connect, the real competitor was "become a payment facilitator yourself," and the advice out there was full of old-industry jargon. So Stripe wrote the complete guide to doing it, ending with the point that it's a huge hassle and you might as well use Connect.
ex: A "reverse RFP": own the PayFac search terms without calling yourself a PayFac
Wiz's brand stands out at SaaS conferences where every booth looks the same

items: Advantage vanishes when models get cheaper

d.verdict: Differentiation is the heart of marketing

l278|534.c: Marketing's job changes with the company's stage; in hypergrowth, re-diagnose every three to six months.
l278|534.e: She spent about eight and a half years at Stripe and was its only marketer for the first three. She credits the two founders, both developers, as the company's first marketers. Phase one was clearing a backlog of features that had shipped but were never announced, and setting the rule that code being done isn't a launch; users knowing about it and using it is. Phase two was expanding launch channels, building developer relations, and running a community. Phase three was helping users navigate a multi-product platform to find the right solution. Confusions surfaced by new hires rotating through support became a list of landing pages to build.
ex: Cristina Cordova handed her a list of features that had never been marketed
Developers will find bugs in your marketing copy, so the bar has to be high

items.d: Help users find the right solution

l278|534.c: The right process makes a company faster: review only at the 20% and 80% marks.
l278|534.e: Marketing is the first place users meet the product, so the experience has to be consistent. As a team grows fast, someone in their second week should be able to get things done as well as a two-year veteran, without learning the unwritten rules or knowing which conference room to ambush the founders outside of. Her approach is a marketing review that's transparent to the whole company, whether a weekly meeting, a Slack channel, or an email list, so people can watch and learn. There are only two gates: at 20%, review goals, audience, and rough direction; at 80%, review the finished work. Showing up at 99% for a rubber stamp is pointless.
ex: Brand isn't just marketing assets; it includes the support and hiring experience
Moving fast and caring about brand aren't in conflict

l278|534.c: A brand is the expectation you set in people's minds; the gap between experience and expectation decides loyalty.
l278|534.e: She believes changing expectations is far easier than changing reality, so she works hard to set them clearly with customers, internal partners, and her own team. Loyalty accumulates this way: exceeding expectations earns credit, falling short costs it. She thinks AI companies shouldn't just race each other on benchmarks and features. What makes a product delightful is the same as for any product, and it takes a long view. Even while moving fast, Stripe and OpenAI slow down for quality and safety, because people try their new launches on trust.
ex: Stripe Relay, a social commerce buy button, failed from bad timing and too little research
The challenge at OpenAI was always being in the eye of the storm, under a magnifying glass

items.d: Be clear about trade-offs, inside and out

l278|534.c: Marketing isn't just the marketing department's job; in the AI era, marketers need wider skills and more taste.
l278|534.e: She separates capital-M Marketing, the department that owns channels, assets, and the acquisition engine, from lowercase marketing: what the company stands for, the story the founders tell, and what product and sales sell to whom. The latter belongs to the whole company. Hire a marketing leader only once there's a spark of product-market fit. The modern marketing leader has to be a chameleon, shifting from T-shaped to comb-shaped, with depth in several areas, and AI lets brand-minded people handle data too. AI will flood the world with mediocre content, which makes craft, real product and customer understanding, and taste scarcer and more valuable. The fundamentals still matter.
ex: PMs and product marketers should run a three-legged race from day one
Her advice to companies: use AI to improve your own operations first

items.d: What the company stands for; founder story
Product decides what; sales decides to whom

l279|537.c: Executives should drive and deliver themselves, log every problem they hit, and assign it to a team to fix.
l279|537.e: Once or twice a month he spends half a day to a full day driving for Uber or delivering food. Afterward he goes through his screenshots and writes up the problems in separate docs for the rider, driver and delivery apps, tagging an owner and adding his suggested fix. Teams filter the list, since not all of his ideas are right, but he follows each one through to the fix shipping. To make it stick, each team commits to about 300 fixes per half-year in its OKRs. The number itself doesn't matter, he says; what matters is having a target and the CEO and leadership genuinely caring.
ex: About 700 to 800 trips and deliveries so far
Every quarter the company runs a week where everyone drives or delivers, with a competition
On his first trip, the rider stood waiting for him to load the luggage

items.d: One doc per app, listing problems
About 300 fixes per team per half-year

l279|537.c: User feedback runs from abstract to firsthand, and doing the job yourself adds what data can't convey.
l279|537.e: From dashboard metrics to surveys, focus groups, one-on-one interviews and finally firsthand experience, each step gets more concrete. Funnel metrics show where the friction is, but they can't measure how strongly users feel about it. A design that looks great on a monitor may not work three feet away in a car moving at 45 miles an hour. He also found that drivers feel real excitement the moment an order comes in, and that the interaction with riders is the heart of the driver experience. None of that comes through in the office.
ex: He holds roundtables with drivers and riders at regional offices
For drivers, every inefficiency means less money earned

marks.d: Metrics like daily and monthly actives

l279|537.c: Documents and brainstorms deliver nothing to users; shrink the time from good idea to users' hands.
l279|537.e: Users only benefit from code that ships, so the point is to shorten the cycle, not to launch recklessly. Product reviews exist to make decisions. Reversible "two-way door" decisions should be fast; only irreversible "one-way door" decisions deserve extra deliberation. When driver supply collapsed during the pandemic, Uber ran cross-functional daily standups for about six months, aiming to decide within 24 hours. A leader can occasionally jump in personally to push something through, but only occasionally.
ex: He wrote a 15-page PRD one weekend to unstick a driver-app project; the result was about half different
Palm took three or four years to respond to the iPhone and Android, a lesson in urgency

d.verdict: Spend decision time according to reversibility

l279|537.c: New PMs should join companies that ship often and build judgment through thousands of small decisions.
l279|537.e: What marks a good PM isn't five brilliant strategic ideas but countless small decisions: where the button goes, how the copy reads, which market launches first. Repetition builds intuition, so the next similar problem gets decided faster, and shorter cycles mean more repetition. His advice is to go through three to five full product cycles in two or three years, and not to rush to be the smartest person in the room. AI is speeding up research and document writing, but understanding users and exercising judgment will only matter more.
ex: The best engineers don't wait for a PRD; they co-create at the whiteboard
He uses ChatGPT and Gemini to condense 50 to 100 pages of user research

items.d: 3 to 5 cycles in two or three years

l279|537.c: Robotaxis will share one network with human drivers, and Uber's demand density keeps them busy.
l279|537.e: Uber spun off its in-house self-driving unit during the pandemic and switched to partnerships, signing about 15 partners in the past year. Robotaxis are expensive, so they need high utilization, and Uber's demand density keeps them from sitting idle, with human drivers filling in at peak times. He estimates full scale is five to ten years away, and people won't be replaced: some pickup and drop-off spots are out of reach for robotaxis, regulation is a hurdle, Uber has committed to providing earning opportunities, and businesses like grocery delivery keep increasing demand for people.
ex: Live in Austin and Phoenix, with WeRide in Abu Dhabi
Sidewalk robots have completed thousands of short deliveries downtown

terms.d: Cover peaks and tricky pickup spots

result.d: One dispatch system, less idle time

l279|537.c: Squeeze efficiency out of the core business first; that earns the right to expand outward ring by ring.
l279|537.e: Uber became profitable about two years ago through a culture shift and a new approach to software. The core business does about 33 million trips a day, so a penny of efficiency gets multiplied enormously. Costs were driven down line by line: batching food deliveries, promotions, customer support, payments, background checks. The savings go back into growth and into riders and drivers. Only a strong core earns the right to expand into food delivery, grocery and reserved rides. When rides fell about 80% overnight in the pandemic, they also shed non-core projects.
ex: Combining several orders in one delivery trip lowers costs
The self-driving unit and Uber Elevate were spun off during the pandemic

l279|537.c: When the data says no, still be willing to bet on your understanding of users' real problems.
l279|537.e: He argues for first understanding what users want and where the problem is, and sometimes that means following intuition. The data didn't support bringing taxis onto the platform, but he saw the drivers' need and motivation and pushed ahead. Teen accounts faced objections over liability and parents' concerns, but as a father of teenagers he knew the pickups were a real pain point. On safety, he pushed the team to track how safe riders feel, not just incident rates, and that measure improved.
ex: Every yellow cab in New York can now be hailed in the app
Teen accounts were shut down in California over regulation, and parents still write asking for them

items.d: Data said no, drivers wanted it
Pickups are a real pain for parents

l280|539.c: Claude Opus 4 can now offer genuinely new strategic angles, and AI timelines deserve to be taken seriously.
l280|539.e: He has long used Claude as a sounding board for product strategy. Its advice used to be safe and predictable, mostly things he'd already considered. With Opus 4 and deep research, it gave him a new angle he adopted on the spot for the first time, which changed his view of whether models can produce original insight. On timelines, Dario Amodei's predictions keep coming true, coding benchmarks are climbing as expected, and progress on agents, memory, and long-running tasks has made him noticeably more confident in the aggressive timelines.
ex: SWE-bench: about 50% when Dario made his prediction, about 72% at recording time
He keeps AI 2027 and his own product strategy open in side-by-side tabs

Dario's call for the end of 2025

l280|539.c: Once AI writes most of the code, the bottlenecks move upstream to decisions and downstream to review and merging.
l280|539.e: Engineering's role has changed, but the mix of people who build products hasn't, and old assumptions linger. PMs and designers can now build working prototypes with Claude, so prototyping happens earlier. But with code volume exploding, the merge queue got overwhelmed and had to be rebuilt. Borrowing from the theory of constraints in The Goal, the new bottlenecks are upstream, in deciding and aligning on what to build, and downstream, in review, coordination, and shipping. He's experimenting with a "minimum viable strategy" that sets just enough direction and lets teams run.
ex: He estimates more than half, maybe 70%, of the company's pull requests come from Claude Code
He guesses Claude Code itself is more than 95% written by Claude Code
Another Claude reviews the code; humans do acceptance testing

l280|539.c: Product's real leverage is shaping the model with researchers during post-training, not wrapping a finished model.
l280|539.e: If what you build could be built by anyone with an off-the-shelf model and a few prompts, that isn't where Anthropic should be. He's increasingly convinced product people need to embed with model teams and work with researchers during post-training, the stage after basic training where the model is taught how to behave, on how a capability should show up. Product feedback then flows back into training. The PMs with the best internal reputation are the ones who sought out researchers early. He also reflects that a few founder-type engineers matter more than simply adding headcount.
ex: Artifacts in Claude 4 was redesigned jointly by the post-training team and product
Claude Code began as an internal project by Boris Cherny

l280|539.c: Consumer hits can't be planned, so a challenger should bet on developers and creators rather than chase ChatGPT.
l280|539.e: He admits that for most people, ChatGPT is synonymous with AI. But Instagram taught him that consumer breakouts are lightning in a bottle, and building a whole strategy around finding the next one isn't wise. AI has room for several generational companies. Rather than envying others, see yourself clearly: the founders' character, the model's strengths in agents and coding, and the existing reputation among developers and builders. So he spent his early months meeting finance and insurance customers and startups, and the next step is serving creators specifically.
ex: A colleague on the legal team used Claude to write custom software for family
The Way of Code, a collaboration with Rick Rubin

Miss the opportunity in front of you
Help people delegate hours of work

l280|539.c: To avoid being crushed by big labs, AI startups need domain knowledge, sales relationships, and new ways to interact.
l280|539.e: He'll only make calls about the next one to three years. First is deep understanding of a specific industry: law, medicine, and biology have workflows and compliance requirements outsiders would never guess. Second is a differentiated go-to-market, knowing not just which company to sell to but which person inside it. Third is entirely new forms of human-computer interaction, which start out looking like geek toys and can take off as models improve, while incumbents are trapped by users' existing habits. On top of that, the do-or-die urgency of a small team is an advantage in itself.
ex: Harvey's product encodes workflows specific to lawyers
Imagine every piece of lab equipment connected through MCP
Is the buyer the CIO, the CFO, or the general counsel?

items.d: Workflows unique to law, medicine, biology
Know exactly who to sell to inside a company
Incumbents stuck with users' old habits
A drive no OKR can instill

l280|539.c: An AI product's usefulness depends on intelligence, context, and interface; MCP fills the context gap.
l280|539.e: He offers a "fake equation": model intelligence, context and memory, and the application and interface, all multiplied together. Whether the model has the right context directly decides how good the answer is. The team noticed every integration was being rewritten from scratch, so they turned it into an open protocol, MCP, that lets developers write a connector once and have it work with any model. The idea borrows from "commoditize your complements": the cheaper and more common the connections, the more valuable the model. He wants every primitive in the product, like projects and Artifacts, exposed through MCP so everything is scriptable and composable. He finds that more promising than computer use.

Shopify's Tobi Lütke and Microsoft's Kevin Scott were early supporters

l280|539.c: Artifact returned one unit for every ten put in, and with several headwinds, shutting it down early was right.
l280|539.e: Artifact's personalized recommendations worked well, but it ran into several headwinds. The mobile web had deteriorated: tap an article and you got a wall of pop-up ads, yet blocking ads would be unfair to publishers. News is consumed privately and doesn't spread naturally the way Instagram photos do, and bolting on sharing hooks crossed a line for them. And the team was fully remote during the pandemic, which made a major pivot hard. Effort and results were badly out of proportion, and with AI changing everything, the opportunity cost was too high. So they shut it down, and most people praised them for cutting losses in time.
ex: Compared with the Instagram days, plotting next moves late at night in a burrito shop
They never set Instagram-scale daily active users as the goal

l281|540.c: Product and engineering aren't separated; engineering leaders who understand both technology and users own product too.
l281|540.e: Mercado Libre assigns responsibility by who is best suited, not by title. It usually lands on engineering leaders, because they know what's technically possible and also understand the business and the users. Fewer than 1,000 people hold a PM title, which he estimates is about 5% of the usual ratio. Hiring tests engineering ability above all, and leaders can't hand off basic technical questions. The reasoning is to keep the full context of problem, technology and user inside one brain. He admits it may not be the only right model.
ex: More than 18,000 developers across 18 countries
Over 5 million packages delivered a day; e-commerce and fintech are similar in size
