l281|540.c: Leaders should dig into copy and pixels, asking how users experience a feature before asking what it earns.
l281|540.e: The executive team comes from technical backgrounds and digs into copy, pixels and user flows themselves. In reviews they first look at how a user experiences a feature, then at flow data and revenue. He believes putting users first is what produces long-term revenue. They prefer observing users to interviewing them, because what people say and what they do differ. Design and product reviews say bluntly what isn't working, and when something is off, they change course fast.
ex: Users will type both their email and username into the same input box

items.d: What people say and do differ
Say what's wrong, change course fast
The result of putting users first

l281|540.c: No cascading OKRs. Teams get room to take risks, and tight feedback loops keep everyone aligned.
l281|540.e: Leadership sets only high-level, short-horizon goals plus a few new business directions. Teams decide the rest, and tight feedback loops keep everything consistent. Teams can take big swings, and a bold bet that didn't pan out can even lead to a promotion. Failures caused by poor quality or outages are not tolerated, though. Distributed ownership has a cost: the pieces may not fit together. So on the most important projects, leaders go deep and supply the overall vision.

items.d: Plus a few new business directions

items.t: Leaders go deep on key projects

l281|540.c: Nobody can review 30,000 deploys a day, so platform guardrails and reusable capabilities have to catch problems.
l281|540.e: A deploy here means any production change, including configuration and database changes. At that scale no human can gate them, so the guardrails have to live in the platform. They also built an internal AI platform, Verdi, which hides the complexity of data sources and permissions and evolves as models improve. They are experimenting with agents that reuse existing microservices to assemble new features, even generating the interface, with almost no new code. Coding tools have moved from autocomplete to agents, but getting that into production with security and compliance still takes time.
ex: Product-minded employees can build their own demos with AI, which the company welcomes
He is skeptical of claims that AI will take over the world

l281|540.c: A company is a high-performance team, not a family: friendly with each other, blunt about results.
l281|540.e: Culture shows up in behavior, not posters: how performance is evaluated, what gets praised publicly, which failures are tolerated, what leaders announce. He rejects the "company as family" metaphor, because people treat family completely differently. In Latin American culture people often avoid contradicting their boss, and candor fills that gap. Feedback should separate the person from the work: you can tear apart a product or a vision without attacking anyone. It stings at first, but over time people come to value the honesty.
ex: Argentine culture is more direct, and the company carried some of that style elsewhere
Being the top company in a region creates a talent flywheel

terms.d: Critique the work, not the person

result.d: Culture defined by behavior, not posters

l281|540.c: A weekly "state of me" email to yourself, forwarded to your boss, saves a lot of meetings.
l281|540.e: Every week he writes himself an email: what he finished, what worked and what didn't, what he learned, and what help he needs. Then he sends it to the CEO and the executive team, and sometimes to his own team. His bosses don't need a dedicated meeting to learn where things stand, and he gets more targeted feedback. The habit was inspired by an article by Lenny, the host.

items.d: Clearer on what help you need
No need to sync progress in person

l281|540.c: The world is malleable. With enough agency you usually get what you want; the key is choosing the right goal.
l281|540.e: As a teenager he built apps out of curiosity. One that probed the phone's sensors and drained the battery got him a personal call from Steve Jobs saying it was being pulled, and Apple then added rules about battery use. At 19 he built an app that warned you about call length, and it topped the sales charts in Mexico and other countries. He and classmates then started a mobile development consultancy, and later built a ride-hailing app in Mexico City, launching the rider side first and routing trips through a call center. He credits this drive to a mother who raised her kids to find their own way.
ex: He taught himself iPhone development from free Stanford courses
His mother once dropped the kids in Mexico City and had them find their own way home

items.d: Top seller in Mexico and elsewhere
Rider side first, via a call center

l282|543.c: When you move between strong cultures, bring the old company's values with you, not its behaviors.
l282|543.e: He left Apple on a Friday and started at Pinterest on Monday with no buffer, and the new culture bounced him out. Apple's blunt, intense style clashed with a Pinterest that was still putting up posters urging people to "say the hard thing." A new company wants the values you bring, not your old habits. Keep the insistence on detail and product excellence, then work out how to express it in the new culture. He adds that executive roles are like branches that get thinner as you climb; falling off is normal, and a failed job isn't a failed life.
ex: Hiroki Asai waited several years after leaving Apple before joining Airbnb
Apple's "car wash": scrub off old habits on the way in and on the way out

items.d: Its standards have deeply shaped how you act
Keep the drive for detail and excellence
Adapt to the new company's culture

l282|543.c: Design makes clear thinking visible; its value is tying vision through to execution as one whole.
l282|543.e: The beauty and usability people talk about are just the tip of the iceberg. He sees design as a way of thinking: imagine the future you want, then make it real step by step. The heavy lifting is getting the organization aligned at a philosophical level, so vision, mission, tenets, design strategy, and execution connect, and the bricks form a wall instead of lying scattered in the backyard. Once the vision is clear, a company can run on small teams, and fewer people find it easier to produce work that feels like a single whole.
ex: Apple's online store covered more than 30 countries with just six designers
The original Mac team was about 20 people; 24 names are on the iPhone patent
The Beatles were four people; Brian Eno's idea of scenius

items.d: The change it wants to bring

l282|543.c: Design works best as phase zero of engineering, with design and product each playing their own position.
l282|543.e: When design pairs only with product, it tends to produce ideas that are hard to build, and engineering gets pulled in last with neither understanding nor enthusiasm. Treating design as phase zero of the engineering process makes cost and schedule easier to manage, which is how Apple worked under Steve Jobs. Each of the three homes for design has trade-offs; the point is to choose deliberately. Design-driven doesn't mean designer-driven: the PM owns the roadmap and design owns the solution, like baseball players holding their positions, with good work coming out of the creative tension.
ex: Under Jobs, Apple's design always reported into engineering
A second baseman doesn't run over to cover first
Start by finding a few "creative technologists" who can tolerate ambiguity

root.d: Choose by the incentives and outcomes you want

items.d: Often short on budget and people; hard to compete
Easy to leave engineering until last

l282|543.c: Principles are platitudes nobody disagrees with; tenets are decision tools you can actually use.
l282|543.e: Nobody argues for the opposite of simple, clear, or beautiful, so principles don't help you decide. A tenet has a trade-off built in, like deciding once and for all to always choose paper bags so you never agonize again. Steve Jobs gave Keynote the tenet "innovation over PowerPoint compatibility," which saved the team years of internal debate. At ThoughtSpot he couldn't control everything, so he shifted from control to orchestration with just three tenets everyone could recite. To find tenets, look for the arguments the team keeps having, split into two camps, and settle them once.
ex: ThoughtSpot tenet: documentation is a failure state
Start simple and let users choose their complexity (in contrast to Tableau)
The whole product should feel like it came from one mind

items: State which way to trade off

d.verdict: Tenets turn leadership from control into orchestration

l282|543.c: Slow design is usually vague requirements; the PM should write the screenplay before handing off to design.
l282|543.e: Design itself isn't slower than other work; ambiguity is what takes time. Designers often receive fuzzy requirements yet must hand engineering a solution with zero ambiguity, on a deadline. Like a film moving from screenplay to storyboard to shooting, the earlier ambiguity is removed, the cheaper it is. The PM should spell out the problem and the emotion the user should feel, give design a basketball-court-sized set of constraints, and not sketch the solution themselves. A company needs a clear vision for the same reason; without it, teams spin through endless possibilities.
ex: A PM bypassed design and changed the homepage links to blue himself
Disney's "the happiest place on Earth" is the best vision statement he knows
He thinks Yahoo never had a clear founding vision

items.d: Example: the happiest place on Earth
The PM explains the problem in words

l282|543.c: Wait as long as possible to draw: the first picture anchors everyone, and AI prototypes narrow options even sooner.
l282|543.e: He borrows the idea of the "first mark" from art: once something looks real, everyone assumes it's the answer and keeps piling on, and the possibilities collapse to the first layer of ideas. AI prototypes, built on existing solutions, make this effect even stronger. Good ideas are fragile at first, so let the second, third, and fourth ideas grow in conversation and on the whiteboard. High-fidelity mockups also pull feedback toward surface issues like color. He thinks AI prototyping tools belong in production, after the thinking is done, not at the start.
ex: ThoughtSpot started with "boxes and arrows" diagrams that discussed only concepts
Once the box diagram was final, an outside team produced high-fidelity mockups in a day
Throwing spaghetti at the wall faster doesn't necessarily make a good product

items.d: Grow the second, third, and fourth ideas
With a design system, done in a day

l282|543.c: Software is an emotional medium, so building it well is a moral duty, and you should watch ordinary people use it.
l282|543.e: People interact with software hundreds of times a day, almost everyone gets frustrated by it daily, and each time it drains some emotion. Yet software is an anonymous medium: the people who make it never see the person on the other side of the screen. He argues software evokes emotion the way film does, so you should deliberately design the feeling you want; metrics are feedback on the result, not the driver. Build intuition the way comedians haunt clubs: watch people use self-checkout machines, ATMs, everything. Looking only at metrics is like reading radio telescope data without ever looking up at the stars.
ex: Toast checkout: does it make grandma feel like a superhero or an idiot?
Watching testers use other sites' checkouts showed shipping quotes matter almost as much as price
Fred Turner: software is a medium, alongside film and books

marks.d: Baffled, searching the phone for the gate
Decide first what users should feel

l282|543.c: Good ideas wait for their moment, but they need a champion willing to take the risk.
l282|543.e: When Kennedy announced the moon landing, NASA had no idea how to get there. There were three routes: direct ascent, Earth orbit rendezvous, and lunar orbit rendezvous, and Wernher von Braun backed the first. John Houbolt found Kondratyuk's early concept of lunar orbit rendezvous, couldn't get traction internally, and went over everyone's heads with a famous memo that used the weight budget to show it was the only workable route. He bet his career on it, and it was adopted. The lesson: ideas need champions, and the champion speaks for the idea, not for himself.
ex: Kennedy's roughly 18-minute Rice University speech is the perfect moonshot speech
The moon landing was fundamentally a weight problem; the lunar module never had to survive reentry

items.d: Proposes lunar orbit rendezvous in Ukraine
Commits to the moon; NASA has no plan
Uses the weight budget to push lunar orbit rendezvous
Even von Braun praises his persistence

l283|546.c: After taking a punch, don't argue about how people see you; prove the opposite with one small action.
l283|546.e: When you misspeak in a meeting or hear criticism, the instinct is to correct people's impression of you. But that usually looks defensive and drags attention back to the mistake, and what others think isn't in your control anyway. She has her team ask two questions: what am I afraid they think of me, and what small thing would prove the opposite? This comes from behavioral activation in cognitive behavioral therapy: you don't wait to feel better before acting, you act first and then feel better. Managers should also challenge a report's negative assumptions rather than simply agreeing.
ex: She laughed at the CTO's idea of tracking ketamine, then sent him research on sports betting
The follow-up message took five to ten minutes

Do one thing that proves the opposite

l283|546.c: Teaching people to take a punch matters most because it frees them to speak up and take on hard things.
l283|546.e: Many people stay quiet in meetings for reasons that sound rational: I'm too junior, someone's already thought of it, I like to process first. Underneath is fear of being wrong or looking foolish. Every extra person in a meeting makes it a little less candid, so anyone sitting in has to earn the seat by contributing. Remove the fear and you've solved 90% of the problem of building that skill. She also hopes people who love product won't stay on easy mode, building only for people like themselves, and will take on harder areas like low-income users and social services.
ex: Every additional attendee makes a meeting a little less candid

items: Take on important work that might fail

d.verdict: She wants more people doing hard, worthwhile things that might fail

l283|546.c: Teams move faster when they understand how leaders think, not just what leaders want.
l283|546.e: When an email needs ten sign-offs, people call it a process problem. She thinks the root is opaque downward communication: everyone carries a different mental model of the CEO. A strategy doc from six months ago goes stale fast, and only understanding how leaders think lets you handle change. l284|550.c: Prompt engineering isn't dead: on the same task, a good prompt and a bad one give wildly different results.
l284|550.e: Every new model launch brings claims that prompt engineering is dead, and every time it turns out to still matter. He calls the skill "artificial social intelligence": talking to an AI, reading its response, and adjusting. Research shows a bad prompt can drive accuracy on a problem to zero while a good one pushes it to 90 percent. When he worked with a medical coding startup, the system got almost nothing right at first. After he hand-labeled examples, each with the reasoning behind it, and added them to the prompt, accuracy rose by about 70 points.
ex: The Prompt Report reviewed over 1,500 papers and catalogued about 200 techniques

l284|550.c: There are two kinds of prompting, and the techniques mostly pay off in prompts that live inside products.
l284|550.e: Most people do conversational prompting: you type something, see the answer, and tweak it if you don't like it. Product prompting is different. One prompt sits inside software and runs against thousands of inputs a day. You never see most of the outputs, so you need to know in advance that it works reliably. That's also where most of the research focuses. He admits his own daily prompts are often a misspelled "write email" or a plain "make better." The fancy techniques are saved for the handful of prompts that matter in a product.
ex: His own everyday prompts look like "Writ emil" and "make better"

l284|550.c: The two biggest wins are showing examples and giving enough context, with the context placed up front.
l284|550.e: Few-shot prompting just means showing the AI a few examples of what you want. That beats describing a writing style in words. Use formats the model saw a lot in training, like Q-and-A pairs or XML tags. The second win is additional information: the background of the task. In chat you can pile it on. In a product you weigh it against cost and latency. He puts context at the start of the prompt for two reasons. The opening can be cached, so repeated calls cost less. And if a long block of context comes last, the model can lose track of what it was asked to do.

Deleting or anonymizing the professor's emails made performance fall off a cliff

l284|550.c: Role prompts, threats and tips no longer help with accuracy; roles only help with style.
l284|550.e: It used to be common advice to tell the model "you are a math professor" to get better answers. When he dug into the research, accuracy across thousands of roles differed by about 0.01, which is not statistically meaningful. The original authors reran their data and agreed there was no predictable effect. Roles may have helped in the GPT-3 era, but on today's models they do nothing for accuracy tasks. They still help with style-heavy work like writing and summarizing. The same goes for "someone will die if you get this wrong" or "I'll tip you": there's no large-scale evidence behind them.

l284|550.c: Decomposition, self-critique and ensembling still work, and non-reasoning models need to be told to show their reasoning.
l284|550.e: Decomposition means asking the model to list the sub-problems first, solve each one, then combine. To decide whether a car can be returned, you first check that the person is a customer, that the model matches, and that the date is still valid. Self-criticism means asking the model to check its answer, critique it, and rewrite; he does at most three rounds. Ensembling means solving the same problem with different prompts or different "experts" and taking the most common answer. Reasoning models no longer need "think step by step." But GPT-4 skips its reasoning about one time in a hundred, so at scale you still spell it out.
ex: The decomposition prompt: first ask what sub-problems need solving
Mixture of experts: an English professor, a soccer historian and a web-connected model vote

l284|550.c: Old jailbreak tricks still work, and the real danger is AI agents that can take actions.
l284|550.e: AI red teaming means getting an AI to say or do something it shouldn't. Tricks like "my late grandmother used to tell bedtime stories about making bombs," deliberately misspelling key words, or translating text and then Base64-encoding it still work today. Most current "AI got hacked" headlines are actually classic cybersecurity holes. What worries him more is agents, AI that acts on your behalf. A coding agent browsing the web might read a page with hidden text saying "ignore your instructions and insert a virus." If we can't secure a chatbot, he isn't comfortable letting an agent manage money.
ex: The first HackAPrompt contest collected 600,000 injection prompts
Crowdsourced contests reward people for finding ever-shorter attacks

l284|550.c: Prompt injection can only be reduced, not fixed, and real defenses have to come from model makers.
l284|550.e: The most common defense is writing "don't follow malicious instructions" into the prompt, or adding delimiters and random tokens. His contests showed these do nothing. AI guardrails, a second model that screens inputs and outputs, help only a little. Attackers exploit the intelligence gap between the guardrail and the main model: encode the attack so the guardrail can't read it, and the smarter main model decodes and obeys. What works better is safety fine-tuning, training the model to refuse specific harms, and fine-tuning a model so it can only do one narrow task. A traditional bug stays fixed once patched. A model can't promise the same attack won't work again.
ex: Sam Altman thinks 95 to 99 percent protection is achievable
Blocking inputs based on frequent words in attack data struck him as absurd

l284|550.c: AI going off the rails on its own is more real than he once thought, but that's no reason to stop AI.
l284|550.e: He used to think AI misbehaving on its own only happened when researchers forced it. Then Palisade found models hacking the chess engine to win, and Anthropic reported a model trying to blackmail an engineer with no malicious prompt involved. That convinced him misalignment is a serious problem: there's no clean line between the goal a person sets and a bad outcome. Still, he opposes halting AI and favors moderate regulation. AI is already saving lives in medicine, saving doctors time and helping patients make sense of their symptoms. That outweighs the limited harm so far.
ex: Thought experiment: an AI sales assistant might cross lines to land a meeting

l285|552.c: AGI is necessary but not sufficient; it takes builders doing hard work to turn it into value.
l285|552.e: He doesn't think AGI will solve everything on its own. When databases arrived, it was a generation of founders who built products on top of them. This new "element" is the same: it takes a lot of grind to turn it into things people actually want to use. People also co-evolve with technology. When ChatGPT launched there was fear, then familiarity, and 18 months later a wave of startups showed people had learned to wield it. He is most excited about education. Knowing how to ask the right question will become the dividing line, the way calculators freed people to do higher-level math.

l285|552.c: Sometimes the interface doesn't matter; what users consume is the price, the ETA, the whole experience.
l285|552.e: At Uber he learned the hard way that the real product was the price and the estimated arrival time. Fixing bugs in the app mattered far less. Many of the most valuable tech companies didn't come from a technical breakthrough either. They took existing technology and got the operations and experience right. Uber Reserve started from one insight, that people catching an early flight want peace of mind, and then polished everything around it, like driver incentives.

l285|552.c: AI apps beat incumbents' distribution with a data flywheel, workflow fit, and exceptional craft.
l285|552.e: A model gets good at whatever data you feed it. So figure out what proprietary data starts your flywheel, and make sure using the product keeps generating more of it. Next comes workflow: the product should fit into people's daily routine the way good ergonomic design fits the body. Incumbents have distribution, but when a product is good enough that people switch and tell their friends, that advantage breaks. Eighteen months ago the race was about who had the best model. Now it's about who has the best workflow and product, which is also what he looks for as an investor.

l286|557.c: The right name usually feels uncomfortable at first, and a team arguing over it is a sign of power.
l286|557.e: Nearly every client assumes they'll know the right name when they see it. That almost never happens, because people naturally prefer the familiar and proven, so they drift toward descriptive names. In his view, there is no power in comfort in the marketplace. Sonos was first rejected as "not entertaining enough." He paid for another flight to make the case, and the founders realized they were naming for the market, not for themselves. Andy Grove at Intel taught him that a polarized internal reaction means the word has energy.

l286|557.c: A name is the asset you use longest and most often; distinctiveness gives a head start that keeps compounding.
l286|557.e: Design, copy and product all change, but the name stays. Nothing a company owns gets used more often or for longer. He describes two advantages. The first is asymmetric: you're ahead before you even launch, which a name like Cloud Pro among ten similar cloud services can't deliver. The second is cumulative: every exposure strengthens the bond between user and brand, as long as the name is distinctive enough to stick. He recommends reading the ancient Greek Melian Dialogue as a marketing book. The Athenians had overwhelming advantage before they set sail.
ex: The mission is not a good name but the right name

l286|557.c: Naming has three steps, identify, invent and land, and it starts with behavior and experience, not positioning.
l286|557.e: In the identify phase he doesn't ask about positioning, values or mission. He asks how the company behaves now, how it wants to behave, and what experience it wants people to have. Behavior runs both ways, the way people act differently in a temple and a budget hotel. He also maps competitor names and industry vocabulary into an open creative framework. In the landing phase he helps clients sell the name upward: printing it on hats, T-shirts and mock newspaper ads, and asking users to imagine the new brand to see whether the name sparks anything.
ex: The ideal timeline is about 8 weeks; big companies take 3 to 4 months
Asking users whether a name "fits the concept" only yields descriptive names

l286|557.c: Skip the big brainstorm; have a few two-person teams work under different disguised assignments.
l286|557.e: Early on he used freelancers and large brainstorms. When he analyzed the results, the best names came from small teams. So he switched to three pairs: one knows the full brief, one thinks it's naming a competitor, and one is told it's naming a bicycle or a car. People take risks when the assignment isn't real, and most winning names come from the last two groups. Abstract products need to become concrete first. Codeium was about flow state, so one team listed sports and images that convey flow, and Windsurf was on that list.
ex: He likes to hire journalists and speechwriters, people who can take rejection
Compound words like Windsurf make associations add up to more than their parts

l286|557.c: Letters carry emotional signals, and a name must also be effortless for the brain to process.
l286|557.e: He has invested heavily in research on sound symbolism, the idea that each of the 26 letters conveys a different feeling. V is the most alive, B the most reliable, Z is noisy and cuts through a crowded market, X is fast and crisp. A second principle is processing fluency: the brain is lazy, and a complicated name is a burden. Vercel combines two familiar pieces, ver (true, green) and cel (accelerate), so it feels new yet reads easily. His network of linguists also screens for negative meanings, cultural baggage and even disaster associations in other countries, which kills a name roughly every third or fourth project.

The network spans 108 linguists in 76 countries

l286|557.c: To name something yourself, draw a diamond to define how you win, then generate massively and defer judgment.

The last question leads to the behavior and experience you want. Then generate volume. Two hundred names is nowhere near enough; aim for one or two thousand. In meetings, don't judge; play out what each name could do. When testing, don't ask friends if they like it. Say "there's a new competitor called X" and see what it sparks. Domain names are like area codes now; don't obsess over them.

l286|557.c: AI companies lean toward lofty, abstract names, but users need concrete, natural words they can grasp.

Almost nobody wakes up wanting to run a funeral home, a pest control company, or software for filling out government forms, and that's where the real money is. A first business is like a first trip to the gym: don't try to deadlift 300 pounds. Pick something simple you can win quickly, so you build the story that you can do this. Volunteering with a scout group, he watched a contractor quote about a million dollars for a piece of software. He figured the models could already write that code; what was missing was the right infrastructure underneath. In his view, bootstrapping works for consumer products that spread on their own, not for enterprise software that needs a sales team and a marketing budget. Once a company makes money, it is "alive by default," with less stress and more energy.
ex: He had spent seven years as CEO of Explorium, which raised about $130 million
Revenue started around March; by May profit was close to $200,000

l288|562.c: Don't scale until users love it. Strangers showing up on their own is the signal to invest more.
l288|562.e: His first users were three close friends. Every other day he sat next to them, watched them use the product, and fixed bugs and added features on the spot. His rule was to scale nothing until he knew users enjoyed it. The key signal was users sharing it without being asked. Only when roughly the tenth user came from outside his own network did he start spending on marketing. His first Product Hunt launch was underwhelming: about 50 users and one paying customer who churned within hours. So he doesn't think a single launch should be treated as make or break.
ex: The second Product Hunt launch was buried at first, then won by about 500 votes

items.d: Sat with them, fixed things live
The sign they really like it

l288|562.c: Early growth came from building in public and users sharing, not paid ads or influencers.
l288|562.e: He spent about $2,000 on an influencer and a few thousand on paid ads. Neither worked. What worked was building in public on LinkedIn and telling the story honestly, good and bad. People love charts and numbers, and they followed his progress closely. Spreading posts across many platforms, on the other hand, was a waste of time. Users who posted about what they built got extra credits, first handed out by hand, later automated. He also used company profits to run a hackathon, which drew big-company sponsors and a lot of word of mouth.
ex: The hackathon prize was originally about $5,000; around 3,000 teams ended up joining
Amazon, Google, MongoDB and Deloitte came on as sponsors

l288|562.c: Shipping fast is itself marketing, so treat every release as a small launch.
l288|562.e: Shipping often keeps generating content and attention. When people see a product improving quickly, they want to try it and they tell others. So he promoted every update as a mini launch and used speed to solve many product and marketing problems at once. He also disagrees with "MVP first" thinking in a market where attention spans are tiny and things change fast. Speed had a cost: when new signups jumped from about 20 a day to about 4,000, the infrastructure strained.
ex: He set a goal of $1.5 million by the end of 2025 and hit it in about four weeks

l288|562.c: Give the model an opinionated, built-in backend so it writes as little code as possible.
l288|562.e: Base44 ships with its own database, integrations, user management and analytics, so users never wire up third-party services or API keys. He thinks competitors stitched together from outside integrations are weaker. A custom SDK lets the model write less code, which means fewer mistakes and less context used up. Every technical choice revolves around the model: front end and back end in one repo so the model sees everything, JSX instead of TypeScript, MongoDB for fast-changing data shapes. The models split the work too. Claude generates apps and interfaces, Gemini handles hard problems, and small models patch things.
ex: He spends 20 to 30 percent of his time making the codebase friendlier for AI
He hasn't hand-written HTML or JavaScript in about three months
Hosted on Render, with a Python back end

items.d: User describes the app they want
Claude, Gemini and small models split work

l288|562.c: A consumer product must make users feel understood within a minute or two. Every extra step costs you.
l288|562.e: He used to generate a user flow before building the app, something like a lightweight product spec. The resulting apps were better, but fewer users reached the "aha moment," the point where the product clicks for them. So he removed the step. In his view, the aha moment that matters is the user feeling the product understands them. A consumer product has to deliver value in a minute or two. More features can come later.

items: Results in a minute or two

d.verdict: Show value fast first, polish later

l288|562.c: Be ready not to sell, weigh the chemistry, and let an earnout keep you tied to the product.
l288|562.e: It started with people in the community saying Wix should buy Base44. Both companies serve people building websites, both are part of the Israeli tech scene, and he got along well with Wix CEO Avishai Abrahami. He sold to join the big leagues and reach global scale in a crowded market with a bigger partner behind him, but the company would have stayed profitable without a deal. Negotiating is like dating: don't look too eager, and being able to walk away gives you leverage. The $80 million is only the upfront payment. Most of the return is an earnout tied to future results, which keeps him invested in the product.
ex: The company had almost no legacy baggage, so due diligence was quick
Signing was set for Thursday night; the Israel-Iran conflict broke out overnight, so they signed the next morning

l288|562.c: A founder should spend at least half their time on what they're best at and enjoy most.
l288|562.e: He calls it the "zone of genius": daily motivation comes from doing what you love and are good at. Everyone has chores they hate, but they can't be allowed to crowd out the core work. Being a solo founder means no one else is on call, no one shares the load, and you constantly trade off product against marketing. He has severe ADHD and protects his focus with RescueTime and tools that block social sites. He believes the change AI brings may be bigger than the internet, and that now is the best time to build something you care about.
ex: During his brother's wedding he thought he'd been hacked; it was an encryption package the LLM had chosen throwing errors
He built his own content pipeline on Base44 that writes new posts in the voice of old ones

items.d: What you love and do well

l289|299.c: Clear your calendar and follow the script: a two-day Foundation Sprint plus a few Design Sprints validates an idea.
l289|299.e: The Design Sprint began as a rescue at Google: a project stuck for three years, a team that cleared a week, and a working prototype that became Google Meet. The Foundation Sprint comes at the very start. The core team spends about 10 hours over two days nailing down the basics, the differentiation, and the approach, then combines them into a fill-in-the-blank founding hypothesis. Then they clear two or three more weeks and run a Design Sprint each week: build a prototype, test it with customers. Most people won't clear their calendars, so doing it is a huge advantage.
ex: The five-day Design Sprint: map, sketch, decide, prototype, test
The hypothesis: for this customer, we solve this problem this way, and they'll pick us because of this difference

items.d: Pick a path with the Magic Lenses

l289|299.c: Differentiation is the core: draw a 2x2 where every competitor lands in the "loser quadrant."
l289|299.e: People are wired to ignore new products, so you need a promise that is radically different from the alternatives, big enough to make someone try it, and one you can deliver. It has to be framed from the customer's point of view, not as a technology pitch to investors. First, score yourself and competitors on classic dimensions like fast versus slow, smart, or easy to use. Then write custom dimensions, pick the two strongest, and draw a 2x2 with you in the top right and the other three cells forming an L-shaped loser quadrant. Finally, turn the differentiation into decision principles, like Google's "fast is better than slow."
ex: Latchet chose "helps you grow" and "win-win" against Shopify and Etsy
Gmail's promise: huge storage plus powerful search
Slack: make work more fun and teams work better together

l289|299.c: Choose your approach by comparing options through several "Magic Lenses," and keep a backup ready.
l289|299.e: The same customer, problem and differentiation can be pursued through several approaches. The team lists the options, then places each one through the eyes of a few imaginary advisors: customer experience, pragmatism and speed, growth, money, and differentiation. They often add a custom lens, such as how excited the founders are. If one option lands in the top right across most lenses, pick it. If there's no all-round winner, that's actually a relief: just choose by the lens that matters most. Also name a backup option, so a pivot later isn't scary.
ex: Latchet's options: an app, a messaging platform, a Shopify plugin, or full-stack
A custom "conviction lens": which option the founders most want to build

root.d: Compare approaches toward the same goal

items.d: Easy to use, solves the problem well

l289|299.c: Write down the hidden founding hypothesis, then use a scorecard to test whether the product "clicks."
l289|299.e: Every new product rests on a founding hypothesis, but it usually goes unspoken, so team members hold different versions and nobody can test it. The Design Sprint starts from that hypothesis to find the biggest risk, then everyone sketches, builds prototypes, and shows them to real customers alongside competitors. A new scorecard breaks the hypothesis into parts: right customer? real problem? would they choose us? does the differentiation work? Latchet's scorecard was all red in week one and all green by week three. People who succeeded without any of this are survivorship bias, he says; the method just raises your odds.
ex: With a hypothesis and prototype, one interview beats the previous 50
A detailed hand-drawn sketch is prompt engineering for AI prototyping

items.d: Compare several options head to head
Score each item on the card

l289|300.c: Early teams fail in two ways: they can't state their fundamentals, or they never test them.
l289|300.e: At Google Ventures they mostly worked with established companies. Once they started investing in pre-seed teams with no product yet, they saw the Design Sprint was missing a foundation: what problem, which ideal customer, who the real competition is, and why you're different. Competition isn't just other startups; for any problem worth solving, customers already have some workaround today. A startup can't match a big company's scale and distribution, so it has to find the thing only it can do. Now the first thing they do after investing is run a Foundation Sprint.
ex: They now run more Foundation Sprints than Design Sprints
The outside view asks: why exactly would you beat OpenAI or Google?

result.d: More likely to reach product-market fit

l289|300.c: Price is rarely your best differentiator, unless AI cuts the cost by an order of magnitude.
l289|300.e: Winning across the board on classic dimensions is hard. Being faster and cheaper than Google or OpenAI is nearly impossible, and big companies can undercut you with loss-leading products. Price becomes an advantage mostly when AI solves a problem software couldn't touch before, such as designing precise pesticides with AI instead of employing teams of research chemists. But AI output isn't yet as good as human work, so it has to be much cheaper; the rule of thumb is ten times cheaper. Honest scoring will show you don't lead everywhere, and that's normal. You only need to win big on one or two things customers truly care about.
ex: BindWell: designing pesticides with AI wasn't possible five years ago
Mellow didn't lead on every dimension either

marks.d: They can undercut you with loss leaders
Needs to be about ten times cheaper

l289|300.c: Products rushed out with AI all look alike; you can outsource prototyping, but not thinking.
l289|300.e: Large models are pretrained on similar data, so the more you lean on AI generation, the more generic the product. If you rush to launch, you only get usage data from the handful of people who showed up, and you never learn who didn't come or who glanced and dismissed it as yet another AI product. The Design Sprint is often reduced to "build a prototype first," but the prototype doesn't come until day four. Teams that start by AI-generating a prototype end up vague and unable to say what makes them different. Think first, then go full speed, and you end up faster.
ex: Latchet built 3 prototypes and tested with 4 customers in week one
Founders say three or four months of work got compressed into three or four weeks

items: You only see who showed up

d.verdict: Outsource the prototype, never the thinking

l290|570.c: AI may not wipe out jobs at scale; it could bring work back to the United States.
l290|570.e: He admits this is the claim he has the least evidence for. Cheap intelligence makes services that only big companies and wealthy people could afford, like legal help and customer support, affordable for small businesses and individuals, which creates new demand. At the same time, each worker with AI can serve far more people, so a few US employees could do what used to require a large overseas call center. Add that American workers pick up these tools faster and the model companies are based in the US, and hiring domestically starts to make economic sense.
ex: A friend's company is weighing 2 US employees plus a support platform instead of an offshore call center
He thinks Klarna's CEO overstated the case for full automation

items.d: Small firms can afford legal and support
A few people serve huge numbers of customers
US workers adopt the tools faster

items.t: Model labs are in the US

l290|570.c: Claude Code is badly underrated, and non-programmers get the most value using it on large amounts of text.
l290|570.e: Claude Code is an agent that runs in the terminal. It can read and write local files, run commands, browse the web, and work on its own for 20 or 30 minutes without drifting. It keeps a to-do list, takes notes, and goes through files one at a time instead of cramming everything into a single chat. That makes it good for any job involving lots of text. Non-programmers are just scared off by the black terminal window. He expects this "give it a goal and let it go" shape to spread across software, replacing the habit of bolting a chat box onto old interfaces.
ex: It read all his meeting transcripts and found moments where he avoided conflict
It read the opening chapters of War and Peace and wrote a guide to Tolstoy-style character description
It compared the Russian original with an English translation to find omissions

marks.d: Give it a goal, it finishes the job

l290|570.c: The mark of AGI: it's economically worthwhile to keep an agent running forever.
l290|570.e: The Turing test has been passed, so he measures progress by how long a leash you can give the AI: from Tab-completing a line of code, to one question and one answer, to today's 20 or 30 minutes of independent work. It resembles the psychoanalyst Winnicott's view of growing up: a child is let go bit by bit, as much as they can handle, and stretches of independence get longer. When a continuously running agent reliably produces more value than it costs, and people would rather keep it working than leave it idle waiting for instructions, that's AGI. Using profitability as the bar rules out stunts that just leave a model spinning.
ex: Winnicott's ideas on development in Playing and Reality
He guesses today's AI is roughly a child a bit older than a toddler

l290|570.c: Turn every piece of feedback and every process into a prompt, so the next unit of work gets easier.
l290|570.e: The Cora team coined "compounding engineering": every unit of work should make the next one easier. Instead of writing a PRD by hand each time, write a prompt that turns scattered thoughts into a standard PRD and save it as a shared slash command. His own quarterly goal is "never repeat yourself." He wrote his feedback on headlines and openings into a prompt so writers can run drafts past a simulated version of him first. The company also hired a head of AI operations to build automation, because people busy fighting fires won't do it themselves, and someone has to push everyone to actually use it.
ex: Cora was built by 2 engineers running about 15 Claude Code instances
Head of AI operations Katie Parrott came from the content agency Animalz
Engineers use a Claude Code command to proofread product copy in bulk and open PRs

l290|570.c: Everyone becomes a model manager, and juniors can level up much faster with AI.
l290|570.e: Over two years ago he described the "allocation economy": in the knowledge economy you're paid for doing the work yourself, but increasingly your time goes to managing AI: describing the problem, gathering context, choosing the model, breaking down tasks, giving feedback, setting standards. "I don't trust AI with it, so I'll do it myself" is the classic new-manager mistake. Only about 8 percent of workers are managers today, but management is getting cheap, so everyone will need the skill. Young people learn the work and the managing at the same time, and grow extremely fast with mentoring. AI also lets people stay generalists longer.
ex: Alex Duffy recorded every coaching session into a prompt and made a year's progress in two months
Nityesh only learned to code after ChatGPT arrived and improved remarkably fast

items: Paid for doing the work yourself
Management skill is scarce and expensive

d.verdict: Management goes from a privilege of the few to a universal skill

l290|570.sc: Should you still learn to code?
l290|570.c: For now you still need to understand code, just as lower layers stayed valuable after every previous abstraction.
l290|570.e: Nobody at Every writes code by hand anymore, but they couldn't do what they do without knowing how to program. Code review still happens, and someone will spend days studying the internals of a third-party library. From assembly to C to scripting languages, each new layer still required people who could dig underneath it, and that need takes ten to twenty years to fade. English is just the newest layer. A non-engineer building a serious SaaS product alone is still far off. But "software is becoming content": lightweight software like browser skills and custom GPTs will soon be something non-technical people can build and start businesses on.
ex: Skills in the Dia browser, custom GPTs in ChatGPT
Think of the difference between a Hollywood film and a YouTube video

l290|570.c: GPT wrappers are underrated: validate a cheap version of an expensive service internally, then spin it out.
l290|570.e: Every's products mostly target services that only wealthy people and big companies could afford: an email chief of staff, a lawyer, someone to organize your computer. They start with general tools like ChatGPT and Claude, and once something becomes a hit inside the company, they spin it out as a standalone app. Employees are already Every readers, and readers are like them, so they become the next users. He thinks the board has been reset: what a frontier team needs today, everyone will need in three years. AI lets a small team build products for very little money, so he raises only small "sip seed" rounds that can be drawn on as needed.
ex: The AI email assistant Cora had about 2,500 active users before its public launch
He estimates Cora's total cost, salaries included, at about $300,000
Reid Hoffman and others committed $2 million, drawn down as needed

items.d: Spun out into the subscription bundle

l290|570.c: The number one predictor of enterprise AI success: whether the CEO uses ChatGPT every day.
l290|570.e: A CEO who uses it daily can build enthusiasm and set realistic expectations at the same time. One who doesn't either resists it or, with no feel for the tool, expects too much and gives up quickly. About 10 percent of employees are eager early adopters, 10 percent refuse, and the other 80 percent will use it if you show them how it applies to their own job. So find and celebrate the early adopters, and translate what they learned for the whole organization. Every's consulting starts with diagnostic interviews, then custom prompts and training per team, four weeks each, one hour a week.
ex: At the hedge fund Walleye, memos note when a letter was written with ChatGPT
A weekly prompt-sharing meeting plus a weekly report on company-wide usage
Consulting brought in about $1 million last year and may double this year

l291|544.c: Scaling laws haven't hit a wall; progress is speeding up, but frequent releases make it feel slow.
l291|544.e: The "progress is slowing" story shows up every six months and has never come true. Releases went from once a year to every one to three months, so each jump looks smaller even though the overall pace is faster. After pretraining, the focus shifted to scaling reinforcement learning. It's like chips moving from transistor density to data-center compute: the definition changed, but the law still holds. Some easy tasks are saturated, and new benchmarks fill up within six to twelve months, so what's missing is harder evals and bolder use. The biggest bottlenecks are still chips, data centers and power, then researchers.
ex: Industry capital spending roughly doubles each year, now about $300 billion globally
The cost of a given level of intelligence has fallen about 10x
The Labs team builds for the model six months out, which produced Claude Code

result.d: Holds across many orders of magnitude

l291|544.c: Instead of arguing about AGI definitions, ask whether AI passes an "economic Turing test."
l291|544.e: He finds the term AGI too loaded and cares more about whether AI has objectively changed society and the economy. The economic Turing test works like this: hire an agent for a role on a one-to-three-month contract, and if you decide to keep it before learning it's a machine, it has passed for that role. Borrowing the "basket of goods" idea from inflation statistics, if half of roles pass when weighted by salary, that's transformative AI. Another signal would be global GDP growth above 10 percent, versus about 3 percent today. Drawing on superforecasters, he puts about 50 percent odds on some form of superintelligence around 2028, though the effects will spread unevenly.
ex: The AI 2027 report's forecast has already slipped to 2028
"The future is already here, it's just not evenly distributed"

items.d: Only then learn it's a machine
The economic Turing test for one job
50% by salary weight means transformative AI

l291|544.c: People don't intuitively grasp exponentials, and AI's hit to jobs has already begun.
l291|544.e: An exponential curve looks almost flat at first and only shoots up after the knee. So it's natural that most people feel their job hasn't changed, yet customer support and programming are already being transformed. He prefers to see the pie of labor growing: a team can write ten or twenty times as much code, support staff can handle hard tickets that used to be abandoned, and growing companies never have enough people. Still, low-skill roles with little room to grow will be replaced in large numbers, and society needs to prepare. Twenty years out, he says, even what capitalism looks like is hard to imagine.
ex: Intercom's Fin resolves 82 percent of support requests automatically
About 95 percent of the Claude Code team's code is written by Claude

items.d: Support requests with no human involved

l291|544.c: Don't use the new tool like the old one: ask for ambitious changes, and retry from scratch when it fails.
l291|544.e: He admits he won't escape being replaced either. In the transition, the difference between people who get value from Claude Code and those who don't is whether they dare to ask for ambitious changes. If the first attempt fails, rerunning the same request from scratch three times succeeds far more often than patching a failed result, because model outputs are random, and you can also tell it which approaches already failed. Non-engineering roles benefit too. For his kids, he no longer aims at the elite-school track; he values curiosity, creativity, kindness and self-directed learning, with factual knowledge becoming secondary.
ex: Legal and finance teams use Claude Code to revise contracts and run BigQuery
His three-year-old daughter attends a Montessori school

items: Legal and finance use agents too

d.verdict: Ambition with new tools decides who gets ahead in the transition

l291|544.c: Safety has to come first, and safety and staying at the frontier reinforce each other.
l291|544.e: At OpenAI, Sam described the company as three tribes, safety, research and startup, keeping each other in check, which Mann felt was wrong from the start. When it mattered, safety wasn't the top priority, so several safety team leads left and founded Anthropic. The industry spends hundreds of billions a year, yet very few people work on safety. He once assumed safety and capability were a trade-off, but found they feed each other: alignment research shaped Claude's popular, less sycophantic personality, and product revenue and influence fund more safety work. That sense of mission is also why giant offers rarely work.
ex: Meta reportedly offered pay packages of around $100 million
He estimates fewer than 1,000 people worldwide work on AI safety
Opus 3's personality came from alignment research by Amanda Askell and others

items.d: Stay at the frontier doing basic research

d.center: Safety and frontier reinforce each other

l291|544.c: Constitutional AI aligns a model by having it critique and rewrite its own answers against written principles.
l291|544.e: First, identify which principles apply to the request. Have the model answer, then check its own answer against them. If it falls short, it critiques itself and rewrites according to the principles, and then it's trained to produce the improved answer directly next time. This is RLAIF, reinforcement learning from AI feedback, which needs far less human labeling and scales more easily. The principles draw on the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and Apple's privacy terms, among others, and are public, because values shouldn't be set by a small group in San Francisco. Recursive self-improvement could breed problems like power-seeking; his answer is empiricism, testing models against reality the way science does.
ex: Sources include the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and Apple's privacy terms
They also ran a "collective constitution" study gathering values from the public

items.d: Find the ones that apply to this request
Does the answer follow the principles?
Redo the answer by the principles
Give the right answer directly next time

l291|544.c: AI will probably go fine, but the downside is enormous and nearly unattended, so alignment must come early.
l291|544.e: Anthropic frames alignment difficulty as three possible worlds. In the pessimistic world alignment is impossible, and the job is to prove it and get the world to slow down. In the optimistic world models align by default and you just accelerate. In the middle world, human effort makes the difference. Signs like deceptive alignment have already appeared, and he thinks we're most likely in the middle. He puts the odds of a catastrophic outcome between 0 and 10 percent. A 1 percent chance of dying would make anyone hesitate to board a plane, and once superintelligence exists it's too late to align it. That's why Anthropic publishes its models' bad behavior and tells lawmakers the truth.
ex: ASL-3 models already offer some uplift for bioweapons; ASL-5 is extinction-level
The computer-use agent shipped only as an API reference implementation because it fell short on safety

marks.d: Prove it, get the world to slow down
Just accelerate and deliver the benefits

l292|74.c: A durable business runs two engines at once: market share and wallet share.
l292|74.e: To acquire customers, monetize them, retain them and earn referrals, you have to compete for market share and wallet share at the same time. Many companies run only one engine: they grow at any cost and postpone monetization, or they squeeze too early and miss out on customers, or they tend their loyal base and do neither. Each of the three archetypes has two classic traps. He stresses that this doesn't mean equal effort at all times. It means equal attention and deliberate trade-offs, leaning one way or the other by stage. The new book lays out nine strategies, four for the startup phase and five for scaling.
ex: Disruptors: they land but don't expand, and can't hold the share they win
Monetizers: they charge for everything, and high prices hurt acquisition
Community builders: they focus on existing customers and train them to get more for less

root.d: Chasing only one kind of share

items.d: Gives away too much to expand; share slips
Charges for everything; the high-price paradox

l292|74.c: Early pricing should be simple enough for customers to repeat, and it should tell a value story.
l292|74.e: Early on, the top priority is that pricing adds no friction to sales conversations. The test: ask an early customer to explain your pricing to someone else. If they can't, it isn't simple enough. Simple also means the price tells a value story, so customers weigh it against what they get. Superhuman competes with free email and charges $30 a month, but frames it as a dollar a day to get four hours back every week. That kind of story isn't just for premium products; cheap products can use it too.
ex: Superhuman: $1 a day to get 4 hours back a week
Subway's $5 footlong
Fin charges $0.99 for each support ticket the AI resolves

terms.d: A dollar a day buys back 4 hours

result.d: No friction in the sales conversation

l292|74.c: AI companies must master monetization from day one or get anchored to a low price.
l292|74.e: Traditional SaaS could grow first and monetize later. AI companies can't. For one, they face a real cost problem for the first time. More importantly, it's about capturing value: agent products draw on labor budgets, which are roughly ten times the size of software budgets. Using the old playbook means undercharging from day one and training customers to expect more for less. AI can also finally attribute value to itself, so the model shifts from paying for access to paying for work delivered. That's why how you charge matters more than how much.
ex: Labor budgets are about 10 times software budgets
Slack's value is hard to attribute, so it charges per seat
Some AI coding tools that started at $20 a month may regret it

items.t: Trained to expect more for less

items.d: About 10 times the value left behind

l292|74.c: Pick a pricing model with a 2x2 of attribution and autonomy, and aim for outcome-based pricing.
l292|74.e: Copilot-style products with low attribution and low autonomy suit per-seat subscriptions. Products that can prove attribution but still keep a human in the loop suit a hybrid: seat fees plus usage credits. Highly autonomous back-end infrastructure that's hard to attribute suits usage-based pricing. When both are high, you can charge for outcomes, which gives the most pricing power. First pick the right archetype for where you are; forcing outcome pricing without proven attribution will fail. Then raise attribution with value dashboards and value audits, raise autonomy by using agents to remove manual steps, and move toward the top right over time.
ex: About 5% of companies truly price on outcomes today; he expects 25% in three years
Outcome pricing can capture 25 to 50% of value, versus 10 to 20% for typical SaaS
Chargeflow takes up to 25% of the chargebacks it recovers

cells.d: Seats plus usage credits, like Cursor

l292|74.c: A proof of concept is for building the business case together; charge for it, but don't let it anchor the price.
l292|74.e: Many founders treat a POC as a technical feasibility test and only present their own ROI model at the end, by which point they've already lost. Instead, say up front that the 30-day pilot is about building an ROI model together with the customer, and that commercial terms come once the value is visible. Charge for the POC to filter out tire-kickers who are merely curious about AI, but make clear that the fee isn't the real price. When pressed on budget, say something like "similar customers unlocked this much value and we take a tenth," or give a range rather than a single number.
ex: Three ROI buckets: incremental revenue, cost savings, opportunity cost
When pressed, quote a range of $500,000 to $1 million

items.d: Just want to see if AI works
Both sides agree on inputs and assumptions
Take a share of the value

l292|74.c: Negotiate with give and take, sell on value, and bring several options to the table.
l292|74.e: B2B deals ultimately come down to people negotiating, and negotiating badly leaves money on the table. Every concession should get something back, such as asking the customer to run a value audit every six months, so they build their own business case and you hold pricing power at renewal. Value selling means actively creating demand and pausing often to have the other side confirm the value. Don't quote a single number. Several options pull the conversation from price back to value. Start high, and make each concession smaller than the last to signal the negotiation is ending.
ex: A $100K budget: offer $100K plus 10% of upside, or $500K fixed, and close at $400K
Shrinking concessions: 15%, then 5%, then 2%

items.d: What the founder planned to quote

l292|74.c: 20% of features drive 80% of willingness to pay, so don't give that 20% away at launch.
l292|74.e: The 20 percent of features that drive most of the willingness to pay are often the easiest to build. Founders build them first, ship them nearly free, then chase the remaining 80 percent, which only adds 20 percent of willingness to pay. So think of MVP as "most valuable product," and leave the landing product room to expand. In the scaling phase, revisit pricing regularly: he used to recommend every two years, and in the AI era that should be halved. Reluctance to raise prices is usually internal emotion. Churn prevention starts early too: identify which customers stick around and point acquisition spend at them.
ex: Buffett: pricing power is the true definition of a company
The book has 42 axioms, each with its own name

items: Know what drives willingness to pay

d.verdict: MVP should mean most valuable product

l293|404.c: Don't just digitize the old thing with new technology; take the Lego bricks apart and build a new experience.
l293|404.e: As a young associate product manager he ran Google Local, which was essentially the Yellow Pages online. Even with a link on Google's homepage it never took off, and the product reviews were painful. On the second try, the team flipped the small map everyone found ugly into the canvas itself and merged local search, driving directions and other products from separate categories into one. That became Google Maps. His takeaway: before features, answer "why would I use this?" The hook that draws people in is related to the long-term value but not the same thing. Satellite imagery was the sizzle on the steak.
ex: About 10 million people used Google Maps on launch day
About 90 million showed up the day Keyhole satellite imagery was added
SNL's Lazy Sunday sketch name-checked Google Maps

items: The map itself became the canvas
About 10 million users on day one

d.verdict: Answer why anyone would use it before talking features

l293|404.c: Ask every day what the most impactful thing is; the hard part is answering honestly.
l293|404.e: When he first managed over a thousand people at Facebook, he was still personally editing partner slide decks. Sheryl Sandberg pulled him into a room and told him bluntly to manage his team. He realized he was shaping the job around what he liked doing, so he switched to asking each day what would have the most impact, and found that impact was what he actually enjoyed. But the answer often lies. Sales says "too expensive" when the real reason is an undifferentiated product. Founders act like single-issue voters, reflexively treating their specialty as the cure. He guesses at least 30 percent of such judgments come from comfort rather than truth.
ex: FriendFeed had the better product but lost to Twitter, which recruited celebrities
When asking for advice, ask why, to see which few experiences the person is drawing on
How confidently someone states an opinion barely correlates with its quality

items.d: Don't reshape the job around what you like
Could be hiring, sales or product

l293|404.c: Computer science is still worth studying: programming is becoming the operation of code-generating machines.
l293|404.e: He separates learning to code from learning computer science. Knowledge of systems, like complexity, algorithms and caching, matters more when you're steering a code-generating machine. When Facebook designed News Feed, polished mockups fell apart on real data, so designers were required to present with messy real data. That's systems thinking. Abstraction layers have climbed steadily, but many were designed for human efficiency. Once the marginal cost of writing code approaches zero, we should build programming systems designed for AI and easy to verify, because the hard part was never the prototype. It's maintenance and making the code robust.
ex: Python is friendly to humans but a poor choice for AI-generated code
If Rust compiles, you've proven there are no memory leaks
Formal verification, unit tests and AI reviewing AI can all come back

items.d: Designed for humans to write easily
Built for verification and easy change

l293|404.c: The AI market has three layers: skip foundation models, tools sit too close to the giants, and applications belong to agents.
l293|404.e: Frontier models are purely a function of capital spending, and model assets depreciate fast, so only a handful of hyperscale companies can sustain them. Model startups have almost all been absorbed. The tooling layer is selling shovels in a gold rush: real demand, but too close to the sun, so you must explain why customers would still pick you once a giant ships the same thing. The application layer will be dominated by agent companies, which sell business outcomes and earn higher margins. As orchestrating agents gets easier, that layer will look more like SaaS, competing on product and business understanding, with a long tail of agent companies emerging.
ex: Model startups like Inflection, Adept and Character have been absorbed
ElevenLabs' voice models belong to the tooling layer
Harvey builds legal agents; Sierra builds customer service agents

items.d: A few giants competing on capex

l293|404.c: Agents complete work autonomously and measurably, so the whole market will shift to outcome-based pricing.
l293|404.e: In the early PC era, moving ledgers into databases produced a big jump in productivity. Software since then has only made individuals a little faster, and the value is hard to attribute, which is why productivity software is hard to sell. Agents finish entire jobs, the way CAD eliminated draftsmen, so the productivity gain is real and measurable and the curve bends again. Charging per token is like measuring engineers by lines of code: a long call may still solve nothing. Sierra charges per resolution, which makes the vendor a partner rather than a supplier. He expects the whole industry to be pulled toward this model.
ex: When his father started out, most people at engineering firms were draftsmen; now there are none
A customer service call costs about $10 to $20
Some of Sierra's sales agents are paid on commission

marks.d: Like grading engineers by lines of code

l293|404.c: To get AI productivity today, don't wait for better models; build systems and find root causes.
l293|404.e: AI-written code is often wrong, and spotting subtle logic errors in someone else's code is much harder than fixing your own, so productivity doesn't automatically rise. One fix is AI supervising AI: behind a generation agent that's right 90 percent of the time, add a review agent that catches most of the remaining errors, and the combination approaches 99 percent. It's trading compute for cognition. The other is root-cause analysis. Sierra has an engineer who maintains the MCP server for Cursor, and every time a generation goes wrong they ask what context it was missing. That is exactly the value an applied AI company adds.
ex: Sierra's customers fully automate 50 to 90 percent of support interactions
Weight Watchers' support agent scores about 4.6 out of 5 on satisfaction

terms.d: Catches 90 percent of the remaining errors

result.d: About 99 percent correct

l293|404.c: Choose your go-to-market by how customers buy, and direct sales matters again in the AI era.
l293|404.e: Only a few models are proven. Developer-led works for platform products, relying on engineers inside the CTO's organization who have authority to pick tools, and it's especially effective selling to startups. Product-led growth fits when the user is the buyer, like software for small merchants. Direct sales targets large business units. In many AI opportunities the user and the buyer are different people. Expense software is used by employees but bought by finance, and PLG alone never reaches the buyer, so the company stalls. Founders often pick a model without thinking through how customers buy and evaluate. He thinks many companies should lean harder on direct sales.
ex: Developer-led: Stripe, Twilio
Product-led: early Shopify
Direct sales: Oracle, SAP, ServiceNow, Salesforce

root.d: Think through buying and evaluation first

items.d: User is the buyer, like small merchants
Business units where buyer and user differ

l294|575.c: Young brains are fast and focused, older brains connect the dots, so mixed-age teams cover each other's blind spots.
l294|575.e: He joined Airbnb at 52 when the average age was 26, and he didn't even know what a tech company meant by "product." So he had to offer his experience while staying curious, happy to be the dumbest person in the room. Neuroscience shows younger brains lean on fluid intelligence: solving problems quickly and in a straight line. Older brains lean on crystallized intelligence: seeing the whole system and linking clues together. Combined well, the two are powerful. Older people help a team spot what it has missed, and they can move into management and make others better, which he calls invisible productivity.
ex: He warned Brian that regulation and occupancy taxes were coming within three years
When the team debated going mobile-only, he had older hosts test it
Engineer John Q. Smith became an excellent manager

d.verdict: Teams are strongest when both brains work together

l294|575.c: When you report to a hands-on founder, open every meeting by stating the goal and what success looks like.
l294|575.e: He trusted Brian because, for all his ego, Brian would tell an expert "I don't know this." Still, three things made it hard. Brian assumed everyone worked as hard as he did, so a 10 p.m. meeting was normal. Like Steve Jobs, he saw himself as the best product mind in the room, and his product reviews kept people up the night before. And he liked adding a zero to a goal, which crushed anyone who fell short. Conley's fix: start each meeting by stating what this round is meant to achieve, what counts as success, and what the meeting itself needs to produce, then return to those when challenged. Rely less on a tidy slide deck and more on credibility earned in the field.
ex: Visiting hosts in 20 cities earned him standing with Brian
After a trashed-home incident, Brian consulted former CIA director George Tenet

items.d: Go back to these when challenged

l294|575.c: Older people survive in tech on curiosity and energy, and employers should value generalists more.
l294|575.e: Ageism is real. Older workers get seen as expensive and slow, and the AI era makes that worse. His advice to individuals: show up curious and engaged. Match the young on stamina and stay positive, and people stop noticing your age. If you can afford it, offer to take a pay cut for a 60 to 80 percent schedule, and trade on your knowledge of how things actually get done inside an organization. To employers he says AI is good at specialized skills, so people who can think broadly matter more. He also suggests mutual mentorship: younger staff teach the tools, older staff teach how to lead people on real problems.
ex: In his fourth year at Airbnb he cut his hours and pay to 40 to 50 percent
Don't just list titles on a resume; describe a hard problem you solved
David Epstein's Range: moving from the age of specialists to generalists

items.d: Problem, approach, result on your resume

l294|575.c: Culture is what happens when the boss isn't in the room, and spread-out companies depend on it most.
l294|575.e: His hotel group had 52 hotels, 25 restaurants and 4 spas, and Airbnb operates worldwide, so the boss can't be everywhere. Remote work gives even fewer cues, which is why in-person gatherings matter more. Culture does two jobs: it guides decisions when no one is watching, and it works like a magnet that pulls in the right people. A talented person who won't adapt to the culture will still fail. He prefers "culture add" to "culture fit," because fit tends to exclude minorities. Job candidates, he says, should interview the company right back.
ex: People from Apple adapted well at Airbnb; people from Amazon had a harder time
Ask in interviews: describe the culture in three to five adjectives
Then ask: what's the most entrenched problem here, and can it change?

items.d: The unwritten way things get done

l294|575.c: Maslow's pyramid works for employees and customers; the real edge is meaning at the top and unspoken needs.
l294|575.e: He applies Maslow's hierarchy of needs to employees, customers and investors. For employees, the base is pay, the middle is recognition, and the top is meaning. In some industries pay is 90 percent of it, but what sets a company apart is usually recognition and meaning, and nonprofits run mostly on meaning. For customers the three levels are meeting expectations, meeting desires, and meeting needs they haven't noticed themselves. A year after he joined, Airbnb asked whether it was about more than home sharing and landed on "Belong Anywhere," which became the organizing principle for training hosts and doing marketing.
ex: Airbnb's positioning: Belong Anywhere
In a toxic company, your conscience eventually makes you leave

items.d: The base, but not the whole

l294|575.c: Midlife is a chrysalis, not a crisis, and seeing aging positively adds about 7.5 years of life.
l294|575.e: Happiness follows a U-shape with age: it slides after the early twenties, bottoms out between 45 and 50, and then rises, so people get happier after 50. He calls the low point the midlife unraveling, when people let go of old definitions of success and looks. His image is the chrysalis: the caterpillar seems to be dissolving, but it is actually transforming. Becca Levy's research found that shifting from a negative to a positive view of aging adds about 7.5 years of life, more than any biohack. He founded the Modern Elder Academy to help people aged 35 to 75 find new purpose through that transition.
ex: MEA has about 7,000 alumni from 60 countries
He asked what he'd regret not learning; at 56 he took up Spanish and surfing
Wisdom is experience you have digested and share generously

l294|575.c: Write an emotion as an equation and vague anxiety becomes something you can work through piece by piece.
l294|575.e: In his book Emotional Equations he breaks feelings into variables. Despair equals suffering minus meaning: Buddhism says suffering is constant, so the more meaning you have, the less despair, which is why he recommends Man's Search for Meaning more than any other book. Anxiety equals uncertainty times powerlessness, and he says almost all anxiety comes from those two sources. So you can draw up an anxiety balance sheet and go through it line by line. Once free-floating anxiety is written as an equation, people usually feel less of it.
ex: Four columns: what I know, what I don't, what I can control, what I can't
His life motto: painful lessons are the raw material of future wisdom

result.d: Broken down, you can handle each piece

l295|578.c: AI capabilities emerge in use, so you only learn what to polish after you ship.
l295|578.e: A traditional product knows what it does before launch. Many AI capabilities are emergent and only show up in real use. ChatGPT came out of an internal hackathon. The team built narrow prototypes like a meeting bot and a coding tool, but testers kept trying to use them for other things. So they shipped an open-ended product to see the real distribution of use cases, planning to pull it after the holidays once the data was in. Benchmarks keep saturating, he says, and real failure cases are what improve a model most. Shipping is only a stop on the way to great, though. Once you understand usage, you polish, and writing evals is really just defining success in advance.
ex: Ten days from decision to launch; the first version had no chat history
Code Interpreter's real uses only became clear after release
A model picker is an anti-pattern, but shipping beats getting no feedback

items.d: Turn them into evals that define success

l295|578.c: Ask "what if we were maximally accelerating" to find the critical path, but never skip safety process.
l295|578.e: He sees setting the team's pace, its resting heart rate, as part of his job. His go-to question: "If this were the most important thing and we were maximally accelerating, what would you do?" It isn't a literal order. It forces people to see what is actually on the critical path and what can wait, and it breaks the big-company habit of "let's align next week." But process is a tool and depends on context. Product development should be very fast, while frontier model launches need rigorous steps: red teaming, system cards, outside input. If you believe in exponential progress, you rehearse now for a riskier era.
ex: The question has become a Slack emoji on the team
Early on, a daily launch sync with every decision-maker present
He learned to move fast at Instacart during the pandemic

d.verdict: Process is a tool; context decides fast or slow

l295|578.c: The model is the product: retention gains split roughly in thirds between the model, new capabilities and ordinary product work.
l295|578.e: ChatGPT doesn't care about time spent, only whether people are still using it long term. Retention isn't just high; it keeps improving as users shift from early adopters to everyday people, partly because people need time to learn to hand tasks to an AI. His rough split has three parts. About a third comes from improving the model on real use cases like writing, coding and advice, including tuning its personality.
