About a third comes from research-driven capabilities like search and memory. The rest comes from ordinary product and growth work, such as letting people use it without logging in.
ex: Search fixed the "as of my knowledge cutoff" problem
Logged-out access lowered the barrier dramatically
A model behavior team shapes how it talks and its personality

items.d: Iterate on real use cases, including personality

l295|578.c: The end state is a personal AI that knows you and acts for you; chat is a transitional form like MS-DOS.
l295|578.e: The original goal was a "super assistant," but he finds the metaphor limiting. What he imagines is something that helps you in any context. It knows your long-term goals and life situation, so you don't spell everything out. It has more room to act, like a smart person who can use a computer. And it builds a relationship with you over time. Natural language will stay, but back-and-forth chat was simply the easiest thing to ship at the time, and an AI can generate its own interface. As it acts more on its own, keeping the user in the driver's seat matters even more.
ex: The codebase is still called SA Server, for super assistant
Agent mode lets you watch it work, like the screen inside a Waymo
He's surprised so many companies copied the chat format

terms.d: Like a smart person using a computer
Memory makes it know you better

result.d: The user stays in the driver's seat

l295|578.c: Many rushed decisions turned out to matter enormously, like launching free and the $20 subscription.
l295|578.e: GPT-3.5 had been available through the API for over six months, so anyone could have built something similar. What mattered was free access plus a usable interface. With no waitlist, everyone arrived at once and shared what they were doing with it, which skipped the blank-box problem that general-purpose products usually face. The subscription wasn't designed as a business model either. The service kept going down, and a paid tier was a way to filter out less serious demand. The price came from a survey posted to Discord. The enterprise product happened because companies had started blocking ChatGPT, and waiting would have meant missing a generation of workplace products.
ex: The name changed from Chat with GPT-3.5 to ChatGPT the night before launch
It spread organically into about 90 percent of the Fortune 500 early on
Enterprise seats grew from 3 million to 5 million in a month or two

l295|578.c: Because the business doesn't run on engagement, they can take on high-stakes uses like health and relationships.
l295|578.e: One update made the model too agreeable, telling users things like "you should break up with your boyfriend." They treated it seriously: a public postmortem, a sycophancy measurement on every release since, and a public statement that ChatGPT is optimized to help you reach your goals, not to keep you around. His line is "show me the incentive and I'll show you the outcome." Because the business model doesn't reward time spent, they could call flattery a bug. Many big companies back away from high-stakes questions. He thinks you should face them well: help people think, don't decide for them, and point to outside resources when needed.
ex: GPT-5 improved on both the sycophancy metric and HealthBench
Some users say ChatGPT saved their marriage

marks.d: Refuse sensitive questions once you're big
Offer a framework, help you think it through
Only says what you want to hear

l295|578.c: Keep the team small, fill gaps team by team like executive hires, and put curiosity first.
l295|578.e: Research labs traditionally take hiring seriously, and he models the ChatGPT team on WhatsApp: lean. Hiring isn't an assembly line. He looks at each team and asks what's missing. If an engineering lead already has strong product sense, that team may not need a PM but may need a front-end engineer or a data scientist. The goal is more barrels, Keith Rabois's term for people who move things forward, with ammunition to support them. Research, engineering, design and product should blend rather than work in silos, and product is everyone's job. In interviews he looks for first-principles thinking and curiosity over whether someone has done it before.
ex: Keith Rabois's barrels-and-ammunition idea
The test: if the model gets twice as smart, the feature should get twice as good
He uses whiteboarding sessions to break down functional boundaries

items.d: Don't hire first and find a team later
Product sense, front end, or data?
Prioritize people who move things forward

l295|578.c: AI search should send readers back to good content, so making good content is the best optimization.
l295|578.e: The original ChatGPT just answered questions with no links, so users who wanted to go deeper had no path back to creators. Adding search fixed the knowledge-cutoff problem and also lets good content reach the people who need it. Asked how SEO works in the AI era, his answer is plain. The model should represent only the user's interests, so winning over the model should look the same as winning over a real reader: make high-quality content and provide enough information and metadata. He's skeptical of new labels like AEO and GEO.
ex: Lenny's newsletter now gets more traffic from ChatGPT than from Twitter
GPTs were a bit early, but enterprises adopted them heavily

items.d: Answer and keep people inside the product
Push good content to people who need it
Win the model by winning the reader

l296|579.c: Every team should ask: if I were the CEO, would I fully fund this team?
l296|579.e: More and more PMs and product teams are being laid off. Spotify's layoff memo said outright that too many teams were doing work around the work. Once the zero-interest-rate era ended, a team became a line item, and sooner or later someone looks at a spreadsheet and asks whether these expensive people are necessary. Most people he asks can't answer right away. If the team can't answer, nobody else in the organization can answer for it. So raise the question inside the team on purpose. If there's no good answer, change the team's remit or goals, or go talk to the right people. A PM's job is to get the whole team thinking like a CEO, not to own that thinking alone.
ex: Daniel Ek's layoff memo: too many teams doing work around the work
Gentler version: what's the one thing you'd want to tell the CEO at year end?
Melissa Perri: product management enables the value exchange between business and customer

items.d: Change remit, goals, or who you work with
Don't wait for someone else to answer

l296|579.c: Low-impact work feeds on itself and eventually drags the whole team into a death spiral.
l296|579.e: Teams gravitate to small features and cosmetic tweaks because they're low-risk and nobody scrutinizes them. His analogy: when fixing a car, it's easier to bedazzle the body than to reach into the engine. But if ten teams all bedazzle, the hood gets too heavy to lift. The product becomes a loose pile of features with growing dependencies, so the company adds program management layers and reorganizes. That makes high-impact work even harder, teams retreat to small changes again, and the cycle runs until the next round of layoffs. Breaking it usually takes one team with the courage to claim the most important goal.
ex: A Mailchimp team raised first-email send success by cutting steps
That PM told the team: if we don't take this goal, I'll haunt your dreams

items.d: So teams keep making small changes

l296|579.c: Obsessing over getting the middle layers "right" disconnects a team's work from business impact.
l296|579.e: For twenty years the product world has prized best practices, and most of the discussion sits in the middle layers between business impact and daily work: goals, initiatives, bets, strategies. Teams spend three weeks writing five to seven objectives, each with five to seven key results, aiming for scores of 0.6 to 0.7, yet can't explain how those add up to the company's goals. Every extra layer of abstraction adds another layer of assumptions and risk, until all that's left is a feature list. He says he has never seen a company that could trace cleanly from daily work all the way back up.
ex: A team spent a full day debating whether a key result scored 0.6 or 0.7
When a company fails, nobody keeps paying you because your OKRs all hit 0.7

items.d: Ends up as just a feature list

l296|579.c: A team goal should sit no more than one step from the company goal, connected by a single calculation.
l296|579.e: The idea comes from Christina Wodtke's Radical Focus: don't cascade goals down through layers; let each team's goal orbit the company goal directly, like a satellite. He gives the example of a fintech feature team that used to take requests, build, and celebrate. Asked to show how it contributed to revenue, he pressed on why the team existed and learned that customers using multiple products had far higher lifetime value than single-product customers. So the team set its annual goal as converting a certain number of single-product users to multi-product. Leadership got it instantly, and the team felt free to make bolder decisions. Whether to use a revenue goal depends on the company's stage.
ex: The test: one "why" or one calculation gets you to the company goal
A startup with no path to hypergrowth pivoted to profit and raised on steady revenue

result.d: Feeds the company revenue goal directly

l296|579.c: Put impact first at every stage so the goal doesn't get diluted layer by layer.
l296|579.e: One growth team did OKRs by the book and spent a full day scoring them at quarter end. He asked a single question: how much did all this add up to against the company's goal of a million new users? The lead immediately drew a timeline on the whiteboard from today to one million and made it the starting point for every discussion. On an ad-tech platform, someone wrote a goal of 20 percent profit growth. Digging in, the team found executives had actually set a target of going from 20 million to 100 million pounds. Once the launch date was placed on that timeline, the team started talking about shipping earlier, rebuilding in pieces, and charging sooner.
ex: "If there's a 51 percent chance it gets us 1 percent closer, push for it"
Best practices only get used once the goal is clear and concrete

items.d: Someone wrote the goal as just 20 percent growth
What the existing business can deliver

l296|579.c: Estimate impact in the same units as the goal instead of ranking work by abstract scores.
l296|579.e: Many teams agonize over ICE, RICE or MoSCoW, but without a concrete definition of impact, no framework ranks things well. Back on the multi-product conversion team, the PM had been scoring impact, confidence and cost and multiplying them. He suggested rewriting impact as: how many users could this option convert, at most? A rough guess is fine. A landing page change could only reach a few hundred people. Rebuilding the whole onboarding flow was harder and had many dependencies, but it could hit the goal in one move, so it was worth coordinating with other teams and marketing.
ex: The ICE vs. RICE vs. MoSCoW debate isn't what matters
"It's called impact estimation, not precise impact calculation"

items: Multiply a few factors to rank
Looks smart, disconnected from the goal
How many users each option converts
Onboarding rebuild might hit the goal

d.verdict: Estimate impact in the goal's own units

l296|579.c: Don't say yes or no to an executive request; offer options, explain trade-offs, and recommend one.
l296|579.e: He describes himself as conflict-averse and a people-pleaser, and says a flat "no" to someone in power has never worked for him. Executives may also know things you don't, like an acquisition or financial pressure, so digging in just burns trust. Better to lay out the team's goal, priorities and expected impact. If the new request has more impact, do it gladly. If not, explain how much the impact forecast would drop and hand the decision back. A single proposal invites nitpicking; several options plus a recommendation turn the back-and-forth into a way of making the plan clearer.
ex: A Mailchimp role-play: one proposal versus options plus a recommendation
His favorite idea from his previous book

marks.d: Hand the decision back to them
Without explaining the cost to impact

l296|579.c: Constraints aren't excuses but the shape of the work, and accepting them is freeing.
l296|579.e: Most PMs don't work at big tech companies. They often say they can't do product "properly" because they're regulated, or B2B, or under quarterly earnings pressure. He sees those constraints as guidance. Regulation applies to competitors too, so mastering the rules is an edge. B2B gives you direct access to customers. Quarterly targets tell you exactly what the company cares about. People naturally fear being accountable for what they can't control, but a company's success was never in anyone's control anyway. In his research he was surprised to find the most business-minded PMs were also the happiest and best at separating work from life.
ex: Don't fight a quixotic battle to turn a bank into a search engine
Alan Watts's The Wisdom of Insecurity: trying harder makes it worse

items.d: Rivals face it too; mastering it is an edge
Direct access to the whole customer system
Tell you what the company values most

l297|229.c: A great product is necessary but not enough; startups win by getting distribution before incumbents copy them.
l297|229.e: He quotes a16z's Alex Rampell: a startup's job is to get distribution before the incumbent copies the product. That race is harder now. Incumbents copy faster. Free traffic from SEO and social platforms is shrinking. AI makes software easy to write, so competitors multiply. The rare exceptions are products where AI itself fired up early adopters. Historically, every major technology shift came with a new distribution platform, and the distribution shift usually arrives a few years after the technology shift. The AI shift has been running for a few years, and the conditions for a new platform are lining up.
ex: Cursor passed GitHub Copilot in share in under nine months
Casey Winters: the AI technology shift hasn't yet brought a distribution shift
Organic reach collapsed after LinkedIn changed its algorithm and Twitter became X

root.d: Get distribution before incumbents copy you

items.d: SEO, LinkedIn and X are all tightening
AI makes software easy to build

l297|229.c: Every new distribution platform follows the same cycle: open up to attract usage, then tighten to monetize.
l297|229.e: Step zero: the market agrees a new category matters, but five to seven players are fighting it out, and the ending is usually a monopoly or a duopoly. Step one: someone finds a durable advantage. Step two: to build that advantage faster, the platform opens to third parties, trading distribution for the use cases and engagement developers bring. Step three: to monetize and avoid being disrupted, it tightens. It shuts things down, builds the most popular use cases itself, or throttles organic reach so people have to buy ads. He stresses this isn't evil; it's competitive and growth pressure. And each cycle is getting shorter.
ex: Facebook opened its platform at a fourth or fifth of MySpace's size
Udemy cut instructor revenue share sharply from about 80 percent
Early Twitter shut down Vine and Periscope

items.d: Like the friend graph or data
Trade distribution for use cases and engagement
Shut down, build it yourself, or throttle reach

l297|229.c: ChatGPT is the likeliest next distribution platform, and its durable edge is context and memory.
l297|229.e: Model outputs alone are roughly similar across labs. What separates them is who holds more user context: the more you use it, the more it remembers, the more personal its output, and the flywheel spins. ChatGPT is furthest along there. Historically the winner was never the platform with the most distribution at the time but the one with the best retention and engagement. Data shows ChatGPT's retention curve is higher and rising each year, with a rare smile curve where lapsed users come back. It's hiring for an agent platform and lining up first partnerships with big companies. If not ChatGPT, he thinks Apple is best positioned, then Google.
ex: He estimates ChatGPT has at least 10 times Claude's monthly active users
He suspects many Gemini monthly actives are accidental visitors
He expects 10 to 20 launch partners to be announced within six months

items.d: Context plus model shapes the output

l297|229.c: It's a prisoner's dilemma with no way to sit out, and startups must concentrate their bets.
l297|229.e: Once people learn that platforms always tighten, the first instinct is "then I won't play." Companies really have died from the Facebook platform collapse, Apple's 30 percent cut, and dependence on SEO. But if you don't play, your competitors will, and customer expectations shift with them. So get in early rather than late, and look for your exit while you play. Later-stage companies can spread their bets and double down once a winner is clear, at the risk of waiting too long. Startups have scarce resources and scarce market attention, so they must go all in on one platform. Early-stage companies that played several games at once almost all failed.
ex: HubSpot integrated early with ChatGPT's deep research connector
Lenny bet early on Substack and earned outsized returns
Betting only on Android usually loses; iOS is where you can win

items: Double down once a winner is clear
Must go all in on one

d.verdict: Whoever you back, get in the game and focus

l297|229.c: Pick a platform by retention and monetization quality, not user counts, and plan your exit from day one.
l297|229.e: He uses four criteria. First, retention and depth of engagement on the platform, not vanity metrics like monthly actives. Second, user quality and how monetizable those users are. Third, the value exchange the platform offers; whoever understands the rules best and arbitrages them fastest gets ahead. Only fourth comes raw scale, which decides things when the gap is huge. As soon as you're in, start planning how to get out, because tightening is coming. Three ways: own a critical step in the user experience or workflow, build proprietary data and context the platform lacks, or create a small network effect of your own.
ex: Android has about 70 percent of devices but only about 30 percent of revenue
If you can land a launch partnership, play that card

items.d: A better signal than monthly actives
User quality, what the platform offers
Pick the big one when the gap is huge

l297|229.c: Hard constraints work best for AI transformation, and you have to confront the anchors holding things back.
l297|229.e: Plenty of CEOs have issued "AI-native" memos, but the force behind them varies enormously. Communication, named owners, and writing AI into levels and performance reviews all help, but hard constraints are what actually move things. Employees fall into three groups: catalysts who experiment on their own, converts who change once given structure, permission and budget, and anchors who quietly create resistance. Fewer than one in ten companies set a deadline for anchors and let them go if they don't change. It sounds harsh, but those companies move fastest, because this is culture change and culture depends on density.
ex: One company caps each function at a fifth of the headcount of a comparable company
New headcount is approved only after proving AI can't do the job
No PRD gets reviewed without three prototypes attached

marks.d: Experiment on their own, lead the change

l297|229.c: Executives are often disconnected from the front line, and AI output is capped by the slowest part of the system.
l297|229.e: They interviewed executives and front-line staff side by side and found a huge gap. Asked who else on their team used prototyping tools, nearly 90 percent of PMs said "just me and one other person." A principal PM at a well-known tech company had a prototyping experiment stuck for a month until she ran into the CEO at a happy hour; it was fixed the next day. He borrows a line from his partner Fareed Mosavat: output is limited by the slowest part of the system. Speed up only engineers and the bottleneck moves to PMs and designers. IT, legal and procurement often slow things too. Go to the front line, find the real blocker, and attack it.
ex: Shopify and others measure real AI adoption and usage directly
"PMs are the new bottleneck" because only engineering got faster

items.d: The system's goal is shipping product
Find real friction on the front line

l298|582.c: AI will disrupt every category, so incumbents either commit fully or get knocked out.
l298|582.e: He sees the history of digital technology as a handful of waves, each of which disrupted almost every category, and AI as bigger than any before it. Intercom's growth had stalled and the company had little to lose, so it could push all its chips in. He insists you can't do it halfway. Sprinkling a bit of AI into the product while keeping the old culture doesn't work. You also have to bring in real AI scientists and learn how the younger generation works.
ex: A Fin beta shipped about six weeks after GPT-3.5 came out
Intercom announced nearly $100 million of its own cash for AI
Fin's ARR went from $1 million to $12 million in its first year

items.d: Bigger than all of them, he says

l298|582.c: A turnaround needs a CEO who decides alone and owns the consequences, not a committee.
l298|582.e: After returning, he cut a huge amount of spending and projects and bet the strategy on customer service alone, even though the other businesses still brought in about $80 million in ARR. He believes great companies are built on clear hierarchy: the CEO takes expert input, then makes the hard calls alone. Get it right and you're rewarded; get it wrong and you should be fired. Founders have moral authority and an appetite for risk, while professional managers are usually told not to screw things up. That, he says, is why founder-led companies do better.
ex: He halted a new office fit-out and ran the company more frugally than ever
He judged that Zendesk had lost its energy after being acquired, leaving an opening

items: Play it safe, don't screw up

d.verdict: In a turnaround someone must make hard calls and own them

l298|582.c: Sharpen the values and enforce them with hard scoring; it hurts, but you get a deeply aligned team.
l298|582.e: He rewrote the values: resilience, high standards, extreme effort, shareholder value first, deliberately making comfortable people uncomfortable. Quarterly reviews scored behavior against those values alongside results. He wrote the formula himself, and anyone below the threshold got a respectful exit, with no manager discretion. Along the way people wrote to the board and some attempted what he calls a soft coup. But those who stayed were more motivated, and the company hired more people like them. He calls it employee-founder-product-market fit.
ex: About 40 percent of staff turned over across a few years
After 15 or 16 months, anonymous surveys showed 98 to 99 percent approval of leadership
His Glassdoor rating when he returned was the lowest he had ever seen

items.d: Amid pushback and a soft coup

l298|582.c: AI products should charge for outcomes, with prices anchored to value rather than cost.
l298|582.e: The old pricing billed by seats, messages and leads at once, plus tiers, and got so complicated it became a meme. The root cause was an unfocused strategy and a fear of trade-offs. He would rather give up a lot of revenue for a simple, fair price, because ripping off customers also erodes employees' belief in putting customers first. Fin charges only for tickets it actually resolves, so revenue lines up exactly with the value customers get. People value digital labor below human labor, so he picked the point between most profitable and most acceptable. Early on every resolution lost money, but he judged costs would fall, and cost is his problem, not the customer's.
ex: Simplifying the old pricing gave up about $50 million in ARR
Research showed SaaS companies spend about $20 to $30 per human-resolved ticket

items.d: Cost of one human resolution in-house

l298|582.c: AI beats people at efficiency work, which makes beauty, story and human touch more valuable.
l298|582.e: Intercom's mission used to be making internet business personal, and the company disliked bots. Now he thinks an always-available, expert and friendly agent is more personal than waiting days for a templated reply. Technology has always replaced work that is repetitive, dangerous or demeaning, and support jobs that amount to pressing macro buttons fit that description. Junior sales roles will shrink sharply too. But efficiency isn't what people value most. As AI pushes automated content toward free, work with a personal point of view and real craft will command higher prices.
ex: Waymo's crash rate is roughly one 3.5th of human drivers'
He disagrees with Benioff: sales will shrink too, but trust still needs humans

marks.d: AI is faster and more consistent

l298|582.c: Repetitive work will go to agents, organizations will get smaller and flatter, and the economy more deflationary.
l298|582.e: He points out that customer experience actually spans service, success, sales and marketing, the largest headcount in most companies. Repetitive mechanical work like invoicing, collections, onboarding and offboarding will be automated too. The future has general operations bots, expert agents for law and accounting, and a glue layer that connects them. Organizations will mix humans and agents, and not necessarily with humans on top and agents executing. Many managers will become individual contributors who configure and supervise agents. The surge in efficiency will bring strong deflation and fierce competition, which ultimately benefits consumers.
ex: He imagines an AI chief of staff that aligns priorities and chases progress daily

items.d: Like an AI chief of staff

l298|582.c: Good therapy sands off the edges that make you ineffective, and that is the recipe for leadership.
l298|582.e: Many founders fear therapy will blunt their edge. His experience is the opposite. More than a decade of weekly sessions wore away the parts that got him triggered, made him miscommunicate, and made him lash out from insecurity. It left him able to admit weaknesses and understand other people better. The two years when he stepped down sick and was attacked in the press shattered his self-image, which was painful. But if you see yourself as the perfect leader, he says, every challenge feels terrifying. The ego never really disappears; recognizing it and seeing it is enough.
ex: He has long worked with Yosi Amram, a therapist who only coaches CEOs
Ram Dass: the ego never disappears, its edges just get sanded down

terms.d: Let go of the perfect-leader image

result.d: Less defensive, better connected to people

l299|585.c: Pre-training has drained the internet, so model progress now comes mainly from new post-training data.
l299|585.e: Labs used to make progress by feeding models all the text, video and books on the internet, a step called pre-training. About a year or two ago those gains started to flatten, because most of the available knowledge had been absorbed. Today's gains come mostly from post-training: collecting high-quality data for specific capabilities like code, math, law and finance. Research teams run it like a science experiment. They test a hypothesis with a small batch of data, and if it helps, they scale up collection.
ex: SFT: pairs of questions and answers
RLHF: pick the better of two responses
Trajectory data: recordings of a person solving a problem step by step with tools

items.d: Absorb the internet's text, video and books
A year or two ago, usable knowledge ran out
Add high-quality data by capability area

l299|585.c: Models are now too good for generalist labelers; only domain experts can find their mistakes.
l299|585.e: The labeling industry used to rely on low-cost generalists overseas for basic tasks. Today an ordinary person can rarely get a model to answer wrong. A physics PhD, though, can show exactly where a model's reasoning breaks in a narrow subfield, spot a flawed reference answer, and write out the correct step-by-step solution. Labs care most about advanced STEM fields and the most economically valuable skills: accounting, law, medicine and finance.
ex: The GPQA paper approach: provide a reference answer and step-by-step reasoning
An education PhD with 20 years of teaching improves instructional design
Hundreds of conservatory students help models understand music

items.d: Break the model in a narrow field
Wrong answer or wrong reasoning step
With every correct step written out
Delivered as JSON and similar formats

l299|585.c: Labs need data that is high quality, at scale, and fast, and all three at once.
l299|585.e: Quality comes first. As with teaching a student, bad data is hard to undo later. Second is scale: producing thousands of examples in cutting-edge chemistry, math and physics while keeping quality high. Third is speed. Researchers bet on several hypotheses at once, double down on whichever shows a gain, and kill the rest, so delivering within days is critical. To support that, Handshake built its own post-training team, rented GPUs, and evaluates how much lift each piece of data provides.
ex: Hired a research lead from Meta's post-training team
Reached out directly to top physics students at Stanford, Berkeley and MIT

items.d: Researchers back 3 to 4 directions at once
A little data to check for a gain
Deliver lots of quality data within days

l299|585.c: In human data, the only durable edge is access to the right experts, and Handshake reaches them at near-zero cost.
l299|585.e: To find 200 physics PhDs, competitors rely on hundreds of recruiters sending LinkedIn messages, spend tens of millions a month on performance ads, and then drop the experts into projects like cheap labor. Handshake has worked with universities for years, building trust and academic data, so it can reach the right people precisely and convert them at high rates. It then trains them through community, peer groups and instructional design, starting them on its own data projects before moving them to client work. Lifetime value in this business depends on retention and how many projects each expert can join.
ex: 500,000 PhDs and 3 million master's students on the platform
Partnerships with about 1,600 universities, covering 92 percent of the top 500
A self-produced data package can be sold to several labs at once

items.d: Schools and students know the brand

l299|585.c: To incubate a new business inside a mature company, separate everything from the team to the processes.
l299|585.e: He leads the new business himself, putting more than 80 percent of his time into it and handing the core business to senior executives. The new unit has its own engineering, design, finance, recruiting, all-hands and onboarding. Anyone pulled from the core business must drop their old responsibilities completely. He tells candidates plainly that this is a 24/7 early-stage startup, and pay is tied to the new business's milestones. The structure is extremely flat: whoever can push something forward owns it, regardless of function. Weekly, monthly and quarterly metrics were tracked from day one. The team's motto is "leave nothing to chance."
ex: The new team grew from four or five people to more than 75
Already working with seven frontier labs
From zero to about $50 million in revenue in four months

items.d: More than 80 percent of his time

l299|585.c: AI-native young people have the advantage; AI is their Iron Man suit.
l299|585.e: He believes in GDP growth more than universal basic income. From employers covering the entire Fortune 500, what he hears is not that they've stopped hiring young people. Social media marketing used to need separate people for photo editing, video cutting and analytics. Now one young person fluent in AI can do all of it. Just as people once put "knows how to use Google" on a resume, being AI-native is an edge. He also expects AI to rebuild the hiring process itself, so nobody has to read 200 resumes by hand.
ex: An intern submitted a first pull request the afternoon they started
PhDs earn $100 to $200 an hour finding model errors, versus about $25 as teaching assistants

items: One person for photos and editing
Data analysis needed a specialized degree

d.verdict: AI multiplies individual output; jobs evolve rather than vanish

l299|585.c: Data won't run out, only change shape, and humans stay in the loop for the next decade.
l299|585.e: As long as models keep improving, he says, they will need human input, and he relays that lab researchers expect that to hold for the next ten years, until superintelligence. The data needed will spread from academic fields to the professional workflows of knowledge workers, then to CAD files, scientific instruments and drug discovery, and audio is in high demand right now. Synthetic data helps in verifiable domains but won't dominate. Where there is no single right answer, experts write rubrics and the model acts as judge.
ex: Rubrics: like an essay grading guide, so the model can score automatically
Demand for audio data is high right now

l300|588.c: Products are turning from static finished goods into organisms that keep learning, and that loop is the new advantage.
l300|588.e: Building a product used to mean having an idea, shipping it, watching dashboards and making small fixes. Models are now strong enough to be tuned directly for outcomes like price, performance and quality. The product team's core metric becomes its metabolism: how fast it digests data and reward signals and turns them into results. Research she cites says that past 30 billion parameters, paying for your own pre-training stops making sense, and optimizing the closed loop is worth more. She expects post-training spend to match or exceed pre-training, and favors combining several models rather than one model for everything.
ex: Dragon, the product for doctors, was trained on 600,000 expert-labeled patient conversations
Dragon's character acceptance rate rose from 30 to 60 percent to about 83 percent
A survey she cites says about half of developers already fine-tune

items.d: New data, and the product improves

l300|588.c: Companies that succeed with AI first get everyone fluent, then transform a process, then use it to drive growth.
l300|588.e: Step one for successful companies is getting everyone to use AI in daily work and stop fearing it. Step two is picking an existing process, rebuilding it with AI, and seeing the effect on the P&L. Only then, step three, do they use it to improve customer experience, lift retention, or create new categories. The ones that fail do AI for its own sake, launch many projects with no blueprint, and lack measurement, observability and evals. Because the technology moves so fast, she advises betting on a platform layer where components can be swapped at any time, and planning for the slope of change rather than a snapshot.
ex: Process changes like cutting fraud case handling from 15 days to 10
She says about 70,000 enterprise AI tools launched last year

items.d: See the result on the P&L

l300|588.c: Hand-off-heavy organizations can't keep up with AI; full-stack builders own the loop, not a lane.
l300|588.e: Every technology shift creates new roles: garage engineers in the move from mainframes to PCs, then SEO, growth PMs and front-end versus back-end in the cloud and mobile eras. Now, she argues, it's the generalist's turn again. A typical organization needs about 10 steps, five or six functions and six or seven layers to ship a product, several hundred touchpoints in all, while new models and techniques appear every week. Whatever your function, you need to understand cost efficiency, reward and system design, and how interfaces serve both people and agents.
ex: Her phrase: the loop, not the lane
Dragon's big improvement came from one small cross-functional team

result.d: Too slow for weekly new technology

l300|588.c: Interfaces are moving from canvases to composable parts, so make your product readable and callable by agents first.
l300|588.e: The instinct is to start by drawing a GUI, but history keeps repeating: databases went from desktop software to SQL, and the cloud went from consoles to Terraform. Text streams are a natural fit for large language models, which is why coding in the terminal feels so good. She thinks product people spend too much time on how things look and should think more about how things compose, how agents can read and call them, and how they scale without limit. Conversation is a powerful interface, but people also work in email, documents and slides, so chat matters but isn't enough.
ex: Databases: desktop to SQL
Cloud: console to Terraform

items: Embedded in docs, email and more

d.verdict: Future products are about how they compose, not just how they look

l300|588.c: Once the marginal cost of good output nears zero, org charts give way to work charts.
l300|588.e: When one more unit of good output costs almost nothing, demand for output grows exponentially, and only agents can keep up: some embedded in tools, others taking on tasks like employees. At that point people stop thinking in terms of who reports to whom and organize instead around how tasks get routed, who handles them, and how they're observed and tuned, with fewer layers. Humans still decide where AI is used. Managing huge numbers of agents can borrow from existing systems for managing devices, policies and permissions. She wants employees to bring their own agents the way they bring their own devices, massively expanding their skills.
ex: You can already assign a pull request directly to Copilot
About 15,000 customers have built agents on the platform, millions in total
Imagine 20 million people 20 percent more skilled; the GDP impact would be huge

l300|588.c: AI moves too fast for long plans, so align on a "season" first, then drive with short-cycle goals.
l300|588.e: Microsoft product teams used to plan in six-month blocks, but six months out is now hard to predict. Instead she starts by naming the current season, defined by a long-term shift in the industry or in customers, lasting anywhere from three months to a year. Everyone aligns on the customer problem to solve, what winning looks like, and the north star metric. Below that sit loose quarterly OKRs, and small squads set their own four-to-six-week goals. The system needs slack, not just for surprises but to invest in disrupting your own platform.
ex: Season one: AI prototypes; season two: models and reasoning models
The current season: the rise of agents

items.d: Long-term shift, customer problem, what winning means
Pave the way toward the goal

l300|588.c: Platforms and products usually win on invisible foundations, not on how many features they have.
l300|588.e: She admits her learning curve would have been much shorter had she known this earlier. At Porch, the home services marketplace, what mattered wasn't the features but the engine that precisely matched providers, service types and zip codes. WhatsApp won on the address book, reliable speed and end-to-end encryption, not stickers or dark mode. Instacart ran on real-time updates to an enormous product catalog. AI platforms are the same: what enterprises really care about is data residency, availability, reliability, the right choice of tools, and knowledge retrieval.
ex: Porch: 6 million providers x 1,300 services x 37,000 zip codes
Instacart: a billion items updated 3,000 times a minute
A German hospital fine-tuning a model with data that never leaves the region

items.d: The matching engine earned the first $500M valuation
Huge catalog updated in real time

l301|376.c: An established company should rethink its mission as if founding it today, and sell if its old assets don't help.
l301|376.e: He argues AI isn't a one-time, predictable shift in form factor like desktop to mobile. Every model upgrade calls for inventing new forms and interactions, so every software product has to be refounded. Sprinkling AI across the website and the feature list isn't enough. You start from zero: if you pursued the same mission today in an AI-native way, what would you build? Then judge honestly whether your existing building blocks are an advantage or a burden. If they don't help, find a buyer and go found the next version of that mission.
ex: He decided Airtable's no-code components were an advantage, which is why he kept running it this way

items.d: Go all in on the new form
Then found the mission's next version

l301|376.c: Having an agent assemble reliable building blocks suits business apps better than generating all the code from scratch.
l301|376.e: Airtable has always wanted to let more people build software, focusing on business apps like CRM, inventory and case management. If an agent writes all the code from scratch every time, the result is unreliable and buggy, carries data and security risks, and collapses under its own context once the app gets complex. Airtable's data layer, views, layout engine and automations act like a domain-specific language for business apps, and an agent assembling those is far more stable. Non-technical users can also drop back into the graphical interface to inspect and change things, instead of staring at code they can't read.
ex: Omni is now the default way to do everything in Airtable
New capability: code generation for last-mile needs like custom maps

items: Can fall back to the GUI

d.verdict: Business apps need reliability and inspectability

l301|376.c: The CEO should get back to hands-on work with AI as an "IC CEO," not a pure delegator.
l301|376.e: In the early days he wrote the front end and back end himself; as the company scaled, process and people management pulled him away from the details. Now every model upgrade can rewrite the product's form, and judging from screenshots and recordings at a distance isn't enough. As he puts it, to taste the soup you have to help make it. He canceled many routine one-on-ones in favor of just-in-time meetings driven by new insights, with separate time for deeper conversations. He tracks the AI sprint personally every week and deliberately "wastes" compute digging for insights. Taken to the extreme, though, it becomes micromanagement.
ex: He is Airtable's biggest spender on AI inference
He used an LLM map-reduce to read a year of sales calls for a few hundred dollars

marks.d: Deep in key details across teams

l301|376.c: Split R&D into a fast-thinking group that draws users in and a slow-thinking group that grows the seeds.
l301|376.e: Early on, Airtable organized by surface area, and each group only made incremental improvements. Later it moved to business pillars like enterprise, teams and AI, which allowed bigger bets but still couldn't match the pace of a company like Cursor shipping major features weekly. The latest reorg borrows Kahneman's language. The fast-thinking group ships impressive AI capabilities almost every week. The slow-thinking group builds the infrastructure and enterprise-grade capabilities that need careful thought. Fast brings in new users and use cases; slow turns those seeds into large-scale deployments, which addresses the retention weakness many AI-native companies have.
ex: The slow group's HyperDB storage handles hundreds of millions of records
About half of R&D works on AI capabilities

items.d: Search, mobile and so on; incremental
AI platform group plus slow-thinking group

l301|376.c: People have to feel AI's value firsthand: prototypes beat documents, and open trials beat explanations.
l301|376.e: What AI can do, and what users want to do with it, often only becomes clear once it's out there. A promise in a PRD or a slide deck is just words, while an interactive prototype can be tried immediately with messy real prompts, so you feel how fast it is and whether showing its reasoning helps. Sales-led approaches can work, but an open trial hits harder, and ChatGPT is the proof. He also thinks today's AI products generally show off their capabilities poorly; an empty chat box lacks a visual metaphor and guidance.
ex: ChatGPT reached about 700 million weekly users in under three years
Palantir's AIP and Harvey took the sales-led route
Airtable's homepage now simply asks what you want to build

items.d: More convincing than a deck or PRD
Learn the limits and the needs

l301|376.c: Explore a brand-new AI capability by feel first, and add evals once the use cases converge.
l301|376.e: He agrees evals matter, but for a brand-new form factor, defining "good" on day one limits exploration too early. Start by trying all kinds of prompts to see which tasks it handles well. Once the use cases cluster and the product scaffolding settles, use evals to compare changes to prompts, models and workflows programmatically. By then the product has usually narrowed into a more specific capability. Big companies have the scale to A/B test everything; early teams don't.
ex: A web-scraping agent: listing every Marvel movie, or companies of a certain type
Only after finding people and company searches worked best did they narrow it

items.d: Pin down entity types and conditions

l301|376.c: Role boundaries are collapsing, and everyone needs baseline competence in the neighboring functions.
l301|376.e: He has found that who uses AI most effectively depends more on attitude and range than on job title. PMs need to become prototyping PMs with design sense, designers need to understand models and tool calling, and engineers need product judgment. One marketer can run an entire campaign, and salespeople need to demo the product themselves. He encourages people to play: cancel a day or even a week of meetings just to try AI products, the way an industrial designer studies famous chairs before building one. He believes all of these skills can be learned.
ex: Early Google required APMs to understand both engineering and design
As he understands it, Stripe sometimes makes an engineer the DRI
The ground is covered in watermelons; no need to climb tall trees for coconuts

root.d: Deep in one area, able in many; judged on results

items.d: One person runs the whole campaign
AEs who can demo the product themselves

l301|376.c: Look at the reasoning behind advice rather than copying the conclusion.
l301|376.e: As the company scaled, operators and investors kept urging him to industrialize everything: hire more executives and give each a lane. He concedes the logic, but it loses the value of thinking holistically and making big leaps. His meta-conclusion: every person is like a model trained on a different corpus, so the priors behind their advice differ. Instead of "do this," ask "why are you recommending it," then work out what that reasoning implies for your own situation. Looking back, the advice he most wishes he'd given himself is not to drift away from the product details he loves.
ex: Brian Chesky: the CEO has to play the role of chief product officer
Interrogate advice the way you'd read a reasoning model's chain of thought

result.d: Apply the reasoning, not the conclusion

l302|214.c: The fixed split between product, engineering and go-to-market is coming apart, and static PRDs can't keep up.
l302|214.e: For twenty years the share of time going to product, engineering and go-to-market work stayed roughly stable. Now the middle part, designing a solution and building it, has been sped up enormously by AI. The PM's three jobs remain: define a sharp problem, support the build, and support the often-neglected go-to-market. But writing long PRDs is too slow and too static. He says PMs shouldn't get hung up on being called the bottleneck. Instead, put the freed-up time into customer insight and add value elsewhere using the PM's view of the whole picture.
ex: One company says it goes from a sales demo to a working prototype in about four hours

items.d: PM, dev and GTM time gets reshuffled

l302|214.c: The best predictor of success is the problem you pick: an old human need, new technology, a 3-to-10x improvement.
l302|214.e: He has watched many startups fail because the founders pivot aimlessly, again and again. The companies that succeed usually start from a core human need that has existed for a long time, then redesign the solution with new technology. The test for a sharp problem is whether it delivers a 3-to-10x improvement or a big cost reduction, so customers are eager to pay. The more often a pain shows up, the more real it usually is. He argues for solving market needs rather than personal passions, and admits he has gotten this wrong himself.
ex: Bezos spotted a large, real need early on
For B2B problem selection, see the Unicorn framework discussed on an earlier episode

result.d: 3-to-10x better; customers rush to pay

l302|214.c: A team should work like a shipyard: about six skills working closely, with tentacles out to the market.
l302|214.e: He borrows a metaphor from Joff Redfern of Atlassian. A shipyard looks chaotic, but high skill and careful communication keep it moving in order. The core is six capabilities, not six people: product, engineering, design, user research, data and AI, and product marketing. They can be part-time, or a group of engineers can cover them. Tight collaboration around a problem beats daily standups. The team also needs connections to support, sales and customers, so it feels the market the way skin feels temperature. He expects roles to keep blurring, with everyone needing more data skills.
ex: Calendly brought support managers into design reviews, where they caught problems design and engineering had missed

items.d: Links to support, sales and customers

l302|214.c: Coding has become describing architecture in plain English, so PMs should learn by building software for themselves.
l302|214.e: He has a master's in engineering but has mostly done product work for years. In the past year he wrote more code than in the previous ten, because programming increasingly means describing an architecture in natural language. He turns PRDs straight into prototypes, writes his own APIs and tests them in Postman, treats AI tool subscriptions as tuition, and is learning MCP. He predicts high-agency people will write lots of software to automate their own lives, and that small indie SaaS products may shrink as a result. It's day one, he says, and the fast starters won't necessarily win.
ex: He automates his home with Home Assistant, a locally fine-tuned model and his own MCP server
The AC turns off when the kids leave a room and pre-cools before they return

items.d: Build it directly with AI tools

l302|214.c: Build simple products for distracted users, and have the nerve to take a clear stance.
l302|214.e: Users stopped being amazed by technology itself long ago, and AI is no exception. Their attention is scattered. So start simple and add complexity only as needed. Simplicity is genuinely hard, and PMs need a bit of anthropology and psychology. Many products are bloated because the team wouldn't make a call and piled on options, and then learned nothing useful from the result. Ship with a clear point of view, be willing to be wrong, and iterate. The confidence to do that comes from actually spending time understanding customers.
ex: In one designer's complex interface, only about 20 percent of users could find the key element

d.verdict: Simple and opinionated is how you learn

l302|595.c: The PM's core job is still de-risking delivery, but software is now a living system that must keep learning.
l302|595.e: She thinks the PM's fundamental value hasn't changed: reduce the risk of what you ship so the investment earns the biggest business return. What's different is that engineers now come to PMs more often to validate customer judgments, and PMs have more time for customer insight. There is also more to orchestrate, with software, feedback loops and LLM touchpoints all woven together. A product is no longer a finished artifact; it has to keep learning. So PMs need data literacy, they need to design guardrails for behavior, and they need to ask the ethical questions that few people asked in the social media era.

l302|595.sc: Hiring PMs in the AI era
l302|595.c: Hire PMs for curiosity, humility and agency, plus the skills to write evals and work across models.
l302|595.e: On attitude, she looks for curiosity, the humility to learn from anyone at any level, and the ownership to act without waiting for permission. Her image: be the thermostat that changes the room's temperature, not the thermometer that just reads it. On skills, writing prompts isn't enough. PMs need to write evals to validate outputs and keep hallucinations down, understand what different models are good at and combine them, and fine-tune when necessary. She rejects the idea that AI makes PMs disappear. She sees AI as a toolbox that makes big mistakes and needs PMs to constrain and tune it.
ex: She is helping a Los Angeles company build a PM curriculum and hiring process

items.d: Learn from anyone at any level
Be a thermostat, not a thermometer
Know how data is organized and flows

l302|595.sc: Do we still need a CPO?
l302|595.c: The tension between CPO and CTO is healthy: one hunts for opportunities to grow the pie, the other optimizes resources.
l302|595.e: Some VCs and private equity firms have started asking whether a company needs both a CPO and a CTO. She thinks many product leaders respond too defensively without explaining their value. In her view, the CTO is good at optimizing existing resources, while the CPO explores and decides which opportunities to chase. The pull between them is where innovation comes from. She wants leaders who grow the pie, not ones who divide an ever-smaller slice. She also urges senior leaders not to skip the beginner AI courses, so they understand how frontline PMs actually work now.
ex: The trend of merging technology and product into a single "CTPO" role

d.verdict: The tension drives innovation; don't just merge them

l302|595.c: Companies that bolt AI onto old systems won't lead. Put AI at the core and redesign the workflow around it.
l302|595.e: She reminds people that AI is a set of capabilities, not magic. If the problem is poorly defined, AI won't save it. Hanging an LLM on an existing software's connection points is AI at the edges. Rethinking the workflow around AI, with the LLM in the middle and a codebase that may even shrink, is AI at the core. Her judgment is that companies only adding to old code will struggle to lead their industries. The winners tend to build specialized capabilities first, then tie them together with a layer of intelligence.
ex: Oji adds: a small Typeform team rebuilt a pre-sales lead agent from scratch
Clay reshaped its product around LLMs

marks.d: Adding on at the connection points
Tied together by an intelligence layer
LLM in the center, less code

l302|595.c: Interview transcripts can't replace watching users in context. See what they actually do.
l302|595.e: AI can transcribe interviews, but people often can't articulate their real intentions or why they behave as they do. She believes ethnographic observation, watching users in their real setting and understanding the motives behind their actions, is still the most reliable method, and warns that some people want to shortcut it with AI interviews. When driving change, she argues for explaining the why over and over and managing it with the crossing-the-chasm model: early adopters have already moved on to the next strategy while laggards are still asking why anything needs to change.
ex: The NASA moonshot story, where even the janitor could explain the mission
Martin Eriksson uses the crossing-the-chasm model to talk about change management

l303|596.c: The deadliest flaw in a leader is hesitation. When both options are bad, pick the slightly better one.
l303|596.e: Real CEO decisions, he says, are not like business school cases. Often both options are bad. Rewriting your architecture means missing features and the quarter's targets, but not rewriting means the company can't go far. So people instinctively avoid choosing. Yet when you don't decide clearly, the whole company gets anxious. The mental muscle to build is staring into the abyss and picking the slightly better path. Much hesitation, he finds, is really not knowing how to say something. Replace a vague accusation with a specific expectation and the conversation becomes possible. A leader's value lies precisely in making the decisions most people dislike.
ex: LoudCloud went public at 18 months old with about $2M in revenue, because the alternative was bankruptcy
The press called it "the IPO from hell," but it beat going bankrupt
Instead of "you're a jerk," say "you're not yet a good enough CTO"

items: Face the worst, pick the better path

d.verdict: A leader only adds value by making decisions most people dislike

l303|596.c: Founders usually fail by losing confidence. Hesitation follows, executives grab for power, and politics takes over.
l303|596.e: Most founders have never run a large organization, he says, so they will make mistakes, and each one is expensive. Slowly they lose confidence. Once confidence goes, hesitation follows. Senior executives feel someone has to fill the gap and start competing for power. The organization sinks into politics, and at that point the founder usually can't steer anymore. Much of how a16z is built is about helping CEOs build confidence. His reminder: the median score on the CEO test is 18 out of 100. A D-minus is fine, as long as you don't flunk out or run out of cash.
ex: A team of about 600 at a16z builds a CEO's network to rival Bob Iger's
"CEO barbecues" put founders at the table with top CEOs
Hiring a wave of senior executives right after product-market fit can train a CEO to defer

items.d: Never ran a big org, so mistakes are certain
Doubt you can do the job

l303|596.c: A CEO's job isn't to develop people into stars. Hire people with standout strengths who give you leverage.
l303|596.e: As a VP of engineering you can develop engineers, he says. But as CEO you don't know finance, HR or marketing, so expecting to turn a non-star into a star is unrealistic, and the company can't afford your time. His test for an executive is who is pushing whom. If you're always telling them what their department should do next, you have no leverage. If they come to you with how to move the company forward, you do. The moment you have to ask "why aren't you doing this," it's time to replace them. Judge people by whether they have a world-class strength, not by whether they have weaknesses.
ex: This was his advice in his first one-on-one with Ali Ghodsi as Databricks CEO
Don't judge someone by their worst moment: he backed Adam Neumann's new company
An experienced sales leader could speed up Databricks

marks.d: Always asking why not; time to replace
They tell you how to move the company

l303|596.c: The only reliable reason to start a company is an irrational desire. Doing it for money rarely lasts.
l303|596.e: John Reed, the former CEO of Citibank, once told him that starting a company isn't worth the money, and the only reason to do it is an irrational desire. When he sold his own company for $1.6 billion, he felt it hadn't been worth it either. His reasoning: so many bad things happen along the way that without a purpose bigger than yourself, you can't keep going. If you only want money, a well-paid job at a big company is a better deal. So as an investor he pushes teams to think bigger. Only if the company gets genuinely big is it worth dropping out of school for.
ex: Databricks wanted to raise $200K; he offered $10M
His partner Marc Andreessen says it's best when the product forces you to build a company
HP started from "what does the engineer at the next desk need?"

terms.d: Make the world a bit better

result.d: Otherwise it's hard to last

l303|596.c: A product manager is a leader with no direct reports, and the only goal is making the product win.
l303|596.e: When he managed product managers at Netscape, he saw them buried in tasks: writing specs, giving talks, handling press. That's why he wrote the essay. Tasks, he argues, are not the job. The job is shipping a product customers love more than anything else in the world. Nobody reports to a PM. A PM can't promote or fire anyone and can only work through influence, which is the essence of leadership. Like a CEO, the PM is the keeper of the vision. Not every idea has to be theirs; their job is to gather the ideas, rank them, and make sure everyone understands them accurately.
ex: If you're yelling at someone, you probably haven't explained what you want
Something written in five minutes is often better than something written over five weeks

items.d: Competitors and where technology is going
Each side understands the other precisely
Gather and rank the good ideas

l303|596.c: When everyone is calling it a bubble, it isn't one. The economics of AI businesses actually work.
l303|596.e: His logic: a bubble needs everyone to believe it isn't one and give up doubting. As long as many people are shouting "bubble," prices are unlikely to run away. He looks back at the dot-com bubble. The problem wasn't that the internet didn't matter. It was that there were too few users and building was too expensive, so the businesses didn't add up. Today's AI products work, and their revenue is growing faster than anything seen before, so the valuations have a basis. He admits the technology is early, today's leaders could be displaced, and bad companies will get funded. But that's normal venture capital, not a bubble.
ex: Evite, the online invitation site, needed about 300 engineers back then
One AI company went from zero to $800M in revenue within a year

items.d: About 55M people online, half on dial-up
The economics didn't work; companies went bust
Products and revenue growing like never before

l303|596.c: AI opportunities sit in inference infrastructure, a handful of foundation models, and an almost unlimited application layer.
l303|596.e: He splits the opportunity into three layers. In infrastructure, whoever runs models at the lowest cost and latency is extremely valuable. At the foundation model layer you must be extremely picky: the bar is raising at least $2 billion before the product has made much progress, and fewer than ten founders worldwide can do that. The application layer is far stickier and more complex than people think. The "GPT wrapper" line is wrong, he says, like calling Salesforce a database wrapper in the 1980s. Scaling gains in large models are slowing, reinforcement learning doesn't generalize well, and the long tail of human behavior is enormous, so every domain needs dedicated work.
ex: Cursor built 14 of its own models behind the product
Waymo's hardest problem is rare, dangerous human behavior
Inside companies, even the definition of "customer" differs

items.d: Almost unlimited companies; sticky with users
Need $2B in funding; very few winners

l303|596.c: AI is this century's industrialization, and the US has to stay in the leading group.
l303|596.e: His starting point: society doesn't need to be perfectly equal, but everyone needs opportunity, and that requires power to be reasonably spread out. A system with too much concentrated power is evil in itself, regardless of who holds it. The American system puts rules above individuals and, flaws and all, is still the best. Last century, the countries that industrialized first gained economic, military and cultural power, while the laggards slid into dangerous regimes. This time, he believes, the decisive technology is AI. So the US must not over-regulate too early, which is why a16z is deeply involved in policy.
ex: People from many countries, he says, are asking the US not to fall behind in AI
He sees crypto as a network technology that complements AI

items.d: First to industrialize gained national power

l304|72.c: AEO and SEO share the same foundation; the differences are at the head and the tail.
l304|72.e: After 18 years in SEO, he calls this the second biggest shift since Google's crackdown on spam pages. But what works in SEO also works in AEO. He points to two differences. At the head: on Google, the top blue link wins. An LLM instead pulls together many citations, and whatever is mentioned most often lands first in the answer. So a new company can show up the next day thanks to one Reddit thread or video. At the tail: people ask longer questions in chat and follow up more, so a huge number of specific questions nobody ever searched for are surfacing.
ex: Per Perplexity, the average prompt is about 25 words, versus about 6 on Google
Early-stage companies: skip SEO for now, but work on citations and long-tail AEO

d.verdict: Same core craft; head and tail play out differently

l304|72.sc: How much the channel is worth
l304|72.c: LLM traffic is smaller but far more qualified, converting at up to six times the rate of search.
l304|72.e: By the time someone clicks through, he says, they've already worked out exactly what they need over several turns of conversation, so intent is very high. The channel is still smaller than search and paid, but it already matters. The turning point came this January: usage climbed, and answers started showing clickable modules like maps and shopping cards. B2B answers often have no links, so you measure with answer tracking plus a "how did you hear about us" survey. If you worry about your content training models, block the training crawlers in robots.txt and allow the indexing ones. Blocking indexing entirely just hands your spot to competitors.
ex: About 8% of Webflow's signups come from LLMs
In e-commerce, review counts and structured data affect shopping cards

l304|72.c: Start AEO by turning search keywords into questions, then work through each type of cited source.
l304|72.e: The hard part, he says, is that LLMs don't publish search volume the way Google does, so there's no ground truth. His workaround: feed your own and your competitors' paid search keywords to ChatGPT and have it rewrite them as questions. Then mine sales calls, support tickets and Reddit for long-tail questions. Each page should cover hundreds or thousands of questions on one topic, and the more follow-ups it answers, the more likely it gets cited. On-site work can go to your SEO team. Off-site video and community work usually needs a separate community-minded marketer.
ex: Help center: move it to a subdirectory, add internal links, fill in the long tail
Long-tail example: which meeting transcription tool integrates with Looker

items.d: Use an answer tracker to see where you stand
Who gets cited, and what page types
Group sources and work each one

l304|72.c: Work each type of off-site source differently. On Reddit, helpful answers under your real identity work best.
l304|72.e: Which sources get cited depends on the industry, he says: tech review sites for B2B, fashion media for e-commerce, review platforms for local businesses. Paying affiliate publishers to mention you is the simplest and most controllable route. Video is easy too, because almost nobody has covered the obscure but valuable B2B topics. Reddit is cited heavily, and a growth mindset tempts people to spin up fake accounts and flood threads, but those accounts get banned and the comments deleted. What works is behaving like a real user: say who you are and where you work, then give genuinely useful information. A few comments are enough.
ex: Dotdash Meredith may be the most-cited source across LLMs
Webflow employees answer relevant Reddit threads under their real names

items.d: Obscure B2B topics are wide open
Real name, helpful; fake accounts get banned

l304|72.c: Answers are drawn from a distribution, so track many times and many ways, and test against a control group.
l304|72.e: Ask the same question twice and you get different answers, he explains. It's like weighted sampling from a distribution. Change the phrasing or the product and results shift again, so what you track is share of voice and average rank across platforms. Because answers fluctuate and LLM traffic is rising overall, a simple before-and-after comparison will mislead you. You need a control group. He says most "best practices" in SEO and AEO have never been tested, and he wants the field to aim for reproducibility, like academic research. Tracking tools are commodities now, so buy the cheapest one that does the job.
ex: Overlap with Google results: about 35% for ChatGPT, about 70% for Perplexity
Roughly 1 in 20 landing pages drives about 85% of traffic
They catalogued around 60 answer-tracking tools

items.d: Post, make videos, pay for mentions
Watch a few weeks before and after
Keep what works, drop what doesn't

l304|72.c: Purely AI-generated content doesn't work, and if it did, answers would collapse into a single viewpoint.
l304|72.e: Back in 2007 he built scraped, stitched-together spam pages and watched Google wipe out the whole category, so he's confident content with no human involvement won't work. His team first checked how accurate AI detectors are, then ran them on content cited by Google and ChatGPT. Only about a tenth was AI-generated. His reasoning: if pure AI content worked, everyone would do it, LLMs would keep summarizing their own derivatives, and the diverse wisdom of crowds would narrow until "ice cream only comes in vanilla." AI-assisted content edited by humans is the future.
ex: The detector's false-positive rate on pre-ChatGPT content was about 8%
About 10-12% of cited content is AI-generated
There's now more AI-generated content online than human-written

l304|72.c: New discovery channels won't kill Google. Its slice stays the same; the whole pie gets bigger.
l304|72.e: Every two years, he says, someone declares Google search dead: first Facebook and YouTube, then Instagram and TikTok, now AI. People really do search and discover in those places, but it adds to Google rather than replacing it. Google's head of search has said traffic to publishers is even up slightly. He warns that this field has an unusually high share of misinformation. Some people pay a premium for tools that are really just keyword trackers, and others oversell how novel AEO is to sell services. He expects LLMs and search to merge, ending with agents that make decisions for you.
ex: AOL and Yahoo were huge once too; he expects about three winners worth optimizing for

result.d: Total search and discovery grows

l305|510.c: The model is the product and the eval is its requirements document. What you can measure, you can automate.
l305|510.e: A researcher's day, he says, is running dozens of experiments against an eval set, chasing small gains. Reinforcement learning is now strong enough that once an eval exists, the score will climb. Math olympiad problems and SWE-bench saturated quickly once labs cared about them. So the barrier to pushing agents into the whole economy is figuring out how to measure success. Companies should start by building systematic tests for their own core value chain. Evals also double as sales collateral: labs and application companies will increasingly prove themselves with evals of practical skills.
ex: An architecture firm: how do you grade the drawings an AI produces?
Academic evals like GPQA are giving way to tests of practical ability

items.d: Written as an eval or rubric
Reward the model against the eval
Also used to prove it externally

l305|510.c: Post-training is shifting to experts defining the standard, then AI grading the model against it.
l305|510.e: Training data used to come in two main kinds, he says: input-output pairs for supervised fine-tuning, and human preference data, where people pick the better of several model answers (RLHF). The trend now is for humans to define what success looks like. In code that's a unit test; in other fields it's a rubric written by an expert. AI then does the grading, which scales better and needs less data. A lawyer who writes down what a contract revision must catch creates both a way to measure progress and a training reward. He sees evals and RL environments as essentially the same thing, used for different purposes.
ex: A radiologist defines rewards and penalties for diagnoses
He notes Andrej Karpathy has said the two are the same kind of data

items.d: Pick the better of several answers
Unit tests or rubrics, graded by AI

l305|510.c: What labs really need is a labor market of top experts, and the key is finding the top 10%.
l305|510.e: The human data market started as crowdsourcing, he says: hire lots of low-skill workers to write passable sentences. Now it's a search and screening problem: how do you find senior engineers, investment bank analysts, doctors and lawyers? Out of a hundred people, the top 10% usually drive most of the model improvement. Being able to identify and match those people creates an advantage that's hard to compete with. This isn't an expert network doing one-off phone consultations. It's closer to an Uber-style, long-term labor market, just with far more senior talent and far higher pay.
ex: Found an award-winning screenwriter for a customer within 24 hours
Hired Harvard Lampoon writers to make models funnier
Tens of thousands of people work on the platform at once

l305|510.c: As long as humans can do things models can't, experts will be needed to write evals.
l305|510.e: Some people say superintelligence arrives within three years and humans drop out of the economy. He disagrees. Models are still bad at many things; they can't even manage his calendar, write his emails or use basic tools well. Tool use, long-horizon reasoning, and eventually having a model spend 30 days starting a company all need evals to reward them. He expects most knowledge-work tasks to be automated within ten years, but the road there is paved with evals and efficient post-training data, not ten times more pretraining data. He sees eval writing as an overlooked new category of job, much as the industrial revolution created new work.
ex: Some researchers think the whole economy could become a machine for building RL environments

l305|510.c: Fields where demand grows with output benefit most, and using AI to multiply your output is the key skill.
l305|510.e: His reasoning: when productivity rises tenfold, demand rises in some fields and not others. The world doesn't need 100 times more accounting, but software can ship 100 times more features. So product managers and engineers who use AI to do more are in the best position, and operations and consulting have similar room. On skills, what matters is using AI to do your actual daily work. Just as you shouldn't ban calculators once they exist, Mercor's interview lets candidates use any AI tool to build a website in an hour. Companies that embrace an abundance mindset will win; those afraid to measure their own business will fall behind.
ex: Marc Andreessen: software is the most demand-elastic industry of all

marks.d: One person can do far more

l305|510.c: Don't force product-market fit. Find customers who are surprisingly easy to sell, and watch leading indicators.
l305|510.e: He spent a long time trying to force product-market fit before realizing that if even the marginal customer is extremely hard to sell, you can't build a big business. Look instead for customers who buy surprisingly easily because their pain is enormous. Be firm on your thesis about the future and open on what the product looks like. Mercor started as AI-powered hiring matches. Meeting xAI's founding team made them realize the human data market was about to change dramatically. Then a crowdsourcing company hired over a thousand people through their platform and didn't pay them, which showed the opportunity to serve labs directly. For the first year and a half there was no sales or marketing, only word of mouth.
ex: He met xAI's founding team in August 2023, while still in college
Bootstrapped to $1M in annualized revenue and stayed profitable

items: Marginal customer is very hard to sell
Watch leading indicators in a fast market

d.verdict: Firm on the thesis, open on the form

l305|510.c: Audacious goals, high standards and high intensity are the cultural base of hypergrowth.
l305|510.e: They always set goals that look crazy, and the company's trajectory takes shape around them. High standards show up most in hiring: the first ten hires were slow and deliberate, and that group's quality shaped everything after. But he also admits a mistake: once it was clear demand far exceeded supply, they should have hit the gas, and scaling from ten to a hundred people was too slow. On intensity, the company never dictates hours; it looks at output and commitment, though the most committed people tend to work hardest. He spends most of his own time on hiring and customers.
ex: At $1.5M annualized he said they'd hit $50M by year end, and they did within two weeks of it
Sundeep Jain, Uber's former CPO and CTO, joined as president
Reselling donuts in middle school taught him: if you want to do it, you can

result.d: The fastest growth curve

l306|17.c: Managing agents and managing people use the same skills, and the hardest part is defining success clearly.
l306|17.e: She defines management as achieving an outcome with the resources you have, and the levers are people, purpose and process. The resources used to be people; increasingly they're models. Different models are like different personalities: you learn what each is good at, assemble the team, then give them enough context and high-level direction. The hardest part is stating success without any ambiguity. Big companies struggle to align because everyone carries a different picture of success in their head. The same is true for agents, which is exactly why you write evals and set metrics. She sees this as more art than science.
ex: "Make a great episode" is too vague; be specific enough to judge success or failure
Deciding which tools an agent may use is a management decision too

l306|17.c: Break down role boundaries so everyone builds. A small team can be better off without a PM.
l306|17.e: AI, she says, can quickly lift someone from the bottom to the 60th or 70th percentile in a field they're weak in, so work that once took a full cross-functional team now takes two people. Her company found that when a PM or designer is present, engineers habitually hand off product definition. Without a PM, communication and user value become everyone's job. The team still needs product judgment somewhere; it just doesn't need to staff roles from a fixed template. Having engineers also do front-end work and teach themselves data analysis is slower at first and pays off over time.
ex: Hand a 12-week course to ChatGPT and have it tailored to how you learn
After learning, explain it back in your own words and let AI catch your misunderstandings

items: Engineering, PM and design in separate lanes
Staff every role from a template
Two or three people, AI fills skill gaps
Product and communication are everyone's job
Staff by the skills the situation needs

d.verdict: More learning up front; faster and broader over time

l306|17.c: Diagnose with data and treat with design. Data shows reality but won't tell you what to build.
