l306|17.e: She thinks many fast-growing AI companies aren't using data well. It used to take years to reach a hundred million users, enough time to build logging and a data team. Now a dozen people can reach a hundred million in revenue running on intuition. But growth always stalls, and without observability you end up scrambling. Data isn't just A/B tests; user interviews and social media spread count too. Which metric to watch, and whether a 5% lift is good, still takes judgment. New technology also needs new analysis: conversational products have no clicks, so you use a model to classify user intent.
ex: The mobile era created new metrics like session length
Every great designer she's met is obsessed with what users really think

l306|17.c: As change speeds up, managers should be like a willow tree: firmly rooted, flexible in the branches.
l306|17.e: Managing change has always been part of the job, she says, but the pace is accelerating. Nobody knows what AI will look like in two years, and many people fear tools will replace their careers. Leaders have to make the team understand that clinging to old ways means being left behind, and that both the product and the way of working must change, without scaring people. Hence the willow: it survives storms precisely because its branches bend. Embracing opportunity matters, but pretending nobody is hurting is wrong. Acknowledge that change is hard, then turn people's eyes toward what's possible.
ex: She agrees the image may come from Dr. Becky's idea of being "sturdy"

terms.d: Change the product and how you work

result.d: Survives the storm without breaking

l306|17.c: Every strength is also a weakness. Feedback is about one dimension and doesn't define your worth.
l306|17.e: Management starts with managing yourself, she says. People can be measured on countless dimensions, and each person's mix of strengths and weaknesses is as unique as a fingerprint. Nobody scores full marks on everything. Any criticism concerns just one dimension and says nothing about your worth; seeing that is what lets you take feedback objectively. She's often praised for being thoughtful and criticized for being slow to react in discussions, two sides of the same trait. Growth isn't rejecting your strengths but learning to read the situation and be decisive when it calls for it. Whether to fix a weakness depends on your goals.
ex: To be a VP, practice thinking on your feet; to master a craft, maybe not
Treat your manager as a guide, not a judge, and talk about your goals

marks.d: Say what you think right now

l306|17.c: Make feedback routine: agree up front to exchange it, check your motive, and admit when you're nervous.
l306|17.e: A team's long-run success depends on how fast it improves, she says. A team that gets 1% better every week soon overtakes one that gets 1% better every month, and feedback is the best tool for that. People misjudge themselves, through overconfidence and impostor syndrome alike, so they need others to show them what they can't see, like a leaf stuck to the back of their head. Her method: agree on mutual honesty at the start of a working relationship. Before giving feedback, confirm you want to help the person rather than prove you're right. If you're nervous, say so; showing vulnerability brings people closer.
ex: About 70-80% of people think they're above-average drivers
Letting someone go can be a win-win; the wrong role only prolongs the pain

items.d: Coming to help gets you to 80%
Show them what they can't see

l306|17.c: When you disagree with a plan from above, break it into hypotheses, find the real disagreement, and test it small.
l306|17.e: Middle managers rarely set the vision, she says, yet they have to execute it. Not one project led by a manager who didn't believe in it ever succeeded big on her teams, so first examine what you actually believe. If you disagree, talk to your boss and understand why smart people support it. Break the plan into hypotheses, and you'll usually find you agree with most of them; the disagreement is one or two points. Then design the smallest test that checks that hypothesis. Bring it to the team as "let's find out together," and people can commit for real.
ex: A lemonade stand: test in one market first whether college students even like it

items.d: You agree with most of them

l306|17.sc: Kids in the age of AI
l306|17.c: AI offers too many shortcuts, so kids especially need to regulate emotions and choose hard things on purpose.
l306|17.e: What she most wants her kids to learn is emotional regulation and self-reflection, because tools and environments change while human "hardware" hasn't in thousands of years. Technology's strength is also its weakness: it makes life easier, and it lets people avoid relationships and uncomfortable feelings, like scrolling short videos instead of facing tension with a colleague, partner or child. AI is more personalized, so the temptation is stronger. People who avoid hard things end up suffering in another way, she argues. Real freedom is choosing your own hard things and being proud of them, so AI should be a tool, not a shortcut.
ex: Her contrarian view: every direction holds infinite depth, and boredom means you haven't seen it yet
She builds apps on Replit and writes parody game songs for her kids

items.d: Lose the freedom to choose hard things

l307|600.c: Start evals by looking at your data and analyzing errors, not by writing tests.
l307|600.e: LLM applications are random and cover a huge surface, he says, so unlike traditional software you can't know in advance what to test. Writing tests straight away tends to miss the real problems. The right move is to sample traces (logs of real conversations), read each one with a product lens, and write one note recording only the first, most upstream error before moving on. The first few are painful; then it gets fast. Looking at data is the highest-return activity there is, so it's worth spending a few hours having AI build a custom labeling interface to remove friction. When you see an obvious problem, just fix it.
ex: Nurture Boss, a property-management assistant, ended chats when no units were available instead of handing off
A reply promised a virtual tour that didn't exist
Aim for about 100 traces, until you stop learning anything new

items.d: Product lens; only the first error

l307|600.c: Hand labeling to one domain expert, a "benevolent dictator," and always grade pass or fail.
l307|600.e: Many teams want everyone involved in labeling, he says, and the process becomes too expensive to sustain. He recommends appointing one domain expert with trusted taste, often the product manager. The goal is fast signal, not perfection. By the same logic, don't let judges score on a 1-to-5 scale. That's avoiding a decision, and when a report says 3.2 or 3.7 nobody knows what it means. The judge has to answer: good enough, or not.
ex: A lawyer for a legal product, a psychiatrist for a mental health product
For property management, someone who understands apartment leasing should judge

d.verdict: Simple enough to keep doing beats perfect

l307|600.c: Before trusting an LLM judge, check it against human labels, and don't stop at the agreement rate.
l307|600.e: Many people write a judge prompt and then treat its output as truth, he says. Once the eval disagrees with reality, the team stops trusting you along with it. So compare the judge's verdicts with human labels one by one. Reporting only an agreement rate is dangerous: if errors are 10% of cases, a judge that always says pass still agrees 90% of the time. Look at the confusion matrix instead, and drive down both kinds of disagreement: real errors the judge lets through, and good outputs the judge flags as wrong.
ex: A Google Sheets pivot table is enough for a human-versus-judge matrix
Someone saying "75% agreement is good enough" is a red flag

cells.d: Real error, judge let it through

l307|600.c: Evals are old-school data science. No tool or generic metric replaces looking at your data.
l307|600.e: The most common mistake, he says, is assuming you can buy a tool, plug it in, and have AI evaluate itself. The second is never looking at the data at all. The first thing he does with consulting clients is read traces with them, and it pays off every time. Error analysis has existed in machine learning for years; the new vocabulary just makes it sound new. The generic evaluation tools from big vendors mostly offer things like cosine similarity and hallucination scores, and benchmark scores have nothing to do with your product's specific failure modes.
ex: Andrew Ng was teaching error analysis eight years ago
Benchmarks like MMLU say nothing about problems like "should this hand off to a human"

root.d: Trying to skip looking at data

l307|600.c: Coding agents can get by on vibes, but that lesson doesn't generalize to other AI products.
l307|600.e: Coding agents were the first AI products to reach scale, and many people conclude from them that evals are unnecessary. But with code, he points out, the developers are themselves the domain experts and use the product all day. Domain judgment and dogfooding collapse into one, so far less data and exploration are needed. A product team in medicine or another field doesn't have that advantage. He also warns that many people who claim to be dogfooding are nowhere near the depth needed to close the loop.
ex: The Claude Code team has said they mostly go on vibes
Developers can tell at a glance whether generated code is good

d.verdict: Don't generalize the coding-agent approach to every AI product

l307|601.c: Evals are a whole spectrum of ways to measure quality. Unit tests are only a small slice.
l307|601.e: She defines evals as the spectrum of ways to systematically measure an application's quality. Unit tests cover hard functional requirements. Beyond that you want to discover unexpected new user groups, track product metrics like thumbs-up rates over time, and run A/B tests, which are evals too. The online "anti-eval" debate mostly comes from defining evals too narrowly, or from being burned by scale-based judges that didn't match human judgment. Products that claim to run on vibes are actually standing on hidden evals: base-model benchmarks, monitoring, and internal dogfooding.
ex: She'd bet the Claude Code team runs some form of eval
A/B tests without prior error analysis often measure the wrong thing

marks.d: Find new users and new problems

l307|601.c: Humans must write the notes. Categorizing and counting them is what to hand to an LLM.
l307|601.e: Ask an LLM directly whether a trace has a problem and it will usually say "looks great," she explains, because it doesn't know the product has no virtual tours. So humans write the notes. Once notes accumulate, have an LLM cluster the open codes into axial codes (failure modes), then a human edits them to be specific and actionable. Next, the LLM assigns every trace to a category, with a "none of the above" option to reveal gaps in the taxonomy. Finally, count. When do you stop? At theoretical saturation, when no new types appear.
ex: Open coding and axial coding come from social science methods
Notes must be specific; "sloppy" on its own isn't enough

items.d: Humans write notes one by one

l307|601.c: An LLM judge checks one failure mode and answers pass or fail, so it's reliable and you need few.
l307|601.e: People worry a judge is as hard to build as the original agent. But a judge handles one narrow failure mode and outputs only pass or fail, which an LLM can do consistently. Anything checkable in code, like valid JSON or length, should be checked in code, which is cheaper. Most problems are solved by changing the prompt. Only stubborn problems that keep recurring after they're in the prompt deserve a judge. Judges can run in CI and also sample production traces daily to monitor failure rates.
ex: Her projects typically end up with only 4 to 7 LLM judges
Sample 1,000 production traces a day and run the judges

items.d: Run in CI and production monitoring

l307|601.c: You can't write all your criteria up front. They grow as you look at the data.
l307|601.e: In her research on "who validates the validators," she found that even experts who had built many LLM pipelines changed their minds about what good looks like after reviewing a batch of outputs. Many failure modes only occur to you once you see them. So the judge prompt is really a requirements document grown from the data, and it ends up more specific than the original PRD. You should still write a PRD, but expect it to change. The investment is modest: about a week for the first round, then about 30 minutes a week.
ex: The research began with developer user studies in late 2023
First-round error analysis takes 3 to 4 days, then about 30 minutes a week

items.d: Criteria you thought of in advance
You notice them only once you see them

l308|603.c: Delight means meeting functional and emotional needs at once, not sprinkling confetti on the screen.
l308|603.e: Drawing on emotion research, she defines delight as joy plus surprise. Animated decoration with no value behind it is what she calls the "confetti effect." Only a celebration with a real reason counts. Emotional connection matters because when products have similar features, users who feel something stay. In a crowded market that becomes a source of differentiation, and it turns into retention, loyalty, word of mouth and revenue. The reverse is true too: she stopped using Instagram because opening it no longer felt good.
ex: Airbnb's celebration when a Superhost re-qualifies every three months
Spotify's Discover Weekly makes people feel understood

items: Drives retention and word of mouth

d.verdict: Delight has to come with value

l308|603.c: There are three ways to create delight: remove friction, anticipate needs, and exceed expectations.
l308|603.e: Making a dreaded chore easy is delightful in itself. Understanding a group of users' situation and having something ready before they ask creates surprise. Proactively giving users a benefit they never requested exceeds expectations. None of the three depends on visual decoration. Each saves users effort, money or worry at a moment that matters.
ex: Charged a wait fee after an Uber driver canceled, she got a refund in two taps
When she traveled to Singapore, Revolut offered a local eSIM inside the app
Edge applied a coupon automatically at checkout, saving about 15 percent

items.d: Give a benefit nobody asked for

l308|603.c: B2B products need delight too, because humans use them, and it matters more as competition heats up.
l308|603.e: She calls it B2H, business to human: behind every piece of enterprise software are people who use it every day. In a new market with a strong pain point and few rivals, a feature that simply works may be enough. Once competition intensifies, the quality of the experience decides who wins. Her favorite technique is personification: if the product were a person, how would it make this experience better? GitHub, Atlassian, Snowflake and Dropbox, all of whom she interviewed, have their own delight principles.
ex: During the pandemic, Google Meet benchmarked itself against face-to-face conversation, not Zoom
Buffer proactively refunded inactive users and earned trust
Dyson compares its robot vacuum to hiring someone to clean

l308|603.c: Four steps: find motivations, turn them into opportunities, sort ideas on a grid, then check them against a list.
l308|603.e: Step one: segment users by why they use the product, not by demographics, and list functional and emotional motivations. Emotional ones split into personal (how I want to feel) and social (how I want others to see me). If motivations are hard to name, start from frustrations. Step two: rewrite each motivation as an opportunity to solve. Step three: place candidate ideas on the delight grid. Step four: check each against a list covering user impact, business impact, feasibility, familiarity, inclusivity and sustainability.
ex: The emotional motivation behind Uber is feeling safe
Miro makes users feel like better leaders
An emotion wheel helps find the right feeling words

l308|603.c: Deep delight meets both functional and emotional needs. Split the roadmap roughly 50-40-10.
l308|603.e: Meeting only emotional needs is surface delight. Meeting only functional needs is low delight. Meeting both is deep delight. She wants to end the "delight or features" debate by building delight into the features themselves. On the roadmap, about half should go to functional improvements, forty percent to deep delight, and ten percent to surface delight, like arranging a bouquet.
ex: Deep delight: Discover Weekly and Spotify Jam
Chrome moves tabs untouched for 21 days into an inactive group instead of closing them
Surface delight: the birthday balloons on Apple Watch

l308|603.c: Delight must pass the familiarity and inclusivity tests and keep being refreshed, or it backfires.
l308|603.e: Brand new isn't always better liked. Discover Weekly was meant to be all new songs, but a bug that mixed in tracks users had already liked made it more popular, and metrics dropped when the bug was fixed. Delight also has to work for everyone and every situation, or it hurts or annoys people. And surprise dulls with habit, so plan a series of ongoing upgrades rather than a one-off Easter egg.
ex: Deliveroo's Mother's Day "call from mum" notification hurt users in France who had lost their mothers
Apple's gesture-triggered video effects popped up in the middle of a medical consultation
Meet's backgrounds went from blur all the way to AI-generated

items.d: Plan the next round of surprise

l308|603.c: Don't try to convince leaders. Tie delight to the goals they care about and build it into team routines.
l308|603.e: Her first piece of advice is not to persuade. Find out what leadership cares about, then show how delight serves those goals, and if necessary leave the word "delight" out at first. To make it stick, set it up as a standing product pillar, write it into the team's routines, and get leaders to back it publicly. She has also noticed an often-overlooked benefit: PMs working on delight features tend to be more motivated and more productive.
ex: A startup funding musicians found users felt "small," so it shifted to emphasizing pride
Spotify's quarterly squad health checks and hack days
She ran a "delight day" for the Swiss supermarket chain Migros

items.d: Ask what they care about first
Health checks, hack days, delight days

l309|606.c: Growth means switching between exploring and exploiting, and spreading one experiment's insight across the company.
l309|606.e: Exploring is finding the right mountain to climb, he says, and exploiting is concentrating resources to climb it well. Only exploring leaves you scattered; only exploiting traps you in a local optimum. He applies the framework at the level of insights. When one experiment reveals something about user psychology, neighboring teams apply it too and the impact multiplies tenfold. When more and more experiments come back insignificant, the juice is running out and it's time to diverge again. AI prototyping and summarization tools have made exploring cheaper.
ex: 80% of game reviews happened after wins, so after losses they now lead with your best moves
That change lifted reviews 25% and subscriptions 20%
Duolingo tracked screenshot hotspots, then had illustrators amplify those shareable moments

items.d: E.g. people review only after wins

l309|606.c: The free version should show the product's full value and let users taste premium features.
l309|606.e: More than 90% of Grammarly users are on the free plan. Free users used to see only spelling and grammar fixes, and the brand was seen as just that. Data also showed few people accept every suggestion in one go, so few ever hit the paywall. The team wove a handful of premium suggestions (tone, clarity, full-sentence rewrites) into free users' text, a kind of real-time reverse trial while writing. They worried that giving away too much would kill purchases. Instead, the upgrade rate nearly doubled.
ex: The upgrade rate nearly doubled
Core value stays free forever, with a taste of premium layered on top
Reverse trials suit B2B, where switching is costly; consumer products mostly use standard trials

items: Taste tone and rewrites in real time
Upgrade once the daily quota runs out

d.verdict: Showing free users your best side usually pays for itself

l309|606.c: Once a subscription product matures, retaining current users and bringing back old ones are the big levers.
l309|606.e: With poor retention, he says, you're forced to make users pay on day one and survive on paid acquisition and aggressive upsells, which is hard. Day-one retention of 30-40% for new users is solid. For a daily-habit product, what matters most is retaining existing users who already have the habit, because that compounds. A mature company also accumulates a huge pool of dormant and occasional users, so the resurrection experience deserves dedicated work. Grammarly is the exception: once installed you don't open it daily, so activation and the aha moment matter most.
ex: About 80% of Chess.com's active users are existing users; new and resurrected users are similar in size
Duolingo wins people back with social pushes like a friend joining, then re-runs the placement test

items.d: Similar in size to new users

l309|606.c: Brand marketing and growth experiments aren't opposites. Together they're rocket fuel.
l309|606.e: He used to be skeptical of marketing until Duolingo. The owl mascot Duo first grew a personality in push notifications and inside the product. Then the marketing team amplified the meme on TikTok and other social platforms, and when the product asked "how did you hear about us," social brought in 20-30% of new users on some days. His view: experiments are steady, continuous iteration, while brand and cultural waves occasionally create a huge swell. When a wave hits, signups can multiply overnight, and not catching it would be foolish.
ex: Social media brought 20-30% of new users on certain days
Chess.com saw signups quadruple overnight with the pandemic, The Queen's Gambit and streamers

result.d: A solid base that can catch big waves

l309|606.c: An experiment target exists to force the conditions you need. The system matters more than any single test.
l309|606.e: Chess.com's employees love chess, and building for themselves and the community can take you far, but growth ends up lumpy. He set a goal of a thousand experiments a year, admittedly a made-up number, to force the conversation about what it would take: running experiments in lifecycle marketing and app store assets too, and making places like the homepage configurable without code. The prerequisites are a growth model and complete instrumentation. You also need founder support, and you should celebrate wins publicly.
ex: One company's internal tool had retention configured backwards, so every positive result was actually negative
He estimates experiment win rates typically run 30-50%

l309|606.c: Learning products start out full of frustration, so design the experience to carry beginners past it.
l309|606.e: Duolingo's gamification rests on three pillars, he says: a core loop of daily lessons, rewards, streaks and push notifications; a long-term metagame of learning paths, leaderboards and achievements; and a profile that accumulates everything you've put in. Chess.com found that most new users are beginners who usually lose their first game, and people who lose retain worse. Without changing the rules of chess, they built a friendlier onboarding and hid ratings for the first few games.
ex: Over 75% of new users call themselves novices or beginners
Under a third win their first game, and retention is 10% worse after a loss
Ratings are hidden for the first five games so people don't watch their score crash

l309|606.c: In the AI era, hire for agency and speed over experience. Experience can be a crutch.
l309|606.e: Standard hiring means writing a job description and finding people from similar companies. But at Duolingo and at smaller companies he kept seeing that the best performers had enormous agency, quick reactions and drive, not necessarily matching experience. His reasoning: AI is shifting the ground so fast that many old habits have to be deliberately dropped. These traits show up outside the interview questions: whether someone has used your product deeply, what questions they ask, how they communicate while scheduling, and what references say.
ex: He's most comfortable at mid-sized companies of 500-1,000 people, 10-20 years old
An early failure at Chariot: dynamic routing built solution-first, with a press release too early

items: Tick boxes on the job description

d.verdict: The fastest-learning companies survive

l310|607.c: Training data changes with every model generation, and has now moved to expert tasks and RL environments.
l310|607.e: Scale's history, he says, is a series of fresh starts: as models get stronger, the data they need changes. Eighteen months ago a task was comparing two short stories. Now it's a top developer building a website from scratch and annotating every decision, or explaining subtle questions about cancer to a model, with a single task taking a professional several hours. Competitors' descriptions of Scale as cheap crowdsourcing are nonsense, he says. The next step is RL environments, sandboxes that simulate real work. There are endlessly many combinations, so data that generalizes is worth the most.
ex: About 80% of the expert network has a bachelor's degree or higher; about 15% have PhDs
Meta invested over $14B for a 49% non-voting stake, and only about 15 people went with it
Example environment: completing a business process in a heavily configured Salesforce

items.d: Labeling for the US Department of Defense
PhDs and professionals working for hours
Agents learn to do things in sandboxes

l310|607.c: Enterprise AI isn't useless, but going from demo to reliable usually takes 6 to 12 months.
l310|607.e: A proof of concept quickly gets you to 60 or 70%, he says, and people assume the rest is easy. In fact it's like data center uptime: each extra nine costs an order of magnitude more. The claim that 95% of pilots fail has a denominator problem: pilots are so easy to start that everyone starts one. Actually automating a critical process takes engineers who understand models working for months, plus legal, compliance and regulatory approvals, plus change management. AI fits best where a process previously ran at 10 or 20% accuracy. Taking 98% to 100% isn't possible yet.
ex: Processes like insurance claims and medical record analysis
His summary: easy to learn, hard to master

items.d: Each extra nine costs far more

l310|607.c: Digitizing human judgment is the new bottleneck, and humans will stay in the loop for a long time.
l310|607.e: A tool they built for a hospital picks out the five to ten things a doctor should notice in a 200- or 300-page record, and once caught an allergy that conflicted with a drug about to be prescribed. But an off-the-shelf model with RAG and fine-tuning only gets you so far. The hospital's own experts have to label and evaluate, defining what good looks like, and the same document means different things at different institutions. He doesn't think human knowledge will stop flowing into models, and he doesn't expect white-collar jobs to be replaced at scale within a year; even two years is a stretch.
ex: Most labeling for enterprise and government customers is evaluation
Models are moving from knowing to doing; he guesses they'll approach decision-making in two or three years

d.verdict: The truth is in between: the tech will get close; adoption depends on change management and policy

l310|607.c: Being close to customers means seeing their real incentives and urgent needs, not taking words literally.
l310|607.e: Incentives aren't only money, he says; status and career matter too. When building Uber Eats, restaurants wouldn't share their costs, so the team ordered lots of food, weighed ingredients against supplier catalogs, and worked out that food and labor each ran roughly 20-30%, then cross-checked with industry sources. The conclusion: what restaurants wanted most was incremental demand, since extra orders with the same staff are highly profitable. That gave them the confidence to charge a 30% commission and build delivery fees and courier pay around it. Saving a restaurant a few points on food cost is valuable, but it isn't the owner's most urgent problem.
ex: Restaurants initially balked at 30%; the actual rate landed slightly lower
A marketplace doesn't need every side happy, just willing to show up

l310|607.c: Screen new businesses by business model and gross margin first. Kill the bad ideas, then talk about passion.
l310|607.e: Success, he thinks, comes either from a founder who persists for years like a force of nature, or at least from knowing which models are good: marketplaces, SaaS, network effects, lock-in. Gross margin is a crude but fast test. If someone claims 40%, ask why not 60%. That usually exposes a substitute right away, and if the substitute runs at 20% margins, your profits will get squeezed fast. Founders should also ask why they in particular have this insight, and why they're willing to spend five to ten years on it.
ex: Ten trucks in DC stocked with 250 convenience items drew almost no orders
Uber Eats launched in Toronto in 2015 and sold $20K in two hours
About $20B in four and a half years, then about $50B after one pandemic year

items.d: Stay open as long as possible
Willing to do five to ten years

l310|607.c: Not losing comes before winning. Weigh the risk of every decision and take asymmetric upside bets.
l310|607.e: "Go for it" is the investor consensus, he says, because investors think in portfolios, but a founder only gets one life. Good operators examine the risk distribution of each decision, because what matters most is surviving until timing, insight and product all line up, and many people quit before that. In a hype cycle everyone bets bigger and bigger, but the customers will still be there in five years, and you need to be too. Early on he sold used golf clubs on eBay without thinking through how low the barriers were and how fast margins would compress, and it was miserable.
ex: Scour was sued for $250B and settled for $1M
Scour's funding terms kept shifting, teaching him that everything is negotiable
His life motto: the ending is never the ending

cells.d: A wrong bet leaves no way back

l310|607.c: He hires on three things: curious problem-solving, working across teams, and being able to lead people.
l310|607.e: He interviews people from every specialty and can't be an expert in all of them, so he looks at just three things: whether they solve problems out of curiosity and can explain how, whether they're humble enough to work across teams, and whether they're a good leader. The world changes fast, so past experience may not fit and adaptability matters more. About 5% of roles are exceptions, such as researchers, where the market moves too fast to train someone and you need matching experience or customer relationships. In building a leadership team, he treats it as one organism with complementary strengths and minimal conflict.
ex: The Uber Eats leadership team barely changed from zero to $20B
He uses AI voice mode daily as a private tutor on technical topics

items.d: And can explain it out loud

l311|610.c: AI is expanding search demand, not replacing it. Basic needs like phone numbers and prices haven't changed.
l311|610.e: People come to Google for an enormous range of things, he says: phone numbers, price comparisons, directions, the page to pay taxes. That breadth is often underestimated, and AI hasn't changed those basic needs. What's changed is that AI can satisfy more complex questions and curiosity that people couldn't express before, so total queries are growing. AI search has three parts: AI Overviews at the top of the page, the multimodal Lens for asking with a photo, and AI Mode, which ties everything together and supports follow-up questions. The goal is that users never have to pick an entry point.
ex: Lens visual searches are up 70% year over year, already in the billions
The shopping graph holds 50 billion products, updated 2 billion times an hour by merchants
Maps covers 250 million places

marks.d: Quick AI answer at the top

l311|610.c: AI answers still run on lots of searches. To get cited, write the most useful content for AI use cases.
l311|610.e: When AI Mode generates an answer, he explains, it does a "query fan-out": the model uses Google Search as a tool, issuing dozens of related queries in the background and pulling real-time data, then pairing each query with content. So decades of quality signals still apply: does the page satisfy the intent, does it cite sources, is it original rather than the 500th retelling. His advice is to study what people use AI for, such as advice, tutorials and complex needs, and make your content the best answer to those needs.
ex: Google's published rater guidelines are a useful reference
Anti-spam signals also filter which content gets cited in answers

items.d: Each query gets pages and data
Send users to the source to verify

l311|610.c: Great products come from never being satisfied. Improvements compound until, at some point, things suddenly take off.
l311|610.e: He says you should embody two things: always going all-in on what's working, and always making things better, never satisfied. Outsiders often credit a product's takeoff to a reorg or one person. He thinks it's mostly the compounding of month after month of polish, until the product crosses the threshold of being net useful. AI Mode came from exactly this dissatisfaction: they saw users manually typing "AI" at the end of their queries and often not getting an answer, and felt they were letting users down every day.
ex: His wife describes him in one word: "unsatisfied"
Tony Fadell's TED talk about fruit stickers that pierce the fruit

items.d: Feel the pain on users' behalf
Users start to truly love it

l311|610.c: Intuition sets direction and metrics are the dashboard. Together they tell you whether to optimize or find a new curve.
l311|610.e: A product starts from a problem or a vision, he says, but you need a dashboard to know if you're on track. First check whether the retention curve flattens at days 7, 30 and 90, then whether it can grow by word of mouth, then how big it can get. For mature products, metrics drive root-cause analysis: slice a decline by region, device, audience and use case. Every business runs on an S-curve, and when more investment yields almost nothing, it usually means the outside world is changing and it's time to go back to first principles and find the next growth engine.
ex: A core metric drops 5% one week: slice it by dimension to find the cause
On a new growth engine, each change can deliver a 4-20% lift

items.d: Born from a problem or vision
Good enough that people recommend it

l311|610.c: When a mature product adopts a new format, make it a distinct but coherent addition, not a forced change to the core.
l311|610.e: Before Stories, the team tried making posts in the main feed disappear. Forcing a core product that users already have a fixed mental model of into a new use is usually a bad recipe, he says. New formats become universal primitives, the way every product has a feed, and refusing to adopt one deprives your users of a better experience. The key is making it your own: keep a similar aesthetic and connect it to the existing system, but give it a clear, separate form and improve it around your own users' frustrations.
ex: Instagram Stories allowed high-resolution photos from the camera roll and press-to-pause
Stories, Reels and AI-powered Google are all additions, not replacements

items: Break users' expectations of the space
A separate Stories bar at the top

d.verdict: A new format should expand the product and feel like your own

l311|610.c: Product work has three chapters: understand the user, rigorously find the root cause, and prefer clarity to cleverness.
l311|610.e: Chapter one borrows from jobs-to-be-done theory: users "hire" a product to do a job, so ask about the specific situation that triggered the first use, and remember that emotional jobs are often underestimated. Chapter two is using data to dissect a problem until you reach the real root cause. Chapter three is following conventions users already understand rather than reinventing icons and interactions to stand out, like door handles that leave you unsure whether to push or pull. The epilogue is staying humble. Close Friends flopped at first and only turned around through this approach.
ex: "Favorites" got mistranslated as "best friends," so people added one person and nobody replied
Renamed Close Friends, suggested 20-30 people, and moved the green ring outside the avatar
The feature took two or three years of iteration

items.d: What job are you hired for?
Data down to the root cause

l311|610.c: Use a small team to build conviction, then invest heavily. Don't worship lean teams.
l311|610.e: He pushes back on the cult of lean, scrappy, fail-fast teams. Products built on a technical breakthrough and meant to serve huge numbers of people often die from underinvestment, and projects inside big companies are especially prone to staying too scrappy for too long. The right approach is a small team building a prototype, then, once there's internal conviction and external validation, staffing it at whatever level a great version requires. Close Friends took years partly because the team stayed too small.
ex: AI Mode started with 5-10 people and went from idea to full launch in about a year
Friends testing your product won't keep using it for 30, 60 or 90 days out of politeness

l312|314.c: The easier software is to build, the more design and craft decide who wins. Good enough is mediocre.
l312|314.e: His instinct when he started Figma was that value was moving up the stack, closer to the user. Servers became the cloud, software moved into app stores, and developer tools kept improving, so building software stopped being the hard part. At the same time, products like the iPhone and Gmail raised everyone's expectations, so companies had to compete on design. AI, which can generate huge amounts of code quickly, makes this trend stronger. So he argues against picking markets purely by size. Early data showed there were few designers, but once design became the differentiator, the number of people who care about it, and the market, grew.
ex: Bureau of Labor Statistics data at the time showed only about 250,000 designers worldwide
For existing codebases, he estimates AI's productivity gains are only small to moderate

items.d: Building it is no longer scarce
More people take part in design

l312|314.c: Add products along the user's workflow. The second one is hardest; FigJam found itself by being fun.
l312|314.e: Figma follows one complete workflow: brainstorming, design, development, and launch. Most new products come from things users were already forcing Figma Design to do. Cramming those into the main product makes both sides more complicated, so it is better to split them into a separate surface. Going from one product to two is the hardest step. He pushed a whiteboard product for years without a convincing case, until the pandemic drove demand and the team built it in a roughly six-month sprint. A month before launch he found it boring, so they decided to win on fun, giving remote teams with cameras off a reason to speak up.
ex: A one-day design sprint produced about 20 ideas, and Cursor Chat came out of it
Buzz: the brand team sets templates, marketing produces on-brand assets in bulk
Figma Design should stay out of the way; FigJam can be playful. Context decides.

items.d: Sites; Make spans the whole flow

l312|314.c: Shorten the time to value and remove what blocks users, but don't delay launch like Figma did.
l312|314.e: He is obsessed with time to value: new users should experience what makes the product special as soon as possible, like editing a design with someone else in real time for the first time. Early Figma even had a team called "Blockers" that knocked out, one by one, the basic gaps that stopped people from adopting it. Each fix produced a visible lift in activation and retention. But basics alone are not enough. A launch also needs something exciting that shows where the product is going. His biggest regret is how slowly Figma got to market.
ex: Founded in August 2012, Figma didn't earn its first dollar until summer 2017
His advice: don't copy us, get to market faster

l312|314.c: An older company stays fast by questioning timelines, matching people to interests, and switching projects decisively.
l312|314.e: The Adobe acquisition fell apart after 16 months. He announced it before the holiday break, then came back with a "Detach" program: anyone who thought they had joined Adobe, or was simply worn out, could leave with three months' severance and return within six months. Day to day, speed comes from a few habits. Ask about timelines with curiosity, to find the padding people add with good intentions. Move on decisively when a project isn't coming together. Keep the organization flat. Figure out which constraints are real. And balance paying down technical debt against pushing forward.
ex: Slightly more than 4% of employees took the Detach offer
People placed on projects they truly care about perform far beyond expectations

root.d: Still a startup at 13 years old

items.d: Don't let old architecture slow you

l312|314.c: AI prototypes bring more people into early discussions, but AI gives you average work that still needs polish.
l312|314.e: In his product reviews, a working prototype beats a static mockup, and a mockup beats a wall of text. With AI prototyping, product managers no longer need a designer for a rough sketch, designers can dig into harder problems, and everyone can explore more options. But AI still produces the average. Make is a starting point, and the work has to move back and forth between Make and Figma Design to get refined. Plugging in a design system matters too, or an idea gets killed early just because it looks off. AI features also need rigorous QA and evals, not gut feel.
ex: Make Design once produced an app that looked like Apple Weather; he called it a QA failure and pulled it
Nail prototyping first, then production apps and internal tools

l312|314.c: Taste means forming and refining your own point of view. Anyone can practice it; few invent a new style.
l312|314.e: He defines taste as having a point of view. You build it in a loop. Whenever you experience something, ask whether you like it and why. Then broaden your exposure: learn the context behind it and the classics, and decide which paths you agree or disagree with. Finding connections across fields is especially useful. Most people can learn to match an existing framework, but he thinks only one in ten thousand truly creates a new style. A good product designer can also switch between personal taste and what the brand needs.
ex: Figma's new chief design officer, Loredana, used to be a musician
Taste implies judgment: you have to be willing to say what's good and bad

l312|314.c: Roles will keep blending, and AI should be treated as a chance to grow, not a way to cut staff.
l312|314.e: The blending of design, engineering, product, and research over the past five years will speed up. Everyone is a product builder, he says, just with different specialties. Figma's demand for development is nowhere near saturated, and AI's productivity gains have been light to moderate, so engineering hiring plans haven't shrunk and most departments are still growing. In a world where software is easier to build, judgment, the ability to hold a team together, and design matter more. He believes designers will become the leaders of the future.
ex: Non-designers who regularly do design work rose from 44% to 56% in one year
Only about 16 to 17 percent of designers feel AI threatens their jobs

items.d: Credit AI tools as the main reason

l313|191.c: Most productivity metrics lie. In the AI era, pick metrics by purpose and add a trust dimension.
l313|191.e: Lines of code was always a bad metric, and now it is trivial to have AI produce enormous, heavily commented code that also brings complexity and technical debt. But if you can tell human-written code from AI-written code, line counts become useful in a new way: you can track how long that code survives, its quality, and whether machine-generated code is flowing back into training. DORA is a prescriptive set of metrics, good only for judging the speed and stability of the delivery pipeline. SPACE is just a framework, which is why it stretches to new situations. She suggests adding one more dimension: trust.
ex: The four DORA metrics: deployment frequency, lead time, time to restore, change failure rate
Trust means: does it hallucinate, is it reliable, does it match the team's style

root.d: Add trust for the AI era

items.d: A: counts help, don't worship them
C, including human-machine division of labor

l313|191.c: AI both interrupts flow and can sustain it, so the shape of the workday deserves a redesign.
l313|191.e: She breaks developer experience into three things that reinforce each other: flow state, cognitive load, and feedback loops. AI turns coding into prompt, wait, review, which is interrupt-driven and breaks flow. But some senior engineers work differently. They lay out the architecture, the tech stack, and the constraints first, then send several agents off to build in parallel while they stay in flow at the level of goals. People get roughly four hours of high-quality deep work a day. It used to take a long uninterrupted block to get there; now the machine can help you recover context, so even 45 minutes can be productive.
ex: She cites attention researcher Gloria Mark's work
Upfront system planning gets AI output much closer to production-grade code

items.d: No mental energy wasted on plumbing
AI makes the loop earlier and faster

l313|191.c: Almost every team can go faster, but first figure out what the speed is for.
l313|191.e: She says she has never seen a team that was already as fast as it could be. The signs are obvious: builds break often, tests are flaky, getting an environment takes a long approval process, and moving to another team means paying the new-hire tax all over again. But faster is not the same as better. A team can absolutely ship garbage faster every day. AI shrinks prototypes and user-facing experiments from months to a day or two, so strategy, experiment design, and data readiness matter more than ever. That, she says, is where product managers earn their keep.
ex: AI is also good at writing unit tests and cleaning up documentation
The better the docs and comments, the better AI tools perform

items: Launch A/B tests on a whim
Decide what to build and in what order

d.verdict: Speed has to rest on the right decisions

l313|191.c: Improving developer experience starts with listening, and often a simple process change does the trick.
l313|191.e: Frictionless, the book she wrote with Abi Noda, lays out seven steps: start with a listening tour, land a quick win, use data to optimize, set strategy and priorities, sell the strategy to stakeholders, drive change within your own scope of authority, then evaluate progress, show the value, and repeat. The best first step, she says, is to ask developers what they did yesterday and where they got stuck, rather than building a tool. The payoff tends to follow a J-curve: after the quick win there is a dip, and only once infrastructure and telemetry are in place does the return start to compound.
ex: One company's approvals meant printing a form and walking it up three floors; email fixed it
A small team can start by cleaning up its test suite; a whole org can change its processes
Run developer experience and metrics like a product, and retire outdated metrics

items.d: Fix a small pain, share it publicly

l313|191.c: To prove the value of AI and developer experience, use leaders' own language and the metrics they care about.
l313|191.e: Start by listening for what leaders keep repeating. If they care about market share, measure how fast an idea gets to an experiment or to a customer. If they care about margins, convert saved time into labor cost, or count the vendor and cloud spend you cut. If they say "productivity" or "transformation," use those words. With developers, talk about saved time, less drudgery, and more focus. When attribution is murky, be honest: AI tools and developer-experience improvements rolled out together and both contributed, but without the developer-experience work, AI's impact would be much smaller.
ex: Cleaning up test and build suites saves developers time and saves the business cloud costs
Gains can reach hundreds of thousands of dollars at small companies and billions at large ones

items.d: Don't make them work to understand
AI and developer experience work together

l313|191.c: With no data, interview first, then survey: ask for the top three blockers and how often each hits.
l313|191.e: Existing telemetry usually wasn't designed for your question, so a survey is the fastest way to see the whole picture. She suggests asking about satisfaction, the three biggest blockers, and how often each one occurs. Some hit every day; others only at quarter end but are brutal. Finish with one open-ended question. Limiting people to three forces them to rank, which keeps the data clean and lets you compute a weighted score as a subjective baseline. Avoid questions that ask several things at once. She also advises against asking about happiness, which depends on family, hobbies, and much else; satisfaction is more actionable.
ex: Bad example: "Were builds and tests slow and complex last week?" is really four questions
Rule: don't collect data that can't answer any question

items.d: Hear it in people's own words
A menu of tools or processes

l314|614.c: Better AI products come from users, data, and prompts, not from chasing news or swapping frameworks.
l314|614.e: Her widely shared comparison table makes the point. People think they will improve by following the latest news, switching to the newest agent framework, agonizing over vector databases, or debating which model is smartest. What actually works, she says, is talking to users, building a more reliable platform, preparing better data, tuning the end-to-end pipeline, and writing good prompts. On technology choices, she suggests two questions. First, how big is the gap between the best option and the second best? If it is small, stop arguing. Second, how hard will it be to swap out later? Think twice about new, lightly tested technology that is hard to replace.
ex: Example: agonizing over MCP versus agent-to-agent protocols
People ask her how to keep up with AI news; she asks why they need to

items: Switching to the newest agent framework

d.verdict: Spend effort where it moves results most

l314|614.c: Pre-training data is nearly used up, so the differences between models now come mostly from post-training.
l314|614.e: She thinks of a language model as an encoding of the statistical patterns in language. The idea goes back to Shannon's 1951 paper, and it is how Sherlock Holmes cracked the dancing men cipher using letter frequencies. Pre-training scales capability with huge amounts of data, but the internet's text is basically exhausted, so everyone's pre-training data looks similar and the differences come from post-training. Supervised fine-tuning teaches the model to imitate expert demonstrations. The open-source world often distills by having a strong model generate answers, but imitating a good model is not the same as knowing how to train one. Sampling strategy, she adds, is badly underrated.
ex: A token sits between a character and a word, like podcast plus ing
A friend tried a pre-trained model without post-training; the output was absurd

l314|614.c: Reinforcement learning hinges on the reward signal, and asking people to compare beats asking them to score.
l314|614.e: Reinforcement learning means giving the model a signal about whether its output was good or bad, so it produces better answers. Asking someone to rate a song out of ten gives unstable scores, but picking the better of two songs is easy. So labs usually train a reward model from human preference comparisons. The judge can also be an AI, or a verifiable reward. That is why labs need large numbers of domain experts in accounting, law, physics, and more to create data. She is curious about the economics of the labeling industry: only a handful of frontier labs are customers, there are many vendors, and the labs are happy to watch them undercut each other.
ex: Verifiable reward: the correct answer is 42, so a wrong answer gets penalized
Some labeling companies earn a lot but depend on two or three customers

terms.d: Human comparison, AI judge, or verifiable check

result.d: Steer toward better outputs

l314|614.c: Evals are a cost-benefit call: mandatory at scale, when failure is costly, or when the feature is your edge.
l314|614.e: Some companies skip evals for a rational reason: the feature shipped, users are happy, and two engineers spent on evaluation might only lift quality from 80% to 82 or 85%, which is worth less than a new feature. But when the scale is large, failure is costly, or the feature is a core strength you intend to be best at, rigorous evaluation is non-negotiable. There is no fixed number of evals. The goal is enough coverage to find where the system performs badly, and complex applications need every intermediate step evaluated.
ex: For deep research: are search queries diverse, and are results broad, deep, and relevant
Evals once revealed a user segment doing poorly; the cause was just the wrong phrasing
She has seen products with over a hundred metrics

cells.d: Know exactly how far ahead or behind you are
If it's good enough, hold off

l314|614.c: The biggest RAG gains come from preparing the data, not from agonizing over which vector database to use.
l314|614.e: RAG means retrieving the context a model needs and handing it over before it answers. The hard part is that real documents are not tidy like Wikipedia, where each article sticks to one topic. A definition appears in the first sentence, and once the document is chunked, the later chunks become unfindable. So you have to design chunk sizes and enrich each chunk with a summary, metadata, or hypothetical questions it can answer. One company rewrote podcasts into question-and-answer format and saw a big improvement. Documents should also be rewritten for AI, adding context human experts take for granted. The vector database only matters for latency and read-write patterns.
ex: Add an AI-facing note explaining what a function output like "1" means on its scale
Have AI generate the questions each chunk can answer, then match those to user queries

marks.d: Many chunks retrieved, each missing context

l314|614.c: AI productivity gains are hard to quantify, and high performers who understand the system often benefit most.
l314|614.e: Customer-facing AI tends to go where results are measurable, like support or hotel-booking bots where you can compare conversion rates. Internal productivity is much harder to measure; pull-request counts and lines of code are unreliable. She had a VP ask his managers: would you rather buy an expensive coding agent for the whole team, or get one more headcount? Nearly every manager chose the headcount. Executives running several teams watch business metrics and lean toward the tool. A friend's 30-to-40-person company split engineers into three performance tiers and gave half of each tier Cursor; the top tier improved the most. Other companies say senior engineers resist the most.
ex: One company has seniors set standards and review, while juniors write code with AI
AI handles well-defined tasks; debugging across components still takes systems thinking
Out of ideas? Spend a week writing down everything that frustrates you

marks.d: Tends to go on autopilot, smallest gain
Knows how to decompose problems, biggest gain

l314|614.c: Role boundaries will blur, base models will improve more slowly, and gains will shift to post-training and applications.
l314|614.e: Evaluation, she argues, is a systems problem, not a standalone one. You need to understand how components interact and what users care about. So product, engineering, and even go-to-market teams will move closer together, and non-core processes that used to be outsourced will be automated by AI. She leans toward thinking base models won't jump again the way GPT-2 to GPT-3 did; improvements will come from post-training, application building, and inference-time compute, meaning the model spends more effort per answer. Voice and other modalities are far from solved: multi-hop latency and knowing when to accept an interruption are mostly engineering and classic machine-learning problems.
ex: Inference-time compute: generate several answers and vote, or spend more tokens thinking
Regulators may require voice bots to disclose that they are AI

items.d: AI takes over formerly outsourced processes
More thinking and tries for better answers

l315|617.c: To become an AI-native company, first replace business-unit silos with a functional organization.
l315|617.e: He is a firm believer in Conway's law: the way an organization is structured shows up in the products it builds. Block used to run Square, Cash App, and the rest like separate companies, each with its own engineering and design teams, little communication, and no shared technical strategy. Once every engineer reported up one line and every designer up another, tools, policies, and leveling became consistent, people could move between units, and the company could push AI and platform depth in a focused way. It also changed hiring: engineers were no longer treated as a commodity you stack up by feature count.
ex: He wrote to Jack Dorsey arguing the company should concentrate its efforts on AI
He compares it to Steve Jobs returning to Apple and making it functional
A senior engineer now means the same thing across every business line

items.d: Each unit has its own engineers and designers
Engineering and design each under one leader
Focused push on AI and platform

l315|617.c: AI is saving real hours, but the gains shrink as codebases get older and more complex.
l315|617.e: Engineering teams that use Goose heavily report saving 8 to 10 hours a week. Data scientists check those claims against pull-request counts and feature throughput, and estimate the whole company, including support, legal, and risk, is heading toward 20 to 25 percent of human hours saved. Brand-new codebases and apps on new platforms show the clearest gains; large, complex legacy codebases are nowhere near that. For deep design problems like architecture and race conditions, AI still trails senior engineers. So dumping tools onto a big codebase doesn't automatically pay off. You expand use step by step as the models improve.
ex: The risk team built its own self-service system, turning weeks of work into hours
Gosling drives Android through the accessibility interface to automate UI tests
A background tool analyzes vulnerabilities overnight and tries to fix bugs from tickets

l315|617.c: Goose uses MCP to give language models hands, so any internal system can be orchestrated by AI.
l315|617.e: Goose is a general-purpose agent that works with any model. At its core is MCP, a standard interface wrapped around existing tools so a model can operate them. Teams no longer wait for software vendors to add AI features; a few lines of code make a system controllable, and Goose can even write the MCP wrapper itself. When an attempt fails, it backs up and tries another path until it makes progress. Block open-sourced it because the company was built on open source, wants to give back, and hopes to create something that outlasts Block.
ex: A marketing report: pull data from Snowflake, analyze it, chart it, email it
He had Goose use AppleScript to gather his kid's therapy receipts into Notes
Databricks and several other companies use Goose too

l315|617.c: The biggest winners are non-technical employees building their own tools, but demand grows with them.
l315|617.e: The most senior and the most junior engineers are the most eager AI users: seniors happily offload work they have done a thousand times, and juniors pick it up naturally. The biggest surprise is non-technical staff in legal and risk building software for their own workflows, which will keep blurring the lines between roles. But it works like widening a highway, which only brings more traffic. When everyone can write software, there is more software to coordinate, and expectations for delivery speed rise, so hiring demand has not fallen. The key to adoption is executives using the tools themselves every day.
ex: Jack Dorsey and the executive team use Goose daily
Hiring looks for a learning mindset, not day-one AI expertise
Interviews now allow vibe-coding tools

items.d: Non-technical teams make their own tools

l315|617.c: Agents should keep working while you sleep, building several versions in parallel so you can pick one.
l315|617.e: Today's vibe coding feels to him like ping-pong: wait a few minutes, get something half-finished, steer again. Goose sessions currently run about five minutes at the median, and the team wants to push that to hours. Limited people and high coordination costs used to mean picking one path to try. Soon you could describe several experiments in detail, sleep, wake up to all of them done, and throw most away. He even imagines deleting the whole app and rewriting it for every release, as long as AI captures every past incremental improvement in the spec.
ex: He gave Goose a 10-item wish list to improve itself overnight; about 60% worked
A colleague let Goose watch his screen; features he discussed had PRs within hours
Human taste still has to anchor it, or you get AI slop

items.d: Hours of continuous work per session

l315|617.sc: Ask whether to do it at all
l315|617.c: First ask whether the thing needs doing at all. Structure and process matter more than which tool.
l315|617.e: AI lacks holistic judgment about how pieces fit together. A common scene: one team wants to buy a vendor tool, another says building it with Goose is faster. The question a human should ask is whether a process change makes the tool unnecessary altogether. He also argues against building in-house just to save money. It pulls the company away from its core mission of economic empowerment and eats the team's attention, which isn't worth it. Besides, the prototype is only 20 percent of the work; the long tail of edge cases takes much longer.
ex: Smart test selection cut test runs by about half; deleting tests and moving to the cloud saved more
Cash Card took about a week to build, and the edge cases took much longer
Security teams often struggle to protect things that never needed building

items.d: Maybe it's not needed at all
Drop what doesn't serve the core

l315|617.c: Code quality has nothing to do with product success. Start small and solve a real problem.
l315|617.e: When Google bought YouTube, people inside Google sneered at its code and architecture, yet it crushed the more capable Google Video because it was built to solve a specific human problem. Running Cash App engineering, he tolerated controlled chaos: hold the line on what must never break, and give engineers freedom to experiment with the rest. He also argues for starting small. Goose, Cash App, and the bitcoin feature all began as small experiments, while Google Wave, which started with 70 to 80 engineers, never landed.
ex: He grew Cash App engineering from about 10 people to more than 200
He, Jack Dorsey, and one other person built bitcoin buying during a hack week
Failures like Wave, Google+, and Secret taught him humility

d.verdict: Solving real problems beats writing pretty code

l316|620.c: Plan backward from the future you want, instead of stacking up whatever bricks you happen to have.
l316|620.e: She describes two kinds of planning. Column A looks at the bricks around you and asks how high you can stack them. Column B imagines the castle on the hilltop first, then works out how to build it. Most people only do Column A, which limits what they can build. When she started, she had no experience and no product, so her Column A was almost empty. Her approach: spend time picturing what a huge success and a terrible failure would each look like in ten years. Then build a ladder to the moon and climb it rung by rung. The first step can be tiny, because ten years of steps compound.
ex: Her vision for the world in 2050 hangs on the office wall
Solving a few people's problem well beats solving many people's problem badly

items: Stack as high as you can
Define a ten-year triumph and disaster
Then build a ladder and climb

d.verdict: Canva was Column B from day one

l316|620.c: Every idea starts out as chaos, and each step only needs to add a little clarity.
l316|620.e: Any idea, problem, or belief begins at the chaos end. The first step might just be writing it down. Then it becomes a slide deck, a design, a prototype, getting more real and visible to more people at each stage. That first step is often uncomfortable because you don't have answers yet and can't claim mastery. That is why she stresses visual communication: an idea that lives only in your head can't be seen by anyone else, so no one can help make it real. Every new project inside Canva has a vision deck.
ex: Her joke: how do you get from chaos to clarity? Add clarity.
Melissa Tan, a Canva executive, made a vision deck for her own area

items.d: Out of your head, into words

l316|620.c: Break a crazy big goal into mission pillars and yearly goals, and celebrate every rung of the ladder.
l316|620.e: A crazy big goal makes you feel unworthy of it, so you work furiously to earn it. A reasonable goal feels like nothing when you hit it, and you give up more easily when obstacles appear. Canva broke "empower the world to design" into pillars: design anything, in any language, on any device. Each year they set a batch of goals that build on each other. They have hit almost all of them, though it usually took more than twice as long as expected. Every goal reached gets a fun celebration, because climbing a mountain without them is exhausting.
ex: Languages: English, then Spanish, then 20, then 100-plus including Arabic and Hebrew
Devices: web, then iPad, then iPhone, then Android, then full parity everywhere
Celebrations: smashing plates, releasing doves, a tomato festival

items.d: Most valuable company, then most good

l316|620.c: A rejection is free feedback: write the answer to each objection into the deck before the next pitch.
l316|620.e: More than a hundred investors turned her down. She was convinced she was right and treated each rejection as a signal for improvement. If someone said the market was too small, she added a slide on market size. If they said it was like every other product, she added a slide on the competitive landscape and the gap. Investors didn't understand design, so she opened with the current state and the problem. The vision barely changed; the telling did, especially leading with the problem, because otherwise nobody cares about the solution. She focused on what she controlled: deck quality and how many people she met. Some people will never get it, so find the ones who do.
ex: One person listened for hours before it finally clicked
An investor with The Lean Startup on the shelf was never going to like Canva
The 2012 deck still describes Canva accurately today

items.d: Market too small, same as everyone else...
Then they care about the solution

l316|620.c: Every time the company doubles, its systems break. Rebuild them your own way instead of copying big companies.
l316|620.e: Each time headcount doubles, nearly every mechanism that used to work stops working and has to be redesigned for the new scale, while keeping the same philosophy. She compares it to building a house: bricks pulled from someone else's house rarely fit. Several times Canva lacked confidence and copied a bigger company's practices, usually with poor results. The front-end rewrite was another lesson. It was supposed to take six months and instead blocked all new features for two years, but it made cross-platform support, right-to-left languages, and real-time collaboration possible. A rubber-duck game board helped the team get through that dark tunnel.
ex: Daily standups became weekly, then monthly, then a quarterly season opener up to six hours long
Before the rewrite, the editor could only handle five engineers working at once
Canva now has about 2,500 engineers

l316|620.c: Product stands on two legs: building the future toward the mission, and listening to the community and closing the loop.
l316|620.e: Half of product work, she says, is building the future along the mission pillars. The other half is shipping what the community asks for. Canva gets over a million requests a year. A dedicated team counts and breaks them down, hands them to product teams, and closes the loop with the people who asked. Behind every person who speaks up are many silent users who want the same thing. User testing is another loop: watch ten random people online and see where they hesitate, and the feedback is usually very representative. AI follows the same rule. It isn't put at the center because investors are excited; it gets deeply built in only where it genuinely helps users get work done.
ex: More than 200 requests closed this year, from gradient text to Sheets
Magic Write opened to classrooms, with safety controls, only after teachers asked loudly
She has personally run hundreds of online user tests

items.d: A million a year, each closed out
Only where it truly helps users

l316|620.c: Making money and doing good can happen at the same time, and each pushes the other forward.
l316|620.e: Canva's biggest goal has two steps: become one of the most valuable companies in the world, then do the most good possible. She assumed the first step had to finish before the second began, but found the two reinforce each other, and doing good makes employees' work more meaningful. Getting rich was only ever a means for her. The two founders have committed about 30 percent of their equity to doing good, and they urge every startup to sign the 1% pledge: it is easy early on and compounds later.
ex: $50 million already given to GiveDirectly, with $100 million more over the next four years
The education product is free and used by about 100 million people a month
Roughly $1.5 billion worth of product is given away free each year

terms.d: Become one of the most valuable companies
Do good with equity, donations, free products

result.d: The steps reinforce each other; work means more

l317|440.c: The mid-market doesn't exist. You are either marketing-led SMB or sales-led enterprise.
l317|440.e: Everyone defines enterprise differently, but she says selling to a 100-person company and a 1,000-person company are completely different games with no middle path. When you dig into what people call mid-market, it turns out to be either the top of SMB or the bottom of enterprise, and usually the latter, which means hiring and pricing like an enterprise company. Mixing the two playbooks guarantees failure. The choice depends on which game the founder understands better: if you are great at marketing and can win a mass audience, go SMB; if you know how big companies work and are willing to do six-figure deals, go enterprise.
ex: Large companies follow a power law and thin out fast beyond the Fortune 1000
She expects AI to shrink some large companies and shift the dividing lines

marks.d: Really one of the two ends

l317|440.c: Early on, go after the number one company in the industry. They are the real early adopters.
l317|440.e: The usual advice is to sell to startups that decide fast. She argues the opposite. The hardest thing for an industry leader is staying on top, so they try new things constantly. Give them even a small edge and your internal champion gets promoted. They will help shape your roadmap and can take a $100,000 deal to seven figures quickly. Once you land the leader, numbers two through four want to copy them, and investors and talent follow. In the AI era you need to claim your position fast, which is another reason to go straight to enterprise, with the founder personally involved.
ex: Leaders means companies like Walmart, McDonald's, Nvidia, Tesla, and ExxonMobil
She skips AI outreach tools and targets people who aren't in public databases

items.d: Staying number one is the hard part
A little alpha gets the champion promoted
Numbers two to four copy them

l317|440.c: To decision-makers, sell the edge and the opportunity, not the pain point or the feature.
l317|440.e: Problem-based selling is specific and technical, every salesperson uses it, and it sounds scripted. With leaders you should paint the vision: here is where you are, here is where we can take you. It is the "don't sell the mushroom, sell the bigger Mario" picture. Founders naturally talk this way, which is why founders sell well. Once you become one of three options a customer is comparing, you have mostly lost. When someone says "we already have a tool," don't argue. Agree that it solves that problem, then pull the conversation upstream toward bigger value.
ex: High-frequency trading sells being a second faster, not fiber optic cable
Cursor could sell: 10x engineers only join companies that use it
Keep cold emails to three sentences and say something counterintuitive

items: Find a specific problem and anchor on it
Paint the future you can reach

d.verdict: The market hates being sold to but loves to buy

l317|440.c: Price the first enterprise deal at $75,000 to $150,000. Landing cheap kills the expansion later.
l317|440.e: Founders would rather sign ten $10,000 deals than lose nine to win one at $100,000. But a customer who haggles hard isn't really buying, she says. A $10,000 deal gets no attention, needs no executive signature, and no good salesperson wants to work for that commission. Worse is the anchor: if you land at SMB pricing, raising it tenfold later means proving fifteen times the value, and the customer will use AI to pull up the contract history. Getting stuck in procurement usually means you sold too low in the organization. Things move once an executive gets involved.
ex: Walmart wanted three seats at SMB pricing, and that price became the anchor
She has seen a $10,000 deal drag on for nine months
A well-managed $100,000 deal can reach $1 million in three to five years

items.d: Set a range for the start

l317|440.c: Design partners are guides, not a revenue pipeline, and the pricing framework must be clear from day one.
l317|440.e: Design partners are the hardest customers to convert into full deployments, so don't count on them as a seven-figure pipeline. Use them to understand how the product gets used in real life. The right ones are tech-forward, startup-friendly companies in the Fortune 1000, with people who give feedback and tolerate rough edges. Have them pay something, spell out the future pricing path and a permanent discount, and be honest about what you can't do, because overpromising leads to churn. About 80 percent of feedback is rooted in the old way of working, and filtering it is the founder's job.
ex: You can promise early partners a permanent discount of about 30 percent
One founder's rule: feedback is 80 percent noise and 20 percent gold

items.t: Pick the right company and people
items.d: Tech-forward, willing to use rough products
What you can and can't do

l317|440.c: Enterprise sales from 1 to 10 is a craft, and the core skill is designing each deal to fit the customer.
l317|440.e: Zero to one is more like science, she says, validated by experiments. One to ten is about mastering the narrative and tailoring a package for each account. The product isn't just the software you hand over; pricing, the deal structure, and the opportunity are all part of the product. Enterprises know best how to buy services, so you can lead with a tech-enabled service and steer the customer toward the product later. You can also give away things that cost you little but are worth a lot to them. Relationships matter most. Ask the questions they are afraid to ask, decide yes or no on the first call, and treat a no as useful data.
ex: Palantir's forward-deployed engineers are services-first in action
Invite the customer to keynote your event
Co-design pricing: smaller in year one, stepped up in year two

items.d: The buying motion enterprises know best
Let the champion claim a win
Close over text; ask the hard things

l317|440.c: Your first enterprise sellers must be able to play the founder. Big-company sales VPs usually can't.
l317|440.e: Hire the first salesperson around $1 million in ARR, once you have seven to ten customers and can see a pattern. After that the founder can't be on every deal. The ideal hire sells the vision like a founder and fights for every close: a former founder, or someone who understands product and engineering. A sales VP from a big company is used to the brand building trust for them, and SMB sellers don't understand how executives decide. Sit in on the first five calls and you will know whether it's working. About half of these hires fail, so hire two at once.
ex: Compensation is typically half base salary, half variable
Tech commissions run about 8 to 12 percent, averaging around 10
Moving from SMB to enterprise means starting zero to one all over again

terms.d: Feels fresh, not like a pitch
Can qualify and drive the process

result.d: Sells the vision, fights for the close

l318|623.c: Product-market fit shows up as organic word of mouth. Launch-day awards are vanity metrics.
l318|623.e: Gamma's first public beta in 2022 won Product Hunt's day, week, and month, but signups spiked and quickly flattened, which meant nobody was spreading the word. Instead of forcing growth with ads, the team bet the company with little money left, spending three or four months rebuilding onboarding with AI built in. After the relaunch, daily signups jumped from a few hundred to tens of thousands with zero marketing spend. His two tests: is there organic growth, and will users pay?
ex: Daily signups after relaunch: thousands, then 5,000, then 10,000, then 20,000
When the free 400 credits ran out, users asked support how to pay
Pricing drew on Van Westendorp and conjoint analysis, landing around $20 a month

items.d: Pitching over Zoom in the pandemic, often rejected
Won the charts, but growth flattened
Rebuilt onboarding, word of mouth took off
Hit $1M ARR and profitability within months

l318|623.c: New users are selfish, vain, and lazy. The first 30 seconds must feel magical to earn the next 30.
l318|623.e: He treats onboarding and product as one thing. A restaurant has to delight you from the door to the check before you recommend it. New users have no interest in learning a new tool, and attention spans are shorter than a decade ago, so every 30 seconds has to earn the next.
