With only 12 people, the team couldn't rebuild the whole product, so they bet everything on the moment a user walks in. He borrows a line from advertising: toss one egg at a time so the person can catch it. Don't open with five features.
ex: The egg was "generate a slide in seconds"
Inspired by Scott Belsky's idea of the first mile
Internal rule: creating and sharing both have to be dead simple

l318|623.c: Founders should do their own marketing: give value consistently to build goodwill, then spend it on reach.
l318|623.e: For the AI relaunch they skipped Product Hunt and posted a deliberately spicy tweet. When Paul Graham commented, it spread fast, and he realized the copy, the story, and the visuals all needed his own hands. His advice: get over the awkwardness, jot down counterintuitive lessons as they happen, set a weekly time to turn them into posts, and have colleagues read them first. LinkedIn rewards inspirational themes; Twitter wants specifics, contrarian takes, and data, so don't copy-paste between them. Practicing your own hooks is what gives you judgment when working with creators.
ex: The tweet: the most valuable skill in business is about to become obsolete
Look for ideas early in the morning, review the day's conversations late at night
Regularly revisit the most bookmarked and reshared posts to find patterns

l318|623.c: Bet on thousands of micro-creators rather than a few big influencers with millions of followers.
l318|623.e: Hand a big budget and a script to a few million-follower influencers and the content instantly looks like an ad, and the money is wasted. The better approach is lots of small creators whose audiences trust them and who genuinely benefit from the product, like teachers who make slides every day. The founder demos the product to each one personally, lets them tell the story in their own voice, and treats them as an extension of the team. Ninety percent of the reach comes from under ten percent of creators, and you can't predict which, so cast a wide net and then double down on the groups that work.
ex: Try $10,000 to $20,000 a month for six months, split across about 40 people, not one
Each creator earns a few hundred to a few thousand dollars
Conversion on LinkedIn is four to five times higher than other platforms

items: Big budget on a few people
Reads a script, looks like an ad
Dozens or hundreds tested in parallel

d.verdict: Do things that don't scale to get wildfire spread

l318|623.c: Scale paid ads only once word of mouth drives more than half of new users, and build the brand first.
l318|623.e: More than half of Gamma's new subscriptions still come from word of mouth. Creators and social media are second, and paid ads third. His rule: paid acquisition should never exceed half, because that means the core growth engine is broken and you are pouring money into a leaky bucket. Around $10 million in ARR they realized their placeholder brand was holding them back, so they spent months rebuilding its DNA so that thousands of assets a week would still look consistent. Brand marketing, he argues, is performance marketing too, just hard to attribute, and it suits consumer and prosumer products best.
ex: For every user from creator spend, word of mouth brings about 1.5 more
Brand guidelines are public at brand.gamma.app for creators to reuse
They rebranded with the studio Smith & Diction

items.d: Boosters that amplify word of mouth
More than half of new subscriptions

l318|623.c: Have an idea in the morning and put a prototype in front of 20 strangers by afternoon to find the value fast.
l318|623.e: Friends will kindly say your product is great and then never use it. The ideal tester is a real potential user with no stake in whether you succeed. Give them almost no context and have them think out loud as they use it. Watching someone stall on the first screen because they can't find the button makes the team feel it instantly. Gamma tests everything this way, from landing pages and onboarding to export and sharing, and always breaks ideas into small pieces, many of which get killed the same day. His mindset: strong opinions, loosely held.
ex: They recruit testers through services like Voicepanel and UserTesting
The Gammaster program shows early prototypes to power users in a separate Slack
They ran a virtual office product, The Lobby, in parallel and dropped it after six months

items.d: Break it into a tiny wedge
Target users with no stake in you
Several rounds before a real launch

l318|623.c: A "wrapper" can last if you go deep on a workflow you care about and pick the right model per step.
l318|623.e: A thin layer over one model isn't worth much. But go deep into a complete workflow and there is a lot of orchestration and optimization to do. First ask whether this is a problem you want to spend five to ten years on; if not, you won't survive the big labs and competitors catching up. Then break creation into steps, such as brainstorming, outlining, drafting, editing, and images, assign the best model to each, and keep testing new and old models for quality and cost. That is why Gamma has high gross margins and years of profit. The goal is to be the default whenever someone thinks of making a presentation.
ex: More than 20 models are tested in production at once
Early on, Perplexity worked well for generating search-backed outlines
Consultants want dense information, teachers want something livelier, so personalization matters

terms.d: Willing to spend five to ten years
Right model per step, tested for cost

result.d: The default tool in users' minds

l318|623.c: Innovate on the organization too: hire painfully slowly, favor generalists, and make every manager a player-coach.
l318|623.e: Their motto is "hire painfully slowly." Revenue per employee and profitability are outcomes, not goals. Set a goal of doubling headcount next year and the hiring bar inevitably drops. The first ten people set the team's DNA, and every ten after that are copied from the same mold. They prefer generalists and hand specialized work to outside agencies. Every manager still does hands-on work, like a quarterback who can call an audible on the field. When someone exceptional shows up, give them more resources; A-players only complain about not getting enough playing time.
ex: All of the first 10 employees are still there five years later
At one point about a quarter of the staff were product designers
The head of marketing single-handedly ran a show with about 4,000 drones

items.d: No headcount targets, no lowered bar

l319|249.c: Where AI goes depends on people, and no technology should strip away human dignity and agency.
l319|249.e: She calls herself a humanist, not a utopian. Technology has on the whole made human life better, but every technology is a double-edged sword, and societies and individuals can get it wrong. So everyone should care about AI and take part responsibly. Silicon Valley loves to talk about infinite productivity and infinite leisure, but rarely has honest conversations with ordinary people. Her answer is that musicians, teachers, nurses, and farmers all have a role in the age of AI, and human dignity and agency belong at the center of how AI is built, deployed, and governed.
ex: She reminds graduates that nothing about artificial intelligence is artificial; people are behind it
In 2018 she co-founded Stanford HAI, which runs congressional boot camps and the AI Index

root.d: Dignity and agency at the center

items.d: Use AI as a storytelling tool
Smart cameras and robots share the load
Have a say in how AI is used

l319|249.c: Big data was the overlooked ingredient, and modern AI still runs on data, neural networks, and GPUs.
l319|249.e: When she started her PhD in 2000, AI was in a winter. Everyone focused on models, but there was little data to train them on. She realized that both human learning and biological evolution are essentially big-data processes, so in 2006 and 2007 she launched ImageNet, an attempt to collect images of every object on the internet, along with an annual challenge. In 2012, Geoffrey Hinton's team trained a neural network on ImageNet with two GPUs and broke through. That combination became the golden recipe of modern AI. ChatGPT swapped in internet text and more complex architectures, but the three ingredients are the same.
ex: About 15 million curated images across 22,000 concepts, organized using WordNet
Around 2016, many tech companies still avoided the term AI
She stresses AI is a 70-year relay race, not the work of one person

terms.d: Two gaming cards, then massive compute

result.d: The core recipe from 2012 to ChatGPT

l319|249.c: AGI is mostly a marketing term, and AI still needs major innovation before it truly thinks like a person.
l319|249.e: AGI has no agreed definition. People use it for everything from machine superpowers to an economic agent that can earn a salary. For her, the north star of AI has always been whether machines can think and act like humans, so there is no difference between AI and AGI. There is still plenty of room to scale data, compute, and current architectures, but no science ever declares innovation finished, and AI is one of the youngest fields. Today's AI still can't do things humans find easy in spatial understanding, abstract creativity, and emotional intelligence.
ex: Ask a model to count chairs in an office video and it does poorly
Even with better astronomical data, AI couldn't derive Newton's laws of motion
A teacher-student conversation about motivation and confusion is far beyond AI

l319|249.c: Spatial intelligence is the key gap beyond language, and world models must create, interact, and reason.
l319|249.e: Much of human intelligence rests on vision, perception, and spatial understanding, not just language. Firefighters coordinating at a scene rely heavily on instant understanding of objects and surroundings. Through her work in robotics and vision, she came to see spatial intelligence as the hub connecting vision, language, and embodied intelligence. A world model should let you generate a world from a sentence or an image, move through it, pick up and change objects, and reason and plan in it, like a robot planning a route to clean a kitchen. It serves not only robots but also humans, who are embodied agents too.
ex: Watson and Crick inferred the 3D double helix from a single 2D X-ray diffraction image
She gave a TED talk on spatial intelligence in 2024
Applications: robotics, games, design, scientific discovery

items.d: Create, interact with, and reason about worlds

l319|249.c: The bitter-lesson approach of just scaling data isn't enough for robots. It's a long haul, like self-driving.
l319|249.e: Rich Sutton's bitter lesson says simple models plus massive data eventually win; for ImageNet, she says, it was a sweet lesson. But robotics is hard for two reasons. Language models train on text and output text, so the objective lines up perfectly. Robots must output actions in a 3D world, yet most available data is internet video, which has to be supplemented with teleoperation and synthetic data. And robots are physical systems: beyond a brain, they need bodies, use cases, and supply chains. Self-driving took 20 years from prototype to the road, and robots that actively touch objects in 3D are harder still.
ex: Around 2005, Sebastian Thrun's Stanford car won the DARPA Grand Challenge
A self-driving car is a metal box on a 2D surface whose job is to touch nothing
The human brain runs on about 20 watts, dimmer than a light bulb

items: Training data and output are both text
Must output 3D actions, but data is mostly video
Physical system with bodies and supply chains

d.verdict: Robotics may face several more bitter lessons

l319|249.c: Marble turns a sentence into an explorable 3D world, which goes a level deeper than generating video.
l319|249.e: World Labs spent more than a year building the first generative model that outputs a true 3D world, and Marble is the first product on top of it. From text or several images, it generates a world you can navigate and export. She uses Plato's cave to explain why: vision is fundamentally about understanding a 3D world from 2D projections, so spatial intelligence is more than producing flat video. Early users include virtual production teams in film, game developers, robotics simulation, and even psychology researchers. The team is about 30 people and keeps research and product-building tightly coupled.
ex: A virtual production team working with Sony reports a 40x reduction in production time
A psychology team generates messy or tidy immersive scenes for experiments
The point cloud shown before rendering is a deliberate visual, and users love it

items.d: A sentence, one image, or several
As a mesh, or as video along a camera path

l319|249.c: Be intellectually fearless: choose by passion, mission, and team, not by enumerating every risk.
l319|249.e: To make a difference, she says, you have to accept that you are doing something new, and she hires for that fearlessness too. Her own path shows it: she gave up a nearly secured tenure at Princeton to move to Stanford, became the first female director of the Stanford AI Lab while young, went to Google to work with the best people, and then founded World Labs. She doesn't dwell on every way things could fail. Her advice to young AI talent is not to treat job choices as a precise equation, but to ask where your passion is, whether you believe in the mission, and whether you trust the team.
ex: At 19 she ran a dry-cleaning business
The biggest surprise of founding a company was how fierce the competition for talent is

l320|628.c: A feature isn't present or absent. It sits somewhere on an S-shaped curve of effort versus value.
l320|628.e: Put effort or quality on the x-axis and value or convenience on the y-axis. At first, effort produces almost no value. Past a threshold, value shoots up. After that, extra effort yields little. Teams tend to treat features as binary: they ship something half-done, users ignore it, the product gets more complex, and the team wrongly concludes the feature wasn't worth doing. So first figure out where you are on the curve. Layer on what Bezos calls divine discontent: the whole industry keeps raising users' expectations, so even basics like signup and password recovery need constant polish.
ex: A hammer with a handle that snaps is useless; once it's sturdy, reinforcing it adds nothing
Google Calendar lists time zones alphabetically, so searching East shows Australia first

l320|628.c: Taste can be learned, and most people don't care about the experience, which is your opening.
l320|628.e: The word taste comes from food, and chefs improve with training, so product taste can be trained too. Most companies don't invest in it, which means care and thoughtfulness become a real advantage. Walking in the Vancouver rain, he noticed only about a third of pedestrians tilted their umbrellas to make room for others; the rest either didn't care or didn't notice anyone else. "Tilt your umbrella" became a Slack onboarding lesson and a slogan on company swag. Those small conveniences are what make users feel attached, so when they change jobs they bring Slack along, which drove its spread.
ex: Magic-link login by email, so you don't type a complex password on your phone
Using @everyone triggers a "shouting rooster" warning showing how many people you'll notify
Do Not Disturb shipped with sensible defaults that admins and individuals could override

items.d: Carried from company A to company B

l320|628.c: For most products the hard part is making people understand, not cutting friction or clicks.
l320|628.e: Someone buying concert tickets has strong, clear intent and will push through a terrible website. Only a few flows, like signup and checkout, deserve a ruthless war on friction. A visitor to Slack's website has barely enough intent to be there and can't even say what the product is. The challenge is getting them to understand what it is and what to do next, which he estimates is 70 to 80 percent of product design. Forcing users to make decisions they don't understand drains them and makes them feel stupid. Rather than minimizing clicks, put the two or three most common actions up front, tuck the rest under "other," and make every step effortless.
ex: "Turn on Sleep" in Apple's Clock app leaves people baffled
Early Uber's home screen offered only "Where to?" and "Other"
Shopkeeper's delusion: a restaurant site with slow hero images and no phone number or hours

items: Right when intent is strong and clear
Blindly cutting clicks makes things harder
Explain what it is and what's next
Don't make me think or feel stupid

d.verdict: Swap the obsession with friction for making users never think

l320|628.c: Anyone who can't see endless room for improvement in the product shouldn't be in charge of designing it.
l320|628.e: In 2014, the year Slack officially launched, he told the press the product was terrible and they should be ashamed to show it to the public. The next day colleagues printed the quote and plastered it on the walls. His point: you can be proud of individual pieces of work, but overall you should always hunger to improve, and the organization should openly admit it isn't perfect. Like Michael Jordan asking his ski instructor to point out every mistake, collect criticism like gems. The precondition is enough trust that direct criticism from colleagues and users feels like fuel rather than an attack.
ex: He uses Toyota-style continuous improvement, kaizen, as a reference point
The Michael Jordan skiing story from Ray Dalio's book

terms.d: Criticism is about doing the work well

result.d: People appreciate direct feedback

l320|628.c: Organizations spontaneously grow "hyper-realistic work-like activities," so leaders must supply work known to be valuable.
l320|628.e: Work expands to fill the time available, and headcount does the same: most new hires want to hire reports, because team size drives level and pay. That isn't bad or dumb, it's rational. Early in a startup there is plenty of work that is known to be valuable. Later the easy wins are gone while headcount keeps growing, so people hold meetings to pre-review the slides for the all-hands, which looks exactly like work. He insists this is the leader's responsibility: set priorities clearly, say no in advance, and make sure there is enough genuinely valuable work to do.
ex: Defaulting thread replies to @-mention the previous person: 2.17 replies per thread versus 2.14
An A/B test, instrumentation, dashboards, and meetings for that difference will never pay off
If a problem looks simple, you don't understand it yet

items.d: Ask for more people at budget time

l320|628.c: A new product means building a market as well as a product: sell the riding, not the saddle.
l320|628.e: "We Don't Sell Saddles Here" started as an internal memo when Slack had about eight people and was still in private beta, and it was published word for word. The goal was to align on the thinking early so it would carry through as the company grew. Nobody needs to be told why they want a beer or a car, but everyone has to be told why they should use Slack. Whenever your product differs materially from the alternatives, you are creating a market at the same time. As the book Positioning warns, planting a brand-new concept in someone's head is nearly impossible; combining two existing ones is far easier.
ex: Harley sells the open road and freedom; lululemon sells a better you
Analogies work: "X meets Y," or "Uber for pets"

items.d: The experience and results users get

l320|628.c: Pivot only after exhausting every realistic option, and make the decision deliberately and calmly.
l320|628.e: Everyone tells you to persevere, but he thinks the real question is whether you have exhausted every opportunity that isn't crazy. While building the game Glitch, the team communicated over IRC and kept improving it, adding only features that were unbearable to live without or obviously needed. That was the seed of Slack. When they gave up on the game, the company still had $9 million and everyone still loved it. The decision has to be calm and rational because pivoting is deeply humiliating: you convinced investors, employees, and users, and many founders would rather let the company slowly die than admit it. Changing direction in the first few months doesn't count as a pivot.
ex: Decision researcher Annie Duke uses Glitch-to-Slack as an example of a smart fold
Shutting Glitch erased a player community and cost jobs, so he doesn't recommend pivots lightly

l320|628.c: In the long run, success depends only on the value you create for customers. Generosity signals cooperation.
l320|628.e: He had the whole company recite at all-hands: in the long run, the measure of our success is the value we create for customers. Anything that takes slight advantage of customers, or maximizes at the wrong moment, is off the table. That is ethical, and it also attracts better employees and reduces internal friction. In game-theory terms, generosity in a repeated game signals that you will cooperate, so the other side cooperates too. Proportion matters, though: Slack automatically credited 100 times the fee for any outage, and after the IPO one long outage wiped out about $8 million in expected revenue before the terms were changed.
ex: The SLA refunded 100 times the fee for any outage, whether or not a customer was affected
He likens generosity to the cooperation signal in the prisoner's dilemma

root.d: The only long-run measure of success

items.d: Earn trust in a repeated game
100x credits needed adjusting after the IPO

l321|629.c: A leader who always supplies the answer trains the team to bring every problem back to them.
l321|629.e: Technical leaders get promoted for being reliable and smart, so they get used to being the smartest person in the room. But once a company scales fast, the people on the front line often know more than they do. If you always hand out answers, she says, your team brings you every hard problem. Coaching questions instead get people engaged, because people act on plans they came up with themselves. Give direct advice when things are urgent, when the person lacks the skill, or when you already know the answer. Managers don't need to coach like professionals; leaving about 15% of a one-on-one for open questions is enough.
ex: One AI company CEO switched to small groups, biweekly reviews, and shared KPIs; the team sped up
Start by asking: do you want advice, or do you need space to think?
When their conclusion is bad, say with honest curiosity: help me understand your thinking

You already know what you want
Overuse makes people depend on you
Best when they know the situation better
People act on their own plans

d.verdict: Most leaders lean too far toward answers

l321|629.c: Great leaders listen at level three, hearing the emotion and situation underneath the words.
l321|629.e: She borrows a line from Fight Club: most people aren't listening, they're waiting for their turn to talk, and that is especially common in tech. She describes three levels. Level one is internal listening, where your head is full of what this means for you. Level two is focused listening, where you can repeat back what the person said. Level three is global listening: you notice body language, tone, and context, reflect back the feelings they haven't voiced, and ask whether you got it right. She did this live with Lenny, asking how fatherhood feels, and in under a minute he felt seen.
ex: She heard both Lenny's huge joy and the strain of setting limits and bedtime routines
Level-three listening also works for influencing people, selling, and sharing a vision

items.d: Hear the feelings and situation beneath the words
Can repeat back exactly what they said
Only thinking about what it means for me

l321|629.c: Four kinds of open questions from the GROW model help people find their own way out.
l321|629.e: A powerful question comes from real curiosity, has no right answer, and doesn't steer the person toward a conclusion you already picked. She sorts questions with the GROW model: Goal (what does success look like), Reality (where are you stuck, what have you tried), Options (what paths exist), and Way forward (what will you do next). The order is flexible; pick what fits. She coached Lenny live on work that never ends: first he named wanting 25% more free time, then he noticed his habit of saying yes to new things, and finally he agreed to skip one episode and rewrite his rules for saying no.
ex: The key question: if you said no to more things, what could you say yes to?
The more the end state resonates, the easier day-to-day discipline becomes

items.d: Where you're stuck, what you've tried

l321|629.c: To avoid burnout, spend 80% of your time in your zone of genius, and fight for it yourself.
l321|629.e: At Stripe she ran a retention program for the top 50 technical executives and found many were running on empty, while others still had energy. The difference was whether they were doing work they were good at and loved. Her exercise: for two weeks, write down each night the five things that energized you most and drained you most, or ask five to ten people who know you what your gifts are, then look for patterns in your calendar. Nobody owes you a life in your strengths. Your manager's job is to make you good at your current role; your career direction is yours to manage. Tell your boss, move sideways if needed, or as a founder hire a COO to cover your gaps.
ex: As a PM, her colleague Zach Abrams told her: your gift is people, not product strategy
Start small: skip optional meetings, take a 30-minute walk between calls

items.d: Work you're great at and love
There's always some work you don't love

l321|629.c: A co-founder relationship works like a marriage: know each other, make clear vows, and keep dating.
l321|629.e: Conflict exposes each person's core values, she says, and founder problems are hard to raise with the board. She starts by building shared self-awareness, for example with the Enneagram personality test. A common tension: the CEO is great at selling a vision ahead of its time, while the CTO is naturally skeptical and fact-driven. Then, like a marriage, the founders write vows and keep repeating them: how we decide, how we fight. They also need to step off the dance floor onto the balcony regularly and review the partnership weekly, monthly, and yearly. If it can't be repaired, seeing that clearly and parting well also counts as success.
ex: Two PR-firm founders drifted apart on opposite coasts; 360 feedback and set meetings repaired it
She and First Round wrote a list of weekly, monthly, and yearly review questions

items.d: Each person's strengths, gaps, and patterns
How we decide, how we fight
Or part ways well once it's clear

l321|629.c: The goal of a conflict is mutual understanding, not winning; nonviolent communication gives you four steps.
l321|629.e: People walk into hard conversations wearing armor, trying to prove they're right, and all they get back is defensiveness. She uses Marshall Rosenberg's nonviolent communication: state a fact nobody can dispute, name your emotion without blaming, explain the need that isn't being met, then make a small request the other person can easily grant, as an olive branch. "I feel like you..." is not an emotion. Conversations are hard because the issue matters, so treat them as a chance to grow. And take 100% responsibility: don't play victim, blamer, or rescuer.
ex: Example: three sprint plannings without me; I feel anxious; I need clarity; please cc me the roadmap
Stanford's Touchy Feely class uses a tennis-net image: don't reach over the net to blame

items.d: Clarity, collaboration, connection, and so on

l321|629.c: Ask yourself whether you'd enthusiastically rehire this person for the role; if not, act.
l321|629.e: This was her go-to question at Stripe. It works because it is binary: your body gives an immediate, honest answer, and that cuts through procrastination. When a CEO keeps putting off a talk with an underperforming executive, it's usually because they already know it isn't working and don't want to face it. A no doesn't mean firing on the spot. You can have an honest conversation, change the role, or start an outside search. In a fast-growing company, the CFO who fit a year ago may now be a better controller. Beyond timing and real demand, she believes a company's success comes down to talent and the environment around it.
ex: When coaching CEOs, she won't accept "let's give it another six months"
The default state is blind, overworked, and lonely; leaders have to create connection on purpose

root.d: If the answer is no, act

items.d: Spell out expectations and the gap
Find the right person for this stage
More talks won't change the answer

l321|629.c: A one-page plan plus a steady operating rhythm shows everyone how their work connects to the vision.
l321|629.e: In many companies the vision, strategy, goals, and values live in different places. Ask an employee how their three top priorities relate to the vision and few can answer. She borrows the people-first operating rhythm from Alpine Investors: four columns for vision and values, strategic intent and KPIs, annual goals, and quarterly goals, so every priority debate is checked against the whole picture. The rhythm matters more than the page. Publish it at the start of the year, then each quarter review together what worked and what didn't, and ask what truth is hard to say out loud. That gets the executive team off the dance floor and onto the balcony regularly.
ex: Alpine's data shows portfolio companies that adopt this rhythm earn higher returns
A quarterly review question: what is the truth that's hard to say out loud?

items.d: Why we exist, how we treat each other
How we win, which numbers we watch
What exactly we do this quarter

l322|633.c: Go-to-market should include every function that touches customers or revenue, joined into one customer lifecycle.
l322|633.e: Most people think of GTM as marketing and sales. She counts sales engineering, post-sales architects, customer success, support, and partnerships too. Those teams used to run on slightly different segmentations and goals, like circles that only partly overlap. She expects today's 17 or so specialized roles to gradually merge. The right approach is to design the whole journey like a product, from first hearing about you to being a high-value customer five years in with full adoption. In the AI era, ten companies often chase the same opportunity, so GTM carries more strategic weight and looks more like consulting.
ex: With usage-based pricing the first deal is only the start, so sales must understand customers better
Forward-deployed engineers work inside the customer's environment and bring common needs back to product

l322|633.c: GTM engineers turn your best rep's workflow into an agent, so one person does the work of ten.
l322|633.e: At Stripe she had budget for only four SDRs. Back in 2017 she tried to build a database of company attributes and auto-fill personalized emails, but the technology wasn't there. At Vercel today, a GTM engineer shadows the top performer, writes the process down as an agent that scores leads and drafts replies, and has a human review before anything is sent, all while watching the original KPIs. Inbound went from ten SDRs to one person doing quality control; the other nine moved to outbound. Conversion held steady with fewer touches. Her goal is reps spending 70% of their time with customers.
ex: One GTM engineer built the lead agent in six weeks using about 30% of their time
The agent costs about $1,000 a year to run; ten SDRs cost over a million in salary
A lost-deal analysis bot took two days and showed big deals die when nobody meets the economic buyer

items.d: Which tabs they open, what data they check
The parts you can write down and repeat
Free up people only if conversion holds

l322|633.c: As products converge, how it feels to be sold to decides the deal, so design GTM like a product.
l322|633.e: When she joined Gmail in 2004 it was a full year ahead of rivals. A decade later, cloud computing made software increasingly similar, and she realized people often buy on feel. So every step, from first contact to long-term customer, should be designed as an experience, not a transaction. Even if they don't buy this time, leave them with something useful, because lost customers often come back a few years later. Big customers don't want generic docs; they want a best-practice blueprint for their situation. In discovery, the rep should talk less than half the time and keep asking why.
ex: Stripe turned the first meeting into a whiteboard session where customers drew their payments architecture
Vercel's outreach includes data comparing the prospect's site performance with peers
Stripe gave marketplace customers a dedicated blueprint for building payments

items: First call is a string of questions
Whiteboard together; customer leaves with value

d.verdict: Make the buying process itself the differentiator

l322|633.c: About 80% of customers buy to avoid risk, so founders shouldn't only pitch the upside.
l322|633.e: A round-number statistic she has heard: roughly 80% of customers buy to avoid pain or reduce risk, and only about one in five buy for more upside. Painting the art of the possible is exciting, but it mostly lands with other founders. Enterprise buyers worry about missing next quarter's revenue target, being overtaken by a competitor, or damage to their brand. Many startups think that kind of pitch isn't cool. But she finds that gently raising the worry that "I might be in a bad spot," or asking questions that help customers see their own gaps, closes more deals.
ex: Enterprise worries: missing revenue targets, being passed by competitors, brand damage

l322|633.c: Don't segment by company size alone; find the attributes that actually change how customers buy.
l322|633.e: Small, mid-market, and enterprise tiers capture how complex a purchase is, but stopping there misses the important differences. In her first 30 days at Vercel she worked with the head of data science to find which attributes, visible up front, predict whether a customer pays $100,000 or $1 million, and where the company keeps winning. Keep it to three attributes at most, because you only have so many reps. She also treats segmentation as a company-wide matter and teaches it herself in new hires' first week, so product managers know who they're building for.
ex: OpenAI is mid-sized by headcount but top 25 in web traffic, so it counts as enterprise
Stripe segments by business model; marketplaces get sold Connect
Vercel is strong in e-commerce but weaker in enterprise SaaS, where migration costs are high

items.d: Vercel upgrades tiers using CrUX rankings
E-commerce and crypto are nothing alike

l322|633.c: A world-class sales team is both a revenue and an R&D function, with product-manager-level depth.
l322|633.e: Her test for a sales team: put an account executive in front of ten of your engineers, and it should take them ten minutes to realize this person isn't a PM. Product depth earns credibility with engineering and makes sales an extension of the product team. A 20-person sales team talks to far more customers each week than user research does, and if reps can separate signal from noise, that feedback flows into the roadmap. She wants reps to think like general managers: knowing when to overcome an objection and when to push a customer request, and caring about product and pricing strategy.
ex: Treat pricing as a product: Stripe Billing dropped its free tier and lost nothing
Vercel found about half of enterprise users were startups, so it carved out a self-serve option

terms.d: A product that wins the market

result.d: Sales puts on the general-manager hat

l322|633.c: Product-led growth is the right start for most companies, but it caps out; add sales earlier than you think.
l322|633.e: Unless you're Sierra, selling eight-figure deals to global enterprises from day one, most products start with startups, so product-led growth still matters. It remains the main growth engine at Vercel and Stripe. But nobody pays you $1 million through a self-serve checkout, and to keep growing fast you need big deals. Building a repeatable sales process and turning outbound into a predictable engine takes time, and many companies hit a wall because they added sales too late. She also admits that sales compensation, locked in annually, makes it hard for an org to adapt when a new product lands mid-year.
ex: She can't name a $100 billion company built on product-led growth alone
She likes mixing experienced sellers with people from consulting and investment banking

marks.d: PLG with sales layered on top

l323|398.c: Change now outruns how fast organizations react, and the bloated big-company product process has stopped working.
l323|398.e: LinkedIn's data says about 70% of the skills needed for today's jobs will change by 2030, and most of the fastest-growing roles weren't on the list a year earlier. Building a product is simple at heart: research, write requirements, design, code, ship, iterate. But at scale each step splits into many sub-steps, each with a sensible reason, until a small feature needs several teams, several codebases, and multiple sprints. Process complexity breeds organizational complexity and ever-finer specialization. He isn't trying to break the model, he says; the model is already broken.
ex: Researching one problem means checking 10 to 15 sources
Reviews run through design, privacy, security, and more
Design alone splits into interaction, motion, content, research, and other roles

items.d: Each one has a good reason
Even small features take several sprints
Can't keep up with the pace of change

l323|398.c: Builders should focus on vision, empathy, communication, creativity, and judgment, and automate the rest.
l323|398.e: The full stack builder model aims to let great builders take an idea to market regardless of function, tech stack, or team, with humans and machines working together fluidly instead of handing off in sequence. He believes people should spend their time on five skills, and the most important is judgment: making high-quality decisions in complex, ambiguous situations. He also thinks AI's creativity still falls short of a human's. This isn't about working alone. Teams become small pods of cross-functional people who attack a problem for a quarter and then regroup.
ex: He compares it to Navy SEALs: cross-trained, small squads, quickly assembled per mission
AI-native startups naturally start out working as full stack builders

root.d: Hand as much of the rest as possible to AI

items.d: A compelling picture of the future
Most important: good calls amid ambiguity

l323|398.c: The transformation rests on platform, tools, and culture, and off-the-shelf tools never work out of the box at scale.
l323|398.e: A startup with no legacy can simply start this way. At LinkedIn's scale, it amounts to adopting a new production function. The first pillar is platform: rebuilding the core platform and composable UI components so AI can reason over them. The second is tools: agents for the parts of the work outside those five human skills. The third is culture, which he calls the biggest and most important piece. One of his hardest lessons was that external coding and design tools couldn't understand LinkedIn's codebase and design system on their own, so the team had to customize them with vendors almost like a private beta.
ex: They worked with Copilot, Cursor, Windsurf, Figma, and others to adapt the tools
Different teams prefer different design tools, and standardizing is hard

items.d: Incentives, role models, reviews; the most critical
Automate the steps outside human skills
Rebuild code and design systems for AI to reason over

l323|398.c: Specialized agents draw their power from company-specific knowledge; curated golden examples beat opening up everything.
l323|398.e: LinkedIn built agents for trust, growth, user research, data analysis, and other domains, each led by that domain's owner, because outside tools don't have that knowledge. At first they pointed AI at the entire shared drive and it hallucinated badly, since it couldn't tell which old documents mattered or which requirements actually succeeded. So they switched to hand-picked golden examples, much like he curated quality professional posts one by one when rebuilding the feed over a decade ago. Build an agent for a single task first so you can evaluate it, then add an orchestration layer so the agents work together.
ex: The trust agent re-reviewed the old Open to Work spec and found risks missed at the time
A research agent role-played a small-business owner reviewing a marketing spec and changed the team's direction
A maintenance agent now handles nearly half of build failures

items: Plug in the whole shared drive
Can't tell important from trivial, wins from losses

d.verdict: Feed the right data, not all the data

l323|398.c: Measure the gain as experiments times quality divided by time, not just how many shots you take.
l323|398.e: Many people assume AI just lets a team take more shots on goal. He cares more about the organization becoming nimbler and more resilient, so its speed of response can match the speed of change. In the pilots, product, design, and engineering each save several hours per person per week, and spec discussions are noticeably better, which in turn saves more time. Designers now fix bugs straight from tickets and submit code, and PMs build their own data dashboards, neither of which happened before. He expects top-line metrics to move only after a broader rollout in about six months.
ex: Teams like semantic people search and semantic job search use these tools in development
The heaviest users with the most feedback are the company's top talent

terms.d: Divided by time from idea to launch

result.d: A nimbler, more resilient organization

l323|398.c: Shipping tools isn't enough; you drive change through reviews, pilot role models, and training.
l323|398.e: He asked his team: once the tools are ready, will people use them? The answer was no. Only the leading-edge 5% or so adopt on their own; everyone else needs change management, just as when LinkedIn moved from desktop to mobile. The playbook: put AI agency and fluency into hiring, calibration, and semiannual reviews; give executives, who now manage by product area, cross-functional 360 reviews; create real success stories in pilot pods and celebrate them at all-hands; and train newcomers through an entirely new program.
ex: The APM program ends this year; from January it becomes APB, Associate Product Builder
A user researcher used these tools to move into a growth PM role
The head of partnerships built the developer portal himself

items.d: AI skills in hiring and reviews
It becomes a movement people want in on

l323|398.c: Don't wait for a formal reorg; it's a full-stack mindset, not a title, and specialists remain but fewer.
l323|398.e: He doesn't care about your title, only how you work. If you're waiting for a reorg or an announcement before changing how you operate, you've already waited too long. Your career interests and the organization's needs line up: both call for being at the frontier of how things get built. Not everyone has to become a full stack builder. Specialists, and the systems builders who equip them, still have value, just in smaller numbers. For leaders, he advises naming the mountain you're climbing from the start, staying urgent about the goal, patient about the execution, and sharing progress publicly throughout.
ex: Lesson: the core team built behind closed doors too long; let the company see and try it earlier
A big-company transformation won't double productivity in a week

marks.d: Still needed, but fewer of them
Builds the platform that equips full stack builders
Takes an idea all the way to launch

l324|572.c: A small elite team amplified by AI can build a billion-dollar company without raising money.
l324|572.e: Back at big tech companies he felt that cutting 90% of staff would make things faster, because the best people would stop being distracted by busywork. So Surge hired only a few elite people from the start. Fewer people means less capital, which means no need to fundraise, and the founder can be a technical, product-minded person rather than someone good at pitching and hype. The cost of no funding and no hype is no media halo; you have to win on a product ten times better that spreads by word of mouth among researchers. He thinks that filtered for early customers who truly understood data and shared the mission.
ex: Over $1 billion in revenue last year with fewer than 100 employees
No venture capital, and almost no promotion on social media

items.d: Elite team plus AI for efficiency
No need to enter the fundraising cycle
Doesn't win on pitching and hype
Small, obsessive team does real innovation

l324|572.c: Data quality isn't about headcount; it's defining "good" deeply and measuring it with thousands of signals.
l324|572.e: Take the task of writing an eight-line poem about the moon. A shallow view of quality checks whether it's a poem, has eight lines, and mentions the moon. He wants unique imagery, something that moves you and leaves you with an insight. That kind of quality is subjective, complex, and hard to measure. So Surge collects thousands of signals on every annotator and every task: keystrokes, speed, review outcomes, even training a model on their output to see if it improves. The approach resembles Google search: weed out the worst on one end, surface the best on the other.
ex: A moon poem: a checklist pass versus Nobel-level poetry
Like Google search, remove the junk and find the gems

items: Done by throwing people at it

d.verdict: Quality data needs deep definitions and fine measurement

l324|572.c: Benchmarks are often wrong and easy to game; real progress needs deep evaluation by top experts.
l324|572.e: He doesn't trust benchmarks at all. Many contain wrong answers. Their questions have clear, objective answers, so models can climb them easily, which is nothing like the messy ambiguity of real work. Labs also tweak system prompts and the number of runs to inflate scores, or simply optimize for the benchmark instead of the real task. He thinks the reliable alternative is to have top experts in each field bring their own real work, talk with the model at length, and check the code and formulas line by line, rather than having casual users pick a winner on a two-second impression.
ex: Models win IMO gold medals yet still can't parse a PDF properly
Have physicists, teachers, and engineers test models on their actual jobs

items.d: Many benchmarks are full of errors
Real tasks are ambiguous and hard to define
Deep human evals by top experts

l324|572.c: Leaderboard gaming and engagement optimization teach models to chase dopamine instead of truth.
l324|572.e: LLM Arena is judged by casual voters who don't check facts and just pick the flashiest answer, so bold text, more emoji, and longer replies raise scores even when the content is made up. Enterprise customers confront sales teams with the rankings, and researchers' promotions are tied to them, so labs game the board even knowing it makes models worse. He worked in social media and saw the clickbait that engagement optimization produced; today's sycophantic models that go along with users' delusions follow the same logic. His principle: you are your objective function. Optimize for hard-to-measure things that enrich people's lives, not proxies like clicks.
ex: Arena shortcuts: bold text, twice the emoji, three times the length
The sycophantic reply: "You're absolutely right, great question"

l324|572.c: Models will diverge because their makers' values and objectives differ, rather than becoming interchangeable.
l324|572.e: A year ago he expected models to catch up with each other and become commodities. Then he realized a company's values shape its model. Post-training involves countless choices: the mix of human and synthetic data, front-end versus back-end emphasis, whether to chase academic benchmarks for publicity, and which aesthetic to prefer. It's more art than pure science. Claude has led in coding and writing for a long time, and data is a big reason, but the objective function and taste matter more. Just as Google, Facebook, and Apple would build different search engines, models will each have a personality.
ex: He once spent 30 minutes and 30 drafts having Claude revise an email
He thinks Anthropic makes more principled choices about model behavior

terms.d: Human vs. synthetic, front-end vs. back-end emphasis
What counts as good design and writing

result.d: Like search engines from different companies

l324|572.c: Post-training moved from imitation to practice in environments; RL environments are the next stage exposing real gaps.
l324|572.e: He compares it to how people learn. Supervised fine-tuning is imitating a master. RLHF is writing many essays and having someone pick the best. Rubrics and verifiers are getting graded line by line. RL environments are being dropped into a simulated world to figure things out yourself. Each new method adds to the others rather than replacing them. Environments contain the real mess of email, Slack, tickets, and codebases, and models that are great at single tool calls fail badly on long chains of tasks. You also have to inspect the intermediate trajectory so models don't luck into answers by flailing or exploiting the reward. He thinks LLMs still need new breakthroughs and his AGI timeline is long.
ex: A simulated startup where AWS and Slack suddenly go down, to see what the model does
He estimates 80% of an L6 engineer's work automated in one to two years, but AGI is 10+ years away

items.d: Pick the best of many attempts
Graded against criteria, told what's wrong
End-to-end practice in a simulated world

l324|572.c: Don't keep pivoting; build only the company that wouldn't exist without you.
l324|572.e: He dislikes the standard Silicon Valley script: pivot every two weeks hunting for product-market fit, chase growth with dark patterns, blitzscale the headcount. To him, a startup is supposed to take big risks for a conviction. Constant pivoting is really risk avoidance and valuation chasing, and failing because the market isn't ready beats pivoting into yet another wrapper company. For big decisions he doesn't consult metrics or the board; he asks what he cares about, because a company is ultimately an embodiment of its CEO. The thing he most wishes he'd known earlier: you can succeed without funding or hype if the product is good enough to cut through the noise.
ex: The founder who did crypto in 2020, NFTs in 2022, and AI today
He'd rather be Terence Tao than Warren Buffett

items.d: He spans math, computer science, and linguistics

items.t: One big idea you believe in

items.d: No trend-chasing, no piling on PMs

items.t: The company only you can build
items.d: No pivoting when it gets hard

l325|638.c: AI capabilities are hard to predict, so OpenAI works truly bottom-up and experiments instead of setting a course first.
l325|638.e: At Dropbox and at his own startup, a PM's job was to point the ship before speeding up. At OpenAI nobody knows when the next capability will arrive, whether it will work technically, or whether users will want it, so humility and fast experimentation matter more. There is still aim, but it's fuzzy: you can discuss a vision a year or more out, like alignment, and you can discuss the next few weeks. The hardest part to reason about is the middle zone around one year. He cautions that this approach depends on very high talent density and personal drive, and most companies can't copy it directly.
ex: Even if models stopped improving, the product layer would still be far behind
Codex grew 10x in a few months, which made him much stricter about time

marks.d: What to build, how it's used: experiment
Around a year out; hardest to reason about

l325|638.c: Codex needs to go from a pairing tool to a proactive teammate that is useful by default.
l325|638.e: He compares today's Codex to a brilliant intern who never reads Slack or checks the monitoring dashboards: however smart, it can only pair with you. A typical user prompts AI a few dozen times a day, while a smart partner could help thousands of times a day. That's why he says today's AI products are actually hard to use: you have to figure out when to call them. The goal is to onboard it like a new colleague, share context, give starter tasks, and eventually let it decide what to do. Proactive help should surface in context, like autocomplete: it speeds you up when right and doesn't annoy you when wrong, instead of pushing a thousand notifications a day.
ex: Autocomplete: faster when it's right, barely disruptive when it's wrong
Tesla Autopilot: you can nudge it any time without turning it off

items.d: Learn the codebase and how the team communicates
Hand off tasks; it finishes asynchronously
It decides what to do on its own

l325|638.c: Codex took off by lowering the barrier to entry and iterating the model and harness together.
l325|638.e: The original Codex Cloud ran asynchronously in the cloud and could parallelize massively, but users had to set up environments and learn a new way of prompting, like hiring a colleague you can never call, only message. People inside OpenAI were used to that; people outside weren't, so internal dogfooding gave biased signals. The team switched to local pairing in the IDE and terminal, with a sandbox for safety, so setup happens naturally during use, and delegation of long tasks comes later. Meanwhile research and product tune the model, API, and harness together. Context compaction, for instance, needs all three layers working in concert before a model can run for a whole day.
ex: Usage grew about 20x after GPT-5 launched
Codex-Max is roughly 30% faster on comparable tasks

terms.d: IDE and CLI plus sandbox; configure as you go
Model, API, and harness tuned in sync

result.d: The most-called coding model in the API

l325|638.c: Whatever agent you want to build, you should probably build a coding agent first.
l325|638.e: A super-assistant has to get things done, and the most effective way for a model to do things is to use a computer. Compared with digging through operating-system accessibility APIs or simulating clicks, writing code is the best way for a model to use a computer. Code composes and can be reused, so a team can turn the things its agent does often into scripts that a new colleague can pick up on day one. He thinks coding agents are already very valuable while non-coding agents are still early, and they'll get much better once they can write code in a composable way. Even financial analysis might get done by writing code, without the user ever noticing.
ex: Data scientists tag Codex in Slack to ask why a metric moved
Each team keeps its own meta-prompts for crash analysis

root.d: A super-assistant has to get things done

items.d: Depends on each app's support; uneven

l325|638.c: The most underrated bottleneck is how fast humans can type, multitask, and review.
l325|638.e: Writing code is the part many engineers enjoy most. Once agents take it over, people get stuck reviewing AI-written code, which is less fun. So the team's principle is to speed up the human as much as possible: build code review features, have the agent verify its own work, and show a preview of the result before the diff. He believes productivity only hits a hockey-stick curve once agents are useful by default and can prove their results. He expects that next year at greenfield startups first, then at big companies with complex systems, and once the speedup flows back into AI labs themselves, we're close to AGI.
ex: Codex code review has already caught errors in training configs
They're trying to have Codex babysit its own training runs

items.d: Limited by typing and multitasking speed

l325|638.c: Coding agents let small teams ship hit products in weeks and compress the boundaries between roles.
l325|638.e: Sora for Android was a brand-new app. Two or three engineers had Codex read the iOS version, write a plan, and implement it. Employees got a beta in 18 days, the public release came in 28 days, and it topped the app store. Cross-platform ports with an existing reference are exactly what Codex is good at. The Atlas team says work that took two or three people two or three weeks now takes one person one week. He borrows the phrase "compressing the talent stack": when each person can do more, there's one less communication boundary. Designers vibe-code prototypes and turn them into PRs; product marketers edit copy directly from Slack.
ex: Atlas: two or three people for two or three weeks became one person for one week
Lots of throwaway code, like a quick interactive data viewer

l325|638.c: As building gets easy, the most valuable skill is deep understanding of a specific customer's problems.
l325|638.e: Building used to be so hard that the ability to build was scarce on its own, and you didn't need to deeply know a customer segment. Now, if he could pick only one skill, it would be truly understanding a particular customer's problems. If you have customers that AI tools have overlooked and the relationships to reach them, a startup is almost a sure thing; if you can only build websites and have nobody to serve, it's a hard road. Ideas are worth less than people think, and execution and distribution remain hard work. His advice to young people: be someone who does things, use the newest tools, and either learn what good software systems and teamwork look like or go deep on some frontier of knowledge.
ex: When hiring early-career people, he looks at how productive they are with new tools
The gap between junior and senior people is shrinking

items: Can spin up a website fast
The barrier to building is disappearing

d.verdict: Scarcity is shifting from building to understanding customers

l326|23.c: In AI, growth is 95% innovation and 5% optimization, and only 30–40% of the old playbook still applies.
l326|23.e: At every past company, about 80% of her problems fit familiar frameworks and most of her time went to optimizing existing user journeys. Lovable is different. The category is in a fast current, so demand mostly needs catching rather than creating, and competitors keep pouring in. Staying ahead means reinventing the solution, not tuning the funnel, so the growth team builds new features and new growth loops. Even activation, usually growth's most important job, is no longer growth-led: the core agent team works around the clock on the first generation, because an agent that understands intent better improves the whole lifecycle. The growth team now helps write agent instructions.
ex: The growth team shipped a Shopify integration so users can build online stores
The growth team launched voice mode to boost engagement

l326|23.c: Shipping constantly and talking about it publicly is itself an acquisition, win-back, and retention strategy.
l326|23.e: Building in public is one of Lovable's core strategies: founders and employees keep telling social media what's happening. Big launches still come in three tiers, with tier-one launches meant to step-change product-market fit. But what matters more is shipping and announcing something every day, sometimes several times a day, so the product feels alive. Users check social media to see what's new. The loop from feedback to delivery is short, which makes people feel heard, and that brings lapsed users back better than any newsletter. l327|550.c: Jailbreaks and prompt injection are different, and injection gets far more dangerous once agents can act.
l327|550.e: A jailbreak involves only the user and the model, like using a long prompt to trick a chatbot into giving dangerous information. Prompt injection adds a third party: the developer's system prompt. The attacker gets the model to ignore the developer's instructions and do something else. Early cases were things like making a company's Twitter bot post threats, or tricking a math-solving site into running malicious code and leaking keys. A chatbot can only do so much damage. But an agent that can edit databases or send email, or a robot driven by a vision-language model, can cause real financial and even physical harm once it's fooled.
ex: MathGPT was tricked into writing code that leaked an OpenAI API key
Splitting an attack into several innocent-looking requests got past Claude Code's defenses

A malicious page or email makes the agent leak data

l327|550.c: Guardrails simply don't work: the attack space is nearly infinite, so blocking 99% means nothing.
l327|550.e: A guardrail is usually a model that judges whether inputs and outputs are malicious, placed before and after the main model. But every possible prompt is a potential attack. For a model like GPT-5, the number of attacks is roughly a one followed by a million zeros. Block 99% and infinitely many remain, and no test sample is statistically meaningful. The reliable method is adaptive evaluation, where attackers adjust to your defenses, and humans are the strongest adaptive attackers. Guardrails don't deter anyone either: whoever can fool GPT-5 can get around a guardrail in passing. Some guardrails don't even support non-English text, and translation is a common attack.
ex: In research with three major labs, humans broke every defense in about 10 to 30 attempts
He considers prompt-based defenses the worst kind

root.d: A classifier model before and after the main model

l327|550.c: The "red-team audit plus guardrails" model sells false security, and a shakeout of those vendors is coming.
l327|550.e: The typical pitch: a vendor runs automated red teaming against a company's model, surfaces hate speech or dangerous information, scares the security lead, and then sells guardrails. But automated red teaming works against any transformer model, and companies mostly use off-the-shelf frontier models, so the audit reveals nothing new. Point the same tools at the vendor's own guardrails and they break too. He thinks these companies have little revenue and open-source options are often better, and he expects a market correction within six months to a year. Around the same time, real-world harm from agents being tricked will start to appear.

Adversarial attacks on image classifiers never became real threats; LLM agents are different

l327|550.c: AI security differs from traditional security: you can patch a bug, but you can't patch a brain.
l327|550.e: Fix a bug in traditional software and you can be 99.99% sure it won't come back. Do the same thing to a model and you can be equally sure the problem is still there. Adversarial robustness is a decades-old problem, and the smartest researchers at frontier labs haven't cracked it in recent years, so an ordinary company with almost no AI researchers certainly won't solve it by buying something. He sees another reason labs underinvest: intelligence comes before security, because an extremely safe but dumb model is worthless. And today's agents are often too dumb to do much damage even when they're fooled.
ex: He sees no real progress on adversarial robustness in recent years
Many security people instinctively assume AI can't be fooled by a single sentence

items: Can't be patched one by one
The problem probably remains after a fix
Any prompt could be an attack

d.verdict: Don't treat AI like traditional cybersecurity

l327|550.c: Defend by capability tier: read-only chatbots need no defense; systems that can act need locked-down permissions.
l327|550.e: A chatbot that only answers questions and only touches the current user's data can, at worst, be tricked into saying something bad. Users can get the same thing from ChatGPT, and guardrails won't stop it, so it needs no defense. But make sure it really is just a chatbot. His rule: any data the AI can access, a user can make it leak; any action it can take, a user can make it take in any order. He suggests designing isolation as if the AI were an angry god out to hurt you, for example running AI-written code inside a container. The most important thing is people who understand both AI security and traditional security.
ex: For MathGPT-style risk, run code execution inside a Docker container
Have a security researcher who understands AI on the team

items.d: Truly dangerous; needs a CAMEL-style architecture

Reputation risk at most; no defense needed

l327|550.c: CAMEL narrows permissions in advance based on user intent; it blocks some injections but isn't a cure-all.
l327|550.e: Google's CAMEL framework works like this: first figure out what the user wants, then grant only the permissions that task needs. If the user asks for a summary of today's email, the agent gets read-only access, so a hidden instruction to "send this to the attacker" can't run. If the user just wants a holiday greeting written, the agent doesn't need to read the inbox at all. But if the task genuinely needs both reading and writing, like reading email and forwarding an operations request to a colleague, the attack conditions line up again. It often requires re-architecting the system, but traditional security people like it, because it's really just setting permissions correctly up front.
ex: The Comet browser once leaked user data because of malicious text hidden in a web page
He sees a plug-and-play CAMEL product as a market opportunity

items.d: By default the agent can read and send
The malicious instruction has no permission to run

l327|550.c: Indirect prompt injection is far harder to stop than dangerous information; the hope is early adversarial training and new architectures.
l327|550.e: To block CBRN information you just tell the model "never." For an action like sending email, you can only say "usually yes, but not when it looks suspicious," and that boundary is hard to describe and hard to train, so indirect injection against agents remains far from solved. Labs report robustness using static datasets built for older models; they should use adaptive evaluations with humans in the loop. More promising is adversarial training early in pretraining, or new architectures, because gains in capability haven't brought robustness. He also urges researchers to stop writing jailbreak papers, and doesn't think asking a human for approval on everything is what the market will ultimately accept.
ex: Anthropic's constitutional classifiers made extracting dangerous information harder, but a human can still do it within an hour

l328|406.c: Extraordinary results require extraordinary effort, and only a company that's winning can ask for it.

Conversely, at a company growing only 30–40% a year, employees can't believe weekend work will pay off. Fast growth gives a leader the standing to ask for the last drop. In a competitive market a team can't relax, because any gap gets filled by a hungrier rival. But that isn't the same as grinding individuals down.

l328|406.c: When you take over product, fix the foundations first, do things in order, and get your hands dirty.

The talent was good, but the team was badly understaffed and lacked a single spiritual leader, so each part optimized locally while the whole fell out of sync. Per Conway's law, the product experience fractured the same way. From the outside he assumed the problem was not tracking adoption; inside, he found there weren't even basics like test coverage standards or a release checklist, and jumping to adoption would have been absurd. The lesson: stay urgent but go in order, and build hypotheses bottom-up from front-line detail. Watching from a distance and assuming you know the answer is the cardinal sin of an executive.

l328|406.c: Process exists only to reduce variance, but it also suppresses outsized returns, so dose it by context.

A zero-to-one product chases alpha and can tolerate variance; a product like payroll must be low-beta, so more process is fine. The only purpose of process is to reduce beta, at the cost of suppressing alpha, so add it only where stability matters. One example is the product quality checklist, or PQL: every launch gets checked line by line, and every incident adds a line. The same lens applies to people: high-alpha people belong in exploratory areas. He also decodes his interview gut feel with six traits: smart, passionate, optimistic, resilient, adaptable, and kind.

l328|406.c: Power laws and entropy mean leaders must keep injecting energy; don't be a hands-off boss.

Entropy pulls everything toward disorder: every extra line of code takes more energy to maintain, and teams will always trade company outcomes for local comfort. So every bug you see gets thrown publicly to its owner, and every skipped reference check gets stopped. The founder-CEO has the highest intensity, and each management layer out can lose an order of magnitude, so managers should replicate that intensity rather than buffer it. A name next to every number

l330|644.c: In turbulent times, leaders needn't have all the answers, but must fire, avoid promises, and put the business first.
l330|644.e: In fast change, she says, a leader's job is not to have answers but to help everyone find them together, and saying "I don't know" takes courage. Don't promise things you can't control: stability, titles, or that you'll never hire above someone. Breaking those promises is the fastest way to crush a top performer. Firing matters as much as hiring. Even the best hirers get it right only about half the time, and the wrong people stick to the team like barnacles on a hull. Hard decisions should serve the business, not please individuals, and being direct is a form of kindness. Spend your energy on top performers and use small experiments to test and expand what they can do.
ex: Claire Hughes Johnson calls such promises letter bombs you mail to yourself
She says even the best hirers are right only about 50% of the time

items.d: You can't control stability or titles
Or barnacles build up on the hull

l330|644.c: About 80% of a company's culture is the founder's personality; operators extend it, not reshape it.
l330|644.e: She once owned culture at Facebook and thought her job was to shape it. Then she noticed one sentence from Mark Zuckerberg at an all-hands did more than months of her effort. To her, Google felt like a paradise built for two PhD students, and Facebook like a 19-year-old hacker's dorm room. Culture is simply "how we do things here," and it shows up in whom you hire, whom you fire, and how decisions get made, not in slogans on the wall. Writing values that don't match the founder only creates a mismatch between words and behavior. Her version of founder mode: build a company that makes decisions the way the founder would, even when the founder isn't in the room.
ex: Zuckerberg: escalating is a tool to unblock things, not tattling
After leaving Facebook she never ran a values exercise again

terms.d: Whom you hire, fire, and how you decide

result.d: How we do things here

l330|644.c: Don't more than double headcount in a year; 50% is comfortable, and more people won't make you faster.
l330|644.e: She learned this from Sheryl Sandberg: growing headcount 50% a year is comfortable, doubling is manageable, and anything beyond that is asking for pain. When you grow too fast, nobody has time to remove duplication. Different teams each hire someone for the same job and only notice the collision once both start. Cleaning that up costs enormous time, energy, and money. Slow down and hire for real needs rather than out of panic, and you often discover that a person, a team, or even a whole function isn't needed. If you truly must grow faster, ask a few extra questions before opening every role.
ex: One founder planned to go from 50 to 150 people in a year
The layoffs after 2021 made everyone care about output per person

l330|644.c: Prove yourself first, then ask what you actually want instead of chasing what you "should" do.
l330|644.e: The first stretch of a career, she says, is the proving phase: you show yourself and others that you're good at something, often chasing titles because family or career books say you should. Eventually you hit a wall that forces the question: now that I've proven it, what do I want to do with it? She spent over a decade proving she could support brilliant founders, then realized it no longer fed her. So she turned down several glamorous executive roles and instead built a safe space where leaders can learn, grow, and connect. Her go-to question: what can this job give me that I don't already have?
ex: "LinkedIn butterflies": you want to post the new job, not do it
Her advice to OpenAI staff: assume a new boss and new job in six months

items.d: What new thing can this give me?
Do the work that actually feeds you

l331|647.c: AI products differ from traditional software in two ways: nondeterminism, and the autonomy-control trade-off.
l331|647.e: Traditional software, like Booking.com, maps what a user wants onto fixed actions through buttons and forms. AI products replace that with natural language. You can't predict how users will phrase things, and a large language model is a black box that's sensitive to wording, so input, process, and output are all hard to pin down. The second difference gets overlooked: every decision you hand to an agent is a bit of control you give up. Autonomy has to be earned through reliability, one step at a time. She also admits natural language is what makes AI so easy to use, and that's exactly its appeal.
ex: Berkeley and Databricks research: about 74–75% of enterprises say reliability is their biggest problem
Reliability worries keep most AI products stuck as low-autonomy productivity tools

items.d: Users phrase things in endless ways
The model is a probabilistic black box
Every decision you hand over is control lost

l331|647.c: AI adoption is a people problem first: hands-on leaders, a culture of empowerment, and deep workflow understanding.
l331|647.e: Every technical problem, she says, is a people problem first. Leaders have to rebuild intuitions they spent a decade forming, which means getting their hands dirty, and this kind of change almost only works top-down. Culturally, the message has to be that AI empowers people, not "use AI or be replaced." Otherwise domain experts fear for their jobs and won't help define what good behavior looks like. Technically, the teams that succeed obsess over breaking down workflows: which steps go to the model, which to deterministic code, and where a human stays in the loop.
ex: Rackspace CEO Gagan blocks 4 to 6 a.m. every day just to follow AI
One leader vibe-coded a prototype and assumed shipping would be easy

terms.d: Domain experts want to take part
Understand workflows, pick the right tools

result.d: All three are required

l331|647.c: Don't trust one-click agents: the race isn't who ships first but who builds an improvement flywheel first.
l331|647.e: She's skeptical of one-click agents that promise results within two or three days. The models aren't the problem. Enterprise data and infrastructure are messy: taxonomies are inconsistent, functions with the same name coexist, and an agent needs time to learn unwritten rules like these. She'd rather pick a vendor who promises to build a pipeline that keeps learning. Even with the best data layer and infrastructure, replacing a critical workflow and seeing a meaningful return takes four to six months.
ex: A retailer's taxonomy had duplicate men's and women's shoe categories, the old ones dead since 2019
Replacing a critical workflow usually takes 4 to 6 months

d.verdict: Pick the option that keeps learning and improving

l331|647.c: Iterate with CC/CD loops: ship with low autonomy, calibrate until surprises stop, then hand over more.
l331|647.e: The development loop: scope what the AI should do, assemble a dataset of expected inputs and outputs (which often reveals the team never agreed on how the product should behave), build the app, design evaluation metrics, and deploy. The calibration loop: study real behavior, find error patterns you didn't anticipate, fix them, and add metrics as needed. Every round starts with low autonomy and high control. There's no rule for when to level up; the signal is that new data stops surprising you. When you swap models or users start using it in deeper ways, you recalibrate.
ex: Customer support in three versions: triage tickets, draft replies, then resolve end to end
Three months after launch, users of a loan-review assistant began asking about past cases
One support agent was shut down because it needed too many hotfixes

items.d: High control; log what humans do
Find new error patterns and fix them

l331|647.c: Implementation keeps getting cheaper; problem definition, design, and judgment are the scarce skills.
l331|647.e: She half-jokes that evals are overrated, when really they're misunderstood: labeling companies, product managers, and benchmark makers have each borrowed the word until it means too many things. What's truly underrated is obsession with the business problem and with design. What's overrated is mechanically building fast, because the cost of implementation is collapsing. Early-career execution skills can now be filled in quickly with AI's help. After that, what matters is taste, judgment, and ownership. Work that looks busy but doesn't move outcomes will disappear.
ex: A new colleague vibe-coded a task tool and replaced a paid subscription
So-called AI engineers and AI PMs spend 80% of their time understanding workflows and data
One client treated checking the LM Arena leaderboard as having done evals

items.d: The core skill over the long run

l331|648.c: Start with high control and low autonomy, then level up; it forces you to define the problem first.
l331|648.e: He compares it to climbing Half Dome: nobody attempts it on day one; you train in stages. Same with AI products. Don't hand an agent every tool and all the context at the start. Begin where the stakes are low and humans stay in charge, learn what the model can actually do today, then add context and tools step by step. Start too complex and you face hundreds of errors that are nearly impossible to fix one by one. Starting small also forces you back to the problem instead of falling in love with a complicated solution.
ex: Support volume spikes whenever OpenAI launches products like image generation or GPT-5
Support: suggest to human agents, then reply to users directly, then issue refunds and file requests

items.d: Humans judge quality and expose blind spots

l331|648.c: Evals versus production monitoring is a false choice; each catches a different kind of problem.
l331|648.e: Evals encode what you reliably know about your product into data, so a change never breaks the things you care about most. Production monitoring uses explicit and implicit signals to tell you which traces to look at, like a user who doesn't hit thumbs-down but does hit "regenerate." A high-traffic product can't review every trace, so monitoring surfaces failure modes, and you build evals for the ones that truly matter. After a fix ships, monitoring is still the backstop. Codex uses both, plus A/B tests and feedback on social media.
ex: Swapping the code-review model means an A/B test to see if users get annoyed and turn it off
