With every new model, team members test their own lists of hard problems
Coding agents are so customizable that evals can't cover every use

items: Point to the traces to read

d.verdict: Complementary; one alone never works

l331|648.c: Multi-agent systems are misunderstood; coding agents are underrated, with adoption still very low.
l331|648.e: He thinks splitting a complex problem across agents by function and letting them chat peer-to-peer is very hard to make work with today's methods and models. In customer support, you can't control which agent is replying to the user, so you need guardrails everywhere. What does work is a supervisor agent dispatching sub-agents, or a human doing the orchestration. The underrated thing is coding agents: Twitter is loud about them, but engineers at ordinary companies outside the Bay Area barely use them, and the potential value is enormous.
ex: Supervisor agent plus sub-agents is a proven pattern
He expects 2025–2026 to be the big years for improving workflows with coding agents

marks.d: A person assigns work to agents
Dispatches sub-agents to do the work
Split by function, talk to each other

l331|648.c: Pain is the new moat: knowledge earned through repeated trial and error beats being first or flashy.
l331|648.e: In a new field, he says, the companies that win aren't the first to market or the flashiest. They're the ones that endured the process of learning what's non-negotiable and then trading that off against what the model can do. There's no textbook. You try one approach, it fails, you try another. That trial and error accumulates into organizational knowledge, maybe in the form of an eval suite or something else, and that's the real moat. The same holds for individuals: information is everywhere, so the people who push through the painful learning are the ones who pull ahead.
ex: The accumulated learning may show up as an eval suite

l331|648.c: Proactive background agents are coming, but only once they're plugged into where real work happens.
l331|648.e: Where AI isn't creating value today, he thinks, it's mostly because it lacks context, and it lacks context because it isn't connected to where the work actually happens. The more it's plugged in, the better an agent understands what metrics you're optimizing and what you're working on, and then it can start nudging you instead of waiting to be asked. ChatGPT Pulse, which pushes you things you might care about each day, is an early version. Extend that to coding, and an agent might greet you in the morning with several tickets already fixed and patches ready for review.
ex: ChatGPT Pulse's daily push
Imagine waking up to patches for five Linear tickets already fixed

items.d: See the metrics and daily activity

l333|651.c: Non-technical people should step up gradually: a chatbot project, then Bolt or Lovable, then Cursor.
l333|651.e: He compares it to exposure therapy: get comfortable one step at a time. He started with a "CTO" project in ChatGPT, agreeing that he owned the problem and the AI owned the technology, and asking it to push back on him. It turned out to be too agreeable. Tools like Bolt and Lovable make many technical decisions for you, which makes them easy to start with but limits your control. Cursor with Claude gives full control, at the cost of making more decisions yourself. The underlying models are much the same across tools; the difference is the harness around them. And code is just files, so you can move it any time.
ex: ChatGPT once agreed with him that Bun and Zustand were the same thing
Bolt got stuck when he tried to add payments

items.d: Give the AI a CTO role
Makes tech decisions for you; easy start

l333|651.c: Reusable slash commands lock in the process: ticket, explore, plan, build, review, update the docs.
l333|651.e: He keeps the commands in the codebase and runs them over and over. Ideas go straight into Linear through MCP. In the explore step, Claude reads the code and asks clarifying questions. Then it writes a markdown plan with a summary, key decisions and task progress. For execution, simple tasks go to the fast Composer model. After that comes a self-review, a cross-review by other models, and finally a docs update so the next agent has an easier time. An AI-written ticket is only a starting point, he says. As a one-person company, he holds all the context in his head and can correct misunderstandings right away.
ex: Adding drag-and-drop fill-in-the-blank questions to StudyMate: about 30% of questions, two blanks, six options
The plan gave the back end to Composer and the front end to Gemini 3

l333|651.c: Have several models review each other like colleagues, with Claude as the lead who defends or fixes.
l333|651.e: He gives each model a personality. Claude is the communicative, opinionated lead. Codex is the quiet senior engineer who can crack the hardest bugs. Gemini is the brilliant but messy designer. Once the code is written, he pastes the other models' review comments back to Claude and has it defend or fix each one. That goes back and forth for a few rounds until nobody can find anything wrong. Each model has different strengths, and combining them is more reliable than relying on one.
ex: Codex (GPT-5.1 Max) is reserved for the hardest bugs
Gemini is a strong designer, but watching it work in Antigravity is scary

l333|651.c: When AI gets something wrong, ask which prompt or tool caused it and fix it at the source.
l333|651.e: Every time the AI makes a mistake, he asks it to analyze which part of the system prompt, docs or tooling led to it, then changes that part so the same mistake doesn't happen again. He considers this one of his biggest sources of efficiency. Continuously iterating on prompts and tools is what separates people who use AI well from those who don't. He treats the money spent on model credits as tuition. He also has a "learning opportunity" command that asks the AI to explain a technical concept using the 80/20 rule.
ex: In two days of one week, he localized StudyMate from Hebrew to English
He built and launched a personal website from scratch in about 90 minutes

items.d: The result isn't what you wanted
Which prompt or tool led to it
Update the system prompt and docs

l333|651.c: AI is a thinking partner, not an outsourced brain, and it lets junior PMs make senior decisions sooner.
l333|651.e: He disagrees that AI lets PMs outsource their thinking. It's more like a mentor on call, but it doesn't take responsibility: if you hand in something AI generated and it's wrong, that's on you. It gives junior PMs earlier exposure to strategy, marketing and other senior decisions, plus more reps. You only get worse if you use it badly. To avoid mediocre output, feed it your style, the problem context and examples. He expects titles to collapse into everyone being a builder, but a large database migration still shouldn't be a PM's job.
ex: A PM can open a PR for a small UI change and let an engineer finish it
An AI-native codebase needs docs for every area of the code

d.verdict: AI amplifies whoever is using it

l333|651.c: AI helps you prepare for interviews, but mock interviews with real people improve you most.
l333|651.e: Preparing for his Meta PM interviews, he built a coach in a Claude project and told it not to make him feel good but to make him ready. He built a small game on Base44 to practice user segmentation questions on his commute, used Perplexity's Comet browser to analyze public question banks for the most frequent questions, and had the AI play the candidate to demonstrate a strong answer. But the biggest gains, he says, came from mock interviews with real people he found through cold outreach on LinkedIn. AI simulations only take you so far.
ex: The coach used a framework based on Ben Erez's method
Many people record their interviews and have AI give feedback, closing a missing feedback loop

l333|651.c: Early in your career, be the best learner in the room. Right now is the best time to be a junior.
l333|651.e: For his first product review at Wix, he prepared alone, hoping to impress the senior team. The format was wrong and he couldn't answer many questions. The team told him they wanted an excellent learner, not a 10x PM. He then matched each senior PM to one strength and learned from each of them separately, which also made them more willing to invest in his growth. Junior roles are scarcer, he admits, but AI lets a person build products independently, so someone curious, hardworking, kind and good at communicating has an unfair advantage.
ex: He sought out colleagues separately for methodology, product sense and systems thinking

result.t: A great time to be junior
result.d: An unfair advantage

l334|654.c: When growth stalls, diagnose in a fixed order. Fixing a downstream problem is wasted if upstream is broken.
l334|654.e: Growth usually slows gradually. The cause might be the economy, AI-driven panic, or sheer company size, but underneath it all, no company doubles forever. His order of diagnosis: churn, pricing and positioning, revenue growth from existing customers, channel saturation, and only then whether you need to grow at all. The order matters because a problem earlier in the chain cancels out any optimization later in it. The same sequence can be run in reverse to look for new sources of growth.
ex: He has founded four companies and made about 60 startup investments

l334|654.c: Churn caps your growth: more customers means more cancellations, but marketing output doesn't grow with them.
l334|654.e: A customer who saw the ad, read the homepage, paid and finished onboarding has shown strong intent. If they leave after that, the product or the marketing failed to meet their expectations. Cancellations scale with the size of the customer base, but new customers from marketing don't automatically scale with it. The bigger the bucket, the more it leaks, until inflow and outflow match. When you're unsure where to start, fix onboarding, because most churn happens early and small improvements at the front compound all the way down.
ex: With 100 new customers a month and 5% monthly churn, the customer count tops out around 2,000
Like video retention: lifting the start from 50% to 55% might lift the end from about 20% to 25%

items.d: Ceiling = monthly new ÷ monthly churn rate

l334|654.c: Churn surveys have to ask the right question, and "too expensive" is almost never the real reason.
l334|654.e: Asking "why did you cancel" invites excuses. Asking "what made you cancel" points people at the product. Even the order of dropdown options creates noise. A paying customer already accepted the price, so "too expensive" usually hides a missing integration, a broken promise or the wrong customer segment. In a complex system there is no single root cause, so keep asking a few layers down. You can also watch early for people who don't upload data, contact support often or stop logging in, and compare their behavior with those who stay. AI is good at summarizing themes, but the raw quotes should be read by humans.
ex: After Groove changed the wording, usable answers rose from about 10% to about 20%
When Smart Bear randomized the option order, each option's share evened out

items.d: Wording and option order add noise

l334|654.c: Early-stage prices are almost always too low. Raising them often doesn't cut signups, because price selects the market.
l334|654.e: Most startups set their price on a hunch and never touch it again. The textbook line, where higher prices mean fewer buyers, often doesn't hold in practice. Too cheap attracts buyers who aren't serious. At the right price, demand holds steady or even rises, and it only drops clearly at a very high price. The shape looks more like a plateau. So raising prices is often an underrated lever, and the value metric and the billing structure deserve the same fresh look.
ex: He cites Patrick Campbell's pricing data from about 4,200 startups
One enterprise founder switched $300 a year to $300 a month, a 12x increase, with no change in signups

l334|654.c: Position around the growth customers value most, not the savings. Changing pricing is changing strategy.
l334|654.e: Take the same product. Pitched as "cut your ad costs in half," the customer saves a limited amount each month and you can only take a small slice of it. Pitched as "same spend, twice the leads," the customer values growth far more than savings and you can charge much more. So position around what customers really care about: growth, retention, competitiveness. But price can't be changed in isolation. Moving upmarket brings new demands around governance, integrations and professional services, and it may clash with company culture. It's a whole-company decision.
ex: He uses Double Down to contrast the two pitches
Citing Jen Abel: enterprise contracts often land between $75,000 and $150,000
Buffer chose not to move upmarket

d.verdict: Sell the outcome customers care about most

l334|654.c: Expansion from existing customers must outweigh churn, but a healthy NRR can still hide customers leaving.
l334|654.e: Net revenue retention measures how much revenue a group of customers brings a year later, counting upgrades, downgrades and cancellations. A healthy company's growth from existing customers outpaces its churn. But NRR can mask lots of customers walking out, and percentages aren't symmetric: lose 20% and you need 25% growth to get back to even. Expansion has a ceiling. Price increases must follow the value customers perceive, ideally with value rising faster than price, and every change deserves an honest question about whether it really helps customers. A second product and in-app purchases are other ways to expand.
ex: He says only about two of a hundred-plus public SaaS companies have NRR below 100%
The median NRR at IPO is about 119%
AG1 sells more products; Duolingo has its gem system

terms.d: Price follows value; add a second product

result.d: Existing-customer growth beats churn

l334|654.c: Every channel eventually saturates and sags. Before it peaks, keep one foot on your strength and step into a new market.
l334|654.e: Audiences get exhausted, ad inventory and search volume have limits, and competitors copy good channels. So every channel follows what he calls the elephant curve: an S-shaped rise, then a droop. Know which channel has saturated, and start testing new ones before the peak. Direct and indirect sales often behave in opposite ways, and usually one main channel carries most of the growth. When expanding, keep one foot on an existing strength and step the other into a new product or market. Don't put both feet into risk at once.
ex: Constant Contact restarted growth by running in-person seminars to reach agencies
HubSpot's agency channel reached about half of revenue after four or five years
WP Engine sells heavily through agencies

l334|654.c: Decide whether you really must grow. You can change the metric or the product, but long stagnation hurts people.
l334|654.e: First define what "growth" means. If the current product or market has hit its limit, the answer may be a different product or market. You can also switch the goal from revenue to profit, or let a product stop growing or even shut it down. Growth shouldn't come from tactics you aren't proud of, or turn the company into something you hate. But long stagnation damages the growth and enthusiasm of founders and employees. He suggests asking the question at least once a year, and making a big change, like leaving or selling, when necessary.
ex: 37signals accepted a ceiling on its size, and the founders take large dividends
He says he'd be sad if his newsletter stopped growing, but flat would be acceptable

items.d: Maintain it or shut it down

l335|656.c: AI is arriving right on time: productivity has lagged for fifty years and populations are starting to shrink.
l335|656.e: He thinks the industry treats AI as a one-way force that sweeps everything aside, and ignores the economic reality. US productivity growth has been sluggish for about 50 years. Everyone feels change is fast, but the statistics don't show it. Meanwhile, fertility rates in many countries have fallen below 2, so populations will shrink over the next century. Without AI, a shrinking population means stagnation and contraction. AI and robots are showing up exactly as labor becomes scarce, which he calls almost miraculously good timing.
ex: Growth over the last 50 years is about half the 1940-1970 rate and a third of 1870-1940

result.d: Fills in for scarce labor

l335|656.c: "AI causes mass unemployment" doesn't hold: jobs outlast their tasks, and workers will get scarcer, not surplus.
l335|656.e: A job is a bundle of tasks. The tasks change first; the job persists longer than any single task, and only later gets reshuffled. Even if AI tripled productivity growth, the resulting job turnover would only match the 1870-1930 period, when new occupations kept appearing. He expects a hiring boom. For mass unemployment, productivity would have to grow 10 to 50 percent a year, which has never happened. And if it did, prices would collapse, which amounts to a raise for everyone and makes social safety nets cheaper.
ex: He calls this basic economics, not a bold prediction
With fewer people and less immigration, the remaining workers become more valuable

marks.d: Only then mass job loss; never happened

l335|656.c: AI is the philosopher's stone: one-on-one tutoring, once reserved for elites, becomes available to everyone.
l335|656.e: Alchemists wanted to turn the most ordinary material into the most precious one. AI turns the most common thing, sand, into the scarcest thing, thinking. In education research, the most effective way to raise achievement is one-on-one tutoring, which only elites could afford. AI can make it cheap and widespread, and he expects a hybrid of school plus AI tutoring. He homeschools his 10-year-old son and wants him to go deep in one field and use AI to become exceptional. Silicon Valley parents, he says, should expose their kids to AI rather than shield them from it.
ex: Bloom's "two sigma" problem
Khan Academy and Alpha School

l335|656.c: Bits are leaping ahead while atoms stand still, and licensing cartels will slow AI's entry into physical industries.
l335|656.e: Looking back at his debate with Peter Thiel, he concedes Thiel was right: the digital world keeps advancing while the physical world has barely changed in fifty years. The buildings, bridges and dams around us are mostly decades old, and new cities and California's high-speed rail never seem to arrive. Protected cartels such as doctors, nurses, hospitals and government systems resist change. AI may diagnose better than many doctors, but it can't get a license or write a prescription. He thinks AI will force these long-standing default assumptions into the open.
ex: He says he puts "it's time to build" on his calendar every morning

l335|656.c: PMs, designers and engineers are in a standoff: each thinks AI lets them do the other two jobs.
l335|656.e: He compares it to three people pointing guns at each other: product managers, designers and engineers all believe that with AI they can take over the other two roles. He thinks each is partly right, and in the end AI may take over all three. A job is a bundle of tasks. Like the executive assistant whose tasks kept changing while the job stayed, the tasks change first and the title changes later. Hollywood's writers, directors and actors are in the same standoff, and the people who can do more than one are the most valuable.
ex: Writer-directors and other hybrids are the most sought after
AI can generate endless icons, so design's value shifts to judging how a product fits into people's lives

items.d: Thinks they can design and code
Thinks they can define and build
Thinks they can do product and design

l335|656.c: Programming keeps moving up the abstraction ladder, but top engineers still need to understand down to the chip.
l335|656.e: Programming moved from machine code and punch cards up to assembly, C and scripting languages. Each time, someone said the new way "isn't real programming," yet every layer of abstraction raised output. Today the best engineers orchestrate about ten coding agents at once and spend their time arguing with them. He stresses that deep understanding of code still matters. To judge and debug what AI produces, you need to understand the stack all the way down to the chip. A mediocre programmer can hand the work to AI, but being top-tier requires knowing how it works.
ex: He says AI coding hit a tipping point over the most recent holiday

l335|656.c: Don't be replaceable: go deep in one skill, get good at a few more, and use AI to tie them together.
l335|656.e: He borrows Scott Adams's idea: being good at two skills is worth far more than twice as much, and three is worth far more than three times, because people who can combine fields are rare and hard to replace. Larry Summers's advice is simply not to be replaceable. AI makes these combinations much easier than before. He likes the idea of the E-shaped person and suggests using spare time to let AI train you: have it set and grade assignments, watch its reasoning, ask where you could do better, then have another AI find the mistakes.
ex: He thinks a young designer with AI has a shot at reaching Jony Ive's level

l335|656.c: The AI landscape is far from settled. Both sides of the moat debate have a point, so stay flexible rather than predict.
l335|656.e: The case for durable advantages: frontier models cost billions of dollars, need vast compute and data, experts are scarce, and the regulatory and legal burden is heavy, so the field could end up an oligopoly. The counter-evidence: about a year after ChatGPT launched, several American and Chinese companies had comparable products, open source followed close behind and soon ran free on small hardware, and the big labs keep few secrets from each other. He notes that most confident predictions about the internet from 1993 to 2010 turned out wrong, so he would rather bet on several strategies at once.
ex: Anthropic reportedly built Cowork with Claude Code in about a week and a half
GitHub Copilot was once overtaken within months

items: Compute, data and talent are scarce
Several caught up within a year
Open source is free and lighter

d.verdict: Nothing structural is settled; stay open to surprises

l336|658.c: Relationships run on repair, not perfection. Going back to fix a mistake is what builds trust.
l336|658.e: In her view, secure relationships come from repair, not from never getting it wrong. Only non-humans are perfect. Repair means naming specifically what you did and how it affected the other person, without excuses, and then saying what you'll do next time. It restores trust and connection, so people cooperate more and stop being defensive. Many parents never received an apology themselves, so it feels awkward at first. She suggests simply asking your kids which one thing you could improve this week, and treating the blunt answers as a window into who they are.
ex: A model repair: I interrupted you and my tone was harsh, and there's no excuse for that
After she asks her kids, she says their behavior that week often improves

items.d: Name what you did, no excuses

l336|658.c: Connect before you correct, and connect without an agenda. People can tell when it's a transaction.
l336|658.e: She uses herself and her husband as the example: a request wrapped in blame goes nowhere, while stepping into the other person's situation first and then inviting them to join you wins cooperation. Connection is a bridge that lets two people move toward a shared interest. But it has to come with no strings attached. Even with the right words, the other person can sense when you only want the deal. She admits that efficiency-minded people find this slow and dull, and it takes deliberate practice.
ex: With a kid: sit closer, say you're glad to see them, describe instead of interrogate
At work: ask a colleague about their weekend and let the conversation slow down

items.d: Understand where they are right now

l336|658.c: Separate behavior from identity and replace judgment with the most generous interpretation, so people don't get defensive.
l336|658.e: "Late means lazy" is a judgment that equates behavior with character, and it makes people defensive instantly, which kills the conversation. Her approach: first signal that you're on the same side and believe in the person's ability, then name the specific behavior, ask what happened, and solve it together. A coach can bench a player and still trust them. She also trains herself to find the most generous interpretation, because judgment and curiosity can't coexist. That practice helped her like her own kids again.
ex: A kid who keeps jumping on the couch after being told to stop may just want some control
Someone who keeps repeating their point in a meeting may feel unheard

items: Good inside; behavior is a signal

d.verdict: Judgment and curiosity can't coexist

l336|658.c: Bad behavior is a symptom of feelings outrunning skills. Punishment widens the gap; teach the skill instead.
l336|658.e: Her training was in reward-and-punishment models, like sticker charts and time-outs, but she found they didn't match what actually helps adults change. Her core view is that kids are born with all their feelings and none of the skills to handle them, and out-of-control behavior is feelings overwhelming skills. Punishment and shame make that gap bigger. Instead, teach the skill the way you'd teach swimming. Boundaries still matter, but lasting behavior change comes from skills.

result.d: A symptom, not the root

l336|658.c: Everyone needs a domain they control. Say who owns what and state your intent, and resistance drops.
l336|658.e: The first things a small child can control are what goes into and out of their body, which is why power struggles over potty training and eating are so intense. Adults also need territory of their own and push back when they feel invaded. That's how micromanagement breeds resistance. She advises managers to spell out what belongs to the other person, what the manager leads, and where the manager will step in. Say your intent out loud too: if you explain that you review their work so they can do it independently later, they'll read your behavior through that lens.

items.d: So your actions are read correctly

l336|658.c: A sturdy leader acknowledges people's feelings, makes the decision anyway, and stays confident.
l336|658.e: Her analogy is the pilot's announcement during turbulence. Telling passengers to stop screaming dismisses their feelings and makes them more anxious. Asking whether anyone wants to come fly the plane is over-accommodating and makes people worry about the leader. The sturdy version acknowledges the turbulence and how people feel, while making a judgment and showing calm confidence. The same applies to a parent turning off the TV or a company announcing a policy change: validate the disappointment and hold the decision.
ex: When turning off the TV, acknowledge the kid's frustration without reversing the decision

l336|658.c: A boundary is what you will do, not what you need from others. When it's time to decide, don't hide behind consensus.
l336|658.e: She separates boundaries from requests: a request depends on the other person complying, while a boundary only describes what you yourself will do. Threats in place of action weaken authority. Handing a kid a decision that belongs to the adult is usually a way to dodge their emotional reaction. The same holds at work. Consensus has its place, but leaders often hold information others don't, and some calls have to be theirs. People want a leader they can locate: even in disagreement, they know where that person stands. Deciding for someone can itself be an act of care.
ex: In an elevator, don't say "don't press the buttons"; stand between the kid and the buttons
A kid refusing therapy: I'll drive you every Thursday, and what you do inside is up to you

l336|658.c: Build resilience, not happiness. Say "I believe you" and "I believe in you" together.
l336|658.e: She believes that making a child's happiness the goal produces anxiety and fragility instead. Adult well-being depends on being able to digest disappointment, jealousy and anger, and that is resilience. So don't rush to erase someone's discomfort; stay with them through it. Validating feelings and believing in capability have to come as a pair, and anxious people usually get only the first. The same goes for work: give feedback early, because avoiding it only raises the cost. The aim is a culture of "this is hard, and I can do hard things."
ex: Don't finish the puzzle for the kid: name the feeling, then say "you can do this"
She cites Kim Scott's example: feedback delayed for nine months left firing as the only option

items.d: See their capable self: I believe in you
One foot in the hole, one foot out
Struggling right now: I believe you

l337|660.c: AI builds faster than people can think, so the real bottleneck is knowing what you want.
l337|660.e: He sees two limits when working with AI agents (AI that does tasks on its own). The model can only hold so much context at once, and people describe what they want vaguely. Tell a genie "make me taller" and it takes you literally. He can't fix the first limit, but the second is entirely in his hands. So he spends most of his time planning and talking with the agent, and only a little actually building. He doesn't read the code itself, but he reads closely how the agent explains what it is doing, to check that it understood him.
ex: Roughly 80% of his time goes to planning and conversation, 20% to execution
He starts with a voice "brain dump," then opens a new project once the idea is clear

l337|660.c: Start the same idea four or five ways at once; the extra credits save days of rework later.
l337|660.e: For one idea, he opens several projects at the same time, each driven by a different kind of input, then picks the one that works best and keeps going. His reasoning: English can't describe a screen down to the pixel, so handing over a reference design or a ready-made code snippet is often more precise than words. The first few rounds do burn credits, but he believes that avoids days of back-and-forth fixes later, and most tools offer free credits anyway. While the agents run, he flips between five or six browser tabs.
ex: Design references come from sites like Mobbin and Dribbble
Code snippets come from component libraries like 21st.dev

items.d: Show what it should look like

l337|660.c: Treat the agent like a new engineer and keep it briefed with a set of documents.
l337|660.e: For each project he writes a few Markdown files. A master plan says why the product exists, who it's for, and how it should feel. An implementation plan sets the order: database tables first, then authentication, then outside integrations. A design spec keeps the AI from over-designing. A user-journey doc describes sign-up and onboarding. A task list says what comes next. A rules file tells the agent to read all of this first, do one task at a time, and report what it changed and how it tested it. After that he mostly just says "next task," and can run several projects side by side.
ex: One task at a time, so the agent doesn't burn its context across 60 or 70 functions
He built a custom GPT that turns a brain dump into a PRD and starter prompts

items.d: Read docs first, one task, report tests

l337|660.c: When stuck, try four fixes in order; the problem is usually your own prompt.
l337|660.e: He finds today's agents obedient but not very honest: they often claim something is fixed when it isn't, so debugging needs a routine. First, click the tool's built-in fix button. Second, have the agent add logging and paste the console output back to it. Third, export the code to GitHub and ask a different model to diagnose only, without changing code. Fourth, roll back to an earlier version, rephrase the request, or just take a break. Once it's fixed, he asks the tool what he should have said in the first place and adds that lesson to the rules file. Getting angry doesn't help; the agent just spends tokens apologizing.
ex: Codex diagnoses only, or Repomix bundles the code for Claude to review
A feature he fought for a week took 30 seconds once the right API shipped

items.d: Use the error the tool flags
Add logs, paste console output back
Roll back, rephrase, take a break

l337|660.c: Everyone can now reach "good enough," so the gap between good enough and world-class is taste.
l337|660.e: He argues that AI makes mediocre output cheap. Users don't care what tech stack is underneath; they care whether the experience feels remarkable. To know what world-class looks like, you have to deliberately increase your "exposure hours": study the best products, designs, and copy. Right now he thinks product managers have the edge, because they are good at spelling out requirements. But the next winners may be designers, since models have learned technical decisions more than emotional judgment. He doesn't recommend learning to code today; judgment is what gets rewarded.
ex: He borrows the idea of "exposure hours" from Guillermo Rauch
He built an app cataloguing about 18 UI styles with prompts to recreate them

l337|660.c: A prototype built in an afternoon moves a decision further than weeks of documents.
l337|660.e: "Demos over memos" was Lovable's slogan for 2025. His reasoning: describing a complex system in writing takes ages, while a clickable prototype lets everyone understand it immediately. Even companies that can't ship AI-built code straight to production use it heavily for internal tools and prototypes. Based on what he has seen, he estimates that at least half of the S&P 500 have employees using Lovable, across healthcare, finance, telecom, and more.
ex: An enterprise prototype built in 4 hours was productionized by engineers 6–7 months later
Examples: a Shopify integration template, a merch store, a feature-adoption tracker

items.d: Instead of a long spec document

l337|660.c: Middle-layer and rule-based jobs are most at risk; engineers, top creators, and people work get amplified.
l337|660.e: He thinks tasks with clear input-to-output rules, and go-between roles that translate between people and tools, are the easiest to replace. Routine journalism, the research and the writing, will also be taken over by AI. But someone still has to maintain, scale, and protect everything being built, so engineers stay essential, even as hand-written code becomes a niche craft like calligraphy. Top writers will see their output multiplied. Comedy and genuine human connection are hard to replace. He also sees engineer, designer, and product manager merging into one role.
ex: He points to the Cloudflare outage as a sign infrastructure is under growing strain
He calls himself a "rapid engineer"

d.verdict: Find the part of your field AI can't replace

l337|660.c: Hire yourself as a professional vibe coder first; building in public is your résumé.
l337|660.e: He studied forestry engineering, did manual labor, ran communities for years, and had barely written code. Not knowing what he "shouldn't" do is exactly what made him bold enough to try. Lovable hired him mainly because he shared his failures and lessons openly on YouTube and LinkedIn. His view: plenty of people can build things now; what's scarce is distribution and attention. So instead of sending résumés, ship an app you made. Don't wait for a company to hire you. Start doing the job you wanted anyway.
ex: He started vibe coding in July 2024, before the term existed
Some companies hire people just to move old CRMs and CMSs onto Lovable

items.d: Post the failures and the lessons

l338|661.c: Engineers are becoming tech leads directing a crowd of agents, a bit like wizards casting spells.
l338|661.e: At OpenAI, almost all code is now written first by AI, and even managers like him hand everything to Codex, OpenAI's coding agent. Engineers often run ten to twenty threads at once, giving feedback and correcting course the way a tech lead would. He borrows a line from the textbook Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs that compares programming to casting spells, and then invokes the sorcerer's apprentice: agents give enormous leverage, but if you can't control them, things get out of hand. The gap in output between heavy users and everyone else keeps widening.
ex: About 95% of engineers use Codex every day
Codex reviews every pull request
Heavy users submit roughly 70% more pull requests

l338|661.c: Agents mostly fail for lack of context, so write the team's unspoken knowledge into the codebase.
l338|661.e: One internal team lets only Codex write code, with no human taking over to patch things. They found that when it failed, the task was usually underspecified or missing background. The fix is to take the tribal knowledge that lived only in people's heads and write it down as comments, code structure, Markdown files, and reusable skills. Code review changed too: Codex comments first, and a person only skims the result. Small changes sometimes skip human review entirely. Chores like fixing lint errors and re-running CI are automated as well.
ex: A review dropped from 10–15 minutes to 2–3 minutes
At Quora he reviewed 20–50 pull requests a day

l338|661.c: AI amplifies high-agency people, so managers should give over half their time to the top 10%.
l338|661.e: He has watched these tools make proactive people wildly more productive, which widens the gap inside a team, so he now spends most of his energy on his strongest people. He borrows the "surgical team" idea from The Mythical Man-Month: the manager's job is to look around corners and clear obstacles so the surgeon can focus. One engineer can already direct twenty or thirty agents, far beyond the six to eight people a human manager handles, and he expects spans of control to grow everywhere. He also uses ChatGPT connected to GitHub and Notion to research performance reviews.
ex: ChatGPT can draw on company knowledge to surface current and potential blockers

items.d: Over half your time to the top 10%
Clear obstacles so the surgeon focuses

l338|661.c: The knock-on effect of one-person billion-dollar companies is a golden age for small business and B2B software.
l338|661.e: Once starting a company gets easy, he cares more about the chain reaction: tens of thousands of ten-million-dollar companies and a flood of custom software built for them. A solo founder might buy services from dozens or hundreds of small vendors, for example outsourcing customer support to a tiny startup that does only that. So small B2B software businesses should thrive. The cost is that venture-style outsized returns may become rarer, and the ecosystem turns into a few big platforms holding up countless small companies.
ex: He imagines tens of thousands of $10 million companies

items.d: Support and more outsourced to small teams

l338|661.c: Many enterprise AI deployments may be losing money, because adoption is ordered from the top only.
l338|661.e: He admits he has no hard data, but suspects many companies' AI spending is currently net negative. Silicon Valley is a bubble; outside it, employees are told to "use AI" without knowing how. Leadership issues the mandate, but nobody on the ground picks it up on their own. His suggestion is a small "tiger team": find the enthusiasts inside the company, often technically minded operations leads rather than scarce engineers, and have them run hackathons, talks, and show-and-tells so adoption spreads from peer to peer.

d.verdict: Let a few insiders drive adoption bottom-up

l338|661.sc: Don't listen too hard to customers
l338|661.c: Models will eat your scaffolding, so build for next year's model, not today's.
l338|661.e: Models and tools change so fast that customer requests are usually small tweaks to whatever works best right now. In 2023 everyone needed vector databases and agent frameworks; stronger models plus simple search and file-based context replaced them, and the file-based approach may be replaced in turn. That is the "bitter lesson": simple methods plus stronger models keep winning. So a product that only works 80% of the time today may become fully usable the moment the next model ships. He also tells founders not to worry too much about OpenAI crushing them; startups mostly die because customers don't care.
ex: The vector databases and agent frameworks of 2023
Cursor shows a crowded market can still be won on product

l338|661.c: The biggest changes ahead: agents working for hours, usable voice, and business-process automation.
l338|661.e: By METR's curve, frontier models are already fairly reliable on software tasks of up to an hour. He expects that within a year to eighteen months they will work coherently for several hours or even a full day, which will need new product forms and feedback loops. Voice is underrated, because so much business happens by talking, and he thinks end-to-end voice models will improve noticeably within six to twelve months. He also believes repeatable business processes, like support scripts and standard operating procedures, could be a market as large as software engineering, even though Silicon Valley pays little attention.
ex: METR's curve of how long a task AI can complete on its own
OpenAI's Responses API, Agents SDK, AgentKit, and Evals

l339|232.c: Starting a company has never been easier, scaling one never harder, and distribution is the bottleneck.
l339|232.e: From cloud services to AI tools, the cost of building a company keeps falling, so he expects far more new companies over the next decade. But more companies means more noise and tougher competition, which makes standing out harder. Most founders are good at building product and have never learned distribution, getting the product in front of customers, and that is now the choke point. In this environment, he says, how fast you learn is your biggest advantage.
ex: AWS, around 2006, sharply lowered the cost of starting a company

items.d: Cloud, then AI, lower the bar
Big jump over the next decade

l339|232.c: Don't trust your interview gut: use backchannel references, hire spiky people, and favor insiders.
l339|232.e: CEOs, he finds, overrate their own interview judgment and underrate backchannel references through mutual contacts. Ask former colleagues whether they would enthusiastically hire the person again, and whether they rank in the top 1% or top 10%. HubSpot used to favor candidates with no weak spots, then switched to people with a standout strength and obvious gaps, and cut the interview panel from eight to about four; the hit rate went up. Executives parachuted in from big companies and consulting firms often struggle, so when candidates are close, pick the insider.
ex: Parker Conrad has CFO candidates critique his board deck
He estimates at least half of executive hires leave within 18 months
The 2004 Red Sox: homegrown talent plus a few expensive veterans

d.verdict: Hire slow, fire fast, and use culture to glue old and new

l339|232.c: Judge a founder on five things: lovable, obsessed, a chip on the shoulder, knowledge, and a student.
l339|232.e: He scores founders with LOCKS. Lovable: do people want to follow them? Obsession: are they deeply attached to the problem? Chip: do they have something to prove? Knowledge: do they know the industry deeply? Student: do they keep studying it like a student? He is skeptical of anyone who only started caring about a problem six months ago. His research with Terence Rohan also found that successful founders are extraordinarily ambitious and often go after things other people consider crazy.
ex: Winston Weinberg of Harvey
James Cadwallader of Profound
Gabe Stengel of Rogo

root.d: Five ways to size up a founder

l339|232.c: Enterprise sales will be the last white-collar job AI replaces, but the top of the funnel changes first.
l339|232.e: AI has already transformed software development, customer support, and legal work, he notes, but sales and marketing have barely moved. The enterprise sales process looks much like it did in the 1990s, and most "forward-deployed engineers" are sales engineers with a new title. Trust between people is hard to automate, so sales roles go last. The change starts at the top of the funnel: buyers now research in large language models first, and the company website becomes an AI avatar that answers questions, qualifies the lead, and hands it to a rep. He calls this AEO, answer engine optimization.
ex: HubSpot has already built a working version of AEO
He used Delphi to clone himself to answer his MIT students' questions

items.d: They research in ChatGPT and Claude
A website avatar answers and qualifies
Reps close with an AI assistant

l339|232.c: AI shortens planning cycles, so CEOs must make irreversible calls faster, without jumping to act two too early.
l339|232.e: People get more done with AI, he observes: a project that took a year now takes two months, and planning cycles have shrunk from a year to roughly a quarter. That forces CEOs to decide faster, especially on one-way-door decisions that can't be undone. He values keeping options open, but warns that trying everything has a cost. A common mistake is pivoting to a second act too early and abandoning the beachhead market. He also worries that AI lets CEOs do more things at once, which can scatter their focus.
ex: OpenAI refocused after Gemini caught up

l339|232.c: Companies mostly die of self-inflicted wounds: deliver bad news once, move on, and rebuild while you can.
l339|232.e: He believes companies die far more often from wounds they inflict on themselves than from outside threats. Do layoffs in one cut rather than nibbling, or morale takes hit after hit. After a mistake, do what basketball coaches teach: play the next play instead of dwelling on it. At the same time, never waste a good crisis; use it to fix the underlying process, and deliberately overcorrect. Every goal should have exactly one directly responsible person, because a plant watered by two people dies. At scale, that person also needs real authority across departments.
ex: After a major outage in March 2019, HubSpot rebuilt how it deployed software
Ruth Porat's layoff rule: don't take small bites

l339|232.c: Decide in this order: customer, enterprise, team, then yourself; he regrets favoring employees early on.
l339|232.e: HubSpot wrote "customer first, then enterprise value, then team, then yourself" into its values and ran quarterly employee NPS surveys by department. The point was to catch leaders who optimized for their own group, who, he says, rarely change. He was once among the highest-rated CEOs by employees and now sees that as a mistake. He would trade ten points of employee satisfaction for ten points of customer satisfaction, so he tied executive pay to retention and customer NPS and brought customers into board meetings to speak. He also warns that a CEO's words get over-read, so repeat them and choose them carefully.
ex: One sales department's NPS fell from about 65 to minus 5
Dharmesh Shah tags emails as "do this week" or "FYI only"

items.d: No favors for your own department

l340|665.c: For the kind of coding he does, writing code is essentially solved.
l340|665.e: He hasn't hand-edited a line of code since last November. He merges ten to forty changes a day, usually with about five agents running at once, though he still reviews the code. Anthropic tends to think in exponentials, so he extrapolated the curve of how much of his own code AI was writing and predicted by mid-year that engineers might not need an IDE by year's end. That came true. The team grew about fourfold in a year while pull requests per person roughly tripled, far beyond the few percentage points he gained at Meta after a year spent improving code quality.
ex: About 4% of public GitHub commits are made with Claude Code
The team grew about 4x in a year; PRs per person rose about 200%

items.d: Predicted no IDE by year's end

l340|665.c: AI is to coding what the printing press was to scribes; people move up to deciding what to write.
l340|665.e: Before the printing press, less than one percent of Europeans could read, and scribes were the gatekeepers of knowledge. Printing slashed the cost, more books were printed in fifty years than in the previous thousand, and literacy rose to about 70% over two centuries. Scribes were happy to drop the copying and focus on art. Programming has always climbed layers of abstraction, from punch cards to assembly to high-level languages, and this is one more layer. Engineers will spend the freed-up time deciding what to build, talking to users, and collaborating. He admits the transition will hurt, and society has to face it together.
ex: Printing cut the cost of books roughly 100x
His grandfather was an early Soviet programmer who used punch cards

items.d: Like engineers deciding what to build

l340|665.c: The most important product principle is latent demand: watch how users and models "misuse" you.
l340|665.e: He believes in building where users already are and paying attention to the workarounds they invent, because those reveal real needs. That is exactly how Cowork came about: people were using a coding tool in the terminal for data analysis, growing tomatoes, restoring photos, even reading MRI reports. The AI era adds a layer: watch how the model itself wants to do something, then make that easier. In other words, fit the product to the model's natural behavior, with as few tools and as little scaffolding as possible.
ex: Facebook Marketplace came from about 40% of group posts being buy-and-sell
Facebook Dating came from people browsing non-friends' profiles
Cowork took about 10 days, built mostly with Claude Code

l340|665.c: Don't box the model into a workflow; give it tools and a goal, and build for the model six months out.
l340|665.e: Carefully built scaffolding usually buys a 10–20% gain that vanishes when the next model ships. That's the bitter lesson, so bet on the general model rather than a small or fine-tuned one. Design the product for what models will do in six months; fit may lag at first, but it takes off when the new model lands. He also advises using the strongest model available, since cheaper ones need more correction and end up costing more tokens. For most tasks he starts in plan mode, confirms the approach, and then lets the agent run.
ex: Sonnet 3.5 drifted after about 30 seconds; Opus 4.6 runs 10–30 minutes
Claude Code jumped twice: with Opus 4 and again in November
About 80% of tasks start in plan mode

items: Betting on small or fine-tuned models
Bet on the more general model
Take off with each new model

d.verdict: Build for the model six months out, not today's

l340|665.c: Keep a small team deliberately under-resourced, give it plenty of tokens, and have everyone write code.
l340|665.e: Scarcity forces creativity, he argues, and engineers' own motivation pushes them to ship faster with AI. Before doing anything, ask whether Claude can do it, and if it can be done today, do it today. Don't skimp on tokens early; once an idea works, switch to a cheaper model to cut costs. At small scale, tokens are far cheaper than salaries. On the Claude Code team, product managers, designers, finance people, and data scientists all write code. He estimates product, engineering, and design now overlap by about half, and the title "software engineer" may give way to "builder."
ex: Some engineers spend hundreds of thousands of dollars a month on tokens
A new hire had Claude build a memory-leak tool and beat him to the answer

root.d: Rules for a small AI-first team

items.d: Hand it whatever it can do

l340|665.c: Safety needs three layers at once; a model that looks good in the lab may not in the real world.
l340|665.e: The first layer is mechanistic interpretability: studying the model's neurons and features, such as activations linked to deception. A single concept is often spread across many neurons in superposition. The second layer is evaluations in controlled settings. The third is watching behavior in real use. A model can pass the first two layers and still misbehave in the wild. That is why Claude Code was used internally for four or five months before launch, and why Cowork shipped early as a research preview, to learn from real use.
ex: Anthropic open-sourced a sandbox that works with any agent
He calls this a "race to the top"

l340|665.c: Coding is just the start; agents will move through tool use to everything done on a computer.
l340|665.e: Anthropic has long expected models to go from writing code to using tools to operating a computer, and Claude Code is an early step on that path. Going in stages also makes the safety research easier. Claude Code already reads user feedback, bug reports, and telemetry and proposes fixes and features on its own, like a colleague. He thinks product management, design, and data science are next, and eventually any work done on a computer. By his estimate, all of this is only about one percent done.
ex: He uses Cowork to pay parking tickets, cancel subscriptions, and fill out medical forms
Claude reviews every PR at Anthropic; humans still double-check

items.d: Cowork gets things done in a browser

l341|666.c: AI is a megatrend you can't fight, and an aging society may depend on it to survive.
l341|666.e: Falling birth rates mean there won't be enough working-age people to care for the elderly, which he says will bring widespread suffering that almost nobody is talking about. AI happens to arrive just as labor runs short, and it could fill that gap. He separates megatrends from hype cycles: don't fight the first, be wary of the second. A quick test: if a use case needs a PhD to explain, it probably isn't a megatrend. Today, he notes, model capability far outruns what companies actually use, a "capability overhang," so the real bottleneck is adoption.
ex: He cites Web3 as an example of a hype cycle
Cisco's next product is expected to be written entirely by AI

items.d: No one to look after the elderly
Matures at just the right time

l341|666.c: Big companies experiment but love to hedge; Cisco chose to bet on AI with no fallback.
l341|666.e: Innovation, he says, is a daily binary choice that has nothing to do with company size. Large companies often run a successful experiment and still hedge. Cisco began its shift before ChatGPT appeared and told employees plainly that their personal success depends on using AI well: AI won't take your job, but people who don't use it will become irrelevant. The company is also changing shape, from a holding company stitched together from about 251 acquisitions into a loosely coupled, tightly integrated platform, and from a walled garden to an open ecosystem that will work with competitors.
ex: OpenAI's forward-deployed engineers advised treating AI as a teammate, not a tool
CEO Chuck Robbins wants Cisco to be both classic and innovative

d.verdict: AI won't take jobs, but non-users fall behind

l341|666.c: AI is held back by three things: infrastructure, a trust deficit, and a data gap.
l341|666.e: First, there isn't enough power, compute, or network bandwidth, and GPUs are only useful when connected together, which makes networking critical. Second, models are non-deterministic and hallucinate, creating a trust deficit that calls for security and observability. Third, public human text is nearly used up, so future gains depend on proprietary, synthetic, and machine-generated data. Cisco is working on all three. Infrastructure work rarely gets glory and always gets blamed, he says, so the team has to care about customers' and partners' success.
ex: The goal: data centers about 800 km apart that act like one training cluster
A healthcare customer said an outage means patients miss dialysis or surgery

items.d: Public human text is running out

l341|666.c: Before entering a market, ask if you have permission to play and a route to customers; reject most ideas.
l341|666.e: When judging a new business, he first asks whether customers would find it natural for you to do it, which he calls permission to play. Then he asks whether there is a route to market, because a good product without distribution can't scale. AI networking and security are a natural extension of Cisco's forty years in infrastructure; consumer electronics would be neither permitted nor reachable. He says he rejects more than 90% of new ideas, because focus pays off far more than spreading out. And as code becomes abundant, judgment and taste matter more.
ex: He estimates 90–99% of new ideas get rejected
Box's Aaron Levie picked up this framework from him

l341|666.c: A company has six ingredients in order of weight: timing, market, team, product, brand, distribution.
l341|666.e: He ranks the six, each outweighing the next. Timing is the hardest to control, and a great product at the wrong time still fails. The market must be big, winnable in segments, and growing. A good team gets lifted by a mediocre market and dragged down by a bad one. Product is the soul of the company, and selling a mediocre one is unethical. A brand, once lost, is hard to rebuild. And "build it and they will come" is false. He also urges anticipating where AI will be in six months, and warns that experience helps you spot patterns but also breeds bias, so you have to be able to unlearn.
ex: Steve Jobs built the iPhone first, then the iPad
Sybase's brand never recovered
Cutting new-grad hiring is a mistake; they embrace AI most

items.d: Hard to rebuild; they won't just come

l341|666.c: Build trust in private, then debate openly and bluntly, rather than only criticizing behind closed doors.
l341|666.e: Information loses packets at every layer of management, he says, so leaders must tell the company story themselves, face the front line directly, explain the why, and be honest about bad news. Clear thinking comes before clear speaking, which is why he turned Cisco's sprawling product line into a story anyone can retell. He disagrees with "praise in public, criticize in private": once trust exists privately, problems should be discussed openly and directly so the best idea wins. He admits he is still working on his tone.
ex: A former board member advised him to own the company narrative himself
He talks with Chuck Robbins several times a day

result.d: Conflict becomes constructive

l341|666.c: Hunger can't be taught; intelligence, curiosity, and persistence can, and stamina beats brilliance.
l341|666.e: Hard, important problems attract the best teams, he says, and business is a team sport. About 30% of any job is unpleasant, so choose something you genuinely hunger for. Pick platforms that work as springboards, and prepare so you can catch luck when it comes. Build relationships by giving value first rather than transacting, and ask for help when you need it. As a young man he washed dishes and cleaned at Sizzler, and cured his stutter so he could greet customers, which is why he recommends service jobs to young people.
ex: Sizzler paid about $2.25 an hour plus tips
Taj Mahal guides speak several languages yet earn about $10 a day

marks.d: Only by choosing what you crave

l342|669.c: The classic design process is mostly dead; design now means helping teams ship and setting short-term direction.
l342|669.e: The discover-then-sketch-then-iterate process, diverging and converging, was fading before AI, and agentic coding sped up its decline. Engineering changed first: anyone can pitch an idea and an engineer quickly builds a rough working version, so designers can't produce polished mockups for every feature. Design work now splits in two. One part is helping teams ship well and stay consistent. The other is setting direction, but not as a five-to-ten-year vision deck; it's guidance for the next three to six months, often shown as a prototype.
ex: Her Berlin talk "Don't trust the design process" felt dated within months
AI products are unpredictable, so you can't mock up every state

items: Help teams ship and stay consistent
Direction three to six months out

d.verdict: Ship early, test with real data, build better products

l342|669.c: Mockup time has halved, while pairing with engineers and editing code by hand keeps growing.
l342|669.e: Her day now looks like this: a lot of time following prototypes and research across teams, planning the next three months, talking with engineers on the fly and critiquing what they've built, then polishing details directly in code. She still does research and mockups, just in different proportions. Figma remains irreplaceable, she says, because coding tools are linear: it's hard to compare eight or ten directions side by side, and they're poor for fine-tuning type and visuals. Tagging Claude in Slack can turn a small tweak into a pull request.
ex: Long tasks go to Cowork; front-end tweaks go to Claude Code

l342|669.c: Shipping early is fine if you label it clearly and commit to fast iteration; speed buys trust.
l342|669.e: Cowork launched as a research preview with known flaws, because internal use had already shown it was valuable. Shipping early only works, she argues, with a public commitment to keep improving, so users see their feedback answered quickly. Go quiet after launch and trust erodes. She finds the pace satisfying because you immediately know what to fix next. She also pushes back on the "built in ten days" story: many components already existed as prototypes, and the ten days were spent assembling them into something shippable.
ex: To-do lists, multiple-choice prompts, and onboarding examples already existed as prototypes
The home screen is becoming a shared to-do list between the user and Claude

l342|669.c: AI's taste will keep improving; what's hard to replace is resolving disagreement and owning the decision.
l342|669.e: She suspects we overrate human aesthetic judgment, and expects AI taste to keep getting better. Having watched how fast AI took over coding, she no longer claims AI will never be good at product judgment. In her experience the hardest part of building software is rarely the code; it's getting a group of people to agree on what belongs in the product and what matters most. AI can supply data and suggestions, but it may not resolve a genuine disagreement. And for now at least, someone has to be accountable for the decision, the way a radiologist still has to sign off.
ex: She compares accountability to a radiologist signing the report

marks.d: AI is very good at this

l342|669.c: She hires three kinds of designers: strong generalists, deep specialists, and exceptional new grads.
l342|669.e: Strong generalists are in the top 20% at several skills and can fill gaps when roles blur, but they're rare. Deep specialists are in the top 10% at one thing, and when anyone can build something, they make the product stand out. The third group is mature, humble, curious new grads with no baggage from old processes, whom she thinks are often overlooked. Since the work changes daily, resilience and adaptability are table stakes. Juniors should build a lot and share a lot. Senior designers don't need to become engineers, but they should use coding tools and speak the language of implementation.
ex: In the Socratica community, students build projects like a science fair
She wouldn't hire Claude as a designer yet

l342|669.c: Designers at frontier labs should act like in-house investors, making exciting but hard-to-read ideas clear.
l342|669.e: She borrows Evan Tana's legibility framework: an idea that's obvious at a glance is usually already well known, and the real opportunity lies in ideas that are hard to explain but have people excited. So when evaluating internal prototypes, a designer should ask like an investor why people are excited, then make the idea legible through a narrative or an interface. One internal prototype she didn't understand at first, but which had a lot of buzz, went on to shape the Skills framework and the Cowork interface that shows plans, to-dos, and the files being read.

items.d: But people around it are excited
Read the signal like an investor
Like Skills and the Cowork UI

l342|669.c: Managers should go back to the front line to learn new skills first; future management is direction plus coaching.
l342|669.e: She joined Anthropic as an individual contributor, managed a team for a few months when needed, then went back to full-time IC. She wanted to be closer to the work, to learn the new skills before managing others, and she isn't sure middle management will remain a stable role. She suggests design managers do what engineering managers do and spend a few months as ICs first. Seemingly low-leverage things, like a leader using the product, triaging bugs, and opening pull requests, turn out to be high leverage. A team that jokes around has psychological safety, and safety makes high standards easier to hold.
ex: Mike Krieger opens pull requests himself too
At Figma she managed 12–15 designers

items.d: A few months leading a team
Learn the skills of the AI era

l343|548.c: Physical AI starts by adding intelligence to existing machines; driver assistance becomes standard like navigation did.
l343|548.e: Over the next 5–10 years, he believes AI's biggest impact will be in farming, mining, construction, and trucking rather than software. The path is to add intelligence to machines whose mechanical engineering is already mature: cars, mining trucks, farm equipment. Humanoid robots are more exciting but not practical. Waymo uses many sensors, lots of compute, and detailed maps, which suits limited areas. Tesla's approach, with fewer sensors, no maps, and cheap compute, is easier to roll out at scale. He expects L2++ driver assistance to become nearly standard within 5–7 years, making full self-driving the default expectation.
ex: Navigation was once a paid option, then CarPlay and Android Auto made it free
Like trying to predict the smartphone's killer apps in 2006
The same path will play out in construction, mining, and defense

l343|548.c: The sooner autonomy arrives the better: human driving is deadly, and dangerous jobs go unfilled.
l343|548.e: About 30,000 Americans die in traffic accidents every year. He says the data shows autonomous vehicles are far safer, and future generations will look back on human driving the way we look at child labor. Few people want dangerous jobs in trucking or mining, the workforce is aging, and working families now have more family-friendly options like ride-hailing. Slowing technology to protect jobs, he argues, hurts low-income people first, because they are hit first when the economy stalls. The answer is to manage the downsides, not to halt AI.
ex: He says the average American farmer is about 58
Recent US growth has come mainly from frontier tech hubs, not Detroit

items.d: About 30,000 US road deaths a year
Few want to work remote mines

l343|548.c: Fear of AI comes from not understanding it; like the industrial revolution, it will reduce suffering overall.
l343|548.e: People fear AI mostly because they don't understand its limits, he says. A video of a humanoid robot swinging nunchucks looks magical because viewers can't tell pre-programmed moves from real autonomy, yet nobody fears the more advanced robots in factories. The industrial revolution brought child labor, monopolies, and wars, but it also brought medicine and goods to ordinary households, and he believes AI will likewise reduce suffering on net. The software stock sell-off is a separate matter: investors were spooked by vibe-coded imitations that look like real products but lack depth and integration. Don't confuse the two.
ex: German POWs' letters home about brightly lit US towns shocked people in Germany
Free autonomous rides would matter enormously to disabled, poor, and rural people

items.d: Can't tell demos from real autonomy

l343|548.c: Comparing US and Chinese AI companies head-to-head is a category error, but never underestimate China.
l343|548.e: He argues that some Chinese companies are partly extensions of the state and may not aim for profit the way American companies do, so judging them by the same business yardstick is misleading. Chinese EV makers look strong partly because outsiders hold them to looser commercial standards, and EVs are a hard business for anyone. He stresses that China is not incompetent and deserves to be taken seriously, but treating it as "another America" is wrong, and the popular understanding is far too simple.
ex: According to House of Huawei, about a quarter of Huawei's employees are party members
Rivian makes good products but is still losing money

d.verdict: No simple comparison, and no underestimating

l343|548.c: If two years in you have no clearer direction, do a hard reset; treat the first company as practice.
l343|548.e: Good companies, he observes, usually get traction early and keep it for a decade or more. If after roughly two years in the market you don't have a more specific direction than when you started, consider a hard reset. The problem is often foundational: the co-founders, the market, your stage of life, or your level of commitment, not just product details. Pivoting is easy before you raise money and hire; afterward it damages employees' trust. Founding is a muscle you can train, so spend the first years learning with low expectations. Good ideas often come from tinkering without pressure.
ex: His third company was the most successful; some funds back only repeat founders
Take it seriously, but don't treat every outcome as life or death

l343|548.c: Derive your values from why the company is winning, then use them to evaluate people and pass them on.
l343|548.e: They asked why the company was winning, listed five to ten reasons, and made those the values, rather than starting from abstract philosophy. First is "speed above all" (fast but safe), judged mainly by decisiveness, and managers are evaluated and paid on it. Others: never disappoint a customer, technical mastery and high output, laugh a lot, half the job is follow-up, and the best work is done quietly and independently. He treats the company as a machine that needs maintenance and tuning, and in nearly ten years it has never spent the money it raised.
ex: He and co-founder Peter teach the values at the weekly new-hire meeting
Employees clean their own areas weekly, and the office is shoes-off
Deliberately low-profile: he admires Berkshire more than the Silicon Valley celebrity model

l343|548.c: Let the best idea win: gather views widely, strip out ego, and once decided, execute firmly.
l343|548.e: He wants ideas to compete on merit regardless of seniority, drawing on customers, employees, competitors, investors, and society. When founders resist input, it's usually ego. Emotion often comes from feeling you own an idea, so ask yourself what you'd choose if nobody cared about your feelings. Companies also miss market shifts through inertia, and small deviations compound, so correct course humbly. But once a decision is made, execute decisively. Judgment and taste, he adds, come from broad experience: read old books that have survived the test of time, and work at a big company first.
ex: Google had about $1 billion a month in cash flow and still lost social to Facebook
He spent over ten years at big companies like GM and Bosch
You seriously read only 50–100 books in a lifetime

terms.d: Best idea wins, regardless of rank
Beware feeling you own the idea

result.d: Once decided, execute firmly

l344|670.c: Treat writing as an experiment: publish every week first, and add a paywall once it works.
l344|670.e: When he left Airbnb, the options he considered were starting another company, being a startup's first PM, being a PM at a big company, or consulting. None was the job he has now. A post summarizing what he learned at Airbnb got featured on Medium and passed around inside the company, and friends urged him to keep writing. He moved to Substack and committed to one post a week as an experiment. Nine months in, he used the Lindy effect, the idea that things that have lasted tend to keep lasting, to conclude it would continue. With Airbnb stock uncertain during the pandemic, he added a paywall and saw meaningful revenue within about a month.
ex: Now about 1.2 million subscribers, and the podcast is often top ten in tech
The podcast came four years after the newsletter
His early startup Local Mine was acquired by Airbnb

items.d: Nine months in, it would last

l344|670.c: The best advice comes from people who have done the thing, not commentators talking in general.
l344|670.e: Rather than hearing people speak in generalities, he would rather have someone who actually does the work share one core lesson, which is why most posts are now guest pieces from practitioners. His quality bar is high: he revises his own posts about 50 times before they go to an editor, a proofreader, and a designer. His advice to creators is the same: write about what you have actually done. Also notice whether you enjoy the work itself, not just whether others find it valuable. And, like David Sedaris, go out and live more so you have something to write about.
ex: While hosting, he keeps writing notes to himself to steer the conversation

l344|670.c: He keeps the business deliberately small and simple, with no full-time staff, to avoid building a job he hates.
l344|670.e: Things get complicated easily, he says. Chase every request and big opportunity and you end up building a job you hate. So he is careful about commitments, avoids hiring full-time employees, and works with a small crew of editors, proofreaders, and designers. One post plus one podcast episode every week is a treadmill that never stops, and it can be draining. He isn't sure what the long run looks like, but he still can't imagine anything more fulfilling or interesting. The cost is that he misses working side by side with other people.
ex: Scammers exploited an API loophole in his product pass; he closed it with Stripe and Substack
He worried the incident damaged readers' trust in him

marks.d: A small crew of editors, proofreaders, designers

l344|670.c: A product manager's job is to deliver business impact by prioritizing the most important business problems, like a mini CEO.
l344|670.e: Asked to define a product manager in a few words, his answer is: deliver business outcomes by prioritizing the business problems with the biggest impact. A PM should think like a mini CEO about what will make the product and the business succeed, not act as a project manager. He didn't expect it, but the structure, high quality bar, and concise communication he built as a PM all carried over into writing and podcasting.
ex: He stresses that a PM is not a project manager

terms.d: The business problem with most impact
Do the most important thing first

result.d: Own it like a mini CEO

l344|670.c: He parents the way he builds products: start with what the smartest people have already figured out.
l344|670.e: He says he isn't someone who runs on instinct. When a problem comes up, he first asks what the smartest people have already worked out. To shorten bedtime, for example, he studied expert advice and set up a star reward system and a fixed three-book routine. With his kids, as with a PM inside an organization, he gets things done through influence rather than authority.
ex: A star reward system plus a fixed three-book bedtime routine

items.d: Lead the way a PM does

l344|670.c: Looking calm is mostly genetic, but your happiness baseline can be raised with practice.
l344|670.e: He says he is more anxious than he looks, and it sometimes shows up as headaches. He figures about 70% of his calm comes from genes; the rest comes from learning to reframe problems and not take things too seriously. A happiness course from the University of Pennsylvania convinced him that people have a happiness baseline, but one that can be raised. Exercise mostly pulls you out of a bad mood rather than making you much happier. He has tried meditation, breathing courses, and a ten-day silent retreat. When his wife's anesthesia went wrong during a C-section, he stood in the hallway telling himself it would be okay.
ex: He has misophonia: open-mouth chewing is a 10, a crying baby an 8
He is also face-blind and often fails to recognize people who greet him

items.d: Reframing, meditation, not taking it too seriously

l345|673.c: Most people get about 20% more just by politely asking if there's room, and that isn't greedy.
l345|673.e: At every level, he has found, a polite question about whether there is any room to move usually yields about 20% more. A proper negotiation typically reaches around 40%, and breaking out of a salary band can more than double the number. Companies get far more value from strong employees than they pay them, so asking simply makes the exchange fairer. Better to ask for too much and be told no than to leave money on the table. He also notices that introverted product, engineering, and design people tend to negotiate worse than marketing and sales leaders.
ex: A simple ask commonly brings about a 20% increase
Done well, about 40%; in some cases 100–400%

l345|673.c: A number given too early, expected or past pay, becomes an anchor; politely defer it to the offer stage.
l345|673.e: Negotiation starts long before the offer, he says: your LinkedIn profile, your photo, and how you post all shape how you get priced. Package yourself as a commodity and you'll be paid like one. A number you give a recruiter early gets written down and can anchor you years later. When asked, say you'd rather discuss it once you understand the role and its value, ask for their range first, and thank them for respecting that boundary. Roles often grow during interviews, and an early number only limits you. Savings, or a current job, give you more leverage.
ex: He once earned a dozen dollars an hour; by deferring the number he landed about $120,000
He turned down a $70,000 content job; six months later the same company offered a $250,000 VP role

items: Hard to adjust as the role grows
Thank them for respecting the boundary

d.verdict: Let them show their hand, then talk value

l345|673.c: Don't negotiate by email or through a recruiter; talk face to face or on video with whoever owns the budget.
l345|673.e: Email gives you no control over tone, he says. A busy executive skimming your counter-offer on the go can easily read it as greed. On video or in person you can see their reaction and reschedule if needed. A recruiter relaying your position is a game of telephone and distorts the message; respect them, but the real counterpart is the person who owns the budget and the P&L. Control time and place too: don't take early-morning calls, offer only a few slots to create scarcity. A walk or a coffee moves the talk to neutral ground, and walking side by side turns confrontation into joint problem-solving.
ex: OpenAI interviews often happen on walks through downtown San Francisco

cells.d: See reactions, adjust in real time

l345|673.c: When an offer lands, show enthusiasm and buy time; don't name a number, say it feels low and ask what would work.
l345|673.e: First, thank them and show excitement to signal you want to close. Then say you need to talk it over with an advisor, a partner, or a lawyer, which is normal for senior roles. Slowing down signals scarcity and leaves time to gather information; haste equals risk.
