Next, instead of naming a number, ask what it would take to reach the top of the range, say the offer feels a little low, and ask how to make it work. If the job is really bigger than its assigned level, ask to rebuild the whole package at the true level.
ex: Several candidates with $185–285k ranges ended up around $1.1 million including equity
Some roles were upgraded from senior director to VP

items.d: What does the top of the range take?

l345|673.c: Treat the interview like an enterprise B2B sale: diagnose the need first, then help them picture your success.
l345|673.e: Job hunting is a long-cycle enterprise sale, he says. You cultivate internal champions. You ask why they're hiring, what problems they have, what they've tried, and what success looks like, so the interview feels like consulting rather than interrogation. Then you help them picture success a few months out, say a great board meeting. You can ask directly what's missing and where a competitor is stronger, and give each interviewer a line they can repeat internally on your behalf. Don't rush to a diagnosis or over-promise. The goal is to grow the pie, not fight over a fixed slice.
ex: A talent agency won a director by arranging a lunch with Spielberg in advance
He uses product language like PRDs, positioning, and reducing friction to explain job searches

items.d: Help them see a few months out
A reason to recommend you internally

l345|673.c: Don't default to meeting in the middle; probe the real ceiling, and when stuck, change the structure instead of pushing cash.
l345|673.e: The other side will often naturally suggest splitting the difference, but once you do, you never learn where the ceiling was. When the cash budget is capped, change the structure: bonuses tied to milestones, extra equity, severance protection, even non-cash items. People confident in their performance are happy with such deals and more likely to stay, and the company keeps talent at lower risk. When a term is clearly unfavorable, first ask whether it's a mistake rather than offering to split the gap.
ex: A screenwriter was offered $700k, the lawyer asked for $1.3M, and they settled at $1M
When a CEO's cash was capped, the contract added a company car worth about $350k
Tom Brady's contract paid bonuses for wins, playoffs, and MVP

terms.d: The part of the budget that can't move

result.d: Risk stays manageable for both

l345|673.c: Frame requests as "we" rather than "I," so decision-makers see their own upside and a precedent.
l345|673.e: Adversarial negotiation is a myth, he argues; treat it as solving a problem together. Pure logic rarely beats a company that negotiates every day, so bring emotion and credibility too. People act when they see their own incentive, so present the request as good for the whole team and let the CEO be the hero. If talks blow up, call proactively and own your mistakes; extreme ownership usually recovers the deal. In most cases an offer won't be pulled; the worst outcome is a no or a final ultimatum.
ex: In a PE buyout, one executive extended protections to the whole leadership team and won retention and severance bonuses
A CMO's $800k offer was pulled after a clumsy negotiation and restored after he called the CEO to apologize

items.d: The ask covers the whole team
The CEO gets to be the hero

l345|673.c: Information and timing are the real leverage; there is no one-size-fits-all script.
l345|673.e: Companies negotiate thousands of times a day while an individual does it a few times in a lifetime, so the information advantage sits with the company. He compares it to the game Werewolf: the side that knows more often wins even when outnumbered. More information shifts the balance, and waiting lets you gather it and build a stronger case. Role, industry, city, culture, gender, and background all change the approach, so any advice promising fixed steps is suspect. Academic frameworks like BATNA and ZOPA can even scare people off; curiosity and empathy work better. When stuck, ask why the obstacle exists.
ex: He mentions that some individual-contributor roles at Meta pay about $1.2 million a year

l346|675.c: Influence isn't office politics. It's keeping good ideas alive, and that is the PM's actual job.
l346|675.e: As a PM at Slack, she noticed that equally well-supported ideas sometimes shipped and sometimes died. So she became chief of staff to April Underwood to watch up close how executives decide. Her conclusion: politics means manipulating people and outcomes for personal gain, while influence means raising the odds that your good ideas survive. When leadership doesn't buy in, it isn't your fault, but it is your problem. Study executives the way you would study a key user, with curiosity and empathy. The headcount and budget you get is an investment, so winning support is simply part of the job.
ex: Annie Pearl's line: it's not my fault, but it is my problem
Noah Weiss wrote down the product principles he learned from Slack founder Stewart Butterfield

d.verdict: Influence is the PM job itself

l346|675.c: An executive's day is a strobe light, so open with thirty seconds of context, then stop.
l346|675.e: Executives jump between finance, hiring, legal, and product reviews all day. The topic you spent weeks preparing may not have crossed their mind since you last met. They also optimize for the whole company, while PMs often see only their corner. So she suggests opening with under a minute of context: why this meeting, where you left off, why it matters now, and what's on the agenda. Then stop talking and ask what else they want to cover. Many mistakes come from ignoring what the executive heard in higher-level meetings.

items.d: What else is on your mind

l346|675.c: Don't go to an executive for a rubber stamp. Go to learn, close information gaps, and build the plan together.
l346|675.e: Treating executive feedback as a formality is already a failure, she says. When an executive says something that sounds wrong, ask what makes them think that. They often decide fast on very little data and sound certain, but a no usually just means you have different information. Before proposing anything, ask colleagues, assistants, and the chief of staff what the executive cares about right now. Instead of asking what's on their mind, ask what the board is pushing and what they most fear getting wrong. Book time early and shape the plan together before it hardens.
ex: Webflow runs office hours before a one-pager even exists
Slack had a 30-minute meeting literally called "Hey Stewart, what do you think"
A colleague trained GPT on review notes to predict executive pushback

items.d: Book time before the plan is set
Turn their instinct into a framework

l346|675.c: Lead with your recommendation, then the alternatives, with evidence in an appendix, formatted to each executive's taste.
l346|675.e: Don't bury executives in proof. Doing the homework is assumed, so put the details in an appendix. And don't bring only one option. Showing a few alternatives you seriously considered signals rigor. She mostly agrees with the pyramid principle: conclusion first, then alternatives, then evidence. But she stresses tailoring it. Some executives hate slides, some only want data, some want to pre-read, some read silently in the meeting. Just ask. If a document gets lots of comments, list the ones that need live discussion at the top and answer the rest offline.
ex: Rachel Wolan sent back a doc with one option; the team returned two days later with alternatives
Slack's "Stewart plus two": build what he wants, plus two things the team believes in

l346|675.c: Tie your proposal to what the executive is measured on, and offer a version that goes ten times faster.
l346|675.e: Executives want to succeed too. Find out what metrics they're held to, then use a metric ladder to show how your team's numbers roll up into company results. If incentives don't line up, say so early. At Slack, leadership felt the product had lost its craft, so the team paused for two weeks and let engineers pick their own improvements. They shipped 65 of them, which matched the company's goal of standing out. Executives have more levers than you: they can move people, find resources, escalate or kill projects. So present a constrained plan first, then an accelerated version, and spell out what it would take.
ex: Slack's Customer Love Sprint shipped 65 improvements in two weeks

root.d: Tie the executive's success to your proposal

items.d: Connect team metrics to company results
Spell out what resources it needs

l346|675.c: Trust comes from working with executives' existing beliefs, shrinking the change, and being willing to kill projects.
l346|675.e: Start from what the executive already believes. If an idea is too far from their worldview, push other ideas that fit first. When they're firm, push back with data once or twice, then let it go. Deliver results first, then trade those results for bigger bets. Shrink a six-month commitment into a one-week test, ask what failure would look like to them, and red-team your own plan. Proactively killing or scaling down a project is a strong trust signal. Follow up on small hints in executive feedback the same day, and ask how strongly and how urgently they feel about it.
ex: Her favorite business book is Switch, whose core idea is to shrink the change
Webflow's design lead produced a risk framework for design changes within an hour

marks.d: Once or twice, then let go

l346|675.c: AI makes building cheap, so the bottleneck shifts to choosing and aligning, and influence gets more valuable.
l346|675.e: She thinks this is a golden age for PMs. Building gets easier every month, so deciding what to build and bringing people along becomes the bottleneck. Tasks AI does well, like organizing data and taking notes, are no longer where you add value. The anthropology of digging up new insights from users and markets still needs humans. She disagrees that the PRD is dead: the faster decisions and shipping get, the more a clear strategy matters. AI agents are like teammates who need onboarding, so write down your product philosophy, success criteria, and past lessons, and put guardrails where taste is required.
ex: Distribution and trust are underrated bottlenecks; brands and existing customers have the edge
Use AI as a tireless sparring partner to find holes in your plan

result.d: Influence becomes the core skill

l346|675.c: Influence doesn't require one personality type. Growth means widening your view from a feature to the whole business.
l346|675.e: She describes herself as a people person with a bit of achievement drive. Early on she was told to be more forceful, but she later found her own style was the strength. To move up, widen your view from the feature you own to the whole business, the industry, and the ecosystem around it. That shift is itself a sign of strategic thinking. Webflow's PM career ladder rewards product citizenship: mentoring others, sharing methods, connecting work to business results, and being willing to say a project isn't the best use of effort and change course.
ex: Webflow's PM career ladder includes product citizenship

l347|328.c: Don't judge an AI tool on first use. Stick with it for weeks to see the real value.
l347|328.e: Her first OpenClaw install took about eight hours and deleted her family calendar. But she could already see enough usefulness to keep going, and today she finds it more useful than almost any tool she has tried. She treats other AI tools the same way, returning until she finds the value. Complaints like "it's buggy" or "it forgets things" are actually signs of product-market fit: people only tolerate breakage when the value is high. It is not low-maintenance, though. Setup is painful, so lower your expectations and narrow each agent's job.
ex: First install took about 8 hours and accidentally deleted the family calendar
She finds OpenClaw warmer in tone, without engagement hooks everywhere

l347|328.c: Onboard it like an executive assistant: its own machine, its own accounts, delegated access instead of your passwords.
l347|328.e: Don't install it on your main computer. An old laptop or a cloud machine is enough, and physical separation limits the damage if it deletes a folder or sends the wrong file. Buying a Mac mini was mostly a commitment device to make herself do it. Give the agent its own system account, email, and calendar, then share or delegate your calendar and inbox to it. Never hand over your own passwords; move keys through a password manager. Choose the personal-use-only mode and use frontier models, which resist prompt injection better and are worth the extra cost.
ex: Telegram is the easiest first chat channel
She names frontier models like Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, and GPT-5.4

l347|328.c: Grant access gradually, and tell the agent to take orders from only one channel: yours.
l347|328.e: Her biggest worry is prompt injection: instructions hidden in an email or web page, or a faked emergency meant to trick the agent into acting. The maintainers have hardened the defaults so agents treat all outside content as dangerous. She goes further and restates in every soul file (the document that defines who the agent is and its rules) that it only takes instructions from her in one specific Telegram channel. Anything in email, Slack, or web pages is ignored. Permissions open up gradually, like with a new assistant. At first she didn't even enable email reading, since an attacker could use it to extract information.
ex: The agent knows where her kids go to school, so operational security matters

l347|328.c: Several agents with narrow jobs beat one do-everything assistant, because context gets overloaded.
l347|328.e: Her biggest breakthrough was splitting roles. One agent stuffed with unrelated tasks starts forgetting things and losing track of its tools. She divides agents the way a team divides Slack channels, crossing over only when needed. In effect she hires different people for different jobs. Non-sensitive work can share a machine. Once the family manager got access to her personal email, it moved to its own machine, physically separated from work. She now runs eight or nine agents across three Mac minis and other machines.
ex: A sales agent scans new signups daily, finds decision makers, and sends personalized emails
She estimates Sam replaced about 10 hours a week of outsourced work

items.d: Family manager on its own machine

l347|328.c: An agent feels alive because of an identity file plus a scheduled heartbeat. The mechanics are simple.
l347|328.e: Onboarding is a conversation, not a form. The agent asks who it is and who you are, then interviews you about your goals, family routines, and boundaries, and writes its own identity into a markdown file you can edit later. The sense of initiative comes from two mechanisms. A clear identity gives it personality. A heartbeat roughly every 30 minutes makes it check its task list, and scheduled jobs handle routine work like fixing code overnight, the way an employee clocks in. She often says thank you, because models trained on human text produce better work when treated politely.
ex: Her soul files say: have opinions, and try to solve it yourself before asking
A new agent reads an old agent's soul file, a kind of brain transplant

terms.d: A soul file written in conversation
Checks its list about every 30 minutes

result.d: Feels like someone who works on their own

l347|328.c: Browser automation is still the weakest link. Look for an API first, and if that fails, rewrite the goal.
l347|328.e: She thinks no product has really solved browser use. Websites are hostile to bots by design, so tasks like ordering takeout are unreliable. Her approach: find an API first, then try the browser, and if that fails, accept it and rewrite the goal. Instead of placing the order, the agent plans the menu and reminds her to cook. Forgetting is mostly a context problem: split roles first, then have the agent write key decisions into memory before a session gets compressed, and maintain the tool notes by hand. When something breaks, Claude Code on the same machine can read the docs and fix it.
ex: Each agent gets its own color-coded Chrome profile
She predicts agents will become the main visitors to websites

items: Exa and Brave instead of browsing

d.verdict: API first; otherwise rewrite the goal

l347|328.c: Home life is an underrated place for agents, but the key decisions should require a human.
l347|328.e: Kids' basketball schedules often come out just before the weekend. Her husband drops the whole page into the group chat, the family agent puts it on the calendar, spots a clash with soccer, and asks both parents how to split up. That's deliberate: logistics can be automated, but who goes where must be confirmed by a person. Every afternoon it asks who is picking up which kid and nudges them to leave based on traffic. A homework agent schedules study time around team practice and piano while protecting bedtime and family dinner. Parents need help, she says, and once they taste it they want more.
ex: Jesse Genet, who homeschools four kids, runs it from her phone with voice and photos

marks.d: Which parent picks up which kid

l347|328.c: Running agents well is a management skill: define roles, write down context, and extend trust gradually.
l347|328.e: She credits her success to twenty-plus years of managing people, not technical skill. Claude Code can handle the technical parts. Borrowing Molly Graham's waterline model, she says most team problems are structural: unclear roles, goals, and ownership. When an agent gets something wrong, it's usually missing context rather than being dumb. Instructions written in files are concrete and checkable, while verbal instructions lose information. Yelling doesn't work on people, and it doesn't work on agents either. Individual contributors can build their own operating system this way too.
ex: Agents assign her human-only tasks in Linear, like sending a fax or returning an item
Hilary Gridley: the highest-bandwidth interface to an LLM is just talking to it

items.d: More access once it gets things right
Check structure first when it fails

l348|677.c: November 2025 was the turning point: coding agents went from mostly working to almost always doing what you ask.
l348|677.e: In 2025 the big labs focused their reinforcement learning training on code, and reasoning models turned out to be naturally good at writing it. GPT-5.1 and Claude Opus 4.5, released in November, looked like modest upgrades but crossed a threshold: ask for a Mac app and you basically get one that runs. He argues code was disrupted first because it is the easiest thing to verify. Either it runs or it doesn't. Essays and legal documents are much harder to check. That is why software engineers are the first knowledge workers to feel the impact.
ex: After Claude Code launched, plenty of people were willing to pay $200 a month

items.d: Reasoning models are good at code
GPT-5.1 and Opus 4.5 cross the threshold

l348|677.c: Dark factories are emerging: first humans stop writing code, next nobody reviews it.
l348|677.e: The term comes from automated factories that run with the lights off. Some companies already forbid humans from typing code by hand. The next step is dropping human review entirely. Six months ago he thought that was crazy; now about 95% of his own code isn't typed by him. He reframes the question as "95% of code written by AI" and estimates about half of engineers will be there by the end of 2026. Code quality is already good enough that "the code is too bad" no longer holds up as an objection.
ex: StrongDM stopped having humans read code in August 2025
Simulated employees file requests in fake Slack and Jira, reportedly costing about $10,000 a day

l348|677.c: Personal tools can be vibe coded without reading the code. Professional work needs agentic engineering.
l348|677.e: He sticks to Karpathy's original meaning: vibe coding means not looking at the code. If it only affects you, that's completely fine for personal tools. Once it can hurt others, say a script that hammers someone else's website, it becomes irresponsible. He worries the term is being stretched to cover professional work, so he coined a separate name for professionals building software with AI: agentic engineering. Doing it well, he says, draws directly on his 25 years of engineering experience.

d.verdict: Don't ship vibe-coded work as professional work

l348|677.c: Writing code is no longer the bottleneck. Design, process, and validation are the new constraints.
l348|677.e: Most of the time used to go into writing code. Not anymore. The first idea is usually wrong, so the job becomes testing ideas as fast as possible. Prototypes are nearly free, so he builds three versions of a feature and compares them. AI is good at the first two-thirds of a brainstorm, the obvious ideas. Its value is that you can push it to keep going and mash unrelated fields together. But it can't replace usability testing with real people. His 25 years of instinct for estimating timelines has also broken: a two-week task can now take 20 minutes.
ex: Naming expert David Placek has different groups brainstorm names from different metaphors
Tests and docs no longer signal quality; "people actually use it" does

l348|677.c: AI amplifies both senior engineers and newcomers. People in the middle are most at risk.
l348|677.e: He cites a conclusion from an internal ThoughtWorks discussion: seniors get their experience amplified, newcomers can get productive in a week with AI, but mid-level engineers have neither deep experience to amplify nor the newcomer's boost. His advice is to lean into the tools: use AI to learn things that weren't worth learning before, take on harder projects, and build the initiative AI lacks. Also watch for burnout. He runs four agents in parallel and is exhausted by 11 a.m., and some people stay up all night to keep their agents busy.
ex: Cloudflare and Shopify each reportedly hired about a thousand interns in 2025
He used AI to learn AppleScript, and to learn to cook

marks.d: Productive in a week with AI

l348|677.c: Have the agent write tests first and watch them fail. Use project templates, not long instructions, to set style.
l348|677.e: Agents need to run code, so skipping tests to save time is a mistake. Having the agent write a test, watch it fail, then implement, the red-green TDD loop, works noticeably better. He has never liked TDD himself, but agents don't mind, so a small library with hundreds of tests is fine since the agent maintains them. Every project starts from a template with one passing test and his preferred style. Agents imitate the patterns they see, which works far better than a long instruction file.
ex: His tools collection has about 193 small HTML/JS tools
He had an agent combine PDF.js and Tesseract into a PDF text-recognition tool

root.d: Give it good patterns to copy

items.d: Watch the test fail, then implement

l348|677.c: Prompt injection can't be filtered away. The only fix is removing one leg of the lethal trifecta.
l348|677.e: Prompt injection is a vulnerability in any app built on an LLM: the model can't tell trusted instructions from text pasted in from outside. A filter that catches 97% still fails, because a 3% success rate is enough for attackers to steal data, and attacks can be phrased in any language. An agent is dangerous when it has all three: access to private data, exposure to malicious instructions, and a way to send data out. The only fix is to remove one, and cutting off the outbound channel is usually easiest. Assume anyone who can talk to the agent can trigger anything it's allowed to do, and limit the blast radius.
ex: He regrets naming it after SQL injection, which has a reliable fix
DeepMind's CaMeL paper proposes isolating two agents, but no good implementation exists yet

result.d: Remove any one leg to break it

l348|677.c: The industry is normalizing deviance, and a Challenger-style disaster is coming sooner or later.
l348|677.e: He points to research on the Challenger shuttle: the O-rings kept failing without a disaster, so people grew more confident each time. AI is doing the same. No prompt injection attack has yet caused a headline-grabbing loss, so everyone keeps taking bigger risks. He admits he has made this prediction every six months for three years and it hasn't happened yet. OpenClaw is close to catastrophic on security, yet hundreds of thousands of people pushed through the setup to install it, which shows how badly people want a personal assistant. Big companies haven't built one because they don't know how to make it safe. A secure version, he thinks, is the biggest opportunity right now.
ex: OpenClaw went from first line of code to a Super Bowl ad in about three and a half months
Some users lost crypto wallets because of it

l349|680.c: Anthropic's growth comes mostly from research, compute, and product. The growth team spends most of its time firefighting.
l349|680.e: He credits the company's takeoff to research, inference compute, Claude Code, and the sales team, and says the growth team deserves less credit than people assume. Revenue grows roughly tenfold each year, so a normal linear chart shows nothing and every internal chart uses a log scale. The growth team owns acquisition, activation, monetization, and pricing and packaging. But about 70% of his time goes to systems breaking under the weight of success, and only 30% to proactive planning.
ex: About 70% of his time goes to "success disasters," 30% to proactive work
Internal growth charts all use log scales

d.unit: Revenue scale (billions USD, by his account)

l349|680.c: Activation is the hardest part of AI products: models outrun the product, so users don't know what's possible.
l349|680.e: He calls it a capability overhang: models improve faster than products can show users what they can do. That makes activation matter more in the AI era than ever before. Lessons learned on one model generation may stop applying on the next, so the product has to be retuned constantly. The highest-leverage move is getting the right feature in front of the right person. Things like importing memory from other products attack the cold-start problem, where the product knows nothing about you yet.
ex: Importing ChatGPT memory eases the cold start
The onboarding experience gets retuned after every new model release

root.d: Capability runs ahead of the product

items.d: Users don't know what the model can do
No context about the user yet

l349|680.c: Friction isn't all bad. Steps that personalize the product are worth keeping; cut the ones that don't.
l349|680.e: At Mercury he spent a whole quarter on nothing but the quality of account onboarding, ignoring metrics, and calls it the highest-impact quarter of his growth career. Breaking a dense form into several screens cut the mental load. Masterclass's pre-purchase quiz looked unnecessary, but it made people feel the courses fit them and drove a lot of revenue. Anthropic's onboarding asks about your job and interests. It isn't short, but the data supports it, and the answers later feed lifecycle marketing and lookalike ad targeting.
ex: At Mercury, one whole quarter went to onboarding quality alone
Masterclass's pre-purchase quiz noticeably lifted revenue

l349|680.c: AI-native product value grows exponentially, so growth teams should shift from small tweaks to big bets.
l349|680.e: Traditional growth teams spend 60 to 70% of their effort on small optimizations. He thinks AI-native products are different: their value compounds as models improve and new markets open up. Agentic coding didn't exist a year and a half ago, for example. The product could be worth 100 to 1,000 times more in the future, while a typical app might grow 30 to 50% over two years. So he flips the ratio. Small optimizations still happen because they compound, but he stresses this only applies to products with AI at the core.
ex: The Chrome extension came from a bet one engineer pushed hard for
He estimates product value could reach 100 to 1,000 times today's

items: Tune the funnel step by step

d.verdict: AI-core products should flip the ratio toward big bets

l349|680.c: Claude can now run growth experiments on its own, at roughly the level of a PM with two or three years' experience.
l349|680.e: The team's CASH project has Claude run growth experiments end to end: spot an opportunity, build it, test it against quality and brand standards, then analyze results and record what was learned. Each of the four steps can be evaluated. He says it didn't work before Opus 4.5, and 4.6 is where it started to look promising. Most experiments so far are copy changes and small UI tweaks, with a win rate like a junior PM's, and humans still review everything. Encoding brand guidelines as a skill will reduce review, but cross-team coordination still needs people.
ex: CASH is led by one engineer on the growth platform team
So far mostly copy and small UI changes

l349|680.c: With engineering output exploding, PMs are the scarce resource, so engineers run small projects as mini-PMs.
l349|680.e: AI tools currently give engineering the biggest boost. Five engineers with one PM and one designer now produce like fifteen to twenty engineers, which squeezes the PM and designer. Their rule: projects under roughly two engineering weeks are run by an engineer acting as mini-PM, handling security, legal, and stakeholders, with the PM only advising. Bigger projects still belong to the PM. At a scaled company, he says, the PM's highest leverage is explaining why and what to build, not writing code.
ex: About 60 to 80% of what ships has no PRD
Important projects still get a solid doc plus a 30-minute cross-team kickoff

l349|680.c: Constraints forced focus: betting on coding gave researchers better tools, which made the models better.
l349|680.e: He credits the focus on enterprise and coding to leadership and the company's DNA. Co-founder Ben Mann wrote a document back in 2021 arguing for AI coding. At the time Anthropic had less money, less distribution, and no first-mover advantage, so it had to narrow its front. Coding is also a research flywheel: better coding tools make researchers faster, and faster researchers make better models sooner. He also mentions the company had a chatbot before ChatGPT and held it back over safety concerns.
ex: Ben Mann's 2021 document making the case for AI coding
A pre-ChatGPT chatbot was shelved for safety reasons

l349|680.c: A transparent culture is the hardest asset to copy, and notebook channels carry beliefs through fast growth.
l349|680.e: He says leadership takes the mission more seriously internally than it does publicly, and employees openly challenge executives on Slack. Everyone has a notebook channel for sharing ideas, which leaders use to spread beliefs and prevent strategy and culture from drifting as the company scales fast. He once wrote about being willing to leave money on the table, and a new growth engineer immediately noticed how different that was from the old playbook. As a public benefit corporation, Anthropic has repeatedly paid a commercial price for safety, which he believes becomes a competitive advantage over time.
ex: Someone publicly pushed back on an all-hands point in Dario's notebook channel
Some internal documents also serve as context for Claude

l350|683.c: Team quality matters more than market or product, and hiring is a craft you improve through practice and review.
l350|683.e: He credits PayPal's success mainly to talent density. Early on, his judgment of strangers in interviews was right only about half the time, and it improved only through repetition and reviewing his calls. Senior hires deserve a lot of reference checks, and you keep calling until you hear something negative. How you ask matters too: "Is he a good employee?" and "Could he become a top founder?" can get completely different answers. Thirty days after someone joins, ask whether you'd hire them again. He finds that as accurate as an evaluation a year or two later.
ex: DoorDash founder Tony Xu does about 20 reference checks for senior hires
Max Rhodes of Fair found that rephrasing the question changes reference results dramatically

items.d: Keep asking until you hear negatives
Could they be a top founder

l350|683.c: A company's output depends on how many "barrels" it has. Hiring more ammunition just adds coordination costs.
l350|683.e: A barrel is someone who can take an idea from start to finish: set their own goals and deliver, marshal people and resources, measure results, and surface problems early with a diagnosis. Most companies hire aggressively without adding barrels, so new people only add coordination overhead. Ammunition, meaning design, engineering, and analytics, is still needed, in amounts that depend on the project. A very good company might have only two barrels. Barrels aren't necessarily senior either: a Square intern solved a problem the admin team couldn't crack.
ex: PayPal had about 254 people at acquisition and roughly 12 to 17 barrels
An intern solved Square's late-night smoothie delivery problem

terms.d: People who drive things end to end

result.d: More ammo without barrels just adds overhead

l350|683.c: Startups win by finding talent that standard processes miss. It's the same skill as investing.
l350|683.e: Big companies pay far more than startups, so fighting them for recognized talent is a losing game. You have to get more output from fewer resources, a principle Peter Thiel taught him. The key question is what another company's process would overlook about this person. Young people have few data points on their resumes, so standardized, data-driven evaluations miss them most often. To attract top people, go beyond the mission and show them that their specific strength solves the company's biggest bottleneck.
ex: Told he was one of few who could do the job, he left Google for Square after two weeks

l350|683.c: High-performing teams run on pressure, not psychological safety. The better things go, the harder the CEO should push.
l350|683.e: He thinks a CEO's main job is fighting complacency. The more successful the company, the harder you push, like a coach who nitpicks after a win and only inspires and paints the future after a loss. Top performers actually hate slack. He favors criticizing in public so colleagues know the problem is being handled and can pitch in. Private feedback takes care of the individual but not the whole system. He also dislikes elaborate post-mortems on failures, because they make people afraid to take big bets.
ex: Airbnb's Brian Chesky kept the pressure on; giving people time off left the team adrift
He describes championship teams with the Bulls documentary The Last Dance

d.verdict: The more successful the company, the harder the CEO pushes

l350|683.c: Models change monthly, annual roadmaps no longer hold, and the traditional PM role is losing its meaning.
l350|683.e: He thinks organizations now have to adjust weekly. Deciding what to build and why looks more and more like the CEO's job, and business judgment is the durable skill. Engineers who use AI well can run a fleet of agents directly, and design and code are merging. He isn't sure who wins, so he invests in both. Once building gets easy, the bottleneck moves to distribution and standing out from the noise, so storytelling and design become the real differentiators. A great CMO, he says, may end up as the company's biggest token user.
ex: A Ramp engineering director manages about 20 people and still writes code
Shopify reportedly bans static slides for product pitches; you have to demo

items.d: Hard to get noticed in the noise

l350|683.c: Consumers can't explain why they buy. Good ideas come from insight, not user interviews.
l350|683.e: He says he doesn't like talking to customers and doesn't let colleagues do it for consumer or small-business products. Most choices are subconscious, so asking a Porsche owner why they bought the car rarely gets the truth. To understand human nature, read Shakespeare rather than run customer research. Customer development only works for enterprise products where the decision maker is clear. Ideas your friends mock as ugly ducklings may be the signal of outsized returns.
ex: DoorDash started from the finding that 93% of US restaurants didn't deliver
Airbnb started from the founders' own problem

d.right: Enterprises with a clear decision maker

l350|683.c: Early-stage investing comes down to whether the founder could change an industry and whether the company moves fast.
l350|683.e: His investing is founder-centered. The core question is whether this person has a non-zero chance of changing an industry. Even without proof, an early founder should be able to explain how their advantages will compound. The signal of a great company is tempo: a question raised at one board meeting has shipped before the next one, and talent density keeps rising. He is skeptical that parachuting in senior executives creates value.
ex: Ramp launched card issuing in about 3 months; the norm is 9 to 12
Ramp's board meetings open with "day X since launch"

items.d: The usual cycle, by his account
The usual cycle, by his account

l351|168.c: Builders have never had it better, with record pay, but the whole industry is smiling through exhaustion.
l351|168.e: Two or three years ago, many product leaders were unhappy. They spent their days passing information upward, with responsibility but no authority, which he calls the worst kind of workplace stress. Today builders can do more with fewer people, take ideas straight to customers to test, and earn historically high pay, with more options open to them. The price is that nothing feels stable and everyone fears falling behind. People in their thirties are also hitting peak career demands while their parents age and their kids are still small.
ex: People in their thirties get squeezed by career, aging parents, and young kids at once

items: A few people can ship a product

d.verdict: Builders are happier, but everyone fears falling behind

l351|168.c: Once trying things is cheap, product changes multiply ten to a hundred times, and leaders need judgment to choose.
l351|168.e: At a gathering of about 125 product leaders, he saw everyone showing off AI tools they had built themselves, and the way they made decisions and set priorities had changed completely from a year or two earlier. Mechanical product work will be heavily automated. Testing and changing things gets cheap, so there will be ten to a hundred times more product changes. Judgment means seeing whether a change actually makes the product better and fits a sustainable, differentiated direction, instead of shipping hundreds of variants that damage the brand and become unmaintainable.
ex: At a meetup of about 125 product leaders, everyone demoed tools they built themselves
He hopes there will be no more bad software within two years

result.d: Choosing among a flood of changes

l351|168.c: About half of PMs are information movers and are being phased out. Builders are the ones getting hired.
l351|168.e: He estimates about half of today's PMs mainly move information around, and that role is becoming a dinosaur. The PMs getting hired are builders, often former founders or people who got into the job to make things in the first place. Engineering, design, and marketing are all looking for builders too. His report shows PM openings at global tech companies are the highest in more than three years, so whether the PM market is good depends on how you define PM. People who don't enjoy building may need to leave tech, or use AI tools to start a business of their own.
ex: PM openings are at a three-year high, close to pandemic-era levels

marks.d: Engineering, design, marketing all want them

l351|168.c: A PM's leverage isn't writing features as a cheap engineer. It's automating reviews and reporting.
l351|168.e: He agrees PMs shouldn't prove their worth by shipping features themselves. The real leverage is building internal systems so one PM can keep up with the output of fifty-plus engineers: automating product reviews, standups, and weekly reports, and rebuilding the product operating system. Several CPOs in his community have already fully automated reviews and standups. With AI supplying the facts, leaders can see the situation directly, and there is less of the performance of alignment through reporting and packaging.
ex: Several CPOs have fully automated product reviews and standups

l351|168.c: Companies will cut deep, then rehire AI-first people. A big-company badge matters less than current skills.
l351|168.e: He thinks companies broadly overhired in the last boom. Over the next year or two, they will lay off large numbers and rehire a much smaller, entirely AI-first workforce. Interviewers care more about which tools a candidate uses now and how they make judgment calls. A big-company resume is worth less; a small algorithm improvement at Meta is hard to make impressive. Skills once prized, like leverage, scale, and delegation, may get flipped, while hands-on building and strong opinions matter more.
ex: His example: lay off 30,000, then hire 8,000 AI-first people

l351|168.c: People struggle to reinvent themselves because life rests on old bargains, and new methods expire fast.
l351|168.e: People built stable lives on old bargains: degrees, jobs, company brands, family. Naturally they resist tearing that down. At peak life load you can't cover everything, so you spread your time evenly and disappoint everyone a little. A new method you spent a week learning is outdated months later, so you never reach a state of flow. The people most fluent in the old system resist change the most, which he calls a shadow superpower. His advice is to find the courage to put reinvention ahead of everything else.
ex: His "evenly distributed disappointment" algorithm
Shadow superpower: the better you are at the old system, the more you resist

l351|168.c: Beating burnout starts with joy: solve a small annoyance of your own and get that first win.
l351|168.e: He asks peers to color the meetings on their calendar green, yellow, or red. Most PMs are mostly yellow and red; builders are mostly green and yellow. The shift from fear to joy usually starts with the first thing you build for yourself with AI tools. Joy is the best antidote to burnout, and leaders should pass it on to their teams. You don't need an engineering background to start, just opinions and a sense of what good looks like. He writes code while rewatching familiar shows, automating his own chores one by one.
ex: He built agents for his community that match members and match candidates to jobs
Tools like Claude Code, Codex, or Lovable will do

items.d: Meetings go from red to green

l351|168.c: Today's chaos is a transition, but most people will change jobs within five years, so plan early.
l351|168.e: He compares now to when internet companies like Google invented modern product management. It was chaotic at first, and within about two years the workflows settled into routine. It won't be a treadmill forever. But he expects most listeners to change jobs within five years, by choice or not. His advice: speed up, let go of status and accept a smaller or different role, accept disappointing some people, and think about the step after next rather than the next step. Engineers will shift toward deciding what to build, and designers must move from producing pixels to taste.
ex: PMs may be like dandelion seeds, carrying new practices into other functions

l352|687.c: Feature cycles shrank from six months to days, so PMs should shorten the path from idea to user.
l352|687.e: She says a feature now goes from kickoff to launch in about a month instead of six, and sometimes in a week or a day. At that pace, spending lots of time aligning multi-quarter roadmaps with partner teams no longer pays off. The best AI-native PMs focus on finding the fastest path to get something into users' hands and on defining which core tasks must work out of the box. She and Boris Cherny split the work like this: he sets the direction three to six months out, and she gets the team from today to there and clears cross-team obstacles.
ex: About six months, then one month, now sometimes a week or a day
She and Boris overlap about 80%; the rest goes to whoever cares more

d.verdict: Speed changed, so the PM's time allocation must too

l352|687.c: The speed comes mostly from process and expectations, not the model: clear goals and minimal process.
l352|687.e: She thinks using the model internally sped up shipping only somewhat. Most of it comes from process and team expectations: the company deliberately keeps process minimal and wants to remove every barrier to shipping. In practice that means setting a clear goal that rules out many options up front. Most features launch as research previews, which lowers the commitment and lets them iterate after launch. Engineers post features they've tried internally in an evergreen launch channel, and docs and marketing can announce the next day. Everyone reviews metrics weekly, and written team principles let people decide without waiting for a PM.
ex: Example goal: zero permission prompts for enterprise developers
PRDs are reserved for vague or months-long infrastructure projects

items.d: One sentence rules out most options
Decide without waiting for a PM

l352|687.c: The cheaper code gets, the more deciding what to write is worth. Product taste is the scarcest skill.
l352|687.e: PMs write code, engineers do product work, designers commit code. The roles are merging. Her team prioritizes hiring engineers with product taste, and many can go from user feedback to a shipped feature within a week with almost no PM involvement. Most PMs on the team have engineering backgrounds too. Knowing engineering helps you judge how hard something is, which is how you prioritize well. Where humans still have the edge is common sense, emotional intelligence, and tacit knowledge of what stakeholders prefer and how they communicate.
ex: About 30 to 40 PMs, split across research, platform, core product, enterprise, and growth

l352|687.c: Shipping fast costs consistency. Rough edges that don't block core use wait for the next release.
l352|687.e: She admits the pace can be brutal, so you have to prioritize ruthlessly, sleep well, and accept that some features won't be polished. As long as a flaw doesn't block the core use case, it gets fixed in the next release based on feedback. The cost is lower product consistency: overlapping features sometimes ship in two forms at once, and the team watches which one outside users prefer. New users don't know the best path, and existing users have to keep refreshing Twitter to keep up. The team long refused to build onboarding, but eventually added a built-in /powerup tutorial.
ex: /powerup came from users asking which 10 features they absolutely had to learn

l352|687.c: Every new model is a chance to delete scaffolding. The PM's craft is getting the most out of today's model.
l352|687.e: With each new model release, the team reads through the entire system prompt and removes whatever the model no longer needs. A superhuman model would need almost no product scaffolding, so the real challenge is building for today's model: drawing out as much capability as possible, guiding users onto the golden path, and covering its weaknesses. New models also unlock new features. Multiple review agents can now reliably catch most bugs, so the engineering team requires code to pass their review before merging.
ex: The to-do list exists because early models stopped after about 5 edits
Since Opus 4, the model uses to-do lists naturally on its own

l352|687.c: PMs build model intuition through heavy use, asking the model to reflect on mistakes, and writing evals.
l352|687.e: The hardest skill, she says, is inferring what the product should look like a month from now from patterns in how users push against today's limits. Her approach has three parts. Use the model heavily and ask it to reflect on why it got something wrong. Find about five users who can describe the model's behavior precisely and keep getting their feedback. And build evals, even just ten good ones, to quantify goals and progress. The team also does lunchtime vibe checks on new models, which often surface problems faster than data analysis.
ex: Example failures: skipping UI verification, subagents that don't run tests
The memory feature benefited especially from evals

items.d: Push the tool to its limits
Ten good ones are enough to help

l352|687.c: The next step is hundreds or thousands of agents running remotely. The key is trusting "done" means done.
l352|687.e: She breaks the path into building blocks: first one task completes reliably, then many tasks run in parallel, and finally dozens or hundreds run remotely at the same time. Getting there requires an interface that makes results easy to triage, agents that verify their own work so people trust that done means done, and the ability to improve from feedback without repeating mistakes. Her advice for individuals is the same: push automation close to 100%, because automation that's only 95% reliable isn't worth much.
ex: Running several Claude sessions in parallel took off in late 2025
Her own Gmail spam triage still misses emails

l353|691.c: Software features are easy to copy. Lasting advantage has to come from ecosystems and integrated hardware.
l353|691.e: Snap learned this the hard way about 15 years ago: features got cloned by competitors as soon as they launched, and patents didn't stop it. So the company shifted toward things that are harder to copy: a creator and developer ecosystem, and vertically integrated hardware. Network effects help, but he doesn't think they're enough on their own. Being copied means your innovation worked, but it forces you to make strategic choices more deliberately.
ex: Developers have built millions of AR lenses
He sees Instagram's subscription plan as a copy of Snapchat+
Snapchat+ has about 25 million subscribers and over $1 billion in annualized revenue

items: Cloned as soon as they launch

d.verdict: Build defenses where competitors can't copy

l353|691.c: Distribution is now the hardest problem in consumer tech, and founders should plan it alongside product-market fit.
l353|691.e: When Snapchat launched, app stores were new and people loved trying new apps. That appetite has faded, and new products struggle to get noticed. Recent winners either spent heavily to subsidize both sides, like TikTok paying viewers and creators, or borrowed existing traffic, like Threads riding on Meta. He thinks founders spend far less thought on distribution than on polishing product-market fit, and in the AI era distribution may be the new moat. New platforms like glasses will open windows, but he worries startups will struggle to break through against the giants.
ex: TikTok spent billions subsidizing both viewers and creators
Threads grew by borrowing Meta's existing distribution
Early Snap grew by connecting you with your few closest friends

root.d: New apps get harder to notice

items.d: TikTok paid both sides to start

l353|691.c: Phones are keyholes that isolate people from each other. Glasses can bring computing back into the real world.
l353|691.e: He loves computers, but people spend seven or eight hours a day on screens, and phones pull them out of shared spaces. AR on a phone is like looking at the world through a keyhole, and you have to operate it with your thumbs. Glasses free your hands and keep people face to face. He is skeptical of heads-up-display glasses that just move notifications onto your face, and believes content should be anchored in your surroundings. His contrarian view is that human nature decides how technology gets adopted, and tech leaders underestimate the social backlash against AI.
ex: In 2024 Snap released a glasses operating system for developers to build full apps
With heads-up-display glasses, your eye position looks awkward in conversation

items.d: Took the camera off the phone in 2014
Put digital objects in your view
Launching to the public this year

l353|691.c: Scale needs hierarchy, innovation needs small flat teams, and leaders must keep the two talking.
l353|691.e: He borrows from the book Loonshots: running a service for nearly a billion people requires structure and reliability, but hierarchy makes people avoid risk and chase promotions, while flat teams dare to experiment. Without communication, innovators see the big organization as bureaucratic and the organization sees innovators as undisciplined. Snap's design team has only about a dozen people and no titles. He reviews hundreds of ideas with them every week, believing good ideas come from lots of ideas. New hires present work on their first day, and designers rotate across products.
ex: The design team is about 9 to 12 people with no titles
Snap didn't hire PMs until it had about 200 employees
Nothing ships without design approval

result.d: As long as both sides keep talking

l353|691.c: Listen to users deeply, but don't build the literal thing they ask for.
l353|691.e: He rejects the idea that talking to users hurts the product. Share ideas early and often, and listen through hour-long conversations. But he doesn't trust surveys, and he doesn't think feedback must be followed literally. Users once asked for a "send to everyone" button. The team saw the real pain was the pressure of permanent, public metrics and a reverse-chronological feed. So they built Stories: gone in 24 hours, with no public likes or comments. Screenshot notifications work the same way. Users cared about knowing, not about blocking saves.
ex: Stories came from the posting anxiety behind the "send to all" request
Apple had no screenshot API then, so Snap inferred screenshots from touch events

items.d: Users want a "send to all" button
Public metrics and permanence create pressure
Gone in 24 hours, no public likes

l353|691.c: Roll out AI by listing users' and advertisers' jobs to be done, then staff teams per job and measure business outcomes.
l353|691.e: Snap started by listing the jobs users need done (download the app, add close friends, use lenses) and the jobs advertisers need done (get into the ads platform, set up a campaign). That shows where agents should plug in. Cross-functional teams form around each job, and progress is measured in business outcomes. An app with nearly a billion users needs guardrails: AI code review has already caught close to ten thousand bugs automatically. Designers can write code but aren't required to. He thinks AI shortens the distance from idea to impact.
ex: A go-to-market agent writes specs, finds stakeholders, and runs legal and security risk analysis
He uses a Glean-based agent to scan dashboards and flag what matters

items.d: What users and advertisers need done

l353|691.c: This is the crucible year: prove the core business is profitable first, then earn the right to fight the glasses war.
l353|691.e: Snap has nearly a billion monthly users and revenue approaching Fortune 500 scale, but heavy investment in future platforms means it hasn't yet turned a net profit. He says this year Snap must prove it is a strong, profitable company: drive growth with topic group chats, Spotlight, and games, rebuild the ad platform and sales organization, and speed up small-business acquisition. A solid core business is the precondition for the long-term bet on Specs. As the company stuck in the middle, Snap also sees Specs as its way out of being overlooked.
ex: Games have about 200 million monthly users
Annual revenue is over $6 billion, with no net profit yet

marks.d: Pinterest and Reddit are smaller than Snap
Stuck in the middle, easy to overlook

l354|696.c: AI has flattened skill gaps, so the drive to act is now the scarce thing.
l354|696.e: People used to count themselves out by saying they lacked the skills. Now that AI tools have shrunk that gap, he thinks what separates people is agency: the willingness to just go do things. And agency is not evenly distributed. People who believe the world can be changed will thrive. People who cling to a job description like "what a PM is supposed to do" will struggle. He wants employees to step outside their roles and fill gaps, even at a company that found product-market fit long ago. The way to build agency is to make things: your work gets noticed, and that pushes you to act more.
ex: An engineer-designer stepped up to fill a gap and became a top recruiter
A PM stopped writing long strategy documents and started building prototypes
Most man-made things around you can be learned in six to nine months

items.d: The world is built by ordinary people
Step outside your role to fill gaps

l354|696.c: Designers should work in the final medium, because AI behavior can only be understood by building it.
l354|696.e: Mocking up an AI chat interface in Figma looks lifeless, he says, because how an AI behaves is something you have to feel firsthand. So he and colleagues built a "playground" codebase that works well with large language models, letting designers prototype with AI tools without being scared of the terminal. He doesn't care whether that code ships. The point is that designers face the material they are designing with. He would rather hire someone who deeply understands the agent loop (how an AI plans, acts, checks the result, and repeats) than someone who only tweaks UI styles. And the only way to understand the loop is to build one.
ex: Before LLMs took off, about 10% of GitHub's top contributors were designers
He compares today's coding harnesses to the operating systems of the 1990s

items: Can't show how the AI behaves
Become a step in a handoff line

d.verdict: The goal is to master the material, not ship code

l354|696.c: The first 10% of a project is nearly free now, so explore in parallel and demo instead of document.
l354|696.e: Getting a product to version 0.8 takes almost no effort today, he observes, while the last 10% is as hard as ever. Since the start is so cheap, it pays to try several paths at once. Back at GitHub he pushed "demos, not memos": bring a prototype or a mock changelog to review instead of a requirements document, so iteration starts earlier. But he warns that feature count, tokens spent, and lines of code are all terrible metrics. Notion currently puts almost no limit on token spend. He expects that in 6 to 12 months companies will start asking hard questions about the return on it.
ex: Send 10 agents to test 10 ideas at the same time
For engineers, editing code by hand should count as a bug in the validation loop

l354|696.c: The "SaaS apocalypse" is wildly overstated; software's real value is that someone maintains it.
l354|696.e: He grants that a lot of 2010s SaaS was just a layer of forms wrapped around a database table, and that layer really can be eaten by AI. But the core value of SaaS, as he sees it, is that dedicated people keep the software secure, reliable, and improving. Most people have no desire to maintain their own software stack. He rewrote a version of Notion himself one weekend and knows exactly how heavy that burden is. He expects tools to become more general, like word processors and spreadsheets in the 1990s, but still delivered as services, with specialized tools surviving too.
ex: Anthropic runs on Slack as its company operating system; nobody would rebuild it
He cites Bret Taylor: software is like a garden that needs tending

root.d: Change is coming, but less dramatic than claimed

items.d: Thin apps wrapped around a database table

l354|696.c: Great products have a tiny, excellent core; a weak core can't be rescued by adding features.
l354|696.e: Good design, good engineering, or being first don't guarantee a win, he says. The common trap is believing one more feature will make the product click. What he sees in successful products is a surprisingly small core that is exceptionally good. Being first matters less than people think: AirPods arrived after countless Bluetooth earbuds and won by getting it right. In 2014 he built a Notion competitor with a beautifully polished markdown editor. Early Notion's editor was rough, but its core was right. His lesson: protect the core idea and keep iterating on it instead of piling on features.
ex: The iPhone's multi-touch, GitHub's pull request
Notion's blocks and slash commands
Dropbox's little menu-bar icon quietly syncing files

cells.d: Rough editor, but the core was right

l354|696.c: Taste is a mental simulator that predicts what a chosen crowd will like, trained by practice and feedback.
l354|696.e: He defines taste as being able to run a virtual machine in your head that predicts whether a particular group you've chosen will like something. Building it takes lots of practice plus real feedback, which looks a lot like training a model. Designers with good taste, he notices, tend to have side projects, range widely across fields, and surround themselves with good things. Because taste forms through something like backpropagation (adjusting from feedback), he rejects the idea that taste is humanity's last advantage. Notion's internal rule is to only ship things that are obviously good.
ex: Notion names meeting rooms after classic design objects as a constant reminder of the bar
Good things are obvious on sight, like the ChatGPT launch

items.d: The people you want to please
Side projects, wide range of interests
See how that crowd really reacts

l354|696.c: Software should be reshapeable by its users and serve them, not the vendor, like rearranging a room.
l354|696.e: Most apps lock their behavior and data inside a fixed interface, he says, which is like not being allowed to rearrange your own living room. He believes people should own their computing lives. Full control in the Linux style costs too much for most people, so the middle path is a platform that encourages users to customize. He agrees with Dieter Rams that things must be useful before they are beautiful, and one test of usefulness is whether something can be modified to fit you, the way good buildings evolve with their occupants. He admits Notion isn't malleable enough yet either.
ex: The research lab Ink & Switch is building malleable tools that are collaborative yet secure
Stewart Brand's book How Buildings Learn
He sees Notion as a Unix-like environment that agents can roam around in

marks.d: Behavior and data locked in a fixed interface
A middle path that invites customization
Full control, but too costly for most

l355|241.c: Companies rarely decline because a rival beat them; success makes them a target for extraction.
l355|241.e: He calls the force that drags organizations toward mediocrity and strips founders of control "financial gravity": nobody controls it, yet everybody obeys it. The logic is simple. The more successful a company becomes, the more worth extracting from it is. So quality gets cut after an acquisition, investors replace the founder, and the business pivots to chasing growth and margins. Bridges are safe not because they accept gravity but because they are built from stainless steel. Companies likewise need structures that resist corrosion, rather than relying on good intentions.
ex: A natural-food brand's founder was pushed out by investors; quality fell and share shrank
Harvard Law data: under standard governance, only about 20% of founders are still CEO three years after IPO

root.d: Makes the company worth extracting from

items.d: The board only sees the highest bid

l355|241.c: Mission-protecting structures must be built early; it always feels too soon, until it's too late.
l355|241.e: Lawyers, bankers, and investors keep telling founders to wait, he says, but by the time the IPO arrives the founder has no leverage left. He coached one star company whose advisors found him too pessimistic. After it went public, its whole category collapsed and the founder was out within five months. He sees that as a structural failure, not just a personal one, and notes that the advisors get paid on deal volume whatever the outcome. Most so-called best practices, he adds, are just conventions from the last few decades that have never been tested over the long run.
ex: You have the most freedom before raising money, or when you've only taken SAFEs
Shareholder primacy is only about 40 years old; before that, charters required a declared public benefit

items.d: Most freedom to design the structure
Investors must agree to it too
Standard governance pushes most founders out

l355|241.c: If your charter defaults to shareholder primacy, the board may have to sell to the buyer you hate most.
l355|241.e: Imagine a buyer you would never work for offers a premium for your company. Most founders say they'd refuse, but their charter may already give the board a fiduciary duty to take the highest bid. That is exactly how the board of Vectura, a British inhaler company, sold it to Philip Morris, which wrote it down heavily and broke it up within three years. Delaware charters are public records, he points out, yet most founders have never read their own. A charter that says the company may engage in "any lawful act" gets read as shareholder primacy.
ex: Philip Morris paid about £1.1 billion and wrote down about $900 million within three years
The real premium was about 15 cents a share, even lower than the $1 in his hypothetical

items.d: From the buyer you least respect
Believes it must take the top bid

l355|241.c: The principled path looks harder but is easier: trust is the most underrated asset in business.
l355|241.e: Principled choices always look expensive in an ROI spreadsheet, he says, so unless leaders hold to principles for their own sake, the spreadsheet wins. But trusted companies communicate more cheaply inside, stay better aligned, keep customers longer, acquire them for less, and get forgiven more easily when they slip. Cloudflare adopted an engineer's offhand line, "build a better internet," as its mission and gave away encryption for free. Paid conversion dropped, but the top of the funnel grew about tenfold. Groupon, by contrast, let experiment data push it to send more and more email, and damaged its brand.
ex: Cloudflare's first value is "be principled"; he credits trust for its $70 billion valuation
Groupon's daily emails climbed from 1 to 8

items: Tests say more email means more money

d.verdict: Hold to principles for their own sake; it's easier long term

l355|241.c: Write down whom you'd rather die than betray, then attach an enforcement mechanism to every promise.
l355|241.e: He revives the old term "fiduciary" in place of stakeholders, culture, or values, and asks companies to state clearly whom they owe an unbreakable duty to. Many self-described mission-driven companies, he says, are merely hopeful. The test: can anyone profit by violating the principles? Are the canaries, like quality, safety, and design, the first things cut? Do bonuses and OKRs reward betrayal? Google never misses a quarterly report because a huge machine sits behind it. "Don't be evil" had no machine behind it, so it faded.
ex: Johnson & Johnson's patient-health mission was in practice overridden by growth targets
Devoted Health: treat customers the way you'd want your parents treated
Automated tests and AI can audit whether promises are being kept

terms.d: Write down the mission and whom you serve

result.d: Withstands pressure from inside and out

l355|241.c: A mission needs a dedicated guardian, and the more institutional and renewable that guardian, the sturdier it is.
l355|241.e: Commercial gravity is too strong for a mission to survive on its own, he argues. Someone or something must guard it full time. Founder control works only as a temporary bridge, and it often leaves founders isolated and exhausted. Writing terms straight into the charter, as Costco did, lacks a way to re-strengthen them once they erode. More durable are stewards whose members can be replaced: employee ownership trusts, cooperatives, nonprofit foundations, and perpetual purpose trusts. He groups these as "ethos holding companies" and says the evidence shows they are more stable and invest more in R&D and quality.
ex: Novo Nordisk has been foundation-controlled for over a century; trustees once blocked a sale
Patagonia's perpetual purpose trust has a "purpose guardian" who can sue the trustees
The Mondragon cooperative has about 80,000 employees

marks.d: A temporary bridge; founders burn out
Like Costco, but hard to re-strengthen

l355|241.c: A public benefit corporation costs almost nothing, and Anthropic proves mission governance doesn't slow growth.
l355|241.e: A PBC needs only a two-page document naming a purpose beyond "any lawful act." When investors accuse a founder of breaching fiduciary duty, that document gives legal cover. The main cost is pushback from lawyers and investors. He admits a PBC doesn't guarantee good behavior. Anthropic is a PBC and also has a Long-Term Benefit Trust, and it still became the fastest-growing company in history. He attributes its advantages in cost, speed, focus, and talent to mission alignment, and notes that turning down dangerous models and Pentagon contracts has been a real, paid price.
ex: The Long-Term Benefit Trust's trustees hold no shares and appoint directors
He says declining a roughly $200 million Pentagon contract took courage
Claude Code's product lead credits fast shipping to mission alignment

items.d: Trustees hold no shares, serve only the mission
States the purpose, keeps room to reform
Investors can't easily oust the CEO

l355|241.c: Doing the right thing at a cost is a deposit in the culture bank; self-serving harm is a withdrawal.
l355|241.e: Mission-aligned companies don't need an ROI spreadsheet for every ethical choice, he says, so there is less arguing and faster action. He quotes Clayton Christensen: it's easier to hold your principles 100% of the time than 98%. Doing the right thing when it costs you is a deposit in the culture bank. Hurting others for your own gain is a withdrawal. The rule is deposits only, never withdrawals. The flip side: at a company where a small group of activist investors can fire the CEO at any time, every past promise becomes untrustworthy, and employees and customers stop believing.
ex: Texas grocer H-E-B let customers take goods for free during an ice-storm blackout
Steve Jobs would personally meet "torchbearer" employees who insisted on doing the right thing
The rule comes from Todd Park and traces back to Howard Schultz

items.d: Like H-E-B letting customers go in the storm
Employees and customers believe the promises

l356|699.c: VR never went mainstream, but the spatial-sensing tech it forged now powers robots and physical AI.
l356|699.e: VR didn't take off, she thinks, mainly because headsets cover your face and get in the way of being social, and gaming is a real but niche market. Its true value is the technology: using cameras so a device knows where it is in space (SLAM), sensing depth, and understanding how the human eye perceives images. Robots, self-driving cars, drones, and manufacturing need exactly these parts and capabilities. AR glasses are still the right direction, letting you read information while keeping eye contact, but Orion's waveguides and microLED displays can't yet be mass-produced at reasonable yield and cost.
ex: Orion's roughly 70-degree binocular field of view is immersive in a way words can't capture
Displays that stay off and light up only when needed may become the mainstream design

items.d: Knowing where you are and how far things are
Waveguides and microLED await mass production

l356|699.c: Digital work behind a keyboard may saturate first; AI's next frontier is the physical world.
l356|699.e: Lab progress is moving so fast, she observes, that knowledge work done behind a keyboard may soon be close to saturated, and the frontier will shift to robots, manufacturing, sensing, moving physical things, and eventually space. Interest in hardware is rising while computer science enrollment is falling. Hardware used to be an underpaid, little-seen career you did for love, Apple aside. But change in the physical world will be slower than in knowledge work: supply chains, reliability, raw materials, and domestic high-tech factories all take time. She doesn't expect twenty million robots on the streets within five years.
ex: She expects delivery robots to show up on streets first
She thinks warfare may change more in the next two years than consumer electronics will

items.d: AI takes the keyboard jobs first

l356|699.c: Hardware only "compiles" a few times, so attack the hardest blocker first and lock targets early.
l356|699.e: A major hardware build takes months, she explains, so a product gets maybe four or five "compiles," and nothing can be patched after mass production. That forces a conservative process with thorough testing. Her approach: set targets early and change them as little as possible. Design the riskiest blocker first, such as confirming a cable can actually route through a laptop hinge. Iterate most on what users touch most, the trackpad and keyboard. Do the known work immediately, because surprises always come. At millions of units, you also have to eliminate the last fraction of a percent of tolerance drift.
ex: Launching a few weeks before a rival can be worth millions in attention
Quest 1 cut to 4 tracking cameras; a tolerance misunderstanding surfaced just before EVT

items.d: Can the cable pass through the hinge?
Trackpad and keyboard get touched most
Squeeze out the last tolerance drift

l356|699.c: Set goals from first principles and weight your metrics, and trade-offs become fast and accurate.
l356|699.e: Apple trains you to start from first principles, she says: why are we building this, and which outcome matters most? Designs that follow that discipline often end up looking very simple. Every product category has its key metrics. VR is judged on pixels per degree, with the human eye as the benchmark. Laptops are judged on clock speed, weight, and price. Deciding up front how many dollars a gram of weight is worth speeds decisions enormously. Quest 2's goal was to make VR mainstream, so the team dropped a camera and changed materials and processes to cut cost. It became the best-selling VR headset, with low returns.
ex: The MacBook Air dropped its ambient light sensor to get thinner and lighter
She's heard Elon Musk also puts a price on every gram

terms.d: What a gram of weight is worth

result.d: Quest 2 cut cost and kept quality

l356|699.c: The US must rebuild its supply chain from raw materials to assembly; actuators, magnets, and memory are weak spots.
l356|699.e: Over the past 25 years or so, she says, supply chains were outsourced to China, Japan, and Korea, and Asia won on scale and cost. Alliances, pandemics, and wars can all cause disruptions, so the US needs to relearn manufacturing at scale. Actuators turn electricity into motion, and the US lacks strong suppliers. If magnets are cut off, the only fallback is a bigger or less efficient design. Drone rotors and robot-arm actuators share the same roots, and the military chain needs to be independent too. AI demand is pushing memory prices up, maybe doubling them, she guesses, so startups should stock up early.
ex: Swapping a die-cast part delays you months; swapping a chip or memory may mean a full redesign
She agrees with Palmer Luckey that drones deserve investment more than aircraft carriers

items.d: Asia wins on scale and cost

l356|699.c: Humanoids are still advanced prototypes; most jobs are better done by purpose-built robots.
l356|699.e: Right now the job is just to prove a humanoid can do useful work, she says. Cheaper, easier to build, high yield, and safer all come later. The truly hard part is scale: hundreds of thousands to a million units running reliably day after day with little human repair. Safety is a big problem. Lighter, softer designs reduce impact energy, and a robot that requires people to stay three feet away clearly can't work alongside them yet. She thinks most jobs suit specialized robots, with humanoids handling only the long tail of odd tasks. Top factories are already heavily automated anyway.
ex: 1X's Neo is built lighter and softer to reduce impact
Assembly lines that once had 200 people now have about 10; some PCB lines are nearly unstaffed

marks.d: Standard cells, upgraded step by step
Different shapes for construction, electrical, logistics
Only the long tail of tasks

l356|699.c: AI still can't do real CAD; hardware needs a "Codex for hardware" that understands physics.
l356|699.e: Today's models can generate surfaces or point clouds, she says, but not geometrically precise parametric solid models. Language and video models don't understand friction, weight, or contact, or how a folded piece of paper unfolds. AI is getting genuinely useful for inner-layer PCB routing and basic component selection, and she mainly uses it for planning, mapping dependencies, building competitor databases, and spreadsheets. The biggest obstacle is data: companies treat CAD files as core IP and won't share them. Hobbyist data, or companies training locally on their own files, might be the way through.
ex: Tedious work like tolerance stack-ups and dimensioning is the best fit for AI
She imagines this direction may be built on top of world models

items: Physical reasoning about friction and contact
No access to CAD training data

d.verdict: Needs a physics-aware Codex for hardware

l356|699.c: Robots need social manners: signal before acting, and look soft and approachable.
l356|699.e: Human-robot interaction research shows that when someone enters a room, they expect nonverbal cues from the other party, she says. A robot that gives none feels creepy. So robots should appear soft, attentive, and eager to help. Glancing before turning is far more reassuring than spinning around suddenly, and Pixar and Disney are the masters of conveying intent this way. The trust bar for home robots is high, but Waymo shows trust can be built gradually. Tesla's self-driving, she thinks, comes across as rude at intersections because there is no eye contact or hand gesture.
ex: She cites Leila Takayama's human-robot interaction research
A new category doesn't replace existing products, so its story has to be more convincing

items.d: Earn trust step by step, like Waymo

l357|570.c: Predicting the future means writing down what early adopters already do: everyone gets an agent to delegate to.
l357|570.e: Nearly all of Every's roughly 30 people are AI early adopters, non-engineers included, so he says his predictions come from observation, not fortune-telling. Around Sonnet 3.5 and 3.7, the team noticed Claude Code could handle all kinds of computer tasks, not just coding. From that he predicts: everyone will have at least one agent they can delegate work to, and most work will move into environments like Codex or Claude Cowork, where email and documents get done too. These become the operating system for work.
ex: The "reach test": is it the first thing you open in the morning?
One Codex thread per project, with a built-in browser and an email agent called Cora
