l357|570.c: Build one company-wide super-agent first; personal agents are too fragile and die without care.
l357|570.e: He used to think everyone would have a personal agent that mirrored them. He changed his mind. Personal agents are too much hassle: they break, they need servers maintained, and the moment the owner loses interest, nobody uses them. More realistic is one super-agent for the whole company, maintained by a forward deployed engineer. Team-specific agents come next, and personal agents return only once models no longer need babysitting. The core mechanism is that an agent needs someone who cares about it. Slack, he suspects, may become the main interface for work agents.
ex: He says Shopify and Ramp both have company-level super-agents
Every paused its hosted OpenClaw because configuration was too hard

items.d: A forward deployed engineer looks after it

l357|570.c: The CLI phase got speedrun, graphical agents win, and Codex has caught up with Claude.
l357|570.e: Anthropic was first to notice that a terminal agent running on your own computer has broad permissions, and models happen to be good at using the terminal. That made Claude Code a general-purpose work tool. OpenAI fell behind for a while, but the Codex desktop app followed the same path from Claude Code to Cowork and caught up. Now it's a horse race. The command line won't disappear, but a graphical interface is better, especially for non-programmers. Cursor's cloud product is more advanced, yet serving only programmers may hold it back.
ex: Most of Every's technical staff have moved from the CLI to graphical apps like Codex
Claude Code currently can't browse external websites

l357|570.c: The SaaS apocalypse is dumb: agents give SaaS more users, and software must serve humans and agents together.
l357|570.e: Agents won't replace SaaS, he argues; they add users to it. Every uses AI heavily, yet its SaaS spending is up year over year. He even says he'd buy SaaS stocks now, though not as investment advice. SaaS will increasingly run inside Codex or Claude Code, burning the user's own tokens, so vendors no longer pay the inference bill. Products need agent-friendly interfaces, plus an approval inbox, activity summaries, logs, and rollback. And infrastructure has to withstand bursts of agent requests.
ex: Bug reports written by agents come with reproduction steps and code context
Onboarding becomes pasting a prompt into Codex
GitHub's recent strain comes from agent traffic

l357|570.c: "Automation is a lie": behind every automation there has to be a person with judgment.
l357|570.e: He earlier coined the "allocation economy": working with AI is more like managing, and it demands ongoing attention. Benchmarks make AI look more autonomous than it is, he says, because they only reward problems that can be clearly stated and scored. So he built a senior-engineer benchmark using Every's own app, Proof. Models went from about 30 points to about 62, while senior engineers score in the high 80s to low 90s. The best models only rewrite from the ground up when a person with judgment prompts them; left alone, they just patch. He expects models to reach senior level within a year.
ex: Two senior engineers each rewrote Proof to serve as reference answers
The 62 came from GPT-5.5 executing with Opus 4.7 planning
Make the task a little harder and scores drop back to zero

l357|570.c: The bottleneck has shifted from "can we build it" to "should we merge it"; judgment and pruning are central.
l357|570.e: PR volume has exploded, he says, with even non-technical colleagues submitting code. The hard part is now deciding what to merge: keeping the product coherent and cutting bloated features, something he thinks Anthropic does well. The "what is my job?" confusion will fade, and generalists are especially valuable at small companies. The forward deployed engineer is a new role, keeping agents productively at work. Data science teams now spend much of their time reviewing other people's sloppy AI analyses. The fix is a data science agent that connects to the warehouse and respects permissions.
ex: OpenClaw's author gets thousands of PRs a day and triages them with many Codex instances
Every's consulting business runs on an agent named Claudia

items.d: Bulk first review and merge suggestions

l357|570.c: Building is now a commodity; PMs and designers who can build and have judgment will win.
l357|570.e: Being able to build something is no longer scarce, he says. What's scarce is judging what to build and whether it's good. The lead of Every's writing app Spiral was a PM at Axios, spent a year learning Cursor, and now ships faster than most of the team, despite only a light technical background. Designers can implement their own interactions and submit PRs, and because AI-generated design tends to look the same, people who make distinctive work will stand out. He also predicts CEOs will fall behind quickly: how far a company goes depends on how deeply its CEO uses AI.
ex: Sales changes least because it's face to face; customer support is already transformed
He found a strong job candidate by asking Codex

terms.d: What to build, and is it good
Now available to anyone via AI

result.d: And full-stack designers

l357|570.c: No AI jobs apocalypse: models commoditize yesterday's skills, and people move on to new work.
l357|570.e: Models make yesterday's human abilities cheap and widespread, he argues, and people promptly move past them to do new things. AI output needs human judgment, so demand for engineers has actually gone up, and some layoffs blamed on AI are really corrections for overhiring. He thinks the scare-style messaging from AI companies is both ineffective and wrong. Beyond the horizon lies neither catastrophe nor utopia but a mixed picture where much stays the same. His advice: do real work with each new model, and keep retesting the tasks that failed before.
ex: For quarterly planning, Every has a Notion agent interview every employee
Most of his email is drafted by GPT-5.5 inside Codex, and he's happy to say so

l358|703.c: AI is a shift on the scale of the internet and mobile, and we're at roughly the internet's 1997.
l358|703.e: Arguing whether AI is 20% bigger or twice as big as the internet is pointless, he says. It is a platform shift of that order. Right now it feels like 1997: exciting, but most of the applications haven't been built yet, and nobody can see how it will work once it matures. Adoption is wildly uneven. Some people in tech have stopped using Google, while many outside it use AI less than once a week. The "jagged frontier" of what it can do makes it hard to know in advance where it will work. Software development is having its VisiCalc moment; law and journalism are still feeling their way.
ex: A survey of 13-to-18-year-olds: about 15-20% use it daily, another 20% or so weekly
Developers are like accountants seeing a spreadsheet for the first time

items.d: A few people pick it up first
Exciting, but most apps aren't built yet
Do more of the old things, then new ones

l358|703.c: AI can produce the output of a task, but people pay for the judgment inside a job.
l358|703.e: Clients pay for judgment, organizational politics, and an understanding of their own situation, not for the visible output, he argues. AI can assemble a rough consulting deck, but that isn't what the client is really buying. Amazon can deliver a screw to your door; knowing which screw to use is a different job. So he calls "AI exposure" scores for occupations nonsense, repeating the mistake of expert systems that tried to break expertise into rules. Companies also have no spare people to redesign their processes, which is why consulting and professional services are booming instead.
ex: AI labs are investing in consulting firms, and PE firms help portfolio companies deploy AI
You can't say 17% of a senior law partner's job can be automated

items: Can be broken down and scored
Knowing what the client really wants

d.verdict: Exposure scores miss why people actually get hired

l358|703.c: Automating tasks usually creates more work; the pain is real, but overall prosperity rises.
l358|703.e: When something gets cheaper, people usually do more of it rather than doing the same amount with fewer people, he observes. Bookkeeping was automated by adding machines, mainframes, ERP, cloud, and spreadsheets in turn, yet the number of accountants in the US kept growing. iPhone developers write far less low-level code, and there are no fewer engineers. Every wave of technology kills some jobs and hollows out some towns, but it also creates professions that never existed. He also rejects arguments from the authority of AI lab CEOs: knowing where models are headed is not the same as knowing labor economics.
ex: In 1800, about 90% of people were farmers
OpenAI and Anthropic are still hiring
A 1950s IBM ad: one electronic calculator equals 150 engineers

l358|703.c: AI spreads fast among consumers, but enterprise change will still take 3 to 10 years, industry by industry.
l358|703.e: AI is being adopted faster than earlier technologies because it sits on infrastructure that already exists, he says. ChatGPT has over 900 million weekly users, whereas when Netscape launched there were only 50 to 100 million PCs in the world. But enterprise sales cycles often run 18 months, slower than the pace of venture capital, so change will unfold by industry over 3 to 10 years. Many SaaS companies founded after ChatGPT could have been built years earlier. He thinks that even if model progress stopped tomorrow, the technology would keep rolling out for the next decade.
ex: Products like Frame.io don't depend on any new technology
He mocks the idea that a big company buys ChatGPT and lays people off weeks later

items.d: PCs, phones, and networks were already everywhere

l358|703.c: If models become commodities, value flows to the application layer, as it did in telecoms.
l358|703.e: He rejects the idea of intelligence metered like electricity: utilities have thin margins, and the profits from TVs and washing machines don't go to the power plant. Telecoms is the cautionary tale. Mobile data volume has grown a thousand or two thousand times since 2010, carrier stocks have gone nowhere in twenty-plus years, and the value went to companies like Apple sitting on top. The key question is whether a model can complete an entire task on its own. If the chat box isn't the final interface and no model wins outright, competition will push prices and margins down. He admits this inference could be wrong.
ex: Global mobile revenue is about $1 trillion a year, with about $200 billion in annual capex
Someone spending about $1.5 million a month on tokens is, he thinks, a temporary imbalance
Flat-panel displays: high tech, low margins

items.d: May capture most of the value
Like the power grid or telecom pipes

l358|703.c: When products converge, distribution decides the winner, and the giants are pushing AI into what they already own.
l358|703.e: If the product is a commodity, distribution matters most, he says. A browser is just a thin shell around a rendering engine, with no interface innovation in twenty-plus years. Microsoft won the browser war with IE and got little from it, because the value moved up a layer. Today Google pushes Gemini through search and Android. Meta AI gets no respect in tech circles, yet surveys put its usage in the same tier as ChatGPT and Gemini. OpenAI's scattershot moves in late 2025 were a search for distribution and stickiness. Incumbents treat a new platform as a feature, which is sometimes enough and sometimes not.
ex: Apple Intelligence's 2024 demo impressed him most, but it still hasn't shipped as promised
Meta benefited from the mobile era; Google changed little

root.d: The deciding factor when products converge

items.d: Pushes Gemini via search and Android
In every app, usage in the same tier
Won distribution, but value moved up

l358|703.c: The anti-AI backlash mixes real and exaggerated concerns; the best personal response is to dive in, not avoid it.
l358|703.e: He goes through the complaints one by one. Higher electricity bills in a few places are real; data centers use about 5% of US power. Water worries are exaggerated, and isolated well problems are planning failures. Slowing employment among 18-to-24-year-olds shows up in both AI-affected and unaffected fields, so AI may not be the cause, and the labs publish little usable data. Harms like deepfakes are real; any technology can ruin a life. His advice: don't bury your head in the sand, and don't rely on moral superiority and slogans. Learn what AI can do and become more worth hiring.
ex: Lawrence Livermore estimates data centers use about 0.017% of US water
The UK Post Office Horizon scandal: a software defect wrongly convicted postmasters

marks.d: Affected and unaffected fields both slowing
Genuinely up in a few areas
A teenager can make one in an afternoon

l359|705.c: A 1.0 product in a brand-new category has no comparable data, so a few people with taste must decide.
l359|705.e: In a new category there is nothing to compare against, he says, so most decisions can't be answered by data. A small group of people with taste has to act as benevolent dictators, judging within the whole picture of marketing, ecosystem, and how customers will discover the product. The iPhone's physical-keyboard fight was the team's longest: only one or two percent of people used BlackBerrys, months of typing tests settled nothing, and Steve Jobs finally made the call. Opponents got on board or left. He criticizes using consultants and user research as cover. Leaders should state their opinion and reasoning and take the risk of being wrong.
ex: Only about 1-2% of phone users had a BlackBerry at the time
He'd worked on virtual keyboards since General Magic and doubted them himself at first

cells.d: Quick calls even when comparisons exist
A few people with taste decide and own it

l359|705.c: Micromanagement isn't running daily operations; it's owning the key decisions and the data behind them.
l359|705.e: Early on he managed everything and pushed people away. Now he goes deep only where it matters: the experience customers touch directly, critical manufacturing and cost issues, and the long-term vision. The micromanagement he means is controlling the decision itself and the data that feeds it, not meddling in day-to-day operations. In a complex system, hardware, software, and graphics are all intertwined, so one person has to hold the whole picture. Asking "why" over and over cuts through excuses to the real problem.
ex: Ask "why" repeatedly to puncture the team's excuses

l359|705.c: Start from a pain people have stopped noticing, solve it fundamentally with new technology, and rebuild the whole system.
l359|705.e: To decide what to build, he looks for pain first, especially the kind people have gotten so used to that they no longer notice it. Then he asks whether a new technology can solve it in a fundamentally different way, rather than just improving the old product. Nest targeted heating and cooling, about half of the energy bill, and the programmable thermostat nobody could use, replacing programming with learning. Real innovation also means rebuilding installation, sales channels, and the surrounding ecosystem together. The iPod was the player plus iTunes plus the music store.
ex: Nest sold for $249 and moved from professional installation to do-it-yourself
The iPod relied on tiny high-capacity storage, lithium-polymer batteries, MP3, and low-power ARM chips
The iPhone relied on multi-touch, widespread Wi-Fi, digital cameras, and YouTube

l359|705.c: Almost nobody gets it right the first time: build the product, fix the product, then fix the business, about three generations.
l359|705.e: The first iPod sold almost only to loyal Mac users, under 1% of the market, and the second did the same. It took off only once it supported Windows and connected to the music store. Jobs had firmly opposed Windows support, so the team built it as a secret project. It let people try Apple without spending about $3,000 on a Mac. Without the iPod, he thinks, there might have been no iPhone, maybe no Apple. The first iPhone likewise ran only on AT&T's 2.5G network and only in the US. As long as you keep iterating, it isn't failure.
ex: The Windows-compatible iPod sold for $349, lowering the barrier to trying Apple
The stylus was also built by a secret team after Jobs rejected it

items.d: Windows support and the music store

l359|705.c: Product people must walk the whole customer journey: write the press release first and tell the "why" as a story.
l359|705.e: Builders live inside their own context, he says, but customers meet the product through ads, sales, and marketing, so you need personas and you have to go where customers are. Early adopters, later buyers, and laggards need different messages, and the iPod's US marketing flopped when moved to Europe. He endorses Amazon's working-backwards method: write the press release first, with only three or four key selling points. The story must explain why, and you can borrow infomercial techniques for setting up the pain, then bring it back to reality. He thinks OpenAI treated ChatGPT as a tech demo at first and moved to product marketing late.
ex: "1,000 songs in your pocket" came from Jobs
His father, a Levi's salesman, sometimes talked customers out of buying the expensive option
Jobs rehearsed the iPhone launch speech on friends again and again

result.d: They try it and remember it

l359|705.c: AI-written software is fast but brittle, trading short-term gains for long-term losses; humans must design the architecture.
l359|705.e: A casual prompt can get AI to build a feature, he says, but without real functional expertise you miss the customer definition and the trade-offs. AI code may run and pass tests, yet security, maintainability, and rollback are unknowns, and quick disposable software just piles up technical debt. His advice: use AI for prototypes and well-bounded subtasks, and let domain experts design the architecture. Software splits into fast fashion and luxury goods. The easier it is to build, the more thoughtful, crafted products stand out. The biggest risk is "cognitive surrender" to AI.
ex: After Claude Code's source leaked, he says, engineers found its main loop bloated and hard to maintain
Opinionated 1.0 products like Flighty are hard to replicate by vibe coding

items: A few prompts and it ships

d.verdict: The easier building gets, the scarcer craft becomes

l359|705.c: Hardware is coming back, and the next interface order is voice first, keyboard second, touch third.
l359|705.e: AI makes software ever easier to write, he argues, so pure software companies are easier to copy. Hardware brings sensors, network access, and staying power; Waymo is a hardware-plus-software platform with a long runway. Unless brain-computer interfaces or retinal projection mature, people still need screens, probably foldable or tablet-shaped. The interface priority should flip to voice first, but building trust in voice will take years, and $20 to $200 monthly AI subscriptions won't reach the mass market. Humane's projector, he thinks, was merely different, not better.
ex: Nest has used AI since 2010, then became a neglected stepchild inside Google
Car systems bolt voice on as an afterthought, so almost nobody uses it

l359|705.c: Product people must hold their principles; making money by addicting users eventually loses the users.
l359|705.e: Designers need principles that don't drift with the wind, he says. Just as you wouldn't tolerate a terrible interface, you shouldn't tolerate addicting users. If the company demands it, change jobs. Digital products are like junk food, but without nutrition labels or warnings. Society has been too loose on innovation and needs some balance, though not nanny-state regulation; platforms like Apple and Google could give families better management tools. He also worries that selling chatbots as relationships erodes our humanity. Companies that harm users' health eventually lose them, so the short-term gain is self-defeating.
ex: Someone proposed porn on iTunes, and Jobs shot it down on the spot
He says the iPhone's addictive pull was never the design intent

items.d: Customers are lost in the end

l360|712.c: Instincts are mostly right, ideas mostly wrong: copy what's proven, make it better, bet on one new thing.
l360|712.e: He thinks people's instincts are about 95% right, but the specific ideas they generate from them are mostly wrong. So confine innovation to a small area and try many times. Step one: copy the proven pattern exactly. You only earn the right to innovate once you're an expert on the best existing version, and "proven" must mean the same platform and the same audience. Step two: make small improvements that ten out of ten existing users would endorse. Step three: add just one new selling point for the back of the box, expect it to fail, and try several.
ex: Sid Meier's Civilization skipped the proven onboarding and lost players within minutes
Words With Friends' new thing: your Facebook friends were already there
Slack may be only proven plus better, and it still succeeded hugely

terms.d: Best practice on the same platform and audience
Small improvements every existing user endorses
Just one bet; expect it to fail

result.d: Fail for the right reasons in a small area

l360|712.c: Founders are ashamed to copy, which creates a "moral arbitrage" for people with less ego.
l360|712.e: Founders want to innovate and were taught that copying is cheating, he says, and that leaves a gap. Ambition should be defined by the consumer, like a nurse in Indiana playing FarmVille, not by awards from peers. Consumers reject pure copies too, so be an inch better in places they barely notice. Change too much and you offend existing users who feel the product is theirs. Most successful products, he argues, are evolutions of what came before. His first company, Freeloader, was built on a buried offline-browsing feature in the browser.
ex: Craigslist took about two years to add photos, fearing it would crowd out quick price comparison
OMGPop broke out with Draw Something and was then acquired by Zynga

items: Copied Words With Friends' turn-based play
Number one for about 60 days in 2012

d.verdict: Building on proven mechanics makes success far likelier

l360|712.c: The bigger the vision, the humbler the start: aim at a thousand feet, not a hundred thousand.
l360|712.e: Many big products started embarrassingly small, he says. Facebook began as a Harvard campus app. His own Tribe chased several use cases at once and failed, while Zynga started with a poker game on Facebook that peers found undignified. Big companies chase only billion-dollar opportunities, which lets startups follow small, shaky-looking clues. Founders who have succeeded are often pushed to think bigger. Unless you have unlimited capital like Elon Musk, he thinks you should resist that pressure. At the same time, the team can't settle for a B+.
ex: The Bolt.new team only discovered after open-sourcing that a browser VM plus AI coding was their edge
Slack came out of an internal engineering tool at a game company

l360|712.c: Kill hope before hope kills you: replace hope with evidence, and build the wrong version before the right one.
l360|712.e: Conviction should rest on evidence, he says; hope is confidence without grounds. Great product people cash in a win they've already seen rather than gamble. He wants the "viable" dropped from minimum viable product, because that's exactly where hope sneaks in. AI lets you test a hundred ideas in a day instead of spending three months on one: build the wrong version, learn, then build the right one. Judging whether something is an A or a B+ works the same way. If you're still asking yourself, it isn't an A.
ex: Before a $10 million ad campaign, FarmVille teased in-game and presold about $19 million in keys
He shut down a metaverse project after four years and about $25 million

l360|712.c: Zynga won on retention, not virality; growth without retention is a speedboat that's sinking.
l360|712.e: Zynga's mission was to connect the world through games. He and Bing Gordon added a social dimension to tired game genres: real identity, cooperation, gifting, and creative expression, aimed mostly at middle-aged women and casual players. The core metric was day-365 retention. Almost nobody looks at that today, he says, yet highly valued companies tend to have strong one-year retention. They also tracked an "active social network" metric measuring back-and-forth interactions with friends. The more of those, the likelier a player was to return.
ex: Going from 0 to 1 social back-and-forths meant about an 80% chance of returning the next month

l360|712.c: Chatbots are a lonely cocktail party; the next social product must bring agent-era efficiency.
l360|712.e: Every past social network started by delivering efficiency and only later slid into time-wasting, he observes. Facebook helped people stay in touch; LinkedIn helped them find customers. Today the thrill of social is gone, and quitting Facebook or Instagram has even become a brag. A successful social product is like a lively cocktail party where useful encounters happen naturally. Chatbots like Claude and GPT are quiet, lonely parties. He imagines agents brokering social plans on people's behalf, sharing only the necessary context through a "trust membrane."
ex: Adults wanted to play games but found the barrier high, so he made them free and three clicks away

marks.d: Thrill gone; quitting is a brag
Efficiency of staying in touch first
The next step he hopes for

l360|712.c: Consumer app discovery is broken, so distribution must be part of the strategy from day one.
l360|712.e: AI isn't a true new platform yet, he thinks; people still use browsers and phones. The channels through which consumers discover new apps have nearly stopped working, counting on word of mouth is a "hope strategy," and consumer companies are harder to fund than those serving professionals or businesses. As tokens get cheaper, consumer services built on nearly free intelligence may become viable. He expects the big model companies to launch consumer agent apps, such as an always-on AI travel agent that rebooks your flights and manages your trips, a service that doesn't pay off when done by humans.
ex: About 40,000 new games launched last year, he says, and none held a steady top-25 spot

l360|712.c: Founders should stay close to the work: make everyone a CEO, yet dare to micromanage what matters.
l360|712.e: He gives every team a hill to take, operating control, a plan, and a budget, so they act like CEOs who ask less and invest more. Frontline experts know the most but decide the least, so the founder must own the first-mile and last-mile decisions. At about 50 people, Zynga held a two-hour daily stand-up tracking everyone's commitments, which he believes made the team more efficient: be present when you can, delegate only when you truly can't. He also keeps a backup leader shadowing him for 6 to 12 months. The CEO's number-one job, he says, is being right.
ex: Discord's founder found key UX handed to new hires and flipped the pyramid
Steve Jobs personally picked the conference-room carpet

l361|715.c: Writing code is no longer the bottleneck; the limits are now verification and how big you dare to aim.
l361|715.e: Anthropic engineers now ship about 8 times as much code per quarter as they did in 2025, she says. Back when software shipped on CDs, manufacturing deadlines forced detailed planning up front. Today writing code costs almost nothing, and the hard part is confirming that what got built is correct and that the experience is good enough. The other side is that everyone's capability boundary is expanding: an engineer who has never done mobile can use AI to extend a feature to phones. So the real question becomes how ambitious you are.
ex: Engineers' quarterly code output is about 8 times what it was in 2025
An engineer with no mobile experience used AI to bring a feature to phones

l361|715.c: Keep the spec in the repo so code is checked against it; test-driven development went from burden to cheap.
l361|715.e: Modules that need deep expert judgment still get human review, she says. Everything else should be automated: store the spec in the code repository, keep it updated, and have the code checked against it. Writing tests used to feel like paying taxes, something to minimize. Now the model writes the tests, the cost drops sharply, and test-driven development becomes worthwhile again. She believes quality should be protected mainly by proactive monitoring and tests, not by humans reading every line.
ex: The spec lives in the same repo as the code and stays up to date
Models write the tests, and TDD is making a comeback

items.d: State the standard and keep it current
Code is checked against the spec

l361|715.c: High agency must come with high accountability: let people run, but state the hypothesis first.
l361|715.e: Her team wants to give everyone room to act on their own, but only with a clear hypothesis about the problem being solved and ownership of the result. She's fine with mistakes as long as they're new ones, because making no mistakes at all means the team is too cautious. Each month she has Claude summarize what shipped, how it performed, and where the feedback came from. She uses that to start conversations with colleagues, not to produce pull requests for them.
ex: A monthly review with Claude of what shipped and where feedback came from

result.d: Own the result; new mistakes allowed

l361|715.c: Don't measure AI's return in lines of code or token usage; ask whether it moved real outcomes.
l361|715.e: Lines of code and tokens consumed only show that people are busy, not that they're making progress, she says. The question is what outcomes the output produced. Metrics themselves can mislead. At Facebook Marketplace, an early metric based on seller count misjudged a region that had few sellers but a handful of super-sellers and a healthy market. The team had to change the metric. That's why she wants senior engineers to go on listening tours instead of only watching dashboards.
ex: Marketplace's seller-count metric missed a region with super-sellers
Senior engineers go on listening tours to supplement the dashboards

d.verdict: Don't mistake busyness for progress

l361|715.c: Quality problems are either bad or sad: block the irreversible ones, and stop the recoverable ones from piling up.
l361|715.e: She sorts quality issues into two buckets. "Bad" means irreversible damage, like a crash that loses someone's work. "Sad" means a recoverable but unpleasant experience, like a flickering interface. Each team sets its own thresholds, and enough sad adds up to bad. The team also tracks how often users swear in conversations and treats that as a frustration signal.
ex: A crash that loses work counts as bad
A flickering interface counts as sad
How often users swear is tracked as a frustration signal

l361|715.c: New managers start as individual engineers, and leaders must use their own product.
l361|715.e: On listening tours, people complained about chaotic priorities and too many layers of review. So she now has every manager begin as an individual contributor, relearning the codebase and product before leading people. She herself used Claude to submit code again after many years. Using the product yourself surfaces problems that metrics can't show, she says, and anecdotes and firsthand experience matter as much as data.
ex: On the VR team, she found a floor-height bug only by using the product herself
Marketplace's Chile launch was dragged down by slow LTE, visible only on a field visit

l361|715.c: Six-month roadmaps can't keep up, so plan monthly and cut any process that no longer helps.
l361|715.e: She once introduced a lightweight six-month roadmap to align direction. Three months later nobody looked at it, because things were changing too fast, so she dropped it. Now a simple monthly spreadsheet lists the top priorities, and each person notes how their work maps to them. Every week the team checks whether those priorities still hold, and every six months everyone gathers to set the big themes. Her advice to any team: pick one process that feels dreaded, noisy, or expensive and ask whether it's still useful.
ex: The six-month roadmap went unreferenced after three months and was dropped
She plans to have the monthly priorities sheet update itself

items.d: Set at an all-hands; they change too
A light spreadsheet; people claim items

l361|715.c: Culture is what keeps her up at night: it drifts quietly during growth, so problems must be said out loud.
l361|715.e: Product and engineering problems can be solved with dashboards, hypotheses, and experiments, she says, but culture is a people problem. It shows in how people treat each other, not in slogans on the wall. When you hire fast, culture will drift; the danger is not noticing. What she fears most is a manager who is struggling but says everything is fine, so she asks people, especially new managers, to talk openly about what isn't working. She also quotes Sheryl Sandberg: if protecting culture during growth feels hard, that's a sign the company is growing.
ex: Airbnb's founders stressed culture and values at every all-hands
Look back at the finish line to see whether your teammates are still there: one team

l362|716.c: Building features is cheap now, so the hard part is choosing among many attempts.
l362|716.e: Traditional product process assumed building was expensive, so teams did research, wrote docs and built prototypes to lower the risk first. He says that assumption has flipped: anyone can talk to a model and get a working feature. The result is lots of people building overlapping things. He gives an example: one feature everyone wanted showed up as about 90 separate, uncoordinated attempts. So the scarce step is now curation: deciding which attempts are good, what to merge, how to frame the problem and where to draw the scope.
ex: One needed feature appeared as roughly 90 uncoordinated implementation attempts

items.d: A chat with the model yields a working feature
About 90 duplicate tries of one feature
Pick, merge, frame the problem, set scope

l362|716.c: The PRD isn't dead: pick a doc or a prototype by the question, and beware anchoring.
l362|716.e: He disagrees with the claim that product requirement documents are dead. When the direction is fuzzy and the product still needs thinking through, write a doc. When you want to test how an interaction feels, build a prototype. Both have traps. Engineers often write long documents nobody reads. Prototypes look like finished, shippable products, so people get anchored on them before the basic assumptions are settled. The medium used to signal which stage a project was in, and that signal is now gone. So he thinks teams must say explicitly where they are in the process.
ex: One team keeps a stripped-down version of the product just for quick experiments

items: Good when the direction is fuzzy
Often becomes a long doc nobody reads
Looks finished, anchors people too early

d.verdict: Pick the medium for the point you're making, and name the stage

l362|716.c: Taste is more than aesthetics: it includes systems thinking, direction and choosing the right medium.
l362|716.e: He thinks taste is becoming the most valuable skill, but people often narrow it down to visual style. To him taste covers much more: how a thing fits into a larger whole, which theme or direction it belongs to, how to frame the problem, and which medium to present it in. He jokes that he cares too much about details like animation timing. That is exactly the point: visual polish is only a small part of taste.
ex: He admits he obsesses over small details like animation timing

terms.d: How a thing fits the larger whole
How to ask, how to present

result.d: Becoming the most valuable skill

l362|716.c: AI is still weak at design: it's hard to grade, outside the research loop, and rewards novelty.
l362|716.e: He explains why AI is strong at code but weak at design. Code can be checked automatically, while design needs human taste in the feedback loop, which is expensive. Labs also prioritize skills that speed up AI research itself. Coding is part of that flywheel; design is not. He expects these practical gaps to close. Two harder problems remain. Design rewards novelty rather than everyone converging on the same look, so a model cloning Linear's website is not designing. And there are abstract judgments, like which components in a codebase should share meaning. One redesign he mentions touched 263 components.
ex: A model cloning Linear's website doesn't mean it can design
One redesign touched 263 components

root.d: Practical gaps will close; deeper problems remain

items.d: Needs human taste in the feedback loop
Only coding directly speeds up AI research
Copying a famous site isn't design

l362|716.c: Roles are blending, but scrapping the PM job to make everyone a builder throws away experience.
l362|716.e: On the Codex team, designers understand engineering and PMs write code. What role you are depends on where your time actually goes. But he is wary of companies that abolish the product role and tell everyone to be a builder. That discards the best practices and lessons each discipline has accumulated, and nobody can be great at everything. He prefers a product organization that plays zone defense: people keep their specialties but cover whatever is open. The most valuable people are those with high agency and taste who can carry an idea all the way to a shipped product.
ex: Core team: double-digit engineers, about half as many designers, a few PMs

l362|716.c: Don't kill a failed feature; wait for a stronger model. The further out, the vaguer the plan.
l362|716.e: He thinks features often fail because the model at the time wasn't good enough, not because the idea was wrong. So keep the core shape and relaunch when models improve. At his previous company, the team listed every idea for the next year or two and prototyped all of them. The ones that worked shipped, the rest were shelved and retried with each model upgrade. The Codex app's successful launch in February rode on earlier model progress, while the original cloud web version was ahead of its time. He also says plan detail should shrink with the time horizon: a precise nine-month plan is false precision.
ex: The Codex app's February launch succeeded thanks to earlier model progress
The original cloud-based Codex web app was too far ahead of its time

d.center: Wait for the model to catch up

items.d: Everything for the next year or two

l362|716.c: Developer tool or knowledge-work tool isn't a choice; Codex aims to be home base for all work.
l362|716.e: Codex started as a command-line tool. The desktop app sits between a chatbot and a full coding environment: more than chat, less than an IDE. After internal trials at OpenAI, marketing, PR, finance and legal teams picked it up too. The team tried putting similar features into the ChatGPT desktop app and the Atlas browser, but people kept coming back to Codex. His conclusion: start simple, add complexity as needed, allow several modes, and let people start, track and automate their work there, handing off to specialized tools like an Excel plugin when needed. A videographer had Codex write a Premiere Pro extension to edit markers; he used it to set up Gmail filters for cold emails.
ex: A videographer had Codex write a Premiere Pro extension to edit markers
He used Codex to set up Gmail filters for cold emails

items.d: More than chat, less than an IDE

l363|718.c: The classic 13-person team is giving way to small pods of generalist engineers plus one product person.
l363|718.e: A product team used to be about 13 people: dedicated Android, iOS and backend engineers, plus a PM, a designer, a data scientist and a researcher. The specialization existed so code reviewers knew the codebase they were reviewing. Now Instagram runs pods of four to six generalist engineers and one "product staff" person who, with AI's help, also covers some design, data and research. The core is six or seven people. Senior specialists join only for things like pricing or a brand-new experience. Fewer people means less coordination, more speed and less design by committee.
ex: A senior data scientist joins only for work like pricing strategy
Funnel analyses are now done automatically by internal tools

items: One product person covering several jobs

d.verdict: Small teams move faster with less design by committee

l363|718.c: Once building is easy, taste about what to build and curiosity without ego matter most.
l363|718.e: His starting point: when building takes almost no effort, the key question becomes what to build. That taste is hard to automate, so he is bullish on designers and expects many to move into product staff roles. In hiring he still looks for grit, fast learning and self-awareness. Now he adds curiosity, plus the mindset of a language learner who is willing to say things wrong and be corrected. He himself started coding again after about ten years and calls himself a mediocre engineer. He thinks the skill of managing huge organizations will lose value, and companies that stop developing junior talent will regret it in two years.
ex: He started coding again after about ten years and calls himself a mediocre engineer

terms.d: Willing to try and look foolish

result.d: Managing huge orgs loses value

l363|718.c: Token leaderboards reward incinerators; compute spend should be budgeted like headcount and GPUs.
l363|718.e: The cost per unit of intelligence keeps falling, but he is against ranking people by token usage. That rewards people who burn a huge amount and produce very little. Teams should compare how much they spent with how much value they got back. Instagram has no token caps yet, but he expects them eventually, managed alongside GPUs, storage, labeling budgets and headcount. He estimates that within a year or two a strong engineer's token bill could approach their salary. Costs will rise with usage first, then fall as labs undercut each other on price.
ex: A strong engineer's token bill could approach their salary within a year or two

l363|718.c: A strategy must be something a reasonable person could oppose; AI gives bland answers unless pushed hard.
l363|718.e: He says work increasingly looks like management: set goals, constraints and budgets, then give feedback. Too much control kills good ideas; too little wastes time. Vision is the product state you want. Strategy is a claim about how to get there, and a reasonable person must be able to disagree with it. "Be the best" is not a strategy. A good one weighs technology, talent, competition, regulation and brand. He thinks AI is weak at strategy: a lazy prompt gets you the answer your competitors would also get. You have to go back and forth, ask it to poke holes, and choose a model that argues back instead of flattering you.
ex: Good strategy weighs technology, talent, competition, regulation and brand
The best product leaders are curators of people and ideas

items.d: The end state you want for the product
A debatable path to get there

l363|718.c: Designing a feed is like city planning; pure chronological order rewards volume and crowds out friends.
l363|718.e: Sorting by time looks fair, but he says it creates bad incentives: the more you post, the more space you take, and prolific accounts drown out your friends. Recency matters, but it isn't everything. If his sister gets engaged, he wants to see that first even if she posted hours ago. When Instagram tested making the chronological feed the default, both usage and overall sentiment dropped. He also admits recommendation systems don't really understand your interests; they only have opaque embedding vectors. Now a large language model can translate those into topics that users can add or remove.
ex: Default chronological feed test: usage and sentiment both fell
Using an LLM to turn embedding vectors into editable interest topics

items.d: Post more to hold your spot

l363|718.c: The more synthetic content floods in, the scarcer real people and original views become; AI helps authenticity.
l363|718.e: He sees power shifting from institutions to individuals, the way athletes now matter more than teams. More AI content will compete for attention, and Instagram is not yet good at ranking it by quality. He doesn't plan to filter by creation tool. Instead, label AI content and disclose things like account age. Long term, certifying real footage may be more practical than detecting AI, and when detection gets hard the platform should be honest about its confidence. He likes AI creators such as Plastic Dream Sequence. But undisclosed spam accounts, like a fake AI monk selling supplements, must be cracked down on.
ex: He enjoys the AI creator Plastic Dream Sequence
Fake AI monk accounts selling supplements must be shut down

items.d: Media and brands hold the mic
People seek real voices and views

l363|718.c: The first Reels bet wrongly on extending old features; fast changes need a communication plan ready.
l363|718.e: His first PM project, Facebook Home, flopped badly, but he says shipping it was the best way to learn the idea didn't work. The first Reels was built on top of Stories, and few people watch Stories to the end, so most Reels were never seen. He believed in extending existing features rather than adding new ones, and that was wrong; TikTok took off during the pandemic. Later pushes toward video and recommendations drew a backlash, which he blames on moving too fast and explaining too little. At scale, controversial tests always leak, so plan what you'll say in advance.
ex: Facebook Home: a custom Android system built with HTC
The video test that caused the uproar covered only about 4% of iOS users

root.d: Better to take occasional heat than stand still

items.d: No real demand; shipping proved it
Wrong bet on extending old features

l364|720.c: Whether AI amplifies or diminishes you splits the workforce, with three times the effect of job title.
l364|720.e: This second annual survey covered about 6,000 people in product, engineering, design, research, marketing, data and sales. He focuses on effect sizes rather than statistical significance, because with a large sample even tiny differences become significant. The strongest predictor of how someone feels about work is whether they believe AI amplifies or diminishes them. That effect is roughly three times larger than role, company or seniority. Optimism, burnout, layoff worries and willingness to recommend their career all split along this line.
ex: About 6,000 respondents in the survey's second year
Differences judged by Cohen's d effect size, not significance

l364|720.c: People fall into four emotional types, excited, ambivalent, lost and resentful, and most feel several at once.
l364|720.e: He sorts respondents into four archetypes. The excited, about 41%, find the tools fun and empowering. The ambivalent, about 35%, are happiest when building but most unsure about their future. The lost are the people whose roles are being redefined and who see no clear path. The resentful, about 12%, feel forced to use AI just to keep their jobs. Respondents picked about five emotions each on average, with curiosity and excitement at the top. He agrees with the phrase "smiling exhaustion" and says mixed feelings are normal.
ex: People picked about 5 emotions on average; one picked 13
Open-ended answers: roughly 37% positive, 37% negative

root.d: About five emotions per person on average

items.d: Love building, worry about the future
Role is changing with no clear path
Forced to use AI to keep the job

l364|720.c: AI's extra output became more work rather than less; burnout rose about 10 points in a year.
l364|720.e: The share reporting significant burnout rose from 44.7% in 2025 to 54.7%, while optimism about their career fell from 54.8% to 48.7%. His explanation: output exploded. Some engineers went from a few pull requests a day to 30. But the extra output was treated as new workload, not as time saved. AI is also addictive and hard to step away from. Still, people enjoy the work itself. PMs, for example, get to use hidden skills like design or engineering.
ex: Burnout: 44.7% to 54.7%
Optimism: 54.8% to 48.7%
Some went from a few pull requests a day to 30

items.d: A few PRs a day becomes 30
Extra output doesn't buy free time
Up about 10 points in a year

l364|720.c: The top fear isn't being replaced by AI; it's being asked to do more for the same pay.
l364|720.e: Among all the worries, losing a job to AI ranked second to last. Number one was doing more work for the same pay. Number two was an unsustainable pace, meaning both how fast people work and how fast AI itself changes, which crowds out focus time. Still, 72% have some worry about layoffs, which he links to companies going all in on agents. His advice: employees should talk to their manager when responsibilities grow but pay doesn't, and leaders should set realistic output expectations.
ex: 72% worry about layoffs; 41.2% at least moderately

items.d: Work and AI both move too fast

l364|720.c: 97% say AI makes them better, but mostly it makes them faster, not necessarily higher quality.
l364|720.e: 97.2% said AI improved their work, and nearly half said it improved it a lot. But he thinks "better" here mostly means faster and more output. Many people report their skills getting rusty and their work actually getting worse. He calls this cognitive erosion: accepting AI output without judgment. Outsourcing problems to AI for long enough also weakens people's belief that they can solve problems themselves. His remedy is deliberate practice, keeping your own judgment, and going deep on a few use cases instead of dabbling in everything.
ex: 97.2% say AI makes their work better; nearly half say much better

d.verdict: The honeymoon is over; practice deliberately and keep judgment

l364|720.c: AI pulls out the ladder's rungs from the bottom; design and research feel it most, so raise the ceiling with taste.
l364|720.e: The survey asked an NPS-style question about whether people would recommend their career. Every role scored negative. Designers and researchers were the least likely to recommend theirs and led on feeling shaken, tired and anxious, making them the most pessimistic group two years running. He borrows Scott Wu's description of Devin: AI climbs from high-school level to senior engineer, and the people on the lowest rungs feel the floor drop first. He thinks AI mainly lowers the floor, while design and research add value by raising the quality ceiling through taste, craft and judgment.
ex: Every role's net recommendation score is below zero
Data analysts worry most about job loss, with design and research close behind

items.d: The higher up, the later it hits

l364|720.c: Founders are happiest on almost every measure, and burnout and layoff fear rise steadily with company size.
l364|720.e: Among founders, 71% are optimistic about the future. They report the lowest burnout and layoff worry and the most excitement about AI. Even so, 47% are at least moderately burned out. He notes the sample only includes founders still running companies, so there is survivorship bias. By company size, from 1–10 person startups up to 5,000–10,000 person enterprises, optimism falls step by step while burnout, layoff worry and unwillingness to recommend the career all rise. Even the lowest burnout level isn't low. So he suggests employees consider smaller companies or starting their own.
ex: 71% of founders are optimistic, yet 47% are at least moderately burned out

l364|720.c: Managers are the biggest lever: a good one means about 65% more job enjoyment, yet only a quarter are effective.
l364|720.e: Manager effectiveness has a very large effect size. People with an effective manager report about 65% higher enjoyment of their work and much lower burnout. But only about 25% rate their manager as highly effective, while 36% rate them ineffective, with design and data teams scoring their managers worst. He worries that flattening org charts and "founder mode" are stretching spans of control. His advice: leaders should invest in training managers and protect entry-level roles, while employees should invest in the relationship with their manager and learn to manage up.
ex: Only about 25% rate their manager as highly effective
36% rate their manager ineffective, similar to last year

l365|303.c: AI lets everyone do more, so roles get messy for a while, but don't put AI back in the box.
l365|303.e: Every time a disruptive technology arrives, teams go through turbulence: everyone can do more, yet nobody is sure what their job is anymore. Her stance is to capture the upside and manage the cost, not retreat. Prototyping with AI is healthy, but not everyone should be pushing code to production. Letting go safely requires a few things: trusted data sources, guardrails before anything ships, and review of AI output. And she is clear that even when an agent writes the code, a human owns the result.

root.d: Capture the upside, manage the cost

items.d: Checks before shipping or big changes
Agent-written code is still your responsibility

l365|303.c: Job boundaries are blurring, but each discipline keeps its edge, and great craft is still scarce.
l365|303.e: PMs, designers and data scientists can now get much further through the product cycle without engineers. Business partners in finance, content and ads can form their own hypotheses and then ask a data scientist to validate them. Decades of Netflix experiments and user insights can be queried with AI in minutes to learn what the company already knows. The catch is that the question has to matter to the business, or you just get thousands of unfocused prototypes. PMs still frame the right problems, data scientists judge whether data can be trusted, and engineers own scale, quality and risk.
ex: Decades of experiment records can be distilled with AI in minutes

items: PM, design and data go further alone
Business teams form their own hypotheses

d.verdict: Roles will blur, but great craft stays scarce

l365|303.c: With agents running across every system, paved shared paths matter more than each team's own stack.
l365|303.e: Netflix historically won by letting each team build its own stack. But when many agents work across systems and more people do new kinds of work, the answers on access, identity, security and quality should live in a paved path, not in tribal knowledge. She says platforms can take most teams about 80% of the way, which lets the company place more bets at once. Design is building templates and a design system too, so the product doesn't become a patchwork of clashing styles. That is why she wants to hire people who can abstract across business areas.
ex: Platforms can get most teams about 80% of the way there
Avoid a Frankenstein experience with mismatched design languages

items.d: Judge whether output is high quality

l365|303.c: Narrow, deep expertise is losing value; fast-learning generalists who work across stacks and functions are preferred.
l365|303.e: She says Netflix needs fewer specialists than it did five or ten years ago and prefers fast learners who adapt. A few areas like encoding and playback still need deep experts, but even they must be willing to change methods rather than cling to old tools. Her tip for building systems thinking: when you hit a problem, step back one level and question your assumptions about the bigger picture, but don't linger there. Then think like your manager: how does this work fit the whole, and what is right for the organization overall?
ex: Areas like encoding and playback still need a few deep experts
Tip: step back one level and examine your assumptions first

marks.d: Still needed in a few areas
Learns fast across stacks and functions

l365|303.c: Instead of rewriting every level's expectations, Netflix adds a layer of AI fluency for everyone.
l365|303.e: Netflix didn't rewrite its leveling guide. It added an expectation of AI fluency on top of every role and level, executives included. Fluency means willingness to experiment, judgment about when AI is useful, and an open mind, not using AI for its own sake. The definition keeps changing as the technology moves. Coding interviews allow AI tools. She thinks younger employees often know AI better, so learning flows both ways, but mentors still need to teach what good looks like and how to use tools responsibly. Netflix started hiring new graduates a few years ago.
ex: Candidates may use AI tools in coding interviews
Netflix began hiring new graduates a few years ago

result.d: Applies to every role and to executives

l365|303.c: Treat excellence as the operating system: talent density first, decisions pushed down, little process to patch holes.
l365|303.e: Culture isn't the goal, she says; it's how you produce excellent results through agency and accountability, pushing decisions down, and hiring people with judgment. Talent density is the non-negotiable starting point. Then take risks and recover fast when things fail, as with live programming. Leaders shouldn't overturn decisions that don't matter much; let people learn. Adding process to planning, feedback, levels and pay only burns time without improving outcomes. The aim is highly aligned, loosely coupled. The keeper test, asking whether you'd fight to keep someone who wanted to leave, is mainly a way to start a feedback conversation.
ex: Keeper test: if they were leaving, would you fight to keep them?
Blameless postmortems encourage people to own their mistakes

l365|303.c: AI should help creators realize their vision, not replace them; human-centered stories remain the backbone.
l365|303.e: Netflix has used machine learning for years in personalization, visual effects and localization, without calling itself an AI company. Today AI helps with pre-visualization before shooting, subtitles and dubbing, and producing trailers and posters at scale. Netflix also acquired InterPositive, founded by Ben Affleck, so filmmakers can lead relighting, reframing and even dialogue changes. Hollywood is split on AI; Netflix's position is to let creators choose their own tools. She doesn't believe purely AI-generated content will replace human-centered storytelling.
ex: Acquired InterPositive, the company founded by Ben Affleck

items.d: Show the creator's vision before shooting

l366|726.c: Frontier models only reach users through frontier products; model and product make each other.
l366|726.e: When she joined, the product team had five engineers and one person ran the entire API business. Claude 3 Opus gave a company of under 200 people its first real answer to "why Claude?" At the time Anthropic had nothing to do with coding, but users were already writing long code with the model. Training for that was a small change that created real differentiation. Later, Opus 4.5 needed Claude Code to reach users, and Claude Code spread faster because of Opus 4.5. Golden Gate Claude went from research finding to shipped product in about 24 hours.
ex: Golden Gate Claude was built and shipped in about 24 hours
Opus 4.5 hit its turning point over winter break, with people coding at home

items.d: One person owned the whole API
A frontier model put Anthropic on the map
Research became a product in a day
Model and product amplified each other

l366|726.c: Abilities emerge suddenly and outrun what products expose and users know, so plans need slack.
l366|726.e: Under scaling laws, loss falls smoothly, but certain abilities, like reliable arithmetic, appear suddenly. They're hard to predict and can only be caught with evals, which also makes safety harder. The result is a product gap and a user gap: the model can do more than the product exposes, and users don't know what is now possible. Her answer is adaptability: reason from first principles, keep asking "so what," and replan whenever a new model lands. She hires for first-principles thinking too, rather than reusing consumer or enterprise playbooks. Cowork, skills and Tag are all attempts to close the gap.
ex: Ask yourself: when Claude 8 arrives, does what I'm building still make sense?
Cowork, skills and Tag are all efforts to close the gap

l366|726.c: Token spend is just the input; the real goal is experimentation, and it's a team sport.
l366|726.e: She reframes "maximize tokens" as the cost of experimenting, not the objective. Good prototypers spend a lot of time with every new research model, because good ideas only come from hands-on use. Anthropic has always let staff try early models openly. Nearly everyone tests in one Slack channel, ideas spread, and a useful use case often emerges within a dozen requests. Her advice: pair with enthusiasts, watch what others discover, and go deep on one or two tools instead of chasing every release.
ex: Almost everyone at Anthropic tests early Claude models in one internal Slack channel

items.d: A dozen requests yields a use case

l366|726.c: Labs bets on discontinuous 10x to 1,000x ideas: strong on the theme, loose on the prototype.
l366|726.e: Labs makes big bets outside the core roadmap, aiming at 10x to 1,000x ideas, with the vision set by Ben Mann. The team holds strong opinions about direction and weak opinions about any specific prototype. A bet that doesn't work yet may be restarted a model generation or two later, and the prototype itself leaves behind learning. Labs runs small teams, often starting with a single engineer, because large teams move slower on fuzzy problems. It hires founder-type people who can go from zero to one, and it has to shut down many projects. Claude Code, skills and MCP all came out of Labs.
ex: Labs has shipped Claude Code, skills, MCP and more

items.d: Or wait a model generation or two
Such as Claude Code and MCP

l366|726.c: A PM's core job is translating vague feedback into actionable evals; evals are the new PRDs.
l366|726.e: When a user says "Claude made something up," the cause might be a failed tool call, a bad synthesis of search results, or an alignment issue, and each needs a different eval. So PMs should sweat tokens the way designers sweat pixels: read failed transcripts closely and find the subtle failure patterns. A good eval covers cases that should succeed and cases that must not fail, mirrors real usage, and gives researchers something they can act on. Because outputs vary, evals measure quality rather than exact matches. She calls it test-driven development for PMs. Early on, about 80% of instruction-following complaints traced back to JSON formatting errors.
ex: About 80% of early instruction-following complaints came from JSON formatting errors
Write 30 to 40 golden examples and iterate until the pass rate nears 100%

items.d: Needs a retrieval and synthesis eval
Needs a behavior and alignment eval

l366|726.c: PRDs aren't dead: one per model as the source of truth, and fuzzy opportunities need them most.
l366|726.e: Her team still writes PRDs, especially one per model, which serves as the single source of truth for engineering, legal, safety and everyone else. When the user pain point is still unclear and the opportunity is fuzzy, a PRD is what forces the thinking to be laid out. When the problem is already well defined, evals can act as shorthand. She disagrees with the idea that PRDs are dead, and notes that the head of OpenAI's Codex app holds the same view.

items: Use when the problem is well defined
Source of truth for all parties

d.verdict: Different jobs; the PRD is not obsolete

l366|726.c: Managers must stay hands-on: form your own view first, then use Claude as a sparring partner.
l366|726.e: She thinks managers need to spend time shipping with AI and walking the same path as their teams. At each model launch she personally owns one or two workstreams to keep her judgment about model progress fresh. To avoid over-reliance, she forms her own opinion first and then has Claude challenge it. Standardized writing like the monthly business review goes to Claude, with her doing the review and verification. The test is whether delegating creates asymmetric value. She likes an AI that pushes back, and aims for a thousand times better, not ten percent better. She built a skill based on the book Crucial Conversations to prepare for hard conversations.
ex: She built a skill based on Crucial Conversations to prep for hard conversations
She uses a research version of Opus to help with pricing decisions for future releases

l366|726.c: As building gets easier, human value lies in judgment, taste, persistence and domain expertise.
l366|726.e: She thinks the hard problems are now deciding what to build and whether the result is good, which is exactly the PM's job. Judgment comes from experience and attention to detail, and persistence, initiative and taste matter just as much. Software engineering has been transformed, but fields like biology and life sciences are still early on the exponential curve, so domain expertise remains valuable, and Anthropic is investing in Claude for Science. For her kids, she values curiosity, persistence and developing their own inner voice. She mentions parents who give their children older models so they still have to struggle.
ex: Some parents give their kids older models so they still have to struggle

terms.d: Such as biology and life sciences

result.d: Deciding what to build and if it's good

l367|732.c: Don't give every team a PM by default; staffing by headcount makes engineers and designers atrophy.
l367|732.e: Early internet companies had no PMs; founders talked directly with engineers and designers. The dedicated decision-making role only split off as companies grew, and he doesn't see it as a permanent necessity. Product judgment is a muscle built through repetition. Keep engineers and designers out of decisions and that muscle never develops. So Whatnot doesn't assign a PM to every team. It sends PMs to the high-leverage problems that must go well, lets engineers and designers lead projects too, and runs all work through the same product review. On a team like notification infrastructure, the engineers already understand the problem.
ex: On teams like notification infrastructure, engineers already understand the problem
A common ratio: one designer, one PM and one EM per six engineers

d.verdict: PM is a craft, not a credential, so don't staff it by default

l367|732.c: Leaders should go back to senior IC work; staying close to the facts means faster calls and fewer alignment meetings.
l367|732.e: He thinks piles of alignment meetings and layers of management usually compensate for leaders who can't see the front line. PMs used to stop doing the work once they became directors, and reviews bounced back and forth inefficiently. At Whatnot, most PM managers spend over 90% of their time on individual contributor work, such as reading tickets, pulling data, writing specs and running standups, and he spends about half his own. Senior people decide faster and better; one senior PM is worth three junior ones. At Twitch he gave ads and discovery to the same PM, who optimized overall GMV and saved months of politics.
ex: A VP with 5 L5s and 4 L7s costs as much as 3 extremely senior ICs
IC work: reading tickets, pulling data, writing specs, running standups

d.unit: Share of time on IC work (%)

l367|732.c: Don't hire PMs for alignment and politics; hire for big-picture end state plus fast, detailed validation.
l367|732.e: He says candidates who lead with alignment and stakeholder management are on the decline. That reads as a political skill, not a technical or customer skill. One candidate's failure story was about not briefing the CEO soon enough. He wants people who can describe the end state and also know how to validate quickly and where to push, who can name specific things they got done rather than maintaining legacy systems at a big company. Interviews include a hands-on case plus a verbal defense, and many people fall apart once data and follow-up questions appear. In two years Whatnot received 31,832 PM applications and hired one.
ex: 31,832 PM applications in two years, one hire

l367|732.c: Systems thinking can be trained: plan for green and red outcomes, then imagine what breaks at 1,000x scale.
l367|732.e: He agrees systems thinking is a skill gaining value. His practice: before every experiment, decide what you'll do if the result is green and what you'll do if it's red. Then imagine usage a thousand times larger and trace the knock-on effects and what breaks first. You don't have to solve it all, but you have to think it through, and the team ends up faster because fewer surprises block it. In hypergrowth, chase changes that compound rather than a pile of statistically significant small wins. He also warns that averages lie: a feature only 3% of users touch may be essential to one group. He quotes Bezos: when data and anecdotes disagree, trust the anecdotes.
ex: Bezos: when the data and the anecdotes disagree, trust the anecdotes

root.d: Think it through first, move faster

items.d: Decide what to do either way
A small group may depend on it

l367|732.c: PMs don't need to ship production code; using AI to understand data and the codebase is higher leverage.
l367|732.e: He is mostly against PMs writing production code. Setting up a commit environment as a non-engineer is slow; he spent more time on setup than on understanding the problem, and hit pitfalls engineers had solved long ago. Enabling the team and improving how it works pays off more. The real change, he says, is that PMs can now pull their own data, run regressions and forecasts with AI, and use Claude to understand the codebase without interrupting engineers. After adopting Hex Threads, his requests to data scientists dropped sharply. An analysis that took a senior data scientist a week or two in 2017 is now fast. But accountability doesn't vanish: data scientists are busy reviewing rough analyses by amateurs, and the root cause is underinvestment in data engineering.
ex: After adopting Hex Threads, he asked data scientists for help far less often
Analysis that took a senior data scientist one to two weeks in 2017 is now quick

l367|732.c: Plan and iterate like an accordion: expand to set hypotheses, compress to ship a small v1, then expand again.
l367|732.e: He rejects both pure roadmap thinking and pure iteration. His approach works like an accordion. First expand: plan and write down your hypotheses. Then compress: build the smallest v1 that lets you learn. Then expand again: update what you know and plan the next step. At every step, think through the second-order effects. His example: live commerce initially didn't require sellers to create product listings, so search couldn't work. But forcing listings costs a seller about three minutes per item, which hurts sellers. That trade-off has to be weighed. Changes to the discovery page are likewise validated with the smallest possible experiment first.
ex: Discovery page changes are tested with the smallest experiment first

items.d: Ship a minimal v1 to learn
Update beliefs, set the next step

l367|732.c: AI shopping agents will only take high-intent purchases; browsing and social shopping stay with live commerce.
l367|732.e: He welcomes agents buying high-intent items like replacement parts or a specific cable. But most US retail is low-intent browsing, and e-commerce has never exceeded roughly 20% of it. Malls and store staff provide taste, curation and a social experience. US retail is about $7.5 trillion, and it won't be winner-take-all. Live commerce combines internet scale with the social feel of shopping in person. Its economics also differ from entertainment streaming: a Whatnot stream works with 30 to 50 viewers, while Twitch considered streams under about 1,000 viewers uneconomic.
ex: A Whatnot stream works with just 30 to 50 viewers
Twitch treated streams under about 1,000 viewers as uneconomic

result.d: Low-intent shopping agents can't replace

l368|734.c: Hiring is a tale of two markets: top talent is fought over while narrow specialists and new grads cool off.
l368|734.e: He sees two worlds at once. Competition for certain roles is extreme, which he calls "eleven out of ten." Meanwhile other companies are laying people off, and the cycle has shrunk from years to weeks or even days. He reads this as a reallocation of talent rather than simply good or bad news. Who is heating up? Forward-deployed engineers, who sit with customers and get AI working for them, because companies have shifted from burning money on AI to optimizing the spend, with finance teams now watching the bill. Also product design engineers who combine product sense with design craft. More broadly, judgment, taste and curiosity are rising in value. Overly narrow specialists and inexperienced new grads are cooling.
ex: Today's forward-deployed engineers are often the full-stack engineers of three to five years ago

d.verdict: A reallocation of talent and labor

l368|734.c: Casting a wide net and filtering down only lands the mediocre people who happened to be free that day.
l368|734.e: The usual approach is to contact a hundred people, get twenty replies, filter round by round, and hire whoever is left. He calls this the "funnel of doom." The twenty who replied are just the people who were available that day, not the top twenty percent, and the bigger the funnel, the more it costs. Comparing hiring to a sales funnel is misleading too: a product stays the same, but candidates are people who change their minds and are not always rational. He flips it around: build a "pillar of excellence" by confidently listing the best people first, then use assessment to verify. He also stresses that density is a team property. Drop a 10x person into a bad team and they will not perform.
ex: The term "funnel of doom" came from his first manager at Trilogy

items.d: Just whoever was free that day

l368|734.c: Finding top people takes three steps: define excellence objectively, map the network, then pursue for the long haul.
l368|734.e: Step one is define. Before meeting anyone, rank the skills and experience the role needs, and spell out why the role matters and what success looks like. Do not copy another company's definition or get dazzled by big-company logos on a resume. Step two is map. Ask people you trust specific, pointed questions, cross-check the names that keep coming up, and work systematically through employees' networks with a dedicated recruiter. Step three is pursue. Stay in touch for weeks, months, even years. When someone says "not now," shrink the next step to something like a coffee. And put real effort into finding a mutual contact who can make the introduction.
ex: A good question: who works best with designers?
Use tools to find companies whose job requirements look like yours

items.d: Stay in touch, get warm introductions

l368|734.c: Hiring is a leadership priority: recruiters build confidence, but hiring managers make the decisions.
l368|734.e: He believes talent should be treated as a top priority, with real time and resources behind it, measured the way companies measure uptime and revenue, and with hiring managers and leaders held accountable for it. He is against handing the whole job to a recruiting department. A recruiter's job is to build confidence on both sides. The hiring manager and the committee, who live with the consequences, should make the call. Cursor's founders personally hired the first 80 or so people and are still deeply involved. That sometimes blurs who is responsible for what, but he thinks the trade is always worth it.
ex: Interview debriefs happen the same day or the next, with final approval from the founders

items.d: Makes the decision, leads first conversation

l368|734.c: Caring costs nothing: design the process around the person, not the role, so candidates feel wanted.
l368|734.e: Candidate satisfaction surveys keep showing that feeling wanted matters most, and caring more than your competitors costs almost nothing. Cursor builds the process around each person. Interviewers are chosen to match the candidate's interests, the hiring manager's first conversation runs much longer than a quick screen, and a candidate may meet the team three or four times before they are really in. Key candidates get a dedicated Slack channel and a ten-minute daily stand-up to drive the close. Even people who do not join become advocates if they were treated well, and that brings in new leads.
ex: Anyone in the company can suggest people in a "hiring ideas" channel
A recruiter tracked down a Turkish violin for a candidate who plays

items.d: Interviewers and process vary by candidate
They speak well of you even if they pass
Word of mouth brings new leads

l368|734.c: Work samples predict performance best, paid trials are expensive but worth it, and assessment should run both ways.
l368|734.e: He cites research showing that work samples, where candidates do a slice of real work, are the strongest predictor of performance, yet most companies lean too hard on one-on-one interviews. Cursor uses longer onsite interviews and side-by-side projects, which also gives candidates just as much signal to judge the fit themselves. The company once tried dropping paid work trials, lost confidence in its decisions, and brought them back. Candidates choose from a few problems, and timing is flexible, Saturdays included. He acknowledges the criticism that this is unpaid labor in disguise, but he still defends it.
ex: Go-to-market roles do a trial built around a real customer challenge

l368|734.c: Selling starts on day one, intrinsic motivation beats a bigger number, and offer-chasers often regret it fast.
l368|734.e: He argues that selling is not the last step. From the first conversation you should understand what the person wants and clear up concerns as they arise. Intrinsic motivators like the team, the work and the colleagues last longer than money, and people who chase the highest number are often unhappy six months later. If someone is not the right fit, he would rather let them go than rehire in six months. In negotiations, candidates should state what they want clearly and consistently. Reneging on accepted offers is on the rise, so Cursor warms people up before day one: dinners with other new hires, a laptop shipped early, a community to join.
ex: He respects Anthropic's no-negotiation policy but says it would not suit Cursor

l368|734.c: Don't look for a silver-bullet first recruiting lead: split urgent hiring and system-building between different people.
l368|734.e: Founders often want one head of talent who will fill urgent roles immediately and also build the hiring system. He says those goals conflict and should be split, for example one person building the system while contingency agencies, paid only on success, fill the urgent roles. Good recruiters are curious, understand the business and have lots of energy, and they perform best at 90 to 110 percent load. Strategic recruiters are rare and high-impact, so the recruiting team should be among the best-paid in the company. He also thinks every recruiter should become a "talent engineer" who builds their own tools.
ex: He hires recruiters on three things: excellent, with a chip on their shoulder, and team-first
