root.d: Don't count on a silver bullet

items.d: Different people fill urgent roles and build systems
Strategic recruiting is rare and critical

l369|737.c: AI hasn't rewritten the design process yet, so the anxiety is fair, but nobody is actually behind.
l369|737.e: Engineers are already much faster thanks to coding agents, while design still runs on iteration, feedback and getting teams on the same page, and that process is as messy as ever. The uncertainty makes classically trained designers feel they need to throw everything out. He thinks nobody in the industry has figured out the new workflow, so anyone who starts exploring today is ahead of most people. His advice: build lots of prototypes, try the tools, and focus on the outcome of shipping good software rather than competing on process or token usage. Don't perform AI confidence either. Recovering fast from failure matters more than getting it right the first time.
ex: He estimates engineers are getting 10 to 100 times more productive
After IGTV failed, the Instagram team quickly corrected and built Reels
He agrees with Elena Verna's critique of "performative AI confidence"

l369|737.c: Once anyone can build software, delight and real user understanding become what sets designers apart.
l369|737.e: As a teenager he learned design by viewing page source and using Dreamweaver. Today an idea becomes a working prototype in minutes. He argues that when the barrier to building software nearly disappears, what separates products is the human layer: delight and a real understanding of users. That is exactly a designer's job. Designers are also getting more say at startups. He has heard of teams considering two designers paired with one strong engineer.
ex: The traditional startup ratio was about one designer to 15 engineers
The new idea: two designers plus one engineer

result.d: Experience becomes the main difference

l369|737.c: AI is already an excellent product designer, but inventing new interaction patterns still takes people.
l369|737.e: He thinks AI is already very good at product design and available to everyone, though it may not be top-tier on visuals, typography, information hierarchy and interaction details. What people still own is observing users, understanding their needs, and having a point of view about who a product is for and why. Real breakthroughs have no training data to learn from. Multi-touch, Instagram's mobile-first approach and Snapchat's way of communicating had no precedent before they appeared. How we should talk to AI by voice, or hand tasks to agents, is equally uncharted today.
ex: Multi-touch, Instagram and Snapchat were breakthroughs with no precedent
Voice interaction and delegating to agents have no established pattern yet

l369|737.c: Roles are blending, but big companies still need specialization; good teams are built on complementary people.
l369|737.e: Design and product already overlap heavily, and the sharp line between them is partly an artifact of big-company career ladders. But expecting one person to design, align the whole company and write the code is not realistic. At scale, responsibilities still need to be split, even if people cross boundaries more freely. At a startup he would hire the strongest generalists he could find. For designers at OpenAI, he increasingly looks for curiosity about AI (not AI experience), prototyping ability, a strategic point of view and systems thinking. The team as a whole needs the full range of strengths.
ex: Systems thinking, like the composable building blocks of early Notion
No AI experience required, but candidates must be curious

root.d: No one person is strong at everything

items.d: A view on where technology is going

l369|737.c: Start by doing less: reuse what exists and save the hard grind for experiences that define the product long-term.
l369|737.e: He often tells his team to do less. If you can extend an existing system, component or feature, don't design something new, or you end up with a pile of disconnected features. The old step-by-step design process has been compressed, so you have to pick your battles. Experiences that shape ChatGPT's long-term form, like becoming more deeply woven into someone's life, go through whiteboards, Figma, internal testing and user research, sometimes a hundred options tried for one that ships. A small feature can go from idea to launch in four hours. Products like Codex lean toward fast, public experimentation.
ex: Try a hundred options, throw away 99, ship one
A small feature takes about four hours from idea to launch

d.verdict: Reuse by default; focus effort on lasting key experiences

l369|737.sc: A billion users vs. the frontier
l369|737.c: Most people use a fraction of ChatGPT's abilities, so keep the default simple and give power users the rest first.
l369|737.e: ChatGPT's users span an enormous range. Some ask what a rash is; others automate a farm or build a Salesforce-like tool. Most people use only a small slice of what the product can do, which he calls capability overhang: the model can do far more than people are using. That is not all bad, since many people already get real value. The approach is to keep the default experience simple while opening advanced capabilities first to the people who care most. The long-term goal is to fold them back into one unified experience, so users never have to pick a mode or a model.
ex: The desktop app, Codex and ChatGPT Work serve power users first
User needs range from checking a rash to automating a farm

items.d: For the few who care most

l369|737.c: The chat box works for everyone, but interfaces need to become proactive, voice-driven and unified.
l369|737.e: He agrees with Kevin Weil, OpenAI's chief product officer, that a conversation box can absorb needs at every level of sophistication, which makes it a good interface. The team is helping users express intent better, for example with follow-up questions you can tap. Conversations are no longer just text either: emails and documents appear as writing blocks you can edit directly. Next come proactivity and more natural voice. Eventually one entry point should decide on its own whether to answer quickly, chat, or go work in the background. Users will be able to save reusable workflows, and the interface will adapt to who is using it.
ex: ChatGPT Work already makes proactive suggestions from your calendar and Slack
Emails and documents shown as directly editable writing blocks

items.d: Decides: quick answer or background work

l371|440.c: The five-stage CRM pipeline is a forecasting tool; a real enterprise deal takes about 15 steps.
l371|440.e: The five stages in a CRM (intro, demo, proposal, contract, close) exist to weight deals for revenue forecasts. She estimates nine out of ten people instead treat them as five meetings to run through, and lose the deal. A real enterprise sale has about 15 steps, with several meetings inside each stage, and the process is the same for a $100k deal and a $1 million deal. The key is to slow down and gather all the information. A full cycle typically runs about 90 days.
ex: Running example: selling AI legal tech to SpaceX's legal team
She estimates about 90% of people treat the five stages as a meeting sequence

items: Five steps from intro to close

d.verdict: Slow down to close faster

l371|440.c: Only target the top decision-maker and the level below, approaching both at once in a pincer move.
l371|440.e: Going any lower doesn't work. Your story gets distorted as it is relayed upward, and those people have no budget authority. She has the founder reach out one-on-one to an executive like the general counsel, while the account executive works the VP or director a level down, so the two meet in the middle. The opening message is two or three sentences about "alpha," the information edge the new tool gives that executive, not features or cost savings. The test: could the executive repeat it to the board? Executives mostly ignore marketing campaigns, so be ready to send a hundred handwritten emails and keep refining them.
ex: Use LLMs, LinkedIn and Lemlist to find people and fill in details
Non-technical buyers can simply be cold-called

root.d: Approach from two sides, then converge

items.d: One-on-one outreach to the CLO or GC
An edge they could take to the board

l371|440.c: On the first call, don't demo or record; ask what changes next year instead of asking about pain.
l371|440.e: This is the most important call of all: about 30 minutes, casual, no slides and no recording, or the other side will hold back. Let the buyer talk first about what is changing next year and what their priorities are. "Change" opens people up better than "problems," and fixating on pain points makes you look like every other vendor. In the last 10 minutes or so, pitch based on what you heard, with no script and no budget-need-timeline checklist to qualify them. About a quarter of first calls turn out to be unqualified, usually because the organization is not mature enough. Walking away quickly is a skill too.
ex: About one in four first calls turns out to be unqualified
She is skeptical of sales books and training, which she says breed generic scripts

l371|440.c: Have the buyer help design the demo, then show only the 20% of features that deliver 80% of the value.
l371|440.e: After the first call, book a 15-minute follow-up to agree with the buyer on who attends and what they will see, so the demo becomes their project. You can also preview it with another colleague of theirs and gather intel along the way. Never demo to a room when you know nothing about them; that is just going through the motions. The real demo runs about an hour and is different every time, covering only the most valuable parts. Showing everything dilutes the story. Right afterward, message your champion privately to debrief: who might veto, who needs more time.
ex: The champion is usually one level below the executive and pushes from day one
The follow-up call takes about 15 minutes

terms.d: Agree on attendees and format together

result.d: Debrief with the champion right after

l371|440.c: Keep pilots short and specific, work backward from the signing date, and line up procurement and legal early.
l371|440.e: If the product needs no integration, a pilot of two or three days with three or four frontline users is enough. Onboard them beforehand and agree on success criteria together. If integration is required, run a paid 30-to-60-day pilot credited against the contract. Before starting, work backward from the target signing date and identify your procurement, security and legal contacts. If it won't fit the calendar, don't start. Procurement's job is not to kill deals, but it usually takes about 30 days. Send contracts as Word, not PDF, accept small edits, get on a call with legal for the hard ones, refuse unreasonable terms, and confirm the signer early.
ex: With integration, run a paid 30-to-60-day pilot credited against the contract
A small vendor asked for $10 million in liability insurance should say no

items.d: Compare actual use with the plan

l371|440.c: Price on risk and upside. If you win more than 35% of deals, you are charging too little.
l371|440.e: A low-priority problem only supports a cheap "good enough" price. A high-risk problem like legal compliance can support a first deal of $250k to $500k. Discuss price after the demo, and give a rough range if pressed. Hold the line together with your champion. Rather than discount, agree on step-up pricing in year two, and never negotiate against yourself. Her benchmarks: a healthy win rate on qualified opportunities is about 25 to 35%, and about 80% of pilots should convert; anything lower means the pilot or the qualification was off. The market talks, so mispricing one customer spills over to others.
ex: A high-risk problem can support a first deal of $250k to $500k
About a quarter of lost deals come back within a year

items.d: Below this, check the pilot or qualification

items.t: Lost deals back in a year

l371|440.c: The money in enterprise is expansion; services are often the biggest budget line, and FDEs only fit big deals.
l371|440.e: A healthy enterprise customer should grow from $100k-$250k in year one to $350k-$500k in year two. After early customers sign, founders should stay involved to decide which custom requests become product and which should be billed as services. Services are often the largest line in an enterprise budget, and buyers already purchase consulting, so bundling it is fine. Forward-deployed engineers, who embed with the customer, make sense for complex multi-million-dollar deals like Palantir's. If you need them because the product is hard to use, that is a bad sign. The math fails on a $100k deal, and many so-called FDEs are just account managers with a new title.
ex: From $100k-$250k in year one to $350k-$500k in year two
Palantir's multi-million-dollar contracts can support FDEs

marks.d: Mostly salespeople with a new title
Embed with the customer, then productize

l372|743.c: AI is moving from chat and one-on-one agents toward persistent coworkers that whole teams share.
l372|743.e: She splits AI's progress into three eras. The first is chat: ask a question, get an answer. The second is working alongside agents, AI that goes and does tasks for you, which today happens mostly in coding. The third is a persistent AI coworker that stays around and finishes work with you and your whole team. Right now agent use is almost always one person at a time. Colleagues at OpenAI even paste screenshots of Codex threads into Slack to collaborate, which is awkward. Getting to the third era needs agents that can run long tasks, but practical problems matter just as much: cloud agents need heavy infrastructure, connections to documents, chat and databases, and real reliability.
ex: OpenAI colleagues collaborate by pasting Codex thread screenshots into Slack
Chat may also become the place where agents coordinate with each other

items.d: Always around, shared by the team

l372|743.c: Future work looks more like steering than rowing; direction, judgment and accountability stay with people.
l372|743.e: Her image is that agents row and people steer, and over time the steering seat moves to a higher, more abstract level. Setting direction, making judgment calls, and having a gut sense of what a product should become are hard to hand off. She compares it to fashion and film: when everyone has the same tools, the difference comes from personal expression. Software, she argues, is more like making a movie than building a house. A big budget does not guarantee success; the author's point of view does. People also stay accountable for outcomes, so agents act more like reports. In heavily regulated industries, a human still has to be the point of contact.
ex: She credits Stripe founder Patrick Collison for "software is like film, not real estate"
Product expert Marty Cagan says the first feature idea rarely survives to the end

items.d: What to build and how it feels

l372|743.c: Execution no longer caps ambition; what separates people in the AI era is daring to think bigger.
l372|743.e: AI makes easy things easier and puts hard things within reach, so what one person can do is no longer limited by their own ability to execute. The best users don't just automate their existing tasks. They expand what they can take on, so a single person can design, build and price a product. The hardest part is updating your own beliefs about what can already be done in a short time. That is why she sees raising other people's ambition as a new job for product managers. Inside OpenAI people often ask: has this been sped up as much as possible, and are you already using it all day?
ex: Stripe founder Patrick Collison keeps a list of projects that were finished remarkably fast
Economist Tyler Cowen often asks people whether they could be more ambitious

terms.d: One person can design, build and price

result.d: PMs should raise others' ambition

l372|743.c: In a research-driven market, strategy emerges from fast experiments, and testing itself is the rigor.
l372|743.e: This market is tied to research progress, so predictions go stale quickly and long analysis documents are less useful than evidence. Before joining OpenAI she assumed there was a secret strategy document. There wasn't; internal ideas show up in public products almost immediately. The method is to find the one core question that decides whether a product succeeds, then build something users can test as fast as possible. At first she worried that skipping deep documents meant being sloppy, but she came to see testing as the real rigor. The core job of a product manager hasn't changed, while scheduling, reporting and similar chores have largely disappeared.
ex: She credits Coda founder Shishir Mehrotra for the term "eigen question"
Codex's momentum came from constant internal use and tight iteration
Sutter Hill tests a market by telling the story to people over and over first

l372|743.c: Aim products at the models of two or three months out, and let the system pick modes for users.
l372|743.e: She is firm that building for today's model capabilities fails, because the models improve too fast. Betting on the model a year away is too far out. The right target is two or three months ahead, which requires working closely with the research roadmap. Products should be designed around what the model can do, not force it into rigid structures. ChatGPT Work runs on the same engine as Codex, just without the coding interface. The long-term goal is that users never choose a mode; the system picks the right model and tooling automatically. For a billion people unfamiliar with agents, simplicity matters most.
ex: A finance team built complex financial models with ChatGPT Work
She quotes OpenAI's Kevin Weil: today's models are the worst they will ever be

l372|743.c: Knowledge work can't be verified like code with tests, so AI must show its process and sources.
l372|743.e: Code can be checked by running tests and actually executing it. Knowledge work is different. With a slide deck full of numbers, you cannot tell from the finished product whether to trust it. You need to see the inputs, the citations and the reasoning. So the product should show work in progress, sources and reasoning, and turn the conversation thread into a shared surface where everyone can inspect and edit. The model then behaves like a collaborator whose work can be examined, rather than delivering a black-box result.
ex: Sites lets Codex or Work generate a hosted web page or small app directly
/visualize turns data into charts that tell a story

items: You need inputs, sources and reasoning

d.verdict: Make the thread a shared, inspectable workspace

l372|743.c: Never outsource writing that helps you think; hand status-style writing to the model freely.
l372|743.e: Briefs, strategy and arguments are thinking in written form. Outlining, cutting and revising is how ideas get clear, so she writes the first and final drafts herself. Status updates and summaries are reporting, and she happily gives those to the model. In between, she uses AI for research, organizing data, translation and pushback. Once models can produce long documents easily, length stops being a signal of quality, so she communicates more with prototypes, mockups and experiment results. She shares a brief when it is about seventy percent done so collaborators can finish it; a polished draft leaves people nothing to add.
ex: At Stripe she circulated first drafts and invited colleagues to attack them
Her rule: read anything yourself before asking others to read it

items.d: No AI polish at the end

l373|748.c: Companies are becoming chains of loops, starting with coding and expanding to functions, divisions and the whole firm.
l373|748.e: An agent, in his view, is just a model running in a loop with tools, memory and skill files. A group of agents that handles one kind of work forms a loop. Coding is the most mature case: from bug report to reproduction, fix, review and deploy often takes minutes, with humans approving only risky changes. Next come business loops for marketing, sales, support, legal and growth. Their combined output becomes a bigger loop the CEO optimizes, which can even reshape strategy and the business model. He expects this to cascade level by level until it covers most of how a company runs.
ex: A coding loop often completes in about five minutes
Reportedly OpenAI's go-to-market team uses Codex more than its engineers do

items.d: Bug report to deploy in about five minutes
CEO optimizes the whole and strategy

l373|748.c: Loops only climb to the nearest peak; jumping to the next hill takes human insight the model lacks.
l373|748.e: Automated growth experiments can already generate variants, run significance tests, keep a long-term holdout, and move to the next round. But a loop stalls once it reaches a local optimum. Models are weak at novel thinking that is hard to verify, and they cannot give themselves direction, which is exactly why AI can't just make you a million dollars. The human job is to supply out-of-distribution insight, carry the company to the foot of the next hill, and hand it back to the loop. Skills whose output is hard to verify, he argues, become the rate limiter on the whole loop.
ex: When an agent fails, ask: what do I know that the model doesn't
PMs may find they are weaker at zero-to-one work than they assumed

items.d: A new direction the model can't see

l373|748.c: Bolting AI onto old functions isn't enough; redesign the company around models, like factories around electricity.
l373|748.e: Many companies just attach AI tools to existing functions. The most ambitious ones assume intelligence is nearly unlimited and extremely cheap, then redesign everything. His comparison is electrification: factories took about 40 years to go from swapping steam engines for motors to rebuilding the floor plan around electricity. Employees, he says, are more willing to adopt AI than the stereotype suggests, and CEOs want to grow the pie rather than cut staff. A friend who is a Google executive didn't lay anyone off; he used AI to race through the roadmap, and the hard question became what to add. When an agent gets stuck, it calls a person, records the fix, and doesn't repeat the mistake.
ex: Used-car company Kavak taught every employee, mechanics included, to use AI in a six-week course
Kavak's agents call a human when stuck and remember what they're taught

items: Like swapping steam engines for motors
Redesign the org and its processes

d.verdict: The most ambitious companies redesign everything around models

l373|748.c: A "permanent underclass" is a fantasy; AI separates skill from desire, so opportunity spreads out more.
l373|748.e: Past tech concentrated power through network effects, yet today every layer of the AI stack has several competitors, the opposite of winner-take-all. Employment data doesn't support collapse either: radiologists were predicted to be replaced about 20 years ago, and demand for programmers remains high. Models improve fast, but diffusion through the economy is slow, and many problems were never limited by intelligence in the first place. AI lets untrained people make music and software, which amplifies individual agency. He sees no reason GDP growth has to stay stuck around 2 percent.
ex: A room full of PhDs still can't beat FedEx's logistics or Domino's
He thinks recursive self-improvement is overrated; it's more like autocatalysis than runaway

root.d: Opportunity is more spread out than before

items.d: Many problems aren't limited by intelligence

l373|748.c: Use frontier models where the upside is unlimited, and tuned mid-tier models where it is capped.
l373|748.e: Frontier model pricing is out of proportion to performance; a bit more intelligence can cost roughly a hundred times more, he says. In fields with unlimited upside like drug discovery, where one molecule could be worth a trillion dollars, the strongest model is worth it, and sales and R&D may be similar. Capped work like checkout, legal and finance suits mid-tier or open-source models tuned with reinforcement learning, where the model improves by trial and reward. Still, a single support call might hide a clue that changes the company. Different models have different shapes; they complement each other rather than being interchangeable commodities.
ex: He uses Alibaba's Qwen for long creative projects, like a documentary about a Star Wars planet
His advice: build something with every new model to develop intuition

cells.d: Paying a hundred times more for capped gains

l373|748.c: More people want to spend time than save it; consumer AI is stuck on product design, not model ability.
l373|748.e: The biggest consumer products are mostly entertainment and social, yet AI is built mainly for productivity, like a better spreadsheet. What people actually want is to feel connected, loved, improving and entertained. He sees this as a product design gap, not a model capability gap. Consumer AI is at its 2010 iPhone moment, held back by three things: expensive models, chat interfaces that are too hard for ordinary people, and a fixation on productivity. Open-source models and new interface experiments are loosening those constraints. Startups can also take on the slightly uncomfortable social use cases that big companies avoid.
ex: Companion apps are used heavily by women in their forties and fifties
Wabi lets ordinary people build small apps with coding agents

l373|748.c: Durable advantages are discovered, not designed; distribution and ambition are the new bar.
l373|748.e: Cursor was once criticized for having no defensible advantage, but a product people loved accumulated huge volumes of reasoning traces, which it used to train its own model. The advantage grew over time. Network effects, scale, brand and proprietary data still work, but software being hard to build is not an advantage on its own. With launches everywhere, staying in users' feeds through word of mouth is a new kind of edge. Nobody today has a real growth problem, he argues, only a product problem or a lack of imagination. Three years ago too much ambition counted against you; now thinking too small is the problem.
ex: Cursor: high NPS, then reasoning traces, then its own Composer model
Meeting-notes app Granola was doubted early and later widely loved
Try imagining a version of your product that costs $1,000 a month

l374|749.c: A sequestered small team with a one-month deadline gets the design right better than a big team chasing a long vision.
l374|749.e: Cursor had always served developers, and the team wanted a knowledge-work product for the whole company, so they started from a blank page. A few people were sequestered in a corner of the office with a private Slack channel and one month to produce a prototype. He argues a large group working toward a 6-to-12-month vision couldn't produce the same design, because every day brings many small, non-obvious decisions that need a quick call. After the all-hands opened it to internal testing, non-engineers quickly moved their daily work into it, which was the real adoption test.
ex: About one month from the first line of code to an internal prototype
Public launch came about three weeks after internal testing began

l374|749.c: Build new products separately; adding a tab to an old product is shipping your org chart.
l374|749.e: The team discussed putting it inside Cursor and decided against it. A coding tool is full of small pain points for non-technical users, looks intimidating, and carries a developer brand. He criticizes the habit of adding a tab for every new form factor: users can tell when several visions are crammed onto one screen. Starting from scratch also avoided the architecture and sunk costs built for coding agents, making it easier to create named, persistent agents and the cloud infrastructure behind them.

d.verdict: A patchwork of tabs feels disjointed to users

l374|749.c: Onboard early users by hand, hold back, and reinforce usage patterns only after they emerge on their own.
l374|749.e: Over about two weeks, the core team personally onboarded two to three hundred early users one at a time, watched where things failed, and fixed them before the next session. The list deliberately went beyond the usual influencers. A coffee shop owner's feedback was nothing like internal testing, a reminder that the team lives in a Silicon Valley AI bubble, and a sign the product may be most powerful for non-developers. Internal users often ran 5 to 10 bots, each owning one area. By the end of week two some had, on their own, set up a "chief of staff" bot to manage the others. The team didn't push it; only after it kept recurring did they gently encourage it.
ex: The coffee shop owner cared most about a Shopify integration
Internal users often ran 5 to 10 bots at once

items.d: Two weeks, a few hundred users

l374|749.c: Two early decisions made or broke it: cloud first, and every bot gets its own computer.
l374|749.e: First, bots run in the cloud rather than being tied to a laptop, so users can start a task from their phone and every device shows the same state. He criticizes existing products that leave people unsure where a task is actually running. Second, people do their work through interfaces, not just APIs, so a bot needs its own computer. Having an agent share your machine and your credentials is strange, like a new hire sharing your laptop. The open-source project OpenClaw proved that a model with the right tools is highly capable and that treating AI as a coworker works. Grok Bot's job is to turn that into a product millions can use.
ex: The product was inspired by the open-source project OpenClaw
The goal is millions of users, not a Mac Mini running at home

terms.d: Start from your phone, synced everywhere
Works through interfaces, not just APIs

result.d: Finishes tasks on its own

l374|749.c: When unsure, ask what a human teammate would do: always around, remembers things, doesn't narrate every step.
l374|749.e: When a product debate has merit on both sides, the team asks what they would want from a human teammate. You don't watch a colleague's every click, so the product hides tool calls, step-by-step browser actions and chains of thought, showing only progress status and stage updates. What users really want to see is the bot's to-do list and priorities. Bots should persist, be organized by role or workstream, remember what happened and learn over time, rather than one-off chats where you copy context between sessions. He expects the next shift to be proactive agents.
ex: A chief-of-staff bot filters Slack, email and X and sends a daily report
They imagine voice stand-ups with screen sharing

items.d: Flags what matters, few false alarms

l374|749.c: Capabilities, not buttons: cut heavily before launch and spend the effort on actually finishing tasks.
l374|749.e: Before launch the team cut a lot of experimental features and debugging views; memory and reasoning details meant for developers had leaked into the user interface. The test: if a feature wouldn't be interesting in the launch announcement, question whether to build it. The framing is "Grok Bot can now do X," not "there's a new button." Phase two focuses on getting tasks all the way done, mostly backend reliability for computer use, website logins and browser control, measured week by week against real task categories.
ex: About 99 percent of automations are set up in plain language
Fixing clicks on Salesforce dashboards immediately helped the sales team

items.d: Keep only "it can now do this"

l374|749.c: Cursor wins by never feeling it has won; durable advantages are discovered after the fact.
l374|749.e: Cursor grew from about 15 people to more than a thousand while keeping a startup feel: move fast, trust each other, and "just do it" instead of asking up the chain. Competitors lose, he argues, not from bad decisions or thin resources but from an inability to change quickly. Cursor needs to be able to completely reinvent itself every six months. You don't plan an advantage in advance: obsess over being useful today, pull near-future capabilities forward with scaffolding, tear it down when the models catch up, and distribution and data advantages follow from being loved. Hiring from high-growth companies can slow you down, so resist it.
ex: Two values: "delete the product" and "just do it"
Be able to completely reinvent yourself every six months

items.t: Tear down when models catch up

l375|752.c: Collaboration carries heavy coordination costs, so organize teams around shared beliefs, not a leader.
l375|752.e: Coordination costs mean a team can only move as fast as its slowest node, yet executives rarely say so out loud. He uses a deliberately provocative image: an effective organization is like an underground movement built around an ideology, not a cult built around a leader. Everyone understands why the work matters, the founder's vision is boiled down to a few short slogans, each area has a directly responsible person, and the front line is trusted to move on its own. Then PMs make the decisions the founder would have made a year or two earlier. Principles everyone agrees with, he adds, are usually weak ones.
ex: The org must have room for spiky talents like Nikita Bier
Push more and more decisions onto your strongest people until they start making mistakes

terms.d: Everyone knows why the work matters

result.d: Keeps moving when leaders are absent

l375|752.c: The median PM is weak for structural reasons: low rates drew in mediocre people and the best leave.
l375|752.e: He looks at it statistically: several forces have distorted the distribution of PM ability, so the median is well below what people assume the average to be. In the zero-interest-rate era, product management became a high-paying path for people without technical backgrounds, attracting many who wanted to stay regardless of ability. Meanwhile the best PMs leave to start companies or become executives, so those who remain skew weaker. Higher rates raise the opportunity cost of a hire, so hiring gets more careful. He evaluates both the PM and their environment to make sure every PM is a net positive.
ex: Strong engineers put PMs to work; weak ones hide behind PM decisions; complaints come from the middle

items.d: A high-paying path in the zero-rate era
To found companies or run them

l375|752.c: Snap's ads were structurally hard: young users, a camera-first product, and messaging at the core.
l375|752.e: Advertising to minors faces strict limits on measurement and targeting, and a user's ad value jumps in steps around ages 17 to 18 and again from 18 to 21. Audiences you can't measure are hard to monetize. Ad slots usually live in a feed or in search, but Snap's core action is taking and sending a snap, with no natural place for an ad; he calls monetizing the camera his biggest failure. Messaging apps also lack good ad formats. He thinks the Snapchat Plus subscription has done well, and launching it a few years earlier would have eased the pressure for ads to grow fast.
ex: From memory, he puts Snap at about a billion users
He says Snap reached about $4 billion in ad revenue faster than Twitter and others

root.d: Structural limits from the product itself

items.d: Minors are hard to target and measure
No natural ad slot in the core flow
Snapchat Plus should have come earlier

l375|752.c: Taste is mostly knowing what to say no to, and AI naturally only adds things to a product.
l375|752.e: He wants to turn founders into curators: the shipped product is a small selection from a much larger collection. To judge someone's taste, ask what they built but never shipped. Saying no is one of the few taste muscles you can train deliberately; people with taste stop a step before everyone else and know when a trend has peaked. AI tends to add features rather than remove them, so a new PM skill is resisting AI-generated additions. The easier creation gets, the higher the bar for what deserves users' attention.
ex: He says Snap founder Evan Spiegel has turned down more good ideas than any consumer founder he knows
Instagram copied even Snap's weakest features

marks.d: Ships a small selection from a collection

l375|752.c: Be "long-term greedy" with ads: advertiser returns and user trust today decide tomorrow's revenue.
l375|752.e: Tomorrow's ad revenue depends on the return advertisers get today. The quickest way to boost returns in the short run is cutting prices or quality, which hurts the long run. Centering advertiser returns earns retention and budget growth, and "long-term greedy" gives teams at public companies the backbone to resist short-term pressure. On OpenAI entering ads, he thinks the latecomer has an advantage and argues for a modified VCG auction, a pricing method based on each party's true value, that counts the value users get from an ad in the bid. In conversation, the equivalent variable is trust.
ex: Amazon stuffing ads ahead of search results may erode trust
He's disappointed that OpenAI's top subscription tier has no ads at all

items.d: The ad itself must be useful
Not bought with lower prices or quality

l375|752.c: Start growth with core users: raising existing users' active days often beats acquiring new ones.
l375|752.e: He treats DAU over MAU as a retention metric, and a small lift in that ratio often beats adding new monthly users. After Snap's 2018 redesign, daily actives stalled, so the team optimized Android performance for existing users, which brought years of renewed growth. Discord focused on "intentional co-op gamers," a group already near saturation, and improved their experience before, during and after play; those demanding players raised the quality bar for everyone. When betting on new directions, he maps core strengths onto other groups, watches for unexpected usage, and works backward from an ideal future.
ex: He says this approach borrows from Meta's growth playbook
He sees the biggest risk as a competitor that is ten times better

l375|752.c: Core product value needs a one-sentence statement and metrics causally tied to retention.
l375|752.e: His core product value framework has two steps: define the product's value in one sentence, then break each phrase into measurable parts and use them to prioritize the roadmap. A slogan alone isn't actionable, and metrics alone mean nothing to most people, so both must exist together and connect causally to retention. He gave this talk to every new hire for seven years running. Data scientists once found the work of breaking down the metrics tedious.
ex: Snap: the fastest way to share a moment with people you care about
Discord: the best place to talk and hang out with friends around games

items.d: Like "fastest way to share a moment"
Fastest, share, people you care about
Use it to prioritize the roadmap

l375|752.c: Great PMs hold three pairs of seemingly contradictory traits; one side alone isn't enough.
l375|752.e: The first pair is confidence and humility: confident almost to the point of arrogance, tempered by humility and a readiness to give credit away, since PMs already get too much of it. The second is process and ambiguity: highly organized and process-minded, yet comfortable in uncertainty and even skeptical of authority, something he tests for in interviews. The third is long-term vision and urgency: knowing where the product should be in six months to two years and which building blocks it needs, while setting the company's daily pace with a bias for action.
ex: He sees ambition as a trainable muscle and wants acceleration, not just speed

d.verdict: Great PMs hold both sides at once

l379|570.c: Delivering the roadmap and chasing new AI capabilities conflict, so don't expect one team to do both.
l379|570.e: His starting point is that product teams now carry two jobs at once. One is shipping the features already promised to customers on schedule. The other is keeping up with AI models that change at high speed and seeing what the new ones make possible. Both jobs compete for the same people and the same attention. If the core team tries to do both, either delivery slows down or the opportunities from new models get missed. So his fix is not to work harder but to separate exploration from scaling in the org structure itself.
ex: One chapter of the talk is about balancing roadmap delivery with fast AI innovation

items: Try models the day they launch

d.verdict: Split them with a separate labs group

l379|570.c: Set up a labs group so early adopters can test new models without disrupting the core team.
l379|570.e: His approach is to create a separate group he calls labs. Labs does the exploring, while the core team focuses on scaling the existing product, and the two don't get in each other's way. That means the natural early adopters in the company can start experimenting the day a new model comes out, without throwing anyone else off their rhythm. He thinks this lets a company keep its current promises while building the next version of its product at the same time. Constant disruption in AI becomes an advantage rather than a headache.
ex: One chapter covers using a labs team to separate exploration from scaling

root.d: Must handle today and what's next

l379|570.c: Each lab is a pair: one person finds where the value is, the other builds a system that scales.
l379|570.e: He recommends keeping labs very small, with two people as the basic unit. The two have different jobs. One he calls the pirate, whose task is to roam through new capabilities and find the uses that are genuinely valuable. The other he calls the architect, whose task is to turn that discovery into a system that can scale. The pair gets feedback through dogfooding, meaning they use their own experiments inside the company first to see whether they actually work. That keeps the feedback loop short and direct.
ex: The pirate finds where the value is
The architect builds a system that can scale
Using their own experiments internally keeps feedback tight

terms.d: Finds the value in new capabilities
Turns it into a scalable system

result.d: Uses its own work, iterates fast

l379|570.c: Experiments don't ship directly; a research pipeline filters them and only the successes join the main product.
l379|570.e: He argues that what labs produces should not go straight to users. Instead it goes through what he calls a research pipeline: systematic testing first, then rounds of iteration, and only experiments that prove themselves get merged into the main product. The benefit is that neither side loses. Labs can be bold in its exploration, while the main product stays stable. And the company gets a repeatable way to turn new capabilities into real product value, rather than relying on one-off luck.
ex: One chapter is about scaling innovation through a structured research pipeline

l381|40.c: Product management should shift from following process to solving customer problems and delivering business outcomes.
l381|40.e: He starts by separating two ways of working: the project model and the product model. In the project model, delivering according to process is the goal. Build it, ship it on time, done. The product model uses a different yardstick: did the customer's problem actually get solved, and did the business get the outcome it wanted? He argues that process by itself creates no value. Once a team clings to process, it tends to forget who it is building for and why.
ex: One chapter is devoted to the difference between the project model and the product model

l381|40.c: He admits Inspired underweighted business viability and wrongly treated problem discovery as a gate.
l381|40.e: Inspired came out about ten years ago and shaped a generation of product managers. Looking back, he sees two clear gaps. First, the book did not give enough weight to business viability, meaning whether the thing actually works as a business. Second, it framed discovery, the work of understanding the problem, as a gate you must pass before building begins. As he sees it now, the real purpose of understanding the problem is to lead the team toward better solutions, not to serve as an approval step. He offers both points as corrections to his earlier thinking.
ex: His book Inspired is a classic among product managers

l381|40.c: Heavy reliance on roadmaps and PRDs usually hides a craving for predictability, and that kills innovation.
l381|40.e: He thinks that when companies lean hard on roadmaps and PRDs (product requirement documents that spell out what to build), the real driver is a craving for certainty: when it will be done and what it will look like, all fixed in advance. That craving suppresses critical thinking. Teams push forward according to the document and stop asking whether what they are building actually works. In his view, that is exactly how innovation gets smothered.
ex: One chapter covers customer churn and the dangers of chasing predictability

l381|40.c: Good product work needs humility, an understanding of why customers leave, and leaders who supply strategic context.
l381|40.e: He stresses three things. First, humility: teams must accept that their ideas may be wrong, which is what makes them test those ideas. Second, understanding why customers churn and stop using the product, rather than only watching how many new ones sign up. Third, strong leadership that lays out the company's strategic context, so teams know where to put their effort. He also discusses how to navigate company politics and what that demands of leaders themselves.
ex: One chapter covers navigating company politics and the demands on leadership

items.d: Accept your ideas may be wrong

l381|40.c: Product is a brutal competition, so build to learn what works, not just to ship.
l381|40.e: He compares product development to a brutal sport: the market shifts constantly, and shipping a feature guarantees nothing about its value. So the point of building should be to learn as fast as possible what actually works, so the solution delivers real value to customers and the business, rather than shipping for its own sake. The final chapter touches on using AI to support this outcome-driven way of working, though the episode page does not spell out how.
ex: One chapter compares product development to a brutal sport
The last chapter is about using AI to drive outcome-oriented development

l383|644.c: When a company grows, hand over your Legos on purpose. Standing still is the least safe option.
l383|644.e: People build their identity around what they own at work, so when a company scales they instinctively resist giving it up, like a kindergartner guarding a Lego tower. Her answer: make yourself unnecessary so you can go build something new. Change is scary and hard, and the best response is to lean in rather than follow your instincts. The future belongs to learners, not knowers. At Facebook she watched high performers who refused to let their teams evolve fall behind within a year.
ex: Her group at Google grew from 25 to 125 people in nine months
In her five years at Facebook, headcount went from about 500 to 5,500 and users passed a billion

items.d: New people take over and grow

l383|644.c: The AI transition brings real grief, not just excitement. Face it and say a proper goodbye.
l383|644.e: The leaders she talks to consistently report grief, overload and burnout. An engineer at a fast-growing company told her he no longer enjoys his work. She reads that as grief: losing the joy of writing code by hand, and not knowing what his role is anymore. Engineering has gone from rowing to steering, and many people still want to row. She argues for naming the hard parts out loud. You can mourn what you lost and still be optimistic about what comes next. One idea is to hold a "funeral" for the old job, grieve it, and then move forward.
ex: A product leader said being a "general builder" who works mostly with AI is lonely
She credits the "funeral" idea to Chip Conley

items.d: No longer writing code by hand

l383|644.c: Pulling people out in favor of AI buys efficiency, but also unhappy people and worse work.
l383|644.e: Engineering teams keep shrinking, people spend their days mostly with AI, and loneliness follows. Leaders who simply remove people get efficiency, but also unhappy employees, and unhappy people don't do great work. Survey data shows people on small teams and at small companies are happier. She borrows Cory Doctorow's centaur framing: ideally a human head directs a machine body, and the human is amplified. Her worry is that knowledge work slides into the reverse centaur, where a machine head directs a human body.
ex: Delivery and ride-hail drivers are examples of reverse centaurs
Big companies cutting managers and piling on output pressure leave less room for happiness

d.verdict: Knowledge work must avoid the reverse centaur

l383|644.c: Burnout rose sharply in a year, and the happiest people are those who feel amplified by AI.
l383|644.e: Her annual survey with Lenny shows burnout up significantly, driven by emotional exhaustion, a constantly shifting narrative, and being asked to do more for the same pay. Yet about half of respondents say this is the happiest point in their careers. Happiness clusters on small teams and among people with more decision-making power, and the factor most strongly linked to it is feeling amplified by AI. Designers are the least happy, because design can't be sped up the way coding can and everyone now thinks they can design. Managers are the single biggest lever on workplace happiness.
ex: A friend at OpenAI saw the mood shift from "AI everywhere" to "is it worth the cost?" within six months

l383|644.c: "AI will replace you" is toxic and poorly supported; more likely, your job gets reinvented every few years.
l383|644.e: She thinks many layoffs blamed on AI are really corrections for poor management and over-hiring, with AI as the excuse. Demand for engineering talent is actually higher than ever. She suggests swapping "will my job disappear?" for "what if my job always exists but gets reinvented every few years?" This moment feels to her like the mobile era, which created many new roles. Rather than hoarding niche knowledge to protect yourself, take part in designing the next version of your own field.
ex: She credits that reframing to journalist Manoush Zomorodi
Journalists becoming entrepreneurs on Substack is a model other fields can follow

l383|644.c: AI is more like a lazy intern who needs coaching; producing more is not the same as moving things forward.
l383|644.e: For many people, a growing share of the job is cleaning up AI output that someone else handed in. Treating AI as a superhuman employee is a mistake; it is more like an intern that needs context, guidance and several rounds of revision. People copy, paste and send without owning the result. A CEO who blasts out an AI-written strategy memo is modeling outsourced thinking. She separates productivity from effectiveness: one means producing more, the other means advancing the work. Ranking employees by token usage repeats old bad management like counting lines of code or cars in the parking lot.
ex: One engineering report found code rework rose about 8x alongside AI productivity gains
The same report showed security incidents rising too

cells.d: Little output, but real forward motion

l383|644.c: Handing work to AI differs from handing it to people: you stay accountable, and judgment and taste can't be outsourced.
l383|644.e: When you give Legos to a person, you should let go completely. When you give them to AI, you must keep supervising and stay responsible; the mental tax stays with you. Managing AI uses the same skills as managing people, so everyone is a manager now, though running a large fleet of agents may exceed one person's bandwidth. She has revised her old view: judgment, trust, relationships and the definition of "good" should stay with humans, because you can't outsource quality you haven't defined. Vision and taste should be human too, steering the world toward what we actually want.
ex: She thinks a manager should have about 10 to 12 direct reports
Airbnb vs. Booking: one pursues experience, the other conversion pressure

items.d: What we want and what counts as good
Like a junior employee needing oversight
Check quality and own the result

l383|644.c: Managers should model AI use, acknowledge emotions, and hold the line on accountability and quality.
l383|644.e: She recommends one habit: before doing anything, ask "could AI help me with this?", like the pause between stimulus and response in meditation. How a manager uses AI, and their attitude toward it, spreads to the team. Acknowledge and normalize the emotions of the transition, including grief. However the work gets done, keep accountability and the definition of "good" intact. The survey shows managers are the biggest lever on happiness and good ones are scarce, so cutting management layers is a mistake. She thinks we are still in a slow takeoff, where the distance from novice to expert is short.
ex: She recently published an AI writing policy built around accountability
She expects a wave of "AI slop" startups that launch fast and vanish fast

items.d: Accountability and what counts as good

l384|407.c: The PM role isn't being merged away. It's expanding from coordinating to building things with AI.
l384|407.e: She sees product managers moving from a job that is mostly coordination and admin to one where they build things themselves with AI. With AI tools, a PM can turn out prototypes much faster. With automation, they can write and ship code directly. Afterwards they use data to judge whether the work actually paid off. So the boundaries of the role are pushing outward rather than several roles collapsing into one.
ex: Episode chapter: entering the AI builder era and how the PM role is changing

root.d: In the AI era, the job expands outward

items.d: Submit it with help from automation

l384|407.c: A PM should switch between doing the work and steering the team, depending on the project's stage.
l384|407.e: She splits a PM's work into two modes. "Rowing" means doing the technical work yourself and pushing the output forward. "Steering" means clearing obstacles for the team and setting direction. In her view, neither mode is better than the other. What matters is which stage the project is in, and switching to whichever mode it needs right now.
ex: Rowing: doing the technical work yourself
Steering: removing blockers and setting direction

d.verdict: Switch between them by project stage

l384|407.c: Automate routine work like docs and sorting feedback, so PMs have time for what matters most.
l384|407.e: She argues that repetitive work, such as writing documents and sorting user feedback into buckets, should be handed to automation. Her reasoning is that a PM's time is limited, so the hours saved should go into the activities with the biggest payoff. When that happens, the whole team gets more done. The end result is that features which are secure and meet enterprise standards ship faster, while still staying close to what customers need.
ex: Episode chapter: case studies of AI-driven product development and team throughput

items.d: Spend it where the payoff is biggest

l384|407.c: The goal is still product-market fit. What changes is how you get there.
l384|407.e: In her view, AI changes the means of building products, not the purpose. Finding product-market fit, meaning a product the market genuinely wants, is still the core goal. The real change happens at the execution level. Prototypes come together faster. The bar for a PM to write and ship code is lower. And judging whether something worked leans much more on data.

l384|407.c: Use a company knowledge graph plus dedicated builder weeks to make the whole organization fluent in AI.
l384|407.e: At Atlassian, two things work together. The Teamwork Graph maps how the company's people, projects and documents relate to each other, and its job is to give AI the context of the organization. AI Builders Weeks are dedicated stretches of time for employees to practice and sharpen their technical skills. She talks about building AI fluency and measuring organizational speed in the same breath. Only by measuring speed can you tell whether the transformation has actually made delivery faster.
ex: Teamwork Graph: gives AI the context of the whole organization
AI Builders Weeks: hands-on time to build technical fluency
Episode chapter: building AI fluency and measuring organizational speed

terms.d: Teamwork Graph gives AI organizational context
AI Builders Weeks for hands-on practice

result.d: While continually measuring how fast it moves

l385|23.c: The career ladder that measures a leader's impact by how many people report to them is obsolete.
l385|23.e: The old promotion logic says your impact equals the number of people you manage. So the only way to grow your influence was to become a manager. She argues that once AI multiplies what one person can produce, that equation no longer holds. A single person can now get far more done on their own. Impact and team size have come apart.
ex: Episode chapter: moving from traditional management to high-impact ICs

items: Scale impact without growing a team

l385|23.c: With AI, a high-impact IC can finish complex work alone, without a big team or cross-functional coordination.
l385|23.e: Her observation is that with AI, a high-impact individual can carry out tasks themselves, build their own prototypes, and drive business results directly. All of that used to require assembling a large team first and then working through heavy cross-functional coordination. Now those steps can be skipped. So in her view AI is both a multiplier for personal productivity and a catalyst for changing careers.
ex: Episode chapter: AI as a catalyst for personal productivity and career change

root.d: One person gets it done with AI

items.d: No waiting on a team's schedule
Ideas turn straight into working things

l385|23.c: Companies must separate status and pay from headcount, and give individuals transparency and the right to ship.
l385|23.e: She argues that for high-impact ICs to actually work, company systems have to keep up. First, status and pay can no longer be tied to how many people someone manages. Second, information needs to be transparent enough that one person can gather all the context they need to make a call. Third, individuals need the authority to ship and iterate on their own, instead of going through layers of approval. Only with all three in place does the role truly stand up.
ex: Episode chapter: building organizational systems that support HI-ICs
Episode chapter: decoupling compensation from headcount

terms.d: Status doesn't depend on team size
Launch and iterate on your own

result.d: Individual impact gets recognized

l385|23.c: Management should be an optional career path, not a required promotion. Going back to IC work brings energy.
l385|23.e: She believes management should be one option on a career path, not the step everyone has to take to get promoted. Moving from manager back to individual contributor does shake a professional identity built up over many years. But she thinks the shift can also bring more personal energy and more direct impact. Someone who returns to the craft can still hold leadership-level influence and responsibility.
ex: Episode chapter: rethinking management as a career path

items.d: Letting go of years of professional identity

l386|610.c: In the AI era, a PM's value lies in high-stakes decisions and taste, not just pushing projects along.
l386|610.e: He believes that in the AI era, a product manager's unique value has narrowed to two things. One is making high-stakes calls at critical forks, where the wrong choice is expensive. The other is using mature taste to decide what is worth building and how far to take it. Simply driving a project to ship on time is no longer enough to make someone a top PM.
ex: Episode chapter: how the PM role is evolving and understanding users deeply

marks.d: Focused on key judgment calls and taste

l386|610.c: Building a product takes three steps: dig into real needs, diagnose root causes, and obsess over craft.
l386|610.e: He lays out a three-step framework. First, use the Jobs-to-be-Done method, which asks what job people are hiring a product to do, to understand what they truly need. Second, when a product underperforms, rigorously track down the root cause instead of stopping at the surface symptoms. Third, obsess over the final craft and user experience, down to the details.
ex: The Jobs-to-be-Done method
Episode chapter: diagnosing root causes and raising product craft

items.d: Use Jobs-to-be-Done to find the real need
When a product fails, trace it to the source

l386|610.c: A feature succeeds only when it matches what users actually want to do, as several Instagram changes showed.
l386|610.e: He uses Instagram's evolution to make the point that a feature's success depends on whether it lines up with what users are really trying to do. The podcast summary mentions two examples: Stories shifting toward Close Friends, a way to share only with a small circle, and changes to the format of Reels, Instagram's short videos. The page does not give further detail on either case.
ex: Instagram Stories shifting toward Close Friends, sharing with a small circle
Changes to the format of Reels, Instagram's short videos

The format changed with user intent

l386|610.c: Use AI to scale user research and automate quality checks, and end up with more human products.
l386|610.e: He thinks AI can help teams in a few places. It can take user research to a much larger scale, for example by analyzing large volumes of user feedback at once. It can automate quality assurance. And it can fine-tune interactions based on feedback, so interfaces become more intuitive and more pleasant to use. The ultimate goal, he stresses, is to build tools that are more human-centered and that connect with people emotionally.

items.d: AI analyzes large volumes of user feedback
Interfaces get more intuitive and pleasant

l387|230.c: A team's context and its ability to keep learning are the real product, more than AI-boosted output.
l387|230.e: Once AI and automation make output cheap, simply producing more is no longer an edge. He believes what really determines whether a product is good is the context a team has built up about its customers and the problem, plus the organization's ability to keep learning. So in his view, deep customer intuition and shared quality standards should come before raw efficiency.
ex: Episode chapter: context as the foundation of product success

items: Speed up with AI and automation

l387|230.c: Tools make execution faster, but they can turn a team into a software factory cut off from the problem.
l387|230.e: Modern tools have made execution much faster. But he warns that if the process turns into an assembly-line software factory, the team drifts further and further from the problem it is supposed to solve. He argues for deliberately keeping a learning loop inside automated workflows: the team still talks to customers, sees the results with its own eyes, and forms its own judgment.
ex: Episode chapter: moving beyond the software factory model
Episode chapter: keeping the learning loop inside automated processes

items.d: It becomes the team's shared context

l387|230.c: Don't outsource thinking to agents. Let AI synthesize customer feedback and maintain a shared knowledge base.
l387|230.e: He draws a line. Judgment and thinking stay with people. AI's job is to pull together customer feedback scattered across many places and to maintain a knowledge base the whole team shares. Used this way, he says, AI strengthens the team's understanding of customers and the problem instead of replacing it.
ex: Episode chapter: using AI agents to synthesize customer context

items.d: The whole team can look it up

l387|230.c: Rituals like Quality Wednesdays and feature roasts train a team's collective judgment.
l387|230.e: He believes collective taste and sensitivity to detail have to be practiced deliberately. Linear has a few standing practices for this. Quality Wednesdays set aside a day focused on product quality. Feature roasts bring the team together to examine a feature and pick it apart. Done repeatedly, these build shared standards for what good looks like.

Feature roasts, where the team picks a feature apart

The team picks a feature apart together

l387|230.c: Hiring and culture drive product success, because output quality reflects the team's understanding and taste.
l387|230.e: If context is the product, then who is on the team and how they work together decides everything. He believes the quality of what a team ships reflects how deeply it understands the problem, how good its taste is, and how closely it stays connected to users. So in his view, hiring and culture are the main drivers of whether a product succeeds.

terms.d: How deeply the team knows the problem

result.d: Determined by hiring and culture

l388|755.c: Building AI products means dropping perfectionism: ship imperfect versions and iterate on real usage.
l388|755.e: They believe successful AI products come from fast iteration and evidence from real users, not from polishing behind closed doors. An example is early agent harnesses, the scaffolding that lets an AI carry out tasks on its own, which shipped as imperfect solutions. Only after shipping can a team see how something is actually used in the wild. That is what lets them fix it before competitors catch up.
ex: Early agent harnesses shipped first and were fixed later
Episode chapter: shipping imperfect products and coping with fast change

l388|755.c: To build on non-deterministic models, product leaders need user empathy plus systems thinking.
l388|755.e: Today's models are non-deterministic: the same question can produce a different answer each time. They argue that no single skill is enough for that. Deep empathy for users helps a team judge which experiences are genuinely useful. Systems thinking helps it design agent systems and platforms that can absorb the uncertainty. Only the two together let you build something reliable on top of an unpredictable model.
ex: Episode chapter: design principles for agent systems and platforms

terms.d: Know which experiences are genuinely useful

result.d: Build products on unpredictable models

l388|755.c: Keep a direct, always-reachable relationship with users to catch subtle feedback on agent behavior.
l388|755.e: Problems with agents are often subtle and do not show up in metrics. So they stress that a team should build direct relationships with users, the kind where you can talk to them any time. That is the only way to hear the small observations about how an agent behaves, and then adjust it accordingly.

l388|755.c: Things change too fast, so they plan only two to three months out and skip long-term forecasts.
l388|755.e: They work alongside research teams, and model capabilities keep shifting. In that environment, long-range predictions rarely hold up. So they compress the planning cycle to two or three months. Within that window they set direction, and when it ends they replan based on whatever has changed.
ex: Episode chapter: working with research teams and planning cycles

marks.d: Too much change for them to hold up

l388|755.c: By 2027, products will move toward voice-first interaction and self-driving software.
l388|755.e: They expect products to head in two directions. One is interaction that leads with voice. The other is self-driving software: you hand it a complex task and it runs the whole workflow on its own. This brings two benefits. It lightens the mental load on users. And it solves the blank-input-box problem, where people stare at an empty field and don't know where to start.
ex: The blank-input-box problem: users don't know where to start
Episode chapter: how the PM craft is evolving and predictions for the future

l389|756.c: AI can already do interface and interaction design, but the PM's core duties have become more important.
l389|756.e: Product management sits between what people need and what the technology can do, and the panel thinks that position remains essential in the AI era. UI design and interaction patterns are work AI can already take over. But a few other things have become more critical: getting the whole organization pulling in the same direction, running operations with real rigor, and making judgment calls when the situation is unclear. Those are a PM's core responsibilities, and the part Claude can't replace yet.
ex: Episode chapter: how the PM role is evolving in the AI era

d.verdict: Core duties matter more in the AI era

l389|756.c: To keep up with rapid change, PMs must tolerate change, bring structure to chaos, and let go of old methods.
l389|756.e: Technology is moving extremely fast, and the panel thinks PMs need a few specific abilities. First, a tolerance for constant change, accepting that direction will shift often. Second, the ability to build clear structure for the team in the middle of chaos, so people know how to move. Third, a willingness to abandon methods that have become outdated rather than clinging to familiar processes.
ex: Episode chapter: essential skills for coping with rapid technological change

items.d: Let the team know how to move

l389|756.c: Software is becoming agent-native: agents operate the interface, work together, and manage complex workflows.
l389|756.e: Anthropic's thinking centers on agent-native software, meaning software designed around AI agents that act on a person's behalf. In this model, agents operate the interface directly and coordinate with one another to manage complex workflows. The interface itself becomes malleable, rather than a fixed layout built for a human to click through.
ex: Episode chapter: building agent-native software and malleable interfaces

items.d: Several agents split up the work

l389|756.c: Run parallel experiments on shared infrastructure to explore the frontier while keeping the product coherent.
l389|756.e: The panel suggests a company can run several experiments in parallel, constantly trying new things at the AI frontier. Shared infrastructure then ties those experiments together, so the product users see stays coherent and reliable and meets enterprise customers' demands for stability. The final chapter looks ahead to software development becoming something anyone can do, but the page gives no detail.
ex: Episode chapter: balancing experimental innovation with enterprise-grade stability
Episode chapter: the outlook for democratized software development

l390|758.c: Hand-configured agent workflows are a stopgap; the direction is persistent intelligence that learns your goals.
l390|758.e: Products that have users build loops and flowcharts to orchestrate agents are, in his view, just a phase. The systems that follow will learn a user's goals and preferences on their own. Dots is that kind of persistent agent: it understands your goals, learns from feedback, has no model picker, and only asks which channels to connect. He imagines a continuous intelligence reachable from any device that remembers your meetings, then handles your email and texts, showing up when needed and stepping back when not. ChatGPT and Codex will also merge to reduce complexity.
ex: Five minutes before his DevDay demo, a Dot alerted him that production was down
Users will be able to create several Dots with different jobs, forming a "virtual team"

items.d: Users build their own loops and flowcharts

l390|758.c: Running many agents in parallel is a frontier-pushing stopgap; once the model jumps, they collapse into one.
l390|758.e: Most of his code is now written by Codex, mainly for analyzing trends, business performance and launch results; he only writes by hand on the occasional weekend. When pushing the frontier he expands his team of parallel agents, and once a model breakthrough lets a single stronger agent do the job, he shrinks the team back down. Ultra-fast models let him get back into flow with fewer agents, a state he has missed since his roughly ten years as an engineer. He admits he underestimated how much he would rely on voice, and didn't expect these capabilities so soon.
ex: He says the ultra-fast model costs about the same as Astra

l390|758.c: The open ecosystem is an underrated highlight: apps get recommended for retention, not for exposure tricks.
l390|758.e: He expects most actions on the internet to be taken by agents, models to get cheaper and faster, and modalities to blend together. Builders consistently underestimate how much better models will be a year from now. The open ecosystem is a hidden card: apps get distribution to ChatGPT users, and popular ones will share in the revenue. Recommendations run on quality signals, above all retention, and an app that stops delivering value stops being recommended. Real usefulness matters more than SEO-style exposure tactics. Agent traffic will also put pressure on everyone's systems.
ex: "Sign in with ChatGPT" is live with about 16 partners
Notion's MCP gets heavy agent traffic, forcing economic and interface trade-offs

items.d: Dropped once it stops adding value

l390|758.c: Fast typing is losing value; taste, understanding users and knowing what good looks like are gaining. PMs win.
l390|758.e: Deciding what to build and judging whether it is good is the core of a PM's job, and he thinks that is exactly the skill the AI era rewards, so product managers will do well. Role boundaries are blurring, and people who used to only design or only code now have room to do more. Former founders perform very well at OpenAI. He also values younger people because they adapt to AI fastest. His advice for early-career people: learn fast, collaborate well, focus on important problems, and don't put yourself first.
ex: He says OpenAI has more than 120 former YC founders
Ahmed Ibrahim joined out of school, now runs compute clusters and helped build Codex

d.verdict: People who decide what to build and judge quality win

l390|758.c: The organization runs bottom-up on trust and tolerates mistakes, but safety investment must stay ahead of capability.
l390|758.e: OpenAI works bottom-up: a small Slack group starts building, then opens it to the whole company. Some launches get pushed back or staggered for quality. Autonomy is high, and he can reset a project when needed; it works through trust and learning from mistakes. He himself took down production on day three of Codex. He reads "controlling the pace of the frontier" as investing early in alignment, safety and guardrails. Dots spent months on safety and runs a secondary model that watches the main agent. With roughly 1.2 billion users, the company is unwilling to take chances.
ex: A secondary monitoring model watches for high-risk actions and prompt injection
The Decisions API started as a hands-on experiment in a small Slack group
